Each time pap gets money he gets drunk, each drunk raises Cain round town, and each raising lands him in jail, a round that suits him well. Hanging round the widow's too much draws her warning that she will make trouble if he does not quit. Chapters six to ten leave pap still circling the widow's house and the courts.
71677-the-cambridge-natural-history-vol-:
The Cambridge Natural History runs to ten volumes, and this text holds volume one. Harmer, a fellow of King's College and head of the Cambridge zoology museum, edited the set with Shipley. Both men were fellows of the Royal Society. The set aimed to give the whole animal kingdom in plain, expert volumes for students and general readers.

Volume one opens the series at the foot of the scale of life. It starts with the simplest creatures. Sponges, worms, and sea beasts follow in the plan of the work. Specialists wrote each part from the live science of the day. The books served for decades as the standard survey in English. Readers get Victorian zoology at its fullest and clearest.
71693-the-cambridge-natural-history-vol-:
Cambridge Natural History, volume three, is a work of zoology by specialists. Harmer and Shipley edited the series for Macmillan in 1895. A map shows the spread of land operculate molluscs across the world. Figures on that map mark the number of known species by region. Cooke wrote the molluscs section of this thick third volume.

Shipley wrote the recent brachiopods, and Reed the fossil ones after him. A quote from George Eliot's Middlemarch fronts the work in fun. Conchology, says that quote, must be a light study for any man. Shells, snails, lampshells, and their kin fill the volume in close detail. Students of 1895 got a standard survey of the lower animals.
71891-the-cambridge-natural-history-vol-:
The Cambridge Natural History, volume two of ten, is a zoology survey edited by Harmer and Shipley, two Cambridge fellows. Macmillan published the series, first in 1896 and reprinted in 1901. This volume treats the flatworms and their worm allies, group by group, each by a specialist.

Gamble writes the flatworms and mesozoa, and Sheldon the nemertines. Shipley takes the thread-worms and sagitta, and returns for the gephyrea and phoronis. Hartog, a professor at Cork, covers the rotifers. Benham of Oxford writes the polychaet worms, and Beddard, prosector to the Zoological Society, the earthworms and leeches. A scheme of the classification adopted in the book stands in front. The series aimed to give students a full, illustrated account of the animal kingdom as Cambridge then taught it.
72052-the-cambridge-natural-history-vol-:
Volume five of the Cambridge Natural History covers Peripatus, myriapods, and the first part of insects. Editors Harmer and Shipley ran the ten volume series from Cambridge. Macmillan published this volume in 1895. Adam Sedgwick wrote the Peripatus section. Sinclair of Trinity College wrote on myriapods. David Sharp began the insect survey, which runs through many orders.

The Peripatus chapters work through the whole animal in detail. Outside features, habits, breeding, and anatomy each get full treatment. The gut, nerves, body wall, and breathing system are all described. A summary of the species and their spread across the world closes it. A frontispiece map shows where Peripatus lives. The myriapod part then treats centipedes and their kin. Sharp's insect opening covers the wingless kinds and grasshopper kin. Students of the lower animals were the book's first audience.
72233-the-cambridge-natural-history-vol-:
Harmer and Shipley put out a great set on the life of beasts in ten books. Volume four deals with crabs, trilobites, and their kin. Geoffrey Smith and the late Weldon wrote the crab part. Henry Woods wrote on trilobites and on the sea scorpions. Shipley, of Christ's College, Cambridge, shares the last part.

Crabs, shrimp, and their kin are set in kind and form order. Dead trilobites show a lost world of sea life in stone. Sea scorpions, vast in their day, close the book's scope. Plates and fine print serve pro and keen home reader alike. The set was a crown work of its age in its field. This book holds the hard-shell share.
72331-the-cambridge-natural-history-vol-:
Volume six of The Cambridge Natural History, printed in 1899, covers the second half of the insects. David Sharp, a fellow of the Royal Society, wrote the volume, and Harmer and Shipley edited the series from Cambridge. Bees, wasps, and ants open the book, in their great stinging orders. Beetles, butterflies and moths, flies, fleas, and bugs follow in turn.

Sharp sets out the scheme of grouping used in the book, then works family by family through form, habits, and life history. Solitary wasps that dig, social wasps that build paper nests, and the digger wasps each get their chapters. The set was built as a sound, readable survey for students and keen amateurs, with the weight of the Cambridge museum behind it. Few works of the age put so much insect life, in such order, between two covers.
72936-the-life-of-jean-henri-fabre-the-e:
Augustin Fabre, an abbé who shared the famed bug scholar's name, wrote The Life of Jean Henri Fabre. Bernard Miall turned the life into English for a New York issue of nineteen twenty-one. War-time limits forced the English text to be cut down from two volumes.

Jean Henri Fabre lived from eighteen twenty-three to nineteen ten, watching insects with unmatched patience. The author recalls an uncle who urged him to follow his kinsman of Malaval. Miall hopes the life will send readers to the Souvenirs, the ten volumes of Fabre's own insect tales. Other versions by Teixeira de Mattos are listed. Admiration guides the book.
73702-the-cambridge-natural-history-vol-:
The Cambridge Natural History, volume seven of ten, edited by Harmer and Shipley and published by Macmillan in 1904, covers the hemichordates, the ascidians and amphioxus, and the fishes. Harmer writes the hemichordata himself. Herdman, professor at Liverpool, takes the ascidians and amphioxus; Bridge takes the fishes; and Boulenger of the British Museum gives the systematic account of the teleosts.

The preface, dated July 1904, confesses delay: parts of the volume had stood in type for more than four years, held up by circumstances tied to the founding of a new university. Boulenger's classification of the teleosteans was finished in 1902, and Herdman's ascidians were ready two years before that. A Shakespeare motto heads the volume, from Pericles: the great fishes in the sea live as men do on land, by eating up the little ones.
73885-the-cambridge-natural-history-vol-:
Volume eight of the Cambridge Natural History, edited by Harmer and Shipley of Cambridge, treats the amphibia and reptiles in Hans Gadow's hands. Gadow was Strickland curator and lecturer on advanced morphology of vertebrata in the university. Physical features of the world affecting the spread of amphibia and reptiles form the frontispiece map. The volume first came out in 1901 and was reprinted in 1909.

Linnaeus had but a poor opinion of the Amphibia, the preface begins. One reason this branch of natural history is not very popular is a prejudice against creatures clammy and cold to the touch, some of which may be poisonous, Gadow owns. Frogs, toads, salamanders, snakes, lizards, turtles, and crocodiles are set out with their builds, habits, and homes. Students get a university survey of the cold blooded vertebrates here.
74964-the-cambridge-natural-history-vol-:
Volume nine of The Cambridge Natural History is the volume on birds, written by A H Evans of Clare College, Cambridge. The series was edited by S F Harmer and A E Shipley. Macmillan printed the volume in 1899. In his preface Evans says he has tried to meet a need he believes widely felt.

Many popular works on birds, he notes, touch only lightly on species as regards their plumage or habits. Others pay little heed to correctness of classification. Each group in the volume is prefaced by a brief summary of structure and habits. Further particulars are added where needed, with the main fossil forms yet recorded. Polar charts open the book, showing the range of bird life at both ends of the earth. The volume is a scholar's handbook of birds. It joins exact sorting of kinds with accounts of how they live.
7595-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part ten of The Caxtons keeps Francis Vivian's secret at the novel's center, half guessed and half hidden. A small household comedy opens the business: a captain insists no letter is for him, just as a servant enters carrying one. Around such small scenes, a larger guess takes shape. The narrator's uncle offers a conjecture about Vivian's parentage, and the narrator seizes it as a discovery.

The conjecture runs that a willful boy, thwarted in a headstrong attachment no father would sanction, threw himself on the world in irritation. That story pleases the narrator because it clears up much that had looked discreditable in Vivian. He could never bear to think Vivian mean or criminal, however rash and faulty. The part thus lets sympathy, not proof, shape the mystery.
76212-kate-plus-10:
Edgar Wallace wrote Kate Plus 10, for Small, Maynard at Boston in 1917. Charles Towne drew the front plate for the book. Its caption runs: Why, Kate, I am always meeting you. Chapter one is called Eighty-three Pearls on a String. The Earl of Flanborough presses a bell push by his study table. After exactly three seconds, he presses it again, impatient.

The footman's lobby lies near fifty yards from the library, the tale notes. Lord Flanborough is over middle age, thin, bald, and dyspeptic. His face is mean and insignificant to a stranger's eye. Contents promise an ideal criminal who is a strategist. A chorus girl, a princess beautifully dressed, and shareholders fill the list. A motor car met by a special train, and the chronology of a great theft, come later. Wallace spins theft and pursuit at his famed pace.
76448-the-little-review-april-1917-vol-3:
The Little Review for April 1917 is volume three, number ten, of Margaret Anderson's magazine of literature, drama, music and art. By now the magazine had moved from Chicago to 31 West 14th Street, New York, still at fifteen cents a copy. The issue is thick with poems, war pieces and argument.

A review of Mary MacLane's new book opens the number, under the head I, Mary MacLane. Anderson writes on Isadora Duncan's misfortune, and there is an item on James Joyce. A vers libre contest is announced. Poems include Sea Poppies by the poet H D, Images of Friendship by Maxwell Bodenheim, and pieces by Richard Aldington and Witter Bynner. Horace Holley writes on the soldiers and John Cournos on the assault, as the war enters the magazine's third year. A reader critic column, book talk and a surprise feature close the issue.
7668-what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-10:
Jasper Losely walks toward Fawley Manor in Book Ten of Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It? On the way he glimpses Lady Montfort leaving in tears after a painful talk with Darrell, and wonders whether an old tie broken by his fraud could ever mend.

At the gate he pauses, unsure how to ask for entry or what name to give. A later scene turns to the stage, where a performer in pink satin feeds a manager's dream of owning a great theater. Fraud, pride, and old guilt press hard on every choice in this volume.
7681-harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-:
Bishop Alred of York sits alone in his London cell in Book Ten of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Harold, subtitled The Sacrifice on the Altar. He has just left a sick King Edward, full of dark forebodings for England after his death, when travel-stained Harold bursts in, wild-eyed and livid.

The volume follows Harold's talks with northern chiefs, where Anglo-Dane leaders elect Morcar and seek redress under Tostig's rule. Gamel Beorn calls Harold just, a man who would shed his own blood before another free Englishman's. Oaths, kingship, and sacrifice gather toward the final crisis.
7711-my-novel-volume-10:
Charron's quip that all men think themselves wise opens Book Ten of Edward Bulwer Lytton's My Novel, and the tale proves it. Riccabocca draws daily rules from Machiavelli, Randal turns knowledge into being too knowing, and Dick Avenel climbs with a blow ahead and a kick behind.

Baron Levy, a cold image of gold, compares himself to a magnetic rock. Later Randal drops his aim at Violante once her fortune grows doubtful, sore only at being supplanted by L'Estrange. The volume satirizes self-praise in every rank, from scholar to moneylender to new man.
7724-the-last-of-the-barons-volume-10:
Sibyll and her father find a peaceful farm in Book Ten of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Last of the Barons, subtitled The Return of the Kingmaker. Fields where war dead once lay now hold gentle flocks, and Sibyll sets aside her embroidery to gaze down a winding lane from a room hung in bright blue serge.

Peace breaks at night: Montagu rides through Edward's troops crying for King Henry, and the king leaps from bed crying traitor, not from Warwick but from Montagu. Gloucester enters calm amid peril as cries ring front and rear. Hope, love, and sudden revolt fill this volume.
7746-the-parisians-volume-10:
Graham Vane hears from M Renard after months of silence. This is Book Ten of Lytton's The Parisians. Renard reports one new fact: Madame Marigny and Madame Duval seem to have exchanged names. The woman who died as Duval may have been Marigny, and the survivor may live under the other name.

The lover of the false Duval, a man of rank and perhaps married, may know where the sought lady went. That night Vane, a professed politician, thinks not of France's crisis but of his private life. A mystery of identity drives this late, tense volume.
7910-american-historical-and-literary-cu: The tenth part of American Historical and Literary Curiosities by John Jay Smith and John F. Watson contains, as text, only an editor's note and title page. The note explains the series is illustrations and page images throughout, with few passages fit for scanning, and points to the HTML version for the actual plates.
8480-life-on-the-mississippi-part-10:
Part 10 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 46, Enchantments and Enchanters, and a missed festival. The largest annual event in New Orleans, the Mardi Gras festivities, arrived too late for Twain to sample. He had seen the procession of the Mystic Crew of Comus twenty-four years before, with knights and nobles in silken, golden, Paris-made gorgeousness, planned and bought for a single night's use.

This section gives New Orleans as spectacle and memory, with carnival pageantry as its center. Readers get Twain's city of parades, costumes, and secret societies, recalled across a generation. It is the book at its most festive, and its most aware that the river world it celebrates has passed.
8788-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Cary's Inferno ends in this tenth part, cantos thirty-two through thirty-four, at the frozen pit of traitors. Dante opens by wishing for rough rhymes and hoarse measures to suit a hole of sorrow ringed by rock. Admitting that describing the depth of all the universe is no task for jesting or infant babbling. He calls on the tuneful maidens who helped Amphion wall Thebes, so that his speech may accord with truth.

Traitors stand locked in ice by degrees: to kin, to country, to guests, to benefactors, until Satan himself, vast and winged, chews Brutus, Cassius. Judas in his three mouths. Virgil and Dante climb down Satan's body and out to see the stars again. The ending's cold, silence, and sudden turn to light give the Inferno its famous close. This part lets a reader finish the descent in a single, shattering movement.
88-price-cost-indexes-from-1875-to-1989-:
What did a dollar buy in 1875, and how fast did prices move after that? This United States reference gathers price and cost indexes from 1875 to 1989, with estimates to 2010. An opening column by Michael S. Hart frames the numbers through computers.

Hart notes that a computer bought for three thousand dollars one year could be replaced for two thousand the next. The point is wider: goods gain value faster than price tags suggest. Tables behind the column track long-run change across more than a century. The file serves researchers comparing money across eras.
9772-alice-or-the-mysteries-book-10:
Book ten of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Alice, or The Mysteries, opens with Vargrave coiling his snares round Evelyn, his marked prey. Lytton spares the reader a sickening detail of each trap, but shows their shape: after Maltravers's farewell letter, Evelyn's resentment yields to certainty of his love. She believes some misfortune he would not share drove him away. Vargrave counts on that faith.

The book follows Vargrave's plot against a girl whose trust in Maltravers both shields and endangers her. Lytton's prose favors suspense and moral shadow. A reader gets the tenth book of a Victorian mystery romance, where a villain's patience meets a heroine's loyal heart.
9882-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-:
Issued Saturday, July 7, 1827, this number opens the tenth volume of the Mirror, a cheap London weekly miscellany. Its lead piece, with an engraving, describes King George IV's pony phaeton and his drives through Windsor Forest and Virginia Water.

The rest of the number ranges widely: Byron set beside other poets, a widow's song, notes on judges' pay long ago, and notices of new books, including Scott's life of Napoleon. It is a pleasant scrapbook of what educated Londoners read for entertainment in 1827, mixing poetry, history, and gossip. The Mirror cost only two pence, cheap enough for a wide readership.
9883-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-:
This supplementary Mirror number, the 263rd of the weekly, continues Sir Walter Scott's life of Napoleon Bonaparte, reprinted for Mirror readers. It sketches Robespierre signing death warrants with a shaking hand, Marat rousing Paris crowds through his journal, and the young Bonaparte's rise.

The narrative moves through Napoleon's early life, his first military exploit, his first marriage, plans to invade Britain, and his coronation. For readers in 1827, Scott's history was fresh and thrilling. The number shows how a cheap weekly brought a famous new biography to ordinary readers, week by week.
9884-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-:
This Mirror number, dated Saturday, July 14, 1827, belongs to the London weekly that sold short, illustrated reading for two pence. It opens with a new church in Regent's Park, tracing how Marylebone grew from a small village into a crowded parish of ten thousand houses.

Shorter pieces follow on the months, the peacock, the nightingale, and a warning to fruit eaters, with extracts from other journals. Readers get a compact sample of early nineteenth-century popular knowledge: buildings, birds, seasons, and curiosities, all in a few lively pages for a fireside evening.
9918-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-:
Dated Saturday, July 21, 1827, this Mirror number leads with an illustrated account of Ashby-de-la-Zouch Castle in Leicestershire. The writer traces the town from its early name through the Zouche family to its market-town present, with its bridge over the Gilwiskaw stream.

Other pieces include the author of Lacon, a dead trumpeter, a celebrated French picture, notes on origins and inventions, the Sphinx, and a new Sketch-Book installment. It is the Mirror's usual mix of travel, history, and curiosity, in short articles meant for a quiet Saturday evening at home.
9919-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-:
This Mirror number leads with Croydon Palace, seat of the archbishops, and follows with a survey of English academies for painting before the Royal Academy was founded in London. A churchyard scene and anecdotes and recollections fill the middle pages.

Shorter items note a wonderful peculiarity in the English character, offer select biography, and carry the paper's usual literary notices. Dated to the summer of 1827, the number shows the Mirror's recipe at work: a handsome building, art history, and curious tales, all kept short for weekly readers at home. The Mirror's short articles suited readers with little leisure time.
9922-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-:
This Mirror number, dated Saturday, August 4, 1827, opens with Hadley Church, near Enfield, and its history as a hamlet of Edmonton. The writer traces the village name to Saxon words for a high place, and its manor to the Mandeville family and Walden Abbey.

Further pieces offer a Sketch-Book installment, a butcher's tale, notes on confidence and credit, the story of Jesse Hammond, curious scraps about celebrated persons, and star tables for August 1827. It is a neat example of the weekly miscellany: local history, anecdote, and useful knowledge in short form.
a-thorny-path-volume-10:
Thunder empties the amphitheatre in Volume 10 of A Thorny Path, by Georg Ebers. Ebers shows lightning and rolling thunder sending the crowd home, while Caracalla reads a fighter's escape as a happy omen meant for himself. His thoughts turn at once to Melissa, and he calls out with real anxiety that she should reach shelter fast in this volume.

Chapter XXVIII gives her a small, firm victory. Offered a waiting chariot to the Serapeum, she asks instead to go home under her brother's escort, and the emperor agrees with good humor. With his own hand he wraps her in the hooded cloak meant for his own shoulders. Then he whispers that tomorrow may fill the horn of happiness for them both. His kindness and his claims arrive together, which is the danger.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-:
Chapters 6 to 10 of Twain's novel take Huck out of town by force. Pap, furious at the widow's warning, rows him across the Mississippi to a log cabin on the Illinois shore and locks him in. Beaten once too often, Huck saws his way out, fakes his own murder with pig's blood and a sunken canoe, and escapes downriver alone.

On Jackson's Island he camps, fishes, and watches a steamboat fire a cannon over the water for his supposed body. Then he finds Jim, Miss Watson's enslaved man, hiding on the same island after running away from sale. A flood floats a house and a raft past them, and the pair's river life together begins in earnest.
alcyone-feet-of-master-1910:
At the Feet of the Master came out in 1910 in the name of Alcyone. Alcyone was the pen name of the young J. Krishnamurti. Theosophy heads hailed him as a great soul to come. The short book gives the words of a master to a young pupil.

Four traits mark the path: keen sight of true and false, right acts, good cheer, and love. Each trait gets plain rules a young hand can use at once. The book spread all over the world in scores of tongues. It is a core text of the new Theosophy and its World Teacher hopes.
alice-or-the-mysteries-book-10: Edward Bulwer Lytton shows Vargrave coiling his snares around his chosen prey in the tenth book of Alice, or the Mysteries, as Evelyn's resentment gives way to certainty of affection. The schemer's designs tighten even as Maltravers' letter sows doubt, and the heroine's fate hangs on whom she will trust. Suspense and moral danger dominate this late, dark stretch of the romance.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith closes the first run of American Historical and Literary Curiosities with a tenth part of illustrated plates. Like the rest of the series, it offers page images rather than a narrative, and only scattered text survived scanning, as the editor's note explains. The HTML edition remains the proper way to study the facsimiles in full.
an-adulteration-act-the-lady-of-the-barg: William Wymark Jacobs includes An Adulteration Act among the Lady of the Barge and other stories in this tenth part of the collection. Jacobs' tales of sailors, barges, and Thames-side folk mix humour with quiet irony. This instalment shows his gift for short, well-turned stories of ordinary English life.
an-egyptian-princess-volume-10:
An Egyptian Princess closes its long arc in Volume 10, the last part of the novel by Georg Ebers. Ebers sets the ending in Egypt some months after the Athenian Phanes has vanished. Sappho has given birth to a daughter, and King Cambyses has grown so harsh that his brother Bartja has moved her to the palace at Memphis for safety.

Chapter XIII takes the party on a decorated Nile boat for the festival of the goddess Neith. Croesus sits with Rhodopis, Sappho leans on Bartja, and Darius watches the water in thought. The rising river, the north wind, and the rowers give the book a calm, bright close after years of court cruelty. Family peace, not conquest, ends the story.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-10:
Volume ten of the Ante-Nicene Fathers is the set's own map and key: a bibliographic synopsis and a general index. Roberts and Donaldson closed their 1885 edition with this reference volume. It covers all nine volumes of early Christian writings before it.

The synopsis walks author by author, listing each work, its manuscripts, and its editions. The index then opens the whole set by topic, name, and scripture cited. No one reads an index cover to cover; everyone who studies the Fathers reaches for it. The volume makes a shelf of ancient texts into a usable library. It is the quiet tool that finishes the set's work.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-10:
Volume ten, published in 1885, closes the main body of Burton's Thousand Nights and a Night. Shahrazad's storytelling ends, her pardon is granted, and the frame tale completes its long arc. Burton then adds his famous Terminal Essay, a wide survey of the book's history, sources, and the societies behind it.

The essay treats the geography, folklore, and private life of the East with a scholar's range. With it, Burton's ten volumes stand as both translation and reference work. Later editors plundered the essay even when they bowdlerized his tales. Six supplemental volumes followed with further stories from other manuscripts. The main set, though, ends here, on the thousand and first night.
art-of-war-giles-1910:
Lionel Giles translated Sun Tzu's Art of War into English in 1910, with a long introduction and critical notes. Sun Tzu, a Chinese general of deep antiquity, is credited with the oldest military treatise in the world. Giles's edition introduced the work properly to the English-speaking world for the first time.

Thirteen short chapters treat ground, supply, spies, deception, and the cost of war. Sun Tzu prizes winning without battle above every bloody triumph. His maxims favor knowledge of self and enemy over force alone. Giles set the Chinese scholarship in order and answered earlier, weaker versions. Business and strategy readers later adopted the book far beyond armies. The Project Gutenberg text is ebook number 132.
arxiv-2412-00110:
Guangyao Zheng, Michael Jacobs, and Vishwa Parekh test how much a chest scan's learned summary reveals about the patient, in a 2024 paper. Foundation models now encode three-dimensional CT scans into compact vectors that ace medical tasks. The worry: those vectors may also carry age, sex, or race. Using a national lung screening dataset, the team threw five kinds of classifiers at the vectors to guess each trait.

Age came out within about 3.8 years, and sex was nearly perfectly classified. Race was harder but still well above chance. The authors warn that embeddings leak personal traits even when trained without labels. They call for a closer look at what self-supervised models absorb, so health AI stays fair and private.
arxiv-2412-00510:
Yixuan Jin reports results for the STAR group in 2024 on how light atomic nuclei form in gold-on-gold collisions. When heavy atoms smash together at high speed, loose protons and neutrons can stick together into light nuclei such as deuterons. How often this happens can help physicists tell apart rival models of the hot matter made in the crash.

The STAR detector's second beam energy scan brought much more data and better tools than the first scan. Jin presents the energy patterns and counts for protons, deuterons, and helium-3 nuclei, split by how head-on each collision was. Ratios between the counts, and measures of how readily the particles merge, are included. These numbers serve as tests for ideas about a possible turning point in the phase map of strong-force matter.
arxiv-2412-00610:
Yangxinyu Xie and Bhaswar Bhattacharya study same-color hyperedges in layered hypergraphs in a 2024 paper. Color the corners of a hypergraph at random, and count the hyperedges that end up all one color. When a hypergraph has several layers sharing the same corners, the counts for each layer form a pair whose joint behavior matters.

The authors prove the pair settles into Poisson distributions, possibly linked ones, whenever the mean vector and covariance matrix of the counts settle down. Only the first two moments decide the limit, a broad second-moment principle. The result extends earlier work from graphs to hypergraphs and from single counts to joint ones, with applications to the birthday problem and random coloring counts.
arxiv-2412-00810:
Yan Yan and Yuanchi Ma draft outlines for very long Chinese texts, such as novels, with help from large language models. Their 2024 paper notes that past tools cope with short and mid-length texts but lose the thread in long fiction. Chapter cuts come out muddled and outlines hard to read. Their method first builds a graph for each chapter from named things and sentence links.

A graph-based module turns those chapter graphs into compact codes. A chain-based step then finds where the plot breaks into parts. Last, a large model sums up each part and assembles the full outline. On tests of plot cuts and outline ease, the method beat deep models and large models used alone.
arxiv-2412-00910:
Gaspard Ohlmann wrote a 2024 mathematics paper on half-wave maps, an equation from physics that describes how a wave-like field twists over time. The paper treats a clean class of solutions: rational functions with simple poles. A pole is a point where the function blows up to infinity.

Ohlmann derives an explicit formula for how these solutions evolve. A tool called a Lax pair tracks the motion of each pole. He then uses a half-spin frame and plain linear algebra to write the time law for the spins. The final form rests on a Toeplitz operator and a related adjoint map. Exact formulas like this anchor the study of wave motion.
arxiv-2412-01010: Yui Tomo notes an estimation error bound for the Transfer Elastic Net in two thousand twenty-four. The method mixes two norm penalties to borrow strength across tasks. It fits linear regression while it transfers knowledge in. Tomo derives a non-asymptotic bound on its estimation error. The bound is stated in the l2 norm for the estimator. Scenes where the transfer helps most are spelled out. The grouping effect gets a close look as well. Correlated predictors there win near equal estimates by design.
arxiv-2412-01310:
Anna Fehérkuti, Péter Major, and Gabriella Pásztor gauge a skew in beam-bright reads in a 2024 paper. Bright, the rate of grain clashes, must be known to a hair for fine work, and a famed scan sets the mark.

The scan parts the beams step by step, first side then up, and reads the clash rate at each step. From the two one-line reads hands build the full face, on faith that the face splits clean in two. The trio tests that faith on a year of clash data from a great ring. They weigh the fit forms, hunt skews, and pin the mend and its doubt. The mend feeds the mark's last word on bright for that run.
arxiv-2412-01410:
Peilin Zhou, Bo Du, and Yongchao Xu present CellSeg1 in a 2024 paper on cell image analysis. Tools that outline cells in microscope images usually need hundreds of labelled images to learn a new cell type. That labelling work is slow and costly, and new imaging methods keep appearing.

CellSeg1 adapts a large general image model with a light training method, using only one training image. A few dozen well-labelled cells in that image, packed tight and varied in size, proved to be the key detail. Across 19 data sets, the tool matched models trained on more than 500 images. It also held up well on data from a source it had not trained on, which suggests broad use in labs.
arxiv-2412-01510:
Mikolaj Fraczyk and Ben Lowe prove that thin minimal surfaces inside octonionic hyperbolic spaces must be large, in work from twenty twenty-four. Locally symmetric spaces generalise constant-curvature geometry to richer settings. Waist bounds ask how small a surface through every loop can be. Codimension two minimal surfaces are the focus of the main result. Compact octonionic spaces supply the sharp test cases.

Any such minimal surface has volume at least linear in total volume. Linear waist bounds for octonionic manifolds follow directly from that. First examples of power-law systolic freedom appear in this family too. Small-volume surfaces of that codimension can be squashed to lower dimension. Branched covers gain stability and expansion bounds from those facts. Maps to low-dimensional spaces also force large fibres in general. Lattice action fixed points follow as a further corollary.
arxiv-2412-01810:
Jain, Jankowski, and Slager studied in twenty twenty-four odd move signs of a shape mark in flat multi-gap phases. Those phases hold a mark called an Euler class that bends how charge flows. They read bent Hall-like flows and the rules of move they spawn.

They phrase those flows by space curve paths and how those paths spread apart. Sums back the read in full. Odd flows at the second and third bent steps stem from that mark in their frame. By fields and their slopes one can re-build the Euler mark, they show. A three-touch set-up may read the broad class too.
arxiv-2412-02010:
Tianxiong Han and a large team of co-authors probe a metal where magnetism and topology meet. Their 2024 paper studies a compound of terbium, vanadium, and tin. Terbium ions in it behave like tiny two-state magnets, while the vanadium atoms form kagome layers, a lattice of corner-sharing triangles. The team asked whether a sideways magnetic field could push the material to a quantum critical point.

Neutron scattering showed the terbium ions settle into a two-level ground state, and strong-field tests found a sharp spin reorientation at a field of 25.6 tesla. A model built from the scattering data explains that jump: an excited level crosses near the ground state rather than meeting it cleanly. The same model holds a surprise. Within the range of its measured parameters sit both a quantum critical point and a tricritical point, which may be reached simply by turning the applied field.
arxiv-2412-02810:
Steve Hanneke and Mingyue Xu study in 2024 how fast a classic learning rule improves as it sees more data, under a broad model of learning. The rule, empirical risk minimization, picks the option with the lowest error on the training sample. It underlies many common algorithms and the classic theory of learnability.

Classic theory fails to explain the observed shape of learning curves, the fall of error with sample size. A newer universal model of learning separates two kinds of best possible rates. The gap between them for this classic rule was not understood. Hanneke and Xu study the case where a perfect option exists. Their results clarify when the rule learns at the best universal rate. That sharpens what teachers of the theory can promise about data needs.
arxiv-2412-03110:
Yannick Mvondo-She links orbifold series numerators to classic polynomials in a 2024 math paper. The work grows out of partition functions in log gravity, where two variable Hilbert series for symmetric orbifolds take center stage. Their numerators come out palindromic, reading the same both ways.

Those numerators split into sums of products of Kostka-Foulkes polynomials tied to pairs of partitions. Since the log partition function is also a KP tau function, the result recasts Hall-Littlewood and Kostka-Foulkes polynomials as numerators on a moduli space of KP series. The palindromic forms also turn out to be eigenvalues of a differential operator from a recurrence.
arxiv-2412-03210:
Jorge Vila-Tomás and co-authors built in 2024 an image quality judge whose layers imitate the human visual system instead of learning freely from scratch. Ordinary deep networks fit human ratings well but carry millions of opaque parameters and overfit. Their parametric network hard-wires bioplausible operations and exposes a small set of meaningful knobs.

The lean models matched the black-box versions on regression against human scores while using about a thousand times fewer parameters. They also trained more smoothly and could be read as vision models, layer by layer. A quirk surfaced in training that the authors name feature spreading, which they take as a warning sign about pure regression training. The paper argues for structure first, data second.
arxiv-2412-03310:
Siddhartha Prasad, Ben Greenman, Tim Nelson, and Shriram Krishnamurthi design a small language for drawing diagrams of formal models, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Such models are built with solver tools that find examples meeting a written specification, and users explore the results as pictures.

The default picture tools know nothing about the user's domain, so their diagrams can mislead or confuse. Full custom visualizations take heavy effort and can fail silently. The authors argue for a middle path: a lightweight language that captures just the key facts about a domain's shapes. They ground the design in how people actually read diagrams, drawing on cognitive research. The language is meant to make generated models easy to inspect and debug. It serves users of tools like Alloy, which turn specifications into explorable examples.
arxiv-2412-03410:
Shaping an electron beam with light can squeeze it into bursts short enough to film atoms in motion. Today's methods need intense pulsed lasers and tiny structures for the light to strike. Cruz Velasco and Javier García de Abajo propose a cleaner scheme that works with continuous beams. Two laser beams aimed at each other meet a stream of electrons traveling along their axis, and the electrons trade energy with the light by stimulated Compton scattering.

Because the beams overlap for millimeters rather than nanometers, the recoil on each electron grows dramatic. Energies shift by neat multiples of the photon-energy difference between the beams, and the timing squeeze on the electron stream grows large. All this comes at modest laser power and without any material structure in the beam's path. The authors argue the setup could bring attosecond timing to electron microscopes that run in steady, continuous mode.
arxiv-2412-03510:
Chen and co-authors show in 2024 where a jelly like flow instability is born inside packed beds of grains. Polymer fluids squeezed through tortuous pores build elastic stress and start to wobble past a flow threshold. Past work on single grains blamed spots facing the flow, but packed beds differ.

The team filmed polymer flow through made to order 3D pore spaces of stacked spheres in two layouts. In both, the wobble began at still points where grains touch, not at the poles. One layout spawned swirling, shifting eddies. The other gave a steadier pattern. Geometry, they conclude, scripts the instability.
arxiv-2412-03710:
Taehyeun Kim, Anouck Girard, and Ilya Kolmanovsky teach a new kind of neural network to stand in for a safety governor on spacecraft rendezvous. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. The governor keeps a docking craft within limits by shifting its target path in time. Running the true governor onboard can be heavy, so a learned stand-in is attractive.

Their stand-in is built from Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, a fresh architecture that puts learnable curves on the links. Constraint facts are baked into the training, hence the name CIKAN. Simulations cover rendezvous on stretched, elliptical orbits. The CIKAN version matched the mission limits well. It was compared against both a classic network version and the true governor. The work suits craft that must dock safely with little computing power.
arxiv-2412-03810:
Riley Whebell and co-authors refine a particle based method for predicting the shape of a resting droplet, in a 2024 paper. Droplet shape matters for farm spraying and tiny fluid devices. On rough or patchy surfaces the edge line is hard to guess ahead of time, which strains grid based solvers.

Particle methods skip a fixed contact rule, but their force law was unsettled. The team proposes a pair of simple polynomial force laws and checks them in still and moving tests. The model then handled a ridged surface, a surface with a water loving stripe, and a virtual wheat leaf with fine roughness and mixed wetting.
arxiv-2412-04010:
Xinyuan Zhou, Ziqiang Wang, and Hua Chen study particles called Dirac fermions on a kagome lattice in this 2024 paper. A kagome lattice is a pattern of corner-sharing triangles. On it, these particles move with energy that grows in straight lines from two special points in the pattern's zone map, and the two points carry opposite winding numbers.

When the particles interact, they can scatter between the two points and lock into a shared state that breaks the pattern's shift symmetry. The particles gain mass, and the bonds form a hollow star-of-David texture in a tripled cell. Twists in that mass host zero-energy modes at their cores, tied to a distinct phase value. The work links lattice geometry to deep ideas about fractional states.
arxiv-2412-04210:
Smart surfaces that bounce radio waves can boost both phone service and radar sensing from the same hardware. Yingbin Lin and co-authors design such a system where each surface element can switch between active and passive modes. Their goal is the strongest sensing beam toward several targets. Limits cover signal quality for each user and power at the base station and surface. The joint design problem mixes choices and curves, so they split it in two.

Each half is solved with relaxation methods, and the two halves alternate until they agree. Tests show the design beats current baseline methods by a clear margin. Letting elements switch modes adds freedom that fixed surfaces lack. The work targets future networks that must sense and communicate at once.
arxiv-2412-04410:
Lyubashevsky and co-authors derive formulas for how fast the two halves of a split nucleus spin, in a 2024 paper. When a heavy nucleus fissions, its fragments fly apart with surprising amounts of spin. The authors blame zero-point wiggling of the neck just before the split: bending and wriggling motions that persist even at absolute zero. From those two modes they build the full joint spin distribution in closed form.

Fragment inertia is estimated from a fluid model, using deformations inferred from how many neutrons the fragments emit. Tested on thorium, uranium, and californium fission, the model matches the size and sawtooth pattern of measured spins. Notably, it skips any assumption about frictionless motion earlier in the split.
arxiv-2412-04510:
Five authors build the first taxonomy of system level attacks on self driving cars in this 2024 paper. Deep learning parts of such cars can be fooled by small, crafted changes in their input, and in the real world those errors can cascade into whole system failure.

The team selected twenty-one highly relevant papers and tagged each with twelve top level categories and finer sub-categories. The sorting shows which car parts and systems are attacked most, what threat models attackers assume, and how a small input change grows into system failure. The authors distill lessons for defenders. A shared taxonomy helps the field compare attacks and build cars that resist them.
arxiv-2412-04610:
Row, Shanin, and Fazekas test whether transformer models can repaint jazz piano pieces into fresh variations. Their 2024 paper works on music overpainting, which keeps a piece melody and harmony while varying its surface. Small datasets have held back earlier attempts.

The team builds a training set of over four thousand performance pairs from a larger jazz piano corpus. A semi-automatic pipeline prepares the pairs for learning. Two transformer setups train on the new set and on a smaller prior dataset. Early results show the larger set improves generalization and output quality. The authors argue scale and diversity are the missing ingredients for convincing machine-made jazz variations. The dataset release aims to spur wider work on creative music models.
arxiv-2412-04710:
Norbert Bodendorfer, Konstantin Eder, and Xiangdong Zhang review three lines of work on quantizing gravity, in this 2024 paper. Loop quantum gravity rewrites gravity with linked loops and needs three traits in its setup: a compact gauge group, real variables, and standard brackets. With those traits, a clean quantum space can be built and the remaining rules applied. The authors note that any gravity theory with these traits can use the same route.

The review covers gravity quantized in more than four dimensions this way. It also covers versions with supersymmetry added. A third strand treats modified gravity theories, which change Einstein's rules. The paper gathers scattered results into one map for researchers entering these areas.
arxiv-2412-04910:
Parity functions, where the answer is the product of a chosen subset of bits, are the litmus test of machine learning theory. Gradient-trained networks learn low-degree parities easily and fail as the degree nears the full input size. Emmanuel Abbe, Elisabetta Cornacchia, Jan Hązła, and Donald Kougang-Yombi show the borderline case hinges on how the weights start.

Begin from a discrete Rademacher pattern and almost-full parities become learnable; blur that start with enough Gaussian noise and learning fails, for one fixed function, not just on average. A gradient-alignment measure explains the split. Starting points, usually an afterthought, here decide what is learnable at all.
arxiv-2412-05010:
ZeinabSadat Taghavi and Hossein Mirzaei study a hidden risk in image classifiers in 2024: secret backdoor attacks that change how a model treats odd, out-of-group inputs. Most past attacks fooled a model inside its known classes. The pair point out that spotting outliers matters just as much in real uses like self-driving cars and medical scans.

They build an attack called BATOD with two kinds of triggers. One trigger pushes normal samples out of the group, and the other pulls odd ones in. Tests on real data sets show the attack harms outlier detection more than older attacks do, even after defenses are applied. The authors frame the work as a warning for builders of safety-critical systems.
arxiv-2412-05310:
Ilya Shesterikov, writing alone in a 2024 paper, proposes a way to calm turbulence in fusion plasma. Turbulence and large waves carry heat out of the hot fuel, spoiling confinement in fusion devices. His idea imposes a regular, repeating variation on the plasma's profile, much as layered crystals block certain light and sound frequencies.

The math mirrors a driven oscillator near resonance. By shaping how fast turbulent waves travel at each point, the pattern can weaken them in chosen bands. He suggests three ways to impose the pattern: radio waves, fixed magnetic tweaks, or shaped density profiles. If it works in hardware, the method could add a tunable knob for stability across many fusion designs, rather than a fix tied to one machine.
arxiv-2412-05410:
Adam Fuller and Pradyut Karmakar settle a question about Fourier parts of functions living in the algebras of twisted groupoids, the operator algebras built from symmetry-like structures. Take a function whose support is an open set; when can compactly supported pieces on that same set approach it? The answer turns on how fast the groupoid's elements decay, a property measured by a length function.

The answer is yes in two cases: when the length is conditionally negative-definite, and when it is the square root of a locally negative type function. The results firm up how harmonic analysis on such algebras handles functions spread over open parts.
arxiv-2412-05510:
Diogo Matsumoto characterized travel groupoids on special graphs in two thousand twenty-four. A groupoid is an algebra system weaker than a group. Travel groupoids obey two conditions tied to graphs. Complete multipartite graphs split vertices into independent clusters. Every vertex links to all outside its cluster. Which travel groupoids live on such graphs was open.

Matsumoto classifies them for all finite cases. He also counts how many exist per graph. The count depends on the cluster structure. Such classifications anchor the theory of these systems. They connect algebra with network combinatorics. The paper is a compact, complete treatment. It will serve researchers extending groupoid theory.
arxiv-2412-05610:
Some lattices have a flat band, a range of waves that all share one frequency and so go nowhere. Riva, Marconi, and Braghin study the tightly boxed wave modes that live in such lattices. The modes stay in a small region because neighboring elements cancel each other's motion, and the same cancellation makes them unusually responsive to small changes in the structure.

The team first works through the physics on a simple spring-and-mass chain. They then carry the ideas to a microelectromechanical system of tiny oscillators. In both settings the boxed modes show enhanced interaction with the structure that hosts them. The authors argue that flat-band lattices could serve vibration control, where stillness is wanted, and precision sensing, where a structure's smallest change should ring loudly in the wave readout.
arxiv-2412-06210:
Jiechao Gao and five co-authors published this paper in 2024. It tackles federated learning for the Internet of Things, where phones and sensors train a shared model without sending raw data away. Real device networks are layered and uneven, which strains the usual two-level designs.

Their system, H-FedSN, trims each device's network to a sparse personal version using an on-off mask, so far less data travels between layers. Shared layers keep a common base, while personal layers adapt to local data quirks. A Bayesian merging step at the edge and cloud levels weighs each group's input fairly. On three real device data sets, the system cut communication costs by up to 477 times against rivals. Accuracy stayed high, which suits low-power, slow-link settings.
arxiv-2412-06410:
Bart Bussmann, Patrick Leask, and Neel Nanda published this machine learning paper in 2024. Sparse autoencoders are tools for opening up language models: they split the model's inner activity into a set of sparse, human-readable features. A popular design, the TopK autoencoder, forces exactly the same number of active features for every input. That rigidity wastes capacity on simple inputs and starves complex ones.

The authors relax the rule to the level of a whole batch of inputs. Their BatchTopK method lets each sample use as many or as few features as it needs, while the average across the batch stays fixed. On two models, GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B, it rebuilt inner activity more faithfully than TopK at the same average sparsity, and it matched a leading rival method. A practical bonus: the average feature count is set directly, with no costly tuning search.
arxiv-2412-06610:
Frank Mol and eight co-authors outline tumors in head and neck MRI scans automatically, in this 2024 challenge paper. Precise outlines of the main tumor and of spread lymph nodes guide radiotherapy, and MRI's soft-tissue contrast may beat CT and PET for the job. The work was done for a segmentation challenge with scans taken before and during treatment.

The team used the nnU-Net framework but ensembled fifteen cross-validation folds instead of the usual five, for robustness. For pre-treatment scans they added mid-treatment scans to the training pool. For mid-treatment scans the network also received the registered pre-treatment scan and its mask as extra channels. On the blind test set of fifty patients, their scores averaged 0.81 for the first task and 0.70 for the second. Lymph nodes were segmented much better than the main tumor in both.
arxiv-2412-07110:
Tamang and co-authors, a team of ten listed by initials and surnames, review in 2024 solid materials that use sunlight to make hydrogen. Hydrogen is a clean fuel, and splitting water with light, called photocatalysis, may be the greenest way to produce it. The review compares flat, two-dimensional materials with bulk three-dimensional ones.

Flat materials often win because their thin layers expose far more surface where water can react. The authors explain how the light-driven reaction works and where other hydrogen methods fall short. They survey the main families of light-catching solids and their tricks for better performance. Recent blends of flat materials with partners get special attention as the most promising path.
arxiv-2412-07210:
Jialiang Cheng and five co-authors present EDiT, a distributed training method for large language models, in work from 2024. Standard distributed training suffers from communication stalls, stragglers and poor flexibility in mixed clusters. Local SGD cuts communication, but its use at large scale is held back by memory costs and weak attention to speed and stability.

EDiT pairs a tailored local SGD scheme with model sharding, and syncs parameters layer by layer during the forward pass to overlap work. A pseudo gradient penalty curbs loss spikes. A fully asynchronous variant, A-EDiT, fits mixed clusters. Experiments back the method as a strong option for large-scale training, with code shared in a public codebase.
arxiv-2412-07310:
Wojciech Szumiński and Adel Elmandouh examine when motion systems on curved surfaces can be solved exactly, in a 2024 math paper. The systems are Hamiltonian, the standard frame for frictionless motion, here set on two-dimensional spaces whose curvature varies from place to place.

Using differential Galois theory, a method that reads solvability from the algebra of a system's variations, the authors derive necessary conditions for exact solvability. The conditions come out as arithmetic limits on the numbers that define the system, easy to check. They apply the test to sample systems and exhibit fresh solvable examples. The work extends a powerful test to curved settings, where real motion from atoms to planets plays out.
arxiv-2412-07410:
Manish Kumar and Mateusz Wasilewski study, in a 2024 paper, the equilibrium states of quantum versions of Cuntz-Krieger algebras. These algebras arise from graphs, now quantum graphs, and their KMS states describe how a system settles at a given temperature under a flow of time shifts. Classifying such states is a basic step in the math of quantum systems.

The authors use a known bridge that rewrites the local quantum algebra as a Cuntz-Pimsner algebra built from the graph's edge structure. Through that bridge, the general rules for KMS states turn into statements about the quantum adjacency operator, much as in the classical case. For some gauge actions, the time flows most often studied, they obtain a full classification of the states. Examples round out the account.
arxiv-2412-07510:
Ravindra Kumar and Om Prakash study a graph number in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-four. They work with zero-divisor graphs, built from a commutative ring so that vertices are ring elements linked by a zero product. On such a graph, they study Roman domination, a labeling with values zero, one, and two under a set rule.

The rule says any vertex labeled zero must sit next to a vertex labeled two. The Roman domination number is the smallest total weight over all valid labelings. The authors focus on finding that number for zero-divisor graphs. They also seek bounds for the same number on a related total graph. The work sits in graph theory and ring theory.
arxiv-2412-07610:
Fard and four co-authors show a way to pull out one weak magnetic effect while hiding a strong one, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Atoms in a magnetic field split their energy in two ways. The strong split is linear and can swamp the weak split, which grows with the square of the field. That makes the weak effect hard to study on its own.

Their method cancels the strong split and leaves the weak one clear. They test it on warm rubidium atoms at room heat. With the weak split alone, they can place atoms in a neat mix of two states. The trick should work for any spin size. It may help build precise atom states for sensing and for quantum work.
arxiv-2412-07910:
Erik Connerty and co-authors build a quantum version of an echo state network to forecast chaotic systems, in a research paper from 2024. Echo state networks use a large fixed reservoir to map inputs into rich patterns, which makes hard time-series tasks easier. On classical machines, that reservoir can grow huge and costly.

The quantum circuit runs on any digital quantum computer with a standard gate set. It needs no stopping or restarting, so the quantum state can evolve over long spans. The team simulated it on the chaotic Lorenz system, with and without noise in the model. Results suggest smaller reservoirs may suffice on quantum hardware. The work points toward time-series tools fit for today's noisy quantum machines.
arxiv-2412-08010:
Milan Maksimovic and Ivan Maksymov test a brain inspired neural network in a 2024 paper. Standard machine learning systems classify images well but can fail with confusing outputs or hand hard cases back to humans. Their model draws on quantum tunnelling ideas and on quantum cognition theory, which models human judgment under uncertainty.

The network classifies image data sets while mimicking human perception and decision patterns. The authors report evidence that the model can replicate human like choices. It also outperformed traditional machine learning algorithms in their tests. They present the approach as a step toward systems that express confidence and uncertainty more like people do.
arxiv-2412-08510:
Chengliang Tan and Risto Korhonen prove a form of the Second Main Theorem for the Askey-Wilson operator. Their 2024 paper works with curves in projective space, where this classic theorem bounds how often a curve can meet flat target sets. Here the usual derivative is swapped for a structured difference step drawn from special function theory.

The authors first build a Wronskian-style determinant suited to that operator, since the standard tool checks how the curve's parts depend on each other. With it they prove a general theorem that improves an earlier result by Chiang and Feng. A truncated form follows for targets in wide position. The work pushes value distribution theory deeper into the difference setting.
arxiv-2412-08710:
Chang Qin and four co-authors measure the fractal shape of open star clusters near the Sun. Their 2024 paper, the third in a series, uses three-dimensional positions from the Gaia mission for over two hundred clusters nearby. Fractal dimension gives one number for how clumpy a cluster's stars are. The team computed it by box-counting, for each cluster as a whole and for its inner and outer zones.

In both catalogs, the outer zones scored lower than the inner ones: the outskirts are clumpier than the core. A clustering algorithm split one catalog's clusters into two shape families by this measure. The measure falls as clusters age, which the team ties to the growth of tidal tails. It also rises with cluster mass, hinting that heavy clusters form by merging smaller filament-like groups. The authors offer it as a tracer of star-forming structure across the Galaxy.
arxiv-2412-08810:
Fan Li and co-authors generate fake dynamic graphs with node traits faster than walk-based rivals. Their 2024 paper serves data work from engine testing to app studies, where graphs beat tables at capturing real links. Past generators miss how structure and traits evolve together, drop edge direction, or crawl through slow path sampling.

Their framework reads each snapshot with two-way message passing that keeps direction and traits. A recurrence unit carries the evolution pattern of early graphs forward. A Bayesian sampler then draws hidden draws for the next snapshot, skipping path walks and merges. That shortcut cuts build time sharply. Wide tests on real data sets check the quality of the fake graphs against rival generators.
arxiv-2412-08910:
W Q Chen, K J Li, and J C Xu track the solar transition region over a full activity cycle in this 2024 paper. The transition region is a thin layer between the Sun surface and its hot corona. Daily full disk images at one ultraviolet wavelength cover 2011 to 2022. Those images come from the Solar Dynamics Observatory.

Overall brightness of the layer rose and fell in step with the solar cycle. Polar brightening should therefore peak at cycle maximum. The background layer at middle and low latitudes moved against the cycle instead. Active parts of the layer seem heated mainly by active region fields. Quieter parts seem heated by the magnetic network. Surface field records match that split well, which supports the reading.
arxiv-2412-09010:
Yusuke Sakemi and five co-authors train chip circuits as physical networks, flaws and all, for brain-like computing. Chips that compute in memory save the power that deep networks burn, yet their analog parts drift and skew. Their 2024 approach writes the laws of the chip as the network itself, then trains that network head-on. A trick that cuts spike times in a smooth way cuts cost hard. It gives up to twentyfold gains in speed and a hundredfold gains in memory room.

Large networks trained this way turned the flaws of the chip into gains on a photo test set. Bench simulations of a laid-out chip, flaws included, matched the trained networks tenfold closer than older ways. The team pitches the approach for lean networks on rough, low-power parts such as write-once memory cells.
arxiv-2412-09210:
Twist two graphene sheets at a large angle and the layers nearly ignore each other for tunneling, yet feel each other's electric pull intensely. Dohun Kim and co-authors report fractional quantum Hall physics at one-third total filling when the layers carry equal charge. Simulations say the ground state is an excitonic superfluid, but the excitons are built from fractionally charged pieces rather than whole electrons.

Sweeping an electric field between the layers triggers transitions into states with different topology and symmetry, also matched by simulation. The system offers a clean stage where fractionalization and interlayer coherence, two exotic themes, meet and mix.
arxiv-2412-09310:
Natori and four colleagues chart exotic states in honeycomb magnets that mix two sizes of spin in twenty twenty-four. The base model, from Kitaev, pairs each spin with its neighbors by bond type and can host a liquid like state with no fixed order. Real materials may place small and large spins on the two halves of the honeycomb. The team worked out when Kitaev like forces rule in such a mix.

In the pure limit, they found four distinct spin liquid phases. Spin orbit coupling and a four pole kind of order help keep these phases stable. Their mix of theory and large scale simulation maps the full ground state. The work guides the hunt for real mixed spin materials.
arxiv-2412-09610:
Mehmet Asım Gümüş and co-authors present a theoretical physics paper, published in 2024, using neural networks to explore which scattering laws nature allows. The S-matrix bootstrap tests whether a proposed particle scattering pattern obeys basic rules, building allowed regions from those rules alone. The team parameterizes scattering amplitudes with neural networks and optimizes them with the same gradient methods used in machine learning.

Working in a simplified setting where one hard term is set to zero, they bound the first low energy coefficients of the amplitude and describe the amplitudes that fill the allowed zone. Their neural results matched the classic primal and dual bootstrap calculations exactly, a strong check that learning based search can map this abstract space reliably.
arxiv-2412-09810:
Branton DeMoss and four co-authors track a sudden learning leap in neural networks through the lens of complexity, in a 2024 paper. The leap, called grokking, hits long after a network has memorized its training data: it abruptly generalizes. The team measure complexity using rate-distortion theory, a principled form of lossy compression akin to Kolmogorov complexity. Well-regularized networks showed a sharp phase transition under this measure.

Complexity climbed while the network memorized, then fell as it found a simpler pattern that generalized. Unregularized networks stayed stuck at high complexity, memorizing forever. The authors tie their measure to known generalization bounds, grounding the link between compression and learning. Their tracker compresses thirty to forty times better than naive methods. They also propose a regularizer based on spectral entropy that nudges networks toward the simple solutions that grok.
arxiv-2412-10410:
Shaofei Cai and co-authors present GROOT-2, an agent that follows instructions given in more than one mode, such as video and language, published in 2024. Building agents that follow multimodal instructions is a core challenge in robotics and AI. Large-scale pretraining on unlabeled data teaches diverse behavior, but such agents often fail to follow instructions.

Labeling data with instructions at scale is impractical, so the team frames the task as semi-supervised learning. One component, constrained self-imitation, uses large amounts of unlabeled demonstration to keep behavior diverse. A second aligns a smaller set of labeled demonstrations so the model's latent space reflects human intentions. Tests in four settings, from video games to robot manipulation, showed robust instruction following across modes.
arxiv-2412-10610:
Fussell and co-authors compare language models for grading student lab notes in this 2024 study. Physics education research often needs written work sorted by skill, sentence by sentence. Doing that by hand is slow, so automated sorting is attractive if it can be trusted.

The team fine-tuned two language models and compared them with a classic word-count method and a large model used with a few examples. Models were judged on resource use, sorting scores, and the research trends each one produced. Bigger models often scored better, but not always. All models found similar trends, though their numbers did not always agree within error ranges. The authors discuss how researchers should pick a model type.
arxiv-2412-11510:
Jerzy Kakol and Arkady Leiderman study Asplund locally convex spaces in a 2024 math paper under a second title on the finest locally convex topology. The hosted head uses the shorter title, and the work extends their past study of smoothness spaces.

The authors prove some negative results for free spaces over infinite spaces, which fail key smoothness traits. They also show that barrelled smooth spaces have a Baire-like trait, which rules out some strict limit spaces. A special role goes to a countable-dimension space with the finest topology. For quojection spaces, the Asplund trait holds exactly when each Banach step holds it. Analysts get sharp bounds on where these traits live.
arxiv-2412-11610:
Tatsuya Shibata, Michael Koch, Iason Papaioannou, and Kazunori Fujisawa speed up Bayesian hunting for buried features in the ground. Their 2024 paper estimates a spatial field and the shape of anomalies inside it at once. Older methods re-solve a costly eigen problem on every new domain shape.

A domain independence property of the Karhunen-Loeve expansion breaks the bottleneck. The eigen problem is solved once on a fixed outer box, whatever the inner shape does. Gradient computation for the expansion runs about a hundred times faster. Seepage flow tests in one and two dimensions show sharp conductivity jumps captured with fewer parameters. Boundary and field uncertainty estimates beat field-only rivals. The authors pitch the method for geophysics and engineering scans alike.
arxiv-2412-11710:
Yuanzhi Wang and six co-authors tighten control in video editing in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Text-guided editing lets users change a video by editing its prompt. Large text-to-image diffusion models power most such editors. Yet objects can land in the wrong place or appear in the wrong number.

Their method, ReAtCo, attacks control without extra training. A re-attentional diffusion step refocuses cross-attention responses. Those responses link words in the edited prompt to regions in the frames. Refocusing aligns the spatial placement of target objects with the new text. Readers who edit video get a fix aimed at the most visible failures of prompt-based editing: things showing up where they should not, or in wrong counts.
arxiv-2412-11810:
Wadjih Bencheikh, Jan Finkbeiner, and Emre Neftci present a 2024 paper on training spiking and recurrent neural networks with far less memory. Such networks handle long input chains well, but training them eats memory and fast links to it. A trick called checkpointing stores only some middle states and rebuilds the rest. It saves memory yet adds compute time, so few teams use it.

The authors tailor checkpoint plans for sparse networks on a chip with many small local memory banks. Their best plan, Double Checkpointing, uses local memory well and adds little extra time. It lets them train on chains more than ten times longer, or nets four times larger, than before. The ideas may help brain-like computing grow on many kinds of hardware.
arxiv-2412-11910:
Hongkai Liu and Daiki Ueda plan a hunt for neutrinos that interact with each other at future muon colliders. Muon machines would flood a target with clean, fierce neutrino beams from muon decay. Their 2024 study sets a forward detector in that beam's path. The quarry is a light scalar particle that couples to neutrinos alone. Such self-interactions could hide new physics.

Both the main detector and the forward one were scored for reach. The pair could tighten current limits by about a hundredfold. That leap passes other planned experiments. The study is a feasibility map, not a build plan. It shows muon colliders doing double duty: smashing particles and serving as neutrino factories.
arxiv-2412-12010:
Mohammad Mortezaei Nobahari and Mahmood Rezaei Roknabadi study a thin sheet of a layered crystal in a 2024 paper. The sheet is a form of molybdenum disulfide. It may serve in very small electronic parts.

Using a simple model and response theory, the authors show how spin and motion lock together in the sheet. Spins point one way in one band and another way in the next. As a key value rises past one, the sheet shifts from a state that guards spin flow at its edges to a plain state. They map where each phase holds and note a zero net heat driven signal.
arxiv-2412-12110:
Saloua Zammali and co-authors give recommendation engines a sense of how sure they are. Recommenders guess what users want from tangled patterns of taste and context, and modern neural versions predict well but cannot say how much to trust each guess. Conformal prediction can attach honest confidence sets, if the model's inner features behave.

Their framework fuses neural contextual matrix factorization with deep autoencoders, which compress users, items, and contexts into compact latent codes. On top of those codes they build conformal guarantees for context-aware recommendations. A system that knows its own uncertainty can hedge, ask, or explore instead of bluffing, a trait that matters as recommenders steer real spending and attention.
arxiv-2412-12210:
Akanksha Singh, Shaily, Singh, and Ertan Güdekli build a universe model in a modified gravity theory. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, uses an f(Q,T) theory, where gravity depends on space-time shape and matter trace. Their chosen form is simple: a square term plus a matter term. Real sky data then pin down the free values.

Hubble measures and a large supernova set do the pinning. The model universe slows early, then speeds up late, as ours does. At very high redshift it passes through a bouncing ekpyrotic phase. In that picture the Big Bang is a brane crash, not time's start. Late-time fits also ease the known Hubble tension.
arxiv-2412-12410:
Keshav Aggarwal and co-authors tighten a bound on paired L-functions in a 2024 paper. L-functions encode deep arithmetic secrets, and their central values resist easy sizing. Subconvexity bounds beat the trivial estimate by a small but precious margin.

One form varies with prime level while a fixed partner form stays put. The team improves the best known exponent in the level aspect. Their path runs through hard bounds on sums of Kloosterman fractions. Those sum bounds descend from Duke, Friedlander, and Iwaniec, sharpened by later hands. Each shaved exponent is a foothold toward the grand conjectures nearby.
arxiv-2412-12610:
Gordon Burtch and Alejandro Zentner study gender bias in property tax appeals in this 2024 paper. They analyzed over 100,000 appeal hearings and years of hearing audio. Homeowners plead for lower assessed values, and panels decide the cuts.

Female appellants fared worse than male ones on average. Male outcomes barely shifted with the panel's gender mix. Women's outcomes did: they won smaller cuts before female panels and larger ones before male panels. The team also used a multimodal model to measure how participants behaved in the hearings. The study shows bias can flow through formal, recorded processes, not just private choices.
arxiv-2412-12910:
Salim Amoukou and five co-authors set out a way to spot, step by step, when a shift in data starts to harm a working learning model, with no true labels at hand. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

In live use, a model's world drifts, and harm can creep in unseen. Past work could track harm over time when labels were there to count errors. The new way stands in a trained guesser of the model's error rate for the true count. Tests show the method has strong power to catch shifts, while it keeps false alarms in check. The shifts tried span field shifts, label shifts, and real drifts across place and time.
arxiv-2412-13110:
Takumi Goto, Justin Vasselli, and Taro Watanabe made grammar correction scores explainable in twenty twenty-four by crediting individual edits. Sentence-level metrics grade a corrected sentence as a whole, and reference-free ones especially hide their reasoning. That opacity blocks model debugging and useful learner feedback.

Their method assigns each edit a Shapley value, borrowed from game theory, measuring its contribution to the sentence score. The attributions stayed consistent across edit granularities and matched human judgments about seventy percent of the time. Mining the attributions exposed metric biases, such as a tendency to ignore spelling-level fixes. The work turns a single number into an audit trail for grammatical error correction.
arxiv-2412-13510:
Rui Cai and co-authors built in 2024 a retrieval adapter that reshapes itself for each caption in a low-resource language. Cross-modal search pairs images with text, but poor languages lack labeled pairs. Adapters can carry a big model's alignment from a rich language to a poor one, yet stock adapters are frozen once trained. Their adapter, DASD, is minted fresh for each caption from its traits.

A splitting module pulls apart what a caption means from how it says it, so the minted adapter fits both. On two image-text sets and one video-text set the method beat rivals. It also slotted into several base models cleanly. The team pitches dynamic adapters for search in languages the data giants skip.
arxiv-2412-14010:
N M Jiménez Cruz, Ameek Malhotra, Gianmassimo Tasinato, and Ivonne Zavala pair star maps with pulse clocks to hunt space waves in a 2024 paper. Fine star maps may catch low waves that pulse clocks now hunt. A shared wave wash bends both reads in linked ways, the team shows.

Sharp math forms spell the map reply, with room for a lean in the wave wash. A best pull tool draws the wave marks from the maps at full worth. Cross reads with clock data then lift the hunt in test cases.
arxiv-2412-14210:
Manuel Cebrian, Petter Holme, and Niccolo Pescetelli test a leading multimodal AI as a would-be street organizer, using a children's puzzle as the safe test bed. Their paper appeared in 2024. Asking a model to pick persuadable people out of a real crowd raises ethical alarms, so the team pointed it at crowded Where's Waldo scenes instead. Cast as an agent who must mobilize face to face, the model described scenes vividly and invented creative engagement tactics.

It could not, however, reliably find the key individuals or read the social dynamics of the crowd. The authors offer the setup as a reusable benchmark: a playful proxy that lets researchers grade AI persuasion skills as models evolve, without experimenting on real publics.
arxiv-2412-14310: Tara Holm, Liat Kessler, and Susan Tolman settle a shape question in this 2024 math paper. Their spaces carry a swirling symmetry and a calm geometry, in four dimensions. The question is how far an algebraic fingerprint, built from the symmetry, pins down the space's true form. The answer is fully: matching fingerprints force matching forms, and each match of fingerprints comes from a real reshaping of the spaces. The result closes the question for this class of spaces.
arxiv-2412-14510:
Jiayi Wu and seven co-authors present PA-RAG in this 2024 paper, a way to tune the generator inside retrieval-augmented generation systems. Such systems fetch documents and then have a language model answer from them. General models often give thin answers, break under poor documents, or cite sources badly. Past fixes added extra steps or used plain fine tuning, yet still missed the full set of needs.

PA-RAG aligns the generator from several angles at once. The team built fine tuning data plus preference data by sampling answers of varied quality under varied document quality. They then trained the model in two stages, ending with direct preference optimization. Tests on four question answering data sets and three base models showed clear gains. The authors release their code and data. They frame the work as a full alignment of the generator with what retrieval based answering demands.
arxiv-2412-14610:
Chuang Li and James Jun He study a one-way superflow effect in tiny tubes in this 2024 paper. A superconductor can act like a diode, passing current more easily one way than the other, when two symmetry rules break at once. Twisted tubes break one rule by shape, and a magnetic thread through the tube breaks the other.

Past claims rested on broad theory, so the team builds atom-level models of carbon and crystal tubes. They chart how the effect shifts with tube width, twist angle, field strength, heat, and charge level. The effect flips sign across several of those ranges. Tests with strained and plain grid tubes add more clues. The work pins down the micro roots of the effect.
arxiv-2412-14910:
