Lim and Poncelet propose a sturdier way to estimate the error bars on particle physics calculations, in a 2024 paper. Calculations stop at a fixed order, and the missing orders are the true uncertainty. The standard trick varies an energy scale, but it can badly understate the error.

Their fix adds theory nuisance parameters that stand in for the missing terms directly. Varying those parameters traces the uncertainty. On several collider processes, the method matched scale variation where that trick behaves. Where scale variation understates, the new estimates grew appropriately. The authors offer it as a simple, more honest error recipe.
arxiv-2412-15010:
Özgü Göksu and Nicolas Pugeault tackle uneven data in federated learning in this 2024 paper. In federated learning, many devices train a shared model without pooling their data. When each device's data skews differently, the shared model often learns poorly. The authors show that such skews in how classes look, not just which classes appear, hurt results across test sets.

Their fix prunes weak connections while regularizing training on each client. The aim is a sparser model whose parts combine more cleanly. They also built a new benchmark from celebrity faces, with gender-based shifts inside each class. Across image tests the method beat standard federated baselines and held up better on data unlike the training mix.
arxiv-2412-15210: Whittington, Bachmann, and Pimentel settle a basic question about tokenisation, the step that splits text into the symbols a language model works with. They ask how hard it is, in the formal sense, to compress a data set down to at most a given number of symbols. Two variants are studied: choosing a vocabulary directly, and choosing a sequence of merge steps, as bottom-up tokenisers do. The authors prove that both variants are NP-complete, so no efficient general algorithm for optimal tokenisation should be expected.
arxiv-2412-16110: Callum Deakin and Xi Chen analyse limits of coherent modulation built on lossless unitary transforms in a short note from 2024. Such transforms reshape a signal across spectrum and time without loss, which offers a fresh route to modulation. The note tests how clean the output can stay at set laser power levels. Results show high signal quality above a strong threshold and better scores than standard IQ modulators at equal transmitter laser power. The work frames where this modulation route can beat classic designs on raw performance.
arxiv-2412-16310:
Nima Ghafari Cherati, Anton Pershin, and Ádám Gali simulate how sulfur impurities affect diamond's most famous defect, in a 2024 paper. The nitrogen-vacancy center, a nitrogen atom beside a missing carbon with a negative charge, is a workhorse of quantum technology. Making these centers exactly where wanted, in the right numbers, is a key engineering challenge.

Experiments found that implanting nitrogen molecules into sulfur-doped diamond layers creates the centers with up to about 75 percent efficiency. Why sulfur helps was unclear. Using quantum-mechanical calculations, the authors compare sulfur defects and their energy levels. A tug of war between two sulfur forms limits efficiency: one donates electrons, the other traps them in a sulfur-vacancy pair. Both forms also trap stray hydrogen, which in turn favors center creation in grown diamond layers. The results explain the observed limits.
arxiv-2412-16410:
Md Robiul Islam, writing solo in 2024, explores putting multimodal language models in the driver's seat. Self-driving systems still falter in messy, unusual scenes, and a model that can see, read, and reason in words might handle the long tail of surprises better. The author fine-tunes such a model on a visual question answering dataset built for driving scenes.

The driving task is then broken into stages that mirror a human driver's mind: understand the scene, predict what others will do, and decide the maneuver. A chain-of-thought routine makes the model spell out its reasoning between stages, which exposes mistakes for inspection. Experiments and analysis argue that language-level reasoning is not decoration but a real component of safe driving decisions. The study sketches a path toward cars that can explain why they turned, braked, or waited.
arxiv-2412-16510:
Soren Toxvaerd traces molecular dynamics algorithms back to Newton in a 2024 paper. A recent journal article claimed two standard integrators differ in substance. Toxvaerd argues they are one algorithm in two outfits.

Velocity-Verlet and position-Verlet both restate a scheme from 1687. That scheme appears in Proposition I of the Principia itself. Other simple integrators in wide use join the same family. All share the same motion, momentum, and energy behavior. Hundreds of thousands of simulations rest on this one discrete rule. Readers get a history lesson with practical bite for simulators.
arxiv-2412-16610:
Alireza Maleki and Ahmad Sheykhi ask how quantum jitter changes black hole entropy and the expanding universe in a 2024 paper. The classic entropy formula ties a horizon's entropy to its area. Adding quantum corrections reshapes that link, and through the holographic principle the reshaped entropy rewrites the equations of cosmic expansion.

Their model alters the expansion equations in specific parameter ranges. Fitted against the Pantheon supernova data set, it can pin down the size of the quantum corrections. One sharp finding: fluctuations can swell the horizon area by up to 47 percent. Past that point the theory strains against observation. The authors frame the work as a bridge between quantum gravity ideas and measurable cosmology.
arxiv-2412-16810:
Four mathematicians study a family of curves that arises from meromorphic differential forms on the Riemann sphere. Each form has zeros and poles of set orders, and the isoresidual map records the residues at the poles. When a form has exactly two zeros, a typical fiber of this map is a complex curve carrying a natural flat geometry called a translation structure. The paper describes that geometry in depth.

The authors compute discrete data for these curves, including the orders of their singular points and a quantity that ties the curve's periods to the residue pattern. They also find the Euler characteristic of a typical fiber curve using intersection theory on a compactified space of differentials. The answer turns out to follow a wall and chamber pattern that depends on the chosen partition, and they classify how many connected pieces a typical fiber has.
arxiv-2412-17210:
Hongsong Wang and three co-authors present a 2024 paper on spotting odd behavior in video by watching body poses. Rebuilding what it sees helps a system flag strange patterns, while predicting ahead helps it flag strange trends. Prior pose-based detectors usually picked one route. Their framework, DCMD, takes both: a diffusion model conditioned on the observed motion and on a learned summary of it.

A motion transformer inside the diffusion process reads layered features of the movement. A custom penalty sharpens the gap between normal and abnormal samples, using both time-wise and global links. At test time, a mask completion step strengthens the prediction side. On four data sets the method beat state-of-the-art rivals by clear margins and generalized well. The authors target surveillance and safety monitoring that must respect privacy by using poses, not faces.
arxiv-2412-17310:
Ashutosh Nayak and five co-authors worked on product bundles: sets of goods sold as one. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with advice systems that push bundles, not lone items. Bundles can lift sales and please buyers, yet work on how to form new bundles is scarce. There is also no sound way to tell if a bundle will be popular. The team aimed at both gaps.

They built embeddings that join what a good is with the context it sits in. Those vectors feed both a popularity guess and a bundle builder. Readers who run shops get a way to mint fresh bundles with proof of taste fit. The work treats bundle craft as a task in its own right.
arxiv-2412-17510:
Tomonori Kouya tests a faster way to multiply a sparse matrix by a vector, using many digits and vector lanes, in this 2024 paper. The catalog title carries a funding note. Sparse matrices are mostly zeros, yet key in science and AI. The operation sits at the heart of many solvers that work step by step.

Those solvers can be badly hurt by rounding errors when they use standard floating point. Working with many more digits can steady them, but it costs a lot of speed. Kouya uses SIMD, chip lanes that do the same step on many values at once, to win back much of that cost. The method works for both real and complex numbers. Tests through solver cases show the routines work well. It serves users who need trustworthy answers from ill-conditioned problems, where extra digits are not a luxury.
arxiv-2412-17910:
Vansh Nagpal, Siva Likitha Valluru, and colleagues built a meal planner that weighs health against convenience in a 2024 study. Choosing breakfast, lunch, and dinner means trading nutrition, such as salt and sugar, against cost, access, and cuisine. Groups eating together over long periods make the problem harder, since tastes and health needs differ and repeat.

Their system, BEACON, reasons over recipes described in text and images, composing full meals from starter to drink. Long-term group recommendations keep plans varied and fair across members. The work targets everyday eaters and people managing health conditions alike.
arxiv-2412-18010:
Grèbol-Tomàs and a large team of co-authors pressed and squeezed olivine crystals from a Moon meteorite to see how they differ from Earth olivine, in this 2024 arXiv paper. How planetary minerals bear stress matters for planning future missions. The sample came from NWA 12008, a lunar basalt that fell as a meteorite.

Tiny diamond-point presses showed the lunar grains are softer and springier than their Earth counterparts. High-pressure X-ray scans then tracked how the crystals compress, and one axis of the lunar olivine squeezed more than Earth's. The team also measured three common meteorites for contrast. A simple model mixing grain-scale and chemical-bond effects explains the softening. The authors offer the paired method as a new way to grade space rocks.
arxiv-2412-18110:
Gui Ling, Ziyang Wang, Yuliang Yan, and Qingwen Liu present SlimGPT in a 2024 paper, a low-cost way to prune large language models layer by layer. Big models are hard to run in the field for their vast size. Structured pruning cuts whole parts away, to strike a balance of skill and speed, but the lost skill is hard to win back on a tight budget.

SlimGPT rests on the Optimal Brain Surgeon frame. A batched greedy step prunes fast and near the best point. Grouped math sharpens the error call per attention head, and a shifting group size speeds the feedforward cuts.
arxiv-2412-18410:
Denis Bernardes and co-authors describe the control system of SPARC4, a Brazilian-built astronomy instrument. It photographs the sky in four color bands at once, or measures light polarization in all four. It rides on the 1.6-meter telescope at Pico dos Dias Observatory. Three software pieces divide the work of running it.

One program drives the four scientific cameras. A second runs the sensors and motors of the moving parts. A third gives observers the interface for choosing settings and taking images, while talking to observatory services. Bench tests measured the delays the system adds. In photo mode it can shoot fourteen hundred full frames with only milliseconds of dead time between them, and polarimetry sequences are similarly brisk.
arxiv-2412-18610:
Zixia Wei and Yasushi Yoneta invent a new way to suddenly change a quantum system and watch it relax, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Physicists use such quenches to study how complex correlations build up over time. Most quenches start from simple, nonthermal states.

Their crosscap quench instead starts from highly structured thermal pure states. The authors ask how those states evolve toward typical ones. In conformal field theories they derive universal features of the entanglement entropy's time evolution. Holographic theories, treated through the AdS/CFT correspondence, give a tractable chaotic example. Numerical simulations of quantum spin chains confirm the picture. Both integrable and nonintegrable systems were tested against the theory.
arxiv-2412-18810:
Yilei Jiang and four co-authors present a plug-in method that makes text-to-image models fairer, in a 2024 paper. Image generators learn the biases of their training photos, which can distort who appears in pictures and limit chances for minorities. Older fixes need retraining or hand-built reference sets, which cost money and cap the gains. Their method, FairGen, instead discovers directions inside the model's latent space on its own.

Small adapters each learn one attribute direction, such as gender or race, through a self-guided noise trick. A distribution indicator then weights the adapters to steer output toward a chosen balance. Several attributes can be adjusted at once, with no retraining. In tests on gender, race, and their combination, FairGen beat prior methods by a wide margin. The authors stress it stays light and can attach to other generators.
arxiv-2412-18910:
Situo Zhang and co-authors present AdaEAGLE in a 2024 paper on faster language model replies. Speculative decoding speeds generation by drafting several tokens with a small model and checking them with the large one. Fixed draft lengths waste effort, since the right length varies with context.

AdaEAGLE models the draft structure directly. A light module predicts the best number of draft tokens at each step, guiding the draft model without hand-set thresholds. Speed matched or beat the best fixed-length systems while output quality stayed unchanged. Combined with threshold methods, it ran 1.62 times faster than plain decoding. The authors argue that explicit modelling of the draft shape opens room for deeper optimisation than rule-based tweaks.
arxiv-2412-19010:
People act one way with friends, another at work, and another at home, and Joel Z. Leibo and co-authors ask what makes each choice seem right for its setting. Their twenty twenty-four work sets out a theory of what fits a given case, and then applies that theory to systems that write and answer on their own.

Early pages ask what sets the rules for what fits, and why those rules shift over time. Later pages look at how the rules work in social life and how they might work in the brain. The closing part draws lessons for safe and sound use of new writing tools, since people in the end judge what those tools do.
arxiv-2412-19210:
Matías Godoy, Manuel Torres-Valdebenito, and Emilio Vilches study sweeping processes, a class of evolution problems where a moving set pushes a state along. The sets here are prox-regular, and the motion is perturbed by an operator that depends on the whole past history. The authors ask when such problems have exactly one solution that behaves well.

Their method rests on an improved form of Gronwall's lemma together with fixed-point arguments. The approach covers both state-dependent and state-independent cases in one frame. It recovers all known results for Volterra sweeping processes and adds new insight into the history-dependent kind. As a test of the theory, the authors prove that a viscoelastic model with long memory is well-posed. The paper gives analysts a compact tool kit for a family of problems that shows up in mechanics and materials with memory.
arxiv-2412-19310:
Tsoupidi, Troubitsyna, and Papadimitratos audit the defenses of crypto libraries in a 2024 article. These libraries guard keys and coded messages across the internet, yet they leak through side channels and memory flaws. The team reviews popular libraries and the guards each one carries. Gaps are named, and fixes for the build process are proposed.

Side-channel attacks read secrets from timing or power traces rather than breaking the math. Code-reuse attacks bend flawed memory handling to hijack flow. The authors argue that library teams should bake checks for both into daily work. The article serves builders of security software who want a map of weak spots.
arxiv-2412-19410:
Félix del Teso and Julio Rossi present a 2024 math paper extending a classic averaging property to a nonlinear equation with a source term. For the plain Laplace equation, a function's value at a point equals its average nearby. The nonlinear cousin, the p-Laplace equation, resists that neatness once a forcing term enters.

The authors derive new asymptotic mean value formulas for exactly that forced case, where the usual rescaling trick fails. The formulas frame solutions through a game: two players tug a token, one maximizing and one minimizing, with payoff rules encoding the equation. They prove the game values exist, are unique, and converge to the solution. It is the first game reading of the forced problem.
arxiv-2412-19510:
Koustav Ghosal and co-authors use parameter-efficient fine-tuning to adapt a foundation model for seismic waveform inversion, published in 2024. Full-waveform inversion builds images of the Earth's subsurface from seismic waves. Deep learning has advanced it, but most models are trained for one task in isolation, which limits how well they generalize to new geology.

The team first builds a task-agnostic foundation model that captures general features across tasks. Fully tuning it beat models trained from scratch on several benchmarks. They then tune only a small fraction of its parameters. That light tuning matched full tuning on standard tasks, with far lower memory and compute cost. On out-of-distribution tasks it beat both full tuning and task-specific models, a case for foundation models in this field.
arxiv-2412-19810:
Sam Carey wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four as the sole author. It gives a full analytic form of the Correlated Fermi Gas model for how leptons scatter off a nucleus in the quasielastic range.

Scattering of neutrinos off nuclei is key to the new round of neutrino trials, and nuclear effects are a chief source of doubt in the cross sections. Carey's form lets form factor effects and nuclear model effects be weighed apart. He sets it against the older Relativistic Fermi Gas model on both electron-carbon and neutrino-carbon data. The work speaks to those who must pin down cross sections before oscillation results can be trusted.
arxiv-2412-19910:
Bhabha scattering, where an electron and positron bounce off each other, is a classic test of quantum field theory. Araújo and co-authors study a heavier cousin of that process inside the Rarita-Schwinger model, which describes spin-3/2 particles rather than ordinary spin-1/2 ones. They ask what changes when the scattering happens not in empty cold space but at finite temperature. Using the thermofield dynamics formalism, they compute the fermion-antifermion scattering cross-section at tree level, the first approximation in the theory.

The setup lets temperature enter the calculation directly, so its effect on the scattering rate can be read off. Work of this kind matters for hot environments, from the early universe to dense astrophysical settings, where thermal effects bend the rules of particle collisions. The paper positions the finite-temperature cross-section as a baseline for richer treatments of spin-3/2 scattering.
arxiv-2501-00510:
Zhaoliang Wan and a large team of co-authors introduce VinT-6D, a large-scale dataset for object-in-hand pose estimation. Their paper addresses a scarcity of data for this task, which is crucial for robotic in-hand manipulation.

VinT-6D is the first large multimodal dataset to join vision, touch, and proprioception for this purpose. It holds two million simulated samples made in MuJoCo and Blender, and a tenth of a million real samples from a custom platform. The real split is described as the largest of its kind, given how hard real collection is. Models get whole-hand tactile perception and well-aligned data, which should help close the simulation-to-real gap.
arxiv-2501-00610:
Farinaldo Queiroz and co-authors use public ATLAS data from the Large Hadron Collider to bound a new force carrier, the Z prime boson of the B-L model. The work appeared in 2024, per the text head. Dilepton events, pairs of leptons in the detector, carry the signal.

With no hidden decays, the data push the boson's mass above four trillion electron volts at weak coupling, and above six at stronger coupling. Hidden decays loosen the bounds a lot: at a ninety percent hidden share, the strong coupling bound relaxes as stated in the study. The team also projects the high luminosity upgrade, which should probe masses up to 7.5 trillion electron volts.
arxiv-2501-00810:
Xin Huang and Fangyang Zheng settle a case of an old geometry question in this 2025 paper. The question asks whether a compact space with a set curved shape must be of a special well-known kind, or flat in a set sense. It was solved for surfaces decades ago, but stays open in higher dimensions.

The authors prove the claim for a family of spaces called solvmanifolds whose commutator has a complex form. These spaces are built from solvable symmetry groups. The result extends an earlier proof for a narrower family of such spaces by Li and Zheng. The authors note the algebraic tangle of the curvature measure is what makes the general question hard. Their case adds one more settled family to the map.
arxiv-2501-00910:
Yang Li, Han Meng, Zhenyu Bi, Ingolv Urnes, and Haipeng Chen point out a blind spot in tools that make fake time series, in a paper from 2025. Most tools make each fake series look real on its own, yet miss traits of the whole set, such as how values spread or link.

Their model, PaD-TS, trains with those whole set traits in mind and uses a two path encoder to read series form. On main test sets it cut the shift in a key link trait by a large factor. At the same time it kept single series quality on par with top rival models.
arxiv-2501-01110:
Jimin Park and four co-authors present a defense tool for spotting malware, in a 2025 computer science paper. Detectors trained once tend to forget old threats as new ones appear, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. Their system, named MalCL, keeps learning in steps as fresh malware families arrive.

Instead of storing old malware, the system trains a generator to fake samples of past threats and replays them beside new data. A matching loss helps the fakes stay faithful, and the system picks which fakes to replay based on the detector's inner state. Tests on Windows and Android malware showed clear gains over older replay methods, with accuracy on Windows samples far ahead of rival systems. The authors share their code for other teams to build on.
arxiv-2501-01310:
Peñil, Domínguez, Buson, Ajello, Adhikari, and Rico search twelve years of gamma-ray sky data for galaxies whose jets brighten or fade in a straight line. Jetted active nuclei usually flicker stochastically. A recently noticed pattern, a steady linear climb in one famous blazar, suggested a distinct long-term behavior worth hunting systematically. The sample covers over three thousand jetted sources watched by the Fermi telescope's main instrument.

Forty sources show significant long-term trends, linear or quadratic, each then characterized in detail. Such trends might betray a supermassive black hole binary slowly tightening, or physics inside the jet itself. Either origin would matter for the periodicity debates around these objects. The catalog of forty gives follow-up studies a concrete target list. A decade of patience, mined well, separates drift from noise.
arxiv-2501-01410:
Rishabh Saraswat, Rekha Verma, and Sitangshu Bhattacharya wrote a paper from 2025 on coaxing more light from a sheet one atom thick. The sheet is made of molybdenum and sulfur. It can emit light when energy pairs inside it join with the help of the sheet's own vibrations. In this material that help is weak, since the rules of symmetry block the key vibrations.

The team ran deep quantum sums and checked them against symmetry rules. In the plain sheet, the blocked modes keep the glow off at low heat. A stretch applied in two directions changes the rules. The stretch wakes a new vibration path that lets the dark pairs scatter and then shine. Strength shifts toward the paths that emit light. The team says strain could lift the glow of a whole class of such sheets.
arxiv-2501-01510:
Saurabh Sihag, Gonzalo Mateos, and Alejandro Ribeiro present a 2025 study of brain age gap in degenerative diseases, using covariance neural networks that stay explainable. Brain age gap, how much older a brain looks than its years, flags vulnerability to decline. Black-box predictors of it are hard to trust clinically. The network family used here ties its features to anatomy and to the eigenstructure of the brain's covariance pattern.

Applied to cortical thickness in Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and atypical Parkinsonian disorders, the method found distinct anatomic patterns per disease. The authors trace those patterns to how the network uses different parts of the covariance spectrum. That linkage, they argue, turns a score into an interpretable signpost for clinicians.
arxiv-2501-02010:
Antoine Ledent and Peng Liu present a 2025 paper on neural networks that people can read and trust. Large networks predict well, but their inner steps are hard to follow. The authors build a network called SparXnet that keeps its logic open. Its forecast is a plain sum of a small set of learned features. Each feature comes from one input field alone.

The network learns which few features matter and drops the rest on its own. Tests on fake and real data show it picks out the right features while matching the accuracy of less clear models. The authors also prove bounds on how well it should do on new data. Those bounds grow slowly as more input fields are added.
arxiv-2501-02110:
Jiaqi Zhou, Samuel Poncé, and Jean-Christophe Charlier screen hundreds of atom-thin materials for spin Hall response. Their 2025 paper automates Wannier-based calculations with spin-orbit coupling across 426 non-magnetic monolayers. The set splits between metals and insulators.

One compound shows an unusual canted spin response from its low symmetry. A tantalum selenide monolayer posts exceptionally high spin Hall conductivity among metals. A semi-metal converts charge to spin efficiently through band anti-crossing. Quantum spin Hall insulators in the set show the expected quantized response. The team also releases a database of the computed Hamiltonians. The survey aims to speed the hunt for two-dimensional materials for low-power spintronic devices.
arxiv-2501-02310:
Splitting a hard equation into easier pieces and solving them in turns is a workhorse of simulation. Pushing the method to high accuracy forces some pieces to run backward in time, which can blow up. Siqi Wei and co-authors study the design choices that tame that risk in a 2025 paper. Step order, the solvers used inside each piece, and the error measure all turn out to matter.

They build a three-step, high-order method tuned for steady behavior on a heart-cell benchmark. A general rule follows: run the shaky pieces with cheap, low-order solvers. Methods rebuilt on these principles ran nearly thirty percent better than the best known rivals.
arxiv-2501-02610:
Anne Green revisits limits on early black holes from star watching in a 2025 paper. Surveys of stars in a small neighbor galaxy can show if such holes make up part of the dark matter halo. Past studies disagreed on how much the limits shift with unknowns in how dark matter is spread.

Green reworks the rate of lens events, where a hole passes before a star and bends its light. Long events, tied to light holes, shift only a little with those unknowns. Short events shift far more, since they hinge on how fast nearby dark matter moves. She argues that a sound map of local dark matter speed is key to firm limits.
arxiv-2501-03210:
David Pérez Castro and co-authors simulated in 2025 entanglement-based quantum networks to learn how well they can share entangled states. Entanglement is the core resource for quantum communication, and sharing it over long distances with high fidelity is hard. Switches that link segments are key to building large networks.

They built a switch-based network in a standard simulator and ran many experiments. Factors tested included memory type, gate times, noise, number of switches, distance, and error handling. All of these shaped the end-to-end fidelity of the shared state. From the results, they draw practical guidelines for designing and setting up future quantum networks of this kind.
arxiv-2501-03310:
Edoardo Anastasi, Roberta Angius, Jesús Huertas, Angel Uranga, and Chuying Wang ask whether gravity theories pinned to a boundary must obey the usual quantum gravity rules, in a 2025 paper. The rules, called swampland constraints, ban features like exact global symmetries and some kinds of empty space. The team studies gravity that lives on the edge of a higher-dimensional spacetime, a setup called localized gravity.

Alone, such a theory can break nearly every rule on the list. Joined to its higher-dimensional host, every rule snaps back into force. The authors name this status relative quantum gravity: the small theory is consistent only relative to its host. They work the idea through double holography and through concrete string theory models with branes. The paper reframes several bans as statements about pairs of theories, not single ones.
arxiv-2501-03610:
Xin-Ying Song tests whether quark stars could power gamma-ray bursts in this 2025 paper. One proposed engine is a neutron star that burns into a strange quark star while feeding on a companion. The burst's outflow would then carry little normal matter, mostly crust material from the quark star. Song gathered a special subset of bursts seen over sixteen years. From them, she estimated how much crust mass the engine hypothesis requires.

She then computed crust masses under several models of cold dense quark matter. The set included the MIT bag model and the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, with and without color superconducting condensates. The comparison gave no positive support for quark star engines. One variant fared least badly: the model that allows hybrid stars, part quark and part normal matter. Song concludes the burst record so far does not back the quark star engine idea.
arxiv-2501-04010:
The authors revisit classic work on pairs of subspaces in a real Hilbert space, a topic tied to how quantum theory handles time and energy. They loosen the old assumption that the subspaces sit in the nicest possible position toward each other. From two real projection operators, they build a complex Hilbert space where the modular operator theory applies.

A group of split quaternions, enlarged by a central extension, plays a key role in the build. Two worked examples have subspaces of unequal size, so they fall outside the generic case the older work assumed. The paper appeared in 2024.
arxiv-2501-04310:
Jihao Fan and Min-Hsiu Hsieh pin down in 2025 how well quantum cyclic codes can fix burst errors. Burst errors strike in runs, a pattern tied to memory effects in quantum channels. Cyclic codes are a key family for this task, yet their exact burst limit was not fully known.

The authors study codes built by two standard routes and find their burst correction limit with fast methods. Many codes in this class reach the quantum Reiger bound, the best a code can do. Quantum Reed-Solomon codes turn out stronger than past work had shown. The team also gives a decoder that runs in linear time. It fixes both plain and degenerate burst errors, and trials show it handles the degenerate kind far more often.
arxiv-2501-04410:
Simulating users, building software stand-ins that act like people using an AI system, is growing into a field of its own. Balog and Zhai survey the topic across computing, design, and social science, where the work has been scattered. They cover user modeling, fake data generation, and testing systems with simulated users in place of costly human trials.

The authors trace a shift from older predictive models to modern generative ones, and they give ethics a full treatment. Controlled simulation can expose bias and support fair, safe systems rather than only risking harm. They tie the topic to general intelligence goals and propose a shared ecosystem linking labs and industry.
arxiv-2501-05010:
Min Liu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on making topological superconductors hardier by letting them leak. A one-dimensional p-wave superconductor hosts Majorana zero modes at its ends, prized for quantum computing. Disorder usually shrinks the safe region where those modes survive.

The team studied a generalized Kitaev chain with asymmetric hopping, which makes the system non-Hermitian, plus non-local disorder. Both numerics and analysis show the leakiness enlarges the region where the topological phase withstands disorder. In plain terms, opening the system stabilizes its protected edge states against stronger mess. The authors offer the result as a new angle on how openness and topology interact, with an eye to more robust quantum devices.
arxiv-2501-06010:
Picking Tor guard relays without using location can still blunt routing attacks, Zhifan Lu, Siyang Sun, and Yixin Sun argue in a 2025 paper. Location-aware picking defends Tor users but leaks where clients sit and invites guard placement games. Their design leans on the internet's route certificate system instead.

A light method uses route origin papers alone. A stronger one also demands validation status, raising matched safe client-relay pairs to nearly half in tests. Both avoid location data entirely. Privacy tools face a standing trade between routing safety and location secrecy; certificate-based picking offers a middle path.
arxiv-2501-06110:
A future quantum internet needs hardware that can store light, emit it on demand, and process it. Wolfgang Tittel and co-authors review a promising platform: crystals doped with rare-earth ions. These ions sit still in the crystal lattice and hold quantum states for long times. They interact with light at useful wavelengths.

The review covers single-photon sources, optical memories that catch and release light, and qubits built from the ions themselves. It then surveys the first repeater links, the relay stations a long-distance network requires. The authors judge where the field stands and point to the experiments that should come next. Rare-earth crystals, they argue, fit the network's needs unusually well.
arxiv-2501-06310:
Isabella Khan links two worlds of modern algebra that grew up apart. One is the wrapped Fukaya category, a frame built from surfaces with punctures and the paths on them. The other is a family of algebras born in knot theory's bordered branch, called star algebras, which Khan built in earlier work. Her 2025 paper proves the two sides match.

Khan first shows the star algebras are the only ones with their generators and basic rules, viewing them as deformations of plainer algebras. Cohomology checks pin down that uniqueness. She then computes the surface side's endomorphism algebras and finds the same generators and rules. The match lets tools cross between geometry and knot algebra, to the gain of both.
arxiv-2501-06710:
Ming Dai and co-authors present in 2025 a two stage frame that finds and cuts out a named thing in a photo from a text cue. Past top frames fuse sight and text in one pass. A blur between the find task and the cut task then yields split calls.

Stage one gives rough find and cut calls from split coders. Stage two refines them with a mask led link block and a two way match loss. That loss forces the find and cut calls to agree. Pre trained sight text models add depth to the text read. Tests back the two stage gains.
arxiv-2501-06810:
Kim, Jang, and Kim studied source language choice in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Speech tools for languages with little data often borrow training from richer languages. Picking the donor language, though, was usually done with little care. The team asked how sound-level similarity between languages shapes the payoff.

For phoneme recognition, training with sound-alike languages beat single-language training by a wide margin. It even topped a large self-supervised model. Within one language family, closer sound patterns helped, while distant ones hurt. Similarity across families mattered more than family ties themselves. The authors give a practical way to judge sound closeness before choosing donors.
arxiv-2501-07010:
Mrinmoy Kundu and co-authors design a device that shifts single light particles between colors in this 2025 paper. Quantum networks need such shifts because most quantum memories work in visible light. Signals must move to telecom colors for long trips through fiber.

Their converter joins a ring and a two-path device on a thin lithium niobate film with a striped pattern. It can shift photons both ways, from memory colors to telecom colors and back. The design claims rates near 90 percent at low pump power, with very low noise. The work targets one key link in future quantum networks.
arxiv-2501-07310:
Peigen Cao, writing alone, offers a 2025 algebra paper on modules and the shapes that describe them. In a branch of algebra called tau-tilting theory, two classes of modules stand out for their rigid behavior. Cao asks whether each such module is fixed once one knows a certain polygon built from the sizes of its quotient modules.

The answer given is yes for both classes. Each module of these kinds is the only one that matches its Newton polytope, the polygon in question. The result extends a classic finding by Gabriel, who showed that modules over Dynkin quiver algebras are fixed by their size vectors alone. Readers get a cleaner way to tell these modules apart.
arxiv-2501-07410:
Florian Ederer and co-authors dissect an anonymous forum where economists trade job market talk, and not always kindly. Economics Job Market Rumors is famous inside the field for sharp, nameless posts. The study tracks how the forum leans on outside sources and what that says about the profession online.

Links outward shape much of the forum's diet, and the team maps which domains feed it. Talk driven by Twitter posts has surged since the late twenty tens. The authors sort whose posts get chewed over most, by the poster's traits and fame. The forum plainly moves information through the field. It also stirs hard questions about welcome and ethics, since nameless attention can shade into abuse. Departments may need norms for a space they do not run but cannot ignore.
arxiv-2501-07810:
Finding the object that makes a sound in a video means joining ears and eyes in one model. Sitong Gong and co-authors built such a model on a newer sequence method that handles long clips cheaply. Older attention-based models grow costly as clips lengthen. Their design has blocks that track change over time and blocks that pass detail between picture and sound. A decoder then merges the two streams at several sizes.

The model set new best scores on two standard test sets for this task. The parts each target a weak spot: time flow, scale, and sound-picture matching. Code and trained weights are shared openly. The work may help video editing and robot hearing alike.
arxiv-2501-08010:
Davide Ricci and co-authors describe upgrades to the control software of a telescope instrument during its build and test phase in this 2025 paper. The instrument, SHARK-NIR, will hunt planets by blocking starlight at a large telescope. Its software must run observing blocks built from script templates, in the style of the observatory it will join.

During assembly and testing the team leaned on those same templates to run their many checks, from flexure tests to mask alignment. They built a web system that writes the observing blocks through a simple interface and also exposes single device moves and status panels. A scare emerged when two moving parts threatened to collide. While a hardware lock is explored, they shipped a three-layer software guard that watches for the clash from every control path. The guard has passed its tests.
arxiv-2501-08110:
Oregel-Chaumont and co-authors report the first sighting of a mixed charge pattern in an upward lightning flash, in a 2025 paper. The flash rose from a tower in Switzerland. Such upward flashes start at tall structures and climb into the sky. Fast cameras caught the event, and sensors tracked current and electric fields.

A recoil leader ran down and met the live channel below one kilometer above the tower tip. That meeting triggered the main pulse of the flash. The pattern was known from downward negative flashes, not this kind. The pulse also shared traits with a second pulse type, which blurs current class rules. The authors propose one charge mode whose traits vary with the length of the junction path.
arxiv-2501-08310:
Michał Zakrzewski and Henryk Żołądek wrote this math paper in 2025. It proves new integral formulas for hypergeometric functions. This is a broad family of special functions. The paper then follows where those formulas lead.

The authors use the stationary phase method. They apply it to WKB expansions for differential equations. They study cases with large inputs and large parameters. They also study what happens when an equation is changed by a small amount. A new proof makes clear a known result by Wasow on the Airy equation. It shows how that result differs from the Stokes phenomenon. Two key equations get close study. They link to generating functions for multiple zeta values. The paper also corrects an earlier claim about one such expansion.
arxiv-2501-08510:
Diego Salvador and colleagues mapped how the mix of star masses varies inside galaxies in a 2025 study. The initial mass function describes how many small versus large stars are born together, and it underpins all models of galaxy growth. Evidence has grown that the mix is not universal, so the team asked how it changes from place to place within single galaxies, using the SAMI survey's spatially resolved spectra.

They estimated the high-mass slope patch by patch and for whole galaxies, using population models. Local and whole-galaxy slopes tracked each other closely over most of the range, yet the local slopes spread widely inside individual galaxies. Follow-up analysis probes what local conditions drive that spread.
arxiv-2501-08910:
Gabriella Pangelinan and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, whether uneven lighting in face photos drives unfair results in face recognition. Brightness on the face is a known quality factor, and matching accuracy for paired photos differs between demographic groups.

The team ran three tests that balanced brightness between photos of Caucasian and African American women. Balancing by the middle brightness value alone cut the accuracy gap sharply, and balancing by the full spread of brightness cut it further. Scores within each group also improved. The results suggest that much of the fairness gap in matching may come from lighting, not from the faces themselves.
arxiv-2501-09010:
Alex Chapple, Othmane Benhayoune-Khadraoui, Simon Richer, and Alexandre Blais propose a new way to read out the state of a superconducting qubit. Their 2025 paper tackles a weak point in quantum computing: the standard readout method loses speed and accuracy when the drive power rises, because extra photon effects get in the way.

The team calls its method junction readout. A small junction links the qubit to the part that senses its state, and a second link added beside it blocks unwanted energy loss without an extra filter. Computer tests suggest the method resists the harmful photon effects better than the standard one. The tests reach accuracy above 99.99 percent in under 30 nanoseconds, using hardware much like what labs already have.
arxiv-2501-09210:
Xinying Hou and co-authors test a gentler way to help programming students who ask AI for help, in a 2025 paper. Modern chatbots will happily hand a stuck student a finished solution, and the student learns little. The team instead offered personalised Parsons puzzles: the lines of a correct program, shuffled, which the student must put back in order. The puzzle is built from an AI solution tuned to the student's own attempt.

In an eighty-minute classroom study of Python practice, students were split at random into two help styles. One group got the puzzles as scaffolding whenever they asked for help. The other saw the complete solution at once, copying the usual chatbot reply. The puzzle group stayed engaged in practice far longer than the solution group. The authors argue for AI help that makes students work, not just watch.
arxiv-2501-09410:
Lyudong Jin and six co-authors present a 2025 paper on running large language models cooperatively across edge devices. Phones and small servers differ widely in power, so pooling them could cut cost and delay. Their framework, MoE2, treats the edge models as a mixture of experts and decides which ones answer each request. The selection problem is combinatorial and tangled, harder than in classic mixture-of-experts setups.

The team found a property of the gating choices that lets training and selection be split apart, slashing complexity. A custom optimization algorithm then picks the optimal experts under energy and delay budgets. They built real edge servers on Jetson boards and high-end graphics cards to test it. Across models and resource limits, the method found better delay-energy trade-offs than the baselines. The authors target cheap, responsive AI served near the user.
arxiv-2501-09610:
Some number patterns refuse to behave randomly, and the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence is a classic: built by flipping zeros and ones, it avoids repeats in a way mathematicians have admired for a century. Denis Janković and co-authors ask what that pattern can do for quantum computing in a 2025 paper.

The team shows the sequence surfacing naturally in chains of interacting quantum spins, the Ising X-X systems. There it suggests a sturdy way to encode quantum memories that shrug off noise. The sequence also feeds quantum error correction and offers a window on quantum chaos. Links reach even into pure mathematics, touching the Riemann zeta function from number theory. The authors pitch the sequence as a bridge: one elegant pattern tying together hardware design, error control, and deep theory.
arxiv-2501-09810:
Om Gupta and co-authors used in 2025 a sharpened catalogue of fast radio bursts to ask where in cosmic history these millisecond flashes come from. The Canadian CHIME telescope's baseband update finally gives precise energies for its bursts. The team calibrated how burst energy and signal smearing vary together across the catalogue.

The energy spread follows the classic Schechter shape with a steep slope. Testing how the burst rate evolves with distance favored a mixed parentage: part of the sources track star birth closely, and part lag by roughly two billion years. A purely young population was disfavored. The authors also forecast what future low-frequency telescopes should catch at the universe's dawn. Hundreds of bursts a year from the reionization era are within reach.
arxiv-2501-10210:
Marius Constantin Chirita Mihaila and co-authors propose a light based fix for chromatic aberration in ultrafast electron microscopes. In a normal electron lens, electrons of unlike energy focus at unlike points, which blurs the image. Their 2025 method shapes the electron pulse with light instead of new lens hardware.

A shaped, pulsed ponderomotive lens gives the beam a phase pattern that varies in space and time. Paired with the natural energy chirp of the pulse, the time shifting lens size makes the focal length depend on energy in just the right way. The two effects cancel much of the blur: the team shows aberration can fall by up to seven fold in theory.
arxiv-2501-10310:
Pascal Baseilhac and Rodrigo A. Pimenta wrote a 2025 math paper, the second in a series, on a family of special polynomials. The work uses pairs and triples of operators drawn from algebra to study states that solve a known set of equations. Those states are used in models of linked quantum systems.

The authors show that overlaps between two kinds of states can be written as sums of the named polynomials. The weights in those sums depend on free values in one state. Special choices then give neat formulas for the polynomials and link hard equation roots to roots of a simpler, even form of the same system.
arxiv-2501-10510:
Yang, Liu, and Feng gauge how a slick coat bends jets from burst suds. Burst suds at a gas-wet face can spray fine drops in the air. Those drops bear chem and live stuff to the sky in their wake. What slick coats do to that spray had stayed dim till now. A slick coat that won't mix sits on the sud face here. Jet width strays from the clean-sud tale in the runs.

The team traces crest waves at the air-oil-wet face for the cause. A thin-wave damp frame rests on coat depth and crest spread. A fresh Ohnesorge count with a scale rule fits the runs well. It holds past a wide span of coat depths and flows. The work may hone spray size guesses for sea and sky work.
arxiv-2501-10710:
Ryo Matsuda and co-authors show how to address single quantum bits on a shared wire without waking their neighbors, in a 2025 paper. Wiring one line per qubit will not scale, so several qubits share a line by pitch. When pitches sit close, a pulse aimed at one can spill onto others.

Their shaped pulse carves null points at the neighbor pitches, silencing the spill. On three fixed-pitch transmon qubits, the shaped pulses matched standard pulses on gate quality for the target. Unwanted excitation of bystanders dropped sharply at the same time. Shared-line control, a key scaling trick for quantum hardware, gains a cleaner tool.
arxiv-2501-10810:
Manthey and three colleagues study ant colony methods in twenty twenty-five, a math approach based on how ants search for food. Computer ants build trial answers step by step and leave a scent trail on good paths. The scent fades over time, and the fade rate can change as the search runs.

The team proves that one graph based method still finds the best answer in the end. They then test two changed forms of a second method on a shortest path task. One form can take far too long to finish. The other form solves the same task in a fair span of time. The work helps users pick safe settings for such searches.
arxiv-2501-10910:
Ibna Kowsar and co-authors present a 2025 paper on filling gaps in data tables. Real tables often miss values at random or in patterns, and poor guesses can poison later models. Common fixes break down when the missing share is high or the gaps are not random.

Their method, DeepIFSAC, pays attention along both rows and columns of a table. One attention path links features to each other, and another links similar samples. Training uses a contrastive setup with a data-mixing trick to steady the guesses. Against eleven rival methods on twelve varied data sets, their approach ranked best on average. The edge was clearest when missing rates ran from 10 to 90 percent and gaps followed patterns.
arxiv-2501-11210:
Simon Huttegger, Sean Walsh, and Francesca Zaffora Blando brought computing theory to a classic puzzle in 2025 about when Bayes' rule can be trusted. Two old theorems pull in unlike ways. One says the rule settles on the truth in most cases. The other says a prior view can be built that never settles. A famed open ask was to name for which starting values the rule does settle.

The authors read the puzzle through the lens of randomness that a computer can test. They show that starting values that pass that test do settle, given a map with the right traits. They also show the bad cases are in a sense thick on the ground. Some of them can be computed and still fail to settle.
arxiv-2501-11310:
Abdelrahman Alzarooni and co-authors survey vision-based fault finding in industry, in work from 2025. Camera checks guard quality and speed on production lines, from factories to aerospace shops. Hand checks by operators are slow and dull work. Smart vision systems now read images on their own and flag flaws as they arise.

The survey covers studies since 2019 and walks the full pipeline, from data capture and cleanup to learning and scoring. It also lists open data sets used in the field. Key blocks, such as scarce flaw samples, are paired with fixes. The authors close with paths the field may take next.
arxiv-2501-11510:
Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider and co-authors study a spinning disk in a thin fluid layer in a 2025 paper. The fluid has odd viscosity, a trait absent in normal fluids. The disk sits on a rigid base and turns at a steady rate. The fluid can be compressed, which adds to the puzzle.

Odd viscosity creates a radial flow that points inward or outward by its sign. That flow should shape how two spinning disks pull or push each other. The team map the full flow field around the disk. They also compute drag on the spin and find odd viscosity raises it for either sign. The work guides study of exotic fluids.
arxiv-2501-11810:
Katsumasa Nakayama and Manuel Schneider improve a physics calculation method in a 2025 paper. Their method, a form of tensor renormalization, rewrites physical quantities as networks of small tensors. It can study systems without a flaw that plagues other methods. To use it, workers first need an initial tensor network in a form suited to repeated coarsening.

They give a systematic way to turn a general tensor form into that starting form. They also show how the choice of starting network affects how the method performs. Based on that insight, they propose an improvement to the method itself. The work is method-focused and aimed at specialists in lattice physics.
arxiv-2501-12110:
Entanglement between a full system and an empty reservoir rises, peaks, and falls like a Page curve. A 2025 arXiv paper by Katha Ganguly and co-authors watches it happen two ways at once. Their fermions leak into the reservoir while a dephasing noise scrambles phases. In one setup the noise hits the system alone, and in another it hits both sides.

Two simulation styles trace the full curve in both setups. One jumps between random unitaries, the other diffuses smoothly. The peak's height and time shift with the protocol. Particle counts and currents leaking out track the curve closely, which the authors mine for general lessons.
arxiv-2501-12410:
How well a second detector at the Electron-Ion Collider could tag a certain process is studied by Elke-Caroline Aschenauer and co-authors in a 2025 paper. The collider will explore quarks and gluons inside nucleons and nuclei. Its first detector, ePIC, is a general purpose design, and many in the community back a second interaction region with a second detector to widen the science.

The process in question is incoherent diffractive vector meson production. The layout for the second region offers a secondary focus that gives better forward acceptance at small scattering angles. The team evaluates tagging efficiency in that setup. Readers learn how a second detector could complement ePIC rather than repeat it, by catching particles the first design would miss.
arxiv-2501-12510:
Nathanael Arkor, Philip Saville, and Andrew Slattery published a mathematics paper in 2025 on algebra structures for a generalized kind of monad. Their objects, relative pseudomonads, extend a known theory to a relative setting. The team defines pseudoalgebras for these objects and builds out their theory. For each such monad, they construct a free-forgetful pairing.

That pairing shows the bicategory of pseudoalgebras as the final option among ways to resolve the monad. A coherence theorem follows, with the result that one classic bicategory matches a 2-category of presheaf categories. The theory also covers doctrinal adjunction and related tools. A final result links monads tied to free completions with maps that preserve colimits.
arxiv-2501-12610:
Yahya Yunus, Tianwa Chen, and Gianluca Demartini build a dashboard for Wikipedia's gender gap over time. Their 2025 paper notes that the editor community aims for gender balance, yet lacks a clear view of how biography coverage split by gender across years. The tool draws on Wikipedia, DBpedia, and Wikidata feeds for steady upkeep, and was built in a business intelligence suite for public display.

Women's biographies form under a fifth of the English stock, though the share climbs year by year. Mean age of subjects fell across genders. Most person classes stay male-heavy. Editors can aim fixes where gaps gape widest.
arxiv-2501-12710:
Karaev, Blumenthal, Moshel, Diringer, and Hacohen-Gourgy wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a fresh way to set a microwave cavity mode to a chosen state. Quantum computers with long-lived memory modes must do this chore often.

Their method, Rabi Driven Reset, moves the state of the memory mode into a lossy mode that drains it away. A qubit driven in a Rabi pattern links the two modes through sideband tones. Once drained, the memory mode can be set to any coherent state sought. Computer models of the scheme predict setup times about ten times faster than the current coupling method. The gain could ease a routine but slow step in such machines.
arxiv-2501-13010:
Jingru Fu, Adrian Dalca, Bruce Fischl, Rodrigo Moreno, and Malte Hoffmann train a model to line up brain scans of the same person over time, in a 2025 paper. Lining up two scans by shifts and rotations sounds simple, but small errors spoil studies that track slow change. Learning methods that excel at matching scans across people have lagged at this within-person task.

The team built on a frame that knows anatomy and copes with varied scan types. They trained their model on fake scan pairs made from one subject, with exact shifts and slight warps added. The trained model then beat older cross-person networks on real repeat scans. It held up across scan contrasts as well, which suits long studies where scan settings drift.
arxiv-2501-13110:
Koshelkin reworks the two-body problem for a relativistic world with outside fields in a 2025 paper. Two particles pulling on each other while sitting in external traps sound simple; in Einstein's physics, even Newton's third law needs repair to stay consistent.

Working from the least-action principle, Koshelkin derives exact equations for the pair, for plain particles and for spinning fermions alike, in any frame rather than one special viewpoint. He maps which fields and forces let the pair's inner motion split cleanly from their joint drift. A fresh basis then splits the fermion equation into four manageable parts. Test case: the electron-positron atom in magnetic fields at low energy.
arxiv-2501-13510:
Ian Musson studies in 2025 how to form clean quotient spaces when a group-like object acts on a geometric one. Groupoids widen groups by letting moves start and end at varied points. The case in view is a named Weyl groupoid acting on a plain affine variety, building on Musson's own earlier work.

The map to the quotient was known to carry good geometric traits. Musson now shows, when the base field is uncountable, that the map is a geometric quotient with the strongest sharing trait: it stays a quotient after any base change among schemes. A classic book result is reshaped to fit groupoids and even plain equivalence relations. Closed points and Jacobson schemes do much of the work in the proof.
arxiv-2501-13610:
Meijer and a team including Detterer and Yousefzadeh built a shared wait line in twenty twenty-five to hold signal delays on brain-like AI chips. Delay-tuned nets can be smaller and leaner than plain ones at the same skill. Past delay gear eats memory as nets grow, though.

Their round shared line scales with net sparseness, not just net size. That ties memory cost to how much of the net is live. It also fits joint chip-and-model tuning well. Lag, chip area, and energy per read are scored in the work.
arxiv-2501-13910:
Eleftheriou and co-authors derive formulas for counting states in a leading theory of quantum gravity, in this 2025 paper. The counts, called BPS indices, describe branes that wrap space in a curved five-dimensional world. Similar formulas were known from the dual gauge theory side, but a direct bulk derivation was missing.

The team quantize the space of giant graviton branes using a method that pins the calculation to special fixed points. They show how a known jump in the formulas, called wall-crossing, emerges from shifting the calculation. For some symmetry groups, extra terms appear from stable branes in a mirrored space.
arxiv-2501-14210:
Hammad Ayyubi and co-authors present PuzzleGPT in 2025, a system that guesses when and where a photo was taken. People solve such puzzles by spotting clues, like signs, plants, or building styles, and chaining them together. The team split that skill into parts and built a module for each.

One module spots visual clues, one reasons over them, one merges the chains, one searches the web when stuck, and one filters noise. The system needs no training on the task and explains its steps. On two test sets it beat big vision-language models, including GPT-4V, by wide margins. It even matched models trained for the job.
arxiv-2501-14510:
Faiz Muhammad Chaudhry and six co-authors train a neural network to read a camera's calibration straight from a single photo, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classic calibration needs many shots of a known target from set angles, material that public photo sets rarely have. Their network instead learns from a large synthetic image library built in a simulator, topped up with a few real photos.

The simulator varied focal length and lens warping under the standard Brown-Conrady model, giving the network labeled examples to regress against. A ResNet backbone adapted for number prediction does the reading. The authors report accurate parameter estimates on real images despite the mostly fake training diet, a result aimed at driving, robotics, and augmented reality.
arxiv-2501-14610:
Feyisayo Olalere and co-authors ask how much echoes and room layout help or hinder software that separates overlapping voices for cochlear implant users. Separation tools shine on clean studio mixtures but struggle in real rooms. The team measured that drop, then tested two kinds of spatial help: cues the model can pick up by itself from the sound, and extra location features fed in by hand.

Both kinds helped, especially when talkers sat close together or their voices sounded alike, the cases where tone alone cannot separate them. Hand-fed cues paid off most where the built-in ones were weak, as with a single implant microphone rather than two. The authors stress that training on real-world recordings is what makes such systems carry over to everyday listening.
arxiv-2501-14710:
Charlotte Leininger, Simon Rittel, and Ludwig Bothmann argue that fair machine learning need not cost accuracy, in a paper from 2025. Two trade-offs haunt the field: fairness rules seem to weaken predictions, and popular fairness metrics seem to clash with each other. Recent work blames the bias baked into training data itself.

The authors explain this with the FiND world, an imagined fair world where protected traits have no causal effect on the outcome. In that world, the clashing metrics agree, and fairness walks hand in hand with accuracy. They then show that causal pre-processing of real data can mimic that world. Simulations and real-data tests confirm that the fixes dissolve both trade-offs at once.
arxiv-2501-14810:
Roberts, Roberts, and Tsoukiàs ask when a single summary number can honestly guide a decision. Index numbers compress complex data, from body mass scores to air pollution grades. Their 2025 paper separates three demands a conclusion drawn from such numbers should meet.

A statement is meaningful if its truth does not hinge on arbitrary scale choices. It is useful if it fits the actual decision at hand, and legitimate if gathering and using it respects cultural, historical, organizational, and legal limits. Meaningfulness is formally precise, while the other two are not yet. Working through body mass and pollution examples, the authors map how the three notions relate. They aim to ground future formal work.
arxiv-2501-15210:
Guy Fayolle and Christine Fricker analyze in 2025 limit equations for a large station based car sharing system in France, where users reserve a parking space when they take a car. As the numbers of stations and cars grow without bound, the system is described by equations for the counts of reservations and cars at a station. The authors prove the system has a single solution that settles to equilibrium at a fast rate.

That equilibrium matches a two queue system in tandem, one queue for reservations and one for cars, which is always stable. Each queue's load factor has an explicit form from a conservation law. Two variants with capacity limits are also sketched, one without reservation and one with a fixed total capacity.
arxiv-2501-15310:
Ayo Adedeji and four colleagues test whether language models can fix speech recognition errors in medical dictation, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Automatic speech recognition often garbles critical medical terms. Undetected errors in a transcript can compromise patient care and safety.

The study compares raw and language-model-corrected transcripts of accented English. Speakers came from Nigeria, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Recognition accuracy differed significantly across the regions. The authors identify the conditions under which model corrections help most. They also note where corrections fall short. The findings matter for hospitals adopting voice tools across borders, since an accent gap in transcription could quietly become a safety gap.
arxiv-2501-15510:
Restoring a damaged photo is easier if the model first knows what kind of damage it faces. The four authors propose Degradation Classification Pre-Training: the model learns to name the degradation type of its input image. That label is nearly free, since it is already implicit in every restoration data set, making it an extremely weak but universal supervision signal. An encoder extracts features and a light decoder classifies the damage from those features alone.

After this pre-training, both convolutional networks and transformers restored better, gaining up to 2.55 decibels on a ten-degradation all-in-one task and 6.53 decibels under mixed degradations. Unlike masked image modeling, the method keeps the decoder useful: the learned classifier eases transfer between models trained on different damage types. Code and models are public.
arxiv-2501-15710:
Rasul Shafikov surveys results about Levi-flat hypersurfaces, a special kind of geometric surface, inside complex projective spaces. A long-standing puzzle asks whether such a closed, smooth surface can exist in the complex projective plane. The question matters beyond geometry, since the same object would appear in foliation theory as a special minimal set and in symplectic geometry as a limit of fillings. Writing in twenty twenty-five for nonexperts, Shafikov gathers results that are scattered, with some known only as folklore, and lays out the state of the problem.

For projective spaces of dimension above two, several authors proved no such analytic surface exists, with extensions to wider families of spaces. The survey presents three mostly self-contained proofs of that nonexistence, two due to Lins Neto and one due to Siu. The two-dimensional case remains open and is the focus of the survey framing.
arxiv-2501-15910:
Michael Muehlebach, Zhiyu He, and Michael Jordan study how much data online learning needs in a 2025 paper. Their setting is reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by acting in a system that never pauses. The systems here are nonlinear, with smooth, endless ranges of states and actions.

The analysis covers cases from a short list of candidate models to models set by a compact dial of values, such as neural nets. Bounds on regret, the loss against the best policy, are derived for each case. For the dial-set case the bound matches earlier results found for simple linear systems. The authors note their methods are simple and use prior knowledge well.
arxiv-2501-16010:
Leping Qiu and four co-authors present a mixed reality tool that helps students take notes in live lectures without looking down, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Typing notes on slides or speech is slow, and eyes on a device mean ears off the talk. Key points slip past.

The team first asked students how they take notes and where they struggle. Their system, MaRginalia, pairs a stylus tablet with a headset. The slides, the speech text, and a ghost of the tablet float in view, so students can scribble and grab quotes while their eyes stay up. When fine work is needed, a look down at the real tablet still works. A study with twelve students showed the approach is workable and liked.
arxiv-2501-16210:
Harith Alani and Grégoire Burel argue that the fight against misinformation needs a change of strategy, not just better detectors. Their 2025 paper surveys a crowded field of tracking and detection tools. Despite heavy research, they say, our side is largely losing. False claims still threaten public debate, trust in sources, and political stability. Understanding how and why falsehoods spread has advanced greatly.

The authors call for a broader front. Technology should now serve fresh approaches rather than only spotting false items faster. They urge regular revisits of work plans in a fast moving contest. The piece is a position paper, setting out where effort should shift. It asks the field to weigh what detection cannot do and to design for those gaps.
arxiv-2501-16310:
Dirk Beyer and four co-authors present a framework that rewrites programs so plain reachability tools can check richer properties in this 2025 paper. Software verifiers often specialize in reachability, the question of whether a bad state can occur. Other properties, like termination or memory cleanup, need custom support in each tool. Their framework instead transforms the input program itself, as a preprocessing step any verifier can use. The transforms are driven by instrumentation automata, a script like device inspired by an older query language.

The first version handles three properties for C programs: termination, no integer overflow, and memory cleanup. The authors also show how broader liveness properties fit the same pattern. In tests, reachability tools on transformed programs matched tools with native support, at like efficiency. The authors present it as a way to split effort between transform writers and analysis builders.
arxiv-2501-16410:
Sun, Gong, Nejjar, and Fink teach image-labeling models to work in new places whose label lists do not match the training set. Standard transfer methods assume both sets share labels, yet real target sets often split one class into finer ones or name things differently. Their 2025 framework, DynAlign, leans on large foundation models whose broad prior knowledge can bridge that label gap.

Prior knowledge first maps source labels onto the target list, which may hold new or finer classes. The foundation models then label pixels and reassign classes, while a fusion step adapts choices to each scene. On street-scene tests from a game world to two real photo sets, the method beat prior approaches by a wide margin. No hand labels in the target set were needed.
arxiv-2501-16510:
UngJin Na and co-authors teach an image model to paint heat maps of boiling flow from bubble maps in a 2025 paper. Heat fields in boiling are hard to read and costly to fake with full math. The model learns from a bank of worked-out flow cases in two stages: first a codebook squeezes the maps, then a cleaning net fills in the heat.

The made heat fields match the true ones well at broad and mid scales. Fine scales still drift, the team notes. The shortcut cuts the cost of full runs and sharpens how lab readings are tuned. Next steps aim at finer churn and wider boiling states.
arxiv-2501-16610:
Miguel Rodrigo Castellanos and co-authors argue for reconfigurable antennas in the next mobile architecture in a 2025 paper. MIMO systems, with many antennas at both ends, raised data rates and spectrum efficiency hugely. The cost is hardware bulk and power draw that grow with array size, a wall for 6G ambitions.

The tri-hybrid architecture mixes analog, digital, and antenna-domain processing to cut that cost. Antennas that can reshape their own patterns add a new degree of freedom, steering energy without extra chains. The authors lay out how reconfigurability fits the architecture and where the gains lie. Their roadmap speaks to equipment makers weighing power budgets for dense future networks.
arxiv-2501-16710:
Astronomers mining the NuSTAR archive found a hard X-ray flare so hot it strains the usual picture of stellar flares. Tomohiro Hakamata and co-authors traced the 2013 outburst to a single M dwarf, a binary, or a young star still forming. Its plasma averaged about 95 million degrees, with an emission measure above typical flares. Modeling the flare loop suggested a structure several times wider than the star itself.

The authors instead propose several linked flares firing together across the surface, a pattern known from the Sun as sympathetic flares. The plasma stayed unusually hot long after the brightness faded, which fits that idea.
arxiv-2501-16810:
Pustilnik and Perepelitsyna chart the brightness changes of a rare luminous blue variable star over 36 years. Their paper appeared in 2025. The star sits in a dwarf galaxy with almost no heavy elements, about one fortieth the Sun's share. It is the only known star of its class at such low metal content, so its outbursts test theories of how massive stars shed mass.

The team combined their own monitoring with Hubble telescope photos from 2010 and 2017 to separate the star's light from its glowing gas cloud. After a giant eruption faded, the star kept swinging by more than three magnitudes over a year or so. Its full range spans about five magnitudes. The swings resemble the classic pattern of its class, but at unusually large size.
arxiv-2501-16910:
Roman Ludwig and co-authors present a medical modeling paper, published in 2025, on how throat cancer spreads through lymph nodes. For oropharyngeal cancer, doctors often treat large parts of the neck on the opposite side with radiation, even when no spread is seen there. The authors build a probability model that estimates hidden disease in each lymph node level for a given patient.

The model treats nodes on both sides of the neck as healthy or involved, linked by chances of spread learned from records of more than eight hundred patients. A tumor crossing the midline emerged as the main risk factor for spread to the other side. The authors aim to help doctors tailor radiation fields to each patient's real risk.
arxiv-2501-18710:
Thomas Gilton, writing solo in 2025, introduces two new forcing axioms in set theory. Forcing axioms are souped-up versions of the Baire category idea: they promise that many dense open sets can be met at once, letting mathematicians build objects with delicate properties.

Gilton's axioms concern building blocks, called proper posets, that preserve two qualities of spaces: being Lindelöf and being countably tight. The paper proves the axioms are consistent, meaning they can hold without contradiction, using Neeman's side-conditions iteration method. The heavy lifting is technical, but the payoff is practical for set theorists: new tools whose uses Gilton saves for a sequel. Consistency proofs like these mark out which mathematical worlds are possible.
arxiv-2501-19010:
Lee and co-authors present DyPCL, a learning method tuned for speech that is hard to understand due to dysarthria. Recognition falters because severity varies by speaker and disordered speech differs from typical speech. Their method splits each utterance into sound units called phonemes. It then trains the model to keep the same unit close across speakers. A live alignment method finds where each unit falls in the audio.

Training also ramps up difficulty over time. Easy contrast cases come first, then near-twin sounds that are hard to split. This staged plan handles speaker variety better than flat training. The goal is steadier recognition for people whose speech is often misheard.
arxiv-2501-19110:
The energy map of a big, messy material defeats exact quantum math, and Chen Hao Xia and co-authors teach a graph network to draw it, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their net is strictly local and symmetry-true. A slicing trick trains it on huge structures while keeping each atom's neighborhood whole.

Test systems ran to three thousand atoms and half a million links. Spectrum error stayed under about half a percent. Disorder, seams, and defects, the cases that break small-cell tools, are the home turf here. Chip and material design gain a fast stand-in for the gold-standard math.
arxiv-2501-19210:
Ignace Bossuyt and co-authors test a time-parallel solver for jittery equations in a 2025 paper. Parareal methods split the time axis across processors to cut wall-clock time. Their micro-macro version pairs a costly fine model with a cheap reduced model of slow behavior.

The test case is a linear Ornstein-Uhlenbeck equation with split fast and slow scales. The fine solver runs the full slow-fast system, while the coarse one tracks only the slow drift. The paper measures how error in the reduced model bends the method's convergence. Numerical runs back the theory. Faster stochastic simulation serves fields from finance to cell biology.
arxiv-2502-00310:
Alaa Nfissi and co-authors present SigWavNet in 2025, a network that reads emotion from raw speech. Emotion cues hide in subtle voice patterns, and noise often buries them. Hand-built features miss much of the signal. Their model learns features straight from the waveform.

A fast wavelet transform splits speech across time and frequency at many scales. The wavelet bases and the denoising step are themselves learnable. A hard threshold with a learned shape cleans the coefficients. Dilated convolutions then catch spatial traits, while gated recurrent units with attention track time flow. The design targets robust emotion calls for human-computer interaction and mental health screening.
arxiv-2502-00510:
Yingxuan Yang and co-authors present ShapleyFlow in a 2025 paper on systems built from many AI parts. Such systems link steps for planning, thinking, acting, and checking to solve hard tasks. It is not clear which parts help most, since the parts affect each other in mixed ways.

The method borrows a fair share idea from game theory. It tests many mixes of parts and gives each part a score for its share of the final result. Those scores then guide cuts or upgrades to weak parts. Readers get the first frame of this kind for judging and tuning multi part AI systems.
arxiv-2502-01210:
