Sam Kirkham, Patrycja Strycharczuk, Rob Davies, and Danielle Welburn model how speakers shift their accents during conversation in a 2025 paper. People often drift toward the speech of the person they talk with, a process called accommodation. That short-term drift is thought to drive long-term accent change, but how live input reshapes speech planning was unclear.

Their model uses two linked fields, one for planning speech and one for memory, each changing at its own pace. Because the memory field lags, matching a partner on one turn can push speech away on the next. That rebound matches patterns in a pilot experiment. Differences in the memory effect may reflect social or language pressures that resist change. The work links moment-to-moment talk with sound change over time.
arxiv-2502-01410:
Giovanni Fantuzzi and Federico Fuentes found a new condition in twenty twenty-five. It tells when moment relaxations of polynomial optimization problems end in the exact best value. These steps turn a hard polynomial problem into a ladder of easier matrix problems. Finite convergence means the ladder reaches the true best value. Correlative sparsity keeps the ladder climbable. In it, variables meet only in small cliques.

The condition grows from a sparse form of the classical truncated moment problem. It asks for flat extensions of some moment matrices. It asks for a running intersection property among the cliques of variables. When met, an algorithm pulls out true minimizers. It gets at least as many as the largest matrix rank in the relaxation. The authors also show the intersection property is necessary. They give cases that show how it all works.
arxiv-2502-01510:
Amit Reza and co-authors build a 2025 machine learning tool for estimating how fast planets lose their atmospheres. A planet's air can stream away to space, reshaping the planet over time. Exact physics models of that escape are slow, so modelers rely on grids of precomputed runs and interpolate between them. The team trained a dense neural network on a grid of about eleven thousand such models.

Their tool, called MLink, fills in escape rates for any planet inside the grid. It cut both the number of bad estimates and the worst errors, compared with classic interpolation methods. A test grid of about two hundred fifty fresh models checked the accuracy. When the team evolved sample planets over billions of years, most results matched the classic schemes. For planets near a known gap in planet sizes, though, the predicted sizes diverged past measurement error.
arxiv-2502-01610:
Sander Schouws and co-authors point a radio array at the most distant known galaxy and find no trace of one key gas signal. Their 2025 paper studies a galaxy seen as it was when the universe was very young. The missing carbon line sets a tight cap on its glow.

A sibling oxygen line was seen before, so the ratio of the two now exceeds three and a half. That ratio tops local galaxies but fits other early ones. Modeling points to fierce starlight, sparse gas, and metals built up fast. Gas makes up less than about three quarters of the mass budget. The authors read strong feedback at work in this fast-evolving galaxy.
arxiv-2502-01810:
Angelo Mele proposes in 2025 a neural network shortcut for fitting models of how networks form. Such models, called exponential random graph models, can bend to many shapes, but fitting them is painful since a key constant cannot be computed directly. Standard fits simulate the network again at every step, which is slow.

Mele trains one network on a single large bank of settings paired with simulated network summaries. The trained map can then be run backward: feed in the real network's summaries and read off the settings that match. Extra summary measures can be added to guard against model error. Simple examples show the shortcut works well.
arxiv-2502-02010:
Nguyen Duc Anh and Tran Ngoc Thang proposed a gradient method for hard optimization tasks in two thousand twenty-five. The tasks include minimax problems, where one side seeks a low value while the other seeks a high one, and tasks with more than one goal. The component functions need not be convex.

Their method uses steepest descent steps whose size adapts and need not fall at each step. They prove it converges for several classes of smooth functions, from nonconvex to pseudoconvex. They then apply it to multi-goal problems and prove it reaches weakly efficient or Pareto stationary points. Numerical tests for each case matched the theory.
arxiv-2502-02110:
Ashwini Venkatasubramaniam and Julian Wolfson offer a way to borrow data across studies of treatment effects in a 2025 paper. A single study may be too small to tailor care to each patient well. Borrowing helps most from a study that is much like the main one, yet effects can vary in mixed ways.

Their forest method lends patient-level data from a second source while tracking that mixed spread. Tests on fake data show gains when study setups differ, and a breast cancer case shows gains too. The method can mix trial data, plain records, or both kinds.
arxiv-2502-02310:
Scampicchio, Arcari, Lahr, and Zeilinger review how a flexible curve-fitting method strengthens predictive control of machines. Controllers that plan ahead need a good model of how a system moves, and real models always err. Their 2025 review covers the use of Gaussian processes, which learn the error from data and also state how unsure they are, inside such planning controllers.

The method has powered many working systems in recent years. Still, the authors list open problems: the fitting grows costly with data, shortcuts needed to keep planning solvable can blur the picture, and updating the model live from fresh data is tricky. They gather results on measuring uncertainty that control theory has not yet used. The paper closes with directions for safer learning-based control.
arxiv-2502-02510:
Branding and co-authors classify a special class of curved surfaces defined by a conformally invariant energy, in a 2025 paper. The energy modifies a classic bending measure, and its resting shapes are called conformal biharmonic. Spheres and product spaces host the study.

In a space form crossed with a line, such a surface is either perfectly flat in the geodesic sense or a cylinder over a lower dimensional example. Inside spheres, the team fully describes the symmetric cases and classifies those of steady scalar curvature in low dimensions. A global result covers compact examples in the five sphere. Totally round cases in the product setting must be flat.
arxiv-2502-02810:
Chanhui Lee and eight co-authors teach a language model to read molecules as graphs as well as text, in a 2025 paper. Models trained on letter-string forms of molecules can predict reactions and properties, but a molecule is really a network of atoms, and plain next-token training ignores that structure.

Their model, Mol-LLM, adds a structural pretraining stage that forces the network to use graph information before instruction tuning across many chemistry tasks. The aim is one generalist assistant for molecular work rather than a shelf of narrow tools. Better graph use should sharpen predictions where shape decides behavior, from drug candidates to catalysts, and make the model’s answers more trustworthy across tasks.
arxiv-2502-03010:
Arthur Turrell wrote a 2025 chapter on how data science can help people who set public policy. Economies are complex systems, and they grow more tangled over time. Data science joins coding, statistics, and field knowledge in one craft. Turrell argues that this mix can help officials see the world more clearly and may also save time and effort in their work.

The chapter walks through real uses in five areas. These cover how growth and prices are measured, how funds and staff are assigned, and how the natural world is watched. Two more areas cover forecasts and other day-to-day tasks. Each case shows what worked and what held it back. The chapter ends with steps that could help this work spread further across public life.
arxiv-2502-03410:
Matthew Hagan and Nathan Wiebe warm a quantum system to a set heat with just one spare qubit as the heat bath. The spare taps the system at random, and each tap is drawn from a set of mix moves. In weak-tap lands, the dance provably settles as a step chain whose rest state is the heat state sought. Their bounds price the run time by the chain gap, worked out in full at the cold edge.

Know the system tone gaps and the price falls by a steep count in their maths. Stay blind and the price soars by a set power of size, gap, and error marks. One spare qubit thus buys heat states for quantum rigs. Ignorance, not hardware, is the bill.
arxiv-2502-03510:
Yibo Liu's dissertation builds robot mapping around LiDAR fiducial markers in a 2025 thesis. LiDAR scanners guide self-driving and robotic systems, yet markers made for them lag far behind camera markers. The data are sparse and shapeless, and old marker designs assume flat images. Liu proposes a full framework to close that gap.

First, thin paper-sized markers are read from intensity images, giving the scanner's pose. Next, an enhanced detector finds markers inside full 3D maps, using both brightness and shape, which extends their range. Last, a mapping method aligns scattered, barely overlapping scans by solving an optimization over scan and marker poses. A new data set for multi-view scan matching is released. Tests across scanner models, indoors and out, showed the framework beating prior methods. Uses range from augmented reality to collecting training data.
arxiv-2502-03610:
Giulia Pozzi and six co-authors model how tiny sacs move on the surface of a nerve cell. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. These sacs, called extracellular vesicles, may carry prion protein and help spread brain disease. How they travel, and what the cell's inner frame does to that travel, was not well mapped.

Their model is built from lab data on sacs taken from star-shaped brain cells. They test sacs and cells with a drug that breaks the inner frame. In one case, motion fits a ratchet with flashes. In an other, it fits a rolling move on a wavy track. The full case mixes both. The model matches the data on the whole.
arxiv-2502-03710:
Samyobrata Mukherjee and four co-authors study waves that ride along graphene placed in a magnetic field. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, and its waves, called magnetoplasmons, sit in a band with a gap.

That band has a topological trait, summed up by a number called the Chern number. Where the field flips direction, the number changes, and protected edge waves appear. In practice the field can only flip across a soft border of some width. Such borders host a second family of edge waves, named for Volkov and Pankratov. The authors work out how the two families live side by side, and how the border's width sets the count of the second kind.
arxiv-2502-04010:
Yunxiao Zhang and co-authors show optical interference by amplitude measurement in a 2025 paper that probes a core quantum rule. Standard interference is read by light intensity after paths are merged into one mode.

Wave interference is at heart the adding of amplitudes. If amplitudes are measured and added directly, interference can appear even when paths stay distinct. The team proves this in theory and lab tests for classical and quantum light. A measurement view that stresses wave over particle resolves the clash with complementarity. The trick can restore interference in lopsided setups past the coherence length. Remote sensing may gain a longer working range from the method.
arxiv-2502-04510:
Shangbin Feng and co-authors design teams of language models automatically in a 2025 paper. Pairing several models can beat any single model on hard tasks. Someone must still decide which model does what and how much each counts. Hand tuning those choices is slow and rarely finds the best mix.

Their swarm method tunes roles and weights together in rounds. Roles form a flow chart of models passing work along in order. A score rates each model's true share in the best chart found. Across a dozen tasks, the tuned swarms beat fifteen rival design methods.
arxiv-2502-04610:
Dominik Kwietniak and co-authors swap averages in the study of dynamical systems in a 2025 note. Ergodic theory watches where orbit averages of a system settle over time. Cesàro averages, the plain running mean, are the classic tool for that watch.

The note replaces them with logarithmic, harmonic-style averages along orbits. Unique ergodicity gains a fresh characterization through those gentler means. A new notion, logarithmic mean equicontinuity, is then defined for whole systems. It turns out to match ordinary mean equicontinuity exactly. Two averaging styles thus see the same calm systems after all.
arxiv-2502-04810:
Hakon Pedersen examines a velocity concept in the theory of two fluids moving through porous rock in a 2025 study. The theory treats total flow as homogeneous in the Euler sense and builds a thermodynamics-like structure with a maximum entropy principle behind it. A co-moving velocity links the theory's intensive velocities to the physical seepage speeds of each fluid.

Pedersen shows the relations among those velocities carry a structure readable through affine and projective transformations, tools from geometry. A geometric reading can expose invariants the raw equations hide. Better theory for two-phase flow feeds reservoir engineering and groundwater modeling.
arxiv-2502-05110:
Aisha Aijaz, Raghava Mutharaju, and Manohar Kumar present ApplE, a formal model of applied ethics for computers, in work from 2025. Ethical choices depend on context: who acts, what is done, and where and when it happens. They also rest on ideas such as rights, duties, and virtue, which are hard to state in machine form.

ApplE joins ethical theory and event context in one modular frame. It was built with an adapted agile method for such models. The aim is to turn abstract moral ideas into clear structures a computer can reason with. That could support fairer, more open automated choices.
arxiv-2502-05510:
Luke Rickard, Alessandro Abate, and Kostas Margellos learn safety certificates for moving systems straight from their past paths. Their twenty twenty-five paper covers three checks: can the system reach a goal, stay safe, and reach while avoiding harm? A certificate is a function whose shape proves the trait.

Training bends the function until trajectory data satisfy the proof conditions. The team also bounds, in probability terms, how the learned proof will fare on fresh paths. That step uses compression and scenario ideas from learning theory. Self-driving and robot teams need proofs that survive new roads, not just the test track; data-grown certificates with odds attached fit that need.
arxiv-2502-05610:
Six researchers benchmark the energy cost of running large language models in a 2025 paper. Training costs draw most attention, yet inference runs constantly in deployment and its energy bill is poorly mapped. The team measured energy across models, tasks, prompts, and system settings.

Energy tracked output token length and response time closely. Quantization, tuned batch sizes, and targeted prompt phrases each cut usage sharply. The authors call the study the first broad benchmark of inference energy across so many factors. They close with deployment advice for lower energy operation. The findings frame inference, not just training, as a design target for sustainable language technology.
arxiv-2502-05810:
Barbara Kaltenbacher studies acoustic tomography of a nonlinearity parameter in a 2025 paper. Sound waves in tissue or materials bend in ways that depend on a local nonlinear trait. Imaging that trait could reveal structure that linear sound misses.

Working in the frequency domain with an advanced wave equation, she proves the trait can be pinned down locally from boundary measurements alone. The proof uses a linearization and a perturbation argument in chosen function spaces. A Newton-type reconstruction method builds on the result. The work joins a rich model with a practical imaging goal in nondestructive testing and medicine.
arxiv-2502-06010: Amartya Goswami, Zurab Janelidze, and Graham Manuell connect three ideas that grew up in separate fields, in this 2025 note. Frobenius reciprocity belongs to the theory of doctrines; modular connections belong to homological algebra; principal elements belong to abstract ideal theory. All three rest on special traits of Galois connections, the paired maps that also underpin a classic result: the lattice isomorphism theorem for groups. The note fills a gap in the literature by drawing the links plainly, tying category theory back to its group-theoretic root.
arxiv-2502-06210:
Aojun Lu and co-authors borrow the crowd logic of human groups to fix continual learning in deep networks. A single network tends to forget old tasks as new ones arrive. Their framework, Evolving Continual Learning, keeps a whole population of models instead of one.

In their 2025 paper, each new task triggers a search for the best architecture to serve it. That tailored model is trained, then shelved as a specialist expert in a growing library. Stability comes from the isolation of each expert, while fresh evolution keeps the system plastic. Tests show the collective beats leading single-model methods by a clear margin, a pitch for evolution over solo adaptation.
arxiv-2502-06610:
Federico Campanini, Laura Cossu, and Salvatore Tringali wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It sets up the category of atomic monoids, algebraic systems whose elements split into atoms that cannot split further.

The maps in the category are homomorphisms that keep atoms intact. The authors compute all limits and colimits in it, which shows the category is both complete and cocomplete. They then study the arithmetic of products and coproducts in this frame. Firm formulas come out for key gauges tied to factorization lengths, which count the ways an element can be built from atoms. The work gives factorization theory a category home.
arxiv-2502-07010:
Moradi, Tanneau, Zandehshahvar, and Van Hentenryck addressed renewable forecasting in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Grid operators need forecasts for whole fleets of wind and solar sites. Often each site supplies its own forecast with odds of high or low output. Those forecasts rarely say how sites move together, which fleet planning needs.

The authors join the site forecasts with a copula, a tool that links separate distributions, and Monte Carlo sampling. The result is a fleet-level forecast that stays statistically sound. Tests on synthetic data from several large United States systems checked the method. The authors say grid operators gain a better grip on swing and risk. That helps them blend renewables into the grid with more confidence.
arxiv-2502-07210:
Junyoung Park loosens a key condition in classic results on mean curvature flow in a 2025 arXiv paper. In this flow, a surface moves by its bend at each point, like a soap film settling. Many sharp tools for the flow demand that the surface be convex, which real shapes often are not.

Park proves a broad form of a known slope bound for flows that are merely mean convex, as long as the smallest bend stays above a set share of the mean. He then uses a classic peak argument to pin down old, everlasting flows of this kind. Under a like bound on sums of the smallest bends, such flows must be families of shrinking spheres. The work widens the reach of the theory.
arxiv-2502-07310:
Boštjan Brešar, Sandi Klavžar, and Babak Samadi study in 2025 total coalition splits in graphs where each vertex needs many neighbors in a set. Two disjoint sets form a coalition when neither dominates alone but their union does. The work hunts sharp bounds on how many parts such a split can hold.

Focus falls on the case where each vertex needs two neighbors in the set. Exact values emerge for cubic and four-regular graphs. The same tools answer an open question on double coalition posed by peers. A three-neighbor case also resolves fully for cubic graphs.
arxiv-2502-07410:
Bitcoin's safety rests on costly puzzles, and the network resets the puzzle's hardness to match the power at hand. Roozbeh Sarenche, Svetla Nikova, and Bart Preneel study attacks that smash part of that power in 2025. Once power is gone, the reset drops the hardness, and the smash can pay for itself.

Three attack forms are weighed where the honest pools will bend a little for gain. Hoarding blocks, the oldest trick, bites harder when honest power is spread thin across many pools. A fresh bribe attack pays small pools to orphan rivals' blocks, and for small pools it can beat hoarding outright. A third form lures power away. The study maps when each attack wins, a chart defenders can use.
arxiv-2502-07510:
Florian Beier, Moritz Piening, Robert Beinert, and Gabriele Steidl present a way to align two very different data sets into one shared space, in a research paper from 2025. The data sets come from different domains and share no known matches. Their method is based on optimal transport, which moves mass between distributions at least cost.

The twist is a penalty that keeps the internal distances within each data set sensible. The authors prove that a best solution exists and that it approaches a known distance measure as the penalty grows. They also turn the problem into a form a computer can solve step by step. Examples cover both flat and curved shared spaces.
arxiv-2502-07610:
Cremades and five co-authors open the black box of a neural network that senses turbulence from a wall, in a 2025 paper. Engineers would love to infer flow away from a surface using only wall sensors, and deep learning can do it, but not explain itself. The team trained a model to predict velocity fluctuations just above a wall from wall pressure and shear stress in a simulated channel. Then they applied an explanation method that scores how much each input point sways the prediction.

The important spots clustered into streak-like patches, tens to a few hundred wall units wide. Those patches showed strong, but not the strongest, pressure and shear swings, typically one to two standard deviations. The authors say knowing which wall features the model trusts helps judge when such sensing can be believed. They frame the work as a step toward explainable tools for flow control.
arxiv-2502-07810:
Brian Choi studies wave solutions of a fractional equation in a 2025 math paper. The Rosenau-Hyman equation models tight wave packets called compactons, which end abruptly rather than fading out. Choi works on a fractional version, where derivatives stretch across space and time instead of acting at a point. That stretch changes what waves the equation can carry.

Using a homotopy perturbation method, he builds series solutions and studies their motion. The spatial stretch rules out compactons, so traveling periodic waves take their place. Analysis with a special function shows the wave speed pins to a halt as the time fraction order varies past a split point. Computer runs on the cubic version hint that waves may blow up in finite time. Choi flags cases where the method's series fails to converge.
arxiv-2502-07910:
Yuning Wang and co-authors test ways to stop airflow from separating off a wing and costing lift. Their 2025 paper uses high-resolution large-eddy simulations of a NACA4412 wing section at a steep angle of attack. Separation control matters because stalled flow raises drag and can make aircraft handling worse.

The team compares steady blowing and suction on one or both wing surfaces with periodic control on the upper surface. Steady control delayed separation and raised lift by up to about a tenth, though overall efficiency barely improved. Periodic control helped on neither measure. Detailed analysis shows how the steady jets reshape turbulence in the boundary layer. The authors say this is the first study of its kind at this simulation detail.
arxiv-2502-08010:
Hao Lin and co-authors model energy-as-a-service for networks of devices powered by radio waves. Their 2025 paper looks ahead to the Internet of Everything in 6G networks, where vast numbers of devices need charging without wires or battery swaps. Shared energy stations would recharge devices from many operators, much as cell towers serve phones.

Such stations cost money to build and cover only a limited zone, so gaps are likely. Using percolation theory, the authors derive when device-to-device links can still span the whole network. Their conditions tie together device density, communication range, station density, and charging zone size. The results give planners a way to judge feasible designs.
arxiv-2502-08110:
Jaehun Lee and Hyunchul Park prove a sharp split in how heat drains from a region when the heat moves by jumps. The math frame is a Lévy process, a random walk that can leap. Heat content here counts the heat left in a region after a short time. Past work split by case, with no one rule for a broad class.

The split turns on how wild the small jumps are. When the walk has no bound on its variation, the lead term comes from the top reach of the walk at the edge. When the variation is bounded, the heat drains at a plain rate, in step with time. One proof covers both arms and a wide class of jump laws, even ones that lean to a side. The paper folds three past results into one and trims the proof.
arxiv-2502-08210:
Muhammad Maaz and Adam Strzeboński present a new math method in 2025 for taming problems stated with radicals. Such problems, called algebraic programs, allow roots and ratios in their goals and limits. Turning them into plain polynomial form unlocks strong known solvers.

The plain route adds one new variable for each radical, which can bloat the problem fast. The new route adds just one variable per algebraic function. It first finds a polynomial that defines the function, then adds inequalities that pin down which root is meant, using results from real algebraic geometry. On changed versions of classic test problems, the leaner form proved easier to solve.
arxiv-2502-08510:
Jaakko Pere, Pauliina Ilmonen, and Lauri Viitasaari study how measurement error distorts estimates of the far tail of a distribution. Extreme value theory cares about rare, huge outcomes, but the numbers fed into it often carry error. Their 2025 work asks when that error fades away in the limit and when it bends the answer, for the classic moment-based estimator of the tail index.

They cover the full range of tail shapes, from short and light to heavy, and give conditions under which the error becomes negligible. From the corrected tail index they also build estimates of extreme quantiles, the levels so high they are almost never seen. As a showcase, they treat elliptical distributions in several dimensions and estimate the whole region of extreme outcomes at once. The shape-preserving setup keeps the estimate aligned with the geometry of the data.
arxiv-2502-09310:
Iasson Karafyllis and colleagues published a control theory paper in 2025 on stabilizing chemostats. A chemostat grows microbes in a tank fed with nutrients. Keeping biomass steady from any starting state is the goal. Natural death of the microbes makes that goal much harder.

Earlier simple feedback worked only when mortality was absent. With death present, nutrient-poor starts could wipe out the culture. The authors design stronger feedback laws to prevent that outcome. Their laws are written out explicitly, not left implicit. They cover both a simple two-state model and a richer age-structured one. When mortality is zero, the laws match the older simple forms. Stability is proven for all positive starting conditions.
arxiv-2502-09510:
Markus Faulhuber gives a math result that breaks a hopeful rule of thumb in signal work. Gabor systems build signals from shifted and tuned copies of one wave shape. When the base shape is a Hermite function, a known density rule was thought to be enough to make the system a frame, a stable basis for signals. His 2025 work shows it is not.

Faulhuber proves the point through the zeros of a helper transform, which decide whether such systems hold up as frames. He builds cases with sampling well above the rule's bar that still fail to be frames. The result warns engineers and mathematicians alike: for these wave shapes, density alone cannot promise a sound signal basis.
arxiv-2502-09710:
A stellar stream of very metal-poor stars stretches across more than one hundred degrees of sky, Zhen Yuan and a large team of co-authors report in a 2025 paper. The stream, C-19, is the most metal-poor stream known. It offers a fossil record of a structure born very soon after the Big Bang, so its full extent matters for early galaxy history.

The team searched the whole sky for new members by combining two stream-search algorithms, STREAMFINDER and StarGO. They used low-metallicity samples from the Pristine survey plus Gaia spectro-photometric catalogs. Twelve new members are confirmed, spread over that wide arc, with help from velocity and metallicity data from follow-up spectroscopy. The stream is far longer than once thought.
arxiv-2502-10110:
Hiroki Nakano, Takashi Koide, and Daiki Chiba send a language model out to investigate websites on its own and judge whether they are scams. Fake sites now mimic real ones closely and play on human psychology, which wears down older detectors that need big labeled data sets. Their 2025 agent, ScamFerret, gathers evidence from a suspect address by itself, reading page content, DNS records, and user reviews as needed.

With a leading model inside, the agent sorted four scam types in English at 0.972 accuracy and online shopping sites across three languages at 0.993, with no task-specific training at all. The multi-angle evidence lets it explain its verdicts, not just give them. The authors present the work as proof that language models can patrol the web as analysts, not just classifiers, against fraud that keeps changing its face.
arxiv-2502-10510:
Blending training data from many sources is now standard, yet the best recipe proportions are usually guessed. Anvith Thudi and four co-authors formalize that guesswork in a 2025 paper. Their framing is two-level: the best mixture is the one whose trained model scores best on the target task, a goal that is normally out of reach.

The key insight is that this hard goal turns convex, and therefore solvable, as the model class grows large. Their gradient method, MixMin, optimizes the mixture directly. It was the only method that improved every mixture it touched in their tests. On a mid-size language model, less than 0.2 percent extra compute bought gains of 1 to 5 percent on several test sets. Mixtures tuned on small models also lifted larger ones, a hint that good recipes travel across scale.
arxiv-2502-10810:
Zhenyu Yang and co-authors built a new test set for models that watch video as it plays, in a paper from 2025. Most past tests ask one question about one clip. Real use, like a live stream, needs a model to follow events over time and answer a chain of linked questions.

Their test set, called SVBench, holds close to fifty thousand question and answer pairs drawn from more than a thousand videos. The questions come in chains, so later ones build on earlier ones across the stream. The team tested fourteen models in both chat and live modes. A closed model from OpenAI did best, while most open models struggled with long streams. The team also built a chat model that beat the other open models on the new test.
arxiv-2502-11210:
An exotic black hole that carries charge without a net pull offers a test bed for how matter and light orbit. Bobur Turimov and co-authors analyze paths around the BBMB black hole, a named solution in gravity theory. Its Hawking temperature is zero, they confirm. For heavy particles they locate the key orbit radii where stable circling ends and where bound orbits fail. Energy efficiency of orbiting matter reaches up to eight percent.

Light capture differs from the classic Schwarzschild case. The photon sphere sits closer in, and the critical impact measure runs larger, marking weaker grip. Formulas for orbit precession and light bending complete the picture. Contrasts like these could one day separate rival gravity solutions by observation.
arxiv-2502-11510:
Tess O'Brien, Matthew Moores, David Warton, and Daniel Falster wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It warns that numerical integration error can split a posterior into two humps in longitudinal models, one true and one false.

Such models pair growth equations with data over time, and the equations are solved by numeric steps. The error from those steps can make a bad parameter set forecast as well as the true one. The posterior then shows two clusters, the main one near truth and a stray near the false set. The team shows the split in theory and in tests for a simple linear case. A simulation check can flag it, and a named sampling fix can dodge it.
arxiv-2502-11610:
Renyu Zhao and Yunxin Chen grade two big scholar databases on a basic task: telling researchers with similar names apart. Studies of science itself depend on knowing who wrote what, yet name variants, initials, and spellings tangle the record. OpenAlex and Clarivate each mint their own scholar IDs as a fix. The team sampled 100 scholars per group from top-quartile journals, split by country, field, and output, and hand-built each scholar's true paper list with help from a search-augmented language model.

They then matched those lists against what each database's IDs claim, and scored precision and recall on the same journal set. The design lets readers see where each system shines and where it merges or splits people wrongly. The authors frame the benchmark as a guide for choosing an ID system by use case.
arxiv-2502-11810:
Santos and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on two new atom-thin sheets of metal. The work builds on goldene, a sheet just one gold atom thick. The team uses math models to test twin sheets made of silver and copper atoms. They check if the sheets would hold together, how stiff they would be, and how they handle light. Both sheets prove stable in their tests, even at room heat.

The silver and copper sheets bend and stretch much like the gold sheet. All three act like metals for electric flow, yet handle light in ways more like chip materials. The authors say that mix could suit light-based electronics. The study maps fresh ground for lab work on thin metal sheets.
arxiv-2502-11910:
Work on fooling large language models risks repeating old mistakes from computer security research, warn Leo Schwinn and co-authors in this 2025 position paper. For a decade, attack research chased headline scores while defenses built on tricks later collapsed under honest testing.

The authors sort old and new threat models using a security taxonomy, then urge a reset: split the broad goal into smaller, testable problems. Progress, they argue, needs goals that are simple, repeatable, and measurable, so results can be compared across labs. The fresh start on language models, they say, is a chance to build on hard lessons rather than relive them.
arxiv-2502-12210:
Papa Abdou Karim Karou Diallo and Amal Zouaq brought retrieval into a classic language task in 2025: finding the semantic frames a sentence evokes. Frame semantics describes events through structured scenes, like buying or arresting, each with its own roles. Detecting which frames a text triggers is a first step toward machine understanding. Previous systems usually needed the target word marked in advance.

Their approach, RCIF, is the first retrieval-augmented method for frame detection and works without any marked target span. It embeds frames from several representations, retrieves candidate frames for an input text, then identifies the best fits. Experiments covered zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned settings. The retrieval component significantly improved results, suggesting frames are easier to recognize by comparison than by pure generation. The method points semantic parsing toward the retrieve-then-decide pattern succeeding elsewhere.
arxiv-2502-12310:
Tesshu Fujinami, Bruce D. Lee, Nikolai Matni, and George J. Pappas study how sample-efficient domain randomization is for a classic control problem. Domain randomization trains a controller by averaging performance over a spread of model settings. The method works well in robotics practice, but its theory has lagged. The test bed here is the linear quadratic regulator, a benchmark for learning control laws.

The team proves that, with a well-chosen sampling spread, domain randomization reaches the best possible rate at which extra cost decays. It matches the benchmark method that knows the system exactly. Robust control, by contrast, can overshoot on caution, yet it does better when data is scarce because it can steady an uncertain system from rough estimates. The authors add a gradient-based algorithm for the randomization method and test it numerically. The results point to open questions about wider classes of systems.
arxiv-2502-12510:
Jiatao Li, Yanheng Li, Xinyu Hu, Mingqi Gao, and Xiaojun Wan probed language models used as peer reviewers in two thousand twenty-five. Automated review is tempting, but small changes to a paper, a review, or a rebuttal might sway the outcome. The authors set out to measure that risk.

Their framework makes targeted changes tied to aspects like contribution, soundness, and tone. They found strong reject advice swayed final meta-reviews, harsh reviews could be misread as thorough, and weak or hostile rebuttals could oddly raise acceptance. The biases held under several chain-of-thought prompts. The work gives a practical way to test review systems for such flaws.
arxiv-2502-12710:
Malte Hellmeier and four co-authors hide notes in text by swaps no eye can see. As model text floods in, human and machine prose blur, and marks that tag a source grow in worth. Their 2025 method, Innamark, swaps plain space characters for twin-form code spaces that look the same. Meaning and character count stay whole, which lets it ride on raw, bare text.

Any byte chain can hide in a long host text. A set message wrap adds compression, encryption, checking, and repair steps, each tuned by the user. The kit ships as a shared code base with a command-line tool and a web face. On a million-page set, ten methods faced off; Innamark held its marks firm and kept them hidden. Capacity and toughness limits get a frank reading.
arxiv-2502-12810:
Michael Sorochan Armstrong tackles misaligned chemistry data in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Multidimensional separations split complex samples along two axes, giving rich detail about their makeup. But peaks drift between runs in both directions, so samples cannot be compared one to one without preprocessing. Closely overlapping peaks add a second headache. Armstrong aligns the data in the frequency domain instead of the time domain.

The method uses a complex form of Procrustes analysis, a classic shape-matching tool. Aligning spectra this way can line up runs from different instruments and setups. That makes large studies of biological samples more trustworthy. The paper serves analytical chemists who run two-dimensional chromatography and related methods.
arxiv-2502-13010:
Rezaei and co-authors build a medical question-answering system that keeps its own knowledge graph fresh instead of letting it age. Medical facts change fast, and hand-updated resources lag, which quietly dates the answers of language models. Their 2025 framework, AMG-RAG, sends agents to construct and update a medical knowledge graph on their own, then reasons over it and pulls in live evidence from sources such as PubMed.

On two standard exam benchmarks the system scored an F1 of 74.1 percent on one and 66.34 percent accuracy on the other. It beat rival systems and even models ten to a hundred times its size, without added computing cost. The design also makes its reasoning easier to inspect, since answers trace back through graph links and fetched evidence. The authors argue that self-updating knowledge, not bigger models, is the fix for trustworthy medical answers.
arxiv-2502-13210:
Yifan Zhang and Sarang Gopalakrishnan find phase transitions made of pure information in a 2025 quantum information paper. Orderly states called Markov networks reveal their structure by showing zero conditional mutual information between distant parts, but adding local noise can smear information across the whole system.

The authors prove the noisy case splits by temperature. At high temperature, the shared information between far regions still decays exponentially, for classical systems under any local noise and for a broad quantum class. At low temperature, long-range information can persist. Strikingly, these information-theoretic transitions appear in models with no ordinary thermal transition at all.
arxiv-2502-13310:
Adib Mosharrof, Moghis Fereidouni, and Siddique test whether chatbots can run task dialogues without costly labels, in a 2025 paper. Booking-style assistants are usually trained on conversations marked turn by turn with states and rules, which is slow to produce. The team instead fine-tuned open language models on plain dialogue text alone and asked how well they finish tasks in domains they never saw in training.

The label-free models answered smoothly and stayed on topic, but their real task success, measured by correct calls to outside services, topped out near half. The authors' fix, ZeroToD, enriches the service schemas the model sees, lifting accuracy where it matters. A human study agreed with the machine scores. Small tuned models using the framework even beat large commercial chatbots at finishing tasks.
arxiv-2502-13410:
Siddarth Srinivasan and three co-authors ask how to pay people for the reasons behind their beliefs in a 2025 paper. Common sense says a stated why helps a group land on the truth. Yet no known scheme rewards honest whys, since classic models assume each person's facts are separate, which makes whys needless.

In real life our facts overlap: we read the same reports and hear the same rumors. A why reveals what is shared and what is new. Their deliberation scheme pays for beliefs and reasons in a way that makes honesty the best play. Under it, pooled reasons beat pooled verdicts alone.
arxiv-2502-13810:
Matthew Pugh and co-authors wrote this 2025 mathematics paper linking machine learning to a construction from category theory. A Kan extension is a universal way to stretch a function along another map. Past work had shown efficient ways to compute such extensions and noted their likeness to learning algorithms.

The authors close the gap with a proof: every error minimization algorithm can be presented as a Kan extension. That covers the core of machine learning, since training is the search for low error. A side result reframes error itself as the cost of lossy changes to data, against lossless ones that cost nothing. The paper offers a foundation for improving learning methods through this lens. It also gives category theory a firm claim on the field.
arxiv-2502-13910:
Anastashia Jebraeilli and Michael R Geller simulate a qubit with unusual physics in a 2025 paper. The models at issue use Hamiltonians that are non-Hermitian, meaning energy can leak, as in open systems and certain symmetry studies. Simulating them on quantum hardware has been held back by methods whose success chance shrinks fast.

The authors instead use a fixed-depth variational circuit, a short tunable quantum program, to run the simulation. On IBM superconducting qubits they pushed deep into the regime where the key symmetry is broken, around a special point where states merge. They argue such circuits, joined with machine learning, can widen what near-term quantum machines can explore.
arxiv-2502-14110:
Hernan Bocaccio and co-authors test, in a 2025 paper, whether turning a voice's spectrum into a graph can identify who is speaking. Each speaker's vocal tract shapes the resonances of speech in a personal way. Volunteers recorded the five Spanish vowels, and the team computed each sound's frequency spectrum.

From every spectrum they built a visibility graph, where peaks that can see each other become linked nodes. Graph measures then formed a feature vector per vowel. A forest of decision trees trained on these vectors identified speakers with high accuracy. The authors single out which topological traits carried the identity signal. The method adds a shape-based tool to speaker recognition, one that reads the spectrum's landscape rather than its raw heights.
arxiv-2502-14210:
Amirreza Neshaei Moghaddam, Alex Olshevsky, and Bahman Gharesifard study how much data a controller needs to learn the best settings for a standard control problem, in a 2025 paper. The problem, known as the linear quadratic regulator, balances state error against control effort for systems with unknown behavior. Earlier learning methods needed a starting controller that was already stable, a real limit in practice.

Their new method works in rolling short horizons and is modeled on a classic policy learning rule. It drops both the stable-start demand and the costly two-point gradient guesses used before, while keeping the same order of data needs. A sharper analysis of how errors shrink through the problem's core equation improves the guarantees. The result widens where such learning control can safely be tried.
arxiv-2502-14310:
Shahar Hod wrote a compact paper in two thousand twenty-five about how a ring orbiting a black hole drags the space around it. When a ring circles close to the horizon, the hole's horizon spin rate no longer follows the simple vacuum rule. A recent result for an uncharged spinning hole found a universal shift that ignores the hole's own spin.

Hod asks whether the same universal shift holds when the hole also carries electric charge. Using analytic methods on the combined black hole and ring system, he finds that the shift in this charged case has an explicit form that does not stay spin independent. The paper thus marks a limit on how far the earlier universal pattern extends across black hole types.
arxiv-2502-14510:
Giavaras studies the electric current that flows when two coupled quantum dots are driven by an alternating field. In such double dots, a spin blockade can stop current entirely, until a spin resonance lifts the block and lets a sharp current peak through. That peak carries information about how the paired spin states mix, especially where spin-orbit coupling is present.

Using a Floquet-Markov transport model, he computes the resonant current for a range of drive strengths and frequencies. The current traces out a rich interference pattern rather than a single clean peak. That pattern, he shows, can be read as a fingerprint of how singlet and triplet states blend together. The result offers experimentalists a way to probe two-spin physics in different dot setups by watching the current as they tune the drive.
arxiv-2502-14610:
Jaakko Hällfors and Kari Rummukainen speed up computer studies of how bubbles of a new phase are born. In a clean system, a first-order transition waits for a rare critical bubble, and a metastable state can outlast any practical simulation by absurd margins. Standard sampling tricks help, yet a condensation barrier still chokes them at large volumes.

Their expanded ensemble method steps around that barrier. Instead of forcing one system size to do all the work, the sampling spreads across an ensemble of related setups. Rare bubbles then appear at workable rates even in big volumes. The authors present the method as a general accelerator for nucleation studies, where the physics of the early universe and of materials both hinge on how bubbles start.
arxiv-2502-14910:
Wu and six colleagues present EvoP in twenty twenty-five, a pruning framework for large language models. Large models are costly to run where computing resources are limited. Pruning removes redundant parts, but heuristic rules can cut the wrong ones. Many methods also ignore the traits of the data used for tuning.

EvoP first builds a diverse calibration data set by cluster based sampling. It then searches for the best pruning pattern with an evolutionary method. The search directly optimizes which elements, channels, or layers to remove. Across models and downstream tasks, EvoP beat existing pruning methods. It kept the best performance while also keeping the best efficiency. The authors present it as a practical path to deploy large models.
arxiv-2502-15010:
Mark Russinovich and Ahmed Salem present Obliviate, a method that makes language models forget set texts word for word in 2025. New deals with creators demand fine control over copied text. Past defenses either wreck model skill or leak exact quotes. Obliviate first finds the passages a model has memorized. It then nudges output odds down for each target token.

A penalty term drives exact recall down while a matching term guards normal fluency. Four mid size models were tested on fake and real book excerpts. Exact recall fell by a factor of about one hundred. Scores on standard skill tests dropped by at most one percent. The authors pitch it as a workable copyright guard for live models.
arxiv-2502-15110:
Evan Sidrow, Alexandre Bouchard-Côté, and Lloyd Elliott present a variational method for inferring evolutionary trees in a two thousand twenty-five statistics paper. Bayesian phylogenetics needs accurate, fast approximations of posterior distributions over tree shapes and timings.

Their variational family for ultrametric trees builds on coalescent times from single-linkage clustering, and it has a closed-form density. Unlike existing approaches, the method searches all of tree space, needs no Markov chain Monte Carlo subroutines, and stays differentiable end to end. Experiments on benchmark genomic datasets and on SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA reach competitive accuracy. The method uses far fewer gradient evaluations than current state-of-the-art techniques.
arxiv-2502-15210:
Feizi and co-authors present a 2025 benchmark paper on whether vision-language models compare images reliably. Such models increasingly rank, judge, and fetch pictures, yet no standard test measured their comparing skill. Their tool, PairBench, turns common image sets into pair tests. Four scores grade each model: match with human labels, stability when pair order flips, smooth spread of scores, and steerability by prompts.

No model won on all four fronts, the tests show. The widest flaw was lopsided scoring, where swapping the pair changed the verdict. Scores on this bench still tracked results on harder popular tests. The authors offer the bench as a cheap health check for model judgment.
arxiv-2502-15410:
Cameron Millar, Bernd Schulze, and Louis Theran study self-stress in symmetric frameworks in this 2025 paper. A bar-joint framework, like a truss, can hold internal stress with no load applied. Symmetry is common in engineered structures such as grid roofs, and it shapes which stress states can occur.

The authors define an averaging map that turns a nearly symmetric framework into an exactly symmetric one, using the framework's own symmetry group. They sort self-stresses into local and spread-out kinds and track how averaging treats each. Algorithms follow for building symmetric frameworks rich in self-stress, and for finding spread-out stress states. The tools aim at structural design.
arxiv-2502-15510:
Light is usually treated as weightless, but a tiny photon mass would change how magnetic fields behave around black holes. Dvali, Osmanov, and Zantedeschi describe a process they call vortextrap magnetization. In it, a black hole slowly gathers magnetic flux tubes from the space around it. In a massive-photon world, a galaxy's field is a dense forest of thin tubes. A black hole traps and collects them over cosmic time, winding its own field up toward the highest strength physics allows.

The fit is best for the giant black holes at galaxy centers. Their sizes match the photon masses still allowed by observation. A field that strong could power the particle boosting blamed for some cosmic rays. Even with no gas nearby, such a field should glow and radiate gravitational waves when two black holes merge. The team supports the picture with a computer simulation of the trapping process.
arxiv-2502-15910:
Zheyuan Liu and co-authors propose MANU in 2025, a method for making a multimodal language model forget chosen knowledge. Big models can memorize and leak private data from their training sets. For models that join text and images, knowledge tangles across the two forms, so erasing a fact in one form can leave it alive in the other.

MANU works in two stages. First it finds the neurons that matter most for the data to be forgotten, judged separately within each form. Then it clips just those neurons, cutting the pathways that carry the target knowledge while sparing the rest. Tests across several model designs showed a more balanced erasure in both text and image sides than past methods, with general skill largely kept. The work speaks to privacy duties that now follow such models.
arxiv-2502-16610:
Francisco Caetano and co-authors present a tool that checks X-ray scans before a computer uses them to aid diagnosis. The tool, shared in 2025, is called AdverX-Ray. Scans can shift in subtle ways when they come from a new machine or new settings, and those shifts can throw off a diagnosis program. The team built the tool to catch such shifts early.

The method trains a model on small patches taken from scans made by known machines. It learns to spot the faint high-frequency flaws that fake or shifted images tend to carry. The team then tests whether a new scan matches what the model was trained on. In tests, the tool beat other detection methods and scored well using just 64 patches from one scan. It is light and fast, so it can run in real time.
arxiv-2502-16910: Foivos Chnaras gives an explicit test for smallest Iwasawa invariants on rank one curves, in work from 2025. Iwasawa invariants measure how class group growth behaves along a tower of number fields built over an elliptic curve. For a fixed rank one curve over the rationals, the test works at any good prime, whether ordinary or supersingular in type. It plays a role like Gold's classic test for when the mu and lambda values sum to one. That sum marks the smallest case the invariants can take at that prime.
arxiv-2502-17210:
Victor Los proposes in 2025 a cleaner way to handle starting correlations in the theory of open quantum systems. An open system exchanges energy with its bath, and its motion is ruled by a master equation. The standard equation carries an extra term for the correlations present at the start, which makes it awkward to use.

His projection reshapes the equation so those starting correlations fold into the memory kernel itself. No chaos style shortcut is assumed. The result is a closed equation for the system alone. In the weak coupling limit it takes a familiar time local form, with extra terms that carry the starting correlations. As a test, he applies it to a quantum oscillator. Exact handling of first moments matters for precise quantum devices.
arxiv-2502-17310:
Rohan Chakravarthy and co-authors tame a beam of dysprosium atoms with a single laser color, in this 2025 paper. Dysprosium is a heavy atom prized for tests of basic physics. Before such tests, the atoms must be sorted into one energy state and cooled as they fly. Doing all that with one laser simplifies the setup a lot. The team used light tuned to a single blue line of the atom.

Sidebands added to the laser covered the several states of one isotope, herding atoms into the top state and its extreme sublevel. A standing light wave across the beam cooled the atoms' sideways drift at the same time. The result is a cold, polarized beam ready for precision experiments. Simpler prep means more labs can attempt such tests.
arxiv-2502-17410:
Liming Liu and co-authors build a hybrid optimizer that trains large language models with less memory in a 2025 paper. Standard adaptive methods store heavy state for every weight and miss links between coordinates. Richer methods capture those links but cost even more memory, while cheap projections lose accuracy.

Their method splits the gradient space by importance. The top directions get a rich second order treatment, and the rest get a lean orthogonal method. This split keeps memory low while holding training quality. Tests across data sets and transformer designs support the design for very large models, where memory is the binding limit.
arxiv-2502-17610:
Samuel Yee and a large team of astronomers report new measurements of the planet WASP-193 b in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Planets like it are called super-puffs. They weigh about as much as Neptune but span as wide as Jupiter, so they are oddly light for their size. Plain planet-forming ideas struggle to explain them. Some super-puffs also circle their stars on tilted paths.

The team used the Magellan telescope to track the star's wobble with care. They sharpened the planet's mass and size values. Their data show that this planet's orbit lines up well with its star's spin. That calm path hints that not all super-puffs were knocked around in the past. The result adds a key case to the debate on how these puffy worlds form.
arxiv-2502-17710:
Akhila Yerukola, Saadia Gabriel, Nanyun Peng, and Maarten Sap wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tests how well AI systems read hand gestures whose sense shifts by culture, where a wrong read can cause real offense.

The team built MC-SIGNS, a set of gesture and country pairs marked for offense, weight, and context, spanning many gestures and countries. Image generators showed a strong United States slant, doing worse on offense checks outside that frame. Language models flagged too much as offensive. Vision and language models fell back on United States senses for broad ideas such as wishing luck. The authors call for safety tools that know culture.
arxiv-2502-17910:
Fangyuan Yu proposes growing a language model's vocabulary during pretraining, the way children grow theirs, instead of fixing it on day one. Static vocabularies are the industry habit. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the method alternates two moves. Entropy-guided expansion adds tokens where the model needs finer grain. Optimization rounds then train with the enlarged vocabulary. Representations transfer across token sizes, so earlier learning is not wasted. A natural allocation emerges: long tokens absorb predictable stretches, while short tokens handle the hard, surprising contexts.

Experiments on small GPT-style models showed better scaling efficiency, with gains following a log-linear pattern in vocabulary size. Code is released for follow-up work. The author plans larger models and more domains. The paper reframes tokenization as a curriculum decision rather than a preprocessing afterthought.
arxiv-2502-18210:
Qian Wang, Zhenheng Tang, and Bingsheng He ask in a 2025 paper whether large language models can truly copy human behavior in social simulations. Such simulations are now used to study how people act in groups. Yet recent work shows gaps between what the models produce and how real people behave, and those gaps raise doubts about the results.

The authors look closely at where the models fall short and what would be needed to fix those flaws. They offer clear steps for making model-based studies of society more sound. Readers get a sober guide to when these tools can help and when their output should be treated with care.
arxiv-2502-18310:
Ryan Cooper and co-authors wrote this astronomy paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on gas blasting out of young galaxies. The data come from the James Webb Space Telescope, which can read the light of galaxies seen as they were billions of years ago.

From more than a thousand galaxies flagged by an oxygen glow, the team found forty with the widened spectral line that marks a fast outflow. Most are star-forming galaxies, and about two thirds are starbursts making stars at a furious rate. The typical outflow moves at over five hundred kilometers per second. Still, most flows fall short of escape speed, so the gas likely rains back. Small galaxies fling out more mass than they turn into stars. The authors link their lower count of outflows to stricter rules and the limits of their spectra.
arxiv-2502-18510:
Chuanguang Yang and co-authors improve how a small neural network learns from several large ones, in a 2025 paper. The setup is called multi-teacher distillation: many trained teacher models pass their skill to one student. The catch is balance, since each teacher helps in its own way and helps only so much. Past weighting schemes looked at just one side of that trade-off.

Their method hands the weighting job to a learning agent. The agent sees both how each teacher scores and how far the student lags each one. It sets the weights, then learns from how the student fares in return. Across image tasks, from sorting photos to finding objects and marking regions, the method beat prior multi-teacher tools and set new top scores.
arxiv-2502-18610:
Chambers and a large team weigh manganese atoms to trace a shift in atomic nuclei in a 2025 paper. Below nickel 68, nuclei may flip into stretched shapes as neutron counts near forty, a zone dubbed an island of inversion. Mass reads pin that shift down, but the heaviest manganese forms had never been weighed with care.

A looping flight time scale at the TITAN lab weighed manganese forms from mass sixty four to sixty eight. The runs gave first precision masses for the sixty seven and sixty eight forms. Set against fresh theory, the masses show nuclei growing more collective, more prone to shared motion, as the count nears forty. The authors read the trend as the island's shore coming into view.
arxiv-2502-18810:
Weipeng Jiang and co-authors build a tool that creates audit sets for testing machine unlearning, in work from 2025. Models must sometimes forget private or protected content on demand. Checking that forgetting truly worked needs far larger tests than the few hundred cases in past benchmarks.

Their framework walks a knowledge graph to cover facts in fine detail. It also strips overlap between facts to forget and facts to keep, a common flaw in audits. Applied to a popular benchmark, it built tens of thousands of cases per data set. The audits found thousands of memorized facts the old tests had missed. Providers gain a stricter way to prove forgetting.
arxiv-2502-19110:
Jiang, Liu, and Van Durme proposed this approach in twenty twenty-five for making language model answers more honest. Models can refuse to answer when unsure, which wastes useful output. Or they can hedge with words like maybe, which downstream tools find hard to use. The authors unite both ideas under one frame.

Their method treats hedged claims as answer sets, in the spirit of set prediction with guarantees. A dial controls how loose or precise the response may be. The outputs carry a formal promise about factual accuracy. Models can also be fine-tuned to rewrite claims with the dial in mind. The result is a tunable balance between being right and being specific.
arxiv-2502-19210:
Yi Feng and co-authors give a noise-driven algorithm for hard optimization over portfolio-like choices in this 2025 paper. The search space is a simplex, or several joined together, as in asset weights. Nonconvex problems there hide many shallow local minima.

Their method updates weights multiplicatively while adding shaped noise. The noise follows the curved geometry of the simplex itself. That helps the search escape saddle points and shallow traps. The target use is polynomial portfolio management, a known hard case. Guarantees for noisy gradient methods rarely cover such constraints. This work extends them into the multiplicative, walled world of portfolios. Fund managers solving such problems nightly are the audience.
arxiv-2502-19410:
Xinru Wang and eleven co-authors study how smart assistants should explain their advice on tiny watch screens in a paper from 2025. Large language models can suggest daily actions, but their wordy reasons are hard to read at a glance. The team tried two fixes: sorting each reason into clear parts, and showing reasons only when the model seems unsure.

In a user study, sorted reasons cut reading time and mental effort and sped up choices. Always-on sorted reasons also raised trust in the advice. Yet users liked them less, wanting more detail, and the timed version helped least. Lessons for watch design close the paper.
arxiv-2502-19510:
Bonnetier and co-authors develop tools for optimizing where boundary conditions sit on a physical domain, in work from 2025. Many engineering tasks amount to choosing the best patch of a surface for supports, sensors, or loads.

The team adapts two sensitivity tools to surface patches: one for small smooth changes to the patch's edge, and one for adding a tiny new patch elsewhere. Worked through on the heat-conduction equation, the math extends to sound and elasticity problems. A numerical method combining level sets with remeshing tracks large motions of the patch. Three-dimensional examples show the approach handling dramatic shape changes cleanly.
arxiv-2502-19610:
Matthew Toles and four colleagues present a 2025 paper on chatbots that help people find out whether they qualify for help programs. Eligibility rules for benefits, taxes, or diagnoses are tangled and change often, so hand-built forms go stale. An agent must ask the right questions, because each extra question costs the user time.

The team built a benchmark, BeNYfits, covering overlapping social benefit programs. A leading language model using step-by-step reasoning scored poorly and often invented facts. Their own agent instead writes a small program from the rules and lets gaps in the user's data choose the next question. Accuracy jumped sharply while the number of questions stayed about the same, showing structure beats free-form chat for such tasks.
arxiv-2502-19810:
Qihao Lian and Di Wang present a static tool that bounds the resource use of Rust programs. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Rust is a systems language prized for memory safety with speed. Yet a safe program can still be slow, and its cost in time or memory is hard to call in advance.

Their tool, RaRust, is a type system that infers straight-line bounds on cost. It leans on Rust's borrow rules, the feature that makes its safety work. New prophecy potentials let it track shared and sole borrows in parts. A test build infers bounds for programs with loans, heaps, loops, and self-calls.
arxiv-2502-19910:
Marco Artusa, with an appendix by Takashi Suzuki, proves a duality result for a class of objects that mix curves and tori in number theory. His 2025 paper extends a classic pairing result, first shown for a simpler class of objects, to these 1-motives over fields built from the p-adic numbers. The older proof used Galois cohomology, a tool that tracks symmetry groups.

Artusa swaps that tool for a condensed form of cohomology tied to the Weil group, which keeps track of the field's topology as well. To fit 1-motives into the new tool, he builds a matching condensed form for them. The duality then takes the shape of a clean pairing between two groups of a well-behaved kind. The result sharpens a theorem of Harari and Szamuely.
arxiv-2502-20010:
Alessandro De Vita and a large team of co-authors published a 2025 study of a layered magnetic material. The material belongs to a new class called altermagnets. In these materials, the pulls of tiny magnets cancel out overall, yet electrons still feel a split in their energies based on spin. That mix was once thought impossible for this kind of order. The team's text studies a compound made by inserting cobalt into a layered crystal.

Using light-based tools that map electron energies, the team charted the material's electronic structure in three dimensions. They resolved the split branches of electron states directly. Computer calculations matched the measurements. The study confirms the compound behaves as an altermagnet of a particular wave type. Layered versions of these materials are still little explored. Knowing their structure in detail is a step toward devices that use spin without stray magnetic fields.
arxiv-2502-20410:
Jean-Pierre Tchapet Njafa and co-authors screen glowing molecules for next-generation displays at a hundredth of the usual computing cost. Thermally activated delayed fluorescence emitters harvest triplet energy to light OLED screens efficiently, but testing candidates with full quantum chemistry is slow. Their framework chains three semi-empirical methods: extended tight-binding for structure, and simplified response theories for excited states.

Benchmarked against the full treatment, the shortcut reproduced singlet-triplet gaps, excitation energies, and emission colors in vacuum and solvent alike. Across a series of real emitters, one design rule stood out: the twist angle between donor and acceptor parts tracked how much solvent reddens the glow. The authors pitch the pipeline for high-throughput hunts, with machine learning hybrids as the next step.
arxiv-2502-20510:
Paul Larson, Grigor Sargsyan, and Trevor Wilson build a set theory model where determinacy holds and every set of reals is universally Baire. Their 2025 paper works in ZF with full real determinacy added. The consistency proof leans on strong set theory assumptions.

The baseline assumes a cardinal that limits both Woodin cardinals and strong cardinals. The construction adapts Woodin derived model method, once used for a Suslin version of the theory. A reflection property of the new model is proven with genericity iterations in the style of Neeman and Steel. The authors present the model as evidence that broad regularity for sets of reals can coexist with strong determinacy axioms.
arxiv-2502-20610:
Jesse Lu and five co-authors present a 2025 scheme to speed light wave simulations on graphics chips. Such simulations step electric and magnetic fields through a grid over time. They need much memory traffic but little math, which clashes with chips built for heavy math. Demand for fast light design tools grows with AI hardware.

The scheme passes updates from cell to cell in a chain, like an assembly line. Only edge values between blocks need shared memory, so sync points drop sharply. On one top graphics chip, the full three-dimensional method ran at a high rate of cell updates. The authors see a path to cheaper, faster design checks.
arxiv-2502-20710:
Quantum bits left excited slowly relax, and that drift skews the answers a quantum computer gives. Enhyeok Jang and co-authors counter the skew in this 2025 paper with a trick they call Barber. Alongside each normal program, they run a bit-inverted twin, where the roles of the ground and excited states are swapped.

In the twin, thermal relaxation pushes results the opposite way. By merging the two runs' answer distributions with care, the opposing drifts cancel. The authors present Barber as a practical patch for today's noisy machines, needing no new hardware. It targets one of the most common error sources in near-term quantum computing.
arxiv-2502-20910:
Jerson Caro, Fabien Pazuki, and Riccardo Pengo study special values of zeta functions in a 2025 maths paper. Dedekind zeta functions encode deep facts about number fields, the number systems built by adding algebraic roots. The authors ask when the values of these functions at real points stay away from zero or cluster in bounded regions.

Two classic properties frame the question, named for Northcott and Bogomolov. The team proves the second property fails for all real points from one half upward. For larger points, they build families of fields of growing size whose zeta values shrink toward zero. For points in the middle range, they use quadratic fields and resonance methods instead. For negative real parts, the first property holds in full, extending earlier work.
arxiv-2502-21010:
Jianming Zhou, Xiaoli Hu, Honglian Zhang, and Naihuan Jing give exact formulas for quantum discord in 2025. Discord gauges non-classical links between parts of a quantum system. It was lately extended from pairs to many-part systems, where exact values are hard to get.

Their formulas cover special families of N-qubit states, including a broad class of GHZ states. Cases span two, three, and larger qubit counts in four repeating size patterns. The formulas sharpen how researchers assess quantum links and supply a tool for computation work. The team also finds a freezing effect, where discord holds steady in even-qubit systems under one noise type.
arxiv-2502-21110:
Charles Dawson, Van Tran, Max Li, and Chuchu Fan learn models of rare failures from as little as a single recorded disaster, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Autonomous systems fail seldom, but when they do, engineers may have only seconds of data from before the event, against mountains of normal operation logs.

Generative models trained on so little either memorize noise or wash the failure out under a strong prior. Their framework, CalNF, calibrates normalizing flows with self-regularization tuned for scarce data. It reaches state-of-the-art results on data-limited failure modeling and on inverse problems. The team also runs a first-of-its-kind case study into the root causes of the two thousand twenty-two Southwest Airlines scheduling collapse. Learning from one failure is a strange statistical regime. Doing it well could change how safety-critical systems are debugged.
arxiv-2502-21210:
Daniel Corrales, David Ríos Insua, and Marino González built in 2025 a decision model to personalize colorectal cancer screening. Most European programs screen by age alone, with one rule for everyone. Their model weighs a person's risk factors alongside comfort, costs, complications, and the value of information gained. A multi-attribute utility framework combines these into recommended policies.

The tool can judge whether to screen, which test to use, and whether to proceed to colonoscopy for a given individual. It can also evaluate existing national programs and help design new ones. The authors argue personalized strategies should replace purely age-based ones. The framework additionally lets planners benchmark novel screening devices before adoption.
arxiv-2503-00010:
Zhiwei Zhu and Jiaqun Wei present a 2025 math paper on tilting subcategories. The setting is an extriangulated category, a broad frame that joins two classic algebra settings. The category is assumed to hold enough projective and injective objects. The authors define Wakamatsu-tilting and Wakamatsu-cotilting subcategories inside it. They prove the two definitions pick out the same class.

That class also matches a pair of infinity-level notions from past work. So one concept goes by several names, and all its good traits carry over. The team then glues such subcategories across a special split of categories. The reverse glue holds under stated conditions. Algebraists get a unified account that ends a naming tangle. Unified notions travel better: results proved under one name now serve readers who met the idea under another.
arxiv-2503-00110:
Gabriele Montefalcone and co-authors set new limits on a possible form of dark matter using data from the early universe, in a paper from 2025. The dark matter they study is very light and prefers to interact with electrons. It would slowly decay into light through a loop process.

Such decays would leave a trace in the cosmic microwave background, the faint glow left from the early universe. The team used the newest Planck satellite data to bound how strong the link between this dark matter and electrons can be. Their limits beat space and lab tests in some mass ranges. They report the strongest limits yet for some light mass cases. The study also treats, for the first time, how the decay energy spreads through the early cosmos in a consistent way.
arxiv-2503-01710:
Xinsheng Wang and co-authors introduce Spark-TTS, a 2025 text-to-speech system built on a large language model. Most speech systems predict several codebooks in stages, which slows them down. Spark-TTS instead uses BiCodec, a single-stream codec that splits speech into two token types. One type carries the words, and the other carries traits of the speaker.

Paired with a language model and step-by-step generation, the split gives broad and fine control. Users can set gender and speaking style, or tune pitch and speed more precisely. The team also built VoxBox, a huge speech data set with rich labels for such control. Tests show strong quality with a simpler design.
arxiv-2503-01810:
Nandini Iyer, Massimiliano Luca, and Riccardo Di Clemente compare travel in city and rural areas across three countries. Their 2025 paper uses trip data from location services in Colombia, Mexico, and India. They draw the line between city and rural zones from the trip network itself. That avoids sole reliance on built-up land as the marker.

They score how much longer real trips run than the shortest route. Rural trips were less direct, above all long trips late in the day. In cities, travel ease often did not match access to public transit during commute hours. Rural gaps tied to how areas lean on their nearest city. Weekday and weekend patterns also differed by place.
arxiv-2503-01910:
Cheng Tan and co-authors present a design tool in 2025 for therapeutic antibodies that takes into account how the target protein changes shape as binding nears. Antibody drugs depend on a snug fit with their target. Most computer design tools treat the target as frozen in its final bound shape, yet real targets flex on approach, and that flex can make a design fail.

Their tool first predicts the target's pre binding shape with a well known structure model. It then joins a coarse alignment of the contact surface with a fine flow based method that drafts the antibody. The aim is designs that still fit after the target settles into place. The team reports tests of the tool on design tasks. Antibodies designed against a moving target could reach the lab with a better hit rate.
arxiv-2503-02010:
Kirkpatrick and Liu find the shortest joint paths for two round-shoulder bots on a clear floor in this twenty twenty-five paper. Each bot is full and matched front-to-back, and the two must not touch en route. The grade counts the sum of the two hub paths from start to goal.

Inside, the pair gives an exact form for one such best path for all start pairs. Each bot's path is built from at most six bent parts in a chain. Parts run straight or hug the edge of the pair's joint sum shape. The sum length comes out as a neat closed form from start and goal alone. Paths can run one bot at a time or turn the pair in one smooth sweep.
arxiv-2503-02110:
Xiaohan Zhu and Nathan Srebro chart exactly how much a classic learning rule overfits as its penalty dial turns, in a paper from 2025. The rule picks the model with the shortest two-part description: one part for the model, one for the data given the model. A dial scales the model part.
