Earlier work showed the rule at the standard dial setting fails to settle as data grows, hinting it under-penalizes. The fear was runaway overfitting. Their result gives the worst-case error for every dial value and noise level, in full. At the standard setting the damage is bounded and precisely known. The curve now tells users the price of each turn of the dial.
arxiv-2503-03010:
Elisa Gorla and Flavio Salizzoni wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It develops latroids, a combinatorial structure tied to error-correcting codes, and shows they can recover a code's key weight measures in one uniform frame.

Latroids were introduced by Vertigan, who attached one to each linear block code and showed a certain polynomial of the latroid fixes the code's weight pattern. The original definition ran through a rank function. The authors give matching descriptions built from independent elements, bases, circuits, and flats, for lattices with complements. They then attach latroids to codes over rings or fields with general support rules. From the latroid, the code's generalized weights can be read back. The frame covers block codes, ring codes, and rank-based codes alike.
arxiv-2503-03510:
Yuri Kozitsky adds a short math note from 2025 on when magnetic spin models gain a prized zero-free pattern. For the classic spin model, a famous theorem ties that pattern to how the model’s counting function behaves. A later result said the full pattern follows if the single-spin part already has it.

Kozitsky shows that for some models, the pull between spins can create the pattern even when the single-spin part lacks it. That holds for the Blume-Capel model and for a diluted spin model placed on a grid, plus a version with a layered link structure like Dyson’s model. The note widens the set of magnets where the pattern, and the phase results that rest on it, can be trusted.
arxiv-2503-03810:
Gravitational wave detectors have logged over a hundred black hole mergers, and where those pairs were born is still argued: alone as stellar twins, or assembled in crowded star clusters. Tristan Bruel and co-authors weigh the cluster route in this 2025 paper. They model how massive clusters form across cosmic time inside a cosmological simulation of realistic galaxies.

Cluster dynamics simulations then convert those clusters into merging black hole pairs. Across three formation models, clusters supply a local merger rate of one to ten per cubic gigaparsec per year, potentially up to half of everything detectors see nearby. The authors conclude dense clusters are a major, not marginal, factory of mergers.
arxiv-2503-03910:
Sarah Moon asks, in a solo 2025 paper, how a policymaker should split funds across many programs when the gains of each are known only with noise. A planner who knew the true distribution of policy impacts would need just two quantities for each program: its posterior mean benefit and its net cost. That planner sets the locally optimal rule.

The true distribution is not known, so Moon estimates the posterior means with an empirical Bayes approach, which borrows strength across programs. She derives how fast this rule converges to the oracle planner's decision as data grow. Simpler plug-in methods, by contrast, can fail to converge at all. In an application to 127 policies, the empirical Bayes rules had positive estimated local welfare effects. The plug-in rule had negative estimated effects. The work gives a firm base for choices under uncertainty.
arxiv-2503-04410:
Two authors present a 2025 review article on nuclear magnetic resonance in pulsed magnetic fields. The method probes atoms inside materials using very strong, brief magnetic pulses. It has sharpened the study of solids, above all those with tangled interactions and strong electron links.

The article covers what the method can do, where it is used, and what comes next. High-frequency experiments under pulses pose special technical hurdles, which are discussed in detail. Case studies on three topical materials show how the method reveals magnetic and electronic traits at extreme fields. Future gains in instruments and reach to harsher conditions are also mapped.
arxiv-2503-04510:
Alex Turzillo, Naren Manjunath, and José Garre-Rubio propose a way to detect symmetry-protected topological order in two-dimensional quantum states. These phases hide their topology from ordinary local probes. Their order parameter uses partial symmetries: acting with the symmetry on only part of the system and reading values of finite operators, with no flux insertion needed.

Lattice rotation symmetry is the lever that extracts the on-site invariants. The construction is checked on paper on group cohomology models and in simulations on states that blend between a known topological state and a trivial one. Partial symmetries are also read as building topological partition functions of lens spaces, suggesting strength.
arxiv-2503-04810:
Testing a network protocol against a formal specification usually runs into a wall: real networks change over time, and most test setups cannot track that. Rousseaux and co-authors propose Network Simulator-centric Compositional Testing, a method that puts a network simulator at the center of the process.

Built on the Ivy verification tool and the Shadow simulator, the method checks real protocol code against its specification while network conditions vary, and it allows online debugging of the running implementation. As a case study the team tested picoquic, an implementation of the QUIC protocol, and found a genuine error in how it handled a time-varying rule. The error has since been fixed. The authors present the approach as a step toward more accurate and repeatable protocol testing.
arxiv-2503-04910:
Kelsey Kraus and Margaret Kroll argue that when people must agree with a model's calls, the model should be trained and judged on those people's own choices. Their 2025 paper looks at tasks like flagging toxic posts or picking the main points of a text. Quick automatic scores are cheap, they note, but they cannot replace human judgment where trust is at stake.

Much of the paper sorts signal from noise in human labels. Some disagreement is mere error and best practice can shrink it. Some of it is real, and it can teach a model what users in fact want. The authors close with a case study in which two safety filters were judged by human raters and tuned to match user taste. They offer the steps as a guide for teams that build language tools.
arxiv-2503-05310:
Anna Berryman and co-authors model how skill and place mismatches shape Brazil's green transition for workers, in work from twenty twenty-five. A greener economy needs deep structural change, but headline job gains hide local pain. The team joins a dynamic labor market simulation with farm and green factory scenarios.

Productivity shifts by sector and region are traced through the labor market, with frictions from skills and distance. Poorly managed shocks deepen inequality in the results. Farm workers fare worst, since they move less easily across jobs and places. The authors stress targeted labor policies to keep the transition just. Green growth must plan for who can actually take the new jobs.
arxiv-2503-05610:
Eigenvalues of the Laplacian on a fractal act like the pure tones of a vibrating shape, and how closely they pack together matters for the math of waves and heat. Bernard Akwei studies that spacing in 2025 on the unit interval and the Sierpinski gasket, a triangle built from shrinking copies of itself. On both, a tool called spectral decimation keeps the tones apart by a positive minimum gap. Cousin fractals, like the level-3 gasket, may not share that luck.

Akwei's goal is a simple test: read a few traits of the decimation function and know whether a positive gap must hold. He also gives a condition that forces the gap to close to zero. The results sort fractals into those with separated tones and those without.
arxiv-2503-05910:
Nathan Rethwisch and Heike Hofmann built an interactive visual tool for forensic bullet comparison in 2025. Examiners now judge by eye whether two bullets came from the same gun, a call that is highly subjective. Algorithms can give hard numbers, but many examiners lack the training to read them.

Their visualizer shows each step of the algorithmic comparison as plots in forms examiners know. Applied to data from a Houston lab, the tool exposed an error in the process caused by a mislabeled item. The pair note future uses, such as testing how the gap between shots shifts match scores. The goal is to make complex statistics usable in daily casework.
arxiv-2503-06010:
Self-driving cars must plan a route across a whole city map and still steer smoothly around sudden obstacles. The authors present the InfoFusion Controller, which pairs a global planner with a fused local controller. The global side grows an informed tree search to lay down an optimal reference path. On the local side, two classic controllers, model predictive control and pure pursuit, each propose their own steering. Mutual information then blends the two outputs, balancing their strengths and covering their weaknesses.

Tests cover varied scenarios, including complex maps built from SLAM data. The fused controller beats traditional methods on safety, stability, and efficiency. The authors credit the information-based fusion for cutting uncertainty in local planning and sharpening reactions to moving obstacles. They release the code publicly for other teams to build on.
arxiv-2503-06410:
Alex Casella and Wayne Wang present a framework that keeps voice AI agents on the right path through branching conversation graphs. Businesses now route callers through webs of decision nodes. Language models steering those webs can pick wrong nodes or drown in context and invent steps.

Their system pairs model reasoning with a vector score that ranks the next node mathematically. It balances strict path-following against smart jumps when callers go off script. Tests beat baseline methods on accuracy and speed together. Call centers and voice assistants are the market. Reliable graph walking is what turns a demo agent into a deployable one. The catalog title carries an equal-contribution footnote as junk text.
arxiv-2503-06510:
Zhenlong Dai and co-authors fix code bugs with the smallest change that works in a 2025 paper. Most auto repair work chases a right fix and skips how far the fix drifts from the flawed code. Wide drift can break trust and add risk, so the team sets a new task around tight fixes.

Their two-stage tool first finds the bug site with a self-taught locator. It then writes the patch with a modifier trained to stay close to the source. Tests beat a set of rivals by a wide gap, the team reports.
arxiv-2503-07010:
Kaiyuan Liu and colleagues benchmark coding agents on whole software projects, in work from 2025. Language model agents now write code fast, but tests rarely judge full projects as a user would. Scores also seldom explain why an agent passed or failed a task.

Their benchmark, called ProjectEval, grades project level generation through simulated user contact. Tasks accept three input levels, from plain text needs to code skeletons. Checks run the built project and compare code with set measures for a joint score. Results show that project wide grasp and systems thinking decide success most. The team offers the tool as a guide for building agents fit for real production work.
arxiv-2503-07210:
Jacob Swindell, Madeleine Darbyshire, Marija Popovic, and Riccardo Polvara compare five ways to discretize Gaussian process maps for drone based weed mapping on farms. Exact weed maps drive precision farming, but stitched photo maps are slow to build. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Gaussian models give smooth maps of weed spread, yet real tasks need a grid form. The team tests quadtrees, wedgelets, two binary split trees, and hexagon grids on real weed fields. Scores cover look, error, and speed. Quadtrees won overall, but hexagons and one split tree suit fields with large weed patches, while quadtrees suit scattered small patches.
arxiv-2503-07310:
Asimina Marousi and Vassilis Charitopoulos solve hard quadratic problems under uncertainty in a 2025 paper. Many engineering tasks reduce to quadratic programs, which turn nasty when the curves bend the wrong way and inputs are unsure. Their algorithm braids two traditions: a branch-and-bound search that guarantees the global best, and robust planning that hedges against the worst case in an uncertainty set.

Convex envelopes supply the lower bounds that make the search provable. Robust cutting planes trim away plans that fail under bad inputs. Pooling problems, a classic chemical blending test, served as the proving ground under uncertainty sets of varied shape and size. The braided method converged faster than solvers that chase optimality alone. Robustness and optimality, the authors argue, search better together.
arxiv-2503-07610:
Anyuan Xu, Xiao Yan Chew, and Dong-han Yeom simulate the collapse of a wormhole in a 2025 physics paper. The Bronnikov-Ellis wormhole is a classic tunnel solution held open by exotic phantom energy. Whether such a tunnel survives disturbance or collapses is a basic stability question.

The team fires two pulses into the wormhole in a double-null simulation, one of normal matter and one of phantom field. The normal pulse triggers collapse into a black hole with a singularity. The phantom pulse drives a different instability path. Mapping both fates shows how fragile the tunnel is and which ingredient betrays it. The results inform the broader question of whether traversable wormholes can exist in any realistic physics.
arxiv-2503-07710:
Jake Belton, Nadav Drukker, Ziwen Kong, and Andreas Stergiou map the operator spectrum of a line defect in a 2025 paper. A magnetic line threaded through the O(N) model creates a one-dimensional quantum field theory on the line itself, interesting to theorists and experimentalists alike.

Working in slightly under four dimensions, the team lists operators with sizes near one, two, and three, plus several classes near four and some with large charge. Analytic bootstrap methods do the heavy lifting, aided by new tools for untangling nearly identical operators. Integral identities add constraints on interaction strengths that reach one order deeper in the expansion.
arxiv-2503-07810:
Louis-Bernard St-Cyr and David Sénéchal studied charge spread and superconductivity in the Emery model of cuprates, in a 2025 paper. The model tracks copper and oxygen orbitals in the planes that carry the current. Charge splits between the two sites in ways experiments can measure. Cluster mean-field calculations map that split.

Two knobs steer the split: the copper repulsion strength and the oxygen energy offset. Nuclear magnetic resonance gave occupation values for three real materials. Matching those values pins down the knob settings for each. Density of states runs complete the picture. The work ties model parameters to lab numbers.
arxiv-2503-08110:
Vasil Yordanov derives a famous quantum equation from a control-theory route in a 2025 paper. The Dirac equation describes a fast-moving charged particle with spin. His route treats the particle's path as a random process steered at least cost, a frame called stochastic optimal control.

The build starts from the standard action for such a particle in an electric and magnetic field, plus a term for spin. A key worry is whether the mass-shell rule, which ties energy and momentum, survives the derivation. Yordanov shows it does: the classical limit returns the known rule, and the full theory gives a quantum-corrected version. Tests on an electron in a uniform magnetic field match the known Dirac-Landau values.
arxiv-2503-08310:
Two players fighting over the end state of a moving system pose a hard control problem when the system changes over time. Vincent Liu, Chris Manzie, and Peter Dower build an algorithm that brackets the true value of such a game. One side seeks to lower a final cost, the other to raise it. Runs of a simpler single-player system give an upper bound. A set of flat surfaces gives a lower bound.

Both bounds rest on solid math linked to a classic equation for game values. The cost of the method grows with the number of runs and surfaces used, not directly with system size. That keeps it workable for fairly large systems. Guaranteed brackets matter for control tasks where safety is at stake.
arxiv-2503-08410:
Marcos Cirne and co-authors speed up underground simulation in a 2025 paper. When acid or hot fluid dissolves rock underground, pore shapes change over time. That process matters for carbon storage, geothermal energy, and oil recovery. Direct simulators track it faithfully but cost a huge amount of compute.

Past learning based shortcuts predicted only one field at a time, such as flow speed. Their stacked method feeds each step's output back as the next input, carrying both time and space information. Several fields are predicted together as dissolution proceeds. The aim is a fast stand in that labs and engineers can run many times while testing designs.
arxiv-2503-08810:
Daniel Abou-Ras and Matthias Maiberg revisit how fast charge carriers are lost at grain boundaries in solar cell materials in a two thousand twenty-five paper. In polycrystalline absorbers, the seams between crystal grains can trap carriers. A measure called recombination velocity captures that loss. The authors derive fresh forms of the equations for that speed and for the energy barriers met by electrons and holes.

For a fixed doping level and temperature, a measured speed turns on just two things. One is the excess charge at the boundary, and the other is a single prefactor. In data from two absorber families, both values stay in much the same range for all boundaries in one material. Yet the speeds span orders of magnitude, so the bands must bend both up and down, and by just small amounts.
arxiv-2503-09410:
Jiale Wang and three co-authors harden a classic vision algorithm in twenty twenty-five. RANSAC robustly fits models to noisy data by testing random samples. Learned versions use deep networks to guide it against outliers. Those versions are trained and tested on data from the same generator, so they generalize poorly.

The authors introduce a diffusion-based training paradigm. Noise is progressively injected into ground-truth data, simulating messy conditions. Monte Carlo sampling adds varied randomness at several stages, diversifying the training distribution. Experiments use feature matching on the ScanNet and MegaDepth data sets. The approach aims at models that survive data unlike their training set. Readers in computer vision get a training recipe for robustness where it usually fails: out of distribution.
arxiv-2503-09810:
Talya Eden, Reut Levi, Dana Ron, and Ronitt Rubinfeld count small graph motifs in sublinear time in two thousand twenty-five. Counting motifs, or small subgraphs, is a core task in graph study. Fast rough counts use queries that probe a graph bit by bit. Past best results in the plain model covered only motifs of radius one.

A richer model with edge sampling knew far more, which left a scope gap. The team narrows that gap with counts based on uniform sampling. Their main result counts any Hamiltonian motif fast in the plain model. A variant can sample such motifs near evenly. Simpler counts for stars and cliques follow too.
arxiv-2503-10510:
Classifying a whole microscope slide of tissue is like judging a book from a bag of pages: only some pages carry the verdict. Rajiv Krishnakumar and co-authors compare attention-based methods for that task in this 2025 paper, where a model learns which patches of a slide matter. They apply the methods to hunting rare abnormal cells in blood samples.

Two lessons stand out. Nonlinear steps in the model matter greatly, since removing them tanked both stability and accuracy. Lifting the features into a higher-dimensional space made the model much more robust. Their shortcut learner, an extreme learning machine, trained with five times fewer tuned parts while nearly matching the deep model. The authors eye such speed for single-cell diagnostics.
arxiv-2503-10610:
The authors hunt for strong gravitational lenses where the bending galaxy is a spiral seen edge-on. Most known lenses bend light with huge red elliptical galaxies, leaving spirals rare. Their search covered 3,600 square degrees of sky images from a northern survey, starting from seven million sources.

A neural network trained on fake and real images cut the field to a shortlist for human review. The final haul counts 82 edge-on lens candidates plus 50 of other types, doubling the known edge-on sample. The team estimates it caught about 60 percent of the bright top-grade cases in the area.
arxiv-2503-10710:
Eric Bridgeford and co-authors argue that brain studies should state cause assumptions plainly and check them with set tools, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A running case on sleep quality and white matter health carries the lesson. Hidden bias from mixed factors and from who gets kept in a study are framed in cause diagrams.

Hands-on cases show how to check overlap between groups and how drop rules can skew results. Multi-site data merging gets the same treatment. The frame guides both study design and data choices where random trials cannot run. Readers get concrete steps to make cause claims in brain work more honest and robust.
arxiv-2503-10810:
Robin van Bijleveld and four co-authors computed new jet functions in twenty twenty-five for quantum electrodynamics. When a heavy fermion scatters, its behavior splits into hard and soft parts — a factorization that lets physicists compute precisely. Pushing that split one order finer in the fermion's small mass needs new building blocks.

The authors define jet functions that connect to the hard part in several ways and compute them to second order in the coupling. A region-by-region test confirms the factorization formula holds with these functions in place. They handle delicate points like rapidity regulators and corrections on external lines. A pleasing pattern of relations among the jet functions also emerges. The work sharpens tools for precision tests of QED and its bigger cousin, QCD.
arxiv-2503-10910:
Vasilis Gkatzelis, Randolph McAfee, and Renato Paes Leme study procurement auctions with a best-and-final-offer option in a 2025 economics paper. In their sequential auctions, each seller may freeze a price while staying active. Freezing signals the seller would reject any lower price, to the buyer and to rival sellers alike.

Earlier descending-auction models forced a choice: accept a cut or drop out. The freeze option changes the strategic game completely, since staying in no longer means conceding. The authors analyze what equilibria and outcomes this common real-world rule produces for buyers and sellers.
arxiv-2503-11310:
Igor Travěnec and Ladislav Šamaj study a one-dimensional fluid with unusual thermal behavior in a 2025 paper. Some materials shrink when heated under steady pressure, a quirk called negative thermal expansion. The authors build the simplest setting where the quirk can be solved exactly: particles in a line that repel each other over two distance scales.

When the repulsion range is short enough, each particle interacts only with its neighbors, and the thermodynamics can be written in closed form. Their equation of state links average spacing to temperature and pressure for several repulsion shapes. At low temperature they find spacing jumps at certain pressures and expansion behavior that flips with the potential's shape.
arxiv-2503-11510:
Anton Burnet, Julia Müllner, and Benedikt Sabass study how cells hold on under force in 2025. Cells stick to surfaces in clusters of small links. When force pulls, a cluster can grow by adding more links. The authors build math models of such clusters, based on real sites where cells attach.

Their models show a state where the cluster grows in step with the pull. The load on each link stays low, so the cluster holds. They call this state perfect stabilization, using the head title's own terms for the process. Past a point, the same growth runs out of control. The work gives maps that show when a cluster should hold or fail.
arxiv-2503-11710:
Designers learn what buyers want by asking them to choose among products with mixed features, a method called conjoint analysis. Yanxia Zhang and co-authors argue that the classic math behind it is too simple. It assumes each feature adds a fixed value, while real taste bends and interacts.

Their system, ConjointNet, learns rich internal representations of people and products from choice data. Two new neural designs turn those representations into preference predictions. On two real preference data sets, the models beat classic methods by more than 5 percent. They also reveal how features interact in nonlinear ways, which plain models miss. The authors offer the tool for product teams that need sharper forecasts of market response.
arxiv-2503-12210: Angenent and Knopf show that still solutions of the Ricci flow can wobble in endlessly many directions, in a 2025 paper. Ricci flow smooths a shape by its curvature, and its flat, unmoving solutions are natural resting states. For shapes that run off to infinity, the authors give conditions under which the resting state is unstable along an infinite-dimensional family of changes. They exhibit examples with uncountably many unstable directions. The result warns that flatness at infinity is a knife's edge, not a valley.
arxiv-2503-12610:
Seungwoo Lee, Mouad Ramil, and Insuk Seo derive the Eyring-Kramers law for the underdamped Langevin process, in work from twenty twenty-five. The law gives how long, on average, a noisy particle takes to hop between two wells of a double well landscape at low heat. Such hops model rare shifts in physics and chemistry.

Standard proofs lean on potential theory tools that break down for this process, since noise acts only through momentum. The authors build a fresh route that skips those tools entirely. Their result gives the low heat form of the mean hop time with full rigor. The method may extend to other processes where classic tools fail. The work sits in probability and statistical physics.
arxiv-2503-12810:
Zachary Olkin and Aaron Ames tackle, in a 2025 paper, a speed problem in controlling machines that switch between modes, like a walking robot whose feet strike and leave the ground. Planning optimal control for such hybrid systems over a rolling horizon is usually far too slow for real time. Their answer splits the job into two layers that run at different speeds.

A slow upper layer sketches a stabilizing trajectory, including which modes come in which order. A fast lower layer tracks that sketch with a standard, quickly solved controller. The lower layer wraps its plan in error tubes that tolerate drift. The team proves the re-planning speed of the fast layer ties directly to robustness, which justifies the split. Simulations on a five-link bipedal robot and a bouncing ball illustrate the theory.
arxiv-2503-13010:
Foil windings, made of layered metal sheets instead of wire, behave differently in transformers and shine at high frequencies, but simulating them turn by turn is ruinously expensive. Silas Weinert and co-authors build a coupled simulation in this 2025 paper that smooths the layers into an equivalent material. The trick covers both the magnetic side and the thermal side at once.

The two physics talk to each other: currents heat the foil, and heat changes the material properties. A weak coupling scheme lets each side march at its own time step. The method checks out on a simple test shape and on a pot transformer mixing foil and wire windings. The authors offer it for faster design of high-frequency magnetics.
arxiv-2503-13310:
Matteo Esposito and co-authors survey what generative AI is doing in software architecture, in a 2025 review. Chatbots write code daily, but designing a system's architecture, its load-bearing choices, is newer ground, and no one had mapped it. The team ran a multivocal review, sweeping journal papers and gray sources alike.

Coding the haul by theme found the busiest uses are decision support and rebuilding designs from existing code. OpenAI's GPT models dominate, usually with few-shot prompting or retrieval aids. Work clusters early in the pipeline, from requirements to design and design to code, on monoliths and microservices. Hard testing of the models' output was usually missing, and precision plus made-up content top the complaints list.
arxiv-2503-13510:
Vishal Gandhi and Sagar Gandhi study how the mood of a prompt steers language model answers in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Every prompt carries a tone, warm or harsh, hopeful or bleak. Whether that tone changes the quality of the reply was little studied. The team sorted prompts by sentiment with two analysis methods. They then tested five leading models across six uses, from legal analysis to creative writing.

By rewording prompts to flip their tone, they measured shifts in coherence, factual accuracy, and bias. Negative prompts often cut accuracy and raised bias. Positive prompts tended to improve the replies. The finding matters for anyone who writes prompts for a living. Tone, it turns out, is a quality lever, not a cosmetic choice.
arxiv-2503-13610:
Becca VanDrunen, Juanjuan Ren, Sebastian Franke, and Stephen Hughes build a theory of light emission in media that amplify instead of absorb in a 2025 paper. Two quantum emitters in such a gain medium interact through light, and gain reshapes every rate in that conversation. Their master equation shows exactly how gain modifies the familiar decay and coupling rates of lossy systems, and adds new gain terms of its own.

They write the dynamics in both the bare basis and a dressed basis of bright and dark combined states. As a worked example, a metal dimer in a gain compensated medium yields all rates from its natural modes. Emission spectra and entanglement between the emitters are computed. The authors warn that weak excitation shortcuts fail under gain, producing extra coupling terms that simpler models miss.
arxiv-2503-13910:
Osama Abdel Aal, Necdet Sinan Özbek, Jairo Viola, and YangQuan Chen designed an optimisation method in 2025 that reaches its goal in a set time. The work was first listed with funding text attached to the title. Viewing gradient descent as a control system lets control tools shape how fast it settles.

Their gradient flow uses a time-varying nonlinear feedback gain to drive the state smoothly to the minimum. Unlike older finite-time schemes built on fractional powers, theirs is proven, via stability theory, to converge in a prescribed time. The proof covers strongly convex functions and a wider class defined by a standard inequality. Numerical tests illustrate the behaviour.
arxiv-2503-14210:
Maicon Hespanha and Ademir Pastor prove that some solutions of a coupled wave system must blow up in finite time. Their paper from twenty twenty-five models a light beam and its third harmonic in a Kerr-type material. The system is a cubic nonlinear Schrödinger pair. The energy-critical case, set in dimension four, is their focus.

Radial solutions are the test class. When starting energy sits below the ground state's but kinetic energy sits above, blow-up is forced. A convexity argument drives the proof. The team also proves ground states exist, as minimizers of an action score. Concentration-compactness plus variational tools do that work. A best constant for a vector Sobolev-type inequality falls out as well. The results sort which beams stay smooth and which collapse.
arxiv-2503-14510:
A deep theory of numbers across shifted worlds may yield sharp new bounds on a classic sum puzzle, and Zhong-Peng Zhou reports such bounds in work from twenty twenty-five. The puzzle asks how large a sum of two coprime parts can run against the product of its prime parts. Zhou applies the deep theory, with a slight tweak, over the rational numbers.

The new bound cuts a famous constant in such bounds by many orders of size. Bounds for a widened Fermat-style equation are also given, split by power size. Those bounds prove the classic last theorem for prime powers from eleven up. With old results for small powers, Zhou claims a fresh full proof path. Check runs back the small end.
arxiv-2503-14910:
Jingyi Liao and co-authors tackle, in a 2025 paper, a weak point of factory inspection AI: anomaly detectors trained in one plant often fail when lighting or sensors change at another. Their method keeps the popular memory-bank design, where normal examples are stored and new items are compared against them.

They tune the stored features using a robust distance measure on a small sample of target-site data, aligning the bank without full retraining. Unlike many rivals, the approach needs no advance knowledge of the new site's data patterns and works across model backbones. Tests on two-dimensional and three-dimensional benchmarks with faked shifts beat leading rivals.
arxiv-2503-15010:
Fernández-Martínez and three co-authors propose a new nozzle for spraying charged liquid jets, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such jets are used to print fine lines and to feed samples into lab instruments. With liquids that carry charge poorly, the jet often breaks up unless the flow stays above a floor rate.

Their nozzle is beveled and made of a material that does not conduct charge. That shape steadies the jet and drops the floor rate, so far thinner jets form. It also avoids chemical reactions that metal needles cause, keeping the liquid pure. Tests made jets about one micron wide and printed lines only tens of nanometers high.
arxiv-2503-15210:
Wenxing Guo and co-authors build an online federated learning framework for classification in this 2025 paper. Data arrives as streams at many clients, and it cannot be pooled, for privacy. The method must update the model on the fly without retraining from scratch.

The framework rests on a discriminant technique that weights distances, staying robust when client data differ. A new optimizer pairs a majorization scheme with renewable estimation, so updates reuse summaries instead of stored data. The authors prove the estimator settles down as theory requires, and that its decisions match the best possible risk. Privacy noise is added to protect client information. Tests on simulated and real data show high accuracy with large savings in computing and storage.
arxiv-2503-15410:
Konrad Schlichtholz and Marcin Markiewicz argue that the electromagnetic potential is physically real, under a locality assumption, in this 2025 paper. Potentials were long treated as mere math helpers for fields. The Aharonov-Bohm effect hints they act where fields are zero. A noted critique showed that effect can still be told with local fields alone. The new argument uses flux quantization's causal structure instead. That setup dodges the critique's loophole, they claim.

If locality holds, the potential's reality follows. The debate is foundational for quantum theory. What counts as real guides how effects are explained. The paper is a physics foundations argument. It picks its test case to close old escape routes.
arxiv-2503-15510:
Duc-An Nguyen and co-authors test whether two robot operators deciding together beat one deciding alone, in a 2025 paper. Teleoperation in risky settings forces choices under deep uncertainty. A single operator can hesitate or err. Pairs have beaten singles in static judgment tasks. Dynamic robot control is a different test.

One hundred participants steered two mobile robots in simulation. Some worked solo, while others paired up and shared confidence. Joint decisions improved when partners pooled their certainty openly. The gain echoes the classic two-heads effect in a live control loop. Results matter for disaster response and remote inspection teams. Designers learn how to structure the shared interface. Confidence display turns out to be a key feature.
arxiv-2503-16710:
Yanyan Li and five co-authors present a system that maps moving scenes in three dimensions over time, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Robots and cameras must know where they are while building a model of the world. Most systems erase moving objects and map only still surroundings, losing much of real life.

Their method sorts each pixel as still or moving, then keeps two sets of scene blobs, one fixed and one that shifts. A small network steers the moving set through learned motion fields. A new flow-checking step compares rendered motion between frames to keep the moving parts honest. Tests on real scenes show steady tracking and sharp new views of dynamic scenes.
arxiv-2503-16810:
Yuki Amari, Muneto Nitta, Chihiro Sasaki, Kenta Shigaki, Satoshi Yano, and Shigehiro Yasui model glueballs as knotted field shapes called Hopfions, in a 2025 paper. Glueballs are particles made only of the strong force's carriers. They are hard to spot in experiments. A Hopfion is a stable knot-like lump in a field. The team quantized these lumps and matched their energies to data. Lab results and large computer simulations both served as checks.

A knot with one unit of twist matches a known particle. Knots with two units read as pairs of glueballs bound together. One pair is bound tightly, one loosely. The loose pair predicts a new particle near a set mass. The team computed both binding energies. Spinning the knots predicts a family of higher-spin glueball states. Some of those states are still missing from data. Future experiments can look for them.
arxiv-2503-17410:
Josef Koumar, Timotej Smolen, Kamil Jerabek, and Tomas Cejka compare forecasting models for internet traffic in a 2025 study. Providers need good forecasts to plan capacity, improve service, and spot anomalies early. The team tests leading deep learning models on a large real data set from a national research network, covering many weeks of measurements.

Their comparison weighs accuracy against computing cost at different levels of network detail. A shared, repeatable method lets others rerun the same tests fairly. The study also maps where each model family is strong or weak. That benchmark gives later forecasting work a common starting point.
arxiv-2503-17610:
Prosper Dellah Allo and seven co-authors create light-emitting defects in silicon chips made by a mainstream foundry process, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Silicon photonics thrives on factory production, but silicon itself is a poor light source. Defect centers that glow offer one fix, yet earlier work needed custom fabrication.

Their trick is a simple end-of-line treatment applied after standard production. At the best implant energy, the glowing centers shone as brightly as in lab-made samples. Varied grating devices confirmed the light came from the device layer, not the wafer beneath. The route opens the way to building light sources, classical and quantum, straight into mass-produced photonic circuits.
arxiv-2503-17710:
Yizhou Zhou turns class slides into books made for each student, with help from a language model. A slide deck packs a course into short points. Students need the full text a book gives. Slide2Text pulls text from slides with OCR. It sorts that text into a neat frame. It then writes study stuff to fit: plain takes on hard points, drills, and source lists.

Choice tools let the book fit the needs and the grade of each class. The author casts the rig as a way to cut the grind of book work. Ease of use for all is a top gain it claims. Plans add sound and film inputs, plus deeper fits for each user. The work sits in the fast rush to use big models as course mills. Its bet: a deck and a book should be one short step apart, not a long print run.
arxiv-2503-17810:
Farhan Farsi and seven co-authors release a Python toolkit for computers working with historical Persian texts, in this 2025 paper. Old languages resist standard text tools: scripts vary, texts survive in fragments, and digital forms lack standards. Their toolkit, ParsiPy, targets the pipeline from raw text to analysis.

Modules split text into tokens, reduce words to their dictionary forms, tag grammar roles, convert between sounds and transliteration, and build word embeddings. The team demonstrates the kit on Parsig, the corpus of Middle Persian, the language of pre Islamic Iran. Processing those texts shows the modules working end to end. The authors offer ParsiPy to computational philology at large, noting the design can adapt to other ancient languages whose digital preservation lags behind.
arxiv-2503-18110:
Bingli Jiao, Chenbo Wang, and Zijian Zhou press a bold claim on wave energy in a 2025 paper. Two radio sources, set in mirror posts and humming in step, can send waves that stack as they spread. The pair ask what that stack means for the count of energy in and out.

With a twin dipole model, they track power at the sources and in the joined waves. On their count, both counts clash with the law that energy is never made or lost. They give the math steps and bench tests for the claim. The paper invites checks of a core physics law.
arxiv-2503-18310:
Gernot Akemann, Sung-Soo Byun, and Yong-Woo Lee present a 2025 mathematics paper on random matrices from the elliptic Ginibre ensemble. These matrices model systems whose values, called eigenvalues, can be real or come in complex pairs. The authors ask how likely it is that almost all eigenvalues turn out real. They study the chance as the matrix grows, allowing a fixed small number of exceptions.

They derive full formulas for this probability in two regimes: one where the matrix stays strongly non-symmetric, and one where it nears symmetry as it grows. In the special case of a single allowed exception pair, they obtain the expansion to every order. The proofs use different tools in each regime, from energy methods to special polynomial techniques. The work sharpens knowledge of real eigenvalues in random matrix theory.
arxiv-2503-18510:
Amos Chen and eleven co-authors count brown dwarfs in a James Webb Space Telescope field in this 2025 paper. Brown dwarfs are failed stars, too light to burn hydrogen, and they bridge the mass gap between stars and planets. They are faint, so past searches reached only the Sun's neighborhood. The COSMOS-Web survey pairs Webb's sensitivity with a wide area, letting the team hunt dwarfs hundreds of times farther away. Color rules that catch water absorption picked the candidates.

Strict shape checks and visual review cleaned the list. Spectrum fitting then set each candidate's traits. The haul was twenty-five T dwarf and two Y dwarf candidates, more than any earlier Webb search. They sit from 0.3 to 4 kiloparsecs away. Their counts match a standard model of the galaxy's structure. The authors present the sample as a step toward mapping the low mass end of star formation.
arxiv-2503-18710:
Miguel Albaladejo, Amador García-Lorenzo, and Juan Nieves build Coulomb effects into femtoscopy correlation functions, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Femtoscopy probes how hadrons act on each other. The authors combine strong contact potentials with Coulomb effects as one whole. Derived scattering amplitudes and wave functions then yield the functions.

Finite-range corrections to the strong interaction, tied to off-shell effects, turn out to be a must. Missing them distorts the amplitudes pulled from correlation data. The authors propose an approximate method to include these corrections. Their forms are compared with earlier theory. For proton-proton systems, results match past realistic results and recent ALICE experiment data well. The method computes the functions in full without solving the Schrödinger equation by computer. It also connects easily to amplitudes from effective field theories.
arxiv-2503-19010:
Luis Anchordoqui and a large collaboration describe the Forward Physics Facility proposed for the Large Hadron Collider in a 2025 paper. The facility would sit in a shielded cavern hundreds of meters from the collision point, catching the intense spray of particles that shoot straight ahead. Four complementary detectors are planned, each tuned to different signals.

The science case spans neutrino physics, the strong force, astroparticle questions, and searches for dark matter and other new particles. The contribution reviews the drivers, the engineering studies done so far, and the design of the four experiments. It also reports the state of partnerships and planning. The authors argue the facility would greatly extend what the high luminosity collider can teach.
arxiv-2503-19110:
Sina Feldmann, Juliane Adrian, and Maik Boltes push crowds in controlled experiments in twenty twenty-five. How a shove travels through a standing crowd matters for safety at packed events. The phenomenon is crucial to collective dynamics yet scarcely studied. The team pushed people forward in a measured, repeatable way.

They varied push intensity, spacing between people, preparedness, and crowd formation. A pressure sensor recorded the impulse while cameras tracked head motion. Three-dimensional motion capture added detail. Propagation distance and speed depended mainly on push intensity. Preparedness showed no significant effect, a result with safety implications. Inter-person distance especially shaped propagation speed. Readers get hard data on a hazard usually discussed only after disasters.
arxiv-2503-19410:
Takuma Kuno and fifteen co-authors shield a silicon spin qubit from noise using a shaped microwave drive, in a 2025 paper. Silicon quantum dots are strong candidates for quantum computers. They fit standard chip technology and scale well. Cheap natural silicon, though, hosts isotopes whose nuclear spins disturb the qubit.

The drive modulates the phase of the control signal in a chained pattern. Under it, the qubit's signal decay stretched from just over one microsecond to over two hundred. A protected basis for the qubit was defined, with robust gate operations proposed. Memory time measured by a standard sequence jumped by a similar large factor. Gate accuracy rose from ninety-five to ninety-nine percent in randomized tests. The method suits noisy qubits and idle storage alike, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-19910:
Chuong Huynh and co-authors present CoLLM, a framework for composed image retrieval, where a user gives a reference image plus text describing a desired change. Training data for this task are costly triplets of image, change text, and target image. That scarcity has pushed others toward synthetic data or loose image-caption pairs, both with limits.

CoLLM builds triplets on the fly from image-caption pairs, so training needs no hand labeling. It uses a large language model to fuse the image and change text into a joint code. The team also releases a very large new data set and cleans two standard benchmarks. Their method set new best results across benchmarks.
arxiv-2503-20010:
Seokho Jin and Seungki Kim derive in a 2025 math paper a truncated inner product formula in the geometry of numbers. The work counts primitive sublattices inside the space of all lattices. A core snag is that the second moment of that count blows up for mid ranks.

Their fix studies inner products of cut off pseudo Eisenstein series built from sublattice sums. Formulas are proven for both the standard Arthur cut and a harsh cut that vanishes off a compact set. Side results cover growth control for the series and a new way to resolve relation singularities. Applied back, the count error for most lattices improves to a sharper power bound. The gain beats classic bounds once the rank or its mirror passes eight.
arxiv-2503-20410:
Akylas Stratigakos and Panagiotis Andrianesis published this energy forecasting paper in 2025. Short-term forecasts, such as wind power predictions minutes to hours ahead, assume input data will be there when the model runs. In practice, sensors fail and attacks happen, leaving gaps that hurt accuracy and decisions built on it. Filling gaps with guessed values works for brief outages but degrades as gaps lengthen.

The authors build forecast models that adapt to whichever inputs are available, using robust optimization ideas from adversarial machine learning. Their models learn to partition uncertainty into a few data-driven sets, so they can adjust quickly without retraining. In wind power tests spanning fifteen minutes to four hours ahead, the models matched gap-filling for short outages and beat it for longer ones. A few partitions came close to the impractical best of retraining for every gap pattern.
arxiv-2503-20510:
Athena Picarelli, Marco Scaratti, and Jonathan Tam solve crowd control problems on a computer in a 2025 paper. Mean field control steers a huge crowd where cost and motion rest on the joint spread of states and acts. The value of such a problem lives on an endless space, which blocks direct math. Past tools fix the start state and solve from there. This team want the whole map at once.

Their route swaps the endless problem for a team game of many players. As player counts grow, the game nears the crowd problem. Finite solvers then chew the game in set steps. That trade keeps proof rigor while it gains speed. No functions on the endless space need a shape guess. The method suits crowd flows in traffic, grids, and swarms where the start can shift.
arxiv-2503-20710:
Farshad Nazari, Andrei Potanin, and Hadi Mohammadigoushki test, in 2025, how two-dimensional foams flow between plates. The foams were made from two commercial detergents with matched bubble size and water content, and were sheared against smooth and roughened walls in a custom device that allows viewing while measuring.

One foam was stiffer and slower to relax, pointing to a less mobile bubble surface. Under smooth walls, the other foam showed a yield stress while the first did not, despite higher thick-flow stresses. Stress scaling differed with wall type for one foam only. The authors trace the contrasts to detergent chemistry shaping the bubble skin.
arxiv-2503-20910:
Sergio Barbosa and co-authors revisited a gravity claim using black holes in two thousand twenty-five. The claim says gravity must be the weakest force in nature. It forces even extreme black holes to decay in time. Tiny extreme black holes push electric fields into a strong regime. There, the basic rules for electric fields may change shape.

The authors derived two tests that any decay claim must pass. One gives a needed bound on charge growth versus mass. They applied the tests to several upgraded field theories. Two theories passed the strong test for decay. One popular theory failed even the weaker test. The result ties the gravity claim to clear gains for physics.
arxiv-2503-21310:
Nicolò Barbieri, Kerstin Hötte, and Peter Persoon wrote this 2025 research paper on how green technology gets counted. Counts of green patents are widely used to track new ideas, judge climate policy, and spot fresh chances in clean technology. Yet those counts rest on sorting systems that change over time, so the systems shape which inventions show up at all.

The authors study patent families filed from 1980 to 2016 and compare two large patent data releases. They find that re-sorting old patents and wider coverage each raise the green patent count by roughly a tenth. Common filters, though, cut out between about two fifths and nine tenths of patents. The paper warns that headline trends in green invention partly reflect the counting tools, not just real inventive work.
arxiv-2503-21510:
Samuel Bilson, Miles McCrory, and Anna Pustogvar build a classification framework that carries measurement uncertainty through to its answers, in a 2025 paper. Trustworthy machine learning should say how unsure it is, but most work counts only the model doubt and ignores noise in the input measurements. That noise matters for traceability in measurement science. Their Bayesian framework is built for generative classifiers that model each class directly.

The test case is a Bayesian version of quadratic discriminant analysis, applied to satellite land cover data from two years. Rivals include random forests and neural networks, the usual tools for such maps. Across real and synthetic data, with noise levels varied, the Bayesian model stayed interpretable and modelled the input noise explicitly. It held its class probability quality across data sets of different kinds and sizes. It also ran cheaper than the rivals. The authors present it as the trustworthy option.
arxiv-2503-21610:
Konstantinos Dimopoulos and three co-authors rescue a classic cosmic inflation model inside a modified gravity frame, in a 2025 paper. The model links early inflation to today's slow cosmic acceleration. In standard gravity it clashes with telescope data. The authors place it in a Palatini-style theory. Kinetic energy of the driving field enters the gravity law there.

Such frames are known to flatten the field's energy landscape. Flat landscapes ease the clash with observations. A quadratic version of the gravity law restores the classic model, they show. An exponential variant of the potential also works. That route needs a gravity law of higher order than two. One framework thus hosts both versions. The paper extends earlier results on this gravity family.
arxiv-2503-21810:
Zhenyu Wu, Jiaoyan Chen, and Norman Paton use large language models in 2025 to infer the type structure hidden in data tables. A table's columns carry types, like city or price, and those types form a family tree of concepts. Finding that tree helps people search, merge, and make sense of data.

Older tools lean on word forms and table shape, and miss much of the meaning in the text. The authors offer two model-based routes. One turns columns into learned vectors and clusters them into a tree. The other asks a big model to name types and build the tree step by step. Tests on three real data sets showed both routes give trees that match the true ones well.
arxiv-2503-21910:
Kadaoui and a large team present a test set from twenty twenty-five for image and text models in Arabic. The set covers four Arabic dialects from Jordan, the Emirates, Egypt, and Morocco. Its tasks are writing captions for images and answering questions about them. The content is rich in local culture and daily life. The team use it to judge how well models handle dialect shifts. They test five open Arabic models and one famed paid model.

The Arabic models did poorly on both image sense and dialect text. The paid model ranked best but varied by dialect and lagged on image sense. The authors say current models leave Arabic users underserved. They call for broader training data and fairer test sets.
arxiv-2503-22110:
Stephen Lacina and Grace Stadnyk compare notions of shellability for posets in a 2025 math paper. Shellability is a way to build a structured set piece by piece in a tidy order. Several rival definitions exist, due to Kozlov, Hersh, and Björner and Wachs, and their relations were not fully clear.

The authors give two small posets that satisfy the first two notions but not the third, settling that they differ. They also define a new condition on first atoms that is required for one notion and enough for shellability in general. Under an added condition it matches that notion exactly. Order theorists get a cleaner map of their tools.
arxiv-2503-22510:
Simran Kaur Ghatoray and Yongmin Li build a system that extracts user experience insights from user research videos automatically. Judging a product depends on reading users' emotions, yet little work automates that reading across several channels at once. Their pipeline joins three streams: facial emotion recognition, speech-to-text transcription, and emotion detection in the resulting text.

For the face channel, they evaluate ten pre-trained models on three benchmark datasets and pick the one that generalizes best. Speech is transcribed with the Whisper model, and text emotions come from a pre-trained model with high reported accuracy. Temporal alignment and fusion merge the streams into deeper, contextual findings. Automated analysis through a data library driven by a large language model turns the merged data into answers. The authors present the work as a proof of concept for emotion-aware UX evaluation.
arxiv-2503-22610:
Karamolegkou and co-authors evaluated AI vision assistants for blind and low-vision users, in a study published in 2025. These tools describe photos and video in words, and many users have adopted them fast. The team first surveyed users about how they use the tools and where the tools fail them. Users praised the help but flagged weak grasp of context, cultural fit, and complex scenes. Those gaps matter most for people who rely on the tools as their only view.

Guided by the survey, the team built five tests with images and video. One new test asks the tools to read Braille from photos. Their systematic scoring shows where current models stand on each user-centered task. The study gives developers a target list drawn from real needs. It also warns against treating fluent description as true understanding.
arxiv-2503-22810:
Jonathan Peters and Philippe Talatchian test a brain-style learning rule on hardware that is itself uncertain. The rule, equilibrium propagation, trains networks from local activity alone. No heavy data shuffling is needed, which suits low-energy chips.

Real analog hardware never matches its blueprint exactly. The pair ask how much mismatch the rule can tolerate before learning fails. Deep networks trained fine up to a sharp limit of uncertainty. That limit did not depend on the dataset used. Sampling tricks, borrowed from a classic statistics theorem, stretch the limit further. Self-learning chips need exactly this kind of tolerance map. The results mark where designs stay safe.
arxiv-2503-23010:
Mingqing Liu and four co-authors compare two wireless links in a study from 2025. One link uses terahertz waves, just below infrared light. The other uses light itself, sent from small laser chips or across open air. Both promise fast data but suffer when beams drift off target.

The team built shared models for beam drift, power use, and signal loss, for rooms and for outdoor use. They also test both links for drones, where motion makes aim hard. The results show which link fits which setting, and where each one wastes power or loses signal first.  Their aim is a fair, like-for-like view of two links often sold on claims alone.
arxiv-2503-23110:
Katarzyna Rybarczyk and Grzegorz Serafin prove bell-curve bounds for counts inside a random graph built from shared sets. Their 2025 paper studies intersection graphs, where points link when their sets overlap. Shared sets make links lean on each other, so counts behave less neatly than in the classic random graph. The pair works with a broad family of count statistics that includes small pattern counts.

Their bounds hold under two standard measures of closeness to a bell curve. The team then shows how the bounds apply to counts of small patterns in the graph. Edge count serves as the worked case. For edges, they give exact terms for when the count settles into a bell-curve shape as the graph grows. The results give later workers a firm base for harder patterns in the same model.
arxiv-2503-23710:
Fangzhou Jiang and co-authors propose an origin story for the little red dots, a puzzling class of objects seen in the early universe, in a 2025 paper. The dots look like compact galaxies powered by huge black holes, yet no clear galaxy shows around them. The team tests whether collapsing dark matter halos could have seeded those black holes.

In their model, dark matter that interacts with itself heats and collapses at a halo's core, forming a black hole seed. Running this process through simulated family trees of halos, they find collapse happens mostly in the young universe at a set mass scale. With simple growth rules added, the model matches the counted numbers of little red dots. The match uses interaction strengths that also fit what nearby galaxies suggest.
arxiv-2503-23910:
Chakraborty and three co-authors film how drops burst in a head-on air stream in this twenty twenty-five paper. A drop that falls through fast air can tear into a spray of child drops. How it tears sets the size mix of that spray, a key fact for fuel and rain work.

Inside, shade shots and light-wave films track each burst form as air force climbs. At low force the drop blows into a bag that pops into mixed child drops. Mid force adds a stalk to the bag as it pops in the stream. High force blows two bags at once, which flips the size mix of the spray. A two-part math curve fits the size mix in all three modes.
arxiv-2503-24110:
François Olivier and Zied Bouraoui propose a way to ground machine reasoning in the patterns of body experience. People grasp the world through image schemas, stock patterns built from sensing and moving, such as inside and outside or up and down. Machines lack that base, so their reasoning can feel hollow. Their 2025 plan joins language models with formal logic built on these patterns.

A tuned language model would turn plain descriptions into formal forms based on the schemas. The result is a system that reasons over body-born structures rather than words alone. The authors argue this should make agents faster to steer and easier to read. It may also make talk between people and agents feel more natural, since both sides share the same basic patterns.
arxiv-2503-24310:
Alok Abhishek and co-authors introduce BEATS, a test suite that grades language models on bias, ethics, fairness, and truth, in a 2025 paper. Scores across twenty-nine measures let teams put a number on harms that are often left vague. A high score asks for very even handed replies.

In their runs, close to thirty-eight percent of outputs from leading models held some form of bias. That rate flags a real risk when models feed high stakes choices. The suite is built to scale and to help teams find what drives the bias they see. Fixes can then be aimed with care. The authors share the frame as a tool for safer model work.
arxiv-2504-00210:
Shivan Mittal and Bin Yan wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five on preparing single quantum trajectories without luck. A trajectory is one run of a quantum system under unitary motion and random measurements. Individual runs carry real physics, including sharp changes in entanglement as measurement rates vary.

The trouble is post-selection: any chosen run is so unlikely that waiting for it costs exponential effort. The authors propose a deterministic method that builds a wanted trajectory in polynomial time using imaginary time evolution, a known mathematical trick. The method works for a certain class of states, and they argue no universal method can cover every trajectory. The result opens a path to experiments on this physics at scale.
arxiv-2504-00310:
Rajeev Kumar, Harishankar Kumar, and Kumari Shalini study bias in large language models in a 2025 paper. Such models learn from vast text and can pick up and even amplify unfair links tied to race, gender, and other traits. That risk matters most where models are used in high-stakes work, such as hiring or health.

Their method, called KGAT, adds facts from knowledge graphs to training, giving the model a structured view of the world. They checked bias with public test sets for faces, life stories, and skin tones, using measures of equal treatment across groups. Aimed fixes then cut biased output and improved the scores. The authors argue the approach can scale and help models act in a fairer way.
arxiv-2504-00410:
Dongwoo Park and Suk Pil Ko sharpen blurry photos of signs and labels by trusting the text recognizer less, not more. Super-resolution tools rebuild fine detail from small images. A hint from a text recognizer helps, but a wrong hint poisons the rebuild.

Their fix swaps the recognizer's final answer for a softer signal from its next-to-last layer. That signal guides without dictating letters. They also blend hard and soft labels during joint training to stop the recognizer growing overconfident on blurry input. Reading signs in the wild, from plates to shopfronts, is the use case. Small hints, softly held, is the design moral.
arxiv-2504-00510:
Jianing Huang, Kaixuan Zhang, Youjia Wu, and Ze Cheng teach neural PDE solvers to handle new shapes by splitting the domain into pieces, in a paper from 2025. Neural operators learn maps between function spaces and solve partial differential equations fast, but they are data-hungry and stumble on geometries they never trained on.

Their scheme, Schwarz Neural Inference, cuts the domain into subdomains. A neural operator solves each local piece, and the pieces are stitched and refined in rounds until they agree. Theory in the paper bounds the error and the convergence rate. On several standard equations with varied boundary conditions, the method generalized to new shapes far better than rivals. The authors pitch it as a route to data-efficient, shape-flexible solvers.
arxiv-2504-00610:
Christine Aidala and co-authors describe a service that lets anyone order custom data sets from the LHCb particle experiment, in a 2025 paper. LHCb studies tiny particles made at CERN's collider, and its open data are free to all. But shaping the raw records into usable files once required the experiment's own complex software, a wall for outside users.

The new service takes a user's request through a wizard that writes the needed settings, then runs the production on LHCb systems. The finished files, in the field's standard format, download straight from the service's web page. The team aim to publish the Run 2 open data through CERN's open data portal this way. The service turns a specialist chore into a public counter.
arxiv-2504-00710:
Piotr Kopszak and colleagues reuse entanglement across two rounds of port based teleportation, in work from 2025. Port based teleportation sends a quantum state using shared entanglement and port choice. Running the protocol twice on the same resource raises whether quality survives the reuse.

Fidelity and success chance are derived for set and chance based versions of the scheme. Both versions use a near best measurement and allow non ideal shared states as input. Large resources give two step fidelity close to the best known joint bound. Resource wear is scored by a recycling fidelity for repeat chance based runs. Recycling works with ideal pairs and fails to hold as well with tuned states.
arxiv-2504-01010:
Dylan Lester and five colleagues cut the labeling grind for railroad fault detection by letting a detection model pre-label its own training data, in a 2025 paper. Finding faults in rail videos needs huge labeled sets, and hand labeling runs two to four minutes per image. Their loop starts small and snowballs.

A pretrained YOLO detector labels an initial batch; humans correct its work through exported text files, which is fast; the corrected set retrains the model; and each round needs less human time. Labeling fell to between thirty seconds and two minutes per image. Accuracy rose as the loop iterated. Unlike paid labeling platforms, the pipeline runs on ordinary tools. The authors aim it at fault detection first, but frame it for any detection task with more video than annotators. Labor, they argue, should go to correcting, not drawing from scratch.
arxiv-2504-01710:
Brans-Dicke gravity swaps Newton's constant for a field that can vary, and cosmologists retell its universe in two dialects, as a fluid or as a self-interacting scalar field. Tiago Alves, Júlio Fabris, and Luiz Filipe Guimarães work through both tellings in 2025, in the theory's two standard frames.

The two descriptions yield the same background histories for the universe's expansion. Across the cases studied, the team charts where expansion switches from slowing to speeding, the cosmic acceleration today's data demand. They also back out the scalar field's shape and potential from the fluid picture. Some configurations look realistic enough to court comparison with the observed universe.
arxiv-2504-01810:
Merling, Raptis, and Semikina wrote in twenty twenty-five on scissors congruence K-theory. Scissors congruence asks when a shape can be cut and rebuilt as another. Its K-theory sorts those links into a spectrum with algebra on it. Their new version is parametrized, with added structure data and topology. Oriented manifolds appear as a special case of the frame. They link the theory to cut-and-paste invariants of manifolds.

Links to cobordism categories and the K-theory of spaces are examined. On the lowest homotopy group, their theory matches a cobordism variant. In that variant, cobordisms may have free boundaries. A refined Euler map detects a classic semicharacteristic invariant. The work deepens links between geometry, topology, and algebra. It is a foundational theory contribution.
arxiv-2504-01910:
Frigerio, Paris, Lopetegui, and Walschaers wrote this physics paper in twenty twenty-five. It asks how well one can measure two things at once: a shift in a particle's position and a shift in its momentum. Quantum rules make the two hard to pin down together. States of light or matter shaped in non-Gaussian ways, which bend the usual bell curve, are the tool used here.

The authors show that any pure non-Gaussian state beats every Gaussian state for this joint task. The two shifts can, in principle, be measured with very high precision and very low conflict. Even blends of Gaussian states can help if tuned with care. The result guides the design of future quantum sensors.
arxiv-2504-02010:
Nan Zhang and co-authors ask what model compression costs reasoning in a 2025 benchmarking paper. Shrinking large reasoning models by quantization, distillation, or pruning makes them cheaper to run, but earlier studies rarely compared all three on the same reasoning tasks or explained where the damage lands.

The team tested compressed versions of a leading open reasoning model on four datasets, from contest math to multi-hop questions. A very low-bit quantized model came surprisingly close to the full one's scores. Probing tools adapted from interpretability research then traced which weights matter most for reasoning. The findings map the fine structure of what compression erodes.
arxiv-2504-02110:
Mingyuan Zhong, Ruolin Chen, Xia Chen, James Fogarty, and Jacob Wobbrock present a 2025 tool that hunts screen reader faults in mobile apps. Blind users rely on such readers, and rule-based checkers catch only a slice of the faults. Their system walks app screens on its own, gathers screen data and spoken output, and uses a large language model to flag faults the rules miss.

Six accessibility experts, one a screen reader user, judged its reports across fourteen app screens. The tool covered about sixty-nine percent of the faults on average, against about thirty-one for a widely used checker. Experts also rated its feedback richer and closer to real screen reader use. The authors say such reports could help builders fix access early.
arxiv-2504-02210:
Daiki Takama and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on the infrared fingerprint of solid nitrous oxide, a laughing-gas ice thought to coat distant icy worlds. Worlds past Neptune, such as Pluto, may grow this ice when sunlight or cosmic rays strike nitrogen and carbon monoxide ices. Lab data on the ice at the warmer end of its range were thin. The team froze the gas into fine grains and read their spectra with an imaging instrument.

A strong absorption band stood out, with three weaker bands beside it. Warming the grains made every band grow stronger for good, a sign the ice was settling into crystals. Under ultraviolet light, the nitrous oxide bands faded within about an hour and a half. In their place rose bands of other nitrogen oxides and ozone. The maps can guide readings of telescope spectra from far icy worlds.
arxiv-2504-02510:
Munis Khan and co-authors present a graphene-based sensing method that reads a living layer's electrical traits, in this 2025 paper. A bioactive coat sits on a thin, resistive film, and its charge behavior bends the film's response to a gentle alternating signal.

With graphene as the film, its own charge sensitivity adds a second signal channel. Unlike older graphene sensors, drift in the fluid over time barely troubles the alternating read. A simple low-frequency rig with a lock-in amp does the work. The authors claim quiet, stable reads fit for tiny sensors. Biomarker spotting with high clarity is the target use.
arxiv-2504-03010:
Shaoyuan Xu, Yang Cheng, Qian Lin, and Jan Allebach build a system that reads emotions from faces in this 2025 paper. Faces sort into seven basic expressions: angry, disgust, fear, happy, neutral, sad, and surprise. Teaching machines to tell them apart has been a busy topic for a decade, with uses from communication aids to attentive software.

The team built their recognizer from scratch, covering data collection, cleaning, training, and testing. Given a still photo or a live video feed, the system reports both a label and graded scores for all seven emotions. Tested on two different data sets, it passed eighty percent accuracy. Live video trials confirmed the convolutional network design can keep up in real time. The authors present the system as an accurate and efficient route to emotion recognition on images and video alike.
arxiv-2504-03410:
In some crystals, electrons choose which orbital to sit in, and that choice can order into a pattern or stay disordered. Crawford and co-authors hunted for those patterns in two fluorine compounds in this 2025 paper. The compounds are fluoro-perovskites holding iron and cobalt. X-ray powder patterns were taken at many temperatures with fine detail.

The iron compound showed a pattern-ordering change tied to its electrons' orbital states. Oddly, the change looked like one that should grow gradually, which clashes with the rules for such shifts. The authors argue a hidden symmetry break must ride along with it. The cobalt compound showed no long-range orbital order down to near absolute zero. Since that compound insulates and its orbital motion is frozen there, the lack points to a disordered orbital state.
arxiv-2504-03610:
Will Thacher, Yulong Pan, and Per-Olof Persson published a computer science paper in 2025 on building triangular meshes. Meshes divide shapes into small triangles for simulation and graphics. Good meshes need well-placed points and clean connections. The authors trained a mesh generator with reinforcement learning instead of fixed rules.

A graph neural network moves and adjusts the mesh points. A standard Delaunay method then connects them into triangles. Training rewards whatever quality measure the user chooses. The team tested generation, improvement, and variable-resolution tasks. Learned meshes matched the output of two popular established generators. The result points toward mesh tools that learn from goals rather than recipes.
arxiv-2504-03910:
Zeev Nutov's 2025 paper sharpens the math behind a classic algorithm for covering networks at low cost. The task is to pick the cheapest set of edges that covers every set in a family, and a primal-dual method with a cleanup phase has long been the standard tool.

For pliable set families, which obey weaker crossing rules than the classic case, the method's guarantee had been pushed down in steps from sixteen to ten. A rival claim of eight rested on a faulty proof. Nutov improves the bound to seven for the general case and gives a simple proof of six for graph cuts below a set size, with a slightly better figure for well-connected graphs. Matching examples show the new bounds are tight.
arxiv-2504-04210:
Yaning Fan and co-authors measured in 2025 how droplets change swirling flow in a lab emulsion. Such mixes of two liquids appear in chemical plants, food making, and drug work. Their many scales and surfaces make them hard to measure with light. The team matched the light-bending values of both liquids so cameras could see inside, even at high droplet loads.

Flow ran between two cylinders, and sensors read two zones: near the inner wall and mid-gap. Droplets near the wall blocked plumes of spinning flow, raising drag on the system. In the middle, droplets calmed large swirls yet kept some linked motion intact. Effects ran stronger near the wall, where droplets break up more. The study clarifies how droplets reshape drag and flow patterns.
arxiv-2504-04310:
Weiwei Sun and co-authors build a testbed for language-model agents that design algorithms. Their focus is combinatorial optimization: hard routing, packing, and scheduling puzzles with strict constraints. Progress here has lagged other fields because no shared benchmark existed. CO-Bench fills the gap with 36 real-world problems across many domains and difficulty levels.

Each problem ships with a clean statement and curated data, so agents can be scored fairly. The team runs several agent frameworks against classic human-designed algorithms. The contests expose where agents shine, where they stumble, and which ideas look most promising. The benchmark is public, giving the field a common yardstick for a skill that industry leans on daily.
arxiv-2504-04410:
Walter Ncube and co-authors present a 2025 paper on running indoor light based wireless networks, under a head title on machine learning driven power sharing. The network uses tiny lasers as access points, which beat plain light bulbs on speed and focus. Users move and shift over time, so the network must keep re-tuning who serves whom and at what power.

Exact math can solve that tuning, but too slowly for live use. The team pairs a simple distance based rule for matching users to points with a neural network that sets power. In runs, their mix came close to the best known results, answered in a few thousandths of a second, and held up as users moved.
arxiv-2504-04610:
Qubit devices lose their quantum edge to faint energy drains in their base materials, and Mark Turiansky and Chris Van de Walle finger one drain source in work from twenty twenty-five. Dirt atoms with a magnetic tilt sit in the base crystal. Their two split states can soak up microwave energy at qubit tones.

The pair derives how much each such atom drinks, then runs the math for three dirt types in sapphire. Loss lands in the same range that labs measure. That match marks magnetic dirt as a real cap on how long qubits can hold a state, and it gives builders a target: cleaner crystals.
arxiv-2504-04710:
Kentaro Takahira, Wong Kam-Kwai, Leni Yang, Xian Xu, Takanori Fujiwara, and Huamin Qu build a hands-on tool for live data talks in a 2025 paper. Telling data stories live with network charts is hard to do well. Charts are complex, and real-time control is clumsy with a mouse. The team aims at talks given to a live audience.

Their tool, TangibleNet, uses a projector and augmented reality. Presenters move two-sided magnets to work a node-link chart by hand. Talks with experts and workshops with 14 researchers shaped the design. A user test with 12 people showed the tool felt natural to use. Presenters kept more control of their story. The work shows touch can aid live data talks.
arxiv-2504-05010:
