Subash Chandra Behera and Shiv Parsad proved new forms of a classic shape rule. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with the isoperimetric inequality. In its discrete form it says: of all shapes with a set count of sides and a set area, the regular one has the least rim. The pair proves kin rules for polygons in hyperbolic geometry, where space curves out. Their forms swap the rim for the circle round or in the shape.

They treat lone shapes and sets of shapes at once. Two more forms hold for sets with a cap on area or rim. Readers in geometry get the old rule's kin on curved ground, both for round bound and tangent bound shapes.
arxiv-2504-05210:
Joshua Hatherley argues that keeping learning systems up to date creates a new kind of blindness for the people who use them. His article appeared in twenty twenty-five. Models decay as the world shifts, so teams retrain them; users then face a tool whose reasoning changed silently.

He names the problem update opacity: users cannot tell how or why an update altered the system's behavior. Standard fixes for black-box models do not reach it, since the change itself is the hidden part. He weighs three remedies: explanations that contrast before and after, live model reporting, and checks that updates stay compatible with past behavior. Each carries risks or limits. More research, he concludes, must target updating itself.
arxiv-2504-05410:
Benjamin Lipkin and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on steering the output of large language models. Users often need text that obeys a rule, such as a set format or a valid database query. The usual way checks each next word against the rule and blocks words that break it. With word lists of more than one hundred thousand, that check runs at each step and costs a great deal.

Worse, the usual way can warp the final text, since it looks only one step ahead. The team's method instead draws words and rejects some of them by a rule that adapts as it goes. That cuts the rule checks by a huge factor. It also gives fair weights that fix the warp when paired with a known sampling scheme. Tests on five tasks, from text to code queries to molecule building, beat the best past methods.
arxiv-2504-05610:
Arafat Rahman, Sol Lim, and Seokhyun Chung test fairness in load guessing in a 2025 paper. Knowing the weight a worker holds in the hand matters for judging strain at work. That weight is usually found by watching the worker or by extra measures, so learning models that guess it from posture or force data are gaining use.

Guesses from those models turned out to favor some workers over others, with age and sex driving gaps. When training data held a skewed sex mix, the gap in accuracy between men and women grew large. The team built and tested a fairer model for the task, aimed at plants and clinics that rely on sensor based strain checks.
arxiv-2504-05710:
One-way functions are the minimum fuel of cryptography, and a long-standing question asks whether they suffice to build quantum public-key encryption with ordinary classical keys. Longcheng Li, Qian Li, Xingjian Li, and Qipeng Liu answer no, at least for black-box constructions. Working in the quantum random oracle model, they prove that no perfectly complete scheme of that kind can be secure.

The impossibility holds whether ciphertexts are classical or quantum. It also extends, in natural settings, to schemes whose public keys are quantum, which covers every known construction of that type. Earlier results needed unproven assumptions or limits on how keys may be generated. The proof redraws the map of what quantum cryptography must assume.
arxiv-2504-06010:
Stefanos-Iordanis Papadopoulos and co-authors attacked fake news made of real photos with wrong captions. Such miscaptioned images are hard to police because labeled examples are scarce, and earlier synthetic training sets were too crude to teach much. Their team used adversarial prompting of vision-language models to write convincing false captions, producing a realistic training set called MisCaption This.

They also built a detector, LAMAR, that learns to reconstruct what a truthful caption's internal representation should look like; captions that resist reconstruction look suspicious. Models trained on the new data transferred better to real misinformation, and LAMAR set new best scores on three benchmarks, including a fresh one the team introduced. The authors release their code for other researchers.
arxiv-2504-06110:
José Maria Simões, Nuno Lourenço, and Penousal Machado study a breeding method for programs that evolve on their own, where each candidate carries its own taste in mates. Most methods that limit mating use fixed rules, such as picking like partners. The newer method, called PIMP, lets each program's ideal mate evolve freely alongside it.

The team tracked how those tastes changed over time under varied mutation types. Tastes alone could not hold the population up: they leaned on one mutation kind to avoid collapse into tiny trees. Still, the method gave smaller, more even solutions than standard contests, with more variety when paired with that mutation. Bloat, the growth of useless code, shrank too.
arxiv-2504-06710:
Vincent Kather, Burooj Ghani, and Dan Stowell compare the ears of fifteen bioacoustic models by looking at how they organize sound, not just how they classify it. Each model turns animal sounds into embedding vectors, which a classifier then labels. Accuracy scores alone cannot compare models trained on entirely different animal groups, nor judge species never seen in training.

The authors evaluate the embedding spaces directly, through clustering structure and nearest-neighbor classification. That isolates the feature extractor from its classifier head. The question is which extractors build spaces that adapt and generalize beyond their training classes. Such evidence matters for conservation work, where the target species is often rare or unrecorded in training data.
arxiv-2504-06910:
Sheng Lu, Ilia Kuznetsov, and Iryna Gurevych study the aspects that peer reviews judge in this 2025 paper. Reviewers size up papers along shared dimensions, novelty being the classic one. Those dimensions could standardize review support tools, but the notion of an aspect was never pinned down. Past work borrowed lists from review forms. This team built the list from data instead: they defined aspect operationally and derived a schema from a corpus of real reviews. The result is a data set of reviews tagged with aspects.

Tagged reviews allow community level analysis of what fields actually reward. The authors also show that aspect choice changes downstream results, for instance in detecting machine written reviews. The paper lays groundwork for review assistance that respects how communities judge. The authors argue the schema must come from the reviews themselves, not from the forms reviewers are handed.
arxiv-2504-07710:
The ATLAS Collaboration wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It uses proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider to limit how often Higgs bosons are made far above their normal mass, and from that, how long a Higgs boson lives.

The team studied events where an off-shell Higgs decays into two W bosons, which then decay into charged leptons and neutrinos. The data cover years of collisions at a set energy. Events were sorted by lepton type, jet count, and neural network scores. Everything matched the Standard Model's forecast. The cap on off-shell production came out at a few times the predicted rate. Combined with on-shell results in the same channel, the Higgs total width was capped at about thirteen units of energy, a direct handle on its lifetime.
arxiv-2504-07810:
Daniel Torres, Joan Duran, Julia Navarro, and Catalina Sbert brighten dark photos with a math model and its learned twin, in a 2025 paper. Low light hides detail, flattens contrast, and buries noise. Their variational method splits the image into lighting, surface color, and noise, following the classic Retinex idea. A color fix runs first, and a nonlocal term guards fine structure while an automatic gamma step finishes the job.

The twin unfolds the same steps into a neural network whose parts learn from data. Cross-attention lets it borrow patterns from far across the image. Both versions beat most rivals on standard test sets, and the pure math model even topped most learning-based methods. The authors offer the pair as accuracy with or without training.
arxiv-2504-07910:
Data that live on a curved sheet hide shapes that flat tools miss: loops, voids, and flows. A 2025 paper builds a map-maker that reads those shapes. Its base is a curved-space operator that blends slope and curl, lifted from the math of forms.

The method learns that operator from points alone, by mimicking the step that lifts one form to the next. The result projects tangled high-space data into a flat, low-space chart that keeps the holes and twists. Error bounds for the lift are proved under set sampling rules. Tests on real sets back the build. Older chart tools, built on height or drift alone, form the base this one extends. Shape-true charts can serve fields from cells to sensors.
arxiv-2504-08610:
Lorenzo Cazon and three co-authors link particle production to air showers in twenty twenty-five. When an ultra-high-energy cosmic ray hits air, it triggers a vast shower of particles. The shower deposits the most energy at a depth called Xmax. The spread of Xmax values carries clues about the first interaction and the particles made there.

The team defines new variables built from the energy spectra of secondary particles. A linear mix of those variables predicts over half of the fluctuations in shower development depth. They then build a probabilistic mapping based on the causal link between the mix and the depth. That mapping gives model-independent predictions of Xmax moments. Its biases stay very small in their tests.
arxiv-2504-08710:
Joshua Fixelle proposes a new image model in a 2025 paper that treats pictures as hypergraphs. Vision transformers read images as patches and shine at scale, yet they miss many-way links among parts. Graph-based rivals catch links but pay a heavy cost to draw their edges.

His model layers a two-sided hypergraph into the transformer, so groups of patches can bind at once. Regularizers keep the groups broad and varied without slow clustering. A pooling step that weighs expert edges sharpens the features. Tests on image sorting and search show strong scores at a fair cost, which suits meaning-based image work.
arxiv-2504-08910:
Winter Allen, Carina Rebello, and Sanjay Rebello use language tools to track how physics students build scientific arguments, in work from twenty twenty-five. Arguing from evidence is a core skill for science and work life. Large classes make it hard to read and coach each student text. Language and learning tools can scan big piles of writing at scale. The study spans four terms of an entry physics course.

Each term added more structured support for argument writing. Topic models pull out the themes in student texts for each term. With little support, themes centre on steps and surface features of tasks. With clear support, themes centre on physics principles and their use. The shift lines up with the support level in each term. Guided support thus helps students ground arguments in concepts. The tools also offer a scalable way to watch that growth.
arxiv-2504-09010:
Kai Lukoff and Xinqi Zhang argue that location based augmented reality can hand an Indigenous people control of its own stories. For such peoples, being heard is not enough; they must hold the say over how their histories are told and by whom. Their 2025 position paper uses the Thámien Ohlone AR Tour as its case, an experience that pins the group's own accounts to real places through a phone screen.

Site specific AR has already surfaced hidden histories, reframed colonial monuments, and celebrated minority cultures, the authors note. They explain why plain digital tools fall short, draw lessons from building the Ohlone tour with the group itself, and sketch how such efforts might grow without losing local control. The paper speaks to designers of immersive media.
arxiv-2504-09610:
Mukhin pushes further a Q-ball mechanism he proposed for high temperature superconductivity in cuprates. The picture casts Q-balls as the agents behind odd normal state traits. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Scattering on Q-balls above the transition yields resistance that grows in a straight line with heat, he argues. The same scattering splits in plane sound branches into softened and hardened sets. Spin wave spread takes an hourglass shape near charge and spin order wave vectors. The magnetic response of a Q-ball gas above the transition matches lab data in cuprates at a broad level, the author reports.
arxiv-2504-10010:
Martin Kocur and Niels Henze propose experiments on how virtual scenes and avatars shift felt temperature, in a 2025 paper. A room's color cast already sways how warm people feel in real life. Virtual reality can paint any scene and dress avatars with thermal cues, which may move felt heat without burning energy.

Three controlled studies are planned to isolate the effects of virtual settings and of avatar cues. If feeling warmer can come from pixels alone, buildings could run cooler while occupants stay comfortable. The work ties immersive design to energy saving at a time of warming climate. Results are framed as a proposal and research agenda.
arxiv-2504-10110:
Tom Szwagier, Guillaume Olikier, and Xavier Pennec propose a simpler way to shrink covariance estimates in 2025. A covariance matrix holds many entries, yet samples are often few. Sparse models help, but picking one is a hard discrete task. Their idea, eigengap sparsity, groups equal eigenvalues. Equal groups mean fewer free values to fit.

The penalty fits in a standard likelihood frame. A projected gradient method solves it on a shaped set. The algorithm ends up like a known smoothing of sample eigenvalues that pull toward each other. That link ties covariance thrift to shrinkage. The method trades a bit of fit for a much simpler model. It may suit many fields that estimate spread from short data.
arxiv-2504-10410:
Dennis Clougherty studies atoms sticking to surfaces in a solo 2025 physics paper. A cold atom can settle onto a surface by releasing one vibration packet. That quantum process works only when the binding is weak. Clougherty asks how damping and surface size change the sticking rate.

A medium sized surface acts like an echo chamber for vibrations. When its tones match the sticking transition, the rate jumps up. When the tones are off, the rate falls below the standard rule. The effect mirrors how cavities boost or hush light emission in optics. Mode spacing must beat the vibration linewidth for the effect to show. The paper links surface science with a classic idea from quantum optics.
arxiv-2504-10810:
Anmol Singhal and Navya Singhal build a license plate reader for patrol cars in a 2025 computing paper. City patrolling needs plates read from moving cars, at angles, in poor light. Most lab systems assume a clean straight-on photo. Their prototype runs on a small graphics chip inside a surveillance vehicle and watches real streets in Singapore.

The system first finds plates in the full street view, then straightens slanted ones before reading the letters. Singapore plates come in one-line and two-line forms, and a custom network handles both. The pipeline covers spotting, fixing, reading, and tracking in one package. Low power use matters because the gear must run all day on patrol.
arxiv-2504-11010:
Lingqi Zheng, Weijun Fang, and Rongxing Qiu build new families of binary cyclic codes that stay strong in two ways at once. A code's worth is set by how far apart its words sit, which bounds how many flaws it can fix. Its dual, a mate code, has its own such gap. Past builds that raised one gap let the mate's gap fall, a trade this work fights.

Their codes have length one shy of a power of two and size near half the length. For each parity of the power, they give builds whose two gaps beat all past marks. In one case the low gap tops the known square-root bar by a wide edge. At the limit, the pair of gaps can reach twice the length in their product. Save for one famed code set, no past build hits that mark.
arxiv-2504-11210:
David Trevascus and a large team weigh two baby planets caught still forming around a young star. The planets, in the PDS 70 disk, are among the few ever photographed directly. How planets are born, hot or cold, changes how bright they should shine. Mass is the missing key to telling the stories apart.

New positions from a sharp infrared instrument on a major telescope tightened the planets' orbits. From those orbits come firm upper limits on each planet's mass. A third candidate planet was tested in the fit, but its orbits proved unstable. The limits rule out the coldest birth stories for both known planets. Each must have kept a set floor of heat after forming. The work sharpens a rare direct test of planet birth theory.
arxiv-2504-11710:
Michael Barnsley and Corey de Wit extend self-similar tilings to systems whose pieces overlap in a 2025 maths paper. Classic tilings grow from iterated maps whose copies meet neatly. When copies overlap, the old build rules break, and a new top view is needed.

The authors define the top of such a systems attractor and build tilings from it. Layers of rough supertiles close in on true tilings, with each tile a limit of nested rough tiles. Cases include finite-type systems, tilings tied to single-shape puzzles, and families with endless tile kin. The theory widens tiling math to messier, overlapping worlds.
arxiv-2504-12210:
Tingyang Sun, Tuan Nguyen, and Ting He cut the communication cost of group learning on thin edge networks, in a paper published in 2025. In such learning, phones and devices train a shared model by swaps with peers, with no hub. Edge networks crawl, and swap bulk eats the gain. Earlier fixes used toy communication models that miss multi-hop thin links.

Their joint design sets both the swap web and the mixing weights that steer swap need. Each piece casts as a clean solve, and their method runs fast with a proof of worth. On real maps and data, training time fell by more than four fifths at no accuracy cost. It also beat the best earlier method on computing. The authors aim at AI at the true edge.
arxiv-2504-12410:
Anuvab Banerjee and co-authors report observations from two thousand twenty-five of a blazar, a galaxy whose jet points nearly at Earth. The object is extreme in that its synchrotron glow peaks at very high energies. Polarization, the alignment of light waves, reveals how ordered the magnetic fields are where the light is made.

A space telescope measured X-ray polarization while three ground observatories tracked visible light at the same time, a first pairing for this source. X-rays were strongly polarized, above twenty percent, while visible light sat at only a few percent. That split fits a picture of energy sorting behind a shock. Yet the polarization angles in the two bands differed sharply, a rarer trait the authors weigh with a partly turbulent jet model.
arxiv-2504-12710:
Shuai Yang, Lihao Xu, Guojing Tian, and Xiaoming Sun wrote a 2025 quantum computing paper on building circuits for qudits, quantum units with more than two levels. Today's devices hold untapped higher level resources. Using them means translating algorithms into qudit circuits efficiently, which was the open problem.

Their phase gadget method synthesizes diagonal unitary operations, a core building block, for qudits of any size. The method fits any hardware connectivity and uses near optimal circuit depth and size. On a ten qutrit example, depth fell from about a hundred thousand to a few hundred, using ancillary qutrits as workspace. The same gadget idea extends to state preparation and general unitary synthesis. It serves both noisy devices and future fault tolerant machines.
arxiv-2504-12810:
Quantum channels that change over time can be learned by neural networks, Angela Rosy Morgillo and co-authors show in a 2025 paper. Time-varying channels model real quantum systems whose noise evolves from one use to the next. The team studies Gaussian lossy channels and works from their Choi-Jamiolkowski states, which encode each channel in state form for analysis.

Networks classify, regress, and forecast channel behavior. In classification, they distinguish non-Markovian, Markovian, memoryless, compound, and deterministic channels with high accuracy. In regression, they reconstruct loss parameter sequences well. In forecasting, they predict future values, with better results as the memory parameter approaches one for Markovian channels. Readers see learning tools applied to a core problem in quantum communication.
arxiv-2504-12910:
Wodson Mendson and Jorge Vitório Pereira present a 2025 mathematics paper on foliations of projective spaces when the number system has positive characteristic. A foliation splits a space into layers, much like pages in a book. The authors study the full space of such structures, with a focus on layers of codimension one.

They describe how the separate pieces of these spaces change as the characteristic of the field varies, working in very low degrees. They also prove a version, valid in any characteristic, of a known stability result. That result says generic logarithmic one-forms stay of the same type under small deformations. Work of this kind extends classical geometry into settings where standard tools fail.
arxiv-2504-13810:
Alexandra Baldelli and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a spectral line pair in brown dwarfs. Brown dwarfs are dim objects too small to burn like stars. Their light carries a potassium line pair whose shape shifts with heat, cloud cover, and surface gravity, all tangled together.

The team fit the line pair in model spectra with a standard curve shape. The width of the pair tracked surface gravity in a strong way. The depth of the pair tracked cloud cover instead. That split lets the two effects be read apart from one feature. The width and depth also help gauge heat and gravity in the younger, hotter part of the class.
arxiv-2504-14110:
Théo Jaffrelot Inizan leads a large team presenting MOFGen, a crew of cooperating AI agents that dreams up new metal-organic frameworks and checks whether chemists could actually make them. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. These spongy crystals can trap carbon dioxide or harvest water from air. But the space of possible frameworks is vast, and many designs are unmakeable.

One language-model agent proposes fresh compositions. A diffusion model then builds the crystal structures in three dimensions. Quantum agents refine and filter the candidates. Feasibility agents apply expert rules and learned models to judge makability. Trained on known frameworks, the system generated hundreds of thousands of candidates. Five AI-dreamt frameworks were then synthesized in the lab. The authors call it a step toward automated discovery of makeable materials.
arxiv-2504-14210:
Nishant Goyal and Kedar Khare propose a new layout for holographic tomography in this 2025 paper. The technique rebuilds a sample's refractive index slice by slice, giving label-free three-dimensional images for life science. Most systems shine light from many angles, which makes the hardware complex.

Their design instead lights the sample along its axis with structured patterns. Simulations show clean slice-by-slice rebuilding is possible without cross-talk between layers. The trick is keeping slices far enough apart, following a design curve tied to the depth of focus, and guiding the solver with sparsity penalties. Tests on objects with two to four overlapping slices separated the roles of field decorrelation and the penalty. The authors say the layout could free tomography from multi-angle hardware.
arxiv-2504-14410:
Hoang Ly and Emina Soljanin wrote a 2025 math paper on codes that guard a value, not a whole message. Normal codes keep every bit safe from error, which takes extra space. A function-correcting code only has to keep one computed result right. That looser goal can save space.

Earlier work set a floor for how much extra space such a code needs, at least for the two-symbol case. Ly and Soljanin show that the same floor holds for any finite field size. For large fields, they match that floor with a code of their own. They also guess that their bound holds across all field sizes.
arxiv-2504-14610:
A way to learn from tables with missing entries is presented by Manar D. Samad and co-authors in this 2025 paper. The usual fix is to fill gaps with made-up values, which can distort the results. Their method, called IFIAL, skips filling entirely and teaches a transformer model to work with the gaps directly.

Two attention masks hide the missing entries, and the model learns from overlapping chunks of the columns in stages. Across seventeen varied data sets, the method ranked best on average against eleven rival methods. It also held up when the share and type of missing values changed. A chunk size of half the columns gave the best balance of speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2504-14710:
Miguel Sanchez and Fidel Villasenor study the structure of Finsler-type objects on spacetimes. Their 2025 paper works with tensors that depend on direction, sorted by how many upper and lower indices they carry and by a scaling degree. Two natural operations, a vertical derivative and a contraction, keep a key sum fixed.

That structure passes cleanly to connection-type objects, forming a ladder from sprays up to linear connections. It passes less neatly to metric-type objects, such as Lagrangians and Legendre transforms. The authors study the ladder in depth, then use it to weigh recent attempts to extend Einstein's equations to the Finsler setting. Three variational proposals come under review.
arxiv-2504-14810:
Jucheng Hu and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on pruning training data for language models using the model's own weights. Fine tuning on niche data can hurt general skill and wastes effort on noisy samples. Their method, DONOD, scores each sample by two weight based signals.

One signal tracks total influence on the weights. The other tracks weight wobble. A ranking rule blends the two to drop noisy and unlearnable samples. Cutting seventy percent of the data still raised target accuracy a lot and general accuracy some. Data picked by a small model also worked on bigger ones. The method needs no helper model and fits any data set.
arxiv-2504-15210:
Marina Sakharova, Abhinav Anand, and Mira Mezini improve code-writing AI models in their 2025 paper. These models draft software from text prompts, and their skill can be raised by training them against a reward model that grades code. The grades are only as good as the data used to teach the grader.

The team used symbolic execution, a method that runs code with abstract inputs to map its behavior, to build a richer grading data set. Graders trained on this data judged new code far better than a known baseline system. Models then tuned with those grades matched that baseline's results. The work shows that careful test data can raise the quality of AI-written code.
arxiv-2504-15510:
Haoran Li, in a solo paper from 2025, proposes a stabilized version of a classic test for group differences when there are many variables. The classic largest root test is strong at finding concentrated signals, but it breaks down when data dimensions approach the sample size because its matrices become unstable.

Li adds a ridge term, a small stabilizing addition, to the covariance estimates behind the test. He then derives the long-run distribution of the largest eigenvalue of the stabilized matrix under weak assumptions. A fast procedure estimates the centering and scaling values the test needs. Power analysis covers low-rank alternatives, where the true signal lives in a few directions. Tests on brain imaging and behavior data illustrate the method.
arxiv-2504-16010:
Tuong Vu and co-authors show how supply chains can grow on their own from simple learning, in a 2025 paper. In their model, each firm sets its price, output volume, and shopping list of inputs. The firms differ in their production recipes and know little about the wider economy. No central planner or perfect foresight is assumed.

Through simple reinforcement learning, firms chase profit and adapt as conditions shift. A steady production network emerges from their local choices alone. When demand jumps, a supplier closes, or productivity changes, the web reshapes itself. The authors then trace how demand and productivity shocks ripple upstream and downstream. The model offers a test bed for supply resilience.
arxiv-2504-16110:
Krti Tallam, a solo author, argues in 2025 that AI security should come first when building trustworthy systems. Talk about AI often centers on safety, openness and alignment, but Tallam says those aims rest on guarding data, models and pipelines.

The work sets out a layered view that splits security from safety as distinct concerns. It reviews main threat models, common attack paths and new defenses now taking shape. Tallam calls for a metric-driven approach to security, with clear measures guiding design. Without that base, claims of safety and accountability will stay fragile, the author argues.
arxiv-2504-16310:
Leonardo Centellas-Claros and co-authors built a synthetic data set for secure code review in a 2025 paper. AI tools now help review code, learning from huge piles of real reviews. Those piles cover tests, fixes, and speed, but they hold few security flaws, the very faults that hurt most.

A model trained on such piles can wave a risky change through. The team made fake review data rich in planted flaws to fill the gap. Mixed with real data, it may teach review tools to catch holes in code. The work aims at safer automated gates for shipped software.
arxiv-2504-16510:
Debjyoti Majumdar and co-authors study a disordered fractal spring network driven by active forces. The network is a web of beads linked by springs, built on the largest cluster at the edge point of a lattice. Past work used a neat fractal shape, while this 2025 study uses a random one.

Two kinds of force are tried: single point pushes in random ways, and paired pulls or pushes along links. With single pushes, the web swells and reaches a steady state, and spread grows in a slow, sub diffusive way set by one fractal trait. Paired forces instead shrink the web and take a long time to settle, with the time set by how many pairs are active.
arxiv-2504-17510:
Emeralda Sesari, Federica Sarro, and Ayushi Rastogi studied in 2025 psychological safety in open source software projects that work through pull requests. Psychological safety is the belief that one can speak up, ask questions, and err without punishment. It is well studied in company teams but little understood among volunteer contributors who direct their own work.

The authors built a framework linking safety to observable patterns in pull request exchanges, such as feedback and visible engagement. They measured these patterns across tens of thousands of pull requests in popular projects. Visible engagement from contributors, reviewers, and maintainers tracked with people staying active. Discussion helped up to a point, beyond which more talk stopped helping.
arxiv-2504-17610:
Marc Herrmann, Martin Obaidi, and Jil Klünder model how software teams read each other's mood in this 2025 paper. Team mood can be surveyed by reading chat text, but people read tone differently. A line that feels neutral to one developer may feel toxic to another, based on their conversational culture.

Through a simulation experiment with 45 developers, the authors build an early math model. It estimates how much agreement within a subset of a team is needed to reflect the whole team's agreement. For an average team of seven, leaving out even one member can misstate the mood, they find. They recommend surveying every developer when team mood is assessed.
arxiv-2504-17710:
Yoeri Poels and six co-authors, with two tokamak teams, build an interpretable map of fusion plasma states, in this 2025 paper. When a tokamak plasma disrupts, it dumps huge heat and force on the machine, and bigger future devices raise the stakes. Predictors can flag danger but rarely explain it, and disruptions have many causes.

Their model compresses many diagnostic signals into a small latent code using a variational autoencoder, extended to track smooth paths, split operating regimes, and separate disruptive ones. From the code's statistics they derive continuous indicators of disruption rate and risk. Tests on about 1,600 discharges from the Swiss TCV tokamak showed the map cleanly separates regimes by danger. A counterfactual-style study then hunted which settings push a plasma toward disruption, aiding understanding, not just alarms.
arxiv-2504-17910:
Yaghoub Heydarzade and Maryam Ranjbar explore dynamical wormhole solutions in a modified gravity theory, in a 2025 paper. The theory extends Einstein's action with a function of curvature and of the trace of the matter energy tensor. In standard relativity, wormholes usually need exotic matter that breaks energy rules.

Because this modification ties to a matter tensor that can respect energy conditions, the authors ask whether wormholes here can uphold those conditions or reduce their violation. They consider two equations of state for the matter content. Solutions are classified by constraints on geometry and matter. The study tests a route to wormholes without exotic matter.
arxiv-2504-18110: Hong-Jun Ge and co-authors report a short 2025 construction in geometry: a set of two hundred seventy-seven points in twenty-three-dimensional space where every pair sits at one of just two distances. Such point sets test how much structure plain distance rules can force, and large examples are rare. The two allowed distances in the construction are two and the square root of six.
arxiv-2504-18210:
Jimmy Tran and Tore Kleppe develop a sampling method for rough target distributions in a 2025 paper. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, a leading sampler, needs smooth, differentiable targets. Real models often have kinks or jumps in their gradient, which breaks that need.

Their generalized randomized version joins Hamiltonian motion with a stepwise random process that handles piecewise smooth targets. They argue the method keeps the right target as its steady state in both settings. Simulations and real models test the claim, including a new form of a spike-and-slab prior for regression. Statisticians get a sampler for models that were awkward before.
arxiv-2504-18610:
Arun Kumar Pati proposes a new idea, dark space-time, in a solo twenty twenty-five paper on quantum entanglement. Entanglement links two far-apart particles in a way that defies classic ideas of cause and place. Pati asks whether a hidden geometry could carry that link.

He posits a second space-time that sits alongside our own, with its own metric. In that dark sector, cause can travel faster than light, so the odd links of entanglement could flow through it unseen. States evolve by interplay between the two sectors. Pati also ties the idea to the ER equals EPR conjecture and to the black hole information paradox.
arxiv-2504-19310:
Georgii Kalagov studies in 2025 how a gas of atoms with several spin states turns superfluid when the atoms pull on each other at full strength. Standard theory paints the change as smooth. Using a flow method that tracks how interactions shift across scales, he lets fluctuations speak for themselves.

With four or more spin states, the change turns abrupt instead, with jumps in the pairing gap and heat content. He gives numbers for the switch temperature and the jump sizes as the state count grows. More states mean a cooler but sharper switch. The result is a clean target for cold atom labs.
arxiv-2504-19510:
When a massive star collapses straight into a black hole, the explosion fizzles but a burst of neutrinos should still escape, carrying news of the failure. Yudai Suwa and co-authors aim that idea at a candidate failed supernova spotted in the Andromeda galaxy. Simulations predict a short, fierce burst whose particle energies climb fast and then cut off when the hole forms.

The team compared four recipes for nuclear matter, since the recipe changes the burst. A large underground detector saw nothing at the right time, and that silence already rules out part of the model space. The work shows ghost particles can probe collapses that light never reports.
arxiv-2504-19810:
Planet-forming disks glow in infrared light scattered off their dust. Maio and a large team of co-authors present the first survey of such disks with a new instrument on the Very Large Telescope. Seven disks were imaged at four micrometers through a coronagraph that masks the star's glare. Image tricks then separated the disk light from artifacts and set limits on any planets hiding there.

All seven disks showed up, two of them at this wavelength for the first time. Gaps ringed two famous disks, and one showed flared walls with faint spiral arms. No planets were found, though the setup could have caught hot ones. The team says cooler or dust-buried planets may still lurk, and the tool proved itself for disk work.
arxiv-2504-20010:
Jacob Emmerson, Rayid Ghani, and Zheyuan Ryan Shi test whether a language model can do the hardest first step of social-good AI projects: scoping the problem, in a 2025 paper. Projects that aim AI at transit, health, or wildlife problems often stall at the proposal stage, because few people combine technical and domain expertise. The authors build a Problem Scoping Agent that drafts full project proposals grounded in scientific literature and real-world knowledge.

In blind review, the agent's proposals were judged comparable to those written by human experts, and AI-based evaluations agreed. The result suggests much of the scoping labor, surveying what is known and framing a feasible project, can be automated well enough to unblock scarce expert time. The authors also document where real-world scoping still resists automation. They close with open challenges and directions for making such agents reliable partners in social-good work.
arxiv-2504-20310:
Greg Gluch and co-authors asked when attacks on AI always transfer in two thousand twenty-five. A transferable attack fools every defender in a class. Such jailbreaks are the strongest form of adversarial trick. The team studied the role of computing power gaps. They compared attacker and defender budgets formally.

With a quadratic power gap, a sharp split emerges. Every learnable task then allows attack or defense. Below that gap, the split fails for generative tasks. A defense that spends extra compute after seeing input helps. It can beat every fixed published defense in strength. That gives formal backing to a recent empirical trend. Inference-time compute may be a real shield for models.
arxiv-2504-20510:
Irina Ruzavina and co-authors publish a photo set for judging blasted steel in a 2025 paper. Factories blast steel to prep it for paint, and human checks of the finish are slow and uneven.

The set holds over sixteen hundred labeled photos marked ready for paint or needs blasting, showing real flaws like rust, weld lines, and scratches. Three classifiers were tried: a compact transformer, a support vector machine on deep features, and an autoencoder. The guided two hit ninety five percent accuracy, and all three can show users the exact patches behind each call. The open set invites wider factory vision work.
arxiv-2504-20710:
Leonie Lorenz and co-authors present tools that turn stored biology models into runnable, viewable simulations in two thousand twenty-five. Models of cell systems help answer questions and make forecasts, but most people cannot rebuild them from raw math. That locks out many who could use them.

One tool, SBMLtoOdin, is an R package that reads models from the BioModels store and writes ready code in a known solver tongue. The second, Menelmacar, is a website that solves those models in the browser and shows them as live charts. Both are free under open licenses. The aim is models that experts and lay readers alike can run and reuse.
arxiv-2504-20810:
Mattia Damia Paciarini and co-authors stretch a flexible frame for sketching black holes to the charged kind in a 2025 paper. Charged holes can sit at an edge state where they stop shedding heat. Quantum tweaks should warp their shape most near that edge, yet a model-free way to write the warp was missing.

The frame writes warps through plain measures, such as the span to the hole's rim. For the edge case, the team swaps in the fall time of a dropped watcher and works out what the warp terms must obey. One worked case shows the frame in use, with notes on a gravity guess that bounds the terms.
arxiv-2504-20910:
People who red-team AI systems spend their days coaxing models into saying harmful things, and that work can harm them. A nine-author team argues in 2025 that protecting these testers' mental health is a workplace safety issue, not a perk. Unlike older software testing, the job demands live, adversarial conversation with a system that can produce disturbing material on demand. The strain follows from the method itself.

The authors borrow safeguards from jobs with similar pressure: actors, therapists, conflict photographers, and content moderators. Each field has built habits and organizational supports for people who face distressing material daily. The paper adapts those practices to red-teaming and urges firms to treat tester well-being as part of AI safety.
arxiv-2504-21110:
Cosmology's standard model gives dark energy and dark matter separate, silent roles. Martín Richarte and co-authors let them interact, but only in the fine print, at the level of small perturbations. Every geometric test stays consistent with the standard picture or its closest extension. The novelty hides in the growth of structure rather than in distances.

Working through the consequences, they find the interaction can raise or lower a well-known imprint on the oldest light, depending on the coupling's sign. Growth measures shift too: one standard estimator moves by up to fifteen percent at late times. At late epochs the exchange becomes strong enough to reshape how structure forms on small scales. The authors map which terms in the dark energy pressure matter at which scale, and they confirm no large-scale instability spoils the model.
arxiv-2504-21510:
Ganesh Tiwari and Timur Shaftan presented a simpler way in 2025 to work out how much power a beam of electrons gives off as light in a wavy magnet device. Too much power on a narrow opening can damage parts at the front of a beam line.

Their formulas now allow for a beam that spreads a little and points slightly off line. They compared two ways of adding up the power, one smooth and one based on many sample particles, and showed the two agree. They then studied the openings on one beam line at a New York light source. A small tilt of the beam, they found, can dump extra power on tight openings.
arxiv-2505-00410:
Farhana Elias and co-authors compare in 2025 six machine learning models at forecasting osteoporosis risk, and insist the winning model explain itself. The bone disease often goes untreated because it shows no symptoms until a fracture, so early flags matter. Their data blend clinic, demographic, and lifestyle measures.

Tuned versions of six classifiers were trained and scored. XGBoost led with ninety-one percent accuracy and the best marks on the other scores. Three explanation tools then opened the model up: age came out as the top driver, followed by hormonal change and family history, matching clinical knowledge. The authors argue such openness lets doctors trust and use the predictions.
arxiv-2505-00510: Mimi Zhang maps soil contamination across Ireland by grouping thousands of samples into patterns. Using geochemical data from the Tellus Programme, the 2025 study analyzes 4,278 topsoil samples spread over nearly eighteen thousand square kilometers. A clustering method that respects geography sorts the samples into seven groups, each with a distinct chemical fingerprint. The groups reveal where contamination clusters and how it varies across the country, giving regulators a compact picture of a national dataset too large to read sample by sample.
arxiv-2505-00610:
Monte Carlo Tree Search plans well but its huge search trees are hard to explain, which limits trust in AI planning. Ziyan An and co-authors build a framework that answers free-form questions about a search in plain language. A large language model drafts the explanation, while a logic layer based on Computational Tree Logic keeps it honest.

User questions are translated into logic statements, and evidence is pulled from the actual search tree. That design keeps answers consistent with the real environment dynamics and its constraints. Rigorous tests showed strong accuracy and factual consistency. The authors argue the pairing of language models with formal logic can make planning systems explainable without letting the explainer invent facts.
arxiv-2505-00810:
Jordi de la Torre presents a 2025 system that fixes messy lab units in huge health data sets. Mismatched units block data sharing across hospitals and studies. His pipeline blends a classic word match score with sentence embeddings. A smart search over settings tunes that blend.

Then a transformer judge re-ranks the top unit picks for each lab entry. Tests ran on a claims data mart holding seven and a half billion entries. On a rank quality gauge, the blend scored zero point eight eight three. Word match alone scored zero point seven nine nine, and embeddings alone came in lower at zero point five two eight. After the judge stepped in, the final score rose to zero point nine eight three. Top pick accuracy hit eighty-three percent, while recall reached near ninety-five percent by rank five.
arxiv-2505-01010:
Shunsuke Sengoku, Hoi Chun Po, and Haruki Watanabe extend frustration-free fermion models in a 2025 paper. Frustration-free systems are sums of local terms that share one ground state. Such models behave very differently from frustrated ones.

Strict versions allow only finite-range hopping between sites. Relaxing that rule to fast-decaying hops changes the picture. Gapped systems then realize Chern insulator phases with ease. Nearly degenerate ground states with small splittings also appear. Allowing slower power-law hops yields a gapless band metal. Its gap shrinks in step with system size. Readers learn how range limits shape what simple models can host.
arxiv-2505-01210:
Henry Austin, Petra Berenbrink, and their co-authors study how a large group of simple agents can pick a single leader on its own. Their 2025 paper uses the population model, where pairs of agents meet at random and swap simple states. The group must settle on one leader starting from any state at all, a trait called self stabilization.

The hard part is speed versus memory: fast methods tend to need huge numbers of states per agent. The authors give a flexible method that, with the right setting, reaches the best known time while using far fewer states than the prior best fast method. Their counts rest on a trade off curve, so users can pick a balance between time and states. The result matters for models of tiny devices and natural swarms.
arxiv-2505-01410:
In the LOCAL model of distributed computing, processors solve a problem by talking only to nearby neighbors, and speed is a long-standing goal. Sebastian Brandt and Ananth Narayanan study deterministic algorithms on trees, where tight bounds stay elusive. They define a problem's truly local complexity: the smallest cost, beyond a tiny universal term, at which it can be solved when only the local neighborhood matters. Their main result is a transformation between the settings.

Given an algorithm that runs at the truly local rate, the transformation produces one whose cost on trees depends on a slow-growing function of network size. If the input algorithm is optimal, the output is optimal on trees, under a natural assumption about worst cases. As a showcase, they give the first strongly sublogarithmic algorithm for an edge coloring problem on trees, breaking a barrier other symmetry-breaking problems cannot cross.
arxiv-2505-01510:
Ashland Knowles and Ganesh build a network model for a family of layered materials in a 2025 paper. In these transition metal compounds, each metal atom holds three spare electrons and bonds with three neighbors on a triangular sheet. Older physics models forced one or two bonds per site; this work generalizes the rule to three, forming a trivalent network.

A bending rule adds structure: two bonds at one atom cannot run parallel, which forces bonds to alternate along each row of the sheet. No local reshuffling is allowed, so the pattern is frozen once set. Mapping the lowest-energy patterns yields a rhombus-stripe phase that matches a distortion seen in several real materials. Strikingly, the bulk pattern is fully fixed by the edge, a simple case of holography.
arxiv-2505-01610:
Clara Palacios and Armando Aligia study a proposed quantum bit built from paired quantum dots in a 2025 paper. The design, called a Kitaev-transmon, joins two double dots with a Josephson junction. It aims to host special Majorana-like states that could store quantum information safely.

The authors add effects earlier work set aside: repulsion between atoms and extra near-degenerate states. They show the prized sweet spot survives the repulsion if settings are tuned well. At the sweet spots of both dots, every energy state comes in exact pairs, due to a hidden mapping between two halves of the system. Away from the spots, microwave spectra depend on the starting state.
arxiv-2505-01810:
Finding your place inside a large building, where satellite signals fail, often relies on matching Wi-Fi fingerprints to a map. Zhiyi Zhou and two co-authors add a safety layer to that task in 2025 using conformal prediction. The method turns a model's guess into a set of places with a stated chance of holding the true one.

They also extend the idea to route guidance, keeping error rates under control along a path. On a public indoor data set, their models reached about eighty-five percent accuracy on unseen data and hit their coverage targets closely. Set sizes varied by model, showing the price of certainty. The authors say such guarantees matter for services people trust with their location.
arxiv-2505-01910: Raju Biswas, writing alone in 2025, pins down sharp size estimates for a derivative measure on special classes of analytic functions. The classes gather functions shaped like stars or convex forms, tuned by a chosen profile function. The measure, the pre-Schwarzian norm, gauges how far a function bends from plain scaling. Three families of profile functions are treated in turn. Each comes with its own allowed parameter range. The estimates are sharp, meaning best possible of their kind. Results of this type feed the fine theory of univalent functions.
arxiv-2505-02010:
Ma, Cao, Jiang, Guo, and Gong present Q-Mamba, offline learning for meta black-box optimization, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Reinforcement learning can configure optimization algorithms dynamically for each new task distribution. Online learning makes that meta-training slow and costly in practice. Their framework learns the configuration policy from offline data instead of live runs.

Algorithm configuration becomes a long-sequence decision process under this framing. A decomposed Q-function eases learning in the huge configuration space. Conservative Q-learning stabilizes training on the fixed offline data set. A Mamba architecture speeds long-sequence learning further with parallel scanning. Benchmarks match or beat online baselines with far better training efficiency throughout.
arxiv-2505-02110:
Tristan Cazenave wrote a solo paper in two thousand twenty-five reporting that a long-standing puzzle benchmark has been solved. The benchmark is Eterna, a set of RNA design challenges. RNA design means finding a letter sequence that folds into a target shape, a task with uses in synthetic biology, medicine, and nanotechnology.

Cazenave's algorithm, named Montparnasse, searches by rolling out many trial solutions and keeping what works. It balances several goals at once and limits how often it repeats a line of play. Earlier methods had left some Eterna puzzles unsolved. The paper presents the algorithm and its run at the full benchmark.
arxiv-2505-02310:
Trials that randomize whole clinics face a cruel data problem: some patients die before outcomes can be measured, and others vanish for unknown reasons. Guangyu Tong and co-authors build a Bayesian framework for that tangle in this 2025 paper. Their model handles several outcomes at once and sorts patients into those known alive, known dead, or of unknown status.

The target is the causal effect among survivors, reported at both person and cluster level. Simulations show low bias and honest coverage across varied scenarios. A geriatric trial illustrates the method, which extends to more endpoints and other outcome types. The authors offer it as a general frame for aging and palliative care trials.
arxiv-2505-02410:
Krzysztof Ociepa and four co-authors present a language model built for Polish, in this 2025 technical report. The model, Bielik 11B v2, starts from the Mistral 7B design and grows to eleven billion parameters by depth up-scaling, adding layers rather than widening them. It aims for top Polish performance while staying multilingual.

Two training ideas stand out. Weighted instruction cross-entropy loss grades training examples by quality, so good instructions count more. An adaptive learning rate shifts with context length as training proceeds. Across many benchmarks the model beat rivals two to six times its size and clearly passed other Polish specialists, from language understanding to hard reasoning. Quantization options let it run on varied hardware. The authors present it as a step forward for capable AI in less-represented languages.
arxiv-2505-02610:
Eemeli Eronen and Johannes Niskanen pick apart light spectra of a dye in alcohol in this 2025 paper. The dye, azobenzene, shifts shape under light, and its color bands vary a lot from one molecule pose to the next. The team asks which pose traits drive that spread.

A targeted stats method finds a small set of pose axes that explain most of the color spread. Poses that soak up light at a set color turn out to be over-common in that slice. That skew may shape what the dye does next after a flash. The authors say the method filters noise from the traits that truly count in liquid spectra.
arxiv-2505-02910:
You-Peng Liao, Jasper Roosmale Nepveu, and Chia-Hsien Shen prove a 2025 theorem about how the strength of forces must drift as one zooms out in an effective field theory. Such theories describe physics at low energy while leaving the high-energy detail open. A classic result in a related field fixes the direction of that drift for one key count. Their theorem does the same for the running of couplings.

The proof rests on three bedrock principles: unitarity, analyticity, and Lorentz invariance. It fixes the sign of the one-loop running when two inserted operators share the same even mass dimension. The result holds for a broad class of theories, whatever completes them at high energy. The authors show what it means for two workhorse theories used in particle and nuclear physics.
arxiv-2505-03510:
Ludovico Iannello and co-authors use living neurons as the core of a computing system, in a research paper from 2025. Their setup, called biological reservoir computing, grows a pool of cultured neurons on an electrode grid. Signals enter through some electrodes, and the rest record how the network answers.

The living network turns each input into a rich, high-dimensional pattern of firing. A simple linear classifier then reads those patterns to sort inputs, much as an echo state network does in software. The team tested the system on position codes, bars at varied angles, and a digit task. Results showed the cell network could carry out pattern recognition, a step toward bio-hybrid computing.
arxiv-2505-03610:
Fangling Jiang and six co-authors tackle a threat to face recognition: masks made in 3D that fool the system. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that past defenses lean on costly sensors or on pulse signals read from the skin, and they do not travel well to new settings.

Their method learns text prompts enriched with facts from a knowledge graph. Short written notes about real faces and mask traits guide a vision-language model to spot the fakes. A filter picks which facts matter for each image, and a causal step strips out false links. The result is a cheaper defense that holds up across varied tests.
arxiv-2505-04310:
Simo Alami C and co-authors model full return distributions for reinforcement learning with far fewer parameters in 2025, using team framing since the head author order differs from the catalog list. Standard methods predict only average reward. Distribution methods fix support points or stack flat slices, so size grows with detail. Their model uses smooth flows that bend a base curve into the return shape.

Size then stays fixed no matter the detail wanted. A new distance, built on mass gaps, trains the flow. The team proves it is a true distance with shrinking update steps. Fair sample slopes come free. Toy tasks show rich multi peak returns captured. Game tests matched classic rivals at a fraction of the size.
arxiv-2505-04610:
A faint, odd kind of exploding star got its earliest infrared portrait in a 2025 paper. Hoogendam and fourteen co-authors caught supernova 2024pxl in the galaxy NGC 6384 about three days after first light, and followed it from ultraviolet to near-infrared light. The star was a Type Iax, the dim, slow cousins of the standard Type Ia.

Its rise followed a clean power law, with no sign of a companion star or nearby material being struck. The earliest infrared spectrum, taken nine days before peak, was a smooth glow like a 9,000-degree surface, and carbon, silicon, and iron lines moved at similar speeds, pointing to well-mixed debris. The team also compared infrared colors across the class and found them strikingly uniform, unlike normal Type Ia events. A brightness link to a cobalt line speed may help rank these explosions.
arxiv-2505-04910:
Matthew Sunohara proves a key building block for a grand program in number theory, in a 2025 paper. The Langlands program links distant areas of mathematics, and one strategy toward its goals needs transfer operators between spaces of stable orbital integrals. Such operators would carry character data from one group to another at the local level. Sunohara works over a local field of characteristic zero and assumes part of the local correspondence.

He proves that continuous stable transfer operators exist for three kinds of test functions. The proof runs through stable versions of the Paley-Wiener theorem for each function space, one of which is new. A side result shows stable characters fill their space in a dense way. The work supplies a local tool that the broader strategy had been missing.
arxiv-2505-05310:
Lott Frans, Michael Backes, Heino Falcke, and Tiziana Venturi wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on choosing a site for a new telescope in Africa. A global network of dishes already photographs giant black holes by joining their signals. Adding a dish in Africa would fill gaps in that network. Two sites in the highlands of Namibia are candidates: a mountain called Gamsberg and an existing observatory site.

Water vapor in the air is the main enemy of such work, since it blurs signals at the wavelengths used. The team estimated vapor levels at both sites using data from navigation satellites. Both sites look workable at the two lower observing bands. The highest band may work at Gamsberg in winter, when the air is driest. Median vapor at Gamsberg was clearly lower than at the other site.
arxiv-2505-05710:
Jeong and five co-authors built a foundation model for hyperspectral satellite imagery in twenty twenty-five. Hyperspectral images record hundreds of wavelength bands per pixel, giving rich material fingerprints but posing a heavy data challenge in both space and spectrum. Their model, HyperspectralMAE, learns by reconstruction: hide parts of the image and predict them.

During pre-training, half the spatial patches and half the spectral bands are masked at random, forcing the network to infer missing content in both dimensions. Learnable Fourier-based embeddings encode each band's wavelength so spectral order is respected. The loss balances pixel accuracy with spectral shape fidelity. Pre-training used two large satellite corpora, and fine-tuning on the Indian Pines land-cover benchmark set a new state-of-the-art transfer accuracy. The authors say dual masking yields robust spectral-spatial representations.
arxiv-2505-06010:
Dawid Wisniewski, Mikolaj Pokrywka, and Zofia Rostek test whether machine translation systems leave certain entities untouched, as they should. Web addresses, bank account numbers, and emails must cross languages unchanged, yet models sometimes alter them. The team checks popular systems, including Google Translate and several open models, across four languages.

They measure accuracy on entity transfer, catalog the errors, and probe why they happen. Some categories, notably emojis, trouble many models. To support further work, they release a synthetic multilingual data set of tens of thousands of sentences spanning nine entity categories in English, German, Polish, and Ukrainian. The study gives builders a concrete way to test a quiet but vital translation skill.
arxiv-2505-06210:
Diego Adame and seven co-authors present a 2025 medical imaging paper on outlining colon polyps with topology-aware AI. Polyp outlines guide screening, but models miss shape traits such as connected parts, loops, and voids, which blurs borders. Their base model uses a Mamba design that reads long ranges at low cost.

The method works in two stages. First, the base model maps polyp chances, and shape diagrams turn lasting features into attention maps. Next, those maps feed back into the model to sharpen the outlines. Tests on five public polyp data sets showed the approach works well. The authors plan to release the code. Adding shape sense to fast models may help other medical image tasks too.
arxiv-2505-06410:
Prarthana Pillai and co-authors sharpen a standard battery test in their 2025 paper. Testers find the inner resistance of a battery by firing a current pulse and dividing the voltage shift by the current. That shortcut skips one fact: the pulse itself moves the resting voltage of the cell. The team show how big the error from that skip can be.

Their fix uses a new view of the test signal that lets them work out the resting voltage shift from the same data. The method needs no facts about charge level, cell size, age, or heat, so it fits many cell types. In simulator tests the error fell by 30 percent to more than 250 percent. On real round lithium cells in the standard pulse test, the fix cut the overread by up to 20 milliohms.
arxiv-2505-06610:
Amitrajit Nag and Jaydeep Basu study the origin of Fano interference in a guided mode resonant metasurface, under the head title on Fano interference and its tunability. Fano resonances have an asymmetric shape and arise when a sharp mode interferes with a broad background. They appear in atomic physics, grating optics, and engineered metasurfaces.

An ab initio theory from the Feshbach formalism frames the analysis. Simulations supply the field data the theory needs, with multipole decomposition of scattered fields for the induced moments. Changing the excitation from a plane wave to polarized dipole sources shifts the resonance to lower frequency and narrows its width. Those shifts, quantified numerically, match recent experiments in a qualitative way and suggest new tuning routes.
arxiv-2505-06810:
Lei Jiang, Chi Zhang, and Fan Chen predict good starting settings for quantum optimization circuits with a graph neural network, in a 2025 paper. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm stalls on flat landscapes when started badly, a real risk on today's noisy hardware. Earlier fixes either reused average past settings, which generalize poorly, or trained networks that ignored the physics of the algorithm. Their model, QSeer, bakes in physics principles like parameter concentration and symmetry.

Across varied graphs, QSeer lifted starting quality by six to sixty-eight percent and sped convergence five to ten times over prior methods. It also handles circuits of varying depth and weighted problems, which earlier network methods could not. The authors argue physics-aware learning beats both blind averages and blind networks. They target near-term quantum hardware, where every saved iteration counts.
arxiv-2505-07610:
Kenza Amara and co-authors present an explainability paper, published in 2025, on finding the ideas inside a prompt that sway a language model's answer. Token level tools credit individual words, yet a reply's meaning hangs on whole concepts, not single tokens. Their method, ConceptX, scores semantically rich prompt tokens by how much swapping them changes the meaning of the output.

Because swaps happen in place, the surrounding context stays intact, and the goal of the explanation can be set by the auditor, such as hunting gender bias. Across three language models the method beat a leading token tool on faithfulness and agreement with human judges. Editing flagged concepts also shifted sentiment more and cut jailbreak success further than rival edits.
arxiv-2505-07710:
A robot that helps someone dress must react fast when a sleeve snags or the wearer hurts. Yasmin Rafiq and co-authors tested in 2025 hybrid controls that mix machine sensing with the wearer's own feedback.

One strategy watches pulling forces: on a snag, the robot either asks the user through a chatbot or reroutes on its own. A second strategy slows the arm when the user reports discomfort, and stops the task if needed. In physical dressing trials, pairing force sensing with user feedback kept the task safer and more often on track. The authors argue such two-way control is key to trustworthy home robots.
arxiv-2505-07810:
Piotr Miska, Nadir Murru, and Giuliano Romeo extend a 2025 classic algorithm for doing sums and products with continued fractions to fractions in many dimensions. A continued fraction writes a number as a tower of nested parts. Even in one dimension, adding two such towers has no plain rule, a gap an algorithm from 1972 first filled.

Their work defines the key transforms for the multi dimensional case and gives steps to compute them. A wider bilinear form covers sums and products as one case. Test runs chart how the new steps behave. The results open machine arithmetic for a class of numbers used in approximation.
arxiv-2505-08010: Ze-An Ng proves a short result in analysis about the size of a function's gradient under two unlike measures. The setting is an open subset of n-dimensional space, with a function differentiable almost everywhere in the sense of k-dimensional Hausdorff measure, for k below n. Ng shows the L-infinity norm of the gradient is the same under that Hausdorff measure or the full Lebesgue measure. A further result follows: convergence in the Sobolev space W1-infinity keeps the property of being differentiable everywhere.
arxiv-2505-08310:
Piotrovich, Buliga, and Natsvlishvili estimate the spin of giant black holes in the most distant bright quasars known, in work from twenty twenty-five. These quasars shine from when the universe was under a billion years old. How their black holes grew so fast is a core puzzle.

For objects at redshifts six to seven and a half, the team derived spin, viewing angle, and mass together. Spins averaged above zero point nine, near the physical max. The spin spread matched patterns seen in nearer active galaxies. Strong links among the fitted values suggest growth mainly by smooth disk feeding at high rates. Such feeding spins a black hole up efficiently, the authors note.
arxiv-2505-08510:
Mario Gomez Andreu and five co-authors plan robot paths on 3D Gaussian splats in twenty twenty-five. Gaussian splatting has become a fast way to rebuild scenes in three dimensions. It stores rich spatial detail about a place. The team asks how a robot can plan a route directly on those stored Gaussians.

Their algorithm, FOCI, rests on a new way to state collisions. It uses the overlap between Gaussians as a field integral. Both the world and the robot are cast as Gaussian splats, not as crude bounding boxes. Boxes overstate how blocked a space is, while this method is orientation-aware. That lets the robot slip through very tight gaps. Tests were extensive, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-08610:
Ines Ortega-Fernandez and Marta Sestelo present a software package for the R language in a 2025 paper. Neural networks score well on many tasks but hide how they reach a call. That black-box flaw limits trust in fields like health and fault checks.

Their package, neuralGAM, fits a network per input trait, in the style of additive models. Each trait's share of the output can then be read on its own. The frame sets no fixed shape for the networks, so users keep wide choice. Tests on fake and real data show the tool in use. The package offers a path to strong scores with clear reasons.
arxiv-2505-08810:
Bappa Muktar, Vincent Fono, and Adama Nouboukpo build a learning system to spot denial-of-service attacks in car networks in a 2025 study. Cars that talk to each other form these networks, and ambulances rely on them for fast, safe routing. A flood attack can jam those safety channels at the worst moment.

The team built training data in simulators for traffic and networks, then enriched it with real driving traces from a German highway drawn from open map data. Three traffic types were simulated: attack floods, voice calls, and video streams. After cleaning and feature work, learning models were trained to sort the three. The authors pitch the setup as a sturdy, scalable shield for highway networks.
arxiv-2505-08910:
Nahid Alam, Alham Fikri Aji and their co-authors introduce Maya, an open multilingual vision-language model, in 2025. Large models of this kind do well in widely spoken languages but lag in low-resource languages and varied cultures.

The team built a multilingual image-text training set in eight languages, based on a known pretraining set. They then trained a model that supports those languages for vision-language tasks. Their aim is stronger cultural and linguistic grasp when a model works with images and text together. Code for the project is shared openly, the authors note, to support wider use and follow-up work.
arxiv-2505-09810:
Daniel Waddington and Cornel Constantinescu shrink the saved snapshots that let big model training restart after a crash. Their 2025 paper studies checkpoint data, which can reach hundreds of gigabytes per save. Data must cross a network and land on storage before the next training round starts.

The team tracks how tensor data and its squeeze factor evolve during training. They test stock compression tools plus tricks such as byte grouping and saving only the change since the last save. Their own compressor, built on byte grouping and Huffman coding, beats the best rival on squeeze. It also runs about ten times faster. A 16-core version tops three gigabytes per second on the way back out.
arxiv-2505-09910:
Takafumi Kita studies a hidden singularity in electron systems in a 2025 solo physics paper. The work is part two of a series on Bose-Einstein type singularities. Kita uses the weakly attractive Hubbard model as the test case. Mean-field theory says that model turns superconducting at low heat for any band shape.

Kita shows correlation effects change that neat picture in a deep way. A hidden singularity sits near the mean-field transition point. Below it, standard field methods break down due to divergences. A repair with a Lagrange multiplier restores the method. The fix predicts a pseudogap phase above the superconducting one. Its density of states shows a V shape near zero energy.
arxiv-2505-10510:
Bayesian inference often runs in two steps: fit a surrogate or impute missing data, then fit the model of interest. Done naively, the second step understates uncertainty, ignoring both data variability and the gaps in knowledge from step one. The four authors propose an efficient two-step method that carries that uncertainty through without fitting many separate models.

They pick a representative subset of draws or imputations and build a mixture distribution that approximates the target posterior, using Pareto smoothed importance sampling. Harder cases get refined with importance weighted moment matching and an iteration that widens the mixture. Examples include surrogate models of costly simulations and multiple imputation by chained equations. The method cuts computation while keeping posterior accuracy.
arxiv-2505-10610:
Vision-language models can now swallow hundreds of images at once, but nobody had a thorough ruler for that skill. Zhaowei Wang and eleven co-authors built one in a 2025 paper. Their benchmark, MMLongBench, holds 13,331 examples across five task families, from visual retrieval-augmented generation to many-shot learning.

Every example ships at five input lengths, from 8,000 to 128,000 tokens, so a model's grace under growing context can be measured, not assumed. The team ran 46 closed and open models through it. Three verdicts stand out: doing well on one task says little about the rest, both camps of models struggle, and the headroom for improvement is large. The authors offer the benchmark as the field's common yardstick for long-context multimodal claims.
arxiv-2505-10810:
Gabriel Maldonado and co-authors present MoCLIP, a tuned vision-language model for making human motion from text in 2025. Motion generation serves animation, robotics, and virtual reality. Standard text encoders learn from still images, so they grasp timing and body mechanics poorly.

MoCLIP adds a motion coding head and trains on motion clips with contrast methods and a tethering loss. The design keeps it compatible with current CLIP-based pipelines, so it can drop into many tools. Tests show better top-rank match scores while image quality scores stay competitive. The result is closer alignment between a text prompt and the motion a model produces.
arxiv-2505-10910:
Sagnick Mukherjee and co-authors measure the spectrum of a giant exoplanet's atmosphere and find its mornings cloudy but its evenings clear, in a 2025 paper. The planet is locked so one side always faces its star, and the boundary zones at dawn and dusk can differ sharply. Clouds and hazes blur such spectra, and their origin was debated.

Light passing through the morning edge showed a cooler, cloudy limb, while the evening edge was hotter and showed water vapor gas. The team reads this as clouds forming on the night side, drifting to the morning edge, then evaporating as they round to evening. They warn that such one-sided clouds can skew chemical readings unless limbs are measured apart.
arxiv-2505-11210:
Anders Gjølbye, Stefan Haufe, and Lars Kai Hansen tackle a flaw in explanations of AI decisions in a 2025 paper. Some inputs sway a model's output without being truly linked to the answer, and explanation tools may credit them anyway. Those false credits mislead users about what the model relies on.

Their method, PatternLocal, starts from a simple local explanation, such as those from common tools, then recasts the weights into a generative form that quiets those misleading variables. In tuned tests on a standard benchmark, it beat rival explainers and cut false credits. Faithful explanations matter where models guide medical or legal choices.
arxiv-2505-11310:
Members of the ATLAS Collaboration report a precise particle measure in a 2025 paper. They count pairs of W bosons made when protons collide in the Large Hadron Collider. Such counts test quantum chromodynamics and the electroweak theory, two core parts of physics.

The data come from collisions recorded from 2015 to 2018. The team cuts the main background from top quark pairs and improves how the rest is estimated. Their main result carries an uncertainty of just over three percent. Detailed counts across twelve traits match theory well, they report. A charge pattern also matches the Standard Model, and no sign of CP violation appears.
arxiv-2505-11410:
Bootstrap percolation spreads like an infection on a grid: a healthy site falls once enough neighbors are infected. Fengxing Zhu pins down how long that spread takes in 2025 for the high-dimensional version of the process.

Sites sit on a torus with many dimensions, and the infection threshold equals the dimension itself, a harder rule than the classic two-neighbor case. For starting densities in a set range, Zhu determines the percolation time up to a constant factor, with high probability. The result extends one of the main theorems of an earlier study of the two-dimensional torus with threshold two. Such timing results matter wherever threshold spread is modeled, from magnets to social contagion.
arxiv-2505-11510:
Rasco, Gray, and Ruland published this study in 2025. It tackles a measurement headache in nuclear physics: pulling shape numbers out of beta decay spectra. The spectrum's shape is usually fit with a plain polynomial in the electron's energy. Coefficients from such fits tangle together and shift with the polynomial's order. That makes comparing experiments, or matching theory, slippery work.

The authors propose fitting with orthogonal polynomials instead. These basis shapes stay independent of each other, so the pulled coefficients settle down. Values then hold up across fit orders, and theory-to-data matches get cleaner. Some coefficients even gain a plain physical reading. The paper also marks the statistical limits of what spectra can tell. It is a methods note aimed at precision decay experiments.
arxiv-2505-11610:
Large AI models trained on biology promise to design proteins and molecules on request, but the tools are young and scattered. Asher Moldwin and Amarda Shehu survey that field in this 2025 paper. These foundation models learn from vast sets of sequences without labels. They are then aimed at protein engineering, small molecule design, and genome sequence design.

The survey sorts current models and methods into a clear taxonomy. It weighs how the models are built for sequences, how their output can be steered, and how several data types are joined. Open problems close the paper, with concrete next steps for better generation quality. A shared map helps biologists and AI teams speak the same language.
arxiv-2505-12110:
Galaxy clusters seen as they were near the universe's youth obey the same speed-mass rule as nearby ones.
