Shrouk Abdulshafy and co-authors check that in fourteen clusters, in work from twenty twenty-five. Member lists were built with their team's own weighting tool. Masses came from a classic balance estimator.

The fitted rule links member speed spread to mass with tiny scatter. It matches what universe simulations predict. The match backs both the member tool and the mass estimator at that era. It also means speed spread alone can weigh a young cluster, a shortcut for surveys that cannot linger.
arxiv-2505-12810:
Samy Abbes and Vincent Jugé study, in a 2025 paper, the long-run behavior of concurrent systems, where many actions can occur at once in a shared state model. The catalog title is garbled, but the head gives the clean title and both authors. They model such a system as an action of a trace monoid on a finite set of states.

Starting from a spectral trait of the system, they prove that a single steady random law exists for endless paths, for any choice of weights. They also prove a strong law of large numbers for systems that cannot split into parts. That law lets them define speedup, a measure of how much true overlap the paths show on average.
arxiv-2505-13010:
Himel Ghosh, Ahmed Mosharafa, and Georg Groh build a tool that flags bias in news writing sentence by sentence. Judging bias is tricky because it is partly a matter of opinion, and expert-labeled data is scarce. The team fine-tuned a language model on an expert-labeled dataset of news sentences.

Careful statistical tests show their model beats a strong baseline that had extra training on news text. A look inside the model shows it pays attention to words that carry the slant in context, rather than firing on any charged political term. The authors pair the detector with an existing tool that names the kind of bias, forming a fuller pipeline. They note the sentence-level view and small data remain limits, and sketch next steps.
arxiv-2505-13110:
Zexin Hu, Yong Gao, and Lijing Shao study why some relations among neutron star traits hold for almost any inner makeup, in a research paper from 2025. Neutron stars squeeze more than a sun's mass into a city-sized ball. Their inner matter is poorly known, yet certain links between spin, compactness, and tidal pull barely depend on it.

The team gives a new linear analysis that splits the small deviations from these relations into two multiplied parts. One part reflects how two candidate inner-matter models differ. The other depends only on the star's background structure. The smallness of that second part explains the near-universal behavior, they argue.
arxiv-2505-13210:
Xiaocong Du, Haoyu Pei, and Haipeng Zhang build in 2025 a multi-signal frame to judge feeling in classic Chinese poems. Poems carry deep feeling, yet past tools read only the text. Poems are also recited aloud and paired with paintings, which add sound and image cues.

The frame pulls sound traits from recitals in several dialects, which may keep echoes of old speech. It also builds image traits for each line and blends them with text traits boosted by model translation. On two public data sets, the frame beat past tools on accuracy and a balanced score. Code is shared for others who study multi-signal language work.
arxiv-2505-13710:
Noam Avidan and Rotem Arnon open the study of computational entropy for quantum systems, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. In classical cryptography, such entropy measures how random data looks to an opponent with limited computing power, and it supports tools from random generators to leakage-resilient codes.

The quantum version of this idea had barely been explored. The authors define quantum computational unpredictability entropy by adapting a classical notion. It rests on min-entropy, which captures an opponent's best chance of guessing a value, but here the opponent must guess efficiently. They prove the new entropy behaves well in several basic ways. One key result is a chain rule that survives even when extra leaked information is unlimited before the guess. The work lays groundwork for quantum-safe cryptography built on entropy arguments.
arxiv-2505-13810:
Qi and co-authors give new tests for telling how deeply a multipartite quantum state is entangled. Their paper, Detecting k-Nonseparability and k-Partite Entanglement with Generalized Skew Information and Mutually Unbiased Measurements, addresses two related notions of multipartite entanglement. Both matter because entanglement shared across many parties is a core resource for quantum technology.

The tests are sufficient criteria built from two tools: a generalized form of Wigner-Yanase skew information and sets of mutually unbiased measurements. Worked examples show the criteria catching entangled states and doing so with advantages over older tests. As a further use, the authors show how the same checks can reveal the depth of a quantum network. The result is a practical toolkit for certifying entanglement structure without full state reconstruction.
arxiv-2505-14010:
Pu Wang and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a fast transformer system that clears haze from ultra-high-definition photos. Giant images make dehazing slow and memory-hungry. Their design adds two ideas: a self-scaling normalization borrowed from a recent language model line, and a memory cache that knows the physics of haze.

The cache keeps or drops features based on how haze forms in air, which favors the parts that matter. Training settled about five times faster while using less memory. The system restores fifty big frames per second on a top gaming card and matches leading quality scores. A heat-map tool shows which pixels drove each fix.
arxiv-2505-14110:
Thomas Fernique and Daria Pchelina bound how tightly two sphere sizes can pack in a 2025 paper. Packing spheres of two sizes raises shapes that equal spheres never form. Tetrahedra, four-sided blocks, appear when space is carved into local cells.

The sizes studied are one and the square root of two minus one. At those sizes, a small sphere fits exactly into each hole of a dense large-sphere stack. That stack is guessed to be the densest possible for the pair. The paper lifts the proven density ceiling slightly, by fresh geometry and hard interval arithmetic. Old two-dimensional bounds from the 1960s guided the attack.
arxiv-2505-14410:
Jinzuomu Zhong and co-authors improve how accent likeness is judged in speech synthesis, in this 2025 paper. Making a voice speak with a target accent is only half the task; scoring whether it sounds right has lagged behind. On the human side, they refine a listening test that pits samples against a reference. Listeners get transcripts, mark where accents seem to differ, and pass strict reliability screening.

Those tweaks give stronger statistics with fewer listeners and lower cost. On the machine side, they test distance measures built from vowel shapes and sound-pattern profiles. Several such measures tracked human accent scores usefully. A common pick, word error rate, proved weak for underrepresented accents. The authors offer the paired toolkit for accent work in speech technology.
arxiv-2505-14510:
High-stakes decisions in health care, finance, and security need models that people can inspect and trust. Haishi Bai, Jozo Dujmović, and Jianwu Wang present BACON, a system that trains decision models whose logic stays fully open. It builds on graded logic, where inputs earn scores between full no and full yes.

BACON keeps accuracy high while showing its whole structure, so experts can read, check, and adjust the rules by hand. The authors test it on four tasks: a classic logic puzzle, flower classification, house buying choices, and breast cancer diagnosis. In each case the model performed well and produced short, human-checkable decision rules. The team argues this approach suits settings where a wrong, unexplained answer is costly. It also supports close teamwork between experts and the model.
arxiv-2505-14810:
Tingchen Fu and co-authors test in 2025 whether models that reason longer still obey the user's orders. Following instructions is core to making language models serve their users, yet training that boosts step-by-step reasoning may erode that obedience. The team built MathIF, a test set that pairs maths tasks with explicit directives.

Across models, stronger reasoning often came with weaker rule following, above all in long answers. Models trained on distilled long thought chains or on reasoning rewards slipped most. Simple fixes won back some obedience but cost reasoning power. The authors call for training that guards both skills at once.
arxiv-2505-15410:
Bahar Radmehr, Ekaterina Shved, Fatma Betül Güreş, Adish Singla, and Tanja Käser wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents ClickSight, a pipeline that uses a large language model to read student clickstreams and name the learning strategies in play.

Click logs are rich but hard to read, and past tools lean on hand traits or expert marks. ClickSight takes the raw clicks and a list of candidate strategies, and writes a text account of what the student did. Four prompt plans are tried, and self-refinement is tested for lift. Expert grades in two open learning settings show fair reads, with quality shifting by prompt plan and little gain from refinement.
arxiv-2505-15510:
Zihui Cheng and co-authors take a unified look at how vision-language models reason step by step about images, in a 2025 paper. Such step-by-step methods, called multimodal chain-of-thought, come in two styles: some reason in text alone, and others mix images into the chain. Both styles boost scores, but why they help was unclear. The team argues that the gain comes from what they call visual thoughts.

Visual thoughts are the image facts a model carries into its reasoning, in whatever form the chain takes. The team defines four forms these thoughts can take and compares how clear and compact each one is. Clearer, tighter forms gave bigger gains in their tests. Probing inside the models, they found visual thoughts ferry image facts to deeper layers of the network. The authors hope the idea guides the design of future reasoning systems.
arxiv-2505-15710:
Tianqi Du and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on picking the safest answer from a language model by reading its inner states rather than its words. Safety checks usually grade the final text, yet the model's hidden layers carry richer signals about risk. Their framework ranks several draft answers using those hidden states.

Both the prompt and each draft are encoded from middle layers of the model. A light scorer then orders the drafts by likeness to safe patterns learned at the list level. Across several test sets, the method held up far better against trick prompts designed to jailbreak the model. The team plans to release the code on publication.
arxiv-2505-16010:
Whether cloud droplets collide and merge decides how fast rain forms. A team led by Pijush Patra and Anubhab Roy studies two uncharged water droplets in a squeezing flow, with an electric field added. Textbook theory says a thin air film between droplets should resist contact. The field-induced attraction can beat that resistance and force a touch in finite time.

Real clouds break the textbook assumptions, so the team added non-continuum effects and van der Waals forces to their model. Collision efficiency then depends on field strength, droplet shapes, and those small-scale forces. The results matter for electrified storms, where fields are strong.
arxiv-2505-16310:
Gaurav Kumar, Soham Satyadharma, and Harpreet Singh study image-to-image translation in a 2025 paper. The task turns a picture from one style or domain into another while keeping its core traits. Networks called GANs, where two models spar until the output looks real, drive much of this work. The team covers two settings: paired images, where a match is known, and unpaired ones, where it is not.

For paired work they used a conditional GAN. For unpaired work they added a cycle rule, which forces a round trip back to the start image. They varied loss rules, patch sizes, and model shapes across trials. Scores such as precision, recall, and the FID score graded the results. A look at sample images rounded out the study.
arxiv-2505-16610:
Jing Ye, Lu Xiang, Yaping Zhang, and Chengqing Zong published a 2025 paper on making AI emotional support personal. Large language models can sound caring, but their comfort is often generic. Good support depends on the person: their character, their mood, and their situation.

The authors propose a two-stage framework in which the model improves itself. First it learns basic support skills from a small set of conversations. Then it reflects on its own answers, rewrites them to fit the user better, and trains on the improved versions. Repeated rounds steadily sharpen the fit to each user’s unspoken preferences. Tests showed fewer unhelpful replies and answers that matched users more closely.
arxiv-2505-16710:
Training models on very long texts eats memory, and Wenhao Li and co-authors cut that cost by chopping the text into chunks, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their first method trains on one chunk at a time, keeping just one chunk's working data in memory. A sparse twin then sends learning signals to select chunks only.

A fix-up factor keeps the sparse signals honest, so nothing skews. In tests on one card, the chunk method stretched trainable length from one thousand to sixteen thousand tokens. The sparse twin ran up to three times faster. The pair ships as light wrappers, aimed at teams that need long-context models on modest gear.
arxiv-2505-17010:
Tim Genewein and co-authors explain prompt tuning and in-context learning through the lens of meta-learning. They view a trained model as a kind of odds based predictor. A prompt then acts like new facts that shift what the model expects next in a clear way.

That view sets clear limits on what prompts alone can do. Some tasks need weight changes instead. Small tests with two kinds of networks back the claims. They also show soft prompts, made of number lists not words, can steer even untrained nets in ways word prompts cannot.
arxiv-2505-17210:
Martin Villagrana and co-authors test whether a general-purpose image segmentation model can outline kidney stones in scope images without special training, in a 2025 paper. Drawing stone borders by hand is slow and impractical across the large image sets that urology produces. The model under test, SAM, is known for segmenting almost anything it is pointed at.

The team raced SAM against three U-Net variants, the standard tools for medical outlining, on both familiar and unseen data. On familiar data SAM matched the best U-Net closely. On new data it pulled far ahead, beating every U-Net variant by margins of up to 23 percent. The authors read this as evidence that a general model can travel between hospitals and cameras better than narrow ones, a key step toward automatic stone typing.
arxiv-2505-17310:
Blessing Airehenbuwa and co-authors survey digital twins as bodyguards for electronics. Their 2025 paper reviews how virtual replicas of physical systems can defend a supply chain plagued by piracy, tampering, counterfeits, and leaking hardware.

A twin offers traceability, full visibility, and continuous checks that a chip still behaves as itself. The survey gathers twin-based defenses across cyber-physical systems, connected devices, and cryptographic hardware, plus work on spotting counterfeit parts, intrusions, fault injection, and side-channel leaks. It also covers pairing twins with large language models for stronger monitoring. Gaps remain in scaling these defenses, the authors note, and they close with open challenges and research directions for making twins a standard layer of hardware security.
arxiv-2505-17410:
Natsuo Yamashita and three co-authors improved in 2025 the cleanup step that fixes speech recognition errors with a language model, focusing on rare words. Such fixers often mangle uncommon or technical terms because training data barely contain them. The team generated synthetic training speech errors rich in rare words to teach the fixer. They also fed it the recognizer's top guesses together with sound-based context.

The phonetic hints guard against over-correction, where a right rare word gets replaced by a common one. Tests in English and Japanese showed better rare-word repair and lower overall error rates. The authors present the method as a practical upgrade for domain speech systems, such as medical or legal dictation. It keeps the language model's fluency while respecting what was actually said.
arxiv-2505-17510:
Marcus Ma and co-authors published this language model study in 2025. Many real tasks need several labels at once, such as tagging a text with every topic it touches. How language models handle that setting is poorly understood. The team watched the models' output scores step by step as each label was produced. They found odd habits. The ranking implied by the first label often does not match the final answer.

Models tend to suppress all but one label at each step. Bigger models show sharper confidence in a single label, yet their internal ranking of labels gets better. Extra training strengthens this quirk. The authors then tackle a matching problem: aligning model scores with the spread of human judgments on subjective tasks. Their best fix is simple and free. Take each label's highest score across all steps rather than only the first, which improved both alignment and accuracy.
arxiv-2505-17710:
Rafael Corsi Ferrão, Fabio de Miranda, and Diego Pavan Soler wrote a 2025 paper on a tool that summarizes the code work of each student in class team projects. A large language model holds the pen. Real industry projects teach well: the tasks are authentic and set by outside clients. But their scope varies widely, so staff cannot give fast, detailed feedback to each student.

The tool pulls the code additions of each student from the shared repository, sorts them, and structures text runs for the model. The summaries go out each week of the sprint. The test ran two semesters, in a three-week full-time sprint with over sixty students. Staff and students both found the tool useful for grading and guidance. The summaries reported real activities for the most part, though some work was missed.
arxiv-2505-18010:
Jens De Winne and co-authors test deep learning for tissue oxygen checks in 2025. Surgeons need live reads of tissue oxygen to judge tissue health. Spectral imaging can read oxygen without touch, but true reference values are hard to get. Classic methods lean on straight line unmixing, which can break down in real tissue.

The team trained two network types on spectra made by detailed simulation. A special training scheme then bridges the gap to real clinical data. The learned models tracked oxygen levels more closely than classic methods. Live, contact free oxygen maps could help surgeons spare tissue at risk during operations.
arxiv-2505-18110:
Zinuo Li and co-authors build a model that watches and listens to video at once, in a 2025 paper on finding specific moments in footage. People naturally combine sight, sound, and speech to locate a scene. Most models fuse sound poorly, which limits their grasp of long videos and the moments users ask about.

Their model, TriSense, joins vision, audio, and speech in one large language model. A connector piece reweights each sense based on the question, so the model still works when one input is missing. To train it, the team built a data set of over two million samples using an automated pipeline. Tests show broad skill gains.
arxiv-2505-18410:
Seunghyun Lee and Yuqi Gu tackle a deep question in causal inference: when can the true causal graph be recovered from data if some of its variables are hidden? Hidden, or latent, variables are common in real data, and older guarantees demanded strict patterns, such as several pure child measures for every hidden variable. Real datasets rarely obey such rules.

The authors study a broad model where observed variables can be of mixed types and the hidden ones are binary. They propose a new pattern, called the double triangular condition, that is much weaker than the pure children rule. Under this pattern, the whole causal graph is guaranteed to be identifiable. They also prove necessary conditions that mark the hard limits of what can ever be recovered. Simulations show that hidden structures meeting their condition can be estimated from data with accuracy.
arxiv-2505-18910:
Christopher Coveney uncovers formal links between two pillars of electron theory, in a research paper from 2025. One pillar, coupled-cluster doubles theory, is a workhorse for computing how electrons correlate. The other, the electronic self-energy, frames the same physics in a different language.

Coveney derives the coupled-cluster equations by splitting the self-energy along particle, hole, and time directions. The ground-state energy formula that emerges matches the classic theory exactly. He also connects the setup to a related eigenvalue method for charged states. A tiny two-site model solved exactly confirms the links. The bridge may enrich both frameworks.
arxiv-2505-19110:
Brain scans that trace white matter bundles are rich but hard for learning models to read, and harder still for doctors to interpret. A seven-author team turns the problem sideways in 2025: each bundle's quality score becomes one pixel, and the whole scan becomes a tiny nine-by-nine picture. An autoencoder squeezes that picture into a compact code. Special training keeps the code's axes separate, so each one can mean something on its own.

Against one-dimensional baselines the picture code wins clearly, lifting a sex classification score by about 16 percent. It also separates its factors more cleanly than a full 3D version. The authors present the trick as a path to brain models doctors can actually read.
arxiv-2505-19310:
Robin Pesl, Jerin Mathew, Massimo Mecella, and Marco Aiello study how to feed software service manuals to language models that must find the right service fast. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Modern systems are stitched from many small services listed in a registry. Full manuals are too long for a model's input window.

The team tests retrieval-backed search over chopped-up manuals. They vary how the text is cut and sized, and grade how well the right endpoint is found. A new bench spans many domains to keep the test fair. A helper agent then asks only for summaries first, pulling details on demand. That two-step flow shrinks input length and lifts retrieval accuracy. Tests on both the new bench and a real-world one back the design. The work guides teams that wire services together with AI help.
arxiv-2505-19910:
Tore Gude, Marta Zagorowska, and Lars Imsland refine feedback optimization in twenty twenty-five. Online feedback optimization steers a process toward its best operating point using measurements. It needs the process's sensitivity, which is often unknown. Random perturbations are the usual way to estimate it, but they push the process off course.

Their controller generates persistently exciting inputs with minimal deviation from the descent direction. The design is a bilevel optimization program. A nonconvex rank constraint is relaxed with linear constraints and penalties. Validation uses a simulated resource allocation problem modeled on oil and gas production. Profit matched the random-perturbation controller while inputs were perturbed less. Readers in process control get gradient estimates bought with smaller disturbances to the plant.
arxiv-2505-20110:
Ruishuo Chen and co-authors train generative flow networks without a stand-in reward model. These networks learn to build objects with high scores. In many real tasks, testing each new object is too slow or costly, so training must run offline on stored examples. A learned proxy for the score often misleads the search.

Their method, TD-GFN, mines the stored paths instead. Inverse reinforcement learning pulls fine-grained rewards for each step from expert trajectories. Those rewards prune the search graph and steer sampling, but the final updates trust only real end scores. Error cannot compound that way. Tests beat prior offline methods on speed and sample quality.
arxiv-2505-20210:
Kun Huang, Irene Gamba, and Chi-Wang Shu present a 2025 solver for how particles and waves trade energy in magnetized plasma. Such trades matter for runaway electrons in fusion machines. Plasma waves can be treated as packets with particle-like traits, which yields a paired set of kinetic equations.

Two snags face solvers: uneven plasma makes the system high-sized with many time scales, and the math must keep mass, push, and energy exact. Their solver pairs a local method for the trade step with a path-averaging step for wave flow. Tests on a tube-shaped plasma show all guard laws hold.
arxiv-2505-20610:
Xiaobao Wei and co-authors present a 2025 framework for rebuilding indoor scenes in 3D from a consumer depth camera. Good indoor maps need shape, look, and a labeling of objects all at once, for uses such as robot navigation. A popular rendering method gives fine looks but weak shape, which hurts object labeling.

Their method first fuses many color and depth images into a rough model, then uses it to start and guide the main training. A small network smooths shape and cuts noise, and a spreading step uses object hints to smooth flat surfaces. Joint training of look, shape, and labels gave top results on several data sets for all three tasks.
arxiv-2505-20710:
Kui Wu and six co-authors build a robot tracker that takes orders in plain language in a 2025 paper. The task is user-centric tracking: a person tells a mobile agent whom or what to follow, and the agent must turn vague words into wheel-level moves. Big language models read orders well but answer slowly, while action-tuned models are fast yet brittle on new wording.

Their agent splits the job into layers. A language model first turns each order into a spatial goal marked on the scene. A lower layer then steers toward that goal mark by mark. Spatial goals form the bridge between understanding and action, letting each layer do what it does best. Tests check the stack on varied phrasings and moving targets.
arxiv-2505-20810:
The back of the eye is a window the body leaves open: its tiny vessels mirror damage from diabetes, high blood pressure, and brain disease. Tariq Khan, Toufique Ahmed Soomro, and Imran Razzak review in 2025 how imaging that window, read by artificial intelligence, could catch deadly diseases early.

New scanners resolve the retina down to five micrometers, exposing microvascular flaws and early nerve change. Learning models score above ninety percent sensitivity for diabetic eye disease and predict heart risk from fundus photos with solid accuracy. Phones and telemedicine stretch the reach to community screening. The authors close with the blockers: varied imaging protocols, thin external validation, and awkward fits with clinic workflows.
arxiv-2505-21010:
Hospitals that train models together without sharing patient data still face two gaps: few labeled records, and new sites that differ. Sabbir Ahmed and co-authors present a protocol for both gaps in this 2025 paper. In their setup, only the central server holds a small labeled set. Each client site trains on unlabeled data alone.

Standard versions of this setup assume test data match training data. Real clinics break that assumption as populations and devices shift. The team's Unified Alignment Protocol aims to keep accuracy on unseen domains. Privacy stays intact because raw records never leave a site. Methods that survive domain shift decide whether federated learning leaves the lab.
arxiv-2505-21110:
Machida, Hirano, and Basu simulate the birth of the first stars in a 2025 paper. These Population III stars formed from clean early gas. The team varied magnetic field strength across a huge range, from near zero to strong, and ran each case for over a thousand years after the first seed star lit.

Without magnetism, the disk broke into many seed stars, and the largest grew huge. With even a weak field, spin wound the field stronger, seeds merged into one star, and breaking stopped. Stronger fields built thick disks held up by magnetic pressure, with spiral arms. Outflows came only in a narrow band of strengths. The authors expect the first stars to be single, wrapped in thick spiral disks.
arxiv-2505-21310: Aihua Fan and Shilei Fan prove two results in a short 2025 math paper on exponential Riesz bases. Their setting is a class of locally compact Abelian groups built on a non-Archimedean base, so the usual rules of size and distance change. The first result says such a basis exists for any finite union of balls. The second says that, for some bounded sets, no such basis exists at all.
arxiv-2505-21410:
Boss-and-worker learning splits long tasks well, yet the boss's fixed reach blurs fine control. Shashank Sharma, Janina Hoffmann, and Vinay Namboodiri give the boss several reaches at once, in work from twenty twenty-five. Near goals steer tight but wobble with noise; far goals roll smooth but miss fine marks.

Each reach gets its own goal-guessing part. A meta-boss picks which reach to use at each state. Scores beat fixed-reach rivals across robot and maze tests, and the gap to flat learning shrank hard. The lesson: goal distance is a choice to make moment by moment, not a knob set once.
arxiv-2505-21610:
Luca Tortorelli and co-authors build a universe in a computer to learn how galaxy surveys skew what we see. Their model grows galaxies from physical recipes, paints them into fake survey images, and measures them with the same tools used on real data. Tested on a deep sky field, the fake sky matched the real one closely.

Magnitudes, colors, and redshift tallies lined up within small margins. Galaxy sizes ran slightly large, and one color showed mild tension. Links between mass, size, and star birth also looked right. The authors plan to fit the model to data directly, sharpening redshift estimates for next generation surveys.
arxiv-2505-21710:
Baran Barbarestani, Isa Maks, and Piek Vossen test how well ChatGPT spots targeting and inappropriate language in online comments, in a 2025 study. Moderating huge volumes of user content is a growing challenge for social platforms. The team compare the model against crowd labels and expert judgments.

They find the model does well at flagging inappropriate content. Almost all gains from refining the prompt came from one change: a simpler label scheme paired with a newer model version. Later tweaks to prompt shape or sampling settings added little. Work on targeting language was weaker and less steady. The study gives a clear view of where prompt design helps and where it does not.
arxiv-2505-21910:
Xianbiao Qi and co-authors explain why large Transformer models crash in training in a 2025 paper. Scaling these models with no warm up tricks is hard and draws wide interest. Warm up means a slow rise of the learning rate at the start.

The team trace crashes to energy piling into a few paths in key weight sets. That pile up squashes the spread of scores the model makes, a fault they call entropy collapse. Their fix caps the learning rate when a step grows too sharp next to the last weights. Smooth steps keep energy spread out and the run stays stable, with no warm up needed.
arxiv-2505-22010:
Nasir Hussain and a team of co-authors use large language models to hunt security flaws in stripped program binaries. Their framework appeared in twenty twenty-five. Stripped files lack names and symbols, so human analysts struggle to read them, and automated flaw finding lags.

Their system, VulBinLLM, first improves decompiled code by adding flaw-focused comments without changing how the code runs. Those notes make weak spots stand out. A reasoning stage then works through the code with guided prompts and a memory agent that holds long context. The combination reached state-of-the-art results on binary flaw benchmarks. The authors argue language models can mirror the classic analyst workflow at machine scale.
arxiv-2505-22210:
Nan Liu and Ran Wang study a math model for very short light pulses in fiber in a 2025 paper. The model, called the coupled complex short pulse system, can support steady wave forms known as solitons. The authors ask what a pulse looks like after a long time, starting from data that fades away at the edges.

Using a steepest descent method adapted to this problem, they derive close formulas for two regions of space and time. In one region the pulse fades at a set rate. In the other, the solution looks like a mix of solitons and breathers plus a weaker term from their contact with spreading waves. The results add to the theory of how such pulses settle over time.
arxiv-2505-22410:
Cornelius Brand, Radu Curticapean, Baitian Li, and Kevin Pratt revisited fast convolution algorithms in two thousand twenty-five. A convolution combines two vectors by a rule over a finite domain. Product domains, where each entry is a tuple, appear often in parameterized and exponential-time algorithms.

Viewing the problem through multilinear algebra streamlines older algorithms and their analysis. Using known results from fast matrix multiplication, they derive faster methods that improve the best previous time bounds. They also show that a famous open conjecture on matrix rank would imply near-linear time for these convolutions. The paper is written as a self-contained guide for an algorithms audience, with all needed algebra included.
arxiv-2505-22510:
Thin sheets of ruthenium compounds may turn heat into power with rare strength, and Parbati Senapati, Ajay Kumar, and Prakash Parida chart that promise in work from twenty twenty-five. Their study is pure computing, built on first-principles math plus classic flow rules. Two sheets are tested, one with sulfur and one with selenium.

Both sheets proved stable in the checks. Heat-to-voltage scores ran very high for both charge types, far above most known sheets. Power scores and yield marks were fair, and the best yield came at high heat along one sheet edge. Hole-type doping won in both sheets. The team pitches the pair as picks for high-heat waste-power tools, pending lab proof.
arxiv-2505-22710:
Pouya Asadi and three co-authors propose one mechanism that creates both ordinary matter's excess and dark matter's abundance, in a 2025 paper. The universe holds more matter than antimatter, and about five times more dark matter than ordinary matter. Explaining both numbers together is a standing puzzle.

Their bridge is a family of heavy neutrinos linking the visible world to a dark sector. After the hot early universe reheated to temperatures far below the neutrinos' mass, particle scatterings slowly froze dark matter in. The same scatterings generated the baryon asymmetry, partly by transferring charge from the dark side, a process they call dark wash-in. Dark matter then annihilated within its own sector, thinning the symmetric part while sparing the net charge. With heavy neutrino masses above ten billion giga-electron-volts, the scheme can match both observed abundances.
arxiv-2505-22810:
Zhoufaran Yang and co-authors build a benchmark for reading the words inside videos in a 2025 paper. Street signs, captions, labels, and screens carry meaning that pure vision misses, yet video benchmarks largely ignore text, and text-recognition benchmarks freeze it in still images. VidText closes that gap with tasks built for moving words.

The suite spans real-world scenarios and several languages. Its tasks stack in three tiers: whole-video questions, clip-level probes, and instance-level hunts for one piece of text. Paired perception-and-reasoning tasks separate seeing the words from thinking with them. Eighteen leading multimodal models sat the exam and struggled across most of it. Resolution and raw text-recognition skill mattered from inside the model; giving extra context or chain-of-thought prompting shifted scores from outside. The authors offer the benchmark as the field's missing report card for video literacy.
arxiv-2505-22910:
Chahat Raj and five co-authors probe how language models assign credit and blame for outcomes, in a 2025 paper. People explain events by inner traits or outer luck. Those habits shape stereotypes and decisions. Models may absorb biased versions of the same habits. Most bias tests stop at surface word links. This team built a deeper, cognition-based test instead.

Their framework varies outcomes and demographic cues together. It then reads how the model's stated reasons shift. Reasoning gaps between groups expose hidden bias channels. A failed exam, for instance, may draw effort blame for one group and test blame for another. Fairness stakes are direct: such patterns color hiring and grading tools. The paper offers the framework as a diagnostic. Deeper bias measures should guide fixes better than word lists.
arxiv-2505-23110:
Sugama studies Landau damping in plasmas through a quantum like equation in twenty twenty-five. Landau damping describes how plasma waves fade without collisions. The author transforms the linearized Vlasov-Poisson system into a Schrodinger equation. That form lets him apply tools from quantum mechanics to the plasma problem.

He shows a fluctuation theorem holds for a relative stochastic entropy in this process. That entropy is defined from the probability density of the particle velocity distribution. A time independent invariant emerges from energy and entropy perturbations. It takes a quadratic form and matches the squared amplitude of the Schrodinger state vector. Exact solutions built from Hamiltonian eigenvectors support the claim. Numeric checks validate the theorem for the damping process.
arxiv-2505-23710:
Zeinab Nezami, Syed Danial Ali Shah, Maryam Hafeez, Karim Djemame, and Syed Ali Raza Zaidi see sixth-generation networks as self-evolving systems, not static pipes. In their account, AI-driven intelligence lets the network adapt past mere connectivity. The paper probes what enables autonomous communication systems. The list includes reconfigurable infrastructure, adaptive middleware, and intelligent network functions. It also includes multi-agent work as a team for distributed choices.

The team looks at how these methods align with new industrial Internet of Things frames, for digital manufacturing. Their results stress gains in real-time choices, in efficiency, and in lower latency in networked control systems. The talk also treats ethical tests, research paths, and standards work. It ends with a technology stack roadmap to guide future growth.
arxiv-2505-23910:
David Zarate-Herrada and co-authors read the shape of quantum states from how quickly they forget themselves. Whether a state spreads or stays put is measured by fractal dimensions, usually extracted by scaling tiny systems. Their result shows the correlation fractal dimension equals the exponent in the power-law decay of the survival probability, the overlap between a state and its later self.

Timing that decay directly skips scaling entirely and reaches bigger systems than exact methods allow. The approach checks out on random matrix ensembles, including the Rosenzweig-Porter and power-law banded models, and on two interacting systems: the Aubry-André model and a disordered spin chain. For full random matrices the authors derive the whole time course analytically.
arxiv-2505-24110:
Dhayalkar builds choice machines as unrolled feed nets with shared weights in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such machines read strings and branch on chance picks as they go. Past net takes used loop forms or dug the machine out post-drill.

Inside, states ride as bit strings and moves as sparse grid shifts in his build. Blank moves fold in as shared snap steps stacked by depth in the net. Proof shows each tongue such a machine takes fits one such net. Weight count stays fixed no count how long the string runs. Drill tests then teach fresh nets the same acts with near-full match.
arxiv-2505-24210:
Zheng Tan, Weizhen Wang, Andrea Bertozzi, and Ernest Ryu speed up image and video generation models in a 2025 paper. Diffusion and flow models make strong media, but sampling from them takes many model calls, which makes use costly. Fast sampling methods exist, yet many fail on two fronts: stiff equations and reliance on one model family's structure.

Their method, called STORK, builds on a stabilized Taylor method with an orthogonal Runge-Kutta scheme. It handles stiffness while staying independent of the semi-linear structure that limits rival methods. Across image and video tests, it consistently improved sampling quality at a given budget of calls. The authors share their code in public. Faster sampling could cut the cost of generative media tools.
arxiv-2505-24810: A large collaboration of physicists surveys the hunt for new physics at a proposed collider in this 2025 paper. The machine, the Circular Electron-Positron Collider, is planned as a Higgs factory in China. Its clean collisions would open fresh chances to spot effects beyond the Standard Model of particle physics. The paper lays out the general case for those searches.
arxiv-2506-00110:
Ya-Hui Zhang, writing alone, builds a theory of new states of matter in a twisted crystal material. The paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Recent tests on this material found superconductivity next to a strange insulating state. In that state, electrons split their charge in an odd, fractional way. A key open question is what kind of metal sits next to these states.

Zhang adds a small number of extra charges to the insulator and works out what phases should appear. The answer may be a metal made of charge carriers with no electron-like character. Other options include a striped charge pattern and a chiral superconductor, which breaks mirror symmetry. The theory links this problem to a known spin model by a duality map.
arxiv-2506-00210:
Ziji Zhang and co-authors present a method to sort customer requests at very large scale in work from 2025. Service centers must route each request to the right agent fast. As product lines grow, the list of request types grows and shifts by sector.

Their system pairs sorting with live search over stored knowledge. Fresh facts flow in at run time, so the sorter stays current without frequent retraining. Tests on real service data beat standard fine-tuned models and plain prompt methods. Gains held both inside the home sector and in new sectors. The approach suits firms whose request types change faster than models can be rebuilt.
arxiv-2506-00410:
Ziwen Wang introduces JojoSCL in 2025, a self-taught learning method that groups single cells by their gene activity. Cell-by-cell gene data are wide and sparse, which makes clean grouping hard. The method refines group centers with a shrinkage step drawn from layered Bayes work and tuned by a risk estimate.

Both single-cell and group-level contrast steps use the refined centers, so cells sit closer to their true group. Tests on ten data sets show the method beats common rivals. Added checks on stability and on parts removed one at a time back its use in real studies.
arxiv-2506-00510:
Sujit Jana and Vikash Kumar Ojha map where a quark is likely to sit inside its target, and how that picture looks in three dimensions, in a 2025 paper. They use a tool called a Wigner distribution, which blends place and motion into one map. Their frame does not depend on how the viewer moves, and they work within a model where the quark wears a cloud of other particles.

Their maps show the quark is most likely found near the center of the target. The chance falls off step by step as one moves away, along the beam line and across it alike. The pattern is even on both sides of the center. The authors note the shape looks much like the maps of electrons around an atom's core, with favored zones rather than an even spread.
arxiv-2506-00710:
Valter Hudovernik and co-authors generate fake relational databases with diffusion models in a 2025 computing paper. Real databases link many tables through foreign keys, and that web is the hard part to fake well. Earlier generators flattened the web into single tables or assumed it away. Their model, RelDiff, treats the key graph as a first-class citizen: one diffusion process fills in values across all tables at once, guided by the graph.

A block-model generator separately creates realistic link structure, so made-up rows still point at rows that exist. Tests on eleven benchmarks checked fidelity against real data. Convincing synthetic databases let companies share data's shape without sharing the data.
arxiv-2506-01010:
Hausmann and co-authors test whether a compact frame type speeds up checking of game-based logic formulas. The alternating-time mu-calculus describes what groups of agents can force over time. Its standard meaning rests on concurrent game frames. Effectivity frames carry the same facts in tighter form, at least in many cases. The team built the translation between the two frame types. They then ran a generic checker on both forms.

Benchmarks included set series plus random systems and formulas. The team also compared speed with a leading ATL checker. Gains would matter for verifying multi-agent systems. The study checks whether a theory-level edge shows up in practice.
arxiv-2506-01110:
AlMasri builds a new family of exactly solvable spin models in a 2025 physics paper. The models start from the Richardson-Gaudin family, used for paired particles and small magnetic systems, and bend them with complex-valued fields. The bend keeps a combined symmetry of mirror flip and time reversal, known as PT symmetry, instead of the usual rule that energies be plain real numbers.

Even with the bend, the models stay exactly solvable, and their conserved quantities still fit together in a generalized way. The author builds the matching standard model through a change of variables and finds the rule that sets the true inner product. Computer checks on small systems show the expected pattern: energies are either real or come in mirror pairs, with low states keeping the symmetry longest. Exact formulas for spin motion follow.
arxiv-2506-01210:
Sambrama, Venkata Srirama Rohit Kantheti, Liang Chu, Erik Blasch, and Shih-Chun Lin build a testbed for satellite networks that heal themselves under jamming. Swarms of low-orbit satellites promise fast global coverage, but flying closest to Earth also leaves them exposed to interference and attack.

Their design lets satellites pool their signals across links between them, choosing among three combining methods as conditions change. To prove it works off paper, they built a radio hardware rig that mimics the space network in the loop, and they also ran field trials on an outdoor wireless testbed. The combined signals stayed strong under interference that broke plain links. The authors argue such self-healing designs suit critical communications.
arxiv-2506-01610:
Siarhei Finski proved a structural result in 2025 connecting two areas of complex geometry and operator theory. Toeplitz operators are a central tool for quantizing complex manifolds, turning functions into operators on spaces of holomorphic sections. Finski works on a compact complex manifold carrying a big line bundle, equipped with a Bernstein-Markov measure, a condition controlling how badly polynomials can spike. His theorem: these Toeplitz operators form an algebra, meaning composing two of them stays within the same class.

As an application, he derives a Szegő-type result describing how the operators' spectra distribute in the limit. A key ingredient is the fine asymptotic behavior of the Bergman kernel far from the diagonal, also known as the Christoffel-Darboux kernel. Algebra closure is the kind of foundational fact that later work builds on quietly. It tells geometers their quantization toolkit is internally consistent.
arxiv-2506-01910:
Krishna Acharya, Aleksandr Petrov, and Juba Ziani present a recommendation system that writes its own search queries. Their system, called GLoSS, appeared in twenty twenty-five. It aims to guess what a shopper will want next from the order of past picks.

Earlier systems matched words exactly when searching for items. GLoSS instead searches by meaning, so it can find items that share no words with the query. A small, fine-tuned language model writes the queries, which keeps the cost low on modest hardware. On three Amazon review data sets, the system beat both classic methods and rival language model systems. It did especially well for new users with little history on two of the sets.
arxiv-2506-02110:
Ritam Basu, Pratyusha Chowdhury, and colleagues connect a quantum complexity measure with random matrices and gravity in a 2025 physics study. A discrete Wigner function paints a quantum state as a real distribution over a grid phase space, and its negative patches signal states that are hard to simulate classically. The total negativity is an operational measure of that hardness.

The authors study how negativity behaves for states drawn from random matrix ensembles, the same structures that appear in models of quantum gravity and black holes. Links between simulation cost and gravitational models feed the broader effort to price quantum advantage.
arxiv-2506-02210:
Pu (Luke) Yi and three co-authors trim neural network computation on the fly, deciding per input which parts of the network can be skipped, in this 2025 paper. Networks keep growing, and their running cost grows with them. Their method, ExPrune, needs no change to the model's shape or training.

The trick rests on a statistical property called exchangeability, which links certain weights and intermediate values. Where parts are exchangeable, the network can be partly evaluated, the partial results inspected, and the rest pruned before it runs. Across vision, graph, and language models, the method cut arithmetic by roughly eleven to twenty-seven percent at small accuracy cost. It also stacks on top of ordinary static pruning for further savings. Theory, the authors stress, is what lets one method span such different domains.
arxiv-2506-02310:
Shyam Balaji, Damon Cleaver, Pedro De la Torre Luque and Miltiadis Michailidis use X-ray sky data to limit two kinds of dark matter in 2025. Light particles that annihilate or decay into electrons and positrons, and tiny primordial black holes that evaporate by Hawking radiation, would both add a diffuse X-ray glow.

Working from the first eROSITA data release, they set new bounds on annihilation rates and decay lifetimes for particles between 1 MeV and 1 GeV. Below about 30 MeV these bounds beat older X-ray limits. They also bound the share of dark matter in asteroid-mass black holes. Notably, they show earlier XMM-Newton limits were about ten thousand times too strict because of a solid angle error.
arxiv-2506-02810:
Ziyad Oulhaj, Mathieu Carrière, and Bertrand Michel tackle a measurement problem in topological data analysis. Mapper graphs, a popular tool for picturing the shape of data, approximate an ideal object called the Reeb graph. Yet no existing yardstick for comparing the two could use the fact that data points arrive with probabilities attached.

The team treats both graphs as spaces carrying a measure, which lets them apply Gromov-Wasserstein distances, a flexible way to compare shapes with mass. In that setting they derive how fast the Mapper graph closes in on the Reeb graph as data grows. Computer experiments show the new yardstick behaving well. The work gives the approximation a firmer statistical footing.
arxiv-2506-03010:
Hao Wu and co-authors show in 2025 a sensing trick for measuring an electric field over a wide band. It beats the standard quantum limit, even when the sensor's quantum state decays fast. Quantum tricks can sharpen measures past that limit, but the gain usually dies once the measure runs longer than the state's lifetime. Most top precision work thus falls back on classical states.

Their method drives a quantum oscillator at a subharmonic rhythm, joined with a laser based excitation method shown earlier. That pairing lets the field's frequency be read with non classical gain over long runs. The paper reports the demonstration and its precision. Wide band sensing past the classic limit could serve fields from navigation to the hunt for faint signals in physics.
arxiv-2506-03610:
Dongmin Park and co-authors present a game arena for training and testing language model agents in this 2025 paper. Game characters run by language models are a growing industry aim, but past benchmarks cover few genres and skip the inner modules that gameplay needs. Their benchmark, Orak, spans twelve popular games across the major genres.

A plug-and-play link built on a standard protocol lets researchers swap agent parts and rerun studies cleanly. The team also releases expert play records for fine-tuning general models into game agents. Built-in leaderboards, model-versus-model arenas, and part-removal studies round out the kit. The authors frame Orak as a foundation for versatile gaming agents.
arxiv-2506-03810:
Chang-Hao Fang and seven co-authors simulate how recoiling atoms in silicon share their energy in a 2025 paper. Dark matter detectors listen for tiny kicks when particles strike atomic nuclei, but only part of each kick becomes measurable charge. That fraction, the quenching factor, is hard to pin down at the lowest energies, right down to a single electron hole pair.

Their atom by atom simulations matched experiments remarkably well across a wide energy range. Below a few thousand electron volts, the crystal's binding and structure explain where older theory goes wrong. Very low energy behavior even depends on which way the crystal faces. The results sharpen how light a dark matter particle such detectors can rule out.
arxiv-2506-03910:
Shyam Prabhu and co-authors compare a classic experiment design method with machine learning for tuning a welding-based printing process. Their 2025 paper addresses materials design, where many variables make testing every combination impossible. The classic Taguchi method samples the space with a fixed grid but cannot bend with nonlinear effects.

The rival approach learns a statistical surface model and actively picks the most informative next runs. Both methods suggested settings for an arc welding printer, judged on how well they predicted bead depth, width, and height. On the held-out test cases, the learning model won on both accuracy and efficiency. The authors argue the lesson extends across materials processing, where each experiment costs time and stock.
arxiv-2506-04110:
Dinis Vitorino and Ingrid Vukusic sharpen bounds tied to a number theory conjecture in a 2025 paper. The two-adic Littlewood conjecture says no irrational number can keep bounded continued fraction digits under all doublings. A past result showed any counterexample must allow a bound of at least eight. The authors raise that floor.

Their proof pushes the needed bound to fifteen for the main form of the conjecture. For a variant based on limit behavior, they prove a floor of five. A classic algorithm for doubling continued fractions carries the argument. Families of quadratic irrationals with long matching chains also appear along the way.
arxiv-2506-04310:
Martje Slob and a large team measure stellar motion in 15 quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon, in work from 2025. The galaxies are massive and were observed with the JWST-SUSPENSE program, using deep absorption line spectra. Forward modelling accounts for optics, galaxy shape, slit position and data reduction effects, making this the largest such sample at that era so far.

Ten galaxies were aligned well enough to measure rotation, and all ten counted as fast rotators. The authors read this as proof that stopping star formation did not destroy rotating discs. Combined samples suggest younger quiescent galaxies rotate more. Dynamical masses far exceed stellar masses, and the results support growth into today's massive elliptical galaxies through mergers.
arxiv-2506-04410:
Computer tools can dream up thousands of claims about new materials, but testing each one costs time and money. Peter Jansen, Samiah Hassan, and Ruoyao Wang build a test set for judging which claims are feasible, in a 2025 paper. Their set, Matter-of-Fact, holds 8.4 thousand claims drawn from published papers.

Claims cover four hot fields, from batteries to superconductors, and mix lab, theory, and code results. The task is framed as a check of each claim against older work only, like a back-test. Strong systems that search the papers and write code still scored under 72 percent, while experts call nearly all claims solvable. The gap marks a clear target for better discovery tools.
arxiv-2506-04710:
Lucas Åkerstedt, Harald Hultin, and B L G Jonsson speed up antenna array computations in a 2025 paper. Large antenna arrays are often built from repeating cells, and the standard simulation method produces a huge impedance matrix. That repetition gives the matrix a layered Toeplitz pattern, named for its constant diagonals, which fast solvers can exploit.

The catch is elements that are electrically joined, breaking the simple symmetry. The authors assemble any such array from nine connectable building blocks and still recover the fast structure, including the irregular edges. Their solver then finds the currents with far less memory and time, easing the design of big radar and communications arrays.
arxiv-2506-05010:
Zhenran Xu and nine co-authors build ComfyUI-Copilot, a language-model plugin that helps users assemble workflows in the ComfyUI art platform. ComfyUI is flexible but hard on newcomers, with thin documentation, easy misconfigurations, and complex graph design. The copilot aims to lower that barrier.

A central assistant agent delegates to specialized worker agents, backed by curated knowledge bases about nodes and models. The system recommends components, constructs workflows in one click, and helps debug and deploy them. Offline evaluations and online user feedback showed accurate recommendations and faster workflow building. Case studies found benefits for beginners and experienced users alike. The package and a demo video are publicly available.
arxiv-2506-05210:
Jan Ackermann, Kiyohiro Nakayama, Guandao Yang, Tong Wu, and Gordon Wetzstein test whether a web-trained multimodal model can design clothes. General vision-language models reason well about everyday images and text. Fashion, with its cuts, fabrics, and fit logic, is a sterner test of transfer.

Their model, VLG, builds garments from written prompts and pictures. The team probes zero-shot use: no fashion training, just the model's web knowledge aimed at unseen styles and requests. Early results show the knowledge carries over better than expected. The authors argue specialist domains like garment design may ride on general models sooner than assumed, and they sketch where the approach strains.
arxiv-2506-06110:
Sylvain Courte and Noah Porcelli constrain Whitehead torsion for families of Lagrangian submanifolds in two thousand twenty-five. The work is driven by the strong nearby Lagrangian conjecture. Their families are closed and exact, set in a cotangent bundle. Torsion is an algebraic gauge of how a family twists.

They prove the torsion factors through simpler maps. It thus vanishes on the two lowest homotopy groups. Its image is also divisible by the Euler characteristic. A case on a high dimensional torus shows what this means for monodromy. Twisted generating functions are the main tool, past the reach of past work.
arxiv-2506-06210:
Pavel Komarov wrote a document in two thousand twenty-five that sets out the math behind a Python package for spectral derivatives. Taking derivatives in the Fourier frequency domain is strikingly easy, a happy accident of mathematics. Using that fact on a computer, without creating artifacts, takes extra care and knowledge.

Komarov builds the needed background from the ground up. He touches on core signal processing and calculus ideas as they become necessary, then develops the spectral method step by step. The document serves as the theory guide for the package of the same name. Readers get both the formulas and the cautions that make them work in practice. It is a reference text, not a research report.
arxiv-2506-06310:
Xiaoyu Sun, Yang Yang, and Xunde Dong work on heart signal analysis in a 2025 paper about electrocardiogram, or ECG, models. Labeled ECG data are scarce, so models often learn first from unlabeled traces. One strong idea treats recordings from the same patient as a matched set, since they share traits, but a small training batch holds too few such pairs.

Their answer is a patient memory queue, a large store that keeps past patient traces available during training. They also add two new ways to vary the data, giving the model more views of matched and unmatched pairs. Tests on three public data sets, at three data levels, beat earlier methods and held up better when labeled data were scarce.
arxiv-2506-06510:
Fatibene and Orizzonte work through boundary equations for a model used in loop quantum gravity. Their lecture notes appeared in two thousand twenty-five. This is the third set in their series on the subject. The model is the Ashtekar-Barbero-Immirzi formulation of gravity. A canonical analysis is needed to extract its constraint equations. Those constraints shape any attempt at quantization.

Working in the covariant framework, they use algebraic constraints to fix key fields. The connection and its conjugate momentum then stand as an independent pair. Two parameters, tied to Immirzi and Holst terms, are left unrelated. Still, the constraints depend on only one of them. They match the standard loop quantum gravity result. A quantization scheme is stated for the next notes.
arxiv-2506-06610:
Dongzhe Zheng, writing alone in 2025, builds a chain complex out of differential forms and shows that a mirror-style flip leaves its key numbers untouched. The head title names the work as mirror duality in a Spencer-type complex, while the catalog title differs, though the text is one study. The complex takes values in powers of an adjoint bundle and is governed by a differential set by a section and a real parameter.

Flipping the sign of either input, or stretching the parameter, changes the differential only by a simple conjugation, the algebraic shadow of doing nothing. It follows that harmonic counts survive the mirror flip, and an index formula in the style of Grothendieck, Riemann, and Roch ignores the parameters entirely. Checks on K3 surfaces and elliptic curves pass. The author frames the trick as the hidden reason such deformations are so robust.
arxiv-2506-06810:
Yuan Yin, Sarah L Waters, and Ruth E Baker model how groups of cells invade the matrix that holds tissue. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. How cells and this matrix shape each other matters for tissue building, cancer care, and healing. Two forces get their focus: cues from fibre lay that guide cells, and the cells' own rework of the fibres.

Their model is a two-way hybrid that can be run on a computer with ease. Cells are lone agents, while collagen fibres form a smooth field. The model folds in random motion, fibre guidance, cell sticking, space limits, and fibre making and breaking. A wide sweep of values shows how a cell's traits change the shape of the joint invasion.
arxiv-2506-06910:
Mahnaz Koupaee and co-authors help language models draw the causal wiring between events before they reason, in a 2025 paper. Models still fumble questions like what enabled what, which undermines forecasting and timeline tasks. The authors have the model first build a causal graph, a web of events linked by relations like 'enables'. To draw it well, they stage a panel of simulated experts.

Each expert champions one kind of semantic relation and argues over several rounds. A final expert consolidates the debate into one graph. Feeding such graphs into downstream tasks improved performance across the board. A new prediction task demands explanations as causal chains, and the graph-based explanations came out more informative and coherent than plain generations.
arxiv-2506-07410:
Dongzhe Zheng, writing alone, builds a new theory in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. It grows out of Spencer theory, a tool for studying systems with constraints. Zheng asks when the Spencer operator shrinks down to the standard one used in calculus on shapes.

The answer is a test on symmetric tensors that depends on a chosen number. When the test passes, the two theories line up in an exact way. Zheng proves the test still passes after mirror moves, which hints at a deep hidden symmetry. He then maps the special cases into a classic counting scheme for shapes. On K3 surfaces, the method picks out special classes of curves and cycles.
arxiv-2506-07510:
Solee Im and co-authors (2025) present DeRAGEC, a method that fixes names misheard by speech recognition systems. Names are where transcription errors hurt most. One fix is to match a garbled name against a list of candidates drawn from a database. The trouble is that the list is noisy, full of names that sound right but are wrong. DeRAGEC extends an earlier retrieval-based method by writing explanations, called rationales, that argue for or against each candidate before any correction is made.

The filtering weighs how alike two names sound, and it uses enriched definitions of each candidate. It runs through in-context learning, so no extra training is needed. On the CommonVoice and STOP datasets, the method improves the word error rate and the share of names recovered correctly, beating plain recognition and the earlier method. Word errors fall by 28 percent relative to unprocessed output. The code is available.
arxiv-2506-07810:
Emiliano Tolotti, Enrico Blanzieri, and Davide Pastorello propose a weighted quantum ensemble of classifiers in this 2025 paper. Ensembles combine many models to predict better than any one of them. Diversity is the key: members must err in different ways. Homogeneous ensembles use copies of one model type trained on varied data subsets. Weighted versions give stronger members more say. The authors move this recipe onto quantum hardware. Indexing registers encode the data, letting one circuit hold many internal classifiers in superposition.

Controlled operations subsample features and training points, which creates the needed diversity. Training runs the circuit, then tunes the member weights with classical optimization. At test time, the learned weights sit inside the circuit itself. Tests showed the method works as intended. They offer the design as a step toward practical quantum machine learning that borrows proven classical tricks.
arxiv-2506-07910:
Effects of a time-varying exposure on repeated events, when death can end follow-up, are estimated by Daniel Mork and co-authors in a 2025 paper. The catalog record lists Mork alone, while the head byline lists five authors. Assessing such causal effects is hard, since a terminating event may be correlated with the event process and can bias standard estimators if it is ignored.

Existing estimators based on marginal structural models and proportional rate models cannot estimate delayed marginal effects well, and they do not account for competing risks. The team proposes semiparametric structural nested rate models and two estimators for short-term and delayed effects. Asymptotic linearity is established with modern empirical process and efficiency theory.
arxiv-2506-08010:
Nick Jiang and co-authors fixed vision transformer glitches without retraining in two thousand twenty-five. Some image tokens swell to huge norms in these models. The outliers muddy attention maps and hurt features. A known cure retrains models with register tokens. That cure costs a full training run. The team traced the glitch to sparse neurons.

Few neurons concentrate the runaway activations. Shifting their output into one extra token mimics registers. No weights change and no retraining happens. Attention and feature maps came out cleaner. Downstream scores improved over base models. Tests covered popular vision backbones. The fix applies to models already deployed.
arxiv-2506-08110:
Picking a varied shortlist from a huge pool is a classic computing problem, and fairness adds a twist: each group in the pool must get its share of seats. Florian Adriaens and Nikolaj Tatti study the version where only a few picks per group are wanted. Their method works in stages, first pruning points that sit too close to same-group neighbors, then sorting points into clusters at random, and finally choosing one fitting pick from each cluster.

The random method beats the best known guarantee for how close the result comes to the ideal spread. Tests on large real datasets back up the math. The work suits tasks like fair shortlists, sample panels, and search results that must span groups without losing variety.
arxiv-2506-08210:
Andrew Wang and co-authors study whether modern decoder-only language models make better text encoders for image generation, in a 2025 paper. Many image models still use older encoders. The team build a standard training and testing pipeline to isolate the effect of the text input.

They train twenty-seven image models with twelve different encoders, varying how embeddings are pulled, which model is used, and its size. The common habit of taking last-layer embeddings gave weaker results. Averaging normalized embeddings across all layers did much better. The study gives builders clear guidance on how to draw text features from language models for image work.
arxiv-2506-08310:
Debesh Bhattacharjee, Eduard Kontar, and Yingjie Luo present a solar physics paper from 2025 on electrons in solar flares. Flares hurl electrons to high energies, and X-rays from their braking glow reveal them. A warm-target model can pin down the low-energy cut-off of those electrons, which the common cold model cannot.

The team used X-ray data from two spacecraft to track flares over time. Around each X-ray burst, the cut-off energy traced a high-low-high path. The rate of injected electrons traced the reverse path, low-high-low. Total power followed the injection rate more than the cut-off. Extra heat from the settling electrons peaked near the X-ray peak. The results sharpen how flare energy budgets are drawn.
arxiv-2506-08410:
Ziyang Ma, Qingyue Yuan, Zhenglin Wang, and Deyu Zhou ask whether language models know when they are going wrong, in a 2025 paper. This self-awareness of errors is called meta-cognition, and it is key to trusting a model's reasoning. Simple gauges such as perplexity can hint at answer correctness, but they read only the surface and ignore single steps. The authors build an automated framework, AutoMeco, to benchmark the available gauges fairly.

They then propose a training-free adjustment, MIRA, that sharpens those gauges by treating the reasoning chain as a step-by-step process. Better error awareness lets a model flag its own shaky steps for checking, instead of presenting every answer with the same confidence. That honesty is a precondition for using AI reasoning in serious work.
arxiv-2506-08910:
Octavio Arizmendi, Andrew Campbell, and Katsunori Fujie study what happens to a random polynomial's turning points under repeated differentiation, in a 2025 paper. Earlier work showed that differentiating again and again, with proper rescaling, pushes a random polynomial toward a Hermite polynomial. The roots settle into a fixed pattern in that limit.

The trio extend that result in two directions using finite free probability. First, they prove limit theorems for the wobble around the settled pattern, for both the polynomials and their roots. Second, they drop the assumption that roots have finite spread, and the Hermite limit gives way to a random sequence set by a broader law. Their proofs run through finite free cumulants, which pack the argument tightly.
arxiv-2506-10510:
Heng-Yu Zhang and co-authors verify that a neutron detector array sees cosmic rays steadily. Their 2025 paper reports calibration checks for ENDA-64, sixty-four detectors inside a high-altitude observatory that catch thermal neutrons thrown off when cosmic ray air showers strike the ground.

Across clusters, neutron counts agreed within about seven percent, and rates drifted only modestly over time. Two environmental lessons stood out. Clusters lacking sand cubes under their detectors disagreed by up to eighteen percent, because rain reached the target material; the cubes both shield it and help gather neutrons. Rainy and dry seasons left their own marks. The authors judge the array stable and consistent enough to ground the physics analysis built on it.
arxiv-2506-11110:
Jaeho Lee and Atharv Chowdhary present AssertBench, a test of whether language models hold their ground when users push back on true facts. For each evidence-backed fact drawn from a fact-checking data set, the benchmark builds two prompts. In one, the user claims the statement is correct; in the other, the user claims it is wrong. The desired behavior is that the model judges the fact the same both times.

The benchmark separates framing effects from knowledge by first checking how the model judges the same claims neutrally. It measures how much the user's stance sways the answer. The setup mirrors a common situation: users asserting things with confidence, rightly or wrongly. The authors argue that a model which flips to agree fails a basic duty of consistency. Their code is public, and they frame the tool as a probe of sycophancy in everyday model use.
arxiv-2506-11510:
Anis Benyoub and Jonathan Dupuy advocate tetrahedral grids for volumetric path tracing in rendering. The grids are built by a longest edge bisection method and partition space in a highly adaptive way. That adaptivity limits the memory footprint of volumetric assets, a major cost in production rendering.

Each tetrahedral cell has at most four neighbors, one per face, or fewer at boundaries. Algorithms and data structures exploit that simple connectivity to trace paths on the graphics processor. In practice the implementation runs up to thirty times faster than regular grids on tested assets. Production assets render in real time at a high sample count, which makes the approach attractive for film and interactive work.
arxiv-2506-11610:
Daniel Hove Paludan and co-authors study how chat tools shape early talks between clients and designers, in work from 2025. A poor grasp of the client's needs can waste a hundred hours of work, as one firm put it. The team first spoke with ten design firms about how they gather needs, then built a tool that pairs a chat agent with choice-based answers.

Fifty mock clients tested the tool in a split design. Both the chat agent and the choice format lowered one trust score, yet the input clients gave was clearer. Seven firms then weighed the tool's worth and limits. The authors draw lessons for early joint work.
arxiv-2506-11710:
Systems that chew through live data streams can choke when data arrives faster than they can process it. Ziren Xiao addresses that overload in this 2025 paper. Too much input makes the system unstable and wastes resources. Slowing the sources before the flood hits is safer than cleaning up after.

Xiao's controller learns by trial and error, guided by a graph neural network that reads the engine's live metrics. Graphs suit the data, since a stream system is itself a web of linked parts. The design need not store old states or wait long to see an action's full effect. It can also adapt across several stream jobs at once. Earlier controllers used plain layered networks for the same job. A general controller could run many real-time services more safely.
arxiv-2506-11810:
Kai Dietze and co-authors show that entangled ions can run an optical clock better than separate ions, in an experimental physics paper from 2025. Optical clocks are the most precise timekeepers known, and quantum links between atoms promise still better performance. The team worked with two calcium ions.

The ions were entangled in a state that ignores first-order magnetic field shifts, which stretched their coherence time. That allowed probe times up to 550 milliseconds, near the atoms' lifetime limit. The entangled clock reached the same stability as a plain one in half the probe time, so its cycle ran faster. Its best instability set a record for a calcium ion clock. The authors compared it with a strontium lattice clock as a check.
arxiv-2506-11910:
Eivind Otto Hjelle's work, first written as a doctoral thesis, builds a new object in advanced number theory, in a version published in 2025. The object sorts a family of math structures called Breuil–Kisin modules, which help scholars study whole-number problems tied to symmetry groups. Hjelle adds extra data that tracks how the structures descend between settings. He caps the allowed weights by a chosen bound before stacking the cases together.

Hjelle proves that the resulting stack behaves like a well-formed space in the p-adic world, a number system built around a prime. He also shows it matches, up to smooth change, a twisted form of a known variety from another line of work. That match lets results flow between the two settings. The text is a lightly edited version of his thesis, submitted in 2024.
arxiv-2506-12010:
Nathan Keenan, John Goold, and Alex Nico-Katz bring random matrix theory to quantum state checks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, studies tomography, the rebuild of an unknown quantum state from many measures. Knowing the size and shape of rebuild errors is key for quantum machines. The authors treat the error itself as a random matrix.

They find a deep link between the error and a classic random matrix family. That link lets them swap real errors for samples from the family in many formulas. They derive mean error, spread, and a bound on how many samples a check needs. Numeric tests on common methods back the theory. A standard fix-up step leaves the bound unchanged.
arxiv-2506-12110:
Testing smart agents on money matters needs a world rich enough to fool no one. Qirui Mi and nine co-authors open such a world in 2025, called EconGym. Eleven kinds of player fill it: homes, firms, banks, states, and their kin, each with its own eyes, moves, and pay. Users can wire the kinds and the agent brains in mix-and-match ways.

More than twenty-five tasks run on the frame, from tax and pension pulls to money supply games. Trials show that richer mixes widen the space of plans an agent can find. Brains led by classic money theory fared best when the world grew tangled. The gym scales to ten thousand players at a fair clip, the team say, which puts town-size what-ifs within reach.
arxiv-2506-12510:
Alessandro Ramponi and Sergio Scarlatti extend, in 2025, a standard credit risk model to portfolios mixing green and brown loans. The classic model uses one shared risk factor, which cannot capture how the two loan types react differently to shocks. Their version adds a second factor and lets the shared risk follow skewed distributions.

With uneven loan sizes, they prove the portfolio loss settles to a limit that reflects each segment's traits.
