Simulations show how worst-case loss measures move with portfolio graininess, default odds, factor loadings, and skewness. The authors offer the model as a base for pricing and for studying green loan books.
arxiv-2506-12710:
Yuqi Ping and co-authors explore how large language models could run drone swarms, in a 2025 paper. New models can read text, images, and video in one system. Drone swarms, in turn, fly group missions that need fast grasp of a scene and quick change of plan.

The authors first lay out how drones and such models each work. They then show how the models could sharpen target finding, route choice, and group teamwork. A case study on forest fire fighting walks through talks with human staff, task plans, fire checks, and flight action. The paper closes with open problems and next steps for the field.
arxiv-2506-13810:
Olivier Saidi proposes a framework for using patterns to tame hard optimization problems in this 2025 paper. Problems like the traveling salesman task resist efficient worst-case solutions. Yet real instances often carry structure, such as clustering or symmetry, that a solver could exploit.

The framework measures such regularities and folds them into a meta-learning solver pipeline. A new metric scores how well a solver uses the patterns it finds. On salesman benchmarks from twenty-two to nearly twenty-four hundred cities, solution quality rose by up to seventy-nine percent. The author extends the lens to finance forecasting and large model tuning. He argues pattern-aware complexity offers a practical, unified view apart from worst-case hardness theory.
arxiv-2506-14010:
Gergely Fejos and Daiki Suenaga present a 2025 paper on hot matter made of two colors of quarks. This simpler cousin of real quantum chromodynamics lets theorists study how a key symmetry effect, the axial anomaly, behaves as matter heats up. They model the lightest particles with a sigma model that also includes paired-quark states.

A flow method that zooms from fine to coarse scales drives the calculations. With real pion values as input, the model's couplings all shrink in step, and chiral symmetry returns smoothly as temperature rises. Partner particles grow alike in mass, as restoration predicts. Yet the couplings tied to the anomaly grow stronger in the hot phase, helped by the paired-quark states. The fate of a related quantity is also traced.
arxiv-2506-14110:
Steve Hanneke and Mingyue Xu pin down how fast the workhorse learning rule can improve when no perfect rule exists, in this 2025 paper. Empirical risk minimization picks the rule with the lowest training error. Universal learning asks how quickly its excess risk shrinks for one fixed data source, not the worst case. Earlier universal results assumed a flawless rule is available, which practice rarely grants.

Dropping that assumption yields a neat trichotomy. Depending on the concept class, the rate is either exponentially fast, just faster than the classic square-root pace, or arbitrarily slow. The authors characterize exactly which classes land in each bucket. They do the same for target-based and Bayes-based variants. The result completes a map of what this basic rule can promise.
arxiv-2506-14510:
Gautam Nagaraj and a very large team report a survey's count of a class of young galaxies across cosmic time and across how crowded their homes are. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The galaxies are picked out by a bright line in their light, from hot gas lit by young stars. The count of such galaxies by brightness is a core gauge of how they form. The survey, called ODIN, maps wide fields with a set of filters tuned to that line at many past times. The team reads how the brightness count shifts with time and with the density of the place each galaxy sits in. The work ties galaxy growth to its setting.
arxiv-2506-14610:
Nicole Avans and co-authors ask what a modern C++ face for the world's workhorse parallel programming interface should look like. MPI moves data between the nodes of supercomputers, but its official C++ bindings were deleted in 2008, and a crowd of partial replacements has grown since. Their 2025 paper refuses to add another one, and instead works out the concepts any worthy interface must satisfy.

The tension they name is real: idiomatic C++ wants strict types and clear ownership of objects, while MPI keeps loose lifetimes and global state. A community standard, they argue, must honor the generic programming principles C++ programmers expect without surrendering the speed and portability that made MPI itself. The stakes have risen with graphics processors and machine learning flooding scientific computing. The paper offers design ground rules for the interface the community eventually blesses.
arxiv-2506-14710:
Francis VanGessel and Mitul Pandya show in a 2025 study that deep neural networks can predict the fluid motion set off by an underwater blast far faster than standard solvers. Blasts under water create complex flows with shock fronts and mixing layers. Solvers that track them step by step are accurate but slow, and that slowness limits design work and real-time use.

Their network takes the traits of the explosive material as input and predicts how shock fronts and material borders move over time. In tests it ran thousands of times faster than the standard solver while keeping errors in the fluid measures extremely small. The method works across a broad range of ideal explosive materials. It opens a path to quick design sweeps for fields from ship building to medicine.
arxiv-2506-14810:
Qiwen Zhang routes each shop product to its best demand forecast model, in work from 2025. Sparse demand with long zero spells breaks single model forecasts in supply chains. Wrong stock calls then cause both empty shelves and wasteful surplus in stores.

A router picks among classic, learning, and deep models per product demand shape. Three router types are compared: rule based, tree based, and deep image style. Smooth, lumpy, and gap filled demand each get matched to a fitting model family. Tests on a large retail set cut forecast error by over one tenth. Deep routing also ran far faster than single strong model runs.
arxiv-2506-15010:
Yijun Lin and Yao-Yi Chiang spot text on old maps in a 2025 paper. Map text holds place lore: past borders, names, and land tales set by the maker hand. But old map text is long, spun at wild angles, and set on busy, stained ground, which breaks stock text spotters.

Their spotter bends its read to each text shape, point by point and char by char. That local bend fits map text where one stiff box would fail. With few past tools and thin training sets for this ground, a flex form is the draw. Archive teams gain a reader for a trove that sits locked in script.
arxiv-2506-15710:
Siru Ouyang and co-authors find a cheap way in a 2025 paper to wake the reasoning skill of large language models. The known way, trial-based tuning, works well but needs vast sums of compute and many model copies. Fresh work hints such tuning mostly reshapes what a model already knows, rather than adding new facts.

The team bets that the shift in word odds from tuning is much the same for small and large models. So they tune a small model and move its shift onto a large one. The large model gains sharp reasoning at a sliver of the cost. This shortcut could put strong reasoning in reach of small labs.
arxiv-2506-15810:
Gisell Lorena Osorio, Milica Banic, and Nicolas Quesada set out plans to make photon triplets with clean spectra in waveguides and ring resonators. Triplet sources show non Gaussian traits prized for quantum computing, but linked spectra can blunt their use. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The triplets arise from a third order process that splits one photon into three in photonic gear. The team studies the spectra in theory and gives ways to gauge and cut the links. One plan shapes spread in waveguides, the other shapes the pump in resonators. Both are shown on real designs, a high contrast fiber and a silicon nitride ring. Few mode triplets look within reach of current gear.
arxiv-2506-15910:
Zakria Qadir and co-authors plan drone flight paths over disaster zones in a 2025 paper. Drones help rescue teams and restore a link to the outside world, but rubble and chaos make the shortest safe route hard to pick.

Their scheme groups the problem into clusters and searches with a gas inspired optimization method, named after a law of gas solubility. It was compared with four rival search methods across four scenes: open, tight, tangled, and complex. The gas method won in every scene. In the open scene it cut transport cost by about thirty nine percent and computing time by about seventeen percent against the swarm method. The authors propose it for smart city fleets.
arxiv-2506-16110:
Graph neural networks learn by passing notes between linked points, but distant points often fail to hear each other. Langzhang Liang and co-authors attack that flaw, called over-squashing, in a 2025 paper. Bottlenecks in the graph squeeze too much information through too few links.

Common fixes add links, which costs compute time and can blur each point's own signal. Their method instead thins the graph in a way that keeps its core vibration pattern, the spectrum, nearly intact. The thinned graph connects better while staying sparse. Tests beat strong rival methods on labeling accuracy and on holding the spectrum of the graph, which shows rewiring need not erase what made the graph itself.
arxiv-2506-16310:
Pranav Pawar, Akshansh Dwivedi, Jenish Boricha, Himanshu Gohil, and Aditya Dubey build a text-to-speech system that keeps accents and feelings straight across languages. Their 2025 paper notes that top systems sound natural in one language but stumble on multilingual accents, especially for Indian languages, and flatten emotion. Cultural nuance in speech data is scarce, which makes the gap hard to close.

Extending an existing model, they add a phoneme-alignment encoder tuned per language, emotion layers trained on native speakers, and a code-switching module that flips accent mid-sentence. Accent errors fell by about a quarter, and native listeners recognized the intended emotion eighty-five percent of the time. Two hundred users rated naturalness 4.2 out of 5.
arxiv-2506-16410:
Graham Gibson and co-authors published this forecasting study in 2025. Disease forecasts guide hospital planning and public warnings, yet they often fail right at epidemic peaks, when accuracy matters most. Simple models just extend past trends, while fixed-rule models rest on rigid assumptions. The team built a hybrid method called epimodulation. It folds basic facts about how epidemics behave into existing forecast models.

Tested on simple trend models, the method raised accuracy for COVID-19 hospital admissions by about nine percent on average. Gains for flu admissions averaged near twenty percent. At the peaks themselves, accuracy improved by roughly a fifth to a quarter. The method also strengthened a major ensemble forecast used for COVID-19. The authors present it as a general add-on that makes outbreak forecasts more trustworthy at the worst moments.
arxiv-2506-16510:
Abby Mintz and co-authors study how small galaxies formed stars at cosmic noon, the busy era when the universe was a few billion years old, in a 2025 paper. Star formation in small galaxies is known to come in bursts, but the quiet gaps between bursts are hard to observe far away. The team used 43 spectra from the James Webb Space Telescope covering small galaxies seen as they were one to three billion years after the Big Bang.

Many of the spectra show strong breaks that signal a recent pause in star birth, and these breaks grow stronger as signs of current star birth fade. By matching the data against simple models of bursty histories, the authors find that these galaxies need long burst cycles. Their quiet phases last more than a hundred million years, far longer than a quick lull.
arxiv-2506-16810:
Ryan Campbell, Mihalis Mathioudakis, and Carlos Quintero Noda test in 2025 a transformer model that reads the Sun's atmosphere from its light. Scientists infer heat, motion, and magnetism at each height by working back from split, polarized light, but classic methods are slow and can settle on wrong answers.

Their model learned from synthetic light built by detailed Sun simulations across fifteen spectral lines. An attention step lets the model focus on the most telling parts of the spectrum for each trait. It beat a plain network, above all high in the atmosphere and for magnetic traits, and it held up well as noise rose to real-world levels.
arxiv-2506-17510:
Rafael Ferreira da Silva and co-authors laid out a roadmap in a 2025 paper for linking self-driving labs into one network. AI-run labs can plan and run tests on their own, yet most sit as lone islands at one site each. A find at one lab then cannot spark a test at the next without slow human hands.

Their plan, AISLE, is a grassroots web of such labs with shared rules for data and control. It aims to shrink the path from idea to proof to impact. The authors span labs, computing, and energy science. The roadmap asks funders to back the links, not just the labs.
arxiv-2506-17610:
Davit Aghamalyan and co-authors offer a new route to best-control problems in a 2025 paper. Their tool is the Dirac-Bergmann method, a step-by-step way to handle systems with constraints. The work covers both classic and quantum systems.

Standard control theory finds best paths by testing small changes to a trial path. The new method skips that step. It builds the best answer from the constraint set and the energy function as the algebra closes. They show the method on the classic fastest-descent curve problem. They also apply it to fast control of quantum systems, both closed and open, a task of use for quantum devices.
arxiv-2506-17910:
Mohamed Benkedadra and co-authors propose a multi-camera 3D vision pipeline for interactive spaces in a 2025 paper. Single 2D cameras miss depth, and gaming depth cameras work only at short range. Large, complex rooms defeat both. Their system fuses several stereo cameras to rebuild the whole scene in 3D.

On that rebuilt scene the system can recognize events, track people, and send notices. A feedback loop lets the system learn from the people in the room. That helps it sharpen its choices or adjust to a wholly new setting. The authors report early experiments with the pipeline. They close with a roadmap of steps needed to move it into production use.
arxiv-2506-18510:
Duygu Altinok shows that large language models can turn imperfect transcript hints into disfluency rich transcripts. Detecting disfluencies matters for speech systems and for inclusive language technology. The method writes disfluencies as explicit tokens with timestamps, which yields fully annotated transcripts of real speech.

Acoustic features from an audio encoder combine with text inputs of varying quality. Inputs may be clean transcripts without disfluencies, time aligned transcripts, or phoneme based recognizer output, all possibly flawed. Experiments show the text need not be flawless. As long as timestamp cues survive, the model smooths the input and restores the disfluency annotation. The robustness lowers the cost of building annotated speech corpora.
arxiv-2506-18610:
When a star collapses into a black hole, the vacuum of space itself gives birth to particle pairs, the effect behind Hawking radiation. Exact formulas cover only the quiet late-time case; mid-process moments and messy events like merging black holes resist exact math. Pedro Duarte Baptista and co-authors build a numerical route to the problem. Their method borrows hyperboloidal slices from relativity computing, curved time surfaces reaching both the far past and far future edges of spacetime.

On those slices they evolve quantum fields through flat-space toy models, where stand-in potentials mimic gravity. They then read off the spectrum of particles arriving at the far future edge. Tests show the approach follows a scattering event start to finish in one run. The authors next aim the same frame at real gravitational settings and a stricter treatment of Hawking scattering.
arxiv-2506-18710:
Maxime Lelièvre and nine co-authors benchmark how well large language models know pedagogy, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Most benchmarks test content knowledge, not knowledge of teaching itself. Pedagogy covers method and practice, from teaching strategies to assessment and special needs support.

Their Pedagogy Benchmark draws questions from professional development exams for teachers. It covers cross-domain teaching knowledge and knowledge for special education needs and disability. They tested ninety-seven models, with accuracy from twenty-eight to eighty-nine percent. They also chart cost against accuracy and track the value frontier over time. Online leaderboards let users filter models by cost and openness. The authors argue such benchmarks guide safe use in education.
arxiv-2506-18810:
Siao Tang and co-authors trim the long winded reasoning of large reasoning models while they write. Their paper from 2025 deals with models like DeepSeek-R1 and the o1 line, which gain skill by writing long chains of thought but waste time and compute on excess words. Past fixes act before reasoning starts, by prompts or tuning.

Their ConciseHint frame slips short hints into the text as it forms, nudging the model to stay terse. Hint strength adapts to how hard the query is, so skill is not traded away. On top current models the method cut length while holding scores. It also stacks with older fixes to push the speed and skill bound higher.
arxiv-2506-19110:
Sara Congia and fourteen co-authors make doubly entangled photon pairs on a silicon chip in a 2025 paper. Entangled photons carry quantum links used in secure networks. Hyperentangled pairs are linked in two traits at once, here time and frequency. Such states resist noise and carry more data per pair.

The team drove two tiny ring resonators on the chip with one laser. Pairs formed through a mixing process inside the rings. Tests broke a key quantum bound by wide margins in each trait. A joint witness test confirmed true hyperentanglement by a large margin. The authors call it a first for an integrated silicon device. The chip path suits scale-up for quantum networks.
arxiv-2506-19310:
Sakamoto and Tomizawa present a physics paper, published in 2025, on building systems of several black holes in a curved space. The black holes in question are of a simple rotating kind, strung along a sphere inside a larger space described by string theory. Making such multi-hole solutions by direct means is hard. The authors use a group-based method that turns the problem into a classic puzzle about stitching functions together.

They start from a known string-like solution with no charge. They solve the stitching problem for it, then apply a transformation that adds charges. The result is a family of solutions holding multiple charged black holes at once. Such exotic systems test the limits of gravity theory. They also feed the study of how black holes in higher dimensions behave, a topic with few exact examples to lean on.
arxiv-2506-19510:
Harsh Mathur and co-authors test whether a hydrogen spectral line can read the Sun's chromospheric magnetic field, in a 2025 paper. The chromosphere is a restless layer where fields shape eruptions, yet its magnetism is hard to measure. The team synthesized the line's polarized light inside a realistic 3D solar model. Two established spectral lines served as yardsticks for comparison.

The hydrogen line's core formed about 500 kilometers higher than the calcium line's core, sampling loftier field. A simple approximation recovered the model's field maps from the synthetic signals. Even after adding realistic noise, most magnetic structures stayed visible. The authors say pairing the hydrogen line with standard ones gives a fuller altitude picture of solar magnetism.
arxiv-2506-20010:
Shu Lin and co-authors move database work closer to the data in a 2025 paper. Huawei's cloud database separates computing from storage: data lives on storage servers that hold spare processing power of their own. Shipping every row to the compute layer wastes the network. Their design pushes filtering, column selection, and aggregation down into the storage servers.

The benefits stack up: less data on the wire, freed compute capacity, and faster queries, which together raise throughput. On a standard hundred-gigabyte benchmark, eighteen of twenty-two queries improved. Data shipped fell by about two-thirds overall and compute time by half. One query was transformed, with shipped data down ninety-eight percent and runtime down eighty percent. The paper is a systems account of making the split architecture pay, a pattern other cloud databases share.
arxiv-2506-20310:
Ion Chirica and Mário Pereira give a method to specify and verify higher order iterators in OCaml in two thousand twenty-five. Iterators are central to all languages, yet proving them right is hard. Higher order forms, where functions pass as inputs, add to that strain. Their method is generic and modular in shape.

A spec language states the joint behavior of any iteration schema. A framework then checks each client against its spec by deduction. Case studies run from classic list iterators to graph methods. The graph cases come from a wide used OCaml library. The work shows the approach holds in real code.
arxiv-2506-20410:
Xia, Huang, and Dong build in 2025 a theory of heat engines fed by sources that generate heat at a constant rate, unlike the fixed temperature reservoirs of textbook models. Radioisotope power systems work exactly that way, which motivates the frame. A finite time Stirling cycle serves as the working case.

A universal proportion links average output power and efficiency, free of cycle details or working substance. Their tailored control keeps the substance at set temperatures during key strokes. The hot source temperature oscillates as heat builds and drains. Radioactive decay then drags performance down over the system lifespan, a decline they quantify for designers.
arxiv-2506-20810:
Shashwat Khandelwal and co-authors extend a chip design tool for recurrent networks in a 2025 paper. These networks, in the LSTM form, work well on time based tasks such as stock moves. But they are heavy to run, and chip tools mostly serve simpler feed forward networks, leaving LSTM work to full custom builds.

The team adds support to the open FINN framework so LSTMs can be placed on FPGA chips in a general way. They model the repeating step with a standard scan operator, allow mixed precision, and add compiler steps that map the model to hardware blocks. A test model for mid price stock forecasts ran on a target chip with good speed and low resource use. Its accuracy matched or beat past models at lower precision.
arxiv-2506-21110:
Sheng Dai, Timo Kuosmanen, and Xun Zhou work out the identification conditions for convex regression, a method that fits a curved, bowl-shaped relation to data without fixing its exact form. Standard regression leans on the condition that errors are unrelated to the inputs. For convex regression, the matching condition was unknown.

Using duality theory from optimization, they derive the sample conditions for several model forms, with and without requirements that the relation rise steadily or scale evenly. They then propose a hybrid method that blends instrument variables with a control function to fight endogeneity, where inputs may be entangled with errors. Simulations and Chilean factory data support the approach.
arxiv-2506-21210:
Christian Liedtke and Matthew Satriano give an arithmetic version of Klein's classic list of finite symmetry groups, in a paper from 2025. Klein sorted the finite subgroups of a matrix group over the complex numbers long ago. That list anchors much of modern geometry. The pair ask what the list looks like over the ring of integers of a number field.

They describe and sort the finite, flat subgroup schemes of the same matrix group over that ring. Their sorting keeps only the schemes that stay well behaved under change of base. They also prove finiteness results that cap how many such schemes can occur. Density results then cover the surface flaws tied to those schemes. The work lifts a piece of classic geometry into number theory. It opens new ground for the study of quotient flaws.
arxiv-2506-21410:
Benjamin Cohen and co-authors map the shape of the 300S stellar stream, a ribbon of stars torn from a lost companion of the Milky Way. Streams are fine probes of the galaxy's gravity field, down to its small lumps of matter. This stream runs on a tilted, backward orbit, which sharpens its value as a test.

Their 2025 study fights heavy contamination from the Sagittarius stream in the same sky. Sky survey photos, Gaia motion data, and spectra from a dedicated stream survey are joined. The team resets the stream's coordinate frame and distance slope, then models its shape two ways. Both reads agree where they overlap, giving a clean run of the stream across a wide span.
arxiv-2506-21510:
Ruixiao Yang, Gulai Shen, Ahmed Alahmed, and Chuchu Fan schedule home energy gear under demand charges, in work from 2025. Homes now mix flexible loads, solar panels, and batteries behind one meter. Peak demand charges punish brief high draws, which makes joint scheduling a hard linked puzzle.

The best control rule has a clean threshold shape in the solved model. Branch counts in that rule explode with horizon length due to storage and peak links. A fast approximation hunts the peak under a mild relaxed version of the task. Run time grows in a straight line with horizon under the new method. Open dataset tests beat learning and rule based rivals on cost gaps.
arxiv-2506-21610:
Pronoy Das and co-authors build a quantum picture of light's spin inside a twisted crystal, in a 2025 paper. Tellurium grows in screw-like chains that lack mirror symmetry. That twist gives its electron waves odd spin patterns, but light waves inside it were harder to read. Long-wave shortcuts blur the fine detail. The team built a spin-sorted map of light bands at the scale of the lattice itself.

On the map, crossings that would stay merged in plain tellurium split apart under the twist, which makes light bend in the swirling way labs had measured. The theory matches those measured values closely. Zoomed in, the twist shows up as a spin texture woven through each light wave. The authors say the frame explains where this light play comes from and should serve other twisted crystals too.
arxiv-2506-21910:
Ernie Chang and co-authors present a 2025 trick for picking the right data mix when training language models. A model needs many skills, yet the link between data blends and skills is hard to model directly. The team notices that saved checkpoints along one training run already show different skills blooming at different times. Those checkpoint models can act as mixers, rating which source data fed each skill.

Using a first-order influence estimate pooled across checkpoints, the method builds blends aimed at target skills. On eight reasoning benchmarks in a pretraining setup, scores rose by up to about two percent. The authors frame checkpoints as an untapped signal hiding in plain sight.
arxiv-2506-22010:
Bentert, Fomin, Golovach, and Morelle study in twenty twenty-five how to build backup-proof bases in matroids, a broad frame that captures independence in vectors, graphs, and sets. A fault-tolerant basis keeps spanning the whole set even after any fixed number of elements is removed. The goal is the smallest such set, a problem with roots in networks and robust design.

They give an efficient algorithm when both the fault count and the structure's rank are treated as fixed parameters. They also show the limits are tight. The problem is already hard in general for a single fault. For rank two or less it is easy, while for rank three or more it stays hard even with the parameter fixed.
arxiv-2506-22110:
Shashwat Bhattacharya and four co-authors study swirling hot fluid in a 2025 physics paper. Their setup is a layer heated from below, a classic model of convection. The fluid has a very low Prandtl number, meaning heat spreads far slower than motion. They ask how the mixing of heat and motion changes across scales.

The team ran direct simulations of the layer across a range of heating strengths. They built a scale by scale measure of the mixing ratio from a classic theory. The measured ratio came out near ten, vastly above the molecular value. In effect, the wild flow behaves like a much thicker fluid. The finding backs earlier models of convection inside the Sun.
arxiv-2506-22910:
Paul Vos proposes a new scale for reporting statistical test results, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. P-values express tail probabilities, which many users find hard to interpret. His alternative counts semi-tail units, where each unit halves the remaining tail area.

On this logarithmic scale, familiar percentiles land at memorable values. The 10th percentile sits near 3.3 units, and the 5th near 4.3. A two-sided version extends the idea symmetrically around the median. Critical values then follow simple arithmetic progressions. Evidence from independent studies combines by simple addition. Vos also defines an efficiency measure based on differences of slopes. Examples range from standardized test scores to poker hand rankings, showing one scale serving many fields.
arxiv-2506-23010:
Max Lovig, Tianhao Wang, and Zhou Fan ask when a widely used iterative method behaves the same no matter how the data is spread, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The method is approximate message passing, used to study learning dynamics in statistics.

For methods whose steps split cleanly by coordinate, such sameness was already known. Steps that mix coordinates were understood only for tidy data, such as Gaussian or rotation-friendly matrices. The authors name a condition on the method's building blocks, the Bounded Composition Property. Under it, for steps built from polynomials, the same step-by-step forecast holds for matrices with non-Gaussian entries. The work opens a study of sameness for this harder class of methods.
arxiv-2506-23110:
Yen-Anh Thi Pham, Huynh To Uyen, and Nabendu Pal study how to estimate the association strength of a Frank copula. Their 2025 paper works with a two-variable form of this tool, which joins separate distributions into a joint one. The Frank family is widely used in finance, yet its key parameter has had little direct statistical study.

Three estimators are compared on bias and on squared error, in both plain and relative terms. Near a value of zero, simple moment estimators beat the maximum likelihood estimator. Overall, though, the likelihood method performs best, and the two approaches lean in opposite directions on bias. Some results clash with a classic 1987 account, which the authors discuss. The paper adds careful small-sample guidance for users.
arxiv-2506-23210:
Taehwan Yoon, Bongjun Choi, and Wesley De Neve present FedRef in 2025, a fine-tuning method for federated learning. Federated learning trains one model across many sites without moving private data. When sites differ in data and hardware, training can forget earlier learning and drift without bound, hurting accuracy and raising local computing cost.

FedRef takes a Bayesian approach anchored to a reference model built from past global states. The anchor reins in drift and guards memory of earlier tasks. It also trims the chatter between sites, saving bandwidth. Hospitals or phone fleets that learn together without sharing data get a steadier method that respects both privacy and limited hardware.
arxiv-2506-23310:
Sergey Foss, Masakiyo Miyazawa, and Linglong Yuan present a study from twenty twenty-five on busy spells in a network of queues. In a Jackson type network, work arrives at set rates and each station serves in its own time. A busy spell runs from when work starts to the next idle gap. The team asks how long such spells can get in rare, extreme cases.

They assume the network is stable, with service times that can be very long. For the stations with the heaviest tails, they pin down the exact growth of the chance that a busy spell tops a large mark. One key claim is a single big jump rule. A long spell comes most often from one huge service time, not from many small ones.
arxiv-2506-24010:
Yuxi Lu and co-authors cross-check two ways of dating stars in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. One method reads the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio in a star's spectrum, which shifts as a star ages. The other, gyrochronology, infers age from how fast a star spins, since spin slows over time.

Both methods are calibrated against a shared pattern: older star groups move with a wider spread of speeds. The team maps where each method can be applied, beyond the ranges covered by star clusters and vibration studies. After fixing systematic offsets, ages from the two methods agreed within uncertainty. The authors define the metal and ratio ranges where the chemical method stays reliable.
arxiv-2506-24110:
The most energetic neutrinos ever seen may interact with each other in ways the standard model forbids. Pravin Kumar Natwariya and co-authors ask what such self-interaction would do to the afterglow of the Big Bang. If fast neutrinos scatter off the sea of slow background neutrinos, they dump energy into the young universe. That extra heat would slightly warp the spectrum of the cosmic microwave background.

Two kinds of warp, named mu-type and y-type, arise at different cosmic ages. Existing limits from a past satellite, plus the planned sensitivity of a future one, cap how strong the coupling can be. For muon neutrinos near a peta-electronvolt, the cap lands near three parts in ten thousand. The authors argue future background measurements could settle whether neutrinos talk to each other.
arxiv-2507-00010:
Jia-Yin Peng and Bing-Zhao Li prove new bounds in a 2025 math paper on signal analysis. The uncertainty principle sets a trade off between how sharply a signal can be pinned in time and in frequency. Many newer tools rest on the Fourier transform, and each raises its own version of that trade off. The pair study the version tied to the offset linear canonical transform, a flexible tool in the field.

They prove a key identity for the transform, then build a sharpened bound of Heisenberg Weyl type. A bound of higher order, named for Heisenberg, Pauli, and Weyl, is also derived. Computer simulations back the math and show the bounds hold in practice. The results give engineers who use this transform firmer ground for judging how fine a signal reading can get.
arxiv-2507-00210:
Imene Kerboua and eight co-authors present LineRetriever, a tool that trims web pages down to what a software agent needs, in a 2025 paper. Agents that browse the web for users are fed the full page code, which is often too long for the model to hold.

Simple fixes cut lines from the end or pick lines that look similar to the task, and both can drop facts the agent needs later. LineRetriever instead uses a language model to pick the lines most useful for the agent's next steps. Tests show the page view shrinks a great deal at each step while task success stays steady. The work targets agents that plan ahead, not just react.
arxiv-2507-00310:
Dhruv Agarwal and co-authors present a system that chooses its own science questions in a 2025 paper. Most robot science tools need a human to set the research question first. Open-ended tools exist, but they pick ideas by variety or by vague guesses at what humans find interesting. Both paths can waste effort.

Their system, AutoDiscovery, uses Bayesian surprise as its guide. It measures how much a result shifts the model's beliefs about an idea. A tree search then picks the next test under a fixed budget. Across 21 real data sets, the system found more discoveries than rivals, the authors report.
arxiv-2507-00410:
Tristen Shields and five co-authors measure, in a 2025 preprint, the density profile of dark matter halos under a new definition. A recent proposal defines a halo dynamically: only the particles actually orbiting in the bound structure count. The authors ask how the orbiting matter is spread, halo by halo. At fixed orbiting mass, the whole profile turns out to hinge on one number, the halo radius. That radius sets how far the orbiting profile reaches. Its scatter at fixed mass is about sixteen percent.

Differences in birth time explain only a little of that spread. Late-forming halos sit slightly more compact. Counting birth time cuts the scatter to about eleven percent. The result simplifies how modelers can paint halos: mass plus radius nearly fixes the profile. That economy helps connect dark matter theory to the galaxies telescopes see.
arxiv-2507-00710:
Can Cui and co-authors design a secure task offloading scheme for drone based edge computing under an eavesdropping drone threat, in a paper from 2025. Ground users send computing tasks to service drones, but an enemy drone may listen in. Task difficulty is uncertain in practice, which the design treats directly.

Service drone positions are first set by a clustering method. A robust optimization step then assigns users and split ratios while guarding against the uncertainty, using a risk measure to tame hard chance constraints. Simulations showed the robust design used only about five percent more energy than a perfect knowledge design. The authors present the scheme as practical for sixth generation drone networks.
arxiv-2507-00910:
Ken Abe and four colleagues prove that certain paired vortices must take the Sadovskii shape, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The setting is the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations of fluid flow. A steadily translating vortex dipole is the object of study.

Their variational framework maximizes kinetic energy under fixed impulse and vorticity norm constraints. Notably, no constraint on total mass is imposed. The admissible shape is then dictated by scaling invariance alone. Every maximizer touches the symmetry axis, which is exactly the Sadovskii configuration known from physics. A sharp energy inequality and the concentration-compactness principle drive the proof. The construction explains why this vortex shape appears as the endpoint of steady dipole branches.
arxiv-2507-01310:
Sourav Chowdhury, Indrani Bose, Suparna Roychowdhury, and Indranath Chaudhuri look for shared patterns across epidemic models in a 2025 study. Their model follows people cycling between susceptible and infected states, with newcomers entering the population. Random environmental noise multiplies through the system and can push it between distinct regimes.

In one regime the steady distribution has a single peak, and in another it has two. Transitions between regimes include a critical point matching a well known class from physics. A genetics model shares the same features, suggesting a universal pattern. The authors also examine how vaccination shifts the spread or containment of disease.
arxiv-2507-01410: Abeer Dyoub and Francesca Lisi present a formal way to write down models that make ethical choices based on risk, and to check those models before they are used. Moral choice is hard to grade, since the ideas behind it are tangled. Their models are written as fuzzy rules, which can hold shades of truth rather than a stark yes or no. Nets of a fuzzy kind then serve to verify and validate the models. A case from medicine shows how the method works in practice.
arxiv-2507-01510:
Sadun Bordoni and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-five, how a clumpy ring of mass could bend the orbit of a star near the black hole at our galaxy's core. The star, called S2, loops around that black hole. Its path so far fits the path predicted for a lone black hole. That fit caps how much spread-out mass can sit inside its orbit, if the mass is smooth. The team asks what changes if the mass is made of many lumps.

They ran many simulations with clusters of equal-mass objects around the black hole. Clumps could tilt the star's orbit plane and shift its swing. Hits with lumps also made the black hole wobble a bit. Mock data show such effects might be seen.
arxiv-2507-01810:
Clinical notes hold rich facts, but pulling them out as neat name-value pairs is a job where small language models can stumble on format. Nikita Neveditsin, Pawan Lingras, and Vijay Mago test how well such models keep a set output shape. Their 2025 study tries three common formats for the output.

One format, JSON, came out on top for how often a machine could read the result back without error. Sharp prompts and larger models each raised the share of clean output. Long notes and some note types pulled the share down. The error review finds each format fails in its own repeat ways. The work gives plain advice for teams that run models where patient data must stay private: pick the sturdy format, and prompt with care.
arxiv-2507-02110:
Md Nahidul Islam Opu and co-authors ask whether code measures taken before launch can call how popular a phone app will be, in a paper from 2025. A good call at launch would give makers an edge in a crowded store.

The team built a strict set of more than four hundred open Android apps sold in two stores. Code traits, code smells, and app facts were pulled from source. Exact rating and download calls failed, thanks to skewed and scattered data. A two way sort, popular or not, did far better. The authors say code traits carry real, if blunt, signal.
arxiv-2507-02210: Berta-Thompson and co-authors introduce exoatlas in 2025, a friendly Python toolkit for working with planet populations. Single planets make more sense beside their peers, the authors argue, and solar system worlds gain depth when set next to the growing census of exoplanets in the Milky Way. The toolkit gives researchers a simple interface for fetching population data and placing individual worlds in that broader context with far less manual effort.
arxiv-2507-02310:
Alif Ashrafee, Jedrzej Kozal, Michal Wozniak, and Bartosz Krawczyk addressed drifting data in 2025 for systems that learn task after task; the catalog title carries correspondence notes. Standard continual learning guards old knowledge but assumes old data stays the same. In real streams, the meaning of old classes can shift for good.

Their fix, Adaptive Memory Realignment, cleans the replay memory: stale samples of drifted classes are dropped and a few fresh ones added. That matches full retraining from scratch while using far less labelled data and computing. Four drift versions of standard vision benchmarks were built for testing. Across rehearsal methods, the fix kept accuracy high with minimal overhead.
arxiv-2507-02810: Bernhard Meirose and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on computing advances for a planned experiment hunting signs that baryon number can break. The two-stage program, set at a European neutron source, would also probe ultralight dark matter. The paper reports progress on three fronts. Machine learning methods pick out the rare events of interest. Fast approximate simulations serve detector studies. Detailed models cover the main tracking chamber and its readout electronics.
arxiv-2507-02910:
Geonwoo Cho and co-authors present a 2025 method for ordering training tasks for AI agents by cause and effect. Agents learn best from a ladder of tasks that grow in difficulty. Good middle tasks should invite exploration yet stay close enough to transfer skills. Past work compared tasks by their true causal maps, which are rarely known. Their method estimates those maps from the agent's own interaction data. The gap between task maps then serves as a novelty signal.

That signal is merged with how fast the agent is gaining reward. The joint score picks the next task in the sequence. On a standard point-mass test world, the method beat rival curricula. Learning was faster and reached higher levels in their runs. The authors say causal pacing can work without ground-truth maps. That widens the method to real settings where maps are hidden.
arxiv-2507-03210:
Selin Ahipasaoglu, Stefano Cipolla, and Jacek Gondzio speed up the design of experiments in a 2025 math study. A good design picks which points to test so a model can be fit with the least doubt. The exact form of that task, called D-optimal design, is hard when test points far outnumber planned runs.

Their method works on the smooth form of the task first. A column method grows the set of used points step by step, with a fast inner solver for each stage. That stage work soon shows which points the best design will use. The team then builds a true exact design on those points and proves it sits close to best. On large cases, the method beat branch-and-bound tools on both speed and score.
arxiv-2507-03510:
Jingze Dai and Douglas Down ask whether two energy-saving tricks for servers help more together than apart, in a 2025 paper. Data centers can slow processors down when load is light, or switch idle machines off entirely. Each trick alone cuts power while keeping response times acceptable, but combining them might interact in useful or useless ways.

The authors model a server that can run at full or reduced speed and can power down, with a restart delay when it wakes. For a cost that blends response time and energy use, one trick always dominates at every load. Adding the second buys only a small extra saving. The finding tells operators to pick the stronger lever for their load and not expect synergy from stacking both.
arxiv-2507-03710:
Vieira defends a bookkeeping freedom in particle physics against a famous apparent exception, in a 2025 theoretical paper. When physicists compute loop diagrams, they may route the momentum through the loop however they like; answers should not depend on the choice. The chiral anomaly, the subtle symmetry breaking behind a pion's decay into two photons, seemed to break that freedom: one routing makes the equations look right, others not.

Vieira shows the anomaly itself is routing-invariant after all. The apparent preference comes from which symmetry one chooses to keep visible, not from the physics. The point matters where no experiment can arbitrate, such as supersymmetric theories or models that violate basic symmetries of space and time. Using routing invariance as the guide, the paper works out which symmetry breaks in one such modified electrodynamics.
arxiv-2507-03810:
Jingeon An proves second order estimates for a phase transition in two thousand twenty five. Allen-Cahn minimizers mimic minimal surfaces as the width shrinks. Level sets converge to a minimal surface in that limit. An indicator potential turns the problem into a Bernoulli free boundary one.

The transition layers are uniformly smooth up to the free boundary. Mean curvature bounds improve and decay at an algebraic rate. A simple elliptic equation for the log gradient drives the proof. Curvature terms on the right side expose the geometry cleanly. The argument runs on general Riemannian manifolds as well.
arxiv-2507-03910:
Henry Moss, Sebastian Ober, and Tom Diethe rethink a popular optimization strategy in a 2025 machine learning paper. Bayesian optimization inside the latent space of a variational autoencoder is powerful for structured domains such as molecules. Existing methods, though, weld the surrogate model to the generative model, which can hurt when the latent space does not fit the task.

That coupling has spawned ever more complex algorithms. The authors instead explore a decoupled approach with a playful title, the return of the latent space COWBOYS. Decoupling may recover strong performance with a simpler method, a useful correction for the field.
arxiv-2507-04110:
Yaroslav Ivanashev, a solo author, studies which problem sets are low for classes that count solutions, a term that means adding the set as a helper does not make the class stronger. For three classic counting classes, the exact low sets were already known.

Ivanashev proves the low set for a further counting class is just the class of easy problems. He also gives the low classes for functions, not just sets, for four counting classes. Links between those function results and set results are set out as equal claims. The work ties up when each class stays closed under a kind of composition.
arxiv-2507-04310:
Gyuejeong Lee, Jihwan Shin, and Daeyoung Choi present ProtoNorm, a way for many devices to train one model together without sharing raw data. Their paper appeared in 2025. In federated learning, each device trains locally and shares only small summaries. Problems arise when devices hold different kinds of data or run different models. Their method shares one average pattern per class instead of full models.

The team found these class patterns often sit too close together, which blurs decisions. Their fix has two parts. First, the patterns are spread out evenly on a sphere, borrowing an idea from physics. Second, the patterns are scaled up so gaps grow in plain space. Tests on standard data sets beat rival methods. Since only small patterns travel, the method suits phones and other weak devices.
arxiv-2507-04510:
Yikang Zhao and co-authors present DFFNet, a network that classifies land cover by fusing several kinds of satellite data. Their paper appeared in 2025. Some sensors record hundreds of colors; others use radar or laser height. Each sees the land differently, and joining them is hard. The team's design works partly in the frequency domain, where patterns repeat at different scales.

A dynamic filter block learns its own frequency filters from each input, so it adapts to varied land types. A fusion block then mixes color and space cues across the data types, shuffling channels to force interaction. On two benchmark data sets the method beat leading rivals. The authors will release the code, aiming at better maps for farming, forests, and disaster watch.
arxiv-2507-04610:
Mostafa Elhoushi and Jeff Johnson present any4, a learned four-bit number format for large language models, in a 2025 paper. Squeezing model weights to four bits halves memory and speeds replies, but fixed formats like plain integers lose accuracy. Their format learns the best sixteen values to use, with no need to pre-process weights or activations.

Across several model families and sizes, any4 beat the standard four-bit formats on accuracy. It also rivaled heavier tuning methods that do need extra preparation. Variants at three and two bits stayed competitive as well. A single varied calibration sample sufficed, where most methods need hundreds. The team also released a fast GPU math library that runs the format, making the gain usable in practice.
arxiv-2507-04810:
Alexandre Meneceur, Vincent Lignon, and Martin Rosalie test for chaos in economic data in a twenty twenty-five paper. They use thirty years of data on joblessness, inflation, and the exchange rate. A tool called GPoM searches the data for a set of equations that fits it.

The chosen model has three linked equations, and its path through space forms a chaotic attractor, a tangled loop the path never quite repeats. The model does not fit the data well, but it links the three measures and shows the exchange rate drives the other two. The team maps the shape of the attractor and finds an extra branch, then reads what that branch means for the economy.
arxiv-2507-05010:
Chenfei Xiong and a large team set out Co-DETECT, a joint way for people and large models to find the edge cases in text sorting. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A domain expert starts with a rough codebook and a data set. A large model then tags the data and flags the cases the codebook does not cover well. It sums those cases up in broad, clear terms. The expert is then helped to fold rules for them into the codebook. Round by round, the book grows to fit fine shades of sense that a first draft would miss. The aim is a tag set that both sides can trust.
arxiv-2507-05810:
Sofiia Chorna and three co-authors present a framework for opening up neural networks in a 2025 paper. Explanation tools usually answer small questions: why this one prediction. The team wants the big picture instead, how whole concepts, such as shapes or topics, form, interact, and travel through a model's layers as it decides.

Their method measures how strongly each internal part of the model carries each concept, and how concepts link to the model's output classes. The results are drawn as a structured knowledge graph in an interactive tool the team calls BAGEL. Users can wander the graph to spot hidden circuits, and to catch spurious links, where a model leans on the wrong clue. The authors aim the tool at anyone who needs to trust, audit, or debug a vision model.
arxiv-2507-06110:
Lena Saurenhaus, Francesca Capel, Foteini Oikonomou, and Johannes Buchner estimate how many neutrinos come from a class of galaxies, in a 2025 paper. Seyfert galaxies hide feeding black holes, and the IceCube observatory has spotted high-energy neutrinos from a few of them. The brightest case is the nearby galaxy NGC 1068.

The team models neutrino output from the hot corona around each black hole, keyed to its X-ray brightness. Their model fits the NGC 1068 data and pins the corona's size down using gamma-ray limits. Scaled to all Seyferts, the galaxies could supply a large share of the diffuse neutrino glow below a certain energy. But if every Seyfert matched the brightest one's settings, the total would overshoot known limits. The point sources, they conclude, must be unusual members of their class.
arxiv-2507-06210:
Yuchen Huang and five co-authors built CultureCLIP in twenty twenty-five, teaching a vision-language model cultural nuance. CLIP-style models often miss the difference between look-alike concepts that carry distinct cultural meanings, because cultural training data with context and contrast cases are scarce. The team built a curation pipeline to synthesize exactly that.

Their CulTwin data set pairs concepts that visually resemble each other but differ culturally, with context-rich captions and generated images. Fine-tuning CLIP on these twins with tailored contrastive learning produced CultureCLIP. On culture-specific benchmarks it beat the base model, gaining up to about five and a half points on fine-grained recognition tasks, while keeping CLIP's general ability intact. The work shows synthetic contrast data can teach subtle distinctions.
arxiv-2507-06610:
Abhishek and Suryanarayana Mummidi model neutrino masses in twenty twenty-five. Their framework generates lepton masses and flavor mixing through an inverse seesaw structure. A modular symmetry, S4, organizes the model. Modular forms build the Yukawa couplings, cutting down free parameters.

Numerical analysis shows the model fits current neutrino oscillation data. It predicts the mixing angles and CP-violating phases within set ranges. The Dirac CP phase lands near maximal violation, around plus or minus ninety degrees. The total neutrino mass falls in a narrow predicted band. The effective Majorana mass sits within reach of upcoming double beta decay experiments. The model also respects bounds on charged lepton flavor violation. Readers get sharp, testable numbers from a symmetry-driven model.
arxiv-2507-06910:
Fareya Ikram and co-authors test whether today's language models can forecast what a tutor will do next and how a student will fare. Their 2025 paper uses two datasets of real math tutoring dialogues. Anticipating tutor strategy matters because the moves a tutor makes strongly shape learning outcomes.

Two leading models, one open and one commercial, were asked to predict future tutor moves and student results. Both struggled badly at guessing the next strategy, even though strategy itself proved highly predictive of how students did. That mismatch is the paper's core finding: the signal matters, but current models cannot read it in advance. The authors argue tutoring systems need stronger methods for modeling dialogue strategy. Their benchmarks give the field a concrete target to beat.
arxiv-2507-07310:
Diego Tapias, Benedikt Gruger, Reimer Kuhn, and Peter Sollich extend a cavity method to spot top eigenvalues when the top vector stays localised, in work from twenty twenty-five. Finding the top eigenvalue of random matrix ensembles matters across fields. A stability test on cavity equations finds it when the vector spreads out. That test fails when the top vector concentrates on few sites. A fresh criterion is needed for the localised case.

The real-valued cavity method is adapted to carry the new test. Constraints inside the cavity equations are exploited to flag the top value. The Anderson model, a classic localisation testbed, validates the approach. Results match expectations where older methods go blind. Localised spectra in disordered systems become readable with the tool. Physics and data uses that rely on top modes gain reach.
arxiv-2507-07710:
Maria Giovanna Mora, Luca Rondi, Lucia Scardia, and Edoardo Giovanni Tolotti work on nonlocal energy in a two thousand twenty-five math paper. They study Riesz energies set over probability measures on ellipsoids. The pull from point to point can change with the way it points. A real hold, a physical confinement, keeps the mass in place.

The team pins down the best low-energy shape in each space dimension. In the Coulombic and super-Coulombic cases, that best shape does not care which way the pull points. In the sub-Coulombic case, that is no longer true, and they show a case where it fails. A key step is a formula for the potential inside an ellipsoid. It works in each case and uses the hypergeometric function.
arxiv-2507-07810:
Nhi Hoai Doan, Tatsuya Hiraoka, and Kentaro Inui probe in 2025 tiny units inside language models that fire on repeated patterns, and how they shape learning from examples in the prompt. Past work eyed attention heads for this skill. This study turns to single neurons tuned to repetition, spread across layers.

Turning these neurons up or down changed example learning in ways that depended on layer depth. The team compared their effect with the known copying heads. A split emerged: early and late units play unlike roles. That split suggests ways to cut looped, repeated output while keeping prompt learning strong.
arxiv-2507-07910:
Adhya and Sanyal present in 2025 a free system, called DTECT, for tracking how topics in text change over time. Text data grows fast, and past topic tools came in split parts that were hard to read or use. Their system joins the full path in one place.

Steps span data cleaning, several model types, and scores for topic quality. Language models add auto labels for topics, and trend views use words that stand out at each time. Clear charts, document summaries, and a chat style query box aid search. The system aims to help analysts follow theme shifts without deep technical work.
arxiv-2507-08010: Miroslav Grmela places the standard meaning of temperature inside a wider multi scale frame in a 2025 arXiv note. The word runs through talk of weather, health, food, and even politics. Its sharp sense came from the study of heat engines and balance states. Grmela argues that this balance state sense is too narrow on its own. The note sets it inside multi scale thermodynamics and the rate based form of that field. It also asks how the term can work in settings outside physics.
arxiv-2507-08110:
Saeedeh Mohammadi and Taha Yasseri test AI feedback on community fact-checking notes in a study from 2025. Community Notes on X lets users flag misleading posts together. The system suffers partisan bias and slow verification. AI help could sharpen notes before they go public.

Participants received generated feedback on their notes in three flavors: supportive, neutral, or argumentative. They then revised their notes accordingly. All feedback improved note quality in the study. Argumentative feedback, the pushback kind, delivered the largest gains. Facing a counterargument forces a writer to tighten evidence and tone. Human-AI teamwork, friction included, may beat either side alone at moderation.
arxiv-2507-08210:
Fryderyk Mantiuk, Hanqi Zhou, and Charley Wu ask in 2025 how an inner world model shapes the balance between curiosity and competence in exploration. Smart agents, from a child at play to a scientist, must seek new knowledge while also gaining control of their world. Those two drives can pull in unlike ways, and inner models of the world may mediate the trade.

The team compares two model-based agents in a learning frame. One uses hand-made state groups, and the other learns its own world model as it goes. In the first, curiosity and competence guide search in distinct patterns, and chasing both lifts search. In the second, search and model learning feed each other in a two-way loop. The loop mirrors how the two drives grow up together in a child.
arxiv-2507-08610:
Dutta and Dukkipati use a communication game to improve image captioning without extra labeled data in a 2025 paper. Caption models need huge labeled image sets, and the known sets are already used to train big vision-language models. Gains must come from another route.

Two agents, a speaker and a listener, learn to talk about images for a shared reward. A vision-language model speaks, and a language model listens and judges. After game training, caption scores rose above the plain model with no new labels. A light version built from scratch also beat past unsupervised methods by a wide margin. Conversation itself drove the gain.
arxiv-2507-08810:
Joel Saucedo sets up a fractional stochastic fluid model with memory and proves when its solutions exist. His 2025 paper studies an incompressible flow on a three-dimensional torus. A Caputo time derivative of order between one half and one carries the memory, while a fractional Laplacian supplies spread-out dissipation.

The equation is derived, not assumed: eliminating fast variables from a Hamiltonian system yields memory and noise together. A heat bath picture shows the memory operator is the exact image of scale-free thermal surroundings. Vorticity math ties the stretching term to the strain field sign pattern. Local existence and uniqueness hold for smooth enough data, and the memory threshold is proven sharp. An enstrophy balance then yields a critical exponent splitting calm decay from possible stretching-driven growth.
arxiv-2507-09010:
Chun-Ting Chen, HanGyeol Mun, Jian Meng, Mohamed Abdelfattah, and Jae-sun Seo design a chip, in a 2025 preprint, to run language models at the edge. Running a model on the device itself gives privacy, low delay, and no cloud bill. Edge chips are small, though, and memory is tight. Inference has two phases with opposite needs. Reading the prompt is compute-heavy, while writing the answer is memory-bound. The design must serve both well.

Their accelerator uses a hybrid systolic array that shifts shape between the phases. Weights are stored in a compact four-bit format tuned to the array. The dataflow keeps the hardware fully busy with almost no unpacking cost. Custom units handle normalization and position steps in-chip. On a billion-scale model with long inputs and outputs, throughput per area beat prior designs several-fold. Energy use per token led the field.
arxiv-2507-09210:
Xin Xiang and colleagues use XRISM calorimeter spectroscopy to dissect the wind blowing off the black hole in NGC 4151. The hottest, fastest accretion-driven winds can reshape their host galaxies, and calorimeter-resolution X-ray spectra are the ideal tool for measuring their power. The team analyzed five observations taken with the Resolve instrument in twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four.

In the iron K band, individual spectra require as many as six wind absorption components. Slow warm absorbers, very fast outflows, and ultra-fast outflows are detected simultaneously, indicating a stratified, multiphase wind. Fast, variable emission components suggest the wind is axially asymmetric rather than a smooth shell. All wind components carry mass flow rates comparable to or exceeding the mass accretion rate feeding the black hole. The wind can thus expel as much as the hole consumes, giving it leverage over the galaxy's gas supply.
arxiv-2507-09310:
Dominika Woszczyk and co-authors convert voice style in a 2025 speech paper. People speak louder and clearer in noise, the Lombard effect, and synthetic speech in that style helps listeners in noise and with hearing loss. Recording enough Lombard speech is tiring and variable, so the team shifts style by conversion instead.

Their goal is to change who a voice sounds like while keeping the Lombard traits. Two conditioning styles are compared: one that hands the model explicit sound features, and one that lets the style be learned implicitly. The implicit route matched the explicit one on intelligibility gains while keeping speaker likeness. The work supports building training data for Lombard speech systems without fresh recordings.
arxiv-2507-09410:
Boscoe and co-authors offer in 2025 a low resource guide for processing camera trap photos with computer vision, aimed at small environmental research groups. Camera traps track wildlife without disturbing it, but groups now collect far more images than they can label or sort by hand. Off the shelf learning tools are hard to fit into local workflows with little computing or expert help.

Their pipeline runs on site and covers sending data, running the models, and checking results. Steps are tailored to the needs of the group that will use them. Readers get practical choices for turning a flood of field images into usable findings about species and habitat.
arxiv-2507-09710:
Christine Cheng studies two ways to break a network's symmetry so that every node can be told apart. One way paints nodes with colors so that no nontrivial reshuffling keeps the painting intact. The other picks a small set of anchor nodes whose fixing pins the whole graph down. Cheng focuses on amenable graphs, a class where a fast color refinement test always settles whether two graphs match.

Using a known structural description of such graphs, she shows both quantities can be computed fast. Those are the fewest colors needed and the smallest anchor set. The running time grows only a little faster than the size of the graph. The two notions are linked: an anchor set can be turned into a painting by giving its members distinct colors. Her results place these symmetry measures within reach of efficient algorithms for this graph class.
arxiv-2507-09810:
Arman Nejad, Andrew Zhu, Kesha Sorathia, and David Tew extend a fast electron-correlation method from molecules to repeating solids. The method, DLPNO-MP2, saves time by focusing on local pockets of electrons, but it was built for single molecules. The team rebuilt it under repeating boundary conditions, using localized electron functions spread across the crystal.

Their local fitting scheme for the needed integrals proved stable, with lattice sums settling properly. Benchmarks showed the shortcuts behave just as they do in the molecular version and match a sister periodic approach described in a companion paper. Tightening the accuracy threshold moved results smoothly toward the exact values. The team provides reference energies for two- and three-dimensional solids to check future work against.
arxiv-2507-10610:
Zihe Yan and co-authors defend screen-using AI agents against pop-up traps in a 2025 paper. These agents click and type through real interfaces, but a planted pop-up can hijack their attention and steer them into wrong or unsafe clicks.

Studying how attacks bend the model's focus, the team found a layer-wise pattern: correct and hijacked runs diverge in specific middle layers. Their defense, LaSM, turns up the volume on attention and feed-forward parts in exactly those layers, pulling the model's gaze back to task-relevant screen regions. No retraining is needed. Across test sets the defense success rate rose sharply while normal skills stayed intact, a cheap shield for agents that work in messy, open screens.
arxiv-2507-10910:
Zibin Zhao and co-authors build stable knot-like swirls inside quantum droplets, in a 2025 paper. Hopfions are three-dimensional solitons shaped as twisted vortex rings. Two counts define them: how much the ring spins and how much its core twists. Their product gives the Hopf number, the state's topological fingerprint. Realizing them in matter has been a long-standing challenge.

The team solves the equations for a two-component atomic condensate held in a ring-shaped trap. Quantum fluctuation effects, which make the droplet self-bound, prove essential for stability. Whole families of true hopfions with Hopf numbers up to seven were partly stable. Without the fluctuation term, every hopfion fell apart. The work guides experiments chasing these elusive textures.
arxiv-2507-11510:
Roshan Samuel and Jörg Schumacher simulate heated-fluid turbulence at record intensity, in a 2025 paper. Rayleigh-Bénard convection, fluid heated from below and cooled from above, is the classic model of thermal turbulence. Their direct simulations reach a Rayleigh number of ten to the eleventh in a wide flat layer, with air-like properties. They summarize how velocity and temperature fluctuations vary with height and scale with the driving strength.

Near the walls, coherent and incoherent patches contribute differently to the total heat flow. The team also tested what happens when an added shear flow is imposed at the start, freely decaying or steadily forced. The near-wall layer that forms under steady forcing breaks the standard rules, a finding modelers of weather and industry must absorb.
arxiv-2507-11710:
Jay Revolinsky, Harry Shomer, and Jiliang Tang work on link prediction in graphs in a 2025 paper. Graph neural networks can guess missing links between nodes, such as ties between people or papers. Their skill often drops when the test graph comes from a distinct source than the training graph, a shift known as out-of-distribution change.

The authors propose FLEX, a method that makes new subgraphs to train on. It builds subgraphs that match the shape of the target data, and it trains a graph maker and a network against each other. The aim is to keep the made-up graphs close in structure to real ones. Tests on made-up and real graphs show gains in shifted settings. The authors also probe how added graph data changes link results.
arxiv-2507-11810:
Haoxuan Zhang and co-authors survey, in 2025 work, the growing roles of large language models in science. Such models now help at each step, from finding past work to running tests and judging results. Past surveys sorted them by field or task alone, which blurs the line between help with research and true finds.

Their frame sorts systems by four roles: helper, partner, scientist, and judge. Three lenses — how free the system is, what mind work it does, and what kind of find it seeks — keep those roles apart. Helper tools are the most ripe, they find, but shaky on open tasks. Partner tools widen the hunt for ideas, yet trade newness against grounding. Judge tools stay weak at spotting what is new.
arxiv-2507-11910:
Kaustav Chanda and co-authors release a made-up data set for tracking how people walk, built for traffic cameras. Their 2025 paper uses event-based sensors, which record change rather than full frames. Such sensors react fast and handle bright and dark scenes well, traits that help at busy crossings.

Real data for rare or risky walking scenes is scarce, so the team built scenes in a driving simulator. The set holds many labeled walkers with body joint points, across crowds, weather, and light, at four-way crossings in town and country areas. They trained leading pose models on the set and tested them on real sensor data. The results show that skills learned in the simulator carry over, at least in part, to real streets.
arxiv-2507-12210:
Jialiang Zhu, Sanoopkumar P. S., and Arman Farhang analyze the peak power problem in a spread variant of OTFS, a waveform for high mobility links. Their 2025 paper works on the uplink, where a handset's amplifier limits how spiky the signal may be. DFT spreading across the Doppler dimension is the standard taming trick, and the team asks how pulse shaping and resource layout change the outcome.

They derive an upper bound on peak to average power ratio for two layouts, interleaved and block allocation. Interleaving wins, and it also yields a periodic time signal built from repeated symbols, which eases transmitter design. A root raised cosine pulse raised the worst case peak over a rectangular one. Error rate performance matched plain OTFS.
arxiv-2507-12310:
Takla Nateeboon, a solo author, develops a theory of uncertainty for classical communication channels in a 2025 thesis. Channels carry signals that can be blurred or mixed, and a fair way to compare their uncertainty was missing. The thesis builds on the idea of majorization, which ranks how spread out a probability pattern is.

Three different approaches to ranking channel uncertainty are introduced, and all three turn out to agree. That agreement gives the ranking a firm base from many angles. Channel entropy is then defined as a measure that grows with that ranking and adds up over combined channels. Known entropy measures for states extend in a unique best way to channels under this scheme.
arxiv-2507-13210:
Emanuele Greco and six co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv study of a supernova remnant floating oddly far above the Milky Way's disc. The faint radio ring G118.4+37.0 is thought to be the wreckage of the star that birthed the Calvera pulsar, an unusual neutron star in the same high neighborhood. Earlier X-ray data hinted at glowing gas inside the ring but were too shallow to characterize.

New telescope observations revealed shock-heated plasma at low temperature and thin density, plus one harder, hotter clump. The team estimates the remnant is ten to twenty thousand years old and four to five thousand parsecs away, matching the pulsar's distance within the errors. That agreement seals the pairing: a massive star exploded high above the disc. Filaments of glowing hydrogen and patchy gamma rays suggest the blast wave has run into the old wind of its own progenitor star.
arxiv-2507-13310:
Moyi Tian, Jeffrey Brantingham, and Nancy Rodríguez model how online buzz spills into street protest, in a 2025 paper. Social media now shapes acts from dinner picks to uprisings. Their framework couples an online network, where a topic spreads, to an offline layer where people actually gather. From the full random model they derive simpler average-field versions of several depths, which forecast when surges will hit and how big the spark must be.

One dial rules the spill: the rate at which online heat becomes offline action. Too low, nothing ignites; too high, the heat also fails to build, so outbursts need the middle range. On made-up networks, sparse webs need the deeper approximations, while dense webs are fine with simple ones. On two real networks, added depth did not help. The authors offer the models as planning tools for crowd dynamics.
arxiv-2507-13410:
Cheng-Ting Chou and co-authors published this study in 2025. It shows how to steer the output language of a multilingual language model without prompts or retraining. The method uses sparse autoencoders, tools that split a model's inner signals into readable features. Working with two Gemma models, the team found features that fire differently for English versus four other languages. Those languages were Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, and French.

Changing just one such feature at one layer shifted the output language with up to ninety percent success. Meaning stayed intact, as checked by a similarity score. Steering worked best in middle-to-late layers. Certain attention heads tied closely to the language features made the effect stronger. The authors pitch this as a light, readable way to control multilingual generation.
arxiv-2507-13510: Benoit Jacob shows that the Strassen fast method for two-by-two matrix multiplication comes from a volume form. Strassen's method multiplies small matrices with fewer steps than the naive way. Jacob works on the space of such matrices with scalar multiples identified. That quotient space is three-dimensional in his account. Its volume form yields the classic algorithm directly. The short note gives a clean geometric root for a famous trick.
arxiv-2507-13710:
Jing Chang and co-authors present in 2025 a learning system that builds data preparation pipelines on its own. Getting raw data ready is a core but hard step in machine learning, because the choices combine in a vast number of ways. Learning-based searches often fence off parts of that space with rigid rules, which can cut away the best pipeline.

Their system, SoftPipe, swaps rigid rules for soft guidance. A large language model supplies a high-level strategy that steers the search without locking it. That guidance is blended with a learned ranking score for each step and with the agent's own long-term value estimates. Tests on eighteen data sets showed pipeline quality up to about fourteen percent better than rival methods. The system also reached good pipelines almost three times faster.
arxiv-2507-13810:
Theodore Andronikos and colleagues introduce the Quantum Dining Information Brokers problem. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents an entanglement-based quantum protocol. Brokers in separate regions join a metaphorical virtual dinner. Each must share one unique fact with every other broker at once. All sharing must happen in a single parallel step.

Anonymity and privacy are protected by design in the protocol. No broker can tell who sent any fact they receive. Earlier quantum schemes could not match that parallel reach. Three advances over prior work are claimed by the authors. The setup frames anonymous, untraceable exchange for distributed systems. It extends the spirit of dining cryptographers into quantum form. Information markets and secure voting suggest possible uses.
arxiv-2507-13910:
Pranav Kasela, Gabriella Pasi, and Raffaele Perego present a 2025 system for academic search shaped to each scholar. General search floods researchers with off-target hits. PARK first trains a neural reader for retrieval. It then turns the citation web into a knowledge graph and embeds that graph in the same meaning space as the text model. A user profile can then blend what a scholar wrote with the web's hidden shape.

Tests ran across four academic domains. The system beat older graph and personal models in three of the four. Gains reached a tenth over the runner-up on the deep ranking score. Search that knows a scholar's corner of the web can cut hours of sifting. Knowledge graphs give profiles a memory of the field.
arxiv-2507-14510:
Jürgen Knödlseder examines the harm that astronomy itself does to the planet's environment. His 2025 paper argues that human activity is straining Earth's stability at a scale never seen before. Rather than deny or bargain with that fact, he urges astronomers to accept it and change how their field operates.

The focus falls on research facilities, since telescopes and computing sites drive most of the field's greenhouse gas output.
