The paper traces where those impacts come from, from building and running large sites to the energy they consume. It then proposes changes that could make astronomy sustainable. Travel cuts matter too, but facilities are the dominant source and the main target here.
arxiv-2507-15610:
Marco Fusari, Andrea Previtali, and Pablo Spiga wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on normal coverings of finite groups. A group has a normal 2-covering when two proper subgroups, swept around by the group's own symmetries, cover the whole group. Classifying the groups with this trait is done step by step.

The key targets are the minimal cases: groups that have a covering while no smaller quotient of them does. Past work sorted those groups into four classes drawn from the O'Nan-Scott theorem: product action, almost simple, affine, and diagonal. This paper opens the study of the affine class, for groups of small dimension. The affine case covers groups that act on vector spaces, a rich source of examples. Early results here set up the full classification to come.
arxiv-2507-15810:
Comparing whole patterns, not just averages, is a basic need when lifetimes are the data. Garg, Dewan, and Kattumannil build a new yardstick on survival extropy, a score for the doubt left in a remaining lifetime. Their measure gauges how far apart two survival patterns sit.

They derive three ways to estimate the measure from data, using U-statistics, the sample curve itself, and kernel smoothing. Ranges for the true value come from a jackknife-based method and from a normal curve fit. Tests on simulated data compare the yardstick with older ones and check each method on small samples. The authors close with a twist: the measure is sharp enough to spot small changes between images in image sets.
arxiv-2507-15910:
Jialei Wei, Ao Liu, Dejiang Li, and Cuihong Wen present a 2025 neural network that reads physical values from black hole images. The images are made by tracing light rays through curved space, and reading values back with high precision helps test how space bends near a black hole. Real data are scarce, costly, and uneven, which makes the task hard for simple models.

Their network, MANet, uses an attention step to stress the parts of the image that carry the most physical signal. A multiscale pyramid step keeps fine structures such as photon rings and glowing disks from being lost when the image shrinks. On simulated data sets the method beat standard baselines in accuracy and held up better on new cases.
arxiv-2507-16410:
Shalaka Satheesh and co-authors build GG-BBQ in 2025, a German benchmark for gender bias in question answering by large language models. Fair tests often exist first in English, yet German marks gender in grammar in ways English does not. The team starts from an English bias benchmark and turns its gender templates into German.

Machine translation made errors that a language expert then checked and fixed by hand, a step the authors call crucial. Their final set has two parts, one using group terms and one using proper names in their place. Tests of several models built for German found bias in all of them, both with and against common social stereotypes, with scores for accuracy and bias reported side by side.
arxiv-2507-16810:
Arduin Findeis and five co-authors ask if outside tools can help a language model judge which of two replies is better. Their two thousand twenty-five paper notes that such paired choices are used to train and grade models. On fact-heavy, math, and code tasks, judges can be swayed by style and miss plain errors.

Their system gives the judge web search and code run tools, so claims can be checked from the outside. They test it on known bench sets and on three new ones. Tools help in many cases, but not all. The results also show how much scores can shift with small changes in prompts.
arxiv-2507-17310: Alexander Gladkov studies an equation for flow through porous material, in a math paper published in 2025. The equation includes a term that absorbs material as it spreads, and its edge condition links the boundary to values inside in a nonlinear, nonlocal way. Starting data are taken as nonnegative. He proves that solutions exist for a short time and sets up a comparison rule for them. He then shows when solutions can be extended for all time and when they instead blow up, growing beyond bound in finite time.
arxiv-2507-17510:
Maciej Kucharski, Mateusz Kwasnicki, and Blazej Wrobel study how a cut-off version of a classic transform compares with the full one, in a 2025 paper. Riesz transforms are core tools in analysis. The truncated kind stops the action at a set scale. Whether the full transform controls the cut one, at a cost that ignores dimension, was open for higher orders.

The authors factor the truncated transform through the full one. The middle operator is a smoothing with a radial kernel. They prove that kernel stays positive only for the first two orders. For higher orders, its size grows without bound as dimension rises. One bound still holds for all orders. The result draws a sharp line in harmonic analysis.
arxiv-2507-17710:
Masatoshi Hirabayashi forecasts how asteroid Apophis will spin after its close Earth pass in 2029. The asteroid will skim within six Earth radii, a rare natural experiment. Earth's tides will twist its spin, and if the rock deforms even slightly, the spin change may differ from a rigid body's.

A simplified model tests that idea across stiffness values. If the asteroid is fairly stiff, its spin drifts only a few degrees from the rigid forecast over a year. If it is very soft, the same drift can appear within days of the pass. Telescopes and visiting spacecraft could catch the effect and probe the interior.
arxiv-2507-17810:
A machine learning tool that reads the proton's gluon map from lattice sums is built by Brandon Kriesten and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Gluons are the bits that glue the proton's parts. Their spread is key to how matter holds, but it hides from direct sight. The tool is a type of net that maps grid sum outputs back to that spread.

The read spread matched known fits well where grid data bind most. A check of the net's inner code showed it learned real links, not noise. The team frames the tool as a bridge between grid sums and fit work.
arxiv-2507-17910:
Roman Dmitriev and four co-authors map how a single molecule loses its quantum spin state in a 2025 paper. The molecule can serve as a qubit, and its spin relaxes as it trades energy with the molecule's own vibrations, called phonons, so knowing which vibrations matter guides better designs.

Starting from basic theory, the team built the full relaxation tensor for the molecule, counting both one-vibration and two-vibration routes. Only three vibrations drove most of the slow spin decay, and a single one caused most of the fast phase loss. The computed times matched lab measures with no fitted tweaks. The work shows chemists which motions to stiffen or soften when shaping a molecular qubit.
arxiv-2507-18210:
Simulating fluids with moving particles has a quiet flaw: a consistency error that acts like invisible friction and slows the flow. Feng Wang and Xiangyu Hu chase that flaw in a 2025 paper across two test flows, a long channel pushed by pressure and a sloshing wave pulled by gravity. Background pressure makes the error worse in both.

They vary channel length, resolution, outlet pressure, and wave depth to map what feeds the error. A modern correction technique trims it but cannot remove it at root. A medical nozzle benchmark shows the same drag in complex shapes, which the authors say makes correction schemes hard to avoid in practice.
arxiv-2507-18810:
Charles Gauthier wrote an economics paper in 2025 on family labor and child welfare. Governments often aid families through cash transfers or parent training. Judging those reforms needs a measure of child welfare, which cannot be seen directly. Gauthier uses a shared household model where adults trade off leisure, spending, and child welfare.

He shows the model can partly pin down how parent inputs shape child welfare in panel data. A new estimation method handles measurement error and builds sound confidence ranges. Dutch couple data then reveal how the making of child welfare varies across households. The tools can sharpen the design of family policy.
arxiv-2507-18910:
Agada Oche and three co-authors reviewed retrieval-augmented generation systems that pair language models with search, in a paper published in 2025. Such systems ground model output in retrieved text, which cuts invented facts and stale knowledge. The team traces the line from early open question tools to the newest builds. Each core part receives a close read: the retrieval craft, the generation model, and the fusion step.

A year-by-year sweep shows the fast growth of the field and its turns. Firm use receives its own look, with strain from private data, safeguards, and scale. Side-by-side tests grade builds on retrieval accuracy, generation flow, delay, and cost. Gaps that remain are named: retrieval quality, privacy, and integration cost. New fixes, from mixed retrieval to agent-shaped builds, close the map.
arxiv-2507-19010: Mayank Manjrekar presented in 2025 an experimental, verified clause processor that helps prove multiplier circuits correct inside a hardware check system used at Arm. Integer multipliers appear in designs from division units to matrix engines, and proving them by hand takes great effort. The new processor fits the existing register-transfer proof books and largely automates that proof work. The short abstract frames the tool and its setting, rather than giving test numbers.
arxiv-2507-19210:
Etienne Buehrle, Ömer Şahin Taş, and Christoph Stiller offered a convex route to planning motion for systems that switch between modes, in a 2025 paper. Hybrid systems, such as robots that walk and then jump, mix smooth motion with sudden switches. Exact planning for them is often too hard to solve in practice.

Their method rests on a framework of graphs of convex sets, filled in with a relaxation based on occupation measures. The result is a convex problem shaped like a shortest-path program, which solvers can finish at the global best. The team used it to plan paths under time-logic rules. In tests, the cost bound from their method sat close to the cost from a fixed-sequence nonconvex solver. Their method ran far faster than the mixed-integer route, and the code is public.
arxiv-2507-19410:
Henrik Garde refines a medical imaging math method in a solo 2025 note. Electrical impedance tomography infers inside conductivity from surface voltages. When the region is split into zones of fixed shape, the task gets easier. Garde asks how little boundary data can still pin down the values.

His older method needed the full boundary map and unknown zone shapes. The new version assumes the zone layout is known in advance. Only a finite set of partial boundary measures is then required. No prior bounds on the conductivity values are needed either. The note adjusts the earlier proofs to fit these weaker demands. Such savings matter for scanners that cannot probe a whole surface.
arxiv-2507-19710:
Ronak Upasham, Tathagata Dey, and Pushpak Bhattacharyya wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It turns tables into text that carries a point of view, not just the bare numbers.

Most table-to-text tools state the facts flatly. This pipeline adds judgment, in three stages. First it pulls RDF triples from the table. Then it weaves them into a smooth account. Last it blends in the subjective read. The middle graph form keeps the facts straight and the steps open to check. Small tuned T5 models do the work, yet the scores match GPT-3.5 and beat two open rivals on several counts. Tests, both scored and read by eye, back the claim.
arxiv-2507-19810:
Zosiamliana and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on new materials that might store hydrogen for clean energy. The materials are double perovskite hydrides, crystals that hold hydrogen inside a repeating framework. The team studied six variants built from lithium, sodium, or potassium paired with aluminum or silicon.

All checks were done by computer, using two levels of theory to cross-check the results. Every variant proved stable on paper, with negative formation energies and sound mechanical behavior. The silicon versions act as semiconductors and absorb ultraviolet light strongly, hinting at uses in light-based devices. The aluminum versions behave like metals instead. The results help judge which of these crystals deserve lab trials for hydrogen storage.
arxiv-2507-19910:
Jun Wu, Weijie Yuan, Qingqing Cheng, and Haijia Jin design drone formations that sense, communicate, and save energy at the same time. In low-altitude networks a ground station must steer several drone groups while also running sensing tasks. Flight time is precious, so the design exploits the upwash of air from a neighbor's rotors, the same effect that lets birds fly in a V.

Each drone updates its position estimate locally, then blends it with neighbors' estimates in a distributed learning scheme. The team casts the whole problem as minimizing a control cost under limits on power and sensing quality. A two-step method solves it: a closed-form cost expression, then an iterative approximation routine. Simulations confirm the V formation is the most energy-efficient shape and beat benchmark designs.
arxiv-2507-20010:
Pairing people as roommates by mutual taste sounds simple, yet some groups admit no stable pairing at all. Muge Fidan and Esra Erdem work on that hard case in 2025. A stable pairing is one where no two people would both rather ditch their assigned partners for each other.

When no such pairing exists, the pair aim for a good-enough one that is shaped to each person. Their method weighs more than ranked lists: it counts habits, settled likes, and each person's circle of favoured friends. Worked examples and tests show how the tailored pairings play out. The aim is a fair fallback for real tasks, from dorm rooms to shared flats, where a perfect stable match may be out of reach.
arxiv-2507-20310:
The authors prove that certain models of cells chasing chemical signals stay well behaved forever, in a 2025 math paper. The models mix several forces at once: cells spread, drift up a chemical gradient, grow, and are damped by their own steepness. Without care, such models can blow up in finite time, predicting absurd cell densities.

The system studied adds local and nonlocal growth terms plus a gradient-based brake, all inside a smooth bounded region with no flow through the walls. Starting from smooth data, the authors prove solutions exist for all time and stay bounded when growth dominates in the stated regime. That guarantee lets biologists trust long-run forecasts from the model. It also guides which terms modelers must keep to stay realistic.
arxiv-2507-20610:
Rima Benhammadi, Anne De Wit, and Juan J Hidalgo simulate how uneven rock permeability shapes a dissolving reaction front underground, in this 2025 paper. The setting matters for storing carbon dioxide, where a heavier fluid sinks and reacts as it mixes. The team compares four layouts: even rock, rock layered across the flow, rock layered along it, and a random patchwork.

Layering across the flow slowed everything down, giving the widest fronts and the weakest dissolution. Layering along the flow or using a patchwork sped up mixing and product formation beyond the even case. In the patchwork, short sideways patches made fingers spread sideways, while long ones channeled flow downward. Where the reaction steadied the density, the flow stalled near the density peak. Structure, the authors show, is destiny for this process.
arxiv-2507-20910:
Constantia Alexandrou, Simone Bacchio, Giannis Koutsou, Bhavna Prasad, and Gregoris Spanoudes present a 2025 paper computing the electric and magnetic shapes of protons and neutrons from first principles. Lattice QCD models quarks on a space-time grid. The team used three grid spacings to take the continuum limit directly at the physical pion mass.

Form factors describe how charge and magnetism spread inside the nucleons. Careful fits handled excited-state effects, and high-statistics tricks tamed the noisy disconnected quark loops. Fits to the momentum trend yielded the electric and magnetic radii and their moments. The proton's electric radius came out near 0.860 femtometers. Neutron and magnetic radii are reported with two kinds of error, statistical and systematic.
arxiv-2507-21110:
Kezhen Zhong, Basem Suleiman, Shijing Chen, and Abdelkarim Erradi present SemRAG in this two thousand twenty-five paper on question answering. Retrieval augmented generation feeds a language model with fetched texts. To fit it to a niche field, most ways need costly fine-tuning, which can lead to overfitting. SemRAG works on the fetch side. A semantic chunking method cuts texts where sentence embedding scores say the topic shifts, keeping the sense whole and cutting compute cost.

Fetched facts are set out as knowledge graphs. These catch how entities link. On multi-hop tests and Wikipedia-based tests, SemRAG beat standard fetch ways. It raised how apt and how right the fetched facts were. The team also studies how chunk buffer size should be tuned per data set. The pitch is a sound niche pipeline, with no fine-tuning that eats up resources, suiting it to lasting use at scale.
arxiv-2507-21310:
Gonzalo Palma, Spyros Sypsas, and Danilo Tapia challenge a standard view of quantum fields in the early universe in a 2025 paper. In de Sitter space, the geometry of fast expansion, light scalar fields were thought to develop runaway infrared growth that a stochastic method must tame. The authors say that story mixes two different cases.

When a shift symmetry protects the field, its interactions involve only derivatives, and no physical observable grows. Without that symmetry, loop corrections do diverge as mass falls, yet the results stay fully symmetric and the time behavior of basic correlators does not change. A symmetry-respecting scheme can remove the divergences order by order. Their verdict: no genuine secular growth occurs.
arxiv-2507-21410:
Dzuba and Flambaum compute how the total binding energy of an atom's electrons shifts between isotopes in a 2025 paper. Isotopes share the same number of protons but differ in neutrons, so their nuclei differ slightly in size. That size change, called the field shift, moves electron energy levels by tiny amounts that precision experiments can measure.

Using a relativistic method that includes magnetic effects, they tabulate shift coefficients for neutral atoms and singly charged ions up to element 120. Closed-shell systems from neon to oganesson anchor the table. A simple power law reproduces the computed shifts within about one percent. Because inner electrons dominate, neutral atoms and their ions differ by only a few percent, so the table also serves higher charge states.
arxiv-2507-21910:
Tania Robens and Rui Santos survey added scalar fields beyond the standard model of particle physics. In that model the Higgs part uses just one field. New spin free fields can be added by new terms in the core math that rules how bits of matter act.

Such fields could yield dark matter parts or new sources of the imbalance that left more matter than antimatter. Tests come from big colliders and from dark matter hunts that probe links between seen and dark worlds. The piece maps which added fields are still allowed and which are ruled out.
arxiv-2507-22110:
Thomas Bakx, Mikhail Ivanov, Oliver Philcox and Zvonimir Vlah present a fast, exact pipeline for the one-loop galaxy bispectrum in redshift space. The bispectrum adds shape information beyond the power spectrum, but one-loop theory is slow to compute for each cosmology tried. Their COBRA method expands the matter power spectrum into eight templates that capture cosmology change to very high accuracy.

With that trick, each one-loop bispectrum takes about a second to compute. A full treatment of random terms also improved the match to data. On huge simulations, the theory fit well and recovered dark matter density, the Hubble constant and other parameters with tight errors. Joined with the power spectrum, it shrank key errors by a quarter to nearly a half.
arxiv-2507-22210:
Aviv Spinner, Erika DeBenedictis and Corey Hudson ask whether more data keeps helping protein language models, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Biological data are redundant, noisy and sparse, so scaling behavior is unclear. The team trained models on yearly snapshots of a major protein database from 2011 to 2024 and tested them on protein function prediction.

No saturation appeared: performance improved with added data, though not steadily. Trends differed between unsupervised and supervised setups. On one well-studied enzyme, unsupervised predictions improved year over year but did not yet consistently beat a supervised baseline. The authors call for smarter data acquisition and deeper study of data scaling in protein modeling.
arxiv-2507-22310:
Justin Finkel and Paul A O'Gorman improve a method for sampling rare climate extremes in a 2025 paper. Ensemble boosting takes a simulated extreme event and nudges it slightly to spawn many near variants, saving the long wait for the next natural event. The trick's success hinges on when to split the runs: too early and the event dissolves, too late and the variants stay alike.

Working with a simplified storm-track model, the authors set the choice of split time as an optimization against a known truth. They propose a stand-in goal, based on spread and strength, that can be computed without that truth. With a well-chosen split time, boosting sampled very rare extremes accurately, and the stand-in goal found near-best times that shifted sensibly with place in the flow.
arxiv-2507-22410:
Checking whether a young child understood a story usually means asking good questions, and writing those questions by hand is slow. The authors propose a method that generates reading comprehension questions for children in kindergarten through second grade who are learning English. The method aims to cover the whole story and to match each learner's level.

It can produce many question types at varied difficulty, from recall to simple inference. The team tested several language models inside the framework on the FairytaleQA dataset of story questions. Performance differed across models, which shows where current systems stand. The authors see the approach as a building block for AI reading tutors that can assess children as they learn.
arxiv-2507-22910:
Sergio Di Meglio and five co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv case study on using language models to clean up hotel data. Booking platforms like theirs ingest property details from third parties, and gaps or contradictions in those feeds frustrate travelers and cost sales. The team deployed two open models on a live reservation platform to generate consistent property descriptions with few fabrications.

The bigger model won on quality: descriptions were more complete, more precise, and hallucinated about a third as often, while running shorter. But it cost roughly ten times more per hour and demanded ten times the graphics memory. The fine-tuned smaller model was the bargain, nearly as accurate at a fraction of the running cost. The authors frame the study as field guidance for industry teams: the right model is an economic decision as much as a technical one.
arxiv-2507-23710:
Layered perovskites were supposed to bind their excitons tighter as the layers thin, but silver-bismuth versions break that rule. Pierre Lechifflart and co-authors used heavy-duty quantum math to find out why. Setting real crystal structures beside idealized ones let them isolate the roles of octahedral distortion, layer spacing, and stacking order. Distortions driven by silver's directional bonding decide where the exciton lives in momentum space and what it looks like.

Those distortions, not confinement alone, cause the reversed, non-monotonic trend. Underneath, the confinement physics still mirrors the familiar lead-based materials, giving designers clear levers for tuning these lead-free alternatives.
arxiv-2508-00010:
Ruibo Wang, Baha Eddine Youcef Belmekki, and their co-authors ask when a flat map model is good enough for satellite and high altitude networks. Their 2025 paper notes that non terrestrial networks are growing fast, and stochastic geometry gives a low cost way to study large networks. Flat models ignore Earth's curvature, which skews results at high altitude, yet they are widely used for simplicity.

The team defines a relative error measure to size the gap between flat and spherical models. They build a method that generates matching flat and spherical point patterns side by side, then compares them on several network measures. The measure tells analysts when the flat shortcut is safe and when the sphere is required. That guidance saves computing where the shortcut holds.
arxiv-2508-00110:
Katharine Clark and Paul McNicholas extend a clustering method to functional data that may contain outliers, published in 2025. Functional data are curves rather than single numbers, which makes grouping them hard: the data are effectively infinite-dimensional, and stray curves can wreck the groups. Their method, funOCLUST, adapts an outlier-aware clustering framework to this setting.

The approach clusters curves while trimming the ones that do not belong, instead of forcing every curve into a group. Tests on simulated data, where the truth is known, and on real-world curve data sets checked both sides of the job: finding the right groups and flagging the right odd curves. The authors report strong performance on both counts and offer the method for fields awash in curve data.
arxiv-2508-00310:
Yong Zhang and Xianfeng Chen design a 2025 material that shields objects from low-frequency shaking. The material is a metamaterial, a structure whose behavior comes from its shape rather than its base stuff. It aims for near-zero stiffness: stiff when holding a steady load, yet soft when a vibration hits, which is the mix that blocks slow shaking best.

Older designs reach that mix by joining a part that pushes back with a part that gives way. This design uses single shell pieces alone, whose curved shape and bending give the same effect. The authors test the shells in the lab and in computer models, tuning their shape for the ideal response. The tuned structure showed strong blocking of low shaking, and it can serve as a building block for larger shields.
arxiv-2508-00410:
Zizhuo Zhang and eight co-authors teach language models to reason without any human-labeled answers, by letting two views of a problem grade each other. Standard reinforcement learning for reasoning leans on checked answers, which are costly to make. Label-free methods that reward a model for agreeing with itself often collapse, settling into confident but empty routines.

Their framework, Co-rewarding, seeks agreement across different views instead. One version pairs each question with a semantically similar one and rewards consistent reasoning across the pair. Another keeps a slow-moving copy of the model as a teacher whose pseudo-labels steady training. Combining the two helped further. Across math reasoning benchmarks, training stayed stable and beat other label-free methods, gaining about 3.3 points on average and over 7 points on one smaller model. In some tests it matched or passed training with true answer labels.
arxiv-2508-00810:
Yan Jin and six co-authors build a machine that solves hard choice tasks by the play of hundreds of light pulses in a tiny ring. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such tasks grow too fast for plain digital machines. Light is a swift carrier of facts, but its parts barely touch, which makes direct work hard. Fresh non-linear photon gear gives strong play among pulse states. The team traps hundreds of pulses in one ring and ties them with a feedback web that can be set at will. By a tweak to self-feedback, each pulse takes on a spin-like split. The full set then acts as an Ising machine, a form built for choice tasks.
arxiv-2508-01010:
Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan introduces, in twenty twenty-five, van der Put Neural Networks, a learning architecture built for strictly hierarchical data. Standard networks embed data in Euclidean space, a poor fit for trees such as taxonomies, word senses, or file systems. His neurons are indicator functions of p-adic balls, nested regions from number theory where distance reflects shared ancestry. Every weight is itself a p-adic number, giving exact subtree meaning. A new theorem shows a bounded-depth network of this form can represent any tree of that depth.

Since gradients vanish in this discrete space, he proposes perturbation-based optimizers. On benchmarks, a CPU-only build hit near-perfect leaf accuracy on WordNet nouns, and strong scores on gene ontology and mammal taxonomy tasks. The learned metric is perfectly ultrametric.
arxiv-2508-01110:
Ezequiel Santos introduces an open-source setup that turns an iPhone into a motion controller, in this 2025 paper. The system runs fully offline and uses only Apple's own frameworks. Motion sensors in the phone track how it tilts and moves. A peer-to-peer link sends that data to a second device ten times a second, and a haptics engine answers with a buzz the user can feel.

Built-in logging measured delays end to end without needing synced clocks. The average delay came in near seventy milliseconds on home Wi-Fi, with nearly all delays below seventy-four. A test game ran at a public event with twenty-one players, holding stable links throughout. The work targets fast prototyping for mobile interaction research, where custom hardware would slow things down.
arxiv-2508-01610:
Rhys Bowden and co-authors derive how to size a demanding kind of trial: factorial, longitudinal, and randomized at two levels at once. Their paper appeared in 2025. Such trials test a personal treatment and a group-level treatment together, with clusters of people followed over time, in designs like stepped wedge or cluster crossover. Older sizing formulas cover simpler mixes but not these longitudinal cluster versions.

The team presents dedicated sample size math for continuous outcomes in these split-plot designs. Getting the size right matters: too few clusters wastes the trial, too many wastes money and patient goodwill. The authors say trialists planning combined individual and community interventions, in schools or clinics, now have formulas that match the design they actually run.
arxiv-2508-02210:
George Close, Kris Hong, Thomas Hain, and Stefan Goetze present a tool that scores speech quality with no clean copy to compare. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such scores help judge speech enhancement systems. Past neural tools need large sets of speech with human scores to train on.

Their tool, WhiSQA, takes its input traits from the encoder of Whisper, a speech model trained for transcription. Those traits prove a strong base for quality scores. On all test sets of a known bench, its scores track human ratings better than recent tools. It also adapts to new domains far better than a widely used rival metric.
arxiv-2508-02410:
Lega and co-authors ask how the early solar system kept several rings of dust apart for millions of years in a 2025 paper. Meteorites carry isotope fingerprints proving that inner and outer solar material stayed separate. A young Jupiter explains part of it: the gap it carved blocks drifting pebbles. But that alone cannot preserve dust inside its orbit for so long.

The authors extend earlier work into three dimensions, adding real radiation transport and magnetic effects. In low-viscosity disks with the right cooling times, a giant planet can carve secondary gaps inside the main one, leaving raised rings between them. Those bumps trap dust locally. Whether they form depends on how the disk sheds heat, which the radiation treatment decides. The rings give the meteorite record its missing shelves.
arxiv-2508-02510:
Daniela Thyssens and three co-authors study how the training data's shape decides routing solver performance in this 2025 paper. Neural solvers learn delivery style problems from examples. They still trail hand built heuristics on open benchmarks. The authors change the game: they build one large base distribution of stops, then sample both training and test problems from it. The test cases are new, but they share the base's hidden structure. Classical meta-heuristics and leading neural solvers faced the same task.

Under this planted structure, the gap between neural solvers and the specialists shrank. Learning pays when the world has a stable shape to learn. The authors argue benchmark design has been unfair to learners: random instances erase the very regularity learning exploits. Real fleets do have such regularity, since cities and depots persist.
arxiv-2508-02610:
Sanchita Kamath and co-authors build a virtual reality boxing game that gives blind and low-vision players a real workout, in a 2025 paper. Blind people get less exercise than sighted peers, largely for want of engaging, accessible options. Sound-only games rarely support moving through space or land a satisfying punch. PunchPulse was designed with blind players, not just for them, over seven months.

Three blind co-designers shaped the game through repeated refinement, with more blind testers joining later trials. Players duck, weave, and strike using rich sensory feedback. Every study participant reached at least moderate exercise intensity. Immersion and engagement ran high. The work argues virtual reality can host intensity-driven, inclusive fitness.
arxiv-2508-03010:
Liu, Zhang, Lu, and Chen show a way to send more sound data at once by using all parts of sound speed, in work from twenty twenty-five. Sound must carry data where radio fails, as in nets under water and deep sea work. Sound waves push along their line of travel, and in the past they used just one channel: pressure. That one-channel cap holds back how much sound can carry, at its root.

The speed of a sound wave is a vector, and it has three parts that act on their own. The team uses all three parts as split channels, much like polarization does for light. One vector sensor at the far end reads all three at once. Tests and math show live sending that holds up well. Mixed with frequency and phase, the trick can lift how much sound carries by a lot.
arxiv-2508-03110:
Zizhong Li, Haopeng Zhang, and Jiawei Zhang show how a search backed answer system can be fooled, in a 2025 paper. Such systems fetch outside text to help a language model answer with fresh facts. That open door cuts both ways: bad text in the store can be fetched and steer the reply.

Their attack works word by word. A small open model writes poisoned passages, then tweaks them step by step so they rank high in search and sway the final answer. It works with full or no access to the target system. In tests it beat past attacks on both the search stage and the end reply. The team frames it as a warning for builders.
arxiv-2508-03310:
Giorgia Zaccaria and co-authors propose a safer way to group messy data in a 2025 statistics paper. Standard grouping methods treat a whole row of data as spoiled when even one entry in it is odd. With many variables, that habit throws away much good data. Fuzzy grouping adds a second twist: each item can belong partly to several groups at once.

The new method judges single entries rather than whole rows, so clean entries in a partly spoiled row still count. The group patterns it finds also help it spot which entries are truly off, and it can repair them. Tests on simulated data and two real data sets showed the approach works well. The authors close with advice on setting its controls, so users can tune how strict the cleaning should be.
arxiv-2508-03610:
Michael Mühlbauer and Timo Schmid refine a method for mapping how people spread across a landscape when privacy rules hide exact addresses, in a 2025 paper. Analysts often know only totals per district, shown as shaded maps. Undoing that grouping to estimate fine-grained density is possible but rough. The authors add side information, such as satellite or land-use data, to sharpen the picture.

Their method blends the density guessed from side data with the estimate rebuilt from grouped counts, weighted by how strongly the two agree. Computer simulations test the blend under good and poor side data. Two real cases show it at work, starting with population density from the 2022 German census round. Better density maps feed transport planning, service placement, and emergency planning where headcounts per street matter.
arxiv-2508-03810:
Neural networks can stand in for quantum fields, at least when the network grows without bound. Srimoyee Sen and Varun Vaidya ask whether the trick survives real calculations with finitely many neurons. Using a simple interacting scalar theory as the test bed, they computed the first corrections in inverse neuron number for two basic correlation measures, after the usual cleanup of infinities.

The resulting series leaned too hard on the high-energy cutoff, converging weakly and threatening accuracy. The authors propose a tweak to the network design that improves the convergence. They also map which theory parameters and neuron counts keep the extracted answers trustworthy. The study marks a checkpoint for the young idea of doing field theory on neurons.
arxiv-2508-04310:
A seven-author team proves a clean case where quantum mechanics beats every classical method with certainty. The task is to tell whether an unknown permutation of n objects is even or odd. Classically, anything short of checking all n labels leaves success no better than a coin flip. The authors show that entangled particles settle the question perfectly.

Each particle needs only about the square root of n distinguishable states, far fewer than the classical demand. Below that threshold, quantum methods also collapse to guessing, so the boundary is sharp. For small cases the authors write down the exact states that work. They also measure how much entanglement those states must carry: close to the maximum possible, and in some cases fully maximal. Because the task needs no oracle or contrived setup, they offer it as a simple, rigorous showcase of genuine quantum advantage.
arxiv-2508-04510:
Michael Unger, Oliver Lux, and Oliver Reitebuch report spotting laser pulses from satellites with a cosmic ray observatory on the ground. Their 2025 paper uses the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina, whose telescopes watch faint ultraviolet light. Side-scattered light from space lasers can cross those telescopes.

The team rebuilt laser shots from a wind-measuring satellite taken over three years, and added first shots from a newer atmospheric satellite launched in 2024. Such shots let scientists study local air particles and check telescope calibration. They also give ground truth on how well the satellite instruments perform. The newer satellite's orbit suits joint detection by two observatories, which could align their energy scales. The paper links space climate tools with ground cosmic ray science.
arxiv-2508-04610:
Mia and co-authors build a brain-style defense that keeps learning new network attacks in a 2025 paper. Intrusion detectors usually freeze after training, so fresh attack types slip past until retraining. Spiking neural networks, which fire in brief pulses, promise low power and fast adaptation.

Their two-stage system pairs a static spiking filter with a dynamic classifier that grows new units when required. A tweaked timing-based learning rule lets it absorb novel threats without erasing old ones, the classic forgetting problem. On a standard attack benchmark it reached about 85 percent accuracy overall, and simulations showed sparse activity suited to neuromorphic chips.
arxiv-2508-04710:
Finding past court cases that match a new dispute is hard because search tools match surface facts rather than the legal issue at stake. Vishnuprabha and co-authors build a retrieval system for Indian case law that first turns a fact pattern into targeted legal questions, then searches with those questions. Structured summaries tuned to Indian cases feed the search, and the system explains why each case fits.

On a test set from the FIRE 2019 data, the system far beat the standing benchmark on average precision and reached a mean recall of 0.67. Legal experts checked the summaries and explanations by hand. The authors frame the shift as moving from fact matching to issue matching.
arxiv-2508-04810:
Gravity may not rest on fixed constants. In one view, the strength of gravity and the push of dark energy shift a bit with the energy scale of the scene. Nicolas Bertini and Marcos Novaes test that view in a 2025 study with the standard tools used to check gravity against solar system facts.

They let both constants grow or shrink as a smooth series in the scale, then work out what the view predicts at the first level past Newton. A new term shows up that has no match in the standard frame. That term reshapes how pressure and inner energy are read, but it leaves the paths of heavy bodies alone. Solar system tests, then, cannot yet rule this view out.
arxiv-2508-05110:
Abigail Gentle proves that the best private data-collection schemes must have a combinatorial shape, in a 2025 paper. Local differential privacy scrambles each person's answer before it leaves their phone, so a company can estimate population statistics without seeing anyone's true value. Protocols built on balanced incomplete block designs, tidy arrangements of subsets, were known to achieve the lowest possible error.

The open question was whether anything else could match them. Gentle's answer is no: any protocol reaching optimal error corresponds to such a design. Combined with earlier work, this completely characterizes the optimal protocols. Requiring optimal communication too narrows the field further, to the symmetric designs. For engineers, the theorem ends a search: there is one family of shapes to use, and it is already known.
arxiv-2508-05410:
Manas Bhargava and co-authors build modular robots whose muscles are printed plastic rods that shrink under infrared light, in a 2025 paper. Animals distribute actuation through their whole bodies; robots mostly centralize it and stay tethered. Their building block pairs 3D-printed bones with liquid crystal elastomer muscles. Aiming infrared at one rod contracts it, so control is local, wireless, and spread across the skeleton.

Two design tools complete the kit: one shapes the skeleton to hit several target poses, the other co-designs skeleton and gait for walking. Built robots morphed into complex shapes, switched control schemes, and adapted to their surroundings. The authors frame the system as a step toward robots that, like organisms, change form and function on demand, designed computationally rather than by hand.
arxiv-2508-05510:
Yi-Mei Wang and co-authors work out how a single photon moves through a waveguide coupled to a driven giant atom. Their 2025 paper studies a three-level atom of the lambda type, which touches the one-dimensional waveguide at several points rather than one. Chiral coupling means the atom interacts with light differently depending on the direction of travel.

Using a real-space scattering approach, the team derives formulas valid in both fast and slow response regimes. A driving field splits the dip in the transmission spectrum into two, and widening the drive widens the split. Tuning the coupling lets the system switch between full transmission and perfect reflection. Making the atom larger adds more reflection and decoupling points in the slow regime. Such control is a building block for quantum networks.
arxiv-2508-05610:
Bonelli and co-authors set a 5D high-fill for a class of Argyres-Douglas frames. The fill nests the frames in a flow from 5D field frames on S1. A q-Painleve and gauge tie does the core work in the text. That tie lets one count 5D BPS sums as a spread form. The spread runs in the Wilson loop mean with whole q parts. Those parts come from gauge work on a blown-up form.

A 5D lift of a known tool-state tie builds those parts. Phase charts for the 4D ends get care in the work. AD spots, the odd points of those ends, get pinned there. Worked counts cover one named frame and its H0 end. That end is the (A1, A2) AD frame in the text.
arxiv-2508-05910:
Wayne Aitken, Kimberly Ayers, and Hanson Smith unify two lines of work on Mahler measure. Their 2025 paper starts from the classic Boyd-Lawton theorem, which links measures of one-variable objects to limits of many-variable ones. One recent team pushed the theorem toward multivariable limits. Another pair stretched the single-variable form to broader measures.

The authors build one frame that does both jobs at once. Inside it, the single-variable upgrades of Issa and Lalín gain multivariable forms in the newer style. The result generalizes both source works in a single sweep. Readers in number theory who use Mahler measure get a cleaner, wider tool. The paper is a piece of pure theory, offered as groundwork for later use.
arxiv-2508-06010:
Andrey Sarantsev, Angel Piotrowski, and Ian Anderson build a time series model for three asset classes in a financial simulator. Their 2025 arXiv paper tracks US and international stocks plus corporate bonds. Monthly and annual returns feed an online wealth simulation app. Users can add regular contributions or withdrawals. Four factors drive the model's behavior over time.

The factors span stock volatility, earnings, bond rates, and Treasury spreads. Their value gauge improves on a classic cyclically adjusted ratio. Linear regressions are tuned until residuals behave like white noise. Kernel density methods then model the remaining randomness. Long-term stability results are stated and proved. The app lets savers test plans against realistic market paths.
arxiv-2508-06110:
Yiran Rex Ma introduces PanelTR, a way for language models to reason about tables without any training examples, in a 2025 paper. Table questions and fact checks often rely on labelled data, and plain language models tend to trail simple trained models on such tasks.

PanelTR gives the work to a panel of model agents with five scientist roles. Each agent studies the table alone, reviews its own answer, and then joins a group review with the others. Across four test sets, the panel beat plain language models and matched fully trained ones. Because the method needs no training data, it can be pointed at new tables at once. Ma argues the same staged discussion could suit other hard tasks.
arxiv-2508-06410:
Sean Borneman applies quantum annealing to a splitting problem in twenty twenty-five. Set splitting asks for a two-coloring of elements so no given subset is monochromatic. It is a classic hard combinatorial problem. Borneman casts it as a QUBO problem, the native language of quantum annealers.

The contribution lies in the penalty functions. They are built so the QUBO ground state corresponds exactly to valid splits of every subset. Logical qubit needs grow linearly with problem size in the formulation. Empirical tests converged to globally optimal solutions with high accuracy over repeated trials. Current hardware, though, inflates physical qubit counts exponentially when embedding. Readers get a clean formulation whose promise waits on better annealer hardware.
arxiv-2508-06510:
Davood Momeni builds a method for working backward from gravity's energy density to the Hamiltonian that drives a system. In curved spacetime, observers can often state how energy is spread, while the rules beneath stay hidden. His 2025 paper sets out an inverse route between the two.

Starting from local thermal balance and Liouville dynamics, the method links the coarse energy profile to a distribution function of Boltzmann form. Functional inversion then recovers the Hamiltonian from that function. The tools join relativistic kinetic theory, statistical mechanics, and covariant thermodynamics. Momeni names uses in expanding-universe cosmology, loop quantum gravity corrections, holography, and the SYK model, framing the route as a probe of hidden dynamics.
arxiv-2508-06610:
Vivek Jha, Debbijoy Bhattacharya, and Hum Chand study flickering light from active galaxies in a 2025 paper. Active galactic nuclei shine as black holes feed, and their optical brightness wanders over years. The team asked what drives the size and pace of that wander.

Five years of survey light curves were matched to a hard X-ray catalog of these objects. Variability timescale grew with black hole mass and with luminosity, which points at the accretion disk's own physics. X-ray traits showed no clear link to the optical wander. Radio strength showed only a weak negative tie, so jets seem minor here. The authors read the pattern as heat-driven disk behavior and call for bigger samples.
arxiv-2508-07010:
Roberto Balestri and Guglielmo Pescatore built a multi-agent system to pull story arcs from serial television in two thousand twenty-five. Long shows spread plots over many episodes, which makes arcs hard to track. Their system borrows ideas from how human memory works.

Language models supply a kind of semantic memory for common story patterns, while a vector database stores arc steps as episodic memory. Agent steps mimic working memory as they merge the two. Tested on the first season of Grey's Anatomy, the system found anthology, soap, and genre-specific arcs. It did well on self-contained arcs but struggled with overlapping ones, and a screen lets people refine its work.
arxiv-2508-07110:
Lorenzo Ruotolo and ten co-authors present a 2025 paper on physically designing a specialized machine learning processor for the smallest coming chip nodes. At angstrom-era scales, wires dominate cost and power, so the team designed for short wires and dense cores from the start. Their processor uses specialized memory structures and vector units that process many data lanes at once. Five variants were synthesized and evaluated on an advanced test process.

Against a leading rival design, theirs needed less than half the normalized wire length and packed over three times the density. The numbers barely varied across the five variants, suggesting the efficiency is built into the architecture rather than tuned per case. Little manual layout work was required. The authors pitch the design as a cheap, wire-friendly path for next-generation AI accelerators.
arxiv-2508-07910:
Computing a planet's gravity field when the planet is lumpy and uneven is the task of a 2025 paper by Alex Myhill and co-authors. Their software package gives numerically exact values for the gravity potential inside and outside such a body, plus the derivatives needed to see what the field is sensitive to.

The method rewrites the governing equation on a tidier reference domain and solves it with spectral tools. As a showcase, they compute the gravity of Phobos, the Mars moon, under smooth and patchy density models. The team also derives a companion adjoint equation and the sensitivity kernels it yields for Phobos. A neat identity links the kernels when the computing domain differs from the real one.
arxiv-2508-08110:
Robin Huo and Ewan Dunbar compare two famed speech models to find why they learn speech so well. Both models learn from raw sound with no labels, yet their inner maps of words, sounds, and voices differ. The pair differ in two ways: the goal used in training, and a loop that refines fake labels over rounds. Their 2025 study splits those two traits apart in clean tests.

Round-by-round refinement, not the training goal, turns out to drive the gap between the models. Maps from refined models line up far more with word, sound, and speaker facts. The authors urge more work on why the loop works so well. The finding can steer how next speech models are built and trained.
arxiv-2508-09110:
Alexander Greenwood, Jackson Russett, Hoi-Kwong Lo, and Li Qian run a quantum protocol on real hardware. Random party distillation pulls clean entangled pairs out of a single shared multi-party state, using only local actions and classical messages between the parties. The team built a qubit version of the protocol and ran it on a superconducting quantum processor.

They carried the process through as many as four rounds and drew out about 0.85 pairs per starting state, a rate above earlier lab demos. Multi-round versions of this local-operations approach have seen little lab time so far, so the result gives a proof that repeated rounds pay off on today's machines. Distilled pairs are a basic fuel for quantum networks, where clean shared entanglement does the heavy lifting.
arxiv-2508-09410:
Wei Fan and Yufeng Lin model the magnetic fields of rocky planets, which are made by moving liquid metal in the planet's core. Their 2025 paper studies a case where heat and chemistry both drive the flow, but spread at very different rates. Most past models treat the two drivers as if they spread at the same rate, for simplicity.

The team ran flow and magnetic simulations in a spinning spherical shell, with the two rates set far apart. Without a magnetic field, the flow shapes differed a lot between the two model types. Once a strong field formed, the two models gave much alike fields at matched strength. The results support the simpler model as a fair stand in for planet cores.
arxiv-2508-09510:
Iing Muttakhiroh and Thomas Fevens take on a known flaw of large language models: they forget old lessons when they learn new ones. Their 2025 method, Gauss-Tin, tries to keep past knowledge alive during fresh training. Replay, or mixing old examples back in, is the base idea.

Gauss-Tin pairs replay with a Gaussian mixture model that picks which old samples are worth replaying. Teaching prompts also guide the model to rebuild past lessons. In their tests, the method raised retention scores by about six percent over standard routes. The authors present it as a step toward models that adapt over time without losing what they knew.
arxiv-2508-09910:
Theodoros Assiotis, Mustafa Alper Gunes, Jonathan Keating, and Fei Wei work on random matrix theory, which studies the statistical patterns of large matrices filled by chance. They focus on polynomials tied to each matrix, and on averages of products of them and their rates of change. The matrices come from two symmetry families, one symplectic and one orthogonal, and the question is how the averages behave as matrix size grows.

The authors derive formulas for that large-size limit and tie the leading terms to averages over a third, simpler ensemble. They also uncover an exact link to a differential equation, the Painlevé V equation, that holds at any matrix size. In the large limit a related equation, Painlevé III, governs the leading term instead. These links let them compute some averages exactly and build others step by step. As a payoff, they settle a question raised by earlier researchers.
arxiv-2508-10010:
Ayana Hussain, Patrick Zhao and Nicholas Vincent wrote a 2025 audit of jailbreak attacks that trick language models into producing health misinformation. One model can be used to craft prompts that break another's guardrails. The team examined over one hundred distinct attacks on three target models. They compared the attack prompts with real health queries seen in the wild.

The fake medical claims produced were set beside misinformation found on Reddit. Standard machine learning detectors were tested on both kinds. The results add evidence that models can flag false health content from machines and people alike. Careful design, the authors argue, lets these tools support a healthier information space.
arxiv-2508-10110:
Sushrut Patwardhan, Raghavendra Ramachandra, and Sushma Venkatesh work on spotting face morphing attacks, where two faces are blended into one photo that can fool a check system. Most spotting tools give only a yes or no score. Their tool also gives a short text note that a human can read and judge.

The tool pairs images with text through a large pre-trained model, used here with no new training. The team tried ten text prompts, both short and long, written in plain human terms. Tests used a face set built from a public source, with five ways of making morphs shown in three forms, and compared their tool with top neural networks.
arxiv-2508-10210:
Rahul Jana, Shubham Dixit, Mrityunjay Sharma, and Ritesh Kumar wrote a 2025 paper on explainable AI for monitoring dairy cattle health. Farmers struggle to track every animal in a herd, and illness caught late costs milk yield and animal welfare. Continuous sensing offers a way to watch all animals at once.

The system collects movement data from three-axis accelerometer sensors attached to cows, sent over Bluetooth and 4G networks. Machine learning models classify the cows' activity and behavior, such as feeding, resting, and rumination. Crucially, the methods are explainable: they show why the model reached each conclusion. Farmers get actionable information they can trust, supporting both productivity and sustainable practice on the farm.
arxiv-2508-10410:
Franck Ramaharo computes the Kauffman bracket polynomial for a family of Celtic link shadows. Knot polynomials turn tangled diagrams into algebra that can tell links apart. Celtic links grow from a repeating decorative pattern, so their shadows form a tidy infinite family worth a formula.

He attacks the problem two ways and checks them against each other. The first way uses recursion inside the Celtic framework of Gross and Tucker, leaning on diagram identities. The second builds the link by joining a basic four-strand tangle to itself again and again. The state space then splits over the basis of the diagram monoid. Both routes land on the same polynomial.
arxiv-2508-10810:
Giovanni Alberti, Ernesto De Vito, Bianca Gariboldi, and Giacomo Gigante wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It proves sampling theorems for inverse problems on curved spaces: how many point measurements suffice to rebuild an unknown signal from noisy, indirect data.

The measurements are values of a transformed signal at scattered points on a manifold, plus noise. The authors require the points to form a special family that controls functions well. Their theorems bound the rebuilding error explicitly, in terms of the sample count, the signal's smoothness, and the transform's properties. They work out the case of convolution on compact spaces that look the same from any two points. A corollary covers convolutions on the ordinary sphere. Four examples tie the theory to measurements of the Earth and the sky.
arxiv-2508-11010:
Tausifa Jan Saleem and Mohammad Yaqub set a public baseline for teaching computers to outline uterine fibroids. Their 2025 paper uses MRI scans, the standard way clinicians size up these common benign tumors before choosing treatment.

Outlining fibroids by hand is slow and varies between experts, yet size, number, and position steer care. Earlier deep learning attempts mostly trained on private scans, so results could not be compared across teams. Working from a public uterine myoma MRI data set, the authors establish a standardized starting point for automated segmentation of uterus and fibroids together. They frame it as shared ground: one open benchmark so future methods can be validated against each other rather than claimed in isolation.
arxiv-2508-11110:
Mukul Singh and three co-authors show, in 2025 work, that a code-making model can also fix broken code. Such models build code by clearing noise step by step from a rough draft. Near the end, the last changes look just like small fixes to flawed code. The team asks if that look can be put to work.

Two uses are tested. First, noise is added to broken code and the clearing steps resume, which lets the model patch it. Second, mid-step and final drafts from the model give cheap pairs for training small fix tools. Tests ran on three settings: a broad code tongue, a sheet tool, and a shell tool. The team also weighs traits of the method itself, and backs both uses as sound.
arxiv-2508-11210:
Minghui Sun and co-authors improve early childhood risk prediction by letting models learn from later, richer data, in a 2025 paper. Clinicians judge a child's risks at many stages, from before birth to toddler checkups. Later judgments are naturally more accurate. Care, though, works best when risks are caught early. That tension defines pediatric prediction.

Their framework, Borrowing From the Future, treats each time window as its own modality. Contrastive training aligns early views with later ones. At test time, only early data are needed. The model has already absorbed what the future usually reveals. Tests target early-stage risk scores in child health. Earlier, steadier warnings could trigger support sooner.
arxiv-2508-11410:
Yanpeng Gong and co-authors apply a flexible math method to the heat and stress inside chip packaging, in a 2025 paper. Electronic packages mix tiny features with large ones, which strains standard mesh methods. The virtual element method allows mesh cells of any many-sided shape, so small zones can be reworked without touching the whole mesh.

The team pairs that method with a version that drops extra stabilizing terms. Their mesh plan tiles tricky small regions with many-sided cells and plain regions with squares. Tests on via, ball grid, and plastic package designs matched known benchmarks. The method caught stress piling up at material joints and gave sound heat and force forecasts.
arxiv-2508-11510:
Hui Li and four co-authors study how an unusual quantum material reacts to a sudden jolt in a 2025 paper. Non Fermi liquids break the standard rules for electrons in metals, and their out of equilibrium behavior is poorly understood. The team built an exactly solvable two dimensional model, based on iron based materials, where every answer can be computed without approximation.

After a sudden change, the model's observable quantities followed odd scaling laws at short and long times, unlike both ordinary metals and the best known non Fermi liquid model. The steady state diagram showed strange critical behavior as well. The authors offer the results as fresh insight into how orbital structure shapes the dynamics of these materials.
arxiv-2508-11610:
Shvetaank Tripathi and co-authors simulate collective neutrino oscillations on quantum hardware in 2025. Inside dense neutrino gases, such as merging neutron stars or collapsing stars, neutrinos swap flavors as they interact strongly with each other. Modeling that swapping on classic computers is hard, so the team turns to quantum tools.

They build a model of the interaction energy, split its time evolution into steps a quantum circuit can run, and encode two and three neutrino systems onto qubits. Runs used both a noisy simulator and a real quantum processor. The team tracks how the chance of staying in the starting state changes over time, and gives circuits to measure concurrence, a gauge of entanglement between the neutrinos. The work tests quantum machines on a real physics problem.
arxiv-2508-11810:
Seven researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on making synthetic health data that is both faithful and fair. Fake patient tables let researchers work around privacy rules, but training generators usually needs expert skill and heavy computing. Skewed fake data can also bake in bias against some groups.

Their framework, FairTabGen, uses a language model with in-context learning and curated prompts to build tables from a small sample of real data. On a major hospital data set it used far less data than rivals and improved one fairness measure by half. A racial skew remained, which preprocessing bias fixes then reduced.
arxiv-2508-12410:
Researchers present a deep learning network for outlining diseased livers in MRI scans in this 2025 paper. Cirrhosis is a late, dangerous stage of chronic liver disease. Catching it early and acting in time can cut deaths, yet the liver's complex shape and varied damage make its scans hard to read.

Past methods underuse the spatial layout inside a full 3D scan, which hurts both accuracy and trust. The new network, SRMA-Mamba, is built on the Mamba architecture, a fast sequence model. A key module scans selectively within liver tissue while weaving in anatomical knowledge. A spatial reverse attention step then sharpens the borders of the outlined regions. The aim is segmentation that follows the organ's real structure, so doctors can measure damage with more confidence.
arxiv-2508-12510:
Zetai Cen, Kaixin Liu, and Clifford Lam fix an identity problem in models of matrix-shaped data over time in this 2025 paper. Such models split each table into row effects, column effects, and shared factors. Without a rule pinning down the split, the parts can slide into each other and the model says nothing definite.

The standard fix forces row and column effects to average to zero. The authors replace it with a broad family of anchors, covering weighted means, middle values, and reference rows. They prove this anchor property is exactly what identification needs, and give direct formulas for the parts. Building on the freedom, they choose an anchor that zeroes the smallest effect, exposing true sparsity, and pair it with a doubly adaptive penalty that recovers sparse and dense blocks alike. Tests on jobs and economic data show the method working in practice.
arxiv-2508-13310:
Datta and nine co-authors study shock waves in magnetized plasma in a 2025 experimental paper. Such shocks matter in space systems, fusion research, and aerospace work.

The team used the COBRA pulsed power machine at Cornell University, which drives a fast, strong current through aluminum wires. The blast of plasma that results was pushed against angled blocks, forming shocks across the magnetic field. Cameras and laser tools measured the shock shape, density, speed, and temperature. The shocks sat at shallower angles and squeezed the plasma more than classic theory predicts. A model that adds both energy loss by radiation and the spread of the magnetic field matched the results best.
arxiv-2508-13610:
Basile Pesin, Celia Picard, and Cyril Allignol give a formal meaning to reactive user interface languages. These languages describe screens for machines and let programmers state how a program reacts to events and how data flows through it. They are used in safety critical interfaces, yet few have been made mathematically precise or verified.

Their 2025 paper builds a denotational model for a core language, Smalite. The authors argue the core is rich enough to encode features of larger, realistic languages. Each program's meaning is given as a mathematical function rather than by steps of execution. They present the work as a first step toward a compiler for such languages that is formally verified, so interface code can be trusted by proof.
arxiv-2508-14110:
Zhengqian Cheng and Chris Marianetti find the root of a famed shift in electron flow in a 2025 paper. The shift, named for Mott, turns a metal into a blocker when electrons crowd and push each other too hard.

Their tool is a theory that sums a material by how its electrons pair off, a frame that has done well for small systems but had not met a phase shift. The team built the frame for a model with up to seven electron homes, at no set size. A kink in the math at a whole count of fill marks the shift. They show how a side push between spins can turn a smooth shift sharp. The path may lead to a truer frame for strong-bound materials.
arxiv-2508-14210:
Natalie Allen and co-authors observed a hot rocky exoplanet in two thousand twenty-five. The planet circles a small red dwarf star. It sits so close that its year lasts less than a day. Blasted by starlight, it may have lost any atmosphere. The Hot Rocks Survey tests such worlds for air. This planet receives the strongest heating in the survey.

A space telescope watched two eclipses of the planet. Eclipse depth measures heat glowing from its dayside. The depth matched what a bare rock would emit. Separate data pipelines gave consistent results. No thick atmosphere is needed to explain the signal. An airless surface fits the heat pattern best. The survey will compare this world with cooler rocky planets.
arxiv-2508-14310:
Felix Brandt, Sunčica Čanić, and Boris Muha prove that solutions exist for a three-dimensional model of fluid pushing through a layered, living-style wall, in a 2025 paper. The fluid is incompressible and viscous. The wall couples a thick spongy layer, modeled by the Biot equations of poroelasticity, to a thin springy plate that fluid can pass through. The interface moves with the solution itself, which makes even stating the problem delicate.

A gentle regularization of the wall's displacement makes the coupling well-defined at finite energy. The team builds approximate solutions by operator splitting, bounds their energy uniformly, and passes to the limit with refined compactness tools built for rough moving interfaces. Both the elastic and the poroviscoelastic cases are covered. The result is the first existence theorem for this class of three-dimensional fluid-structure systems.
arxiv-2508-14510:
Arnab Chaudhuri, a solo author, studies neutrinos sent out by tiny ancient black holes in a 2025 paper. Such primordial black holes slowly evaporate, and the particles they emit carry clues about their spin, motion, and charge. Chaudhuri works out how those three traits shape the direction and energy of the emitted neutrinos.

Spin makes the flow uneven around the hole's axis, while fast motion beams the flow forward like a spotlight. Charge slows the loss of like charged particles and changes how long the burst lasts. The resulting patterns are rich and vary with time. The author argues these signatures could help current and future detectors spot such black holes.
arxiv-2508-14810:
Alexander Stoychev, Ulrich Kuhl, and Nicolas Noiray break a wave symmetry in twenty twenty-five. Reciprocity says a wave should pass equally well in both directions through a device. Breaking it is key for isolating signals and protecting sources. Their method uses synchronization of self-oscillators instead of the usual magnetic or resonant tricks.

Aeroacoustic cavities act as weakly nonlinear oscillators when driven by steady airflow. Coupled to waveguides at two ports, they sync differently depending on the wave's direction. Waves from one port trigger anti-phase sync, causing destructive interference and low transmission. Waves from the other port induce in-phase sync and high transmission. The working bandwidth is set by the synchronization region and beats resonance-based methods. Experiments showed robust behavior under parameter changes.
arxiv-2508-14910:
Lepage, Mary, and Picard ask why generative recommender systems, which phrase suggestions as generation over item tokens, still trail classic ID-based models. They blame two weak points. First, tokens standing for items carry no signal about which items people enjoy together. Second, the standard encoder-decoder design is wasteful. Their fixes are COSETTE, a tokenization method baking shared taste patterns into the item codes, and MARIUS, a leaner generative model. MARIUS borrows from audio work and separates timeline modeling from item decoding.

On standard sequential recommendation benchmarks, the pair closes most of the gap with strong ID-based baselines; it sometimes erases it. Inference gets cheaper under the new architecture. The authors frame the result as evidence generative recommenders were held back by fixable design choices, not by the idea. For platform teams, the paper offers upgrades that keep the flexibility of generation.
arxiv-2508-15010:
Alabed and a large team built a fast tool in twenty twenty-five to split large smart models across many chips. Split calls are tied in knots, and past tools can run out of room or take too long to search. Some past tools cut the search and then give splits that break chip room caps.

Their tool, TOAST, pairs a code read with a tree search that tries splits by chance and score. The read finds which parts must share the same split and where clashes need a call. It beat top trade tools on many chip types and model forms. New best splits came up in the search.
arxiv-2508-15110:
Graham Hill and co-authors survey what large language models and AI agents could mean for insurance in Africa, in a 2025 paper. Model performance is rising while deployment costs fall. Open tools widen access further. Insurance markets in Africa, though, carry deep gaps in coverage and data.

The authors map where smart systems could help decisions, from pricing to claims. They also name the local hurdles: thin data, weak infrastructure, and skills shortages. Key local players and partnership openings are identified. The paper closes with a call for actuaries, insurers, regulators, and tech leaders to build inclusive strategies together. The goal is AI shaped by and for Africans.
arxiv-2508-15210:
Joscha Mecke, Yongxiang Gao, and Marisol Ripoll stir a fluid of spinning colloids around patterned obstacles and watch order emerge from turbulence, in a 2025 paper. Near an obstacle's surface, the rotors circle against their own spin, driven by one-way rotational stresses, as theory predicts. That steady background flow competes with the fluid's own active turbulence.

Rotor density and obstacle size set the winner: pinned, tidy vortices around obstacles, or vivid turbulent motion. A little friction with the floor can even strengthen the vortex flow. The colloids also diffuse oddly, steered around obstacles by sideways fluxes, so transport speeds up at moderate blocking. The authors say confinement can be a control knob for active matter.
arxiv-2508-15810:
Nouar AlDahoul and Yasir Zaki test, in twenty twenty-five, large language models on Arabic social media content. Arabic posts and memes are a major form of online expression. They can be funny or useful, but they also carry hate speech and abuse. The team judged how well models spot hope, hate, offensive language, and emotion in such content. They compared base models, fine-tuned models, and embedding models on a shared challenge data set.

Two fine-tuned models led the field. One was tuned on Arabic text posts, the other on Arabic memes. Their scores topped all three tasks, and the team placed first overall in the challenge. The authors say such tools can support Arabic content moderation.
arxiv-2508-16210:
Recommenders like to borrow taste from a data-rich domain to help a sparse one, but most methods need users who appear in both. Ziyin Xiao and Toyotaro Suzumura drop that requirement entirely. Their framework, DUP-OT, first turns reviews into shared embeddings, then models each user's taste as a mixture of Gaussians over item space, a cloud rather than a point.

Optimal transport then matches those clouds across domains, letting taste transfer without any shared users. On Amazon review data, the method beat single-domain baselines even with no source data in training. It also cut the large errors that plague cold-start users. The 2025 paper makes cross-domain help possible between strangers.
arxiv-2508-16310:
Javier Rey-Domínguez and Mohsen Razavi rethink quantum repeaters in this 2025 paper. Repeaters are needed to send quantum signals over long distances. Early designs do not scale well, while advanced ones demand gear far beyond today's networks.

Their compromise uses a connectionless style of entanglement swapping, much like packet switching on the internet. It also uses simple error detection in place of heavy error correction. That keeps device demands modest while the network grows. They test the idea on quantum key distribution across a repeater chain. The results point to trust-free links at continental scale through staged steps of growth.
arxiv-2508-16710: Justine Tang improves snow-clearing routes in a 2025 paper. The snowblower problem asks how a machine clears snow from shapes in fewest steps. An earlier paper split the snow into lines and combs and gave clearing methods. Tang finds leaner ways to clear both shapes. Fewer steps are needed per line and per comb than before. The overall complexity class stays the same, so the gain is in constants, not growth rate. The note is a compact optimization of a classic puzzle in motion planning.
arxiv-2508-16810:
A signal that fires its neighbour, which fires the next, sweeps a tissue as a wave — the cell world's alarm bell. Brandon Schlomann and three co-authors ask what it takes to light that wave in 2025. The match point, the stimulus bar for a sweep, is a core number for any such circuit.

Their model uses a switch curve of the kind real circuits show. The bar is solved in full for a line, and by simulation on sheets and in solids. At high sensitivity the bar splits into two dials of the self-firing loop: its grip strength and its steepness. A lab can read those dials in bulk and forecast the bar. Waves run from wounds to heartbeats, so the rule travels far.
arxiv-2508-17010:
Hu, Cao, and Liu built this protein alignment tool in twenty twenty-five. Comparing the 3D shapes of two proteins is a basic task in biology and drug design. The classic method solves the best overlay exactly, but only for one standard score. Their framework, Lie-RMSD, turns the overlay into a learning problem.

Rotations and shifts are packed into a six-number vector from Lie algebra. The mismatch score then becomes a loss that gradient methods can shrink step by step. Four standard optimizers all reached the same best fit as the exact method. The test case was a well-known enzyme in two shapes. The authors say the setup can extend to richer scores with no exact solution.
arxiv-2508-17310:
Yuanchun Wang and co-authors study student dropouts in an AI-driven interactive online course, in a 2025 paper. The course platform uses language model agents to turn passive lectures into active, text-based lessons. Even lively courses lose students along the way. The team asks three linked questions about that loss.

First, what factors lead students to drop out? Second, can dropout be predicted from interaction logs? Third, can timely action reduce it? Chat patterns turned out to link strongly with dropout behavior. The authors build a prediction approach on those patterns. They also test ways to re-engage students at risk. Course designers gain tools to keep learners enrolled. The lessons extend to online learning at large.
arxiv-2508-17410:
James Tian develops a theory of ridge kernels, a family of functions built by running one-dimensional kernels along many straight-line projections of the data and averaging. Such averaged kernels are positive definite, and Tian shows the function class they generate matches its reproducing kernel Hilbert space exactly. Varying the averaging weights sweeps out a family he characterizes fully.

He proves that family is exactly the uniform closure of all positive combinations of single ridge pieces, which yields a sharp test for when the class can approximate any function. A dividing line between polynomial and non-polynomial slices governs how expressive the class is.
