He then studies random networks built from these kernels, proving error bounds that decay like one over the number of units, both on average and with high probability.
arxiv-2508-17610:
Nannan Huang, Haytham Fayek, and Xiuzhen Zhang ask whether shrinking language models also skews their fairness in a 2025 paper. Pruning trims a model's size cheaply, and opinion summaries shape public views, so hidden bias shifts matter. No one had mapped how pruning choices move fairness.

Across three pruning methods, several calibration sets, and three open models, the pruning method itself moved fairness scores far more than the calibration data did. Guided by that insight, the team designed a pruning rule that cuts weights with strong output influence but weak input use. Their method held or improved fairness where rivals degraded it, across four fairness metrics. Human judges agreed the summaries were fairer. Code is public.
arxiv-2508-18110: A large Super-Kamiokande collaboration reports measuring how often muon capture produces four specific isotopes. Maekawa is first author among a very long author list. Muon capture is a reaction in atomic nuclei. A muon, a heavy cousin of the electron, is absorbed and changes the nucleus. The giant underground water detector in Japan records the faint signals. The branching ratio states what share of captures ends in each isotope.
arxiv-2508-18710:
Nandita Chaturvedi, Charuhansini Tvishamayi, and Shashi Thutupalli model in 2025 how yeast populations adapt to extreme stress when growth and survival pull in opposite directions. Stress such as starvation, antimicrobials, or freezing forces this trade off. Their model ties growth rate, lag time, the chance of entering a resting state, and stress survival to one trait linked to a sugar that protects cells in freeze thaw cycles.

Simulations of growth and stress cycles, plus direct calculation of long term growth, locate the outcomes evolution favors. How strong the trade off feels depends on how long the growth phase lasts. Strikingly, stress ready populations can hold their own next to growth tuned ones even with no stress at all.
arxiv-2508-18810:
Yonghwi Kim, Sang-Hyun Park, Siyun Yang, Kai-Kit Wong, Linglong Dai, and Chan-Byoung Chae confront near-field beam squint in ultra-wideband integrated sensing and communication systems. Their paper from twenty twenty-five frames sixth-generation networks around ISAC for driving, extended reality, and smart factories. Giant arrays plus huge bandwidths drag users into the near field, where beams smear across frequencies. True time delay hardware fixes it but costs too much to scale.

Their answer is codebook craft across analog and digital domains, bending beams to cover users and sharpen sensing despite squint. Large simulations on three-dimensional city maps validate the strategies. Communication throughput and sensing accuracy hold together under harsh near-field conditions. Open hardware and algorithm problems close the survey.
arxiv-2508-18910:
Tsiry Avisoa Randrianasolo analyzes a numerical scheme for a classic pattern forming system in a 2025 paper. The Gray-Scott equations model chemical reactions that grow spots and stripes. The scheme treats part of each step implicitly on a finite volume grid. Randrianasolo proves the discrete problem always has a valid solution.

Solutions stay positive and bounded under the scheme, as physics demands. A compactness argument shows grid answers converge to a true weak solution. With added smoothness, error bounds in the square norm follow. Computer runs confirm first order convergence in practice. The runs also reproduce the classic patterns the system is famed for.
arxiv-2508-19010:
Wireless links can mint secret keys from the channel itself, since two partners see the same fading pattern while an eavesdropper sees another. At millimeter-wave frequencies this trick falters: channels are sparse, noisy in phase, and lossy. Mollahosseini and Ghasempour present mmKey, which uses antenna arrays to stir randomness into a quiet channel by shaping the beam.

A genetic algorithm evolves the beam weights step by step. The winning shapes suppress the direct line-of-sight path while respecting the channel's sparseness and signal strength, balancing secrecy against reliability. In simulations, mmKey widened the secrecy gap by about thirty-nine percent over random beamforming and thirty-four percent over null beamforming. The authors pitch the method for securing next-generation wireless networks where keys must be born from the air itself.
arxiv-2508-19110:
Carla Piazza, Riccardo Romanello, and Sabina Rossi go back to a trait of stochastic systems called persistent stochastic non-interference. The trait asks that a high-level process cannot shape what a low-level viewer sees, not even in fine numeric detail. Their aim is a view of that pledge built around how well the system runs.

They bring in weak-exact equivalence, a way to match how systems act that treats quiet inner steps in a loose way while it keeps what can be seen exact. Built on it, exact persistent stochastic non-interference mirrors how the first trait is described. The new form takes the same bisimulation-based and unwinding-style descriptions, and keeps much the same way its parts fit as a whole. The team present this match as a firm base to reason on interference in stochastic process algebras.
arxiv-2508-19310:
Yıldız, Kaykı, and Güdekli showed in 2025 that a universe can bounce instead of beginning in a singularity, if its matter is a thick fluid with a causal sense of time. A bounce needs matter to break a rule that healthy theories guard, which is where viscosity earns its keep.

An older fluid theory broke causality; its modern successor, with a finite relaxation time, stays lawful. In that frame the authors built exact bounce solutions and read off the viscosity and relaxation values that keep entropy growing and wobbles stable. The trick worked in plain gravity, in a modified gravity, and in a quantum geometry cosmology. Each frame adds its own safety net for the bounce.
arxiv-2508-19910:
Lasers modulated directly by the signal are cheap and simple for short data links, but their messy physics makes tuning hard. Sergio Hernandez and co-authors let the hardware teach its own model. They train a stand-in model on real measurements from the lab setup, then optimize the whole chain against it.

The tuning covers pulse shaping, equalizer filters, laser bias current, and radio power all at once. On the bench, the tuned system beat four rival schemes across speeds and distances. It did so with lower radio power, fewer filter taps, and less signal bandwidth. The 2025 paper shows end-to-end learning squeezing more from humble lasers.
arxiv-2508-20210:
Xiaodi Li and co-authors build a system that animates a person from sound alone, for long stretches of video. Such tools can dub films or drive virtual hosts, but long clips tend to drift. Faces change, colors shift, and hands warp or fall out of step with the voice. Their 2025 system, InfinityHuman, works in stages from rough to fine.

First it lays down motion that matches the sound. Then a refiner uses body poses and the first frame as anchors to hold the look steady. Poses do not decay over time the way raw frames do, so drift drops. A hand-focused reward, trained on clean hand data, sharpens gestures. Tests on two data sets put the system ahead on quality, lip match, and hand form.
arxiv-2508-20310:
Atit Pokharel, Ratun Rahman, Shaba Shaon, Thomas Morris, and Dinh Nguyen turn the flaw of today's quantum computers, their noise, into a privacy shield. In federated learning, many devices train a shared model without pooling raw data, but the updates they exchange can still leak information to attackers.

Working with quantum models on noisy near-term hardware, the team shows the noise itself can be tuned to meet formal privacy guarantees. Adjusting the number of measurement rounds and the strength of a scrambling channel dials the privacy level up or down. Simulations traced the trade between privacy, accuracy, and resistance to attack: stronger privacy cost some accuracy but blunted attacks. The authors present the scheme as a practical route to safer shared quantum learning.
arxiv-2508-20410:
Sam Jung, Agustin Garcinuno, and Spencer Mateega introduce UI-Bench, a benchmark for judging whether AI text-to-app tools actually design well. Such tools promise high-quality applications and websites in minutes, yet no public benchmark rigorously verified those claims. UI-Bench evaluates visual excellence across competing tools through expert pairwise comparison.

The benchmark spans ten tools, thirty prompts, three hundred generated sites, and more than four thousand expert judgments. Rankings come from a TrueSkill-derived model that yields calibrated confidence intervals, so differences between tools carry uncertainty estimates. The authors release the complete prompt set, an open-source evaluation framework, and a public leaderboard, with the rated sites to follow. UI-Bench establishes a reproducible standard for a fast-moving product category. For buyers and builders alike, it replaces vendor demos with expert-judged evidence about which tools produce the best-looking results.
arxiv-2508-20810:
Jessica Lundin and co-authors turn clinical guidelines into self renewing tests for language models in a 2025 paper. Fixed test sets go stale and leak into training data, so scores fade in meaning. Their harness builds a queryable graph from a guideline's structure, then walks the graph to spin fresh test items on demand.

The design promises three things: full coverage of the guideline's links, leak resistance through sheer mix and match variety, and soundness inherited from the expert written source. Built on the WHO child illness guide, it made grounded choice questions on signs, cures, severity, and follow up. Five models were strong on spotting signs but weaker on treatment and care calls. The frame refreshes as guides update and ports to other rule bound fields.
arxiv-2508-21810:
Jessica Liang and Anirudh Bharadwaj present a machine learning paper, published in 2025, on fine tuning giant language models with a radically small set of trainable numbers. Low rank adaptation already trims fine tuning costs by learning small update matrices, but popular versions seed those matrices with a costly factorization of the original weights. The authors instead pull an orderly basis from the weights using QR decomposition with column pivoting.

The update is then written as a blend of those basis vectors, and only the blend weights are trained. On standard language benchmarks the method matched or beat full fine tuning and rival adapters while training only a few hundred parameters. The structure also makes the learned change easier to read.
arxiv-2509-00010:
Shuchang Liu and Paul A. O'Gorman present CERA in 2025, a framework to help climate models work in warmer worlds they never saw in training. Machine models often fail when the climate shifts past their training range, and they lean heavily on costly warm-world sim data. Hand-built climate-invariant inputs help, but they demand hard manual work.

CERA pairs an autoencoder, which squeezes data into a compact code, with clear alignment of that code across climates. A predictor then reads the code for the target task. For moist physics, CERA learns from labeled mild-climate data plus unlabeled warm inputs. It beats raw and physics-guided baselines on key moisture and energy traits, with no warm labels used.
arxiv-2509-00210:
Jinzhou Tang and five co-authors present VEME in 2025, a method to give video-based embodied models a richer sense of the physical world. Vision-language models read still scenes well, but they reason poorly over time and space in moving, open settings. Tasks such as task-oriented navigation and embodied question answering expose that gap.

VEME aligns objects, spatial representations, and visual semantics with spatio-temporal cues in one cross-modal frame. A dynamic, implicit cognitive map, centered on the agent's own viewpoint and past experience, supports the reasoning. The world model aims to generalize to unseen scenes. Better space-time grounding could help embodied agents act sensibly in new homes and work sites.
arxiv-2509-00310:
Yuxuan Ding, Shuangge Wang, and Tesca Fitzgerald present TReF-6 in 2025, a method that lets robots generalize a skill from a single demonstration. One-shot learning is hard without a transferable, interpretable spatial frame. Their method infers a simplified six-degree-of-freedom task-relevant frame from one trajectory, which is the path a hand or tool follows.

An influence point, drawn purely from trajectory geometry, sets the frame's origin. That frame then parameterizes a Dynamic Movement Primitive, a standard motion model, beyond plain start-goal copying. A vision-language model grounds the frame in meaning, and a grounding tool locates it in new scenes. Real manipulation tests show functionally consistent transfer.
arxiv-2509-00510:
Li Weigang, with two co-authors, proposes SuperBrain. SuperBrain is a plan for group intelligence. It grows from large language models paired with human users. Each user and model pair forms a Subclass Brain. That pair builds memory from steady contact. It learns to adapt over time.

Pairs refine their prompts and their task work step by step. A search method modeled on evolution helps them improve. Many pairs then coordinate through swarm rules. Swarm rules copy how groups in nature act as one. Their shared habits merge into a Superclass Brain. It is meant to generalize and improve itself. Early uses include drone scheduling and keyword filtering. A shared registry is proposed for knowledge from all pairs.
arxiv-2509-00710:
Albert Sadowski and Jaroslaw A Chudziak build a multi-agent system for legal reasoning. Legal work needs precise reading of statute language. It also needs rules applied in a consistent way. AI systems that answer end to end hide their steps. That opacity makes their legal answers hard to trust or check.

Their system splits the work into clear stages. Specialized agents first extract legal concepts from statutes. They formalize the rules into checkable intermediate forms. A second stage maps case facts onto a concept schema. Symbolic inference then draws the conclusions that follow. Final answers are generated by a program, not free text. On tax calculation tasks, base models improve sharply over baseline. The gap to reasoning models narrows, with far better transparency.
arxiv-2509-00810:
Jose Roberto de Toledo leads a team of fifteen authors on energy and charge transfer in a layered stack. The stack pairs a tungsten diselenide monolayer with a chromium sulfur bromide crystal. Such stacks join a dichalcogenide layer with a magnetic semiconductor layer. They offer ways to tune exciton and valley traits.

The team uses light emission under magnetic fields to probe the stack. Each emission peak behaves in its own way under a field. That behavior differs from the pristine monolayer alone. Emission grows sharply at certain field values. At those values, an exciton in one layer matches an optical state in the other. They read this as resonant energy transfer controlled by the field. The effect could aid light harvesting and brighter thin materials.
arxiv-2509-00910:
Yuta Ito, writing alone, explains the power-law profile of core-collapsing globular clusters. Globular clusters are dense balls of stars. Observed clusters show power-law profiles in their inner halos at core collapse. The origin of that power law lacked a good explanation. Ito applies Buckingham's Pi theorem to the problem.

The model is an orbit-averaged Fokker-Planck model of equal masses. He first proves an infinite model evolves self-similarly. That follows from the principle of covariance. He then shows the inner halo must form a power-law profile in a finite model. Complete similarity makes covariance and conservation laws hold there. The usual assumption of self-similar, stationary halos is not needed.
arxiv-2509-01010:
Hai-Jun Su, writing alone, presents solvers for equations that arise in robot kinematics. Four common types are covered in the paper. They include single trig equations and single-angle systems. Two-angle systems and bilinear two-angle systems are also covered. Such equations come up often when joint angles must be found.

Detailed methods are given for each type. They include closed-form solutions and numerical steps. Robustness is discussed as well. The solvers handle general coefficients and manage singular cases. They list all real solutions in an efficient way. The code lives in Python packages for reuse. Sample prompts can rebuild working code via a coding agent. Tests and benchmarks show the methods are sound.
arxiv-2509-01110:
Language models trained on recent text can leak future knowledge into studies of the past, skewing results in economics and finance. Ali Kakhbod and Peiyao Li present NoLBERT, a small foundation model trained only on text from 1976 to 1995. By freezing its knowledge in that window, the model avoids both lookahead and lookback bias.

NoLBERT beat domain baselines on language tests while staying true to its time window. Kakhbod and Li then applied it to patent texts, building firm-level networks that show how companies link through new ideas. Firms that gained a more central place in those networks tended to see higher long-run profit growth. The work gives social scientists a tool that respects the flow of time.
arxiv-2509-01310:
Women live longer than men but report worse health, a puzzle often blamed on women using more healthcare. Nadja van 't Hoff, Giovanni Mellace, and Seetha Menon challenge that view with causal evidence from Denmark. They use the near-random timing of first non-fatal heart attacks and strokes in administrative records.

After such a shock, men raised their statin use and doctor visits far more than women did. The gap was not about willingness: both sexes filled the same number of prescriptions, but women got lower doses per fill. The gap also grew where doctors had more discretion in prescribing. Despite extra treatment, men did no better on death, illness, or work outcomes, raising the question whether women would fare even better with equal intensity of care.
arxiv-2509-01410:
Sparse signal recovery rebuilds a signal from few measurements, but noise in the dictionary, the set of building blocks, degrades the result. Debraj Banerjee and Amitava Chatterjee introduce JS-gOMP, an algorithm that strengthens a standard greedy method called generalized orthogonal matching pursuit. Their addition is the James-Stein estimator, a classic shrinkage method that balances fitting the signal against suppressing noise.

By tuning that trade-off inside the pursuit steps, the algorithm resists noise that would mislead a plain greedy search. Comparative analyses show JS-gOMP beats the traditional version, especially in noisy settings. Banerjee and Chatterjee offer the method for signal and image processing tasks where noise is significant and clean recovery matters, such as sensing and imaging systems that must work outside quiet laboratories.
arxiv-2509-01510:
A light particle bound to a heavy one is usually described by the Dirac equation. An outside potential does the binding. Yet that potential breaks translation symmetry, while the bound state's momentum stays well defined. Paul Hoyer studies this tension in a simplified theory of the strong force. The theory has two dimensions and is taken in the limit of many colors.

Hoyer finds the light quark's wave function does not depend on the bound state's frame. Only an irrelevant Lorentz contraction sets them apart. The discrete energies of the full theory fix matching energies for the Dirac equation. For a linear potential, that matching allows a continuous spectrum instead. The result clarifies a puzzle. A bound state can be held in place by a potential, yet still move cleanly across frames.
arxiv-2509-01610:
Aligning large vision and language models usually needs human preference data, which is costly, while machine-made data are weaker and self-training can breed hallucinations. Jefferson Hernandez, with four co-authors, proposes Panel-of-Peers, a framework where a panel of models evaluates and learns from each other's outputs. The idea mimics collaborative learning and peer review among students.

Models generate, assess, and refine answers to a curated set of prompts in an iterative loop. No extensive human-labeled data are required. Experiments show significant gains across several benchmarks, and the authors report a clear rise in average score from the peer process. Hernandez and the team present peer evaluation as a scalable alternative to self-supervised alignment, using the diversity of a model panel to catch errors that a single model would miss in itself.
arxiv-2509-01810:
Rajibul Islam, Shakeel Ahmad, and Fei Xue show that electric torque can flip the magnetic order of a layered topological material. The material is a two layer form of a manganese bismuth telluride compound with antiferromagnetic order, meaning neighboring layers point in opposite magnetic directions. Such materials host exotic effects but resist direct electric control. The team uses first principle calculations, meaning counts from basic physics laws.

A symmetry allowed torque persists even inside the energy gap where no free carriers flow. It reverses the layer order and a marker of topological state without heating losses. Adding carriers boosts both torque types and cuts the needed field by a hundredfold. The results open a route to electric control of edge states in this material.
arxiv-2509-01910:
Furong Jia leads five co-authors on a geo-localization system that explains its guesses through clear concepts. Geo-localization finds where a photo was taken from cues like climate, landmarks, and building style. Strong prior models align images with locations but cannot say why. Concept methods that explain other models fit poorly with that alignment goal.

Their module projects both image and location codes onto a shared bank of geographic concepts. Examples include tropical climate, mountains, and cathedrals as named concept slots. A concept level loss sharpens alignment inside that shared space. Tests beat a leading prior model on accuracy and lift other geospatial tasks too. The concept view also reveals richer reasons behind each location call.
arxiv-2509-02010:
Susanta Ghosh leads five co-authors in measuring giant magnetoresistance in iron based kagome metals. Kagome lattices weave corner sharing triangles, hosting flat bands and Dirac states. Their compounds order antiferromagnetically at a high temperature, with a weak ferromagnetic turn at low heat. Resistance in a magnetic field is the core probe here.

Resistance jumps by thousands of percent at low temperature under a strong field in one compound. A two band fit of Hall data shows near perfect balance of electrons and holes plus high mobility. That balance explains the huge response. The effect also varies strongly with field direction, and its angular pattern shifts with temperature. Those shifts signal changes in the Fermi surface shape over the same range.
arxiv-2509-02310:
Frankie Higgs wrote a 2025 solo probability paper on the random connection model, where points scattered at random link to nearby points and form clusters. The question is how fast the chance of a huge cluster at the origin fades when the system sits below its critical density.

Higgs proves that this chance drops exponentially, under weak assumptions and even when links can reach arbitrarily far. The proof adapts a recent method from percolation on highly symmetric graphs. A sparse model is built inside a very dense one, which becomes almost symmetric at high intensity. That trick, the paper notes, may help with other problems where symmetry is only approximate.
arxiv-2509-02510:
Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Seyedarmin Azizi, Souvik Kundu, and Massoud Pedram wrote a 2025 natural language processing paper on sampling text from language models without losing coherence. Truncated sampling methods cut off unlikely words, but they use the model's confidence crudely.

The authors frame the creativity-coherence balance as an entropy-constrained optimisation problem and prove it equals a mass maximisation problem that is NP-hard to solve exactly. Their Top-H decoding is a fast greedy method for that problem. It uses the full probability distribution rather than a single top token. On creative writing tests, Top-H beat the leading min-p sampler by a wide margin. It also held up on question-answering sets, and judge-model checks confirmed coherent output even at high randomness settings.
arxiv-2509-02610:
Jonathan Feldman and Tal Feldman present a 2025 biosecurity paper warning that AI protein design has outrun the filters meant to catch dangerous outputs. Generative biology can create novel proteins for medicine, but the same tools could aid synthetic bioweapons.

Current defences lean on prediction tools that flag risky protein interactions. The authors tested three leading interaction predictors on known viral-host pairs, including hepatitis B and SARS-CoV-2. Despite training exposure to those viruses, the tools missed many confirmed interactions. None caught any of four proven SARS-CoV-2 mutant binders. The authors argue screening alone cannot carry biosecurity. They call for response-oriented infrastructure: fast experimental validation, adaptable biomanufacturing, and regulation that moves at AI speed.
arxiv-2509-02710:
Gabriel A. B. do Nascimento and eleven co-authors wrote a 2025 medical imaging paper. It seeks breast lesions in contrast-enhanced MRI scans of high-risk women. Early, accurate spotting matters most in that group. Lesions vary a lot in look, though.

Their pipeline adapts a pretrained foundation model, the Medical Slice Transformer. It turns each scan slice into feature embeddings. Its training used self-supervised DINOv2 methods. A Kolmogorov-Arnold Network then judges the embeddings. That network uses spline curves that adapt as it learns. It gives flexible yet readable decisions. The joined system beat the foundation model's own classifier on ranking accuracy. Attention heatmaps keep the logic visible. The authors aim at robust screening tools for hard clinical data.
arxiv-2509-02810:
Stanisław Kurzyna and three co-authors wrote a 2025 quantum optics paper. It demonstrates a hybrid quantum memory. The memory stores light in atomic coherence and reads it back. Two established protocols merge: gradient echo memory and electromagnetically induced transparency.

The two parts complement each other. Their mix converts signals between time and frequency forms, in both directions. The modes vary across spectrum and time. Such conversion helps quantum networks work as one system. Their parts often speak incompatible encodings. The authors also point to basic science uses. One is studying Rydberg polaritons, collective atomic excitations. Another is mapping ionic impurities or lone Rydberg excitations. A single device that translates encodings could simplify future links.
arxiv-2509-03710:
A 2025 research paper from Yineng Chen and one co-author examines seasonal and periodic patterns in ischemic heart disease hospitalisations in New York. Ischemic heart disease restricts blood flow to the heart, and its hospital visits have long been reported to vary by season. Their tool is a new bootstrap method designed for signals with several overlapping rhythms.

The Variable Multiple Bandpass Periodic Block Bootstrap first filters a time series to isolate one periodically correlated component, then resamples it in blocks that preserve its correlation structure. That yields tighter confidence intervals than existing periodic bootstrap methods. Applied to hospitalisation records, the method finds significant weekly and annual patterns, plus several harmonics, meaning repeating sub-patterns at fractions of the annual cycle. Aggregating only the significant components builds a confidence band holding several rhythms at once. The approach suits noisy series with many periodic patterns, such as environmental or health data.
arxiv-2509-03910:
Christoph Brune and three co-authors' 2025 research paper takes up an invertible generative model handling both forward and inverse problems in one object. Inverse problems infer hidden causes from data, framed here in Bayesian terms. A model able to simulate data from parameters and infer parameters from data is what the authors call a Reversible Simulator.

Their design joins two triangular normalising flows, one suited to each sampling direction, into a single invertible map. Structural properties of that design are established, and its non-uniqueness is explored: many reversible simulators can match the same problem. A variational form then shows how to train the model directly from paired samples. Tractable examples and stylised tests illustrate the framework. The authors present it as one reversible object replacing forward and inverse machinery for conditional modelling.
arxiv-2509-04310:
Yunbo Long and four co-authors evolve emotional strategies for language-model negotiators in a 2025 research paper. AI agents now bargain over prices across many turns, yet they usually show emotion passively, leaving them open to manipulation. Their framework, EvoEmo, treats emotional expression as a policy to be optimized rather than a byproduct. Emotional state changes are modeled step by step, and a population-based genetic search evolves better emotion policies across many bargaining scenarios.

Two baselines anchor the tests: plain agents and agents stuck on one fixed emotion. EvoEmo agents won more deals, closed them faster, and saved buyers more money across experiments. Ablation tests, which remove parts one by one, confirmed each piece mattered.
arxiv-2509-04410:
Matteo Ippoliti and one co-author, David M Long, build static quantum systems whose states act as if endlessly hot, even at zero energy, in a 2025 physics paper. Driven systems, called Floquet systems, can thermalize to effective infinite temperature. The authors adapt the Feynman-Kitaev clock, a device that encodes a computation's history inside a Hamiltonian, the energy rule of a quantum system, by giving its clock register wrapped-around boundaries.

Assuming the input circuit thermalizes as expected, every eigenstate of the built system shows infinite-temperature traits, including maximal entanglement spread. Exactly solvable driven circuits then supply the needed thermal behavior with proof. The combined families yield local Hamiltonians whose lowest-energy states are volume-law entangled with proof, a first with that property across all subsystems.
arxiv-2509-04510:
Michele Materazzini and six co-authors combine virtual reality with machine learning to flag dyslexia in university students in a 2025 research paper. Italian and Spanish students completed VR tasks measuring silent reading performance and self-esteem. Statistical tests first compared students with and without dyslexia. Completion time on the reading test differed significantly between groups, while accuracy and self-esteem did not. Supervised learning models then classified dyslexia status from the VR data.

Accuracy reached high levels for Italian students, lower for Spanish, and in between for the pooled group. Speed differences carry the signal, the results suggest, while language-specific factors sway how well classification transfers. VR assessment could support traditional dyslexia screening, especially where specialists are scarce.
arxiv-2509-04610:
A triple sum built from generalised divisor functions sits at the centre of a 2025 number theory paper by Bikram Misra and one co-author. The divisor function counts how many ways a whole number can be written as a product of a fixed number of factors. The sum shifts that function in three linked places.

Misra and his co-author first note a predicted size for the sum, supported by Dirichlet series and probability arguments. They then derive a lower bound of the correct order and recover the predicted constant. A final part restricts the sum to primes, using results about primes in arithmetic progressions.
arxiv-2509-04710:
Differential privacy protects data, yet its decentralised forms depend heavily on network communication that privacy research rarely examines. Zhou Li, lead author with three co-authors, open that intersection in a 2025 paper on network-aware differential privacy. They survey the gap and argue network research can shape how privacy tools are deployed.

The authors identify two focus areas where networking can contribute: network security and network topology. Local and shuffle models of differential privacy both rely on collecting data across networks. Their aim is to encourage mechanisms designed explicitly for real network environments, rather than assuming communication is neutral or free.
arxiv-2509-05110:
A tissue closing over an egg must rearrange its cells while staying mechanically coherent. Maryam Setoudeh and one co-author model that epithelial gap closure in a 2025 biomechanics paper. Inspired by serosa closure in a beetle embryo, their minimal continuum model has a circular gap bounded by a contractile actomyosin cable.

Two closure mechanisms appear, depending on the energy barrier to cell intercalation versus the energy it releases. When the barrier dominates, cells intercalate into the gap. In a fluidised tissue, cells instead leave the boundary for the bulk, and cable inhomogeneities gain a mechanical role. The work explains tissue fluidisation in development and healing.
arxiv-2509-05310:
Identity appeals outran issue appeals in 2024 campaign TikTok posts, Sabina Tomkins and two co-authors report in a 2025 political science paper. Short video platforms reward content shaped by recommendation algorithms, so campaigns must adapt how they fundraise, mobilise, and persuade.

The study covers the last six months before the 2024 United States presidential election, using posts from the Harris and Trump campaigns plus a two-wave voter survey. Trump disparaged Harris more often and stressed Republican identities and issues, while Harris stressed Democratic ones. Identities appeared in about a third of posts and issues in about a quarter. Most posts mentioned neither, yet issue positions still predicted party ties.
arxiv-2509-05710:
Learning a chosen property of an unknown quantum operation, without learning all of it, is given exact cost limits by Daiki Suruga in a solo 2025 quantum information paper. Fully mapping a unitary needs samples growing with its size, which explodes with the number of qubits.

Suruga frames estimation of any square-integrable function of the unitary, given controlled access to it, in one scheme. The optimal sample count is pinned down tightly when error is averaged over all unitaries. An algorithm then achieves the optimum under a learning criterion for several function classes. Uses include matrix elements, trace, determinant, and polynomial functions, via a generalised Hadamard test.
arxiv-2509-05810:
The zeros of L-functions, deep objects that encode prime number patterns, are the subject of a 2025 paper led by Lawrence Dillon with eight co-authors. A famous conjecture by Katz and Sarnak says zeros near the center of a family mimic eigenvalues of a classical symmetry group. Which group appears can depend on how family members are weighted.

Knightly and Reno had shown that weight dependence for one-level densities; this team extends it to centered moments, averages that capture how the density spreads. Handling products of many primes forced them to widen a weighted trace formula from primes to all positive integers. A combinatorial rewrite then separates main terms from errors, letting the authors match both orthogonal and symplectic symmetry against random matrix predictions.
arxiv-2509-06110:
Curved shapes that flow until they solve a Minkowski-type problem are studied in a 2025 paper by Jinrong Hu and two co-authors. The setting is capillary geometry in the Euclidean half-space, where surfaces meet a boundary at a set angle, as droplets do. The team analyzes anisotropic capillary Gauss curvature flows, evolutions driven by curvature with direction-dependent speed.

They prove long-time existence and describe the asymptotic behavior of these flows. As a payoff, the flow method yields smooth solutions to the capillary even Lp Minkowski problem across a wide range of exponents, and to the capillary Lp problem for large exponents. Flow methods thereby settle existence questions that direct methods had left open.
arxiv-2509-06410:
Dice rollers that sample fairly from loaded inputs are verified formally in a 2025 paper by Daniel Zilken and three co-authors. Sampling algorithms resist proof because of chance, intricate loops, and inputs that vary by case. The authors present a Hoare-like framework for discrete probabilistic programs, built on distributional invariants, statements about whole output distributions rather than single values.

They apply it to two non-trivial algorithms: Lumbroso's fast dice roller and Saad and co-authors' fast loaded dice roller. The framework adds to existing proof rules and establishes both total and partial correctness for the two samplers. Verified sampling matters wherever randomness must be trusted, from cryptography to randomized algorithms.
arxiv-2509-06510:
When should someone supplying funds to a crypto trading pool pull their money out? Philippe Bergault and two co-authors study that timing question in a 2025 finance paper. In an automated market maker, providers earn trading fees but can lose value when prices move, a drawback called impermanent loss. Earlier work mostly assumed fixed deposits or exits decided from outside.

Here the exit time is part of the problem, set up as a stochastic control task where chance drives prices. The authors show the provider's value obeys a special inequality and that its solution is unique in a weak sense. Two numerical methods solve it, one based on operator splitting and one on regression. Calibrated simulations show the best exit depends on price volatility, fee levels, and how arbitrage traders and noise traders behave.
arxiv-2509-06610:
Simulating thin, fast gas flows more cheaply is the aim of a 2025 kinetic theory paper led by Veronica Montanaro, with three co-authors. Particle methods for the Boltzmann equation describe gases far from equilibrium well, but they grow costly when collisions pile up near the continuum limit. Fokker-Planck models replace collisions with diffusion and run faster.

A good Fokker-Planck model must match the Boltzmann equation's key moments and must obey the H-theorem, the law that entropy behaves correctly. The authors add a constraint based on Fisher information, a measure of how sharply a distribution is determined, and expand the drift term as a polynomial. With that design they achieve weak moment matching and correct entropy behavior at the same time. Numerical tests on a shock problem support the theory.
arxiv-2509-06810:
People learn goals faster when those goals can be squeezed into a simple rule, argue Gaia Molinaro and one co-author in a 2025 cognitive science paper. Assigning value to new, abstract outcomes is flexible but mentally expensive. The authors propose that goal learning starts in capacity-limited working memory.

As practice accumulates, learners build a compressed reward function, a simplified goal rule stored in long-term memory. Feedback can then be evaluated automatically, freeing working memory and speeding learning. Six experiments support the account: learning suffers as the goal space grows, improves when the space allows compression, and faster reward processing tracks better learning. Computational models echo the behavioral pattern. The findings bear on intrinsic motivation and on interventions meant to help people reach goals.
arxiv-2509-07010:
Ahmed R. Sadik and Mariusz Bujny give a human-in-the-loop way to grade 3D models made by AI in a 2025 paper. Large AI models can now read mixed inputs and draft complex 3D shapes. Yet there are few firm ways to tell how true those shapes are to the source, a gap that blocks uses such as open CAD design, re-drafting old parts, and fast prototyping.

Their suite scores a made shape against the true CAD file on size, surface fit, scale, and how complex its form is. As a test case they use a plain L-shaped bracket. They feed the models four kinds of input: flat views, a sketch-like view, a tree of the shape's parts, and code-based fix prompts. Richer inputs gave truer shapes each time, and the code prompts did best of all.
arxiv-2509-07110:
Arindam Basu, writing alone in 2025, asks whether light dark matter particles could be found without seeing them hit a detector directly. The particles in question are scalar dark matter with masses in the MeV range, far lighter than atoms. Some of them would be boosted, meaning they move fast enough to leave signals in sky surveys.

Within one chosen model, Basu checks gamma ray data from the COMPTEL and EGRET instruments against limits from several neutrino detectors. The results suggest that boosted light scalar dark matter with masses of roughly 20 to 80 MeV could be probed this way. Such particles also match the total amount of dark matter seen by the Planck satellite. Indirect searches may reach cases that collider and scattering tests cannot.
arxiv-2509-07410:
Next-generation mobile networks are being rebuilt as cloud software, raising a worry: does flexibility cost performance? Bilal Saleem and 8 co-authors answer with TEGRA, presented in a 2025 research paper. TEGRA is a mobile core, the control center of a 5G or 6G network. It is built as small services that can run on private or public clouds.

The authors introduce resilient design patterns for these services and new ways to manage their state. In tests, TEGRA answered requests far faster than three existing open cores. It matched a leading high-performance core while staying flexible. Adding new features also took far fewer lines of code than in rival systems. The work suggests mobile cores can serve demanding uses like augmented reality and autonomous driving without rigid, dedicated hardware.
arxiv-2509-07610:
Ahsan Mehmood and 2 co-authors design modulation schemes in 2025 for fluid-antenna systems that send data and power together. Simultaneous wireless information and power transfer, or SWIPT, lets one signal carry both. A fluid antenna can switch among many ports to find the best channel position. Practical energy harvesting circuits behave nonlinearly, which the design must respect.

The authors set a dual-objective problem over the rate-energy region: jointly raise the mutual information for discrete inputs and the harvested current. An epsilon-constraint method solves it, producing optimized signal constellations for several harvesting thresholds. Three port strategies are compared: best port, fixed port, and random port. Simulations show the optimized constellations beat conventional ones on both information rate and harvested energy. Better constellations could stretch battery-free sensors and implants further.
arxiv-2509-07710:
Benjamin W. Ryan and 2 co-authors build a way in 2025 to compare the flickering of young stars against models, in the tenth paper of a small-telescope survey series. Young stellar objects vary in brightness over hours to decades, driven by changing accretion, shifting dust extinction, and evolving starspots. Beyond a few rotation periods, that variability is stochastic, essentially random in detail.

The team converts each light curve into a variability fingerprint: a map of how likely a change of a given size is over a given timescale. Principal component analysis of the fingerprints yields a stable distribution that forms a continuum with no clusters. Adding a model-generated fingerprint to a real sample barely moves the distribution, which makes model-versus-data comparison robust. The method helps judge whether star formation simulations reproduce real stellar youth, not just average brightness.
arxiv-2509-07810:
Brigitte G. A. Pruijt leads an 8-author study in 2025 of the heart of the dwarf galaxy NGC 5253 with the MUSE instrument. NGC 5253 is a nearby blue compact dwarf galaxy with three young super star clusters and nitrogen enrichment. Its likeness to extreme star-forming galaxies of the early universe makes it a prized local analogue.

New adaptive-optics data in narrow field mode reach about 2.3 parsecs per resolution element around the giant ionized gas region near the clusters. The team derives attenuation for the central clusters and maps the extinction parameter R_V across an extragalactic object for the first time, finding it varies between clusters, which suggests differing dust physics. Gas temperatures come out flat, densities structured, and helium and oxygen abundances uniform by the direct method. The maps feed the title's claim: nitrogen enrichment arrives through stellar chemical feedback at parsec scales.
arxiv-2509-07910: Plasma wakefield acceleration uses waves in plasma to push particles to high energies, promising much smaller colliders than conventional designs. Erik Adli and Carl A. Lindstrøm track how one such design evolved, in a 2025 research paper. Their short note summarizes the major design changes since an earlier concept. That concept was presented at Snowmass 2013. The comparison ends at the most recent HALHF 2.0 baseline design.
arxiv-2509-08010:
Overreliance on language models, trusting them beyond their abilities, is measured and addressed by Lujain Ibrahim and 16 co-authors in a 2025 paper on human-compatible artificial intelligence. Models act as fluid thought partners, and people increasingly let them shape consequential choices in healthcare, advice, and other domains. Errors then carry real costs.

The authors consolidate risks at individual and societal levels, from high-stakes mistakes to governance problems, and argue that measuring overreliance should become central to research and deployment. Mitigation strategies follow from the measurement work. Keeping human judgement properly calibrated, neither dismissing models nor surrendering to them, is a design problem this paper tries to make concrete and testable.
arxiv-2509-08110:
Magnets arranged on a triangular lattice cannot all satisfy their neighbors at once, a tension called frustration. Juan R. Chamorro and 8 co-authors study that effect in a neodymium cadmium phosphide crystal in a 2025 research paper. Standard measures suggested little frustration in this material. The team suspected the standard measures were missing something.

Neutron scattering and heat tests revealed hidden signs of frustration. The ground state of the neodymium moments splits even well above the ordering point. Low-energy fluctuations persist in the same range. The ordered moment also comes out weaker than its saturated value. The authors discuss how this frustration, plus bond frustration in the surrounding network, shapes the material. Hidden frustration may be common in triangular magnets judged calm by simple tests.
arxiv-2509-08210:
Huan-Wen Wang's 2025 paper, written with Bo Fu and Shun-Qing Shen, reinterprets the chiral anomaly on a lattice. The anomaly is a quantum effect for massless Dirac fermions, particles that appear both in particle physics and in modern materials. Models usually capture behaviour near the Dirac point but lose the high-energy states at the edge of the Brillouin zone.

Effective models built from higher-dimensional Chern insulators cover the whole zone, keeping low-energy chirality and boundary states in one description. With electromagnetic fields present, the chiral coefficient generally depends on chemical potential, yet it locks to a quantised value exactly at the Fermi surface. A cleaner lattice picture of the anomaly helps both lattice gauge theorists and condensed matter physicists trust their simulations.
arxiv-2509-08510:
Assistive robots for frail older people keep failing to leave the laboratory, and Angela Higgins with 6 co-authors ask the people involved why, in a 2025 human-robot interaction paper. Co-design workshops gathered sixty-one participants across seven sessions: people living with frailty, their carers, and healthcare professionals. A persona-based approach drew out emotional, social, and psychological realities that engineering specifications miss.

Everyday issues about where new technology fits into a life, not just what it does, dominate the findings. Any assistive solution must be designed inside that complex context. Robots that ignore dignity, trust, and household routines will be refused at the door, however elegant their navigation stack may be.
arxiv-2509-08710:
Digital heritage projects describe their example uses in wildly uneven ways, which makes the examples hard to learn from. Gustavo Candela and 12 co-authors propose a stricter method in a 2025 research paper. They reviewed use case writing from outside the field and studied documented examples from heritage projects. The review showed large gaps in depth and coverage between cases.

Their framework documents use cases for heritage computing systems inside Jupyter notebooks. Notebooks keep the work open and reproducible, mixing story with runnable code. Five examples illustrate the step-by-step process. Communities such as the GLAM labs network, which links galleries, libraries, archives, and museums, stand to benefit. The authors aim to help e-infrastructures spread through heritage research by making every example complete, comparable, and reusable.
arxiv-2509-08810:
J. Le Graet and 123 co-authors present a fast method to measure conversion gain in Euclid camera sensors in a 2025 paper. Euclid is a European space mission. Its CMOS sensors need gain values that correct for signal nonlinearity and charge sharing between pixels.

The standard mean-variance method assumes a linear response and is biased. Older corrections are too slow to run per pixel. The new method uses a separate measure of the sharing pattern for a near instant calculation. Tests on flight detector data match slower methods within a tenth of a percent. The nonlinearity fix also removes a gain bias of more than two percent.
arxiv-2509-08910:
Tung Vu and 2 co-authors introduce PromptGuard for principled synthetic text generation for vulnerable populations in a 2025 paper. Language models can produce harmful or biased text for groups such as LGBTQ+ people and single parents. Post-hoc filtering, the authors argue, does not stop harm at the source.

A VulnGuard prompt uses few-shot examples, ethical reasoning steps, and adaptive roles to build protective barriers per population. Six modules handle classification, prompting, principles, tools, validation, and user interaction. Formal analysis claims a harm reduction of twenty-five to thirty percent through entropy bounds. The framework is presented as theory and design for later empirical research.
arxiv-2509-09010:
L. Feenstra and 11 co-authors test a cold vibration shield based on anti-spring blades in a 2025 paper. Fine sensors for microscopy and gravity wave work need both low heat and low shake. Closed cycle coolers, though, pump in strong low rate shake from one hertz up.

Blade anti-spring shields are small and work below one hertz, but had not been tried at cryogenic heat levels. Titanium blades set in a ring form the filter here, tuned in place by a magnet driven part. At seven kelvin, the shield's own rate drops to a very low value. Shake at the cooler rate falls by a factor of ten.
arxiv-2509-09410:
Weisheng Niu and 2 co-authors improve error bounds for multiscale elliptic homogenization in a 2025 analysis paper. Homogenization replaces a material that varies on many tiny scales with a smoother effective model. Older repeated methods gave convergence speeds limited by ratios between neighbouring scales, which can be slow when scales sit close together.

Assuming the coefficients are real analytic and repeat in each variable, the authors define multiscale correctors and sharper effective operators. Their new rate replaces those ratios with a far smaller exponential term, and they prove no larger constant can improve it. A uniform Lipschitz estimate also follows under a mild condition on how the scales separate.
arxiv-2509-09510:
Racquel Fygenson and 2 co-authors bring affordance theory into data visualisation in a 2025 paper on cognitive affordances. In classic work, an object's shape hints at the actions a person can take with it. The cognitive version asks how design steers mental actions, such as how a chart's choices guide what a reader notices and understands first.

Visualisation research uses many near neighbours of this idea, but no formal translation existed. The authors review those constructs, set them beside one another, and build a framework from psychology, human-computer interaction, and visualisation studies. It lists design decisions and reader traits that shape a chart's order of communicated information, then shows how to use it when judging and redesigning graphics.
arxiv-2509-09910:
Poorna Talkad Sukumar and 2 co-authors study how people react emotionally to data pictures in this 2025 paper. The question is racial homophily, the pull toward one's own racial group. An earlier study using bar charts found no such effect in responses to mass shooting data. This team redesigned the test with anthropographics, charts built from human figures. They also used a larger sample.

In a crowdsourced study with 720 people, each viewer saw victims from one racial group highlighted, either their own group or another. Across all conditions, viewers whose own group was highlighted showed a modest but real rise in negative feeling. The authors offer this as early evidence that homophily can surface in responses to data displays, at least with human-figure charts.
arxiv-2509-10010:
Adnan Ahmad and 3 co-authors compare small open-source language models on a dialogue task in this 2025 paper. In task-oriented chatbots, one user message can carry several intents at once, and the system must catch them all. The team tested Llama2, Mistral, and Yi models, each under eight billion parameters, on the MultiWOZ 2.1 benchmark in a few-shot setup.

Mistral came out best among the generative models, leading on most of the fourteen intent classes. A supervised BERT classifier, fine-tuned in the older style, still beat every few-shot model. The paper also records inference time and memory needs, giving builders a practical guide to what small local models can and cannot yet do for dialogue understanding.
arxiv-2509-10310:
Finding every lamp post on a city map sounds simple until addresses blur and records disagree. Evan Murphy, Marco Viola, and Vladimir A. Krylov address precise geolocation of street furniture in this 2025 paper, a task councils face when monitoring public assets in dense urban areas.

Their framework paints energy maps that encode how likely each spot is to hold an asset, in a format that can absorb outside geographic data such as road maps and placement rules. A stochastic birth-and-death optimizer then searches for the most probable arrangement of objects. Trials built around real street-lighting records from central Dublin show the method can map assets accurately and at scale. The authors promise a public code release alongside the paper.
arxiv-2509-10410:
Pei Liu and five co-authors model how DNA gets knotted inside virus shells in this 2025 applied mathematics paper. Bacteriophages pack a micron-long genome into a capsid only tens of nanometers wide. That tight confinement orders the DNA like a chromonic liquid crystal and tangles it into knots, matching what experiments see.

Their model pairs a vector field, found by minimizing the Oseen-Frank energy of nematic liquid crystals under chromonic rules, with a line tracing the DNA's central axis. A snag: that energy forbids the defects knots require. So they start from the ideal field and a helical line, then add knots through random perturbations driven by splay and twist, simulated with a Langevin system. The resulting knot patterns are compared with published experiments.
arxiv-2509-10910:
Kiyoshi Igusa and Gordana Todorov tell the story of signed exceptional sequences in this 2025 paper. The concept is their own, introduced in 2017. Exceptional sequences have a long history in representation theory, with ties to combinatorics. The signed variant is newer. It was realized after the fact that the category of noncrossing partitions is a special case.

As a short history, the paper traces how the idea grew. It grew out of the authors' work on cluster combinatorics, link invariants, and algebraic K-theory. Hereditary algebras are the focus. The paper also acknowledges the sequel. Buan and Marsh introduced tau-exceptional sequences. They carried the definitions and theorems over to every finite-dimensional algebra. For readers entering the area, the paper doubles as a map. It shows who proved what, and why the signs matter.
arxiv-2509-11410:
Roberta C. R. Mota and 4 co-authors present a lens tool for exploring three-dimensional data in virtual reality in this 2025 paper. Complex scenes often mix surfaces and flow lines, and analysts need to inspect one region closely without losing the wider picture. Their 3De lens fuses two older lens ideas, a volumetric 3D lens and a surface decal lens, into one instrument that works across geometry types.

Placed inside a virtual environment, the lens supports direct hand manipulation, so exploration feels like handling the data itself. Two domain examples show the lens building custom views that combine surfaces with streamlines. The authors offer the technique as a flexible focus-and-context aid for exploratory analysis of layered 3D data.
arxiv-2509-11510:
Rishab Parthasarathy, Michael Popik, and Noah Haefner built a radio converter as an analog electronics project. This 2025 engineering paper seeks a circuit that turns AM signals into FM ones. Both signals must stay inside their proper radio bands.

The incoming AM signal is first demodulated to its audio envelope. The envelope then drives a voltage-controlled oscillator. The oscillator re-modulates it as FM, far up the dial. The leap is about eighty-six megahertz. Audio fidelity stays high through the jump. The team built, measured, and showed the working system. They note its teaching value too. The project exercised design, analysis, and building skills for radio-frequency circuits.
arxiv-2509-11610:
Michal Botur and Tomasz Kowalski generalize a classic construction of semigroup theory. This 2025 algebra paper extends the two-sided wreath product. That product combines semigroups in a layered way. The authors develop the base of a broader construction.

For groups, the new construction matches the usual wreath product. Nothing is lost in that case. The payoff comes in decomposition theory. The Krohn-Rhodes theorem breaks finite semigroups into simple pieces. Their version sharpens that theorem. The three-element flip-flop monoid in the standard statement is swapped out. A two-element semilattice takes its place. A finer building block gives a finer account of assembly.
arxiv-2509-11910:
Markus Teller and three co-authors store qubits in an array of crystal memories. This 2025 quantum optics paper treats random-access quantum memory. Any stored qubit can be fetched on demand in such a memory. Quantum repeaters and photonic processors could use one. Solid-state memories are a leading platform.

The team stored path and time-bin qubits across ten memory cells. The cells are temporally multiplexed with controllable addressing. Weak laser pulses at the single-photon level carried the qubits. Arbitrary combinations of cells held them. Read-out came on demand. Fidelities averaged in the mid-nineties for path qubits and low nineties for time-bin qubits. Classical bounds were beaten for every cell. One time-bin qubit was parked in two cells at once and read out together.
arxiv-2509-12010:
Copying an expert into a new setting fails when many reward functions explain the same demonstrations yet disagree on what to do next. Filippo Lazzati and one co-author confront that ambiguity in inverse reinforcement learning in 2025, and propose picking the average policy.

Their criterion averages, in effect, over the policies induced by a bounded subset of the rewards consistent with the expert's behavior. The surprise is practical: that average policy comes from planning with a single reward, the centroid of the subset, which the authors derive in closed form. An efficient algorithm estimates the centroid from an offline pile of demonstrations alone, and simulations illustrate how the resulting behavior relates to the expert's own.
arxiv-2509-12310:
Old Sun-like stars spin faster than theory says they should, a puzzle blamed on their magnetic braking weakening with age. Federica Chiti and three co-authors test that story in 2025 by mapping the magnetic field of tau Ceti, a nearby Sun-like star already in the weakened-braking regime.

Using polarized light gathered at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope, they build the first Zeeman Doppler image of the star. The field is strikingly simple, stable, and feeble, mostly a tilted dipole with a strength well below what standard braking models predict. The map directly confirms the weakened dipole the hypothesis requires, and sets a sensitivity benchmark.
arxiv-2509-12410:
Expansive operators stretch small differences until they become visible, a basic engine of chaos in linear dynamics. Nilson C. Bernardes and two co-authors widen that theory in 2025 from Banach spaces to arbitrary locally convex spaces, the broader setting where many natural function spaces live.

Their average expansivity notion gets full characterizations for weighted shift operators on Fréchet sequence spaces, the workhorse examples of the field. A partial answer to a recent open problem follows for uniform expansivity on Köthe sequence spaces. The paper rounds out the picture with general properties of the several expansivity flavors and concrete examples of each.
arxiv-2509-12510:
Wei Shao and 5 co-authors propose an unsupervised way to judge the quality of wearable heart signals in a 2025 paper. Photoplethysmography, an optical method used in billions of devices, tracks blood flow from the wrist. Motion, poor perfusion, and ambient light easily corrupt its waveform and endanger downstream health analytics.

Their pipeline first trains a contrastive network on hundreds of hours of raw, unlabeled data from varied devices, learning representations stable across emitters and motion. Each embedding is then converted into a small topological signature using persistent homology, a method that summarizes shape, and clustered. The densest cluster is taken as acceptable signals, yielding a binary quality index without labeled training data. The approach works for any such device, the authors argue.
arxiv-2509-13010:
Christian Kirkham, Dominic Anstey and Eloy de Lera Acedo fit drift over time in 2025 for sky radio hunts of the first stars. The faint global signal needs a rock-steady gauge. Past gauges skip time data and assume match traits of sources.

Their noise-wave gauge fits a surface over time and pitch at once. Fits fill gaps to each antenna read time. On fake REACH data with a drifting amp, drift is cut out. New terms drop source match guesses and cut clashes in fits. Fakes then match truth to a hair, with spectrum error cut by near all.
arxiv-2509-13210:
Ligang Chang, Shengkai Xu and five co-authors detect violence in public camera video in 2025 with Vi-SAFE. Small targets, clutter, and real-time needs strain watch systems. Split spatial and time steps offer a lean path.

A slimmed detector finds human zones first, using a light backbone and focus tricks plus pruning. A time segment net then sorts clips as violent or not. Training stays split by task. On the RWF-2000 set the pair beats the time net alone and prior methods on score and speed. The design suits live public safety feeds.
arxiv-2509-13310:
Liangcai Su and 21 co-authors propose continual pre-training for agent models in a 2025 paper. Language models have grown into agents: systems that use tools on their own and reason through many steps. Built that way, agents keep falling short on agent tasks.

The authors name a root cause. A solid agentic foundation model does not exist yet. So post-training must do two jobs at once. It must teach a wide range of agent behaviours, and it must line those behaviours up with expert demonstrations. Their answer is to put agentic continual pre-training first, as the opening step in training a deep research agent. On that base they built a model called AgentFounder. Across ten benchmarks it reached the best results reported, while keeping its tool use strong.
arxiv-2509-13410:
Ashwat Jain resolves in 2025 a multipartite entanglement gauge by symmetry for all distinguishable particle systems with local symmetry. The gauge is the global entanglement of Meyer and Wallach. Symmetry resolution splits a measure into charge sectors.

For Haar random state ensembles, equipartition holds in full. Leading acts plus finite-size corrections follow a power law in local degrees of freedom. Consequences for the broader symmetry-resolved paradigm are discussed. Lab checks that could test the pattern are sketched. Random ensembles thus obey a tidy split law for this multipartite gauge.
arxiv-2509-13610:
Fabian L. Seidler and three co-authors model the skies of hot rocky exoplanets in a 2025 planetary science paper. Such planets may hold thin mineral atmospheres boiled off magma oceans, and telescope spectra hint that the planet 55 Cancri e has a carbon-rich one. The team asks which spectral features reveal an atmosphere's origin and interior state.

Their coupled atmosphere-interior model computes equilibrium gases from rock-forming and volatile elements, including how gases split between magma and air. Oxygen fugacity, a measure of how oxidized the system is, turned out to control the spectral shape most. Certain features can separate accreted gas from outgassed gas, though total air mass stays hard to pin down, and current data rule out some scenarios for 55 Cancri e.
arxiv-2509-13810:
K. M. Kwan and eleven co-authors demonstrate loss-tolerant detection of squeezed light in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Squeezed states reduce noise in one property of light below the usual quantum limit, enabling sharper measurements, but at wavelengths near two micrometers photodiodes waste much of the signal, erasing the advantage.

The team place a phase-sensitive amplifier before the detector, boosting the squeezed vacuum while it is still intact. Effective detection efficiency rose from about three quarters to nearly ninety-five percent, and observed squeezing doubled to the highest level yet reported at this wavelength, in the audio frequency band. Better shot-noise clearance also widened the useful measurement band toward lower frequencies, a result aimed at future gravitational-wave detectors.
arxiv-2509-13910:
Hao Su and fifteen co-authors hunt ultra-diffuse galaxies with deep learning in a 2025 astronomy paper. These galaxies are large but incredibly faint. Their surface brightness sits below the usual detection comfort zone. Traditional searches miss them across wide sky areas. The Kilo-Degree Survey covers a large patch of sky. It is exactly where automation should pay off.

The team adapted a network built for low surface brightness systems in another survey. They retrained it in steps for KiDS data, starting from a small training sample. Confirmed ultra-diffuse galaxies are rare, so samples stay small. The network flagged roughly thirty-three hundred candidates. Visual inspection kept five hundred forty-five high-quality ones. The keepers include rediscoveries of known systems and new candidates in about fifteen local groups and clusters.
arxiv-2509-14110:
Hans Ringström, writing alone in 2025, builds a local existence theory for Einstein equations coupled to a nonlinear scalar field. The gauge choice is of constant mean curvature type, a way to slice spacetime into time steps. Initial shapes are closed and parallelisable manifolds.

Ringström proves solutions exist for a short time, are unique, and persist under a clear continuation rule. Solutions also vary stably when starting data change slightly, a property called Cauchy stability. Earlier gauge results covered only torus shaped space and missed the scalar field case. The theory is groundwork. A companion work uses it to prove past global stability results for a family of cosmological models, where control near the start matters most.
arxiv-2509-14210:
Seth Farrell, Chenghao Li and Henrik Christensen describe GLIDE in 2025, a team system for search and rescue in places no one has mapped yet. Two drones in the air work with one ground vehicle below. One drone looks for victims, while the other scouts the ground ahead.

Inside GLIDE, the searching drone marks victim spots for the ground vehicle, and the scouting drone sends updates on where the ground vehicle can safely drive. The vehicle mixes those aerial cues with its own sensors and keeps replanning its route. Tests with a golf cart as the ground vehicle, plus separate simulations, showed faster arrival and safer travel than without the split roles and guided planning.
arxiv-2509-14310:
Samuel Patrone, Nikita Blinov and Ryan Plestid revisit axion like particles in 2025, light hypothetical particles that beam dump experiments may create. Two facilities anchor the study: SHiP at CERN and BDX at Jefferson Lab. Past forecasts counted only a few production routes.

Earlier work used particles from the main beam, or high energy photons from meson decays at SHiP. Patrone and colleagues add production inside the full electromagnetic shower that spreads through the target. Including the shower raises predicted visible decays by about tenfold across a wide mass range. Updated sensitivity curves for SHiP and new forecasts for BDX follow. Both facilities could probe regions of axion parameter space that remain unexplored so far.
arxiv-2509-14510:
Sandra Q. Liu, Yuxiang Ma and Edward H. Adelson extend a soft tactile robot finger in 2025, the GelSight Baby Fin Ray. The device mixes a camera with a soft fin shaped structure that bends on contact. Camera based touch captures force, shape and texture richly.

Earlier work showed the finger digging through clutter and sorting nuts in shells. New learning tasks test finer skill: telling nut textures apart through the shell, and estimating contact force and position. Ablation studies with popular neural networks show which design choices drive performance. Soft tactile fingers that can feel texture and force could help robots handle fragile or hidden objects where vision alone fails.
arxiv-2509-14810:
Arpan Bhattacharyya, Sayed Gool, and S. Shajidul Haque study Krylov complexity in open quantum systems in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Krylov complexity measures how an operator spreads under time evolution. Open systems also exchange energy with an environment, so dissipation and decoherence, the fading of quantum coherence, shape that spread.

The authors work with Lindblad master equations for systems coupled to bosonic baths, especially the Caldeira-Leggett model. For a damped harmonic oscillator, complexity shows clear signs of energy loss. At high temperature, complexity settles to a steady value when the full equation is used. Separating the effects, the decoherence part alone keeps oscillating like a closed system. Surprisingly, complexity shows no clear marker when decoherence begins, which the authors trace to the basis used to define it.
arxiv-2509-14910:
Ediline Nguessap, Antonio Roque, and Fernando Ferreira model a ring of heat-sensitive nerve cells linked by mixed synapses, in a 2025 paper. Each cell obeys the FitzHugh-Nagumo rules, a simple two-part model of firing. An outside electric field acts on the ring, and the cells' heat response shapes how they fire.

Runs of the model range from messy, unlinked firing to clean traveling waves. Some runs show chimera states, where synced and unsynced groups live side by side. Links of the chemical kind, spread over a range, are what keep the waves and chimeras stable. Pure local electric links give only disorder. Field rate and reach act as control knobs, while cell size tunes how strongly each cell feels the field.
arxiv-2509-15110:
Dan Zhang and five co-authors train smoother reward models for language models using temporal difference learning in a 2025 machine learning paper. Reward models grade model outputs and drive both reinforcement learning and inference-time checking. Many existing reward models judge inconsistently across steps, which makes policy updates ineffective and training unstable.

Their method, TDRM, penalizes temporal differences so a process reward model's scores evolve smoothly along a solution. At inference, the smoother models lift best-of-N selection and tree search results noticeably. During reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, models guided by these reward models reach baseline quality with a small fraction of the training data. Gains appear across eight model variants from several families and sizes, suggesting temporal consistency is a broadly useful property for reward modeling.
arxiv-2509-15410:
Vishwak Srinivasan, a lone author, studies when a mix of data sources keeps nice math traits. Two traits matter here: one bounds how fast a random walk settles, the other bounds how fast doubt shrinks. Many models are built by mixing simpler parts, and users need to know if the mix keeps these traits. Past checks were split by case.

Srinivasan gives new rules that cover both traits at once, using a broad frame built on a class of entropy measures. The rules hold for many step by step random processes. That lets him track how the traits change as such a process runs. The payoff is a clean error check for estimates made by random sampling methods used in practice.
arxiv-2509-15510:
Danqing Chen leads a team that checks what large language models did to jobs in their first years. Since late 2022, these tools have spread fast, with claims of big gains and fears of lost jobs. The team ask whether pay and joblessness moved in fields more exposed to the tools. They compare fields with high and low exposure over time.

Using a method that builds a fair comparison path, they estimate the effect of exposure after ChatGPT came out. Workers in more exposed jobs saw pay rise, while jobless rates stayed flat. The team read this as an early shift through pay, not through workers moving jobs. The paper covers short term effects only.
arxiv-2509-15810:
Chen Wang leads a team that breeds new test problems for auto designed optimizers. Meta learning can train a neural policy that designs search algorithms, sparing human experts. The training set shapes how well that policy travels. Standard suites are narrow, so policies can overfit and fail on new problems.

Their method, LSRE, first trains an encoder that maps problem traits into a flat, two way space. Even sampling on a grid in that space gives hidden codes for varied problems. A genetic program then searches for formulas close to those codes. The bred problems are diverse by design. Policies trained on them should generalize better to unseen tasks.
arxiv-2509-16010:
Cloning a voice from a few clips can make speech tools feel personal, but sharing voice data raises privacy risks. Qi Wang and four co-authors propose Fed-PISA, a method that trains voice cloning across many devices without pooling raw data. Each device keeps the speaker's tone traits at home and sends only a small style part to a shared server.

A matching step, drawn from methods that pair like users, builds a custom model for each client from peers with like styles. Tests show gains in style, natural sound, and speaker likeness over standard shared training. The gains come with very low data transfer costs.
arxiv-2509-16110:
Mexican cities have grown outward for decades, even as their centers lose people. Gonzalo G. Peraza-Mues and four co-authors study sixty-nine metro areas from 1990 to 2020 with census data. They build a model of city form from size, density, and spatial layout, using a radial curve and an expansion factor to compare cities across time.

Over thirty years the urban population nearly doubled, yet centers lost about two and a half million residents. Average distance from the center grew by more than a quarter. The study gives planners a clear way to track sprawl and its costs.
arxiv-2509-16310:
Objects that mimic black holes but have a hard surface instead of a horizon ring with tones that may shift under tiny changes. Kyriakos Destounis and three co-authors test how a lump of matter placed outside such an object affects those tones. The lump stands in for the messy surroundings real objects live in.

Loosely packed objects lose their main tone under the lump, while ultra-compact ones keep theirs steady. Higher tones shift in both cases, and some outer tones can morph into main tones as the lump moves out. Matter can amplify these shifts but cannot by itself force a full modal breakdown.
arxiv-2509-16410:
Can the richness of a data set foretell when quantum learning will beat classic methods? Christophe Pere builds a frame around that claim and tests it under rules fixed in advance across twenty-seven data sets. The central forecast fails: a combined complexity score did not predict the quantum edge, which swung with the choice of classic rival instead.

Against a weak rival the signal looked real, but against the best of six classic models it vanished. A built-in quantum pattern could still be caught by a matched measure, so quantum-sensitive structure is not ruled out. The null result ties any edge to baseline, encoding, and access.
arxiv-2509-16710:
Kevin Player, working alone, revisits a classic effect in quantum theory in a 2025 paper. A fast-moving observer who speeds up at a steady rate should feel empty space as warm. That claim is the Unruh effect. Player asks how driven, linked excitations change that warm response. The work draws a likeness with squeezing, a trick from quantum optics.

He builds smooth packet models that bridge two views of the effect. One view is tied to wedge-shaped regions of space. The other is tied to tight, local sources. His packets use special functions to blend the two. The result places the classic warm response inside a wider frame where local structure also matters.
arxiv-2509-16910:
Daxiang Li and Zhichao Zhang extend a signal tool to graphs in a 2025 paper. The Hilbert transform builds analytic signals that expose envelope and phase. On graphs, the classic form is stuck in one domain, uses a fixed shift, and lacks tuning knobs. Their fractional version loosens all three limits.

They define the new transform and prove its core traits. A method for analytic signals on graphs follows. Tests cover edge detection, anomaly spotting, and speech sorting. The new tool beat the classic graph form in each test. Flexible graph signals could aid sensor networks, where data live on irregular links rather than neat grids.
arxiv-2509-17210:
