Context-conditioned decoding with multi-tower heads models post-scoring signals like ad position, resolving a chicken-and-egg problem between predicted rate and ranking. Self-gated focus stabilizes training, timestamp-based position codes capture time across scales, and session masking prevents learning from unavailable in-session events. Production engineering enables fast training and serving at scale, and online tests show a clear click lift over the production rival.
arxiv-2602-11610:
When thousands of variables are tested at once, researchers must limit false discoveries without throwing away real signals. A knockoff-based method from Sarkar and Tang tackles that trade-off. Aniket Biswas and one co-author show it is a special case of a broader family, Benjamini-Hochberg testing weighted by e-values that are not normalized. That wider view opens room for finer weights through bounded p-to-e calibrators.

Three procedures follow from the framework, including adaptive versions that estimate how many null hypotheses are truly present. The authors establish false discovery rate control for all three. They are candid that no formal proof of superiority exists. Simulations and a real HIV drug-resistance analysis show large, consistent gains over the earlier method, and an edge over knockoffs when signals are few and weak.
arxiv-2602-11910:
Audio diffusion models synthesize high-fidelity music from text, yet fine control over musical attributes remains hard because internal mechanisms for high-level concepts are unclear. Łukasz Staniszewski and three co-authors use activation patching to show recent audio diffusion models exhibit a semantic bottleneck. A small, shared subset of adjacent attention layers controls distinct musical concepts such as instruments, vocals, or genres.

Building on that finding, they evaluate steering methods, comparing steering against prompt-level, score-space, and weight-space interventions and analyzing how steering interacts with intervention site. A new benchmark, backed by a large user study, shows localized activation steering sets a new state of the art in audio concept modulation. For music generation, that finding matters: control concentrates in a few layers, so steering those layers beats broad tweaks. The work maps where musical meaning lives inside spread models and how to adjust it on purpose.
arxiv-2602-12110:
The Hubble infrared channel responds nonlinearly to incoming light, and its 2009 correction, an average polynomial per detector quadrant, is weakly constrained near saturation. Huynh and five co-authors test a new pixel-based correction against varied image types, sources, and sample sequences.

In nearly all cases the new fix improves linearity above 50,000 electrons, by up to 7 percent near the 80,000-electron saturation limit in final reads. It also sharply cuts cosmic rays wrongly flagged during ramp fitting, improving photometric accuracy and signal-to-noise, especially in the upper-left quadrant. Because the correction makes sources brighter, the team recalibrated five flux standards and found a negligible shift, smaller than the scatter in observed-to-synthetic flux ratios.
arxiv-2602-12310:
Biochemical data live scattered across many databases, each with its own names, formats, and gaps, so a single question can mean many searches. Casper Asbjørn Eriksen led this work with three co-authors, presenting ChemRecon, a meta-database and Python interface that unifies compounds, reactions, enzymes, structures, and atom maps into one consistent ontology.

Unified querying and cross-database analysis let users build graph views by walking links between entries, drawing out facts no single base holds alone. One example is settling conflicting sources to pick the most likely structure for a compound. ChemRecon is open source, installable through pip, with code on GitLab and docs online, giving researchers a single door into scattered biochemical knowledge.
arxiv-2602-12610:
Microlensing can reveal planets in complex stellar systems beyond other methods, and event KMT-2016-BLG-1337 shows that power. Cheongho Han led a large team here, reporting a planetary companion in a microlensing event produced by a binary system of low-mass stars. The light curve shows a short-term anomaly on top of a binary-lens single-source model profile.

Detailed modelling under binary-lens binary-source and triple-lens single-source readings favours the triple-lens case substantially, strongly supporting a planetary companion. Two viable triple-lens solutions fit nearly equally well. One is a Saturn-mass planet near 0 point 3 Jupiter masses at about 4 astronomical units, the other a 7 Jupiter-mass planet at about 1 point 5 astronomical units. Host stars are early M dwarfs of about 0 point 54 and 0 point 40 solar masses. They are separated by about 3 point 5 astronomical units, at about 7 kiloparsecs toward the Galactic bulge.
arxiv-2602-12710:
Two ways of trimming a general vector autoregression for multi-dimensional data look unrelated at first glance. Matrix-valued time series models and global vector autoregressions each cut the parameter count, but from different starting points. Dietmar Bauer and Kurtulus Kidik compare the restrictions each model imposes and ask where the two families overlap.

They show that, under matching restrictions on both sides, the two approaches meet in a shared framework. That shared view lets insights from matrix time series shed light on how global models behave, and vice versa. For practitioners, the result clarifies which simplifications the two model families really share, rather than treating them as separate tools that happen to look similar.
arxiv-2602-12810:
Advertorials are paid ads dressed to look like news, and readers often take them for independent reporting. Emmanouil Papadogiannakis and three co-authors present the first large-scale systematic study of the practice. They built an automated detector, gathered 186,000 ad web addresses over five months, and mapped where advertorials appear and how they behave.

The findings are stark: advertorials show up on one in three news sites, including well-known outlets such as The Guardian, EuroNews, and CNN. Many display traits linked to deceptive practice, hiding or obscuring legal disclaimers so readers cannot spot the paid nature of the content. By borrowing a publication's credibility, advertorials gain trust they have not earned, and the study documents that mechanism at scale.
arxiv-2602-12910:
Single-member districts create a tension: follow each district's majority, or mirror the statewide vote? Yunus Aybas and two co-authors measure misrepresentation as a weighted sum of local and statewide gaps, then find the rule that minimises it. The optimal rule is a cutoff rule: as the weight on statewide misrepresentation rises, the cutoff slides continuously from first-past-the-post's 50% to the proportional cutoff that matches seat share to vote share.

That sliding cutoff makes gerrymandering harder, offering a new lever against manipulation. Using a majorisation-based measure of geographic concentration, the authors show concentration cuts misrepresentation only under the optimal rule. Within this family, first-past-the-post and proportional representation are uniquely picked out by no cross-district spillovers and by gerrymandering-proofness. United States House data then infer weights that rationalise outcomes, giving a fresh metric for reform proposals.
arxiv-2602-13110:
Language models increasingly judge other models' outputs pairwise, but their judgements suffer miscalibration and position bias. Sher Badshah, Ali Emami, and Hassan Sajjad propose SCOPE, a framework that sets an acceptance threshold so accepted judgements keep their error rate below a user-set level alpha, assuming exchangeability. A bias-neutral uncertainty signal, bidirectional preference entropy, queries the judge in both response orders and converts order-averaged preference into an entropy score.

Across pairwise judging benchmarks, the entropy signal beats standard confidence proxies on calibration and discrimination. SCOPE meets its target risk bound, with empirical false discovery rate near 0.097 to 0.099 at alpha 0.10, while retaining substantial coverage. Compared with vanilla baselines, SCOPE accepts up to 2.4 times more judgements under the same risk constraint, showing that better uncertainty signals enable reliable, high-coverage model-based evaluation.
arxiv-2602-13310:
Longer chains of thought help language models, but depth alone can trap a model in one line of reasoning. Running several reasoning paths in parallel widens the search, yet that trick had not been carried over to vision-language models. Visual Para-Thinker is the first parallel reasoning framework for such models, splitting visual input into parts and reasoning over them at once while keeping paths independent and diverse.

Two mechanisms, Pa-Attention and LPRoPE, guard path independence, and a native multimodal build on vLLM keeps the parallel work fast. Benchmarks spanning fine-grained vision, counting, grounding, and hallucination tests confirm the parallel gains transfer to the visual domain. Haoran Xu leads the work with seven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13510:
Variational inequalities are a broad lens for problem-solving, covering finding minima, saddle-point problems, and Nash game solutions as special cases. This paper tackles a harder two-level form, where smooth operators at each level are given as finite sums. The challenge is to design sampling methods that cut variance and provably approach the solution in both Euclidean and Bregman geometries.

The authors claim the first rates and complexity statements for sampling algorithms that cut variance on two-level problems of this kind in these settings. That claimed first fills a gap between general variational theory and practical sampling methods for nested problems. Pavel Dvurechensky leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14310:
Sharan Srinivasan and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv problem in robust filtering for Lévy-driven models. Signal and view runs share Brownian and jump noise, and toughness means the sifter hangs smoothly on the view path. That smoothness matters when paths are rebuilt from discrete samples, yet jump cases were largely open.

The authors build a sifter form and prove smoothness in two regimes. With finitely many jumps on tight spans, smoothness holds in rough p-shift and p-shift shapes on cadlag path space, with no split rule on jump factors. With endlessly many jumps, smoothness holds in a tweaked rough p-shift shape for cadlag shape rough paths, under an added split rule. Stratonovich and tied calculus tools carry both proofs.
arxiv-2602-14410:
Zhi Xiao and two co-authors build a 2026 arXiv differential-form approach to extended electrodynamics. The work derives Newman-Penrose null-tetrad formulas for Lorentz-breaking widenings of Maxwell theory. Change forms state acts and field formulas tightly and with no grid tie, enabling a step-by-step, clear proof of first-order formulas.

Within that form, the authors give a simple algebra build for gauge-safe widened Maxwell acts, dodging plain index juggling up to mass size six. The joined change-form and Newman-Penrose plan offers a deft tool for studying Lorentz-breaking effects on far light travel and twist, a probe of base symmetry in light's far-field acts.
arxiv-2602-14510:
S. Hayashida and 14 co-authors report a 2026 arXiv high-pressure cell for inelastic neutron scattering. The zirconium-based bulk metallic glass clamp cell is built for high-pressure measures, with empty-cell spectra showing broad, plain backgrounds mirroring the glass's shapeless form. That clean background is a key edge.

Test measures with a CsFeCl3 guide sample confirm neutron flow through the metallic-glass cell far tops that of an old monobloc CuBe clamp cell. Raised neutron clarity plus a clean background profile advance high-pressure inelastic neutron hit studies, letting researchers probe matter under pressure with less cell meddling and clearer signals.
arxiv-2602-14610:
A ring can be sorted by how its units look. Zari Vesali Mahmood, with Ahmad Moussavi and Peter Danchev as co-authors, defines weakly square-root-J-U rings, where each unit equals one plus or minus a root of the Jacobson radical. The class widens several older ring types at once.

The authors show such rings are Dedekind-finite and that larger matrix rings over them never qualify. In positive characteristic, the characteristic must be a product of powers of two and three. Group rings get a full test, with the group forced to be torsion. The paper also sharpens recent work by other authors.
arxiv-2602-14710:
Shaojie Jiang, Svitlana Vakulenko, and Maarten de Rijke present Orcheo, a modular, full-stack platform for conversational search. Building such search today means wiring query reformulation, ranking, and response generation into one pipeline, and researchers lack both a shared framework and an easy route to end-to-end prototypes for user study.

Orcheo answers with single-file node modules that make components easy to share and reuse, plus production-ready infrastructure with dual execution modes and secure credential handling to bridge prototype and system. The open-source platform aims to make conversational search experiments reproducible and deployable. Research code becomes a working system with less glue.
arxiv-2602-14810:
Y. Asaoka and others describe the excavation of the Hyper-Kamiokande cavern, six hundred metres underground, now complete at sixty-nine metres across and ninety-four metres high, among the world's largest rock caverns. A vertical, dome-capped cylindrical design was chosen to optimise cost and performance, while great depth and geometry posed major engineering challenges.

The paper outlines the underground works, main cavern design, excavation plan, and the evolution of support design and construction methods, following an information-based observational approach that adapted as digging revealed the rock. A giant neutrino detector's home was carved with care and constant revision. Underground physics gains a cathedral of stone.
arxiv-2602-14910:
Claudiu Cristian Musat and others hold that sound thought grows from talk-fed self-check, learned from rich social play, not from size alone. They lean on Vygotsky's growth lore and push three self-check claims, first that the lone mind is born in talk: sense of the world first forms midst others, then moves in.

Talk-fed self-check, they add, lets agents make sense free of snap reply, as the rub of lining up with a peer hones thought. Schooling, then, should grow talk rooms that teach self-check, not just big models. Thought turns out to be a social heirloom, rehearsed alone.
arxiv-2602-15010:
Mark and colleagues address robot tasks that demand memory, such as finding an item after searching part of a room. Top robot policies usually look only at the current observation, which fails tasks that hinge on history. Feeding in full histories backfires too, since policies latch onto incidental training features that do not survive deployment. The team traces that failure to thin coverage of the history space in training, a space that grows exponentially with horizon.

Their answer, Big Picture Policies, conditions on a small set of key frames flagged by a vision-language model. Projecting varied rollouts onto compact task events cuts the train-to-deployment shift without losing expressivity. Across four real manipulation tasks and three simulated ones, BPP beats the best comparison by 70 percent in success rate on real-world tests.
arxiv-2602-15110:
Egleston and colleagues measure pulsar distances from chirping orbital periods. The observed rate of change of a millisecond binary pulsar's orbital period encodes both the binary's own traits and its environment. Chirp contributions come from intrinsic energy loss through gravitational wave emission, from apparent motion across the sky, and from galactic acceleration. The latter two depend on how far away the pulsar is.

Using chirp data, the team infers ranges for 21 binary pulsars. For four of them, uncertainties beat prior measures. They test several realistic acceleration models to gauge how much the inferred ranges hinge on the chosen potential, finding a significant dependence for four pulsars. The method turns orbital chirps into a distance tool.
arxiv-2602-15310:
Abt and colleagues image the shape of the dead zone of a p-type BEGe unit at bias levels by mapping 3D Compton bounce yield. The bias was raised step by step to full drain. The shape take was found at full drain. Below full drain, the scaled take seen for 2 by 2 by 2 cube mm cells was used to create the image of the dead zone for each bias level.

The images were matched with models from the open software SSD.jl to pull the outward dirt level curve of the unit. The strong outward drop in dirt level obtained in the outer cm was checked using other charge tests. This new method to find dirt level via 3D Compton bounce yield maps gives a strong tool for deep unit study.
arxiv-2602-15410:
Wang tests if magnet caused pion-rho mixing can clarify the steady acts of the charged pion seen in lattice QCD. Using a near-pole working move drawn from the SU(2) Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, he shows that the lowest Landau level charged pion blends with the lengthwise aligned charged rho meson. It holds the same quanta labels in a magnet setting.

The result pushback is hard boosted by the damping of the rho wave-function retune near the pole. As an upshot, the lowest blended mode grows a peak as the magnet field rises, echoing the broad drift seen on the lattice. Check with the plain core answer of the Landau-cast heart shows that the trick is tough, though the exact spot of the peak stays plan tied. These findings back pion-rho mixing as a key hopeful trick for charged meson range in high magnet zones.
arxiv-2602-15510:
Kabgere and Shylaja point to a mismatch at the heart of federated learning on graphs. Standard federated methods average model weights as if they lived in one shared flat space, but graph neural network weights act as message-passing operators whose sense hangs on graph shape. When client graphs differ in shape and in data mix, each local update perturbs a distinct operator, so plain averaging blends directions that do not fit together.

The result, they argue, is a global model that may converge and score well yet lose feel for graph structure, a loss that loss and accuracy scores miss. Their fix is GGRS, a server-side scheme that works on a data-free proxy of operator shifts and enforces fit through alignment, subspace match, and sensitivity control. The aim is to keep message passing coherent while clients keep their data local.
arxiv-2602-15710:
Laude works alone on Bregman proximal augmented Lagrangian methods with second-order oracles for convex composite optimisation. The outer loop is that algorithm with relative errors, applied to the KKT operator for the problem. Like old Lagrange-Newton methods, it again and again solves adjusted KKT inclusions by finding the minimum of a smooth Bregman Lagrangian, formed after dual variables are removed.

Non-flat geometry makes that function generalised self-concordant, placing it within Newton method reach with quadratic convergence when the outer step size is chosen with care. Metric subregularity then yields fast outer-loop rates and a joint cost bound. Special cases include a variant of the Tseng and Bertsekas exponential multiplier method and interior-point schemes close to those of Pougkakiotis and Gondzio.
arxiv-2602-15810:
Sznitman and Widmayer use Gaussian measure on R-N to define coefficients of an elliptic diffusion. That diffusion lives in an open cone of R-2, with one component for enstrophy and one for energy. They show this diffusion has exactly one stationary distribution. Thanks to special properties of its coefficients, they derive a condensation bound. That bound controls how close the ratio of expected energy to expected enstrophy sits to one, a ratio capped at one under their normalisation.

A companion article, offered as a proof of concept, shows this diffusion as the inviscid limit of the enstrophy-energy process from a stationary Galerkin-Navier-Stokes type evolution in N dimensions. That evolution uses Brownian forcing and random stirring, whose strength can tend to zero in the inviscid limit, playing the role of regularisation. The paper thus builds the diffusion whose limit the companion article studies.
arxiv-2602-16010:
Huang and colleagues trim checkpoint costs in high performance computing by asking a sharper question: which data actually affects the output. Checkpoint restart saves program state on a schedule and eats storage and compute, yet much of what gets saved never influences the result, so it need not be saved at all.

Their method uses automatic differentiation to test every element inside each variable, marking pieces as critical or uncritical by whether they touch the output. Visual maps of those regions follow the physics and logic of each code, a useful check in itself. Across eight NAS Parallel Benchmark codes, dropping uncritical elements cuts checkpoint storage by up to twenty percent, a direct saving for long running simulations.
arxiv-2602-16310:
Zhexiao Lin and coauthors introduce the b-value, a tool for combining unbiased and biased estimators from a sensitivity analysis perspective. In empirical research with multiple estimators for the same parameter, a central question is how to combine fair but less precise estimators with biased but more precise ones to improve results. The authors focus on a less studied inference question: how to conduct valid statistical inference with unknown bias.

They propose combining unbiased and biased values from a bias perspective, giving confidence ranges keyed by bias size. . The b-value is the key value of unknown maximum bias at which combining them does not yield a clear result. Applied to three standard combined cases, the authors find bias limits where results change. They advise giving the b-value based on the soft-threshold method, which is robust to unknown bias and achieves the lowest worst-case risk.
arxiv-2602-16410:
Leroy Chew leads a team of three coauthors introducing a PSPACE-complete fragment of first order logic called QEALM. Set against other known fragments, QEALM takes after quantified Boolean formulas in nature, with game-like alternations and room to narrow to complete problems for the polynomial hierarchy. It is a natural first-order analogue of quantified Boolean formulas, just as effectively propositional logic is a first-order analogue of dependency quantified Boolean formulas.

For QEALM, the paper proves completeness results at the PSPACE level and across the polynomial hierarchy, plus traits like closure under Robinson resolution and hardness that holds after meeting Schaefer fragments. They also identify problems in the TPTP library that fall into the fragment and determine each one's level in the polynomial hierarchy. The paper thus gives logicians a fragment that behaves like quantified Boolean formulas while staying inside first order logic.
arxiv-2602-16710:
Ruijie Zheng and co-authors present EgoScale, a transfer frame for dexterous robot manipulation built on large-scale egocentric human data. Human behavior is a highly scalable data source for physical intelligence, yet it was unclear if it could support fine-grained, high-degree-of-freedom hand control. The team trains a vision-language-action model on over twenty thousand hours of action-labeled egocentric human video, far larger than prior efforts.

They uncover a log-linear scaling law between human data scale and validation loss, and that loss tracks downstream real robot scores closely. A two-stage recipe follows: large-scale human pretraining, then light aligned human-robot mid-training. The final policy lifts average success by over half against a no-pretraining baseline on a twenty-two degree-of-freedom hand, with strong long-horizon control and one-shot task adaptation.
arxiv-2602-16810:
Noah Fleming, Anna Gal, Deniz Imrek, and Christophe Marciot prove a separation above TFNP from Sherali-Adams lower bounds. In TFNP, many natural existence problems are incomparable in the black-box setting. In the second level of the total function polynomial hierarchy, by contrast, many natural problems reduce to the Strong Avoid problem. The paper breaks that pattern.

The Linear Ordering Principle is shown not to reduce to Strong Avoid in the black-box setting, the first such problem at that level. The proof uses a link between total search problems and proof complexity. It suffices to rule out a small proof of the principle in a Sigma-2 variant of Sherali-Adams. That is done by extending the pseudo-expectation method to the Sigma-2 setting via a combinatorial covering problem about permutations.
arxiv-2602-16910:
Mike Cummings deepens the link between webs and Springer fibers in the two-column case. Webs and Springer fibers are separately key objects in representation theory: webs give a diagrammatic calculus for tensor invariants, and Springer fiber cohomology builds irreducible representations of the symmetric group. Fung's 1997 thesis first linked sl2 webs to two-row Springer fibers, but that case is far from generic.

Building on Fresse, Melnikov, and Sakas-Obeid, the paper uses webs to characterize the smooth components of two-column rectangle Springer fibers and to describe their geometry simply. It also shows the Poincaré polynomial of the smooth components is invariant under the natural dihedral action on the corresponding webs. Representation theorists get a clean web-based account of smooth components in a substantially more complicated case.
arxiv-2602-17110:
Tanisha Parulekar led a five-author team bridging a gap between rigid and soft robot grippers. Grasp synthesis tools like AnyGrasp are built for rigid parallel grippers. Porting their poses to a soft Fin-ray gripper usually fails to capture compliant behavior, demanding heavy data and yielding poor grasps. The paper maps rigid-gripper poses onto soft-gripper poses with Conditional Flow Matching, a generative model.

A data pipeline pairs rigid and soft grasps. A U-Net autoencoder conditions the model on object geometry from a depth image, learning a smooth map from AnyGrasp poses to stable Fin-ray poses. On a seven-degree-of-freedom robot, the generated poses beat rigid baselines clearly on both seen and unseen objects, with standout gains for cylindrical and spherical shapes. The method offers a data-efficient route to soft grasping.
arxiv-2602-17310:
Dennis N. Schneider led a four-author team on choosing where to grasp tissue in colorectal surgery. Exact grasping point prediction is key for self-run tissue handling in keyhole surgery, yet colon procedures, long and complex, remain rare in research. Their repeated tissue handling makes them a good entry point for machine learning support. The paper offers attachment anchors, an ordered map of local shape and force ties between tissue and its body links.

Anchors recast operating scenes into a steady local frame, cutting doubt in grasping point choice. They can be read from scope images and fed into a machine learning grasping setup. Tests on a dataset of ninety colon cases show anchors beat image-only rivals, with very strong gains out of sample, including unseen cases and surgeons. The map thus offers a useful middle step toward learning-based tissue handling.
arxiv-2602-17410:
Bingqian Li led an eight-author team improving LLM-based recommendation with self-hard negatives from intermediate layers. Large language models show great promise in recommender systems, where supervised fine-tuning usually adapts them, and preference learning later adds negatives to training. Current methods rely on sequence-level, offline-made negatives, which prove less sharp and useful when item spaces grow large.

The paper proposes ILRec, a fine-tuning system using self-hard negative signals from intermediate layers. Self-hard tokens from middle layers supply fine-grained negative guidance that live reflects the model's learning process. A two-stage system of cross-layer tuning and cross-layer teaching lets the model jointly tell apart informative negatives and enhance signal quality from middle layers. Tests on three data sets show ILRec works for LLM-based ranking.
arxiv-2602-17810:
Edson Leonel and team discuss a shared critical behavior in the shift from order to chaos in an oval billiard with a static edge. A warp knob controls the edge shape, from round at zero warp to oval at nonzero warp where wildness emerges. The warp gives rise to a chaotic layer along a well-defined stripe in phase space.

By introducing changes that isolate the chaotic stripe, the authors track spreading of path groups and identify a readout that plays the role of an order parameter. For small warps, the peak value of spreading obeys a scaling law with an exponent near one half, fading smoothly as warp tends to zero. The linked response blows up in the same limit, marking edge behavior like second-order smooth phase transitions in stats physics. The account complements the companion billiard study with a fuller picture of the near-edge regime.
arxiv-2602-17910:
Hanjing Shi and Dominic DiFranzo introduce APEMO, affect-aware peak-end modulation for orchestration, aimed at long-horizon agentic systems. Old matching focuses on individual model outputs, yet self-run agents in long-horizon workflows need steady trust across entire exchange paths. APEMO is a runtime planning layer optimizing compute sharing under fixed budgets by using time-feeling signals.

Instead of changing model weights, APEMO detects path wobble through conduct signs and targets repairs at key parts such as peak moments and endings. Tests across multi-agent runs and language-model-based plan-act flows show APEMO always lifting path-level quality and reuse odds over fixed planners. Results reframe matching as a time control problem, offering a tough building path for long-horizon agentic systems where trust must persist across long interactions.
arxiv-2602-18010:
Jilan Xu and colleagues re-purpose multimodal large language models for audio-text retrieval, the task of bridging acoustic signals and natural language. Contrastive dual-encoder systems like CLAP show promise, but small-scale encoders cap their power. Their text encoders especially struggle with complex queries that need reasoning or world knowledge.

The authors propose AuroLA, a contrastive language-audio pretrained model that uses a multimodal large language model as a single backbone for retrieval. A scalable data pipeline curates diverse audio from many sources and generates multi-granular captions, from long descriptions to structured tags, through automated annotation. The model is adapted by prompting it to summarize the audio or text input, with the hidden state of a special token serving as the embedding. In experiments, AuroLA consistently beat leading dual-encoder models, including the recent PE-AV, supporting the unified-backbone approach.
arxiv-2602-18410:
Tai Huy Ha builds a unified algebraic theory of Łojasiewicz exponents. His 2026 paper treats pairs of graded families and ideal filtrations. Local exponents, gradient exponents, and exponents at infinity all appear as limits between filtrations, ruled by integral closure. In this view, these exponents are valuative optimization problems at heart.

The central contribution is a finite-max principle. Under checkable rules, an infinite supremum bounding the exponent drops to a finite maximum that computes it exactly. Two mechanisms drive this. Finite testing comes from normalized blowups and Rees algebras. Attainment comes via compactness of normalized value spaces under linear bounds. The principle yields strong results and recovers classic toric and Newton cases. The paper also shows why its rules are needed.
arxiv-2602-18510:
Vladimir M. Subbotin and four co-authors test whether early life's building blocks could gather in meteor craters. Their 2026 paper offers lab and numerical evidence for liposome gathering on meteor crater floors on Early Earth. It builds on earlier work showing liposomes sunk in a shallow Archean pond are shielded from harmful UV radiation.

That shield lets liposomes live long enough for self-copying of amphiphiles, plus mutation and selection of assemblies with the most stable membranes. For liposomes to fuse, grow, swap contents and membranes, and divide, they need a population: a dense group in close contact. The study shows such gathering is feasible in bowl-shaped craters on Early Earth, especially under periodic quakes.
arxiv-2602-18710:
Give the same data and the same question to many analysts, and honest analysts often disagree. Martin Bertran, with two co-authors, asks whether autonomous AI analysts can reproduce that structured disagreement cheaply in 2026, and what it means when defensible analyses become almost free to generate.

Each AI analyst runs a full pipeline for a single dataset and question. A separate AI checker then vets every run for sound method. Across three datasets, results spread widely in effect sizes and conclusions, traced to choices in preprocessing, model form, and inference that shift with the analyst persona and the underlying model. The authors argue for multiverse-style reporting and full disclosure of prompts, so that analytic uncertainty stays visible instead of being cherry-picked away.
arxiv-2602-19010:
Type-IIn supernovae interact with material shed by their progenitors, and their spectra record that interaction. Sethulakshmi Vazhayil, with three co-authors, reports a comparative spectroscopic study in 2026 of SN 2017hcc and SN 2023usc, using data from the Himalayan Chandra Telescope.

SN 2017hcc is sampled over seven epochs, from two weeks after explosion into the nebular stage at over a year. SN 2023usc is sampled over five epochs, from under two weeks to about five months. Late spectra of SN 2023usc are nearly featureless except for hydrogen alpha, suggesting a novel explosion route. Assuming a circumstellar medium model from multi-epoch ejection, the authors compare both events with other interacting supernovae. True narrow lines emerge early only in a few events, suggesting progenitors with highly extended, optically transparent outer circumstellar media are relatively rare.
arxiv-2602-19110:
Tokamak scenario design needs fast plasma predictions. Chenguang Wan, with twelve co-authors, builds a transformer surrogate in 2026 for the WEST tokamak. Physics codes give insight but cost too much for rapid design and control tuning. A data-driven model can fill that gap.

The model predicts key global parameters from pre-discharge signals alone. Magnetic coil currents, heating power, plasma current reference, and line-averaged density feed it. Targets include three beta measures, stored energy, and two safety factors. Training uses hundreds of WEST discharges. Error stays low, fit stays strong, and inference runs in well under a second. Discharge planning, scenario evaluation, and real-time control all gain a fast assistant.
arxiv-2602-19510:
Data mixing means strategically reweighting training domains, and it is vital for robust machine learning models. Rudrajit Das and three co-authors analyze it as a bilevel optimization problem. An outer loop tunes domain weights to minimize validation loss, while an inner loop tunes model parameters to minimize weighted training loss. Classical bilevel methods need hypergradients, which in theory require the inner loop to converge.

State-of-the-art methods instead run a finite, often small, number of inner steps before updating weights, and the theory of that shortcut was unclear. The paper proves the greedy approach of a single inner step can fail even in a plain quadratic example. Under a fixed budget of parameter updates, the analysis clarifies when fewer weight updates over a longer horizon converge better, justifying the less-is-more title.
arxiv-2602-19910:
This discovery task asks a model to recognize both known categories, for which some labels exist, and unknown ones, for which none do. A 2026 arXiv paper by Wei He and five co-authors proposes a multi-modal feature-learning framework for that open-set problem, built on semi-supervised rate reduction.

Prior methods lean heavily on aligning representations across modalities, but few shape the within-modality structure of those representations. The new framework, SSR-squared-GCD, aligns within-modality relationships to give cross-modal features the desired structure, and it boosts transfer by integrating prompt candidates through vision-language alignment. Extensive tests on generic and fine-grained benchmarks show better performance. Readers gain a framework that treats within-modality shape as a first-class concern.
arxiv-2602-20010:
Scheduling problems sometimes pair tasks: a second task must start exactly a fixed delay after the first finishes, and the pair shares a due date. A 2026 arXiv paper by Wiesław Kubiak, working alone, studies such coupled tasks on a single machine with the goal of minimizing maximum lateness.

The literature offers hardly any results for coupled tasks with exact delays, leaving the problem open. Kubiak gives polynomial-time algorithms for two structured cases. In the agreeable case, later due dates go with longer second tasks; in the disagreeable case, later due dates go with shorter second tasks. Whether the general problem is tractable remains open. Readers gain efficient algorithms for the two tractable orderings and a clear statement of what stays unsolved.
arxiv-2602-20110:
Dynamical encounters fling black holes together on eccentric orbits. Those orbits should still be eccentric when the merger enters the gravitational-wave band. A 2026 arXiv paper by Mor Rozner and three co-authors argues every dynamic birth channel predicts the same eccentricity pattern.

The claim covers gravity-wave frequencies used for LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA, in the high-eccentricity limit. It rests on a wide gap in scale. The regime where gravity waves create eccentric mergers in those detectors sits far from the formation environment. A formula-based solution from the authors matches computer studies very well. The result guides both theory and ongoing searches for eccentric gravity-wave sources.
arxiv-2602-20310:
Ke Xu and John Gunnar Carlsson offer one method for a whole family of truck-and-drone routing problems. Coordinated routing pairs truck capacity and range with drone speed and flexibility for last-mile delivery. It cuts time and cost. Yet each coordination mode has its own constraints. A small structural change can create a new type needing its own algorithm. This 2026 paper builds a unified three-phase method on the Lin-Kernighan-Helsgaun algorithm.

The method is tested on three types, each benchmarked against an effective algorithm. They are the Flying Sidekick Traveling Salesman Problem, the Traveling Salesman Problem with Multiple Drones, and the Vehicle Routing Problem with Drones. Results nearly match optimal solutions on small instances and improve the best-known solutions for several medium instances. Extensions in the paper show how widely it applies. Planners gain one method instead of a separate algorithm per variant.
arxiv-2602-20610:
Specs are vital for proving programs correct, yet writing them by hand is slow and hard. Cuong Chi Le and six co-authors note that language-model methods can generate specs, but single-pass prompting often yields inaccurate results. Their framework, SpecMind, treats language models as interactive explorers rather than one-shot generators. It uses feedback-driven multi-turn prompting, letting the model refine candidate specs from implicit and explicit correctness feedback while deciding on its own when to stop.

That loop deepens code grasp and aligns outputs with true program behavior through exploratory tries. Tests show SpecMind clearly beats state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and completeness of generated specs. The paper presents interactive refinement, not bigger single-pass prompts, as the key to trustworthy specs.
arxiv-2602-20810:
Yaacov Pariente and one co-author release POMDPPlanners, an open-source Python package for testing planning algorithms under partial observability, where the agent cannot see the full state. It bundles leading planning methods with benchmark tasks, including safety-critical variants, so researchers can compare rival approaches fairly on shared ground.

The package adds automated tuning through Optuna, persistent caching with failure recovery, and parallel simulation, cutting the overhead of large simulation studies. Built for scalable, reproducible research on decisions under uncertainty, it targets risk-sensitive settings where standard toolkits fall short.
arxiv-2602-21010:
Real-time object detection needs high accuracy at low latency, but current real-time detection transformers are hard to reproduce because backbone pre-training is so costly. Jiannan Huang, Aditya Kane, Fengzhe Zhou, Yunchao Wei, and Humphrey Shi show good design can cut that cost in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their EfficientNAT backbones combine modern efficient convolution with local attention, and a redesigned hybrid encoder lifts both performance and speed.

The resulting Le-DETR family reaches state-of-the-art real-time detection using only two standard training datasets, saving about four fifths of pre-training images against previous methods. Experiments report top accuracy on COCO validation with millisecond latency on a high-end graphics card, beating recent rivals on accuracy, speed, or both. Code and weights are promised as open source.
arxiv-2602-21610:
Jiwan Kim and six co-authors present WatchHand, the first continuous 3D hand pose tracking system on off-the-shelf smartwatches using only built-in speaker and microphone. Hand pose tracking on wrist wearables enables rich, expressive interactions, yet remains unavailable on commercial smartwatches, since prior systems need external sensors or custom hardware.

WatchHand emits inaudible frequency-modulated continuous waves and captures reflections from the hand. Acoustic signals feed a deep-learning model estimating 3D hand poses for 20 finger joints. Evaluation spans diverse real-world conditions: multiple smartwatch models, wearing hands, body postures, noise conditions, and pose-variation protocols. Mean per-joint position error reaches under 8 millimetres in cross-session tests with device remounting. Performance drops for unseen users or gestures, but lightweight fine-tuning on small data adapts effectively, lowering the barrier to smartwatch hand tracking without extra hardware.
arxiv-2602-21710:
Motoki Nakata extends out-of-time-ordered correlators, a quantum measure of operator growth and information scrambling, to turbulent fields as an example of non-canonical Hamiltonian systems. Using the Wigner-Weyl transform and Moyal bracket formalism, he derives the semiclassical limit for turbulent plasmas ruled by the Hasegawa-Mima equation. That limit is an ensemble-averaged squared Lie-Poisson bracket between two functionals of the turbulent fields.

The classical-limit correlator measures how a small perturbation to one functional spreads across scales and later affects another. It captures scale- or field-dependent transfer. In a quasilinear setting with strong zonal flow, a closed analytic form describes zonal and non-zonal mode interaction. It grows quadratically at early times, then saturates in the strong-shear regime with an inverse-square tail, as zonal shearing pushes perturbations to higher wavenumbers.
arxiv-2602-22110:
In a permutation flowshop, every job visits machines in the same order, but processing times can wobble from plan. Noam Goldberg and two co-authors study the robust version where only a budgeted number of times may deviate on each machine. They show the robust problem reduces to solving many instances of the plain nominal problem, a surprisingly clean result.

The payoff is immediate: the robust problem becomes solvable in polynomial time for two machines, and approximable in polynomial time for any fixed machine count. The proof adapts a classic Bertsimas and Sim analysis, applying duality to a min-max objective instead of a linear one. Shops gain exact or near-exact robust schedules without resorting to heuristics or heavy integer programming.
arxiv-2602-22210:
On a compact connected Lie group, differential complexes built from real involutive structures raise a basic question: when can their equations be solved globally? Gabriel Araújo and three co-authors study these left-invariant, essentially real structures and their cohomology spaces. They prove that solving the first degree forces a solution in every degree.

A converse holds under a commutativity hypothesis that is always true when the group is a torus. The same holds when the structure comes from the Lie algebra of a closed subgroup. The paper further examines real tube structures over the group as base manifold. Experts gain a clean ladder for these geometric complexes.
arxiv-2602-22310:
Stacking atom-thin materials lets physicists tune quantum matter layer by layer, and Kitaev magnets are a prized target. Pedro M. Cônsoli and four co-authors examine what happens when a Kitaev honeycomb magnet meets a nearly lattice-matched van der Waals antiferromagnet. An effective staggered magnetic field from the neighbor can drive the monolayer into new phases.

Using three methods, perturbation theory, exact solving, and classical energy minimization, the team finds an antichiral Kitaev spin liquid, a nonmagnetic nematic phase, and several skyrmion-crystal types. First-principles tests then check a concrete pairing: a two-layer stack of ruthenium trichloride and manganese phosphorus trisulfide. The work turns proximity effects into a dial for exotic magnetism.
arxiv-2602-22410:
Gamma-ray-emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies are prized laboratories for disk-jet coupling, with soft X-rays hinting at a disk component peaking in optical and ultraviolet light. Aman Kumar and four co-authors study their optical emission with long-term Zwicky Transient Facility observations, discussed against the blazar context. They report long-term flux and color variability in two optical bands.

Fractional variability reaches nearly three-quarters, averaging about a quarter, consistent with earlier ultraviolet variability studies. Color-magnitude trends resemble blazar patterns, redder-when-brighter or bluer-when-brighter. Variability timescales imply an emitting region spanning ten billion to a trillion kilometers, consistent with the inner disk or jet base.
arxiv-2602-22510:
Composed image retrieval pairs a reference image with a text edit, seeking images that apply the change while keeping other relevant visual content. Guoyizhe Wei and six co-authors note that classic fusion pipelines lean on supervised triplets and can lose fine detail. Recent zero-shot methods often caption the reference image and merge caption with edit, missing implicit intent and returning repetitive results.

They present Pix2Key, which represents queries and candidates as open-vocabulary visual dictionaries. That setup enables intent-aware matching and diversity-aware reranking in one embedding space. A self-supervised pretraining part, V-Dict-AE, sharpens the dictionary using images alone, strengthening fine-grained attribute grasp without retrieval-specific supervision. On the DFMM-Compose benchmark, Pix2Key improves Recall at ten by over three points. Adding V-Dict-AE adds about two more points, with better intent consistency and list diversity.
arxiv-2602-22610:
Tao Huang and four co-authors fix a privacy snag in conditional diffusion models. Condition injection lets these models generate context-aware time series, but varied conditions, like patchy histories or outlier inputs, can produce heavy-tailed gradients. Under differentially private training, those rare giants trigger global clipping, skewing updates and wasting the privacy budget.

Their drop-in mechanism, DP-aware AdaLN-Zero, caps conditioning strength without touching the private training algorithm itself. It jointly bounds the conditioning representation and the AdaLN modulation terms through bounded re-parameterization, taming extreme gradients before clipping and noise. Tests on a real power dataset and two public ETT benchmarks show better interpolation, imputation, and forecasting at matched privacy, with no cost to standard performance.
arxiv-2602-23010:
Gorkem Yildiz presents Helmlab, a family of two purpose-built color spaces for UI design systems sharing an eleven-stage analytical structure. MetricSpace, a 72-parameter space, targets color-difference prediction, while GenSpace, a 44-parameter space, targets gradient and palette generation. The forward transform maps CIE XYZ to a perceptual Lab form through learned matrices, per-channel power compression, Fourier hue correction, and Helmholtz-Kohlrausch lightness adjustment.

On COMBVD, about thirty-eight hundred color pairs, MetricSpace scores about twenty-two and a half on STRESS, a twenty-three percent cut from CIEDE2000 near twenty-nine. It also leads on a screen-condition set, about twenty-three versus about sixty-three, though it trails CIEDE2000 on a small 3D-printed set, a regression the author owns. GenSpace wins 65 of 90 gradient and palette metrics against OKLab, and the transform inverts with round-trip errors below one part in ten trillion.
arxiv-2602-23310:
Kelcey Davis and 30 co-authors ask what powers extreme emission-line galaxies in CEERS: young star formation or active galactic nuclei. Using JWST NIRSpec spectra from CAPERS, RUBIES, THRILS, and CEERS, the team studies galaxies picked for extreme equivalent widths above 5000 angstroms in H-alpha or H-beta plus oxygen-III lines. Such galaxies reveal what produced excess ionizing radiation in the early universe.

Six new broad-line active nuclei at redshifts 3.5 to 7 emerge from deep THRILS data, and a Little Red Dot color-color plot removes active nuclei with non-extreme lines. About 10 percent of photometrically picked galaxies show broad Balmer lines, rising to 35 percent in deep spectra. Yet the narrow H-alpha component dominates over the broad one even when an active nucleus is present, above all in the highest-width sources. The verdict is that star formation, not the active nucleus, dominates the extreme emission.
arxiv-2602-23510:
Emma Tien Hwai Medlock and four co-authors build a lab emulator for the optical channel between a satellite and the ground. In a free-space optical link, channel losses shift over time. Characterizing the channel matters for judging how a satellite payload will truly perform.

Their emulator reproduces those dynamics, especially for Low Earth Orbit CubeSats. It covers varied atmospheric turbulence, satellite paths, and ground station settings at a chosen wavelength. It was designed to test the continuous-variable quantum key distribution payload of the SPOQC mission. SPOQC is an in-orbit demonstrator for the UK Quantum Communication Hub, slated for launch in early 2026.
arxiv-2602-23610:
Yu Zhu and one co-author propose an LLM-driven method for making multi-turn task chats grounded in lifelike thinking. Thinking, the ability to analyze, infer, and decide from input data, is key for smart dialogue systems, yet current benchmarks miss real-world depth.

Current thinking data sets are often simple and abstract, cut off from lifelike task flows, domain limits, and day-to-day rules. Leaks from pretrain corpora further weaken test trust, while crowd work for data sets is heavy and hard to scale. The new method makes chats grounded in true task scenes, filled with real-world data and strong context flow, using three-level tuning to lift chat quality. Thinking tasks built around these chats are refined step by step to lift quality and challenge.
arxiv-2602-23910:
Anian Altherr and nine co-authors measure baryon masses in lattice simulations that include both strong and electromagnetic effects. The 2026 paper uses the openQxD code, developed by the RC star collaboration, which enables fully dynamical quantum chromodynamics plus quantum electrodynamics through C-periodic boundary conditions.

The omega-minus baryon is the focus, because its precise mass has served as the yardstick for lattice simulations. C-periodic boundaries add partly connected contributions to its two-point function, which vanish in infinite volume and are computed here for the first time. The paper presents preliminary masses from simulation ensembles at an unphysical pion mass, a step toward isospin-breaking corrections that split up and down quark effects and include photon exchange.
arxiv-2602-24210:
Haritz Puerto and four co-authors study how to keep large reasoning models from leaking sensitive information in their reasoning traces. The 2026 paper notes that reasoning traces often contain private details, resist explicit privacy directives, and can be exposed through prompt injection, creating a direct privacy risk.

The authors treat the problem as controllability: improving instruction-following inside reasoning should cut leaks. They introduce a supervised fine-tuning dataset that teaches models to follow general instructions throughout reasoning. Staged decoding decouples trace and answer generation with separate adapters to maximize instruction-following in each part. Tests on six models across instruction-following and privacy benchmarks show large gains on both, though sometimes at a cost to task utility. In short, rules must hold inside thought. Held rules keep secrets safe. Rules are the shield. Better instruction-following, the paper argues, is a promising path to privacy-aware reasoning models.
arxiv-2603-00210: Majumdar sets out the Universal Clustering Problem, a polynomial-time computable partition utility maximised over a finite metric space that holds the common core of clustering paradigms. He proves its NP-hardness with two reductions, one from graph colouring and one from exact cover by 3-sets. Ten major paradigms, from k-means and DBSCAN to spectral clustering and affinity propagation, map onto this frame and share its hardness. The results explain failure modes like local optima in alternating methods and greedy traps in hierarchical merging.
arxiv-2603-00410: Cao, Yi, and Habiger derive exact bias and variance formulas for a false discovery rate estimator built from published p values, where the assumed publication rule may be wrong. Their expressions show estimates can lean conservative or liberal depending on how well the assumed rule matches true selection. A large psychology replication study with estimable selection traits supports the formulas in practice. A second set of p values mined from medical abstracts shows how the formulas enable a simple sensitivity check when selection is unknown.
arxiv-2603-00510: Fan and three colleagues probe what visual tokens in multimodal language models encode, using an EmbedLens tool. Input tokens split into sink, dead, and alive groups; only the alive share, about sixty percent of input, carries image meaning. Those alive tokens already hold objects, colours, and OCR cues before reaching the language model, while visual computation proves redundant for most tasks. For vision heavy tasks that need it, alive tokens line up with middle layers, so mid layer injection suffices and shallow processing can go.
arxiv-2603-00610: Ma and eleven colleagues build an evaluation ecosystem for music reward models that follow text, lyrics, and audio prompts together. They release CMI-Pref-Pseudo, a large pseudo labelled preference set, plus a smaller human annotated CMI-Pref set for fine grained tuning. CMI-RewardBench then tests reward models on musicality, text music fit, and instruction fit across varied samples. Their efficient CMI reward models track human judgement closely on musicality and fit.
arxiv-2603-00810: Barger derives quark weak mixing from a one flavon, three messenger Froggatt-Nielsen construction behind the companion mass spectrum. One hierarchy parameter, an exponent lattice, and a four phase messenger model account for the four CKM magnitudes and, via Fritzsch-Xing reconstruction, the matrix and Jarlskog invariant. A benchmark Yukawa pair reproduces light quark masses, nine CKM magnitudes within 1.2%, and the invariant close to the global fit. Equal weight messenger interference fixes the CP phase at a right angle, and the lattice parameter fixes the charged lepton ratio.
arxiv-2603-00910: Amaefuna and three colleagues decide how to spread model capacity across layers under a fixed hardware budget. Layers differ wildly in value. They score each layer by a curvature-aware gain that reflects reducible risk. Then they solve two convex programs: one assigning expert slots, one setting pruning ratios while shielding strong layers. Mistral-7B and Gemma-7B tests show clear allocation wins in places and mixed pruning results, replacing guesswork with a budget-feasible procedure.
arxiv-2603-01210: Contré and colleagues present a kinetic-equilibrium forecast workflow for full TCV shots, coupling predict-first RAPTOR transport runs with FBT inverse math. Rapid pre-shot runs from the pulse schedule across shapes and cases feed pressure and heat curves to the solver, meeting in a few rounds. Built into shot planning, the coupling lifts coil-current guesses for target shapes and gives staff a true picture for inductance, pressure, and pulse runs.
arxiv-2603-01710:
Abdur-Rahman Butler and Umar Butler build a full test for legal question systems that fetch law before answering. Their 2026 benchmark draws thousands of passages from a Victorian criminal charge book. One hundred hand-crafted questions demand expert grasp of criminal law and court procedure.

Each question ships with a long-form answer and the passages that support it. A full factorial design lets the team swap search models and answer models in every pairing. A layered error breakdown then shows whether faults come from search or from reasoning. Three search models and two top answer models face the test. Search proves the main driver of correctness, while answer models play a smaller role. Many so-called hallucinations trace back to failed search, which sets the ceiling for the whole system.
arxiv-2603-02010:
Amir Asiaee and Samhita Pal do sound statistics on data that has been made private, without ignoring the added noise. Their 2026 work starts from a split in how private data is shared. Some groups share fake data with no guide to its error, while others share one best guess with no sense of doubt.

Their middle path shares just a few key sums, made private, for a broad class of models. Those sums hold all the facts the data has about the model values, so little is lost. A noise-aware fit then runs on the sums as a pure post-step. The team proves how much the noise swells the spread and gives sound ranges for true values. It also shows the cost of privacy cannot be dodged. Tests on three model types and real census data back the full plan.
arxiv-2603-02110:
Yun Fang asks a sharp question in this 2026 astronomy paper: does faint gravitational wave noise line up with nearby galaxies? Pulsar timing arrays have found a shared low hum across pulsars. If huge black hole pairs cause that hum, its strength should vary across the sky. Fang tests that idea with the NANOGrav fifteen-year data set.

Fang builds sky maps from a large galaxy catalog, split into two distance shells. Those maps enter a Bayesian test as fixed patterns to match. No clear match appears in either shell, alone or combined. Model comparisons favor the plain, even-sky picture instead. The null result still helps, since it limits how much nearby structure can shape the hum.
arxiv-2603-02310:
Rebecca Maria Kuntz, based at Heidelberg, studies the hidden geometry inside jet classifiers in this 2026 paper. Particle jets are sprays from high-energy collisions, and networks learn to sort them by type. Inside each network, jets are mapped into a latent space with its own geometry. Kuntz asks what that geometry reveals about the physics the network uses.

She introduces the core tools needed to read such learned geometries. Curvature and related measures describe how the latent space bends and stretches. Those tools apply to both decoder and classifier geometries. Two physics tasks test the approach: sorting quark jets from gluon jets, and tagging fat jets three ways. The goal is explainable learning that physicists can trust and learn from.
arxiv-2603-02410:
Ryutaro Ichikawa and Mitsuru Shibayama analyze the dynamics of tubular origami in this 2026 mathematics paper. Origami tessellations fold repeating crease patterns into tube-like structures. The number of modules around the tube sets the system's behavior. Its inverse acts as a small perturbation in their analysis.

With many modules, the motion provably settles into an integrable map. That map's generating function equals the total discrete mean curvature of the folds. Simulations show phase space densely filled with the invariant curves theory predicts. Retuning fold signs and lengths creates nontwist maps with new stable folding zones. Those zones appear as elliptic islands from zero-frequency resonances. A virtual extra fold steers expansion and contraction, yielding stable quasi-periodic attractors.
arxiv-2603-03010:
Victor Morand, Mathias Vast, Basile Van Cooten, and colleagues rerun a fair race between recipes for training search rankers. Cross-encoders, which read a query and document together, are the accuracy backbone of modern search. Recent work claimed distillation from large models could lift them to top-tier quality, but training recipes were rarely compared under one roof.

The team reproduced a recent large-model distillation recipe and raced it against teacher-ensemble distillation and other supervised losses. They trained many encoder generations, from the original BERT to the recent ModernBERT, and tested in-domain and far afield. Losses based on relative comparisons won consistently across backbones and test sets. The right objective, they find, can gain as much as a bigger backbone.
arxiv-2603-03110:
Wayne Lawton connects the first digits of numbers across different counting bases to a deep conjecture about transcendence. Write one number in several bases, say base three and base ten, and record its leftmost digit in each. His 2026 paper studies the joint pattern of those leading digits.

He proves that if every combination of leading digits actually occurs, then the logarithms of any two bases must be rationally independent. For two bases he proves the converse outright. For three or more bases, the converse needs the algebraic independence of prime logarithms, a condition guaranteed by Schanuel's conjecture, a famous unproven claim about exponential functions. A humble question about digits thus leans on one of transcendence theory's central open problems.
arxiv-2603-03210:
J. M. Franco-Patino, J. García-Marcos, V. Belocchi, and colleagues interpret a first-of-its-kind neutrino measurement from Japan. The JSNS2 experiment measured the missing-energy spectrum of carbon-12 hit by a pure beam of neutrinos from kaon decays at rest. Missing energy reveals how the nucleus absorbed the blow.

Their analysis uses the relativistic distorted-wave approach, which tracks how the struck neutron's outgoing wave bends in the remaining nucleus. A new parameterization of the neutron spectral function folds in detailed electron-scattering data at high missing-energy resolution. The paper weighs the roles of the recoiling residual nucleus, final-state interactions, and the event generators experiments rely on. Such comparisons sharpen the nuclear models behind neutrino oscillation programs.
arxiv-2603-03310:
Andrew J Kiruluta proposes a different clock for running large language models. Today's inference engines generate text token by token under fixed rules, tuned for speed and low delay. His 2026 design, called entropic-time inference, lets the flow of uncertainty drive the process instead of the token count, treating generation as a thermodynamic process that spends computation where doubt falls fastest.

The design extends the popular vLLM engine in three linked ways. An entropy-aware scheduler orders work, uncertain attention blocks get pruned, and sampling temperature adjusts itself to hold generation near a target uncertainty level. Kiruluta gives the full systems design, pseudocode, and an integration plan. The aim is a self-organizing engine that uses entropy as a first-class control signal at scale.
arxiv-2603-04010: Bezem and others present generalized algebraic theories for type theory with stated universe polymorphism. They first give a theory for kinds with families matching Martin-Löf theory with an external tower of universes. They then give a theory for level-indexed kinds with families matching Martin-Löf theory with stated universe polymorphism, featuring level judgments and level-indexed products. These characterize both theories as initial models, abstracting from grammar and inference-rule details. The work also serves as a categorical logic case study on Voevodsky's initiality conjecture project.
arxiv-2603-04210: Roth and others construct any in-phase moves in optical lattices. In-phase control of ultracold atoms' motional states in optical lattices opens a bright path toward programmable quantum motion with massive particles. They propose and analyze a scheme for in-phase moves of ultracold atoms, realizing any unitary maps on single-particle motional states.
arxiv-2603-05210: Ofir Ben Shoham trims draft-model vocabularies to speed speculative decoding of language models. The draft model often dominates latency, generating tokens in turn with a head growing costly with vocabulary size, so larger vocabularies trade reach for speed. He frames vocabulary choice as tuning balancing reach against latency, measuring reach on training replies and latency from flop counts. A Tree-ordered Parzen Estimator explores the reach-latency frontier under a minimum reach constraint. Domain tasks gain latency cuts and throughput gains while vocabularies shrink drastically with reach kept high.
arxiv-2603-05710: Mozaffari and team warn that current AI building risks widening the divide between North and South in global climate information. Frontier models come almost only from the Global North, and gap persists across inputs, steps, and outputs, from skewed training data to one-sided checks. At-risk regions bear outsized effects. The authors call for a Climate Digital Public base, well-being-centred test metrics, and knowledge co-making building bounce-back rather than gaps.
arxiv-2603-06110: Sinha, Ghosh, Allys, Boulanger, and Delouis develop a statistical method that pulls Galactic dust emission apart from cosmic infrared background anisotropies in Planck 353 GHz data. Template fitting assumes gas and dust correlate, but fails where molecular hydrogen, diffuse ionised gas, and dark gas add emission. The team builds background maps over 25 patches from the dust-HI correlation, then models it with scattering covariance statistics. Applied to Planck data, the method recovers a test dust map richer than the corrected SFD map, split between atomic- and molecular-hydrogen-associated dust.
arxiv-2603-06310: Xiao and his team study speech foundation models for low resource Pacific Indigenous languages, where scarce data bites and fine tuning risks catastrophic forgetting. They look at data volume, tuning plans, and representational drift across sets, plus continual learning for sequential language acquisition. Across three Pacific Indigenous languages, tuning for distant tongues brings severe internal drift, forcing a strict plasticity and stability dilemma. LoRA adapts at first but suffers catastrophic forgetting during step by step learning, showing the need for robust plans for tongues with too little data.
arxiv-2603-06510: Sabbi and colleagues introduce the Galaxy UV Legacy Project, a Hubble Treasury program characterizing stars, OB associations, and young star clusters in star-forming galaxies. With filters plus archival observations, it provides an eight-band view from far-ultraviolet to I-band. The paper details strategy, processing, and results for the dwarf NGC 4449 as a test case. Younger stars and clusters concentrate along the bar, and star formation migrated from northeast to southwest. The ultraviolet bump appears in many areas but not where star formation is intense and recent.
arxiv-2603-06610: Thede and team define forgetting in large language model post-training as model drift degrading ways and user experience, beyond the view of knowledge loss. They bring CapTrack, a tool joining a taxonomy with an evaluation suite centred on capability-specific metrics. They conduct a hands-on study across domains, model families, and post-training algorithms, including large models. Lesson fine-tuning induces the strongest drift, while preference tuning, more careful, can recover lost capabilities, family gaps persist, and no fix emerges.
arxiv-2603-06710: Sam Nicholas Kouteili and colleagues widen spec mining from bare true-false events to data-aware behavior. They first find candidate functions that cover the traces with syntax-guided synthesis. They then give a finite-prefix semantics for TSL_f, a temporal stream logic with first-order predicates and functional updates. That pairing unifies learning of data transforms and time-based specs. On Gymnasium ToyText tasks, mined specs beat passive learning baselines on sample use.
arxiv-2603-06810: Chen and colleagues study team multi-agent reinforcement learning where the joint reward is submodular, capturing diminishing returns as agents join a team. Unlike simple summed rewards, submodular rewards fit cases where agent efforts overlap, such as multi-drone watching and joint scouting. They give a frame for this setting with proofs on sample use and regret. With known dynamics, greedy policy tuning gives an approximation in polynomial time in agent count, escaping the exponential curse of tuning. With unknown dynamics, a UCB-based learner achieves a regret bound.
arxiv-2603-07310: Liu, Zhou and Livingstone show that a Metropolis-Hastings chain inherits slow mixing when its proposal mixes slowly and acceptance nears one fast enough. Their conditions look strong, but a counterexample shows they cannot be weakened. Turning to random-walk and guided-walk variants, they find the guided walk doubles the polynomial convergence rate under heavy tails. With a strictly convex potential, the random walk instead trails the guided walk at a similar ballistic pace.
arxiv-2603-07510: Yang proves a conjecture about chromatic polynomials at negative inputs. Dong and colleagues had conjectured that a certain log derivative stays negative for all orders from two upward on the negative axis. Yang proves the claim for x far enough below zero, with the threshold scaling in the maximum degree and the derivative order. The result covers the conjectured sign pattern in that far-below-zero range.
arxiv-2603-08410: Hazinedar and colleagues study a simple f(R, T_phi) gravity model coupled to a scalar field. They show that the theory admits classical broken metric solutions, like those known in GR. In particular, they find a class of solutions showing a smooth shift from a Euclidean to a Lorentzian domain. That yields a moving case of signature change.
arxiv-2603-08910: Hexuan Wang and colleagues build SciTaRC, a benchmark for question answering over scientific tables. Each question ships with a hand-built plan and complexity scores, enabling diagnosis beyond final accuracy. Top models fail on at least 23 percent of questions, and even oracle plans give only limited gains, exposing an execution bottleneck in long computational chains.
arxiv-2603-09310: Ashkan Panahi links the training dynamics of algorithms fed Gaussian mixture data to a simpler surrogate system that is easier to analyze. The proof uses Gordon's comparison theorem and holds without asymptotic limits for a stated family of algorithms. The result confirms dynamic mean-field formulas in the large-limit regime and suggests an iterative scheme for sharper finite-size versions. A perceptron trained by a full-batch first-order method shows extra fluctuation terms beyond the mean-field kernels.
arxiv-2603-09410: T. Baird and colleagues simulate the infrared spectra of protonated water clusters, from one molecule up to four. Spectra reveal cluster structure and motion, but good simulations usually need costly quantum methods. They pair machine-learned potential and dipole surfaces of high accuracy with the quantum thermal bath method, which adds nuclear quantum effects to dynamics at low cost. The pairing matches past theory and experiment while costing far less.
arxiv-2603-09510: Ido Feldman and Miguel Moreno work in generalized descriptive set theory on the continuous reducibility of isomorphism relations. Their setting is the space of regressive functions on kappa to the kappa. For inaccessible kappa, they compare theories with few non-isomorphic models of size kappa against unstable or superstable non-classifiable theories. The isomorphism relation for models of the tamer theory proves continuously reducible to that of the wilder one.
arxiv-2603-09710: Tomasz Kania and Grzegorz Lewicki settle the open range of a theorem of Pełczyński about injective Banach spaces. A prior joint paper covered smaller values of the parameter, leaving all values above two unresolved. Their construction builds, for each such value, a space with the weaker injectivity property but not the stronger one. Repeated use of one zero sum subspace drives the proof.
arxiv-2603-10010: Mehrabi and coauthors build FERRET, a self driven red team tool that grows its own attacks in stages. A first stage improves the opening moves that shape a hostile chat. A second stage turns those openers into full attacks that mix text and images, while a third stage finds better attack plans mid chat. Across tests, FERRET makes stronger mixed media hostile chats than leading prior red team tools, and it does so with less hand work.
arxiv-2603-10410: Taehyung Kwon and co-authors present STemDist, the first dataset distillation method built for spatio-temporal forecasting, as in traffic and weather data. Such data are huge in both space and time, so training deep models gets costly. Distillation replaces the full data with a compact synthetic set, yet past methods squeezed only one dimension. STemDist compresses both in balance, works at cluster level to cut cost, then adds subset refinement. On five real datasets, training on its output ran faster, used far less memory, and gave lower error.
arxiv-2603-10510: Maria Axenovich and Raphael Steiner settle the size of Ramsey numbers for minors in the two-color case. The question asks how large a complete graph must be before any coloring of its edges in two colors forces a monochromatic minor of a given graph. Thomason, and Myers with Thomason, had found the leading constants for such problems years ago. For two colors the authors now give the exact asymptotic form for every graph. They also handle many colors when the color count and clique size both grow large.
arxiv-2603-10610: Balázs Patkós studies anti-Ramsey numbers for posets, asking how many colors a coloring of all subsets of an n-set can use while avoiding a rainbow copy of a given poset. Copies come in weak and strong forms, depending on whether order is preserved one way or both ways. He links these numbers to the well-studied extremal La numbers. The strong anti-Ramsey number is then pinned down asymptotically for every tree poset, and for every crown poset with an even number of elements.
arxiv-2603-10910: Shuaiqi Duan and coauthors present GLM-OCR, a compact multimodal model built for real-world document understanding. It has under one billion parameters. It pairs a vision encoder with a language decoder. It predicts several tokens per step. That speeds the fixed-output transcription work that plain step-by-step decoding handles slowly. A layout stage first maps each page. Then regions are read in parallel. Benchmarks show top-tier results on parsing, formula and table recovery, and key information extraction.
arxiv-2603-11110: Jseen Zhang and coauthors rethink world models for visual reinforcement learning. They predict the future from residual actions, small adjustments to the previous action, rather than absolute actions. Absolute action distributions are task-dependent and unknown in advance, which destabilizes optimization. Residual control matches the smoothness of real movement and shrinks the search space. Paired with an encoder that models changes between adjacent frames inside a Dreamer-style latent model, the approach improves sample efficiency, returns, and control smoothness on a standard control suite.
arxiv-2603-11210: Jonas Mirlach, Sonia Laguna, and Julia Vogt argue machine unlearning should aim for indistinguishability, not damage. A model should treat forgotten examples like data it never saw. It should not merely perform worse on them. Their Reference-Guided Unlearning builds a class-conditioned reference distribution from disjoint held-out data and trains the model toward that non-member behavior. Across architectures, datasets, and forget fractions, it matches retraining-like membership inference behavior while keeping a good balance between forgetting and utility.
arxiv-2603-11710: Apter, Kaplan, and Poveda study how many normal measures a measurable cardinal can carry in settings beyond inner model methods. Their tools come from consequences of the Ultrapower Axiom. One result joins the classical Kimchi-Magidor theorem with any prescribed pattern of measure counts on the first n measurable cardinals. Another shows the first such cardinal above a supercompact can carry any given number of normal measures. The same holds at the first measurable limit of supercompacts. The work also strengthens results of Goldberg, Woodin, and others.
arxiv-2603-11910: Shinjo and co-authors demonstrate quantum synchronization and a quantum chimera state on programmable superconducting processors. They run stroboscopic Floquet evolution of a two-dimensional Heisenberg model on IBM heavy-hex devices. Spins started with random phases fall into lattice-wide oscillations on their own. On 28 qubits the sync holds even for strongly scrambled starts, guarded by SU(2) symmetry. At 156 qubits the picture splits: weak randomness still syncs globally, while strong randomness leaves only local patches in step. Simulations confirm both regimes come from the Floquet dynamics itself.
arxiv-2603-12310: Song, Pfister, and Song improve generated videos through an agentic question-answering loop named VQQA. Aligning video output with complex user intent stays hard for current generators. Test-time methods often cost too much or demand white-box access to model internals. VQQA instead poses dynamic visual questions and turns VLM critiques into semantic gradients. That feedback drives closed-loop prompt refinement through a plain black-box interface.
