arxiv-2604-15610: Gouru, Felner, and Li tackle the Multiple Watchman Route Problem, finding paths for M watchmen so every map location falls under at least one watchman's view. Pruning areas guaranteed visible en route shrinks the search space, and their MWRP-CP3 optimal planner cuts it by more than 95 percent while running over 200 times faster than existing optimal methods. Suboptimal variants with quality bounds solve maps 3 times larger.
arxiv-2604-15910: De Nitti, Wang, and Zhang study the three-dimensional incompressible MHD system for conducting fluids. They show any weak solution obeying a strong energy inequality is asymptotically stable around a Landau solution in the L2 sense. With an extra integrability rule on the initial change, they also obtain an explicit decay rate for flow and magnetic perturbations.
arxiv-2604-16410: Xia untangles a confounded comparison in adapting CLIP, where full fine-tuning and LoRA are usually run at different learning rates. Using eighty matched runs across two image datasets, four shared learning rates and five seeds, he tracks how attention patterns drift and how much zero-shot transfer survives. Learning rate strongly shaped structural change, and LoRA preserved far more transfer than full fine-tuning at the same rates. Attention drift, Xia concludes, best serves as a descriptive gauge of preservation, not a causal explanation of transfer.
arxiv-2604-16610: Lin and Booth build fairness-aware linear models for settings where the key trait is hidden. Most methods assume seen attributes, which privacy or legal limits may block. Proxies use bell-curve mixtures for number inputs and multi-choice mixtures for grouped inputs. Later group odds then strip inputs of their link to the latent key structure. Capped least squares serve number outcomes, penalty logit fit serves binary ones, and SEMMS pick serves wide cases. Tests and real-data uses show good accuracy trade-offs.
arxiv-2604-16710: Retnaraj and colleagues study global asymptotic stability in linear networks with uneven links and loss. Such networks capture neuron group action and interest control experts for their richness. A one-knob family keeping LDS has a fixed rest set. The fast limit settles to a moving system, and the slow limit to a jumpy hard-pick system. Under diagonal stability, the fast limit is strongly stable and the slow limit stable in the long run. Settling calm at both endpoints offers a grounded path toward global calm for likely networks.
arxiv-2604-16810: Yang and colleagues propose Gleaner, an online tail-sampling framework for microservice diagnostics. Tail-based samplers model traces as graphs, but expensive graph analysis blocks online use. Gleaner treats each trace as a bag-of-edges enriched with log semantics, using set operations. An alarm-driven quota and diversity strategy prioritize rare traces for root cause analysis. Gleaner processes traces in zero point seven four milliseconds each, improving pattern coverage by about 129 percent. At a 1 percent sampling rate, root cause accuracy improves by 42 to 107 percent over the next-best sampler.
arxiv-2604-17110: Zhao and six colleagues let clinicians drive AI development directly with coding agents, closing the gap between medical experts and AI developers. A clinician states the task in plain language, and the system builds a pipeline, refines it through repeated experiments, and returns a model meeting the stated goal. Across five clinical tasks it matched requests with competitive performance. It sharply cut reliance on chest drains, a shortcut for pneumothorax classification, from 60 percent to 31 percent on one dataset and from 50 percent to 18 percent on another.
arxiv-2604-17210: Bach and Tran introduce safety token regularization, a lightweight method for preserving safety alignment when fine-tuning aligned models on new domains. The approach picks salient tokens from rejection templates of aligned models and constrains their logits during training, blocking the loss of critical safety behaviors. Unlike reinforcement learning or preference optimization, it needs little extra compute and works with efficient methods such as LoRA. Experiments show safety on par with top methods while preserving task utility, plus gains in training stability and overall performance.
arxiv-2604-17310: Kollovieh, Ayadi, and Günnemann introduce IDDM, a discrete diffusion model that generates text and molecular graphs by partly resetting probability toward a prior distribution. The reset curbs errors that pile up when masked models unmask too early, while keeping the self-correction that uniform models offer. Its steps blend staying put, resampling, and moving toward the target, and tests show competitive results against leading discrete diffusion models.
arxiv-2604-17510: Bajaj and nine colleagues study reachability in chemical reaction networks, asking whether one mix of molecular species can turn into another through allowed reactions. General reachability was recently proved Ackermann-complete, far beyond feasible computation, but restricted rules like deletion-only or volume-preserving reactions pull it back down. The paper extends that analysis to inhibitory networks. There, a reaction is blocked while certain species are present, and the paper maps where reachability stays tractable under restricted unimolecular and bimolecular reactions.
arxiv-2604-17610: Floden, Granados, and Mandic offer a method to estimate the angular power spectrum of the anisotropic stochastic gravitational-wave background without inverting the Fisher matrix. Such searches split the sky into spherical harmonics, but the Fisher matrix holds small singular values, and regularization biases the result. Working in dirty-map space avoids inversion fully, with inference carried out there. Applied to mock signals in noise from LIGO's third run, the method recovers parameters for strong signals up to order 10, for both auto-correlation and cross-correlation with electromagnetic tracers.
arxiv-2604-17910: Chuhan Qiao introduces PI-CMDP, a framework for constrained decision processes whose constraint links form a layered graph under a lifecycle ordering assumption. Its identify-compress-estimate pipeline finds causal edge weights, compresses the state space through a Markov abstraction, and estimates with a physics-guided doubly robust method. On the TPS benchmark of 4,206 episodes, it repairs 76.2 percent of cases with only 300 training episodes, against 70.8 percent for the best baseline, and keeps a smaller edge at full data.
arxiv-2604-18410: Bell examines crossed-product C*-algebras from free non-minimal actions on the circle by infinite discrete abelian groups. Building on Putnam, Schmidt, and Skau, he obtains a large class of unital separable nuclear non-simple algebras that are quasidiagonal with stable rank one and a unique tracial state. He determines their ideal structure and improves the uniform upper bound on nuclear dimension. For integer-lattice groups, he computes K-theory and the trace pairing map.
arxiv-2604-18510: Kabir and Tiganj compare three routes to unsafe open-weight language models: harmful supervised fine-tuning, harmful reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and refusal-feature abliteration. All three reach near-ceiling harmfulness in Qwen and Llama models, but their side effects differ. Fine-tuning causes the broadest skills loss and drift, while feature removal suppresses refusal features in patches. That training preserves skills, safety judgments, and internal layout. It also induces capability-blind compliance, with models claiming missing actions and making up facts about fake things.
arxiv-2604-18610: Xu and eight colleagues offer SpikeMLLM, the first spike-based frame for multimodal language models, where spike nets save power but mixed inputs resist a shared code. Their frame folds ANN quantization into spike form, adds per-type time scales, and squeezes LIF units to cut steps from linear to log scale. Four test models keep near-full scores under step cuts, with gaps of 0.72 percent and about 1 percent on the FP16 base. A chip for the spike path gives about 9 times the throughput and about 26 times the power efficiency.
arxiv-2604-18710: Jiang, Surace, and Motrunich introduce charge transport capacity, a cap on how many particles can cross a central cut of a one-dimensional lattice, as a probe of many-body localization. For ergodic systems it grows linearly with size, while for localized models it should stay of order one. In the interacting Anderson model, the average capacity is small but grows with size at a rising rate, even at very large disorder. The authors trace this growth to resonances that move more charge across the cut as size grows.
arxiv-2604-19110: Ali, Khan, and Abdel-Hafiez review crystal growth control of quantum materials in transition metal dichalcogenides. Growth sets chemical potentials, defect counts, polytype stability, and metastable phase access, shaping the landscape behind effects. They build a unified thermo-kinetic framework linking growth to phase stability, defect costs, and texture. Potentials define stability windows, supersaturation and transport govern nucleation and shape, and off-balance pathways enable trapping and polymorph choice. Synthesis methods sit in one map, showing how growth regimes yield disorder patterns and phases.
arxiv-2604-19210: Hovatta and seven colleagues attempt first near-infrared blazar resolution. With VLTI-GRAVITY, they observe flaring Ton 599 and four quiet blazars in wide mode with a bright star as tracker. Ton 599's visibilities fit no single point source without unknown loss, and cannot distinguish a point source plus extended emission or loss from a single Gaussian component. They suggest an unresolved or partly resolved jet base. Wide-field mode struggled with fainter targets, yielding non-detections or unmodelable data. The work demonstrates jet emission in infrared.
arxiv-2604-19610: Fang and colleagues formalize conflict reasoning for Open Radio Access Networks. Multi-vendor xApps running within and across layers, subnets, and domains can trigger conflicts latent during building. Current conflict handling relies heavily on joint runs, which are often missing in practice. That means identifying conflict-causing conditions given only marginal datasets from each individual xApp. They propose ZODIAC, a three-stage framework for zero-shot conflict inference with uncertainty-aware surrogate training, trajectory-level diffusion training, and compositional guided denoising.
arxiv-2604-20210: Zhang and five colleagues present Vibrotactile Preference Learning, a tool that maps what each user likes in buzz settings. Learning based on Gaussian process doubt scores picks test pairs with a best first rule over 40 rounds of side by side picks, plus user noted doubt. A trial with thirteen people using Xbox buzz pads shows it learns each person's likes fast. Use stays easy and low strain, pointing to wide scale custom buzz tuning.
arxiv-2604-20510: Kinikar and five colleagues build a model for flopping-mode spin qubits, quantum bits whose electron shuttles between two wells. It tracks well shape and field gradient rather than a two-site picture. Simulating electrically driven control, they find a trade-off between fast driving and clean Rabi oscillations. They show the two-site approximation can overstate the Rabi frequency by up to about 20 percent in some regimes. For two coupled qubits they derive the exchange interaction, showing how well shape, field gradient, and Coulomb repulsion set coupling strength.
arxiv-2604-20710: Yang, Lee, and Kuzmin develop a local thermal non-equilibrium model that maps the heat of inflow as it moves through rock. The key is a tracer tracking inflow and giving a three-way coupling among rock, resident, and inflow heat. That framework shows how inflow parcels warm through conductive and convective exchange, and forecasts well temperatures without relying on bulk means. Numerical experiments for enhanced geothermal systems show that the framework captures inflow heating paths and breakthrough trends not seen by standard models.
arxiv-2604-20910: Ono and colleagues map a new way to explore worlds beyond Mars, where decade-long cruises make repeated missions impractical. Their roadmap, drawn from a Keck Institute workshop, calls for single missions with software-defined craft. Such craft reshape their own functions in flight, doing first surveys and then follow-up science from their own data. Three example missions sketch a Neptune and Triton flyby, an ocean-world explorer, and a sweep of the Oort cloud.
arxiv-2604-21010: Zheng, Bécsy, and Mingarelli turn pulsar timing terms into gravity echoes of a black hole binary. Each array records an Earth term and a pulsar term from the wave passing each pulsar earlier. A future microhertz detection of a nearby binary would date those echoes. For an equal-mass binary of one billion solar masses at 80 megaparsecs, the signal-to-noise ratio reaches 33. Up to 24 pulsars resolve it on 50-year baselines, and one alone localizes it to roughly 10 to 100 square degrees.
arxiv-2604-21710: Zhao and nine colleagues model ionized gas flowing out of the Seyfert 1 galaxy NGC 3783, using 2024 spectra from XMM-Newton and XRISM alongside older data. They find eight warm absorber components, with outflow speeds from 480 to 1230 kilometres per second. Total column density in 2024 is 1.5 times the 2000-2001 level, so fresh material must replenish the flow. The absorber population has shifted markedly over 24 years.
arxiv-2604-21810: Fu and three colleagues show that combining low-resolution images at different scales can make super-resolution well posed, without image priors. Scale differences come from sensors with different pixel sizes or from zoom magnification. Images with pairwise coprime pixel sizes yield a stable inverse, and reconstructions proceed efficiently by Fourier methods or iterative least squares. One- and two-dimensional experiments with CCD binning validate the analysis and its noise-resolution trade-off.
arxiv-2604-22110: Kallel argues standard supervised sorting trains models to copy exact oracle labels in one pass, forcing certainty and too-sure predictions. He proposes Reinforced Iterative Classification, swapping copying for reinforcement learning: a looping agent updates class odds step by step, earning reward for gains. The value function gives a natural stopping rule by gauging leftover gains. Kallel proves the iterative form recovers the same best predictions as cross-entropy while yielding an anytime sorter. On image tests, it matches supervised accuracy with truer confidence and flexible compute.
arxiv-2604-22710: Tusha, Palathinkal, and Ghosh measure how a 5G base station radiates power in three dimensions under the 3GPP Release-18 standard, instead of relying on simplified beam-nulling theory. They find interference depends on many beam directions through side lobes, not only the worst one, and that antenna design shapes average radiated power. They also propose two nulling methods cutting power toward a chosen direction.
arxiv-2604-23110: Kulagin and Petti analyze deep-inelastic scattering data from deuterium to lead, finding nuclear modifications to bound nucleon structure functions minimal where valence quark distributions peak. Across isoscalar cross-section ratios, a global analysis shows a striking cancellation of nuclear effects across all nuclei. The mean value is 0.9988 overall. The authors discuss these results and explore interpretations within a microscopic model for nuclear modifications of structure functions.
arxiv-2604-23510: Liu and colleagues measure the magnetic traits of test masses for Taiji, a planned space mission to sense gravitational waves, with a physics-guided neural method. Their system pairs a neural noise gauge with an exact physics solver, so it can spot and drop tainted test data. Checked on real test-stand noise, it meets Taiji's ground-test accuracy needs on every magnetic trait at once.
arxiv-2604-23610: Woszczek, Teuerle, and Wyłomańska study Lévy walks whose speeds vary randomly, extending classic models that assume constant speed. They derive scaling limits showing that diffusion depends on the interplay of heavy-tailed waiting times and velocity distributions. Three distinct scaling regimes emerge, including a critical case with logarithmic corrections, giving a precise framework for anomalous transport in heterogeneous systems.
arxiv-2604-24010: Xia, García-Fernández, and Svensson speed up extended object tracking with Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture filters. Data association is the hard step, so they build blocked Gibbs samplers on an augmented state space that yield high-weight global hypotheses for the filter update. A collapsed variant that marginalizes object existence runs faster still, notably when new objects first appear. Simulations match baseline tracking quality while needing substantially less runtime.
arxiv-2604-24310: Lu and five colleagues present Vib2Conf, a deep learning model reading molecular shapes from vibrational spectra. Earlier models recovered flat structures, but three-dimensional conformations stayed hard to tell apart because similar shapes blur spectra. An attentional resampler distills shape-sensitive features from sparse signals, and Mixture-of-Experts splits conformation space for mapping. The model tops 95 percent top-1 recall on benchmarks. It reaches 82.06 percent on near-isomeric conformers differing by about 1 angstrom.
arxiv-2604-24810: Papanikolaou, Kontopoulos and Tserpes compare Upper Confidence Bound strategies for adaptive deep networks on edge devices. Adaptive networks use the bandit framework to pick thresholds for early exits without losing accuracy. Prior work used only the first Upper Confidence Bound strategy. The authors add four more, UCB-V, UCB-Tuned, UCB-Bayes and UCB-BwK, and test them on ResNet and MobileViT on CIFAR benchmarks. All achieve sub-linear regret, with UCB-Bayes fastest, while UCB-V and UCB-Tuned lead accuracy-latency and accuracy-energy trade-offs.
arxiv-2604-24910: Veneziani and four colleagues outline a math roadmap for Digital Twins in coronary artery disease. Data plus models, enhanced by AI, form the Digital Twin approach for personal medicine. The roadmap centers on data assimilation and graph models for twin communication. A key quantity is Wall Shear Stress, the tangential part of normal stress on the arterial wall. By personalizing and synthesizing Wall Shear Stress estimation, they propose a Digital Twin system that may help prevent infarcts, among the most lethal diseases.
arxiv-2604-25010: Raghavan-Chitra, Koner and Yuen-Zhou show nonlinearities of individual emitters can appear in linear spectra of quantum emitter arrays. Recent polariton work shows cavity linear response can encode nonlinear traits, and the authors show the phenomenon is more general. Emitter-emitter interactions let single-emitter nonlinear effects emerge in the array linear response, without cavities or special symmetry. Linear spectra for coupled dimers and linear chains show Raman features of single monomers as sidebands of collective peaks. Tuning Raman effects enables precise control of spectral features.
arxiv-2604-25110: Wang argues that task scores alone cannot judge a distilled student model. A student may match its teacher on chosen tests yet lose the deeper skills that make the teacher safe to trust. He groups these hidden losses into a clear taxonomy. Then he proposes a Distillation Loss Statement that lists what was kept, what was lost and why the rest is fine.
arxiv-2604-25610: Mantilla and four colleagues study autoresearch, in which coding agents tune programs that can be run and scored automatically. Ground-state preparation fits that pattern, since candidate protocols rank by estimated energies and other proxies for convergence. The team applies it to choices for variational quantum eigensolver, density matrix renormalisation group, and auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo protocols. They validate it on simple spin models and molecular Hamiltonians. Across all three settings, the agent mutates simple baselines into protocols with better energy proxies under tight space-time budgets.
arxiv-2604-25810: Constantinou, Shorttle, and Nicholls ask whether Venus's massive carbon dioxide atmosphere points to one past. Earth stores much carbon as crustal carbonates; Venus holds a similar stock almost entirely as gas. The authors model three routes: magma-ocean outgassing, stagnant-lid degassing, and carbonate remobilization after breakdown. A once-habitable Venus could have banked about 20 bar as carbonates, freed over tens of millions of years. Stagnant-lid degassing reaches only about 25 bar. Venus-like totals need enrichment, delivery, or recycling, so the atmosphere alone does not prove a temperate past.
arxiv-2604-26110: Tran and five colleagues compare three hybrid quantum neural networks: convolutional, recurrent, and vision-transformer variants built on variational circuits. They test generalization, accuracy, and robustness. All three shine on low-feature data such as handwritten digits but degrade sharply on high-feature datasets. The convolutional variant proves weakest on high-dimensional data. Traditional architectures resist adversarial noise better, while the transformer variant best withstands quantum measurement, channel, and finite-shot noise. That split should guide model choice on today's noisy hardware.
arxiv-2604-26310: Siregar and five colleagues benchmarked PyCaret AutoML tools against BiLSTM models for sorting text into 20 emotion classes. On 79,595 English sentences, logistic regression, naive Bayes, and support vector machines ran on TF-IDF features, while BiLSTM, GRU, and a light Transformer ran as deep rivals. BiLSTM won overall at 89 percent accuracy, just ahead of the best classic model at about 88 percent. Sequence models caught emotional context better, though classic models stayed cheap and competitive.
arxiv-2604-26410: Ortholand, Lee, and Bind reviewed causal estimands, the precise targets of a causal claim, for longitudinal outcomes cut short by death in randomized trials. Once a participant dies, the outcome stops being a real-valued measurement, muddying both definition and interpretation when treatment affects survival and results together. They split into two classes by whether they need extra assumptions to compare results beyond death. Simulations with Bayesian estimators and an ALS trial example led them to pair the survivor average causal effect with restricted mean survival time.
arxiv-2604-26510: Savin ran computer models of flat two- and three-layer builds from polyglycine beta-sheets and parallel Kevlar strands on a graphene sheet. The beta-sheets kept their shape through parallel hydrogen-bond chains up to 800 kelvin, while Kevlar builds proved even stabler, keeping bonds between molecules at higher heat. The models showed adding graphene can lift Kevlar fibers' heat tolerance a lot. The result points to graphene as a handy helper for hydrogen-bonded molecular assemblies.
arxiv-2604-26810: Belgacem replaces Hill functions, the standard sigmoidal curves in gene-network models, with logistic-based models that avoid three flaws. Hill curves can blow up, turn complex-valued, or trap a network in its off state when fitted at non-integer powers. His logistic forms stay smooth, real-valued, and positive at zero input while keeping the familiar S-shape. On a two-gene network with delayed mutual activation and self-repression, he derives matching rules, locates the single feasible steady state, and maps where stability gives way to oscillation.
arxiv-2604-26910: Malacarne and three colleagues present a planning pipeline for rope-assisted robots that climb vertical walls. The plan splits into two levels: picking feasible landing spots, and choosing rope tensions, leg forces, and landing points for dynamically feasible motion. The outer level uses the Cross-Entropy Method, while the inner level uses gradient-based nonlinear optimization. The approach is tested on ALPINE, a new climbing robot platform, across varied tough terrain setups.
arxiv-2604-27110: Gautam and Blair examine conference writing as assessment in an intro quantum mechanics course for engineers using project-based learning. From post-course surveys in a pilot run, they assess effects on understanding, communication, research readiness, and views on the writing requirement. Students found the project good for engagement, confidence, and skill growth, while the conference paper felt demanding but meaningful. They argue that once project-based learning is set, conference writing can extend the model, especially for graduate students, and back keeping the requirement with better support.
arxiv-2604-27410: Zhu, Vedula, and Malmasi tackle entity search in shopping, where the most similar products to a query product vary by category and context. In an offline stage, they pull structured product attributes from unstructured text and build a reusable attribute graph with category schemas. Online, they rank candidates by reasoning over that graph instead of text, cutting per-product token use by 57 percent while improving ranking precision. The approach beats baselines with no training data, gaining over 5 percent in average precision, and it generalizes across product categories.
arxiv-2604-27510: Ali and Brattain offer FMCL, a single-pass, class-aware client grouping tool for federated learning. Old plans rely on raw stats, model values, or simple matches that miss class meaning structure and often need looping teamwork. FMCL uses a frozen foundation model to compute class samples for each client, judging likeness by cosine distance between profiles. Grouping happens once before training, adding no traffic during training and staying neutral to downstream design, and tests show better, steadier grouping than methods under uneven partitioning.
arxiv-2604-27610: Yadav and Mohanty review recent work on physics-informed neural networks for portfolio management. They present these networks as a way to build finance principles directly into learning, aiming for results that respect established financial rules and processes. The review surveys portfolio optimization with mathematical models, deep learning, and these networks, weighing the strengths and limits of each approach. It closes with open gaps and future paths for investment management research.
arxiv-2604-27810: Teufel and three colleagues introduce hyperdimensional prints, training-free molecular codes from algebra on high-dimensional vectors. Conventional prints lose shape detail through hash squeeze, at low sizes, while learned graph nets need task training and cost. Across trait forecast benchmarks, HDF beats older prints in most tasks with even results. At 32 sizes, HDF gaps hit a 0.9 Pearson link with graph edit distance, versus just over half for Morgan prints. Simple nearest-neighbor fit stays useful with as few as 64 parts.
arxiv-2604-28010: Singh and colleagues reframe doctors overriding clinical AI advice as preference data from experts whose choices carry real consequences. They sort overrides into five types, tie each type to a different model update, and build a twin system that learns both rewards and clinician capability together. The design blocks a failure where correct but hard advice gets suppressed when capability falls short, a pattern drawn from live value-based care work.
arxiv-2605-00310:
Zhili Li and 8 co-authors challenge how super-resolution models for satellite imagery are usually judged. Sharpening a blurry satellite image helps monitoring work in farming, ecology, city planning, and disaster response. Yet models are normally scored on fidelity measures of pixel closeness, not on whether the sharpened images help real tasks.

Their benchmark, GeoSR-Bench, pairs images from about thirty-six thousand locations across many land cover types and a wide span of resolutions. Nine super-resolution models were tested across hundreds of settings, on image quality and on downstream tasks such as land cover mapping and biomass estimation. Gains in the usual fidelity scores often failed to match gains in task performance, and sometimes pointed the wrong way. The authors argue downstream tasks belong inside model development itself.
arxiv-2605-00510:
Mengke Zhao and 3 co-authors build a test kit for testing whether AI models that make up tangled physical systems have learned physics or only statistics. Standard probing tools poke single pixels, which creates inputs no real system would give and pushes the model outside valid data. Their method instead splits data across scales with a bounded diffusion method, allowing changes that stay true to physics at chosen scales.

Applied to a denoising diffusion model, the test steps in inside that scale space. Under mild physical nudges, the free model did not respond smoothly as a physical law would. It showed freezing in spots and sudden wobbles, losing smoothness across scales and drifting when pushed into unseen physical states. The authors offer the continuum of coherent test states as a proving ground for future model designs that must respect how causes chain across scales in nature.
arxiv-2605-00810:
Sumana Hatui, Tony Nixon Mavely, and Sahanawaj Sabnam describe how to compute the Schur multiplier of certain finite p-groups, where p is an odd prime. They focus on groups of nilpotency class two whose abelianization is a direct product of copies of a cyclic p-power group. Their method generalizes an approach by Blackburn and Evens, who handled only the simplest case.

As an application, the authors ask which abelian p-groups can appear as the Schur multiplier of a non-abelian p-group. They also introduce s-special p-groups of rank k, extending the notion of special p-groups. Structural properties are studied, and Schur multipliers are computed for the rank-one s-special case.
arxiv-2605-01510:
Huy Duong and five co-authors make subject-driven image generation run in a single step. Given a photo of a person or pet, personalization tools redraw that subject in new scenes, but they lean on slow fine-tuning, long optimization, or many denoising steps that block real-time use.

SwiftPie is presented as the first one-step diffusion tool for the job. A dual-branch identity injection feeds the subject's look into the single pass, and a mask-guided rescaling step strengthens how the subject sits in its new context. Across tests it runs far faster than multi-step rivals while matching them on keeping the subject's identity and following the prompt. The authors frame the speed as the missing piece for interactive tools, where a user can steer a personal image as fast as they can type.
arxiv-2605-01610:
Eunchae Jang and S Shyam Sundar ask what happens to user communication when AI stops chatting and starts acting. Agentic systems pursue workflows on the user's behalf, so routine back-and-forth should shrink; the authors argue oversight talk must grow instead, since a system that acts proactively must also explain itself.

From a communication angle, users judge whether the system is the source of an act or just a channel, and that judgment shapes trust. Agentic systems blur the reading by playing several roles at once. The remedy offered is three kinds of explanation: how an action unfolded, how sure the system is, and how it coordinates with others. Controls that let users pick when and which explanations appear may be the key guard of human agency as autonomy rises. The paper is a perspective piece for interface design.
arxiv-2605-02010:
Hengyu Liu and colleagues argue that reliable artificial intelligence needs a way for humans to check knowledge that is normally left implicit. Models learn from papers and databases, but also from reasoning traces, debugging steps, and other work habits. Those implicit sources carry both good judgement and harmful bias, and current checks can only verify explicit sources.

The authors propose Knowledge Objects, structured artefacts that state implicit knowledge in a form people can inspect, verify, and endorse. That change alters the economics of checking, making validation that was once too costly feasible over time. Accumulated human approval could then improve reliability, rather than leaving the most valuable model skills outside any review process.
arxiv-2605-02410:
Sihan Chen and colleagues improve shared autonomy by letting a robot show its intent through how it physically responds, not through an extra screen. Shared autonomy helps a human reach a goal the robot has inferred. Most work improves that inference, but humans also need to read the robot's intent in return, or collaboration and task performance suffer.

Their system builds an impedance-driven anisotropic guidance field. It modulates the robot's dynamic response to human input, which both communicates intent in a continuous, embodied way and naturally guides the human's actions. User studies across three scenarios and two teleoperation interfaces evaluate the approach. The authors present the channel as more intuitive and expressive than explicit interface displays.
arxiv-2605-02810:
David Mumford compares agency in humans with the agency that might be built into AI programs, in a short essay. Human agency, he notes, takes many years to develop, tied to the slow maturation of the frontal lobe. Machines have no such childhood, and early attempts to give language models agency have run into serious obstacles.

Mumford's conclusion is architectural. Progress, he argues, requires a new design in which actions and plans are formed jointly with the human actors in each real-world setting, rather than by the program alone. Agency, on this view, is not a module to be added to a model, but a shared process between people and systems. The essay is a position piece, setting out the contrast and the design demand in brief form.
arxiv-2605-03110:
Stephen J. Thomas speeds up representative token selection in transformer attention by reusing choices across layers. One attention method picks a small set of key tokens per layer, but building the full similarity matrix each time is costly.

The cascade inherits the prior layer's set, checks it with a smaller cross-matrix, and adds or drops a few tokens as needed. That cuts the selection cost sharply. On three model families, tests saved a large share of Gram work, and the key token sets overlapped strongly between layers. The result suggests informative tokens persist through network depth.
arxiv-2605-03210:
Erin McGurk and David Khachaturov argue that proving work was done by a human should be treated as labor infrastructure, not a luxury label. As AI cuts the cost of routine cognitive and creative work, standard mid-tier knowledge jobs lose the scarcity that supported their pay.

They predict a barbell outcome: cheap synthetic output at scale on one side, and scarce verified human presence earning a premium on the other. Human value then rests on presence, provenance, and accountability that are core to what is bought, not extras. Policy, they argue, should fund verification systems accordingly.
arxiv-2605-03310:
Maksym Nechepurenko and Pavel Shuvalov argue that coordination should be a separate, configurable layer in multi-agent language model systems. Production failures in such systems are common and stem mostly from coordination faults, not raw model skill, yet fixes so far are catalogs or engineering frameworks.

On prediction markets with one fixed model, tools, and prompt, they vary only the coordination setup across five configurations. Score decomposition separates calibration from discrimination, giving each setup a distinct signature. Two setups led on the cost-quality frontier in this regime, and live agents replicate the test in parallel.
arxiv-2605-03410:
Shawn Li, You Qin, Jiate Li, Charith Peris, Lisa Bauer, Roger Zimmermann, and Yue Zhao propose train-once, deploy-anywhere detection of out-of-distribution inputs. Their method uses diffusion geometry instead of density alone. Standard detectors are tied to one training domain. Real deployment faces new domain pairs, with only a handful of known-good samples.

Their UFCOD method reads two energy features from diffusion score paths. The features are path energy and dynamics energy, forming a Sobolev-style signature. Each new task needs about a hundred unlabeled in-domain samples, and no retraining. Across twelve cross-domain benchmarks, accuracy was strong, rivaling methods trained on vastly more data.
arxiv-2605-03510:
Fengyuan Yang, Yongqian Peng, Yuxi Ma, Chenheng Xu, and Yixin Zhu ask why languages settle on one morpheme combination over other plausible ones. New words are built by compounding and affixation. Yet morphological choice, as a situated speaker decision, has rarely been modeled directly.

They work within a rational speech act framework. A time-indexed lexicon comes from historical and contemporary American English corpora. Across thousands of words over two centuries, attested forms ranked above available unattested rivals. Models that balance listener recoverability against speaker cost beat meaning-only and cost-only baselines. The edge grew as candidate sets grew.
arxiv-2605-03610:
Lorenzo Beltrame and six co-authors address a missing resource in satellite imaging: paired examples of the same ground scene with and without shadows. Shadows from terrain and tall buildings degrade classification, detection, and 3D reconstruction, yet public paired data for shadow removal barely exist. Their deSEO method builds such pairs from an existing shadow detection dataset.

For each tile, deSEO picks a lightly shadowed image as a weak reference and pairs it with shadowed views using time and geometry filters, orientation normalization, and careful registration. A validity mask marks reliably aligned pixels. The team also trains a depth-aware deshadowing model, giving satellite shadow removal a replicable data pipeline.
arxiv-2605-03910:
David Hambraeus and four co-authors demonstrate an inverse-designed optomechanical crystal that largely closes a known performance gap. Optomechanical devices couple light to mechanical motion, linking optical and microwave signals. Release-free crystals anchor heat better than suspended nanobeams. But they have historically shown weaker photon-phonon coupling. Strength and thermal robustness seemed to trade off against each other.

The team combined physics-guided human intuition with a multiphysics inverse-design algorithm for resonant structures. They built a release-free silicon crystal with a record vacuum optomechanical coupling rate for its class. That rate is comparable to suspended state-of-the-art devices. Its scattering rate is nearly twice previous release-free results. The design framework itself is presented as reusable for co-optimizing optical and mechanical properties in other devices.
arxiv-2605-04310:
Reza Farahani and six co-authors present a system for running serverless workflows across several edge computing clusters that must together meet strict end-to-end deadlines. Running close to data sources helps, but existing tools were designed for a single cluster, not a federation.

Their method handles the full life cycle, from analysing task dependencies to choosing how each function runs and where it is placed. A leader-based coordination layer links the clusters. Built on open tools for functions and workflows, the system was deployed on a testbed of six clusters with sixty-four varied edge nodes to check it under realistic conditions.
arxiv-2605-04410:
Rokas Gipiškis and Olga Kurasova argue that research on explainable artificial intelligence has a reporting problem: measures of explanation quality are defined inconsistently, reported incompletely, and rarely checked against shared baselines. That fragmentation makes results hard to compare or trust.

They propose an evaluation card, a standard document that should accompany any study introducing such a metric. The card declares what property the metric targets, its assumptions, the validation evidence behind it, how it could be gamed, and its known failure cases. Adopting the template as a community norm, they argue, would support meta-analysis and accountability.
arxiv-2605-04510:
Leonard Boussioux and three co-authors develop an optimisation approach for fighting wildfires, where commanders must assign scarce crews across a wide area as fires evolve. The difficulty is circular: assignments change how fires spread, and spread determines where crews are needed next.

Their model links crew routes on a time-space network with fire dynamics on a state network through shared constraints. A specialised algorithm generates suppression plans and crew routes together, strengthened by new cuts that exploit the structure of those linking constraints. A data-driven method estimates fire spread from conditions and suppression effort while correcting for confounding in historical records.
arxiv-2605-04910:
Soumya Sinha Babu and Aaron Welters give a short algebraic proof of a realization theorem for systems theory in the special setting of characteristic two. Bessmertnyĭ realizations write certain matrix-valued functions as corners of larger symmetric linear systems. A recent proof of the symmetric case in characteristic two was algorithmic in style.

Using differential algebra, the authors define formal derivatives for rational functions over such fields and study their constants. That reduces the matrix problem to checks on diagonal entries alone. As a bonus, they prove a new result on the field extension problem and, in the scalar case, count how abundant counterexamples in characteristic two can be.
arxiv-2605-05310:
Debtosh Chowdhury, Rounak Nath, and Sudipta Show use the NANOGrav pulsar timing results to constrain the early universe's inflation era and the reheating that followed it. Pulsar timing arrays recently found strong evidence for a background of gravitational waves, which could come from cosmic inflation. Assuming that origin, the authors fit the fifteen-year dataset for the tensor spectrum's tilt and strength.

The data prefer an extremely blue-tilted tensor spectrum and a reheating era that was not instantaneous. The team also test non-standard initial vacua beyond the usual Bunch-Davies choice, finding the observations favour one subclass, the alpha-vacuum, and narrow its defining parameter sharply. Their analysis shows gravitational wave backgrounds can probe both inflation and reheating together.
arxiv-2605-05810:
A medical vision-language model that answers "no consolidation" while consolidation is plainly visible has not just erred; it has contradicted the image in clinical language. Zhengru Fang and co-authors name this failure negated-option attraction. The model is drawn to a negated answer option despite both the picture and the question pointing the other way.

Their benchmark, CXR-ContraBench, diagnoses the failure on chest X-rays across internal and external protocols. It centers on questions about findings that are present, where choosing the negation creates direct clinical risk. The work separates polarity confusion from ordinary misreading.
arxiv-2605-06010:
Yuchen Guo and four co-authors give ordinary visual systems a thermal sense without slowing them down. Models that see only visible light often fail at night or in fog, where heat based infrared images carry vital extra cues. High quality fusion methods exist, but their delay rules them out for real time use on edge devices.

FusionProxy is a plug in fusion module trained from a diffusion teacher's sample spread. Pixel level spread weights its image supervision, while feature level spread routes alignment inside frozen backbones. Once trained, it drops into any perception system with no joint retraining. Tests show gains on static recognition and stronger robustness in dynamic tasks, including closed loop driving, at real time speeds.
arxiv-2605-06110:
Xinglin Wang and eleven co-authors allocate models and tools to agent workflows under hard budget and deadline limits. Agentic systems split a request into subtasks run by specialized models, coordinated by their dependencies. Real deployments often demand completion on time and within budget, not just good average efficiency, which changes the goal entirely.

The team frame the task as a finite horizon stochastic allocation problem. Their planner, Monte Carlo Portfolio Planning, simulates whole workflow executions to estimate the chance of finishing within both limits. It then replans in a closed loop after each observed outcome. On code and proof workflow benchmarks, the planner consistently raised constrained completion rates over strong baselines across a wide range of budget and deadline settings.
arxiv-2605-06210:
Sacha Braun, Michael Jordan, and Francis Bach introduce super-level-set regression for building small prediction regions with guaranteed coverage. In multivariate regression, users want the smallest region that still contains the truth at a set rate, conditional on the input. Standard routes estimate the full conditional density first and then threshold it, a plug in process that is fragile and costly.

Their framework instead parameterizes and optimizes the region's boundary directly. A mathematical construction resolves the coupling between the volume goal and the quantiles of the model's own error, which had blocked direct approaches. Flexible volume preserving frontier functions let the regions take complex, multimodal, or disjoint shapes. The result reframes conditional quantile regression as direct geometric optimization rather than density estimation plus cutting.
arxiv-2605-06310:
Siru Zhong and five co-authors add dynamic pattern recalibration to time series forecasting models. Real series shift their local patterns constantly, yet deep forecasters apply one fixed set of weights to every time token. That static response forces a compromised average, blind to changing local dynamics. This holds whether the backbone is modest or huge, the authors argue. Their mechanism attacks the bottleneck directly at the token level.

A light perceive, route, and modulate pipeline computes a soft routing over a learned basis of response patterns for each token. The resulting time aware vector rescales hidden states through a residual product, recalibrating the model moment by moment. As a plug in it improved forecasting across diverse architectures with minimal overhead. As a standalone model it stayed competitive across twelve benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-06610:
Jakub Stępień, Marcin Mazur, Jacek Tabor, and Przemysław Spurek propose SoftSAE, a sparse autoencoder that chooses how many features to activate for each input. Sparse autoencoders unpack neural activations into understandable features for interpretability research. Fixed top-k versions force the same feature count on every input, though simple inputs need fewer features and complex ones need more.

A differentiable soft top-k operator learns an input-dependent sparsity level, so explanation length tracks the information in each sample. Experiments confirm the model finds meaningful features and picks sensible counts per concept. The work targets language models and vision transformers, where fixed sparsity can add noise or miss structure.
arxiv-2605-06910:
Jaime Morales, Sergio Pastrana, and Juan Tapiador benchmark how well language models recover hidden indicators of compromise, such as IP addresses, from obfuscated and encrypted JavaScript. Attackers hide these traces to frustrate analysis, and model resilience against such hiding was largely uncharted. Their dataset holds 336 programs put through twelve rising levels, from simple renaming and Base64 encoding up to XOR and AES-256 encryption.

A test harness queries diverse models in a repeatable way. Models handle light transformations well, but encryption-based hiding badly hurts detection. The authors frame encryption as a key frontier for model-driven code analysis and threat intelligence, marking both present limits and paths to improve.
arxiv-2605-07110:
Zejian Chen and eight co-authors survey computer-use agents, programs that operate browsers, desktops, phones, and terminals on a user's behalf. As these agents leave narrow benchmarks for real software, success alone no longer captures reliability. Perception errors, drifting plans, memory, permissions, and oversight jointly decide whether actions match user intent.

The article organizes the field by architecture, covering perception, decision, and execution layers, and by lifecycle, from creation through maintenance. It separates where failures become visible from where their enabling conditions arise. Open challenges include grounding, preserving limits over long tasks, binding authority safely, and keeping assurance as systems drift.
arxiv-2605-07210:
Shuai Wang and four co-authors use diffusion language models as document retrievers in a way that matches how those models actually work. Earlier diffusion retrievers squeezed each text into one averaged vector, ignoring the masked-prediction training that gives these models their strength. DiffRetriever instead appends masked positions and reads their outputs as retrieval signals.

One masked position already beat the earlier diffusion approach on the same backbones. Several masked positions, processed together in one pass, enable fine-grained matching at little extra cost, unlike autoregressive retrievers that must decode in sequence. In matched comparisons, DiffRetriever achieved the strongest overall effectiveness among the methods tested.
arxiv-2605-07310:
Ning-An Lai and three co-authors estimate how long classical solutions survive for a one-dimensional wave equation with spatial-derivative nonlinear terms. Lifespan bounds for space-derivative terms are harder than for time-derivative ones, especially the sharp upper bound, because iteration must handle weights that depend on position. The paper derives both upper and lower bounds.

Part of the analysis lands on the same ordinary differential inequality known from damped wave equations studied decades ago. The authors give a simple blow-up proof from that inequality, using iteration and slicing, in a more general situation. The work sharpens understanding of when small wave disturbances must break down.
arxiv-2605-07410:
Ayumi Ukai proves that simpler effective Hamiltonians for quantum spin systems stay accurate independently of system size. For bounded, short-range forces on lattices of any size, Ukai builds an energy cut-off Hamiltonian for any finite target region. A spectral-overlap bound controls how much its low-energy states leak into the original system's high-energy space.

The cutoff-dependent error decays exponentially, giving stable low-lying eigenvalues in finite volume. In infinite volume, the same estimate holds for the ground state itself. The result extends and strengthens an earlier effective-Hamiltonian mechanism by replacing operator-norm control with a volume-uniform spectral form suited to the large-system limit.
arxiv-2605-07510:
Bohan Hou and seven co-authors benchmark agents whose searches must interleave text and visual evidence, each round shaping the next. Existing tests keep visual evidence in the input or treat it as a final answer, missing that back-and-forth. InterLV-Search holds over two thousand examples at three levels, from active visual seeking to open-web search.

Some samples force comparison between several entities during the search itself. An accompanying agent framework standardizes tool use, logging, and scoring. The best current model scored below fifty percent overall. That exposes weaknesses in seeking visual evidence, controlling search, and integrating multimodal findings.
arxiv-2605-07610:
Jeongho Kim studies steady flows of a compressible fluid with a capillarity effect, described by the spherically symmetric Navier-Stokes-Korteweg system. The setting is the region outside a unit ball, with given boundary and far-field data, and three kinds of boundary behavior: an impermeable wall, inflow, and outflow.

When the boundary data are small enough, Kim proves a unique smooth stationary solution exists for each case, and pins down how fast it settles to its far-field state. The wall case decays exponentially, while the inflow and outflow cases decay only algebraically. The paper also tracks what happens as the capillarity coefficient vanishes, and numerical experiments confirm the theoretical convergence rate is optimal.
arxiv-2605-07710:
Jakub Kopystiański and Jan Otop speed up the exact learning of tree automata, the machines that recognize sets of trees. In the classic Angluin-style setup, a learner asks membership and equivalence queries about the target language, and the number of queries drives the cost. Many natural properties of tree data, like subtree order not mattering, are known in advance.

Their extension hands the learner a term rewriting system that encodes such properties of the target language. The learner uses the rewrite rules to deduce some answers itself instead of querying, cutting the query count. They present example rewrite systems expressing natural properties of tree-structured data that yield significant reductions, making exact learning practical for richer targets.
arxiv-2605-08010:
Bhaskar Dutta and four co-authors propose a new source for the gamma-ray glow at the center of the Milky Way. The Galactic Center excess is usually blamed on dark matter annihilation or on unresolved millisecond pulsars. Their alternative: cosmic-ray protons scattering off dark matter in the galactic halo, converting some of that energy into photons.

Two model versions are worked out. In the inelastic one, cosmic rays excite a lighter dark particle whose heavier partner decays into two photons; in the elastic one, the photon appears directly in a two-to-three scattering. For viable parameter ranges both fit the observed excess spectrum comparably to the annihilation and pulsar explanations. The mechanism opens a fresh interpretive avenue for gamma-ray observations of the center.
arxiv-2605-08110:
Dario Coscia, Sindy Löwe, and Max Welling add Bayesian uncertainty to LoRA, the popular low-rank method for fine-tuning large models. Plain LoRA gives a single point estimate, leaves a persistent accuracy gap against full fine-tuning, and offers no measure of confidence, which limits its use where reliability matters.

BaLoRA reparameterizes the LoRA matrices with an input-adaptive Bayesian form that adds few parameters and little compute. The adaptive noise it injects not only calibrates uncertainty well but also raises accuracy, narrowing the gap to full fine-tuning on language reasoning and vision tasks. Applied to band gap prediction for metal-organic frameworks, it also supports zero-shot test-time use.
arxiv-2605-08210:
Sanaz Karimijafarbigloo, Armin Khosravi, Alireza Kheyrkhah, Reza Azad, and coauthors model rater disagreement head-on. Expert outlines in medical scans truly differ from one reader to the next. Scanners add their own artifacts. Consensus labels can hide real doubt and yield overconfident outlines.

Their framework separates the two sources of variation. A small harmonizer network models scanner effects. It modulates features so latent maps match one shared form. The doubt that remains then reflects anatomy, not noise. High-frequency prompt modules in the spectral domain encode each rater's edge precision. They also encode texture response. The system can thus speak in single expert styles, not one blurred average.
arxiv-2605-08410:
Amanda Cook, Kaitlyn Shin, Ziggy Pleunis, Maxwell Fine, and coauthors report thirty new repeating fast radio burst sources found by the CHIME telescope in Canada. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from other galaxies, and only a small share of sources are ever seen to repeat, which makes each new repeater valuable for follow-up.

The discoveries raise the CHIME total to eighty repeating sources. The team assembles uniform statistics for the whole sample: repeaters stay rare, at roughly two to three percent of sources, with no clear change over the survey years. Four repeaters show steady, linear drift in their dispersion measure over years, a clue to slowly changing environments around the sources.
arxiv-2605-08710:
Dongxin Guo, Jikun Wu, and Siu-Ming Yiu ask when a human and AI team can beat both members working alone, a result most studies fail to reach. For confidence based ways of combining judgments, they derive tight bounds joining signal detection theory with information theory. Teamwork helps exactly when human and machine errors correlate less than a threshold they compute.

Beyond that threshold, no confidence based rule can achieve complementarity at all, an impossibility guarantee. Predicted accuracies match human data on two image labeling sets closely, and the multi class threshold scaling also holds. Team design gains formulas that explain why synergy is rare and when to stop expecting it.
arxiv-2605-08810:
Yang Xiao and nine coauthors press short clips into one code each for film picks. Their module is the Compressed Video Aggregator. It does not feed each frame to the taste model. It sums frame codes from a frozen vision model into one pact point. It then squeezes that point into a small space. Light self focus polishes it. One code per clip goes to the pick model.

The team found the base test set had too many near same frames. They picked key frames with the help of titles and a text image model. That step lifted all plans on test. Their module gains score while training time and memory fall a lot.
arxiv-2605-08910:
Hira Nasir and four coauthors harden network intrusion detectors against adversarial examples crafted to slip past neural classifiers. Standard adversarial training improves robustness blindly, with no view of how attacks spread layer by layer. Their LARAR method first scores each layer's vulnerability, then weights regularization adaptively during training and adds auxiliary classifiers that help expose attacks early.

On a widely used intrusion dataset, the system keeps clean accuracy near ninety five percent while resisting gradient based and transfer attacks better than conventional training. Layer scores make the defense interpretable, and focusing effort on weak layers cuts computing cost. Security teams gain a detector that explains where it is fragile while becoming harder to fool.
arxiv-2605-09010:
Manoranjan Singha and Rohan Pradhan write on ultrafilters, a tool in set theory used to judge which sets count as large. They define a quotient-like operation between two ultrafilters and study what happens when one ultrafilter divides another in a strong sense.

Much of the work centers on ultrafilters that divide themselves, and on how that property links to the quotient construction. The authors also present results on the stability of special ultrafilters tied to multiplication, and they connect the theory to sets in combinatorics called multiplicative delta sets. Readers get a focused piece of pure mathematics that ties several strands of ultrafilter research together.
arxiv-2605-09110:
M Archita and Karim Johannes Becher work in pure algebra, on a question about symmetries of special algebraic structures. Over fields whose characteristic is not two, and which carry a certain anisotropic form, they apply a construction due to Merkurjev to build an algebra with an orthogonal involution of degree six.

The algebra they produce admits proper projective similitudes that fail a property called R-triviality, which is the point of the result. Such examples, they show, exist over every finitely generated field extension of the kind they list, including extensions of local and global number fields and certain extensions of the real numbers. The work adds concrete counterexamples to a corner of the theory of algebraic groups.
arxiv-2605-09210:
Machado and Seade study vector fields holomorphic on hypersurface singularities, deriving global blocks on compact shapes. For a germ with a lone singularity, they map generic fields through the GSV-index. They prove a lower bound on the minimal index, given by a formula in the Tjurina-Greuel number and the dimension, with parity based sign.

A match holds when the field extends to complex space with a clean singularity at the origin, and such cases form an open dense set. That sorts generic fields on weighted homogeneous germs, and sorts those germs too. For singular hypersurfaces in complex manifolds, the results constrain compact shapes admitting holomorphic fields. In one case, an irreducible compact singular curve with a nontrivial field that is zero somewhere is rational, with at most two flawed points. For singular surfaces in Kähler 3-folds, genus is at least irregularity when positivity holds.
arxiv-2605-09310:
Li and two colleagues put ESG limits on step by step portfolio optimisation without touching the financial policy's inputs or reward, treating ESG as preference, risk exposure, or hedge. Static ESG scores are noisy, vary by provider, come out rarely, and lag behind step by step choices, so adding them to observations or rewards fits step by step control poorly. Their Multimodal Action-Conditioned Constraint Field derives ESG costs tied to mechanisms, from point in time multimodal evidence and planned portfolio moves.

MACF-X, a set of optimiser tuned adapters, turns MACF costs and uncertainties into native constrained optimisation links through one shared pressure layer that tracks slack and doubt. Across many integration setups, MACF-X cuts tail ESG budget pressure while keeping financial results strong. Ablations show the gain needs dynamic evidence inputs and three head decomposition. Static ESG score proxies look almost like score shuffled noise baselines.
arxiv-2605-09410:
Liufu and eighteen colleagues build RePO-VLA, a recovery-driven policy framework for vision-language-action models that treats success, recovery, and failure trajectories differently. Such models stay brittle in contact-rich manipulation because success-only imitation barely supervises drift and failed rollouts are discarded. Recovery-Aware Initialization slices segments and resets history so fixes depend on the bad state rather than the failure.

A Progress-Aware Semantic Value Function aligns features with instructions and good examples. The resulting labels salvage useful failure prefixes through reliability decay, while weak labels mark drift and breakdowns. A data engine turns bad states into rollouts, teaching recovery to the success manifold, and refinement trains the policy to favour high-progress moves. At deployment, a fixed high value of 1 point 0 biases actions toward the success manifold with no failure detectors or heuristic retries. FRBench adds standardised error injection and recovery-focused evaluation.
arxiv-2605-09610:
Goel and three colleagues introduce SmartEval, a benchmark for judging Solidity smart contracts made by language models from plain word specs. It pairs 9,000 made contracts with expert written ground truth from the FSM-SCG data set. It adds a five part rubric covering code quality, business logic fidelity, state machine correctness, variable fidelity, and functional completeness. It supplies a repeatable generation and scoring pipeline. Three studies check the benchmark's trustworthiness.

An ablation study isolates each pipeline part. Human experts confirm auto scores track expert judgment closely. The Slither static analyzer agrees with the model auditor about 79 percent of the time. Study of the full corpus finds logic gaps in about 35 percent of contracts and state transition errors in about 23 percent. Made contracts score higher overall, traced to literal spec following. SmartEval gives the field a checked base for contract synthesis research.
arxiv-2605-09710:
Chatterjee and three colleagues studied a strange quantum effect in which states with no entanglement still resist being told apart by separated parties. Their paper works with antidistinguishability, the task of ruling out at least one state a system was not prepared in, using only local work plus ordinary messages. It introduces a related task called local state antimarking, where parties must rule out a whole sequence that was not supplied.

The authors show that any set of mutually orthogonal multipartite pure states can be ruled out locally. They then build a set of product states whose sequences behave differently under local versus global checks. That gap reveals nonlocality without entanglement, a case where separated parties fall short of a joint measurement. They also show no strict ranking holds between antimarking and related local tasks, since some sets allow one task but forbid the other.
arxiv-2605-10010:
Bhangale and Zhang study constraint satisfaction, where variables take values from a finite set and local rules must be satisfied as widely as possible. Their rules are generalised linear equations over a finite group: sums of variable values, or products for non-abelian groups, must land in a chosen set. The goal is an assignment satisfying the largest possible share of rules.

For satisfiable instances the pair gives an approximation algorithm and proves it optimal for certain sets, assuming P differs from NP. The predicate is rare in two ways at once: it resists approximation on nearly satisfiable instances, yet still admits a non-trivial algorithm on fully satisfiable ones. That combination makes it one of very few known cases of its kind.
arxiv-2605-10210:
Pizzolato, Pasti and Bellotto build a framework for binary terrain segmentation on a low-cost microcontroller, a capability tiny outdoor robots need but state-of-the-art models cannot fit. Memory and compute limits on microcontrollers block deployment on small platforms. At the core sits Nano-U, a highly compact segmentation network with only a few thousand parameters.

To offset minimal capacity, Nano-U trains via Quantization-Aware Distillation, combining distillation with quantization-aware training. The quantised model performs excellently on the Botanic Garden data set and very well on TinyAgri, a custom field set with harder scenes. Deployed on a commodity microcontroller via extended MicroFlow, a Rust compiler-based inference engine for TinyML, the model runs on an ESP32-S3 with minimal memory footprint and low latency. It eliminates interpreter overhead and dynamic memory allocation. The result is a viable, energy-efficient perception route for low-cost robots.
arxiv-2605-10310:
Ruben Laukkonen and fifteen colleagues argue that AI alignment research has aimed too narrowly. Most work focuses on safety and harm prevention: safeguards, control, and compliance. They liken that stance to early psychology's illness-centered view, which left flourishing aside. Their 2026 paper proposes Positive Alignment, an agenda for AI that actively supports human and ecological flourishing.

Positive Alignment means systems that help people flourish in a plural, context-aware, user-led way while staying safe and cooperative. The paper argues that flaws such as engagement hacking, lost autonomy, weak truth-seeking, and low humility may respond better to this positive agenda than to more safeguards. It closes with design rules favoring dissent and shared control: grounding in context, local customization, ongoing adaptation, and many centers of oversight rather than one choke point.
arxiv-2605-10810:
Daniel Ranard's 2026 paper offers a label-free way to judge language models on technical writing. It tests whether a model's forecast helps a separate scoring model predict hidden text. The core task hides the tail end of a displayed equation from a physics or mathematics paper. It then measures whether the forecast raises the score the true ending receives.

Forecasts are checked against controls that feed the scorer nearby context instead of a real prediction. A gain must therefore come from genuine foresight rather than extra words. Trials on more than thirteen hundred equation endings show leading models beating those controls. Extra tests probe shortcuts in which a forecast merely primes the scorer. Readers who build or choose benchmarks get a statistical yardstick that needs no human grading.
arxiv-2605-10910:
Richie Yeung, Aleks Kissinger, and Rob Cornish teach a reinforcement-learning agent to synthesize Clifford quantum circuits for fully connected devices. The agent must find a short gate sequence that reduces a circuit's symplectic matrix form to the identity, learning from random walks outward from that identity.

A new network design respects qubit relabeling symmetry and works for any qubit count without splicing or resizing. One policy therefore scales across sizes. On six-qubit circuits it lands within one two-qubit gate of optimal and finds true optima in over 99 percent of cases. It then scales to thirty qubits with fewer gates than Qiskit's standard synthesizers. Compiler teams get a fast, size-flexible route to lean Clifford circuits.
arxiv-2605-11010:
Antonios Makris and four colleagues compare ways to combine model updates in federated learning, where training runs across scattered devices. The server's combining rule strongly shapes learning quality, toughness, and system behavior, and its best choice may depend on how alike the devices' data are.

Using image-classification test sets, the team measures how widely used combining rules respond to varying data mix, tracking central accuracy and loss plus combining, training, and communication time. Rules show distinct trade-offs that shift with data set and operating conditions, so no single rule wins everywhere. Federated practitioners get an experimental map for matching the combining choice to data conditions.
arxiv-2605-11410: Tang and eight colleagues ask what EEG foundation models actually capture from human brain signals. Clinical EEG work leans on a hand-built feature catalogue refined across decades. Modern foundation models learn directly from raw signals and match or beat feature-engineered baselines. Using ridge probing, subspace erasure and a transparent classifier, the team audits three foundation models across five clinical tasks and a sixty-three-feature lexicon. Of 945 model-task-feature units, 68 point 6 percent prove representation-causal and 21 point 1 percent encoded-only.
arxiv-2605-11510: Sasaki, Nakamura and Nozaki give a decoding method for mixed deletion and insertion errors in Hagiwara codes. Hagiwara codes are quantum codes built from quantum Reed-Solomon codes. Though they can correct mixed deletion-insertion errors, a fast decoding method for such errors stayed an open problem. This paper supplies that method for Hagiwara codes, closing a gap between the codes' known correction power and usable decoding.
arxiv-2605-11610: Wang and thirteen others benchmark 15 stand-in models for lattice thermal conductivity. New models have opened vast matter spaces, but high-quality thermal conductivity work still needs exact anharmonic treatment. Using the Phonix base of 6,966 entries from theory work, they group stand-ins into physics-aware features, end-to-end deep networks, and trained MLIP codes. MLIP-based models excel at filling gaps, while deep networks prove most robust on new data. Stand-ins cut compute costs many times over for high-throughput heat-power screening.
arxiv-2605-11710: Phu-Quy Nguyen-Lam and five colleagues tackle continual few-shot learning, where a model must absorb new concepts without forgetting old ones. Their framework trains slot reps toward whole-class identity using self-supervised vision transformers. At inference, those frozen slots are composed to match new scenes. The strict split between learning reps and composing them gave state-of-the-art transfer to unseen concepts with minimal forgetting.
arxiv-2605-11810: Olivier Massicot, Giulia Cervia, and Maël Le Treust extend empirical coordination, the study of how agents align actions under communication limits, to short message blocks. Using Shannon's random coding argument and the method of types, they study how a random codebook performs on average and prove that coordination at some rate is achievable. Their bound on the best achievable rate comes both exactly and as an asymptotic expansion, matching standard finite-blocklength characterizations.
arxiv-2605-12010: Aybüke Ulusarslan, Niki Kilbertus, and Nora Schneider set limits on learning linear motion from tests. Old rules for steered linear time-fixed systems assume full control and steady prodding, leaving open what stays pinned down when those fail. They show the test setup itself, the actual initial state and control input, sets what information the seen path can recover. They give a shape-based account of this limit and a closed-form list of all fitting systems, proving reachable-subspace motion stays fixed.
arxiv-2605-12110: Di Liu and eight colleagues present AB-Sparse, a training-free system for fast long-context inference. As context grows, KV cache loading drags speed down, and fixed block sizes assume all heads behave alike. Heads differ widely in how block size affects them, so AB-Sparse gives each head its own block size. It offsets the extra memory with lossless centroid coding of blocks, plus custom GPU code for mixed block sizes. Tests show accuracy gains up to 5.43 percent over block sparse baselines, with no speed loss.
arxiv-2605-12210: Yanqing Liu and Jie Wang build a moment-sum-of-squares system for tuning over quaternions. The hard part is hybrid algebra: products do not commute, while values obey extra rules from four real slots. They present sums of squares with ideals, and prove Archimedean Positivstellensätze for real forms. Dual problems are solved with Riesz-Haviland accounts and a flat-growth theorem, yielding ladders that close with exactness rules. For square-limited programs, the moment relaxation matches the real value, and tests show equal values with shorter times.
arxiv-2605-12410: Su, Banerjee and Klabjan propose a bootstrap method for transition kernels of finite controlled Markov chains. The setting covers nonstationary or history-dependent control policies. It arises in offline learning where the data policy is unknown. They prove distributional consistency in single long-chain and episodic regimes. The proof uses a new bootstrap law of large numbers for visit counts. It also uses a martingale central limit theorem for increments. The delta method extends this to policy evaluation and optimal policy recovery, giving valid confidence intervals.
arxiv-2605-12510: Dos Santos and eleven colleagues release WhaVax, an expert-labelled set of vaccine-related WhatsApp messages from large Brazilian public groups across pandemic years. The build combines keyword collection, semantic deduplication and multi-stage annotation by medical specialists, yielding a gold-standard corpus with strong annotator agreement. The paper also maps WhatsApp misinformation patterns in language, structure, timing and group behaviour, including a layer of genuinely ambiguous cases. Benchmarks test classic models, small tuned models and large models under scarce-data conditions.
arxiv-2605-12610: Kumar and three colleagues test whether open language models can give good code review feedback after light tuning. Proprietary models raise cost, compute and ethics concerns around sharing student code, yet open models lag them out of the box. The team distils knowledge from a larger, stronger model into Code Llama using parameter-efficient fine-tuning and prompt engineering. Feedback on buggy Java code is judged by students, manual annotation and automated metrics including BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore. Results show fine-tuning notably improves feedback quality over prompts alone.
arxiv-2605-12810: Bissonette and eight colleagues present metallicities for 40 stars in Segue 1, a dwarf galaxy of 500 solar masses. They measure the CaII K feature in Keck spectra, covering red giant branch and turnoff stars. The sample is sixfold larger than earlier Segue 1 data. The metallicity distribution averages [Fe/H] -2.52 with dispersion 0.59, fitting a single Gaussian with no sign of multiple peaks. That pattern fits a star-formation episode before reionization, and its spread confirms Segue 1 as a galaxy.
arxiv-2605-13010: Huang and Zhou study image inpainting, filling masked regions, with generative diffusion models. Instead of training a dedicated model or adapting a pretrained model per image, they introduce Amortized Inpainting with Diffusion. It fixes the diffusion backbone and trains one small reusable guidance module offline. They frame guidance as a deterministic problem with a supervised terminal goal. A Gaussian bridge they derive yields a principled continuous-time actor-critic learner. Tests show a better quality-speed trade-off with under one percent extra trainable parameters.
arxiv-2605-13110: Alexandrou and Pramatari present a fully automated multi-agent setup for venture capital due diligence and market analysis. The system pairs language models with live web retrieval on an event-driven orchestration design, turning messy data into tidy investment intelligence. Its key technical piece reverse-engineers the Greek Business Registry's frontend-to-backend traffic to pull official filings, parsed with layout-aware OCR. A structural fallback flags gaps plainly instead of inventing figures, directly targeting hallucination in money contexts.
arxiv-2605-13210: Wang and colleagues build PoisonCap, a scheme guarding CHERI memory against use after freeing. A poisoned capability token marks freed blocks and tells hardware how to handle quarantined memory. Nested memory managers can pass poisoning rights down without disturbing managers above them. It replaces an older shadow bitmap, clears memory on reuse, and matches the cost of a clearing baseline.
arxiv-2605-13810: Ying Feng and four colleagues prove fair noised rounding with a single shuffled Hadamard transform, matching the mean squared error bounds of truly random spin grids. Their rounder feeds HD to the input vector then subtracts a random scalar offset before rounding, adding extra chance at tiny cost. A noised TurboQuant hits mean squared error (pi times square root of 3 over 2 plus o(1)) times 4 to the minus b at b bits per slot.
arxiv-2605-14010: Guterman and Yurkov work out how to compute the Cullis determinant, a spread of the plain determinant to rectangular matrices. It sums maximal minors with alternating signs. The paper writes it as a Pfaffian of a matrix built from X by multiplication and transposition. That rewrite yields a fast polynomial-time algorithm that needs no division, for entries in a commutative ring. The authors also weigh its cost against the definition-based route and add formulas for horizontal expansion.
arxiv-2605-14310: Mahdizadeh and four co-authors propose CoRDS, coreset picks for streaming video. Streaming video understanding needs compact memory for future reasoning. Existing streaming methods rely on local heuristics, without optimizing cache representativeness. CoRDS treats KV-cache compression as coreset selection: it picks a small subset covering the cache's shape. A bicriteria goal balances key-value coverage, with diversity favoring new picks. Across four VLMs and five benchmarks, the method beats heuristic methods under a fixed budget.
