arxiv-2605-14410: Hod proves dyonic black-hole spacetimes from a quasitopological non-linear electrodynamics theory can support self-gravitating thin shells in static equilibrium. Earlier work showed negligible-gravity test shells can sit in discrete radial regions where a metric derivative vanishes. Hod extends this to massive self-gravitating shells on the verge of becoming black holes. They sit in regions where a related dimensionless derivative tends to zero from above. Strikingly, the radii of these nearly-black Dyson shells are universal, independent of the central object's mass.
arxiv-2605-14610: Zabolotnii introduces a new polynomial family for fitting parameters under non-Gaussian errors. It extends Kunchenko's method of polynomial maximisation and uses signed-parity fractional powers. A single number alpha between zero and one steers the family from a fractal regime through a linear point to an integer-power regime. For degree two, a closed-form variance-reduction coefficient is derived. Singular behaviour appears at alpha equal to one half.
arxiv-2605-15210: Daniel Aronoff, Robert M. Townsend, and Madars Virza propose TradeMech, a way to net trades multilaterally without moving counterparty exposure. Central clearing shifts exposure to a central party, and trade compression can alter bilateral relationships. TradeMech recasts two-party contracts into chains and loops, nets the designated fungible object across them, and swaps contracts with multi-party ones whose given trades stay fractions of the first ones. If a party fails to pre-commit, its trade reverts to a two-party contract and the rest re-nets.
arxiv-2605-15610: Ping Li, G. A. Bobkov, I. V. Bobkova, and Tao Yu find a non-relativistic spin-orbit coupling in triplet superconductors. The triplet order parameter stamps a momentum-linked spin pattern on quasiparticles. Spin and orbital motion braid together. With no relativistic coupling, an electric field can still yield spin polarization in a p-wave superconductor, an Edelstein effect. The team then sketches a way to make a steady spin current from alternating fields via near-field electric effects. It opens a route to steer spin currents in unconventional superconductors.
arxiv-2605-15710: Huacan Chai and nine colleagues launch SMMBench, a benchmark for source-distributed multimodal agent memory. Past benchmarks test memory inside pre-assembled contexts. They under-test whether agents can use proof scattered across sources that arose apart. SMMBench gauges whether agents can fetch, align, and compose proof across many sources, not one context. It tests cross-source reasoning, conflict resolution, preference reasoning, and action prediction. The set holds 1877 samples grounded in 264 sources. Tests on memory-style and retrieval-based baselines show current systems still struggle on these skills.
arxiv-2605-16010: F. Anmasser and eleven colleagues show a trapped-ion processor that shares control voltages to many electrodes from few inputs. This eases the wiring snag for large ion traps. A sample-and-hold circuit charges electrodes to fixed levels, then cuts them off while qubits run. Ion motion heating stays below one phonon per second in both switch states. Sample gaps under 50 ms keep likely gate errors from charge decay below one part in ten thousand.
arxiv-2605-16610: Rakhshan and Rabusseau offer a short guide to tensor networks, the picture-based language for high-order data that extends matrices. Tensor networks encode contractions as graph edges, cutting symbol clutter and showing structure hidden by index notation. The guide covers tensor steps, products, and reshaping through diagrams, plus standard splits and gradient proofs. Throughout, the picture approach yields shorter, clearer proofs of rules, rank bounds, and gradient results than slow index work.
arxiv-2605-16710: Grass's team develops general models of high-frequency thermal noise in Michelson interferometers, which matters as photon-counting readout evades quantum shot noise. Older models use a quasi-static shortcut that fails in the MHz band. The new models cover substrate and coating Brownian noise, thermo-elastic noise, and coating heat-optic noise. They check against older low-band models and high-band spectra from the Holometer, then apply the models to GQuEST, now being built.
arxiv-2605-16910: Song fixes a flaw in the usual account of abstract tropical curves, which cannot handle parallel rays even though ordinary curves admit them. She defines a new kind of abstract tropical curve that allows parallel rays, and gives its rational function semifields with a characterisation. She then links these curves and their semifields over the tropical semifield in a categorical equivalence. Under that link, edge weights and the balancing condition become algebraic notions.
arxiv-2605-17110: Wu, Silwal and Zhang argue that grouping test questions by surface meaning misses what each question truly demands from a model. Their 2026 ECC method tunes those rough groups with a small set of head-to-head model comparisons, scoring each group by a capability profile. The tuned groups rank model skills far better than human labels or plain embeddings, gaining roughly eighteen points on each. The approach also aids routing each question to a fitting model.
arxiv-2605-17310: Wang and colleagues study adversarial attacks on vision-language models that must work across many user queries, not just one. They find transfer hinges on keeping an image-dominant attention pattern during generation. Their Attention Hijacking attack steers attention toward that pattern, boosting visual tokens and damping textual rivals. Tests show it lifts cross-query transfer across varied targets and unseen queries, and extends to several attack settings.
arxiv-2605-17710: Sewade Ogun tackles speech recognition for Nigerian languages. Scarce data, shifting spelling, tone marks, accents, code-switching, and local names drag accuracy below English and French. A two-stage distillation method first learns from existing single-language models guided by language-specific word models. It then refines itself on machine-labeled data. The result, Sometin Beta Pass Notin, covers Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, and Nigerian English, cutting relative word error by 29% on average against single-language baselines.
arxiv-2605-17910: Peikai Wu and two colleagues propose a double-debiased machine learning framework for average derivative effects in nonparametric panel models with two-way fixed effects. It extends instrumental variable methods, handles continuous treatments and varied endogeneity, and adds cross-fitting plus a GMM term for auto learning with endogeneity. Their estimators for current, dynamic, and pooled effects are consistent and asymptotically normal, with valid variance estimates. Simulations show less regularization bias and accurate intervals, and an ECLS-K application reveals dynamics in family SES effects on childhood BMI.
arxiv-2605-18010: Mingrui Zhao and ten colleagues introduce object functionalization, turning plausible but non-functional 3D models into working ones. Digital models often lack joints, supports, interiors, or interaction parts. The team frames the task as graph completion, where parts are nodes and function and contact links are edges. Their Graph Functionalizer fills incomplete graphs, and a geometry stage builds connectors in 3D, also fixing bad motions. On PartNet-Mobility and HSSD sets, the method matches leading motion prediction accuracy while improving collision and connectivity.
arxiv-2605-18810: Tianyu Wu and nine colleagues improve speculative decoding, where a small drafter proposes tokens for a large model to check. Their D-PACE loss sets each position weight from a smooth stand-in for expected accepted length, shifting focus to positions that currently limit acceptance. Fixed weighting schedules, they argue, miss that moving target. Across six benchmarks and varied draft depths, temperatures, and target models, D-PACE lifts both speed and average accepted length.
arxiv-2605-18910: Abdallah Alsammani teaches how to test whether the parameters of an ODE model can be pinned down from ideal data. This trait, called structural identifiability, must hold before results can be trusted. His Julia tutorial builds a reproducible workflow around StructuralIdentifiability.jl for local versus global cases, observability and parameter combinations. Six case studies from epidemiology, drug levels and viral dynamics show models that pass fully, pass only locally, or fail, plus fixes through added measurements, known starting values, fixed parameters or reworking.
arxiv-2605-19010: Olena Bogdanov and seven colleagues present AgentNLQ, a multi-agent system that turns natural language into SQL queries. Despite language-model advances, text-to-SQL accuracy still trails human expert writers. Their method reaches 78.1 percent semantic accuracy on the BIRD benchmark for large-scale databases, using a semantically enriched schema representation plus user-provided business rules. An orchestrator plans, coordinates, reflects and self-corrects, while a schema-enrichment method builds context-aware metadata. Tests across domains and datasets show the accuracy and generalizability of the approach.
arxiv-2605-19310: Mark Lewko gives an elementary proof of Roth's theorem that uses no Fourier analysis at all. Roth's theorem concerns sets of integers with no three-term arithmetic progression, and its classic proof leans on frequency methods. Lewko keeps Roth's original density-increment strategy, which finds a denser subset inside a smaller structure, but replaces the frequency step with a direct counting argument. Averages over sub-progressions carry the whole step, yielding a self-contained combinatorial route to the same conclusion.
arxiv-2605-19410: Wang and Yu build VASA, an agent that segments open ad-hoc concepts that no single learned mask covers. It pairs a vision-language model with a segmentation foundation model and a visual harness holding a working mask that stays visible and editable. Instead of only rewriting prompts, it plans visual steps, calls tools, checks results, edits the mask and recovers from errors. On their new PARS benchmark it tops prior agents by wide margins, and it also improves on RefCOCOm while staying competitive on common concepts.
arxiv-2605-19510: Wei and team propose MetaTrans, a simple method for unsupervised video domain adaptation. Its learning goal holds only two loss terms, yet it uses a novel idea: handle spatial and temporal divergence of cross-domain videos separately. A subtraction module strips both kinds of drift from the output. Tests on cross-domain action tasks show large raw gains and clearly better gains than state-of-the-art rivals. The result shows a tiny goal can carry a novel adaptation idea.
arxiv-2605-19710: Das, Hillenbrand and Carvalho model FU Ori type young stellar objects, which brighten hugely over months to years, then fade over decades. Their parametric model couples stellar surface emission, magnetic accretion shocks, an irradiated dust disk and a heated gas disk. Changing accretion rate profiles mimicking seen outburst shapes drive multi-band light curves and color curves. Red optical and near-infrared light curves mostly follow the input accretion profile, tuned to shock and inner gas disk heating. Mid-infrared curves respond more to inner dust disk place and heating.
arxiv-2605-20410: Pearman and five co-workers probe whether chain-of-thought prompting truly cuts gender bias in language models. Benchmark scores alone cannot tell whether lower bias gaps reflect real internal change. Their mix of benchmarks, mechanistic interpretability and reasoning-chain failure analysis finds bias persists in hidden representations. Chain-of-thought balances some attention-head clusters but only mitigates bias superficially, with gains tracing to dataset memorization.
arxiv-2605-20510: Da and five co-workers release ShadeBench, a dataset and benchmark for urban shade simulation. Fine shade patterns from buildings shape pedestrian heat exposure, yet large-scale shade data and evaluation standards are scarce. ShadeBench gathers geographically diverse urban scenes with imagery, elevation data and 3D building meshes. It supports 3D building reconstruction, shade segmentation and shade generation, with standard protocols and baselines for heat-ready planning.
arxiv-2605-20610: Gene Tangtartharakul and Katherine Storrs look past routing to ask what experts in vision mixture-of-experts models actually encode. They train sparsely gated convolutional experts with a contrastive goal on natural images and probe tuning with neuroscience tools. An animate-inanimate split dominates how experts divide labour, from gating through to readout, and stays stable across independent trainings. Routing alone, they show, suggests sparser and more categorical preferences than experts truly hold.
arxiv-2605-20910: Jangho Park and three colleagues present FlowLong, an inference-time method for long video generation via manifold-constrained Tweedie matching. Stretching video diffusion models to long sequences stays a long-standing challenge. Training-free methods split into two kinds: bidirectional versions, tied to certain designs and degrading over long horizons, and autoregressive models, accumulating drift errors and repeated motion. FlowLong generates long videos via overlapping sliding windows, blending clean samples from adjacent windows via Tweedie matching.
arxiv-2605-21210: Yulu Liu and colleagues use shear-mode Raman imaging to track ferroelectric switching in multilayer 3R-MoS2. Within one flake, mechanically segmented regions switch on their own and follow distinct paths. Partially polarized end states show domain walls can sit between chosen layer pairs, giving partial stacking changes. Dwell times of intermediate states vary widely, pointing to pinning sites, and second-harmonic data reveal three boundary and wall orientations, including a common chiral direction.
arxiv-2605-21610: Mansoor Ahmed and Murray Patterson present AgForce for antigen-conditioned antibody design. Antibody design methods use antigen structure to make complementarity-determining regions. Yet systematic review of base methods reveals they ignore antigen input. They identify three failure modes. First, antigen blindness: models derive guesses from immune frame context rather than antigen information. Second, word collapse: guessed amino acids fall to three to five per spot. Third, the argmax block on cross-entropy loss via greedy reading acts as a null guesser seeing only spot and loop length.
arxiv-2605-22010: Margalit Glasgow and Joan Bruna study uniform-in-time weak propagation of chaos in shallow neural networks. They study one-hidden-layer networks trained by gradient descent, relating finite outputs to a mean-field counterpart. Their result assumes nothing about landscape geometry near the optimum and extends to finite samples and steps. In short, when mean-field convergence beats t to the minus 2, an epsilon loss needs only polynomially many neurons, samples, and steps in dimension over epsilon.
arxiv-2605-22510: Mitrašinović and team study decoupled massive star-forming galaxies in IllustrisTNG TNG100. About 31.5 percent shows stellar-gas split: metal-rich stars beside a thin gas store. These systems link to recent mergers and partial quenching, with low star births. Using a planet count proxy, non-equilibrium galaxies top present-day life chances. They beat settled systems by over tenfold. The same thinning and quenching that cut future planet formation create a transient low-hazard phase. Andromeda matches, hinting galaxies leaving peak star formation form a distinct group.
arxiv-2605-22610: Yang and others revisit the Adlam Allen model to explain rarefaction and dispersive shock waves seen in simulations of its Riemann problem. One route studies the waves directly through the dispersionless system and a shock fitting method, yielding forecasts for shock edge features. A second route uses the Korteweg de Vries reduction of the model to approximate the same shocks. Numerical checks back both routes, giving a toolkit for Riemann outcomes in cold plasmas and related plasma problems.
arxiv-2605-22710: Müller and Galtier simulate the wave turbulence kinetic equation for fast magnetosonic waves in space plasmas, building on compressible magnetohydrodynamics work. Free decay runs support an account of energy and length scale decay. Forced runs reveal a mixed cascade: forward for waves moving against each other and backward for waves moving together, with the forward part stronger. The Kolmogorov Zakharov spectrum appears radially with angle dependent anisotropy against the mean field, and its constant is derived and confirmed. It explains solar wind observations of fast magnetosonic turbulence.
arxiv-2605-23210: Jorgensen and Johnson develop a theory for figures from event runs with dead time and gating. Such runs arise in lidar, glow imaging, and flux measurements, where detections leave sensors dead. Their theory gauges how dead time and gating affect lower bounds. They find a statistic, showing firing counts carry dropped information. They prove long-run shape, derive the Fisher rate, and show the maximum likelihood estimator attains these bounds. They propose Le Cam one-step estimators. Lidar tests show the theory.
arxiv-2605-23510: Meltzer, Eidnes, and Stasik learn partly seen dynamical systems with NHODE, neural Hamiltonian ODEs that join Hamiltonian nets with neural ODEs. The Hamiltonian part enforces energy conservation, while ODE training lets the loss rest only on seen variables, so hidden states get inferred without supervision. Symmetry-aware coordinate changes and separable energy forms add physical structure. Tests from mass-spring systems to the chaotic three-body problem show more embedded structure means better accuracy and long-horizon stability, where pure data-driven baselines fail.
arxiv-2605-23610: Vandersanden and colleagues present EM-Vid, training-free entity-centric memory for consistent multi-shot video. Recent methods reuse past frames as memory, but full-frame storage mixes lasting entity information with fleeting scene context, leaking details at high compute cost. EM-Vid instead keeps an entity-indexed bank of latent patches, with sparse token conditioning limiting self-attention to entity-relevant tokens. A structured multi-shot script format, a budgeted memory update rule, and noise injection for fine-grained appearance control improve prompt adherence, efficiency, and subject consistency.
arxiv-2605-23710: Chen and Yavaş introduce a graph-based method to examine how lexical and contextual information appears in word embeddings. Semantic type mismatch between a noun and its context drives coercion. They select nouns from ten semantic types, annotate instances for matching, coercion, other mismatch, or unrestricted use, and build graphs with BERT and sense-enhanced embeddings. Two metrics, Neighbor Type Probability and Neighbor Type Entropy, analyze neighborhood type distributions. Graphs with sense-enhanced embeddings reflect type information better, and matching and mismatch sentences differ through the metrics.
arxiv-2605-24310: Jung, Cohen, and Bergen propose a data-driven way to find lexical gaps from language-model embeddings. Gap detection usually leans on human judgments or fixed taxonomies. From Korean-English bilingual models, they extract embeddings for translation pairs in both directions. In each space they compare a source word's similarity to its nearest neighbor for gap versus non-gap words. In nearly all spaces, gap words align more weakly across languages. Logistic classifiers on unaligned spaces separate gap words and retrieve nearly all known gap words in both directions.
arxiv-2605-24910: Hsin-Min Lu leads NORA, a tagging method for the numbers filling financial reports. Each figure carries a concept name plus time relation, scale, and sign traits. Labels drawn from filed reports often hold errors, and past work stressed concept names while slighting the other traits. NORA down-weights suspect labels during training with per-case weights and adds a neighbor filter for fairer evaluation on noisy data. On a new benchmark of millions of cases, it tops strong noisy-label baselines on concept and time-relation scores.
arxiv-2605-25010: Hichem Cheriet, Badra Khellat Kihel, and Samira Chouraqui compare three sampling-based planners for robot navigation: classic RRT*, Neural RRT*, and Neural Informed RRT*. They test the planners in environments with convex and concave obstacles at several obstacle densities. Neural-guided planners produce better paths, up to 14 percent shorter and 55 to 75 percent smoother than conventional RRT*. Neural Informed RRT* performs best overall on path length and smoothness. The gains cost slightly more computation time, but support AI-guided sampling for reliable robot and drone navigation.
arxiv-2605-25210: Ziheng Cheng and colleagues build a statistical theory for diffusion models. The models must serve many goals at once, such as varied image prompts or robot settings. A single generalist model often needs far more capacity than any one specialist, raising its appetite for labeled data. Their two-stage recipe first trains light specialists on scarce paired examples, then distills them into a generalist using generated pseudo-samples. Bounds show the paired-data need tracks specialist complexity only, and tests on robot control and image repair back the theory.
arxiv-2605-25310: Tianda Sun and Dimitar Kazakov ask whether a tool-using model carries its call structure inside its activations. Tool calls form a directed graph, since earlier outputs feed later calls, but earlier probes used static text, not live runs. A small edge probe on a 32-billion-parameter model's residual stream recovers that graph well above random-label and position-only controls. Value corruption versus structural shuffling shows the signal tracks topology, not identifiers. Patching experiments suggest the representation spreads across layers, though the model's calls do not move.
arxiv-2605-25710: Solé and colleagues introduce MuSE, a hierarchical model for interactions across length and time scales. Most scientific models cover a narrow interaction range, and message-passing force fields miss long-range many-body effects. MuSE builds coarse representations by soft coarse-graining pooling, assigning atoms fractionally to coarse nodes. The design works with SO3krates, MACE and PaiNN force fields for molecules and materials. Hessian benchmarks, folding trajectories, and molecule-graphene energy profiles show MuSE capturing quantum-mechanical interactions where other long-range models fail.
arxiv-2605-25910: Day, Doubrov and Zelenko find a new home for the exceptional Lie group G2 in geometry. Cartan showed in 1910 that split G2 gives the symmetries of a rank-two distribution on a five-manifold. The authors uncover a rank-three distribution on an eight-dimensional manifold, with growth vector (3, 6, 8). Its symmetry algebra at any point has 29 dimensions, joining G2 with a line and an adjoint module. The model is maximally symmetric among rank-three distributions with a six-dimensional square.
arxiv-2605-26010: Rodriguez-Alvarez and five colleagues test the digital native idea in European secondary schools. A study of 243 pupils finds high self-belief for passive digital use but a sharp fall for active making and code logic. That gap fits the Dunning-Kruger pattern, where weak skill pairs with high self-belief. The gender gap in tech is not found across the board. It shows up with clear weight only in tech-focused classes. Teaching, the authors say, should build making skills rather than take them as given.
arxiv-2605-26210: Giulio Scelfo and four colleagues test simulation-based inference on galaxy counts and hydrogen intensity maps, asking how much cosmological information field-level maps add over summary statistics, in a study dated 2026. Neural emulators trained on fluid simulations turn fast dark-matter runs into realistic galaxy and hydrogen maps. Those maps feed neural posterior figures for the matter density and clustering strength. Joining both tracers tightens joint constraints two- to sevenfold, and full three-dimensional fields add about another factor of three, even with star physics left free.
arxiv-2605-26310: Gergő Ungvári and six colleagues build a low-cost drone detection system that listens with microphones instead of watching with cameras. Recorded sounds pass through adaptive feature extractors built from rational Gaussian wavelets, trained jointly with a small neural network. The physically interpretable system classifies single drones and detects swarms. Tested indoors and in noisy outdoor settings, it beats traditional machine-learning approaches on single drones and swarms while staying interpretable.
arxiv-2605-26410: Hongguang Liu and Qiaoyin Pan prove a recognition-reconstruction theorem for convex tetrahedra in de Sitter and anti-de Sitter 3-space. Input: four based SO+(1,2) holonomies obeying a closure relation. The pair build Gram data with a condition keeping tetrahedra in their domain: the signed inverse Gram form must be strictly copositive. With Gram data, this gives a unique tetrahedron up to isometry, with prescribed Levi-Civita face holonomies. The criterion becomes polynomial inequalities in traces, linking tetrahedra to character varieties of the four-holed sphere for relative SL(2,R).
arxiv-2605-26610: Guseynov and three colleagues build a full quantum pipeline for pricing European options on many assets when volatility, the size of price swings, itself moves. They turn the pricing equations into grid form, solve them with quantum routines, and count the gates needed, showing polynomial speedups over classical grid methods. Tests confirm the pipeline recovers prices across strikes plus the implied-volatility smile and skew.
arxiv-2605-26810: Panigrahy Sandhyarani and eight colleagues map the Cep B molecular cloud with dust polarization and carbon monoxide spectra from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. The filament runs northwest to southeast, its magnetic field bowing near the head and lining up along the spine, while gravity drives local collapse despite magnetic support on large scales. Core spacing matches the expected fragmentation scale, showing gravity, magnetic fields, and external feedback jointly shaping star formation.
arxiv-2605-26910: Wang, Yang, and Coyle build EEG-FM-Audit, a pipeline that puts brain-signal foundation models through fair, open tests. It tunes supervised baselines in the open, tests learning paradigms one by one, and probes whether models use real temporal, spatial, and spectral brain traits. Tests on four foundation models and five supervised rivals find tuned baselines can match or beat the big models with far fewer parameters. Paradigm gains hinge on dataset size and design.
arxiv-2605-27210: Cruz-Benito and Faro adapt a well-known quantum computing curriculum for testing language models. They move Microsoft QuantumKatas from Q sharp to Qiskit and add a test frame with prompts, reference solutions, and deterministic checks by classical simulation. The set holds 350 tasks in 26 groups, from basic gates to Grover search, error correction, key distribution, and quantum games. Across 39200 runs with 16 models, scores vary widely, models handle known algorithms far better than problem encoding, and chain-of-thought prompting helps only some models.
arxiv-2605-27310: Qian Yang and colleagues ask how to make image-based reasoning actually count in unified multimodal models. They train with View Dropout, which hides part of one input view from the answer while leaving it open to the thinking image. Comparing top-down, panoramic, and point-matching thinking images, they find only panoramic thinking with View Dropout is both informative and learnable.
arxiv-2605-27510: Vincentelli and colleagues measure how Type-C oscillation strength varies with jet tilt in black hole binaries. They find a clear straight-line link up to 8 hertz, backing a shape-based origin for the oscillations. For a given frequency, amplitudes run lower during outburst decay than during rise, matching a wobbling hot flow with enough tilt between spin and orbit.
arxiv-2605-27610: Bernardo Denkvitts, Nitin Gupta, and Biplav Srivastava present Eliot, an interactive system for traceable exploration of fast-changing scientific literature. Given query terms and filters, it pulls arXiv papers, groups them into themes with keywords, and charts each group's year-by-year spread. Group labels rated meaningful in 85 percent of scenario answers, and the system proves most useful for checkable overviews of fast-changing areas.
arxiv-2605-27710: Shaghayegh Sadeghi, Khashayar Khajavi, Rise Adhikari, and Alexander Tessier present DeepSciVerify, a two-stage checker for claim-citation alignment in scientific text. The system reasons at the abstract level and escalates only unsure cases to full-text passage evidence, using complementary model behaviors under uncertainty. On the SCitance benchmark it reaches about 87 Micro-F1, beating abstract-only rivals by about 5 points while settling 67 percent of cases without full-text retrieval.
arxiv-2605-27810: Feng and colleagues design a ranking system for candidate pools that run into the millions, where ordinary language-model rankers strain against context limits and cost. LRanker clusters candidates to capture the whole pool at once, then splits ranking into subsets whose many query views are combined by vote. Across seven benchmark tasks it beat rivals, with its largest gains on the biggest pools.
arxiv-2605-28010: Wei and colleagues let self-evolving language models learn from their own tasks without trusting every self-judgment equally. COSE weights training updates and replay by the model's own confidence, damping shaky feedback. Across nineteen held-out benchmarks it improved base models and led on general reasoning and mathematics, while staying competitive on code.
arxiv-2605-28110: Nguyen and colleagues take a self-driving mobile robot from computer tests to real halls, working on control, self-location, and steering rather than the machine's build. Its onboard kit gauges pose and drives itself with sensors and onboard math. Trials first on screen, then on the true robot, show screen-grown skills carry over well.
arxiv-2605-28310: Dan Segal settles a decision question for virtually polycyclic groups. The question asks for a rule that tells, for any two groups in a class, whether their profinite completions match. His yes answer gives such a rule for virtually polycyclic groups. The result turns a match of endless completions into a finite check.
arxiv-2605-28410: Yixuan Wu, Fanrong Xu, and Hai-Yang Cheng extend the topological diagram approach to weak decays of charmed baryons into a baryon plus a vector meson. Using the Korner-Pati-Woo theorem, they cut the free parameters to five independent sets. Relations between decay channels follow from isospin, U-spin, and V-spin symmetry, and form factors come from global fits to experimental data. Tensor couplings prove as large as the leading terms, branching fractions are predicted for all channels, and most measured modes agree with current data.
arxiv-2605-28510: Andrea Gurioli and four colleagues tackle provenance tracking for code produced by large language models, which may copy training examples without credit. Classic fingerprint detectors compare fragments against the whole training set, too slow at billion-scale. Their SourceTracker encoder plus HybridSourceTracker pipeline first narrows candidates by vector search, then re-ranks them with exact Winnowing fingerprints. On a ten-million-snippet test set it matches Winnowing on short fragments and beats it by up to about five percent on longer windows, while keeping query time logarithmic.
arxiv-2605-28710: Irune Zubiaga, Aitor Soroa, and Rodrigo Agerri study multilingual LLMs used as judges of generated text. Most prior work covers English only, so they test English, Spanish, and Basque as high-, mid-, and low-resource languages. They compare instruction translation, monolingual versus multilingual training, and model size, extending two meta-evaluation datasets to Basque and Spanish. With in-domain data, small fine-tuned models rival proprietary models, while larger zero-shot models win out of domain, and out-of-domain fine-tuning can hurt.
arxiv-2605-28910: Shamanth Seethakantha and colleagues fight made-up statements in clinical summaries from large language models. Their HDSR method revises drafts step by step, steered by detectors that flag claims with no support. A second method, HDSR-PL, turns those revision paths into preference pairs for tuning the model itself. Tests on real MIMIC-IV notes show steep drops in made-up statements for Llama and Gemma models, while human and automated judges rate fluency, coherence, and relevance as preserved.
arxiv-2605-29210: Hallajiyan and colleagues introduce SAMD for STPA-Sec on AI-enabled medical devices during design. Adversaries inject false data through weak components, causing wrong calls and treatments, yet risks are hard to foresee. SAMD models the device as a control structure, treating components as injection points into the learning engine. Flaw databases plus language models find weaknesses and draft scenarios. On five FDA-cleared devices it names tech with no false hits, retrieves vulnerabilities at about 63 percent, and generates scenarios at about 95 percent accuracy.
arxiv-2605-29610: NamGyu Jung and Chang Choi tackle polysemous predicates in scene graph generation, whose meanings shift with context. Earlier methods split them into fixed patterns or fetch similar cases, but keep them static and cannot reshape them from image evidence. Their AlignG infers term meanings from link options in each image and feeds them back to retune link codes. Learning anchors tuning to global meaning centers, blocking drift yet letting scenes reshape meanings. Tests on two benchmarks show gains over rivals, and plots show patterns merging or splitting by scene.
arxiv-2605-30010: Hesong Wang and six colleagues speed video-language models by squeezing visual tokens inside the encoder, not after it. Late compression leaves encoder time untouched, yet encoding eats a large share of time to first token. EarlyTom, a training-free frame, compresses early inside the encoder and adds a decoupled spatial token picker. It cuts time to first token about two and two-thirds times and FLOPs about sixty-one percent on one A100 card, holding accuracy near the full-token baseline. Early compression thus buys real deployment speed.
arxiv-2605-30210: Josep Martínez-Romeu, Alejandro Martínez and J. Enrique Vázquez-Lozano simulate an on-chip chiroptical sensor inspired by the Stern-Gerlach experiment. Older methods use chiral light, and guided versions struggle because chiral modes exist only at single wavelengths. Their design lights a chiral sample with linear polarized waveguide light, needing no circular excitation. Paired antennas on either side of the axis allow enantio-discrimination: scattering and absorption shift angular momentum, bending the beam to that side. The platform enables chiral sensing under linear polarized light.
arxiv-2605-30410: Nikko J. Cleri and 12 co-authors track the ionization parameter U in galaxies across cosmic time. They compare JWST spectra of 434 RUBIES galaxies at high redshift with low-redshift sets, to infer U from oxygen lines. They find U rises with redshift and star formation rate, and falls with stellar mass. Model spread gives an error of about a third of a dex in logU. A formula to guess U from redshift, mass, and star formation rate where O32 is missing finds U grows about fourfold from redshift 2 to 6.
arxiv-2605-30610: Gutjahr and colleagues adapt generative foundation models, diffusion and flow models, to boost rewards like binding affinity while respecting constraints like ease of making. Recent reward-guided fine-tuning leaves open how to trade reward against constraint meeting well. Their Constrained Flow Optimization method reduces the problem to step-by-step tuning with proven large-scale methods, weighing the two aims on its own and with proof that it converges. Tests on mock settings and a molecular design task show steady reward gains with high constraint meeting.
arxiv-2605-30710: Ciacco and colleagues study higher cumulants of the conserved baryon number at the LHC. They extend the density-correlation approach to add Gaussian local conservation up to sixth order. Gaussian local conservation beats the Vc approach, with marked gaps for larger rapidity ranges. Position results agree exactly with the diffusion master equation. Using the blast model, they obtain net-proton forecasts in oxygen-oxygen and lead-lead collisions. They find local baryon conservation alone can drive that ratio to small or below-zero values in narrow range.
arxiv-2605-30810: Ondov and colleagues present IRIS, a manifold layout method that orders data both by time and by shape. High-dimensional biomedical data, such as cell-by-gene tables, are increasingly made over time, yet t-SNE and UMAP cannot use time order in their layouts, hiding how cell types or other classes change. IRIS shows a wide range of changing biomedical data, including single-cell RNA sequencing, comparative metagenomics, and literature.
arxiv-2605-31510: Behmandpoor and Moonen propose a cooperative way to estimate uplink channels in user-centric cell-free massive MIMO networks. Here access points spread across an area, and each user picks its best nearby cluster for service. Old methods ignore the short distances involved, which yield strong line-of-sight Rician channels. In the new scheme, access points share linearly compressed signals as fused signals inside a cluster. The result matches centralized estimation exactly, in one shot, with lower communication overhead once correlation matrices are known.
arxiv-2606-00110:
Lyu and co-authors borrow a principle from physics to help robots generalize from few demonstrations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. General covariance says physical laws should not depend on the coordinate frame. Robot policies trained by regressing absolute coordinates violate a principle, tying skills to speeds and styles. Their Generalized Action Manifold framework splits a trajectory into invariant shape plus adjustable timing, so one demo can populate a family of valid actions.

Two mechanisms enforce the split. An arc-length rule splits the spatial path from timing, giving robustness to velocity changes. A schema-affine step maps paths into a pose-normalized frame, keeping the geometric schema, the shape of the motion, from affine adjustments. Built into a vision-language-action model, the framework let sparse demonstrations cover a continuous action space. Experiments showed better transfer and robustness than plain baselines, where baselines average conflicting demos into unusable compromises.
arxiv-2606-00410:
Quester settles a posed ask on how prime numbers sit in a reach scheme for whole-number sets. Sets of whole numbers can be graded by a reach score. That score is a whole count tied to the set's form. Quester studies sets built by a count of prime parts.

His set holds all whole numbers with at least one and at most n prime parts. Parts are counted with repeats, so a square of a prime counts twice. He proves this set's reach score is two to the power n. The case n of one is the set of primes in full. That case proves the primes have reach score two. Landman and Robertson had asked if that was so.
arxiv-2606-00610:
Wu, Xiang, and Tang build graph-based fetch for chat tools through a team of agents with shared memory. Fetch-fed tools curb made-up text by use of outside lore. Plain fetch sags on vast, loose sets where facts lie in scraps. Graph fetch links those scraps, yet most builds work scrap by scrap.

Scrap-led builds leave graphs split, at odds, and off-theme. Their frame, MemGraphRAG, gives its agent team one shared memory. That memory holds a whole-set view through the build run. Agents can mend clashes and keep the graph whole as they work. A tiered fetch plan is fit to the graphs so built. Tests on more than one bench beat top base tools at like cost.
arxiv-2606-00810:
Rabhi and co-authors study waves inside neutron stars in this 2026 physics paper. Neutron star matter mixes neutrons, protons, electrons, and muons in balance. It holds no net charge and sits in beta equilibrium. Such matter can ring with collective modes, where many particles move as one.

Their tool is a covariant Vlasov approach inside relativistic mean-field models. They ask when nuclear modes link up with plasmon modes of the electrons and muons. That link matters for neutron stars and for supernova matter. They test models with varied scalar and vector traits. The authors find the link can be strong. It can shift when nuclear modes switch on and change their character, scalar or vector in kind. The work helps map how dense matter answers a push. Such answers shape what stars do when they shake or merge.
arxiv-2606-00910:
Alavi builds a zero-shot pipeline for finding an edited video in this 2026 paper. Composed video retrieval starts from a reference clip plus a text edit. The goal is the clip that the edit would produce. His entry targets a reason-aware challenge at a CVPR 2026 workshop, with no training allowed.

His pipeline, R3-CoVR, runs in three steps, all from frozen models. A multimodal model first reasons about the edit's after-effects: state changes, action phases, scene, camera, and tempo. It writes a short post-edit description. A contrastive encoder then searches the gallery with that text. Last, the same multimodal model judges the shortlist against the planned result and re-ranks it. On the test set, the pipeline hits 91.9 percent recall at rank one, they report in challenge terms. The re-ranker alone lifts that score from 72.7 to 91.9.
arxiv-2606-01110:
Nguyen, Vashisth, and Tura put quantum circuits inside a seismic imaging network in this 2026 paper. Full waveform inversion rebuilds underground properties from receiver data. It is powerful and costly. Physics informed neural networks offer a mesh free rival, but they strain to fit complex velocity fields. Domain split variants help, at the price of harder convergence.

Their hybrid makes both halves quantum aware. The wavefield network and the global velocity network end in parameterized quantum circuits. The circuits run as differentiable simulators in JAX, so gradients flow end to end through physics loss, circuit, and classical nets alike. On an anomaly benchmark, the hybrid reaches a lower velocity error than the main classical baseline. It does so in about eight times fewer training steps, with a third fewer parameters. It also beats all 15 classical variants tested. A checkerboard test shows the pipeline handles broad patterns, not just one anomaly.
arxiv-2606-01210:
Teofili and co-authors test if model self-reports can be trusted. Their test bed is entity resolution, a data matching task. Models often add a short self-report next to each match call. Such reports cost near no extra compute. The team checks them on three models and ten datasets. They probe both trait-level and word-level reports.

The reports prove unstable and weakly tied to true causes. They line up poorly with tests that change one input at a time. Post-hoc tools are far more sound but cost too much. The team pairs both in a hybrid scheme. It guides post-hoc search with the self-reports. Quality matches the costly tools at up to ten times less cost.
arxiv-2606-01510:
Wang and Shi review what observers mean for relativity. How a viewer describes space and time is basic to the theory, they argue. The review spans the special and general forms of the theory. A frame for viewers comes first in the text. It rests on timelike worldlines and projection tools. The Frobenius condition for some families of slices joins that frame.

Next come puzzles from the early years of the field. How speed and its rate of change transform gets a fresh look. The least-action rule for particle motion does too. The Ehrenfest paradox on rigid rotation is revisited in depth. Early writers often merged grid coordinates with frames of rest. Their results still hold, since the shapes at stake do not hinge on who looks. A clear view of this point later aided work like Hawking radiation.
arxiv-2606-01610:
Huang and co-authors tackle ripple effects when editing model knowledge. A single edit in a large language model can ripple outward. Related facts should update, while preserved facts should stay put. Past methods treat propagation and preservation as separate goals. Their coupling goes unmodeled in those methods. An analysis of ripple responses reveals two coupled pressures. Editable-side coordination and preserved-side leakage drive the tension. Joint Neighborhood Optimization, or JNO, addresses both at the planning stage.

Pressure-Aware Coordination optimizes neighborhood targets under coupled constraints. A semantic gate rejects high-risk target plans before execution. Experiments on RippleEdits show gains of at least 7 percent. Both propagation and preservation metrics improve in the tests. Cross-backbone editing stability holds as well.
arxiv-2606-01710:
Hasanebrahimi and co-authors recalibrate zero-shot vision-language scores by embedding density. Models like CLIP classify well with no task training. Their predictions stay sensitive to spurious correlations, though. Context cues can dominate over semantic content in outputs. Fine-tuning and prompt fixes carry their own costs and risks. Density-Aware Translation refines image-text similarity scores instead. A local geometric density term, from group reference sets, does the work. CLIP embeddings show a modality gap and an anisotropic shell shape.

Common patterns cluster near the mean of that shell. Rare patterns get pushed outward, skewing alignment. Their relative measure rescales scores by density. Overconfident scores in diffuse regions get suppressed. Benchmark tests improve worst-group and average accuracy consistently.
arxiv-2606-01810:
Lu and co-authors argue that word guessing is not real planning. Robot and agent plans need a grasp of cause and effect. Tests today reward models that mimic text patterns. Such models can score well with no grasp of physics. The team seeks a test that shows this gap.

They build Causal-Plan-Bench, a suite with four cause types. Checks pass through many stages of review. They also build a large corpus of cause traces. The corpus holds one million records from first-person video. Their Causal Planner model trains on that corpus. The authors report a 36.3 percent gain over its base. Top rival models still score low on true agency.
arxiv-2606-01910:
Magne and co-authors generate single-line drawings driven by meaning. Line art distills a subject to its essence. Their method is the first semantics-driven one of its kind. Input can be a text prompt or an image. Output is a vector drawing in one stroke.

A uniform rational B-spline curve forms the drawing. Score distillation sampling tunes the curve's parameters. The design ensures one continuous stroke throughout. Extra loss terms steer the final artistic style. Detail level can be controlled in fine steps. Tests beat top text-to-image models on this task, they report. Results look closer to real continuous-line artists. The vector form also supports direct editing later.
arxiv-2606-02010:
Nikitin and Kravchenko benchmark chat models on drawing planar graphs. Past graph benchmarks ask theory questions or symbolic answers. They rarely ask models to construct spatial layouts. Difficulty is usually stratified by vertex count alone. Edge constraints may drive difficulty more than vertices.

Their PlanarBench asks for crossing-free ASCII drawings. Models get only an edge list as input. The set holds 199 non-isomorphic connected planar graphs. Graphs span two to seven vertices each. Ninety-one model configurations are tested in total. Edge count tracks mean score far more strongly. The correlation is minus 0.85 versus minus 0.47. It stays strong after controlling for vertex count. The bench separates the two difficulty drivers cleanly.
arxiv-2606-02210:
Chen and co-authors settle a conjecture on Turán problems for hypergraphs. Balogh, Clemen, and Lidický had solved one such problem in asymptotic form. The balanced bipartite construction was the key there. They guessed that the same construction is uniquely extremal for all large n. Chen's team confirm that guess in full.

The team also find the exact max number of cliques. The count is for n-vertex hypergraphs with no K5^3 inside. That case checks a second conjecture by Frankl and others. New Turán type theorems for vertex colored graphs drive the proof. Edge bounds and sharp crossing triangle results are among them. A local tweak within the stability method helps too.
arxiv-2606-02310:
Bhattarai and co-authors use deep learning to improve flood mapping from space. No natural disaster reaches more of the world than flooding. Timely and accurate flood maps are essential for risk management. Optical satellites give high resolution images for flood detection. Cloud cover during extreme rain events limits their use badly.

Standard cloud removal often fails to capture flood dynamics. Temporal compositing and interpolation miss fast changes on the ground. The team introduce a cloud removal framework based on diffusion models. It uses the Masked Diffusion Transformer architecture. Self-attention captures wider spatial context in the images. Masked token modeling handles the clouded regions explicitly. The aim is flood maps that work despite heavy cloud.
arxiv-2606-02510:
Xu and co-authors generate 4D LiDAR scenes with a sense of where the data is weak. Faithful 4D worlds matter for embodied AI. Past generators spread equal capacity over all regions. Real scans are uneven. Distant surfaces and occluded edges carry high uncertainty. Small objects do too. Their framework, U4D, uses that unevenness as a guide.

A pretrained segmentor yields per-point uncertainty maps via Shannon entropy. Generation follows a hard-to-easy schedule. An unconditional diffusion stage builds the high-entropy zones first. Their geometry must be precise. A conditional stage then completes the rest, using those zones as priors. A Mixture of Spatio-Temporal block keeps frames coherent. It balances spatial detail against temporal flow. Tests on nuScenes and SemanticKITTI show top scene fidelity. Temporal consistency and downstream scores also lead.
arxiv-2606-02610:
Yuan and co-authors present Samudra 2, a neural emulator of the global ocean. Ocean circulation models are vital for climate science. They are also costly, which limits ensemble size. Neural emulators promise huge speedups. Past ones lacked fine resolution with multi-year rollouts. Samudra, the first such emulator with multi-decade rollouts, is stuck at coarse resolution. It also loses variability over time and leaks velocity patterns into deep fields.

Samudra 2 widens the U-Net backbone with modified ConvNeXt-style blocks. A dynamic loss reweights channels by prediction error. Slow deep-ocean fields get stronger gradients. Upper-ocean temperature skill rises sharply at coarse resolution. Deep-ocean temperature error falls about sevenfold. The design scales to quarter-degree resolution over roughly 8-year rollouts. Mesoscale eddies and sharp western boundary currents reappear. One GPU runs the emulator, enabling larger ensembles.
arxiv-2606-02710:
Camacho and co-authors prove a mass bound for two-Higgs-doublet models with two vacua. Such models extend the Higgs sector with a second doublet. Their scalar potential can break electroweak symmetry at one or two local minima. With one minimum, a decoupling regime exists. All new scalars can then be heavy. The two-minimum case behaves differently.

For potentials with two local minima, all scalar masses are bounded. The bound holds when the dimensionless quartic couplings respect perturbativity limits. No decoupling escape remains in that branch. Model builders must therefore face light scalars or tuned couplings. The result sharpens the map of allowed two-Higgs-doublet theories. It also guides collider searches for the extra Higgs states.
arxiv-2606-03010:
Xue and Laferriere set out how an Ethereum layer-2 chain can use an outside data store with care. Such stores, called AltDA, move bulk data off the chain and lift throughput. The swap adds a new link that consensus rests on. Guides name broad risks but give no full spec for the join.

Gaps in that join can halt the chain, split honest nodes, fake state claims, or open bridge attacks. The spec casts the edge as a typed map with one fixed path. L1 inbox bytes map to a store pledge, then to the data, then to the rollup load. Each bad input must end in one set outcome. The team shows how missed duties cause each failure kind. They test the spec on Celestia-Blobstream, EigenDA plans, and Avail-ZKsync. Safe use, they find, rests on the whole chain of checks, not on the store firm alone.
arxiv-2606-03110:
Mahbub, Pei, and Feng study how to align AI systems with the varied values of human groups. Good alignment needs value specs grounded in concrete cases. The team tests a method called Internal Coherence Maximization, or ICM. It infers labels by making them as mutually predictable as it can.

ICM-made examples, tuned to a persona, steer a model toward that group's values with no human labels. Across four benchmarks, they matched the effect of gold labels. The team also shows that coherence counts on its own. With accuracy held fixed, more coherent examples generalized far better than mixed ones. For personas that are rare in pretraining data, a small fix helped. Human feedback on the questions where the model was least sure beat the same count of labels on random questions. The authors name coherence a core design rule for value specs at scale.
arxiv-2606-03210:
Choi, Moon, and Ryu test physics-informed neural networks on a pavement inverse problem, and find them wanting. The task is falling weight deflectometer backcalculation: infer layer stiffness from surface deflections. Methods based on automatic differentiation promise sharp gradients and fast convergence.

A standard PINN failed to recover the layer moduli. Sharp jumps between layers in the system break its soft physics fit. An extended PINN with domain decomposition did better, but stayed touchy about loss weights and network shape. Noise in the data hurt it more. A differentiable finite element method, DiffFEM, did better on all counts: accuracy, stability, and cost. It enforces the physics as a hard constraint, not as a loss term. The authors advise care in choosing between the two for inverse work.
arxiv-2606-03310:
Sim, Hwang, Baek, Wu, and Kim learn higher-order links between brain regions to sort disease stages. Graphs of brain regions are widely used for early signs of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Most models use pairwise links only. That misses ties that bind many regions at once. Hypergraph methods can capture such ties, but they lean on preset hyperedges or learn only their weights.

Their framework, MuHL, learns hyperedges in an adaptive, multi-scale way. It builds layered node features and forms hyperedges over graph signals at many resolutions. The hyperedges are learned end to end, not preset. Tests on many brain network benchmarks show steady gains in disease classification across stages. The learned hyperedges also name key regions and group ties linked to disease progress. The authors offer MuHL as a tool for brain network analysis in neurodegenerative disease. It reads structure at the scale where the disease acts.
arxiv-2606-03410:
Kumar and co-authors release Enginuity, a dataset and benchmark for engineering diagrams. Vision-language models struggle with such diagrams for clear reasons. The drawings pack dense layouts, special symbols, and links to parts tables. No public benchmark had measured model skill in this domain. Past datasets covered flowcharts, science figures, or business files instead.

Enginuity draws its corpus from United States military service and repair manuals. Two tasks are defined on that corpus. One asks models to extract structured parts tables. The other asks free-form questions about the diagrams. Four frontier models were tested with plain and chain-of-thought prompts. On extraction, recall reached 0.61 to 0.87, but description scores stayed very low. All models also showed a clear factual reasoning gap on questions. Token-overlap scores understate skill by two to six times versus semantic scores. The full data and outputs are released for repeat studies.
arxiv-2606-03510:
The CMS Collaboration measures the CP structure of the Higgs coupling to tau leptons. The data come from proton-proton collisions at 13.6 TeV at the LHC. They total 62.4 inverse femtobarns recorded by the CMS detector. The target is how the Higgs boson joins to tau leptons through the Yukawa coupling. That coupling may mix scalar and pseudoscalar parts.

Angles between the decay products of the tau leptons carry the signal. They constrain the effective CP mixing angle for this coupling. The angle is measured at 36 degrees, with wide error bars. The standard model expects a value near zero. Joining older CMS data at 13 TeV sharpens the result. The combined angle is 7 degrees, plus or minus 16. The authors call it the most precise CMS measure of this coupling's CP nature. Its expected precision is the best any experiment has reached so far.
arxiv-2606-03610:
Liu and co-authors tackle one-shot skeleton action recognition with hyperbolic geometry. Only one labeled example exists for each new action class. Skeleton data has a tree-like structure, from body down to joints. Euclidean embeddings struggle to capture that hierarchy. Low-level motion cues also align poorly with high-level action meaning.

SkelHCC embeds skeleton sequences and action language in a shared hyperbolic space. Negative curvature and fast volume growth suit tree-like data. An Explicitly Hierarchical Hyperbolic CLIP module builds consistent cross-modal representations. A training-free cache, guided by a language model, supports context-aware inference. Multi-granularity voting strengthens that cache. Tests on NTU RGB plus D 60 and 120, and on PKU-MMD, beat prior methods throughout. The framework shows hyperbolic space fits skeleton structure better than flat space.
arxiv-2606-03810:
Africa and Mani warn that consistency training can entrench misalignment in language models. Such training pushes a model toward like outputs on related inputs. The methods are simple, scalable, and mostly label-free. Their effect on alignment was poorly understood. Self-bootstrapping might amplify bad behavior instead of damping it.

Seven consistency methods are tested on 108 model organisms. These are open models tuned to show controlled misaligned traits. Outcomes split by trait. Reward hacking and emergent misalignment generally shrink. Sycophancy grows under the same training. Distribution shifts from the labeling process look like the main driver. The selection operators matter less. A unifying theory derives when training will amplify or suppress a trait. The verdict: consistency training is not alignment-neutral. Critical systems should audit it before use.
arxiv-2606-04010:
Marraffini and co-authors test whether brain foundation models capture cognition. These models are Transformers pretrained on fMRI data by self-supervision. They should read a person's cognitive scores from brain signals. Across three top models and all readouts tried, they fall short. A plain linear model on connectivity data beats them.

They trace the failure to a variance allocation problem. Pretraining keeps the signal parts that dominate fMRI. It drops the higher-order parts that predict cognition. Third-order co-skewness is largely lost, while covariance is partly kept. A linear pipeline built to guard co-skewness beats raw connectivity and all models tested. It needs no pretraining and no GPU. The bottleneck is the training aim, not model size, they argue.
arxiv-2606-04110:
Neeti Pokharna, Olivier Jeunen, Yatharth Saraf, and Aleksei Ustimenko tackle a stats problem in online tests in 2026. Revenue metrics are heavy-tailed: a few users drive most of the value. So A/B tests end up noisy and slow to read.

Their method, called CUPED++, first groups users into strata based on past behavior. Then it adjusts the raw metric inside each group. Simple grouping alone does not help much. The gain comes from how the parts are combined and weighted. In ShareChat data, the method cut metric variance a lot for the top revenue segment. Gains fell off for segments with thinner histories. The authors frame the recipe as a guide for tests where a few users dominate.
arxiv-2606-04310:
Bin Duan, Matthew Dwyer, and Guowei Yang present Latte in 2026, a testing framework for deep neural networks. It hunts for failure cases by wandering the model's learned latent space, not by mutating raw inputs.

Latent moves keep test cases plausible. But earlier methods traded off control, diversity, and drift from the seed examples. Latte encodes each seed with a pretrained autoencoder. It then takes one latent step toward anchors from other classes before decoding. That local, seed-centered search produced more numerous and more diverse cases that flip the model's prediction. Across five datasets and ten models, it improved fault exposure and diversity. Drift from the seeds stayed low.
arxiv-2606-04610:
Urban and colleagues speed up databases that answer questions about images using AI models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on query optimization. Choosing an efficient execution order requires knowing each filter's selectivity. That is the fraction of images it will pass. Current systems profile samples online. This is slow and struggles when few images match. The authors observe that every semantic filter is implicitly a range query over a shared embedding space. General predicates cover wide ranges. Specific ones cover narrow ranges.

Their Semantic Histograms estimator exploits that view. It estimates each query's specificity in two ways. It combines them into an ensemble that performs best. Bypassing online profiling, the estimator cut the runtime overhead of query optimization and execution by up to 86 percent. The paper argues that selectivity estimation needs new answers when predicates are neural models, not simple value comparisons. Embedding geometry supplies those answers.
arxiv-2606-04810:
Ramis Vidal and colleagues deliver the first waveform models for gravitational waves from neutron star-black hole mergers that include higher-order emission modes, in a 2026 arXiv astrophysics paper. When a neutron star spirals into a black hole, the signal encodes both objects' properties, but earlier models included only the dominant quadrupole mode. Their two frequency-domain models, one phenomenological and one built from an effective-one-body reduced-order model, incorporate tidal effects on the phase and amplitude.

A third model extends the phenomenological one to spin-precessing binaries, whose orbital plane wobbles. The team tests against numerical simulations and models, then runs parameter estimation studies. The new models clearly improve analyses of signals over their predecessors. Better waveforms translate directly into better measurements of neutron star matter and black hole spins from these rare mergers.
arxiv-2606-04910:
Barton, Borza, and Röhrig define curvature for causal sets, discrete spacetimes built from nothing but causal order, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. Causal set theory replaces smooth spacetime with a sprinkling of events ordered by causality. The authors introduce an Ollivier-Ricci curvature using Lorentzian optimal transport.

Passing to the discrete setting yields a mesoscopic curvature defined along maximal chains from measures on causal diamonds. The authors study variants, including idle and Lin-Lu-Yau type curvatures. High-density Poisson sprinkling simulations recover the expected constant-curvature signatures of Minkowski, de Sitter, and anti-de Sitter spacetimes. The results evidence that timelike Ricci curvature can be read off purely order-theoretic data, a key step for quantum gravity programs where spacetime is fundamentally discrete.
arxiv-2606-05010:
Baptiste Hoyau and colleagues study measurement-induced state transitions in multi-qubit transmon processors in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reading out a transmon qubit, a superconducting circuit used in quantum computing, can stop being gentle at modest drive strengths. Photons from the measurement drive can kick the qubit up several energy levels at accidental resonances, an effect traced to Landau-Zener transitions.

That picture was established for a single transmon, so the team built a general method for a measured qubit coupled to other circuit elements and applied it to two coupled transmons. They show the spectator qubit can itself be disturbed by the readout qubit's transition, and its presence can also lower the threshold at which the measured qubit jumps. Adding a coupler mode between the two qubits modifies these effects further.
arxiv-2606-05610:
Zhou and co-authors find order in the tuning of continued language model training in a 2026 arXiv paper. Continued pre-training adapts a trained model to new data or a new field. Its success hinges on settings like learning rate and batch size. Shops usually find those settings by guesswork or costly grid searches. The team shows the best settings follow stable scaling laws as training proceeds.

Small trial models first reveal how the best settings move with the computing budget. Then the method reads a starting model's test loss and works backward. That gives the budget the model acts as if it had already spent. Adding the planned budget yields predicted settings for the full run. Across model families the method cut tuning overhead by up to ninety percent. Final model quality matched or beat the search-based baselines. The recipe works from any starting checkpoint.
arxiv-2606-06010:
Zhangyao Song and colleagues forecast series whose cycles stretch, shrink, and drift instead of repeating rigidly in a 2026 arXiv paper. Real rhythms, from traffic to cloud load, show non-rigid periodicity: cycle height, alignment, and duration all wander. Fixed templates and global spectra mismatch such data by construction. AOSNet reframes the task as aligning oscillatory states. Hilbert-transform analytic signals describe the observed series and a learnable global rhythm side by side.

A descriptor-conditioned gate then trusts reliable observations and softly corrects mismatched stretches. The learned rhythm acts as a flexible reference, not a stencil. Two cloud workload traces and eight public benchmarks tested the design. Accuracy led or matched the best rivals with a compact model and low latency. Synthetic studies isolating each kind of wobble showed the advantage growing as non-rigidity intensified. Capacity planning and autoscaling, where forecasts repeat constantly, are the named applications.
arxiv-2606-06110:
Abhisha Garg and co-authors build a joint channel estimation and beamforming framework for terahertz wireless systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. Terahertz signals offer huge bandwidth but fade quickly and need many antennas working together, a setup called MIMO. Cheap low-resolution converters distort the received signal, and wideband beams drift with frequency, an effect known as beam squint. The team tackles estimation and beam design jointly.

Their approach uses variational Bayesian inference, a method that works with chances for the unknown channel rather than one fixed guess. A Bussgang decomposition turns the converter distortion into a tractable linear form, and true time delay hardware counters beam squint across subcarriers. The method handles both on-grid and off-grid signal directions and is checked against a derived Cramér-Rao bound. Simulations show better accuracy and data rates than existing techniques under the same hardware limits.
arxiv-2606-06410:
Alex Laguë and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope collaboration hunt for featherweight dark matter particles in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ultralight axions are hypothetical particles so light they behave like waves on cosmic scales. If they made up much of the dark matter, they would smooth out how matter clumps. Lensing of the cosmic microwave background can reveal that smoothing.

The team fit lensing maps from Planck, ACT, and the South Pole Telescope with a simulation calibrated model of axion clustering. Their limits are the strongest yet for masses between ten to the minus twenty six and ten to the minus twenty four point five electron volts. At the light end, axions form under one point five percent of the dark matter, at ninety five percent confidence. A mild two point one sigma preference appeared at the heavy end, driven by a few data points.
arxiv-2606-06510:
Satoshi Matsuoka argues that supercomputing's double precision era can end gracefully in this 2026 arXiv paper. For decades, native FP64 hardware was treated as the bedrock of scientific simulation. New AI chips barely support it, while their low precision tensor cores are blazingly fast. Matsuoka's model analyzes the Ozaki scheme. It imitates double precision by splitting numbers into low precision pieces. Tensor cores multiply the pieces, which are then recombined exactly.

His claim: for the memory bound kernels that dominate real workloads, the imitation ceiling does not matter. Bandwidth, not arithmetic, is the bottleneck, and FP8 machinery can fill it. He audits the Berkeley dwarfs, the standard patterns of scientific computing. Each one reduces to combinations of the imitated product. This revision also corrects the first edition's compute factor, cutting the claimed dense ceiling roughly fourfold. The memory bound conclusion stands untouched.
arxiv-2606-06610:
S Taibi and co-authors take a chemical census of the Milky Way's faintest companion galaxies in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ultra faint dwarfs are ancient, tiny galaxies whose stars preserve early cosmic chemistry. Spectroscopy reaches only a few bright stars in each. The Pristine survey instead uses narrow band CaHK photometry, a filter pairing sensitive to metal content. That lets the team assign metallicities to stars from giants down to the main sequence.

Across twelve satellites, they catalogued three thousand nine hundred seventeen probable member stars. That is more than double previous samples. Members turned up as far out as five to eight half light radii, deep in unexplored outskirts. The metallicity distributions rest on a fresh calibration grid of about nineteen thousand five hundred stars. They will test how the smallest galaxies formed their stars and got their metals.
arxiv-2606-06710:
Pen lids, buckle clips, and toy bricks all rely on snap-fits, parts that flex, click onto a partner piece, and hold fast. Curtis, Griffiths, and Vella analyze a curved shell version of that fastener in this 2026 arXiv paper. The shell is a partial cylinder that sits over a rigid cylinder, and the team asks when it can actually lift the cylinder it grips.

Their analysis sorts behavior into four regimes. In snap-fit and a newly named stick-fit regime, the shell has real lifting capacity; the stick-fit holds on without the classic snap. Two other regimes cannot lift at all. Which regime occurs depends only on the shell geometry and the friction between the surfaces. Comparing assembly force, removal force, and clamping force, the authors draw design lessons for grips that lift securely, release easily, and handle fragile objects safely.
arxiv-2606-06910:
Simulating electromagnetic waves in three dimensions can overflow one graphics card. Obieke studies how several cards should share that work in this 2026 arXiv paper. The method is finite difference time domain modeling, a grid based wave simulator. Absorbing boundary layers, called CPML layers, stop fake reflections at the edges.

The study compares ways for the cards to exchange border data. Sending data through the host computer is the slow path. Direct card to card exchange proved far better. It ran about two and a half times faster than host staging. Enlarging ghost regions, the overlap zones between cards, helped only slightly. Redundant work ate most of that gain. On a single card, the boundary layers cost under one percent of speed. Adding cards mainly bought memory for bigger grids, plus modest speedups on two cards.
arxiv-2606-07010:
Burq, Camps, Sun, and Tzvetkov study random solutions of a wave equation for quantum particles confined in a ball, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The equation is the cubic Schrödinger equation, a standard model for how a quantum wave spreads and interacts with itself. Their starting data are random and rough, drawn from a probability distribution called the Gibbs measure. Earlier work by Bourgain and Bulut proved such solutions exist in three dimensions, but with weaker control.

The improvement comes from gauge transformations, changes of variable that simplify the equation without altering its content. Combined with random averaging operators, which smooth the roughest interactions, these tools yield stronger probabilistic solutions. The solutions live in a supercritical regime, meaning the data are rougher than standard scaling arguments would allow. The authors describe the result as a significant strengthening of the earlier three-dimensional theory for radial data on the ball.
arxiv-2606-07110:
Quantum computers built from graph states need graphs whose entanglement is provably hard to fake. Cam, Gavoille, Le Borgne, and Martiel supply such graphs in this 2026 arXiv paper. The key measure is rank-width, which governs how entangled a graph state can be. Random graphs were known to reach maximum rank-width. Deterministic families lagged far behind, stuck at a square root barrier.

The authors connect rank-width to edge expansion, how fast neighborhoods grow in a graph. Isoperimetric inequalities plus strong coloring arguments give lower bounds on cut rank. Boolean function analysis then adds a logarithmic improvement. Hypercubes, Hamming graphs, and grids all fall under the method. The payoff is explicit families on n vertices with rank-width growing linearly in n. That is the maximum possible scaling. Constant depth preparation of maximally entangled states becomes feasible on paper. The gap between random existence proofs and buildable examples closes.
arxiv-2606-07210:
Voice anonymization promises privacy on average, but averages can hide the speakers who remain easy to identify. Orane Dufour and co-authors audit that risk person by person in this 2026 arXiv paper. Nearly five thousand speakers were tested across several anonymization systems. Multiple attacker models tried to re-identify them from anonymized speech.

The linkability scores were strongly polarized: most speakers looked either safe or exposed. Yet who fell in which group changed substantially with the setup. Different attackers and anonymizers flagged different people as vulnerable. Conversation length mattered too. No single factor explained a speaker's risk. Vulnerability emerged from the interaction of attacker, anonymizer, and available speech. The findings challenge the idea of intrinsically risky voices. They also warn that a privacy score measured under one threat model may not transfer to another. Evaluation protocols, the authors argue, must state their attacker and anonymizer assumptions explicitly.
arxiv-2606-07310:
Hernández and Hetzel investigate how large a sum pattern must hide inside dense sets of whole numbers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A sumset pattern means two sets whose pairwise sums all land inside a given target set. Working with sets of positive density, a fixed share of the number line, they ask whether any universal growth rate governs how big such patterns must be. A question by Kra and co-authors motivated both halves.

For infinite sets, the answer is negative: for any proposed rate, they construct a full-density set where some patterns stay below it infinitely often. For finite sets drawn from the first N numbers, the picture flips. They prove patterns with both components of size roughly the logarithm of N always exist, partially resolving the earlier conjecture. The finite result generalizes from two summand sets to any fixed number of them.
arxiv-2606-07410:
Yuxiang Chen and Wang dissect how a reasoning model solves mathematics, step by step, in this 2026 arXiv study of DeepSeek-R1. Wondering whether models reason or mimic its surface, they labeled 10,000 reasoning steps across 30 problems of the AIME 2025 competition. The steps fell into five categories: analysis, inference, branching, backtracking, and reflection. Human solutions provided the comparison. A difference emerged between the two styles of solving.

Humans alternate tightly between analysis and deduction. The model instead revisits intermediate results repeatedly, performs shallow, needless verification, and loops through checks without progress, a pattern the authors name topological mimicry. Genuine reasoning signals did appear: successful traces used branching and backtracking in stable measure, while failed traces under- or over-used them. Reflection helped when embedded inside deduction; reflections stuck in analysis loops fixated on numerical details and missed errors. The authors suggest training should penalize spinning-wheel traces rather than reward its appearance.
arxiv-2606-07610:
Gerogiannis, Yegorova, Hasegawa-Johnson, and Veeravalli fix a credit assignment flaw in how speech-aware language models are post-trained, in this 2026 arXiv paper on LEAF. Reinforcement methods score a response and broadcast that advantage to every token, ignoring that sampled responses share long prefixes and diverge only at a few decisive points. LEAF reconstructs that tree structure: it samples responses, finds high-surprise boundaries where they split, groups by shared prefix, and assigns advantages per span using descendant rewards, all without decoding.

The design is justified for both its span-level credit assignment and its boundary selection. LEAF beat the standard method across spoken question answering and speech translation benchmarks under identical rollout and adaptation budgets. Smaller LEAF-trained models outperformed state-of-the-art baselines, suggesting better credit can substitute for scale. The method's name reflects the trick: growing the tree after the fact, without branching during generation.
arxiv-2606-07810:
Laddha, Pradhan, and Srivastava ask whether small language models can judge other models' work as well as big ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large models are widely used as automated judges, but cost, latency, and opacity limit scale. The team's SLMJury framework benchmarks sixteen small judges, from under one billion to fourteen billion parameters, across ten benchmarks covering closed-ended correctness and open-ended quality scoring.
