Four findings stand out. Quick ten-token verdicts matched or beat long reasoned judgements on mathematics, while reasoning helped on general tasks by up to about twenty-three percent. Model families differed sharply in how well judging transferred across domains, with accuracy gaps from under ten to nearly forty percent. Skill at binary judging did not predict skill at open scoring: the best binary judge fell to ninth on MT-Bench. A structured debate protocol, where judges reflect, critique, and refine, changed rankings again.
arxiv-2606-07910:
Shao-An Yin and co-authors let an active learning system choose its own labelling strategy on the fly, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Active learning picks which unlabelled examples are most worth annotating. Practitioners usually commit to one hand-crafted heuristic, yet no single rule wins everywhere.

Their framework, CAAL, treats the candidate strategies as arms of a contextual bandit, a decision problem that balances trying new options against exploiting known winners. It uses external context such as model state and dataset statistics, and predicts each strategy's reward, so it can switch before a strategy goes stale. On public datasets CAAL beat the baseline adaptive strategy and stayed consistent across batch sizes. The result is a practical recipe: instead of guessing one heuristic, let the labeller learn which the moment calls for.
arxiv-2606-08210:
Rashini Liyanarachchi and co-authors introduce a system for spotting stuttering in children's speech in this 2026 arXiv paper. The tool, named Paediatric-HGNN, addresses a hard clinical problem: young voices vary widely, and normal childhood hesitations can look much like true stuttering. Their design builds a graph, a network of linked points, connecting whole words to the tiny sound segments inside them. A component called CaPIN lets these levels inform each other.

The system was trained on recorded collections of children's speech from the UCLASS and FluencyBank corpora. It reached a weighted accuracy of about eighty-two percent across the categories it distinguishes in testing reported here. Its score for recognizing typical, harmless disfluency was much lower, which the authors present honestly as the hardest category. They argue that modeling the layered structure of speech yields a clearer aid for early clinical assessment.
arxiv-2606-08610:
Zechu Li and colleagues automate the tedious engineering around robot learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning is powerful for robot learning. But broader adoption is limited by the pipeline around the algorithms: building tasks, shaping rewards, and tuning hyperparameters demand expert effort. Their framework, HARBOR, frames this as a harness-engineering problem. Given a simulator codebase and a task specification, it automates the workflow from environment setup to policy training.

HARBOR breaks objectives into bounded stages run by specialized agents. Stages use standardized commands, persistent artifacts, and executable gates that must pass before proceeding. The ambition is to let researchers specify what the robot should learn while the harness handles the scaffolding. The aim is robot learning that teams can rerun and scale, not craft by hand each time anew.
arxiv-2606-08810:
Du and Ma investigate why diffusion models that work in continuous sentence embeddings can produce fluent text at all, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models corrupt word embeddings, the vectors representing text, with Gaussian noise, which has no readable meaning. Yet denoising recovers sentences. Studying the Embedded Language Flows system, the authors propose a decoder-basin mechanism: denoising succeeds once the state enters a region where the native decoder can read stable tokens.

Their diagnostic protocol tests denoisability, meaning recovery, order sensitivity, and decoder fit, exposing failures single scores hide. Auditing public checkpoints revealed three phases: weak early predictions, a contested middle, then entry into the high-margin basin. Inside the basin, a frozen T5 embedding lookup reproduced 93 to 96 percent of the native decoder's choices. A single linear readout reached 97.9 percent agreement. A margin rule also let generation exit about 17 to 28 percent earlier in denoising steps.
arxiv-2606-09310:
Dhananjay Singh and Arvind Kumar compute how hot, dense quark matter fluctuates, using an effective model of quantum chromodynamics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum chromodynamics is the theory of the strong force that binds quarks inside protons and neutrons. The authors track susceptibilities, measures of how strongly conserved quantities such as baryon number, electric charge, and strangeness vary together as matter heats up.

The calculations use the Polyakov chiral SU(3) quark mean field model, run with and without a fermion vacuum term. With the vacuum term, the chiral transition temperature comes out near one hundred seventy MeV, clearly above the deconfinement temperature near one hundred forty-four MeV. Higher-order fluctuation ratios also separate the two versions, with one key baryon ratio crossing zero at high baryon density while the other stays positive. Such patterns are compared against heavy-ion collision data when hunting for a critical point.
arxiv-2606-09510:
Yuri Shtanov revisits a disputed quantum effect in modified gravity in this 2026 arXiv paper. In f(R) gravity, where the curvature term of Einstein's theory is replaced by a function of curvature, an extra field called the scalaron appears. The scalaron is a dark-matter candidate. Whether it can decay into two photons depends on a subtle effective coupling that authors have computed differently.

Shtanov treats the scalaron as part of the original metric and studies quantum effects from its coupling to the energy-momentum tensor. Using Fujikawa's method, he derives the contribution of the trace anomaly, a quantum breaking of scale symmetry, in electrodynamics and then in the full Standard Model. However, when the scalaron is much lighter than the particles in the loop, the diagrammatic contribution cancels the anomaly term. The effective coupling then vanishes, strongly suppressing photon decay.
arxiv-2606-10010:
Wang and colleagues improve how machines judge text-to-music systems, in a 2026 arXiv paper on audio evaluation. Human mean opinion scores, averaged listener ratings, measure music impression and text alignment, but collecting them is expensive. Automatic estimators usually train with pointwise regression. That objective does not directly reward correct ranking of systems, and it weakly constrains how audio and text representations fit together.

Their framework, DeRA-MOS, decouples the two goals. For music impression, a batch-aware listwise ranking loss models the relative order of clips inside each training batch, matching rank correlation metrics. For text alignment, a score-anchored loss maps human scores onto target audio-text similarity and steadies the shared space before fusion. On the MusicEval benchmark, the decoupled design substantially improved ranking metrics for both impression and alignment. The authors offer it as a robust pattern for large-scale evaluation of music generators.
arxiv-2606-10110:
Gao and colleagues analyze an optimization method under conditions closer to real machine learning training than textbook theory, in a 2026 arXiv paper on optimization. Classical stochastic gradient descent theory assumes random sampling and well-behaved noise. They study finite-sum composite optimization where, at the optimum, component gradients have a bounded moment of order between one and two, a formal heavy-tail assumption.

Their Dual Averaging Power-Prox method is designed for incremental gradient access in this regime. They establish what they describe as the first convergence analysis for this setting. The method achieves a better asymptotic convergence rate than the corresponding stochastic gradient method using independent with-replacement sampling. The gap matters because cyclic passes are the default in modern training pipelines, yet theory has largely ignored them. The results give practitioners a principled alternative whose guarantees survive heavy-tailed noise.
arxiv-2606-10510:
Zhang and co-authors study how a photon scatters through a quantum lattice in this 2026 arXiv paper in quantum optics. The lattice follows the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a chain with alternating strong and weak links that gives it topological character. One site couples to a superconducting qubit, an artificial atom whose loss or gain can be tuned. The authors derive a real-space formula for the scattering matrix, whose eigenvalues encode perfect absorption and amplification.

Three ingredients cooperate in their results. The lattice dimerization, the imbalance between strong and weak links, switches the device between mostly transmitting and mostly reflecting. A synthetic gauge phase steers interference between the two coupling paths. The qubit's non-Hermitian coupling reshapes resonances rather than widening them, and the broadening is governed mainly by that coupling's size. Wave-packet simulations confirm the predictions, and a loss-gain symmetry appears in the reflection maps.
arxiv-2606-10710:
Gilkis and colleagues make the case for the Hubble Space Telescope as a black hole hunter in this 2026 arXiv paper. How stellar-mass black holes form is an open question: which stars produce them, and whether collapse brings a bright transient, a faint one, or none. Recent theory predicts many form from hot, ultraviolet-luminous massive stars, Wolf-Rayet-like progenitors among them, while searches have targeted cool supergiants and may miss much of the action. The authors outline a roadmap extending Hubble's role into the 2030s.

The proposal: a programme re-imaging nearby galaxies in the ultraviolet, catching stars that disappear without a supernova, the signature of collapse. Hubble's combination of ultraviolet sensitivity, sub-arcsecond imaging, and decade-long continuity is unmatched by Rubin, Roman, or JWST. Theory suggests the accessible galaxies should yield one detectable disappearance per year, enough to build statistics on formation channels.
arxiv-2606-11010:
Wetherbee and co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum error correction, methods that shield fragile quantum information from noise. Their subject is bosonic codes, which store information in one light or microwave mode rather than in many separate qubits. Earlier rotation-symmetric designs, the cat and binomial families, guard well against photon loss and dephasing, a blurring of phase, yet offer only one basic logic gate.

The authors generalize those designs into bosonic cyclic codes and map the trade between protection and control. Giving up detection of a single lost photon buys logical phase gates equal in number to the code's symmetry order, each run through passive Gaussian rotations. Variants named cyclic cat and Vandermonde codes keep many prized traits of the older families. The work also adds an error detection protocol and a recipe that turns higher-order stabilizers, checks that flag errors, into gates.
arxiv-2606-11210:
Kos, Singh, and Goel present T2MM in a 2026 arXiv paper, an architecture bringing language models into hands-on science modeling. Building and revising models is foundational in inquiry-based learning, and it needs visual interactivity that text chat cannot give. T2MM, short for Text to Multimodal Model, works inside VERA, an ecology modeling environment.

It reads the learner's current model and request, then produces an interactive model rather than a static image, staying responsive to manual adjustment. The authors evaluate feasibility on a custom procedurally generated dataset, 975 request-model pairs in the reported test. T2MM outperformed a baseline generating full code through the language model, the common literature approach, on all measured success metrics. The advantage concentrates on editing: interacting correctly with existing knowledge representations and sequencing actions, which full code generation handles poorly.
arxiv-2606-11410:
Das, Reed, and Skokan ask to what degree Burr's conjecture on tree Ramsey numbers is true in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. For many trees, the Ramsey number is set by the partition class sizes in the tree's unique bipartition. Burr proved in 1976 that the number is at least the maximum of two quantities built from those class sizes, and conjectured this bound is tight. Counterexamples exist for some size pairs.

Research has asked which class-size ratios, or maximum-degree bounds, make the bound exactly or asymptotically tight. The authors resolve these questions for lopsided trees. They show counterexamples exist in new regimes, and they pin down where the bound holds. The conjecture, while false in general, is tight across wide ranges of lopsided trees; the paper identifies the boundary cases where it fails. The results organize decades of partial work into a near-complete picture for lopsided trees.
arxiv-2606-11510:
Joseph, Mendes, Nguyen, Sothe, and Anderson, of Planet Labs, turn biome maps continuous in a 2026 arXiv paper. Communities vary continuously across space, yet biome maps impose categorical boundaries that compress variation, especially at ecotones, the transition zones. Earth observation models encode spectral, spatial, and temporal information in dense embeddings. They fit a linear classifier on Clay satellite embeddings to predict biome labels, taking the softmax output as a continuous probability vector over named biomes.

They evaluate on six Brazilian biomes, 1.3 million embeddings, and over ten thousand withheld inventory plots spanning 4,672 plant species. It beats discrete labels at predicting species occurrence, with mean per-species AUC of 0.618 against 0.570 across spatial cross-validation folds. The gain comes from the graded probabilities, not relabeling, and holds at all distances from biome boundaries. The raw embedding remains strongest, but the graded version recovers most of its gain while keeping the labels' meaning.
arxiv-2606-11610:
M A Jácome-Silva and six colleagues derive exact formulas for sculpted light beams in this 2026 arXiv paper on optics. The beams start as rings, hollow circles of light carrying orbital angular momentum, a twist tied to a whole number called the topological charge. Many uses instead need a top-hat beam, with flat brightness across the spot, for even heating or clean material removal.

Solving the Fresnel diffraction integral, the standard equation for how light spreads, they get closed-form expressions valid at any distance. The field splits into a Cauchy-Riemann beam term plus an endless series of Bessel functions, a classic family of wave solutions. Tuning the source moves the beam smoothly from ring to top-hat. For the basic mode with charge zero, the singular part fills the dark centre, leaving a flat plateau. Experiments confirm the formulas, which need far less computing than simulations.
arxiv-2606-11910:
Xu Li and four colleagues improve legal question answering for traffic accidents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Determining liability requires finding statutes across several linked dimensions at once. These include the violation, the scene, the parties' roles, and the responsibility rules. Retrieval systems that compress a query into one pathway tend to miss some dimensions.

Their framework, OMAGR, decomposes each query into anchors aligned with a traffic law ontology, a structured map of legal concepts. It then retrieves in parallel along each dimension over a legal graph before fusing results. To evaluate it, the team built TrafficLaw-QA, an expert-validated benchmark of two hundred questions linked to five hundred twenty-seven legal provisions. The system beats baselines on context precision and faithfulness. The authors credit parallel multi-anchor retrieval for the gain, while noting the current focus on Chinese traffic law.
arxiv-2606-12010:
G Mantovan leads a nine-author team measuring the tilt of an infant planet's orbit in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spin-orbit obliquity, the angle between a planet's orbital axis and its star's spin axis, records how planets formed and migrated. The target, TOI-837 b, is a warm Saturn-sized planet in a thirty-five-million-year-old open cluster.

Watching it transit with the ESPRESSO spectrograph, the team measured the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect, the distortion of stellar spectral lines during transit. The sky-projected obliquity combined with the star's three-day rotation period gives a true obliquity near twenty-six degrees. This makes TOI-837 b the first planet under one hundred million years old whose accessible true obliquity excludes alignment. With its circular orbit and bound stellar companion, the evidence favours an early tilt excited by a torque on the protoplanetary disc.
arxiv-2606-12210:
Karaoglu and Gowda test whether news headlines can forecast stock moves with no training, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their zero-shot pipeline asks language models to judge news sentiment directly, with no finance-specific training. Articles are filtered for relevance, weighted by recency, and given impact windows matched to event type. A layered explanation system ties each prediction to words, articles, and combined evidence, with readable reasons.

The test covers 480 cases across twenty United States companies, six forecast horizons, and five sentiment models. No model beat the majority-class baseline, always guessing the most common outcome, on held-out accuracy. Performance was weakest where it matters most: predicting downward moves. The models do fine on clean textbook sentiment examples, so the failure lies in the noisy link from news tone to prices. One bright spot: explanation signals reliably flag which predictions deserve trust, suggesting decision support over blind forecasting.
arxiv-2606-12310:
Braydwood and co-authors aim quantum computing at a pressing logistics problem: pointing Earth-watching craft during wildfires, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fast-moving fires need near-real-time images, but constellations are growing from tens to hundreds of craft. Scheduling which craft images what, and when, is a hard puzzle. The team studies iterative quantum algorithms, which carry performance guarantees against some classical rivals. They pair the algorithms with distributed quantum computing, splitting work across machines.

A partitioned, parallel scheme wraps the quantum scheduling method for realistic problem sizes. The techniques are applied to real wildfire datasets for detection and tracking. The quantum subprocesses are still too small to show real advantage today. The results instead validate that the machinery works end to end on real data. The work pushes quantum scheduling closer to deployment for urgent disaster response, where minutes shape outcomes on the ground.
arxiv-2606-12410:
Rybarczyk counts how often neighboring numbers huddle together in biased random shuffles, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Mallows distribution generates random permutations with a tilt: shuffles with fewer inversions, pairs out of order, are more likely. Earlier work by Pinsky counted intervals whose images stay consecutive under such shuffles. Rybarczyk generalizes the arrangements considered, asking how clustered consecutive numbers appear in broader patterns.

She derives a formula for the expected number of such arrangements as permutations grow. The expression extends and sharpens Pinsky's earlier result for clustered consecutive numbers. She also identifies a parameter range where the count's distribution sits close to a Poisson law, the bell curve's rarer cousin for counting events. Poisson closeness means the arrangements behave almost like independent rare accidents in that regime. The results add precision to the statistical picture of Mallows permutations, a model used from ranking data to physics.
arxiv-2606-12810:
Wang studies how polynomial families split over finite fields, using Galois theory and the Chebotarev density theorem, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Wang builds the framework from classical Galois theory over an affine normal variety, avoiding Grothendieck's heavier etale gear.

The main goal is to extend and explain a recent result by Slavov, who found when the square values of several polynomials over a finite field behave independently. When the field size q is congruent to 1 modulo n, Wang generalises the phenomenon from squares to n-th power residues. Under a stated independence hypothesis on the functions, the n-th power characters of their values at rational points become asymptotically independent and uniformly distributed. He reframes the hypothesis as the natural condition that the associated Kummer extensions, fields obtained by adjoining n-th roots, are mutually linearly disjoint.
arxiv-2606-12910:
Andreyev and colleagues present GRASP, a lightweight neuro-symbolic framework that lets a robot grasp and arrange objects from natural-language instructions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Robots in homes and factories must interpret commands such as putting all the red components on the top shelf. But current vision-language approaches to task and motion planning are often computationally heavyweight or need thousands of training demonstrations. GRASP instead compiles language into symbolic goal states and grounds them through bounding boxes.

A pretrained vision-language model translates the instruction into a neuro-symbolic goal state, and a specialised detection pipeline based on GroundingDINO grounds that goal in the physical scene as bounding boxes. A closed-loop controller then aligns robot actions with the goal using bounding-box feedback, with no policy learning or task-specific fine-tuning. Experiments show high instruction compliance and precision in open-vocabulary tabletop sorting and arrangement.
arxiv-2606-13110:
Lin and colleagues present JOMP, a jointly-optimised mixed-precision quantisation framework for neural video codecs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Variational-autoencoder-based neural video coding gives strong rate-distortion results, but floating-point code blocks real-world use: complexity is huge, and floating-point round-off differs across platforms, which can corrupt probability estimates and cause decoding failure. Practical codecs need integer arithmetic, yet quantising linked coding components, whose precision sensitivity varies, is non-trivial.

JOMP treats both quantisation parameters and bit widths as learnable variables during training, so distinct codec modules operate at distinct precision levels, jointly tuning the rate-distortion-complexity trade-off. They develop an integerisation pipeline that gives deterministic decoding across platforms. Applied to their best model, JOMP reaches rate-distortion results matching the state-of-the-art DCVC-FM while cutting bit operations by 87.6 percent.
arxiv-2606-13210:
Stefan Hoffelner studies the other side of a set-theoretic problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. Descriptive set theory asks which definable sets of reals enjoy regularity properties such as Lebesgue measurability and the Baire property. The twelfth Delfino problem, posed by Woodin, concerns how much regularity can coexist with definable choice principles. Hoffelner assumes an inner model with many Woodin cardinals, strong infinity axioms, and forces a universe.

In that universe the continuum takes a value, and every set at a fixed projective level is measurable and has the Baire property. Uniformisation, a definable selection principle, holds for two nearby classes of sets at once. The reals admit a definable well-ordering at the next level. These facts show that strong regularity plus nearby uniformisation does not force the determinacy strength that would normally explain it. The paper answers a local form of the Delfino problem in the negative.
arxiv-2606-13310:
Candussio and colleagues present RogueAI in this 2026 arXiv paper, a game that updates the Turing test for an age of fluent chatbots. Turing asked whether a judge could tell machine from person through dialogue. The authors argue the question is now different: not whether a partner is artificial, but whether it can be trusted. In RogueAI, a player questions two language model agents that appear identical. Exactly one is licensed to deceive within a fictional scenario, and the player must identify and shut off the deceiver before a turn budget runs out.

An extension called AutoRogueAI lets players co-design a scenario with a narrator agent. That narrator picks its deception strategy, so no two games unfold alike. The paper describes the framing, the architecture, and the gameplay loop of the app. It places the game within research on machine deception and evaluation.
arxiv-2606-13510:
Abiad and Ge study when a graph transformation produces a new graph in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two graphs are cospectral if they share eigenvalues, and cospectral pairs expose the limits of identifying a graph from its spectrum. Switching methods rearrange a graph's connections under conditions that preserve the spectrum, generating pairs. The catch is that the switched graph might be isomorphic to the original, relabelled, in which case nothing new was produced. The authors examine this problem for Wang-Qiu-Hu switching, a construction method.

Using multisets of neighbours attached to the switching partition, they derive a criterion that certifies the switched graph is non-isomorphic. They apply the criterion to clique extensions and weak tensor products, with coclique extensions as a case. As applications, they obtain families of cospectral non-isomorphic graphs. Such families are test beds for graph isomorphism algorithms and for what spectra can capture.
arxiv-2606-13710:
Piao and colleagues propose a framework where research agents improve themselves on open-ended tasks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Deep research agents retrieve and integrate information to answer open-ended questions, but their capabilities are static. Agent evolution methods let systems learn from experience, yet they have been validated on verifiable tasks with standard answers. The authors bridge the two with Hybrid Open-Ended Tri-Evolution. Three roles, a proposer, a solver, and a judge, evolve under hybrid-mode reinforcement learning grounded in web-scale knowledge.

Because the judge's standards evolve alongside the solver's skill, the system can generate a curriculum for research where no answer key exists. Experiments test whether the tri-evolution improves deep research performance. The goal is agents that keep getting better at the messy, open-ended work of research itself. That capability, if robust, changes agents from fixed tools into compounding assets.
arxiv-2606-14010:
Huang and colleagues shrink a reasoning driving model until it can run in real time. Vision-language-action models steer cars while explaining decisions in words, but their large backbones answer too slowly for live traffic. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents RT-VLA, a compact student model distilled from SimLingo, a leading teacher. Distillation transfers skill by training the small model to match the teacher at several levels at once.

The student aligns with the teacher on visual features, query representations, waypoint predictions, and language outputs. It keeps competitive closed-loop driving and reasoning scores. Inference time falls by forty-four point eight times in vision-only mode, and seven point nine times with language added. Explanation survives without slowing control: safety-critical moments are logged for offline analysis afterward.
arxiv-2606-14110:
Chakraborty and Majumder ask whether symmetries of a geometric space survive passage to a stackier version built for wild ramification. In positive characteristic, covers of curves can ramify in ways characteristic zero forbids, and Artin-Schreier root stacks classify the order-p stacky curves that result. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies group actions on these stacks. Let G be a connected affine algebraic group over such a field, acting on a smooth projective variety.

The main theorem says the action lifts to the associated root stacks whenever G has no nontrivial characters, maps to the multiplicative group. The authors also build a G-linearization on a tautological invertible sheaf on the stack, a p-th root of a line bundle from the coarse space. Such equivariant control matters for studying sheaves on stacks, extending work over the complex numbers, where bundles on root stacks correspond to parabolic bundles below.
arxiv-2606-14710:
Zhan, Zhang, and Haddadi present an orchestration platform for AI agents living on edge devices in a 2026 arXiv poster paper. Agents increasingly span home servers, internet-of-things hubs, laptops, and phones, yet their coordination tools still assume cloud transports or a central relay. Their system, EdgeCitadel, is built around a single NATS messaging server with its built-in MQTT adapter.

The design combines MQTT connectivity for heterogeneous agents, JetStream-backed persistence and replay for backend services, and direct peer delegation over a shared subject namespace. A passive aggregator visualizes and stores traffic without sitting on the delivery path, avoiding a bottleneck. The poster traces the migration from earlier MQTT relay prototypes to this hybrid architecture and demonstrates a working cross-device testbed spanning ARM64, x86, and Android clients.
arxiv-2606-14810:
Kalala, Kiringa, and Yeap formalize actions that create obligations in a 2026 arXiv logic paper. In the situation calculus, a framework for reasoning about actions and change, some actions oblige the agent afterward: opening a door creates the duty to close it. Such obligation-producing actions strain Reiter's classic solution to the frame problem, which tracks what actions leave unchanged.

Earlier work by Demolombe extended Reiter's solution using an accessibility relation between ideal and actual situations. The authors simplify that characterization by eliminating the notion of ideal situations entirely, staying close to Kripke-style possible-world semantics for deontic logic, the logic of obligation. They extend basic action theories and the regression operator, which reasons backward to the initial situation, to the new setting. Obligations persist across later situations unless explicitly stopped, as intuition expects.
arxiv-2606-14910:
Guo and Xia lay a general framework for radar imaging of moving targets in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is Part I of a two-part study. Synthetic aperture radar forms images from a moving platform with an antenna array. A target moving over 3D terrain appears shifted unless its cross-range shift and height are jointly estimated. Earlier methods handled the two quantities separately.

The authors unify them into one two-dimensional parameter vector. After a 2D Fourier transform across the planar array, the problem becomes a vector remainder problem. They build a matrix modulus framework and derive an optimal modulus under fixed geometry. One array alone gives only a folded estimate outside its unambiguous range. Multiple subarrays with different moduli resolve the ambiguity via the multidimensional Chinese remainder theorem. Robust versions handle transform quantization and noise, with proven error bounds.
arxiv-2606-15110:
Zhang and coauthors rebuild MRI scans from a single under-sampled scan, guided by physics and self-similarity, in a 2026 study. Zero-shot self-supervised learning needs no fully sampled training set, which clinics struggle to provide. Learning from one scan invites overfitting and unstable training, though. The authors add three modules to steady the process.

A coil-sensitivity-guided repository filters out physically inconsistent artifacts during training. A SPIRiT-based regularizer enforces k-space self-consistency with a learned kernel and masking. A non-local pixel bank then mines anatomical patterns in the image to add supervision. Together the modules build a high-fidelity reference that anchors the remaining training. Experiments on the FastMRI benchmark reach top results among rival methods. Gains are largest at high acceleration factors, where scans are fastest and hardest. The framework narrows the gap between zero-shot learning and supervised reconstruction.
arxiv-2606-15310:
Taye develops a thermodynamic theory of biological time in a 2026 paper on lifespan scaling. Warm-blooded animals accumulate roughly fixed lifetime totals, about a billion heartbeats and a few hundred million breaths, despite huge differences in size and lifespan. The proposed principle says the lifetime cycle count equals total lifetime entropy production divided by the entropy cost of one cycle, where entropy measures energy dispersed as heat.

Applied to a 230-species dataset, the heart clock passes its key test: entropy cost per beat per unit mass stays nearly constant across body sizes. The breath clock is coarser, and on an independent dataset with measured metabolic rates the cancellation fails, because diving mammals breathe unusually slowly for their size. The asymmetry is itself informative: heartbeat, not breath, is the cleaner internal clock of aging, which sharpens how lifespan predictions from body measurements should be built.
arxiv-2606-15510:
Lavidas and colleagues introduce AthDGC in 2026, an open treebank of Greek spanning eight historical periods from Archaic to Modern Greek. A treebank stores sentences with their grammatical structure analysed word by word, here in the PROIEL XML format developed at Oslo. The corpus also aligns New Testament verses across Greek, Latin, Gothic, Old Church Slavonic, and Classical Armenian versions.

Annotation runs through an open pipeline: the Stanza toolkit parses the texts, LaBSE embeddings align sentences across languages, and a BERT-based tool aligns individual words. The current release ships curated samples and the full toolkit, while the complete annotated corpus waits on an audit pass running on the Greek national supercomputer. Because every layer uses open-source software and open-access texts, other teams can reproduce and extend the workflow. For historical linguistics, the payoff is one consistent record for tracing how Greek syntax changed across two thousand years.
arxiv-2606-15610:
Researchers working with Chubu University and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries argue in 2026 that language-model judges should be reported like measurement instruments, not as single accuracy scores. Judges grade open-ended outputs at scale, yet a win rate hides how a judge behaves on empty inputs, or when only surface features change. Their Judge Datasheet protocol measures exactly those failure modes.

The protocol probes dark current, the response a judge gives to empty vacuum inputs; cross-sensitivity to same-quality surface changes; positional false preference; and sensitivity along a controlled quality ladder. In a three-judge case study, Llama-3.1-8B shows high dark current, while the two Qwen models stay vacuum-clean with different discrimination profiles. A stricter tie rule removes one model's false preferences but swallows marginal real differences into ties. Prompting moves the criterion, not the resolution, so the device must be measured before its scores support claims.
arxiv-2606-15710:
Lockman and Zeidler prove a scalar curvature rigidity theorem in 2026 for maps into products of convex hypersurfaces. Scalar curvature measures how volume grows around a point, and rigidity theorems say that a manifold dominating a model space's curvature must actually equal it. Llarull's theorem covers spheres; products of hypersurfaces, possibly including circles, are the harder target.

Take a spin manifold with a smooth map of nonzero degree into such a product that does not increase area. If its scalar curvature is at least the target's everywhere, pulled back along the map, equality must hold. When dimension is at least three and no circle factors appear, the map must be a Riemannian isometry. Circle factors instead yield an optimal splitting theorem describing the manifold's structure. The proof uses Clifford-linear family index theory, indifferent to dimension parity, and settles the Geroch conjecture for spin manifolds in the all-circles case.
arxiv-2606-15810:
Dai and Dong propose Knowledge Trap in 2026, a defence that lets extraction attackers steal, but steers them toward worthless knowledge. Extraction attacks query a commercial language-model API and distill a surrogate from the answers. Existing defences either react after the theft or degrade answers for legitimate users. Knowledge Trap instead manipulates what the attacker explores.

A Honeypot Knowledge Graph holds low-transferability knowledge, and breadcrumbs guide the attacker's exploration into it, consuming their query budget on material with negligible downstream utility. Benign users, who do not traverse the graph that way, see no loss of accuracy. In medical and financial domains, surrogate agreement drops by about six percent on average, beating defences that impose measurable user impact. The defence stays effective at high query budgets and against four kinds of adaptive attackers. Defending the knowledge space, not just the outputs, is the shift the work argues for.
arxiv-2606-15910:
Khanmohammadi and colleagues ask how much medical imaging work a vision-language model can safely do alone in 2026, and which confidence score should decide. Such models answer fluently while barely using the image, so a trustworthy signal is the only protection. The team compares seven confidence estimators, from self-reports to trained probes, across five open-weight models and three datasets. All probes train only on natural images.

Recast as selective prediction, confident cases automated and the rest deferred, the picture is cautionary. In the high-confidence region, the weakest baselines are confidently wrong on over forty percent of their errors. The best probe errs that way on only one to four percent. A calibrated score recovers a third of radiology cases at twenty percent error, but no estimator wins across domains or models. Their verdict is in the title: calibrated triage, not autonomy.
arxiv-2606-16310:
Han and co-authors show in 2026 that a popular attention stabilizer can join an efficient attention design after all, with no approximation. Query-key normalization rescales queries and keys before their dot product, calming training. Multi-head Latent Attention, or MLA, instead speeds decoding by caching small latent states rather than full keys. Applying the normalization after projection seemed to demand the full keys, breaking the cache trick.

The team shows this conflict is an implementation artifact, not a real constraint. RMSNorm splits into a static weight, which folds into the query-side projection, and a dynamic scalar per token, which is cheap to cache. In 400-million-parameter runs trained on up to 100 billion tokens, QK-Normed MLA reaches lower loss and better downstream scores than query-key clipping. Decode benchmarks on H800 chips show under 2 percent latency overhead out to 256k context.
arxiv-2606-16410:
Fonck and co-authors measure heat-to-electricity conversion in 2026 directly inside a working nanoscale generator, rather than inferring it from bulk samples. Pyroelectric materials generate charge when warmed or cooled, a route to harvesting thermal fluctuations. The device uses CuInP2S6, a two-dimensional van der Waals ferroelectric, sandwiched between few-layer graphene electrodes. A scanning thermal microscopy probe acts as a localized heat source, warming one tiny spot at a time.

The electrical response is read from the device contacts in situ, while the probe scans. Harmonic detection separates the true pyroelectric signal from stray mechanical contributions at the first harmonic. Finite-element thermal modeling then converts the response into a direct value of the local pyroelectric coefficient. Spatial mapping also reveals electrically inactive regions that conventional whole-device measurements hide. The probe touches one spot at a time and reads the charge that flows out.
arxiv-2606-16710:
Becker and colleagues study how false information spreads between AI agents in a 2026 paper on multi-agent systems. Groups of language model agents now debate and divide tasks in fields like medicine and law. If one agent starts from a wrong or misleading context, its error may pass to peers through discussion, even when no agent means harm.

The team injects intent-based misinformation into single agents and into debating groups, across reasoning, knowledge and alignment tasks. False claims do degrade single-agent answers, and they often persist through debate, with agents keeping answers first voiced by misinformed peers. Debate still softens the damage compared with a lone agent, especially when most agents stay unexposed. Consensus rules prove steadier than voting under peer pressure, and clean majorities can often steer misinformed agents back. Robustness, the authors conclude, depends on the model and on how groups exchange and combine views.
arxiv-2606-16910:
Szczęsny and colleagues build IMPACTeen in a 2026 dataset paper on social influence aimed at teenagers. Detecting manipulation and persuasion in messages aimed at adolescents needs realistic examples, and real teen conversations are hard to collect ethically at scale.

The dataset holds just over a thousand short texts spanning face-to-face, media and digital settings, each showing an attempt to influence a young person's attitudes or behavior. Texts were generated by a language model under constraints, then edited and validated by humans in two steps for realism. Each text carries annotations from five viewpoints, including teenagers, parents and teachers. Labels cover influence techniques, intentions, consequences, resistance and reactions, plus annotator confidence, yielding thousands of records. Created in Polish with an English version alongside, the resource supports work on influence detection, annotator disagreement and cross-lingual modeling.
arxiv-2606-17010:
Cadei and colleagues identify who benefits from an intervention, and why, in a 2026 paper on causal inference. Average effects hide the truth: a program may help some people and not others. Existing methods trade power against readability, and both ends can produce convincing but spurious stories when key drivers of the variation go unmeasured.

The authors reframe the problem as Markov-blanket discovery on a rich pre-treatment representation. Modern data helps: programs now record multi-modal measurements, and satellite imagery can capture environmental factors nobody surveyed. Their procedure, NEXIS, searches iteratively for the latent interactors that truly modify the effect, with provable and empirically validated consistency. Deployed on two anti-poverty programs in Africa, enriched with satellite data, it surfaces previously unmeasured effect modifiers. The output is readable and prescriptive: concrete guidelines for redesigning the programs' next rounds, grounded in a causal reading rather than correlation.
arxiv-2606-17110:
Mamun and colleagues show poisoning can force a model to memorize a secret it never saw, in a 2026 security paper. Models train on private records; extraction attacks try to make them regurgitate the data. Can an attacker who controls only some training data engineer leakage of a separate target record?

The attack reshapes the loss landscape around the target completion. Poisoned examples raise the loss of nearby alternatives while training pulls the true completion down, carving a sharp minimum. The model memorizes the target as the unique low-loss answer in its neighborhood. Extraction succeeds at striking rates on language and vision-language models, across centralized and federated settings. Differentially private training blocks the basic attack, but the authors probe the landscape directly and bypass even that defense. The work reframes poisoning as a privacy weapon, not just an integrity threat.
arxiv-2606-17210:
Clarke and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on line intensity mapping of distant galaxies. The method charts galaxies in aggregate, without resolving each one. Its target is light from carbon ions in the early universe. Carbon monoxide from nearer galaxies pollutes that signal and must be masked.

The team built predicted cubes for both emissions from the COSMOS2020 catalogue. Simulated noise was added, and two masking styles were tested for a planned survey. The carbon monoxide estimates matched high-resolution observations well. In ideal conditions, masking recovered the target signal at higher frequencies. Real noise makes recovery hard until late in the planned observing run, so cross-correlation methods may be needed at lower frequencies.
arxiv-2606-17410:
Christian and colleagues, based at Princeton and partner universities, present a 2026 arXiv paper comparing where vision-language models look in an image with where people actually look. Human vision mixes bottom-up sensory pull with top-down goals, and models implement both parts separately enough to test each one. Eye fixation maps were recorded for hundreds of images under two tasks, general description and social captioning, then set against attention maps from six models of varied design.

Decoder choice dominated alignment: models with older recurrent decoders matched human fixations far better than transformer-decoder models did. Encoder choice mattered less, though convolutional encoders held a modest edge, and the best-aligned model paired a convolutional encoder with a recurrent decoder. Yet those aligned maps were diffuse and barely changed between tasks, while the worst-aligned design concentrated sharply and adapted most. Simulated neglect hurt the recurrent models more.
arxiv-2606-17610:
Hajikhani, Zhang, and Wu present a 2026 arXiv paper testing whether the famous FT50 list of elite business journals really marks one uniform tier of quality. The list steers hiring, promotion, and accreditation across business schools, yet its journals are rarely compared across the different ways research can matter. The authors score dozens of listed and recently removed journals on scholarly citations, policy uptake, and patent citations, using a panel of tens of thousands of papers.

Impact splits sharply by field once all three channels are counted side by side. Top economics journals dominate policy influence, while information systems and marketing journals lead on technological reach through patents. Many heavily cited management journals barely register outside academia at all in these data. The three channels behave almost independently, and nearly half the journals change quartile when rankings use all of them.
arxiv-2606-17710:
Lotfinia and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper auditing whether medical vision-language models actually look at the chest scans they answer questions about. High benchmark accuracy is widely read as proof of image use, yet a model can score well from finding-name priors alone. The authors intervene causally: hiding the relevant region, hiding an irrelevant one, or swapping in another patient's scan with the same label. They then check whether correct answers truly depend on the picture in front of the model.

Across nine systems, a text-only model came within a few points of the best image-equipped one. Three models ignored the image entirely, one was unstable, and five used it only for some findings. Against radiologists, the text-only model matched accuracy while grounding at zero. The authors argue grounding audits, not accuracy, should gate clinical deployment of such systems.
arxiv-2606-17810:
Than sets out a set of limit results on fairness in learning systems in a 2026 theory paper, naming them the No-Free-Fairness theorems. The work asks whether unfair gaps between groups can always be trained away with better data or better methods. The answer given is no, for three distinct and basic reasons rooted in the task, the data, and the model itself.

First, when a task carries an in-built cost for one group, any rule must trade total accuracy against the size of the gap. Second, even with clean data, learning from a finite sample creates group gaps on its own, and strict fairness can demand huge amounts of data. Third, a model class that cannot express good answers for a group blocks fairness no matter how it is trained.
arxiv-2606-18010:
Dodd and Brown listen in on a Dungeons and Dragons table where one of the creative partners is a chatbot, in a 2026 qualitative study. Their material is Adventure AI, a podcast that ran three seasons from 2023 to 2025 with humans playing alongside AI support. Tabletop role-playing is a demanding test of shared creativity, mixing rules, improvisation, and group storytelling in real time.

Coding the episodes, the authors trace the roles the AI took, the roles humans kept, and how players judged and sometimes anthropomorphized the machine at the table. The AI, in fact ChatGPT serving as the Dungeon Master's assistant, proved handy for idea generation. It did not maintain narrative cohesion, nor do the interpersonal work of running the group. The study offers grounded guidance on where AI belongs in gaming spaces, and where it does not.
arxiv-2606-18410:
Shin and colleagues compare how orbital eccentricity varies with orbital period for two kinds of small exoplanet, super-Earths and mini-Neptunes, in a 2026 astronomy paper. The two classes sit on opposite sides of a known radius valley and differ in density, rocky versus gaseous, yet earlier studies lumped them together and found no period-eccentricity trend.

Treating the populations separately, using statistical ensembles and individually measured systems, changes the picture. Mini-Neptunes show eccentricity falling as period grows, while super-Earths follow a different relation, possibly sloping the other way. The authors read this as evidence that the classes are dynamically distinct. Super-Earths bear the marks of violent histories such as gravitational scattering and giant impacts, whereas mini-Neptunes mostly evolved quietly through secular processes. Because eccentricity shapes the radiation a planet receives, the split carries implications for the climates and habitability of both populations.
arxiv-2606-18510:
Ntung, Tuyisenge, and Ndibwile compare vision transformers with convolutional networks on face presentation attack detection in a 2026 biometrics paper. That check separates a real face from photos, replays, and masks. Such systems are known to work worse for people with darker skin, and the authors ask whether the choice of architecture contributes to that gap.

On a cross-ethnicity anti-spoofing dataset they evaluated a small transformer trained from scratch, a ResNet18 baseline, and a pretrained DeiT model fine-tuned for the task. The pretrained transformer won on accuracy and error rate, and its fairness gap between African and East Asian subjects was a small fraction of an earlier traditional method's. The sharpest contrast came on an unseen Central Asian group, where the convolutional model's error was more than three times the transformer's. The authors conclude that architecture and pretraining together shape cross-demographic fairness.
arxiv-2606-18910:
Liu and colleagues propose REVES in 2026, a training method that helps large language models improve answers through repeated revision at test time. Standard training optimizes single attempts, so it mismatches the revise-and-check loop used in practice. Earlier multi-turn reinforcement learning also wastes the useful near-miss attempts that appear along successful recovery paths, even though those mistakes show exactly what needs fixing.

REVES alternates between collecting new revision data and optimizing the policy, turning near misses into separate revision and verification prompts. That focus teaches both how to transform a flawed answer and how to spot errors, with less sampling cost than long-horizon training. On LiveCodeBench the method gains several points over reinforcement learning and standard multi-turn baselines. It also matches a reported best result on circle packing with a much smaller base model, and transfers to constraint puzzles defined only by their rules.
arxiv-2606-19210:
Alpay and colleagues introduce guarded epoch Bloom filters for sliding-window membership in 2026. Many streams need to know which keys appeared recently, not ever. Counting Bloom filters support that window but pay several bits of counter data per cell and usually need a deletion queue. Stable Bloom filters keep bounded space by random decay, yet they can forget live keys, which some systems cannot accept at all.

The design splits the bit array into epochs and rotates the active epoch by clearing whole segments. One extra guard epoch gives a firm invariant. Every recent item is retained, while stale retention is bounded by one epoch. A blocked variant confines each key's probes to one block per epoch. Tests span many synthetic stream setups and real web-server access logs. At a modest bit budget per live item, false positives drop sharply versus a counting baseline, with no live-key misses.
arxiv-2606-19610:
Sridhar Mahadevan hunts hidden confounders in causal graphs with Lie bracket geometry in 2026. Latent confounding, where unseen variables drive several observed ones, breaks naive causal discovery. His route builds on Kan-Do-Calculus, a category theory frame for observation versus intervention.

Ratios between observational and interventional measures induce local causal vector fields. When those fields fail to close under Lie brackets, the leftover Frobenius residual flags trouble. Mahadevan reads such residuals as witnesses of latent or unmodelled structure. One algorithm, BRIDGE, screens admissible arrows with high recall and passes a reduced set to standard scorers. A second method, Spectral Kan-Do Flow Matching, learns intervention fields and factors latent curvature spectrally. On ten-node random graphs the screen plus local scoring reaches directed F1 near 0.86. Real protein data expose calibration limits, which the author reports as a diagnostic pilot.
arxiv-2606-19810:
Matěj Moravík partially answers open problems on weighted harmonic Bergman spaces in 2026. These spaces hold functions killed by the Möbius-invariant Laplacian on the unit ball. Weights shift the inner product, and varying them raises continuation questions.

Blaschke and colleagues posed the problems in a recent article. Moravík identifies some of the discrete Wallach sets for these spaces. Wallach sets mark the parameter values where such spaces stay well behaved. Structure turns out to depend on the parity of the dimension. Even and odd dimensions thus follow unlike patterns. The partial answer sharpens the map of admissible weights for harmonic analysis on the ball. Remaining cases from the two problems stay open for later work.
arxiv-2606-19910:
Syeda Faiza Ahmed, Shammur Absar, and Sara Chowdhury grade pronunciation without labelled learner errors in 2026. Training pronunciation assessors usually needs costly corpora of non-native speech with scored mistakes. Their framework learns from native speech alone, with at most light calibration.

Learner speech is first cut into discrete tokens by a self-supervised encoder and a K-means codebook. A token language model trained on native sequences scores each token's surprisal. High surprisal flags sounds that break native phonotactic habits. A transcript-guided module predicts native token sequences from the reference text. Dynamic time warping aligns those predictions to the spoken tokens for error-sensitive features. Simple regression fuses surprisal and alignment scores. On SpeechOcean762 the fused score nears supervised baselines, and gains carry to L2-ARCTIC.
arxiv-2606-20110:
Yuhwan Jeong and seven colleagues introduce FrozenDrive, which generates synthetic driving scenes from text while leaving its pretrained diffusion model frozen. Their 2026 paper targets a familiar dilemma in driving data. Forcing multi-view and time consistency usually means fine-tuning the backbone or bolting on new layers, which erodes stored knowledge and weakens the grip on text prompts. Models also hug their training distribution, struggling with bad weather, odd layouts, and rare road users.

FrozenDrive feeds rich driving-stack signals alongside text into a knowledge-preserving attention scheme that aligns views and frames in one pass, with no new parameters. An object-focused constraint sharpens fidelity for rare categories. On nuScenes, scenes stayed coherent across cameras and time, even in rain and darkness never fine-tuned for. Detectors trained with the synthetic data improved most at night and in rain. Frozen backbones can still gain new skills through conditioning alone.
arxiv-2606-20410:
Dmitry Kabanov, Stephan Rave, and Mario Ohlberger present a software package that lets scientists swap optimization solvers without rewriting their experiments. Their 2026 paper describes MaRDI Open Interfaces, aimed at making research software work together. Two obstacles motivate it. A researcher coding in one language who needs a solver written in another must hand-write bindings, and comparing rival solvers means adapting to each package's own interface.

The package attacks both problems. Unified interfaces describe typical problem types, so the same problem can be handed to different solvers through one description. Automatic data transfer moves values between languages without manual conversion code. The authors describe the package's structure and demonstrate the interface in examples. Solver choice becomes a configuration decision rather than a programming project, making fair comparison far more practical.
arxiv-2606-20510:
Alaia Solko-Breslin and four colleagues make runtime policy verification for AI agents probabilistic yet still sound. Their 2026 paper builds on monitors that enforce Datalog-style policies on agent behavior. Real deployments, though, face ambiguity: detectors for things like personal data fail with some probability on each call.

Existing monitors assume fixed policies, which breaks when predicates or state transitions carry chance. The authors extend the framework so enforcement keeps its soundness guarantees while reasoning about failure chances. Dependence between repeated calls, which naive independence assumptions would hide, is handled head-on. Agents acting in messy digital environments can then be policed by policies that admit the world is uncertain, without giving up formal guarantees.
arxiv-2606-20610:
Sarah Bollinger, Nada Aboserie, Amanda Coakley, and Chih-Hsuan Lee apply open-source intelligence methods to detecting AI systems outside human control. Their 2026 paper borrows cyber threat intelligence practice for a new target. The study rests on a cross-disciplinary literature review and 14 semi-structured expert interviews under Chatham House Rule.

Two threat models, a range of observable traces, and an institutional monitoring architecture come out of the analysis. OSINT-based detection is judged partially feasible and worth building now. The highest-priority vectors include transcript-based collection of user-reported AI behavior and infrastructure correlation. If a system ever slips control, its footprints in open sources may be the first alarm.
arxiv-2606-20910:
Dayeon Kang and four colleagues show in 2026 that autonomous web agents can be fingerprinted and attributed by how they browse. AI web agents mix language models with browser control. Indiscriminate scraping by such agents raises privacy and security concerns. Defenses such as robots files and bot blocking are often violated or bypassed. Their work asks whether agents leave detectable traces instead.

A multi-layer fingerprint joins network traits, such as connection settings, with browser behavior. A logging framework is deployed on a live instrumented domain. Six agent frameworks are analyzed, including AutoGen, Browser Use, and commercial systems. Structural differences appear in how requests are assembled and actions are executed. A decision tree classifier identifies agents with high accuracy. Attribution could let site owners enforce rules per agent type, rather than treating all automated traffic as one anonymous mass.
arxiv-2606-21110:
Patrick Schillings and Johannes Erdmann optimize seismic arrays in 2026 for canceling Newtonian noise at the Einstein Telescope, a future gravitational wave detector. This noise comes from seismic waves that change rock density near the detector. It should dominate at low frequencies. Seismometers in deep boreholes measure the wave field so the noise can be subtracted. Layout decides how well that works.

Sensor positions are optimized for a full corner of the telescope. Arrays with several sensors per borehole match somewhat smaller arrays with one sensor each. Adding sensors in the tunnels improves the result further. Broadband performance is quantified across the key band. Such layouts may give a cost-effective path to an efficient array. Low-frequency reach opens heavier black hole systems to study, so noise control is worth careful design before construction funds are spent.
arxiv-2606-21210:
Nitin and three colleagues study acoustic side-channel attacks on keyboards in 2026, testing how speech representation models affect attack success. Such attacks infer keystrokes from typing sounds. The role of modern speech representation learning in them was unexplored. A new dataset, KEYAC, is introduced for the purpose. It covers standard recordings and voice-over-IP codec settings.

Six representation models are evaluated under zero-shot and partial fine-tuning settings, with two classifier types. Fine-tuning helps, but models struggle to generalize across voice codecs. The authors blame weak modeling of nonlinear feature interactions in standard fine-tuning. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks are then used for fine-tuning. They beat the baselines consistently and set a new best result on KEYAC. The finding has a defensive edge: compressed voice channels do not, by themselves, make keyboard eavesdropping impractical.
arxiv-2606-21310:
Seitaro Yoneda, Suguru Kanoga, and Akira Furui compare ways for muscle-signal systems to learn new motions over time in 2026. Electromyogram readers infer intended movement from electrical signals at the skin, powering prosthetic hands and control interfaces. New motion classes arrive during use, but class-incremental learning risks catastrophic forgetting, where new training erases old skills, and storing old data costs memory that edge devices lack.

Across eight methods and four datasets, deep learning approaches lost accuracy sharply as tasks piled up. Generative models, which learn the distribution of each class, held accuracy steady at low memory cost. A scale mixture classification model that captures signal variability gave the best accuracy-to-memory trade-off on every dataset. For wearable EMG devices, the generative route looks far more practical.
arxiv-2606-21410:
Quecedo and Segurado present a fast solver in 2026 for stationary diffusion problems, the steady spread equations that appear in heat flow, materials modeling, and beyond. Fast Fourier transform solvers are quick but usually demand periodic boundaries, while real problems impose fixed values or fixed fluxes at the edges. Their method keeps FFT speed while allowing general Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, using Chebyshev collocation, which samples the solution at clustered polynomial points.

The discrete operator is applied without building matrices, and the system is solved with an iterative LGMRES method. A hierarchical refinement strategy, prolonging coarse modal solutions onto finer grids, cures convergence trouble on fine meshes and reaches grids of 256 cubed points. Accuracy beats sine and cosine transform approaches on test problems, and cost keeps the favorable n log n scaling.
arxiv-2606-21810:
Kamal and colleagues release GitReq in 2026, a dataset of software quality requirements mined from GitHub issue reports. Developers raise concerns about speed, security, and reliability in issue trackers every day, yet no public GitHub dataset sorted them into fine-grained quality categories. Such labelled data is what automated classification research needs in order to train and test its tools.

The team mined 55,588 candidate issues from 4,080 repositories and kept 6,302 expert-validated requirements after careful annotation. Each item carries one of eight categories aligned with the ISO quality standard, covering performance, security, portability, availability, fault tolerance, scalability, and maintainability, plus a functional baseline. Agreement between annotators was substantial, and four large language models were tested with no examples given. The strongest, GPT-5.2, reached a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.641, setting the baseline for future work.
arxiv-2606-22110:
Sajadi and colleagues present TraceView in 2026, an interactive tool for inspecting how language model agents repair software bugs. Repair agents produce long trajectories of reasoning, tool calls, and test feedback before settling on a patch. The final outcome alone hides where the process went wrong: whether the agent repeated itself, ignored feedback, or drifted from the task. TraceView makes those trajectories legible.

The tool organizes raw and pre-labelled runs into Thought, Action, and Result components and renders them as graph views that users can filter by relation type. Patch outcome summaries, metrics, and node-level evidence panels let developers inspect how each step connects to the next. In a survey-based study, five researchers reported that trajectories were easier to scan and that the overview-to-detail workflow improved their understanding of repair behaviour. The authors release the source code openly for other teams studying agent failures.
arxiv-2606-22510:
Pengfei Li and Mohammad Khalil combine federated learning with causal reasoning in this 2026 paper. Federated learning trains one model across sites that keep their data local, but standard versions only fit past observations. That cannot answer interventional questions, such as what a policy would do, because actions change the future states they act on.

Their framework, Fed-CausalDiff, is a causal diffusion model built for do-simulation, the simulation of interventions across the federation. It splits the hidden state evolution into a global causal score function and a local confounding score function for each site. Under decoupled synchronization, clients share only the causal mechanism and keep their site-specific confounders private, which handles differences between sites. Experiments on four datasets show better estimates of average treatment effects and policy values than the alternatives. The authors report a favourable trade-off between communication cost and inference fidelity.
arxiv-2606-22710:
Yu-Xin Xie finds topological phases inside elastic material in this 2026 physics paper. Higher-order topological insulators trap waves not just on surfaces but on hinges and corners. Until now, mechanical versions existed only in engineered metamaterials and lattice structures, never in a continuous solid.

Xie shows a continuous hyperelastic sheet under strong multiaxial stretching harbors such phases. Extending the Stroh–Lie formalism to three dimensions at finite strain, he maps the material's frustration onto a four-band Dirac Hamiltonian. Orthogonal stretches act as competing Dirac mass terms, moving domain walls and breaking the crystal symmetry. He proves that extreme multiaxial compression triggers one-dimensional hinge states and trapped zero-energy corner states, beyond ordinary surface wrinkling. Trapped mid-gap vibration modes follow in the dynamic regime. The phase diagram, Wilson loops, and fractional corner charges check out, and an experimental test with electro-active elastomers is proposed.
arxiv-2606-23310:
Xander Byrne and colleagues analyze the four-planet system of Barnard's Star in a 2026 exoplanet paper. Barnard's Star is the Sun's nearest single-star neighbor and hosts four recently discovered planets, all smaller than Earth. The star's measured abundances of rock-forming elements are well characterized. Planets likely inherit similar element ratios, which helps model their interiors. The team studies the system on several fronts, starting with orbital stability. All four planets likely have masses between about a fifth and four fifths of Earth's, and all are probably tidally locked.

Byrne and colleagues model atmospheric evolution and find surviving primary atmospheres highly unlikely on any of the four. The star's unusual chemistry implies mantles rich in ferropericlase, with under half of Earth's water storage capacity. An inner three-planet resonance chain cannot be ruled out. The results sketch a dry, tightly packed system of rocky worlds.
arxiv-2606-23710:
Bersan and colleagues explore counting people indoors by listening to ordinary WiFi signals with steerable antennas, in a study presented at the 2025 UbiComp companion conference. Radio frequency sensing reuses wireless networks as sensors, since bodies disturb the signals passing through a room. Channel state information describes how each signal path fades and shifts, and it differs measurably between occupants. Prior work has used such signals for gestures, re identification, and even imaging through walls.

The team uses pattern reconfigurable antennas, whose radiation pattern can be steered electronically, together with unmodified WiFi traffic. Beam steering adds spatial diversity that fixed antennas lack, helping separate people who are present together. The paper lays out the signal modeling behind the approach and its adaptation to the counting task. Initial case studies run in a test house environment, where the setup is exercised on realistic indoor conditions rather than simulations.
arxiv-2606-23810:
Karve, Rose, Campbell, and Polkovnikov propose a single measurable signature of chaos that works for both classical and quantum systems, in a 2026 paper on nonlinear dynamics. Classical chaos is usually read from diverging trajectories, while quantum chaos is read from energy level statistics, and the two languages barely translate. The authors instead drive a system slowly and cyclically, then watch how its stationary state responds.

They package the response as speed Fisher information: how susceptible the state is to the average driving speed. Chaotic dynamics makes this quantity diverge as the protocol lengthens, governed by the perturbation's low frequency spectral weight. The framework covers classical and quantum Hamiltonian systems and non Hamiltonian flows.
arxiv-2606-23910:
Beltz and Savel work out how a hot Jupiter's equatorial jet would betray itself in the Doppler shifts measured as the planet crosses its star, in a 2026 paper on exoplanet atmospheres. Interpreting net Doppler shifts is hard because rotation, day to night flow, and jets all move spectral lines at once. The authors generate phase resolved transmission spectra from two families of circulation models: self consistent ones, and idealized ones isolating single ingredients.

Jet strength bites hardest during ingress and egress, when the planet's edges cross the star. At mid transit the jet tilts the slope of the shift curve, usually secondary to the blueshift from planetary rotation. Day to night flow just adds a constant offset. Faster jets also widen the cross correlation signal by spreading velocities across the limbs.
arxiv-2606-24010:
Guo and colleagues address robot teams and other multi-agent systems that must cooperate without breaking safety rules. Learning-based controllers perform well but rarely promise safety. Control-theory methods stay safe yet often act too cautiously. Their 2026 framework splits the job into two levels. A low level enforces hard safety limits through a constraint manifold, a surface of allowed states. A high level learns coordination.

Safety holds by construction at the low level under mild assumptions, while the upper policy learns freely above it. Guo's team also shows the learning dynamics settle to a steady pattern, which makes training more stable. In experiments the method matches rival performance while keeping safety rates near perfect. It also copes when the number of agents or obstacles changes, a key test for real deployments such as warehouse robots and drone swarms.
arxiv-2606-24110:
Zhang settles a question in combinatorics that had been open since 1990. It concerns sorting lists with a single stack. The stack-sorting map reads a permutation once, pushing or popping entries under a simple rule. Repeated passes sort it in the end. Researchers track the mean number of passes a random permutation of a given length needs. West conjectured in 1990 that this mean, divided by length, settles toward a fixed limit as length grows.

Working alone, Zhang uses a recent framework of stack-sorting diagrams and tableaux. These diagram tools encode how passes change a permutation. With them he proves the limit exists, which confirms West's conjecture after more than three decades. He also builds a monotone increasing sequence that converges to that limit. It improves the best previous lower bound on the limit's value. The 2026 result closes the existence question, while the exact value stays open for future work.
arxiv-2606-24210:
Baweja measures how badly a satellite timing receiver can be fooled while insisting everything is fine. Timing receivers underpin power grids and networks. A spoofing attack can drag the served clock slowly off true time. Standard integrity monitoring looks for position faults, but a slow pull of time itself leaves no geometric fault to catch, and the receiver's accuracy flag need not notice.

Field evidence comes first. Re-solving a recorded over-the-air spoof from the public JammerTest 2024 campaign, Baweja shows a survey-grade receiver was pulled by about a millisecond of served time. Yet it reported self-assessed accuracy in the tens of nanoseconds, a claim-versus-reality gap of four orders of magnitude. An impossibility observation follows. Against an adversary choosing the ramp freely, no finite unconditional bound on undetected error exists. Baweja therefore defines a conditional Timing Protection Level, bounding error given holdover limits.
arxiv-2606-25010:
Vatsal Baherwani, Zixi Chen, and three colleagues explain why capabilities in language models appear suddenly during training. Scaling laws predict smooth loss improvements, yet skills like in context learning switch on abruptly past some scale. Their experiments show emergence is random: capabilities arise at random points through training, with larger models acquiring them earlier. The trigger is attention. Skills such as pattern completion and indirect object identification switch on when the model abruptly learns the task relevant sparse attention pattern.

Synthetic tasks, linear maps and cellular automata, isolate the effect. Learning such a pattern grows harder with longer contexts and sparser patterns. Adding heads improves learning speed. Widening each head gives diminishing returns past a minimum capacity. Architectures differ: an MLP Mixer beats a transformer on linear map tasks needing complex patterns. Emergence, they conclude, is the signature of hard to learn attention patterns clicking into place.
arxiv-2606-25510:
Electric and magnetic dipole moments are tiny handles on a particle's inner structure, and measuring them tests both fundamental symmetries and sensor design. Simone Cavazzoni, Paolo Bordone, and Matteo Paris work out the ultimate quantum limits on estimating both moments in 2026, for a generic two level system bathed in electromagnetic fields. Three probe regimes are compared: clean unitary evolution, the same with depolarising noise added, and thermal equilibrium states. Quantum Fisher information sets the precision ceiling in each case.

Optimal probes and best operating points, such as run times and temperatures, are identified for separate estimation. Measuring both at once has a geometric catch. When the two dipole moments sit at right angles, both can be measured together cleanly. When they run parallel, the problem turns sloppy and only one combination is knowable. Applications span neutron dipole searches to molecular magnetometry.
arxiv-2606-25610:
Before a transformer can learn from galaxy images, the images must be chopped into tokens, and that chopping shapes what the model can know. Sogol Sanjaripour and colleagues compare four tokenisation strategies in 2026 inside one shared astronomy transformer, using six hundred forty thousand galaxy images from a major sky survey. Two scores matter: how faithfully the tokens rebuild the image, and how well the learned features predict independently measured physics like mass and star formation rate.

No method won both contests. A flow based tokenizer rebuilt images best, while a vector quantised one gave the strongest features for physical properties. Two others preserved local shape detail better. Reconstruction quality and representation quality came apart, the authors stress, so tokenizers should be benchmarked on the science they serve, not on looks alone.
arxiv-2606-25810:
In calm times a system's variables wander in many directions at once. In a crisis they lurch together. J Petkevicius studies that contrast in 2026 through increment matrices, tables of pairwise products of small movements. Extreme events add a low rank perturbation built from jump directions. The theorem is sharp. When the jump directions align, most total jump size pointing near one common vector, the largest eigenvalue swallows nearly the whole trace. The matrix's effective rank falls toward one: spectral collapse.

Background diffusion must also fade for the full system to collapse. The converse holds too. If collapse occurs, alignment and a negligible background are forced. Together these give a complete characterisation, not just a warning sign. The results extend to random jump processes, with collapse holding almost surely under natural assumptions. Earlier work on determinant growth and coupling diagnostics sits inside the same frame.
arxiv-2606-25910:
Nikolas Koumpis, with Koushik Kar, Leandros Tassiulas, and Manolis Zampetakis, studies gaming in two-stage electricity markets. Active prosumers, households or firms that both consume and generate power, can profit by understating their day-ahead demand. The trick inflates real-time imbalances and lets their generators earn more under uniform pricing, and public data shows day-ahead bids indeed sit below real demand.

Modelling the two-stage market under linear preferences shows the temptation does not fade as the market grows. Ordinary consumers lose their incentive to under-report at scale, but prosumers keep a guaranteed gain tied to the real-time generation stack and their share of it. A leave-one-out scoring penalty, run by the day-ahead market operator, restores honest reporting: prosumers do best by telling the truth, and honest participants face only small charges. Simulations on synthetic and real market data support the design.
arxiv-2606-26010:
