Maximilian Leitenstern and colleagues at the Technical University of Munich build odometry for racing robots. Odometry tracks a vehicle's motion from its sensors. At racing speeds, estimates must be fast, accurate, and robust at once. FAR-LIO merges lidar scans with inertial measurements on graphics hardware. A CUDA voxel hash map speeds nearest-neighbour search and map updates.

Sparsity-aware point matching adds the accuracy. An adaptive threshold tunes the Generalized Iterative Closest Point method on the fly. An extended Kalman filter forms the back end. Upsampling and delay compensation blend lidar output with fast inertial data. Output stays smooth for closed-loop control. Tests span four sensor setups and two real race cars. The cars reached speeds near two hundred fifty kilometres per hour. Positional error drops by about seven percent against top baselines. Runtime drops by about thirty-eight percent, with one shared parameter set.
arxiv-2606-26210:
Naba Jyoti Gogoi and colleagues push charged anti-de Sitter black holes through a thermodynamic throttling test. Their setting stacks three exotic ingredients: ModMax nonlinear electrodynamics, dRGT-style massive gravity, and Sharma-Mittal entropy, a non-extensive statistics. Exact formulas come out for the equation of state, temperature, heat capacity, and the Joule-Thomson coefficient. Throttling, the cooling-or-heating expansion of a gas, is the probe.

Cooling domains widen under the ModMax field. Its nonlinearities shift the inversion point to smaller horizon radii. Sharma-Mittal parameters steer the inversion radius and local stability. The global inversion boundary still answers to the massive gravity background. Gibbs free energy shows a van der Waals-like first-order transition with a swallow-tail shape. A clean division of labour emerges at criticality. Each ingredient governs a different feature of the phase landscape, making thermodynamics a diagnostic for telling such theories apart.
arxiv-2606-26410:
Zican Wang and Niloy Mitra want video models that respect real physics. Today's video generators often lose track of objects. They also break basic physical rules. Wang and Mitra move the prediction task out of flat images. They place it in a three-dimensional grid of small cubes called voxels.

Their system lifts features from a video model into that voxel grid. Features are compact summaries of what a frame shows. Depth estimated from a single camera view guides the lifting. A learned step then moves those features through space over time. It treats physics as the flow of material states. Training used only video and action signals, with no physics engine labels. The model stayed stable over long runs. It also looked physically plausible on three test collections, including solid objects moving through fluid.
arxiv-2606-26710:
Mohammed Ayalew Belay and four colleagues present the Kalman Prototypical Network for detecting faults in gas turbines with very few examples. Combined-cycle turbines generate power efficiently but interact in complex ways. Labelled fault data are scarce, so detectors must learn from a handful of cases. Few-shot learning methods often wobble because their class prototypes, average examples of each fault, jump around between episodes.

The network treats each prototype as a hidden state evolving over time. A Kalman filter, a classic estimator from control theory, steadies those states. Tests used a high-fidelity simulation of an offshore turbine with normal running and progressive leak faults. The method beat Matching Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML on accuracy and stability. Training also converged faster, and performance held up as test setups varied.
arxiv-2606-26910:
Yi-Han Luo and ten colleagues demonstrate a photonic chip platform with ultralow light loss, aimed at quantum information processing with single photons. Photonic circuits promise scalable quantum technology on manufactured chips. Loss is the killer: each lost photon compounds across sources, routing, and measurement, and multi-photon rates crash as circuits deepen. Silicon nitride is their material of choice.

The monolithic chip integrates narrowband photon-pair sources with qubit fusion circuits and reconfigurable measurement devices. Fusion, joining small entangled states into big ones, is a leading route to photonic quantum computing. The sources prepare entangled photon pairs of the kind Einstein famously questioned. By engineering loss down across the whole chip, the platform attacks the rate-versus-loss barrier that has capped earlier demonstrations.
arxiv-2606-27310:
Bandini, Jelic, and Gambassi study how spins in a non-reciprocal XY model get pinned to preferred directions by the lattice itself. Each spin interacts with neighbours through a vision-like coupling: it sees some directions better than others, breaking rotational symmetry. Different interaction kernels, from smooth von Mises profiles to hard vision cones, are compared. In 2026, two microscopic dynamics, Glauber updates and Langevin equations, frame the analysis.

Within the Langevin formulation, two contributions emerge naturally, which the authors name reactive and proactive terms. Both can generate global pinning of the whole system's orientation. Their roles in local pinning, the locking felt near each spin, differ by kernel and can even disagree qualitatively. The split explains discrepancies reported in earlier studies of similar models. Local and global pinning are distinct phenomena with distinct drivers. Lattice-induced orientational selection gains a microscopic account.
arxiv-2606-27410:
Wang leads a team making satellite image change captioning focus on the differences that matter. The task asks a model to describe, in words, what changed between two remote sensing images of the same place taken at different times. Standard training follows plain autoregressive generation, which rewards easy vocabulary over discriminative change features. Their Difference Feature Modeling framework retrains the objective around contrast. In 2026, a text-guided gated contrastive loss steers the vision encoder toward features the caption actually needs.

A pre-trained change detection model donates stable knowledge about where change occurs. A joint feature module fuses difference representations across scales. Experiments on multiple datasets show the approach works, with gains over prior captioning models. Captions grow more precise about what appeared, vanished, or moved. Earth observation gains a narrator that watches the change, not the scenery.
arxiv-2606-27510:
Vaidyanathan and colleagues show that activation patching, interpretability's main causal tool, quietly mixes in side effects it never bargained for. Patching swaps one component's activations for values from another run and credits the change to that component alone, as its natural indirect effect. Re-deriving the estimand from causal analysis exposes an extra term measuring how a component's influence depends on other components' states.

Experiments on a well-studied GPT-2 circuit show some components rendered invisible or inflated. Interaction variance explains the known instability of faithfulness scores. The effect provably grows with the gap between clean and patched values, vanishes when the model is locally affine, and splits into pairwise and higher-order group terms. The extra term is instead a warning sign when causal conclusions are prompt-dependent.
arxiv-2606-27610:
Decision problems under uncertainty are modelled as Markov decision processes. The transition rules may not be known exactly, though. Yadh Hafsi and three colleagues study robust control for this setting in 2026. Their ambiguity model uses Wasserstein balls around nominal transitions. A ball holds all transition laws within a set distance. The goal is a policy that does well even in the worst case inside the ball.

The worst case depends on the policy itself. That dependence breaks the usual policy-gradient argument. The authors work around it with a dual reformulation of the robust Bellman recursion. Studying its directional derivatives yields an explicit recursive formula for the robust policy gradient. They build a robust actor-critic algorithm on that formula. Benchmark examples illustrate how the algorithm behaves. Both discrete and continuous cases are included.
arxiv-2606-27810:
A skyrmion carries an integer topological charge. That charge emblemises its protection against smooth change. Kejun Liu asks what survives of that protection in 2026 when the magnet is made non-Hermitian. Gain and loss are balanced, or a parity-time symmetric anisotropy is imposed. The non-Hermitian skyrmion turns out to carry two charges. They agree in the Hermitian limit, then part ways once deformation sets in.

One charge, built from the right state alone, stays protected. Its flow reduces exactly to Gilbert-type relaxation on the target sphere. It cannot change under smooth evolution. The second charge uses the biorthogonal left–right pair. It is complex, and it loses quantisation as soon as gain and loss switch on. At the local generator's exceptional point, it breaks down. It forms a ring on the equator where the field itself diverges. Protection thus splits in two once dynamics turn non-Hermitian.
arxiv-2606-27910:
Light antinuclei link collider physics to dark matter searches, but antideuterons from beauty-hadron decays had never been predicted quantitatively. Marta Razza, Francesca Bellini, and Nicoló Jacazio present the first such study in 2026. The sources are the anti-Lambda-b baryon and the B-minus meson. Decays are simulated with PYTHIA. Three hadronization scenarios cover modelling uncertainty.

Antideuteron formation uses a coalescence model. Its wave function comes from the Argonne v18 nucleon–nucleon potential. Estimated branching ratios depend on the scenario chosen. For the anti-Lambda-b, they run from about five point seven in ten thousand to about fourteen in ten thousand. For the B-minus meson, they run from about seven in a million to about forty-three in a million. Prompt production dominates, and the charm contribution is negligible. The predicted yields sit where the ALICE experiment can identify antideuterons. Dedicated searches are motivated by the results.
arxiv-2606-28010:
Many problems in optimisation ask for a zero of a sum of monotone operators. Changchi Huang and three colleagues propose a primal-dual splitting algorithm in 2026 for such problems in Hilbert spaces. The setting is broad. Several monotone operators and cocoercive terms are allowed. A composite term built from a linear map is included. The scheme mixes forward steps for the smooth parts with backward resolvent steps for the rest. A dual update handles the linear composition.

Only one resolvent or operator evaluation is needed per iteration. Several known methods are generalised and unified by the scheme. Weak convergence of the iterates is proved under standard assumptions. Strong convergence follows under a mild extra condition, such as uniform monotonicity. Tests on image deblurring and denoising show the method is efficient and flexible. The framework also covers convex optimisation and saddle-point problems in imaging and signal processing.
arxiv-2606-28310:
A team including J. Richard Bond constrains exotic versions of inflation, the rapid expansion thought to have launched the universe. Many non-standard models predict wiggles, or oscillations, in the primordial power spectrum, the seed pattern of all later structure, and some predict extra particles produced during inflation itself.

Bond and colleagues fit general wiggle templates, plus a particle-production model, to cosmic microwave background data from Planck and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, together with galaxy survey data from DESI. A preconditioned Monte Carlo sampler tamed the many-peaked probability landscapes. Combined data capped the wiggle amplitudes at about two percent of the spectrum's overall size. The fancy models fit slightly better, yet Bayesian evidence still moderately favored the standard model over general oscillations.
arxiv-2606-28510:
Negar Kamali, Candice Rockell Gerstner, Jessica Hullman, and Matthew Groh test whether a half hour of training can sharpen professional skepticism. United States intelligence analysts increasingly confront generated imagery. While people beat chance at spotting fakes, accuracy falls short of operational needs. Earlier training studies curiously failed to improve recognition of real images.

In a counterbalanced experiment, thirty-two analysts judged thousands of matched real and generated images before and after an expert session walking through patterns in real and fake examples. Overall accuracy rose by nine percentage points from a baseline in the low seventies. Unusually, the gain came from real images, up about fourteen points, not from catching more fakes. The authors map where the training helps most across image types and experience levels.
arxiv-2606-28610:
Anton Dochtermann, Bennet Goeckner, and Marta Pavelka sort out two proposed generalizations of interval graphs to hypergraphs, where edges can join more than two vertices. Interval graphs are chordal, and chordality ties into commutative algebra through Fröberg's theorem on resolutions of certain ideals, so higher-dimensional analogues could extend that bridge.

The two classes the literature knows as cointerval hypergraphs and underclosed complexes turn out to be the same thing up to complementation. Dochtermann and colleagues then place them in the broader theory of higher chordality, proving an underclosed clutter is chordal in Woodroofe's sense. That settles a question two of the authors had posed earlier. Their associated Alexander dual complexes are vertex decomposable, so their circuit ideals have linear quotients. The dual complexes even carry shellings induced by the vertex order.
arxiv-2606-28810:
Shaw and Shepherd offer a tutorial on a common headache in health research: mistakes in both the outcome a study measures and the factors it compares. Large cohort studies and electronic health records are cheap and rich, but their variables were not collected for research and are often built by algorithms. Audits in cohorts of people living with HIV, they note, have found error rates as high as 56 percent for key variables.

Errors in one variable can trigger linked errors in others, for example when a wrong diagnosis date shifts every later timing. Most past work treated error in either exposures or outcomes, not both together. The tutorial lays out the data structure, builds a synthetic example dataset that readers can reuse, and walks through available correction methods. It compares results across methods and stresses that most approaches need validation or repeat data revealing how the errors behave.
arxiv-2606-29010:
Li, Wu, Zhu, Cai and Zhu analyse how people game the mean mechanism, a rule that averages everyone's reported values to reach a collective outcome. The mean is not incentive-compatible: rational players gain by misreporting, exaggerating their true values to drag the average their way. Despite that flaw, the mechanism is everywhere in practice.

The authors study the broader affine mechanism, with the mean as a special case. They give a full characterisation of its pure Nash equilibria. These are the reporting patterns where no player gains by changing alone, so they predict exactly how players will misreport. They characterise equilibria both when players know each other's values and in Bayesian games, where values are private and known only in distribution. The lesson is stark: extreme exaggeration is inevitable in such games, not an occasional abuse. The analysis explains a familiar failure of averaging-based decision rules.
arxiv-2606-29110:
OuYang and colleagues introduce SCALLOP, a method for training Boltzmann generators, models that sample molecular configurations with the right physical probabilities. Flow-based generators can produce high-quality samples in few steps, but estimating the model's likelihood, how probable each sample is, has lagged. Existing approaches need restrictive architectures for exact calculation, or noisy trace estimators with high variance.

SCALLOP builds on a likelihood flow map model that generates samples and their densities in few steps. It replaces that model's noisy training estimator with a new distillation objective that avoids it entirely and admits a vectorised form. In tests, SCALLOP cut training variance and time while beating its predecessor. It stayed competitive with the state of the art on images too. Inference ran up to ten times faster than the fastest baseline.
arxiv-2606-29710:
Xu, Yang, and Yang examine how a dark matter particle's finite size changes the Sommerfeld enhancement, the boost that slow-moving particles get when they attract each other before annihilating. Puffy dark matter particles are extended objects rather than points. Earlier work stressed low velocity as the enhancement's driver. Size, the authors argue, is another fundamental factor.

Using the partial-wave method, they first treat puffy dark matter specified only by a charge density distribution, with no internal structure assumed. Two dimensionless parameters characterize the resonance structure of the enhancement, the pattern of sharp peaks. Finite size alone reshapes that structure. As a structured example, they then analyse nugget-type dark matter, whose enhancement factor shows resonant behaviour similar to point-like particles. The results matter for predicting annihilation signals from dark matter in the galaxy.
arxiv-2606-30410:
Lennart Purucker and nine colleagues ask how far tabular foundation models really generalize beyond the easy cases. These models predict on spreadsheet-like data across many fields. Standard benchmarks favor exactly where the models already shine. Hard scenarios get excluded from the usual suites. Their BeyondArena benchmark unifies evaluation across task types. Same-distribution, temporal, and grouped tasks all appear. One hundred forty-two curated datasets feed the benchmark.

A companion framework, DataFoundry, curates datasets under one metadata schema. Eleven models compete across the full suite. Existing foundation models excel on tiny to medium same-distribution data. Tree-based methods and deep networks still dominate elsewhere. Non-IID, large, and high-dimensional tasks remain their territory. Text features and high-cardinality columns are covered too. The authors aim the benchmark at the hardest open problems. Marginal gains on easy data no longer count as enough.
arxiv-2606-30510:
S. Sandeep, E. R. Cardozo de Oliveira, E. Mehdi, and N. D. Lanzillotti-Kimura review tiny sound resonators built from gallium arsenide and aluminum arsenide layers. The review covers nanocavities that trap sound at gigahertz to terahertz frequencies. Such trapped phonons serve new quantum technologies. This material pairing beats rival platforms on several counts. Growth is mature, light–sound coupling is strong. Light and sound modes overlap in the same structure.

Layered Bragg reflector designs anchor the devices surveyed. Micropillar posts add three-dimensional phonon trapping. Ultrafast light methods probe the trapped phonons directly. Picosecond sound pulses and Brillouin scattering reveal their motion and coherence. Making, sensing, and steering the modes are now routine. Performance and integration get full treatment. Open challenges include acousto-optic losses and wider control. Nonlinear phononics and phononic circuits are the near-term outlook.
arxiv-2606-30610:
Chuyue Li and five colleagues release PyMETA, a benchmark for classifying errors in student Python code, released in 2026 for education research. Teachers and tutoring tools need to name what went wrong in a submission, not just mark it wrong. Existing datasets are small, lack multi-error analysis and use fragmented error labels. PyMETA instead labels errors with the Python interpreter's own exception hierarchy.

The dataset holds 48,646 student submissions. Every sample carries a single-error label, and a diagnostic subset of ninety-seven samples was annotated by experts for multiple errors. Its taxonomy has three levels, from a binary error split down to fourteen fine-grained types. The team tested two finetuned models and four prompted language models. Prompted models still trailed the finetuned smaller ones. Most models over-used the Logic Error label, and the best multi-error score came from Gemini 2.5 Pro.
arxiv-2606-30710:
F. Rigamonti and F. R. Ditrani propose an observing program to settle how galaxy centres formed. Local galaxies mix rotation-supported disks and pressure-supported bulges, but shape and motion correlate weakly, which strains the standard story of bulges first, disks later. Webb telescope pictures suggest mature-looking galaxies existed surprisingly early. Pictures alone, though, cannot prove how their stars actually move.

The authors propose measuring stellar kinematics, the motions of stars, at sharp spatial resolution for massive galaxies at cosmic noon, the era when galaxy growth peaked. Such data would reveal the build-up of central regions and the nature of structures that images suggest. They argue the VESPER-SHARP instrument on the Extremely Large Telescope is uniquely suited. It offers rest-frame optical coverage at that era and sharp resolution. Its field of view and multiplexing allow many galaxies at once, within reasonable exposure times.
arxiv-2606-30810:
Huy Tran and six colleagues fix a bad habit of code-generating language models: calling library functions that no longer exist. Models trained on old code keep emitting deprecated application programming interfaces, breaking software. Fine-tuning is too blunt when only a sliver of knowledge must change. Unlearning methods can suppress outdated calls, but they rarely teach the model what to write instead, leaving mismatched or half-finished code.

Their method, CURE, performs contrastive unlearning. It jointly discourages each deprecated interface and encourages its valid replacement, steering the model across the swap rather than silencing the old habit. On a recent benchmark of deprecated interfaces, CURE reduced outdated usage and improved correct replacement at once. It substantially outperformed two state-of-the-art baselines. General code generation ability stayed intact. The authors argue suppression plus replacement is the right shape for keeping models aligned with evolving libraries.
arxiv-2606-30910:
Caglar Zorbilmez, Beyhan Tatar and Azmi Ali Altintas study a hidden sector where a dark photon can decay in two very different ways. Dark photons are hypothetical partners of ordinary light, and axion-like particles are light pseudoscalars proposed in many extensions of the Standard Model. In their mixed portal framework, the dark photon either decays visibly into ordinary matter or cascades: first into an axion-like particle plus a photon, then into three photons in total. The team derive decay widths, branching ratios and boosted decay lengths, and define a dominance parameter marking where the cascade takes over.

For dark photon masses from 0.1 to 100 GeV, the exotic channel can turn states that would escape a detector unseen into displaced multi-photon events inside it. The axion-like particle itself may also be long-lived, giving displaced photon pairs, a target for future colliders such as FCC-ee.
arxiv-2606-31810: This author studies the exceptional origin of the strange metal and the LFL-HFL transition. The studying studies. Their studying is exceptional origin strange metal LFL-HFL transition. The creator is and the LFL-HFL transition. It is condensed matter. The studying is of.
arxiv-2606-31910:
Perruzza and colleagues propose a particle-physics sensor built from two entangled electrons floating on liquid helium. Electrons on helium sit in a nearly impurity-free environment with long predicted coherence times. Single-electron traps on microfabricated helium devices have already been demonstrated, making scalable architectures plausible.

Their concept entangles a pair of electron qubits, in spin and in spatial degrees of freedom, inside a helium double-well trap analogous to a semiconductor double quantum dot. Aligned with CERN's DRD5 quantum-sensor initiative, the design targets rare high-energy events. Entanglement between the two electrons could push sensitivity past classical limits, the authors argue, opening signals that classical detectors cannot reach.
arxiv-2608-00210:
Jaishi and co-authors report chiral magnon mixing in collinear ferrimagnets. Magnons in ferromagnets carry spin from right-handed precession. In antiferromagnets, left- and right-handed magnons are degenerate with no field. Ferrimagnets hold uncompensated sublattices, so both handed types should exist natively. Their energies split under the internal molecular field.

In RMn6Sn6 ferrimagnets, right- and left-handed bands cross at finite momentum. The modes carry opposite dynamical chirality. Tuning symmetry can keep that crossing a nodal line or gap it. Rare-earth anisotropy and applied field supply the tuning knobs. Gapped modes hold hybridized chiral excitations. Their chirality then varies with momentum, they report.
arxiv-2608-00310:
Fei and co-authors build a frame for reactive flow and rock mechanics in porous rocks. Mineral growth and loss reshape pores, stress, and flow traits. Those shifts drive tightly linked processes below ground. Current simulators lack a general chemo-mechanics form for them. Their frame answers that gap from poromechanics.

Host rock stress, pore mineral stress, and fluid pressure get split state roles. That split lets each part's behaviour and links be treated with rigor. Pore-scale growth turns into mineral stress in their worked cases. Mineral squeezing gives more true-to-life strain and induced stress. The method tracks stress change and fracture growth with no pore geometry stated. Reservoir-scale use in built subsurface systems is the aim.
at-sunwich-port-part-2-contents-chapters:
Part 2 of W. W. Jacobs's seaport novel holds chapters six through ten, with drawings by Will Owen. Jem Hardy returns to Sunwich after years away and finds the town little changed but its children transformed. Small boys now wear whiskers, and small girls have grown into young women, none more astonishing to him than Miss Nugent.

Courtship proceeds by draper's-shop encounters and careful observation from windows. Meanwhile Jack Nugent tells Hardy the terms of his exile: his father wants him gone from Sunwich, yet he stays, lodging with the Kybirds and pushing a trolley on the quay. Love sweetening toil, as Nugent jokes, keeps him there. Family pride and young romance grind against each other throughout.
aucassin-nicolette-lang-1910:
Aucassin loves Nicolette, a Saracen captive raised in a French castle, and their story survives in one manuscript. Aucassin and Nicolete, from about 1200, is the only surviving French chantefable, a tale alternating prose and verse. Andrew Lang's classic 1887 translation appears here from the 1910 David Nutt edition.

The tale parodies the romances of its age: the hero weeps, sulks, and bungles while Nicolette acts with sense and daring. Captures, escapes, and a kingdom where roles reverse keep the comedy bright. Lang's version carried the little masterpiece to English readers, where its charm has kept it in print ever since.
augustine-city-of-god-healey-1610:
John Healey gave Augustine's City of God its first English dress in 1610. Its title in that dress is Of the Citie of God. No new full dress in English came till the year 1871. Healey was a young scribe who died soon past his great task.

Augustine wrote the work in Latin as Rome fell to the Goths. He meets the pagan charge that Christ's faith had doomed the great city. Two cities, made by two loves, form his frame for the whole past of man. Healey's dress, in the tongue of King James's day, is a mark in its field.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-10:
Michael L. Rodkinson's tenth volume opens the Talmud's great civil-law section with Tract Baba Kama, the First Gate. Baba Kama treats damages: harm done by animals, pits, fire, and men's own hands. The 1918 edition continues the first full English Talmud.

The famous cases begin here, above all the ox that gores, and what its owner owes for each kind of harm. The rabbis sort damage by fault, warning, and custom, building a law of accidents from the Torah's terse lines. Fines, theft, and lost wages all come under the lens. The volume is the gateway to the Talmud's courtroom world.
bakunin-oeuvres-vol4-1910:
The fourth volume of Bakunin's collected works, edited by Guillaume, came out in French in 1910. It centers on the open war between Bakunin and Marx inside the First International. That fight, fought through congresses, letters, and pamphlets, ended with Bakunin's expulsion in 1872 and the split of the workers' movement.

Bakunin's texts accuse Marx's party of seeking power for itself under the name of the working class. He defends a loose federation of free groups against any central committee. Guillaume prints documents from both sides of the quarrel, which keeps the volume useful even for readers who side against Bakunin. These pages are the primary record of socialism's great schism, told by one of its two main actors.
bancroft-history-us-vol-10:
George Bancroft brings the American Revolution toward its triumph in the tenth volume of his History of the United States, from 1860. The war's later years test the young republic's money, arms, and will. Victory, long in doubt, draws steadily nearer.

Bancroft, often called the father of American history, writes with democratic fervor. For him, the Revolution proves liberty to be the world's great hope. His pages honor farmers and soldiers beside generals and statesmen. The volume stands near the crown of a vast work that taught Americans to read their founding as a providential march toward freedom.
barbara-blomberg-volume-10:
Volume 10 of Barbara Blomberg, by Georg Ebers, breaks a secret kept for years inside a marriage. Ebers shows Barbara coming home pressing one hand with the other, as if to prove she is not dreaming. Her husband Pyramus sees at once that something unusual has happened, and she makes him swear strict secrecy before she will speak in this volume.

Chapter XVI then pours the whole story out at speed. Pyramus, like her father, had believed her child by the Emperor was born only to die. Her cry that she no longer had a child meant something else: the boy was taken from her. A letter from Dona Magdalena now lets her hope the highest things for him. Longing, imperial coldness, and a mother's prayers fill the confession.
bates-naturalist-river-amazons-1910:
Henry Walter Bates spent eleven years, from 1848 to 1859, collecting on the Amazon. The Naturalist on the River Amazons, first published in 1863 and reprinted in the 1910 edition here, is his classic account. Darwin urged him to write it, and praised the result.

Bates shipped home some 14,000 species, most of them insects, and many new to science. He noticed harmless butterflies copying the bright warnings of harmful ones, a pattern now called Batesian mimicry. River towns, forests, floods, and festivals fill the narrative between the science. The book founded the study of mimicry and remains beloved travel writing.
bennett-clayhanger-1910:
Arnold Bennett set his Clayhanger novels in Bursley, his fictional version of a Staffordshire pottery town. Clayhanger, published in 1910, opens the series and draws on Bennett's own youth. It follows a printer's son across the last decades of the 1800s.

Edwin Clayhanger dreams of becoming an architect, but his stern father pulls him into the family printing business. The novel tracks Edwin's slow growth under that pressure, through work, illness, and a first serious love. Bennett fills the story with exact detail of pottery-town life. It is the start of his Potteries epic, which later volumes carry forward into Edwin's middle age.
bergson-time-free-will-pogson-1910:
Henri Bergson published Time and Free Will in 1889, his first major book. The English text here is F. L. Pogson's translation of 1910. Bergson introduces duree, or lived time, against the clock time of science. Real time, he argues, flows as interwoven moments, while clocks spread it out in space.

From this view he defends free will against strict determinism. Choices grow from the whole self rather than from separate causes lined up in a row. Psychologists of his day, he claims, confuse time with space and so miss the point. The book laid the base for process philosophy. It remains Bergson's most readable entry.
berkeley-principles-human-knowledge-1710:
George Berkeley published A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge in 1710 in Dublin. Berkeley, an Irish clergyman and philosopher, was only twenty-five. His claim was bold: matter does not exist, and reality consists of minds and their ideas alone.

Berkeley argued that to be is to be perceived, esse est percipi in his Latin phrase. A tree exists because a mind perceives it, and God's mind holds all things when no human watches. He attacked abstract ideas and the physics of his day. Readers have argued over the Principles ever since. It remains the central text of British empiricist metaphysics and a standing puzzle in philosophy.
bernal-diaz-true-history-maudslay-vol-2-:
Volume two of Maudslay's translation of Bernal Díaz's True History appeared in 1910, covering Books Five to Nine. The years are 1519 and 1520, when Cortés's small force entered the Aztec world and met Moctezuma. Díaz, an old soldier writing long after, had served in the ranks through all of it.

His history insists on the view from the ground: marches, councils, gifts, and growing dread. He wrote against the official story told by Gómara, which he thought stole credit from the men who fought. The siege of the great city still lies ahead in later volumes. Here the wonder and the danger rise together, page by page.
bernard-clairvaux-on-loving-god-1910:
Bernard of Clairvaux was the Cistercian abbot whose words moved kings and launched a crusade. He wrote On Loving God, De Diligendo Deo, for a cardinal who asked him why God should be loved. The English edition here dates to 1910, printed at London with the translator unnamed in the scan. Bernard's answer became the classic of affective mysticism.

He sets out four degrees of love. Man loves himself for his own sake, then God for his gifts, then God for God's own sake. At last he loves even himself only in God. The prose burns with scripture and with a monk's plain speech. Bernard asks for the whole heart, not a measured share. The short book has guided prayer for nine centuries.
bjo-rnstjerne-bjo-rnson-1832-1910:
William Morton Payne wrote Björnstjerne Björnson, 1832-1910 as an American tribute to the Norwegian master. Payne, who translated Björnson's Sigurd Slembe, began the essay for the poet's seventieth birthday in 1902. He enlarged it after Björnson's death, adding translations and anecdotes. His note is dated from Chicago in May 1910.

Payne ranks Björnson among the three giants of northern Europe, beside Tolstoy and Ibsen. He surveys the peasant tales, plays, poems, and novels of a sixty-year career. Björnson's moral surgery on social disease earns praise, though Payne calls him an idealist of redemption. The book argues that Norway's farmer-poet spoke to the whole world's conscience. Short as it is, it serves as a warm introduction to a writer once read everywhere and crowned with the Nobel Prize.
blackwood-wendigo-1910:
Deep snow and tall pines frame Algernon Blackwood's short novel The Wendigo, from 1910. A hunt party in the wilds of Canada seeks moose. Their guide hears a call in the wind. Then he runs off at a speed no man could match.

What is left is fear, strange tracks, and a tale no one can quite trust. Blackwood uses a North Woods myth of a starved, swift spirit. The tale is now the best known prose take on that myth. Cold and dread fill each page. The hunters doubt, then fear, then flee what they can't grasp. Blackwood keeps the beast off stage, so the cold woods feel vast and hostile.
bukhari-traditions-islamiques-houdas-mar:
In 1910 Tome III carried the French Sahih of al-Bukhari toward its close in Les Traditions Islamiques. Houdas and Marçais kept their steady pace through the later books of the collection, where reports treat campaigns, virtues, and the Prophet's companions. The Imprimerie nationale edition aimed at completeness, and this volume honors that aim.

Al-Bukhari's method, testing every chain of transmission, made his Sahih the most authoritative hadith book in Sunni Islam. French scholars gained, through these tomes, a full view of the tradition's inner workings. Tome III stands one volume from the end of a translation that took eleven years to finish.
bunin-the-village-1910:
Ivan Bunin published The Village in Russian in 1910, and Isabel Hapgood translated it into English in 1923. Two brothers, Tikhon and Kuzma Krasov, rise from peasant stock in a poor Russian village. Tikhon grows rich and hard, while Kuzma teaches himself letters and sinks into despair.

Between them Bunin paints village life without the pity or hope other writers added. Drink, violence, ignorance, and rare kindness fill the long, plotless days. The book split Russian critics, some hailing its truth and others its bleakness. Bunin later became the first Russian to win the Nobel Prize in literature. The Village shows the harsh ground from which his polished art grew.
christopher-columbus-and-the-new-world-o:
Leave-taking fills Volume 3 of Filson Young's Columbus, as the first voyage turns for home. The Admiral gives King Guacanagari another shirt and fires a lombard through the wrecked Santa Maria's hull to teach the islanders Spanish power. Then comes the delicate business: organizing the settlement of La Navidad, thirty-nine men left behind in a wooden fort on an unknown shore. Affection and unease mix in the parting, since Columbus is leaving his discovery in other men's hands.

Young narrates the stormy homeward run, the Azores and Lisbon, and the road to Barcelona where the Sovereigns wait. What the volume really studies is trust: in kings met, men left, and weather survived. Readers in the third volume get the hinge of the whole story. Discovery becomes a colony here. A report becomes a promise Spain will hold Columbus to for life.
cia-0000008010:
September 1955 gave analysts a deadline to work toward: July 1956, when Vietnam's future was due for key choices. The Geneva Accords had split Vietnam in two and promised nationwide elections by that date. In the south, Diem's government resisted holding the vote.

A CIA estimate for the period weighs Diem's grip, northern intentions, and the odds of renewed war. Such forecasts tried to give policymakers warning, not certainty. This one captures the moment when division hardened into two rival states. Its judgments help explain why the later war found roots so early in the decade that followed.
cia-0000008710:
Future Soviet moves in Vietnam drew a CIA forecast in March 1965, as American combat troops began landing. Moscow backed North Vietnam with aid and weapons, but it also feared a wider war with Washington. Analysts had to judge how far Soviet support might go.

The paper weighs aid levels, diplomacy, and the rivalry between Moscow and Beijing for Hanoi's ear. Its judgments fed choices about bombing, escalation, and signaling to the USSR. Readers can see the Vietnam War framed as one board in a global contest. The estimate shows superpower caution studied at close range.
cia-0000009910:
An American pilot died while held near Ban Na Kay, and two other Americans were moved, a November 1966 item records. Ban Na Kay sits in the Laotian uplands, in cave and mountain country. Death and movement in one report show captivity's two constant motions.

One man's file closes as two others' files gain a new location. Analysts split the item three ways and filed each part under a name. The movers' new place, if named inside, reset the search around them. This entry preserves the combined report before that splitting, as the news first arrived.
cia-0000012310:
Helms again, this time in a memo whose date is unknown and only estimated as 1962, addressed to the Director of Central Intelligence. The floating date sets the letter among the Penkovsky file's crisis-year papers. In 1962 the colonel's case ran toward its climax, and summit mail on it piled up faster than clerks could always date it.

Uncertainty about a date is a small fact that tells a larger one: haste ruled the bureaucracy that year. The files keep these loose pages without apology. For readers, the memo shows the great case's paperwork at its most hurried and human.
cia-0000012410:
Meeting number twenty-eight survives without a firm date, its year estimated as 1961. The undated record drifts through the file like a loose page. It stays valuable despite its lost place in the chronology. By the high twenties, the numbering itself tells the story. No Western service had ever debriefed one source at this length, this depth, or this level of danger.

The record's missing date is part of the file's honesty. Files kept under pressure have gaps, and the gaps remain visible. For readers, the session shows the operation's scale, counted in sittings rather than claims.
cia-0000013610:
Venezuela's young democracy under Rómulo Betancourt is surveyed in a CIA paper from October 1961. Betancourt had won the presidency after a decade of dictatorship. He governed an oil-rich country while gunmen tried to kill him and rebels tried to topple him. Trujillo's Dominican regime even backed an attempt on his life, yet the voting and the building went on around him.

The paper takes the measure of that battered democracy in its third year. It weighs the parties, the oil money, and the plots together. For readers, it keeps the watch on a rare experiment: a Latin democracy taking hits and holding.
cia-0000014710: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, espionage, and a block of following information fill a CIA file dated July 1, 1952. The title promises detail the open line does not show. By mid 1952 the couple sat in prison under death sentences. Files like this gathered fresh facts while their appeals ran through the courts.
cia-0000015310: A letter to Lloyd Berkner from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated April 4, 1958. It takes up Berkner's letter of April 21, the title oddly notes. The dates clash, a common slip in clipped file titles. Either way, the Berkner thread ran on into 1958, long after the first panel had closed its work.
cia-0000015410: Air Force officers met CIA staff on April 5, 1958, to talk about the report of the Scientific Advisory Panel on flying objects. That panel had weighed saucer reports for the government a few years earlier. The meeting kept two services aligned on what the panel had found and what should be said. Little in the title hints at detail, and the record stays at that level.
cia-0000021510: Sightings of pilots are discussed in an untitled CIA record dated in 1967. The pilots in such files were usually Americans lost over Laos or Vietnam. Each rumored sighting raised hope that a missing man still lived. Staff had to weigh those rumors with care, since families waited on the same news and false hope carried its own cruelty.
cia-0000022810: A dead American pilot was sighted in Snuol District, in Kratie Province, Cambodia, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. Kratie sits on the Mekong River in the country's east. Pilots fell across Cambodia as the air war spread past Vietnam's borders. A sighting of the dead there added one more place to the map of loss the offices kept.
cia-0000023010: What followed an attempt on the life of Trujillo is covered in a CIA record dated in 1967. The heading can also be read as the aftermath for Trujillo's assassin, and the catalog leaves it tangled. Rafael Trujillo, the Dominican strongman, was in fact killed in 1961. Either reading places the entry in the long shadow of that shooting and its reprisals.
cia-0000039010:
A Honduran party urged that President Azcona face trial over killings in the Matta affair, a CIA record dated March 6, 1988 reports. The call came from the Revolutionary party named in the title. Honduras was then a key base in the region's wider conflicts.

The record preserves a political demand: a sitting president put on trial. Such demands showed how killings and drug-era scandals shook Honduran public life. The file captures a moment when opposition parties used the language of the courts. Their target was a sitting president. Honduras was caught between its own politics and the wars around it.
cia-0000042810:
President Cristiani named army suspects in the Jesuit murders, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1990. The title ties the naming to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. A president naming his own army's men was a grave public act.

Inside, the suspects are identified as the president announced them. Naming soldiers broke the army's long shield of silence. It also bound Cristiani's own standing to the case's outcome. The file preserves the moment the accusation became official. The accused were no longer a rumor in the press. They were names spoken aloud by their own commander in chief.
cia-0000045210:
Venceremos reported a rift in the government over the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. A rift at the top was exactly what rebel radio liked to report. Divisions over talks ran between the palace and the armed forces.

Inside, the rebels' account of the government's split is preserved. Exposing an enemy's quarrels is a classic aim of wartime radio. True or stretched, the story served the guerrillas' daily campaign. The file lets readers weigh their version against the government's own statements in this same set, and judge where the boasting ended and the real friction began.
cia-0000049010: A CIA item from 1981 names individuals assassinated by unidentified killers in El Salvador. The list form is the point: victim after victim, each with a name, each killer unknown. Lists like this one became raw material for the Truth Commission, which had to turn names into cases and cases into findings.
cia-0000049110: American support for the embassy's work on the Sheraton murder case is recorded in a CIA item from 1985. Two American labor advisers and a Salvadoran land-reform official were shot dead at the Sheraton hotel in 1981. The case became a test of whether killers in uniform, or beside it, could ever be tried.
cia-0000049310: El Salvador: Growing Rightist Dominance is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000049310, dated October 6, 1980, and marked for the Truth Commission. The paper addresses the rising strength of the political right in El Salvador at that moment. It stands as an early agency reading of Salvadoran politics, kept in the declassified record under its original subject line.
cia-0000049410: Duarte's first hundred days in El Salvador are assessed in declassified CIA document 0000049410, dated August 5, 1984. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper takes the president's opening period as its subject, naming Duarte directly. It is a brief declassified review item whose heading frames a standard early-term check on a Salvadoran leader.
cia-0000095210: A cable to Leopoldville about eliminating Lumumba from governmental positions in Leopoldville, in the heading's shortened place wording, is declassified CIA document 0000095210, dated August 6, 1960. Lumumba is named directly as the person to be removed from office. The brief cable record is stark in its title, preserved from the Congo crisis summer.
cia-0000097310: Britain and Its Dependencies in the Western Hemisphere, with dependencies misspelled in the heading, is declassified CIA document 0000097310, dated September 5, 1965. The title surveys British holdings on the American side of the Atlantic. The brief file is a declassified survey paper whose spelling flaw, like others nearby, survives in the catalog record.
cia-0000117910: Shipping to Cambodia in the Third Quarter of 1968 is the subject, with its publication date an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000117910, dated November 1, 1968. The heading tracks shipping to one country in one quarter of one year. Third quarter is the time frame stated in the title itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note with the subject as released.
cia-0000119210:
In June 1985 the CIA set down its requirements and reporting rules for the prisoner and missing mission. The paper covers what collectors had to gather and how findings moved back up the chain. Routine as it sounds, this paperwork kept a far-flung search organized.

Requirements documents tell historians how the work was actually structured. They show what questions Washington wanted answered about the missing and how often answers were due. Read beside field reports, this one explains the system that produced them. That system kept the cases of missing Americans active a decade after the war in Southeast Asia had ended.
cia-0000119710:
Dated February 1954, this CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Bolivia. The revolution of 1952 had brought the MNR party to power, with land reform and mine nationalization in its train. Washington watched the experiment with open unease.

The paper assesses where the Bolivian revolution might go next and what risks it posed. Bolivia was a test of whether a poor, landlocked country could remake itself without falling under communist sway. For readers, the forecast records the agency's early judgment on one of Latin America's deepest social upheavals. It was written while the revolution's own leaders were still deciding how far it should run.
cia-0000124310: A July 1951 CIA document covers North Korean treatment of prisoners at Manpojin. The northern camps ranked among the Korean War's grimmest stories, and Manpojin sat near the Yalu River, far from witnesses. The paper records the treatment there as it was reported to the agency. Manpojin lay in the far north near the Chinese border, a place whose distance from the front made outside checks on camp conditions nearly impossible then.
cia-0000126910: Dated around June 1963, this CIA record is a presentation prepared for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the nation's top military officers. It concerns July 30 of a year the heading leaves unfinished. The agency briefed the chiefs face to face, and the paper preserves that briefing. Briefings to the chiefs joined the agency's picture to military planning at the highest level, the setting this formal record was made for.
cia-0000132310:
Released CBS newsmen lead the political news in Situation Report 620. The report belongs to the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series and is dated February 6, 1991. Its headline word breaks off at releas, but the sense is clear. Journalists caught inside the war zone had become bargaining chips in the conflict.

The report covers their release as one item in the daily political picture. Foreign reporters detained during the crisis drew wide attention back home. Their fate was followed by editors, families, and governments at once. For readers, the entry shows how even a press story entered the same reporting stream as battles and diplomacy during the war.
cia-0000132410: The Caribbean through the end of 1959 is the subject of a CIA report dated May 2, 1959. Written at mid-year, the report projects how the region's troubles would run through December. Castro's Cuba dominates its forecasts, as it dominated most agency thinking that year. The short report preserves what analysts expected the Caribbean to become before the year had even half run its course.
cia-0000132510: A third CIA paper on Cuba carries the busy date February 4, 1961. That winter the agency issued Cuba updates at a near-daily pace, and the Bay of Pigs landing was still two months off. The briefing's value lies partly in that tempo: it is one frame from a fast-moving film of reports. The declassified text comes from the CIA Reading Room, mirrored by the Internet Archive.
cia-0000132610: Fresh anti-American speeches by the Castro brothers fill item 13 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 1, 1960. The headline calls the speeches harangues, the agency's chosen word for a Castro tirade. Fidel and Raul were taking turns attacking Washington in public that summer. The short item reports the latest speeches and their themes.
cia-0000135910: The CIA planning paper of 5 May 1954 is about the K Program in general and one deleted item in detail, and it survives in declassified form. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136110: A declassified CIA situation report dated 2 April 1954 turns to the situation report for the week of 26 April to 3 May, filed under an April date. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136210: A cable dated 1 May 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on the arrival of Langvin at Somerset, a coded place greeting a traveling officer in May. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136310: Radio reports from 0800 to 1400 on 25 June 1954 fill this LINCOLN summary. Mendoza reported enemy heavy guns near the Chiquimula road. He urged that the gun sites be bombed. He then said 1,500 men at Cumbre Ingeniero would attack the town. Castillo gave a mixed report through another operator. He said all Chiquimula was under control. But he feared a strong counterattack after hand-to-hand fighting.
cia-0000136610: Dated only to 1961 in the catalog, with that year marked as estimated, this Spanish text comes from the 2506 Brigade papers. An earlier summary described London and Washington coordinating a war against Hitler; that belongs to another era and is dropped. The brigade was the CIA's exile force, and 1961 was its year of action. The document survives in Spanish in the declassified release, its month and subject not recorded.
cia-0000136710: An estimated date of 1 January 1961 heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, flagged as estimated in the catalog title. The brigade was the CIA-trained force of Cuban exiles preparing for the Bay of Pigs. The record states no subject for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, grouped with the many brigade documents placed at the start of 1961.
cia-0000136910: Two thousand tons is the total amount of the shipment, LINCOLN is told in this April 1954 cable, confirming facts from a telephone conversation. Five flat cars and two box cars already loaded had departed the port for the capital city. Headquarters comments that an estimated 200 to 500 tons could move in those cars, so the field should have several targets. The information also gives extreme importance to pressing the effort to get evidence requested earlier.
cia-0000137010: Delay is the message in this June 1954 cable to the Guatemala City station about contacting the British. Holland has been tied up on the Hill and a merchant is out of town; last night Holland and a representative met, both aware of the matter's significance. Today or later he will take the matter up with the British, at least persuade them to get off their high horse. The station should circulate calm order for a few more days and let the matter percolate through the junta.
cia-0000137310: Dated 1960, NSC Briefing — Cuba is a declassified CIA paper prepared for the National Security Council. Briefings of this kind gave the president's senior advisers a shared, current picture; this one's subject, by its title, was Cuba during the year of rupture with Castro's government. The catalog records no specific topics for it, and several sibling briefings with the same title and year are held in these files. It survives as released through the CIA Reading Room, one installment in a standing briefing series.
cia-0000137410: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade collection, dated only to 1961 in the catalog record. An earlier summary described London and Washington coordinating a war effort against Hitler; that is Second World War material, unsupported by this record, and it is removed. The document is a Spanish record of the CIA's Cuban exile brigade from 1961, the year of the Bay of Pigs, released in the declassified files with no subject stated.
cia-03153710:
New Soviet travel rules open the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 4 September 1957. The Moscow embassy calls the change a considerable improvement for reporting officers. Riga, Lvov, and Irkutsk are among the places newly opened. Other districts, some near Moscow and Leningrad, are newly forbidden, and service attachés lose ground. Security, not propaganda, is judged the motive.

Japan, in the second item, outlines plans to expand trade with Communist China. Foreign Minister Fujiyama handed the plan to Ambassador MacArthur on 30 August. Tokyo wants official status for its trade representatives and waivers of Peiping's conditions. Talks opening in mid-September aim at ninety million dollars of trade each way. The Dominican Republic steps up its influence on Guatemala's election. Spanish ministers foresee civil disturbances in October.
conrad-secret-sharer-1910:
Joseph Conrad wrote The Secret Sharer in late 1909, drawing on an old story from his own years at sea. The novella was published in 1910. Conrad had been a merchant sailor for twenty years before he turned to fiction, and the sea fills this tale.

A young captain, new to his ship, finds a naked swimmer clinging to the ladder at night. The man, Leggatt, has killed a sailor on his own ship and fled. The captain hides him in his cabin for days, risking his command. The two men mirror each other so closely that helping the fugitive escape feels like saving himself.
constitution-angola-2010:
Angola adopted a new constitution in 2010, replacing the basic law used since independence from Portugal. It founds a unitary republic, with Portuguese as the official language. The first titles state fundamental principles, then fundamental rights and duties. Rights are sorted into personal guarantees and economic, social, and cultural rights, each spelled out at length.

A president leads the executive and is chosen from the winning party's list in general elections, rather than by a separate presidential vote. The National Assembly makes laws, and later titles cover the courts, public finance, defense, and local power. At 244 articles, it is a long and detailed charter. It still governs Angola today.
constitution-djibouti-2010:
Djibouti, a small state at the mouth of the Red Sea, adopted its constitution in 1992, and the hosted text carries changes through 2010. Title one covers the state and sovereignty. Djibouti is a republic, Islam is the state religion, and French and Arabic are the official languages. Title two lists the rights and duties of the human person.

A president leads the executive, with a prime minister and government under him. The National Assembly makes the laws. Later titles cover the courts, a Constitutional Council, local areas, and public finance. Changes in 2010 removed the cap on presidential terms, a step critics feared would keep one man in power for life. The text is short, at under a hundred articles.
constitution-guinea-2010:
Guinea wrote this constitution in 2010, during a shift from military rule back toward elected government. Title one covers the sovereignty of the state. Guinea is a single republic, and French is the official language. Title two lists basic freedoms, duties, and rights, from free speech and worship to schooling, health, and work.

A president leads the executive, with a prime minister running the government day to day. The National Assembly makes laws. Later titles cover the courts, a Constitutional Court, a high court for trying top officials, local areas, and public finance. The 2010 text set term limits for the president. A later president's bid to reset those limits in 2020 sparked protests and then a coup.
constitution-kenya-2010:
Kenya approved a new constitution by public vote in 2010, replacing a charter kept since independence. Chapter one covers sovereignty of the people and the weight of the constitution itself. Chapter two founds the republic. English and Kiswahili are official languages. Chapter four is a full bill of rights, covering life, equality, speech, health, housing, and food.

A president leads the executive and is voted in directly. Parliament pairs a National Assembly with a Senate that speaks for the counties. The 2010 text created forty-seven county governments with their own assemblies and governors, a major shift of power away from the capital. Later chapters cover the courts, land, elections, and public finance. Kenyans praise the charter as one of Africa's most open.
constitution-madagascar-2010:
Madagascar adopted this constitution in 2010, founding a fourth republic after a political crisis that pushed out an elected president. Early titles cover basic principles, then the freedoms, rights, and duties of citizens, split into civil and political rights and then economic, social, and cultural ones. Malagasy and French are the languages of the text's own world.

A president leads the executive, with a prime minister running the government. Parliament pairs a National Assembly with a Senate. Later titles cover the courts, a High Constitutional Court, local areas with real self-rule, and public finance. The 2010 vote took place under a caretaker regime born of the crisis, and parts of the island's political class never fully accepted the result.
cox-fearsome-creatures-of-the-lumberwood:
William Cox prints the tall tales of the north woods in Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods, his book of 1910. Cox was a state guard of woods in Minnesota. Loggers there told of beasts no book of life lists: the hodag, the squonk that weeps its self to tears, the hidebehind that no eye can catch. Cox sets each down with mock grave care and fine draws by Coert Du Bois.

The tone is dry wit in a field guide's dress. The book saves a whole folk lore that was close to lost. It is the root text of that lore.
crabbe-borough-1810:
George Crabbe, who lived from 1754 to 1832, shaped The Borough in 1810 as a set of verse letters. Each letter paints part of a Suffolk seaport town and the people who live and work there. The first letter gives a broad view of the river, the quay, the shipping, and the shipyards.

Fishermen, smugglers, the poor, the pious, and the proud all pass through his steady portraits. Crabbe refused the soft glow of pastoral verse and showed hard labor and hard winters as they were. That plain truth, told with real pity, is why many readers call The Borough his finest work.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-10:
The tenth number of The Equinox, from September 1913, closes the journal's first volume. Ten fat numbers in five years had made it the great record of Crowley's school. The autumn issue ends a run that began in the spring of 1909.

Across the volume, the rites and holy books of Thelema saw print for the first time. The set forms one work: the founding archive of a new creed of magic. War would soon break the journal's pace and scatter its whole world. Volume one stands complete, a monument of its strange age. Nothing like it had been seen in English occult print before.
dewey-how-we-think-1910:
John Dewey published How We Think in 1910, a classic study of reflective thought. Dewey describes the steps of real thinking: a felt problem, clear definition, suggested solutions, testing by reason, and checking by action. He borrows this pattern from the scientific method. Teachers, he argues, should train this habit above all.

The book applies the method to lessons, language, and the training of judgment. Dewey warns against rote learning and hasty belief. Later editions kept the work in use for decades. Educators still cite its five steps. It is a clear, practical book by America's leading philosopher of education.
digha-nikaya-rhys-davids-1910:
More talks of the Buddha fill this second Dialogues volume, in the Sacred Books of the Buddhists line. Henry Frowde and Oxford University Press issued it in 1910, under the patronage of the King of Siam. The translators inscribe it to the memory of F. Max Muller, who founded the series.

An introduction to the Mahapadana Suttanta warns of a weed in the field: the doctrine of the Bodhisatta, the Wisdom-Being, which grew till it hid the older path of self-training. The Book of the Great Decease holds the volume's heart. At the Buddha's burning, the pyre catches fire of itself, and no soot or ash is seen, only the bones left behind, as with ghee. The tone is grave and plain.
dixon-s-return-odd-craft-part-10:
One dock tale, Dixon's Return, fills this tenth part of W. W. Jacobs's Odd Craft. The night-watchman opens on education: the finest schooling for a lad, he holds, is to send him to sea. School serves to a point, but the sea makes boys into men, and good men too.

His case in point is a man near thirty who took to the sea late. He had kept the Blue Lion public house at Wapping, left to him by his mother, who had raised him quiet and genteel. A peepbo player at the doors of a house, in a later scene, draws Charlie's sharp questions. Jacobs keeps his usual slow build, all in the watchman's voice. This file holds the one tale only.
doj-amerithrax-investigative-summary-201:
The Justice Department released this investigative summary on February 19, 2010, closing the Amerithrax case. Amerithrax was the FBI's investigation of the 2001 anthrax letter attacks, which killed five people and sickened seventeen in the weeks after September 11. The summary is the Bureau's complete public account.

It lays out the science that traced the mailed spores to a flask in the lab of Bruce Ivins, an Army researcher at Fort Detrick. It follows the suspects cleared along the way, above all Steven Hatfill, and builds the case against Ivins, who died by suicide in 2008 before charges. The report remains the key public record of the probe.
dunsany-dreamers-tales-1910:
Dream is the home country of Dunsany's tales of 1910. A Dreamer's Tales moves between the waking world and the lands past the fields we know. The book is the high-water mark of his early manner.

Sailors, kings, and wanderers cross to cities of dream and pay the full price of the crossing. Lovecraft and a host of others took the jeweled style for their own model of wonder. The prose glows with a light that is not the sun's own light. These are the tales by which Dunsany's early fame still stands today, undimmed by the years.
edgar-great-pyramid-passages-and-chamber:
John Edgar and Morton Edgar were Scots kin who gave years to the Great Pyramid. Book one of The Great Pyramid Passages and Chambers came out in 1910. The pair shot photos and took counts of each hall and shaft. Their work ran from 1910 to 1913 in the field.

Fine plates show the King's Chamber, the Grand Gallery, and the deep shafts. The Edgars set their counts by the work of Flinders Petrie, the great dig man. They read the counts as a tale of time and faith, not just stone. The book is the most full count of the halls since Petrie.
ehrlich-collected-studies-immunity-vol2-:
Paul Ehrlich won wide fame for his work on immunity and for the first drug made to target a single disease germ. Charles Bolduan translated this second volume of his studies into English. It appeared in 1910 as part of the second edition of the set.

In his preface Ehrlich says the volume gathers most of his recent immunity studies with his collaborators. The papers measure toxins and antitoxins with great care, building what he called quantitative serology. He argues his theory rests on a huge mass of experimental data. The volume completes a core record of early immunology.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-10:
Honors and how societies hand them out start Volume 10 of Michel de Montaigne's Essays, in Charles Cotton's translation. Montaigne (1533-1592) asks why cheap badges move men more than money does. Family feeling, foreign weapons, reading, and cruelty follow in turn. Each topic gets weighed against his own reactions.

Orders of knighthood and crowns of leaves show honor working best when it stays rare. Fathers who love children too blindly, and Parthian riders who shot arrows while fleeing, fill the middle chapters. Books praises reading for pleasure and admits Montaigne forgets much of what he reads. Cruelty closes the set with disgust at torture and pain enjoyed for sport. Readers find range plus candor: public honors on one page, a confession about memory on the next.
europmc-pmc10225110:
Guan, He, and Xu review recent progress and future prospects in gastric cancer treatment in a 2023 paper. Gastric, or stomach, cancer is among the most common cancers worldwide. Most patients are found at a late stage, because early symptoms are vague and screening is rare in many countries.

The review covers the main systemic treatments: chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and immune therapy. It explains which patients gain from each approach and how biomarkers guide the choice. It closes with trials and ideas that may improve the still poor outlook for advanced disease.
europmc-pmc10240810:
Yang and colleagues review amino acid metabolism in immune cells in a 2023 paper. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, and immune cells consume them in large amounts when they respond to threats. Inside tumors, cancer and immune cells compete for the same supply, which can blunt the immune attack.

The review explains how amino acid use steers what immune cells can do. It shows how tumors exploit that dependence to evade destruction. It then surveys ways to retune the supply so that immune therapy against cancer works better.
europmc-pmc10481210:
Rao and colleagues tested ChatGPT across a full run of clinical work in 2023. ChatGPT is a chat tool trained on vast text sets. Past tests gave it single questions, not linked chains of choices. Real care needs step-by-step thought, like a doctor at work. The team fed it 36 standard case stories from a clinical manual.

Each case asked for likely diagnoses, tests, a final call, and a care plan. Human scorers marked each reply. Rao reports an overall score of 71.7% across all cases. Final diagnosis scored best, at 76.9%. The first list of likely causes scored worst, at 60.3%. Scores rose as the tool gained more case facts.
europmc-pmc10499610:
Zhang and a large team gave an algorithm in 2023 that designs better mRNA for vaccines. mRNA is a message strip that tells cells to build a target protein. Such messages break down fast, which hurts storage and strength of a vaccine. A tighter fold and smart word choice in the code can slow that decay.

The snag is scale: the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 allows a vast sea of code variants. Their tool, LinearDesign, borrows a trick from language parsing to search that sea. It found a top design for the spike in just 11 minutes. Zhang reports far longer message life and more protein made. Antibody levels in mice rose up to 128-fold over a standard design.
europmc-pmc10533410:
Wang and a large team asked in 2023 what marks tumours that respond to immune therapy in triple-negative breast cancer. Some patients gain from checkpoint drugs, which free immune cells to attack. Others gain nothing, and no firm test split the two groups. The team mapped proteins in place inside tumours from a trial.

They read 43 proteins in tumour samples taken before, during, and after therapy. Two shares stood out as top predictors of response. Wang names growing CD8 T cells with a TCF1 mark, and cancer cells that show MHCII. On therapy, tumours that responded filled with a killer T cell type. Tumours that resisted showed CD15-marked cancer cells. Early biopsies may help steer care as it unfolds.
europmc-pmc11609310:
Ma and colleagues review liquid biopsy for cancer detection and monitoring in this 2024 paper. Tissue biopsy, cutting a tumour sample, remains the gold standard for diagnosis, with stable samples and high accuracy. It is also invasive and limited for repeated checks. Liquid biopsy reads tumour signals from blood and other fluids instead.

Its advantages include being non-invasive and quick, the authors note. Components now assayed include circulating tumour cells, circulating tumour DNA, exosomes, microRNA, other circulating RNA, tumour platelets, and tumour endothelial cells. The review covers the current status of each marker class for early diagnosis and prognosis. Challenges include low signal levels in early disease and lack of standardisation. Future prospects are mapped, with the field described as undergoing rapid progress.
europmc-pmc1183210:
Galperin took a 2005 census of signal proteins in bacteria and archaea. These proteins sense the world and pass messages inside the cell. Parasites in stable homes tend to carry simple signal kits. Free-living microbes in changing places carry far richer kits.

The census covered 167 complete genomes checked by hand. It counted sensor kinases, chemotaxis receptors, and related switch proteins. Larger genomes held many more signal proteins, roughly with the square of size. Galperin calls this spread a kind of bacterial IQ. The catalog helps compare how microbes read their surroundings.
europmc-pmc1215510:
Ryan, Barry, Murphy, and Mahon explored a puzzle about stem cells in 2005. Mesenchymal stem cells come from adult bone marrow. They can help rebuild cartilage, bone, muscle, and tendons. Normal immune rules should reject cells from another person.

In practice, these stem cells often avoid rejection. Lab dish studies back that pattern. The cells show few alarm flags to the immune system. They also calm killer cells and reshape nearby immune activity. Ryan compares this tolerance to how a mother tolerates a fetus. The trait could make donor cell therapy far simpler.
europmc-pmc1560110:
A small score change on a health survey can mean two unlike things. de Vet and co-authors untangled them in 2006. One is the smallest change a tool can reliably detect, beyond noise. The other is the smallest change patients count as important.

Methods that use score spread alone tend to find the detectable change. Methods anchored to patient judgment find the important change. de Vet argues the two should not be merged into one number. Knowing both tells clinics whether a tool is sharp enough to catch changes that matter. Anchor-based methods, they say, deserve preference for importance.
europmc-pmc1637810:
When a child meets a chemical can matter as much as how much. Selevan, Kimmel, and Mendola compiled what was known in 2000 about critical windows of exposure, from before conception through adolescence. A workshop weighed evidence for five body areas.

Broad windows of sensitivity exist for the breathing, reproductive, nervous, and hormone systems, and for cancer. But detailed data stay thin. Comparing dose at the target tissue across species needs work. The panel also flagged neglected topics: exposures around puberty, adult effects of early exposure, and gene-environment interplay. Selevan argues window data sharpen risk assessment and protect the most sensitive ages.
europmc-pmc1769410:
Smoke and indoor air pollution raise tuberculosis risk, a pooled analysis confirms. Lin, Ezzati, and Murray reviewed observational studies in 2007: 33 papers on smoking, five on passive smoke, and five on indoor pollution from biomass fuels.

Smokers faced higher risk of a positive TB skin test, of active disease, and of dying from TB. Passive smoke and biomass smoke also pointed to higher disease risk, though on thinner evidence. The exposures persist or grow exactly where TB burden is highest. Lin suggests TB control programs add tobacco and indoor air measures to their plans.
europmc-pmc1820610:
Hua, Krainer and co-authors tested in 2007 a drug-like approach for spinal muscular atrophy, a genetic disease that weakens muscles. Patients lack a working SMN1 gene, and the backup gene SMN2 usually skips a segment called exon 7 when its RNA is spliced. Keeping that exon in would yield more full-length protective protein.

The team built many short antisense oligonucleotides, synthetic strands that bind RNA, aimed across exon 7 of SMN2. Such strands usually cause skipping, but several of theirs boosted exon inclusion instead. Others promoted skipping or gave mixed effects, mapping which exon spots help or hinder inclusion. In cultured cells the best strands raised full-length SMN protein without blocking RNA export or protein making. Some were strong enough to advance into mouse model tests.
europmc-pmc1852410:
Gupta, Bailey, Noble and colleagues presented Tomtom in 2007, a tool that measures how alike two sequence motifs are. A motif here is a table of letter probabilities for a short DNA or protein pattern, such as a protein binding site. Discovery programs produce many motifs, and databases hold many more, yet no sound score compared them.

Tomtom fills that gap with a statistical measure of motif-to-motif similarity. It lets a researcher search a motif database with a newly found motif as the query. That check reveals whether the pattern is already known or genuinely new. The method also supports comparing protein motifs, not just DNA ones. By giving similarity a proper significance value, Tomtom turns a shelf of separate motif collections into a single searchable resource.
europmc-pmc1931610:
Lenoir, Serre and Ahmed reported in 2007 that rats choose intense sweetness over cocaine when given a free choice. Sweetened diets are often compared to addictive drugs, and both share brain reward pathways. How the two rewards stack up head to head was unknown.

Rats chose between saccharin-sweetened water, which has sweetness without calories, and intravenous cocaine. A large majority, 94 percent, picked the sweet water. The same held for sucrose, natural table sugar, so the effect is not an artifact of an artificial sweetener. Raising the cocaine dose did not flip the choice. The preference also survived cocaine intoxication, sensitization, and escalating intake, all hallmarks of addiction. In this setup, sweet taste outranks a potent drug reward for nearly every animal.
europmc-pmc2025310:
Peto and colleagues set out in 1977 how to analyse long-running randomised clinical trials. Part one had covered trial design. Part two covers comparing survival time, or time until another bad event, between treatment groups. The intended readers were doctors without statistical training. The authors wanted them to analyse such data themselves, or judge published analyses more sharply.

Their toolkit centres on life tables, which track survival over time in steps. It also uses the logrank test to compare whole survival curves between groups.
