Retrospective stratification, grouping patients after the fact by risk factors, refines the comparison. The authors explain how prognostic factors should and should not be used. Worked examples show each method in practice.
europmc-pmc2124710:
Russell L. Cecil examined the pancreas in ninety cases of diabetes mellitus and reported the anatomy in 1909. Lesions of the gland, he found, occur in more than seven-eighths of all cases. Where diabetes came with pancreatic lesions, the islands of Langerhans always showed changes: sclerosis, hyaline degeneration, invasion by white cells, or overgrowth.

In twelve of the ninety cases the lesion was limited to the islands alone. Durations differed by lesion type. Sixteen cases with hyaline change averaged three and a half years of disease. Forty-six with sclerosis averaged three years and eleven months. Six with white-cell infiltration averaged only eleven months. In bronzed diabetes, pigment destroyed the islands. Readers get strong evidence, counted case by case, that diabetes lives in one small part of the pancreas.
europmc-pmc2124810:
Peyton Rous of the Rockefeller Institute reported in 1910 the first bird tumor that could be transplanted into other birds. The growth was a spindle-celled sarcoma of the common hen. Rous carried it into its fourth tumor generation, using fowls of pure blood from the small, closely related stock where the tumor first appeared.

Success was narrow and picky. Market-bought fowls of similar variety would not take the tumor. Neither would mixed breeds, pigeons, or guinea pigs. Young chickens proved more susceptible than adults, and birds that failed once never grew a tumor on a second try. The sarcoma stayed true to type, growing into and destroying tissue. It spread to the heart once. Repeated bacterial examinations found nothing. Readers get the founding report of a transplantable bird cancer, cautious about what it does and does not prove.
europmc-pmc2125010:
Richard M. Pearce and J. H. Austin published the fifth paper of their spleen series in 1912, on the cells that step in when the spleen is gone. Dogs without spleens received hemolytic serum, and their lymph nodes and livers were examined. A large share of dogs spleenless for two weeks or more showed a great increase in the endothelial cells of the lymph nodes.

Normal dogs given the same serum show nothing of the kind. The liver's star-shaped capillary cells often did the same eating. The cells seem to be formed on the spot, not carried in. The authors read the finding as compensation: the lymph nodes, and perhaps the liver, take over the spleen's red-cell destruction work. Readers get a clear case of the body reassigning an organ's job.
europmc-pmc2125210:
Rufus Cole reported in 1914 that pneumococci turn hemoglobin into methemoglobin, the brown, useless form of the blood pigment. The change requires the living germ in direct contact with the hemoglobin. Neither the fluid the germs grew in, nor extracts of the bacteria, can do it.

Washed pneumococci in salt solution also fail, until a trace of sugar arrives. Minute amounts of dextrose switch the reaction on quickly. Other sugars, and certain other organic substances in larger amounts, can substitute; glycerin works even at one part in ten thousand. No special molecular shape explains which substances serve. The effect of free oxygen's presence fits that scheme. Readers get a pneumonia germ caught performing a small, exact piece of chemistry on blood.
europmc-pmc2128510:
Paul E. Howe, of the Rockefeller Institute's animal pathology department at Princeton, traced colostrum proteins from a newborn calf's meal into its blood and urine. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. He analyzed the proteins of the blood before and after feeding, in calves given colostrum and in calves given plain milk.

Two globulins, euglobulin and pseudo-globulin I, appeared in blood and urine after colostrum feeding and were absent when milk was fed. Their arrival supports the view that colostrum causes the newborn calf's proteinuria, the protein leak Smith and Little had described. In the passage through the gut wall the proteins are in part unaltered, a striking fact for whole proteins. Blood serum proteins fed the same way were also absorbed and excreted. Part of the high protein in young calves' droppings, Howe adds, is simply colostrum passing through.
europmc-pmc2128610:
Twenty generations of transplanting their rabbit malignant tumor are summed up by Wade H. Brown, Louise Pearce, and Chester M. Van Allen. Their report is the sixth study based on that tumor, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. All the transplants went into the testicle, and the team charted growth and malignancy from clinical and post-mortem records.

Many changes in the tumor's behavior appeared across the twenty generations, but they ran irregularly, seldom holding one direction for long. The evidence even contradicts itself. Much of it shows the tumor cells growing more active and capable with passage. Yet, a few generations apart, secondary tumors became rarer in both frequency and spread, while the death rate stayed flat or rose. Continued passage, the record says, does not simply sharpen a tumor. It makes its behavior wander, and any single trend is soon broken.
europmc-pmc2222610:
Petrus and co-workers showed in 2007 that blocking an ion channel called TRPA1 reverses mechanical hyperalgesia, an exaggerated pain response to pressure. TRPA1 senses pungent chemicals and may detect harmful mechanical and cold stimuli. Its role in sensitised pain was unsettled. The team developed a specific small-molecule blocker, AP18, and tested it in mice with inflammation caused by complete Freund's adjuvant, a standard pain model.

AP18 reduced pain behaviour triggered by cinnamaldehyde, a TRPA1 activator. It also reversed the inflammation-induced mechanical hyperalgesia in normal mice. In mice genetically lacking TRPA1, hyperalgesia developed normally, yet AP18 had no effect there, proving the drug acts on target. The authors infer that TRPA1 helps sensitise pain, and that lifelong knockout mice compensate in ways that mask that role.
europmc-pmc2235210:
Jusko and co-workers followed children in 2008 to test whether low blood lead levels harm intelligence. The official threshold for elevated lead was 10 micrograms per decilitre, but effects below it were disputed. The team measured blood lead eight times from six months to six years of age. At age six, 194 children took a standard preschool intelligence test. Models adjusted for maternal IQ, home environment and other confounders.

Lifetime average lead, with a mean of 7.2 micrograms per decilitre, linked inversely to full-scale and performance IQ. Those associations were statistically significant in the adjusted models. The cohort consisted of young children. Children averaging 5 to 9.9 scored 4.9 points lower than those under five. Peak lead levels linked to lower IQ down to 2.1, the lowest peak observed. The authors conclude impairment occurs well below the official threshold.
europmc-pmc2289810:
de Groot and co-workers validated the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, in its Dutch version, in 2008. This questionnaire, built in Sweden, measures patients' own view of knee problems and had been validated in several languages, but not Dutch. The team translated it by a standard procedure, then tested it in patients with mild, moderate and severe osteoarthritis, and in patients after first or revision knee replacement surgery.

Internal consistency exceeded 0.70 on all subscales in every patient group. Repeat-test reliability also exceeded 0.70 for mild and moderate osteoarthritis and revision groups. At least sixty percent of predicted relationships with other measures held for mild, moderate and primary replacement groups. For severe and revision patients, under forty-five percent held. Ceiling and floor effects appeared in some groups. The score suits mild-to-moderate disease best.
europmc-pmc2323710:
Green cells photosynthesize faster in brighter light up to a point, and Robert Emerson tests how that curve depends on chlorophyll amount and temperature. His 1929 Harvard study uses the alga Chlorella vulgaris at several chlorophyll concentrations, varying light, heat, and exposure to prussic acid.

Photosynthesis tops out at about the same light intensity across all chlorophyll levels studied. The temperature relationship also stays the same, though the temperature characteristic shrinks gradually as temperature climbs. Prussic acid depresses the rate more strongly when chlorophyll is scarce. Emerson reads these patterns as signs that photosynthesis may involve a self-accelerating reaction, and that chlorophyll does more than simply soak up light.
europmc-pmc2363610:
Jenkins, Fallowfield, and Saul asked over two thousand UK cancer patients how much they wanted to know in 2001. The survey ran inside a bigger study of communication training for cancer doctors. Some clinicians still held back bad news, assuming many patients prefer not to hear details.

In total 2,331 patients answered. A striking 87% wanted all possible information, good and bad, and 98% wanted to know whether their illness was cancer or not. Only 58 of 440 patients in one subgroup preferred to leave details to the doctor, and they tended to be over 70. Even they still wanted specific facts. Women more than men wanted the exact name of the illness and every treatment option listed. The authors called withholding information on preference grounds untenable after these results.
europmc-pmc2543010:
Montazeri reviewed three decades of research in 2008 on quality of life among women treated for breast cancer. The term covers how patients feel and function day to day. It had grown into a major outcome in cancer care. He searched English-language journals from 1974 to 2007 and examined 477 full papers after screening out meeting abstracts, letters, and duplicates.

Two questionnaire families dominated measurement: the European EORTC scales and the FACIT scales, each with a breast cancer module. Different operations gave broadly similar quality of life, though mastectomy patients reported worse body image and sexual functioning than breast-conserving patients. Chemotherapy brought side effects that dragged quality of life down. In advanced disease, quality of life scores also predicted how long patients survived, and anxiety and depression stayed common years after diagnosis.
europmc-pmc2633610:
Sánchez-Vargas and co-authors asked in 2009 how the mosquito Aedes aegypti fights off dengue virus type 2, the virus it passes to people. Their focus was RNA interference, a defense in which the cell chops viral genetic material into tiny pieces and uses them to destroy matching viral messages.

In infected mosquito cells and in live adult mosquitoes, the virus did trigger this defense. Small virus-specific RNA pieces appeared, yet the virus still copied itself and spread. When the team blocked key defense genes named dcr2, r2d2, and ago2, the virus grew even faster. It also needed less time inside the mosquito before it could be passed on. The defense thus slows dengue, even though the virus partly slips past it.
europmc-pmc2642810:
Fisher-Wellman and Bloomer reviewed in 2009 thirty years of research on exercise and oxidative stress, the strain placed on the body by reactive oxygen molecules. Close to 300 studies had appeared since the first work in 1978. A single hard workout, whether endurance or sprint based, was known to raise this strain for a short time.

Across the studies, the size of the rise depended on the type of exercise, its intensity, and how long it lasted. Who was tested mattered too, as did any antioxidant pills they took. The authors note a twist: the brief rise seems to be a useful signal. It prompts the body to strengthen its own antioxidant defenses over time, a pattern known as hormesis. Short-term strain, in this view, trains long-term protection.
europmc-pmc2654510:
Ma and colleagues watched in 2009 how the germ Pseudomonas aeruginosa builds the glue that holds its biofilms together. Biofilms are city-like clusters of bacteria stuck to a surface, hard for drugs and immune cells to clear. This germ's clusters cause stubborn infections, especially in the lungs.

The team colored one glue ingredient, a sugar chain called Psl, and filmed it as clusters grew. On single cells the sugar wrapped in a spiral pattern that helped cells stick to each other and to the surface. Pulling the sugar off with chemicals broke the cluster apart. As clusters matured, the sugar gathered at the edges, leaving a hollow center. Swimming cells later appeared in that hollow, ready to spread. Dead cells and loose DNA filled the same space, and genes controlling cell death shaped the whole layout.
europmc-pmc2687710:
Ma and co-authors profiled in 2009 how the tissue around a breast tumor changes as the cancer advances, not just the tumor cells themselves. The stroma, the supporting tissue, is now known to feed and shape tumors. The team used a laser to snip pure samples of tumor and stroma from fourteen patients, each matched across normal, preinvasive, and invasive stages.

Stroma changed its gene activity as extensively as the cancer cells did, starting before invasion. Tumor-linked stroma turned up genes for scaffolding material, for cutting enzymes that clear paths, and for cell division. The step into invasion brought a fresh rise in three cutting enzymes, MMP2, MMP11, and MMP14. Even tumor grade, the pathologist's measure of aggression, left a readable signature in stroma, rich in immune genes for high-grade tumors. The surroundings, the authors conclude, are a partner in the crime from its earliest stage.
europmc-pmc2707010:
Liberati and co-authors published in 2009 the explanation for PRISMA, a set of rules for reporting systematic reviews and pooled analyses of health studies. A systematic review gathers all studies that fit set rules to answer one question. Poor reporting had often left out key facts, which made reviews hard to judge or reuse.

As an update to the older QUOROM guidance from 1999, the text walks through each PRISMA item and shows what good reporting looks like. It stresses clear notes on what was planned, what was done, and what was found, plus any changes to the plan. The goal is full, open reporting that lets readers weigh strengths and flaws for themselves.
europmc-pmc2781110:
Ramsköld, Wang, Burge, and Sandberg analyzed in 2009 deep RNA sequencing data across human and mouse tissues to map which genes each tissue uses. The set of active genes in a tissue reflects the jobs it performs. Their gene-level survey asked how many genes run everywhere, as housekeeping, and how tissues differ beyond that core.

Roughly eight thousand protein-coding genes were switched on in every tissue. Together they supplied about three quarters of all message copies in most tissues. These core genes mostly made intracellular proteins for metabolism, transcription, RNA handling, and translation. Genes for secreted or surface proteins, by contrast, ran in only some tissues. Expression levels formed one broad continuum, with no sign of separate expression classes. Muscle and liver ran the simplest programs, while brain, kidney, and testis ran the most complex.
europmc-pmc2816710:
Larsen and colleagues compared gut bacteria in 2010 between men with type 2 diabetes and men without it. Hints from animal work tied gut communities to weight and blood sugar control, but human diabetes data were thin. Their study covered thirty-six adult men with wide ranges of age and body size, eighteen of them diabetic.

Diabetic men carried smaller shares of one major bacterial phylum, Firmicutes, and of its class Clostridia. The balance between two big groups tracked blood sugar levels closely, yet showed no tie to body mass. Another class, Betaproteobacteria, ran higher in diabetic men and also rose with blood sugar. The authors say sugar control, not weight alone, should frame future gut studies.
europmc-pmc2821410:
Ghosh, McBurney, and Robbins showed in 2010 that SIRT1 puts a brake on a major growth pathway called mTOR. SIRT1 is an enzyme tied to calorie restriction and longer life in model animals. The mTOR pathway senses nutrients and stress and drives cell growth, and its role in aging made any new brake worth finding.

Cells lacking SIRT1 ran mTOR signaling high, and stress could not switch it off. A SIRT1 activator, resveratrol, lowered mTOR activity, while a SIRT1 blocker raised it, and both effects vanished without SIRT1. The team found SIRT1 binds TSC2, part of a complex that restrains mTOR, and the brake failed when TSC2 was missing. The work ties two aging pathways together through one contact point.
europmc-pmc2873910:
Mefford and a large consortium searched in 2010 for missing or extra DNA chunks behind unexplained epilepsy. Epilepsy affects about one in a hundred people, yet most cases have no known genetic cause. Such chunks, called copy number variants, were already tied to autism and intellectual disability, so the team scanned five hundred seventeen people with epilepsy that showed no lesion on scans.

Rare gene-bearing chunks appeared in about nine in a hundred patients and were absent from nearly twenty-five hundred controls. A few patients carried two rare chunks at once. Some chunks removed genes already linked to other brain development disorders, including one tied to autism-related traits. Rare chunk changes look like one shared root across several brain conditions, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc2890410:
Ahmed, Creanga, Gillespie, and Tsui examined in 2010 how women's wealth, schooling, and say in decisions shape use of maternal health care. They call those three factors the three Es. The analysis spans the developing world. They pooled the most recent national household surveys from thirty-one countries. Separate models tracked modern contraceptive use, antenatal care, and having a skilled attendant at birth.

All three Es pushed service use upward in most countries. The gaps were stark: women in the poorest fifth of households had odds of a skilled birth attendant more than nine tenths lower than women in the richest fifth. Completing primary school alone multiplied those odds several fold. Raising quality and access will underdeliver, the authors argue, unless women's economic and social position rises too.
europmc-pmc2903510:
Jordan and colleagues counted in 2010 how often people consult British general practitioners for regional aches like back, neck, and knee pain. Such problems hide under thousands of different record codes, so four doctors first sorted nearly six thousand codes by body region. The team then extracted a full year of consultations from twelve practices into a research database.

One in seven of all recorded consultations concerned a muscle or joint problem. The back led by far, with about five hundred ninety-one people per ten thousand consulting yearly, and the knee came second at roughly three hundred twenty-four. In children the foot topped the list instead. Women and older adults consulted more for most regions, giving planners a firm denominator for services.
europmc-pmc2942810:
Kooij led a European expert network in a 2010 consensus statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults. The childhood condition carries into adult life in most cases, yet adult services across Europe lacked skill and facilities for it.

Drawing on research and clinical experience from eighteen countries, the statement covers the biology of the disorder. It then answers three questions. How does adult ADHD look, how should it be diagnosed, and how should it be treated? The authors warn that the condition stays under-recognised and undertreated, raising illness costs. They call for better training and proper screening tools in psychiatry.
europmc-pmc2946910:
Huynh-Thu and colleagues presented GENIE3, a method for rebuilding gene control networks from expression data, in a 2010 article. Working out which genes switch which others on or off from large datasets is a core problem in systems biology.

GENIE3 splits the puzzle into one prediction task per gene, using tree-based ensemble methods to forecast each gene's activity from all others. Genes that help most in a forecast are scored as likely regulators, and the scores combine into a ranked network. The method topped a major simulation challenge and compared well against rivals on real data from the bacterium Escherichia coli.
europmc-pmc3012610:
Goldstone and co-authors catalogued the full set of cytochrome P450 genes in zebrafish in a 2010 study, a family of enzymes that transform drugs, poisons, and the body's own signals. Zebrafish were rising fast in drug discovery and toxicology, so their enzyme roster mattered.

The fish carry ninety-four such genes in eighteen families shared with mammals. Many match human genes handling hormones and regulatory molecules one to one, with matching chemistry confirmed for several. The drug and pollutant families are far more tangled, with extra fish copies. Developmental tracking showed when each gene switches on as embryos grow.
europmc-pmc3048210:
Yokota and colleagues reported in 2011 that one gene mutation marks a far worse outlook in advanced colon and rectal cancer. The team typed tumors from more than two hundred patients receiving chemotherapy for advanced or returning disease. Two related genes were checked, since both can lock a growth pathway on and blunt the effect of targeted drugs.

Tumors carrying the rarer mutation, in the BRAF gene, clustered on the right side of the colon and spread to the belly lining more often. Patients with that mutation lived far shorter on average than patients whose tumors carried neither mutation. After adjusting for other factors, the mutation remained one of the strongest predictors of poor survival. A specific change in the partner gene also trended toward worse outcomes. The authors say mutation typing should guide prognosis talks and treatment planning.
europmc-pmc3055910:
Erickson gathered in 2009 a practical guide to judging the size and shape of protein molecules, the tiny machines of the cell. Three classic methods are covered: how fast proteins sink in a spinning tube, how they filter through gel beads, and how they look in electron microscope images. The review collects simple calculations for turning those measurements into structural sense at the nanometer scale.

One popular equation for shape is shown to mislead and is set aside for a simpler check that flags whether a protein is round or stretched out. Gel filtering, he reminds readers, sorts by effective radius, not by weight, though pairing it with sinking speed yields weight. Microscope methods that shadow or stain single molecules resolve shapes directly. Combined, these bench methods give a medium detail picture of proteins too small or flexible for crystallography.
europmc-pmc3102710:
Decroly and coauthors solved in 2011 the three dimensional structure of a two protein machine that the SARS coronavirus uses to cap its RNA, a step its copying machinery requires. The cap finisher, nsp16, works only when its partner, nsp10, is attached. The team crystallized the pair together, with and without a blocking compound, and mapped the contact surface in detail.

The partner grips a broad patch and switches the finisher into its working shape. Functional tests pinpointed the residues that hold the pair together, grip the RNA, and perform the chemical step, apparently by a direct hand off mechanism. A single letter change in the partner tightened the embrace and sharpened the picture further. Because human capping uses different machinery, the viral complex is an attractive drug target. The structures show exactly where a blocking drug could sit.
europmc-pmc3116910:
Jonas Warringer and colleagues mapped natural trait differences in yeast for a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Yeast is a workhorse of genetics, yet how its wild strains differ in behaviour, and why, was poorly charted. The team measured many traits across the common yeast and its closest wild relatives and traced the history behind the patterns.

Farmed and wild yeast strains differed more in traits than their modest genetic differences would suggest, and trait patterns followed population history rather than local habitat. One West African group stood out as weak on many traits, including a broken gene that blocks use of a certain sugar. Even the standard lab strain proved highly unusual. The authors argue drift after population crashes shaped many traits, warning against generalising from lab strains.
europmc-pmc3135510:
James Adams and colleagues compared body chemistry in autistic and typical children in a 2011 paper in Nutrition and Metabolism. Links between metabolism and developmental conditions were drawing growing interest. The study enrolled fifty-five autistic children and forty-four typical peers in Arizona, none taking supplements at the time, and ran a wide panel of blood tests.

Autistic children showed lower levels of several vitamins and protective chemicals, higher signs of oxidative stress, and weaker markers for energy transport and detox routes. Common vitamin and mineral levels, though, mostly sat within normal ranges in both groups. Groups of markers also tracked with how severe a child's autism rated on three scales. The authors suggest nutrition trials are warranted, since many gaps look correctable.
europmc-pmc3171010:
Françoise Farace and colleagues compared two machines that count tumour cells circulating in blood in a 2011 paper in the British Journal of Cancer. Such counts forecast patient outlook and treatment success, but no universal detection method exists. One system fishes cells out by a surface marker; the other filters by cell size. Sixty patients with spreading breast, prostate, or lung cancer gave samples to both.

The two systems agreed in just over half of breast and prostate cases, and in only a fifth of lung cases. Size-based counts often found cells the marker method missed. The authors warn that marker-only capture can overlook tumour cells that have shed the marker while turning more aggressive, a bias worst in lung cancer. Counts from the two methods should never be treated as interchangeable.
europmc-pmc3261210:
Dennys Cintra and colleagues showed that unsaturated fats can reverse obesity-linked inflammation in the brain's appetite center, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. In animal models, inflammation of the hypothalamus is an early driver of obesity, and drugs or gene tricks can restrain it. Whether ordinary nutrients could do the same was unknown.

In mice fed a fattening diet, swapping part of the fat for flaxseed oil or olive oil corrected the hypothalamic inflammation. It restored insulin sensitivity there and body-wide, and it reduced fat stores. Injecting pure omega-3 or omega-9 fatty acids into the brains of obese rats cut food intake and weight gain. It restored responses to the satiety signals leptin and insulin. It also switched on appetite-suppressing genes. A recently found fatty acid receptor helped relay the effect. Nutrients, the authors conclude, are credible candidates against this inflammation.
europmc-pmc3291410:
Thomas, Keating, Hulse-Post, and Doherty made the case in 2006 that flu vaccines should do more than raise antibodies. Shots built on antibodies work well only when the vaccine matches the circulating strain closely, because flu changes its outer coat often. T cells, another arm of the immune system, instead target inner parts of the virus that stay similar across strains.

The authors explain how two broad kinds of T cells help clear infected cells, one by guiding other immune cells and one by killing infected cells directly. Mouse studies of flu lung infection show how these responses form, persist, and return during a second infection. Vaccines that also train T cells, they argue, could protect even when strains drift.
europmc-pmc3304110:
Nicolas-Alonso and Gomez-Gil reviewed systems that let people control computers with brain activity alone, in a 2012 article. Such brain computer interfaces aim to restore communication for people left fully paralyzed by conditions like motor neuron disease, brain stem stroke, or spinal cord injury. The review walks through the standard chain of stages every system uses.

Stages covered include recording brain signals, cleaning them, picking out the features that carry intent, translating those features into commands, and running the device. The authors compare ways of sensing the brain, from scalp electrodes to measures of blood flow, and survey the math used to decode signals. They close with the range of devices these systems can drive, from spelling aids to assistive appliances.
europmc-pmc3315510:
Risso, Schwartz, Sherlock, and Dudoit tackled a hidden bias in gene activity measurements, in a 2011 methods paper. RNA sequencing counts how many reads come from each gene, but the counts skew with a gene's content of the DNA letters G and C. That skew differs from sample to sample and can fake or hide real differences between conditions.

The team proposes three simple corrections that adjust each gene's count within a single sequencing run before runs are compared. On two datasets from different species and designs, their approach cut the bias and gave more accurate estimates of how much gene activity changed. It also kept error rates honest in tests for differing activity. The methods ship in a free software package, and the authors stress that careful cleanup is essential before drawing biological conclusions.
europmc-pmc3404110:
Suthar and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2012 whether antiretroviral therapy for HIV also prevents tuberculosis in adults. Tuberculosis is the great killer riding alongside HIV in much of the world. If treating the virus cuts tuberculosis rates, one program could fight both diseases at once.

Pooling the available studies, the review found therapy tied to a large drop in tuberculosis cases, about two thirds lower across all levels of immune cell counts. The protection was not confined to the sickest patients. That breadth matters for policy, since it supports starting therapy earlier rather than waiting. The analysis gives tuberculosis programs a firm number to plan around.
europmc-pmc3440110:
Boxall led a worldwide expert exercise in 2012 to name the biggest open questions about drugs and personal care chemicals once they escape into nature. A decade of work had traced these chemicals through water and soil, but research money needs aiming. Questions were solicited globally, workshopped down to a top twenty, then ranked.

The priorities fell into seven baskets. They covered which substances to assess first, how exposure happens, uptake by living things, harm, relative risk, antibiotic resistance, and managing the problem. The ranked list is meant to steer future research programs toward the gaps that matter most. With evidence mounting that these everyday chemicals reach ecosystems worldwide, the authors argue focus beats breadth now.
europmc-pmc3477710:
Datta and co-authors modeled how brain stimulation dose varies from person to person, in Frontiers in Psychiatry in 2012. Transcranial direct current stimulation passes a weak current through scalp pads to nudge brain activity, and it is being tested for many disorders. People respond unevenly, partly because head shape steers the current. The team built computer models from MRI scans of three adults.

Standard pads spread current widely, and the peak spot in the brain shifted from person to person. A ring-style setup kept current inside a tighter zone for everyone. Fine folds of the cortex bent the flow in each model. Datta's group argues that dose should be tuned to each person's own scan for steadier results.
europmc-pmc3514210:
Memory turns short-lived into lasting through a chain of molecules, and Eric R. Kandel traces that chain in this 2012 lecture-style review. Six steps take center stage: the messenger cAMP, the enzyme PKA, the CRE DNA element, the regulators CREB-1 and CREB-2, and CPEB, a protein that helps lock changes in place.

Kandel first retells the clinical and behavioral work that separated implicit memory, for skills, from explicit memory, for facts and events, and made a molecular approach possible. He then gives the discovery history of each molecular step and its role in explicit memory. The result is a personal map of how synapses store experience.
europmc-pmc3514310:
Some health interventions work in one clinic and fail in another, and Jo Rycroft-Malone leads an eleven-colleague team demonstrating realist synthesis, a review method built to explain such puzzles, in 2012. Instead of asking whether a program works, it asks what mechanisms make it work, for whom, and under what conditions.

The worked example asks which strategies enable evidence-informed healthcare, focusing on change agency. The team mines concepts, builds an outcome-focused framework, searches and scrutinizes evidence, then extracts and synthesizes it into hypotheses. Few detailed examples of the method existed, so the paper doubles as a how-to, weighing the approach's strengths and its practical challenges.
europmc-pmc3526310:
MicroRNAs dampen thousands of genes, and Charles E. Vejnar and Evgeny M. Zdobnov built miRmap in 2012 to rank how hard each one pushes. Their open-source library predicts repression strength, not just target identity, using eleven features drawn from thermodynamics, evolution, probability, and sequence.

Three features are new, including one scoring evolutionary conservation with PhyloP. Benchmarked against four kinds of large experimental datasets, the features are compared fairly, without cherry-picked thresholds. How reachable a target site is proves the single most predictive feature. Combined in one model, the features explain more variance than the standard TargetScan score. The tool targets the ranking problem every microRNA study faces.
europmc-pmc3563110:
Damien Fair and colleagues, writing for the ADHD-200 Consortium in Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience in 2012, tested whether brain scans can separate the two main subtypes of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Resting-state MRI measures which brain regions vary in step with each other. Tiny head movements distort those measures, and children with this hyperkinetic disorder move more than most, so movement control was central to the design.

Pooling scans from five centers, the group stripped out micro-movement effects and then trained pattern classifiers on the cleaned data. The classifiers could tell the combined subtype from the inattentive subtype by their connectivity patterns. Network analysis showed overlapping changes in sensorimotor systems alongside points of difference. The paper offers a careful case that subtype signals survive once movement noise is handled honestly.
europmc-pmc3565910:
Lucie Heinzerling and colleagues set out European standards for the skin prick test in Clinical and Translational Allergy in 2013. Skin prick testing confirms allergy driven by IgE antibodies in hay fever, asthma, hives, eczema, and food and drug allergy. A drop of allergen extract is placed on the skin and pricked in; a raised wheal signals sensitivity. Methods varied widely between clinics, making results hard to compare.

Standard procedure, the paper states, means proper extracts, positive and negative controls, and reading the skin after fifteen to twenty minutes, with a wheal of three millimeters or more counting as positive. A standard panel for European inhaled allergens follows, from birch and grasses to house dust mites and cockroach. Matching panels for other regions are urged, so diagnosis and research can be compared across borders.
europmc-pmc3570210:
Andrew McDavid and colleagues built a statistical framework for single-cell gene tests in Bioinformatics in 2013. New microfluidic machines can measure gene activity in hundreds of single cells at once, using a method called qPCR. No two cells are truly alike, so these data expose useful variety. They also bring quirks: many readings are zero because a gene is simply off in that cell, not because the test failed.

Their framework explores the data, sets quality rules to drop unreliable cell readings, and models each gene as off, giving zero, or on, giving a graded value. A combined test built on that model detects treatment-driven changes better than tests using only the graded or only the on-off part. The tools were built on one machine brand but are written to transfer to other multi-measure data. Labs gain cleaner reads on how single cells differ.
europmc-pmc3614510:
Nitika Pant Pai and colleagues reviewed HIV self-testing in PLoS Medicine in 2013. In July 2012 the United States approved the first over-the-counter self-test for an infectious disease, an oral HIV test people can buy and run at home. The hope was plain: lower the stigma and logistics that keep status unknown. The open questions were whether people test accurately alone, prefer the option, and link to care afterward.

Their systematic review gathered studies of supervised and unsupervised self-testing in high- and low-risk groups. Self-testing proved broadly acceptable and often preferred, with accuracy acceptable especially when some supervision or support stood by, though the oral test's lower sensitivity than blood tests framed the trade-offs. Evidence on what happens after a positive home result, the link into treatment, was the thinnest part. The review maps where programs can build and where proof must catch up.
europmc-pmc3661910:
Clumps of protein inside nerve cells mark a wasting disease, Blokhuis, Groen, Koppers, van den Berg and Pasterkamp review in a 2013 Acta Neuropathologica article. The disease, ALS in short, kills the nerve cells that drive muscles. Fresh studies had named new clump parts, among them proteins called FUS and TDP-43 and a gene-stretch product. Faults in the genes for these proteins run in some family cases of the disease.

Clumps appear in patients with no such fault, and in other brain diseases, hinting at a shared path. The review weighs three routes to clumping: parts of proteins that self-clump, faults in RNA grain handling, and breakdown of the cell's quality control. Whether clumps harm by gaining a toxic role or losing a needed one is unsettled. Sharper facts on clumping, the authors say, may open new treatment paths.
europmc-pmc3668610:
Phone-based health research grew fast and changed shape over a decade, Fiordelli, Diviani and Schulz map in a 2013 study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Their net caught 117 articles from 2002 to 2012 on mobile health, called mHealth in the text, across 77 journals. Output almost doubled between 2007 and 2008. The review sorted each study by audience, health topic, method and outcome type.

Chronic conditions drew the clearest focus among many topics. Over the decade, studies shifted from judging the gadgets themselves to judging their health impact. Outcome measures were mostly clinical, mixing self-reports and hard measures. Research designs grew more complex and aims more sharply set. Yet the newest phones' tricks, such as built-in sensors, had barely been put to use. The map, the authors say, shows a field maturing in method while leaving fresh tools untested.
europmc-pmc3696910:
Noble and colleagues review why abnormal tagging of the tau protein with phosphate groups matters in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Tangles of heavily tagged tau are a hallmark of these diseases. Yet evidence increasingly suggests the tangles themselves may not kill neurons; changes in soluble tau beforehand may do the damage.

This tagging alters tau's shape, location, and jobs. Those jobs extend beyond steadying microtubules to protecting DNA and supporting synapses. Tau pathology also appears to spread between connected neurons. Because enzymes drive the tagging, the reviewers discuss whether adjusting it is a realistic treatment lever for these diseases.
europmc-pmc3879010:
Susan L. Prescott leads a team of co-authors in a world food allergy survey in The World Allergy Organization Journal in 2013. Food allergy and eczema rank among the most common long-term diseases of childhood. Yet solid counts of food allergy are scarce, above all in poorer countries.

The team surveyed allergy societies across dozens of countries in 2012, gathering published counts and care burden data. Over half the lands had no prevalence data at all. Only a small share had counts proven by the gold-standard food challenge test. Parent reports, which overstate rates, filled most gaps. Where challenge-proven, rates in young children in rich lands ran high. Fast-growing Asian societies show rises too. The survey maps a data desert that policy must fix.
europmc-pmc3881510:
Kassem Makki, Philippe Froguel, and Isabelle Wolowczuk review fat tissue and insulin resistance in ISRN Inflammation in 2013. Fat tissue is no longer seen as a mere fuel store. It holds many immune cells and sends out hormones and signals, which puts it at the crossroads of metabolism and immunity.

In obesity, the cell mix inside fat shifts. Attack-type immune cells build up and the tissue's signal output changes. Those shifts drive a low, steady body-wide inflammation and blunt insulin's action, the core of type 2 diabetes risk. The review sums the literature on how fat-resident immune cells steer that process through their secreted signals. Big open questions close the piece, such as what first calls the immune cells in.
europmc-pmc3935310:
Janos X. Binder and colleagues present COMPARTMENTS in the journal Database in 2014. It is a resource that unifies facts about where proteins sit inside cells. A protein's place shapes its job. But the proof was scattered. Some came from papers curated by hand. Some came from large microscopy screens. Some came from computer guesses based on sequence.

COMPARTMENTS pulls all of these sources into one place. It adds results from automatic reading of papers. It maps all entries onto shared protein IDs and standard terms. Each fact gets a confidence score. That lets users compare kinds of proof fairly. For each protein, the facts are drawn on a sketch of a cell. The picture gives a quick summary at a glance. The resource also updates itself from its sources.
europmc-pmc3965110:
Robert D. Finn and colleagues update Pfam in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014, the database of protein families. Pfam groups proteins that share a conserved region into families, each with a curated alignment and a statistical model used to recognize new members. Release 27.0 holds 14,831 hand-curated families. Since the previous update paper, 1,182 families were added, and coverage of the UniProt knowledgebase held near 80 percent even though that database grew by half.

The team also audited every extra feature the website offered, weighing use and computing cost. Some features were dropped, others improved, and new ones built, including family alignments drawn from four representative proteome sets and an interactive search for DNA sequences. The paper documents the content growth and the reasoning behind the service changes.
europmc-pmc3965210:
Adam P. Baker and colleagues report in eLife in 2014 that the resting brain flickers through network states far faster than standard scans suggested. For thought to work, brain networks must reorganize in well under a second. Using magnetoencephalography, which times brain activity precisely, the team recorded spontaneous activity and developed a method to spot the moments when a distinct whole-brain pattern returns.

The brain cycled through short-lived states lasting only 100 to 200 milliseconds, whose shapes matched the familiar resting-state networks seen in slow scans. Activity within each network rose and fell in coordinated bursts at that fast pace. The team also showed the default mode network and attention regions avoid direct switching between their states, a pattern behind their known opposition. The work reframes resting networks as rapid, repeating events.
europmc-pmc4008810:
Shona L. Halson reviews sleep in elite athletes and foods that might improve it, in Sports Medicine in 2014. Sleep supports body repair, learning, memory, and clear thought. Signs suggest top athletes often sleep less, or sleep worse, than they need.

Poor sleep cuts endurance in long, steady exercise and dulls learning and memory. It can also shift pain sense, immunity, and inflammation. Long-running partial sleep loss changes sugar handling and hormone signals, which can alter appetite, food intake, and protein building. Those shifts can drag down an athlete's diet and form. Halson then weighs food-based aids that act on brain signals tied to sleep. Studied options include carbohydrate meals, the amino acid tryptophan, valerian, and melatonin. Each shows some promise, but the evidence base is thin. More trials in athletes are needed before firm advice can be given.
europmc-pmc4053810:
Andrew E. Jaffe and Rafael A. Irizarry warn that blood cell mix can fake epigenetic findings, in Genome Biology in 2014. Studies of DNA methylation in whole blood are booming. Blood, though, is a blend of cell types, and each type carries its own methylation pattern.

Using a method that estimates cell proportions from the methylation data itself, the pair re-examined five published studies of aging. Cell composition itself changed with age. Much of what had been read as age-linked methylation shift was really that blend shifting. At single sites, the two effects tangled badly. The lesson reaches beyond aging: any study on mixed tissue can mistake a change in the recipe for a change in the cells. The authors supply software for the standard array platform so teams can estimate and correct the mix.
europmc-pmc4132710:
Antoine-Emmanuel Saliba, Alexander J. Westermann, Stanislaw A. Gorski, and Jörg Vogel reviewed single-cell RNA sequencing, a technique that profiles gene activity in one cell at a time. Their review appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Cells that look identical can behave very differently over their lives, and those differences show in their RNA.

Bulk sequencing averages millions of cells and hides this variation. The authors compare the single-cell protocols on offer, each with strengths and current limits. They survey the questions already tackled, from tracing cell lineages to exposing hidden diversity inside organs, and the major findings so far. Remaining challenges include capturing tiny RNA amounts faithfully. The review maps a fast-growing field with broad basic and clinical promise.
europmc-pmc4229610:
Frances Bunn, Carol Brayne, and six co-authors mapped what is known about dementia plus other illnesses in BMC Medicine in 2014. People with dementia very often live with further long-term conditions, from diabetes to failing eyesight. Care systems built around single diseases serve them poorly, yet the evidence on the overlap was scattered.

Their scoping review gathered 54 primary studies, eight reviews, and three guidelines. Most work counted how common added conditions are, or described patchy care quality. Some studies found patients with dementia got less monitoring and treatment for eyesight and diabetes than similar patients without dementia. Far less is known about how services should be organized, or about what patients and family carers themselves experience. The authors chart those gaps for future research.
europmc-pmc4240310:
Selene K. Bantz, Zhou Zhu, and Tao Zheng reviewed the atopic march in the Journal of Clinical and Cellular Immunology in 2014. Many children follow a set sequence of allergic disease: eczema in infancy, then hay fever and asthma in later childhood. That sequence is called the atopic march, and it was long unclear whether the steps truly cause each other.

Newer evidence supports a causal chain. A leaky skin barrier, often from filaggrin gene faults, lets allergens and bacterial products in through eczema patches. The exposure trains the whole immune system toward allergy, priming nose and airways to overreact later. Early, severe eczema raises the risk most. The authors highlight a possible early window when repairing the infant skin barrier might stop the march before asthma starts.
europmc-pmc4248310:
Stephen N. Sansom, Georg A. Holländer, and seven co-authors profiled the thymus's teaching cells in Genome Research. In the thymus, epithelial cells show developing T cells the body's own proteins, so the cells learn not to attack them. A gene called Aire drives much of that show in mature medullary cells, and its failure causes autoimmune disease.

Deep RNA sequencing of mouse cell groups and of 174 single cells found these epithelial cells can express up to 19,293 protein-coding genes, more than any other cell type known. Aire alone switched on 3,980 tissue-restricted genes, many of them normally silenced elsewhere by Polycomb marks, which Aire seems to override. Single cells each displayed only a scattered few of those genes, at random. The picture explains both the breadth and the patchiness of self-tolerance training.
europmc-pmc4297610:
Hiroyuki Kuwano heads the author list of the Japan Esophageal Society guidelines for cancer of the esophagus, in the April 2012 edition. The guidelines appeared in the journal Esophagus in 2015. They set the standard practice for doctors who diagnose and treat this cancer across Japan.

Built on evidence based medicine, the document covers how the cancer is found, staged, and treated, and what follow up care should look like. The stated aims are safer treatment, smaller gaps in results between hospitals, less wasted cost and effort, and care that patients can face without needless anxiety. The text is a working reference for Japanese practice rather than a research report.
europmc-pmc4308910:
Kirsten M Timms and eleven co-authors tested whether genome wide scar scores can spot breast tumors that lack working BRCA1 or BRCA2 repair. Their study appeared in Breast Cancer Research in 2014. When this repair path breaks, tumors leave characteristic patterns of chromosome damage, and such tumors respond better to platinum drugs.

Just over two hundred tumors of all receptor subtypes were profiled for mutations, gene silencing, and three damage scores. Harmful BRCA changes turned up in every subtype, while silencing of BRCA1 clustered in triple negative cancers. All three scores tracked deficiency tightly, and their average caught cases each single score missed. The work supports score based screening for repair defects beyond direct gene tests.
europmc-pmc4329810:
Michele Milella and ten co-authors review PTEN, one of the most important tumor suppressor proteins in human cancer. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Oncology in 2015. PTEN is best known as the main brake on the PI3K growth pathway, and losing it frees cells to grow, which is why it is so often altered in tumors.

The protein does more than that one job. It also works through other enzyme actions and non-enzyme roles, touching gene control in the nucleus and teaming with other suppressors and growth pathways. The review maps this network of functions and the evidence from a decade of studies. The breadth explains why PTEN status shapes tumor behavior and treatment response in so many cancer types.
europmc-pmc4337710:
Lauran Madden, Mark Juhas, William E Kraus, George A Truskey, Nenad Bursac, and Amy J Wagers grew working human muscle in the lab that answers drugs the way real muscle does. Their study appeared in eLife in 2015. Flat cell cultures of muscle lack the aligned fibers and force of the real tissue, which limits drug and physiology studies.

Their myobundles, built from primary human cells, formed striped, multi-nucleated fibers with a reserve pool of stem cells. The bundles twitched on their own, answered electric pulses, and grew stronger and better at handling calcium as they matured. A calcium reporter let the team watch drug effects without touching the tissue. Responses matched known clinical effects of several drugs.
europmc-pmc4342410:
Fumiaki Imamura, Renata Micha, Shahab Khatibzadeh, Saman Fahimi, Peilin Shi, John Powles, and Dariush Mozaffarian graded the world's diets in 1990 and 2010. Their assessment appeared in The Lancet Global Health in 2015. Diet drives much of the global burden of chronic disease, yet no consistent picture existed of what nations actually eat or how that changed.

Hundreds of surveys covering nearly ninety percent of the world's adults fed two diet quality scores, one built on ten healthy items and one on avoiding seven unhealthy ones. Patterns varied sharply by region, income, age, and sex, and improvements in healthy eating were partly offset by rises in unhealthy items. The atlas gives policy makers a baseline for food programs.
europmc-pmc4348510:
Jordi Sunyer and a large team followed Barcelona schoolchildren to test whether traffic pollution at school slows mental development. Their study appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2015. Air pollution is a suspected developmental neurotoxicant, many schools sit beside busy roads, and traffic peaks exactly when children are in class.

Nearly three thousand children aged seven to ten, in schools paired by neighborhood wealth but split by traffic exposure, took computer tests four times over a year. Pollution was measured inside classrooms and in courtyards. Children in high traffic schools gained working memory and attention more slowly than peers in cleaner air schools. The design separates the pollution effect from family income, a common confound in such studies.
europmc-pmc4402510:
Matthew Ritchie and co-authors reviewed the limma software package for gene expression analysis, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Limma, written for the R environment, became a popular choice for finding genes whose activity differs between conditions, first for microarrays. Its strengths include handling complex experimental designs and borrowing information across genes to steady estimates when samples are few. The article explains the package's philosophy and its newest expansions.

Limma now analyzes RNA sequencing data as well, for both gene activity and alternative splicing, using pipelines closely parallel to the microarray ones. It can also move beyond one-gene-at-a-time tests, examining sets of co-regulated genes and higher-order expression signatures that aid biological interpretation. A single, familiar workflow across old and new data types is the package's selling point for labs in transition.
europmc-pmc4451910:
Trong Ao, Nicholas Feasey, Melita Gordon, Karen Keddy, Frederick Angulo, and John Crump estimated the world burden of invasive nontyphoidal Salmonella disease for 2010 in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2015. Salmonella bacteria of this group are famous for gut infection and diarrhea. A separate, invasive form enters the blood, often without diarrhea, and had been left out of earlier global counts.

Drawing on reviews of bloodstream infections, especially in Africa, the authors calculate the invasive form's toll. It accounts for millions of illnesses and hundreds of thousands of deaths in a year. Africa bears most of that toll. In many African regions, these Salmonella strains cause most bloodstream infections found in community studies. The paper argues that prevention, diagnosis, and treatment plans built only on diarrheal disease miss a major killer.
europmc-pmc4499410:
J Gambini and ten co-authors reviewed resveratrol, a plant compound found in red wine, in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2015. Plants containing it have served in traditional medicine for over two thousand years. It can be taken by eating grapes and other foods, drinking wine, or swallowing supplement pills. Its structure lets it bind many biological molecules, which may explain its wide range of reported effects.

Studies in cells, animals, and humans credit resveratrol with anticancer, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-aging actions, among many others, and with effects on platelets and allergy. The sticking point is availability in the body: absorption is efficient, but the liver transforms it so fast that little free compound remains in circulation. The review gathers evidence on its metabolism, stability, and biological effects and judges which claimed benefits rest on solid ground.
europmc-pmc4508810:
Alison Beauchamp leads a nine-author team in a 2015 BMC Public Health survey of health literacy in Victoria, Australia. Health literacy covers how well people find, grasp, and use health information and services. The team asked which social groups hold strengths or gaps, since such gaps can drive unfair health outcomes and shape where help should go.

Clients of eight health and community care groups, 813 people in all, filled in the Health Literacy Questionnaire. The group averaged 72 years of age, 63% were women, and nearly half had not finished secondary school. Scores differed across most groups compared. People who did not speak English at home scored much lower on several scales. The pattern gives services a map of where support is most needed.
europmc-pmc4510710:
Zhenlan Fang, Bart Bueken, Dirk E. De Vos, and Roland A. Fischer review defect engineering in metal-organic frameworks for Angewandte Chemie in 2015. These frameworks are crystal sponges built from metal joints and organic links, with ordered pores. Real crystals always carry flaws, and the review argues those flaws can be designed rather than merely tolerated.

Flaws can tune how the material soaks up gases, speeds reactions, or carries charge and magnetism. The authors sort defect types, explain how to detect and measure them, and gather uses reported over past decades. They compare the approach with work on zeolites and related network solids. The review closes with where deliberate flaw design in these materials may lead next.
europmc-pmc4552010:
M. A. Bellis and five co-authors measure the adult disease toll of bad childhoods in England, in the Journal of Public Health in 2015. Adverse childhood experiences, such as abuse and household violence, are known to track with risky adult behavior. This national survey went further, linking them to major diseases and to early death, using sibling deaths as a stand-in measure.

The survey covered 3,885 adults aged 18 to 69 in 2013. Nearly half reported at least one adverse experience, and 8.3% reported four or more. Disease risk climbed steeply with count: four or more experiences went with far higher rates of cancer, diabetes, and stroke before age 70. The work frames childhood adversity as a driver of lifelong health costs.
europmc-pmc4562710:
Augustine T. Choko leads a twelve-author team trialing HIV self-testing in Malawi, in PLoS Medicine in 2015. Home testing by visiting counselors reaches many people but costs too much to sustain. Self-testing, where people test themselves with support nearby, could be cheaper and easier to repeat yearly.

In 14 neighborhoods of urban Blantyre, resident volunteers offered oral self-test kits to 16,660 adults, with demonstrations, counseling, and help linking into care. Over two years the team tracked how many tested, how accurate results were, and what happened after positive results, investigating every death. The study tests whether annual self-testing can run safely at community scale.
europmc-pmc4614810:
A. Murat Eren and colleagues presented a 2015 software platform called anvi'o for exploring microbial 'omics data. Sequencing now lets researchers read whole communities of microbes without growing them. Making sense of the resulting genomes needs tools that non-specialists can also drive. The paper appeared in PeerJ.

Anvi'o links data from several sources into one interactive display built around assembled genome pieces. Users can inspect single-letter DNA changes over time and place cultivated or single-cell genomes beside community data. The team re-analysed public datasets to show these uses. Because the platform is open source and visually guided, it aims to let more researchers perform and present deep analyses of large microbial datasets.
europmc-pmc4647710:
Huabin Zhang and Shao-Cong Sun published a 2015 review of NF-kappaB in inflammation and kidney disease. NF-kappaB is a family of gene switches central to immune responses. Kept inactive in the cell body, they activate through two pathways when infection or stress signals arrive. The review appeared in Cell and Bioscience.

While NF-kappaB is essential for fighting infection, runaway activation drives inflammatory disease. Evidence links it to kidney inflammation from infection, injury, and autoimmune attack, including conditions such as IgA nephropathy. The authors review how activation works in each kidney disease type and what is known about its targets there. The synthesis helps researchers judge where blocking this pathway might help kidney patients.
europmc-pmc4653610:
Abhishek D. Garg and a large group of colleagues published a 2015 classification review of damage-associated molecular patterns, or DAMPs, in immunogenic cell death. Some cancer treatments kill tumour cells in a way that alerts the immune system. Dying cells release DAMPs as the alert signals. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology.

When DAMPs are released, immune cells can mount tumour-targeting responses that mop up resistant leftover cells and leave lasting immune memory. The authors sort DAMPs by molecular type and trace their immune, laboratory, and clinical aspects. They also tabulate what is known and list open questions for the fast-growing field. The synthesis aims to help researchers design treatments that deliberately provoke this helpful form of cell death.
europmc-pmc4660210:
How mutations in the protein FUS drive ALS and frontotemporal dementia is the subject of a 2015 study by Takahiro Murakami and colleagues. FUS is an RNA-binding protein whose disordered tail lets it form liquid droplets and soft gels inside cells. These assemblies are part of normal RNA granule work. The study appeared in Neuron.

Disease mutations pushed the droplets into stiff, poorly soluble fibrillar gels unlike classic amyloids. Those gels trapped other granule components and disrupted granule function, including protein making at nerve endings. In a worm model, the assemblies were enough to cause nerve toxicity. Blocking their formation reduced the harm. The authors propose treatments that keep FUS assemblies reversible, a strategy that may extend to other RNA-binding proteins in these diseases.
europmc-pmc4702910:
Michael Ryan, Wing Chung Wong, Robert Brown, and five colleagues built TCGASpliceSeq, described in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. Alternative splicing lets one gene yield several protein versions, and cancers often rewire those choices. The Cancer Genome Atlas holds RNA data from over ten thousand tumors across thirty-three types, a rich splicing record that was too heavy for most researchers to process. The team's SpliceSeq software computed splicing measures for every sample in advance.

The website serves those precomputed values through a visual interface. Users can inspect one gene, hunt for the strongest splicing differences between tumor types, or compare tumor with nearby normal tissue. Charts show splicing patterns, read counts, and statistics together, and data can be downloaded for bigger analyses. Access is free to academic, government, and commercial users alike. The resource turns an intimidating archive into something a bench scientist can query in minutes.
europmc-pmc4707510:
Michele Zanoni, Filippo Piccinini, Chiara Arienti, and five colleagues studied reproducibility in 3D tumor spheroid testing, in Scientific Reports in 2016. Spheroids, balls of tumor cells with mixed growth states, promise more realistic drug screening than flat cell layers. Yet almost nothing was known about how repeatable spheroid data are. Using new open-source software that measures spheroid images automatically, the team hunted for sources of scatter in treatment responses.

Size and shape both mattered: large spheroids of uneven volume or outline answered treatments inconsistently. Comparing commercial viability tests built for 3D models, they picked and validated one that reports damage faithfully in spheroids up to a stated size. Their prescription is simple: pre-select spheroids of uniform volume and shape before any drug test. That discipline, they argue, is what will make 3D screening data worth trusting in drug development.
europmc-pmc4717410:
Paul D. Morris, Andrew Narracott, Hendrik von Tengg-Kobligk, and eight colleagues reviewed fluid-flow computing in heart medicine, in Heart in 2016. Computational fluid dynamics simulates how fluids move, a routine tool in safety-critical engineering. Applied to scans of a patient's vessels, it can compute pressures and flows no probe can measure directly, such as the stress blood exerts on vessel walls. The review weighs the method's benefits and obstacles.

Device design already leans on these simulations for stents, valves, and heart pumps. The frontier is personal: models built from one patient's imaging can forecast risk and rehearse treatments virtually. Combined with population models, they could make trials cheaper and safer. The authors also name the blockers, from methods to training, that groups are working through. Their verdict: a new era is coming, provided the groundwork is done honestly.
europmc-pmc4718210:
Stephen P. H. Alexander, Anthony P. Davenport, Eamonn Kelly, and eight colleagues plus the CGTP Collaborators compiled the G protein-coupled receptor section of the Concise Guide to PHARMACOLOGY 2015/16, in the British Journal of Pharmacology in 2015. The guide condenses knowledge of more than 1,750 human drug targets into short overviews, with pointers to a free online knowledgebase. These receptors form one of its eight target classes and the largest class of membrane proteins in the genome.

Each entry gives the official name, a pharmacology summary, the best probe compounds, and key references. The print edition is a fixed snapshot from late 2015, while the website version updates constantly. Produced with the international pharmacology union, the guide carries the official classification for these targets. For students and drug researchers, it is a citable map of the receptor family that modern medicines most often aim at.
europmc-pmc4736110:
Kazuto Yoshimi, Yayoi Kunihiro, Takehito Kaneko, and three colleagues achieved large CRISPR knock-ins in rat embryos using short single-stranded DNA donors, in Nature Communications in 2016. Inserting new genes into animal embryos is far harder than knocking genes out, especially for big inserts. The team combined CRISPR cutting with short single-stranded DNA pieces that bridge the cut ends to a donor. In rats, a one-thousand-base donor placed a glow gene at a chosen site.

Two guides plus two short donors then steered a 5.5-thousand-base construct into the Rosa26 safe harbor. The boldest test swapped in a two-hundred-thousand-base human gene cluster, and another replaced a fifty-eight-thousand-base rat gene cluster with its human counterpart. No custom homology arms were needed, which removes the slowest design step. The protocols promise genetically engineered rats, prized in drug research, carrying human-sized genetic cargo.
europmc-pmc4761110:
Javier Herrero leads a team of many co-authors in Database in 2016, setting out the comparative genome resources held by Ensembl. Comparing genomes across species is a basic way to read evolution, yet building the alignments and gene trees takes heavy computing. Ensembl maintains one shared, free set so labs need not rebuild it.

The resources align whole genomes in pairs and in groups, from which shared blocks, conserved spots, and locked-down stretches are drawn. Gene trees sort genes into families and mark which copies in which species count as the same gene. Special views show these links as tree plots and side-by-side maps. The paper stresses that the whole set updates on one steady frame, so results stay comparable across species and releases.
europmc-pmc4786410:
Diana M. Mitrea leads eleven authors in eLife in 2016 on how the nucleolus, the cell's ribosome factory, holds together without a membrane. The factory forms like oil drops in water, by a process called phase separation. A key protein, nucleophosmin, is rich in its outer zone, and the team asked what grips pull it into the drop.

They show nucleophosmin binds in several ways at once: to proteins carrying arginine-rich tags and to ribosomal RNA, the factory's product. Those same tags appear in the address labels that send proteins to the nucleolus. Pairs of sticky patches on the protein, plus its folding into five-part units, proved needed for drop forming in the dish and for settling in living cells. The work gives a parts list for how the factory assembles.
europmc-pmc4817710:
A. Murat Eren leads six authors in The ISME Journal in 2015 with a sharper way to sort microbe sequences. Surveys of a community read a marker gene from every member, then cluster near-identical reads into units. Fixed similarity cutoffs blur close kin, even when a single letter separates species that live in different niches.

Their method, minimum entropy decomposition, splits the data only at the letter positions that carry real information, a measure borrowed from information theory. Applied to sponges from the deep sea, it split one broad cluster into units faithful to each sponge species. On human mouth data it separated kinds differing by under one percent that nonetheless kept to distinct mouth sites. The method needs no hand tuning and little computing.
europmc-pmc4823510:
Young-Sun Lee and Hee-Sook Jun review diabetes drugs that also calm inflammation, in Mediators of Inflammation in 2016. The hormone GLP-1, released from the gut after eating, steadies blood sugar: it prompts insulin release, slows the stomach, and cuts appetite. Two drug families built on it, direct mimics and blockers of the enzyme that destroys it, are standard care for type 2 diabetes.

The review gathers evidence that these drugs also fight chronic inflammation far from the pancreas. Benefits have been reported in vessel disease, fatty liver, kidney damage, asthma, psoriasis, and brain disorders. The authors trace the molecular routes of the calming effect in lab and animal work, and argue the drugs' value may outgrow glucose control alone.
europmc-pmc4877810:
Jiyoung Kim, Jung-Hee Park, and Sujin Shin pooled trials in 2016 on simulation training in nursing education. Simulations let students rehearse care and choices on fake patients, from simple models to lifelike high-fidelity manikins. From 2,279 candidate papers, 40 studies fit the rules for pooling. Overall gains were solid, with the largest effects in hands-on skill.

Gains also appeared in knowledge and judgment, though sizes shifted by outcome type. Higher fidelity did not always beat lower fidelity by much, which matters since top models cost more. Schools can thus mix price levels with care. Simulation earns its place in nurse training, the pooled proof suggests, when matched to the skill taught.
europmc-pmc4886210:
Shorena Janelidze and co-authors measured amyloid protein pieces in blood plasma in Scientific Reports in 2016, in the Swedish BioFINDER group of 719 people. Blood tests for Alzheimer's markers would speed clinic use, since spinal fluid taps and brain scans are costly. The group covered healthy older adults, people with mild memory loss, and Alzheimer's patients, using an ultrasensitive test.

Blood levels of the two amyloid pieces tracked spinal fluid levels only weakly. Blood Aβ42 fell as brain amyloid rose on scans, a faint but real link. Plasma amyloid alone will not diagnose the disease, the data suggest. Its best use may be as one cheap screen among several, flagging who needs the costly tests.
europmc-pmc5029010:
Hasan Rehman, Ann W. Silk, Michael P. Kane, and Howard L. Kaufman review the first approved oncolytic virus therapy, in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer in 2016. Talimogene laherparepvec, or T-VEC, is a modified herpes virus injected straight into melanoma tumors. Regulators in the United States, Europe, and Australia had just approved it for advanced melanoma, yet community oncologists were slow to take it up.

The virus kills cancer cells it infects, and the dying cells prime a wider immune attack on tumors elsewhere in the body. A large randomized trial showed real benefit, and side effects were mostly mild flu-like symptoms and sore injection sites. The authors give hands-on advice on storage, handling, dosing, and judging response. They note the fit for older patients and those who cannot take other melanoma drugs, and look ahead to pairing T-VEC with checkpoint drugs.
europmc-pmc5031610:
Bin Ma and Michael O. Hottiger review the crosstalk between two master signaling pathways in Frontiers in Immunology in 2016. The Wnt/beta-catenin pathway guides embryo growth and tissue renewal, while NF-kappaB is the central switch for inflammation. Each can raise or lower the other, and both go wrong in cancer, immune disease, and metabolic disorders.

The review works through the contact points. Wnt signaling can quiet NF-kappaB's inflammatory gene sets in some settings and feed them in others. NF-kappaB returns the favor by steering beta-catenin's level and activity. Which way the balance tips depends on the cell, the tissue, and the trigger at hand. The authors caution that blanket claims about the pair mislead, and they map the links so future work can test each in its proper setting. For drug design, the network warns that pushing one pathway will move the other.
europmc-pmc509410:
Yong-Xu Wang and eight co-authors reported a mouse study in PLoS Biology in 2004 on PPARdelta, a gene switch in muscle. Exercise training can shift muscle toward slow, tireless fibers, but no single factor had been shown to direct that shift. The team switched on an active form of PPARdelta in mouse muscle.

The engineered mice grew more type I fibers, the slow kind rich in oxygen-using machinery, and could run up to twice as far as normal littermates. A drug that activates PPARdelta gave normal mice a similar fiber profile. The changed muscle also resisted obesity and showed healthier metabolism even without exercise. The study shows that traits like stamina and running capacity can be taken apart and adjusted at the molecular level.
europmc-pmc5127510:
Marlieke E. A. de Kraker, Andrew J. Stewardson, and Stephan Harbarth questioned a famous forecast in PLoS Medicine in 2016. A high-profile 2014 review for the United Kingdom government projected that drug-resistant infections could kill ten million people a year by 2050 without a global response. The figure is quoted everywhere, usually without its caveats.

The authors agree the burden of antimicrobial resistance is large and growing. But they argue the number rests on shaky ground. Data are weak on how many infections occur, how often they resist drugs, and how many deaths resistance itself causes. Building future models on unreliable present-day estimates, they warn, can mislead and even undermine the fight. They call for solid surveillance in rich and poor countries alike.
europmc-pmc5133610:
Anoop Babu Vasandan, Sowmya Jahnavi, Chandanala Shashank, Priya Prasad, Anujith Kumar, and S. Jyothi Prasanna studied how stem cells retrain immune cells, reporting in Scientific Reports in 2016. Mesenchymal stem cells are thought to help repair at sites where macrophages, the immune system's clean-up cells, meet injury.

Growing human macrophages together with the stem cells, they found naive macrophages became stronger germ killers, while inflammatory macrophages were calmed and shifted toward a repair state, which was itself boosted. The stem cells rewired the macrophages' energy use, and blocking a stem cell signal called PGE2 erased the effect, proving its central role. The retrained macrophages also spared human vessel-lining cells from inflammatory injury, showing the shift has practical protective value.
europmc-pmc5157710:
Meg Fluharty, Amy E. Taylor, Meryem Grabski, and Marcus R. Munafò reviewed smoking, depression, and anxiety in Nicotine and Tobacco Research, with the hosted text dated 2017. Many studies link smoking with mental illness, but which comes first has stayed murky. The team limited their review to studies that followed people over time.

Across 148 studies, sorted by outcomes such as starting to smoke, heaviness, dependence, and quitting paths, evidence ran both ways. Nearly half found that earlier depression or anxiety predicted later smoking behavior, while over a third found smoking predicted later depression or anxiety. Few studies tested both directions at once, and almost none reported no link at all. The authors call for stronger designs, such as gene-based methods, before any causal story is believed.
europmc-pmc5183610:
Pavel Pospíšil reviewed harmful oxygen chemistry in photosynthesis in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2016, writing solo. Photosystem II, the plant machinery that splits water for oxygen, inevitably leaks reactive oxygen species under strong light and heat, and those species can damage the cell.

The review maps each production route. Singlet oxygen arises when excited chlorophyll passes energy to oxygen, and also from damaged fats. On one side of the system, electrons leaking to oxygen form superoxide. That becomes peroxide and then hydroxyl radicals. On the other side, incomplete water splitting makes peroxide. Manganese converts that peroxide to hydroxyl radicals. Heat adds its own dark routes through fat breakdown. Knowing the exact chemistry, Pospíšil argues, shows how plants survive harsh conditions.
europmc-pmc5227110:
Zhen Qi and many colleagues showed how BMP signaling limits intestinal stem cells in Nature Communications in 2017. The gut lining renews itself every few days from Lgr5-positive stem cells at the base of small pockets called crypts. Bone morphogenetic protein, or BMP, acts as a brake on that growth, but the exact mechanism was not settled.

The experiments show BMP signaling in the lining is essential to stop stem cell overgrowth, both in normal upkeep and after damage. BMP switches off a large set of stem cell signature genes, including Lgr5 itself, through Smad proteins that recruit a gene-silencing enzyme, HDAC1, to those genes' control regions. The effect does not run through the rival Wnt pathway. Deleting Smad4 erased BMP's restraining effect entirely. The findings explain how the gut balances fast renewal against the cancer risk of unchecked growth.
europmc-pmc5253810:
D. P. D. Wilkie, assistant to the professor of clinical surgery at Edinburgh, tested retrograde venous embolism as a cause of acute stomach and duodenal ulcers in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1911. The experiments were done at the Royal College of Physicians laboratory in Edinburgh with Carnegie Trust funding. Surgeons knew the omentum, the fatty abdominal apron, seals off inflamed areas; Wilkie asked whether it could also carry disease to the stomach.

Earlier cases pointed that way: after hernia operations where omental pieces were tied off and removed, patients vomited altered blood the next day.
