Wilkie's experiments showed clots form readily in omental veins under mechanical, heat, and bacterial insults. Clot fragments can break free, ride backward up the gastric veins, and lodge in the vein web under the stomach lining, producing an ulcer there. He presents this as a proven route, with wider suggestions left for later work.
europmc-pmc5288410:
Ludger Klimek and a large team of colleagues issued a position paper on visual analogue scales for allergic rhinitis in Allergo Journal International in 2017, for German allergy and ear, nose, and throat societies. Allergic rhinitis, hay fever and its year-round kin, needs quick, repeatable measures of symptom severity and disease control for everyday care, not just for trials.

A visual analogue scale is a line on which the patient marks how bad symptoms feel, giving a fast score that research has validated against standard severity classes and quality-of-life questionnaires. Treatment studies have adopted it as an outcome measure. Digitization suits the scale well: it now sits inside a smartphone app, the Allergy Diary, offered in fifteen languages, which feeds a decision support system that helps direct treatment. The paper reviews the scale's history and methods and weighs the strengths and weaknesses of its forms.
europmc-pmc5359410:
Kelly L. Wyres and co-authors mapped the capsule gene sets of a hospital germ in Microbial Genomics in 2016. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a rising cause of ward infections, and many strains resist key drugs. Its sugar capsule is a prime attack tool and a typing mark. But lab typing of the capsule needs rare reagents, and many strains cannot be typed at all.

The team read the capsule gene sets in more than two thousand and five hundred genomes. They found more than a hundred distinct set types, dozens of them new. Gene parts swap between sets at a brisk rate, and two genes used by old typing schemes vary too much to trust. They built a shared naming scheme, a clean reference store, and a free tool called Kaptive that reads a strain's capsule type straight from its whole genome.
europmc-pmc5408810:
Jean-Philippe Fortin, Timothy J. Triche, and Kasper D. Hansen update a software package for DNA methylation data in a 2017 paper in Bioinformatics. Methylation arrays read chemical marks on DNA at set sites across the genome. A new array from Illumina covers nearly twice as many sites as its forerunner and reaches more gene control regions, but the old package, minfi, could not read it.

The authors describe the changes that let minfi handle the new array and mix data from both array types in one study. They add a cleaning method that works one sample at a time, which suits studies that grow bit by bit, and they advise using it when merging array generations. Old data sets can also help guess the cell mix of new samples. The update is free through Bioconductor.
europmc-pmc5422210:
Haarhuis and co-authors show how a release factor keeps chromosome loops from growing too long. Their research article appeared in Cell. Chromosomes fold into loops inside the nucleus. A ring-shaped protein complex called cohesin builds those loops. It links anchor sites marked by the protein CTCF. How far a loop can grow was not clear. Two partner factors pull in opposite ways.

The loader complex SCC2/SCC4 puts cohesin onto DNA. It also helps loops extend. WAPL does the reverse. It opens cohesin's ring and frees the DNA. The team found that WAPL limits loop size. Without it, loops grow larger and link wrongly aimed anchor sites. How long cohesin grips DNA sets how far loops enlarge. The results support a loop extrusion model of folding. They also frame domains called TADs as groups of loops in progress. Balance between loader and release factor keeps the structure right.
europmc-pmc5446110:
Snyder and co-authors hunt for signs that foretell who gains from a bladder cancer immunotherapy. Their exploratory analysis appeared in PLoS Medicine. The drug atezolizumab blocks the PD-L1 brake on immune cells. It can give lasting benefit in metastatic bladder cancer. Known markers predict that benefit poorly. The team layered several omic tests on trial patients. They sequenced tumor DNA and RNA.

The study drew on 29 patients from the IMvigor 210 trial. Patients with lasting benefit had more T cells inside their tumors. Low T cell clonality in blood before treatment linked to longer survival. After treatment, benefiters showed growth of tumor-linked T cell clones in blood. High blood clonality plus strong PD-L1 staining spelled poor outcomes. Mutation load alone failed to predict benefit. The authors stress the small sample. Their results raise hypotheses for larger prospective work.
europmc-pmc5534210:
Wilkinson and co-authors present a systematic review in Burnout Research on burnout and empathy among health workers. Empathy anchors good care, yet it is hard to define. Burnout drains staff through exhaustion, detachment, and lost pride. Whether the two feed or fight each other was unclear. The team screened the literature and kept ten solid studies.

Eight studies found a negative link, they report. More burnout came with less empathy. Only one study found the two rising together. Every included study passed the quality checks. Burnout itself proved a stable concept across cultures. Protecting empathy may start with easing exhaustion.
europmc-pmc5590510:
DeSalvo and co-authors issue a call to action in Preventing Chronic Disease. Health in the United States has improved for a century, yet gains have stalled. Life expectancy can differ by 20 years between neighborhoods a few miles apart. A person's zip code may shape health more than their genes.

Their answer is Public Health 3.0. Local health leaders act as chief health strategists. They partner across housing, transport, education, and business. The targets are the social and economic conditions that drive health and equity. The article sums up listening sessions held across the country in 2016. It ends with steps to spread the model. Readers get a plain case for broader public health work.
europmc-pmc5683310:
Cassandri and co-authors present a review in Cell Death Discovery. It surveys zinc-finger proteins in health and disease. These proteins form one of the largest protein groups known. A zinc ion holds each finger domain in shape. The domains can bind DNA, RNA, and other proteins. That reach puts the family inside many cell processes. Examples include gene control, DNA repair, and cell movement.

The review first sets out the classification scheme. Thirty zinc-finger types are now approved for naming. Structure and known functions are described for each. It then traces roles in normal development and tissue growth. Disease links follow, spanning cancer and brain decline. Skin disease and diabetes are covered as well.
europmc-pmc5695910:
Steger and co-authors report a proteomics study in eLife. It maps which Rab proteins the Parkinson's kinase LRRK2 modifies. LRRK2 mutations cause inherited Parkinson's disease. The kinase tags Rab GTPases at a conserved site. Rab proteins steer vesicle traffic inside cells. The team tested the full Rab family in turn. Mass spectrometry tracked which ones gained the tag.

Fourteen Rab proteins were tagged by LRRK2 specifically. Ten showed the tag at natural levels too. Tagged Rab8A and Rab10 bound a cilia regulator, RILPL1. Cilia are hair-like cell structures for signaling. Cells from mutant knock-in mice formed cilia at half rate. The work links LRRK2 to cilia building. Faulty transport at cilia may feed the disease.
europmc-pmc5715110:
Bankhead and co-authors present free software for studying digital pathology images. Their paper describes QuPath, built for whole slide image analysis. Scanned slides can be huge, and hand scoring is slow and uneven. Existing open tools did not handle such images well.

QuPath offers tools to find tumors and score biomarkers at high speed. Batch processing and scripting let users handle many slides at once. The design is flexible, so new methods can be added and shared. A tile-based viewer handles the very large files with ease. The platform also suits other kinds of biomedical image work. The authors aim to make tissue analysis more exact and repeatable.
europmc-pmc5746410:
Deng and co-authors review how single letter DNA changes, called SNPs, affect cancer risk. Many cancer linked genes carry such changes. They sit in promoters, exons, introns, and the untranslated ends of genes. Each site changes gene activity in its own way.

Promoter changes alter factor binding and gene switching. Exon changes can quiet a gene, while intron changes reshape splicing. Changes in the tail ends affect translation and small RNA binding. Marks laid on DNA add a further layer of effects. The authors weigh the use of SNPs as signs for diagnosis and care.
europmc-pmc5754410:
Cortez and co-authors review advances in ovarian cancer therapy. This cancer is usually found at an advanced stage. Surgery and chemo bring full remission for many patients. Still, relapse is common, and care becomes a cycle of quiet spans and returns.

The review covers the current standard of care first. It then takes up new forms of standard treatment. Targeted drugs include anti-angiogenic agents and PARP inhibitors. Growth factor and folate receptor blockers are covered, as are immune based methods. The authors also weigh costs and better matching of patients to treatments.
europmc-pmc5773910:
Chaput and co-authors review how sleep length links to health in children under five. The review gathers studies on many outcomes, from body fat to growth and mood. No date or design limits were set on the search. Evidence quality was graded with a standard framework.

The team kept 69 studies with close to 150,000 children from 23 countries. Shorter sleep tied to higher body fat in most studies that checked. It also tied to weaker mood control, slower growth, more screen time, and more injuries. Links to thinking, movement skills, and life quality stayed unclear, they report.
europmc-pmc5785010:
Zhang and co-authors study a guidance protein, Semaphorin3A, in corneal nerve repair. Corneal nerves are easily hurt by trauma, surgery, infection, or diabetes. In the embryo, this protein repels growing nerve fibers. After corneal injury, its levels rise fast. What it does in adult nerves stayed unclear.

In adult mouse neurons, the protein did not block growth, they report. Given alone, it spurred growth much like a classic growth factor. In living mice with scraped corneas, pellets of the protein sped nerve regrowth. The protein seems to switch roles, from repellent in development to helper in the adult.
europmc-pmc5825910:
Bridi and Hirth review how alpha-synuclein damages synapses early in Parkinson's disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. The protein normally sits at nerve terminals and aids signal release. In disease it clumps into Lewy bodies, and its small toxic clumps gather at terminals first.

The authors trace several failures that follow. Vesicle pools shrink and their movement falters. Proteins of the SNARE fusion machinery get scattered or misregulated. Vesicle recycling slows, so transmitters release poorly. Dopamine control also slips, feeding still more toxic clumps. This cycle of failing synapses, they argue, starts the wider nerve loss.
europmc-pmc5826010:
Tainio and co-authors pool studies on watching, not treating, CIN2 lesions. CIN2 marks moderate abnormal cell growth on the cervix. Standard care removes the tissue, but many lesions vanish alone. Removal can harm later pregnancies, so the trade-off matters.

Their review joins 36 studies and 3,160 women under active surveillance. At 24 months, half the lesions had regressed. About a third persisted, and 18 percent progressed. Women under 30 fared better, with 60 percent regression. About one in ten women skipped follow-up visits. Readers get the numbers behind a watch-and-wait choice for younger patients.
europmc-pmc5833710:
Schaaf, Garg, and Agostinis review how a tumor's blood vessels help it hide from the immune system. Their review appeared in Cell Death & Disease. Tumors grow crooked vessels to feed their hunger. Those vessels leave the tissue short of oxygen and hard to enter.

Vessel walls block T cells from reaching cancer cells. Endothelial cells also dampen T cell recruitment and action directly. Remodeled lymph vessels ease spread and deepen immune suppression. This shield helps explain why checkpoint drugs often fail. The authors survey vessel-fixing treatments that could reopen tumors to immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc5884210:
Lee reviews the double role of zinc in cell oxidative stress. The review appeared in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Zinc is an essential trace metal for human health. Lack of it harms nerves and immune function. Zinc itself does not change redox state. Yet it supports enzymes and shields proteins from harm.

Too little zinc can raise oxidative stress, Lee reports. Too much zinc can raise it as well. Zinc helps a key superoxide enzyme work. It also lifts levels of metallothionein, a metal-binding protein. The review covers how cells control free zinc inside. Mitochondrial balance and inflammation are also addressed. Readers learn when zinc protects and when it harms.
europmc-pmc5923710:
González-Bueso and co-authors review links between gaming disorder and other mental conditions. Their comprehensive review appeared in an environmental and public health journal. They searched five databases for studies on internet gaming disorder. Twenty-four articles met their rules for inclusion. Most were cross-sectional and based in Europe. Effect sizes were gathered or computed anew.

Gaming disorder correlated most often with anxiety, they report. Depression showed the next strongest pattern of links. ADHD symptoms and social anxiety also appeared often. Obsessive-compulsive symptoms were linked in three quarters of studies. Men showed higher rates in most work. Few long-term studies exist, so direction stays unclear.
europmc-pmc5960010:
Broadhurst and co-authors give guidelines for system suitability and quality control samples in untargeted clinical metabolomic studies. Their tutorial review appeared in Metabolomics. Such studies use mass spectrometry to measure many metabolites at once. Quality assurance and quality control keep the data trustworthy. System suitability samples check the platform before real samples run. They reveal contamination or poor operation early.

Isotope-labelled internal standards track stability for each sample, the authors explain. Pooled quality control samples condition the platform during a study. They also measure reproducibility and correct systematic errors. Reference materials support checks across studies and laboratories. The review shows how to apply each sample type and report data quality.
europmc-pmc6004510:
Boateng and co-authors offer a primer on best practices for developing and validating measurement scales. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Public Health. Scales underpin much health, social, and behavioural research. Building a good one demands many varied techniques. Graduate training often skips that skill set entirely. The primer lays out three phases spanning nine steps. First, items are generated and their content validity checked.

Next, the scale is built through pre-testing and surveys. Item counts shrink and factor structure is explored. Last, dimensions, reliability, and validity are tested formally. Worked examples of good practice fill each step. The guide serves both researchers and practitioners.
europmc-pmc6041410:
Moreno-García and co-authors review lipofuscin and its role in brain aging. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Lipofuscin is a glowing pigment that builds up inside nerve cells. It mixes lipids, metals, and misfolded proteins. Doctors long treated it as a harmless mark of aging.

New evidence points to a more active role. The pigment disturbs the cell skeleton and internal traffic. It is linked to neuron loss and glial activation. The authors argue it may drive neurodegeneration, not just follow it. Diseases in view include Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Readers get a case for studying this pigment as a risk factor. It reframes a classic aging sign as a possible cause.
europmc-pmc6131510:
Maiullari and co-authors present a research article in Scientific Reports on 3D bioprinting of heart tissue with blood vessels. Heart muscle works only when its many cell types act in concert. Lab-grown heart tissue has lacked vessel networks. That limits its size and its use in repair.

The team printed strands of gel holding two cell types. One type forms vessel linings. The other, grown from stem cells, forms heart muscle cells. A custom printing head placed the strands with fine control. The muscle cells aligned well along the print paths. When grafted into animals, the vessel-like shapes linked with host vessels. The authors see a step toward working heart patches.
europmc-pmc6143810:
Karl and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Microbiology on stress and the gut microbiota. Stress is a daily part of human life. It can shift the mix of microbes living in the gut. Those microbes, in turn, shape how the body handles stress.

The review covers mental stress, broken sleep, and shifted daily rhythms. It also covers heat, cold, high altitude, noise, and pollutants. Diet and hard exercise are included too. Animal studies show these stressors change gut microbe makeup and output. Human proof is still thin. The stressors were picked with military life in mind. The authors call for studies that test these links in people.
europmc-pmc6155610:
Sharifi-Rad and co-authors wrote a review in Molecules on the biological activities of essential oils. Essential oils are complex mixes made by plants, stored in glands on flowers and leaves. They play a key role in plant ecology, shaping dealings with insects and microbes. Humans have used them in healing systems since ancient times.

The review moves from that plant role to lab evidence of health effects. Preclinical studies report antimicrobial, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory actions. Traditional uses around the world are surveyed as well. One section follows lavender oil used for pain relief and wound care after childbirth. Readers get a broad map of what these oils do and how they are used.
europmc-pmc6166610:
Mollan and co-authors present joint guidelines in Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry on a condition where pressure inside the skull rises with no clear cause. It is called idiopathic intracranial hypertension. It can harm sight if it is not caught. Care spans many fields, and practice varied a lot.

A large expert group met from 2015 to 2017 to build national guidance for the United Kingdom. It drew on brain, eye, and surgery specialists, nurses, front-line doctors, and patient voices. The group first surveyed doctors who treat the condition. Then it reviewed the published studies in full. The guidelines cover how to spot, track, and treat the condition, aiming for one shared standard of good care.
europmc-pmc6186810:
Sakr and co-authors wrote an updated review in Frontiers in Microbiology on Staphylococcus aureus living in the human nose. Up to 30 percent of people carry this bacterium in their nostrils permanently, without symptoms. To settle there, it must grip nasal lining cells and beat host defenses. Other nasal bacteria can help or hinder it.

The review covers the mechanisms of colonization and who is at risk. Host traits and environmental factors both predispose some people to carriage. Carriers face higher chances of later infections, including surgical site infections. Those infections raise illness, deaths, and health-care costs. The update pulls mechanisms, epidemiology, and risk factors into one reference for clinicians and researchers.
europmc-pmc6251310:
Glantz and Bareham review e-cigarettes, their risks, and what policy should do. Their review appeared in the Annual Review of Public Health. E-cigarettes heat a liquid to make a nicotine aerosol, with no burning. Some experts have backed them as a safer path away from smoking. They do deliver lower levels of cancer causing chemicals than cigarettes. But they still give high doses of fine particles and other toxins.

The authors argue that heart and lung risks may stay close to those of smoking. Those risks drive more than half of smoking deaths. Rather than helping smokers quit, the products may be slowing quit rates. Youth uptake is also widening the nicotine market. The review weighs use patterns, health effects, and policy options together. Its stance favours tighter control of the products.
europmc-pmc6305110:
Long and co-authors review LAG-3, a promising immune checkpoint in cancer. The review appeared in Genes and Cancer. Checkpoint drugs like PD-1 blockers changed cancer care. Yet many patients do not respond to them. LAG-3 offers another target in the tumor setting. It calms T cell activity and cytokine release.

The authors explain how LAG-3 acts on several lymphocyte types. It pairs closely with PD-1 to deepen immune restraint. Trials now test LAG-3 blockers on their own. Combined LAG-3 and PD-1 blockade shows strong early results. It may even beat resistance to PD-1 drugs. The review maps where this therapy could head next.
europmc-pmc6316710:
Santana-Codina and Mancias review ferritinophagy, a process that frees stored iron in cells. The review appeared in Pharmaceuticals. A protein called NCOA4 guides ferritin to destruction. Ferritin is the cell's iron storage cage. Breaking it down releases iron on demand. This balance supports red blood cell making.

The process also feeds into ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. Iron problems appear in brain disease, cancer, and infection. Little is known about this pathway in those settings. The authors map how NCOA4 itself is regulated. They weigh turning the pathway up or down as therapy. Such drugs might correct iron imbalance in patients.
europmc-pmc6343010:
Liu and co-authors identify a circular RNA that pushes breast cancer forward. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Disease. Circular RNAs often work by sponging microRNAs. The team screened breast cancer circRNAs by computer first. One, hsa_circ_001783, ranked at the top. Tests confirmed it runs high in cancer tissue and cells.

Higher levels meant heavier tumors and poorer survival. Silencing the ring slowed cell growth and invasion. It acts by soaking up the microRNA miR-200c-3p. That microRNA normally restrains cancer cell behavior. Freeing its targets lets progression resume. The authors propose the ring as a prognostic marker. They also name it a possible treatment target. The work adds breast cancer to the circRNA map.
europmc-pmc6365110:
Zheng and co-authors present a research article in Science Advances on gut bacteria and schizophrenia. The team first compared gut microbes from 63 patients with 69 healthy controls. Patients showed lower microbial diversity and distinct bacterial groups tied to symptom severity.

The team then transferred patient gut microbes into germ-free mice. Those mice became hyperactive and showed stronger startle responses, unlike mice given control microbes. Chemical tests found disturbed glutamate, glutamine, and GABA levels in blood and brain. The authors argue that gut microbes may take part in schizophrenia through the gut-brain axis. They propose the pathway as a route toward new diagnosis and treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc6366910:
Broman and co-authors present a software article in Genetics. They introduce R/qtl2, an R package for mapping quantitative trait loci in experimental populations. The tool extends the widely used R/qtl package to modern datasets and breeding designs.

The new package supports multiparent populations such as Collaborative Cross and Diversity Outbred mice. It handles high-dimensional data, including gene expression traits used in eQTL mapping. It also reconstructs founder haplotypes and imputes whole genomes for study animals. The authors describe the data structures and workflows in detail. Geneticists get an open, extensible system for crosses that the older package could not handle.
europmc-pmc6367010:
Senzai and co-authors present a research article in Neuron on the layered structure of mouse visual cortex. They recorded from all layers at once in awake, freely moving mice. Their aim was to link broad electrical patterns, called local field potentials, to the firing of single neurons in each layer.

Gamma rhythm coherence and spike coupling defined six physiological layers, plus sublayers. Firing rates and burst patterns differed by layer and by brain state. Signals from layer 2/3 to layer 5 grew stronger during waking than in non-REM sleep. A subset of deep neurons fired only in the DOWN state of sleep. The results tie mesoscopic signals to laminar anatomy.
europmc-pmc6394610:
Sochocka and co-authors offer a critical review in Molecular Neurobiology on gut microbes and Alzheimer's disease. Gut bacteria talk to the brain in both directions. Some call this community a second brain, the authors note.

Gut bacteria make brain-active compounds like serotonin, and even amyloid proteins. Changes in the gut community may feed inflammation that harms the brain. The review weighs evidence for that chain and its weak points. It also asks how diet and daily habits shift gut microbes. Firm proof in humans is still missing, they caution.
europmc-pmc6401010:
Lu and co-authors report a materials study in Nature Communications. A conducting polymer called PEDOT:PSS can link electronics with living tissue. Past hydrogels mixed it with other polymers, which weakened its key traits.

Their method forms a pure hydrogel from tangled polymer nanofibrils. A solvent is mixed in, then the gel is dried, heated, and soaked again. The result conducts well while staying soft and stretchy. Such traits suit sensors and stimulators placed on or in the body. The authors present it as a cleaner base for bioelectronic devices.
europmc-pmc6432010:
Le and co-authors survey the electrical and electrochemical behavior of conducting polymers, plastics that carry current much like semiconductors or metals. Mild synthesis, flexible shapes, and adjustable conductivity make these materials attractive for electronics and energy devices. Nanostructuring has widened their uses still further in recent years.

Early sections explain how charge moves through the polymer chains and which factors, from chain length to crystallinity, raise or lower performance. Size and shape of the material receive close attention as design levers. Closing sections track two fast-moving applications, electrochemical capacitors and sensors, through the standout studies published since 2003.
europmc-pmc6433910:
Zhong and co-authors test soluble TREM2, a protein fragment shed by microglia, as a treatment in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. TREM2 variants raise Alzheimer's risk, and the soluble form rises in spinal fluid alongside markers of neuron injury. Its actual role in the disease was unresolved.

Delivered into the brains of 5xFAD mice, soluble TREM2 cut amyloid plaque load and restored spatial memory and synaptic plasticity. It pushed microglia to multiply, migrate, cluster around plaques, and eat and degrade amyloid. Removing microglia erased the benefit entirely. Raising soluble TREM2 therefore looks like a plausible therapy route worth pursuing.
europmc-pmc6444510:
Li and co-authors review the cGAS-STING pathway as a sensitizer that could make cancer immunotherapy work in more patients. The pathway senses stray DNA inside cells and answers with type I interferon, which matures dendritic cells, sharpens killer T and natural killer cells, and protects effector cells from death. That bridge between innate and adaptive immunity is the attraction.

Resistance, both immediate and acquired, still limits vaccines, checkpoint blockade, and CAR T cell therapy. Pairing a STING activator with each approach is surveyed, along with lessons from failure. The early agent DMXAA killed mouse tumors, yet it failed in a phase III human trial because it binds only mouse STING.
europmc-pmc6463810:
Höglund and co-authors compare how tryptophan handling feeds brain serotonin across backboned animals, from fish to mammals, and how stress reroutes the supply. Tryptophan is the raw stuff of serotonin, and extra tryptophan in food often calms aggression and blunts post-stress cortisol in many species. Only hindbrain neurons that use the TPH2 enzyme, though, seem limited by how much tryptophan arrives.

Most tryptophan in fact flows down the kynurenine pathway, opened by liver TDO and by IDO, which inflammation switches on. Long stress and infection can thus starve serotonin making by stealing the pool. Sharp stress may do the reverse, through the stress nerves. Fish data and effects of dietary fat round out the comparison.
europmc-pmc6487510:
Feng and co-authors read China's cancer ledger for 2018, asking whether the news is good or bad. An estimated 4.3 million new cases and 2.9 million deaths made cancer the country's leading killer. Incidence runs lower than in the United States or United Kingdom, yet mortality is 30 to 40 percent higher, a gap demanding explanation.

Part of it is case mix: digestive cancers of stomach, liver, and esophagus supply 36.4 percent of China's cancer deaths against at most 5 percent in either Western country, and they carry grim prognoses. Late diagnosis and uneven treatment add to the toll. Smoking drives about 24.5 percent of male cancers and chronic infection about 17 percent, while roughly 40 percent of risk is judged preventable.
europmc-pmc6591610:
Diekema and co-authors chart twenty years of bloodstream infection microbiology from the SENTRY surveillance program, writing in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. The program collected 264,901 infection isolates from over 200 medical centers in 45 nations between 1997 and 2016, all identified and drug-tested at one central laboratory.

Two organisms dominate throughout: Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli together caused over 40% of infections. Their balance shifted, though — E. coli's share climbed from about 19% to 24% while S. aureus slipped from about 23% to 19%, and Gram-negative bacteria gained ground overall. Pneumococcus faded to under 2%, and drug-resistant staph rose until the mid-2000s before retreating in every region. The tables break the patterns down by region, age and where infection began.
europmc-pmc6611910:
Czystowska-Kuzmicz and co-authors show how ovarian tumors ship an immune brake in tiny vesicles. Their research article appears in Nature Communications. Ovarian cancer resists immunotherapy in most patients. Its tumors build a strongly suppressive local setting. The enzyme arginase-1 is one known suppressor of T cells.

The team found arginase-1 inside small extracellular vesicles from patients. The vesicles occur in both ascites fluid and plasma. They curbed CD4 and CD8 T-cell growth in lab tests. In mice, vesicles reached draining lymph nodes and entered dendritic cells. They then blocked antigen-specific T-cell responses. Tumors rich in arginase-1 grew faster in mice. An arginase inhibitor could block that effect.
europmc-pmc6688310:
Huria and co-authors present the CONSIDER statement for reporting health research with Indigenous peoples. Their guideline paper appears in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Indigenous communities face severe health gaps. Research on them carries a legacy of abuse. Reporting rules improve research quality generally. None targeted Indigenous involvement head-on. The team merged seven national rule sets. Sources spanned Australia, Canada, and New Zealand. Hawaii, Taiwan, the United States, and Sami regions gave sets as well. Eighty-eight draft items were merged down.

Eight domains frame the final checklist. Seventeen points cover oversight through sharing results. Relationships, taking part, and capacity feature strongly. The statement aims to strengthen research practice. Clear reporting should advance Indigenous health.
europmc-pmc6738410:
Lu and co-authors built a DNA-based estimator of telomere length. Telomeres are the caps on chromosome ends, and their length tracks with aging diseases. The new estimator reads 140 chemical mark sites on DNA in white blood cells. It works across the full human age span.

The estimator tracked age far more strongly than directly measured telomere length. It also beat direct measures in predicting time to death, heart disease, and heart failure. Links to smoking history were stronger too. Validation used about 10,000 samples from seven large studies. Cell experiments suggest the marks partly record how often cells have divided, not length alone.
europmc-pmc6751310:
Guzman-Martinez and co-authors argue that neuroinflammation is a shared feature of neurodegenerative diseases. These diseases begin with proteins that unfold and clump inside neurons. Tau in Alzheimer's, alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's, and huntingtin in Huntington disease all follow this pattern. The clumps are toxic and the damage spreads across the brain.

The authors trace the trigger to inflammation between glial cells and neurons. Activated microglia and astrocytes release signals such as TNF-alpha and interleukins. Those signals overactivate enzymes inside neurons and push proteins toward clumping. The same sequence, they propose, runs in several diseases. That would make brain inflammation a common treatment target across them.
europmc-pmc6838110:
Fok and co-authors report a study in Nature Communications on a drug called AZD7648. The drug blocks DNA-PK, an enzyme that repairs double-strand breaks in DNA. Cancer cells under attack by radiation or chemotherapy lean hard on such repair. Blocking it should leave damage unrepaired and kill the cell.

AZD7648 proved potent and selective in lab tests. Combined with radiation or the drug doxorubicin, it caused lasting tumour shrinkage in mouse models, including tumours grown from patient samples. Paired with the PARP inhibitor olaparib, it strongly harmed cells lacking the repair gene ATM. Normal cells were less affected. The authors present the drug as a booster for existing cancer treatments.
europmc-pmc6841710:
Liao and co-authors report a study in Nature Communications on an inflammation-calming compound. When macrophages switch on, they change how they make energy, favouring fast sugar burning called aerobic glycolysis. That switch fuels their attack mode. A natural metabolite, itaconate, reins them in. The team used a form that enters cells, 4-octyl itaconate, to find out how.

The compound latched onto the glycolysis enzyme GAPDH at one spot, cysteine residue 22, and cut its activity. Sugar tracing showed the flow of glycolysis blocked at that step. With glycolysis curbed, inflammatory output fell. Other glycolysis blockers copied the effect. The result names a precise lever for calming harmful inflammation.
europmc-pmc6855510:
Creamer and co-authors report national tobacco figures in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Cigarette smoking remains the leading preventable cause of disease and death in the United States. Its rate has fallen for decades. New products such as e-cigarettes, though, have reshaped the market. Federal agencies analysed the 2018 National Health Interview Survey to take stock.

An estimated 49.1 million adults, 19.7 percent, used some tobacco product in 2018. Cigarettes led at 13.7 percent, their lowest level since 1965. Cigars, e-cigarettes, and smokeless tobacco followed. Most users, 83.8 percent, used products that burn. The report also tracks quit attempts and success among smokers.
europmc-pmc6859310:
Clark and co-authors report a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences comparing foods on two scoreboards at once. What people eat drives both disease and environmental harm. Food choices threaten global climate and health goals together. Yet foods are usually judged on one side only. The team set out to join the two.

They linked 15 food groups to 5 health outcomes and 5 measures of environmental damage. Foods tied to better adult health, such as whole grains, nuts, and vegetables, also tended to burden the planet least. Unprocessed red meat scored badly on both counts. The authors argue one dietary shift can serve both agendas.
europmc-pmc6868810:
Zhao and Shilatifard review histone marks in cancer, in Genome Biology. DNA in a cell is wound around spools of protein called histones; 147 base pairs wrap each spool. Chemical marks on the histones help decide which genes are read. Those marks are versatile and tightly tied to development. When the marking goes wrong, cancer can follow.

The review catalogues the main kinds of histone modification and the enzymes that add or remove them. Many of those enzymes are altered in tumours. Small-molecule inhibitors against them now exist as research tools, and some are in clinical study. The authors explain how the tools reveal what each mark does.
europmc-pmc6915110:
Quintero-Fabián and co-authors review matrix metalloproteinases in angiogenesis and cancer. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Oncology. These enzymes, called MMPs, break down tissue scaffolds. That step lets new blood vessels form. It also helps tumours spread.

The authors trace how MMPs degrade basement membranes. They show how the enzymes remodel the matrix around cells. Endothelial cells can then migrate and multiply. Tissue inhibitors, called TIMPs, rein in MMP activity. The balance of pro- and anti-vessel factors shifts as a result. The review gathers recent work on these steps. It links them to tumour growth, vessel growth, and metastasis.
europmc-pmc7026710:
The GBD 2017 Cirrhosis Collaborators assess cirrhosis and other chronic liver diseases in The Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology. Cirrhosis kills and disables large numbers of people, yet its causes differ widely between places and groups. The collaborators report burden and trends from 1990 to 2017 for 195 countries and territories, broken down by cause, sex, and age.

Estimates rest on vital registration and verbal autopsy data for deaths, and on hospital and claims data for prevalence. The team split cirrhosis into five causes: hepatitis B, hepatitis C, alcohol-related liver disease, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, and other causes. In 2017 cirrhosis caused more than 1.32 million deaths worldwide. Comparing observed burden with levels expected from development status highlights where prevention and treatment lag behind.
europmc-pmc7084410:
Havis and Duprez review the transcription factor EGR1 and its control of matrix production in tendons and other connective tissues, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. EGR1 switches genes on and off, and many signals can trigger it. Its activity keeps turning up in tissues built around extracellular matrix, the scaffold between cells.

EGR1 helps shape tendon, cartilage, bone, and fat tissue as they develop, maintain themselves, and heal. It drives genes for collagens and other matrix parts. When matrix is overproduced, as in fibrosis, EGR1 is often involved, which makes it a possible drug target. Tendon repair is flagged as one use needing more study.
europmc-pmc7113510:
Prado, Purcell, and Laviano review nutrition strategies for treating low muscle mass in cancer, in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle. Many cancer patients lose muscle severely, at any stage of illness, and low muscle worsens outcomes. It often hides alongside obesity, so weight alone misses it.

Evidence for nutrition treatment is patchy, partly because few studies measure body composition well. The authors give working targets: 25 to 30 kilocalories and 1.0 to 1.5 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight daily. Supplements such as leucine, creatine, and fish oil are weighed, as are combined plans pairing nutrition with exercise and drugs. Longer, better-designed trials are the main need.
europmc-pmc7147910:
Schillie and co-authors issue the CDC's updated hepatitis C screening recommendations for United States adults, in MMWR Recommendations and Reports. Hepatitis C spreads mainly through contact with infected blood, most often from injection drug use. No vaccine exists, but direct-acting antiviral courses of 8 to 12 weeks cure most infections.

Two recommendations are new. All adults aged 18 and over should be screened at least once in their lifetime, and pregnant women should be screened in every pregnancy, except where infection prevalence is under 0.1%. Testing of people with risk factors continues regardless of age, and anyone who asks for a test should receive one, since many hide stigmatised risks.
europmc-pmc7215310:
Yang and co-authors review how skin barrier failure and immune dysfunction combine in atopic dermatitis. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The disease brings inflamed, chronically itchy skin that keeps returning. It was once seen as mainly a childhood condition. Evidence now shows adults carry it more often than assumed.

Barrier defects let irritants and microbes through the skin. Immune responses then skew toward the Th2 pattern, with its signature cytokines. A signal called TSLP helps drive that skewing and activates other immune cells. The disease also raises the risk of asthma, food allergy, and hay fever later. The review ties genetics, experiments, and clinical findings together. It highlights TSLP as one promising treatment target.
europmc-pmc7232010:
Lukassen and co-authors locate the lung cells that carry both entry factors for SARS-CoV-2. Their study appeared in The EMBO Journal. The virus binds ACE2, then uses TMPRSS2 to prime its spike. Which airway cells hold both was a key question for understanding infection. The team sequenced single nuclei from lung tissue of 12 donors.

They counted 39,778 cells in that dataset. A second set held 17,521 cells from bronchial branches of 4 donors. TMPRSS2 was widespread, but ACE2 was rarer and unevenly spread. Both factors concentrated in transient secretory cells of the bronchi. A third factor, FURIN, may also help prime the virus. The map points to the cells first in the virus's path.
europmc-pmc7277610:
Knight and co-authors describe every pregnant woman admitted to hospital with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in the United Kingdom during the first pandemic weeks. Their national cohort study appeared in The BMJ. Data came from all 194 obstetric units through the UK Obstetric Surveillance System, covering March 1 to April 14, 2020.

The cohort held 427 women, an admission rate of 4.9 per 1000 maternities. More than half were from black or other ethnic minority groups, and 69% were overweight or obese. Most women who gave birth did so at term. Forty-one women needed respiratory support and five died. Twelve of 265 infants tested positive for the virus, six within the first 12 hours after birth.
europmc-pmc7320010:
Schmidt and co-authors sharpen a genetic method, Mendelian randomisation, for judging whether a protein is a good drug target. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications. The method uses genetic variants as natural instruments to test whether a risk factor truly causes disease. Its weak spot is horizontal pleiotropy, where a variant influences disease through a second, unrelated pathway.

When the risk factor is a protein, that worry shrinks. Proteins are the direct products of genes and the proximal effectors of biology, and most medicines target proteins. The authors build a mathematical framework contrasting protein targets with risk factors further down the causal chain. It guides key model decisions, boosts statistical power, and tests how robust a target-validation result really is before money is spent on drug development.
europmc-pmc7323510:
Guo and co-authors map how widely SARS-CoV-2 contaminates hospital wards in Wuhan, testing both air and surfaces. Their study appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. Knowing where the virus lands matters for staff safety and for judging transmission routes. Contamination was heavier in intensive care units than in general wards.

Viral traces were widely distributed on floors, computer mice, trash cans, and bed handrails. The virus was also detected in air about 4 meters from patients, further than classic droplet guidance assumed. Intensive care areas, packed with the sickest patients and the most procedures, carried the greatest load. The findings supported stronger cleaning, distancing within wards, and attention to airborne precautions around COVID-19 care.
europmc-pmc7333410:
Huang and co-authors review advances in CAR-T cell engineering in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. CAR-T therapy retools a patient's own T cells with a synthetic receptor so they hunt cancer. Early products worked well against blood cancers but faced relapse and resistance.

The review walks through upgrades to each part of the receptor, from the targeting head to the signaling tail. Fourth-generation cells add an immune modifier to help them work inside solid tumors. Better manufacturing and new cell sources also promise stronger, longer-lasting cells. Readers get a clear tour of how engineers are trying to widen a powerful therapy beyond its first successes.
europmc-pmc7375210:
Koyama and co-authors catalogue the genome variants of SARS-CoV-2 in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. Between February and May 2020 they downloaded 10,022 viral genomes from patients in 68 countries. Each genome was aligned against the reference to list its changes.

They found 5,775 distinct variants, including 2,969 that change a protein and 1,965 silent ones. The commonest included the spike change D614G, seen in 6,294 samples, which later swept the world. The genomes sorted into six major clades and 14 subclades. C-to-T base changes were the most frequent type. Readers get an early family tree of a new virus, built while the pandemic was still young.
europmc-pmc7413410:
Huang and co-authors compare emotional responses of nurses and nursing students during China's COVID-19 outbreak in PLoS ONE. More than 3,000 medical staff in China had been infected, and nurses stood closest to patients. An online survey ran in Anhui Province from 1 to 20 February 2020, spread by snowball sampling.

Women reported more severe anxiety and fear than men. City participants showed more anxiety and fear, while rural participants felt more sadness. Living nearer an outbreak zone intensified anxiety and anger. Frontline nurses were hit harder than students, the authors found. Coping styles differed between the groups as well. The study argues that emotional support should be graded by exposure, not offered uniformly to everyone in a white uniform.
europmc-pmc7501310:
Ning and co-authors give a framework, iCAMP, that measures what builds microbial communities. Selection, dispersal, diversification, and drift all shape communities. Weighing their shares has been very hard.

The method sorts microbes into family bins and runs null models on each bin. On fake communities it scored high on accuracy and allied measures. It beat whole-community methods by wide margins in those tests. Applied to grassland microbes under experimental warming, it found two dominant forces. Steady selection drove 38% of assembly and drift 59% in the warmed plots studied. Warming cut drift over time and raised selection, tied to drought and plant growth. The tool may serve plant and animal ecology too.
europmc-pmc7529510:
Sun, Liu and Yang review ubiquitination in cancer metabolism. Cancer cells rewire how they build molecules and make energy. This rewiring helps them grow under stress.

Ubiquitination tags proteins through a multi-step enzyme process. Removing those tags is called deubiquitination. Both steps can tune metabolic pathways in cancer cells. The review tracks effects on energy use and redox balance. It also covers effects on making large molecules. Faults in these systems help drive disease. The authors argue that the pathways offer drug targets. Readers get an overview of a fast-moving field in cancer research.
europmc-pmc7589810:
Everts, Onishi, Jayaram, Lana and Mautner review platelet-rich plasma therapy and new findings on its action. PRP uses a patient own blood fraction rich in platelets. It may aid repair in muscle, spine and wound care.

Platelet growth factors support the three phases of healing. Those phases are inflammation, growth and remodeling of tissue. Many PRP formulas have been tested in labs and animals. Human results often differ from lab-based guidance. The review covers platelet dosing and formula makeup. White cell effects on immunity and pain are discussed. Serotonin effects and drug interactions are covered too. Pairing PRP with rehabilitation plans is also reviewed for care.
europmc-pmc7610710:
Peng, Gong, Beckmann, Vedaldi and Smith present a light deep network for predicting brain age from MRI. Deep learning can predict disease from brain scans. Small datasets and memory limits often hold it back.

Their model is called Simple Fully Convolutional Network. It has fewer parameters than popular deep models. That suits small samples and 3D volume data. Tricks included data augmentation and pre-training steps. Ensembles and bias correction also boosted results. On UK Biobank data with 14,503 people, error was 2.14 years. Sex classification reached 99.5% accuracy there. The model won a 2019 prediction challenge as well. Code was released for other imaging tasks.
europmc-pmc7616810:
Romanello and co-authors lead the 2023 Countdown report, calling for a health-centred climate response. It is the eighth report in the series. Findings show few signs of the progress urged before.

A total of 114 scientists and health experts contributed. They came from 52 research bodies and UN agencies. Mean heating stood at 1.14°C above pre-industrial levels. Heat records broke on all continents through 2022. Older adults and infants now face twice the heatwave days. That compares with what they would have seen in 1986–2005. Over 60% of hot days in 2020 were made far more likely by human-caused change. Heat deaths in older adults rose by 85% versus 1990–2000.
europmc-pmc7665310:
Wolff and co-authors image the hidden compartment where coronaviruses copy their genome. The virus builds a network of changed membranes inside the host cell. Its core parts are double-membrane vesicles, sacs thought to have no opening. Yet new viral RNA must exit to be used and packed.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team found a crown-shaped pore that spans both membranes. The work used a mouse coronavirus as a safe model for its human kin. The pore likely lets viral RNA pass into the cell body. This solves a long-standing puzzle about how these closed sacs support the viral life cycle.
europmc-pmc7697710:
Gordon reviews how cut peripheral nerves regrow and reconnect to muscle. Unlike central nerves, peripheral nerves can regenerate after injury. After a crush or cut, fibers past the injury break down. Support cells called Schwann cells line up to guide new growth.

These support cells switch on growth genes and release factors that feed young axons. But this support fades with time. Regrowing fibers also miss their old paths and targets, which limits recovery. The author covers surgical tricks in current use, such as nerve transfers. Brief electric stimulation and a local drug, FK506, may speed axon growth.
europmc-pmc7896410:
Gong and co-authors report a study of blood cell ratios as predictors after stroke treatment. Patients with acute ischemic stroke often receive clot-busting treatment by vein. Some improve fast, while others worsen within a day. Simple blood measures taken before treatment might flag who is at risk.

The team studied 1060 patients who had thrombolysis. They computed three ratios from routine blood counts before treatment. Early deterioration struck 18.2% of patients, and early improvement came for 37.5%. All three ratios were linked to deterioration. The neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio also predicted early improvement. The authors say these cheap ratios may help staff spot risky cases early. The neutrophil ratio performed best of the three. The study points to inflammation as a clue to how a stroke will unfold.
europmc-pmc7900110:
Li and co-authors report a laboratory study of a liver cancer driver linked to low oxygen. The cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma. Cells in low oxygen switch on a factor called HIF-1α. The team traced how that switch feeds a self-cleaning process called autophagy, which helps tumours survive.

The authors show that HIF-1α turns up YTHDF1, a reader of the m6A mark on RNA. YTHDF1 then boosts production of two autophagy genes, ATG2A and ATG14. High YTHDF1 levels in tumours were tied to poor outcomes for patients. Removing YTHDF1 slowed autophagy, growth, and spread in cell, organoid, and mouse models. The chain offers new points where drugs might cut off a tumour's survival trick.
europmc-pmc7902610:
Zhang and co-authors present a systematic review of alternative splicing in cancer. Splicing is the step that cuts and rejoins RNA messages before they are read. Faulty splicing can produce abnormal protein forms. Such faults often appear as tumours form and grow. The review sets out how the process works and where it goes wrong.

The authors explain the rules that govern normal splicing choices. They then trace the effects of abnormal splicing on tumour growth, cell death, invasion, and new blood vessel growth. Changes in splicing factors found in tumours get full cover. So do odd splicing events in long non-coding and circular RNAs. The review closes with treatments that target splicing itself. These include drugs that reshape spliced products and immune therapies built on tumour-specific forms.
europmc-pmc8012210:
Granja and co-authors present ArchR, a software suite for single-cell chromatin accessibility data. Profiling open chromatin in single cells has grown faster than the tools to read it. ArchR runs in R and aims at speed plus depth. It handles the full workflow on ordinary hardware. The authors report analysis of over 1.2 million single cells on a standard laptop.

The suite removes doublets, clusters cells, and names cell types. It builds unified peak sets across samples. Users can trace cell trajectories and link DNA elements to genes. Transcription factor footprinting is built in. ArchR also predicts gene expression from accessibility. It can merge chromatin data with single-cell RNA sequencing for multi-omic work.
europmc-pmc8066110:
Sève and co-authors give a clinical overview of sarcoidosis, from first symptoms to settled diagnosis. The disease seeds granulomas in many organs, and its cause stays unknown. It strikes adults most often between 30 and 50 years of age. African Americans and Scandinavians face it more than most groups. Nearly any organ can be involved.

The chest bears the brunt, with involvement in 90% of patients. Swollen chest glands and fine lung nodules mark the classic picture. Skin lesions, eye inflammation, and joint pain are also common. Heart and nerve involvement stays under 10% but can mislead. Diagnosis rests on three legs working together. The clinical picture must fit the disease. Tissue must show non-necrotizing granulomas under the microscope. Other causes of granulomas must be ruled out. New organ-specific criteria sharpen the call.
europmc-pmc8158510:
Zhao and co-authors survey bone grafts and substitutes used in dentistry. After tooth loss, bone shrinks and does not grow back on its own. Grafting is the standard fix and is needed for many implants.

The review sets out what an ideal graft material should do. It sorts grafts and substitutes into natural and synthetic classes. Properties of each class are weighed in detail. Products now on the market are named for each group. The authors track new materials and fabrication methods. Readers can match graft choices to implant needs.
europmc-pmc8304710:
Bao and Wong survey hypoxia, metabolic rewiring, and drug resistance in liver cancer. Low oxygen marks solid cancers, above all liver tumours. Drug resistance is the main cause of poor treatment results.

The review centres on hypoxia-inducible factor, or HIF. HIF rewires metabolism so cells thrive on little oxygen. Those same shifts blunt drug action. The authors sort the molecular routes one by one. They also sum up combination therapies that target hypoxia-driven enzymes. Such pairings aim to break resistance. Fresh routes against stubborn liver cancer are the goal. Combination therapy is the practical response they favour.
europmc-pmc8369710:
Wilson and co-authors map what helps or blocks older adults when they use e-health services. Their scoping review covers adults aged 60 years or older. It asks why older people take up technology-based care, or fail to take it up.

The review included 14 papers, grouped into five themes. The main barriers were low confidence, little knowledge, weak support, and poor information about benefits. Design faults in the tools also held people back. What helped was involving older users in design, support that eased privacy worries, and services joined up across care settings. The authors say these points must be fixed for e-health to reach its promise.
europmc-pmc8583510:
Andrieux and co-authors review how mitochondria act as a hub in infection and inflammation. Mitochondria make energy for the cell. They also help drive the response to germs. Their work links cell energy, defense signals, and tissue harm in one organelle.

The review traces the origin of mitochondria and their role in host defense. Mitochondria make reactive oxygen species that help kill germs. Too much of this output can damage the cell and its tissues. Germs can also disrupt energy flow and the signals sent to the nucleus. The authors close with targets in mitochondria that could guide new treatments for infection and long-term inflammation.
europmc-pmc8595410:
Zhao and co-authors present a thin film that helps zinc anodes last longer in water-based zinc-ion batteries. These batteries are cheap and safe, but zinc grows sharp spikes as it charges. The spikes and corrosion cut battery life. The team coated the zinc with a fluorinated porous film.

The film guides zinc to grow in flat plates on one crystal face. Its small channels let ions pass but keep the liquid out. Cells with the coated zinc ran for over 750 hours at high current. Full cells also cycled for hundreds of rounds at high zinc use. The work points to longer life for a low-cost battery type.
europmc-pmc8788510:
Miranda and co-authors review the properties and applications of PDMS, a silicone elastomer widely used in biomedical engineering. The material has strong optical, electrical, and mechanical traits. It is also safe for use with living tissue. These traits drove its spread into many lab and medical devices.

PDMS enabled soft lithography, a fast way to prototype micro and nano structures. That method advanced microfluidics, electronics, and biomedicine at once. The review covers the material's core traits and common surface treatments. It then surveys uses such as biomedical microchips and heart flow models. Medical implants built from PDMS are also covered.
europmc-pmc8891310:
Peng and co-authors review how mouth microbes connect to diseases across the whole body. Oral bacteria cause tooth decay and gum disease directly. The mouth also talks constantly with distant organs. Its microbe mix mirrors immune and metabolic states. Disturbed oral communities now link to many systemic diseases. The review gathers that fast-growing evidence. It aims to widen clinicians' view beyond the mouth.

Digestive diseases come first in the survey. Cancers linked to oral bacteria follow. Heart and vessel diseases get a full section. Alzheimer's disease and diabetes each earn one too. Rheumatoid arthritis and preterm birth close the list. For each, the authors weigh how oral microbes might contribute. They stress two-way traffic between mouth and body. Dental research, they argue, is whole-body research.
europmc-pmc8996410:
Li and co-authors review PROTACs, engineered molecules that destroy cancer proteins rather than block them. A PROTAC has two linked heads. One grips the target protein. The other recruits the cell's tagging machinery. The tag marks the protein for the proteasome shredder. The approach can remove proteins that drugs cannot inhibit. Many cancer drivers sit in that hard class. The review explains the design logic first. It then traces the method's growth since its first proof in 2001.

Target sections march through famous oncoproteins. BRD4, cell cycle kinases, and EGFR each get a chapter. BRAF, PARP1, and BCR-ABL follow. PD-L1 closes the target list. Design rules for new molecules are set out. Problems get plain treatment too. Size, delivery, and resistance all limit the class. The authors compare PROTACs with older targeted drugs. Destruction, they argue, widens the druggable map.
europmc-pmc9018410:
Andrews and co-authors measured how well COVID-19 booster shots worked in England during the Delta wave. Using a test-negative design, they compared boosted adults with people who had two doses or none. Against symptoms, a booster after either main vaccine course raised protection to around 85% to 95%. Overall effectiveness soon after boosting reached 94% to 97% across age groups.

Protection against hospital admission or death was higher still, at around 97% to 99%. Waning stayed limited through ten weeks after the booster. The authors conclude that boosters restored strong protection against both mild and severe disease.
europmc-pmc9096710:
Buetti and co-authors update expert guidance on stopping bloodstream infections tied to central lines in acute-care hospitals. Central lines are tubes placed in large veins to give drugs and fluids. Germs can enter the blood along these lines and cause grave harm. This update replaces advice last set out in 2014.

The guidance sorts steps into essential practices for all hospitals and extra approaches when infections persist. Essential steps cover staff training, hand hygiene, site choice, sterile care, and quick removal of lines no longer needed. Extra steps can be tried in units where rates stay high. Hospital teams get a short, ranked list to put into daily use.
europmc-pmc9243210:
Sun and co-authors review how metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic changes drive each other on the path to cancer. Both are well-known hallmarks of cancer and are closely linked. Many metabolites serve as raw materials or helpers for enzymes that modify chromatin. Enzyme and metabolite placement inside the cell matters too.

The review focuses on acetylation and methylation of histones and DNA. It also covers newer marks like succinylation and lactylation. These shifts can help tumors escape immunity or block immune watch. The authors update progress on therapies that target metabolism or epigenetic marks. Readers get a current view of two intertwined systems and how drugs might break their alliance in cancer.
europmc-pmc9331210:
Sarhadi and Armengol review molecular biomarkers in cancer. A biomarker is any measurable molecular sign of cancer risk, presence, or outcome. Signs can hide in genes, gene activity, or proteins. Samples may come from tumor tissue or, more gently, from blood, saliva, urine, or stool.

The review sorts biomarker types and the tools that detect them. Uses span risk checks, screening, diagnosis, outlook, and therapy choice. Precision oncology depends on them, since targeted drugs work only in patients with matching mutations. New tests read tumor DNA floating in blood or tiny vesicles called exosomes. The authors say better sensitivity and accuracy are still needed. Faster detection tech keeps widening what can be measured.
europmc-pmc9640110:
Nelson writes a 1910 journal article on Ehrlich's new cure for syphilis, made with Hata's dioxydiamidoarsenobenzol. Syphilis was then one of the great plagues of the age. It had killed and scarred people in vast numbers for centuries. A one-shot cure claim stirred the whole medical world.

Nelson reports Ehrlich's aim of sterilisatio magna, a full kill of the parasite. Animal tests came first, checked by the Wassermann method. One injection in human cases was the stated manner of use. Observers across Germany reported strong and uniform success, he writes. Praise ran high among those who tried the remedy. Effects were said to show within ten to fourteen days. The drug was reported to work at all disease stages. That spread ran from the first lesion to late tertiary signs. The piece conveys the era's hope more than hard proof.
europmc-pmc9671810:
Bowe, Xie, and Al-Aly measure the added health risks that come with SARS-CoV-2 reinfection. A first infection raises later risks in many organ systems. Whether a second infection stacks more risk on top was unclear. The study drew on the US Veterans Affairs health database.

Three cohorts were built from the national records. One held 443,588 people with a single infection. The reinfection cohort held 40,947 people with two or more. A noninfected control group held 5,334,729 people for scale. Reinfection added clear risks of death and hospital care. Aftereffects spanned lung, heart, kidney, and brain systems. Diabetes and mental health harms also rose after reinfection. The added risks showed with or without vaccination. They peaked in the acute phase yet lasted six months. Total burden grew with each added infection a person had.
europmc-pmc9728410:
Ahn and co-authors review the state of COVID-19 knowledge on spread, testing, treatment, and vaccines. The disease first surfaced in Wuhan, China in late 2019. It causes hard lung illness, pneumonia, and lung failure. Within months the virus reached pandemic scale worldwide.

The review opens with the virus itself and its likely animal source. It then walks through test kits built to find the virus fast. Repurposed drugs with early clinical promise get a survey. Vaccine efforts by firms and institutes round out the tour. By late March 2020 over 400,000 cases were confirmed. Deaths had passed 18,000 across the world by then. The authors stress that containment needs fast shared knowledge. Their summary gathers what was known at that early point. It maps the gaps that work still had to close.
europmc-pmc9977110:
Rossaint and co-authors present the sixth edition of the European guideline on major bleeding after trauma. Severe trauma is a major global public health burden. Bleeding and trauma-linked coagulopathy can cause preventable organ failure and death. Fast, correct early care is vital for these patients.

A pan-European task force from six professional societies updated the guideline. They used structured searches and an evidence-based consensus process. The advice covers the first diagnostic and treatment phases. It speaks to clinicians who manage bleeding trauma patients early. Topics span detection, resuscitation, and control of coagulopathy. The edition replaces the prior version with current evidence. Its aim is more uniform, timely care across Europe.
flaubert-temptation-st-anthony-hearn-191:
Saint Anthony sits in the Egyptian desert while wonders and horrors crowd his night in Flaubert's Temptation of Saint Anthony. Lafcadio Hearn's 1910 translation renders the work Flaubert called his life's own, rewritten across thirty years. Gods, heretics, monsters, and Death itself parade before the hermit's eyes.

Each vision tempts the saint with a different offer: power, pleasure, knowledge, rest. The book reads more like a vast stage dream than a novel, rich with the lore Flaubert loved. Odilon Redon's dark images, noted in this edition, suit a text where faith wrestles every phantom it can name.
for-better-or-worse-ship-s-company-part-:
Jacobs opens this Ship's Company tale in the King's Head, where George Wotton cadges a drink from Ben Davis. Davis has had a shock: news of the wife who left him long ago. Wotton is sent to sound out how the land lies with her.

The old lady he finds gives the story a sharp turn. In her telling, Davis went off like a cur and left his young wife to manage alone. Now she has come into a bit of money, and she guesses exactly why two gentlemen came calling. W. W. Jacobs lets the deserter's version collapse in a few lines of dialogue.
forster-howards-end-1910:
E. M. Forster published Howards End in 1910, and it became his first widely praised novel. Forster, a Cambridge graduate, wrote about the England he knew: cultured liberals, rich business families, and the clerks caught between them. A country house gives the book its title.

Two Schlegel sisters, Margaret and Helen, befriend the wealthy Wilcox family and a poor clerk named Leonard Bast. Margaret marries into the Wilcoxes, while Helen's rash choices pull Bast toward ruin. The house, Howards End, passes slowly toward the person who understands it best. Forster's famous plea, only connect, sums up the novel's hope for bridging class and feeling.
francis-little-flowers-1910:
The Little Flowers of St. Francis came down from the 1300s in Italy. T. W. Arnold gave the tales English dress in 1910. Francis of Assisi was the rich youth who wed Lady Poverty. His friars roamed the roads with songs and tales of his deeds.

Short tales tell of the wolf of Gubbio, the birds who heard his preach, and his scars of Christ. Joy, love of beasts, and scorn of gold shine in each tale. The book won hearts far past the Church that bred it. It is the most loved book of tales on the saint.
freud-three-essays-brill-1910:
Sigmund Freud published Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality in German in 1905. The English text here is A. A. Brill's translation of 1910, titled Three Contributions to the Theory of Sex. Freud argues that sexual life begins in infancy, not at puberty. Children, in his theory, pass through stages centered on the mouth, anus, and genitals.

He treats perversions as fixations or detours in that growth. The libido, or sexual drive, is the energy behind the process. The book scandalized its age and remains psychoanalysis's most daring founding text. Later editions grew with notes and changes. Its claims still provoke debate among clinicians and critics.
froude-history-england-vol-10:
Spain sends its great fleet against England in the tenth volume of Froude's History, from 1865, covering the Armada year. Drake and Howard lead the sea fight in home waters. Storms then scatter the Spanish ships along wild coasts, completing England's deliverance.

Froude treats the victory as the climax of his whole Tudor epic. Protestant England, in his telling, survives by courage, seamanship, and God's weather. The fate of a nation hangs in the balance through the summer's fighting. His account reads as patriotic pageant, done with great narrative skill, and it crowned his reputation with the reading public of his day.
frus-1861-d10:
Joseph Wright wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 June 1861. The dispatch is document 10 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861, the first year of the Civil War.

By late June both sides were in the field, and Europe watched for a quick result. Wright's reports kept his corner of that watch. The letter shows the plain, dated rhythm by which far posts fed a capital that could not see events for itself. Each dated page added one more fixed point to a map Washington drew from afar. Fixed points like this one let later readers chart the war's foreign course.
frus-1861-d110:
A letter of 24 October 1861 went from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons at the British legation.

The matched dates show the machine in motion: the Navy chief reports, the State chief answers abroad. Seward's note to Lyons carries the product of that inner talk. It is a small, clear case of how the Union turned sea power into diplomacy. Such matched dates let readers watch the inner talk become foreign policy in a day. One day from inner talk to foreign note was swift work for the age of sail and steam.
frus-1861-d210:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Mr. Wood on 22 August 1861. It was printed as Document 210 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d310:
Writing on 7 September 1861, Mr. Dryer sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 310 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d10:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 31 January 1862. It was printed as Document 10 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d110:
A letter home from Charles Francis Adams, dated 25 July 1862, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 110 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d210:
Lord Lyons replied into the file on 21 February 1862 with a note to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 210 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both men wrote on the same day, a sign of active business between them.

Same-day exchanges usually mean a matter was moving fast or a deadline pressed. Lyons wrote as Britain's eyes in Washington as well as its voice, reporting home on all Seward said and did. A note from his hand in February belongs to the routine that kept a hard relationship workable through the war's first full winter. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d310:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward opened the September Paris mail with a dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 15 September 1862, printed as Document 310 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-September found Lee's army in Maryland and the Union's foreign standing at its lowest point of the year. France had drafted a plan to propose a truce, and Britain was considering it. Seward's letter to Dayton that day went out two days before Antietam, into the most dangerous fortnight the Union faced abroad during the war. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d410:
An instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Horace J. Perry in Madrid on 15 September 1862. It is Document 410 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Mid-September 1862 was a hinge of the war: Lee's army was in Maryland, and Lincoln waited on a victory before issuing his emancipation order. Foreign courts held back, waiting on the same news. Seward's letters in these days armed his agents with the Union's reading of events. For the Madrid legation, that meant pressing Spain to see a government that meant to win, and to keep its ports closed to Confederate use.
frus-1862-d510:
On 23 July 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote again from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward, a week after his previous report. The dispatch is Document 510 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Weekly reports in a bad month had a hard job. They had to be truthful. Yet they must not give Washington fresh cause for worry it could not act on. Pike's July letters did that job plainly, recording Dutch steadiness while Union arms regrouped. He also tracked the war's naval fringe, where Dutch colonial ports had rules to enforce. The letter continues a correspondence notable for its regularity. In the whole of 1862, few American posts wrote home as often as Pike's. Fewer still wrote as frankly.
frus-1862-d610:
Thomas Corwin received the year's closing Mexican order from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 21 October 1862. It is Document 610 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

October's instruction reached Mexico as the French settled in for a long war and as Washington, steadied by Antietam, took stock of its foreign position. The policy Seward repeated to Corwin had not changed in a year: friendship for Mexico's republic, refusal to accept the European enterprise, and patience. Within two years a freed Union army would stand on the Rio Grande and the patience would end. The letter is a fitting close to the volume's most principled American file.
frus-1862-d710:
On 13 September 1862, Andrew B. Dickinson wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second day in a row. Dickinson was the American minister in Nicaragua. The letter is document 710 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Two reports on two days point to a post with much to tell. From Nicaragua, an envoy tracked the transit route, the local government's acts, and the safety of Americans passing through. Dickinson's letters fed that watch. Kept in the volume, they show the pace of a small legation's work when events moved fast and mail home was slow.
frus-1863p1-d10:
On 8 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London. A second letter to Adams bears the same date in the volume. This one is document 10 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote as the year turned, with the war at a grim point and Europe still weighing its course. His letters told Adams what to say and what to hold back in talks with the British. Paired sheets like these show the secretary working a brief in parts. This letter belongs to that pair, and to the long chain that bound Washington to its London post.
frus-1863p1-d110:
On 6 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 110 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Early March found the legation deep in the ship question, as Southern warships took shape in British yards.
