Luisa Molina, Sasha Madronich, Jeffrey Gaffney, and colleagues published this overview in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics in 2010. The project studied where emissions come from, how they travel, and how they change in the air.

Three ground supersites, mobile labs, lidars, seven research aircraft, and satellites all took part. Forecasts and computer models ran alongside the measurements. Together they produced the fullest portrait yet of the region's air composition, with lessons for megacities everywhere.

That run, from September 2015 to January 2016, delivered history's first gravitational-wave detections.

The search combed the run's data for the chirp pattern of two black holes spiraling together. Its confirmed events opened an entirely new branch of astronomy. Beyond the detections themselves, the analysis measures how sensitive the instruments were and how often such mergers occur. The paper stands as the complete record of that first harvest, methods, candidates, and all.

Research in this field suffers from inconsistent definitions and testing methods, the authors say. That inconsistency helps explain why effective treatments remain limited. The paper recommends full head and neck examination, including nasal endoscopy, for suspected cases. It warns against trusting self-reported smell alone and backs validated tests of odor threshold and identification. Taste screening should accompany smell assessment, they add. Dmitrii Bogdanov, Javier Farfan, Kristina Sadovskaia, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2019. The paper opens by noting that fossil fuel emissions are a major cause of global warming. It reviews how expert groups differ in their energy outlooks, with some forecasting far more renewable power than others. Solar power is widely expected to become a main source of electricity at very large scale. The study offers its own long-term pathway toward a sustainable system.

Simon Martin, John Davey, Camilo Salazar, and Chris Jiggins published this study in PLoS Biology in 2019. It examines how genes flow between three species of Heliconius butterflies in South America. When species cross-breed, foreign DNA can enter a genome, a process called introgression.

The team read the whole genomes of ninety-two butterflies and compared family relationships across the genome. They found that species relationships vary in a predictable way at the scale of whole chromosomes. Rates of introgression were predicted by how much the local recombination rate varies. That pattern suggests the barriers keeping species apart involve many places in the genome, linked to how DNA is shuffled each generation.

Gabrielle Canonico, Pier Luigi Buttigieg, Enrique Montes, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Marine Science. It sets out what the world needs in order to observe marine biodiversity well. Healthy ocean ecosystems feed and protect billions of people, yet their wildlife is changing under climate change and other human pressures.

The authors argue that forecasting where, when, and how ocean life will change requires a stronger shared base of observations. They survey the resources already in place, from observing systems to data networks, and name the gaps that remain. Their aim is a global picture of marine life that is steady enough to guide policy and protection work.
openalex-w3039077710:
Mehdi Sharifi-Rad, Nanjangud Kumar, Paolo Zucca, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Physiology in 2020. It traces the back-and-forth between lifestyle, oxidative stress, and antioxidants in chronic disease. Everyday body processes, from breathing to digesting food, produce unstable molecules called free radicals.

A healthy body's antioxidant system normally destroys those radicals. When it cannot cope, radicals set off chain reactions that damage cell membranes, block enzymes, injure DNA, and stall energy production. This oxidative stress is tied to metabolic disorders, chronic diseases, and cancers. The review weighs how habits such as diet and alcohol use feed the problem, and how antioxidants may counter it, in the long-running debate over their benefit.
openalex-w3096967710:
Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo, Yisela Pantaleón, Irene Dios, and Daniel Falla published this study in Frontiers in Psychology in 2020. It builds a predictive model for depression among university undergraduates during COVID-19. The predictors are fear of the virus, stress, and anxiety.

Depression is a leading cause of disability, and past epidemics and disasters raised its levels for years afterward. The pandemic hit some Latin American countries hard, where coping resources are thin. The authors surveyed students to test how fear, stress, and anxiety combine to forecast depression scores. A working model helps universities spot students at risk early, when support can still change the outcome. The study adds student data to the pandemic's mental health record.
openalex-w3129541210:
Jamie Caldwell, A. Desiree LaBeaud, Eric Lambin, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2021. It shows that climate predicts where and when mosquito-borne diseases flare on two continents. The diseases covered include dengue, chikungunya, and Zika, all carried by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.

Climate can seem to help the virus in one place and hinder it in another. The team built a model from lab measures of how climate drives mosquito body functions. With little local tuning, it captured the number, timing, and length of outbreaks in Ecuador and Kenya. It matched mosquito counts and confirmed case patterns with fair accuracy. Such models can guide control efforts and forecasts of disease under climate change.
openalex-w3214960410:
Khalid El Bairi, Harry Haynes, Elizabeth Blackley, and colleagues report on tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes in breast cancer in npj Breast Cancer in 2021. These lymphocytes, shortened to TILs, are immune cells found inside and around tumours. Their presence seems to show the body fighting the cancer. The report comes from an international working group on immune biomarkers in cancer.

TILs are believed to predict how well patients respond to immunotherapy, chemotherapy, and other targeted drugs. They also carry information about a patient's outlook. Checkpoint drugs have changed breast cancer care, but choosing who benefits needs better markers. The report gathers what is known about measuring TILs, so labs and trials can use them in a shared, reliable way.
openalex-w4225890110:
Caroline Junqueira, Ângela Crespo, Shahin Ranjbar, and colleagues report how the coronavirus infects blood monocytes, in Nature in 2022. Monocytes are immune cells that patrol the blood. The team found the virus enters them through Fc gamma receptors, the docks that grab antibody-coated particles. That route turns a defence cell into a source of inflammation.

Inside infected monocytes, two alarm systems, the NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes, switch on. The cell then dies by pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death that spills inflammatory signals. Those signals include cytokines that can drive severe COVID-19. The work helps explain how infection of blood cells can fuel dangerous whole-body inflammation.
openalex-w4308150510: Rosa Paolicelli, Amanda Sierra, Beth Stevens, and colleagues discuss the states and naming of microglia, the brain's resident immune cells. Muhammad Javed Iqbal, Ayesha Kabeer, Zaighum Abbas, and colleagues review how oxidative stress drives cancer through cell signalling. Their review appeared in Cell Communication and Signaling in 2024. Oxidative stress means an overload of reactive oxygen species inside cells. These harsh molecules disturb the cell's balance and damage its genome's stability. Raised levels are tied to the start and growth of many cancers, from liver and breast to lung and prostate.

The review traces the signalling pathways that oxidative stress disturbs. They include famous cancer guardians such as p53 and the Keap1-NRF2 system. When these pathways fail, cells grow unchecked, repair DNA poorly, and dodge death. The authors discuss therapies that aim to restore redox balance and so improve standard cancer treatment.

They made it by a topochemical reaction from a lithium-containing precursor. The product has a spinel structure with ordered empty sites.

Cobalt ions sit only on one site type, forming a diamond lattice. On that lattice, magnetic interactions compete and frustrate each other. Measurements show antiferromagnetic order setting in near four kelvin. That ordering point is strongly suppressed compared with the interaction strength. Strong frustration can hide exotic magnetic states. New materials like this give physicists fresh ground for finding them.

Lucimar Graf led a Portuguese-language study, in Brazil in 2026, on teacher mental health: contemporary problems and plans for promoting teacher well-being. Teacher mental health is essential for career permanence, teaching quality, and welcoming school environments. The research reads research papers, global organizations' records, and Brazil's norms on schooling, work, and mental health.

Long hours, accumulated functions, excessive records, scarce resources, weak support, conflicts, violence, and ongoing tools use can deepen professional wear, the authors find. Plans centered only on individual self-care are insufficient, since teacher suffering is tied to the concrete problems of the work. Promoting mental health requires permanent prevention policies, professional valorization, participation in choices, manager training, intersectoral support networks, and revised school organization.

Fabrizio Jose Serafini Coronel leads a team describing ultrasound findings in younger gallstone patients at the Coronel Bogado District Hospital in 2025. Gallstones are among the most common diseases of the liver and bile system and a leading reason for laparoscopic gallbladder removal, and ultrasound is the standard tool for checking them before surgery. The team reviewed charts and ultrasound reports for thirty-one patients aged eighteen to forty.

Most patients were women, and the largest group was aged thirty-five to thirty-nine. Stones were usually multiple, mobile, and of medium size, and every case showed the dark shadow behind the stone that confirms it on a scan. A thickened gallbladder wall was the most common added finding, while bile sludge and duct widening were rare. The study gives surgeons a clear picture of what to expect in patients under forty.

Marcia de Almeida Fraga, Ana Maria Filgueira Cabral Lins, and Suenya Talita de Almeida write on talk as an answer to harm, with child neglect at the core. They draw on Jurgen Habermas. One kind of talk aims at shared sense; the next aims at a win. The first kind, they hold, fits a group cure built on talk rings, where folk sit in a round and speak as peers.

Neglect, they argue, is not just a flaw of lone homes. It marks talk nets torn among home, state, and town. That tear can leave kids with no guard at all. It can even cost the home its rights to the child. State plans, they close, should prize shared sense, close heed, and shared blame. Then the base rights of kids and teens can be made real, not just writ.

The redo group was the more young, but its risk score ran high. More of them had Marfan's ill or a long-torn main road. Their cuts ran long on each count. Still, deaths in the house matched the first group. Long life past the cut matched too. Math checks blamed long pump time, the female sex, and haste, not the fresh sawing of the chest. With the right plan, the team holds, a redo arch cut can match a first one.

Nurses hold a strategic watch role in prenatal care.

Daniel Ortega Oliveira da Silva and three fellow dentists reviewed the literature on cone-beam computed tomography. This three-dimensional dental scan helps diagnose periapical lesions, the damaged areas around a tooth root tip. Studies from the past decade show the scan detects more root-tip changes and reveals their size and relation to nearby structures, which helps planning and follow-up. The fund redistributed education money according to elementary school enrollment, leaving high school outside its automatic formula — the gap their title names.

Programs such as PROMED, Projeto Alvorada, and Viva Educação filled part of that hole in certain years, expanding places and resources. Yet high school spending beside elementary spending swung sharply, because temporary projects cannot substitute for a stable funding base. Their documentary study shows a lasting lesson of Brazilian education finance: what the formula skips, improvisation must carry.
original-short-stories-volume-10:
Volume ten of Maupassant's Original Short Stories opens with brandy and a warning. In The Christening, an old ship's surgeon holds his glass to the lamp. He savors the golden drops. Then he calls alcohol the charming poison, the seductive murderer. He has watched it exterminate a whole people, he says, where traders unloaded it by the barrel.

Fourteen tales fill the volume, including The Farmer's Wife, Walter Schnaff's Adventure, That Pig of a Morin, Pierrot, and A Normandy Joke. The mix is classic Maupassant: war's absurdities, peasant cunning, desire and its punishments, and the bottle never far away. The surgeon's toast frames the book darkly, as if the christening cup itself carried the germ of the stories' undoing.
pascal-pensees-trotter-1910:
Blaise Pascal, the French thinker and scientist, died in 1662 leaving behind bundles of short notes. Friends published the notes in 1670 as the Pensées, or Thoughts. W. F. Trotter translated the book into English in 1910, and his version long served as the standard one.

The fragments argue that reason alone cannot settle the deepest questions of life. Pascal's famous wager urges the doubter to bet on God's existence. He calls man a thinking reed, weak in body yet great in mind. Other notes treat custom, boredom, pride, and the hidden God. Few books of fragments have been quoted so often or read so closely.
plaw-111-126-2010:
Public Law 111-126 speeds up tax gains for gifts to Haiti earthquake relief. The 111th Congress acted in January 2010, days after the quake in Haiti on January 12, 2010.

A taxpayer may treat a covered cash gift as if made on December 31, 2009, not in 2010. The rule covers cash gifts made after January 11, 2010 and before March 1, 2010 for relief of victims. The gift must be one that earns a charitable tax deduction under section 170. The act also sets recordkeeping rules for such gifts. Speed matters because donors give most in the first weeks after a disaster.
plaw-111-127-2010:
Public Law 111-127 is the Emergency Aid to American Survivors of the Haiti Earthquake Act, passed by the 111th Congress in January 2010. It amends section 1113 of the Social Security Act.

The act raises total fiscal year 2010 payments for short-term aid to United States citizens returned from other nations. That aid helps Americans brought home after the Haiti quake. A third section covers funding for the QI program, which helps low-income people with Medicare cost sharing. The act aims to avoid shortfalls in that program as well. The QI part shows the act pairs quake aid with a funding fix.
plaw-111-128-2010: Somerville, Tennessee is home to the post office renamed by Public Law 111-128, a 2010 act of the 111th Congress. The building at 116 North West Street becomes the John S. Wilder Post Office Building. Under the act, any federal mention of that site in a law, map, or record means the new name.
plaw-111-129-2010: Public Law 111-129, enacted in 2010, gives the post office at 76 Brookside Avenue in Chester, New York a person's name. The building becomes the 1st Lieutenant Louis Allen Post Office. As with like acts, a mention of the site in a United States law, map, or other record is deemed a mention of the Allen name.
plaw-111-130-2010: St. Louis, Missouri gains the Coach Jodie Bailey Post Office Building under Public Law 111-130, a 2010 act of the 111th Congress. The honored site stands at 9810 Halls Ferry Road. The act states that references to that Postal Service site in federal laws, maps, and records shall be read as references to the new building name.
plaw-111-131-2010: In Portola, California, Public Law 111-131 names the post office building at 440 South Gulling Street. Passed in 2010, the act calls the site the Army Specialist Jeremiah Paul McCleery Post Office Building. Federal maps, laws, and records that name the site now name it under the McCleery title. The honored name is Jeremiah Paul McCleery, with his Army rank.
plaw-111-132-2010: Public Law 111-132 designates the post office at 427 Harrison Avenue in Harrison, New Jersey. The 111th Congress acted in 2010 to name the site the Patricia D. McGinty-Juhl Post Office Building. A reference to the site in any law, map, or federal record is a reference to the McGinty-Juhl name under the act.
plaw-111-133-2010: White Springs, Florida is home to the building renamed by Public Law 111-133 in 2010. The Postal Service site at 16555 Springs Street becomes the Clyde L. Hillhouse Post Office Building. The act provides that mentions of the site in United States laws, maps, and records count as mentions of the new name.
plaw-111-134-2010: Public Law 111-134, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010, names one post office building in Smithfield, Utah. The Postal Service site at 170 North Main Street shall be known as the W. Hazen Hillyard Post Office Building. Any mention of that site in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-111-135-2010: Naming a post office building in Stow, Ohio is the whole job of Public Law 111-135, from the 111th Congress in 2010. The Postal Service site at 3900 Darrow Road shall be known as the Corporal Joseph A. Tomci Post Office Building. Any mention of that site in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-111-136-2010: Small business programs gain three more months here. Public Law 111-136, from the 111th Congress in 2010, gives small business programs another short extension. It swaps January 31, 2010 for April 30, 2010 in the earlier extension law, as most lately amended. The change takes effect on January 30, 2010, one day after approval, so the Small Business Act and Small Business Investment Act programs do not lapse.
plaw-111-137-2010:
Emergency care outside VA walls gains wider repayment. Public Law 111-137, from the 111th Congress in 2010, amends title 38 to widen who can be paid back for emergency care. The Secretary of Veterans Affairs may repay more veterans for emergency treatment in a non-Department facility.

The act strikes the words or in part from one test in section 1725, and strikes a subpart as well. It adds rules on repayment limits when a veteran has a claim against a third party. If that claim would only partly wipe out what the veteran owes the provider, the new text governs the payment.
plaw-111-138-2010:
Public Law 111-138 deals with papers tied to Franklin Delano Roosevelt. The 111th Congress acted in 2010 on claims by the United States to certain documents in one collection.

If a person or group gives such property to the National Archives and Records Administration, the federal claim counts as waived. The waiver takes effect the day before the gift. The property must be part of the documents, papers, and keepsakes tied to Roosevelt, his family, or his staff. It must have been held by Grace Tully and kept by her at her death.
plaw-111-139-2010:
Public Law 111-139 is a joint resolution of the 111th Congress raising the legal cap on the public debt. It also carries Title I, the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010.

The resolution moves the debt cap in section 3101 of title 31 to $14,294,000,000,000. The pay-as-you-go title aims to restore a legal process to enforce budget neutrality. That rule means new tax or direct spending laws must not add to the deficit. Key terms in the title draw on the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985. The two parts pair new borrowing room with a new budget rule.
plaw-111-140-2010:
Public Law 111-140 is the Nuclear Forensics and Attribution Act, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010. It strengthens work in the Department of Homeland Security to build nuclear forensics skill.

Congress finds that a nuclear terrorist attack is among the gravest threats to national safety. After an attack, naming who was to blame would matter most. Since a nuclear blast leaves little proof, the radioactive material in the weapon itself may be the key clue. Forensics means testing that material to trace its source, and the act backs that work. Tracing a weapon's source can shape the whole response to an attack.
plaw-111-141-2010: Sunset dates in two terror laws move by a year. Public Law 111-141, from the 111th Congress in 2010, extends expiring parts of two anti-terror laws until February 28, 2011. The laws are the USA PATRIOT Improvement and Reauthorization Act of 2005 and the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004. In each law the act strikes February 28, 2010 and inserts February 28, 2011. That one-year delay of the sunset dates is the whole act.
plaw-111-142-2010:
Public Law 111-142 carries the long name Social Security Disability Applicants' Access to Professional Representation Act of 2010. The 111th Congress made two trial fee rules permanent.

First, the attorney fee withholding steps under title II of the Social Security Act are extended for good to title XVI. Withholding means the agency holds back part of a won benefit to pay the lawyer. Second, those same steps are made permanent for qualified non-attorney helpers as well. Claimants gain steadier access to skilled help with disability claims. Fee withholding spares claimants from paying helpers up front.
plaw-111-143-2010: Public Law 111-143 bears the short title Criminal History Background Checks Pilot Extension Act of 2009, though the 111th Congress passed it in 2010. Like an earlier act with the same name, it extends the pilot program that lets volunteer groups obtain criminal history background checks. The act amends the PROTECT Act by changing a 78-month pilot period to a 92-month period. That edit is the whole law.
plaw-111-144-2010:
Public Law 111-144 is the Temporary Extension Act of 2010, a short stopgap law from the 111th Congress. It gives a brief added span to certain programs that were set to lapse.

Section 2 extends unemployment insurance rules. It moves February 28, 2010 to April 5, 2010 where that date appears in the Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2008. It also moves a July 31, 2010 date to September 4, 2010. The edits keep jobless aid flowing while Congress weighed longer bills. Later parts extend more programs in the same date-swap form. Stopgap acts of this kind often run only a few weeks at a time.
plaw-111-145-2010:
Public Law 111-145 is the United States Capitol Police Administrative Technical Corrections Act of 2009. The 111th Congress made small fixes to the laws on how the Capitol Police run their office work.

Section 2 deals with the powers of the Chief of the Capitol Police. It clears up hiring powers, starting with the Chief Administrative Officer. There shall be an Office of Administration inside the force, led by that officer. The officer reports to the Chief and serves at the Chief's pleasure. The act is housekeeping, not a change in police duties.
plaw-111-146-2010:
Public Law 111-146 is the Trademark Technical and Conforming Amendment Act of 2010. The 111th Congress made small technical fixes to the Lanham Act, the main trademark law.

The act first defines its key term: the Trademark Act of 1946 means the Lanham Act of July 5, 1946. Section 3 then lists the fixes. An early fix deals with certificates of registration in section 7 of that act. It inserts the words United States before Patent and Trademark in the text. Such fixes align wording across the law. Trademark owners rely on exact register text in court fights.
plaw-111-147-2010:
Public Law 111-147 is the Hiring Incentives to Restore Employment Act, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010. Most of its edits land in the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

Title I gives incentives for hiring and keeping jobless workers. It offers payroll tax forgiveness for hiring unemployed workers. It also offers a business credit for keeping certain new hires through 2010. Later titles raise expensing for business assets and allow a refundable credit for certain tax credit bonds. The aim stated in the title is to restore jobs. Most edits land in the tax code, as the act's own rule states.
plaw-111-148-2010:
Public Law 111-148 is the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, the large health law of the 111th Congress from 2010. Title I is called Quality, Affordable Health Care for All Americans.

Its first part brings quick gains in health coverage. New rules bar lifetime or yearly caps on coverage and bar firms from dropping coverage by rescission. Coverage of preventive health services is required, and dependent coverage is extended. The act also calls for plain, uniform summaries of coverage, with standard terms, so buyers can compare plans with ease. Later titles of the act reach far past this first coverage part.
plaw-111-149-2010:
Wetlands projects in Canada gain clear cost rules. Public Law 111-149, from the 111th Congress in 2010, amends the North American Wetlands Conservation Act. It sets rules on paying the non-federal share of costs for wetlands projects in Canada funded under that act.

The new text says that share may not come from federal grant programs. For a project in Canada or Mexico, the share may include cash from non-United States sources used to pay project costs. For a project in Canada, funds from Canadian sources may count as well. The rules keep cost sharing honest across borders.
plaw-111-150-2010: Old funds are freed to keep a loan program going. Public Law 111-150, from the 111th Congress in 2010, lets old funds be used to extend the Small Business Loan Guarantee Program. Up to forty million dollars from the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2010 may also be used for fee cuts under the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009. The money may also cover the cost of guaranteed loans under that act. A second part extends the sunset date for the program rules.
plaw-111-151-2010: Public Law 111-151 renews the Satellite Home Viewer Extension and Reauthorization Act of 2004 through April 30, 2010. The 111th Congress passed it in March 2010, and its short title in the sample reads Satellite Televison Extension Act of 2010. The act amends section 119 of title 17 by moving March 28, 2010 to April 30, 2010 in two places. It makes a like date change for the end of a license in an earlier law.
plaw-111-152-2010:
Public Law 111-152 is the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010. The 111th Congress passed it under the budget rules for fiscal year 2010, as a companion to the main health law.

Title I covers coverage, Medicare, Medicaid, and revenues. Its coverage part deals with tax credits, personal duty to hold coverage, and employer duty. A Medicare part works on closing the prescription drug gap known as the donut hole. It also deals with Medicare Advantage payments and savings from caps on plan office costs. School aid sits in later titles of the same reconciliation act.
plaw-111-153-2010:
Public Law 111-153 is the Federal Aviation Administration Extension Act of 2010. The 111th Congress amended the tax code to extend funding for the Airport and Airway Trust Fund by one month.

For fuel taxes, the act moves the end date from March 31, 2010 to April 30, 2010. Ticket taxes gain the same new date. The act also extends the fund's spending power under the tax code. It extends clearances for the airport improvement program under title 49 in the same short form. One month is a short bridge while a longer aviation bill is weighed.
plaw-111-154-2010:
Public Law 111-154 is the Prevent All Cigarette Trafficking Act of 2009, or PACT Act, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010. It aims to stop tobacco smuggling and to ensure that all tobacco taxes are gathered.

Congress finds that sales of illegal cigarettes and smokeless tobacco cut federal, state, and local revenues by billions each year. Web sales alone are blamed for much of that loss. The findings also state that groups such as Hezbollah, Hamas, and al Qaeda have gained from trade in illegal cigarettes and fake tax stamps. Lost tax money and terror funding are the two harms the findings stress.
plaw-111-155-2010:
Public Law 111-155 is the Prevent Deceptive Census Look Alike Mailings Act, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010. It guards the honesty of the United States census, which the Constitution requires.

The act sets rules for mail that bears the word census on the envelope or outer cover. It amends section 3001(h) of title 39, which deals with mail that solicits the purchase of a product or service. Mail that uses the census term to mislead falls under the stated limits. The aim is to stop fake census mail from tricking households.
plaw-111-156-2010: Public Law 111-156 is a joint resolution of the 111th Congress honoring the Blinded Veterans Association. It marks the group's 65th anniversary of speaking for blinded veterans and their families. The group was formed on March 28, 1945, at Avon Old Farms Army Convalescent Hospital in Connecticut. One hundred blinded service members who served in World War II formed it at 8:45 that morning. The resolution praises the founders as heroes who shaped care and schooling for the blind.
plaw-111-157-2010:
Public Law 111-157 is the Continuing Extension Act of 2010, another stopgap law from the 111th Congress. It gives a brief added span to certain programs, as its near-twin act did weeks before.

Section 2 extends unemployment insurance rules. It moves April 5, 2010 to June 2, 2010 where that date appears in the Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2008. It also moves a September 4, 2010 date to November 6, 2010. The edits follow the same pattern as the Temporary Extension Act of 2010, pushing jobless aid dates forward once more. The pattern of short bridges ran through much of that spring. Each new bridge buys time for a longer deal.
plaw-111-158-2010:
Public Law 111-158 is the Haiti Debt Relief and Earthquake Recovery Act of 2010. The 111th Congress acted after the January 2010 earthquake in Haiti.

The act urges the Secretary of the Treasury to direct United States leaders at world lending bodies to press for full debt relief. The bodies named are the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and the Inter-American Development Bank. The goal is to cancel Haiti's debts to such bodies at once and in full. A new section 1628 on debt cancellation is added to the International Financial Institutions Act.
plaw-111-159-2010:
Public Law 111-159 is the TRICARE Affirmation Act, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010. It amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 on health coverage from the Department of Defense.

The act makes sure that Defense health coverage counts as minimal essential coverage. That term matters under the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act. The new clause names medical coverage under chapter 55 of title 10, including coverage under the TRICARE program. Service families thus know their military health plan meets the coverage test in tax law. The clause it writes names TRICARE coverage in so many words.
plaw-111-160-2010:
Public Law 111-160 is a joint resolution granting the consent of Congress to changes in a transit pact. Maryland, Virginia, and the District of Columbia made the changes to the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Regulation Compact.

The three parties first joined the compact in 1960, with consent from Congress. They amended it in 1962 and 1990, each time with consent as well. The new changes touch article III of title I, on appointments, and rest on state laws passed from 2007 to 2009. Section 1 of the resolution grants the needed consent. Transit for the capital area is the compact's long-standing work.
plaw-111-161-2010:
Public Law 111-161 is the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2010. The 111th Congress amended the tax code to extend funding for the Airport and Airway Trust Fund once more.

For fuel taxes, the act moves the end date from April 30, 2010 to July 3, 2010. Ticket taxes on persons gain the same new date, with a like edit for property. The act also extends the fund's spending power. It extends clearances for the airport improvement program under title 49 as well. Summer travel season falls inside the added span of weeks. Airport taxes of this kind are paid by flyers and fuel buyers.
plaw-111-162-2010: Small business programs gain a further three months. Public Law 111-162, from the 111th Congress in 2010, gives small business programs another short extension. It swaps April 30, 2010 for July 31, 2010 in the earlier extension law, as most lately amended by Public Law 111-136. The change takes effect on April 29, 2010, one day before approval, so the Small Business Act and Small Business Investment Act programs do not lapse.
plaw-111-163-2010:
Public Law 111-163 is the Caregivers and Veterans Omnibus Health Services Act of 2010. The 111th Congress amended title 38 to aid caregivers of veterans and to improve health care for veterans.

Title I covers caregiver support. It provides aid and support services for caregivers, plus medical care for family caregivers. It also covers counseling and mental health services for caregivers, and lodging and food for attendants. Title II turns to women veterans' health care. It opens with a study of blocks that keep women veterans from care. Caregivers often give daily help that clinics cannot give at home.
plaw-111-164-2010: A Long Beach center for blind veterans gains a name. Public Law 111-164, from the 111th Congress in 2010, names one veterans center in Long Beach, California. The Department of Veterans Affairs blind rehabilitation center there shall be known as the Major Charles Robert Soltes, Jr., O.D. Department of Veterans Affairs Blind Rehabilitation Center. Any mention of that center in a law, rule, map, or other federal record counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-111-165-2010: Lawmakers vote to skip their own pay raise. Public Law 111-165, from the 111th Congress in 2010, freezes lawmaker pay for one year. It provides that Members of Congress shall not receive a cost of living adjustment in pay during fiscal year 2011. Despite any other law, no adjustment shall be made under section 601(a) of the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1946 for that year. That single bar is the whole act.
plaw-111-166-2010:
Public Law 111-166 is the Daniel Pearl Freedom of the Press Act of 2009, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010. It amends the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 on human rights reports.

The act adds facts about freedom of the press in other nations to the Annual Country Reports on Human Rights Practices. Section 2 makes the edits in section 116(d) of that act, adding a new item at the end of a list. The reports must now cover how free the press is in each nation, a wider lens on rights abroad. Press freedom joins the list of rights the yearly reports must weigh.
plaw-111-167-2010:
Public Law 111-167 is the Blue Ridge Parkway and Town of Blowing Rock Land Exchange Act of 2009, passed in 2010. The 111th Congress cleared a land swap to gain lands for the Blue Ridge Parkway.

The other party is the Town of Blowing Rock in North Carolina. The act defines the map for the swap as a National Park Service map from April 2008. That map is titled Blue Ridge Parkway, Proposed Land Exchange with Town of Blowing Rock. Section 3 then clears the exchange itself, on the terms the act sets. Parkway land gains protect views and access along the scenic road.
plaw-111-168-2010:
Cemetery land in Utah carries an old federal claim. Public Law 111-168, from the 111th Congress in 2010, provides for the sale of a federal interest in land in Salt Lake City, Utah. The land, about 60 acres, first went to the Mount Olivet Cemetery Association under an act of January 23, 1909.

If the Association offers to buy the federal reversionary interest within one year after the needed appraisal, the Secretary of the Interior shall convey it. A reversionary interest is the federal right to take the land back if set terms fail. The sale would end that old federal claim on the cemetery land.
plaw-111-169-2010:
Public Law 111-169, from the 111th Congress in 2010, extends the power of the Adams Memorial Foundation to set up a memorial work. The work honors former President John Adams and his legacy.

The act amends Public Law 107-62, which first cleared the memorial. It ties the end date in that law to December 2, 2013, in place of the standard seven-year span. Small technical fixes to the older law follow. The extension gives the Foundation more time to plan and build the tribute in the capital area. Memorial work in the capital needs long lead time for design and funds.
plaw-111-170-2010:
See-through envelopes raise a census mail question. Public Law 111-170, from the 111th Congress in 2010, amends title 39 to clear up when the word census may appear on mail. It deals with mail that asks the reader to buy a product or service.

The act covers mail where the word census can be seen through the envelope or outer wrapper. It adds that case to the rule for mail that bears the term on the envelope itself. A like part covers mail that solicits facts or gifts of funds. The point is to keep census-like mail honest and easy to spot.
plaw-111-171-2010:
Public Law 111-171 is the Haiti Economic Lift Program Act of 2010. The 111th Congress extended the Caribbean Basin Economic Recovery Act and cleared customs support services for Haiti.

The findings describe the blow that made the aid urgent. On January 12, 2010, Haiti was hit by a 7.0 magnitude quake, the worst in its recorded history. Aftershocks up to 6.0 followed for days. The quake wrecked homes, offices, factories, roads, ports, and other systems across the nation. The act notes that Haiti was the poorest nation in its region even before the quake. Trade aid is the tool the act uses to lift Haiti's economy.
plaw-111-172-2010:
Public Law 111-172 is the Lord's Resistance Army Disarmament and Northern Uganda Recovery Act of 2009, passed in 2010. The 111th Congress backed steady peace in northern Uganda and nearby areas hit by that armed group.

Congress finds that Uganda fought the Lord's Resistance Army for over two decades. The war drove more than two million people in northern Uganda from their homes. The act backs a regional plan to guard civilians and end the threat of the group. It also clears funds for relief, rebuilding, and justice work. Guarding civilians comes first in the plan the act describes.
plaw-111-173-2010: VA health programs are named as coverage that counts. Public Law 111-173, from the 111th Congress in 2010, clears up which veterans health care counts as minimal essential coverage. It rewrites one clause in section 5000A of the tax code, as added by the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act. The new clause names a health care program under chapter 17 or 18 of title 38, as the Secretary of Veterans Affairs decides with two other secretaries. The change takes effect as if it had been in the health act.
plaw-111-174-2010:
Public Law 111-174 is the Federal Judiciary Administrative Improvements Act of 2010. The 111th Congress passed it to improve how the federal courts run day to day.

Section 2 fixes senior judge governance by striking a long aside from section 631(a) of title 28. Section 3 rewrites the legal description of the District of North Dakota. It states that North Dakota forms one judicial district and says where court shall be held. Later parts split the judgment and statement of reasons forms, and cover pretrial services for juveniles. Housekeeping acts of this kind keep court law clear and current.
plaw-111-175-2010:
Public Law 111-175 is the Satellite Television Extension and Localism Act of 2010. The 111th Congress extended the statutory license for secondary transmissions under title 17, the copyright code.

Title I covers statutory licenses. It changes the license for satellite carriers and the license for carriers in local markets. It also changes cable system rights for secondary transmissions under section 111. Waivers for providers of local-into-local service, meaning local stations sent back into their own market, are covered as well. Copyright Office fees get a section too. Local stations on satellite are the localism half of the title.
plaw-111-176-2010: Public Law 111-176, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010, names one federal building in Washington, District of Columbia. The United States Department of the Interior Building at 1849 C Street, Northwest shall be known as the Stewart Lee Udall Department of the Interior Building. Any mention of that building in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-111-177-2010:
Public Law 111-177 has one of the longest titles in this set, on extending immunities to two overseas offices. The 111th Congress passed it in 2010 for the Office of the High Representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the International Civilian Office in Kosovo.

The act lets the International Organizations Immunities Act reach both offices. It adds a new section 17 to that act for this purpose. Immunities of this kind shield the offices and their staff in like ways to other world bodies. A final part covers budget compliance for the change.
plaw-111-178-2010:
Public Law 111-178 is the Special Agent Samuel Hicks Families of Fallen Heroes Act, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010. It amends title 5 on help for the families of fallen federal workers.

A new section 5724d covers travel and moving costs for the immediate family of certain workers. It applies when a federal worker dies in the performance of duty. Under rules set by the President, the agency head may find that a worker is covered. The family may then gain paid transport and moving help at a time of loss.
plaw-111-179-2010: Riverhead, New York gains a renamed post office building under Public Law 111-179, passed by the 111th Congress in 2010. The Postal Service site at 1210 West Main Street is designated the Private First Class Garfield M. Langhorn Post Office Building. References to that site in any United States law, map, or record are treated as references to the Langhorn name.
plaw-111-180-2010: Public Law 111-180, enacted in 2010, gives the post office at 109 Main Street in Swifton, Arkansas a person's name. The building becomes the George Kell Post Office. As with like acts, a mention of the site in a United States law, map, or other record is deemed a mention of the Kell name.
plaw-111-181-2010: Roper, North Carolina is home to the post office renamed by Public Law 111-181, a 2010 act of the 111th Congress. The building at 101 West Highway 64 Bypass becomes the E.V. Wilkins Post Office. Under the act, any federal mention of that site in a law, map, or record means the new name.
plaw-111-182-2010: Public Law 111-182 renames the Postal Service building at 43 Maple Avenue in Shrewsbury, Massachusetts. Enacted in 2010 by the 111th Congress, the act designates the site as the Ann Marie Blute Post Office. Later federal records that point to the building point to it under the Blute name. The honored name is Ann Marie Blute, as the act states.
plaw-111-183-2010: Overland Park, Kansas is the setting for Public Law 111-183, a postal naming act from the 111th Congress in 2010. The site at 9727 Antioch Road shall be known as the Congresswoman Jan Meyers Post Office Building. The act adds the standard rule: mentions of the site in laws, maps, and federal records mean the new name.
plaw-111-184-2010: Public Law 111-184, enacted by the 111th Congress in 2010, names the post office at 7464 Highway 503 in Hickory, Mississippi. It shall be known as the Sergeant Matthew L. Ingram Post Office. Any law, map, or federal record naming that Postal Service site names it under the Ingram title after the act. The site stands on Highway 503, as the act states in full.
plaw-111-185-2010: Public Law 111-185, passed by the 111th Congress and approved on June 9, 2010, gives a Palm Desert post office a new name. The Postal Service site at 45300 Portola Avenue in Palm Desert, California, is named the Roy Wilson Post Office. From then on, any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, or record means the Roy Wilson Post Office.
plaw-111-186-2010: In Public Law 111-186, the 111th Congress renamed a post office site in Greeley, Colorado, in 2010. The Postal Service site at 930 39th Avenue is now the W.D. Farr Post Office Building. The act adds that any later mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name.
plaw-111-187-2010: Public Law 111-187 of the 111th Congress, approved June 9, 2010, names a post office in North Troy, New York. The site at 2-116th Street is named the Martin G. 'Marty' Mahar Post Office. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record after that date uses the new name.
plaw-111-188-2010: With Public Law 111-188, approved June 9, 2010, Congress named a post office in Cheyney, Pennsylvania, for an Army Air Forces captain. The Postal Service site at 119 Station Road is now the Captain Luther H. Smith, U.S. Army Air Forces Post Office. Federal laws, maps, rules, and records must use that name for the site from then on.
plaw-111-189-2010: Public Law 111-189, from the 111th Congress in 2010, names a post office building in Westwood, New Jersey, for a sergeant. The site at 216 Westwood Avenue is now the Sergeant Christopher R. Hrbek Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name.
plaw-111-190-2010:
Public Law 111-190, enacted by the 111th Congress in 2010, extends a 2004 antitrust law. That law, the Antitrust Criminal Penalty Enhancement and Reform Act, was set to lose effect after six years. The new act stretches that span to sixteen years instead.

The act also guards firms that seek leniency from the Antitrust Division for reporting price fixing. It defines a marker, a pledge from the division that holds a firm's place in line while it completes its leniency request. Firms that got a marker or signed a leniency deal before the end date stay covered after it passes.
plaw-111-191-2010:
After the Deepwater Horizon rig blew up and sank in 2010, Congress passed Public Law 111-191. The law amends the Oil Pollution Act of 1990. It deals with how the Coast Guard pays for the spill response. The spill at issue began in 2010 with the blast on the rig.

The act lets the Coast Guard take advances from the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund without waiting for a new spending bill. Each advance can reach 100 million dollars, within the fund's legal cap. Within seven days of each advance, the Coast Guard must tell Congress the amount and why it was needed.
plaw-111-192-2010:
Public Law 111-192 of 2010 carries the long title Preservation of Access to Care for Medicare Beneficiaries and Pension Relief Act. The 111th Congress passed it to fix doctor pay under Medicare and to give pension plans relief.

In its health title, the act sets the update to the Medicare payment rate for doctors at 2.2 percent for June through November 2010. It also states that this bump does not change how the rate is figured for the rest of 2010 or for later years. The pension part of the act, named in its title, gives funding relief to pension plans.
plaw-111-193-2010: Public Law 111-193, approved June 28, 2010, names a post office building in New Orleans, Louisiana. The Postal Service site at 2000 Louisiana Avenue is now the Roy Rondeno, Sr. Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill had passed the House in late 2009 and the Senate in June 2010.
plaw-111-194-2010:
Public Law 111-194 is a joint resolution of the 111th Congress from 2010. It concerns the draft constitution written for the United States Virgin Islands. Congress had let island voters write their own constitution under a 1976 law, and the draft reached Congress in March 2010.

Justice Department lawyers found parts of the draft that clashed with the United States Constitution and federal law. Their list flags a missing statement of United States sovereignty, perks tied to birth or ancestry, and rules on local waters, among other points. The resolution sends the draft back so those parts can be reworked and fixed.
plaw-111-195-2010:
The Comprehensive Iran Sanctions, Accountability, and Divestment Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-195. The 111th Congress passed it to widen United States sanctions on Iran. It builds on the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996. The first of its titles is devoted to sanctions.

The act orders sanctions on banks that carry out banned deals with Iran and on people blamed for abuses after Iran's June 2009 vote. It bars federal contracts with firms that sell sensitive tech to Iran. It also lets the president enforce United Nations Security Council sanctions on Iran. Its contents list also covers steps to fight unlawful and terrorist financing.
plaw-111-196-2010: Public Law 111-196, the National Flood Insurance Program Extension Act of 2010, keeps a flood cover program alive a bit longer. The 111th Congress moved the end date of the National Flood Insurance Program to September 30, 2010. It also set the program's borrowing cap at 20,725 million dollars, and made the change count as if it took effect on May 31, 2010.
plaw-111-197-2010:
Public Law 111-197, the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2010, Part II, is a short stopgap from the 111th Congress. It extends the taxes that feed the Airport and Airway Trust Fund. Those taxes cover jet fuel and air travel tickets.

The act moves the end dates for the fuel and ticket taxes to August 1, 2010. It lets the trust fund keep spending through August 2, 2010. It also covers the grants program that helps airports make upgrades, so airport aid does not halt in mid-summer of 2010. The changes take effect in early July 2010.
plaw-111-198-2010:
The Homebuyer Assistance and Improvement Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-198. Congress passed it to help buyers who had signed a contract but could not close in time to claim the homebuyer tax credit. It became law on July 2, 2010.

The act lets buyers with a binding contract signed before May 1, 2010, still claim the credit if they buy the home before October 1, 2010. The credit at stake was the federal credit for buying a main home. The act also extends the penalty for a bad check to other payment tools used to pay a tax bill.
plaw-111-199-2010:
Public Law 111-199, the Formaldehyde Standards for Composite Wood Products Act, amends the Toxic Substances Control Act. The 111th Congress passed it in 2010 to cut formaldehyde fumes from composite wood goods.

The act adds a new title to the older law with set limits for these goods. The new part is numbered Title VI of the older act. It covers hardwood plywood, particleboard, and medium-density fiberboard, plus finished goods made from them. It leaves out loose parts used to build a finished good, antiques, and used furniture that was bought in good faith. Some terms, like hardboard, are left for the agency head to define by rule.
plaw-111-200-2010:
Public Law 111-200 reauthorizes the Congressional Award program in 2010. Its short title calls it the Congressional Award Program Reauthorization Act of 2009, though it became law in July 2010. The program is run under the Congressional Award Act.

The act sets the terms for the board that runs the program. Appointed members serve four-year terms and may serve at most two full terms in a row. A member who chairs the board is exempt from that cap while in the chair and may take one more full term after. Terms start on October 1 of an even-numbered year.
plaw-111-201-2010:
Public Law 111-201 is a joint resolution of the 111th Congress marking sixty years since the Korean War began. North Korea invaded South Korea on June 25, 1950, with about 135,000 troops. President Harry Truman then ordered United States forces to help defend the South.

The text recalls that about 1,789,000 United States troops served in the war, beside South Korean and United Nations forces. It lists 54,246 United States dead and more than 103,284 wounded. The fighting ended with a cease-fire signed at Panmunjom on July 27, 1953, and the resolution reaffirms the United States alliance with Korea.
plaw-111-202-2010:
Public Law 111-202 makes Radio Free Asia a permanent service in 2010. Radio Free Asia, or RFA, began in 1996 as a private nonprofit based in Washington, D.C. Congress had first authorized it in 1994, in the hope that free media growth would one day make it needless.

RFA sends news, commentary, and culture shows to Asian countries whose rulers block a free press. It broadcasts each day in Mandarin, Tibetan, Korean, Burmese, and other tongues. Because those states jam its radio signals, RFA leans on shortwave and the internet to reach its listeners.
plaw-111-203-2010:
The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, Public Law 111-203, is the 111th Congress's big answer to the 2008 financial crash. Its stated aims are to steady the nation's finances, end the idea of too big to fail, shield taxpayers from bailouts, and guard buyers from abusive money services.

The act's first title sets up a Financial Stability Oversight Council to watch for risks across the whole system. It gives that council power to place large nonbank firms under stricter watch by the Federal Reserve. The titles that follow, listed in its long table of contents, reach deep into banks, markets, and home loans.
plaw-111-204-2010:
Public Law 111-204 is the Improper Payments Elimination and Recovery Act of 2010. It amends a 2002 law on mistaken payments by federal agencies. Congress aimed to stop the loss of billions in taxpayer dollars.

The act orders each agency head to review all programs on a set cycle and flag those prone to large mistaken payments. Agency heads must follow guidance from the Office of Management and Budget when they do these reviews. Reviews start the year after the act and repeat at least once every three fiscal years. A program counts as high risk when its bad payments may top ten million dollars in a year.
plaw-111-205-2010:
The Unemployment Compensation Extension Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-205. The 111th Congress passed it in July 2010 to keep jobless aid programs from lapsing. It amends the tax code and several past aid laws. The programs at stake gave extra weeks of benefits to workers who had lost their jobs.

The act pushes key end dates for extra jobless benefits from June 2, 2010, to the end of November 2010. Related cutoffs move to April 30 or May 1, 2011. One change covers the Assistance for Unemployed Workers and Struggling Families Act, part of Public Law 111-5. The act also updates the funding rules so the extended benefits can be paid.
plaw-111-206-2010:
Public Law 111-206 carries the title Shasta-Trinity National Forest Administrative Jurisdiction Transfer Act. Passed in 2010, it swaps control of some federal land in California between two agencies. One side is the Forest Service; the other is the Bureau of Land Management.

Land inside the Shasta-Trinity National Forest, shown on a 2009 map, moves from the Agriculture chief to the Interior chief. A second tract moves the other way, from the land bureau to the Forest Service. Land that moves to the bureau is then run under the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976.
plaw-111-207-2010:
The Cruise Vessel Security and Safety Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-207. It amends title 46 of the United States Code to set safety and security rules for cruise ships. Congress wrote it after crimes on cruise voyages drew public concern.

Congress found about 200 overnight ocean cruise ships worldwide, each carrying some 2,000 riders and a crew of about 950. It noted that riders often do not grasp their risk of crime at sea or know their rights after a crime. The act then sets rules meant to guard riders and crew, in a part titled for cruise vessel security and safety needs.
plaw-111-208-2010: Public Law 111-208, approved July 27, 2010, names a post office in Columbus, Ohio. The Postal Service site at 1981 Cleveland Avenue is now the Clarence D. Lumpkin Post Office. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in March 2010 and the Senate in May of that year.
plaw-111-209-2010:
Public Law 111-209 of 2010 changes one date in the Credit Card Accountability Responsibility and Disclosure Act of 2009. The change concerns the gift card rules in Title IV of that act. Most of those rules still took effect 15 months after the 2009 act.

For gift cards made before April 1, 2010, the act delays some notice duties until January 31, 2011. In the gap, issuers must treat card funds as if they never expire and swap a card with funds left at no cost. They must also tell buyers of these terms through store signs, service calls, web sites, and ads.
plaw-111-210-2010:
Public Law 111-210 is a joint resolution of the 111th Congress from July 2010. It approves the renewal of import limits set in the Burmese Freedom and Democracy Act of 2003. Those limits target goods from Burma, also known as Myanmar.

The resolution counts as a renewal resolution under the 2003 act. It also shifts a customs user fee date by one week in August 2018. A third part raises a corporate tax payment rate set in a 2010 jobs act by a quarter of a point, as a budget offset. The tax rate at issue sits in section 561 of the Hiring Incentives to Restore Employment Act.
plaw-111-211-2010:
Public Law 111-211 of 2010 opens with a title called the Indian Arts and Crafts Amendments Act of 2010. That title aims to guard real Indian arts and crafts from fake goods sold as genuine. It amends an older act that set up a board to aid Indian craft work.

The title rewrites the part of the older act on court cases and civil suits. It states that any federal law enforcement officer may probe a claimed breach of the act inside the United States. Its contents list also covers the false labeling of goods as Indian made.
plaw-111-212-2010:
The Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2010 is Public Law 111-212. It adds extra spending for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2010. The text opens with the Department of Agriculture and its farm loan programs.

In that opening chapter, the act backs farm ownership and farm operating loans run by the Farm Service Agency. It sets loan totals in the hundreds of millions of dollars for backed and direct loans. It also adds one million dollars for the cost of running those loan programs, before moving on to forest repair work. A following part of the same chapter funds the Emergency Forest Restoration Program.
plaw-111-213-2010:
Public Law 111-213 is the Independent Living Centers Technical Adjustment Act of 2010. It tweaks how grant funds for centers for independent living are split in some states. The centers are funded under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973.

In a state where federal funds for the centers top state funds, the act fixes the fiscal year 2010 split. Each center in the state gets the same share of the funds as it got in fiscal year 2009. When that math is done, funds that came from the 2009 Recovery Act are left out of the count.
plaw-111-214-2010: Public Law 111-214 of 2010 gives small business programs a short extra lease on life. It moves the end date for programs under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 from July 31, 2010, to September 30, 2010. The change took effect on July 30, 2010, the day the act was approved. The bill passed the House and Senate on the same day, July 27, 2010.
plaw-111-215-2010: Public Law 111-215 of 2010 pushes back the date when ship discharge permits can be required. It amends a 2008 law that barred the EPA and states from asking for permits for discharges tied to the normal running of a vessel. That bar now runs until December 18, 2013, instead of ending two years after the 2008 act.
plaw-111-216-2010:
The Airline Safety and Federal Aviation Administration Extension Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-216. Title I of the act extends the taxes that fund the Airport and Airway Trust Fund. It also extends the airport improvement program and other FAA powers for a short span.

Title II turns to airline safety and pilot training. Its contents list a pilot records database, a task force on air carrier safety and pilot training, and more safety inspectors. It also covers how the transport chief should answer safety board advice. It was approved on August 1, 2010.
plaw-111-217-2010: Public Law 111-217, approved August 3, 2010, names a post office building in Chicago, Illinois. The Postal Service site at 1343 West Irving Park Road is now the Steve Goodman Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in April 2010 and the Senate on July 14 of that year.
plaw-111-218-2010: In Public Law 111-218, approved August 3, 2010, Congress named a post office building in Hornell, New York. The Postal Service site at 23 Genesee Street is now the Zachary Smith Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in May 2010 and the Senate on July 14 of that year.
plaw-111-219-2010: Public Law 111-219, approved August 3, 2010, names a post office in Sharon, Massachusetts. The Postal Service site at 15 South Main Street is now the Michael C. Rothberg Post Office. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in May 2010 and the Senate on July 14 of that year.
plaw-111-220-2010:
The Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-220. Its stated aim is to restore fairness to federal cocaine sentencing. For years, crack cocaine drew far harsher prison terms than the same weight of powder cocaine.

The act raises the crack amounts that trigger set prison terms, from 50 grams to 280 grams and from 5 grams to 28 grams. It ends the mandatory minimum term for simple possession of crack. At the same time, it raises the fines that can be imposed on major drug traffickers. The text makes the same threshold changes in the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act.
plaw-111-221-2010:
Public Law 111-221 is the National September 11 Memorial & Museum Commemorative Medal Act of 2010. It marks ten years since the September 11, 2001, terror attacks on the United States. It also marks the founding of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum at the World Trade Center.

The act orders the Treasury chief to strike up to two million silver medals for sale. Each medal holds one ounce of silver and bears the years 2001-2011 and the words Always Remember. The design must honor the courage of those who died, those who risked their lives to save others, and those who lived through that day.
plaw-111-222-2010: Public Law 111-222 of 2010 makes a single small change to the National Law Enforcement Museum Act. It strikes the words 10 years in that act and inserts 13 years. The change extends the end date for the museum project by three years. The act was approved on August 6, 2010. The bill had passed the Senate in May 2010 and the House on July 21 of that year.
plaw-111-223-2010:
Public Law 111-223 is the Securing the Protection of our Enduring and Established Constitutional Heritage Act, called the SPEECH Act for short. It amends title 28 of the United States Code. The subject is foreign libel suits against United States writers and publishers.

Congress found that some claimants sue United States authors in foreign courts whose libel laws guard speech far less than the First Amendment does. The act bars United States courts from honoring foreign defamation judgments that clash with that protection. It also covers some foreign judgments against firms that run interactive computer services.
plaw-111-224-2010:
Public Law 111-224 is the United States Patent and Trademark Office Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2010. It adds funds for the patent office for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2010. The stated amount is 129 million dollars for salaries and expenses.

The extra sum is meant to be offset by patent and trademark fees the office collects, leaving a net cost of zero from the general fund. To balance the books, the act cancels 129 million dollars that had been set aside for the Census Bureau's periodic census work. The patent office funds stay open until spent.
plaw-111-225-2010:
The Cell Phone Contraband Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-225. It amends title 18 of the United States Code. The subject is phones and like wireless gear held by federal prisoners.

The act adds a phone or other device used on a commercial mobile service to the list of banned items in federal prison law. It thus makes holding or using such a device by a federal prisoner a crime under that section. The act also orders a study, due in one year, of phone rates charged inside federal prisons. The study also covers the costs of running inmate phone services and what providers pay to supply them.
plaw-111-226-2010:
Public Law 111-226 of 2010 is a spending law whose enrolled text left its own short title blank. Its opening lines speak of updating air traffic control and renewing the Federal Aviation Administration. The first title that follows does something else entirely.

Title I creates an Education Jobs Fund and puts ten billion dollars into it. The fund is run by the Education chief under terms drawn from the 2009 Recovery Act. Half of one percent is set aside first for schools run or funded by the Bureau of Indian Affairs. A further share of the fund's terms is drawn from sections 14001 through 14013 of that act.
plaw-111-227-2010:
The United States Manufacturing Enhancement Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-227. It amends the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States. The aim is to change, for a limited time, the import duties on a long list of goods.

Title I lists new duty suspensions and cuts item by item. Early entries cover reusable grocery bags and many kinds of synthetic staple fibers used in textiles. Each entry names one product and the temporary rate change that applies to it. The schedule is the master list of United States import taxes. Congress passed the act in August 2010.
plaw-111-228-2010: Public Law 111-228 is the General and Special Risk Insurance Funds Availability Act of 2010. For fiscal year 2010, it lets the Housing and Urban Development chief pledge to guarantee loans tied to the two funds named in the title. Total loan principal under those pledges may reach 20 billion dollars. The pledges rest on two sections of the National Housing Act.
plaw-111-229-2010:
Public Law 111-229 of 2010 gives the Housing and Urban Development chief more freedom over FHA mortgage insurance premiums. The premiums at issue are those charged for single family home loans insured by the Federal Housing Administration.

The act raises the cap on the yearly premium from 0.50 percent to 1.5 percent of the loan balance. A second cap rises from 0.55 percent to 1.55 percent. The chief may set the actual rates by a notice in the Federal Register or a letter to lenders. The act also calls the FHA chief to testify before Congress on FHA finances within 270 days.
plaw-111-230-2010:
Public Law 111-230 of 2010 makes emergency extra appropriations for border security. The money is for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2010. Title I funds the Department of Homeland Security, above all Customs and Border Protection.

The largest sum, about 254 million dollars, covers salaries and expenses. Of that, about 176 million dollars pays to hire more Border Patrol agents for the Southwest border. Other parts fund more customs officers at ports of entry and background checks. Further sums cover border fencing tech, tactical radios, and air and marine operations. The sums stay open past the fiscal year, most until September 30, 2011.
plaw-111-231-2010: Public Law 111-231, approved August 16, 2010, concerns federal easements on land in Caseyville, Illinois. It lets the Agriculture chief end any easement the chief holds on land owned by the Village of Caseyville. The chief may also end the linked contract terms with the Village. In return, the Village must enter into offsetting arrangements that the chief finds fitting. The easements at issue were held through the Natural Resources Conservation Service.
plaw-111-232-2010:
The Star-Spangled Banner Commemorative Coin Act is Public Law 111-232, passed in 2010. It orders the Treasury chief to mint coins for the 200th year since the writing of the Star-Spangled Banner. The song later became the national anthem of the United States.

The act's findings retell how Francis Scott Key watched the British shelling of Fort McHenry in September 1814. Seeing the huge flag still flying at dawn, he began the song first called The Defence of Fort McHenry. The coin part of the act then sets the terms for the new coins, starting with one-dollar silver coins.
plaw-111-233-2010: Public Law 111-233 carries the short title Agricultural Credit Act of 2010, though its whole work is one date change. It reauthorizes state farm mediation programs run under title V of the Agricultural Credit Act of 1987. To do so, it strikes the year 2010 in the funding section of that act and inserts 2015. The act was approved on August 16, 2010.
plaw-111-234-2010: Public Law 111-234, approved August 16, 2010, names a courthouse annex in Atlanta, Georgia. The annex, then under construction for the Elbert P. Tuttle United States Court of Appeals Building at 56 Forsyth Street, is named the John C. Godbold Federal Building. Any mention of the annex in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name.
plaw-111-235-2010: A post office building in Dixon, Illinois, took a president's name under Public Law 111-235. The building stands at 405 West Second Street and serves Dixon for the Postal Service. Under the act, approved August 16, 2010, its name is the President Ronald W. Reagan Post Office Building. Federal laws, maps, and records must call it by that name. The House passed the bill in June 2010, and the Senate followed on July 30.
plaw-111-236-2010: Public Law 111-236 gave the Maitland, Florida, post office building the name Paula Hawkins Post Office Building. The building stands at 151 North Maitland Avenue. Congress approved the act on August 16, 2010. The House had passed the bill in June, and the Senate acted on July 30. From then on, federal laws, maps, rules, and records use the new name for the site.
plaw-111-237-2010:
The Firearms Excise Tax Improvement Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-237. Despite the short title, its terms cover the makers' excise tax on recreational equipment in general. It amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

The act states that this tax is due on the date the tax return for it must be filed, a shift the act's title frames as a move to quarterly payment. It also tells the Treasury chief to assess and collect court-ordered criminal restitution for unpaid taxes in the same way as the tax itself. That rule reaches orders made under title 18 of the code.
plaw-111-238-2010: Public Law 111-238 of 2010 extends Navy power to sign multiyear contracts for three aircraft types. The planes are the F/A-18E and F/A-18F fighters and the EA-18G Growler. The act amends the defense act for fiscal year 2010, changing a date in its approval step from March to September. It also states that the section counts as meeting two tests set in title 10 of the code for such contracts.
plaw-111-239-2010:
Public Law 111-239 is the Mandatory Price Reporting Act of 2010. It amends the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946. Its subject is the reporting of prices for livestock and dairy goods sold in the United States.

The act extends the livestock price reporting power from September 30, 2010, to September 30, 2015. It adds a new duty for meat packers to report the price and volume of wholesale pork cuts to the Agriculture chief. The chief must publish that data and must set up a joint rule-making process with the trade to write the pork rule.
plaw-111-240-2010:
The Small Business Jobs Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-240. Its first aim is a Small Business Lending Fund Program run by the Treasury chief. The fund puts capital into banks and like lenders so they can lend more to small firms.

The act also amends the tax code to add tax breaks meant to spur small business hiring. Its contents list widens Small Business Administration loan programs, among them 7(a) business loans, 504 loans, and microloans. It raises the top loan amounts under several of those programs. The act was signed on September 27, 2010.
plaw-111-241-2010:
Public Law 111-241 is the Multinational Species Conservation Funds Semipostal Stamp Act of 2010. It tells the Postal Service to issue a special stamp for wildlife conservation funds. A semipostal stamp sells above the normal postage price, with the extra going to a cause.

The stamp costs the price of a one-ounce letter plus a markup of at least 15 percent, and buying it is a free choice. The act says the sum raised from sales goes to the Multinational Species Conservation Funds. Those funds back work to protect species shared across national borders.
plaw-111-242-2010:
The Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011 is Public Law 111-242. Congress passed it on September 30, 2010, to keep the federal government funded into fiscal year 2011. It is a stopgap measure used when the regular yearly spending acts are not yet law.

The act funds each agency at the rate set by its fiscal year 2010 spending act, under the same terms. Its opening section lists the 2010 acts that supply those rates, from farm and defense spending to homeland security and interior. It covers work that was already under way in 2010. It was approved on September 30, 2010.
plaw-111-243-2010: Public Law 111-243, approved September 30, 2010, names a federal building in Jackson, Mississippi. The building at 1220 Echelon Parkway is designated the James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, Michael Schwerner, and Roy K. Moore Federal Building. The head of the General Services Administration must ensure the name is used. While the building is federally occupied, any mention of it in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name.
plaw-111-244-2010:
Public Law 111-244 of 2010 deals with two island topics. Its stated subject is the use of existing funds for political status education in the Territory of Guam. A second part concerns the minimum wage in American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.

Section 1 states the sense of Congress that the Interior chief may aid Guam's status education only for options that fit the United States Constitution. Section 2 then delays set wage rises in the two territories, with no rise in 2010 or 2011. It also orders the Government Accountability Office to report on the effect of past wage rises.
plaw-111-245-2010:
The First Responder Anti-Terrorism Training Resources Act is Public Law 111-245. It amends the Homeland Security Act of 2002. The subject is the Center for Domestic Preparedness, which trains first responders for terror attacks and disasters.

The act lets the Homeland Security chief accept and use gifts for the center's lawful training work. Gifts may be land, goods, or services, even guest lectures. The chief may not take a gift whose use would harm the honesty, or the look of honesty, of a department program. Each year the chief must report to Congress on gifts taken under the act.
plaw-111-246-2010: Public Law 111-246 of 2010 widens who may receive care in state veterans homes. The Veterans Affairs chief must let a state home give nursing home care to a new class of parents. The class covers a non-veteran parent whose child died while serving in the Armed Forces. The rule sits in title 38 of the federal regulations, at section 51.210. The act was approved on September 30, 2010.
plaw-111-247-2010:
Public Law 111-247 is the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2010. It raises the rates of pay for veterans hurt in service, starting December 1, 2010. It also raises payments to the survivors of some disabled veterans who have died.

The sums raised cover wartime disability pay, extra pay for dependents, and the clothing allowance. They also cover dependency and indemnity pay for spouses and children of veterans. Each sum rises by the same percent as the rise in Social Security benefits under title II of the Social Security Act. It is the 2010 entry in a yearly series of such acts.
plaw-111-248-2010:
Public Law 111-248 of 2010 improves the running of some House of Representatives facilities and programs. Section 1 concerns the exercise facility, or gym, built for House staff. Section 2 concerns the House Child Care Center and how its money is held.

Section 1 lets active duty service members posted to a military liaison office at the House join the staff gym on the same terms as House staff. Section 2 turns the child care center's account into a revolving fund in the Treasury. That fund becomes the sole source for the center's pay and costs.
plaw-111-249-2010: Public Law 111-249 is the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2010, Part III, a further short stopgap for air travel programs. It moves the end date for the fuel and ticket taxes that fund the Airport and Airway Trust Fund from September 30, 2010, to December 31, 2010. The trust fund may keep spending through January 1, 2011. The act also extends the airport improvement program, and its changes take effect on October 1, 2010.
plaw-111-250-2010: Public Law 111-250 carries the title National Flood Insurance Program Reextension Act of 2010. In two short changes, it moves the end date of the National Flood Insurance Program from September 30, 2010, to September 30, 2011. The same one-year shift applies to the program's financing terms. The act was approved on September 30, 2010, the very day the old end date fell.
plaw-111-251-2010: Public Law 111-251 of 2010 grants small business programs one more short extension. It amends the same 2006 extension law that Public Law 111-214 had amended weeks before. This time the end date moves from September 30, 2010, to January 31, 2011. The programs covered sit under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958. The change counts as effective from September 29, 2010.
plaw-111-252-2010: Public Law 111-252 of 2010 concerns a narrow group of federal workers: Customs and Border Protection staff serving abroad on limited appointments. It lets the Commissioner of that agency move such a worker into a permanent post in the competitive service. The worker must first complete at least two years of steady service on one or more overseas limited appointments. The worker's ratings must also have stayed at fully successful or better for that whole span. The power applies despite the normal exam and hiring rules in title 5 of the code.
plaw-111-253-2010:
