Jeremy R. Haag, Olga Pontes, and Craig S. Pikaard studied two plant-specific polymerases in 2009. Plants have five nuclear RNA polymerases, more than other eukaryotes. Polymerases IV and V are found only in plants. They drive small-RNA-guided DNA methylation, which silences genes.

Their PLOS ONE article tests the metal-binding sites of Pol IV and Pol V. Both metal A and metal B sites proved required for silencing. Without them, siRNA-dependent methylation failed. The result confirms these polymerases work as true enzymes in the pathway. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004210:
Han-Jun Jin, Chris Tyler-Smith, and Wook Kim published this population genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Koreans are generally classed as a northeast Asian group based on geography. Yet Y-chromosome studies had shown that the Korean population carries lineages from both southern and northern East Asia.

To untangle that history, the team analysed mitochondrial DNA, inherited from mothers, alongside Y-chromosomal markers inherited from fathers. Comparing the two sides of ancestry sharpens the picture of how Korea was peopled. The study weighs how much of the population came from each direction.
plos-pone-0004310:
Sarah Louie and colleagues published this signalling study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Wnt signals guide cell fate, proliferation, polarity, and movement as vertebrate embryos grow, acting through beta-catenin-dependent and independent pathways. Wnt signals are among the oldest in animal life. Dishevelled is a scaffold protein required for this signalling, gathering other proteins around it.

The team studied Hipk1, a protein that associates with Dishevelled. They report that Hipk1 tunes the beta-catenin signalling pathway. A modulator attached to the central scaffold can tune one of the embryo's most important signals up or down. Tuning it changes how cells read Wnt messages.
plos-pone-0004410:
Two opioid receptors push impulsivity in opposite directions. Mary Olmstead, Abdel-Mouttalib Ouagazzal, and Brigitte Kieffer report that split in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. Impulsivity is a primary feature of many psychiatric disorders, including ADHD and drug addiction.

Impulsivity covers failing to delay rewards and failing to withhold a motor response. Using a signaled nose poke task, the authors show mu and delta receptors regulate motor impulsivity oppositely. That contrast could guide drugs that tune one receptor but not the other. It refines models of addiction and self-control. Motor impulsivity is the urge to act, distinct from choosing delayed rewards.
plos-pone-0004510:
Two typhoid-causing Salmonella types arrived at the same deadly trick by different roads, show Wei-Qiao Liu, Ye Feng, Yan Wang, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. More than fourteen hundred Salmonella types cause gut illness that usually passes on its own. A few, including Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi C, cause typhoid, a whole-body infection that can kill.

It was not known whether the typhoid agents came from one common ancestor or evolved separately. Comparing their genes, the team found paratyphi C diverged from a gut relative, Salmonella choleraesuis. Its disease style converged with typhi's. In plain terms, nature invented typhoid more than once. That matters for vaccines, which may need to cover separate lineages.
plos-pone-0004610:
Thyroid hormone switches genes in the developing cerebellum, and Hongyan Dong, Carole Yauk, Andrea Rowan-Carroll, and co-authors mapped where it binds, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Thyroid hormone is critical to normal brain development, but the mechanisms operating in this process are poorly understood. Without enough of it, a child's brain development suffers lasting harm.

The team used a method called ChIP-on-chip, which fishes out DNA regions bound by a protein and identifies them on a chip. They sampled the cerebellum of mice fifteen days after birth and captured regions bound by the thyroid receptor beta. The resulting list of binding sites and target genes shows, concretely, which genes the hormone throws its switches on during a key window of brain growth.
plos-pone-0004710:
Chehani Alles and colleagues compared gene activity in breast cancers that lack the estrogen sensor, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Such cancers tend to have worse outlook, higher grade, and distinct traits under the microscope. Within them, one subgroup stands out for its own gene pattern and course.

The team merged many studies and ran gene set tests split by sensor status. They found raised activity of two growth drivers in the basal subgroup. Clear driver maps can help split breast cancer into truer types. That split guides which drugs to test for each type. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004810:
Stefan Koestler and colleagues measured F- and G-actin concentrations in lamellipodia of moving cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells protrude by polymerizing monomeric G actin into polymeric F actin at the tip of the lamellipodium. Filaments depolymerize toward the rear in a treadmilling process, supplementing the G actin pool for new rounds of polymerization at the advancing front edge.

Direct concentration measurements test that classic model. Values show how much building material is available locally. Quantitative data constrain models of cell crawling. Crawling underlies wound healing, immunity, and cancer spread. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004910:
Simon Reinke and colleagues studied influence of recovery and training phases on soccer players body composition and immunity, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Professional soccer players endure lengthy seasons with high physical stress maintained throughout. The recuperation period before next pre season is generally considered short but sufficient. The team tracked peripheral vascular function and immune system markers across recovery and retraining in elite athletes.

Recovery restores most markers but not all equally. Short off seasons may accumulate fatigue across careers. Monitoring guides individualized load management. Elite sport science informs occupational health. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0005010:
When a cell dies by apoptosis, its DNA is chopped into pieces. The first cuts were thought to land randomly. Miriam Di Filippo and Giorgio Bernardi showed otherwise in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used an entirely new approach on chicken liver cells. Their focus was early apoptotic DNA fragmentation.

The early cuts strike only a few specific regions. Those regions are open chromatin, where DNA is loosely packed. The precision suggests a programmed first strike. Random shredding comes later, if at all. The finding rewrites the opening chapter of cell death. It raises new questions about how the cutting machinery chooses its first targets.
plos-pone-0005110:
Dried bloodstains hold DNA that forensic scientists prize. Ancient DNA researchers prize it too. A worry was that aging hemoglobin damages that DNA. April Marrone and Jack Ballantyne tested the worry in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hemoglobin is the iron-carrying protein of red blood cells. In the dry state, it changes over time.

Those changes did not increase oxidative DNA damage. Dried blood keeps its DNA safer than feared. The finding reassures anyone reading genes from old stains. Crime labs can trust aged samples a bit more. Ancient DNA work gains the same reassurance. The study turns a plausible fear into a tested non-issue.
plos-pone-0005210:
Macrophages are immune cells that swallow invading bacteria, a process called phagocytosis. Staphylococcus aureus can survive that swallowing, turning the macrophage into a refuge. Koziel and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that the swallowing also changes the macrophage itself.

After taking in the bacteria, macrophages raised their levels of anti-death factors that keep the cell alive. A living host cell shelters the bacteria inside it. That bargain helps explain why staph infections can persist, and it points to the host cell's survival program as a treatment target. If the host cell stays alive, the germs inside it stay safe too, so drugs that break that truce could clear infections that now come back.
plos-pone-0005310:
For a synapse to release its message, vesicles must dock at the membrane in a precise molecular embrace. Camoletto and colleagues studied one docking partnership in PLOS ONE in 2009, between the proteins syntaxin1 and Munc18. A lipid called sphingosine turned out to regulate it.

Mice lacking an enzyme that breaks down sphingolipids model a disorder with mental retardation, making them useful for this question. The work shows lipids are not passive packing in synapses. They actively tune docking, which links lipid balance to healthy brain signaling. Fat and sugar signals share the stage at the synapse, so a fault in fat balance could dull the mind in ways that pure protein views would miss at first glance.
plos-pone-0005410:
Antibodies against two malaria parasite surface proteins, MSP3 and MSP6, help a protective mechanism that stops parasite growth. Both proteins share a small signature section at one end. Singh and colleagues extended that story to a whole gene family in PLOS ONE in 2009.

A conserved multi-gene family in Plasmodium falciparum induces cross-reactive antibodies. Cross-reactive means the antibodies hit several family members, not just one variant. Broad coverage is precious in malaria, where the parasite often escapes by varying its surface. Parts of this parasite stay the same while the rest of its coat shifts,. Those fixed parts are the spots where one vaccine might guard a child in Mali and a man in Brazil at the same time.
plos-pone-0005510:
Svenja Günther, Kai Matuschewski, and Sylke Müller knocked out a malaria gene in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Lipoic acid is a helper that lets key enzymes in cells handle fuel. The malaria parasite must attach this helper to its enzymes to keep growing in blood.

The team removed a parasite gene for one attaching enzyme and watched what happened. The parasites fared poorly in the blood stage, the stage that makes people ill. A step the parasite cannot do without is a promising target for new malaria drugs. The blood stage is also the stage that spreads back to mosquitoes, so weakening it could cut transmission as well.
plos-pone-0005610:
Adeel Safdar and co-authors studied small RNAs in mouse muscle after hard exercise in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. MicroRNAs tune gene activity after genes are read, and a few are known to guide muscle cell growth. What a single bout of endurance exercise does to them was less clear.

The team ran mice through acute endurance exercise and measured microRNAs in their skeletal muscle. The profile shifted with the workout, pointing to which genes muscle adjusts first. That helps explain how one exercise session starts the body's adaptation to training. Endurance exercise reshapes muscle over weeks, and this early response is where that reshaping begins.
plos-pone-0005710:
Heather Miller and colleagues sorted out the true job of a helper protein in HIV in 2009. The protein, Tat-SF1, was thought to help HIV's Tat switch on viral genes. It was found through lab mixes that rebuilt viral gene reading step by step.

Careful tests showed Tat-SF1 is not needed for Tat's switch-on work after all. Instead, it sets the balance between two forms of HIV RNA, cut and uncut. That balance decides which viral proteins get made. Correcting an old assumption keeps HIV research aimed at the right targets for drugs.
plos-pone-0005810:
Philip Liu and co-authors untangled in 2009 how two immune signals converge to arm human cells against germs. When a sensor on monocytes detects germs, the cell mounts a vitamin D dependent attack. A cytokine called IL-1 beta is part of that same defense web.

The team showed the IL-1 beta path and the vitamin D receptor path meet and reinforce each other. Together they drive the antimicrobial response triggered by the sensor. That meeting point helps explain why vitamin D status affects infection risk. It also suggests combined ways to boost innate defense.
plos-pone-0005910:
Liz Allen and co-authors compared in 2009 two ways of judging which research papers truly matter: expert review and citation counts. Funders need to know which outputs were landmarks. Shortly after publication in 2005, nearly seven hundred Wellcome Trust papers were rated by experts.

The team checked how well bibliometric indicators matched those expert judgments of quality and importance. Agreement was imperfect, which matters when money follows metrics. Counts are cheap and experts are costly, so the trade-off needs evidence. This study supplies it for a large, real cohort of biomedical papers.
plos-pone-0006010:
The eye sharpens an image before the brain ever sees it. Jacques Demongeot, Yannick Fouquet, Muhammad Tayyab and colleagues borrowed that skill for image processing in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies how natural vision works, in healthy eyes and in failing ones, and turns those mechanisms into contrast and contour operators for pictures.

Their models rest on neural networks with lateral inhibition, where active cells quiet their neighbors and edges stand out. Such flows can raise contrast and trace outlines in an image. By copying the retina's own tricks, the work links biology to software and may help both: better image tools, and a clearer model of vision itself.
plos-pone-0006110:
What a young rat eats can echo in its adult pancreas. Nicolas Theys, André Clippe, Thomas Bouckenooghe and colleagues followed that echo in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies rat islets, the pancreas clusters that make insulin. These islets start life with a weak antioxidant defense. They hold plenty of one guard enzyme and too little of the two that finish its work.

An early low-protein diet worsens that imbalance, and the islets falter. A defense left lopsided leaves insulin cells open to oxidative harm for life. The work links early nutrition to later diabetes risk by a named mechanism, giving the broad idea of developmental programming a concrete, testable chain.
plos-pone-0006210:
Smoking makes Crohn's disease worse, raising the risk of narrowed bowel, abnormal tunnels, and surgery. Ole Haagen Nielsen and colleagues asked what smoking does to gene activity in the colon, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of Crohn's patients. Genes and environment together drive the disease, and smoke is its best-known environmental harm.

The team profiled which genes were switched on or off in smokers versus non-smokers with Crohn's. Those shifts point to the pathways through which smoke aggravates the bowel. Knowing the pathways strengthens advice to quit with hard biology. It may also reveal drug targets that mimic the benefit of quitting.
plos-pone-0006310:
Brain responses to food pictures differ between lean people and those who have lost weight. Marc-Andre Cornier and colleagues tested short-term overfeeding in thin and reduced-obese volunteers in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Energy intake is regulated by body signals mixed with sensory input from the outside world.

The study examined how overfeeding changes the neuronal response to visual food cues in both groups. Comparing people who were never heavy with those who slimmed down isolates weight history effects. Such effects may explain why keeping weight off is so hard. The work maps appetite circuits under deliberate excess.
plos-pone-0006410:
Maps of protein interactions grow faster than anyone can test them by hand. Hua Li and Shoudan Liang showed that local network topology in human protein interaction data predicts functional association, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. High-throughput techniques generate huge interaction volumes, needing methods that suggest functional relationships automatically.

In yeast networks, neighbourhood patterns had already hinted at shared functions. The human analysis extends that principle. Proteins whose local map positions resemble each other often work together. Automated hints let experimentalists spend bench time on the likeliest pairs. Such maps help labs choose which pairs of proteins to test first at the bench.
plos-pone-0006510:
Catherine Dostert and co-authors linked a leftover of malaria to fever and immune alarms in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria brings back fever attacks again and again. The germs that cause it feed on blood. As they feed, they leave behind a dark crystal waste called hemozoin. The team asked what this waste does to the body.

Their title says the crystal acts as a danger signal that sets off an immune alarm called the Nalp3 inflammasome. That alarm may help drive the fever and harm of the disease. The waste thus keeps the body on alert even as germs are cleared. Blocking that alarm could be a new way to treat severe cases.
plos-pone-0006610:
Corinne Berthonneche and co-authors charted cardiovascular traits across mouse strains in PLOS ONE in 2009. They report characterization of many cardiovascular-related traits in twenty-three inbred mouse strains. Mice were phenotyped either in response to chronic administration of a single drug or at baseline. The drugs blocked or activated beta-adrenergic signaling, a core heart control pathway.

Strain differences show how strongly genes shape drug responses. Such a panel helps researchers choose the right strain for a study. It also models human variability in response to beta blockers. The dataset is a resource for cardiovascular genetics.
plos-pone-0006710:
Liang-I Lin, Shih-hui Chao, and Deirdre R. Meldrum built a simple device for isolating single cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microfabricated devices are powerful for cell-level studies. Building them, though, requires clean rooms and special training. Most biology labs cannot make or afford them easily. The authors wanted high-throughput single-cell analysis without microfabrication.

Their device is called the Microscale Oil-Covered Cell Array, or MOCCA. It is low-cost and simple enough for ordinary labs to assemble. Cells settle into an array where each can be studied alone. Single-cell work reveals differences that mixed samples hide. A practical device like MOCCA widens access to that kind of analysis.
plos-pone-0006810:
Mojgan Rastegar and colleagues designed gene therapy vectors for Rett syndrome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rett syndrome is an autism spectrum disorder. It is the leading cause of intellectual disability in females. Mutations in the MECP2 gene cause the condition. No treatment exists.

The team built viral vectors carrying the MECP2 gene. Their vectors are isoform-specific, matching particular versions of the protein. Expression from the vectors can be regulated. Control matters because too much MECP2 is also harmful. Regulated, specific delivery is a step toward safe gene therapy for Rett syndrome.
plos-pone-0006910:
Rikke Bæk Sørensen and colleagues found the immune system attacking a cancer-helping enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme is indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, or IDO. IDO suppresses immunity inside tumors and their draining lymph nodes. It helps establish tolerance toward the cancer. That makes IDO a villain in tumor immunology.

Patients nevertheless carried cellular immune responses against IDO itself. The immune system strikes back, as the title puts it. Such spontaneous responses suggest IDO can serve as a vaccine target. Turning a tolerance promoter into a target is an elegant reversal. The finding supports vaccines designed around IDO-derived peptides.
plos-pone-0007010:
Rudolph Spangler, Noel Goddard, and David Thaler fine-tuned a detection test in PLOS ONE in 2009. PCR can in principle detect a single target DNA molecule. In practice, stray bacterial DNA hiding in reagents sets the real limit. That contamination plagues efforts to find sparse bacteria in environmental and health samples.

The team varied the amount of Taq polymerase in the reaction. Their aim was the best signal-to-noise for broad range detection. A cleaner test matters for water safety and hospital screening. When bacteria are rare, cutting background noise is the difference between detection and a false answer.
plos-pone-0007110:
Oliver Baumann and Mark Greenlee studied attention and eye tracking in PLOS ONE in 2009. Smooth pursuit lets the eyes follow a moving target. Older views treated it as nearly automatic. Newer evidence showed attention matters for accurate pursuit. What attention does during pursuit, though, was unsettled.

The pair had subjects attend to moving sounds while tracking with their eyes. They measured the resulting activity in the cortex. Attention to auditory motion changed pursuit-related brain responses. The study shows the senses cooperate during tracking, rather than the eyes working alone. That matters for understanding attention disorders.
plos-pone-0007210:
Anna T. Reinicke, Kyla D. Omilusik, Genc Basha, and colleagues studied immunity to a foodborne bacterium in 2009. The bacterium is Listeria monocytogenes, which can cause serious illness. Dendritic cells can start CD8 T cell responses by cross-presentation, showing outside material in a special way.

That process lets a small number of dendritic cells start primary immune responses. The authors ask whether cross-priming by dendritic cells is essential against Listeria. Their PLOS ONE paper tests the requirement in living infection. The result matters for vaccine design, where dendritic cell pathways are a common target.
plos-pone-0007310: Mihaela E. Sardiu, Joshua M. Gilmore, Michael J. Carrozza, and colleagues presented a proteomics method in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject is protein complexes, groups of proteins that work together as machines inside cells. Knowing which proteins connect within a complex is essential for mapping cell function. The authors build a probabilistic deletion network from quantitative proteomics data, using protein removal patterns to infer how complex members connect with each other.
plos-pone-0007410:
Xi-Qin Ding, Alexander B. Quiambao, J. Browning Fitzgerald, and colleagues tested eye gene delivery safety in mice in 2009. Delivery under the retina of compacted DNA nanoparticles produces efficient gene expression in retinal cells. The nanoparticles use a polyethylene glycol substituted peptide to compact DNA into tiny particles that cells can take up.

The authors evaluate ocular safety of those compacted nanoparticles. They report delivery does not elicit toxicity in the mouse retina. Safety is the gate for retinal gene therapy, because the eye cannot tolerate inflammation well. Their result supports further development of non-viral eye treatments.
plos-pone-0007510:
Ildefonso De la Fuente and colleagues published a theoretical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the stable core of cell chemistry. Studies of single-celled organisms show a set of enzymes that stays active at all times. That set is called the metabolic core. Around it, other reactions switch on and off. The team asked what makes such a core appear in the first place.

Their models point to the number of catalytic elements as the crucial factor. When enough reacting components are present, a stable core emerges on its own. Below that threshold, the chemistry stays unsettled. That rule of thumb could help predict how real cells organize their metabolism. It also speaks to deeper questions about how orderly chemistry arises from many simple parts. The core is an outcome of numbers, not design.
plos-pone-0007610:
José López-Bao and colleagues published a field study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was the Iberian lynx, one of the world's most at-risk wild cats. Teams that guard such animals sometimes leave out extra food. The food may be meant for cats whose lives or litters are most at risk. Whether cats of each sex and age use that food in equal shares was not known. The team watched who ate at the feeding sites.

The strongest lynx took over the extra food. Access skewed by sex and age, so the gains were not shared alike. A plan meant to help the neediest may instead feed the strongest. That warning holds for feeding plans aimed at many kinds of wildlife. Good aims need checks on who truly gains. The study shows a care tool can widen gaps inside the very group it aims to save.
plos-pone-0007710:
Nobuaki Kono and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It introduces a web tool called Pathway Projector for viewing biochemical pathways. Pathway maps give context for the flood of data from modern experiments. They show how the parts of a cell work as a system.

The tool builds on the KEGG Atlas maps and the Google Maps interface. Users can zoom and pan across huge pathway charts, much like a street map. Layers of experimental data can be placed on top. The browser aims to do for pathway research what genome browsers did for DNA sequences.
plos-pone-0007810:
Dian-Bing Wang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It develops a fast test for the anthrax bacterium, Bacillus anthracis. The germ can be used as a biological threat agent. Quick, simple detection is vital for defense and for medicine.

Anthrax exists as hardy spores and as growing vegetative cells. Most tests catch one form or the other. The team raised monoclonal antibodies that detect both forms with the same reagents. They report three antibodies with high affinity and specificity. A single test for both forms would speed field screening in an emergency.
plos-pone-0007910:
Marjo den Broeder and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It creates a zebrafish model of fragile X syndrome. Fragile X is one of the most common known causes of inherited intellectual disability. The mutated gene, FMR1, is conserved from humans to fruit flies.

To study FMR1 during vertebrate development, the team knocked the gene out in zebrafish. They describe the generation and characterization of the mutant fish. Zebrafish develop fast and can be watched under a microscope. A fish model lets researchers screen drugs cheaply. It also tests what FMR1 does as a body is being built.
plos-pone-0008010:
Jeroen Pennings and colleagues mined data for better pregnancy screening markers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Screening for Down syndrome uses proteins in the mother's blood, drawn from the placenta or the baby's liver. The current set misses some cases and flags others wrongly.

Rather than test proteins one by one in the lab, the team sifted gene and protein data for strong candidates first. Their short list gives labs a focused set to check. Better markers would mean fewer mothers sent for risky follow-up tests and fewer cases missed before birth.
plos-pone-0008110:
Kwadwo Kusi and colleagues mixed several forms of a malaria protein to widen a vaccine's reach in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, AMA1, helps the parasite break into red blood cells. Its shape varies by strain, so a vaccine built on one form may miss others.

Animals given the mixed vaccine made antibodies that knew all the forms in the mix, not just one. Breadth is the whole game against a shape-shifting foe. The result backs the cocktail approach for malaria vaccines, even though mixing raises the work of making and testing them.
plos-pone-0008210:
Paola Sebastiani and colleagues studied genes linked to extreme old age in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Living to very old ages runs in families, which suggests genes play a role. Most genes found so far act in fat metabolism or insulin signaling. Many more longevity genes likely remain undiscovered. The team looked in an unexpected place: RNA editing genes.

They linked these genes both to extreme old age in humans and to lifespan in roundworms. Using two species strengthens the case for a real effect. RNA editing changes RNA after it is copied from DNA. The findings open a fresh angle on the biology of aging.
plos-pone-0008310:
Kanae Iijima-Ando and colleagues modeled Alzheimer's disease in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. Amyloid-beta 42 is thought to play a central role in the disease. How it causes neuronal dysfunction and degeneration remains elusive. Mitochondrial problems are seen in Alzheimer's brains. Whether those problems cause the damage was an open question.

In the fly model, mitochondria ended up in the wrong places within neurons. That mislocalization underlay the dysfunction caused by amyloid-beta 42. Neurons need mitochondria positioned where energy demand is high. The study links a small transport failure to large brain effects.
plos-pone-0008410:
André Ouédraogo and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about how malaria spreads by mosquito. For a mosquito to pick up malaria, the blood it drinks must hold the sex stage of the germ, called a gametocyte. These stages are most times few and far in the blood. Counts too low for a scope to see may still be high enough to infect a biting mosquito. How much weight such low counts carry was not known.

In a land where malaria comes with the rains, they weighed the share of these faint carriers. Such carriers gave a large part of all the spread to mosquitoes. Plans that find just the cases a scope can see will miss this pool. The work backs the use of more keen tests.
plos-pone-0008510:
Claire Salzer and co-authors map eye change hot spots in fruit flies in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A gene network called the retinal determination network governs early eye growth. It is conserved across the animal kingdom. Switching its members on in the wrong tissue can transform that tissue toward retina. Such ectopic eyes have long fascinated biologists. The team ask which tissues are most prone to transform.

They identify hot spots in developing fly epithelia where transformation occurs readily. Epithelia are sheets of cells that cover body surfaces. Hot spots reveal where the network's signals meet a receptive state. The map helps explain how organ identity can be reprogrammed.
plos-pone-0008610:
Nicole Meyer-Morse and co-authors study a cell defense during listeria infection in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The defense is autophagy, where cells digest their own parts and invaders. Past studies said it helps protect cells from Listeria, a germ that causes foodborne illness. The team find it has no clear role in the germ's escape or growth in macrophages. Instead they focus on a toxin the germ makes, called listeriolysin O.

They show that toxin alone is enough to trigger autophagy. No other germ factor is needed for that effect. The toxin lets the germ escape its compartment in the cell. Autophagy in this infection is thus a response to the toxin itself.
plos-pone-0008710:
Raquel López-Fontal, Miriam Zeini, Paqui Través, and colleagues asked what a thyroid receptor does during liver repair. Their mouse study ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. A liver can regrow after part of it is surgically removed. Thyroid hormone T3 was suspected to help that regrowth. Which receptor carries the signal was unclear, though.

The team used mice lacking the beta form of the receptor. After surgery, those livers showed more cell death. They also started their regrowth program later than normal livers. The delay names the beta receptor as a real player in repair.
plos-pone-0008810:
Farhad Karbassi, Veronica Quiros, Vijay Pancholi, and colleagues took apart an eight-piece bacterial enzyme. Their structural study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enolase is a workhorse enzyme in sugar breakdown. Most versions join as pairs of subunits. The Streptococcus pyogenes version stacks eight subunits in a ring of pairs. What held that bigger assembly together was unclear.

Breaking the octamer apart showed its interfaces support each other. Weakening one contact destabilized another contact far away. Cooperating interfaces explain the assembly's toughness. The lesson extends to many multi-part protein machines, including drug targets in germs.
plos-pone-0008910:
Celina Montemayor, Oscar Montemayor, Alex Ridgeway, and colleagues hunted the true target genes of a lonely receptor. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. NR2F1, also called COUP-TFI, is a nuclear receptor with no known natural activator. Such orphan receptors still control many body processes. Finding their direct gene targets in living tissue is hard. Binding alone does not prove control.

The team intersected genome-wide binding maps with gene activity data. Only genes passing both tests counted as direct targets. A verified target list grounds the receptor's role in development. The method itself can be reused for other orphan receptors.
plos-pone-0009010:
Anne-Katrin Rohlfing and co-authors found that salt stress can fool a worm's immune alarms, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans lives in soil and is a favourite lab animal. Infection by bacteria or fungi switches on a clear set of defence genes. The team studied genes that respond instead to osmotic stress, meaning water imbalance.

Turning on the salt-stress genes copied much of the infection pattern. The similarity suggests the two alarm systems share wiring. That overlap makes sense for a worm meeting germs and drying soil together. It also warns researchers that a defence signature may not always mean infection.
plos-pone-0009110:
Judith Reinhard and co-authors worked out how honeybees make sense of blended smells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A bee meets dozens of complex floral scents on her rounds every day. Each flower's perfume is a blend of many different odorant chemicals. How the bee's small brain unravels those mixtures was still unclear.

Bees, the team found, latch onto a few key odorants within a blend. They learn the whole mixture through those standout parts alone. The rest of the scent simply fades into the background for them. A key-odorant shortcut keeps the bee's crowded world of smells manageable.
plos-pone-0009210:
Ziad Al Tanoury and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines L-plastin, a protein that bundles actin fibers inside cells. Actin bundles give cells shape and help them move. L-plastin was first found in white blood cells and in many cancers, where it serves as a marker.

A phosphate tag on one spot of L-plastin makes it grip actin more strongly. The team measured the speed and strength of that bundling in detail. They also tracked how L-plastin changes the turnover of actin fibers. Those numbers explain how a single small tag can reshape the cell's skeleton, a process that matters in cancer spread.
plos-pone-0009310:
Lisa Rohan and co-authors published this HIV prevention study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tenofovir gel was in clinical trials as a microbicide, a gel women could use to block HIV infection. Oddly, no published pre-clinical testing of the gel existed. The team set out to supply that missing groundwork.

They tested tenofovir in lab dishes and in human tissue kept alive outside the body. In both models, the drug proved effective against HIV-1. Having lab results lets researchers validate what the clinical trials find in people. The study fills the bench side of the record for a leading prevention candidate.
plos-pone-0009410:
Yali Hou and co-authors published this dog breeding study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Canine hip dysplasia is a common inherited fault that cripples hips and burdens owners. A screening program for breeding dogs began in the United States in the 1960s. The team asked whether decades of screening actually improved hips.

They analyzed records of Labrador retrievers born from 1970 to 2007. The long cohort lets genetics separate steady improvement from year-to-year noise. Breeding programs are often run on faith; this audit checks the payoff. Its lessons reach any breed where inherited joint disease is selected against.
plos-pone-0009510:
Rita Guerreiro and colleagues examined a gene tied to Alzheimer's disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. Large genome scans had just flagged a gene called CLU as a risk factor. Such scans give a first hint, not a full account. The team read the gene in detail in patients and in controls. They hunted for variants that change risk.

Their work refined which parts of CLU matter for the disease. Confirming a scan hit with close reading helps separate true signals from noise. Each firm risk gene adds a clue about how the disease starts. CLU is thought to help clear harmful proteins, so its variants may point to new care ideas.
plos-pone-0009610:
Richard Gardner studied the first cell divisions of mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2010. The body's left and right sides are set very early in development. In mice, the young embryo normally rotates in a set direction as it grows. Gardner asked what decides that direction. His work points back to the embryo during its earliest cleavages. At that stage it is still a small ball of cells, and their makeup matters.

The way those first cells are composed biases which way the embryo turns. So a basic body pattern may be seeded before any organs form. The finding links the chemistry of the egg to the anatomy of the adult. It gives developmental biology a very early handle on left right patterning.
plos-pone-0009710:
Glaucoma slowly steals side vision, which can make driving risky. David Crabb and colleagues tracked eye movements in glaucoma patients as they viewed a driving scene. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Eye movements show where a driver looks and what they might miss.

Where the gaze goes matters when part of the visual field is gone. The team mapped scanning patterns and compared them with safe driving needs. Patterns like these could inform fitness-to-drive checks. They also matter for designing road scenes that are easier to scan.
plos-pone-0009810:
Jamie J Kirkham, Doug Altman, and Paula Williamson examine bias in medical reviews in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. A systematic review gathers all trials on a question under a plan written in advance. Changing the main outcomes, the results a review tracks, after seeing findings can tilt its verdict.

The team compared plans and finished Cochrane reviews for two hundred and eighty-eight pairs. Over a fifth differed in at least one outcome, most often the main one. Few reviews explained the change. In some, the switch came after trial results were known, and promoted outcomes were more often positive. The authors urge full, open reporting of every outcome change and its reason.
plos-pone-0009910:
A growth pathway inside cells can be switched on by bringing two proteins together. Zhiyong Ding and colleagues tested whether that contact alone is enough to fire the pathway. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The proteins are PDK1 and AKT1, both key links in cell growth signaling. Their physical association proved sufficient for pathway activation. That held independent of membrane localization and of phosphatidylinositol 3 kinase, two steps long thought required. AKT pathways help control cell survival and growth. The result simplifies a famous pathway's wiring diagram. Each partner is a kinase, an enzyme that switches other proteins on.
plos-pone-0010010:
Roy Malka, Eliezer Shochat, and Vered Rom-Kedar offered a math-based study of bacterial infection in PLOS ONE in 2010. Infections take hold when invading bacteria overwhelm the body's defenses. Neutrophils, a front-line white blood cell, do much of that defense, so low counts or poor function raise risk sharply.

The authors used bistability, an idea where a system can settle into one of two stable states. In their framing, a body can sit in a healthy state or tip into an acute infection state. That view helps explain why similar exposures can end very differently, and why early treatment can matter so much.
plos-pone-0010110:
Abigail Fisher and colleagues use twins to split genes from surroundings in a 2010 PLOS ONE study of children's activity. Twin studies act as natural experiments, since identical twins share all genes and fraternal twins share half. The team studied nine to twelve year olds, measuring daily movement with motion sensors.

Shared home surroundings explained most of the gap in measured daily activity, with no clear gene effect. By contrast, fidgetiness and enjoying activity were mostly under gene control, by both parent and child reports. Day-to-day activity, the authors argue, is set mainly by shared settings such as home and school, so programs aimed there should pay off.
plos-pone-0010210:
The authors were Biaoyang Lin, Anup Madan, Jae-Geun Yoon, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study profiled glioblastoma, the most deadly common brain tumor. Better treatments need a full picture of which molecular pathways go wrong in this cancer. The team applied a next-generation sequencing method called massively parallel signature sequencing to tumor samples.

Combining those reads with bioinformatics, they found two genes turned up in tumors. The genes, TGFBI and SOX4, were up-regulated compared with normal tissue. Each up-regulated gene is a candidate marker or drug target for a cancer with few good options.
plos-pone-0010310:
Thierry Baron, Anna Bencsik, and Eric Morignat studied prion spread in sheep-like mice in 2010. Prion diseases, such as scrapie and BSE, are caused by misfolded prion proteins. Agents differ in how they target brain regions and lymphoid tissues, and the pattern depends on the host. Their PLOS ONE model used transgenic mice carrying sheep prion genes.

They analyzed resistant prion protein in the spleen of those mice. Ruminant prions showed distinct splenotropisms, distinct tastes for spleen tissue, by strain. Such patterns can help identify which prion strain is present in an animal.
plos-pone-0010410:
Marcel Schmidt am Busch, Audrey Sedano and Thomas Simonson tested whether computer-designed proteins can help recognize protein shapes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Recognizing a protein's fold usually relies on statistics from natural examples of that fold. The authors tried a different supply of examples: sequences invented by computational design. Designed sequences follow the same physics but are not found in nature.

If designed sets work as well, they could fill gaps where natural examples are scarce. The study validated the design method against known cases. It also weighed uses in searching for similar proteins and spotting folds. Protein shape predicts protein job, so better recognition speeds biology broadly. The work treats design as a way to learn, not just to build.
plos-pone-0010510:
Erbin Dai and colleagues blocked a chemical attraction system in donor tissue to protect mouse transplants in PLOS ONE in 2010. Immune cells home to grafts using chemokines, chemical beacons stuck to sugars called glycosaminoglycans. That binding builds the gradients cells follow. Most research targets chemokine receptors on cells. This team instead broke the beacon-to-sugar link inside the donor tissue itself.

Treated grafts suffered less vessel disease and less rejection. Protecting the graft before transplant is attractive, since the recipient's whole immune system stays untouched. Vessel disease in grafts is a leading cause of late transplant failure. A treatment applied once, to the organ, could have lasting benefit. This study demonstrates that strategy in mice.
plos-pone-0010610:
Joshua Cohen, Maria Staroselsky Dibner, and Andrew Wilson checked whether new drug money for neglected diseases was working, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Earlier studies blamed low funding for the lack of treatments. Funding then rose sharply, and the authors asked what it bought.

They tracked products in development and whether finished drugs reached patients. More projects had started, but access in poor countries still lagged. Price, delivery, and local health systems blocked many finished products. The lesson is blunt: funding research is only half the job if medicines never arrive.
plos-pone-0010710:
Casey Richardson and colleagues questioned gene labels in the model plant Arabidopsis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some listed genes are orphans with no known relatives or clear job. The team suspected some were wrongly labeled as protein-coding genes at all.

Genome-wide chips measured RNA read from both strands of DNA. Silencing tests then checked which readings were real. Several orphan genes matched antisense patterns, not true protein messages. Mislabels waste years of follow-up work across the field. Cleaning the catalog is slow, unglamorous labor that makes every later plant study more reliable.
plos-pone-0010810:
Stephanie Adams and colleagues studied how two forms of the tau protein interact, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tau normally supports the cell's internal tracks. In several dementias it piles into tangled filaments. The protein comes in three-repeat and four-repeat forms, named for a repeated segment, and diseases differ in which form piles up.

In test systems, the three-repeat form blocked the four-repeat form from building filaments. Mixing the forms thus slowed the very process that defines these diseases. The balance between forms may decide whether tangles form at all. Therapies that nudge that balance, even slightly, gain a clear rationale from this result.
plos-pone-0010910:
Atsushi Niida, Seiya Imoto, Rui Yamaguchi and co-authors published this bioinformatics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Each human tissue runs a different program of gene activity, written partly in regulatory codes near the genes. Earlier tools hunted those codes by comparing one tissue against all others, or by grouping genes that share a code, but both miss programs active in only some samples.

Their new method, BEEM, starts from gene sets sharing common regulatory motifs and then extracts tight expression modules across many tissues at once. Niida and colleagues designed it to catch programs switched on in a subset of tissues, exactly the blind spot of older tools. Decoding these shared codes helps explain how the same genome produces a liver cell and a neuron, and where that control breaks down in disease.
plos-pone-0011010:
Nelson Cuamba, John Morgan, Helen Irving and co-authors published this malaria vector study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Anopheles funestus is a major African malaria mosquito, hard to breed in laboratories, so resistance in wild populations is under-studied. The team collected and reared thousands of larvae from Mozambique's Chokwe District to test the adults against insecticides.

Standard susceptibility assays showed extreme pyrethroid resistance: no deaths after the normal exposure time and under half even after more than double it. Resistance to a carbamate insecticide also appeared, but the mosquitoes stayed fully sensitive to DDT, ruling out one classic resistance mechanism. Cuamba and colleagues document a population that front-line bed net insecticides barely kill. Such field evidence is what malaria programs need before resistance turns into failed control.
plos-pone-0011110:
Lehmann, Lafferty, Garzino-Demo and colleagues studied HIV patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. They focused on a rare immune cell type that makes large amounts of interferon alpha, an alarm signal. In people with HIV, these cells were found gathering in the lymph nodes.

There, the cells kept releasing their alarm signal over time. Constant alarm may wear down the immune system instead of protecting it. That pattern helps explain why HIV causes lasting immune stress even as the virus attacks defenses. The finding may point to ways to calm harmful arousal while keeping real defense intact.
plos-pone-0011210:
Verde, Ruiz, Santiago and colleagues built a dosing tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. A blood thinning drug related to warfarin needs exact dosing: too little invites clots, too much risks bleeding. Two genes are known to shift how much drug a person needs.

The team combined variants of both genes into a single algorithm that predicts the right dose. Gene guided dosing could prevent dangerous bleeding events in new patients. It replaces early trial and error with a test based starting point. That is a concrete example of medicine tailored to a patient's DNA.
plos-pone-0011310:
Lindberg, Wijbrandts, Van Baarsen and colleagues profiled joint tissue in arthritis for PLOS ONE in 2010. A biologic drug helps many rheumatoid arthritis patients, but not all. The team read gene activity in the inflamed joint lining, called synovium, before treatment and tested whether that profile predicts who responds.

Gene patterns in the tissue did carry predictive signal for clinical response. A tissue based forecast could spare non responders months of ineffective treatment and side effects. It moves joint care toward matching drugs to patients in advance. Biopsy guided choice is demanding, so the study also motivates a search for simpler blood based versions.
plos-pone-0011410:
Wei Yao and co-authors reported in 2010 a surprising way to raise peak bone mass in female mice. Most of a lifetime's bone strength is built during the growth years, and hormones steer that building. The team blocked the progesterone receptor, a hormone sensor, only during the fast linear growth phase, then measured the adult skeleton.

Mice treated during growth ended with higher peak bone mass than untreated mice. Blocking a hormone signal lifting bone mass was unexpected, since progesterone is usually cast as a supporter of the skeleton. The result uncovers a hidden brake on bone building that acts during youth. If the same brake works in people, easing it at the right age could raise the bone reserve that protects against fractures and osteoporosis decades later.
plos-pone-0011510:
Marc Ancrenaz and co-authors surveyed forests in Sabah, Malaysia, in 2010 and found orang-utans holding on in lightly logged woods. Conservationists had assumed the apes need untouched old-growth forest, which would leave them little room as logging spreads across Borneo. The team surveyed the Ulu Segama Malua forests, where selective logging had taken some trees but left the forest standing.

Orang-utans of the local subspecies persisted in those slightly logged forests at levels suggesting the habitat can maintain them. That softens a doom narrative without removing the threat: heavy logging and clearing remain deadly. Carefully managed logging may buy time and space for the apes while stronger protection is built. For conservation planning, managed forests count as part of the solution, not only as part of the problem.
plos-pone-0011610:
Michelle Carey and colleagues tested common anti-inflammatory drugs during flu infection in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drugs block enzymes called COX-1 and COX-2, which help drive inflammation. Earlier work showed mice lacking COX-1 fared worse with flu, while mice lacking COX-2 fared better, raising questions about drug use during infection.

Carey and colleagues gave flu-infected mice blockers aimed at each enzyme and tracked illness and inflammation. Their results help separate helpful inflammation from harmful excess. For doctors, the findings matter because pain and fever drugs are widely used by flu patients every season.
plos-pone-0011710:
Valentina Neplioueva and co-authors mapped the reach of an RNA-binding protein across the genome, in PLOS ONE in 2010. RNA-binding proteins guide every stage of a message's life and let cells adjust gene activity quickly when conditions change. Their grip on target messages shifts with where the proteins sit inside the cell.

The team studied a double-stranded RNA-binding protein called protein 76, whose levels vary by tissue. They charted its tissue pattern and used genome-wide methods to list the messages it binds. That hit list shows how far one such protein's regulatory reach extends.
plos-pone-0011810:
Ondřej Kott, Radim Šumbera and Pavel Němec tested light perception in underground rodents, in PLOS ONE in 2010. African mole-rats live strictly below ground, are born with tiny eyes and are hardly ever exposed to light. Because they show no obvious reaction to light, they were long considered blind.

The authors examined two strictly subterranean species for any retained light sense. Their tests probe whether the animals live truly in the dark or still register blue light. Whatever vision lingers in such eyes informs how senses decay when evolution stops using them.
plos-pone-0011910:
Britta Muster and colleagues imaged living cells in 2010 to see how the energy machinery is arranged inside mitochondria. Mitochondria supply most of a cell's energy and constantly merge and split. Blocking that movement is tied to several nerve-degenerating diseases.

Inside these shifting organelles, the respiratory chain complexes, the protein machines that make energy, were not spread evenly. They sat in a patchy distribution across the inner membrane. A patchwork layout changes how scientists picture energy production: output may depend on where the machines cluster, not just how many exist. That view matters when explaining why disturbed mitochondrial movement leads to disease.
plos-pone-0012010:
Hideo Matsumura and colleagues combined in 2010 a digital gene-counting method with next-generation sequencing to handle many samples at once. The base method, SuperSAGE, cuts a short tag from each gene message, and counting tags gives a digital readout of gene activity. Sequencing had become fast enough to count tags for whole sets of samples in one run.

Their high-throughput version keeps the counting honest while scaling up to multiple samples. Digital counts avoid some distortions of older analog measures of gene activity. For projects comparing many tissues, treatments, or patients, a scalable counting method is the difference between a pilot and a real study.
plos-pone-0012210:
Scott Heron, Bette Willis, William Skirving, and co-authors modeled coral disease outbreaks on the Great Barrier Reef in PLOS ONE in 2010. White syndrome, a tissue-destroying coral disease, has struck the reef in waves, and hot water stress was already suspected as a trigger. Their model added the other half of the year, asking how winter conditions set the stage for summer outbreaks.

Linking hot snaps with the cold season before them gives forecasters a longer lead time on outbreak years. Reef managers could then watch the most at-risk areas closely or cut other stresses, like pollution, ahead of a predicted outbreak. For a reef under climate pressure, advance warning is one of the few tools left.
plos-pone-0012310:
Jean-Philip Truman, Mónica García-Barros, Matthew Kaag, and co-authors studied how precise radiation treatment interacts with vessel-blocking therapy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Combining anti-vessel drugs with radiation was a popular hope, yet trials had gained little, mostly because nobody knew exactly how vessel blockade changes radiation's effect. Their setting was radiosurgery, the tightly focused high-dose radiation used on small tumors.

They found the tumor's vessel lining must remodel its membranes for the anti-vessel drug to sensitize the tumor to radiation. A required step like this explains uneven trial results and tells doctors which tumors and timings should benefit. It turns a failed combination into a recipe with conditions attached.
plos-pone-0012410:
Marc Pearton, Sang-Moo Kang, Jae-Min Song and colleagues examined skin immune cells after a flu-like vaccine shot, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Langerhans cells sit in the skin and are first responders when a vaccine enters through it. How they change shape and move right after vaccination in human skin was largely unknown, a gap for teams designing needle-free skin vaccines.

Using human skin samples given virus-like particle vaccines, the team tracked early changes in these cells. The particles stirred the cells and set them moving, a good sign for skin delivery. The work gives vaccine designers concrete early readouts to compare delivery methods before large trials.
plos-pone-0012510:
Jianzhong Ma and Christopher Amos set out the math behind a key fix used in gene studies, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When scientists hunt for genes tied to a disease, they compare large groups of people. If the groups differ in ancestry, that gap alone can fake a gene link. A method based on principal components, a way to sum up big data sets, is used to spot and remove that bias.

The authors give the firm math base for how the fix works and when it can be trusted. Gene hunts now use the method as a matter of course, so its limits matter a great deal. Their work helps study teams choose how strong a fix to apply, and when a weaker or stronger one is the right call.
plos-pone-0012610:
Loebig, Klement, Schmoller and co-authors tested a link between body weight and a growth factor called VEGF. VEGF helps blood vessels grow, and its blood level may shift with body mass. Their 2010 study used healthy young men of similar background to keep the test clean.

Each man went through a glucose clamp, a careful lab method that holds blood sugar steady while insulin response is measured. Even after that control, VEGF still tracked with body mass index. That points to a weight link that does not run through insulin alone, a clue for obesity research.
plos-pone-0012710:
Yu, Zeng, Xiong and co-authors warned that some epigenetic cancer drugs may also help cancer spread. Ezrin is a protein raised in many tumours, where it helps them invade new tissue. Their 2010 study asked whether drugs that change gene tags, used to wake silenced genes, also wake ezrin by mistake.

They found such drugs can raise ezrin through changes to its gene control region. A treatment that fights a tumour while feeding its spread would be a bad trade. The warning tells drug developers to screen for this side effect early.
plos-pone-0012810:
Yen, Le, Bansal and co-authors compared ways of measuring fat in the tiny worm C elegans. The worm is a stand-in for human obesity studies because its energy pathways match ours closely. Judging a worm's fat stores, though, needs methods that are exact and fair.

Their 2010 study ran dye-based methods, which stain fat, against label-free methods that need no stain. Stains can mislead, so a checked label-free option strengthens every obesity screen done in worms. The comparison gives labs a clear guide for measuring worm fat.
plos-pone-0341210:
Xiaocui Yuan and colleagues built an automated system that both finds defects in railway fasteners and measures their parts precisely. Fasteners hold rails in place, and worn or broken ones threaten train safety. Inspectors can spot defects with cameras, but careful measurement of each part still relies on slow hand work.

A 3D line laser scanner captures color images and matching depth maps of each fastener. One neural network spots defects and locates sound fasteners, while a second segments the parts so the system can compute block sizes, pad thickness, and bolt height. In tests the defect finder reached very high precision, pointing toward faster and more consistent track inspection.
plos-pone-0342410:
Sabine Pur, Stefan Huesig, and Christoph Schmidhammer trace how online lending marketplaces in three countries grew alike, in this 2026 PLOS ONE case study. These platforms match borrowers with lenders directly online. The authors followed the market leaders in Britain, the United States, and Germany from 2005 onward, comparing who they served and what they promised customers.

All three drifted toward the same shape: funding from institutions rather than small savers, aimed at underserved borrowers such as small firms and the self-employed. Regulation, technology, and institutional money drove the sameness. The authors turn the pattern into a general model of how platform business models standardise across borders.
plos-pone-0343610:
Ada R. Miltz and her team tested a chain of harm for people with HIV in the UK. The chain runs from slights in daily life to shame, then to lone days, then to low mood. They used a UK-wide survey from 2022 and 2023. It held more than twelve hundred straight men and women with HIV.

More than half felt shame about their state. Slights in health care fed that shame the most. Next came fear of public spots and slights from kin. Lone days were the top link to low mood. Cash strain hurt too, while grit helped. The chain fit the data well, the team says.
plos-pone-0345710:
Jorge Quiroga-Canaviri and colleagues argue that standard measures of output misjudge Latin American economies. Those measures ignore the limits of nature. They also ignore the slow loss of natural wealth. The team proposes a bioeconomy frame rooted in Andean and Amazonian thought. It joins an entropy-aware view of production with ancestral knowledge. Six countries were studied across three decades. Human development stood in for well-being.

The new model explained far more of the well-being pattern. It also surfaced a paradox. Saving the shared fund of ecosystems and cultures predicted higher well-being. Normal accounts book that saving as a pure cost. In these results, care for nature reads as an investment that pays in human development.
plos-pone-0345910:
Xia Li and Maho Niwa examined how the fat makeup of cell membranes affects stress control in yeast cells. They focused on the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell structure that folds proteins and must pass intact to new daughter cells. Their 2026 study changed membrane fat saturation in a controlled way and watched three linked safety systems.

Changing fat saturation affected whether the stressed reticulum was passed to daughter cells. Yet it affected the other two systems, which repair the reticulum and destroy bad proteins, in different ways. A fat signal also helped trigger the checkpoint that pauses cell division under stress. The findings suggest membrane fats help coordinate how cells protect this key structure during division.
plos-pone-0347210:
Zhichao Jiang, Xiaorun Wang, and Pengling Liu ask whether digital tools can raise the quality of farm goods that China sells abroad. Their 2026 study uses yearly data from thirty-four Chinese provincial regions covering more than two decades. They build an index of farm digital growth and track how it lines up with export quality over time.

Digital growth did go with better export quality, and the link held up under extra checks. The gains ran through faster farm technology, better trained workers, and smoother shipping. Effects were stronger in eastern regions, big grain areas, and places with more open markets. Government support and trade openness made the link stronger still.
plos-pone-0347410:
Long Zhou, Litao Zhu, and Faming Zhang ran pot experiments to free phosphorus locked in iron-rich red soils, where maize often starves despite fertiliser. They combined organic phosphorus with two helpers: phytase, an enzyme that releases phosphorus from plant residues, and bacteria that dissolve mineral phosphorus. The 2026 study measured plant growth, root shape, and how much phosphorus the maize actually absorbed.

The combination outperformed either addition alone, and the enzyme proved the stronger partner, raising phosphorus uptake by more than half in one comparison. Roots grew longer, thinner, and more branched where phosphorus flowed better. The authors offer the recipe as a sustainable way to farm phosphorus-poor red soils.
plos-pone-0347810:
Hyeonji Song, Yusik Lim, and Jaechul Lim describe a laboratory panel that can tell apart dozens of mouse cell types in one run, in this 2026 PLOS ONE methods paper. Flow cytometry sorts cells by fluorescent tags, but overlapping colours and scarce mouse-ready reagents have limited how much can be measured at once. Their panel uses twenty-seven colours across three lasers.

The panel resolves sixteen immune cell families plus several non-immune cell types, and it works across spleen, blood, gut, and other tissues. In a test inflammation model it tracked body-wide shifts in white blood cells and spotted a previously unnoticed cell subset. Such panels speed up immune research in mice.
plos-pone-0348110:
Yangyang Chen leads a team of eight reading ten thousand years of climate from a pillar of black soil in northeast China, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The Songnen Plain holds one of the world's three black soil belts, vital to national grain supply, yet how its rich layer formed is still debated. The team sliced a sediment profile and combined grain size fingerprinting, chemical weathering measures, and luminescence dating to build a dated history of the whole Holocene.

Five stages emerged. Dust piled up fast in the early Holocene, then a cooling spell arrived near the transition to the middle period, echoing a known global cold snap. The middle Holocene optimum, warm and humid, did the decisive work: weathering peaked and the black soil began in earnest. Late Holocene cold and dryness then slowed the process. The profile ties a farming treasure directly to an ancient climate window.
plos-pone-0348510:
Aboa Paul Koffi and co-authors carried out a huge hunt for yaws, a poverty-linked skin infection that mostly strikes children in the humid tropics, across fifteen districts of Côte d'Ivoire. The country is one of the few where yaws remains endemic, and planners needed its true extent before attempting eradication. Their 2026 campaign visited nearly four thousand villages and targeted close to half a million children in schools and homes.

About fifteen percent of examined children had skin lesions of some kind. Blood tests flagged two hundred ninety-one possible yaws cases, and a confirmatory test verified about half, mostly in children aged five to fourteen. Confirmed cases received a single antibiotic dose. Teams also catalogued other common skin conditions, giving health authorities a fuller map for the eradication push.
plos-pone-0348610:
Zhiqi Huang, Yizhang Jiang, and Kaijian Xia present a fuzzy logic classifier that learns from several views of the same data at once. Fuzzy systems sort items by degrees of belonging rather than hard lines, which suits messy real-world data. Their 2026 model lets each rule's center shift to fit the data and weighs rules by importance for each new sample.

Across five public datasets, from handwriting to brain signals, the model beat strong rivals at sorting accuracy. Removing either new part hurt results, and using both helped most. Brain signal sorting gained the most from the pairing. The design offers a clearer, more flexible way to classify when information arrives from mixed sources.
plos-pone-0349110:
Yingjie Kuang and co-workers train machine learning models to predict which leg vein clots confined to the calf will fail to clear. Such clots are common, and doctors lack good tools for judging their course. Their 2026 study gathers records for sixteen hundred patients, builds six competing models, and tests the best on patients the models never saw during training.

All six models sorted outcomes acceptably to strongly. A boosted-tree model won overall, pairing high accuracy with honest probability estimates. An explanation method then ranked which patient features drove its calls. A tool like this could help doctors decide who needs closer watching or longer treatment, and who can safely be left to heal.
plos-pone-0349310:
Jean-Marc Perone and colleagues mined data from a large cataract surgery trial to learn why eye pressure falls after the cloudy lens is removed, even in eyes without glaucoma. The drop is well known but unexplained, and knowing its drivers could sharpen glaucoma care. They tracked pressure at one, three, and twelve months, sorting eyes by starting pressure into high, middle, and low bands.

A wide set of eye measurements and surgical details was tested for what predicted the size of the drop at three months, in the whole group and each band. A literature review checked the regression approach against prior traps in this kind of analysis. Since cataract surgery is the world's most common operation, its pressure side effect is a therapeutic lever hiding in plain sight.
plos-pone-0349410:
Breast cancer that starts young tends to behave worse, and Le-Wei Zheng and colleagues searched tumor DNA for why, focusing on the hormone-sensitive luminal type. Their 2026 PLOS One study combined gene fusions, mutations, and missing DNA segments across many tumors.

One pairing stood out: a fused gene joining two partners, together with deletion of a gene called KDM6B, marked tumors with aggressive traits and shorter survival. Young patients' tumors also carried more fusions overall and distinct mutation patterns. The authors propose the pairing as a warning marker that could help doctors single out young patients needing closer watching and stronger treatment.
plos-pone-0349510:
Kaleab Fikre, Abeje Berhanu Kassegne, and Getnet Tadele interviewed forty one people in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: cancer patients, family caregivers, and religious leaders. In depth talks explored how faith shapes what cancer means and what care people seek. Beliefs in Ethiopia had drawn little study despite their central place in daily life.

Illness was often read as divine or supernatural in origin: a punishment, a test of faith, Gods will, or spiritual attack. Views shifted over time with teaching, custom, and reflection. Faith brought comfort and strength while also steering treatment choices, sometimes toward prayer first. Clinicians who grasp those frames, the authors argue, can plan care patients will actually follow.
plos-pone-0349610:
Alba Roldan and colleagues examined how shaky movement affects learning in adults with severe cerebral palsy of the athetoid or ataxic types. Thirteen adults with the condition and eighteen without practiced motor tasks that taught through two channels: correcting errors and chasing rewards. Extra movement noise might open exploration, or it might drown the signals learning needs.

The cerebral palsy group moved far more variably, made larger absolute errors, and adjusted less precisely within tasks. Yet the two teaching channels were not equally blocked. Error-based practice produced substantial improvement after training, while reward-based learning lagged further behind. For therapists, the split is practical guidance: build drills around clear error feedback, where these learners demonstrably gain, rather than around reward signals their motor noise obscures.
plos-pone-0350010:
Xue Zhang, Xiaoya Ba, and Bo Li studied seven major cyberattacks that spread through supply chains, hitting sectors from retail and logistics to energy and health care. Attackers in these cases slipped in through trusted third-party connections instead of breaking front-door defenses. The team mapped how each attack entered, spread inside, and was eventually stopped.

Across the cases, four spread patterns kept recurring, including flattened networks that let intruders roam and alert overload that paralyzed defenders. Damage grew worst when systems were tightly linked and teams failed to coordinate. Recovery worked only where firms shared information early and were organized before the crisis, which the authors call synergy dependency.
plos-pone-0350110:
Marleen G A M van der Velde and co-authors introduced a new Dutch registry tracking urgent internal medicine care in 2026. The registry follows how hospitals handle urgent medical admissions, so units can compare themselves with a shared benchmark and find bottlenecks.

The report covers a single centre pilot at one teaching hospital, drawing records for more than six thousand emergency patients aged sixty-five and over between late 2019 and mid 2023. Data cover complaints, ward organisation, and measures like time in the emergency department. The pilot proves the dashboard works locally before national use, and shows the case mix such registries must handle.
plos-pone-0350510:
Chidozie Ezechukwu and colleagues interviewed the people charged with delivering Nigeria's new HPV vaccine in Kano, Kaduna, and Lagos states, asking what keeps the program from running steadily. The vaccine prevents cervical cancer, and Nigeria added it to the national schedule recently, but early rollout stumbled. Policymakers, immunization officers, agencies, community groups, and partners described the friction from their seats.

The analysis organizes the barriers by the machinery of delivery: how policy is implemented, how the program is financed, and how services reach girls in practice, with community-level obstacles woven through each. Interview studies like this cannot weigh the barriers, but they name them in the words of the people hitting them, which is where fixes start. Sustaining a vaccine program is a systems problem, and this is a systems map.
plos-pone-0350610:
Ika Saptarini and colleagues in Indonesia followed dengue patients through fever and early recovery in 2026, measuring immune signals in blood. Severe dengue often declares itself as fever fades, and doctors lack early warnings of who will worsen.

Paired blood samples from more than one hundred patients at five hospitals were tested for a set of messengers and complement parts. Two signals ran higher in the severe form during early recovery, while none separated the groups during fever. Links among the signals also shifted. Tracking how immune signals move, not just their level on day one, may sharpen dengue care.
plos-pone-0350810:
Medical students in Tunisia will soon treat people living with HIV, and Imen Mlouki and colleagues tested whether hands-on workshops can cut the stigma those patients face from health workers. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered all fifth-year students at the Monastir medical faculty across two academic years.

Two hundred sixteen students completed anonymous questionnaires before and after each workshop, using validated knowledge and stigma scales. Most already knew the facts about HIV well. The team measured how far attitudes moved after active sessions, and which student traits traveled with lingering stigma. Findings should help faculties design training that changes behavior, not just knowledge.
plos-pone-0350910:
Vivat Keawdounglek, Anuttara Hongthong, and Warapon Paenkhokuard built a community-run food safety system in Wiang Kaen District, a rural area of northern Thailand, and documented its first steps in 2026. Their mixed-method study surveyed 204 households, interviewed local stakeholders, and tested food from eight establishments for chemical and microbial contamination while residents co-designed the management approach.

Testing found contamination generally low, though pesticide traces turned up in garlic bought from outside markets, beyond local control. Food safety knowledge varied with gender, age, and rice growing. The process's concrete product was a standing Community Food Safety Committee linking households, vendors, and officials. The authors present the model as a workable template for rural districts with informal food systems.
plos-pone-0351110:
Jaya Kshatri and colleagues lay out a planned trial of joined-up primary care for older adults in urban India. The patients live with several chronic diseases at once, plus growing frailty. Indian primary care still tends to treat one disease per visit. Ten public health centers in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, will take part. Whole clinics will be assigned by lot. Half will give a monthly package of combined care. Half will give standard care as usual.

The trial will judge health-related quality of life and well-being. It is built from parts a public system could truly staff and fund. As a protocol, it reports no results. If the package works, its design is the point. It shows other cities a model that does not depend on private money or rare specialists.
plos-pone-0351210:
Olanrewaju Onigbogi and four co-authors study how depression drugs link body weight and smoking in American adults. They used a 2023 national health survey. Their model asked whether taking drugs for depression helps explain smoking habits. They compared adults who were underweight, normal weight, overweight, or obese.

Use of depression drugs played the largest connecting role in underweight adults. It played the smallest role in obese adults. Underweight adults on such drugs were more likely to smoke than obese adults were. Obese adults on the drugs also showed raised odds of smoking, compared with underweight peers. The authors say weight group should be part of the picture. Clinicians should weigh it when they design quit-smoking support for people treated for depression.
plos-pone-0351310:
Jingjing Ma refines how forecasters combine predictions about a country's energy mix. The 2026 study works with compositional data: shares of coal, oil, gas, and renewables that must sum to a whole. Single forecasting models shine at different times. Combining them helps, but only if the weights adapt. Ma proposes an aggregation method built on an ordered weighting operator, informed by each model's recent accuracy. A genetic algorithm searches for the weight set that minimises error against the real series.

Two combination schemes resulted: one with time-varying weights, one built on the new operator. Both were tested on China's primary energy production structure. The varying-weight model beat the benchmark on prediction accuracy. Energy planners live and die by share forecasts: grid investment, import contracts, and carbon budgets all hang on them. A demonstrably better way to blend rival forecasts is a quiet but consequential upgrade.
plos-pone-0351410:
American law reviews are edited by students who must pick a few articles from thousands, and they lean on the author's school as a quality shortcut. Chad M Topaz simulated that market with a computer model, in this 2026 PLOS One study, and compared it with centralized matching like the system placing medical residents.

More than sixty percent of top placements differed from what quality-based matching would give, and article quality lined up only loosely with journal rank. Partial fixes such as longer deadlines barely helped; the scattered structure itself caused the waste. The model also shows prestige bias persists even between equally strong articles, an inequity built into the system.
plos-pone-0351510:
Brittany Lee Vermeulen and three colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS One case study on short online courses, called microcredentials, inside university teaching. The setting was a large undergraduate science subject in 2024, where students also completed a brief sustainability course on thinking, caring, and acting. The authors focused on a smaller group of students and studied their final reflective writing.

Reading those reflections, the team found students understood sustainability more deeply, rethought daily habits, and saw their future science careers differently. Engagement with the self-paced course varied widely, as the authors expected. They offer the case as a workable model for universities that want to build sustainability literacy into existing subjects rather than adding whole new courses.
plos-pone-0351610:
Editorial Note: PLOS One corrects a greenhouse tomato study after data from another institution was included by mistake. This 2026 note replaces the wrong figure and fixes sentences describing the test of micro-fog systems, which cool greenhouse air by spraying fine mist during summer heat.

The corrected values describe midday conditions with and without fog: the fogged section ran cooler and far more humid, with much lower dryness stress on the plants. The original paper argued the gentler air improved leaf photosynthesis, growth, and yield. Readers should rely on the corrected figure and numbers given here rather than those first printed.
plos-pone-0352110:
