Yu Zhao and six colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One nationwide study of colorectal cancer deaths in China's cancer registration areas from 2005 to 2018, with forecasts to 2035. The team combined trend analysis, an age-period-cohort model, and spatial statistics to separate the roles of aging, calendar time, and birth generation, and to locate high-risk regions.

Mortality rose, then fell significantly for several years, then flattened into a slight rise, with urban rates falling over the later years while rural rates crept up. Risk grew steeply with age, and hotspots concentrated in eastern coastal and northeastern provinces. The forecast shows a slow upward drift ahead. The authors offer the patterns as a basis for targeting screening and prevention where deaths cluster.
plos-pone-0352310:
Mengxuan Liu and five colleagues search public gene data for shared sparks between sepsis and diabetes. Their 2026 bioinformatics study concerns pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death that bursts cells open. Both diseases kill many people, and they worsen each other in practice. Two gene expression datasets supplied the raw material. The team filtered for genes that change in both conditions and belong to the pyroptosis machinery. Network and pathway tools then mapped their neighbourhoods.

Seven genes survived the sieve. Most specialise in killing cells or sounding immune alarms. Their pathways centred on cell bursting and an inflammatory signal family. A separate enrichment pass flagged another immune signalling route. Immune cell mixtures in blood correlated with the genes' activity too. None of this treats a patient yet. It nominates molecular markers where two major diseases overlap, giving laboratory researchers concrete suspects for the crosstalk clinicians see at the bedside.
plos-pone-0352810:
Josheil Boparai and seven colleagues test a simple fix for weak concussion teaching in medical school. Their 2026 study starts from a known gap. Concussion barely appears in undergraduate medical curricula. Poor knowledge then follows graduates into clinical practice. Students first completed a knowledge survey. Next came a single didactic lecture on concussion.

Knowledge scores jumped sharply right after the lecture. Students were surveyed again within two days. A final survey came two weeks later. Scores at two weeks matched the immediate scores, showing the learning had stuck. No extra teaching happened in between. One focused lecture, the authors argue, earns its place in a crowded curriculum. Better-trained graduates should then recognise and manage concussion more safely in real patients.
plos-pone-0353010:
Faith Logan and six colleagues published this 2026 protocol for a pilot trial helping teenagers who live with chronic muscle and joint pain stay active. Many such teens avoid movement for fear of hurting more, which can seed lifelong pain. Their program, called PREP-Y, builds confidence and motivation alongside activity for forty adolescents at a children's hospital in Ohio.

Surveys, activity measures, and pain scales will track functioning, fear of movement, and resilience. As a protocol, the study promises no results yet; Logan's team designed it to shape a later full trial.
plos-pone-0353110:
Amr Sobhy led a team of six authors on this 2026 randomized trial of pain control for young children having penis repair surgery. Thirty children aged one to five received either the standard caudal epidural block or a newer ultrasound-guided block near the sacrum, both using the same local anesthetic. Nurses recorded how long relief lasted and how much rescue medicine was needed.

Children with the newer block waited longer before needing extra pain relief and needed less of it, with similar safety and body readings. Sobhy suggests the technique as a dependable alternative for this surgery.
plos-pone-0353610:
Toqeer Ali Syed and four colleagues propose giving city infrastructure a self-managing digital twin, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. A digital twin mirrors bridges, roads, and water systems in software, fed by live sensors. Their design adds artificial intelligence agents that perceive problems, plan responses, and act through official city systems, while a permissioned blockchain seals every observation, approval, and action against tampering.

Eighteen thousand simulated incidents tested the framework across five designs and three difficulty levels. The paper characterises how the system behaves under stress rather than proving it in a real city. The stakes are accountability: when software orders a road closure or repair, someone must be able to audit why.
plos-pone-0354510:
Sabrina Al Bukhari and colleagues built a closed-loop pain therapy in which brainwaves drive a virtual reality healer. Their 2026 study trained lightweight machine learning classifiers on an open dataset where volunteers rated laser-induced pain. One-second slices of scalp signals became an eleven-step pain scale. The live prediction was then piped into a game engine, where a digital avatar responds with tailored therapy.

The best classifier sorted pain levels with accuracy in the high nineties in cross-validation. It beat comparable published systems. The avatar reacted in real time across slight, moderate, and severe bands. Nothing here treated a real patient yet; the work proves the loop runs. Drug-free, self-adjusting pain care is the stated destination.
plos-pone-0354610:
Fahimeh Alsadat Hosseini and three colleagues published this 2026 trial of positive psychotherapy delivered through virtual reality to people with major depression. Seventy-eight patients were split between headset sessions and the same therapy face to face, three sessions each. Mood, life satisfaction, and suicidal thoughts were measured around every session, followed by interviews.

Both formats improved emotions, satisfaction, and suicidal thinking by similar amounts, and patients found the headset version workable. Hosseini calls the trial preliminary and asks for larger groups and longer follow-up before clinics adopt virtual delivery.
plos-pone-0354710:
Michael Getie led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of bloodstream infections at a public health institute in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. Four full years of blood culture records, from 2020 through 2023, were reviewed to see which bacteria grew and which antibiotics still worked reliably, using standard lab methods.

Half the suspected cases grew true pathogens, dominated by hard-to-treat Gram-negative and notorious hospital bacteria, hitting males, newborns, and young adults hardest. Getie calls for immediate antibiotic stewardship, refreshed treatment guidelines, and stronger lab testing to track resistance.
plos-pone-0354810:
Yüksel Peker led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study linking a mixed sleep disorder to heart and blood vessel disease in Türkiye. The condition, called COMISA, pairs insomnia with sleep apnea. Drawing on a national sleep registry of nearly thirteen thousand adults sent for sleep testing, they compared four sleep groups.

The mixed disorder appeared more often in patients who had cardiovascular disease than in those without it, even after adjusting for many other factors. The link was modest, though. Peker treats COMISA as a distinct, burden-heavy pattern shaped by both body and behavior.
plos-pone-0354910:
Ziyang Luo led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of the HIV strain dominant in Ningxia, China. They analyzed just over two hundred local virus sequences of the CRF01_AE recombinant to trace where it travels and who drives its spread. The strain is known for faster disease progression.

Spread radiated strongly from the capital, Yinchuan, toward other cities, carried mainly by people in their twenties and thirties. Transmission remains above the level where the epidemic shrinks, while the virus's mutation pace stays steady. Luo urges prevention aimed at this strain's actual hubs and groups.
plos-pone-0355210:
Tonya Campbell led a team of eight authors charting deaths tied to benzodiazepines in Ontario, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These sedative drugs are widely prescribed, and deaths involving their toxicity have been rising. The team ran a descriptive cross-sectional study of trends and patterns in those deaths.

Campbell's data give coroners and policymakers a clear picture of who is dying and how. Patterns by age, setting, and drug combinations point to where prevention can work, from prescribing rules to safer supply debates. Benzodiazepine deaths often hide inside wider drug toxicity figures, mixed with opioids. Separating them out, as this study does, is the first step toward policies aimed at the right problem.
plos-pone-0355410:
Rownak Jahan and colleagues check in 2026 whether fresh fruit skins in their study area carry a gut bacterium that can cause severe infection and resist many drugs. Washed samples from seven fruit types were cultured and tested for the bacterium, its harm related genes, its ability to form slimy layers, and its drug resistance.

More than three in five samples carried the bacterium, most often on oranges. Resistance was high to several common drugs and worrying even for last resort drugs, and most isolates resisted many drugs at once. Harm genes and slime forming were common. Thorough washing and wider monitoring are urged.
plos-pone-0355710:
Theres Mühlberg and three colleagues build a classroom observation tool for identifying which teaching principles a teacher is actually using, in this 2026 German study. Many observation instruments exist, but few are valid, reliable, subject-independent, and rooted in constructivist ideas about learning rather than simple evaluation. The team developed their protocol, called OPTIS, from a comparative review of teaching principles and refined it through expert rounds.

Piloting used both video-recorded lessons and live observation. Two independent observers reached almost perfect agreement with each other, and each stayed consistent over time, as measured by a chance-corrected agreement statistic suited to the data. Expert review supported the tool's foundations and its power to predict what it aims to capture. The authors present OPTIS as a psychometrically sound lens for researchers and school developers studying teaching quality across subjects.
plos-pone-0356910:
Xiaoxia Jia and colleagues model how city firms might cooperate to cut waste when the costs of doing so can be shared. Cities need industry to shrink its waste stream, but each firm weighs its own costs and gains. The study first maps material flows and life cycle impacts. That finds the nodes where cuts matter most. Then it runs a game model in software. Firms linked in a network copy or abandon cooperative moves over time.

Moderate penalties and positive spillovers between neighbors encouraged cooperation most reliably. Cost sharing and fair benefit splits also helped, but only within sensible ranges, and effects shifted with network size. Jia and colleagues advise cities to tune incentives to the local business network rather than copy one national recipe.
plos-pone-0357010:
María Carmen Martínez-González leads a team of eight testing whether needling a deep calf muscle changes how the foot bears weight, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The tibialis posterior, buried behind the shin, steers the arch when walking, and hidden trigger points in it may distort foot loading. Eighty-two adults with such trigger points were assigned to real deep dry needling or a simulated version, with foot pressure measured on a walking platform before treatment and at three points afterward.

Right after needling, pressure under the heel rose in the treated group. A day later, average pressure rose while contact areas shifted, including less forefoot contact. By seventy-two hours, every difference from baseline had vanished. The authors conclude a single session rearranges foot loading only briefly, which matters for clinicians deciding whether the technique can support longer term gait correction plans.
plos-pone-0357110:
Sarah Al-Rihaymee leads a systematic review of whether a little-studied mouth bacterium belongs on the list of gum disease suspects. Known gum pathogens do not fully explain why disease severity varies so much between people. The review gathered observational studies in healthy adults that compared the bacterium's presence in people with gum disease against people with healthy gums, in spit or in plaque below the gumline.

Across eight studies from three continents, the bacterium turned up more often, and in larger shares, in disease than in health, with enrichment clearest in advanced stages. The authors rate the certainty as low, since most studies were snapshots rather than follow-ups. Al-Rihaymee and colleagues call for stronger designs before the bacterium earns a firm causal label.
plos-pone-0357310:
Weirui Zhang and three colleagues studied what Chinese school textbooks teach about the nature of science, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They read senior secondary geography textbooks in light of sustainable development, a theme the books are meant to carry. Textbooks shape whether students see science as fixed facts or as inquiry.

Zhang's team identified gaps between what the books claim about science and how they present it. They also pointed to reforms that would show science as argument and testing, not just lists to memorize. In a country teaching millions of students, textbook wording matters at huge scale. Better books can shape how a generation judges evidence on climate and resources.
plos-pone-0357410:
Rena Hidaka and fellow researchers pilot a monthly program in Tokyo that teaches children about mouths, chewing, and food at community cafeterias. These cafeterias serve local families, and the team added a chewy meal plus a short talk on teeth and balanced eating. About fifty children and thirty parents joined six sessions, answering surveys before and after the program.

Children looked inside their own mouths more often and used fluoride more after the program. Fewer children said they ignored balanced eating, and parents reported serving more meat, dairy, and root vegetables at home. Because there was no comparison group, Hidaka and colleagues treat the gains as promising early signs and call for a fuller trial to confirm them.
plos-pone-0357910:
Atefeh Allahbakhshian and three colleagues traced how uncertainty affects heart patients' lives, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. People with coronary artery disease live with gnawing doubt about their future. The team ran a pathway analysis linking quality of life in these patients to their coping strategies, perceived stress, and illness uncertainty.

Allahbakhshian's pathways reveal where support could break the chain from uncertainty to poor quality of life. If coping strategies carry much of the effect, teaching better coping becomes a concrete intervention. Cardiac care often stops at the artery; this work insists the mind's burden is part of the disease. Nurses and counselors gain a map of which link to strengthen first for each patient.
plos-pone-0359210: Aujla and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on gene copy changes in a national Canadian data bank. HostSeq holds genetic data from people across Canada. The team charted the full spectrum of copy number variation, places where chunks of DNA are missing or repeated. Such a spectrum gives doctors a baseline: which changes are common and harmless, and which stand out in disease.
plos-pone-0359310:
Jie Wang and co-authors set out a protocol in 2026 for comparing three sets of criteria used to classify antiphospholipid syndrome. This autoimmune condition makes blood more likely to clot and complicates pregnancies, and classifying it consistently is essential for research. The planned study is a systematic review with network meta-analysis, a method for comparing several options across many studies at once.

The criteria under comparison are the Sapporo criteria, their revised version, and the newer 2023 criteria from two major rheumatology bodies. The protocol fixes the questions and methods in advance, so the eventual results can be judged against a public plan. Which set performs best shapes who counts as a patient in every future trial of this disease.
plos-pone-0359810:
Kulthoom Qureish and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about dengue fever in Kenya. It tests vector competence, whether mosquitoes can pick up and pass on dengue-2 virus. The mosquitoes are Aedes aegypti sampled at selected sites in Lamu County, split into groups resistant or susceptible to the insecticide permethrin.

Comparing the two groups matters because spraying programs assume resistance only affects survival, not virus spread. If resistant mosquitoes also differ in how well they carry dengue, control plans need rethinking. Malaria and dengue control teams in coastal Kenya are the readers who must weigh insecticide choices against disease transmission.
pmc-10653410:
Salleh and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-three translating an implementation survey into Malay. Programs need measures of whether communities accept and can use them. Malaysia lacked such tools in its national language. The team translate and adapt a three-part outcome questionnaire. Two samples, of one hundred seventy and two hundred thirty-five people, test it. The Malay version settles into one factor with seven items. Content checks and reliability scores run strong.

The single scale fits the data well by standard indices. All items load cleanly on the one factor. The authors back it for community program evaluation. Dialect variety across states merits more testing, they note.
pmc-10654810:
An EFSA expert panel assessed a food enzyme called catalase in 2023. The enzyme comes from a fungus strain. That strain was not genetically modified. Food use requires a safety verdict first. Production and exposure were examined closely. Allergen matching was also performed.

One match with known allergens was found. Allergy risk could not be fully excluded. Likelihood was judged low, though. Genotoxicity results raised unresolved questions. Absence of living production cells was unproven. Safety could therefore not be established. The panel withheld a clean verdict. More data would be needed.
pmc-10655210:
Sarah Monshi and co-authors present a 2023 study on whether cultural occasions spur smokers to quit in Saudi Arabia. Tobacco use stays high in the country. The team surveyed 742 Saudi tobacco users between 2021 and 2022. It asked about desire to quit and past quit behavior around Ramadan, Eid feasts, and birthdays.

Thinking about quitting at any of the three occasions linked to a stronger desire to quit. It also linked to far higher odds of a past quit attempt. Ramadan led on both counts, with about eightfold odds of an attempt. Only Ramadan linked to calling the national quitline. The authors urge timing quit campaigns to such occasions. Faith and culture, they say, are levers for health programs.
pmc-10655310:
Dazhi Fu and co-authors map the father-line genetics of the Hui people in Liaoning Province, China, in a 2023 paper. The Hui are China's second-largest ethnic minority, spread across the whole country, yet earlier work on their paternal lines had skipped Liaoning. The team typed 282 unrelated Hui men at two sets of markers on the Y chromosome, the piece of DNA passed from father to son.

The men's lineages proved highly varied, sorting into 46 branch groups. Comparing marker patterns with other regions split China's Hui into three broad clusters. The Liaoning Hui grouped with those of the northwest, apart from groups in the southwest and in two other provinces. Measured against other Chinese peoples, the Hui showed the closest kinship with the Han, the majority group. The authors offer the data for both population history and forensic work, where such marker profiles help identify people.
pmc-10655410:
Sulaiman Lakoh and co-authors count the extra diseases carried by tuberculosis patients in Sierra Leone. Their 2023 study covers two hundred forty adults with confirmed TB at the country's largest hospital in Freetown. TB kills on a vast scale worldwide and often travels with chronic illness, yet co-disease counts stay thin. Charts and checks logged each patient's lasting conditions over three months.

About two thirds of patients carried two or more chronic diseases. High blood pressure led, with diabetes next. Younger adults were far less likely to stack illnesses than older ones. The team backs joined-up care that treats TB and its chronic partners in one plan.
pmc-10656010:
Tatjana Nazir and co-authors ask in 2023 how social robots should look to be welcomed by people. Cases of robot abuse hint at a risk: people may treat human-like machines as rivals and act with aggression. The team guessed that trouble starts when people can compare their own body skills with the robot's.

Pairs of robots varied in how human they looked and in how they moved. Some walked or jumped, moves a body can copy; others rolled or floated. For copyable movers, less human looks meant lower ratings of human-like traits. For the others, the least human-looking scored highest. Welcome followed those trait ratings.
pmc-10656410:
Shielding electronics from stray electromagnetic waves calls for materials that soak up energy yet stay light. Eight materials scientists build such a sponge in 2023 from chitosan, a biomass polymer. They freeze-shape it into an aerogel, bake it into carbon, and seed it with nickel and manganese oxide particles. Nitrogen doping and the mix of magnetic and dielectric parts tune how waves enter the material instead of bouncing off.

The aerogel absorbs across a band 7.36 gigahertz wide, with a deepest loss past minus 64 decibels. It also hides objects from radar and infrared sensors and helps manage heat. The authors offer the recipe as a cheap, flexible route to protection for devices and aircraft.
pmc-10656510:
Sebastian Metz and nine co-authors trawl global DNA surveys for a mostly parasitic branch of single-celled life. Perkinsea sit inside the Alveolata, and some species invade and kill marine animals, yet their true diversity is barely sampled. The team mined the EukBank metabarcoding set, keyed to one gene region, across thousands of environmental samples. They found 1,568 distinct sequence variants in the group.

Soil alone held 269 variants, which breaks the old assumption that Perkinsea stick to sea and fresh water. Variants sorted by habitat preference across many settings. The authors frame the haul as the visible tip of a much larger hidden diversity.
pmc-10657010:
Ed Day, Ifigeneia Manitsa, Amanda Farley, and John Kelly surveyed recovery identity in the United Kingdom in a 2023 national study. Among people who have beaten a drug or alcohol problem, how many call themselves in recovery? The label guides services and policy, yet lived usage may differ from professional usage.

A representative survey covered about thirteen hundred seventy people who had resolved a serious problem. Just over half currently identified as in recovery, about twenty-nine percent never had, and nineteen percent no longer did. Current abstinence, treatment history, and support group use predicted adopting the label. Those who skipped it often saw their problem as mild or fully resolved. Services should not assume the label fits everyone.
pmc-10657410:
Tyler W Dunn, Xiaotang Fan, and their co-authors studied calcium channels in the touch sensing nerve cells of the sea slug Aplysia. Their 2023 paper starts from a puzzle: these cells release less signal after repeated touch, a simple form of learning called habituation. Most other connections in the animal do not fade this way, which hints at a special release setup.

The team found that touch cells favor certain splice forms of the channel gene needed for signal release. Yet no single splice form proved required for the fading response. The tail end of the channel binds two partner proteins and is needed for full presence of the channel at the release site. The results narrow how the special release setup is built.
pmc-10669010:
Alexandra Louise Møller and co-authors test whether pairing two drug classes lowers a scarring signal in people with type 2 diabetes, in a study from 2023. The signal, endotrophin, reflects the building of a stiff collagen type and marks risk for kidney decline. It was measured in blood from nearly three hundred patients in a kidney-focused project.

Among all blood markers tested, this signal best predicted later kidney function loss. Patients on both drug classes together showed a clear drop in the signal, compared with one class alone. Higher starting levels of the signal also meant higher risk of kidney decline. The authors suggest the paired treatment may slow kidney damage, with the signal as a way to watch it.
pmc-10669310:
Horațiu Roman, Adelina-Gabriela Niculescu, Veronica Lazăr, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It tests tansy essential oil against the ESKAPE gang, the hospital superbugs most notorious for dodging antibiotics, and checks whether the oil makes standard drugs hit harder.

Drug-resistant infections are among medicine's worst problems, and multi-target plant compounds are promising allies. The team distilled the oil and charted its chemistry by gas chromatography. Its main components include thujones, eucalyptol, camphor, and germacrene. Standard disk and dilution tests measured killing power against resistant Gram-positive and Gram-negative strains on the ESKAPE list. The authors tied activity back to the isolated compounds. Pairing the oil with antibiotics showed synergy in the study's framing. The paper builds the case for tansy as an adjunct worth developing, not a folk remedy to shrug off.
pmc-10675410:
Charalambos Michaeloudes and co-authors review why fish oil compounds help some heart patients and not others, in a 2023 paper. The two compounds, known as EPA and DHA, come from omega-3 fats and can lower blood fats and calm vessel inflammation. Yet large trials of these supplements have given conflicting results, which confuses the public and clinicians.

The review traces how the two compounds act in shared and unlike ways inside cells. They swap into cell membranes in place of more inflammatory fats, steer gene switches, and leave marks on DNA control. Trial design flaws may explain part of the clash in results. The authors propose better trial and lab design, better supplement mixes, and markers that predict who will respond, so treatment can be matched to the person.
pmc-10687210:
Kangjie Li, Jielian Deng, and four colleagues untangle a confound in HIV research, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. Gut microbe changes blamed on the virus may partly belong to the study population instead. Many HIV gut studies enroll men who have sex with men, whose microbiomes differ from other men's even without infection.

The team gathered the published changes linked to HIV and to this population separately, using databases of microbe genes and metabolites. They then asked, with bioinformatics and single-cell data, what the population-linked changes do to immune balance. Their synthesis argues that dysbiosis tied to this group can itself disturb immune homeostasis and raise HIV infection risk. That reframes a literature: some effects credited to the virus may precede it. Untangling cause, consequence, and coincidence is essential before microbiome therapies for HIV can be designed honestly.
pmc-10692110:
A team of researchers maps the microbes living in the bladders of baby boys in a paper from 2023. Doctors once thought urine held no germs, but the bladder hosts a small community now called the urobiome. Samples were taken with a thin tube during care, so they stayed clean. The team used both lab growth and gene reading to name the microbes present.

Many microbe types appeared in all samples, which points to a shared early pattern. Birth type and past antibiotic use did not change the mix. The team also grew nine strains of one germ linked to infections in older men. Their gene maps add a base for later health studies.
pmc-10692210:
Franco Angelini and co-authors publish a dataset gathered by a four-legged robot in the high Italian Alps. The robot, ANYmal C, surveyed siliceous scree slopes, a protected European habitat that people normally monitor on foot. Its cameras recorded eight plant species typical of the habitat or signalling trouble, along with four detailed survey plots. The records pair species footage with the robot's own state data and images gathered to judge the habitat's condition.

The authors aim the openly archived data at two audiences. Ecologists can use the plant material to devise new measures of habitat health or to train image classifiers. Roboticists can use the machine's state records to validate their control and perception algorithms. The dataset shows what a legged robot can already contribute to monitoring fragile mountain habitats.
pmc-10693410:
Wang, Chen, Deng, and Jiang study second cancers after prostate radiotherapy in work from twenty twenty-three. Radiation can cure prostate cancer, but it may raise the later risk of new cancers in the pelvis, such as bladder or rectal cancer.

The team used a large United States cancer database that spans decades. They picked men whose first cancer was prostate cancer treated in the pelvis region. Standard risk models weighed the chance of a second pelvic cancer against other causes of death. A hospital group in Nanchang gave an outside check. Knowing who faces the most risk can guide long term checks after treatment.
pmc-10693610:
Kunjing Qu and co-authors publish the genome of a high-plateau grass and compare it with a close cousin. Their 2023 paper assembles the full chromosome set of Orinus kokonorica. Both genera descend from an ancient genome doubling some ten million years ago.

Neither copy of the doubled genome dominates the other in use or survival of genes. The two species differ by many rearrangements and structural changes. Gene-by-gene comparison suggests fresh roles for old genes drove much of their split. Flower and rhizome genes vary in copy number between them, matching their unlike looks. The work links genome doubling to later diversity.
pmc-10693710:
Yao Yang and co-authors map the research landscape around kneecap joint replacement, a narrower operation than full knee replacement. The surgery suits arthritis confined to the kneecap joint, but reports of implant failure and complications keep it controversial. The team searched five databases for work from 1950 to 2022 and charted 241 papers with mapping software.

Publications climbed steadily over the years. The journal Knee carried the most papers, while Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research drew the most citations. Clinical outcomes dominated the field: implant survival, revision surgery, and complications drew the most study. The authors read the map as a guide to who leads the field, which questions are crowded, and where collaboration clusters sit.
pmc-10694910:
Martijn van der Steen, writing alone, follows one Dutch nursing home through four years of market-style reform in a 2023 study. Western governments trusted New Public Management to spark business energy in care. Whether local dementia care homes actually respond that way was untested.

Interviews with managers and staff, plus piles of official and internal papers, traced the home's moves. Three strategies came in sequence: cutting care services, teaming with neighbors on non-care ventures, and specializing in care niches. Two of the three aimed at the office, not at better care. The case shows reform energy flowing into survival tactics the policy never intended.
pmc-10695110:
Alex Cebrian-Ponce and co-authors track body water and muscle strain across trail races of three lengths in a 2023 study. Ninety-two runners at fourteen, thirty-five, and fifty-two kilometer events were measured before and after racing. Electrical impedance mapped whole-body fluids, and blood enzyme levels gauged muscle damage.

Vectors shifted toward dehydration in nearly every group, men and women alike. Starting hydration predicted finishing time in some groups, and a muscle-localized probe followed quads, hamstrings, and calves in a small subset. Longer races wrung the body harder, as expected, but even the shortest left marks. Race doctors gain numbers for fluid advice.
pmc-10695610:
Youlin Yu and three co-authors built a risk score for liver cancer from cell death patterns, in a 2023 study. Treatment often fails as this cancer grows and resists drugs. Programmed cell death helps control cell balance, and its genes may carry clues. The team studied twelve known death patterns in tumor data.

They found seventy-five death-related genes tied to outlook. A score built from eleven of them split patients by risk. High-score patients fared worse in both the main data set and a check set. The score also tracked immune features in the tumor. High-score tumors responded more to some common chemotherapy drugs in their analysis. Joining the score with clinical traits gave a strong prediction chart. The authors offer the score as a guide for prognosis and drug choice.
pmc-10696010:
Michał Bełcik and four co-authors tested whether what birds hear changes how forest fragmentation affects the song thrush in Central Europe. They played recordings in 150 forest patches of varied size and isolation. Some patches heard thrush song, an attractive signal. Others heard predator cues, a repulsive one. Some heard both, and some heard only a control.

Predator cues lowered thrush numbers and changed how patch size and isolation related to abundance. Thrush song alone did not raise numbers, but it flipped the usual link between patch size and abundance. The mixed signal changed nothing. Most effects faded by the next breeding season. The authors conclude that landscapes of fear and attraction can bend the effects of fragmentation, but probably only briefly, which complicates simple habitat rules.
pmc-10697810:
Oscar Delaney, Andrew Letten, and Jan Engelstädter rethink a lab staple: growing microbes in cycles, each time keeping only a small share to seed the next round. Tight cuts risk losing good new mutants, while long growth rounds force tight cuts. The standard daily cycle with a harsh cut has little theory behind it, the authors say.

Their math flips the usual answer. Measured per hour of experiment, not per round, adaptation runs fastest with very frequent, very gentle cuts, near steady growth in the limit. Adding food limits and rival mutants did not change the verdict. They suggest robots or steady-flow vessels to put the idea to work.
pmc-10698910:
Bigirinama and co-authors probe how lead works at ward tier in long-crisis Congo. Care webs in low and mid lands strain to give good care to all. Lead aids web grace and true change in past tales. Yet lead in the Congo had thin print till this work. Eight farm health zones in east Congo ground the work. Facts came in 2021 by deep talks and plain watch runs.

Key health hands in each zone gave the talk facts. Six lead themes frame the hunt in a bent set form. That form stems from a known lead frame in the text. Talks span how lead is lived and seen by zone hands. Watch runs add what talks can't catch in the zones. The work is one-cut and word-based in its build.
pmc-10699410:
Vicky Chang leads an eleven-author team testing whether a common herbicide damages farmers' chromosomes, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. Glyphosate is the world's most used herbicide and is suspected in some blood cancers. Human evidence for its genotoxicity was scarce.

The marker studied is mosaic loss of chromosome Y in blood cells, a measurable sign of genomic damage. DNA came from 1,606 farmers aged fifty and over in an agricultural health cohort. Lifetime glyphosate use was reconstructed from self-reported spraying histories. Men who spray more can be compared for Y loss rates. Such biomarker studies probe possible mechanisms long before cancer counts could settle the question either way.
pmc-10699610:
Yakup Yildirim and Yeşim Yilmaz gather teacher views on fostering creativity in preschool. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, works in Alanya, Turkey. Twenty-five working preschool teachers and twenty-five trainees took part. All answered open-ended questions about the current preschool program.

Both groups prize creative thought that lets a child express feelings well. Problem solving and cause-and-effect thinking also rank high. A fresh viewpoint on events rounds out the valued traits. For growing creativity, trips out of class lead the suggestions. Art, drama, science, and math activities follow close behind. The findings can steer teacher training.
pmc-10700110:
Ronald Bronson and co-authors chart how vessel lining cells change into scar like cells, in a 2023 study. The shift, called EndoMT, feeds a growing list of human diseases. Knowing its gene pattern could point to new drug targets.

The team built an atlas of gene activity across vessel lining cells and traced how the shift rewires it. The program touched cell stickiness and white cell traffic. Patterns differed across artery, vein, and tiny vessel cells, yet shared hub genes linked them. A short chain fat, acetate, strongly blocked the shift in all cell kinds. The atlas is offered as a resource for drug hunting.
pmc-10700210:
Lucia Brodosi and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-three, the risk of binge eating disorder in patients with fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction. Few data link the liver disease to eating disorders. The team assessed one hundred twenty-nine patients sent by general doctors to a hospital metabolic unit. Most had obesity, with a mean body mass index in the mid-thirties. A standard binge eating scale scored risk: mid scores meant possible disorder, high scores meant probable disorder. Liver fat and scarring were checked with blood markers and scans.

About eighteen percent scored as possible cases and about eight percent as probable cases. Those rates did not link to sex, obesity class, diabetes, liver fat, or scarring. Daily calorie intake did link to possible cases.
pmc-10700610:
Jun Suzuki and fourteen co-authors present a 2023 study of a fat handling protein and noise caused hearing loss in mice. The protein helps cells take in and move fatty acids in the nervous system. Whether it shapes the ear's response to loud noise was unknown.

The team bred mice that lack the protein and compared their hearing with normal mice. Hearing was tested before noise, a day after a loud blast, and two weeks later. At the start, the groups heard alike. After noise, the mice without the protein kept lower hearing thresholds and more of their sound sensing cells survived. Gene and chemical readouts from the inner ear filled in the picture.
pmc-10701610:
Odeya Barayev and co-authors ask whether statins help older veterans with kidney disease in a 2023 cohort study. Proof for statins to prevent heart disease and death in people with kidney disease has been thin.

The study used a trial-like design on health system and Medicare data for veterans over sixty-five with moderate kidney disease. All were within five years of diagnosis, with no past heart disease or statin use. Close to fifteen thousand veterans were tracked for death and major heart events. The design weighs statin starters against non-starters with care for bias. Readers get a large, real-world test of a common drug choice in kidney care.
pmc-10702410:
Winter Roth, David Dadiomov, and Michelle Chu audit off-label antipsychotic use at a large teaching hospital. Their review from twenty twenty-three covers one year of quetiapine dispensing. The drug is often prescribed outside psychiatry at low doses. Side effects include weight gain, blood sugar rises, and falls.

A safe-use protocol was drafted from labels and guidelines first. Every dispensed strength over the year entered the review. Charts were then checked against the protocol criteria. Inappropriate uses were counted and their harms costed. The audit tests whether a stewardship programme is needed. Antipsychotic stewardship mirrors antibiotic stewardship logic. Hospitals can target the commonest misuse patterns found.
pmc-10704610:
Every pregnant woman in one Turkish study used social media, and most scored high on a hook scale. Merve Bağrici Bozan and Eda Cangöl surveyed five hundred women in 2023 at two hospital clinics in the west of the land. Face-to-face talks logged why the women went online and how long they stayed. Mean daily use ran to three and a half hours.

More than seven in ten women crossed the line for high hook scores. The pair do not treat the apps as pure harm: mothers seek facts and peer comfort there. Their worry is wrong facts and lost hours. They urge health staff to teach sound, even use of the apps at each stage of care, and to point women to sources that can be trusted.
pmc-10704810:
Yanyan Wang and co-authors trace how tiny gene regulators called microRNAs change in goat ovaries as the animals grow up. The ovary drives sexual maturity and breeding ability, and these small molecules help control that growth. The team sampled ovary tissue at four ages, from one day old to six months old.

Blood tests showed seven breeding hormones were lowest at birth and peaked at four months of age. Gene reads found 667 of the small regulators in total, with 254 changing a lot between ages. Groups of them rose and fell in clear patterns across the stages. The work gives goat breeders and researchers a map of the signals tied to maturity.
pmc-10707010:
Emanuele Piccinno and co-authors track a small RNA that controls cell joining in colorectal cancer, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. Desmosomes are the rivets that hold surface cells together, and they fall apart as this cancer turns disordered. The team focused on miR-195-5p, a tiny RNA that tunes gene use, and on JUP, a gene that codes for a rivet part called gamma-catenin.

Restoring the small RNA in colon cells lowered JUP output and shifted two partner proteins of the rivet system. It also changed key parts of the Wnt signal path, which drives growth in this cancer. The work names a fresh control route over cell adhesion in the gut lining. The authors suggest the small RNA could one day serve as a base for treatment.
pmc-10707510:
Lois Daamen, Quintus Molenaar, and Vincent Groot review recent advances in pancreatic cancer care in a 2023 article. Survival for this cancer stays poor even as surgery and care around it improve. The authors survey bold directions across the full span of care, from early detection to treatment planning.

Blood based liquid biopsies may aid early detection, guide therapy, and watch for return of disease. Precision approaches target gene changes with matched drugs, such as PARP blockers for BRCA linked tumors. Artificial intelligence is entering imaging, marker search, and planning, though ethics, data safety, and proof of reliability remain concerns. The authors stress joint work between clinicians, researchers, and AI specialists to make these tools pay off.
pmc-10708410:
Patrizia Picerno and a large team of co-authors turn almond skins into a health extract, in a paper dated twenty twenty-three. Sicilian almond peels, a food industry waste, are rich in plant compounds that fight free radicals. The team made a dry water extract and coated it with a natural polymer.

Tests showed strong antioxidant action and a clear block on nitric oxide. The extract also curbed an enzyme that breaks down tissue and slowed sugar damage. The coating helped the powder dissolve and release better. A food supplement with added health value came out of the work.
pmc-10708510:
Christopher Lobban, Britney Sison, and Matt Ashworth name new tiny sea plants in a 2023 study. Diatoms are glass-walled algae that feed sea life, and one group lives on sea floors across Micronesia. Field sweeps found clusters of unknown kinds that vary around shared themes of shell build.

With fine scope views of shell detail, the team names 17 new kinds in three groups. One group bears thick ribs and framed pores on its shell face. A second holds large, straight kinds kin to two known ones. The names grow the known flock of this group and sharpen how kinds are told apart.
pmc-10709310:
Four researchers from Iran simulate what happens when runaway electrons slam into the tungsten wall of a fusion reactor. In a tokamak, some electrons escape control and race around the chamber. When they strike the wall, they dump heat that can melt or crack it, and they can make the wall radioactive.

Using a Monte Carlo code, the team tracked electrons through the metal and measured where their energy lands. Steeper hit angles drove energy deeper and spread it wider. A magnetic field boosted deposits most for slow electrons striking at a slant. Fast electrons, in the fifty to one hundred MeV range, often passed clean through the wall. The study warns that gear behind the wall needs shielding too.
pmc-10709610:
Maristella Canovai and ten colleagues showed that resistant prostate cancer cells can export their drug resistance to neighbors. Docetaxel failure is a main reason metastatic prostate cancer treatment collapses. The team found that resistant cell clones release three specific microRNAs into their surroundings. When other cancer cells take up these molecules, the chemotherapy works less well on them too. The twenty twenty-three study traced this sharing mechanism in cell experiments.

Computer analysis and lab tests identified genes the microRNAs suppress, including FOXO1 and PDCD4. Two further genes, PPP2CB and INSIG1, carried much of the resistance effect. Tiny vesicles called exosomes ferried the microRNAs between cells. Blocking this traffic could be a future strategy for keeping docetaxel effective longer in advanced prostate cancer.
pmc-10709810:
Huazhen Liu and co-authors present a portable printer for printing hydrogels and cells directly at a wound site in a 2023 paper. Skin lesions break appearance and barrier function and can lead to severe infection and immune reactions. Printing in place deposits bio ink to repair tissue within a clinical setting. Their handheld device patterns and molds hydrogels on surfaces as needed.

Using two hydrogels of high and low thickness together, the team achieved cell laden printing with the thinner gel. Cells stayed viable while the gel gained structure. The approach can package drugs, proteins, and cells with control at macro and micro scales. Readers see a step toward wound repair that adapts to each lesion in real time.
pmc-10709910:
Novika Purnama Sari and co-authors published this study in 2023 on autistic traits in mothers and children. Past work showed the two run together in families. The team asked whether a mother's weight before pregnancy changes that link. They drew on two cohorts: a Dutch one with 4,659 members and a Cambridge one with 179. Traits were scored in mothers and in children from toddler age to the early teens.

Higher traits in mothers went with higher traits in children at every age checked. Higher pre-pregnancy weight also tied to higher child traits in the Dutch cohort. But weight did not change the strength of the mother-child link in either cohort. Children of underweight and overweight mothers scored higher than those of healthy-weight mothers. The authors say the family link stands on its own, and the brain paths behind it still need work.
pmc-10710310:
Ann-Elin Synnes and co-authors compared fish communities under different protection regimes in Norway in two thousand twenty-three. When top predators vanish, mid-level predators can multiply and reshape the food web, an effect called mesopredator release. Cod is a likely top predator in these coastal waters.

They sampled fish with fyke nets over three seasons in national park waters open to fishing and in a nearby seascape with protected zones. Cod in the protected seascape were much larger on average. Open waters held more mesopredator fish. The pattern fits the release hypothesis: protecting top predators helps them control mid-level fish. The authors link today's coastal fish state to long fishing pressure on large predators.
pmc-10710710:
Maria Moralidou and co-authors ask whether cement gives surgeons better control of stem angle in hip replacement than press-fit fixation. The femoral stem's twist, its version, affects stability and wear, and surgeons aim near twenty degrees. Cementless stems lock to the inner bone, following its natural twist; cement lets the surgeon set the angle freely.

The series covered ninety-five patients and one hundred six hips, eighty-one uncemented and twenty-five cemented, all planned with 3D CT and done through the same approach. Comparing achieved version between the two groups tests whether cement's freedom delivers accuracy in practice. The answer guides fixation choice when a patient's anatomy fights the target angle.
pmc-10711810:
Gangbin Han and a large team of co-authors survey mental health during China's Omicron wave in a 2023 study. The pandemic's first years strained minds worldwide through lost income, closed services, and isolation. When the fast-spreading Omicron variant hit Shanghai in early 2022, a new round of disruption followed. The team measured the psychological toll of that outbreak on the Chinese public.

Their introduction frames why this wave differed: a variant that mutated and spread quickly, meeting a population under strict controls. The study explores how anxiety, depression, and stress patterned across groups during the outbreak months. Such surveys guide where counseling and support should aim when the next wave comes. The work adds a China-specific record to the global pandemic mental health archive.
pmc-10711910:
Daniel Freeman leads a large team presenting the protocol for the Phoenix trial of automated virtual reality therapy, in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Young people with psychosis often have low confidence and heavy negative self-beliefs. Many pull back from day-to-day life. And a lack of therapists means few of them get psychological help at all.

The therapy was built with young people who have lived experience of psychosis. A virtual coach inside VR gives the treatment. Staff help the user, in place of a full therapist. The randomized controlled trial will test if it lifts positive self-beliefs and psychological wellbeing. This protocol paper sets the design out in advance. If it works, automated VR could widen access to therapy that builds confidence, and by a lot.
pmc-10712110:
Dalia H El-Kashef and Mona Abdel Rahim tested whether an allergy drug can protect rat lungs from a harsh cancer drug, in a study published in 2023. The cancer drug is used worldwide but can badly damage the lungs. The allergy drug is known to calm swelling and allergic responses, which made it a candidate shield.

Rats given the cancer drug alone showed clear lung harm: more swelling signals, more damage markers, and worse tissue under the microscope. Rats that also received the allergy drug for two weeks, starting a week before, showed much less of each harm. The authors credit the drug's mix of calming, protective, and anti-scarring effects. The work is early, animal-only evidence, but it points to a possible guard for patients who need the cancer drug.
pmc-10713310:
Xiaomei Cao, Kun Wang, and Huizhi Zhu report a 2023 rat study of a traditional Chinese herbal granule used for asthma. The granule, called Yanghepingchuan, is known to ease airway inflammation, but how it works at the molecular level was unclear. The team set out to trace the chain of signals the treatment affects.

Rats were made asthmatic with standard triggers, then treated with the granule, a pathway-blocking drug, or both. Lab checks showed the granule raised levels of a small RNA called miR-328-3p. That change quieted a signaling chain, running from a protein called HMGB1 through a receptor called TLR4, that drives inflammation. With the chain calmer, a cell self-cleaning process slowed and lung inflammation eased. The authors conclude the granule fights asthma mainly by calming this pathway.
pmc-10713610:
Reeve and co-authors trace how mountain birds spread across the Indo-Pacific in a 2023 study. Two rival stories explain mountain populations: birds hop straight from peak to peak, or they climb from nearby lowlands. The team asked whether a species' homeland decides which story fits. Island songbirds at the crossroads of Eurasia and Australo-Papua gave a clean test case.

Family trees and range maps showed both stories at work, split by origin. Species from Eurasia spread by hopping between mountains, aided by a taste for cold seasons and short migrations. Species from the Australo-Papuan side rose from lowland stock instead. Once settled in highlands, those birds rarely spread to new island peaks. Origin, not chance alone, shapes how the region's mountain bird life took form.
pmc-10714210:
Jorunn Kirkeleit and co-authors traced lung decline to early life in two thousand twenty-three. Lung power peaks in youth and falls with age. Some people's lungs fall faster than normal. The team asked whether early exposures speed that fall. Their pooled cohort held about eleven thousand adults. Follow-up ran for more than twenty years.

Two long-running population studies supplied the data. Lung measures were taken up to three times each. Exposures spanned from conception through puberty. Parental and childhood factors were weighed together. Faster decline tied to several early exposures. The findings argue lung health is set partly in childhood. Protecting children's airways may pay off decades later. The study is among the largest of its kind.
pmc-10715010:
Anita Grootemaat and co-authors report, in 2023, that a viral protein lingered in the kidney of a patient who had recovered from COVID-19. Many patients develop kidney injury during the illness, yet whether the virus itself reaches kidney tissue is debated. The team examined kidney tissue from a recovered patient.

A protein from the virus's shell was found built up in the kidney's tubule lining, without signs that the virus was copying itself there. Because that protein is made in large amounts during infection, its persistence could affect later kidney health and the immune system. The finding adds a piece to the long-term effects puzzle.
pmc-10716010:
Gorka Sesma and co-authors study the center of the retina in 2023 in Saudi children treated for lazy eye. A lazy eye develops when one eye is misaligned or focuses differently, and the clear center zone of the retina has no blood vessels. The size of that vessel-free zone may mark how the eye responds to treatment, so the team tracked it with a vessel scan.

Twenty-three children were followed for a year of patching treatment, with scans every three months. The vessel-free zone was about the same size in lazy and healthy eyes at the start, and it did not change clearly in either group. Starting vision and eye alignment did track later changes in the zone.
pmc-10716110:
Yao Lu and co-authors test robot help for fixing a hard knee fracture, in a 2023 feasibility study. The fracture dents the back-outer corner of the shin bone's top, a spot that is hard to reach and set. One group of patients received robot-assisted surgery through small skin cuts. Another group had the classic manual screw method.

Records covered a few dozen patients treated over four years, all with fresh, closed, one-sided fractures. The team compared cut length, operating time, blood loss, and X-ray use. Hospital stay, timing of weight training, and complications were also tracked. A standard X-ray score graded how well each joint surface was restored. The study weighs whether robot precision earns its place in this niche.
pmc-10716410:
Cezary Grunwald and twelve co-authors published a 2023 case-control study of an immune gene variant and multiple sclerosis risk in Poland. Earlier work on the IL-13 variant rs20541 and MS had clashed. The team genotyped 94 relapsing-remitting MS patients and 160 healthy volunteers. One allele, A, and the genotypes carrying it appeared significantly more often in patients.

Carrying A raised the odds of MS by about 1.7 times per allele. The variant showed no link, though, to age at onset or disability scores. The authors conclude the variant may predispose Poles to MS without shaping its course. They frame the result as one piece of the disease's genetic puzzle, needing replication in larger cohorts.
pmc-10716810:
Longwu Wang and co-authors present a 2023 study on why cuckoos remove host eggs from nests they parasitize. Cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds' nests and let the hosts raise the chicks. A female cuckoo usually removes one or two host eggs as she lays, and the benefit of that habit has long been debated.

One idea says biting an egg speeds up her laying, shrinking the time she is exposed to host attack. The team timed common cuckoos laying in empty nests, nests with host eggs, and nests with blue stick models. Biting an egg or a stick cut laying time by about thirty-seven percent. This is the first direct experimental support for the speed hypothesis.
pmc-10717010:
Shuxi Liu and co-authors test lentinan, an active ingredient from shiitake mushrooms, against cognitive deficits caused by chronic Toxoplasma gondii infection in mice. Their 2023 study notes that this parasite is increasingly seen as a risk factor for neurodegenerative disease.

Mice were infected by gavage with parasite cysts, and lentinan was given by injection two weeks before infection. The team ran behavior tests and used RNA sequencing, microscopy, and staining to check cognition and brain pathology. Lentinan is known for boosting anti-infective immunity. The study asks whether it can also protect the brain, in a field where drug options for this infection are limited.
pmc-10717110:
Yingjie Liu and co-authors surveyed men in China about a long-acting shot to prevent HIV, in this 2023 study. The men had taken a daily or event-based pill form of prevention in an earlier study. Shots that last for weeks could help those who find pills hard to keep up.

Of 612 men who answered, 77.8 percent said they would take the free shot form. Willingness was higher in men with more partners, partners of unknown HIV status, drug use for recreation, or a past herpes infection. It was lower in event-based pill users and in men whose pill use had been less steady. The authors say shots could widen coverage, but steady-use groups need care.
pmc-10717210:
Farhad Sheikhnia, Vahid Rashidi, Hossein Maghsoudi, and Maryam Majidinia review a black seed compound as a possible helper against colon and rectal cancer. The compound, thymoquinone, comes from Nigella sativa and has a long history in traditional medicine for many ailments. The review gathers dish and animal studies of its action on colorectal tumors. Across those studies the compound slowed cancer cells through several pathways.

Paired with standard anti-cancer drugs, it strengthened their effect while softening their side effects in the reported work. The authors call it a promising partner therapy rather than a stand-alone cure. Big gaps remain: its exact molecular targets and pathways are not yet pinned down. More work, they argue, could turn the compound into a tool against drug resistance, one of the hardest problems in treating this cancer.
pmc-10717810:
Majid Mokhtari, Samane Khoshbakht, Mohammad Esmaeil Akbari, and Sayyed Sajjad Moravveji published a precision medicine study in twenty twenty-three presenting a protocol that picks drug combinations patient by patient. Cancer drug screening for individuals is slow and costly. Their bioinformatics system instead reads each patient's disturbed gene pattern like a fingerprint and matches drugs against it.

Data covered over six thousand breast cancer patients, healthy controls, and nearly seven hundred drugs. Combinations mixing cancer and non-cancer drugs outperformed cancer-only sets in their analysis, a win for drug repurposing. Every patient's perturbed pattern proved unique. The protocol is offered as the front end for laboratory platforms that validate personalized combinations before treatment.
pmc-10717910:
Cervical cancer is rising in young women, and early warning signs are hard to spot with standard tests. Yuhan Jia, Kun Zou, and Lijuan Zou review a fresh angle in a 2023 paper: the study of small molecules in the body, called metabolomics. These molecules shift as cancer forms, and their pattern can act like a fingerprint.

The team searched four databases for studies up to 2022. The review maps how key molecules change as tumors grow and spread. It also weighs how well the method could serve for screening, diagnosis, and tracking treatment. The authors see the field as young but fast-growing. Better tools here could catch the disease sooner and guide care.
pmc-10719310:
Jérôme Levallet and co-authors pinned in 2023 a low-oxygen switch that helps lung cancer spread to the brain. Lung tumors and their brain offspring both bear marks of oxygen want. In bronchial cells starved hard of oxygen, a growth signal named YAP woke while its usual brakes faded. One kinase, NDR2, bucked the trend and ran hot. Such cells crawled in a amoeba-like way and seeded brain growths.

NDR2 ran higher in spread lung tumors than in contained ones. Muting it in the cells blocked brain growths in mice. The team names NDR2 as the hypoxia-driven engine of this spread. A simple stain for it on tumor samples could flag patients at risk, they suggest.
pmc-10720010:
Muhammad Ali and co-authors test a common blue dye as a tool to free trapped oil from sandstone in Pakistan, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Much oil stays stuck after standard recovery, and rock soaked in organic acids repels water. The team aged rock samples in acid, then soaked them in dye solutions.

Heat, pressure, and salt all pushed the rock toward oil-loving behavior. Dye soaks flipped the rock back toward water-loving, which favors oil release. The strongest dye bath gave the biggest flip. Since the dye is a waste product in huge amounts, the authors pitch it as a cheap recovery aid.
pmc-10720210:
Sengo and six co-authors study eye strain from screens in Mozambique, in work from twenty twenty-three. Computer vision syndrome is a set of eye and vision problems tied to screen use. Screen use surged for students and teachers during the pandemic.

The team surveyed students and teachers at a university in Nampula in late twenty twenty and early twenty twenty-one. They used a tested eye strain survey plus questions on desk setup and habits. More than three in four people met the mark for the syndrome in their results. Odds tests linked risk to certain work conditions. The study gives local proof for eye health steps in schools.
pmc-10722510:
Arran George Plant and co-authors make chemicals with reactor radiation in a 2023 paper. Ethylene glycol, derived from a biodiesel byproduct, is the starting feedstock. Irradiation inside a fission reactor converts it into methanol or acetaldehyde.

Nuclear power offers low-carbon energy but faces high costs. Making valuable chemicals could improve the economics of reactors. The team varied radiation quality, dose rate, and total dose. Yields were measured as standard radiochemical values for each setup. Low dose rates with gamma rays alone favored selective output. Readers see a route to use spare radiation capacity for green chemical production.
pmc-10724810:
Emily Ganek and six co-authors review how nurse educators can build diversity, equity, and inclusion into their work. Their review is from two thousand twenty-three. As patient populations grow more diverse, nurses need training that matches that reality. Faculty lead that training, so their own practice is the place to start.

The team searched four global databases and selected twenty-six strong sources from sixty-one found. Recurring best practices fell into clear themes. Schools should recruit more faculty from underrepresented groups and state inclusion in their mission. Curricula should treat these topics directly, backed by a written plan and real leadership. Mentoring, outreach partnerships, and credit for this work in hiring also mattered. Data-driven steps and policy change round out the list.
pmc-10730010:
Ruszkowski and Pfrommer give a teaching-style review of cosmic rays in galaxies and galaxy clusters. Knowing what shapes galaxy growth is a core problem in astrophysics. Recent work suggests cosmic rays, fast charged particles, may play a far larger role than once thought in that story.

Cosmic rays cool slowly and couple strongly to gas, so their pressure can rival heat, magnetic, and turbulent pressure in interstellar space. They can drive large galactic winds that reshape whole systems. The review covers how cosmic rays are sped up, how they travel, what telescopes see, and how they push back on galaxy growth.
pmc-10731210:
A 26-year-old man in Saudi Arabia had lived with Graves' disease for two years when a check found a lump in his thyroid. Naweed Alzaman tells the case in this 2023 report. Scans showed a 2.6-centimetre nodule with rich blood flow, and a needle sample looked highly suspicious for cancer.

Surgeons removed the whole thyroid and found multifocal micropapillary thyroid cancer, several tiny tumour foci of the commonest thyroid cancer kind. He then received radioactive iodine treatment and thyroid hormone replacement. Cancer is uncommon in Graves' disease, though nodules are not, and the two conditions have been linked before. Alzaman urges careful checks and ultrasound screening of nodules in Graves' patients, since this pairing had not been reported from his region before.
pmc-10731310:
Rachel Deere and colleagues ran a small crossover trial in 2023 on exercise and long-term knee pain. Many people with sore knees find that leg exercise makes pain worse for a time, which can push them to stop exercising. The team asked whether arm exercise could ease knee pain without working the painful joint. Volunteers with knee pain lasting at least three months each did one session of arm cycling and one of leg cycling, a week apart, and rated their pain for days afterward.

Arm exercise lowered knee pain the next day, while leg exercise did not. Both kinds of exercise changed how pressure felt at test spots, and responses to light touch varied widely. The authors say the reason for the arm effect is not yet clear. Still, they suggest arm exercise may offer a useful extra option for people whose knees limit leg workouts.
pmc-10732010:
Anna Manvell and co-authors test the role of a single water molecule in the magnetism of lanthanide complexes. Their 2023 study uses a well-known ring ligand that wraps the metal ion. Theory had flagged the bound water as the part that breaks the ideal fourfold symmetry.

The team built versions with no bound water, keeping the ligand itself the same. Careful crystal growth held the strict symmetry in the solid state. A mix of measures and theory then mapped the electronic shape and magnetic axes. One angle from the crystal form predicts the ground state across the series. Results prove the water sets the magnetic direction and slow relaxation, and give a clean test bed for theory.
pmc-10733810:
Losing one night of sleep shifts the blood levels of proteins tied to brain degeneration, but the plumbing behind the shift is unclear. Eide and co-authors compared volunteers who stayed awake all night with others who slept freely. In the morning they measured five such proteins in blood. They also used a tracer injected into the spinal fluid to gauge two clearance systems: the lymphatic vessels of the brain's membranes and the glymphatic flow inside the brain.

After the sleepless night, blood levels of the two amyloid-beta forms fell, while the other markers held steady. In the sleepers, overnight amyloid changes tracked the membrane lymphatic clearance measure, not the glymphatic one. A tau marker instead tracked the glymphatic measure in the sleep-deprived group. The authors conclude that the biomarkers answer to sleep through different routes, so one mechanism cannot explain them all.
pmc-10733910:
Lee and colleagues studied in 2023 how glucose and d-amino acids shape the work of rodent islets of Langerhans, the pancreatic cell clusters that manage blood sugar. Certain d-amino acids sit in insulin-making beta cells or glucagon-making alpha cells and bind receptors tied to insulin release. How glucose changes their levels was little known.

Isolated islets were exposed to low or high glucose, and levels of three d-amino acids were measured inside and outside the cells. Inner levels varied a lot and barely moved with glucose. Outer levels of two of them fell at high glucose. Adding those two also changed the calcium waves that signal insulin release, while their mirror forms did not. The work adds detail on islet signaling.
pmc-10734010:
Rafał Nowaczyński and six co-authors wrote a 2023 study on preparing glass microspheres to work as biosensors. Tiny spheres of doped glass trap light in whispering gallery modes, circulating it many times. That makes them exquisitely sensitive detectors of single biomolecules. New low-melting glasses for these spheres need surface chemistry that lets antibodies stick.

The team made three glasses: two phosphate types and one tellurite. Each was coated by silanization, using protocols based on ethanol or toluene. Spectroscopy and a glowing DNA probe confirmed the coating took. Aluminophosphate and tellurite samples survived without damage. Tellurite glass treated by the toluene route glowed strongest, marking it the most efficient functionalization. The result guides fabrication of sensitive, low-cost optical biosensors.
pmc-10734310:
Building surfaces coated with proteins or sugars at exact densities is a basic need for lab-made membranes and binding tests. Oksana Kirichuk and co-authors give a recipe for dialing that density up or down in a 2023 paper.

Molecules carry an anchor that sticks to a surface packed with anchor sites. By mixing the target molecules with loose free anchors in set ratios, the team can preset how many targets land. They back the recipe with theory that links the mix to the final density, and prove it with the common biotin anchor across many densities and molecule sizes. Flipped around, the same trick can measure leftover free anchor in a sample, a handy purity check.
pmc-10735510:
Amy Thierry presents work in 2023 on why thought skills fade faster for Black older adults in the United States. This group faces twice the risk of a dementia finding compared with white peers. Yet which mix of body, mind, and place drives that gap, seen from inside the group, was not well mapped.

Drawing on a large national aging study, the work links thought scores with traits from the home area, social and mental life, and body marks. Phone-based thought tests give the scores. By studying one group in depth, the work avoids mere contrast with others. Health teams gain leads on what guards or harms thought in this group.
pmc-10735810:
Nancy Karlin compares older adults in rural Wyoming with those on the frontier, the emptiest country of all. She asks which services they use, how satisfied they are, and what they expect to need. She interviewed seventy rural and seventy-two frontier residents, all over sixty-five. Frontier respondents had less schooling, lower incomes, and fewer savings. They also had far less contact with computers and the internet, which cut their promise for telehealth.

Use of meal programs, dental care, and senior centers differed. So did future hopes for food services, hearing and vision clinics, and housing. The gaps, Karlin argues, should guide funding for senior housing, care, transport, and food support.
pmc-10735910:
Jaime Goldberg and Jooyoung Kong ask why adults who were harmed by a parent in childhood choose to care for that parent in old age, in a 2023 study. Such care can raise low mood, stress, and poor coping in the caregiver. Yet many survivors stay in touch and take on the role. The team ran deep interviews with twenty-two adults aged twenty-four to seventy.

Five themes came out of the talks. Duty mixed with mixed feelings led the list. Others cared to prove they were unlike the abuser, or saw a second chance in the task. Faith and worldview shaped some choices, and money played a role for others. The authors urge care plans that honor this tangle.
pmc-10736010:
Walter Boot surveys recent studies on using virtual reality to keep older adults engaged and connected at home, in a 2023 talk summary. The audience includes elders with and without cognitive impairment. Limits on movement and thinking can cut them off from enriching activity, which speeds further decline. Virtual reality could restore some of that engagement if it is designed with users, iteratively.

The talk walks through fresh data on usability snags and on which experiences elders prefer. It asks whether shared virtual spaces support real social contact, how present users feel, and how far attitudes toward the technology can shift. Mood and social connection are the target outcomes.
pmc-10736110:
Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength with age, is easier to prevent than to reverse, yet clinics had no tool to flag who is at risk. Researchers built and checked a prediction model for that risk in 2023, aimed at older adults living in the community.

The model grew out of a prospective cohort of 1,042 older residents without sarcopenia, of whom 87 developed it within a year. Seven factors carried the prediction: age, sex, body mass index, low activity, malnutrition, pain, and calf size. The model sorted high-risk from low-risk people with strong accuracy and stayed stable under internal checks. A cutoff of ten percent risk or more marked the group for follow-up.
pmc-10736310:
Dianne Oladejo, Joyce Chapman, Tonya Roberson, and Rachel O'Conor describe work with Black dementia caregivers in two thousand twenty-three. Their team joined two local groups and a medical center on Chicago's Far South Side. Black families face gaps in diagnosis and health that add to the load of care. Few care programs fit their needs or their culture.

The local groups helped design interview guides and spoke with thirty caregivers. Most cared for a parent or grandparent and shared tasks with kin. They named stress, the need to learn how dementia changes, racism, family duties, and a wish for rest and local help. Their views will shape a new family care program.
pmc-10736610:
Cynthia Hancock and co-authors question a school custom for the hundredth day of class in 2023. Some teachers ask young children to dress as if they were one hundred years old. Photos online show stiff, frail, and confused images of old age. The team argues this teaches bias at a young age.

With early years experts, they built a toolkit for teachers. It gives true facts about people who reach one hundred, plus facts on aging and age bias. Class tasks meet learning goals for the youngest grades. They also support respect for all ages. The team shares early pilot results from the new lessons. Next steps aim to grow aging education for very young learners.
pmc-10736910:
Emily Heilbrunn and co-authors present a 2023 study of mood in nursing home residents across the COVID-19 years. Lockdown rules cut visits and group life to curb spread, with loneliness as the feared side cost. The team mined the national care data set, scoring low mood with a standard nine-item form. Scores were set beside the home's four-week case counts in bands from none to heavy.

Odds of low mood ran higher in every band with cases than in case-free spans. The lift was largest in the lightest band, a third higher, and stayed raised in heavier ones. The pattern hints that fear and disruption, not just illness counts, weighed on minds. Pandemic playbooks should budget for mood care, the data suggest.
pmc-10737010:
Karin Wolf-Ostermann and co-authors ran a German trial to keep people with dementia out of hospital, in a 2023 study. Hospital stays often harm patients with advanced dementia, yet admissions run high. The program mixed movement and thinking training for residents with coaching for caregivers and family doctors. Ninety-seven shared-housing homes took part, with 341 residents tracked over six months and beyond.

Admissions fell clearly during the program, and challenging behaviors eased. Caregivers later reported warmer social interaction in the homes. Quality of life, falls, and cognition were also tracked. The team draws practical recommendations, arguing simple non-drug programs belong in everyday care.
pmc-10737110:
Natalie Pope, Abigail Latimer, Debra Moser, and co-authors share lessons from research with older adults who lack housing in this 2023 paper. Adults in their late fifties and sixties are the fastest growing group among homeless people, and their numbers are expected to triple by 2030. This group carries heavy illness burdens and unmet health needs.

The authors draw on two completed interview studies with unhoused older adults and clinician groups. They describe trouble finding and screening participants, and hard calls about memory problems and mental health seen during the work. They also cover the emotional load on the research team, building ties with local partners, and paying participants fairly. Their advice urges researchers not to skip this hard-to-reach group. Studies shaped around these hurdles can bring the voices of unhoused older adults into services meant for them.
pmc-10737310:
Rafael de Cabo reports in 2023 on how daily fasting and calorie cuts affect health in female mice. Earlier work of this kind used mostly males, leaving a gap. A carousel feeder let the team control how much food mice got, and when.

Mice on calorie restriction responded strongly: cancers progressed less and lung inflammation eased, compared with mice that only ate in a set time window. Blood chemistry after an overnight fast also differed between the two regimes. Late-in-life daytime feeding with long fasts helped most when paired with lower energy intake. The study guides how diet timing studies should be designed.
pmc-10737510:
Kate Crary, Melissa Mandrell, and Laura Davie describe a certification program that trains counselors to put nursing home residents' own choices first. Person-centered care is the stated gold standard for older adults and people with dementia, yet low-resource communities often lack a clear route to it. The program answers with a mentoring model and a competency framework.

Their 2023 paper reports the pilot in rural New Hampshire. Professionals gain set knowledge, skills, and abilities through guided mentorship, using ready-made teaching materials instead of costly degrees. Trainees in the pilot rated the training relevant to their own communities. The authors present the framework as a cost-effective way to spread person-centered practice where budgets are thin.
pmc-10737710:
Austin Oswald and Karen Fredriksen-Goldsen study thinking health among older sexual and gender minority adults in a 2023 paper.
