Their focus is African American and Hispanic elders, whose combined identities are rarely studied in this field. Data came from a national study of health, sexuality, and gender in later life.

Everyday discrimination and identity stigma tracked with worse cognitive scores in both groups. Outdoor leisure protected African American participants, while social support protected Hispanic participants. Gender split the patterns further: stigma hit African American women's cognition harder, and Hispanic women were more exposed to discrimination effects. Activity and leisure guarded African American men's scores in particular. The authors call for programs shaped to each subgroup rather than one plan for all.
pmc-10737810:
Sofhia Ramos and co-authors link diabetes to fitness and muscle energy in older adults in a 2023 study. Nearly nine hundred participants of a muscle and aging study, averaging in their late seventies, underwent deep phenotyping. About one in seven reported diabetes.

Muscle bulk itself looked similar between groups, but fat inside the belly and inside muscle ran higher with diabetes. Peak oxygen uptake and every measure of mitochondrial energy output ran lower. The differences survived adjustment for body size and other illness. The picture blames energy machinery and fat placement, not muscle amount, for diabetic frailty.
pmc-10737910:
Jingwen Liu wrote this research paper, published in 2023, on how often middle-aged and older Americans take part in religious life. It tracks how attendance changes with age and across birth cohorts, and whether the pattern differs by race and ethnic group.

Liu used survey data from 2004 to 2020, covering more than 130,000 person-years. Attendance followed a reversed U shape over life, and newer cohorts attended less and dropped off faster. Black and Hispanic older adults attended more often than White older adults but declined faster in late life. Among Hispanic immigrants, longer exposure to strict immigration policy went with higher attendance. The paper shows faith habits shift with both age and the times people live through.
pmc-10738010:
Reagan Moffit and co-authors test a walking measure in a 2023 study of older adults. The gold test of heart-lung fitness needs a treadmill lab, which is costly and hard for many seniors. A simple corridor walk of four hundred meters at a normal pace might stand in for it.

Eight hundred twenty adults, average age near seventy-six, took both tests in a large aging study. Walk time and peak oxygen use were moderately linked, with slower walks matching lower fitness. A model adding age, sex, body mass, effort rating, and weekly activity sharpened the fit. Each extra half minute on the walk matched a clear drop in fitness. The authors offer walk time as a practical fitness gauge for clinics.
pmc-10738110:
Rodlescia Sneed asks who would gain coverage if the United States lowered the age for Medicare eligibility in a 2023 study. She used data from the 2018 Health and Retirement Study. Her estimates cover how many people would become insured at cutoffs of 60, 55, and 51. She also compared the health profiles of the uninsured with insured peers.

Lowering the age to 60 would newly insure about 1.43 million Americans. Cuts to 55 or 51 would cover 3.45 million and 4.59 million. Among those aged 51 to 64, the uninsured reported less screening for high cholesterol and some cancers, plus lower flu and shingles vaccination. Over a third had no usual place of care. Those with high blood pressure were less often on medication for it.
pmc-10738210:
Soonhyung Kwon, Ellen Benoit, and Liliane Windsor test how support from others and faith in self shape hope in low income older adults, in a study from 2023. The data come from the start line of a trial that sought to lift virus test rates in one New Jersey county in the pandemic years. All in the set were aged fifty or more and lived on low means at the edge of care.

Each kind of support, from facts to hugs to shared time, tied to more hope once other marks were weighed. Faith in self tied to hope most strongly of all. Faith in self also sat on the path from support to hope, and bore part of that lift on its own. The authors call for work that builds both nets of kin and self trust in this group.
pmc-10738310:
Margaret Danilovich, Andy Rapoport, and Meredith Nicholson describe SHARE, a national advisory board that turns long term HIV survivors into research champions. Published in 2023, the paper starts from a shift: HIV is now a chronic condition, and survivors face aging with the virus. Their voices, the team argues, belong inside the research that shapes their care.

Board members trained in research methods, then ran a community needs assessment to set priorities on HIV and aging. Each member then carried findings home through talks, webinars, infographics, podcasts, and photo projects. The speakers present the model as a route to person centered care, where dissemination is done by the community, not just to it.
pmc-10738410:
Chung Lin Kew and co-authors examine what drives burden in partners caring for someone with dementia, in a 2023 study. Baseline surveys from a state-funded program captured problem-solving style, care circumstances, mood, and burden among care partners, most of them women around sixty living with the person they supported.

High burden came with more resentment of the role, more anger at the care recipient, and more depressive symptoms, alongside less felt social support. Surprisingly, a positive problem-solving outlook and even positive aspects of caregiving also tracked with higher burden, while family conflict ran lower. The authors argue that help must address carers' inner conflict and the relationship itself, not just skills and services.
pmc-10738510:
Breder and three co-authors ask how old queer folks used tech for friend webs in the plague years in this twenty twenty-three study. Such folks oft live lone and lean on peers for care. Far rules in the plague cut those webs at their most frail hour.

Inside, deep talks with a mixed crew of old folks feed the checks. Three themes rose: a want for true touch, web bound rules, and age gaps. Touch lack topped the list, with screens a poor fill for hugs. Web bounds took care as folks set who could reach them there. Age-gap tech skills barred some from care calls and meets.
pmc-10738610:
Li-Mei Chen examines older volunteer organizations in Japan in a 2023 study, twenty-five years after the country's nonprofit law passed. The law sparked rapid growth, and by 2022 Japan counted huge numbers of volunteer groups and millions of volunteers. Many groups that give community social services lean heavily on older members, yet how they have fared as organizations was little known.

Chen surveyed five hundred such groups and grouped them by strength across areas such as leadership, funds, and staffing. Types ranged from achievers, strong on all fronts, to challenged groups, weak on all. Some leaned on government programs, some prized flexible roles, and some were tight circles no longer seeking members. Strong groups gained volunteers and rarely lacked them, while weak groups showed the reverse pattern.
pmc-10738710:
Eight authors, led by Daniella Chusyd, compared stress biology in orphaned elephants and wild controls in this 2023 study. Poaching leaves young elephants motherless, and wild herds thus form a natural test of what early loss does to a body over time.

In 2021, the team collected dung samples from rescued orphans and from similar-aged wild elephants, in both the early and late dry seasons. The samples revealed levels of a stress hormone byproduct and of a thyroid hormone, T3. Body condition was scored at the same visit. Ages were known closely for orphans and estimated for wild calves by dung size. Statistical models adjusted for age and season. Orphans showed higher thyroid hormone levels than controls, a hint that early hardship tunes the body's energy system for years.
pmc-10738810:
Sheena Pubien and co-authors used, in a 2023 project, human-centered design to fight loneliness among older tenants of subsidized housing. Social isolation harms body and mind, and communal living does not by itself cure it. The team worked inside two Baltimore housing communities for five months.

Over 50 residents, service coordinators, and managers joined listening and brainstorm sessions. Their talk surfaced six themes: feeling excluded, weak community ties, hard moves into shared living, shifting building rules, and worries about the physical space. From those themes the group built responses, from welcome materials for new tenants to cultural inclusion events and better engagement routines. The approach treats residents as designers of their own social world. It offers a template other housing providers could copy.
pmc-10738910:
Eunju Lee and Kyungmin Kim studied married couples in Korea in a research paper from twenty twenty-three. Their subject is whether husbands and wives agree on moving home after they retire. The authors note that where a couple lives can shape health and well-being in later life.

Most couples in the large sample agreed with each other, either both wanting to move or both wanting to stay. Couples were more likely to agree when they solved problems together as a team. Agreement was also more common when the wife felt happier in the marriage. Talking about life after retirement also helped couples agree to move.
pmc-10739010:
Michelle Paulsen and three co-authors test whether a drug burden score helps cut risky medicines in older veterans in a 2023 paper. Many medicines raise fall risk by sedating patients or scrambling balance. A burden index totals a patient's exposure to those drug classes.

A pharmacist reviewed fall-risk medicines for veterans in a prevention program, in two rounds. In the second round, the burden score was shared with each patient's main prescriber. Three months later the team counted medication changes and score drops. Nearly every participant, ninety-five percent of forty-four, took at least one risky drug. The comparison asks whether one extra number in the chart moves prescribers to act. Safer prescribing for fall-prone elders is the practical prize.
pmc-10740210:
Yangyang Wu and co-authors present a 2023 study on how two cycad species cope with sudden freezing. Cycads are old plant lineages, and late spring or fall freezes may grow more common as climate shifts. One species is known to bear cold better than the other. The team asked whether energy use and stored food explain that gap.

Both species were put through sudden freeze treatment in the lab. Light use, energy charge, stored sugars, and fats were all tracked. The hardier species kept its light machinery more stable. It also shifted sugars and fats in a distinct pattern over time. The weaker species broke down key membrane fats. The authors link the contrast in cold tolerance to these energy patterns.
pmc-10740410:
Yaowalak Panyasing and co-authors tested a new blood and saliva assay in 2023 that can tell vaccinated pigs from infected ones in classical swine fever control. Telling the two apart matters because marker vaccines let herds stay protected while watch teams hunt real infection. The team checked the test on hundreds of known samples.

Panels covered clean pigs, pigs infected with a wild strain, and pigs given two kinds of vaccine, on farms and in the lab. At the chosen cutoff, the test caught about ninety-seven percent of true cases in blood and ninety-five percent in saliva. It raised no false alarms in either fluid. Pen-level saliva sampling also worked. The authors offer the assay as a fast, easy partner for marker vaccine programs.
pmc-10740510:
Serena Dattola and co-authors map brain activity during mental arithmetic in a 2023 paper. Most prior work used fMRI scans, but this team used EEG signals instead. They rebuilt source activity with a method called eLORETA.

Thirty-five healthy young adults performed a serial subtraction task. The team split them into good and bad counters by score and compared brain activity. A clear difference appeared only in the beta band. The left limbic lobe was more active in the better counters. That region links to memory, fact retrieval, and emotion. The authors offer the finding as a start for deeper study.
pmc-10740810:
Tefal and co-authors feed young seabass on organic protein swaps in a 2023 study. Organic fish farms need feeds that meet organic rules without losing growth. Nearly five hundred young fish ate six diets over 125 days. Protein came from standard fishmeal or from pig byproduct, trout byproduct, insect meal, and blends of them.

Standard fishmeal gave the top growth, with trout blends close behind. Pig and trout mixes digested protein best, while insect blends lagged. Fish on insect diets grew less and digested worse across the board. Liver cells were largest on the standard diet. The authors say trout and pig byproducts can carry organic feeds, but insect meal needs care.
pmc-10740910:
Earth's magnetic field never sits still: storms from the sun shake it, and human technology hums inside it, all at extremely low frequencies that wash over every living thing. Ruslan Sarimov, Dmitry Serov, and Sergey Gudkov review the biological effects of those fields in 2023. Decades of data exist, they note, but no unified picture of how the effects work.

The review takes a fresh quantitative pass over the literature, summarizing effects from molecules to whole organisms for both natural storms and man-made fields. It also walks through the leading theories of mechanism. The authors aim the survey at biologists, physicists, and physicians who need common ground on a contested topic.
pmc-10741110:
Crescenzi and co-authors profile in 2023 the chemical contents of extracts from a plant used in teas and supplements, and test their antioxidant power. Two green extraction methods, alcohol based and a boiled water method, were applied to the fruit and its outer husk. A high resolution instrument chain named fifty eight compounds across the samples.

The extracts proved rich in plant compounds such as flavonoids and carotenoids. Cell tests showed the extracts cut free radical production in gut cells. An combined approach pairing full chemical profiling with cell assays was applied to this plant for the first time. The authors argue the plant is a good source of helpful compounds, with the boiled extract closest to home tea practice.
pmc-10741210:
Tanja Maisenbacher and four co-authors reviewed mouse models used to study how diabetes slows bone healing, in a 2023 narrative review. Diabetes raises the risk that a broken bone heals poorly, and type 2 diabetes keeps spreading worldwide. Labs use diabetic mice to probe why healing fails, but the models differ a lot.

The review sorts the models into three families: drug-induced, diet-induced, and gene-based. Each family has its own strengths and limits, and each shapes bone and healing in its own way. Because studies pick such different models, their results are hard to compare. The authors find few models that mimic how adult type 2 diabetes builds over years. They suggest a high-fat diet, with 60 percent of calories from fat for at least 12 weeks, as the closest match.
pmc-10741510:
Małgorzata Knapp and colleagues reviewed in 2023 what myostatin, a protein best known for limiting muscle growth, does to the heart. Myostatin is secreted mainly by skeletal muscle, with smaller amounts from heart muscle and fat. It switches on signaling pathways that restrain growth. Animal studies show the heart shrinks when myostatin is overproduced and enlarges when the protein is removed.

The review gathers evidence on myostatin's diagnostic and prognostic value across heart conditions. It discusses how myostatin-null mice develop larger ventricular chambers and volumes, and how the heart may release myostatin as a brake on its own growth signals. For clinicians, a circulating factor linking skeletal muscle and heart size could become a blood marker of disease or a drug target. The authors weigh that promise against what is still unknown.
pmc-10742210:
Ioanna Akrida and co-authors review a glowing dye for breast surgery in a 2023 paper. Finding the first lymph node a tumor drains to guides breast cancer care. The standard pairing of radioactive tracer and blue dye works well but brings allergy risk and radiation logistics. Indocyanine green, a water soluble dye that glows under near infrared light, offers a third way.

Trials have lately extended node biopsy to more patient groups, raising the value of simpler tracers. The review sums the dye's accuracy and safety record against the standard pair. A tracer that drops the radiation suite could spread good staging to smaller hospitals. The update helps surgeons weigh a switch with current evidence in hand.
pmc-10742410:
Wenqiu Lin and co-authors traced how a spray forces pineapple plants to flower in a 2023 study. Growers spray ethephon, which sheds ethylene gas, to make a whole field bloom at once for a timed harvest. The gene and chemistry shifts that the gas sets off inside the plant tip were not well mapped.

The team read both the gene activity and the small-molecule mix in shoot tips across the days after spraying. Samples ran from day zero to the first bud parts. Joined maps show which genes wake and which pathways shift as the tip turns to bloom. The map may help breeders time or boost flowering.
pmc-10742510:
Katherine Quispe-Medina and co-authors map lung microbes in critically ill patients in southern Peru in two thousand twenty-three. Gene reads of the 16S marker can chart whole microbe communities. Whether the lung mix marks who will recover was the pilot question.

Patients on breathing machines for non-lung reasons gave airway samples, read by next-generation sequencing. Three phyla led the mix: Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Bacteroidata, with the order shifting between those who lived and those who died. Friendly resident microbes fell in the group that died, while hospital germs rose over time. The team frames the profile as a candidate early marker, pending larger studies to confirm it.
pmc-10742710:
A team of co-authors presents a trial from two thousand twenty-three on diet and premenstrual syndrome in Omani teenagers. The syndrome affects mood and well-being in women worldwide, and evidence on diet's role conflicts. The trial tested a healthy diet plus motivational support.

Two schools in the Muscat region took part. Students in grades ten and eleven with regular cycles and PMS symptoms were split between groups. The diet group got a personal face-to-face consultation and follow-up motivational phone calls. The study tracked symptom severity and quality of life, asking whether eating advice can ease the monthly burden.
pmc-10742810:
Bailing Chen, Huilin Lai, Chuandong Lin, and Demei Li model how a tilted boundary between two fluids changes a classic mixing instability, in a twenty twenty-three paper. The Rayleigh-Taylor instability grows when a heavy fluid sits over a light one. Most studies start with a flat boundary. This team started with an inclined one and used a particle-based flow method that tracks effects beyond normal fluid theory.

They found several measures of imbalance first rose and then fell as mixing grew. A steeper starting tilt made the density gradient, the out-of-balance strength, and the affected region all larger. Three rival effects explain the pattern: the growing wavy boundary spreads contact, waves fade with time, and the fluids blend. The work aids designs where tilted fluid layers mix.
pmc-10743310:
Pingliang red cattle, a prized Chinese breed known for tender, well-marbled beef, get their first full genome reading from Wang and a large team. They compare SNP chip data across seventeen breeds to place the breed's origins and trace the genes that flowed into it. The breed stands apart with its own genetic signature, a hybrid of the two great cattle lineages.

Its ancestry mixes roughly half East Asian taurine with a fifth Chinese indicine, plus smaller Eurasian and European shares. Its closest Chinese relative is Qinchuan cattle, and European South Devon and Red Angus blood also entered the line. The authors say the map supports smarter breeding of the resource.
pmc-10743510:
Beata Krzykowska and seven co-authors tried to improve a plant based plastic in a 2023 study. The plastic, called P3HB, breaks down in nature, which makes it prized. On its own, though, its traits fall short of common plastics, so the team blended it with other parts to lift its strength and heat range.

They mixed in a soft polyurethane at four dose levels. Heat traits got better at each dose, and strength rose too. A five percent mix gave the best gain in impact traits, so they added a treated clay at low doses on top of it. The smallest clay dose, one percent, gave the best mix of strength and heat traits in the whole set of blends.
pmc-10744910:
Simone König and co-authors ask whether oxidized parts in insect hormones are natural marks or lab artifacts in 2023, using team framing since the head byline is shorter than the catalog list. These hormones steer key body tasks in insects. They are short peptides with a set tryptophan spot. Changes to that spot or to a proline spot have been reported.

Extracts from many insect species were read with a high grade mass method. Fresh glands were taken with care against oxidation. The proline change showed in fresh samples and could be released on demand. Made copies of it worked in a live assay. The tryptophan change, by contrast, fits easy oxidation in handling. The authors split the two cases.
pmc-10745010:
A class of cancer drugs saves lives but strains the heart, and the standard guards all lower blood pressure, which frail patients bear poorly. Čiburienė and co-authors test a different guard in 2023: a drug that slows the heart alone. Their trial takes women, mostly with breast cancer, whose resting pulse ran high before treatment.

The women were split by lot to get the drug or not, in an open trial. Heart scans and strain reads track harm as the cancer drugs run their course. A fast pulse, past work shows, flags higher death risk in cancer on its own. A guard that spares pressure while it calms the pulse could widen who can be shielded. The trial is among the first to test that bet head-on.
pmc-10745610:
Wahid Rizaldi Akili, Ari Hardianto, Jalifah Latip, Afri Permana, and Tati Herlina screen plant compounds by computer for use against germs, in work from 2023. The compounds are flavonoids from coral trees, long known to fight germs in the lab. The target is a bacterial enzyme that twists DNA, a proven weak point.

Of 378 compounds screened, forty-nine bound the target better than known blockers and the natural fuel. Toxicity screens narrowed the set to six with low predicted harm. One compound stood out for how the body is predicted to handle it. The authors offer it as a lead for new drugs against resistant infections, pending lab tests.
pmc-10745910:
Rachelle Mendoza and co-authors study a vessel signaling path in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, in a 2023 paper. The virus harms the vessel system as well as the lungs. Two related proteins guard vessel walls: one steadies them, and the other rises during swelling and new vessel growth. A known immune signal can trigger the second protein's path.

The team measured both proteins, the immune signal, and virus antibodies in patient blood. Samples spanned mild to severe disease, with healthy controls for contrast. The second protein was high in patients at every severity level. The first protein fell. The pattern fits the vessel injury seen in serious COVID-19 and may mark patients at risk of worse disease.
pmc-10747210:
Milica Djapovic and co-authors make tiny plastic particles in the lab and check what leftover soap in them does to human cells. Their 2023 study uses PET, the plastic of drink bottles, shrunk to bits about 300 units wide. Such clean test particles are hard to make, since plastics repel water and cling to aids used in their making.

A magnetic resonance method let the team measure how much of the soap stayed in each batch. Across a wide range of soap shares, the particles' surface charge shifted only a bit. In rich lab media, human blood cells showed no clear harm up to a set dose. In plain buffers, though, the leftover soap did sway the tests, even bursting red blood cells.
pmc-10747510:
Gum disease can destroy the bone and tissue that hold teeth, and full regrowth of that support is still hard. Luana Epicoco and co-authors review a promising material for the job in this 2023 paper. The material is a membrane made of ultra-fine spun fibers, called an electrospun membrane. Such membranes can be loaded with helpful substances and placed where tissue must regrow.

The tissue in question has four parts: jaw bone, a root coating, the gum itself, and a linking ligament. Each part heals at its own pace, which makes full repair tricky. Guided repair methods use a membrane to hold space and steer growth. The review covers recent versions of these fiber membranes and what has been added to them. The goal is a repair that restores both form and function.
pmc-10747710:
Current hepatitis B drugs hold the virus down but rarely clear it, so cure research turns to gene tools. Nadiia Kasianchuk and co-authors review two families of such tools. Gene editors, from zinc fingers to CRISPR, aim to cut the virus's stored DNA. RNA interference drugs instead silence the virus's messages. The review weighs the promise and the problems of each route, including safety and delivery.

RNA-based candidates have already reached human trials, though bigger and longer studies are needed. CRISPR cures remain pre-clinical, with high hopes and open safety questions. The elimination goal for twenty thirty will not be met on current tools alone, the authors warn. Vaccination stays the strongest lever while cures mature.
pmc-10747910:
Marta Guadalupi and co-authors used a pressure-sensing walkway to judge lameness in dogs after knee surgery, in a 2023 study. Twenty dogs had torn the main stabilizing ligament in one knee and received an operation that shifts the shin bone's top with a porous implant. The dogs walked across the walkway before surgery and at one, three, and four months after.

The walkway gives each limb a lameness score and a pressure share. The treated limb lagged the healthy one at every check, so full recovery was not complete even at four months. Even so, scores for the treated limb improved clearly by three months and held at four. The authors say the walkway gives vets an objective way to follow healing, beyond what the eye can judge.
pmc-10748010:
Yang and co-authors test computer models that predict how pregnancy and cancer together change the handling of cancer drugs, in a study from 2023. Treating cancer in pregnancy is hard because pregnant patients are rarely in drug trials, so dose and safety data are thin. Body-based models can fill part of that gap.

The team checked a pregnancy population model against real data for two drugs, paclitaxel and docetaxel, in pregnant patients with cancer. The model fit docetaxel well, while paclitaxel needed a boost to one liver enzyme that rises in pregnancy. Changes in blood protein binding in cancer had little effect. The model then forecast much lower exposure to a third drug, acalabrutinib, in pregnancy. The authors urge wider checks with more drugs.
pmc-10748210:
Florence Mukamanzi and co-authors proposed this 2023 method for hiding where a sensor sits in a wireless network. In such networks, an attacker who tracks message flow can find the source sensor, which may guard something precious. Random-walk routing confuses trackers, but often at the cost of draining batteries faster. The new scheme aims to raise privacy and battery life together.

Packets first wander backward at random, then loop around rings, then take short hops to the base station. The mix spreads paths widely and evenly. The team also studied, for the first time in this setting, how radio range itself affects both privacy and lifetime. Models and simulations showed gains in the safe period before discovery and in how long the network lasts.
pmc-10748410:
Qian Zhao and co-authors compare the chemistry and strength of a Chinese medicinal plant by plant part, in work from 2023. Roots of Duhaldea nervosa are the prized drug part, while stems, leaves, and flowers are mostly discarded. That waste ignores a large share of the plant's bulk.

Two mass spectrometry tools profiled each part, finding 45 volatile and 174 heavier compounds. Certain acid compounds clustered in roots and flowers, while others favored stems and leaves. Dozens of compounds differed sharply between parts. Antioxidant strength ranked flowers first, then roots, then leaves or stems. A compound network tied key chemicals to the observed effects. The work supports fuller use of the plant.
pmc-10749410:
Mohammadi, Hadian, and Olyaei test whether Wii game training improves brain-based skills in athletes with unstable ankles. Ankle sprains lead to lasting instability in about 80% of cases. Standard rehab often skips the thinking and reaction problems that come with the injury. The trial enrolled 25 athletes with instability in one ankle and 25 without. Athletes were split at random into training and no-training groups.

The training group played balance and strength games three times a week for 12 sessions. A computer test measured reaction time before and after the program. The study asks whether game-based rehab can restore mental sharpness along with ankle control. Results bear on how sports rehab should be designed.
pmc-10750410:
Izuhara and co-authors test whether how long people sleep affects antibody gains after COVID-19 mRNA shots. Sleep is known to boost vaccine responses, but data for mRNA vaccines were thin. The study followed 48 healthy adults who got one of two mRNA vaccines in 2021 and 2022. Sleep was tracked with wrist devices and written diaries. Tracking covered the first shot and the booster periods.

After accounting for other factors, longer measured sleep after the booster linked to stronger antibody levels. The link showed at both three and seven days after the booster. Self-reported sleep showed a weaker pattern than device data. The findings suggest sleep in the days after a booster matters for immunity.
pmc-10751610:
Sagila Gangadharan and Swapna Raveendranath report three cases of a fungal infection seen in cancer patients at a large centre in South India. Their 2023 paper deals with cryptococcosis, a rare infection that can show in many guises. All three patients were men with weakened immune systems. Some had solid tumors and some had blood cancers, and all took drugs that suppress immune work, such as steroids or chemo.

Each patient had the fungus in the blood and in the lining of the brain. Proof came from lab tests of the infection. Outcomes were poor in this small group. The authors stress that late spotting drives high death rates, and that early antifungal care gives the best hope.
pmc-10752610:
Jing Zhang, Dehuan Liu, Linwei Ding, and Guankui Du report a 2023 survey of depression among teens in Hainan, China. Depression can stall a teen's growth and make adult life harder to meet. The team used a standard nine-item form plus a social survey across six schools.

More than eight thousand teens aged thirteen to eighteen took part. A sorting method split them into three groups: no, low, and high depression. About a tenth fell in the high group, and near half in the low group. The youngest junior students joined the high group far more often than seniors did.
pmc-10753710:
Xingxing Li and co-authors tested twice-daily mild electric brain stimulation in patients with Alzheimer's disease, in a 2023 trial. The current was aimed at a front brain area tied to planning and memory. One hundred twenty-four patients were split at random between real and sham treatment. Sessions ran twice a day, five days a week, for six weeks. Thinking was scored at the start, at two weeks, and at six weeks.

Real treatment improved thinking scores, with the clearest gains in memory tasks such as word recall and word recognition. A measure of how readily the motor cortex fires, blunted in these patients, rose after real treatment. The size of that rise tracked with the size of the thinking gain. The authors say the work is the first to show gains from a twice-daily schedule. They link weak thinking in the disease to weak brain plasticity.
pmc-10753810:
Rakshyakar Giri leads a team on charge states of diamond NV centers. Their study from twenty twenty-three deals with shallow nitrogen vacancy centers. Spin based uses need an efficient spin readout.

One route maps spin onto charge states for reading. Stable charge allows long measures with less noise. Sensing needs centers just nanometers below the surface. Surface effects there can harm charge stability. Four shallow centers passed the conversion protocol tests. Readout noise fell well below fluorescence based reads. Initialization of charge states was also shown.  Charge starts were shown on the same centers.
pmc-10753910: The editors of Open Forum Infectious Diseases thank the peer reviewers who read and judged papers for the journal. The thanks cover one year of work, from the start of November 2022 to the end of October 2023. The notice names each reviewer in one long list. It notes that the quality of the journal rests in large part on their skill and unpaid time.
pmc-10754510:
ChaoFeng Zhang and co-authors analyze in 2023 the role of a protein called CISD2 in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, the most common B-cell lymphoma in adults. The protein helps cell growth, and abnormal levels appear in several cancers. Its role in this lymphoma was unclear before this study.

Using public data and lab tests, they found CISD2 raised in patients and cell lines. High levels tied to poor prognosis. They built a risk signature from one hundred related genes and a prediction chart for survival. The signature also linked to immune cell patterns in tumors and drug sensitivity.
pmc-10756910:
Qiu and five co-authors set two reed kin side by side in mixed soils in this twenty twenty-three study. The two reeds grow side by side in salt meadow and in sand on one plain. Mixed ground can push kin apart in form and gene code as time runs on.

Inside, gene proof backs the pair as two true split species, not one loose kind. One reed reads as a broad guest that shifts form a lot from soil to soil. The other reads as a soil-bound type with tighter form shifts across ground types. Small gaps in shape, code, and soil use add up to let both reeds thrive in harsh ground.
pmc-10762310:
Yang leads a team reporting a rare liver tumor case and its imaging fingerprints in a 2023 paper. Perivascular epithelioid cell tumors are uncommon and often mistaken for liver cancer. The patient was a man in his early sixties whose lesion turned up by chance.

Scans showed solid tissue mixed with fat inside the tumor. The solid part took up a tracer strongly on PET imaging. Magnetic resonance signals confirmed the fatty component. Contrast scans showed a fast-in, fast-out pattern typical of richer blood flow. The authors argue these combined features can separate this tumor from true liver cancer. Careful multimodal imaging is their message. Misdiagnosis can lead to wrong treatment.
pmc-10763510:
Liam Shaw and Richard Neher build a way to draw and measure the neighborhoods of genes that jump between bacteria, in a 2023 paper. Mobile resistance genes ride elements like integrons and transposons into new genomes, and the DNA flanking them records that travel history. Reading those flanks had been a manual, expert craft. Their method uses a pangenome graph tool to find matching blocks around a gene and turn the variety into pictures and numbers.

Applied to twelve important beta-lactamase genes, the approach showed that faster-changing genes sit in more varied neighborhoods, with extra variety upstream. Interactive charts are published online. The framework aims at general rules for how new genes spread.
pmc-10768410:
Marija Kocic and eight co-authors review the causes of upper gut bleeding in children by age. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. The cause shifts a lot from newborn to teen, though some causes span all ages. Where a child lives also shapes the most likely cause.

Some causes bind to one age band, such as vitamin lack in newborns or milk protein allergy in infants. Others, such as a sore food pipe or stomach lining, can show at any age. The worst bleeds come from swollen veins, ulcers, or a blood clotting crash. Care starts with a fast check of how grave the bleed is, then a scope. Surgery is held for the worst cases.
pmc-10768510:
Ivan Budimir and co-authors present a 2023 case report of a rare stomach wall blood pocket with no clear cause. Such pockets form when blood pools inside the stomach wall. Clotting ills lead the known causes, with gland disease, artery bulges, and scope injuries behind them. No set care path exists.

The patient was a 22 year old man with two weeks of left flank pain. He had no injury, blood thinner use, or past scope work. His blood counts sat a touch low. Scans and a scope exam confirmed the pocket. With no active bleed or shock signs, the team chose watchful care over surgery. He responded well on that plan. The case adds a data point for a hard to spot cause of acute belly pain.
pmc-10773810:
Zhaoliang Geng and five co-authors measure the aroma precursor chemistry of cigars across tobacco parts and origins, in a two thousand twenty-three food chemistry paper. Which leaf and which terroir produce which flavors had not been systematically mapped.

Sixty-nine precursors were quantified in sixty-one tobaccos. Plant part mainly shifted amino acid content, while origin influenced amino acids, organic acids, fatty acids, and sugar alcohols. Middle leaves from different origins varied widely in style and quality, with woody aroma prominent. Dozens of precursors correlated strongly with flavor, style, and quality scores. The authors offer the map for steering blending and cultivation toward desired sensory profiles.
pmc-10786210:
Sandeep Karna and Ki-Woon Kang review why fat around the heart grows too large in heart failure, in a twenty twenty-three article. This fat hugs the heart and acts like a hormone-making tissue, not a passive store. Too much of it is tied to heart disease and to worse heart failure. The authors set out to sum up each path that links the fat to the failing heart.

Their review covers fat-made hormones in excess, swelling signals, stem cell growth, cell stress from oxygen damage, and sugar harm. It also covers faults in the nerves that tune the heart. The fat serves as an energy store and talks closely with heart muscle. The authors argue this two-way talk helps drive the disease.
pmc-10786710:
Tadaharu Shiozumi and co-authors report a case from 2023 of a muscle weakness disease that first appeared as breathing trouble. The disease is an immune attack on the link between nerves and muscles. A rare form of it is marked by antibodies against a protein that helps that link work. This form often brings less typical signs than the common form and can weaken the breathing muscles to failure.

Their patient was an eighty-four-year-old woman who came to emergency care after three days of worsening breathlessness. Her breathing was shallow and strained, and tests showed a failure to clear waste gas. No nerve or muscle signs stood out on exam. A blood test found the marker antibodies, which confirmed the rare form. The authors urge doctors to weigh this disease in older patients with unexplained breathing failure, even when classic signs are absent.
pmc-10790410:
Rare diseases that inflame many organs at once are hard to study one clinic at a time. A 2023 paper by Cynthia Stapornwongkul and co-authors describes a German registry built for that task. The GAIN registry gathers data on people born with multi-organ autoimmune diseases.

The registry belongs to a national network that links care and research for this patient group. Its data set maps each person's complex clinical state in depth, and it ties records to stored biosamples. Data from 486 people had been documented at the time of writing. Planned additions include patients reporting their own quality of life. The authors present the registry as a base for better studies and better therapy choices.
pmc-10792710:
Henish Shakya and co-authors studied screen habits in young children at a large hospital, in work published in 2023. They asked caregivers of children aged two to five about how much time the children spent with screens each day. Heavy screen use in these early years can harm thinking skills, social growth, and health.

Among 310 children, about seven in ten had high scores for problem screen use. Many first saw a screen before their first birthday, and most watched shows not made for their age. More than six in ten spent over two hours a day on screens. The authors urge parents and caregivers to set firm limits early.
pmc-10809810:
Sayan, Kankoc, Valiyev, and Celik present cases in twenty twenty-four showing varied uses of a thermal camera in chest surgery. The camera maps temperature as colour in real time, with no contact, no radiation, and easy repeat use. Medicine has applied it to wounds, diabetic feet, and heart surgery checks, but chest uses were less documented.

In one case, the camera marked the boundary between blood-fed and starved lung tissue during cancer surgery, guiding where to cut. Measured temperatures confirmed the visual gap. In another, it checked whether palm temperature rose after a nerve-cut operation for sweaty palms, a sign the procedure worked. The authors argue the tool is safe and handy across chest procedures.
pmc-10811210:
Maria Tsagiopoulou and Ivo Gut wrote this review, whose text is dated 2023, on machine learning for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The blood cancer varies widely from person to person. New tools read many layers of cell data at once, from genes to proteins, a stack called multi-omics. The pair ask how learning models can turn that stack into care fitted to each patient.

They survey models trained on single data layers first, noting where each helps diagnosis or forecasting. They then turn to the newer work that fuses layers, and weigh its promise against its flaws: small cohorts, messy data, and hard-to-read models. The authors see real hope for precision care, if the field solves data sharing and proof in clinics. The review maps a young field for doctors and data scientists alike.
pmc-10825010:
Shun-Yao Liao and Yuan-De Tan present a new statistical method in a paper whose text dates to 2023. Their topic is haplotypes, the sets of gene variants a person inherits together on one chromosome. Studies often link haplotypes to complex diseases, but mixing between chromosome copies can distort the results.

The method pairs each haplotype with its sister copy, a matching form built by restating the gene data. It then checks whether the pairing pattern differs between patients and healthy controls. Applied to past data, the method confirmed a link between one gene region and Alzheimer disease. It also showed that some reported links to breast cancer and heart disease may have been artifacts. The authors argue their check should come before strong claims are made.
pmc-10854010:
Hannah Varkey and co-authors map research on screening baby movement in a study published in 2023. Disorders of brain development are often found only after age four, which delays help. Watching how infants move on their own can flag risk far earlier. A classic method, General Movement Assessment, scores those movements by eye. Digital tools that track movement with sensors have grown fast over two decades.

The team mapped close to three hundred papers with bibliometric software, charting keywords, co-authors, and citations. Observation still rules the field's standard method. A few classic groups have added digital tools, but few teams have gone fully digital. Sensor use stayed rare in the maps. The authors propose blending trained observation with digital tracking. That mix, they argue, could yield earlier diagnoses and earlier therapy for infants at risk.
pmc-10871110:
Arianna Yglesias-Rivera and co-authors measured how a Cuban scorpion's venom retunes immune signals in tumor cells, in a 2023 study. The venom of Heteroctenus junceus slows tumors, and cytokines may carry the effect. Mouse tumor cells bathed in venom doses, and mice bearing the tumors fed venom for twenty-four days, supplied the test beds. Assays tracked a panel of inflammation messengers in fluid, blood, and tumor tissue.

Venom lowered three messengers that feed tumor growth while raising two that fight it, shifting with dose and time. Tumors in treated mice grew slower, and their tissue showed less of one growth messenger. The venom acts partly as an immune conductor, not just a poison.
pmc-10901110:
Xianqiang Yu and co-authors reviewed virus-caused pancreas disease in two thousand twenty-three. The pancreas helps digest food and control blood sugar. Its sudden swelling is more often blamed on gallstones or alcohol. Viruses are a rare cause that doctors can easily miss. Missing it can lead to severe harm for the patient.

The review sums up what is known about how viruses injure the gland. Viruses enter pancreas cells and trigger swelling and immune attack. The gland's own juices can then start to digest its tissue. Most past reports describe single patients rather than large studies. The authors urge doctors to keep viruses in mind when causes are unclear. They also map open questions for future research.
pmc-10909110:
Nasrulla Shanazarov and four co-authors hunt for inherited markers of breast cancer risk in Kazakh women. The team first mined databases for gene variants already tied to breast cancer. They then typed those variants in women with confirmed breast tumors and in healthy women for comparison. Nine variants showed frequencies that differed clearly between the two groups.

Those nine tracked with higher risk in this population and could serve as warning signs during screening of women with loaded family histories. A second set of variants appeared in over forty percent of the cancer patients. The authors suggest those could flag raised risk even without a family history. They recommend folding the markers into national early-screening programs, to catch tumors sooner and group high-risk patients for closer watch.
pmc-10918310:
Sanat Gupta, Kaushik Nayak, and Saikiran Pendem test how CT slice thickness affects lung tumour measures in a 2023 study. Radiomics extracts numbers from scans that may reflect tumour biology. If the slice thickness changes those numbers, studies cannot be compared, and this effect in lung tumours was little studied.

Scans of thirty-two patients were rebuilt at two thicknesses, five and two millimetres. Of one hundred seven features, about sixty-two percent changed significantly between the two. Only twenty-nine features reproduced well across thicknesses. Shape features held up best, while one texture family barely reproduced at all. The authors urge care in fixing scan settings for radiomic work.
pmc-10994610:
Mukhripah Damaiyanti and co-authors review how ready family caregivers are when stroke patients go home, in a 2023 paper. Most stroke survivors return home after hospital and rehab care, and kin then handle daily tasks and treatment routines. The team searched four databases and kept fourteen studies on caregiver readiness for that handover.

Four needs stood out across the studies. Caregivers' own needs should be assessed and named. They need clear, fit information during the move home. They should be part of care planning up to discharge, not handed a fait accompli at the door. And support should continue after the patient is home. The authors argue that planned steps to build readiness are key to safe home care after stroke.
pmc-11081110:
Megan Kennedy wrote this editor's message for the December 2023 issue of a Canadian journal for health sciences librarians. She had just taken over as editor. The message appears in both English and French, matching the journal's two working languages.

Kennedy thanks the outgoing editor for getting the journal indexed in a major citation database, which will bring it an impact factor starting in 2024. She also thanks the departing production editor and welcomes new staff. She describes the board's planned work on fair and inclusive peer review. The message closes by previewing the issue, which covers Wikipedia in health teaching, two book reviews, and a product review.
pmc-11146010:
Horste and co-authors show that where a message RNA is translated inside the cell steers how much protein it makes, in a 2023 paper. The team sorted particles from two neighborhoods, TIS granules and the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and compared their RNAs with the free pool. Among genes for non-membrane proteins, fifty-two percent parked their messages in a preferred spot.

Parking followed a code of message length, exon length, and bound proteins. Granule messages made scarce proteins such as transcription factors, while reticulum messages made large, abundant ones. Moving a message to the reticulum raised its protein output, proving location itself is a control knob. The map gives cell biologists a new layer to add to gene control.
pmc-11502110:
Jose Luis Pura and co-authors proposed in 2023 a light trap built from graphene disks, whose trapping quality can be tuned live with voltage. Bound states in the continuum are resonances that, in theory, never leak, storing light with endless quality factor. Making such states, and then adjusting them on demand, has been the hard part.

Earlier designs used graphene only as a passive layer under or over the structure. Here pairs of graphene disks are the active atoms themselves, laid in a square array and hosting their own plasmons. Applying different voltages to the two disks of a pair switches the bound state on and steers its quality factor, shown in their analysis. Readers get an active metasurface sketch: a resonance you can dial, drawn in carbon one atom thick.
pmc-11532310:
Walaa El Gazzar and nine co-authors quiz Jordanians on cancer causing substances in the environment in this 2024 study. Knowing which everyday exposures can cause cancer is a first step toward preventing it.

Their survey collected 579 answers from adults. Just over half scored in the good knowledge range overall. Awareness ran thin, though, for wood dust, nitrosamines, aflatoxins, formaldehyde, naphthalene, asbestos, benzene, and arsenic. Many respondents also failed to class infection causing microbes as cancer risks. The authors say the gaps mark exactly where health authorities should aim future awareness campaigns, since broad knowledge alone hides weak spots that matter for prevention. Better teaching on those weak spots, they argue, could lift prevention across the country.
pmc-11532410:
Gao, Fu, Li, and He test a case based, staged teaching plan for jaw surgery students in twenty twenty-four. The plan walks each lesson through six steps, from a hook to a summary, with real cases at its core. Thirty-eight master's students were split by chance into the new plan or classic lectures. Scores for theory and clinical thinking were compared at the end.

The new plan group scored higher on theory and on case analysis. On a scaled clinic exercise, they led on four of five skills. Teachers also rated their own teaching as stronger after the switch. Students said the method sharpened their thinking, though some felt more pressure. The authors back wider use of the plan.
pmc-11533210:
Azeez Oyemomi Ibrahim and co-authors review fourteen years of breast cancer cases at a rural hospital in southwestern Nigeria in this 2024 paper. Most past Nigerian studies came from city hospitals, leaving rural care less known. The team examined what raised risk and what raised the chance of death.

The study covered two hundred sixty patients admitted between 2010 and 2023. Older age, family history, smoking, and hormone-based birth control were linked to the disease. About thirty-eight percent of patients died. Death was more likely for older or obese patients, for late-stage cases, and for those whose follow-up drug treatment was stopped or never started. The authors call for teaching that pushes early diagnosis and steadier access to treatment.
pmc-11533310:
De Freitas and co-authors test a new antibody that blocks the Notch1 signal in melanoma, in a 2024 cancer study. Skin melanoma often resists immune checkpoint drugs, and earlier work tied Notch1 to tumors that shut immune cells out. The team built an antibody that stops Notch1 from being switched on by its partner proteins. They tested it alone and with checkpoint therapy in human and mouse melanoma models.

The antibody cut Notch1 activation and slowed tumor growth in mice at a set dose. Tumors became more inflamed, meaning immune cells moved in more freely. That shift made checkpoint drugs work better than before. The findings suggest that blocking a single growth signal can warm up a cold tumor and widen the reach of immune therapy.
pmc-11533410:
Erica Ryu and co-authors sample in 2024 the mouth microbes of sixty-three people in Nepal whose lives span foraging to city work abroad. Gut microbes clearly shift with lifestyle, but the mouth's response was muddied by geography in past studies. The Nepali groups hold place roughly constant while lifestyle varies, from foragers to recent farmers to expatriates in the USA.

Against the usual expectation, overall mouth microbe diversity did not differ firmly across lifestyles once geography was controlled. Still, the mix of species shifted, and the team pins specific microbes and lifestyle factors to the gaps. The work separates place from way of life in the vanishing-microbiome debate.
pmc-11535110:
Fatemeh Bamarinejad and seven co-authors look for predictors of a heart procedure complication in a study from two thousand twenty-four. After emergency stenting for a severe heart attack, blood flow through the reopened artery can stay slow or fail, a problem called slow flow or no reflow. It affected about thirty percent of their patients.

The study included four hundred sixty patients treated for ST-elevated heart attacks. Early analysis tied the problem to age, heart pumping strength, kidney function, and lesion traits. In the final adjusted model, three factors stood out on their own: long diffuse lesions, weaker pumping, and poorer kidney filtration. The authors say these markers can warn clinicians before the procedure.
pmc-11535210:
Yuanyuan Lian and co-authors map how warming varies with height in China's Qinling-Daba Mountains, using satellite land surface temperature from 2001 to 2021. Published in 2024, the study first confirms the satellite readings track air temperature well in the range. It then asks whether higher ground warms faster, and what role surface brightness and airborne particles play.

From 2001 to 2010 the mountains showed clear height linked warming, mostly in spring. The next decade flipped the pattern, with negative height trends in autumn and winter. Surface brightness damped warming mainly above 2,500 meters, while particle load mattered most at low and middle heights. The authors read the two forces as a combined control on the mountain climate signal.
pmc-11535510:
Sazedur Rahman, Jon Adams, Wenbo Peng, and David Sibbritt followed in 2024 what shapes healthy habits among stroke survivors in Australia. The team used a large long-running study of older adults, comparing a first survey from 2005 to 2009 with a follow-up in 2017. Their sample held 576 survivors. Habits tracked were activity, drinking, smoking, and supplement use.

Activity at a fair or high level fell over time and ran lower in people with diabetes, but higher in university graduates. Smoking ran higher in women, heavier drinkers, and people with depression, and lower in supplement users. Risky drinking fell over time and was lower in women. Supplement use also fell, though women and people with asthma used more. The authors urge more support for lasting healthy routines.
pmc-11537410:
Jili Qu leads a team on zeolite and palm fiber in treated soil. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with cement treated soil strength. Additives may raise strength while cutting cement use.

Compression tests tracked strength across mix levels. Cement, zeolite, and fiber shares were all varied. Curing time also shaped the strength results. A best swap rate of zeolite for cement was sought. A best fiber share for strength and bend was probed. Regression models tied strength to the mix shares. All factors showed strong effects on strength.  Software aided the search for best shares.
pmc-11538310:
Mauro Passari and a large team of co-authors study how a gene called RNASET2 is controlled in neutrophils during rheumatoid arthritis. Neutrophils are front-line immune cells that dump granule contents and cast DNA traps when they attack. RNASET2 makes an enzyme recently cast as an alarm signal in inflammation. Their 2024 study traces the protein as neutrophils mature in the marrow. It appears in the segmented, mature cells and sits inside two kinds of granules.

The team then maps what switches the gene up or down in this joint disease. Knowing where the alarm sits and when it fires could point to new ways to calm arthritis flares. It also adds to the picture of neutrophils as active drivers, not mere foot soldiers, in chronic inflammation.
pmc-11538510:
Xuequn Luo and six colleagues published a genome study in two thousand twenty-four on the Chinese grouse, a rare bird found only in China. Its subspecies boundaries were poorly settled, above all in Sichuan. The team sequenced the bird's full mitochondrial genome from a nature reserve population.

The Sichuan birds' mitochondrial structure and sequence closely matched birds from Gansu, suggesting one shared subspecies. A control region differed clearly in length from the hazel grouse, a close relative. Family trees built from the full data led the authors to propose splitting the hazel grouse group into two genera. The work is the first Sichuan sequence for the species and feeds conservation planning.
pmc-11540110:
James Vienneau, Camden Burns, Anto Boghokian, and Varun Soti compare two ways to repair a swollen abdominal aorta before it bursts. Open repair replaces the weak section through a large incision, while the endovascular method threads a graft inside the vessel through small cuts. The review gathers studies that compare the two head to head.

The inside method gave a survival edge for up to four years. After that the balance shifted toward open repair. Graft problems such as leaks led to more follow-up procedures and lifelong checks. Open repair patients more often needed breathing support and transfusions, and stayed longer in intensive care. They also recovered to normal life more slowly at first, though quality of life ended up similar. The authors stress that the choice should weigh each patient's health, anatomy, and odds of long-term success.
pmc-11548910:
Wendell Rodrigues Oliveira da Silva and four co-authors asked who really pays for basic medicines in Brazil in a 2024 paper. Brazil's public health system splits duties among federal, state, and municipal governments, but the money tells a messier story. The team analyzed spending from 2016 to 2020 across regions.

Municipalities spent more on medicines than the federal contribution in every year studied. Per-person municipal spending rose over the period, most steeply in poorer municipalities. A federal pharmacy subsidy program, meanwhile, mostly reached large, better-off cities. The authors conclude that inequality is widening: the places least able to fund medicines carry the heaviest load, raising illness and death risks in primary care.
pmc-11549910:
Allison Morse, Hana Kurz, and Donald Moore review a cell product for patients who need a stem cell transplant but lack a matched donor. Cord blood has long served as a backup donor source, yet it has limits. The product, called omidubicel, is made from cord blood cells grown with a form of vitamin B3 and was approved in the United States in 2023.

A large trial compared the product with standard cord blood transplants in patients with high-risk blood cancers. Blood counts recovered much faster with the new product, in about twelve days against twenty-two. Serious bacterial and fungal infections were also less common. The review weighs which patients may benefit and what care teams should expect.
pmc-11563210:
DNA origami folds a long strand of DNA into tiny shapes that can carry cargo, and placing each one exactly where it belongs is the hard part. Tingting Zheng, Caoimhe O'Neill, John Marshall, Thomas Iskratsch, and Matteo Palma use a heated scanning probe to pattern a surface so the folded shapes stick only at chosen spots. As a proof of concept they placed origami carrying gold particles and quantum dots, tiny light-emitting crystals.

The shapes landed at the planned positions in neat arrays, with control down to single molecules. The team says the method could build mixed arrays where different spots carry different cargo. Such platforms could serve in sensing and in the study of single molecules and new materials.
pmc-11563410:
Tyler Rollman and co-authors studied which T cells guard against a virus in pregnancy, in this 2024 paper. The virus kin infects guinea pigs and mirrors a human virus that is a top cause of birth defects. The team removed one T cell type at a time with antibodies.

Removing the helper type, called CD4, made illness worse, raised virus levels, and raised infection of pups before birth. Removing the killer type, called CD8, was well tolerated and did not change virus levels in blood or tissue, though more virus signs appeared in the placenta. The results stress the helper cells' role and show other defenses can cover for the killer cells.
pmc-11566110:
Abrahams and co-authors introduce a microphone that hears sound in a completely new way. Most microphones track a membrane wobbling under sound pressure. Their device instead watches how sound pressure changes the stiffness of a thin trapped air film under a graphene membrane driven at resonance.

As sound waves shift the air pressure, the film's stiffness shifts, and the membrane's resonance frequency moves with it. A tracking loop follows that frequency, turning it back into sound, and the team used it to record sound and music. The graphene disc is over a thousand times smaller in area than the membranes in standard micro-electromechanical microphones. The authors see room for wider dynamic range and tougher, smaller devices.
pmc-11569210:
Microplastics in soil change its chemistry and enzyme activity, Yanan Cheng and co-authors report in a 2024 study. Microplastic-induced changes in nutrient cycling and microbial activity may risk soil ecosystem health. Mechanisms behind those effects remain underexplored. The team exposed soil to polyethylene microplastics of two particle sizes at five concentrations, from none to ten percent by weight, and measured biochemical properties and ecosystem function.

The smaller particles significantly reduced soil respiration and two enzyme activities. They also enhanced another enzyme and lowered pH and several nutrient measures in most cases. The larger particles barely affected some measures, though high concentrations still mattered. Size and dose both shape the harm. Readers in soil science get a response surface rather than a single-dose snapshot.
pmc-11570610:
Seeing the same doctor over time may keep young asthma patients out of hospital, and Iyn-Hyang Lee and co-authors test that claim in South Korean insurance data. Their cohort held 136,296 children and teenagers newly diagnosed with asthma in 2015 and 2016. A continuity index sorted them into high, medium, and low groups by how consistently they visited one primary care provider.

Over two years, about eight percent were hospitalized for asthma. The high-continuity group fared best at about five and a half percent, against eight and a half in the low group. After adjustment, low continuity carried thirty percent higher admission risk and medium continuity fourteen percent higher. Repeated checks across subgroups told the same story.
pmc-11570810:
Peikai Ding and eight co-authors build a survival model for an aggressive breast cancer in a 2024 paper. This subtype lacks the usual hormone and growth receptors, so treatment options are few and outlook poor. The team focused on genes tied to a cleanup process that removes damaged mitochondria. Single-cell data from public databases helped find the relevant genes and build a risk score.

Nine genes formed the model, which split patients into high and low risk with clearly different survival. It predicted well across several independent cohorts. High gene levels also tracked with more immune cells in tumors and possible sensitivity to certain drugs, aiding personal treatment choices.
pmc-11571810:
Jennifer Hurtig, Catherine Stuart, and Ambro van Hoof studied an enzyme family in yeasts in 2024. Most eukaryotes carry one member of this family, which trims odd ends from RNA. One yeast group carries two, and the second copy gained a role in maturing a ribosomal RNA piece.

The team shows that this maturation role is not shared across kingdoms but arose in budding yeasts. Its origin matches the event that doubled the gene, and single copies lack the role. Two apart yeast lines each doubled the gene and, in parallel, one copy in each gained the same new job. Many like sequence changes came with it, a striking case of repeatable new function.
pmc-11572110:
Yukiko Miyoshi and co-authors test if sleep drugs bar wild mind states post stroke in a 2024 study of stroke care. Stroke-born wild states hit a large share of cases and drag ends down for the ill. Two drug kinds have shown worth at barring such states in ward care of late in the field.

Past charts of old stroke cases at one hub form the base of the work at hand. Three drugs, one sleep-onset kind and two wake-block kinds, are the picks on trial in the charts. Their bar worth is read from the charts for the stroke group in care.
pmc-11574410:
Antoine Bola Siafa and co-authors set out a 2024 protocol to measure unjustified antibiotic use for acute tonsillitis in low and middle income countries. Tonsillitis often clears on its own, and rich countries use rules to decide who truly needs an antibiotic. In poorer settings, doctors tend to prescribe for nearly every case, likely feeding drug resistance.

Their planned review will gather observational studies on tonsillitis diagnosis and care in those countries over a recent span of years. Searches will cover major databases plus grey literature, with study picking under standard review rules and bias scored by a set tool. Like studies will be pooled in a meta analysis, with splits by study period and quality. The goal is a firm estimate of how much tonsillitis prescribing is needless, to guide stewardship where resistance is rising fastest.
pmc-11574910:
Kazuki Ohashi and co-authors count, in a 2024 study, whether Hokkaido has enough clinics able to give a new Alzheimer's drug. Lecanemab was approved in Japan in 2023, but it demands brain scans and close monitoring, so only some hospitals qualify. Using map data, the team sorted hospitals into three scenarios by how fully they met the treatment rules. Then they measured how much of the population could reach one within thirty, sixty, or one hundred twenty minutes.

Coverage swung widely with the rules. Under the most workable scenario it reached fifty-six, about seventy-four, and eighty-eight percent at the three travel times. The far north and south were worst served, while Sapporo was flagged as likeliest to overflow. The authors call for new treatment centers placed where access and capacity are thinnest.
pmc-11575010:
Ming Liu and five colleagues published case reports in two thousand twenty-four on redoing root canal work in oddly shaped upper molars. Some upper molars fuse their roots into a C shape, hiding extra canals. Missed canals are a common reason root treatments fail.

The first case had three canals in the palate root merging into a C shape, a pattern not previously reported in a first molar. The second fused all cheek-side canals of a second molar into a C ending near an extra tooth. Both patients were free of symptoms at later checks, and scans showed healed tissue. In one case, sinus swelling from the tooth also settled. The authors stress scan and microscope use.
pmc-11575210:
Cynthia Henley-Smith and four co-authors test a plant-based blend against the bacterium that drives tooth decay. Streptococcus mutans colonizes enamel and starts cavities; stopping its adhesion is a prevention strategy older than modern dentistry, since plants like Heteropyxis natalensis have long treated oral infections. The study examined that plant, green tea, and tea tree and peppermint oils.

After forty-eight hours the blend cut bacterial load by about a hundredfold, while sparing a friendly Lactobacillus species much more. Microscope images of enamel blocks showed fewer attached bacteria, broken chains, and damaged cell shapes. Human macrophage tests found low to no toxicity for the mixture and its parts. The authors call it a selective first candidate for caries prevention.
pmc-11576410:
Anthony Rendall and co-authors measure animal escape at night in a 2024 paper. Flight-initiation distance tells how close a threat can get before an animal flees. The method was built for day-active birds, since light is needed to watch animals. Light itself can change behavior, so night species were hard to study.

Thermal cameras solve that problem, the team shows. They give a full method, report night distances for birds and mammals, and compare day and night values. The known link between escape distance and starting distance holds at night too. Most species need twenty-five to fifty samples for a solid reading.
pmc-11576610:
Gesa Beele and co-authors present a 2024 pilot study on treating school anxiety in teenagers with virtual reality exposure. Facing feared settings in small steps is a proven therapy idea, and virtual schools let teens practice safely. Most evidence, though, comes from adults, leaving teen use untested.

Ten adolescents aged fourteen to seventeen, with social anxiety or school-linked phobia, took part in five virtual sessions. The team tracked self-rated anxiety, heart rate, and the feeling of being present in the scene during each session. They also checked whether repeated sessions dulled the fear response and eased wider anxiety symptoms. Links between presence and response were explored. The pilot gauges whether a larger trial is worthwhile.
pmc-11577110:
Yi-An Hsieh and six co-authors trace how house dust mites push airways toward the stiff, thickened state seen in asthma. Working with human bronchial cells, they found mite exposure switched on a receptor called PAR2 and raised production of TSLP, a signaling protein. A specific internal pathway carried the signal; blocking the receptor cut both the pathway activity and the protein output.

The team then asked what that protein does to lung fibroblasts, the cells that lay down structural tissue. Medium from mite-treated airway cells made fibroblasts multiply and produce collagen, and so did the pure protein. Antibodies against the protein, or the receptor blocker, stopped those effects. The results sketch a chain from mite to receptor to signal to scarring. Drugs blocking the receptor are floated as candidate treatments.
pmc-11577710:
Zaib Un Nisa Mughal and Abdul Malik write a 2024 note on a study of a heart lung aid and a bleed ill. The aid is a machine that takes over for the heart and lungs for a short time. The study looked back at sick people whose hearts stopped out of a ward. It asked if the aid raised the odds of the bleed ill, in which blood fails to clot well.

The note praises the study in clear terms. The plan was told in full, the sums were sound, and the fate of each sick person was set out well. The note then turns to flaws. A look back can bend the finds, and the team said too little on that risk. No group was on hand who did not get the aid, so the aid share of blame stays hard to split off.
pmc-11577810:
Ha Na Cho and co-authors present work from two thousand twenty-four on predicting how long sick patients stay in hospital after surgery. The patients studied needed general anesthesia, which puts them to sleep for the operation. Knowing the likely stay in advance helps hospitals plan beds, staff, and care.

The team used records from a very large group of patients treated between two thousand eighteen and two thousand twenty. They tested four kinds of machine learning models, and one called XGBoost gave the best results, with an average error within three days. The paper also shows which factors shaped each forecast, so doctors can see why a stay was predicted to be long or short.
pmc-11577910:
Wenlong Zou and co-authors build a chance-web model to call stroke risk after heart bypass surgery done off the pump. Their 2024 study mines records for more than ten thousand patients at a Beijing hospital from 2018 to 2022. Stroke struck about one and a half percent during the hospital stay.

Seven traits tie straight to stroke: female sex, past stroke, tight neck artery, and four blood marks. Diabetes links in by an indirect path through two of the marks. The web model called cases more truly than standard regression on both build and test sets. Early flags could steer watch and prevention for high-risk hearts, the authors say.
pmc-11579510:
Soohyun Oh and five co-authors study how some plants spot a broad family of crop pathogens, in a research paper from 2024. The pathogens, called Phytophthora, attack many plants. They share families of proteins, called effectors, that they inject into plant cells.

The team tested sixty-nine effectors from six pathogen species against immune receptors in nightshade plants. About three in five were caught by receptors, grouped by effector family. Three receptors each gave broad protection against several species. The authors say matching shared effector families is a fast way to find useful resistance genes for other crops facing similar threats.
pmc-11579910:
Ellery Hayden, Jack Leoni, and Frank Culicchia report a brain-covering tumor that turned out to be a rare blood-vessel growth, in a 2024 case report. Such growths usually appear in bone or inside brain tissue. Only a small share start in the dura, the brain's tough outer cover. The patient was a forty-six-year-old woman.

Her left frontal mass had been found by chance and grew over four years. Scans suggested a common meningioma: even enhancement, a broad base, and a dural tail. Surgery removed it in one piece. The purplish-red mass proved to be a capillary hemangioma under the microscope. The case warns that rare mimics can wear a textbook disguise.
pmc-11580310:
Yuna Uchi and co-authors read, in a 2024 study, the death records of a city hit by the Fukushima nuclear disaster. Deaths tied to a disaster can come late and by indirect paths: the stress and disruption of evacuation can kill months later. The team read all 520 certified disaster-related deaths in Minamisoma City, north of the plant, from 2011 to 2021.

Heart and vessel diseases led, at 27.7% of deaths. Lung diseases came next, at about a quarter, and cancers third. Older people bore the brunt of the heart and lung toll, which points to evacuation strain. Cancer led deaths for those in their fifties, a hint that evacuation cut screening and care. Self-harm led for the young and could strike years later. The authors urge better shelters, evacuee care networks, cancer care during evacuation, and long suicide watch.
pmc-11580510:
Mihretu Tarekegn and co-authors survey malaria mosquitoes in north-western Ethiopia in a 2024 study. Malaria remains a major health problem in the country despite wider control work. Local data on mosquito habits are needed to aim prevention where it counts.

For a year, adult mosquitoes were caught indoors and outdoors in two sites with traps, sprays, pit shelters, and aspirators. Each mosquito was identified to species, and lab tests showed what blood it had fed on and whether it carried the parasite. The survey covers feeding choice, biting site, and resting habits. District programs can use the picture to time and place their efforts.
pmc-11584510:
Mayar Al Mohajer and co-authors ask in 2024 whether doctors from higher ranked medical schools prescribe antibiotics less often to older patients. Overuse of these drugs is a known concern in outpatient care in the United States.

The team linked Medicare drug claim data from 2013 to 2021 with records on each provider. Nearly two hundred thousand providers were included. School rank showed no link with the rate of antibiotic days per one hundred patients. Provider type did matter: hospital and emergency doctors supplied fewer days than family doctors. Students, women, and those more than twenty years out of school supplied more. The authors call for stronger stewardship in outpatient care.
pmc-11584710:
Heng Du and co-authors present a genome data set for Chinese native pigs in a 2024 paper. Pigs are central to farming in China, yet large scale sequencing of local breeds lagged behind. Gaps in the record held back studies of pig traits and breeding.

The project sequenced more than one thousand pigs from fifty populations across about two thirds of China's regions. Deep reads found over sixty million variants and built a reference panel that sharpens trait mapping in these breeds. Signals of an old mixing event track a wave of human migration in the thirteenth century. Other findings touch high altitude adaptation and body size. The resource opens fresh work on pig biology and breeding.
pmc-11584810:
Yu and co-authors profile cervical tumors with joined gene and protein data from 139 Chinese women. Cervical cancer has fallen where vaccines and screening spread, but it still threatens women in poorer nations. Tumor samples got deep proteogenomic reads. The joined analysis links gene faults to the pathways they disturb. It also maps how HPV infection reshapes the tumor at many levels. One finding ties the protein EP300 to faster tumor growth through a partner protein.

Protein patterns split patients into three groups. The groups differ in outlook, gene faults, and likely drug response. The atlas aims to guide both biology and treatment picks.
pmc-11585110:
Zhenkun Yang and co-workers study blood sugar swings in patients with both diastolic heart failure and type 2 diabetes, in a 2024 paper. Wide swings in glucose can worsen heart and vessel problems. Their effect on survival in this combined group was unclear.

Using a large ICU database, the team followed more than two thousand patients, plus a later group for outside checks. Patients with the largest glucose swings had higher death rates at three months, one year, and three years. The team also built machine learning models to predict one-year death. Those models were checked on held-out and external groups.
