pmc-11585510:
Macarena Artigas-Arias and co-authors ask whether breast cancer survivors gain as much from strength training as healthy women, in this 2024 study. Both groups were past menopause, when muscle mass and strength tend to fall. Weight training is known to help healthy women of this age, but evidence for survivors was mixed.

Thirteen healthy women and eleven survivors followed the same twelve-week whole-body weight program. Before and after, the team measured thigh muscle thickness, top lifting strength on several exercises, grip strength, and daily movement tasks. Both groups improved on every measure. No gap appeared between the groups on any outcome. The authors conclude that a structured strength program brings the same gains in muscle, strength, and physical performance whether or not a woman has had breast cancer.
pmc-11585610:
Yi Shen and co-authors studied how wedge-shaped deformity across the spine relates to its front-to-back curves in teens with scoliosis, in a 2024 study. In this condition the spine curves sideways for no known cause. Past work tied the main sideways angle to those front-to-back curves, but the wedge shape of the bones and discs was less studied.

The team looked back at 122 patients treated at their hospital from 2018 to 2023. They measured the main angle and a long list of wedge angles for bones and discs. In 102 patients with side X-rays, they also measured the upper and lower back curves. The main angle rose with many wedge measures, while the upper back curve moved the other way.
pmc-11586310:
Yi-Peng Gao and co-authors review a protein family called CREB3 as a drug target in a 2024 paper. The family helps run cell programs tied to fat handling, inflammation, and blood vessel function. Those same processes drive heart, vessel, and metabolic diseases such as diabetes and fatty liver. The review sums up recent work on how each family member acts in these diseases.

Studies show the proteins sit at control points for lipid metabolism and inflammatory signals. That position makes them attractive targets: adjusting one protein might shift several disease pathways at once. The authors gather the evidence for each member's role and weigh what is known about drugging them. They present the family as a promising set of targets and map questions that future therapy research should answer.
pmc-11586510:
Health students prove their clinical skills in OSCEs — structured exams where they rotate through simulated patient scenarios. Tuba Sengul and co-authors built a scale in 2024 to measure how students themselves perceive that exam format, a view missing from most assessment research. They tested the new 19-item scale on 220 medical and nursing students from 2022 to 2023.

Factor analysis supported the scale's structure, and its internal consistency was very high, with a reliability coefficient of 0.943. Model fit indices landed in the acceptable range. The authors conclude the instrument is a valid and reliable way to capture student perceptions of the exam. That matters, they argue, because a trusted exam is one whose results educators can act on — and student experience is part of that trust.
pmc-11586610:
Supattra Changsuphan, Boonjai Srisatidnarakul, and Holli DeVon present a 2024 study that builds a short scale for nurses to judge when older patients can go home after hip surgery. Poor readiness can mean pain problems, weak movement, and too little help at home. A clear checklist could cut those risks and lower readmission.

The team drafted items from past research and from talks with experts and patients. They then tested the nine item scale in four large public hospitals with 200 older adults who had hip joint surgery. The paper reports how sound the scale proved: how well its items hang together and how well it sorts patients.
pmc-11587010:
Enrico Armato and co-authors follow patients with vestibular neuritis, a sudden inner-ear problem that causes strong dizziness, to learn what predicts recovery. Recovery can mean the ear heals fully or the brain compensates. The team tested patients within days of onset and again about three months later.

They combined balance organ tests at several frequencies with a questionnaire on dizziness handicap, forming four recovery groups. Heart and vessel risk factors, especially high cholesterol, went with poorer recovery, while age and body weight did not. Only a minority of patients had normal test results at follow-up, with little difference between high- and low-frequency tests. Some patients felt unwell even after tests normalized.
pmc-11587710:
Rubén Cuevas-Martínez and ten colleagues published a mouse study in two thousand twenty-four on intermittent fasting and rheumatoid arthritis. Fasting calms inflammation in several conditions, but its mechanism in arthritis was murky. Sixteen mice with induced arthritis were split between normal feeding and alternate-day fasting for four weeks.

Fasted mice developed milder, less frequent joint disease, confirmed by tissue and imaging checks. Gene activity shifted broadly: hundreds of genes rose or fell, with inflammatory pathways turned down. One mediator, IL33, stood out as central to the benefit. Gut microbe profiles changed too. Master metabolic regulators were implicated in the response. The authors propose fasting as a probe and possible adjunct in arthritis.
pmc-11589710:
Ayan Chatterjee and co-authors pair single immune cells of very different sizes in tiny channels. Their 2024 paper builds a microfluidic sorter that traps one macrophage with one T cell, though the two can differ fivefold in size. Pairing topped forty percent. The rig then watches their talks live under a microscope.

They test a drug combo: immune triggers plus rapamycin, a drug that curbs a growth switch. The combo shines in mice but lags in clinics. Single-cell views showed rapamycin damping the T cells' inflammatory output over time. Bulk tests would have blurred that signal. The authors argue such rigs can explain why immune combos help some cells and hush others.
pmc-11590310:
Sini Siltanen and co-authors compare outdoor mobility in senior housing residents and older people living at home, published in 2024. Getting outdoors supports function and an active life in old age. Little was known about how residents of senior housing move outdoors, or whether the density of the area matters.

The team pooled data from two Finnish studies, one a housing survey and one a population cohort. They scored how far people ranged in daily life and how free they felt outdoors. Community dwellers scored higher on both measures than housing residents. Area density changed the gap between the two groups. In the most and least dense areas, housing residents ranged less far than their peers at home.
pmc-11590810:
Yohei Kamikawa asks whether the job market moves the number of ambulance rides in Japan. He tracked monthly data from 2003 to 2021, a span covering more than 108 million dispatches. His main measure was the ratio of open jobs to applicants, a standard gauge of how tight the labor market is. He adjusted for the older population, the average temperature, and the total population.

Months with more open jobs per applicant saw slightly more ambulance calls, and the link held up in the statistics. A model that included the job ratio also tracked the real trend better than one built only on age, heat, and headcount. Kamikawa argues that emergency planning should watch the economy, not just demography and weather. Busy labor markets, it seems, send more people into ambulances.
pmc-11591910:
Jessica Angelina Trejo Vazquez and co-authors show how lung tumor vesicles switch on nearby fibroblasts. Their 2024 study uses vesicles shed by lung adenocarcinoma cells. Lung cancer kills more patients than any other cancer, mostly through spread. The tumor's neighborhood helps drive that spread.

Vesicles were spun out of cell cultures and checked by standard methods. Resting lung fibroblasts then bathed in vesicles, a growth factor, or plain buffer. Vesicles woke the fibroblasts into a cancer-linked state, raising marker proteins. Their gene patterns partly matched the growth factor's effect. Vesicle-woken cells favored tissue remodeling and invasion-linked genes more strongly. Tumor messages in tiny parcels may recruit local help for growth.
pmc-11596210:
Jennifer Narro-Serrano and co-authors study scent chemicals in urine as possible signs of COVID-19, in this 2024 paper. Infection changes body chemistry, and urine carries volatile compounds that reflect those shifts. Past studies named varied candidate markers. This team wanted a firmer set, so they tested urine in several ways and compared the results.

They gathered urine from thirty-five hospital patients with the disease and thirty-two healthy people. A fiber-based method fed the samples into a gas analysis machine, with some samples dried or acid-treated first. Statistical models separated patients from healthy controls, and the split grew sharper with the treated samples. Yet treatments could also create or destroy compounds. The authors advise mixing methods when picking markers of viral illness.
pmc-11597310:
Three Mexican salvias carry folk reputations as painkillers, and chemistry can test whether the reputation is earned and shared. Nancy Ortiz-Mendoza and six co-authors profile the three species' methanol extracts in 2024 by untargeted metabolomics, then test each in animals for pain relief and safety. Forty-six compounds were annotated, mostly diterpenes and phenolics.

Only four compounds appeared in all three plants, yet all three extracts eased pain significantly at the tested dose and showed no acute toxicity even at the highest dose tried. The authors conclude the salvias reach the same relief by different chemistry. A shared use, they show, need not mean shared ingredients. Each species keeps its own recipe.
pmc-11597410:
Lea Schuh and co-authors follow COVID-19 inside the body, asking what the antiviral drug remdesivir really does. Trials had suggested it speeds recovery, but only modestly. The team tracked 369 patients of all illness levels, treated and untreated, and used a process-based math model to reconstruct the infection's course in 88 of them.

Among untreated patients, those who ended up in hospital showed weaker early immune responses and higher total virus loads than those who stayed home. Among treated patients who died, hospital arrival came later after symptoms began than among survivors, a sign that timing matters. The model's verdict on the drug itself was restrained: its antiviral activity looked rather limited. The authors argue the findings point to a need for different or added treatment plans.
pmc-11599610:
Cosme Ayani and seven co-authors present a 2024 study of electrons in a flat material that normally traps them in place. Such materials, called Mott insulators, owe their behavior to strong pushes between electrons. Stacking a single layer of one on a metal base lets scientists watch how the layers sway each other.

The team mapped how electrons scatter in the stack as the temperature fell. Below eleven degrees above absolute zero, a sharp contour emerged in the maps. That signals electrons breaking free and moving as a coherent group, a state tied to a known lattice effect. Math models of the material backed the reading of the data.
pmc-11600610:
Salhadin Mohammed and co-authors describe a man whose inherited nerve disease announced itself as a tremor, sending diagnosis down the wrong road. Their 2024 case report concerns Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A, confirmed by genetic testing. The classic picture is distal weakness, high arches, and numbness; tremor belongs to a different subtype and is seldom seen here.

Their patient, a thirty-four-year-old Eritrean man, came with six months of hand tremor plus walking difficulty and wasting of the far limbs, and no family history. The report warns clinicians in similar settings that a tremor does not rule this disease out, and that genetic confirmation can end a long diagnostic wander.
pmc-11600710:
Megan Coe and co-authors ask why health staff in western Kenya stray from national rules for children born to mothers with HIV. Their 2024 study is based on group talks and deep one-to-one talks with staff at two sites. The rules cover both HIV care and food support, since poor diet and HIV harm these children together. Staff were picked to give a wide mix of roles and views.

Team work and shared sites helped staff link the two kinds of care. Gaps still came from split know-how across staff, too few workers, and patchy supplies. Referrals between services often stalled. Staff felt strong drive to help, but they lacked steady checks and support.
pmc-11600810:
Khushbu Shah and co-authors review the care of US veterans with opioid use disorder who inject drugs, in a 2024 study. Records covered 502 veterans seen at one Long Island center between 2012 and 2022. Of them, 216 injected drugs. That group mixed in stimulant use more often than the rest.

Injectors also landed in the hospital with infections far more often, and they were admitted more times in all. The team compared who got each kind of help by group: drugs that treat addiction, kits that reverse overdose, and drugs that block HIV. They also charted the worst injection infections and what followed from them.
pmc-11600910:
Shunqing Shu leads a team on whether a scope step is needed in colon checks. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with entry to the last gut part. That step proves a full check, but its worth is in doubt.

Records came from a large set of folks at one center. Half had the extra step and half did not. Odd finds in that gut part were quite rare. Rates of polyp and growth finds were compared by group. Score matching was used to make groups more fair. The team finds the step not needed as routine.
pmc-11601910:
Liqiu Wang and seven co-authors find a fat-tagging checkpoint that the antiviral hub MAVS must pass before it can switch on, in a study from 2024. When RNA viruses infect cells, MAVS clumps on mitochondria into prion-like aggregates that launch interferon defenses. What licenses that clumping was unknown.

A fatty acid tag placed on one cysteine of MAVS, mainly by one named enzyme, proved essential for aggregation and immunity in macrophages. A lupus-linked mutation at that very spot blocks the tag and weakens interferon output. Mice lacking the tagging enzyme made poor interferon responses and died more easily from viral infection.
pmc-11602810:
Yi Chen and seventeen co-authors show in 2024 that tiny parcels shed by lab-grown liver cells can restart a failing liver. The parcels, extracellular vesicles, carry molecular messages between cells. Their parent cells, grown from liver tissue, were already known to aid recovery from acute liver failure in animals.

In mice poisoned by two standard liver toxins, the vesicles sped regeneration. Human liver cells in dishes divided faster after vesicle treatment. One small RNA inside the vesicles proved key: it silences a brake gene, switching on a growth pathway. The work points to a cell-free therapy for liver failure built on packaged signals.
pmc-11602910:
Hanaa Hassan and co-authors test natural boosters for garlic crops, in this 2024 study. Farming must raise yields while cutting the harm that heavy fertilizer and pesticide use does to ecosystems and health. Biostimulants, substances that nudge plant growth without being fertilizers themselves, are one candidate. The team tried two: potassium citrate sprayed on leaves, and humic acid worked into the soil.

They measured how the treatments changed garlic growth, yield, and the healthy compounds in the bulbs. Garlic essential oils were also checked for power against fungi, a bonus use for the crop. Pairing a leaf spray with a soil treatment tests whether the routes reinforce each other. Results of this kind help growers cut chemical inputs while keeping the harvest strong.
pmc-11603210:
Julie Noah and six co-authors test whether a crop fungus can adapt to a plant it normally cannot infect in a 2024 paper. The fungus causes stem canker in oilseed rape, while a close cousin plant resists it strongly in France. Field trials and lab tests confirm that cousin as a true nonhost for now.

Rare fungal strains with mild adaptation were found on a related plant in fields. Crossing one such strain with a normal strain bred offspring even better adapted to the resistant plant. The trait rests on many genes, the cross showed. The new strains will help reveal how such adaptation works and why the plant resists.
pmc-11603310:
Cutting the steel cladding of fast reactor fuel rods is slow work for saws, which wear fast and leave rough edges on the springy metal. Tianchi Li and fifteen co-authors test laser cutting on mock fuel rods in this 2024 study. A laser cuts without contact, at high speed, and suits radioactive settings where hands-off work matters.

The team varied four settings: cutting speed, focal point, power, and gas pressure, and judged each cut by speed, surface roughness, and slag left behind. The best balance came at a speed of one meter per minute, a deep focal setting, power in a stated mid range, and high gas pressure. The authors say the tuned recipe can guide real fuel rod processing, including reprocessing and plant decommissioning work.
pmc-11603710:
Health technologies promise safer care, yet they can also create new risks that no one planned for. Shahd Abdelaziz and eight co-authors asked patients, carers, and health workers in the UK about those side effects in 2024. Forty people joined five online focus groups held in late 2021 and early 2022.

Five themes came out of the talks: unfair access, extra burden on users, loss of the human touch, over trust in the tools, and unclear duty when things go wrong. Some harms were known, such as alert fatigue, while others were newer, like patients growing dependent on their devices. The authors say these themes should shape how new tools are checked for safety.
pmc-11603810:
Si Chen and co-authors set out a 2024 protocol for a teaching trial on spinal ultrasound. Pain doctors and anesthesiologists use lumbar ultrasound to guide needles. The images are complex and the learning curve long. Their team built a route map that charts the scan path step by step.

The trial will randomize forty trainee clinicians. One group learns with the map, the other without. It also tests when in training the map helps most. Learning scores and satisfaction are the outcomes. A proven map could shorten training for a tricky skill.
pmc-11603910:
Haibin Yu, Wenjian Wu, Weihsun Tai, Jing Li, and Rui Zhang test whether flat feet cut jump height, in a review from 2024. Some selectors bar flat footed athletes on a belief that arches drive power. Past studies split on that claim, so a pooled check can settle the jump question.

Nine studies met the strict entry rules for pooled jump height analysis. Study spread was low, which supports one joint effect size for the pool. Jump height showed no real gap between flat and normal feet overall. Teen and adult splits also showed no gap in either age band. Athlete and amateur splits matched that null result across training levels.
pmc-11604010:
Jingyan Sun and four co-authors examine how clashing work and family demands feed depression in Chinese prison officers. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Depression runs high in this workforce, and role conflict theory predicts stress is the bridge between the clash and the low mood.

Four hundred seventy-two officers completed standard scales for conflict, stress, and depressive symptoms. Mediation analysis tested whether stress carries the effect from conflict to depression. A network analysis then mapped which symptoms sit at the center and which link the three clusters together. Naming those bridge symptoms points to precise targets for support programs. The authors aim their findings at interventions built for this overlooked group.
pmc-11604710:
Ying Shi and co-authors tie food habits to sleep breath blocks in a 2024 study of sleep health. The work asks how daily food maps to the breath ill's depth in folk at night. Two hundred folk gave food tales by a set form for the pool of the work.

Cases sort into mild, mid, and grave bands by their breath scores at night in the lab. Maths ties food traits to the ill while it holds other traits firm in the frame. Force shares of the three food fuels are set next to sleep marks too in the end.
pmc-11605010:
Jing Shen and Chuang Jiang hunt for genes shared by heart disease and schizophrenia, in a 2024 study. The two conditions co-occur far more than chance allows, and shared heredity may explain why. The team combined genetic data across seventeen cardiovascular diseases and schizophrenia. A battery of statistical methods probed correlations genome-wide and region by region, then tested cause in both directions.

A clear genetic correlation emerged between the disease families. Hundreds of DNA variants appeared to influence both sides of the pairing. A few genes, including TRIM27, CENPM, and MYH7B, stood out as hubs. The shared pathways touch immunity, metabolism, and early brain development. Untangling them could yield treatments that help heart and mind together.
pmc-11605610:
Kengo Yamada and co-authors engineer natural killer cells that keep killing inside oxygen-starved tumors in a 2024 study. Solid tumors like glioblastoma run low on oxygen, and the adaptation switch HIF-1α dulls the immune cells sent against them. The team deleted that switch in human killer cells with CRISPR.

Edited cells, even under low oxygen, slowed the growth of donor-mismatched glioblastoma cells more strongly and pushed tumor spheres into programmed death. Gene readings tied the boost to higher output of perforin and a death signal molecule. The authors present the knockout as a route to hardier cell therapy for brain tumors.
pmc-11605810:
Shamila De Silva and co-authors (2024) measure how well the Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine worked in Sri Lanka's real rollout. Trial efficacy numbers existed, but real-world evidence for this vaccine was scarce. The team ran a test-negative case-control study at ten large state hospitals. Adults coming to clinic departments were tested for the virus; those positive became cases, and those negative, controls. Histories came from interviews.

Of 1,829 enrolled, about half were men, the mean age was forty-five, and 89.3 percent had received two vaccine doses. Comparing vaccination rates between cases and controls shows how well the vaccine blocked infection in everyday conditions, with all the messiness of a national program included. Such estimates mattered for countries that built their campaigns on this vaccine and had to decide on boosters with local data, not foreign trials.
pmc-11606010:
Frederick Chan and co-authors validate in this 2024 study a slightly longer questionnaire for catching thinking troubles in dialysis patients. Memory and thinking faults are common on dialysis and harm health, but full testing takes time and trained staff. The short scale they extend has three items; the team adds a memory question that the original lacked and tests the four-item form on 268 patients in Singapore.

The extended scale held together as one factor with good consistency. It flagged objective impairment fairly and self-reported complaints better, and it beat the original at predicting daily function faults and missed treatment. The authors offer it as a workable screen for busy kidney units.
pmc-11606110:
Lukas Müller-Wirtz and co-authors reply in 2024 to a comment on their review of inhaled sedation in intensive care. The exchange concerns whether gases used to keep patients calm can also help the lungs and the main breathing muscle. The authors stress that their review weighed early signs, not firm proof.

They agree that extra dead space from the gear should stay low, above all at small breath sizes. They also argue that care should fit each patient, since these gases let breathing drive stay on and be tuned. More close clinical data, they say, must come before strong claims.
pmc-11607310:
Yuanqi Wang and nine co-authors track how Arctic surface waters mixed as sea ice waned. Their 2024 study covers the Pacific Arctic shelves from 1996 to 2021. These seas feed rich ecosystems, yet ice loss is reshaping their upper layer. Ship data and model records gauged the summer mixed layer.

Before 2006, the mixed layer grew shallower as ice melted and surfaces warmed. After 2007 the trend flipped to deepening. Longer open water, stronger wind stirring, and less meltwater drove the change. Control thus passed from surface buoyancy to wind. The shift may explain odd fall plankton blooms and faster acidification. Ice loss, in short, now stirs the sea it once calmed.
pmc-11607910:
Parivash Jamrasi, Mia Tazi, Nur Afiqah Zulkifli, Jun Bae, and Wook Song review whether exercise can shield fertility during immune cancer therapy, in a 2024 paper. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs have transformed cancer care but can inflame glands and damage the gonads. Many patients are young enough for parenthood to matter. Exercise already helps patients feel better and may improve treatment response, and it supports reproductive health in other settings.

Direct evidence for the therapy pairing, though, is thin. The review gathers what is known about fertility-related side effects and the paths by which the drugs might harm reproduction. It then argues exercise is a plausible, low-risk shield worth testing. The authors urge that fertility counseling become routine beside these drugs.
pmc-11608210:
Zhifeng Wang and co-authors study an enzyme that helps liver cancer evade immunity in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The enzyme adds sugar units to cell molecules, and its levels are abnormally high in HCC tumors. High levels also mark a worse outlook for patients.

The team traces a chain from this enzyme through two signaling proteins to a secreted factor. That factor reshapes the immune cells around the tumor, favoring types that suppress attack. Silencing the enzyme in mice made an immune therapy work better at killing tumors. The authors propose the enzyme as both a prognostic marker and a helper target for immunotherapy.
pmc-11608310:
Si Chen and co-authors test a fiber-spiked black tea against after-meal sugar swings in type 2 diabetes, in a 2024 trial. The drink adds inulin and a resistant dextrin to black tea powder. Thirty-five patients took part in a crossover design: each person tried both the active drink and a look-alike placebo before a standard test meal, in random order. Blood sugar was followed for hours after eating.

The fiber tea blunted glucose rises at every checkpoint compared with placebo. Far more patients kept their two-hour swing small on the active drink. The odds of a large swing fell by about two thirds. The authors present the drink as a simple dietary aid for smoothing post-meal glucose. Longer trials would test whether the effect lasts.
pmc-11609310:
Liwei Ma and seven co-authors review blood based cancer tests in a 2024 paper. Cutting tissue remains the standard way to diagnose tumors. It is accurate but invasive and sometimes slow. A liquid biopsy reads cancer traces floating in blood instead.

Those traces include whole tumor cells and scraps of tumor DNA. Small sacs shed by cells and tiny RNA pieces also count. The review walks through use in several common cancers. It weighs speed and comfort gains against lab hurdles. Test results can guide treatment choice and track its effect. The authors see the method moving toward routine care as detection improves.
pmc-11609410:
Mihrican Yeşildağ and co-authors test body measures in a 2024 study of sleep apnea and heart risk. People whose breathing stops in sleep face higher odds of heart and metabolic disease. Two newer body indices, one for shape and one for roundness, might flag that risk better than older measures such as body mass index.

The team reviewed records for two hundred eighty-one patients at a sleep center. Most had sleep apnea, split among those with heart disease, those at risk, and controls. The roundness index predicted risk status better than older measures, while neck size alone predicted actual disease. The shape index showed no clear value. The authors back the roundness index as a handy extra check in clinic.
pmc-11610310:
Xia Shan, Ruoyu Huang, Kuanyu Wang, and Pei Yang build a prognosis score for glioma brain tumors out of nineteen genes tied to reactive oxygen species. These molecules are double agents: moderate levels sustain cells, high levels feed tumors. Mining gene expression profiles, the team first split patients into two groups with distinct clinical features and survival.

The nineteen-gene signature predicted prognosis robustly in both training and validation datasets. High-risk tumors showed raised immune checkpoint and M2 macrophage markers, painting an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Functional analyses tied oxygen species levels to that immune landscape. The authors propose the score as an independent prognostic factor and a hint that redox biology helps gliomas hide from immunity.
pmc-11611510:
Evelyn Goicochea-Rios and three colleagues study which factors link to kidney disease in people with type two diabetes, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The team reviewed 371 diabetes patients seen in primary care between twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-four. Kidney disease harms quality of life and raises heart risk. Records covered age, sex, disease length, other illnesses, and lab values.

Being male, being over sixty, poor sugar control, and more than twenty years of diabetes all linked to kidney disease. High blood pressure was the most common extra illness, in seventy percent. The middle kidney stage was most frequent. The authors urge screening of older men with long, poorly controlled diabetes.
pmc-11611810:
Javed Iqbal and co-authors track how one long stress session reshapes gene use in rat brains and raises anxiety-like acts. Their 2024 study samples two nearby zones of a front brain area tied to emotion and thought. Gene reads come from rats sorted by how strongly they react to the stress.

Sixty-two genes shifted in the prone group across the two zones. In one zone, genes for synapse parts and signal paths faded. In the other, genes for nerve growth and learning faded instead. Disease-linked paths for brain decline lit up in one zone, and stress and habit paths in the other. Split responses may explain why some brains cope and some do not.
pmc-11612110:
Ji-Eun Lee and co-authors probe the surface states of a semimetal called TaSb2 in a 2024 paper. Such states sit on the surface of topological materials and are kept safe by symmetry. They drive odd traits in how the stuff acts with charge and with magnets. This compound shows an effect called negative magnetoresistance, but the small-scale picture was not yet clear.

The team used photoemission spectroscopy to map its electronic band structure. They then set that map next to results from density functional theory. Their work pulls bulk states apart from surface states. That split is the step needed to explain the odd transport traits and to judge its promise for future devices.
pmc-11612310:
Xie and four co-authors studied in twenty twenty-four how water weakens red mudstone, a soft rock in red beds. The rock is hard when dry and soft when wet, which can shake slope safety. They ran shear and fine-view tests across the full range of wet levels.

Strength and stiffness fell along a smooth S curve as water rose. Stick force fell more than rub force, then both leveled off. Cracks from swelled grains drove the fast fall in the mid range. Their harm model, with load and start harm joined, fit that fall well and can shift form by its parts.
pmc-11612410:
Wade Ghribi and co-authors made a new dual-acid catalyst in 2024 and put it to work on a family of fused-ring compounds. The catalyst is a hybrid salt that holds two kinds of acid sites at once, a metal-based Lewis site and a sulfonic Brønsted site, two of each per unit. A full kit of scans and tests proved its build. The team then ran a one-pot, three-part reaction that builds the ring family in one go.

Run warm with no solvent and a small load of the salt, the reaction gave high yields in short times. The dual acids work as a pair, which the team credits for the pace. The salt was fished out and reused six times with no clear loss.
pmc-11613410:
Peng Bao and seven co-authors ask whether food state before heart bypass surgery forecasts grave kidney harm after it in older patients. Kidney harm is a common and grave side issue of this surgery. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Records came from a large US care database and held about a thousand older bypass patients. Two scores rated food state from blood protein and body measures. Over half the patients had mid to grave kidney harm after surgery. Worse food scores linked to higher harm risk after other factors were weighed. The authors also test how well the scores alone can flag who will be harmed.
pmc-11613810:
Charlotte Veser and four co-authors argue that lab-grown kidney models should build in sex differences, in a 2024 review. Kidneys clear drugs and toxins, so models of them guide drug tests. Yet kidney work varies much by person, and sex shapes that work in deep ways. Most lab models still skip sex as a factor.

Skipping sex risks missing how disease starts, how it runs, and how drugs act or harm in each sex. The review maps known sex-linked traits of the kidney, from cells to whole tissue. It then lays out design rules for models that carry those traits. The goal is sharper models and safer, more tailored care for each patient.
pmc-11614010:
Sony Varghese, Shaikhan Al Hashmi, and Al Anood Al Hadhrami reported facial reanimation surgery results from Oman in a 2024 study. Facial palsy freezes one side of the face, and the goal of surgery is to restore both resting symmetry and movement that mirrors the healthy side. A free muscle transfer from the thigh was their method.

Patients treated at Khoula Hospital in Muscat between 2019 and 2022 were reviewed. Younger children had two-stage surgery, while older patients had a single stage. Recovery appeared at about three months on average. Single-stage transfers powered by the jaw muscle nerve recovered earlier than cross-face nerve grafts. Satisfaction was high, and mouth corner symmetry ended near normal.
pmc-11615510:
Yuki Suzuki leads a team on how a transplant drug is absorbed. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with kidney transplant patients. The drug, mycophenolic acid, varies a lot from person to person.

Data came from a small group of transplant recipients. Models of uptake were tested with a mixed effects tool. A two part model with two uptake steps fit the data best. Weight, kidney work, and days since surgery shaped drug levels. The last model was used to work out dose advice. Good models help keep drug levels safe.
pmc-11615810:
Faten Moassass and co-authors study a gene mutation that marks a distinct form of acute myeloid leukemia. Their 2024 paper covers Syrian patients whose leukemia cells had a normal chromosome picture. The gene, NPM1, is mutated in a large share of such cases worldwide and shapes how the disease behaves.

The team sequenced samples from one hundred newly diagnosed adults. About a fifth carried the mutation, most of a common type, with a few new variants found. They also tracked two partner mutations that often travel with it. The mix of mutations shapes prognosis and treatment choices for this leukemia subset. Local data matters because mutation rates and pairings can differ between populations, and care plans borrow strength from pooled global figures.
pmc-11616010:
Athanasios Tasis and co-authors read single bone marrow killer cells in blood growth diseases to find marks of drug response, in a study from 2024. Killer cells guard against tumors, but their edge dulls in the high risk forms of these marrow states. The team read over a hundred pre care marrow samples with mass and flow tools and deep cell reads.

One cell set, marked by two face tags, ran high in patients who went on to fail the lead drug. A share past a set line of that set also tied to short life span. Cell reads tie drug gain to a spark signal path and drug fail to a calm growth path. The authors urge a pair of the lead drug with a block on the calm path for high risk cases.
pmc-11616110:
Poor sleep is common in menopause, and steady aerobic exercise is a drug-free aid worth testing. Yan Jing and co-authors pooled trial results on that aid in a 2024 review. They gathered sixteen papers with nineteen randomized trials from seven databases. Study quality was checked with a standard bias tool. The pooled effect covered low and moderate effort levels.

Exercise gave a moderate gain in sleep for women in menopause. The strongest gains came with three sessions a week and longer sessions of seventy to ninety minutes. Programs of eight to ten weeks also scored well. Results varied a fair amount across trials, which the team notes with care. The authors shape their findings into a practical program of what to do, how much, and how often.
pmc-11616710:
Jie Qi and five colleagues design a new family of alloys that stay both very strong and bendable at extreme heat, in a 2024 study. Refractory high-entropy alloys suit hot structures, but their huge recipe space makes phase control and ductility hard to win together.

The team screened recipes with machine learning, atomistic simulation, and quantum calculations in one loop. The winning aluminum-rich alloys formed a single ordered phase. They reached compressive yield strengths up to 1.7 gigapascals, bent past fifty percent strain before breaking, and kept strength when hot. In tension they still yielded at a gigapascal. The authors also map which electron counts spell ductile versus brittle behavior.
pmc-11617110:
Spanish-speaking parents often struggle to use online health portals for their children, even when they want to. Jennifer Gutierrez-Wu and co-authors pilot a support package: a tablet preloaded with health resources plus two coaching calls from a navigator. Twenty-five parents from pediatric specialty clinics took part, and surveys tracked their technology habits and wishes.

Every parent wanted to know more about their child's health. Interest in health technology ran high, yet only 12 percent had activated a portal before the study. Afterward, portal uses such as booking visits and viewing results rose, though not significantly. Tablets saw real use, above all for video visits at 56 percent. The authors call for stronger Spanish-language support inside portals themselves.
pmc-11617310:
Mind traits in medication-overuse headache are gauged by Franz Riederer and co-authors in work dated 2024. The state grows when pain drugs are taken too often for migraine. It has been tied to habit-like behavior and a weak control zone in the brain. The team gave self-control and feeling-blindness scales to thirty patients and forty-seven healthy peers. Brain scans joined the checks.

Patients scored higher on both scales than peers. Nine in ten met a drug-dependence rule set. In healthy peers, self-control tied to one control-zone patch, but that link was gone in patients. The two scales did not tie to the shrunken control zone itself.
pmc-11618210:
Daniel Frynta and co-authors test which snakes scare people most in this 2024 study. Fear of snakes runs deep in primates, likely an old defense against venom. But snakes fight back with threat displays, and the team asked which display works best.

People in Somalia and Czechia rated photos of snakes at rest and in threat poses. Both groups ranked the snakes much the same way. Threat poses scared people more than resting poses overall. Hooding cobras topped the list, even though resting cobras looked mild. The hood, a wide warning flare aimed at mammal predators, seems to hijack ancient fear circuits. The authors call it a display that outruns the snake itself.
pmc-11618410:
Ren Goto and co-authors probe how slanted micro-teeth keep surfaces water-repellent under pressure in a 2024 study. Lotus-like periodic textures shed water well until pressure forces drops into the grooves. The slant, or taper angle, of each tooth was suspected to guard against that collapse, but proof was thin.

Laser carving built samples with varied slant and spacing. Instead of the usual contact angle, the team judged surfaces by how high test drops bounced off them. Bounce height cleanly separated the slants, favoring shapes that held their air pockets. A simple model of pressure on slanted walls explains the bounce pattern.
pmc-11618510:
Qikun Hu and colleagues recycled polyethylene plastic chemically in two thousand twenty-four. Breaking plastic down with hydrogen yields fuels and waxes. High hydrogen pressure usually suppresses unwanted methane gas. Their catalyst mixes a little ruthenium into platinum. This dilute alloy changes where bonds break. Plastic sticks to both metals on the surface.

Bond cutting runs faster on ruthenium sites. Isolated sites prevent repeated end-cutting of fragments. Methane stayed very low even at ambient pressure. Fuels and lubricant oils formed instead. Low-pressure hydrogen sources could feed such plants locally. Decentralized plastic upcycling becomes more feasible. Spectroscopic studies backed the mechanism proposed.
pmc-11619210:
Jinbo He and co-authors study what people with eating disorders in China see as the causes of their illness, in a paper from 2024. These disorders are common in China yet often go unnamed and untreated for years. The team read posts on a large question-and-answer platform. They kept more than two thousand posts from users who reported an eating disorder.

Coders sorted the claimed causes into personal and social groups. More than nine in ten users named a personal cause. Worry about body image and food was the most named cause, with mood problems close behind. A third to a half also named social causes like media ideals. Trauma, genes, and sports were named far less. The mix of causes shifted by disorder type. The authors say the patients' own views can guide better care.
pmc-11619410:
Yan Zhao and co-authors lay out, in a 2024 trial protocol, a test of gentle ear stimulation for depersonalization-derealization disorder. People with this condition feel detached from themselves and the world, often without relief, and few proven treatments exist.

Patients will be assigned at random to real stimulation through the ear's vagus nerve branch or to a sham version, for six weeks. Scores for detachment, depression, anxiety, thinking, and social function are compared before and after, alongside safety checks. The trial, registered in China in late 2023, aims to show whether this non-drug approach is safe and whether it eases symptoms enough to matter.
pmc-11619610:
Hands-on therapy can ease a worn knee, but only if the therapists offering it know it well and reach for it at the right times. Ahmad Alghadir, Zaheen Iqbal, and Amir Iqbal survey that knowledge in Saudi Arabia in a 2024 study. Close to two hundred physical therapists answered a long questionnaire about their training and habits with knee arthritis patients.

About a third had no formal training in hands-on therapy at all, and only a third held a certificate in it. Most said they pick the method case by case. Pain relief and wider motion led their goals for using it. Attitudes were warm overall, yet the therapists named exercise paired with hands-on care, not either alone, as the best plan. The authors see a training gap worth closing.
pmc-11620610:
Abdisalam Mahdi Hassan and co-authors count how many Somali households still drink from unsafe water sources, and why, in this 2024 study. Safe water is a basic right, yet Somalia's infrastructure leaves many families drawing from unprotected wells, rivers, and vendors. The team mined the 2020 national demographic and health survey, covering more than thirty-two thousand participants. Statistical models then hunted the traits that travel with unimproved sources.

Wealth, region, and household features were all weighed for their pull on water choice. Knowing which factors matter most tells aid programs where pipes, wells, or money will change the most lives. Studies like this turn a national survey into a targeting map for one of public health's oldest fights.
pmc-11620810:
Liang Hou, Jinli Liu, Yuhui Yuan, and Yanchun Ding study how oxidized LDL cholesterol switches on inflammation in macrophages. These immune cells drive artery plaque growth, and their state can lean toward attack or repair. The team focuses on a sensing pathway built around the proteins NOD1 and Rip2.

Human macrophages in culture were exposed to varied doses of oxidized LDL for varied times. Pathway genes and proteins rose with dose and time, and two inflammatory signals rose with them. Blocking Rip2 with a silencing RNA cut those signals back. Oxidized LDL also shifted cell surface markers away from the repair state. The work names this pathway as a possible drug target in plaque disease.
pmc-11621710:
Zahra Siahpour and Maryam Hajjami turn food waste into a chemistry tool. Their 2024 study converts leftover bones into bone char, a mix of calcium phosphate and carbon, then treats it with a strong acid to make a solid acid catalyst.

They put the catalyst to work building pyrimidine carbonitrile compounds, a drug-relevant family. A battery of imaging and analysis methods confirmed the material's structure and surface. The catalyst drove the reactions efficiently and could be fished out and reused several times without losing strength. The authors highlight the novelty: bone char had never served as a catalyst support in organic synthesis before. Waste bone, they argue, can anchor green chemistry.
pmc-11622610:
Geoffrey Bove, Holly McMillan, and Mary Barbe test massage therapy against radiation-caused tissue scarring in rats, in this 2024 study. Radiation fibrosis stiffens and thickens tissue months after cancer treatment, and nothing now prevents or cures it. The team's earlier work showed hands-on therapy stopped like scarring in rats doing repetitive tasks, since the two conditions share marker patterns. They asked whether the same therapy helps after irradiation.

One forelimb of each rat received a damaging dose of X-rays. Some rats then got manual therapy on that limb, and markers of fibrosis were tracked. A simple touch test by hand, palpation, was also scored for how well it reads the tissue state. Early findings of this kind could justify trials in cancer survivors whose stiffened tissue limits daily life.
pmc-11623310:
Ben Reader, Deborah Zerkle, Renata Fabia, Rajan Thakkar, and Dana Schwartz reviewed how massage therapy was used for children with fresh burns, in a 2024 study. Burn care increasingly treats pain, stress, and anxiety alongside the wound itself. The team examined records of one hundred and ninety-eight children admitted to a verified pediatric burn center over eighteen months, excluding intensive care cases.

Every child was referred for massage, but only about one in seven actually received it, across forty-three sessions with a median length of twenty-five minutes. Three quarters of children who reported pain beforehand felt relief, and nearly all were calm or resting afterward. Sessions were most often missed because the child was asleep, off the unit, or busy with other care, and short or weekend stays missed out most. The authors urge more weekend staffing and better timing to widen access.
pmc-11624210:
Raúl Mateos and a team of co-authors built a test to spot when a cell stress system is stuck on. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with the KEAP1-NRF2 system. This system guards cells against harsh chemical stress. When it breaks, genes below it run too high, a known mark of cancer. A good test for this stuck state can guide both study and care.

Their test reads splicing joints in gene reads, since overactive genes leave extra odd joints. A simple Bayes based sorter reads the pattern. It held up well across large data sets. Readers who study cancer get a new way to flag this state from gene data they may already hold.
pmc-11625510:
Chengcheng Yue and co-authors review atopic dermatitis, a common itchy skin disease, in a 2024 paper. The disease affects people of all ages and backgrounds. Its causes mix genes, environment, a weak skin barrier, and a skewed immune response. Faults in barrier genes let alarm signals escape, which switch on a type-two immune path and draw immune cells into the skin.

The review sums up lab models of the disease and the treatments in common use. It traces how skin immune cells talk with each other and with the barrier, step by step. The authors aim to give a clear picture of that crosstalk at cell and molecule level. Their stated goal is to suggest new clinical approaches that could cut how often the disease occurs and how much harm it does.
pmc-11625810:
Ivana Stevic and co-authors survey pharmacy students about nuts and nutrition teaching in a 2024 study. Nuts prevent chronic disease in study after study, yet people eat too few. Five hundred nine Serbian students, three quarters of them pharmacy trainees, answered questions on attitudes, knowledge, and habits.

Attitudes ran positive overall, and pharmacy students outscored peers on knowledge, though the whole sample averaged only about four right answers of thirteen. Lectures and media supplied most of what students knew. Over half wanted more teaching on the topic, and wanting more moved attitudes more than knowledge did. The authors argue nutrition deserves a firmer place in the pharmacy curriculum, since pharmacists counsel the public daily.
pmc-11626010:
Amelewerk Gizachew, Sabura Shara, and Asfaw Kifle test fertilizer rates for orange-fleshed sweet potato in southern Ethiopia in a 2024 field study. The orange roots carry pro-vitamin A, which aids health. Yields stay low in much of the land for want of site-fit feed plans and strong root types.

Three root types were grown at four feed rates in two zones during the 2022 season. The best sale-ready yield came from the Kabode type at the top feed rate in one town. The same type gave the best profit at a mid rate in the other town. Using feed well fell as rates rose, so the team backs Kabode with a mid rate in one zone and a low rate in the other.
pmc-11626110:
Fatema Hashem Rupa and Mosharop Hossian map the health fallout of the August two thousand twenty-four floods in Bangladesh in two thousand twenty-four. The floods hit over five million people, swamping latrines, sewers, and farm land. Dirty water then raised the risk of cholera and other gut diseases, while still pools bred mosquitoes that spread malaria and dengue.

Broken clinics slowed emergency care, and fear, grief, and stress spread through displaced communities. The authors call for fast steps: restore clean water, watch for outbreaks, and repair health sites. Longer work should brace the system for the next flood. The piece is a perspective, blending impact data with a review of risk factors.
pmc-11626710:
Mengxin Tu and co-authors use electron beam radiation to break apart a lead compound that poisons industrial wastewater. Lead bound to EDTA slips past standard cleanup, since the cage keeps the metal dissolved and mobile. A method that cracks the cage and recovers the metal in one pass would solve two problems.

Beam tests show a mild dose clears over ninety percent of the compound, though most lead stays caged at that stage. A stronger dose lifts compound loss a bit more and frees near seventy percent of the lead as metal. Radical trapping tests pin the work on hydroxyl radicals that chew the cage down to small acids. Leftovers test as far less toxic than the start mix. Beam plants could thus detox water and reclaim lead together.
pmc-11626810:
Matthew Humar and co-authors review an emergency airway cut in cardiac arrest in a 2024 study. When standard airway methods fail during resuscitation, medics can cut through the neck into the windpipe, a procedure called cricothyroidotomy. Australian records over eighteen years held eighty such cases, fifty-six of them during cardiac arrest. The team measured how often the cut is used and how often it works.

Use in arrest ran at about one per thousand resuscitation attempts and rose over time. Success reached about sixty-nine percent overall but only fifty-nine percent during arrest, against ninety-two percent outside it. A surgical cut beat the needle method by a wide margin in arrest cases. Male patients fared better. The study gives rare hard numbers for a last-resort airway move.
pmc-11627110:
Adel Moalwi led a large team making wound-healing particles from a plant in a 2024 study. They used water extract of a high-altitude flower to make zinc oxide particles in a green way. Such particles are cheap, easy to make, and known to fight germs. The team measured the particles and tested them on cells and rats.

The particles were tiny and killed a broad range of bacteria plus a fungus. In cell tests, treated wounds closed far faster than untreated ones. In rats, treated wounds shrank much more than untreated wounds, matching a standard iodine treatment. The authors see promise but call for more work on how the particles act and their long-term safety.
pmc-11629010:
Zongshi Qin and seven co-authors present a free software macro that checks whether trial patients truly stayed blind to their treatment, in a 2024 methods paper. Blinding keeps patient and staff guesses from skewing trial results. Bang's Blinding Index turns guess counts into a score for each trial arm. The macro, built for the SAS statistics package, computes the score and draws it as a chart.

Users need no ready data set; they just type in how many people guessed right, wrong, or were unsure in each group. The tool covers two-arm, three-arm dummy, and four-arm factorial designs. The team shows it on guess data from three past trials, on topics from weight gain to depression care. Charts make the success or failure of blinding plain at a glance. The authors aim the tool at trial teams of all sizes.
pmc-11629210:
Elys Mwigamba, Clavery Tungaraza, and Mariam Nguvava review why pollution studies in Tanzania's Geita mining region report wildly different metal levels. Gold mining there, from small diggers to large firms, raises concern about metals in soil, sediment, rice, and water. Mixed findings hamper public action and policy.

Two studies of soil near one mine reported mercury levels thirty times apart, and arsenic and lead also swung widely. The authors trace the gaps to varied sample drying, digestion, and mix ratios, plus unreported season and weather. Lab tools themselves were standard. They call for national standard methods so results can be compared. Shared methods would sharpen health and environment decisions.
pmc-11629910:
Jiaying Li and co-authors hunt the genetic roots of angle-closure glaucoma in the iris itself, in a 2024 study. The disease was long blamed on a shallow eye chamber and short eyeball, yet pooled data showed its risk genes do not track those traits. In 2,161 people from an eye study, odd iris features stood out as risks on their own.

The team then read which DNA stretches lie open in iris tissue and tested 202 risk variants for regulatory punch. Iris open regions carried a rich share of the disease's heritability. Twenty-two variants shifted enhancer activity, and two tuned genes tied to the cell skeleton. The authors say the iris, not just eye shape, drives this glaucoma, and they offer their enhancer-first approach to other eye diseases.
pmc-11630610:
Liu, Ma, Wang, Cui, and Shen study risk spillovers among Chinese financial sectors, in work from twenty twenty-four. Shocks in one sector, such as banking, can spread to insurance, securities, and multifinance. COVID was a sharp test of those links.

Daily closing prices from mid twenty seventeen to the end of twenty twenty-three fed a time varying model. Three stages were split: before, during, and after the epidemic. Total spillover rose then fell, with far bigger swings during the epidemic. The securities sector was most exposed both ways, while banking stayed most stable. Regulators can use such maps to watch the weakest links.
pmc-11631210:
Alexandros Patsouras and a large team of co-authors report a 2024 case of a very large skin cancer of the scalp. The cancer, a basal cell carcinoma, grows from the skin's base layer and is usually mild as cancers go. Left alone, though, it can eat into quality of life and even kill. A tumor wider than twenty centimeters earns the label super-giant.

The patient was an elderly man whose tumor covered most of his scalp. It had left him with severe anemia and a general worn-down state. The report walks through his case and the care he received. The authors use the case to warn against letting this common cancer grow unchecked, since early removal is a small task beside what neglect demands.
pmc-11631710:
Bernard Coetzee and Layla van Zyl gauge whole light scenes in Ugandan woods cut in unlike ways, in a 2024 study. Light drives woods life, but its full mix of tone and span is hard to catch. A new field way shoots whole scenes and reads tone and span as one set.

Prime woods, young woods, picked cut woods, and a bare clear patch stand in line. Glow drops by vast folds from clear patch to prime woods. Blue light rules the sky part of the clear patch shots. Picked cut and prime woods read most alike of all pairs. The way may serve woods heal work well.
pmc-11631810:
Podgorska asks if plant flags for old iron mines flag old lead mines too. The field is a left mine plot from the 16th age in age. Heaps from lead ore digs still scar the plot's face. The team set 41 plots: 21 on heaps, 21 off the heaps. Each plot got a full list of leaf plants with cover shares. Soil bits from each plot went to lab checks for traits.

Checks read soil sour marks and the stock of key salts. Lead, lime, and three food salts got counts in the lab. Soil shifts drove the plant mix split twixt heap and field. On the heap plots, 18 leaf-wood flags for iron plots showed up. Those flags lean hard to heap soil in the counts. The flags thus serve for lead heaps as well.
pmc-11631910:
Tawffeek Mohammed, a solo author writing in 2024, maps research on the aims of Islamic law. That field guides legal theory and modern uses of Islamic law in many parts of life. Knowing the shape of its scholarship helps judge its growing reach.

The study drew four hundred papers from two large databases for the years 2000 to 2022. Several tools were used to trace shared citations, sources, and keywords. Work in the field spans religion, business, science, and medicine, among other areas. Output rose over the period in both databases, with distinct patterns in each.
pmc-11632010: A 2024 correction notice fixes two small errors in a study of metal buildup in bats from a cacao region of Brazil's Atlantic Forest. The study linked worn landscapes to metals stored in bat tissue. The notice states that a chemical name was printed with a wrong capital letter, and that a bat species name in a table was misspelled, though the main text had it right. The publisher notes the original article has been corrected.
pmc-11632110:
Ze-Yun Xu and co-authors type a fever germ found in ticks in Gansu, China, in a 2024 paper. The germ causes Q fever in people and animals worldwide. Ticks carry it and pass it when they feed. The team gathered one hundred ninety-two fed ticks from one city and tested each one.

All ticks were one species, and ninety carried the germ, near half the sample. Gene checks placed the local strain near known strains worldwide. A ten part typing code gave a fresh pattern, logged as a new type in the shared database. Spread of a new type in local ticks signals risk for nearby people. Watch and control steps follow from that find.
pmc-11632510:
Rajshekhar Thippana and Adarsh Bhat report a hip surgery case from two thousand twenty-four. A man aged seventy-five had a bent upper thigh bone and bad arthritis in his right hip. He had also had bone surgery on that leg some thirty years before. The bend made it hard to place a new hip stem in the usual way.

In the past, surgeons would cut and reset the bone first, then fit the new joint. This team instead turned the sleeve of a modular stem around and placed it in reverse. That trick gave a firm fit without the extra bone cut. They argue the method is safe and reliable for this rare shape.
pmc-11633310: Michael Trimble reviews the four principles approach to medical ethics in this 2024 paper. The approach, proposed by Beauchamp and Childress, judges hard cases by four principles and is now standard practice in the United Kingdom. Trimble traces the history of this framework, called principlism, then weighs its impact and reviews the main criticisms of it. A later paper, he notes, will take up the deeper philosophical problems. Readers get a compact map of how one framework came to guide bioethics debate, and where its weak points lie.
pmc-11634610:
Siva Chamarthi and co-authors map gene spots tied to water thrift in soybean. The study appeared in 2024. Drought is the top brake on soybean yield, and most fields in the United States rest on rain. A carbon mark in leaves tracks water thrift well.

Over two hundred bean lines grew in seven site-year mixes, some with added water and some in drought. Gene scans found over one hundred marks in near one hundred spots. Most spots matched past work, while a share were new. Zones near the marks held hundreds of stress genes. Gene-based calls could guess the mark across sites with care.
pmc-11635610:
Simin Liu, Sydney Hu, and Lanxin Su ask whether parents who talk with teenagers as equals raise happier teens, and whether trust in society carries the effect. Data come from a national Chinese family panel: 691 high school students split at age eighteen. Structural models trace democratic communication to subjective well-being directly and through mediators. Societal trust emerges as the heavyweight mediator in both age groups. For the younger group it works directly and in a chain through negative emotion and pleasant experience.

For eighteen-year-olds, trust is the only channel that carries the effect. The measurement model holds across ages while the pathways differ. In a lonely era, the team argues, family talk that respects the teen may build the outward trust that well-being stands on.
pmc-11636010:
Fabiana Vieira Duarte de Souza Reis and colleagues, with the Diamater Study Group, ask whether gestational diabetes diagnosed early in pregnancy harms newborns in a different way from the usual late diagnosis. Terms and diagnostic rules for pregnancy hyperglycemia are being made standard. Women diagnosed by twenty-four weeks or earlier face higher risk of postpartum prediabetes. But the link to bad newborn outcomes was disputed.

The look-back cohort ran at a perinatal diabetes research center in São Paulo state, Brazil. Early-onset women had fasting glucose in the diabetic range, below the line for overt diabetes, before twenty weeks. Late-onset women screened negative in the first trimester. They tested positive on the standard glucose tolerance test at twenty-four to twenty-eight weeks.
pmc-11636310:
Hanna Poulsen and five co-authors study gum disease in women who once faced a high risk of diabetes in pregnancy, in a 2024 paper. Both gum disease and metabolic syndrome involve inflammation, and each may feed the other. The team checked whether women with the syndrome show worse mouth health years after delivery.

They examined 112 women from an earlier group of 348, four to six years after their pregnancies. About a fifth had metabolic syndrome by standard criteria. Full mouth checks, X-rays, and questionnaires measured gum bleeding, pocket depth, plaque, and tooth loss. The authors compare these signs between women with and without the syndrome. Links found here could push joint care of teeth and metabolism after high-risk pregnancies.
pmc-11637310:
Ground sink risk in Hangzhou is scored with the help of a large language model by Bofan Yu and co-authors in work dated 2024. Past scores for sink and collapse risk leaned on expert weights set by feel. The team first fed nine risk factors to a joined neural model. That stack beat a lone model on test scores. They then let ChatGPT-4 set the factor weights in place of experts.

Land experts checked those weights by a paired-compare method. The two weight sets sat within a few percent of each other. A final risk map built on the model-set weights scored well. Data-driven weights may thus stand in for slow expert rounds.
pmc-11638010:
Primary cilia may help steer skin immunity, Jingwei Sun and co-authors review in a 2024 paper. Primary cilia are signaling hubs needed for proper epithelial formation and skin homeostasis. They sit on most cells in the body, including skin cells. Through several pathways, they let ciliated cells interact with the immune system and help maintain immune balance in tissue that meets the outside world daily.

Cilia change with microenvironmental stimuli and take on matching regulatory roles. Ciliary pathways are involved in immune processes across various skin lesions. The review compiles evidence from cells, tissues, and disease models. Key pathways and ciliated cell types in skin are discussed with a focus on immune modulation. Readers get an organelle-level view of skin defense that textbooks rarely give.
pmc-11638410:
Zekai Wang and eight co-authors wrote a 2024 study on a shoreline bacterium built to survive a punishing habitat. The intertidal zone swings in temperature, salt, and oxygen stress as tides turn. Strain LCG004, a new Palleronia species from a Western Pacific harbor, thrives there anyway.

Its genome shows broad metabolic range: organic acids, amino acids, sugars, and complex carbohydrates all serve as food, alongside inorganic nutrient handling that feeds local cycles. Defense kit abounds: transporters that stockpile osmoprotectants, a light-activated DNA repair enzyme, and layers of antioxidant enzymes. Oddly, the strain grew better and clumped more under nutrient-poor conditions when light was present. The study reads the genome as an adaptation manual for life between the tides.
pmc-11638710:
Pham and six co-authors report a new record and diet study of a poorly known treefrog in Vietnam, in work from twenty twenty-four. The white lipped treefrog Zhangixalus pachyproctus was described only in twenty nineteen. It had long been confused with a similar species across China, Vietnam, and Thailand.

Misidentified records were corrected when the new species was named from form and DNA evidence. The Vietnamese record extends its known range. Dietary ecology, what the frog eats, was documented from field samples. For a species known from few specimens, each record sharpens range maps and conservation assessments.
pmc-11639810:
Dorota Wloga and co-authors review tiny beating hairs, called motile cilia, in human fertility in a 2024 article. Rows of these hairs line parts of the male and female reproductive tracts. Their synced beating moves fluid, particles, and cells along the tract walls, steps that conception depends on.

The review maps where the ciliated cells sit in each tract, from the fallopian tube and uterus to male ducts. It explains how flow from beating helps move eggs, sperm, and early embryos. When cilia beat out of sync, move weakly, or fail to move, the result can be reduced fertility or full infertility. The authors gather what is known and where gaps remain.
pmc-11640010:
Maria Carolina Souza and co-authors study a protein fragment in dog breast tumors that may help the tumors invade nearby tissue, in a 2024 paper. The fragment is snipped from a larger matrix protein by scissor-like enzymes, and it can shift immune behavior in some cancers. The team compared two kinds of spontaneous dog mammary tumors with different outlooks.

The fragment clustered near invasion fronts in one tumor type, and one enzyme stood out as its likely cutter. A certain collagen type moved opposite to the parent protein in early tumor areas. The authors suggest the fragment and its enzyme shape the tumor's surroundings, and that the pair could inform diagnosis and care in dogs and people.
pmc-11640110:
Sepideh Hosseininejad and co-authors turn a problem fruit into a snack bar in this 2024 study. The 'Rojo Brillante' persimmon is too astringent to enjoy raw, and large amounts of the harvest go to waste. The team dried the fruit and built it into an energy bar with walnuts, hazelnuts, and chia seeds.

The finished bar carried more healthy fat, protein, and fiber than other fruit bars they compared it with. The dried persimmon held the bar together on its own, so no syrups or gums were needed. During storage, the bitter tannins fell while color compounds and antioxidant activity held steady. A lab digestion test showed the tannins survived digestion well, while the color compounds mostly did not. The authors present the bar as a natural snack that also cuts farm waste.
pmc-11640210:
Radiation to the brain can prevent lung cancer spread there, but it also clouds thinking, and its value is being rethought in the immunotherapy era. Alice Daumas and co-authors reviewed real-world care in 2024 for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer at a French center. Fifty-six patients who qualified for preventive brain radiation were split between those who got it and those who did not.

Survival and time free of brain spread did not differ significantly between the groups. Patients without radiation lived longer on median, but they also received immunotherapy more often, which muddies the comparison. Starting fitness and a blood ratio predicted outcomes better than the radiation choice. The authors say the study found no benefit for the preventive treatment in this real-life mix.
pmc-11640310:
Bartłomiej Zieniuk and co-authors test farm and food waste as cheap homes for a working enzyme in this 2024 study. The enzyme is a lipase, widely used in food work, and pinning it to a solid support makes it stabler and reusable. Their candidate supports were buckwheat husks, pea hulls, loofah sponges, and yerba mate waste.

The materials were cleaned in different ways, from solvent washing to acid and alkali baths for the loofah. The team then loaded them with a commercial lipase or with yeast cells that make their own, and measured how well each setup broke down and built up fats. Alkali-treated loofah gave the best fat-breaking activity, while brewed yerba mate leaves led on the building side. The authors present the waste supports as a working example of a circular economy in food processing.
pmc-11640610:
Chijioke Emenike and co-authors track how the chemistry of haskap leaves changes as the plant grows, across three varieties of the berry shrub. Haskap fruit gets the attention, but its leaves also carry sugars, acids, amino acids, and polyphenols worth harvesting. Timing decides their value. Their 2024 study samples leaves of Indigo Gem, Wojtek, and Jolanta at successive growth stages.

A targeted mass spectrometry panel quantifies the mix at each stage. Nearly every prized compound class peaked early and fell by fruiting. The leafing stage, before fruit takes over the plant's budget, offers the richest leaves. Growers sitting on pruned foliage get a harvest calendar for a byproduct they currently throw away.
pmc-11641110:
Jie Chen and co-authors found the enzyme behind a lone ribosome mark in two thousand twenty-four. Ribosomal RNA carries many chemical marks. One mark, on the large subunit's RNA, lacked an owner. It appears in humans and frogs but not yeast. Fruit flies carry the same mark, the team showed. An enzyme called Ptch writes it there.

The human counterpart, SPOUT1, does the same job. Both enzymes proved necessary and sufficient in tests. The marked base sits at a functional hub. Mutant fly cells lost ribosome performance without it. Protein building suffered in those cells. The finding closes a basic enzymology gap. It may matter for human ribosome diseases.
pmc-11641310:
Mehmet Onur Aksoy and co-authors probe in a 2024 study how a gene switch drives fat cell growth in pigs. The switch, tied to a gene called SREBF1, steers fat use and cell fate and comes in two forms. Pig fat work had mapped fat use well but left the forms' roles in growth unclear.

The team cut a control region for the growth linked form with a gene editing tool. That cut left one gene alone but dropped two fat genes and raised a third. Two more genes key to fat cell fate were blocked by the cut. With those shifts, fat cell growth halted in the tests. The results assign the growth linked form a clear driver role in pig fat growth.
pmc-11641410:
Zhe Yang and co-authors find the storage sweet spot for rice meant for fresh noodles. Paddy rice is often stored for months before milling, and storage time changes the grain. Their 2024 study used fourteen rice varieties stored for six, nine, or twelve months, then milled into fresh rice noodles.

Noodles from nine-month rice beat both fresher and older batches in quality tests. The team linked the edge to gel consistency, a measure of how cooked rice paste behaves. When that value sat near 32 millimeters, noodle quality peaked. Statistical methods that weigh many traits at once confirmed the pattern. The results give noodle makers a clear rule for picking and timing their raw rice.
pmc-11641510:
Tomasz Chmiela and co-authors ask how often blood sugar control goes off track in people with Parkinson's disease. Both Parkinson's and type 2 diabetes grow more common with age, and past work hints at a link. One guess blames faults in the autonomic nervous system, which helps steer sugar levels. Their 2024 study ran for 14 days of round-the-clock glucose checks.

The group held 35 people with Parkinson's and 20 matched healthy controls. The Parkinson's group leaned toward lower morning glucose. Those with autonomic symptoms swung more widely and dipped lower in the mornings. Signs such as blood pressure drops on standing stood out. The work ties shaky sugar control to the spread of autonomic faults.
pmc-11641610:
Xiaolan Zhang, Lingbo Liu, and Antonio Campese review, published in 2024, whether worn-out T cells quietly drive acute myeloid leukemia forward. This fast blood cancer kills through relapse and drug resistance, and immune therapy often fails against it. The review gathers signs that T cells in the marrow age early: they slow, change their surface marks, and stop killing well. Leukemia itself seems to push that aging. Aged T cells then shield the cancer instead of fighting it.

The authors chart the signals that drive the aging and the traits that mark it. They also weigh treatments meant to slow, dodge, or reverse the wear. Options range from drugs that clear aged cells to ways of shielding fresh immune cells. The piece is a map for trial designers rather than a trial itself. Its claim: fixing T cell youth may be the missing half of leukemia immune therapy.
pmc-11641710:
Niti Sharma, Seong Soo An, and Sang Yun Kim published a review in 2024 on common drugs and dementia risk. Older adults often take many drugs for long-term ills like high blood pressure, diabetes, and poor sleep. Some drugs may harm thinking or speed decline, even as they help the body.

The review covers five drug classes: pain drugs, drugs that block a nerve signal, sedatives, stomach acid drugs, and cholesterol drugs. It sums up cohort studies, trials, and past reviews for each class. The findings clash across studies, so no clear verdict on risk emerges. Blood tests for early disease signs may help future work, the authors note. They call for open weighing of gains and harms for each patient.
pmc-11642010:
Hebe Al Asadi and a large team study aspirin response in patients with a HeartMate 3 heart pump, in a 2024 paper. Pump patients usually take drugs that prevent clots, yet clots, bleeding, and stroke still occur. The team asked whether poor aspirin response raises those risks.

Thirty-two patients had their aspirin response tested twice with a standard assay. Resistance was common at the first test and somewhat lower at the second, without a clear change over time. Event rates did not differ between responders and non-responders. The authors suggest aspirin may play only a small role in this pump's drug regimen.
pmc-11642110:
Twenty-five years of outcomes for a lesser surgery on benign growths near the bile duct are reported by the authors in work dated 2024. Full removal of the pancreas head is the norm for cancer there, but it is harsh for benign growths. The lesser cut, done through the gut wall, suits small benign lumps when scope care fails. The team tracked fifty-three patients treated from 1996 to 2023.

About a third had problems in the first month, with few harsh ones. Deaths by ninety days were rare. Some lumps proved to be early cancers on lab checks, and a few growths came back. Lifelong scope checks are urged after this kind of surgery.
pmc-11642210:
Sadettin Uslu and co-authors report a 2024 study of a biosimilar drug in spine arthritis. Ankylosing spondylitis stiffens the spine through inflammation. CT-P13 is a biosimilar copy of infliximab, a proven antibody drug. The team asks how well it works and how long patients stay on it in real practice. Data come from a national Turkish registry of biologic drugs, covering 2014 to 2021. Patients split into first-line users and those on it after other biologics.

Drug persistence, safety, and effect are tracked in both groups. Registry data answer questions trials cannot: what happens over years, in mixed patients, after switches. Rheumatologists get persistence numbers that guide counseling when a cheaper biosimilar is offered. Payers care too, since biosimilars cut costs only if patients stay on them. First-versus-later line splits show whether prior failures dim the copy's value.
pmc-11642310:
Maciej Wilczak and co-authors looked back at the records of women who received a surgical mesh for pelvic organ prolapse, in a 2024 study. Prolapse, where pelvic organs slip from their place, affects three to four in ten women, and one or two in ten need surgery. The team judged one lightweight plastic mesh brand, placed through the belly or the vagina at several centers. Eighty-one patients aged twenty-eight to eighty-three were followed.

At three check-up visits, patients reported high satisfaction and little pain or discomfort. Many said their quality of life had clearly improved. No serious implant-linked problems appeared in the records. The authors conclude the mesh worked safely for the conditions treated, which include bladder, bowel, and womb prolapse. They note the study is a look back, not a trial, so stronger designs should confirm the picture.
pmc-11642610:
Claudia Massaccesi and a large team of co-authors tested whether hormone levels in hair predict social choices, in a 2024 study. Past work tied testosterone to social behavior, but results from blood or saliva measures were mixed. Hair measures capture hormone levels built up over time. The sample held just over one thousand young adults from a community cohort.
