Hair testosterone linked weakly to lower trust in a money game. It also linked weakly to self-reported aggression. Both links faded once factors such as hair color and drug use were taken into account. No other social behavior showed a clear link. Hair cortisol, a stress hormone, did not change any of these patterns. The authors conclude there is no real evidence for a role of hair hormone levels in social choices.
pmc-11642710:
Esra Kayacan Erdoğan, Hakan Babaoğlu, and Eugen Feist published a pilot study in two thousand twenty-four pitting trainee doctors against AI on rheumatology cases. Ten junior residents and two GPT-4 models, one specially trained and one not, worked ten cases of inflammatory arthritis.

Cases were scored for reasoning quality and staged management choices. The trained model beat the residents at every stage, from first impression to second-line treatment. Residents then reviewed its answers and answered attitude questions. Sixty percent favoured AI as a support tool, expecting gains in competence and relief from fatigue and burnout. The authors frame AI as an assistant, not a replacement. The study was small and single-specialty.
pmc-11643310:
Chojnacka-Brożek and co-authors study how two flowable dental filling materials behave when squeezed. Dentists use these tooth-colored composites to repair teeth, and a filling that is too weak or too stiff can fail in the mouth. Knowing the elastic properties helps predict how a repair will hold up.

The team compressed samples of EverX Flow and Flow-Art and measured strain with both strain gauges and a camera-based method called digital image correlation. EverX Flow proved stronger and stiffer, while both methods gave near-identical Poisson's ratio values. A computer model fed with the measured values matched the camera results well, showing the camera method can reliably test such materials.
pmc-11643410:
Zannara Mustafa and co-authors tuned production of a dye-eating enzyme from engineered bacteria in 2024. Laccase enzymes can break down textile dyes in wastewater. The team cloned a laccase gene from a Bacillus strain found in Punjab soil into a workhorse laboratory strain of Escherichia coli.

Growth tuning set sugar, yeast extract, copper, acidity, and timing for best yield. The crude enzyme then attacked five commercial dyes in test runs. Removal ranged widely, from about seven percent for one dye to over eighty percent for another. Spectral checks confirmed chemical change in the dyes. The process points to cheap enzyme supply for dye clean-up.
pmc-11643510:
Sergio Caprara led a team that tested, in two thousand twenty-four, a new view of cuprate superconductors. Cuprates are copper oxide wares that carry current with no loss at quite high heat. How their electrons act just above that point is still in dispute.

One view is the marginal Fermi liquid. The team's own view is the shrinking Fermi liquid. In their view, near a quantum critical point, swings of the order term scatter electrons near evenly across the Fermi surface. That gives the odd metal act seen in tests. Past light tests were read as a win for the first view. The team shows the heat range was too slim to split the two views. At high wave rates, their view fits the light data just as well.
pmc-11643610:
Bunka Son and three co-authors built a way to grade earthquake damage in concrete columns from crack photos in a 2024 paper. The columns are a resilient type, reinforced with weakly bonded ultra-strong bars, meant for quake-prone regions like Japan and China. Judging their damage by eye is slow and uneven.

The team photographed cracks on eight tested columns and measured each pattern's fractal dimension, a number for how wiggly and branched the cracks are. The number rose in step with how far the columns had drifted sideways in testing, and one column property, the shear span ratio, shaped the link. They fit simple equations tying crack pattern, past drift, and leftover drift together for quick assessments.
pmc-11643710:
Mila Milenkovic and co-authors turned fruit brandy waste in 2024 into a carbon shield against electromagnetic waves. Modern life leaks radio signals everywhere, and interference is a pollution of its own, so demand for green blocking materials is rising. The team started with the stillage left after distilling apple and quince schnapps.

Mixed with potassium hydroxide and baked at 850 degrees under nitrogen, the waste carbonized into a porous char. Such carbons can swallow microwaves instead of letting them pass or bounce. The study weighs the shield's performance alongside the full modern checklist: cheap feedstock, low energy, and little new pollution. The byline is long; the work is framed by its lead author. Readers get a circular-economy material: orchard waste, charred once, standing guard against stray signals.
pmc-11643810:
Sha Ni and co-authors report a 2024 study of copper state in a catalyst that turns carbon dioxide into fuel with light. The catalyst pairs copper oxide grains with titanium dioxide. Copper can sit in varied charge states, and those states steer which product forms, but they shift easily and their roles were fuzzy.

The team grew the catalyst in place with a reduction method to pin set copper mixes. Two charge states proved to be the main active sites. One state favored methane output, while the other favored carbon monoxide. How carbon monoxide sticks to and wakes on each surface set the split. The work gives builders a lever for product choice.
pmc-11644010:
Pipeline steel rusts at rates that depend on the water around it. Daniela Buruiană and co-authors soaked a common grade in salt water and drinking water for six months, in work from twenty twenty-four. Coupons were pulled at set hours and read by scopes, ray scans, roughness and hardness tests, plus weight loss and current measures.

Weight-based rust rates in salt water slowed over time as a skin formed, while drinking-water rates held near steady. Current-based rates ran higher in salt water. The pair of methods brackets the truth from both sides. The aim is shop-floor guidance: where this steel lasts, where it fails early, and what that costs.
pmc-11644110:
Erica Wiborg, Amber Manning-Ouellette, and Melissa Rocco write about pushback in leadership training in a 2024 article. They set out what such training looks like and how resistance shows up in the room.

The authors describe resistance as a knowing act, spoken, thought, or physical, that stands against a person or an idea. Stories from training sessions show the forms it can take. They stress that trainers need to know the setting, what is being resisted, and who is involved before they respond. The article then offers practices trainers can use when resistance appears. It serves as an entry point for people who run or study leadership programs.
pmc-11644210:
Jing Wu and co-authors use drilling signals to spot weak roof rock in mine tunnels in this 2024 study. As crews drill anchor holes, layered gaps and soft bands in the roof threaten tunnel safety. The team asked whether the drill itself can warn of those zones in real time.

Push force, twist force, and shaking signals each changed in clear ways over different rock layers. Lab tests, computer simulations, and field runs agreed on the patterns. A learning system built on the signals found every layered gap in tests and flagged weak zones with high accuracy. The method could let crews add support exactly where the roof needs it, before trouble starts.
pmc-11644310:
Itraconazole kills a broad range of fungi but dissolves so poorly in water that little of an oral dose reaches the blood, and high doses bring side effects. Huang and co-authors attacked both problems by locking the drug into water-loving polymers as an amorphous dispersion, which raised its solubility and speed of dissolving. They screened five polymers, extruded the mixes, and checked the products with heat, X-ray, and microscope tests.

One polymer, soluplus, won out and was extruded into printing filament. Tablets were then designed and 3D printed, and their release tests showed the dose curve could be programmed by changing the tablet's printed structure. The authors argue that pairing hot-melt extrusion with 3D printing is a strong route to personalized antifungal doses, printed to fit each patient's needs.
pmc-11644410:
Rehab Mahdy and seven colleagues present a 2024 field study on feeding peas with fulvic acid, a natural soil compound sold as a growth booster. Over two growing seasons they compared two delivery routes: soaking seeds before planting, called priming, and spraying leaves, each at two doses plus a water control.

Both routes helped, and the higher dose helped most, but seed priming won overall. Primed plants gave the most pods, the most seeds per pod, and the heaviest hundred-seed weights and yields. Spraying did edge ahead on leaf pigments and leaf carbohydrates. The authors recommend priming pea seed at three grams per liter as the cheap, effective way to lift productivity.
pmc-11644610:
Paulina Spanu, Bogdan Felician Abaza, and Teodor Catalin Constantinescu build in 2024 a neural network that predicts the heat generated when milling glass fiber reinforced plastic. Such composites are shaped by milling to tight tolerances, and the temperature in the cutting zone strongly shapes the quality of the finished surface.

Their model was built with a graphical virtual instrument and trained on machining data. A reliable temperature forecast lets operators choose speeds and feeds before scarring a costly part. The study links a smart model to a practical workshop problem in composite manufacturing.
pmc-11644710:
Andreas Economides, Md Niamul Islam, and Konstantinos Baxevanakis study 3D printed plastic parts strengthened with short carbon fibers, in a 2024 paper. They varied how the parts were printed, including the internal pattern, the amount of empty space, and whether parts were heat treated after printing. They then tested stiffness, strength, and response to vibration.

Empty space inside the part had the largest effect on most traits, while the internal pattern mattered most for stiffness under pulling. Heat treatment raised stiffness in all samples tested. Microscope images showed fibers pulling out of the plastic, which points to weak bonding, but also showed better bonding between printed lines after heat treatment. The findings can guide design of printed parts for specific loads.
pmc-11644810:
Zhipeng Li and six co-authors study a display flaw called friction greening in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Polyimide is a flexible base used in foldable OLED screens. After long use, friction can build charge in the base and shift green pixels, making the screen look green.

The team tested how heat during making changes the inner structure of the material. Higher heat made chain segments more ordered, raised conductivity, and made charge traps more shallow. Tests with X rays, light, and electric measures backed this up. With less charge stored over time, the voltage drift that drives the flaw fell. The work points to a clear fix in how the base is made.
pmc-11644910:
A sensor that reads a material's insides without cutting it open can ride along a drying wall or a curing slab of cement. Floriberto Diaz-Diaz and three co-authors build such a sensor in this 2024 paper, modeled on the NMR MOUSE. A permanent magnet array plus a radio coil listens to hydrogen nuclei a centimeter and a half above its face.

Sliding the probe builds one-dimensional profiles of how fast the nuclei relax, a fingerprint of water's state inside. Test erasers of layered rubber resolved at one-millimeter steps, and cement pastes, white and ordinary, told apart cleanly at a week old. The team also profiled an avocado and a beef steak. The report is an instrument paper: design, calibration, and proof on pantry and construction alike.
pmc-11646210:
Frazer and a large team reviewed in twenty twenty-four when a single drug is the best first care for spread kidney cancer. Mix care with two drug kinds is now common, but it is not right for all. They focus on one drug, tivozanib, that blocks a growth switch for blood vessels.

For folks with a good outlook, long-term data back single-drug care with fair life and life quality. This drug matches peers on strength but has fewer off-target side harms. The choice turns on risk class, age, other ills, and what the patient values most. Guides still list single-drug care as a norm for the good-outlook group.
pmc-11646810: Mohammad Dehbozorgi and six co-authors report a severe fungal infection after COVID-19 in a 2024 paper. The mold invades nose, eye socket, and brain, and it can kill quickly. Their case report walks through one patient's full management. The authors stress keeping suspicion high in anyone with a recent COVID-19 history, even without the usual risk factors like uncontrolled diabetes. Fast diagnosis, aggressive surgical removal of infected tissue, and antifungal drugs together gave the case its successful course, and they urge the same bundle elsewhere.
pmc-11646910:
Yuko Matsui and co-authors presented a heart rhythm puzzle in two thousand twenty-four. A very long gap between heart signals is rare and hard to read. In this case the upper chamber signal fell right after the main beat. That odd placement made the rhythm easy to misread. The tracing mixed in early beats from the lower chamber as well.

The authors show how close attention solves the puzzle. The shape of the upper chamber signal gives a key clue. Early lower beats that merge with normal ones help confirm timing. Getting the rhythm right guides safe treatment choices. Misreading could lead to the wrong device or drug plan. The case trains clinicians to slow down on odd tracings.
pmc-11647310:
Lorenzo Zanasi and co-authors lay out a trial plan for worn knees that lack a key cushion. Their 2024 protocol covers knee arthritis in one compartment, caused by loss of the meniscus plus bowed leg alignment. Bone cutting surgery plus a donor meniscus has shown promise, but proof is thin.

The trial will assign 52 patients aged 20 to 60 by chance to one of two arms. One arm gets the bone cut plus the donor tissue, and the other gets the bone cut alone. Knee scores, pain scales, scans, and walking tests track patients for a year. The main score comes at 12 months. The design aims to show if the added tissue truly helps.
pmc-11647410:
Junhyung Lee and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, how long a play object should stay in the pen after piglets are weaned. Weaning is a stressful break for young pigs, and a richer pen may ease it. Two hundred forty weanlings were split into four groups: no object, or an object kept for one, two, or four weeks. Growth, feeding, and behavior were tracked for four weeks.

Pigs with the object for two or four weeks gained weight faster than the rest. The two-week group also ate more early on. Diarrhea in the first week fell under the longer enrichment plans. Fighting behaviors, such as biting at penmates, tails, and ears, dropped as well. Keeping the object for at least two weeks looks like the sweet spot for growth and welfare.
pmc-11647810:
Md Asif All Azad and three co-authors check water and soil near a coal mine in Bangladesh, in this twenty twenty-four study. Mining can load water and soil with heavy metals and change their quality across seasons. Local people depend on that water for drinking and crops.

The team sampled nine spots in summer and winter, taking water and soil to labs for testing. Surface water was broadly fit for watering crops, though haze and chemical load meant it needed treatment before drinking. Metal build-up and soil fertility were scored with set indexes. The results give a base for guarding health near the mine.
pmc-11649410:
Yoana Estrada-Reyes and co-authors study serotonin loss and flexible learning in rats in a 2024 paper. The prefrontal cortex steers behavior when rules flip. Serotonin there helps animals switch, and its loss delays reversal learning. How it tunes brain rhythms during the switch was not clear.

Male rats did a spatial reversal task in a water T-maze after serotonin depletion. Learning the flipped rule took longer for depleted rats. Theta rhythm power rose in two prefrontal subregions. Coupling between the orbitofrontal area and its neighbors also grew. The results say serotonin shapes flexibility by tuning both the strength and the sync of prefrontal rhythms.
pmc-11649710:
Hubert Hörterer and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on repeat surgery for a painful heel tendon problem. The tendon joins the calf muscle to the heel bone, and it can wear down where it meets the bone. First-time surgery for this problem follows a clear plan. Much less is known about what happens when that first surgery fails and a second one is tried.

The team tracked patients at one large center who had the repeat surgery and checked on them at least a year later. Nineteen of the twenty-four patients took part in the final check, about four to five years on. Their pain and function scores were far better than before surgery. Still, only about one third felt as well as healthy people do.
pmc-11649910:
Waqas Faridi and four colleagues work out exact wave solutions for a plasma system of ion sound and Langmuir waves, in a twenty twenty-four mathematics paper. The system describes an electric field and a density ripple shaped by a nonlinear force in a charged gas. The team used three forms of fractional math, which track memory effects in the medium. A newer algebraic method then built the solutions.

The solutions came in many shapes: bright and dark solitons, mixed forms, and sharp singular waves. Graphs made with a math software package compared how the forms behave under picked settings. The authors note the method is fast and simple and can serve other nonlinear systems.
pmc-11650310:
Afsaneh Moghaddam Jafari and co-authors test a modified chitosan material in 2024 as a binder that could pull aflatoxins out of food and feed. Aflatoxins are mold poisons with strong toxic effects, and a safe binder could cut exposure. Their material joins chitosan with a common sulfate compound through ionic cross linking to raise its pull on the toxins.

Imaging showed a porous network that filled with toxin molecules after use, and light based tests confirmed new bonds in the joined material. Raising the binder share lifted toxin uptake greatly for several aflatoxin types, and acidity shaped the result. Cell harm tests were run before and after toxin removal to check safety. The authors present the material as a candidate binder whose pull and cell effects both need to be weighed.
pmc-11651510:
Zhang Hongxing and co-authors test in a 2024 study if low blood sodium causes bone thinning. The link between the two is disputed, and past ties may just reflect shared causes. A gene based method can pull cause apart from mere correlation.

Traits set at birth stand in for sodium levels in a two sample design. Bone density at four sites, from forearm to heel, forms the outcomes in view. Data came from large gene studies in European groups, with near half a million people for sodium. The main method found no causal effect of low sodium on bone density. Four backup methods agreed, and bias checks held firm, so the null result looks robust.
pmc-11651910:
Amy Balanoff reviews the study of dinosaur brains and senses, in this 2024 paper. Fascination with what dinosaurs could do began with the first fossil finds. The field reads brain cases from fossils to infer sight, smell, balance, and behavior.

Balanoff argues the field is maturing but faces three limits: a stable family tree, better methods for building brain casts, and fossil experts trained in neuroscience. Progress on all three now lets the field feed findings back into brain science. Most examples come from meat-eating dinosaurs and the origin of birds and flight. The review maps where the science stands and where it can go.
pmc-11652010:
Yinquan Ye and co-authors test whether a special MRI measure adds value to the standard prostate scoring system for finding important prostate cancer. The measure tracks protons on amide groups, and a second measure tracks how water moves in tissue. Both differ between important and less important cancers.

In men who had a biopsy or surgery soon after their scans, important cancers showed higher values on the first measure and lower on the second. Adding the first measure to the standard score clearly improved accuracy. Adding the second helped only a little more. Checks on new patients and decision curves supported the combined model's use in care.
pmc-11652110:
Ejgil Gravesen and co-authors report a 2024 study of food webs on land newly freed by a shrinking glacier in Greenland. The Arctic has warmed fast, and ice retreat leaves bare ground that life slowly claims. Small animals such as spiders and beetles are among the first hunters in such places.

The team read DNA from gut contents to learn what each hunter ate. They paired that with counts of animal activity on the ground, then joined the data in one model. The model shows chains driven from below by prey supply and chains driven from above by hunters. Which pattern ruled changed as plants grew in over time.
pmc-11652510:
The antibiotic cefotaxime saves lives but can injure the liver and kidneys. Shaimaa Azzam and co-authors tested in 2024 whether geranium oil shields rats from that damage.

Thirty rats were split into five groups: controls, antibiotic alone, oil alone, and the combination. After fourteen days, rats on the antibiotic alone showed the expected harm in blood markers and tissue samples. Rats also given the oil fared far better: liver enzymes and kidney markers dropped, inflammation signals fell, and protective compounds recovered. Microscope and staining checks confirmed healthier tissue. The authors conclude the oil blunts the drug's collateral damage.
pmc-11653710:
Dingwen Zhang and co-authors trace how pancreatic cancer spreads along nerves, in a study from 2024. Spread of this kind is a mark of poor outlook, above all when a key cancer gene is changed. The team finds a small round RNA, packed in tiny sacs shed by tumor cells, whose level rises with nerve spread in patients.

The sacs carry the RNA to nerve cells and prompt them to grow new fibers toward the tumor. The team shows how the RNA helps the sacs form by a side route that skips the normal sorting path. In a mouse model with the same gene changes, the loaded sacs drove strong nerve spread. The authors name the RNA as a target for new care.
pmc-11653810:
Lisa Guthardt and co-authors ask dental students in Germany what stresses them, what helps them cope, and what fixes they want. Their paper from 2024 notes that past work counts stressors but seldom asks students in their own words. Such views can shape better support and prevention.

Fifty seven students took part in seven group talks in the summer term of 2019. Stressors named ran from program planning and poor digital tools to hands on tasks, exams, the work setting, and social strain. Help came from good planning, hands on courses, patient work, and valued feedback. Students asked for regular joint meetings, clearer talk with staff, a central planning unit, and fixed grading rules.
pmc-11653910:
Hu and seven colleagues hunt for genes tied to a form of cell death in a kidney disease in twenty twenty-four. The disease harms the kidney's filters and is a top cause of kidney failure. The cell death form, called necroptosis, is planned by the cell and stirs inflammation. Its role in this disease was unclear.

The team mined public gene data from patients and healthy controls. They found seven hub genes that set patients apart and built a test from them. The test worked well on a second data set. Gene patterns also hinted at how immune cells act in the disease. Four known drugs were flagged as possible treatments to try.
pmc-11654310:
Biruk Zerfu and three co-authors survey chikungunya knowledge in Ethiopia's Afar Region in a 2024 study. The mosquito borne virus causes fever and joint pain across the tropics. Prevention leans on community behavior, so what people know matters. Two districts hosted the mixed methods study in late 2022 and early 2023.

Nearly three hundred adults answered a household survey. Focus groups added over a hundred voices in discussion. Two thirds had heard of the disease before. Among them, under half knew a virus causes it. Most believed the disease could be prevented. Knowledge gaps sat beside fairly positive attitudes. Regression analysis tied knowledge scores to social factors. The authors argue targeted teaching should precede control campaigns in the region.
pmc-11654410:
Dion Gajadin, Wouter van der Heijden, and Maarten van den Berg wrote a letter in two thousand twenty-four about an ultrasound score used in critical care. The VExUS score grades venous congestion from flow patterns in several veins. The authors respond to a report on how reliable that score is between observers.

They add a caution for patients on venovenous ECMO, a form of life support that moves blood outside the body. In one such patient, they saw a high-speed wave in a liver vein, which they name the B-wave. They think the wave comes from steady flow through the ECMO circuit. Its presence could mislead the congestion score, so vein choice and settings matter.
pmc-11654710:
Ulrich Heininger and co-authors reviewed in 2024 the rise of whooping cough germs that lack one key protein. Whooping cough has come back even in lands with high child vaccine rates. The missing protein, pertactin, is part of the germ that some vaccines train the body to attack. The team swept the world literature to mid-2023 for reports of such germs, with no bounds on place.

Such germs grew more common where the newer, part-based vaccines are used. They seem absent where whole-germ vaccines are used. That split backs the view that the new vaccines push the germ to shed the protein. Shots still guard well against illness, the team finds. They call for closer watch on how much the shift matters for care.
pmc-11655810: Madger published this 2024 letter clarifying what right atrial pressure means inside the circulation model of Guyton, replying to comments on an earlier review of fluid management. The letter insists on one distinction: the pressure does not measure venous return or cardiac output, which are flows. It shows instead how well the function of the heart matches the venous return offered to it. The same zero reading can mean a healthy person standing upright, or a heart starved by severe hemorrhage; context, not the number alone, tells which.
pmc-11655910:
Kim Cocks and co-authors review how cancer trials use time to deterioration of patient-reported outcomes, and how to do it better. Their review appeared in 2024. Such endpoints measure how long patients keep a given quality of life before it worsens. Trials define and analyze them in many ways, which muddies comparisons. The team gathered trials published from 2017 to 2022 and extracted every endpoint definition they found.

Seventy trials yielded 849 single endpoints across seventeen cancer types. Full definitions were often missing from reports. Choices about what counts as deterioration and how to treat side events changed results. The authors give best-practice advice: define the endpoint fully, state the assessment schedule, and report methods plainly. Their goal is trials whose quality-of-life claims can be trusted and compared.
pmc-11656110:
Daniel Adrian Lungu leads a team of eight authors in 2024 in testing who understood pandemic health videos, and why. During COVID-19, video carried much of the public guidance, in many formats and voices, and studies had mapped which video features work, but not which viewer traits change comprehension.

In a randomized experiment, viewers watched short health videos, and the team tested six personal characteristics for their effect on understanding. Traits like prior knowledge and trust may matter as much as production polish. The findings help health agencies design messages for the audiences least likely to absorb them the first time.
pmc-11656410:
Pallavi Priya and four co-authors report, in 2024 work, a hip-muscle abscess that aped a nerve ill. Such pus sacs are rare and oft missed, since the deep muscle sits near many parts and signs point astray. Late finds can kill. Their patient was a woman of fifty-four.

She came with right flank pain and signs like a lower nerve flaw. First tests told no tale. A scan then found a large pus pool by the right kidney and in the hip muscle, of likely urine-path birth, with a clean spine. Vein drugs began, and a scan proofed the pool. A sound-guided drain with a soft tube, plus aimed drugs, cleared it.
pmc-11656610:
Shitong Xie and co-authors, for a China study group, test a home-grown health survey for the Chinese public in a 2024 study. The survey, called CHROME-G, is the first of its kind built in China to turn health states into values for policy use. The team set it against two widely used foreign surveys to see how it stacks up.

A sample matched to the nation by age, sex, schooling, and town or country residence filled out all three surveys online. A repeat round came two weeks later to check steadiness. The team looked for ceiling and floor effects and for agreement with related and unrelated measures. Head-to-head results help health economists choose a survey whose values reflect Chinese views.
pmc-11656710:
Muhammad Sheraz and co-authors survey the burden of neurodevelopmental disorders in the Lakki Marwat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Published in 2024, the cross-sectional study ran from 2022 to 2023. Teams recruited families through district hospitals and door to door visits in both rural and urban areas, and recorded health, family, and social data.

In all, 276 cases or families were found. Most cases were sporadic, not passed down in a clear family pattern, and about 38 percent of families had low income. Traits such as marriage between kin, family type, and age of onset varied a lot between major and minor groups. The authors say non-genetic factors may play a large role, and better health care could cut the burden.
pmc-11656810:
Freddy Gnangnon and co-authors assessed breast cancer care in Sub-Saharan Africa in two thousand twenty-four. Death rates from breast cancer there are among the highest in the world. Yet rates of new cases are among the lowest. The team asked whether hospitals doing breast surgery can offer full care. Full care spans testing, surgery, and follow-up drug or radiation treatment.

The study reused data from a large global surgery project. It covered hospitals across the region that treat breast cancer. The authors checked which tests and added treatments each hospital could offer. Gaps in testing and follow-up care were common. The findings point to where health systems should invest first. Better linked care could improve survival for many women.
pmc-11656910:
Yun Yao and co-authors present a 2024 study of a stress protein in the blood as a warning marker for lung patients whose blood vessels are failing. The tougher group has chronic lung disease plus high pressure in the lung arteries, a serious pairing. Lung tissue and blood from hundreds of patients and controls were compared.

The protein ran high in the paired disease, in tissue and blood alike. It rose and fell with inflammation signals and vessel strain markers, and against oxygen levels. Statistical checks gave it strong predictive value for the pairing. The authors propose it as a blood test candidate to flag vessel trouble early in lung disease.
pmc-11657210:
Kelin Mou and co-authors weigh a protein family in lung cancer in a 2024 study. The proteins, called cavins, build tiny flask-shaped pits in cell skins that run food intake, signals, and fat store. Past work ties cavins to tumor growth, spread, and new vessel growth, with two-faced roles by cancer kind.

Their role in the most common lung cancer was unmapped. The team read cavin levels, survival links, immune cell mix, and pathway work in patient data banks. Some cavins track with better outlooks, others with worse. The study flags cavins as marks and maybe targets.
pmc-11657510:
Jacob Blindenbach and co-authors present SQUiD in a 2024 paper on safe storage of genetic data for precision medicine. Gene and trait datasets keep growing, and the cloud is a cheap place to hold them. Their private nature, plus mixed laws across places, calls for stronger guards than a plain database gives.

SQUiD lets many users store and query such data on a low-cost public cloud while it stays encrypted. The method used lets the cloud run searches on locked data without opening it. Tests with made-up data and with UK Biobank data show the system works in practice and scales to large sets.
pmc-11657610:
Huanyu Zhang and five colleagues published a 2024 cross-sectional study from China on parents of autistic children. Behavioral interventions work best when parents carry them out consistently at home. Sticking to the program improves children's behavior and parents' own outcomes, yet the burden on parents is heavy and multidimensional.

Earlier studies measured mainly health-related well-being, which misses much of that burden. This study instead used capability well-being, a broader measure of what a person is able to do and be. The researchers surveyed caregivers and tested how strongly adherence to the intervention was associated with this wider well-being. Their approach gives services a fuller picture of what supporting parents should achieve.
pmc-11657810:
Jianfei E and five co-authors test blood measures that might catch deep vein thrombosis early after a leg fracture. Their twenty twenty-four article deals with a common risk: clots in deep leg veins around the time of surgery for traumatic fractures. Ultrasound is the standard check, but a blood-based early flag would help.

The team reviewed patients from one year of admissions and split them by ultrasound proof of clots. Sixty-one had clots and one hundred ninety-one did not. Several clot-related markers and a clot-strength test ran higher in the clot group. A risk model kept eight factors, among them hip fracture and a clinical risk score. The markers showed real diagnostic value.
pmc-11658210:
Heewon Kang and Dong Ha Kim examine what shapes how the oldest South Koreans rate their own health, comparing city and country dwellers. People in their eighties and nineties are a fast growing group, and self rated health guides policy. Their 2024 study analyzes a national survey of 21,896 adults aged eighty to ninety nine.

Among those in their eighties, city dwellers more often rated health good than rural peers, while the pattern flipped slightly in the nineties. Education and higher income linked to better ratings in the eighties, less so later. Across all groups, regular walking, good oral health, and social activity tied to better self ratings. The authors offer the patterns as guidance for aging policy in both settings.
pmc-11658410:
Zhigang Li, Siqi Peng, Decong Zhang, and Lulin Liu present a 2024 study on heavy metals in the blood and fecal incontinence in American adults. Losing bowel control is common and distressing, and metals are known to disturb gut microbes and the gut wall. Whether blood metal levels track with the condition was unknown.

Data came from national health survey cycles between 2005 and 2010, covering 12,142 adults. Bowel health answers were paired with lab measures of cadmium, lead, and mercury. Higher cadmium and lead each linked to more incontinence in raw models. After full adjustment, both links stayed significant, with the top cadmium group at notably higher odds. Mixture methods checked the metals acting together.
pmc-11659210:
Taizhi Lin, Qianhui Wang, Zixuan Tan, Wen Zuo, and Rong Wu analyze how neighborhood social life affects older adults' mental health in China. Older adults' living space shrinks as physical function declines, making the neighborhood social environment a major influence. Using the twenty eighteen China Labor Dynamics Survey, the authors modeled neighborhood ties, trust, and security as the social environment. Subjective well-being was the mediator and green space the moderator.

Structural equation modeling found social trust and community security directly and positively associated with mental health. All three social factors also promoted mental health indirectly, by raising subjective well-being. Green space strengthened the link between neighborhood ties and mental health. The mechanism matters for policy: neighborliness works partly by making older people feel their lives go well, and greenery amplifies the social benefit. Community investment should be social and spatial together.
pmc-11659510:
In twenty twenty-four, de Lorenzo reported a science outreach effort that brings microbiology lessons into Spanish prisons. The effort is run by Spain's National Research Council with a development charity. It aims to raise inmates' grasp of microbes and their weight in daily life. It follows a world drive for microbial literacy.

Talks use plain metaphors to turn inmates from passive listeners into people who join in. The core points are simple. Earth is a microbial planet, and each body hosts vast microbiomes that shape health and social life. Microscopes open up the hidden microbial world and spark curiosity. Cases from microbial biotechnology, like bioplastics and skin bacteria bred against acne, show the useful side of microbes. The author argues such literacy helps shut-out groups bear their time inside and rejoin life outside.
pmc-11662210:
Arianna Poli and co-authors study who skips digital health studies among older adults in a 2024 paper. Older adults join such research unevenly, by age, sex, health, and digital skill. Little was known about how that uneven mix bends study results, or how to correct it, so the team used data from a Swedish day surgery monitoring study.

First, effects were tested in a sample of 281 people aged fifty and older with two standard unweighted methods. Then the team weighted the effects using known chances of joining at each selection step. Effects proved too high, due to over joining by groups that gained most. The weighting method offers a fix for future digital health trials.
pmc-11662910:
Xiangyong Li and co-authors build a survival chart for rectal cancer from two blood ratios in 2024. One ratio weighs a protein against an enzyme. The other sums inflammation load. Three hundred fifty six surgery patients were split into training and check groups. Machine learning picked the strongest forecast factors.

Low ratio patients fared worse, and one mixed group fared worst of all. Five factors entered the final chart. Its accuracy scores ran high in both groups. Fit curves and benefit checks backed the chart. The authors say both blood marks can flag risk before surgery. The chart may help doctors counsel patients on outlook.
pmc-11663710:
Jitka Široká led a large team on a plant study in twenty twenty-four about how plants keep a stress hormone's raw stock in check. The raw stock, called cis-OPDA, can act on its own, apart from the main hormone path. Years ago, one tagged form of it was found in hurt leaves. The team went looking for more.

They found five tagged forms in a small lab plant, each built by linking the stock to a common building block of proteins. The tagged forms piled up when the plant faced attack or harsh stress. Their levels rose and fell through the work of two enzyme groups, one that tags and one that frees. The tagged forms acted much like the raw stock itself. Plants, it seems, bank the signal for later use.
pmc-11664110:
Sughashini Murugesu and co-authors survey London trainees in women's health on remote care after the COVID years in a 2024 study. Phone and video visits spread fast during the pandemic. Training bodies wanted to know how junior doctors view that shift and its effect on learning.

The survey reached the 2022 group of trainees, and 118 of 255 replied. Nearly all had used remote care in clinic, and most backed its place in future practice. Time saved was the top plus; language gaps were a top snag. Many said remote visits gave weak hands-on training. Most favored online teaching for class work. The results can guide how programs blend remote care with the training doctors still need in person.
pmc-11664910:
Bacteria lack the membrane rooms that bigger cells use, so many build protein shells instead, tiny cages that hold enzymes and keep risky chemistry penned in. Tobias Giessen reviews one large family of these shells in a 2024 paper. The shells snap together into ball-like forms with twenty faces, each shell able to pull in its own chosen cargo.

The review tours how the shells differ across species: how they assemble, how their symmetry varies, and how they flex as they work. Pores in the shell wall let small goods pass while the cargo stays trapped. Some shell parts carry extra domains fused or tucked inside, which widen what the cage can do. Giessen closes with open questions and the structural work still needed to grasp these cages in full.
pmc-11667610:
Sion Cha and Wooksung Kim model the inner ear's balance sensors when the head spins off-center. Most studies assume the rotation axis passes through the canals' center, yet daily motion rarely obliges. Testing a real offset is hard because the canal's sensing membrane is too soft to mimic well in physical mock-ups.

The pair instead built a computer model coupling fluid and structure inside the canals, then ran step and waving motions through it. As the offset grew, the sensor's gain rose while its slow response constant shrank. That drift exposes blind spots in the simple filter models engineers use today. The authors offer a corrected transfer formula that carries the offset, aimed at virtual reality and motion-sickness work.
pmc-11668610:
Jun Zhu, Yuanda Zhang, Guangxian Yang, and Shuxian Liu race three models that predict pepper plant development under drought. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Growers need timing forecasts that survive water stress.

Peppers grew under set soil moisture bands for varying days. Mild shortage sped development briefly; severe or long shortage delayed it. Three clocks were tested: physiological development time, a heat-and-light product, and simple degree days. The physiological clock fit best across growth stages, with errors near a day. It was then used to build forecast models across the full moisture range, giving growers a drought-aware calendar for flowering and harvest.
pmc-11668810:
Zhao Wu, Chengyu Yuan, and Xue Peng asked in 2024 whether joint diseases raise the risk of heavy bleeding after childbirth. They used a genetic method that mimics a trial, testing the link in both directions. Gene data came from a large open database.

Forward tests suggested joint diseases do act as a risk factor for such bleeding. Reverse tests found no link running the other way. Checks for bias and mixed effects supported the result. The team also found thirty-three linked genes, tied to defence responses and cell killing pathways. The work offers clues for study of the body process behind the link.
pmc-11669010:
Pamela Reyes and co-authors name two new fungus species from Mexico, in a paper published in 2024. The fungi belong to a family found worldwide, richest in the tropics, whose members live on dead wood, inside plants, or as plant pests. The team rechecked herbarium specimens and fresh finds from the Yucatan Peninsula.

One new species is marked by spindle-shaped spores, and the other by wine-colored fruiting bodies and dark pigments that show in alkali tests. pmc-11669510:

pmc-11670810:

pmc-11670910:

pmc-11671110:

pmc-11671910:

pmc-11672510:

pmc-11672910:

pmc-11673010:

pmc-11673210:
Edward Madara and Achintya Bhowmik review the stigma around hearing aids in this 2024 paper. Hearing aids work better than ever, yet few who need them wear them. pmc-11673410:

pmc-11673610:
Ziyu Liu and Liyao Xiao surveyed college students about scrolling through social media in a 2024 study. Just browsing posts without posting, called passive use, has been tied to lower well-being. The team looked at the role of comparing oneself with others, which can cut in several directions.

pmc-11673710:
Mijun Noh and Jaehong Kim compare two ways of making thin zirconia veneers for teeth, in a 2024 study. One way mills the veneer from a solid block. The other prints it with a light-based printer. pmc-11674210:
Le Thi Nhu Ngoc and co-authors review a tree extract for cosmetics in a 2024 paper. Extracts of Dendropanax morbifera, a Korean medicinal tree, are sold for skin care. Claims include skin whitening, calm of inflammation, and germ control, plus safety on skin.

pmc-11674310:
Narongchai Autsavapromporn and co-authors present a 2024 pilot study hunting blood markers of lung cancer risk in a Thai area with high natural radiation. Radon gas indoors is a known driver of lung cancer. A chemical scan of blood might flag who is at risk before disease starts.

pmc-11674610:

pmc-11674710:
Yujie Zhang and co-authors test a spray-based method to fight false smut, a destructive rice disease, in a 2024 study. The fungus behind the disease is now a top threat to rice crops. pmc-11674810:
Pamela Ochoa-Lantigua and co-authors review a thin ribbon of brain tissue that may drive one kind of epilepsy in a 2024 paper. pmc-11674910:

pmc-11675010:

pmc-11675410:

pmc-11675910:

pmc-11676110:

pmc-11676310:

pmc-11676410:

pmc-11676510:

pmc-11676810:

pmc-11679710:

Ebba Könighofer and co-authors read the full sugar coat of the shell protein of the tick-borne brain fever virus in 2024. The virus rides tick bites across the north of Europe and Asia. Its shell protein wears one known sugar chain that helps it infect. The team used a fine mass-reading tool to map all chains on the protein, not just the known one.

They found three new chains of a second kind, each worn by few copies of the protein. One of the new chains sits close to the known site, near a loop that may steer how the shell works. The known site itself was near always dressed, in two chain styles. Some chains bore shapes seen when a cell's sugar line is jammed. That hint says the virus bends the host's coat works as it grows.
pmc-11680710:
Seven surgeons in India ran a small trial on whether a saliva gland can be spared during neck surgery for early mouth cancer, in work published in 2024. The surgery clears lymph nodes near the jaw, and the gland often comes out with them. Losing the gland can leave the mouth dry. The team compared twenty patients, some with the gland removed and some with it kept.

Keeping the gland made the operation a bit longer and raised blood loss by a small amount. The number of nodes found near the gland was the same in both groups, which eased fears about missed cancer. Dry mouth scores did not differ between groups in the first four weeks. No cancer came back in the glands that were kept, so the authors call sparing the gland a sound choice in early cases.
pmc-11681610:
Jiemei Ji and co-authors follow kidney injury in children after liver transplants, in a 2024 study. Kidney harm after this surgery is common, yet its long shadow was poorly charted. The team tracked 132 children, aged three months to twelve years, for a year after transplant.

About 45 percent developed acute kidney injury, split among mild, moderate, and severe grades. Half of those children had chronic kidney disease a year later, against 23 percent of children who escaped early injury. Moderate, severe, and long-lasting injury each raised the odds of chronic disease several-fold. Death within a year ran at 9.8 percent overall, higher after severe or prolonged injury. Guarding young kidneys in the first days after transplant looks vital.
pmc-11683610:
Kabir Rishi and co-authors measure in this 2024 study the tiniest silica dust thrown off when workers cut engineered stone countertops. Breathing crystalline silica is a rising job hazard, yet the nano-sized share of the dust was unmapped. The team made dust in a test chamber, sorted it by size, and read its crystal forms with X-ray and infrared tools.

Crystals made up seventy percent of the mass in the finest fraction, in two forms whose shares shifted with size. That finest share is only about one percent of the dust by mass, but up to a quarter of it by surface area that can land in lungs. The authors warn that mass-based safety checks may understate the risk.
pmc-11685010:
Chenhao Deng, Zhiyi Zhao, Nur maizura Ahmad Noorhani and Arniatul Mustapha wrote a 2024 paper framing how childcare room design shapes young children's play. They build the frame from ecological psychology, which studies how beings perceive and act in settings. Two ideas anchor it: what a setting invites a child to do, and how stable behavior patterns form in a place.

Past work, they argue, misses quick in-the-moment actions and treats settings as static. Their frame joins both ideas to guide study of indoor childcare rooms. They call for field checks: watch free play and test how well rooms match what children try to do.
pmc-11689010:
Wesley Browning, Mustafa Yildiz, and Carolyn Pickering track how youth trauma echoes in Black dementia carers, in a study from 2024. Black carers oft show less strain than white peers on crude sums, which can mask true risk. In-group reads, the team argues, see the spread that group sums hide.

One hundred one carers kept daily logs in three waves of 21 days each, more than five thousand days in all. Three youth harms were scored: care neglect, word abuse, and blows. Each was set twixt true ill-grade gloom, daily gloom weight, and daily death thoughts, in its own math run. The head shown here ends ere the scores land; the frame stands: youth wounds, split by kind, steer the carer mind years on.
pmc-11689310:
Rahul Malhotra, Ha-Linh Quach, and Jeremy Lim-Soh published this study in 2024. It looks at sleep among family caregivers of older adults in Singapore. Data covered 167 caregivers and 135 non-caregivers. Sleep quality was scored with a standard index, where higher marks mean worse sleep. The team also measured psychological resilience, the ability to bounce back from strain.

Caregivers slept worse on average, and nearly half had poor sleep, against about a quarter of non-caregivers. But the gap shrank as resilience rose. Among caregivers, better sleep went with more schooling, fewer chronic conditions, and fewer limits in daily function. Higher resilience also helped on its own. The authors point to resilience as a trait programs could strengthen to ease the sleep cost of caregiving.
pmc-11689410: Fabrisia Ambrosio's 2024 presentation abstract summarizes her laboratory's work on the youthful factors carried by parcels in the blood. Swapping blood between young and old animals shows that circulating factors steer how tissues age and heal. Attention has shifted from proteins to extracellular vesicles. These membrane-wrapped packages ferry messages between distant tissues. Her team found that ageing disrupts how these vesicles deliver their cargo to target cells, weakening tissue maintenance and repair. The talk describes engineering and exercise-based strategies meant to restore youthful vesicle communication in older people.
pmc-11689610:
Meneka Johnson Nicholson and Peter Martin studied what predicts long life in African American older adults in two thousand twenty-four. Longevity research has rarely focused on this group. Their data came from the Health and Retirement Study, a large national survey.

They followed seven hundred twenty-three African American participants from wave two and predicted age at death. Parents' ages at death did not predict longevity. Education and number of children mattered, as did body mass index and smoking. Four health markers, from self-rated health to diabetes, added further predictive power. Daily function and depression did not. The full model explained about thirty-five percent of the variation in age at death.
pmc-11689910:
Lyn Holley and Kenneth Hites presented a framework on the marginalization of drag artists in two thousand twenty-four. More than fourteen states had passed or weighed laws that restrict or criminalize public drag performance. Some bills label the art as adult cabaret, which the authors call a false conflation.

The presentation sets the bills in a wider wave of anti-LGBTQ measures that year. It argues the language of drag bans is also designed to oppress transgender people, a distinct community. Drawing on the idea of othering, the authors clarify what scholars alone can add. They can supply valid data on drag artists and their social and economic effects. That data can inform law and policy on free expression.
pmc-11690010:
Jacob Kimmel reports a screen for ways to make aging human immune cells act young again. Brief use of transcription factors, the proteins that switch genes on and off, can restore youthful gene activity in old cells. The few factors used so far also blur a cell's identity, though. Kimmel built a screening method called Partial-seq that tests thousands of factor sets at once in aged human T cells, a core part of the immune system that weakens with age.

Screening more than four thousand factor sets, he found many sets beyond the classic ones that restored youthful gene patterns without erasing T cell identity. Combinations worked better than single factors, and many gains lasted after the factors were switched off. The results suggest that the age of human T cells can be rolled back in a lasting way with a wide choice of tools.
pmc-11690310:
Ning Kang and four co-authors study what drives exercise among older adults who live at home in Beijing. Their twenty twenty-four survey drew seven hundred seventy valid replies, most from women. Four in ten people had low levels of activity. The team used a standard activity form and built a path model to sort direct from indirect effects.

Support for exercise, drive to move, and knowledge each had a direct link to activity. Belief in one's own skill worked in a less direct way, through support and knowledge. Drive shaped by health and by goals stood out as well. The authors say programs should build support and drive, not just give facts.
pmc-11690510:
Yasin Abul and co-authors report a 2024 study of how often the long COVID diagnosis code is used for United States nursing home residents. The code was added in late 2021, but its use in long-term care was unmapped. Claims data linked to pharmacy records gave a monthly view over a year and a half.

Each month held more than two hundred thousand residents, most of them women in their early eighties. Coding peaked early in 2022 and fell to its low a year later. Residents with a fresh COVID case got the code most, and rates swung widely by region with the waves of illness.
pmc-11690610:
Michelle Kimzey (2024) studied what happens when a person living with dementia helps teach a dementia course. Such teachers are called experts by experience, since they know the condition from inside. The study followed one undergraduate class for health profession students. The researcher interviewed student focus groups, the teacher with dementia, and the teacher's care partner. The aim was to see how the shared teaching affected each side.

Students said the experience raised their awareness and skills and lowered stigma. Hearing daily life described by the person living it taught lessons no textbook gave. The teacher described real gains alongside real challenges, and found the role meaningful. The care partner saw benefits for the teacher and the family. Kimzey argues that giving people with dementia a teaching platform lets them speak for themselves. That voice, the study concludes, improves both student learning and the teacher's own life.
pmc-11690710: Kezia Scales, Adam Glickman, and Mariana Morante present how union power lifted Washington State's direct care workers, in a 2024 conference abstract. Recruiting and keeping home care workers is a national problem, and Washington is a labor-led test case. The panel, with input from union SEIU 775 leadership, reviews the union's reach across long-term care. City living-wage laws and negotiated raises interacted to lift pay. Health insurance grew cheaper and paid time off expanded. The panel closes by co-designing research and policy agendas with its audience.
pmc-11690810:
Xiaoling Xiang grades a web mood cure with lay coach aid for old folks with low mood, in a 2024 study. The cure packs nine web drills and a print book for home use. Past loose work showed the cure can run and may help, so a strict trial came next.

Seventy old folks were split to cure plus coach calls or pal calls for ten weeks. Cure folks did most drills and felt much more good than pal call folks. Skill gain, more acts, and self rule growth sat mid path of the gain. Talks show drills, coach trust, and mixed print and web as plus points.
pmc-11691010:
Justin Farmer and five co-authors test whether prosociality predicts later cognitive health. Volunteering and caregiving have been linked to better brain health in older adults. Less work looks at prosociality as a broad trait in its own right, as shown by items on altruism and collectivism.

Data cover 7,844 people aged fifty or older from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. A nine item scale of this trait is built from scales that past work has used and checked. Mixed models track executive function and verbal memory over eleven years, and survival models compare time to dementia. Higher scores link to brain health that holds up better, even when age, schooling, wealth, and health at the start are held in the model. The high group shows 24 percent slower verbal memory decline than the low group.
pmc-11691110:
Fatemeh Adelnia, Feng Wang, and John Gore test a gentle MRI method that watches muscle blood vessels age in rats, in a 2024 conference paper. Aging stiffens the small vessels that feed muscle, starving it during and after work. Old ways to read that micro-world cut tissue or carry risk. Their method reads a spin signal, R1rho, across weak locking fields, and the spread of that read sizes the capillary bed without a needle.

Female rats at six and fifteen months had their lower legs scanned. The spread score ran firmly higher in the older group, which the team reads as aged microvessels rebuilt. A second standard measure rose too, in line with more inflammation in old muscle. The authors pitch the spread as a candidate marker of vessel aging. Male rats and tissue proof under the microscope come next to test the claim.
pmc-11691210:
The ACTIVE trial is the largest test ever run of cognitive training for healthy older adults. It enrolled 2,802 people and followed them for up to ten years, with dementia diagnoses tracked through records for twenty. The authors of a 2024 report ask a narrower question: do social conditions, such as schooling, income stability, neighborhood quality, and access to care, change how much training protects against dementia?

Fewer effects appeared than the team expected. Training helped people across most social conditions. Protection ran stronger for those with better access to health care and more education. Better neighborhoods also lined up with lower dementia risk. The authors suggest pairing tailored training with exercise and better access in future work.
pmc-11691310:
Kristina Shiroma, writing alone in two thousand twenty-four, studied how older Uchinanchu adults in the United States make end-of-life choices. Uchinanchu people, an ethnic group from Okinawa, are little studied in health research. She held deep interviews with eighteen older adults, found through community ties and referrals.

Three themes stood out. First, elders aimed to spare their adult children burden. Second, they kept customs of duty toward their own parents. Third, a mindset the author calls shoganai, an acceptance of fate, helped them balance making plans with letting go. The study widens views of how culture shapes care at life's end.
pmc-11691410:
Dorothea Vafiadis recounts how listening sessions with older adults became an Obesity Bill of Rights, in a 2024 symposium paper. In summer 2023, two national groups convened four town halls in senior centers and faith venues across four states. More than two hundred fifty older adults, community leaders, and clinicians described the barriers to decent weight care: ageism, weight bias, and a care system whose coverage rules shut people out.

The themes were distilled into eight core principles. Experts and stakeholders reviewed and validated the bill that fall, and it launched on the last day of January 2024 as a framework for equity and self-advocacy. By the time of writing, nearly fifty health organizations and medical societies had endorsed it. Vafiadis frames the bill as proof that policy language lands better when the affected community drafts it.
pmc-11691510:
Emma Cho and co-authors published a study in 2024 on home sensors and loneliness in older adults. Sensors that track motion, heat, beds, and doors can watch daily life with no effort from the user. Less was known about how older adults feel when such sensors aim to gauge loneliness.

Fifteen older adults lived with seven kinds of sensors for six months. They then sat for structured interviews about the setup. Most had a positive view overall and grew used to the sensors. They liked the thought that the system could spot loneliness and spur healthier habits. They also raised worries: data might be misused, readings might be wrong, and no human might respond. Trust and privacy shaped how each person judged the system.
pmc-11691610:
Duong Huynh, Mary Patterson, and Bin Huang test a digital test of thought, called BC-Assess, as a way to spot early loss of memory and mind. Their pooled study is from two thousand twenty-four.

The team joined data from two past studies and from clinic partners. It held one hundred ninety-three people: some with normal thought, some with mild loss, and some with dementia. Scores on the tool set the three groups apart with clear gaps. The test found most cases of mild loss and dementia, and it was right on most healthy cases too. The authors say such a tool could help front-line doctors screen early, in a form that fits daily work.
pmc-11691710:
Alison Rataj and co-authors study United States nursing homes in a 2024 paper on drug use during the COVID-19 pandemic. Homes with heavy death tolls faced staff loss and strict isolation, which could change how often doctors started dementia or mental health drugs. The team surveyed nursing directors across the country in 2022.

Homes with higher peak death rates were less likely to report changes in starting dementia drugs, in either direction. No link appeared for mental health drugs as a group. Homes that saw more behavior problems in residents, though, were far more likely to start such drugs. The authors tie that rise to the strain of isolation during the pandemic.
pmc-11691910:
Winnie Sun, Lucas Martignetti, and Jen Calver review staff retention frames for nursing in long term care in 2024. Nurses and support workers anchor care in these homes. Unsafe conditions drive high turnover, yet planning guides are scarce. Their review blends proof, theory, and grey sources. Near twelve hundred papers were screened down to seventeen.

Named models include a structural model and a dual driver model. Retention factors fell into five groups. They span organization traits, personal traits, leadership, social systems, and labor markets. The authors plan to build a shared frame with care staff next. Expert rounds will refine the draft. The goal is stable staffing for homes that house frail elders.
pmc-11692110:
Bárbara, Gonçalves, and Lopes present a 2024 study adapting a thinking-skills test for older adults in Angola. Tools built in one culture can misfire in another, distorting care. The team reworked the cognitive section of the OARS resource scale for local fit. One hundred twenty-seven Angolan elders took the draft version.

A first statistical pass flagged items that clashed with local norms. Those items were rewritten and the test rerun. The revised structure held together far better, and a consistency score rose to 0.82, a solid mark. The authors argue that careful cultural tailoring, not direct import, is what makes screening fair for Angola's elders.
pmc-11692210:
Toshiko Tanaka and seven colleagues published a 2024 study on the link between fat inside muscles and thinking speed in older adults. Intermuscular fat, fat infiltrating the muscle, has been associated with worse cognitive function, but the biological mechanism is unknown.

The team profiled blood proteins in 942 participants of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, measuring fat on thigh CT scans and processing speed with cognitive tests. They then validated the protein findings in 2,453 participants of the CARDIA study, where abdominal scans were used. The search focused on plasma proteins that statistically mediate the relationship, carrying the effect from muscle fat to slower thinking. Such mediators could become targets for protecting cognition in ageing.
pmc-11692310:
Jaehyun Kim and co-authors published a 2024 study on tai chi practiced inside virtual reality by older adults. About one in five older people lives with a mental health condition, yet many avoid clinics because of stigma or low awareness. A gentle, game-like program might reach them where they are. Tai chi, a slow exercise of flowing movements, is already known to calm the mind.

Eighteen older adults from senior centers in North Carolina took part. Each did eight fifteen-minute sessions in a headset over one month. Surveys before and after showed clear drops in depressive symptoms, with a large effect. Perceived stress also fell by a moderate amount. Participants rated the program easy and pleasant to use. The authors suggest virtual tai chi as a practical tool for geriatric mental health. They note the small group size as a limit, and call for larger trials.
pmc-11692410:
Mohammed Essioti, Hind Boukaaba, Anouar Titou, and Dounia Kamal present a 2024 case report on a rare jaw disorder. The growth at issue is a harmless mix of bone-like tissue that forms in the lower and upper jaw. It shows up most often in middle-aged women, and in the case here it had become infected.

The authors walk through the signs, the scans, and why this growth is easy to confuse with other jaw lesions. Care stayed cautious: the team controlled the infection, cleaned out dead tissue, and kept watch over time. The report urges care in making the call and steady follow-up to stop new problems.
pmc-11692510:
Alison Stone and co-authors survey rural frontline clinicians on their confidence in elder care. Their 2024 study runs inside a national program that beams geriatric help to rural sites for veterans. A case conference series teaches the five M's of good elder care, and the survey piggybacks on three spring sessions.

Half the attendees answered, 211 in all, from nurses and pharmacists to doctors and social workers. About seven in ten felt confident or very confident across sixteen tasks. Trust ran highest on asking what matters most to the patient. Soft spots were low mood care, cutting needless drugs, and dementia behavior. Rural-heavy staff felt surer than city peers, a hint for where training should aim.
pmc-11692610:
Juliana Smichenko and co-authors compare drug loads for older patients across culture groups in Israel, in a study from 2024. The drugs in focus calm the mind or block a nerve signal, and a heavy load can dull thought. Care in a hospital ward can add such drugs fast, but habits may not be the same for all groups.

The team used data from 672 older adults who were clear in mind and able in body. Groups were Israeli Arabs, Jews who came from the former USSR, and veteran Israeli Jews. A burden score summed the load for each patient. Both the Arab group and the USSR group had lower loads than the veteran group at the same health state. Worse symptoms, worse illness, and more diseases raised load. The authors urge study of doctor-patient talks.
pmc-11693010:
Chiyoung Lee, Juyoung Park, Mindy Fain, James Galvin and Hyochol Ahn wrote a 2024 study on brain stimulation for pain in older adults with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Pain reports can be unreliable in this group, so behavior signs matter too. Forty people got real or sham stimulation for twenty minutes on five straight days. Two scales tracked felt pain and observed pain behavior.

Analysis sorted each person into high or low pain states over time. In the real group, high-pain members had near even odds of dropping to low pain right after treatment. The sham group showed no such early shift. Gains in the real group persisted at later follow-ups.
pmc-11693110:
Roy Noy and Noelle Marie Coloma Javier report a joint aging care training pilot in 2024 for LGBTQIA+ older adults. Care for this group is oft skipped in med school, which leaves gaps in old-age care. A Tel Aviv trainee spent four months at a New York center in the pilot.

The trainee rode with old-age, comfort, rehab, and niche clinics and took one-on-one lessons on group care. Gains span a course plan other schools can copy, joint papers, and firm cross-sea links. Tel Aviv gained its first old-age clinic for the group from the work.
pmc-11693310:
Elise Hu and seven co-authors pilot tested a home exercise program built for frail older adults with dementia in a 2024 paper. Staying active guards health in old age, yet adults with Alzheimer's and kin diseases often sit out due to long stillness, weak bodies, or low drive. Their Gentle Moves program brings guided moves into the home, shaped for inactive and frail users.

The program sets activity goals with each pair, folds moves into daily routines, and lends a tablet that prompts and tracks each day. Eight elders, mean age near seventy nine, joined with a family carer each for three months. Every pair finished the program. Elders felt safe and found the pace right for their strength, with milder cases soon working the tablet alone.
pmc-11693410:
Bárbara Costa and co-authors report three cases of complex knee plateau fractures treated with a calcium based bone filler, in work published in 2024. The fractures were severe split types at the top of the shin bone. Surgery fixed the bone with plates and filled the crushed void with the graft material.

Patients reported high satisfaction and low pain after recovery. Knee function scores were fair to good, and quality of life scores were high. Movement range was good to excellent, with no major complications. No new sinking of the joint surface appeared at follow up. The authors suggest the filler gives support and bonds with bone, aiding recovery in these hard fractures.
pmc-11693810:
Shabnam Khatami and co-authors review the health effects of blood removal, called phlebotomy, in this 2024 article. Drawing blood as a treatment is old in many schools of medicine, yet modern Western practice allows it for only a few set uses. The authors wanted a firm summary of what trial evidence says about its gains and its risks.

They gathered seven reviews that together covered fifty-six trials and more than five thousand people. Blood removal helped in high blood pressure, gout attacks, some skin diseases, and several liver diseases. The most common harm was a bruise where blood was drawn. The authors judge the proof solid for those uses, but call for larger trials before the method spreads to other diseases.
pmc-11700610:
Childress and a large team show that platelet growth drugs speed bone healing in mice, rats, and pigs in twenty twenty-four. Broken bones that refuse to knit remain a clinical headache. The usual growth proteins carry side effect worries, including cancer links. Thrombopoietin, the marrow signal for platelet making cells, was their candidate.

Two fracture models and both local and body wide dosing worked. Gene and cell studies credit richer blood vessel growth for the gain. Vessel growth is a must for bone union. The drugs already serve clinic use for low platelets, with known safety. That head start lifts their promise here.
pmc-11701510:
Masahiro Ono and Tessa Crompton present a toolkit for tracing how young cells change over time inside a living body, in a study from 2024. Starter cells shift their genes and proteins as they split into many cell types. Watching that timing at single-cell level in vivo has stayed hard, even with fluorescent timer methods.

The toolkit blends lab measures with new math based on correspondence and network analysis. It reads high-dimensional flow data to map paths of growth and change. The team tested it on thymic T cells from mice with a fluorescent timer gene. Removing a cell-death gene then showed fresh detail on growth and on the culling of T cells after receptor signals. The method suits other fast-changing cell systems too.
pmc-11702410:
Aysha Rajeev and co-authors test whether low vitamin D at admission shadows the fate of broken hips, in a 2024 study. Records covered 1,440 patients with a fractured thigh bone top, treated over four years at one British trust. Seven in ten were women, and the average age sat near eighty-two. Blood vitamin D was drawn on arrival, and walking state and deaths were tracked after surgery.

Over half arrived with low vitamin D. Their walking fell further in the three months after surgery than that of patients with sound levels. Deaths also stacked against them: higher at one month and higher still as the gap widened at one year. The authors read the vitamin as more than a bystander mark. They urge teams to check and mend it as part of fracture care, since the deficit is common and cheap to treat.
pmc-11703610:
Gurdeep Sagoo and Marina Richardson explain new reporting standards for cost studies of medical AI in a 2025 paper. Health economists judge value with a standard checklist, CHEERS, first issued in 2013 and refreshed in 2022. A new extension, CHEERS-AI, adapts it for artificial intelligence tools in healthcare.

Reviews had found cost studies of medical AI only middling at following reporting rules, with key items often skipped. The extension aims to force fuller, clearer reporting so readers can compare studies and trust them. The paper walks through the checklist's history and why AI raises special questions, such as data and model updates. Journals adopting the extension should lift the field's transparency.
pmc-11704610:
Neha Khetan and co-authors compare two ways to measure noise in gene activity, in a 2024 study. Gene activity varies from cell to cell even among alike cells, and that random flicker is called noise. A common lab method reads RNA in single cells, but how well it tracks noise was unclear.

The team used a drug that boosts noise without changing mean activity levels. Most software tools did report higher noise for most genes after the drug. A direct imaging method, which counts single RNA molecules, confirmed the rise for most genes tested. Yet all the software tools shrank the size of the change. The study gives labs a fair guide to what each method can and cannot show.
pmc-11705610:
Upendra Kaul and co-authors used a light based imaging method to study heart artery plaques in young Indian patients with acute heart problems, in work published in 2024. One hundred patients aged eighteen to fifty were scanned during their artery opening procedure at several centers. Plaque traits in this group were little known.

Fibrous plaques were most common, seen in three quarters of patients. Plaques with immune cells, tiny channels, and calcium nodules were also frequent. Rupture, surface wear, and fat rich plaques each appeared in about a quarter to a third of cases, and clots in about half. Major events after one year were rare. The authors say young patients show a wide mix of plaque forms.
pmc-11709410:
Peter Lichtenberg assesses financial capacity in older adults with early memory loss using real world records in a 2025 paper. Judging money management from office tests misses how people actually handle accounts. National guidance calls for real world assessment, which has been lacking.

About one hundred fifty older adults, roughly half with early memory loss, shared a year of checking account statements. Interviews confirmed who managed each account and mapped income and spending. The memory loss group showed lower daily functioning and memory scores, higher decision making vulnerability, and more excess spending. Thinking measures helped explain the spending gap.
pmc-11709510:
Daphne Gasparre and ten co-authors investigate cognitive reserve, the brain's ability to withstand aging and damage, in patients with mild impairment and dementia. Their study came out in 2025. Reserve is built across a lifetime through education, work, mental activity, and social ties.

Patients took a battery of tests covering attention and memory. Higher reserve went with better test performance, and the link was clearest at the mild impairment stage, before decline deepens. The authors argue that reserve is not fixed: more activity, new languages, new skills, and exercise may all build it. If so, boosting reserve could delay the point where brain changes become disability. They call for more research on how to grow it deliberately.
pmc-11709610:
Victor maps how brain immune cells shift across Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 paper. Single-cell reading of dead brain tissue gives only a frozen frame. Victor pairs that reading with lab-grown human brain cells that can be perturbed. The data set spans over 150,000 microglia profiles from more than 400 brains.

Gene activity and control marks show the order in which inflamed states appear as disease grows. Targeted gene edits in the lab-grown cells test which switches drive each state. Work also probes how overactive brain circuits may feed the symptoms beyond memory loss. Victor offers the map as a stage-by-stage guide for drugs that calm brain inflammation.
pmc-11709810:
Stephen Keegan and co-authors sort Alzheimer's disease traits into a layered map of biological domains to sharpen the hunt for drug targets. Most past drugs for the disease failed to lift its burden. Their consortium seeks targets in underexplored corners of the disease biology, as this 2025 paper sets out.

Experts first sorted Gene Ontology terms into 19 domains, each an endophenotype of the disease. They then redid the process to carve 80 subdomains that name each trait's key functions. Gene lists became protein interaction networks. Reading a target gene at domain level links it to traits, and at subdomain level to the functions behind them. The map guides target choice.
pmc-11709910:
Sanghee Yoo and Ickpyo Hong present a 2025 study on swallowing problems and low mood in United States adults. Trouble swallowing can bring fear at meals, hurt self-worth, and strain social ties. The team asked whether adults with this problem report more signs of depression. They used a large national health survey from 2022.

The survey held 26,810 adults, and the team used careful methods to balance the groups. Adults who reported swallowing trouble had much higher odds of low mood signs.
