Risk also varied by sex, race, schooling, income, and other health problems. Anxiety raised the risk a great deal. The authors call for care plans shaped to each patient, not a single mold.
pmc-11710010:
Tadayuki Ogawa and four co-authors applied several imaging methods to Alzheimer's brain tissue in a 2025 study. Amyloid clumps are a hallmark of the disease, but the events before them and the chemical setting around them are poorly known. New tools can map molecules and elements at fine scale.

Slices of donated brain were examined with standard staining plus three advanced imaging methods. One mapped small molecules, one mapped metals, and one mapped elements, all on the same tissue. Math sorting then highlighted how diseased and healthy brains differ. The molecule maps showed fats of several families spread abnormally in diseased brain. Metal and element maps added their own patterns. The authors say the combined view can expose early changes that single methods miss, and may point to fresh clues about how the disease begins.
pmc-11710210:
Sitong Zhou and nine co-authors present a 2025 study on fat-derived signaling molecules in the brain and liver of people with Alzheimer's disease. Inflammation helps drive the disease, and oxidized fats called oxylipins are potent inflammation signals. An enzyme that converts calming fats into inflammatory ones runs high in the Alzheimer's brain. The team measured these lipids in paired postmortem brain and liver samples from seventy-nine donors.

Both organs showed altered levels of a protective family of fat compounds in Alzheimer's. The liver showed the strongest changes, including a drop in stored inflammatory products of that enzyme, matching reports of raised free levels in blood. A male tilt toward inflammation also appeared. The authors conclude Alzheimer's is a whole-body disorder, not just a brain one. They suggest blood lipids from these pathways might one day flag the disease process.
pmc-11710310:
Himanshi Singh and co-authors linked lasting DNA damage to brain swelling and redness in a mouse model of tau disease, in a study published in 2025. Tau diseases, including Alzheimer's, involve clumps of tau protein and steady nerve cell loss. The team focused on breaks in DNA and on a cell alarm system that reacts to them.

In brain samples from patients and from mice, breaks were more common and repair proteins were lower than in healthy tissue. The alarm system, known by the short names cGAS and STING, was also more active where tau harm was present. The authors argue that unrepaired breaks may help switch on this alarm, driving the harmful swelling that follows. That chain could offer new points for treatment.
pmc-11710610:
August Yue Huang and co-authors found cancer-linked mutations enriched in the brain's immune cells in Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. The cells, microglia, accumulate small somatic mutations as people age. Some of those mutations are the same drivers seen in blood cancers, an overlap no one expected to matter in the brain.

The team sequenced microglia from Alzheimer's brains and found driver mutations at higher rates than in controls. They link the mutated cells to neuroinflammation, the chronic immune activation that harms neurons. The finding suggests rogue, expanding microglia clones may fuel part of Alzheimer's inflammation. It also opens a drug angle, since cancer drugs already target some of these pathways.
pmc-11710710:
Jasper Crockford and co-authors linked remembered menopause symptoms to later thinking and behavior complaints in a Canadian aging study, in a 2025 paper. Menopause has been tied to greater dementia risk, and the team asked whether specific symptoms around it carry the signal. Their sample held 896 postmenopausal participants from an online research platform.

Each woman reported which of eleven past symptoms she had experienced, from hot flushes and sleep trouble to brain fog and mood change. Current thinking complaints and emerging behavior symptoms were scored on standard scales. Statistical models then tied symptom patterns to those later scores, hunting early markers of decline risk.
pmc-11711710:
Finsterer and Gama Marques reported a case in twenty twenty-four of an eighty-six-year-old man whose brain lymphoma returned twice, each time in a different place. This lymphoma of the central nervous system can grow in the brain, the spinal cord, the coverings of the brain, or the eyes.

The man's first tumor, in the back of his brain, was removed and treated with drugs when he was eighty-two. At eighty-four the disease came back only in the gel of his eyes, first the right and then the left, with no sign in the brain. Surgeons cleared both eyes. At eighty-six a second return appeared as new growths in the lower brain, treated with radiation. The authors say the case is the first of its kind they know. It shows one disease can reappear in the eyes alone and later in the brain alone.
pmc-11711910:
Erica Dove, Rosalie H Wang, Kara K Patterson, and Arlene J Astell recruit people with dementia as testers of exercise games in 2025. Motion games can aid activity in this group with human support. What makes the tech usable for them was unclear. Thirty two testers joined weekly sessions at four day programs. They tried several systems and games, from darts to dancing.

Nearly three hundred play turns were logged. Some testers quit games from boredom, confusion, or strain. Handheld controllers proved harder than gesture controls. Games needing many joint moves also shut people out. The authors urge builders to test with this group directly. Design that fits real limits can widen access to activity.
pmc-11712110:
Kunmei Han studies how healthy older adults speak, to set a base line for normal aging. The 2025 paper uses free speech from 243 adults in Singapore aged over 60, all with sound thinking skills. Each person spoke for about 15 minutes, and trained staff wrote down the speech.

Han measured speech speed, word range, and how concrete the main words were. Older speakers spoke more slowly than younger peers in the group. They also used more concrete nouns and describing words as age rose. Schooling, sex, and count of tongues spoken were not tied to each other. The base line can help spot speech changes that go beyond normal aging.
pmc-11712210:
Charline Compagne and co-authors study lost self-awareness in Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 interview study. Many patients do not grasp how much their abilities have shrunk, a problem called anosognosia. That gap can make living at home risky. The team spoke with eighteen pairs of patients with mild dementia and their family caregivers.

Patients argued for staying home in terms of comfort, familiar faces, and keeping their habits and freedom. Many admitted memory loss yet played down the risks that came with it. Caregivers backed the wish to stay home but pushed for planning and outside help. They suggested paid support, home technology, and legal safeguards. The authors say weak self-awareness blocks the flexible planning that safe ageing in place requires.
pmc-11712310:
Asuna Arai and Yuriko Katsumata compare how dementia symptoms unfold in care homes in Japan and the United States. The symptoms span mood, behavior, and thought, and they weigh on both residents and carers. Whether they follow like paths in unlike care cultures was unknown. The team used yearly follow up data from both lands.

Hundreds of residents were sorted into groups by their symptom paths over four waves. Three path groups appeared in each country, and their shapes matched closely. Traits that sorted residents into groups differed somewhat by land. The authors infer that symptom paths are sturdy across settings, even as local traits steer who lands where.
pmc-11712410:
Tatiana Belfort and co-authors compare social skills in people whose Alzheimer disease began early or late in life. Their 2025 study covers 48 people with onset before age 65 and 118 with later onset, plus the family members who care for them. Social cognition means reading other people and getting along with them.

The early-onset group scored worse on general thinking tests and on quality of life. They also showed more mood and behavior symptoms. Yet their social skill losses did not grow in step with those wider losses. The pattern stayed more flat than the team expected. The authors link social skills to other clinical traits to explain the split.
pmc-11712510:
Natalia G Gonçalves and co-authors study work and memory in a 2025 paper on older adults in Brazil and Mexico. Jobs that demand more skill and thought may build a reserve that protects the mind late in life. Most past work came from rich countries, so the team turned to two large Latin American surveys.

The study used health surveys from 2018, with adults aged fifty and over in both countries. Jobs were grouped as unskilled, partly skilled, or skilled, based on the main job each person held. Mind tests were scored against a healthy reference group to flag weak function. The team then weighed the link between job group and mind scores, with social and health factors taken into account.
pmc-11712610:
Alan Kott and co-authors, in a 2025 paper, ask whether small trial sites hurt data quality in early Alzheimer's disease trials. Sponsors depend on sites to pick the right patients and to rate symptoms in a sound, steady way. Sites that enroll few people cost much money and effort, and may add errors.

The team drew data from three large early dementia trials with 834 sites in all. They split sites into those with more than five patients and those with five or fewer. Data quality meant errors in giving and scoring the tests used in the trials. Those error counts were summed per site and compared between the two groups, with trial and size taken into account. Past work in a related field found most sites enrolled very few patients.
pmc-11712810:
William Coath and co-authors estimate in 2025 how much time passes between two stages of Alzheimer's disease in people who still think clearly. First, a protein called amyloid turns positive on a brain scan. Later, a second protein, tau, rises in set brain regions. Knowing the gap between those steps matters for drugs that attack amyloid, since timing may decide how well they work.

The team used a British birth cohort of people born in 1946. Members had two amyloid scans, and a subgroup enriched for amyloid also had a tau scan. A changepoint model marked when each person's amyloid turned positive and when tau rose. The gap it gives can help trial teams pick who to treat and when. It also helps families and doctors read what a positive scan means for the years ahead.
pmc-11712910:
Melanie Matyi and co-authors compare thinking test scores between minoritized and White patients with frontotemporal degeneration in this 2025 study. These brain diseases strike behavior and language first. Minoritized patients are understudied in this research field. The same team earlier found distinct symptom profiles by group. Cognition across groups had not yet been reported. Data came from a national Alzheimer's coordinating dataset.

Patients carried one of two diagnoses: behavioral variant disease or a language variant. Their test battery scores were compared across groups. Care can misfire when norms come from one population only. Knowing real score patterns guards against misdiagnosis. The study fills a named gap in the literature. It uses a large shared United States dataset.
pmc-11713010:
Larry Adams and co-authors study trust in dementia research in a 2025 paper. Social and environmental factors shape Alzheimer risk, and minority groups bear extra burden, yet surveys on such factors can feel intrusive. The team built a fifty-six-question survey and tested it in focus groups with Black American and Hispanic or Latino participants.

Nine themes emerged, from first reactions to fears of data misuse. Black participants tied reluctance to historical mistrust, while Latino participants stressed privacy. Both wanted clear community benefits and guidance to real services. Readers get a trust-first playbook for sensitive research.
pmc-11713110:
Siwon Kim and co-authors test an oral drug for Alzheimer disease in a mouse model in a 2025 study. The drug switches on a receptor called TGR5, and an injected form had helped in earlier work, but a pill form suits long treatment far better.

The pill was given twice a day for twelve weeks to both normal mice and a transgenic model of the disease. Treated model mice did better on a water maze and on a test of spotting new objects. Their brains held fewer amyloid plaques, and the loss of mature neurons slowed. Blood protein scans hunted for markers that track the drug's effect, for use in later trials.
pmc-11713210:
Oonjee Oh, Debra Parker Oliver, Karla Washington, and George Demiris study dementia caregivers in a 2025 paper on the move into hospice care. Many caregivers know little about hospice and feel unprepared for the change. The authors asked how the timing of that move relates to caregiver mental health.

They re-used baseline data from a trial of problem-solving therapy for hospice caregivers, drawn from 156 people. About 40 percent had entered hospice within the prior two weeks. The team compared mood, anxiety, sense of well-being, and quality of life between recent arrivals and those in hospice longer. They also compared how those measures moved together in each group. The work helps services time support for families at a hard point in care.
pmc-11713310:
Lagarde and co-authors study younger Alzheimer's patients whose amyloid scans come back negative, in this 2025 paper. About a quarter of such patients in a large early-onset study lack the amyloid the diagnosis implies. Some other cause must explain their symptoms.

Seventy-four patients had a second scan that shows how active brain areas are. The team sorted scans as normal or low-activity using strict data rules and a matched control group. They then compared the two patient groups on health and personal traits. The split may reveal which patients have true Alzheimer's disease and which have look-alike conditions that need different care.
pmc-11713610:
Most aging research uses inbred mice that are genetic copies of each other, which is nothing like a human population. Seven researchers instead follow UM-HET3 mice in 2025, a stock bred for genetic variety. They compare middle-aged mice at 11 months with old ones at 25 months. Tests cover blood counts, grip strength, balance, vision, startle, wheel running, and fear memory. The team also asks whether blood measures predict memory in old age.

Older mice ran cooler, saw worse, gripped weaker, and remembered less. Their blood shifted on many counts. In old males only, two white cell shares tracked memory strongly. Balance and wheel running held steady. The authors present the stock as a closer mirror of human aging.
pmc-11713710:
Masashi Kameyama and co-authors work on the contrast of early phase images from amyloid PET scans of the brain. Published in 2025, the paper explains that the first minutes of such a scan can give a stand-in image of blood flow. That image flags both amyloid buildup and sites of nerve cell loss. The catch is that the early image is not a true blood flow image, so its contrast suffers.

The team built a method to recover that contrast. They also built a way to set its key parameter, grounded in a literature review. Early images from one tracer tracked a standard glucose scan closely. Mild underestimates appeared where blood flow was high. The authors set out the theory for wider use.
pmc-11713810:
Amanda Denning and co-authors present a 2025 research abstract on Alzheimer's disease. The team asks how tau damage in the brain relates to brain shrinkage seen on scans taken before death. They focus on the medial temporal lobe, a region hit early in the disease. Older rating scales lump tau damage together, so the team uses finer counts that separate tangles from threads.

Brain tissue came from 138 patients whose illness had been confirmed after death. The team compared set ratings and direct counts of tau in the hippocampus with scan measures of cortical thickness. They also checked whether a second protein problem changed the pattern. The work helps link what scans show in life to what tissue shows after death.
pmc-11713910:
Vanessa Guzman and nine co-authors report a 2025 conference study linking the pulse in brain arteries to blood markers of degeneration. Eighty older adults from a long-running Manhattan study had ultrasound scans of neck and brain arteries plus blood tests for Alzheimer's-related markers. The team separated two kinds of vessel aging: stiffening of the body's arteries and pulsing pressure inside the brain's own arteries.

Only the brain measure mattered. Stronger pulsing in the main brain artery went with higher levels of four markers, including a tau form and a nerve damage marker. After accounting for age and sex, only the tau link stayed firm. Stiff body arteries showed no links at all. The authors read this as a hint that the brain's own vessel aging tracks degeneration more closely, while noting the small sample limits certainty.
pmc-11714010:
Deborah Alawode and colleagues independently validated a more sensitive blood test platform. Their 2025 pilot study modifies the Single Molecule Array technology. The upgrade claims up to a hundredfold gain in sensitivity. Independent checks matter before such claims guide research. The team tested an interleukin 17A assay on paired samples.

Serum and spinal fluid came from Alzheimer's patients and controls. Four instruments ran the same samples for comparison. The standard machine missed the protein in all spinal fluid. Modified machines found it in nearly every spinal sample. Serum detection also jumped with the upgrade. Mean levels could then be compared across groups. Ultrasensitive tests may unlock faint brain disease signals in blood.
pmc-11714310:
Mark Gluck and co-authors share ten field-proven tactics for drawing older African Americans into brain health studies, in a 2025 paper. African Americans face Alzheimer's disease at two to three times the rate of white Americans. Yet long-standing barriers keep them out of the studies that could close that gap. The team writes from hard-won success in Newark, New Jersey, where they enrolled more than five hundred older adults.

The tactics all rest on slow trust work. Hire a varied team with deep local roots, and set up a board of community partners. Run steady brain health events, and help with needs far from research. Honor members who live the message, and craft programs that draw in older men. Treat members as VIPs, thank past members as recruiters, and report results back. The authors warn the path is neither quick nor cheap.
pmc-11714510:
Isabelle Foote and co-authors split frailty into genetic pathways in this 2025 paper. Frailty is a state of poor health in older adults, scored by counting health deficits. Lumping all deficits into one score can hide the biology behind them. The team modeled shared genetic signal across 30 deficits from the standard index.

Their model found one general factor plus six more, tied to isolation, lifestyle, multiple illness, metabolism, cognition, and disability. Genetic scans for these factors found 408 risk spots. Risk scores built from the multiple-illness and cognition pathways best predicted frailty in outside groups. The cognition pathway also tied genetically to Alzheimer's disease. The authors say this split can help flag people at risk of dementia.
pmc-11714610:
Stephanie Buss and co-authors measure cortical excitability with magnetic stimulation and brain wave reads in early Alzheimer disease, and tie the numbers to thinking scores. The Alzheimer cortex is known to run hot, but most proof comes from the motor area. Whether the parietal lobe, a seat of cognition, also runs hot was open.

Their 2025 study pulses two sites, motor and parietal, in biomarker-confirmed patients and matched controls. Early response strength near each site is the readout. The team sets those reads against global cognition and a parietal-weighted score built for this question. Linking a brain-physiology dial to specific thinking skills could give trials a fast marker of disease state and drug effect.
pmc-11714810:
Daniela Delphus and five co-authors review in 2025 a puzzle about weight and Alzheimer disease. Extra weight in midlife seems to raise the risk of the disease. Yet extra weight late in life seems to guard against it, a pattern called the obesity paradox.

The team screens close to 2800 studies and keeps 44 human studies for close reading. Brain scans and fluid tests form the core proof in those studies. Many find that heavier older adults face lower risk or slower decline than lean peers. The review weighs how firm that pattern is and what could explain it. Age, illness, and weight loss from early disease all cloud a simple reading.
pmc-11714910:
Muhammad Ali and a large team of co-authors search in 2025 for protein signatures of Alzheimer's disease in spinal fluid. Protein changes appear before symptoms, so fluid profiles may aid diagnosis and therapy. The team measured more than seven thousand protein markers with a broad assay.

Samples came from 2,286 people across four cohorts. A three-stage design covered discovery, replication, and pooled analysis. Proteins that passed strict cutoffs in all stages were used to build a disease prediction model. The multi-cohort design aims to find signatures that hold up across sites, not just in one sample.
pmc-11715010:
Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body disease often appear together, and their symptoms overlap. Sungwoo Kang, Seun Jeon, and Byoung Seok Ye studied four hundred seven people with scans and tests for both illnesses. They measured a brain area that makes a key messenger chemical, plus a scan of the dopamine system. They also counted bright white matter spots that mark vessel damage.

Lower volume in that messenger area and lower dopamine signal each linked to more symptom burden. Both tracked thinking problems, unstable awareness, and seeing things that are not there. The dopamine signal also tied to dream-enactment behavior and stiffness of movement. Bright spots tracked high blood pressure and small bleeds instead. The work helps separate which brain change drives which symptom.
pmc-11715110:
Monica Nelson and co-authors weighed job status against job demands in 2025 as paths linking race to cognitive health in older adults. Gaps in cognition between racial groups persist even after standard social factors are counted. Work is a less studied factor, shaped by long-standing inequities, and it may act through income standing or through mental stimulation.

Participants were 493 Black or White older adults in a Michigan aging project. The team tested memory, language, processing speed, and executive function as outcomes. They asked whether occupational status, a sign of standing, or occupational complexity, a sign of stimulation, carried the racial gap. Readers get a sharper account of how a working life may leave its mark on the aging mind, and which side of work matters more.
pmc-11715210:
Filippos Anagnostakis and co-authors probe brain signatures across body weight and metabolic states in mild cognitive impairment. Their twenty twenty-five study joins obesity, metabolic syndrome, and brain degeneration in one frame. Late-life obesity has oddly linked to lower dementia risk in some past work.

Brain scans, spinal fluid amyloid and tau, and a learned atrophy index were read together. Groups were split by metabolic health to untangle fat from vessel risk. The picture in impairment alone was unknown before this work. A clear split could explain the obesity paradox in dementia and guide which patients need vessel care most.
pmc-11715310:
Samantha LG Paço and four co-authors set out to sharpen gene risk scores for Alzheimer's disease. A risk score adds up many small gene marks into one number for a person. Such scores still leave out what the marks do in the body. The team looks at marks that sit where proteins get tagged after they are built, a step that can change how a protein works.

Their first step was a tool that pulls tag-site data from three big banks into one place. A user can search by gene place, by protein, or by the text that codes it. Whole gene reads from a European study and a Brazilian bank will feed the tool next. The team will then weigh each mark and test if tag-site marks make risk scores read risk more truly in both groups.
pmc-11715410:
Weiquan Luo and co-authors tested ways to clean up brain amyloid scans pooled from many sites in Down syndrome work. Each scanner leaves its own stamp on a scan, which can blur group reads. Two common fixes are a blur to a shared sharpness and a fix for spill between zones. The team ran four fix plans on scans from four scanners in a shared Down syndrome bank.

They then gauged how much stamp each plan left, in one-time and over-time reads. The blur plan did not cut the scanner stamp in any read. The spill fix, on raw or blurred scans, leaned toward a larger stamp. A stats clean-up plan was tried on the zone values as well. The reads warn that the most used fixes may not tame site gaps for this group, and may even grow them.
pmc-11715510:
Zhong Pei tests a fast digital memory test, MemTrax, as a way to detect cognitive impairment in people with Parkinson's disease. The test scores correct answers, response speed, and a blend of the two. Pei compared its scores with scores on a standard clinic test, the MoCA. The 2025 study ran in groups that ranged from healthy adults to patients with dementia.

The groups held 61 healthy adults, 102 patients with normal cognition, 74 with mild impairment, and 52 with dementia. The standard test could not separate healthy adults from patients with normal cognition, but two MemTrax scores could. All test scores fell step by step as impairment grew worse, and they tracked the standard test well. Pei gives cut points for mild impairment and for dementia. The test looks fit for early checks and for tracking change over time.
pmc-11715610:
Narlon Cassio Boa Sorte Silva and co-authors test whether resistance exercise slows white matter damage in older adults with vascular cognitive impairment. Their 2025 report covers a 12-month randomized trial run single-blind. One group did resistance training, while the other did balance and tone exercises as a control. All participants had scan evidence of cerebral small vessel disease and mild cognitive impairment, but no dementia.

At 12 months, 74 people had complete follow-up scans. Whole-brain white matter damage did not differ between the groups overall. Yet sex changed the result: women in the resistance group lost less white matter than women in the control group, while men showed no such gain. Damage also fell in the side and lower back regions of the brain. The team sees resistance training as a useful tool, with the clearest gain for women.
pmc-11715710:
Xiaolei Han and co-authors ask whether cognitive reserve can blunt the effect of microstructural brain lesions on cognition in dementia-free adults. Their 2025 study uses the UK Biobank, a large health resource in Britain. Reserve was built from education, occupation, physical activity, and social activity. The lesions were read from diffusion MRI scans that track water motion in white matter, the wiring of the brain.

The sample held 26,490 adults in the imaging part of the project. Lesion markers such as freer, more spread-out water motion went with slower processing speed, weaker attention, and weaker executive function. In the split by reserve, some lesion links with reasoning and memory appeared only in the low-reserve group. The authors read this as evidence that high reserve can soften the cost of the lesions. They still note that the data are a snapshot of linked traits, not a trial.
pmc-11715810:
Charlotte Jacob and seven co-authors look for links between blood chemistry, behavior changes, and dementia in people with Down syndrome, in this 2025 study. People with Down syndrome face a high risk of Alzheimer's disease, but the timing of decline varies a lot. A behavior scale filled in by caregivers is one early warning tool, and the team compared its scores with blood markers.

The blood panel covered brain signaling chemicals such as dopamine and serotonin, plus standard Alzheimer's markers. Early data suggest ties between parts of the behavior scale and some of these measures. The authors aim to learn whether a blood test could back up caregiver reports when judging if dementia is starting. That would support better daily care and earlier planning for families.
pmc-11715910:
Jose M Aravena and four co-authors compare how Indigenous Mapuche and non-Indigenous older adults in Chile think about dementia and brain health. Their 2025 study notes that no earlier work set the two groups side by side in the same territory. Twenty-four people aged sixty and up gave deep interviews about aging, memory, risk factors, and habits for a healthy brain.

The views parted in telling ways. Mapuche elders who kept cultural religious practice described dementia as a passage toward the ancestors' spiritual plane. They named trauma and grief, poor food, social troubles, and alcohol as chief risks. Non-Mapuche elders named loneliness and depression instead, and prized an active attitude, social life, and mental exercise. Mapuche elders prized balance, avoiding excess, natural food, good sleep, pride in identity, and traditional work such as farming and crafts. The authors urge culturally shaped prevention programs.
pmc-11716010:
Arthur C Macedo and co-authors compare three scan tracers used to stage tau buildup in the living brain, in this 2025 paper from the HEAD study. Tau spreads through the brain in a known order, and doctors grade that spread with the Braak staging system. Different tracers may not grade the same patient the same way, so the team scanned each person with more than one.

One hundred adults at McGill University, half with thinking problems, received at least two of the three tracers. Readings from the tracers moved together across brain regions, most tightly in early stage areas. Agreement on a patient's final stage was strong between pairs of tracers but only moderate across all three. A simpler four step staging scheme improved agreement, which matters for trials that enroll by stage.
pmc-11716110:
Sekh Thanprasertsuk and co-authors report a 2025 study from Thailand on two tests used in Alzheimer's disease. One test is a brain scan that maps tau, a protein that builds up in the disease. The other is a blood test for a changed form of the same protein. Blood tests are cheaper and easier, yet their link to scan patterns in Southeast Asian patients was unclear.

The study enrolled Thai patients with mild memory loss or mild dementia thought to stem from Alzheimer's disease. The team compared blood levels with scan maps region by region across the brain. Their goal was to learn how well a simple blood test reflects where tau has spread. Results could help doctors judge when a blood test can stand in for a costly scan.
pmc-11716210:
Alexandra DiFilippo and co-authors examine how the loss of synapses relates to tau tangles in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 paper. Synapses are the tiny junctions where brain cells pass signals, and their loss tracks closely with failing memory. Tau tangles are a second hallmark of the disease. Earlier scan studies looked only at narrow groups, leaving open how the two changes connect before symptoms appear.

Participants came from Wisconsin studies of Alzheimer's prevention and from the local community. Each person had full clinical and thinking tests to set their status, from healthy to impaired. A special scan tracer let the team measure how dense synapses were in the living brain. They then compared those readings with tau tangle load in people with and without impairment, including cases with disease changes but no symptoms yet.
pmc-11716310:
Mustafa Shehzad and five co-authors report a heart-failure case that unmasked a rare genetic syndrome hiding without its usual signs. Their report appeared in twenty twenty-four. Andersen-Tawil syndrome normally brings muscle paralysis spells, distinctive features, and rhythm trouble together.

The patient, a man in his mid-twenties, arrived with chest pain, breathlessness lying flat, and exhaustion. His mother and brother had both died suddenly of cardiac causes. Tests showed a weak, enlarged heart pumping at fifteen to twenty percent, with conduction delays and a long QT interval. Genetic testing found the KCNJ2 variant behind the syndrome. After a fifty-five-second run of dangerous rhythm, he received an implanted defibrillator and standard heart failure drugs.
pmc-11716410:
Oh and co-authors report in 2025 on how being unable to read may affect the risk of dementia in older men and women. Their study followed 5,217 Korean adults aged 60 and older who did not have dementia at the start. Nurses noted who could not read, and doctors tracked who went on to develop dementia over about eight years.

In all, 283 people developed dementia, and lack of reading skill was more common in women. Among those who could not read, women developed dementia at a higher rate than men. The findings suggest that early schooling gaps can shape brain health late in life, and that help may need to reach women most.
pmc-11716510:
A blood test for Alzheimer's-related change would be far easier to scale than a spinal tap. Ming Ann Sim and co-authors checked how blood markers line up with brain measures in this 2025 study. The spinal fluid markers reflect brain disease closely, but drawing that fluid needs a needle in the back. Their cohort held community volunteers aged fifty-five and over, all free of dementia.

The blood markers covered three themes: amyloid buildup, nerve cell damage, and brain inflammation. The team compared them with thinking test scores, cortex thickness on scans, and the matching spinal fluid values. Each marker was picked to echo a known fluid or scan signal. A blood panel that tracks the brain well could widen screening to clinics without scan or tap services. The study tests that promise in a healthy older group.
pmc-11716610:
Habbiburr Rehman and six co-authors published a study in 2025 on a blood protein score that forecasts thinking decline. Single markers help, but a score built from hundreds of proteins might predict who will develop mild impairment or Alzheimer's disease years ahead. The team built such scores in the long-running Framingham Heart Study.

They used protein data from more than fifteen hundred adults, most of them healthy at the start. One score used 279 proteins for mild impairment and another used 103 for the disease itself. Both scores separated future patients from healthy peers well, and follow-up ran over twenty years on average. A single blood draw might one day rank a person's long-term risk.
pmc-11716710:
Cheryl L Wellington published a project description in 2025 on partner violence as a possible risk factor for dementia. About thirty percent of women worldwide face such violence, and most report blows to the head or strangulation. Yet there is no accepted way to document the brain injury involved, and long-term risks are poorly understood.

A new study at three clinics in British Columbia will follow survivors and test blood markers of brain injury. Survivors and service partners helped design the study forms and materials from the start. The team also plans a living practice guideline for clinicians. The goal is care and research that ask about this hidden cause of brain harm.
pmc-11716810:
Zachary Green and co-authors link metabolic syndrome severity to brain wiring in a 2025 study. Poor metabolic health raises Alzheimer's risk, and the brain's default mode network is an early casualty of that disease. Whether metabolic strain alone maps onto the network's structure was the question.

Data came from a diverse aging cohort: about twelve hundred cognitively healthy and three hundred impaired adults. A continuous metabolic severity score, built from blood pressure, fats, sugar, and waist size, differed by diagnosis and ethnicity. Higher scores tracked with thinner cortex, smaller hippocampi, and altered connectivity in the network's rear subsystem. The authors say metabolic care may be brain care, and the score gives clinics a graded tool rather than a yes-no label.
pmc-11716910:
Sohail Karimi and colleagues tracked blood and spinal fluid markers across the lifespan of squirrel monkeys, a primate that naturally develops amyloid buildup in brain blood vessels with age. That condition, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, is a leading driver of vascular dementia and often overlaps with Alzheimer disease. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team used ultrasensitive assays to measure markers of Alzheimer processes, nerve damage, blood-brain barrier trouble, and inflammation in young and old animals. A touchscreen test system also measured the monkeys thinking performance.

Several markers rose steadily with age, including ones tied to support cell activation and nerve fiber damage in both blood and spinal fluid. Two enzyme markers fell with age, while others showed no simple trend. The authors argue the monkey model mirrors the human disease course closely enough to test future biomarkers and treatments.
pmc-11718110:
Tsuburaya and four co-authors described in twenty twenty-four a valve that may help a brain bleed risk after shunt surgery. A shunt drains extra fluid from the brain, but too much drain can cause a slow bleed on the brain's surface. To treat it, staff must stop the shunt, then build it back later.

The new valve can be set to a near-off state and turned back on at will. Once the bleed clears, flow can restart at the best set level. No new surgery to rebuild the shunt is needed. The team sees it as a fresh way to treat over-drain while keeping the shunt in place.
pmc-11726010:
Mo Y, Zou Z, and Chen E review a form of cell death in liver cancer in a paper from two thousand twenty-four, with the text in Chinese. The death form, ferroptosis, depends on iron imbalance and damage to cell fats. It is closely tied to how the main type of liver cancer grows and spreads.

The review explains how this death pathway affects fat, iron, and energy handling in the cancer. It also shapes tumor immunity, boosting some immune cells and weakening cells that suppress attack. Key control molecules affect how well immune therapy works. The authors discuss drugs and tiny carriers that trigger this death, and they see strong clinical promise in combining such approaches with immune therapy.
pmc-11727310:
Jingyan Liu and co-authors studied what cold storage does inside sweet corn kernels in a 2024 paper. Sweet corn spoils fast after harvest, and chilling is the main defense, yet the molecular side of that defense was murky. Kernels were stored warm or cold for one, three, and five days, then checked for enzyme activity and gene changes.

Cold storage raised two protective enzyme activities. Across all time points, nearly two thousand genes changed in the cold, and many sat in the pathway that builds flavonoids, plant compounds prized for health value. Eleven pathway genes shifted steadily, and three regulator genes tracked the pattern closely. The study explains part of how chilling protects quality and names targets for breeding corn that stores better.
pmc-11727910:
A team of researchers tested melatonin-related drugs on body-clock cells in a dish in this 2024 paper. Daily rhythms govern sleep, thinking, and even DNA repair. Melatonin steers those rhythms by binding its MT1 receptor, which quiets the brain's master clock. Most earlier work used whole animals, leaving open what the drug does to clocks outside the brain.

The team used human bone-derived cells engineered to glow in rhythm, a living clock readout. They applied melatonin and a blocker that reverses MT1's usual action. The cells' rhythms shifted in response, showing their clocks answer to the receptor without any brain input. The setup lets drug hunters screen clock-shifting compounds cell by cell. It also matters for tissues everywhere that keep their own time.
pmc-11728010:
Marta Obremska and co-authors compare two ways of sewing in a donor heart in a 2024 study of sixty-six transplant patients. The two methods, called total and bicaval, join the heart at different points. The team asked how each method affects the left upper chamber of the new heart.

Half the patients had each method, matched for sex, age, and time since surgery. Ultrasound scans measured chamber size and how well the chamber filled and emptied. The total group showed a smaller chamber index and better emptying. Strain measures of stretch and squeeze also favored the total method. The results may help surgeons weigh the two options.
pmc-11728110:
Miodrag Janić and co-authors review whether gut hormone drugs could aid lung disorders. The drugs mimic two gut hormones and are best known for blood sugar control. Their effects also reach the heart, kidneys, and body weight. Lung diseases rank third among causes of death worldwide, so new options are sought.

The review weighs direct actions on lung cells and indirect gains through metabolism. It covers long-term lung disease, asthma, pneumonia, and sleep apnea. Lung pressure illness, lung cancer, and lung transplant care also get sections. Proof splits by disease, with some areas richer than others. The authors map where trials should aim next to firm up the case.
pmc-11728410:
Néstor Báez-Ferrer and co-authors published a cohort study in twenty twenty-four on heart failure patients sent home from emergency care without a structured follow-up plan. Most such patients in their hospital were simply referred back to ordinary primary care. The team tracked who bounced back within a year.

Seven hundred seventy-nine patients, averaging eighty-two years old, were followed prospectively. Those who suffered new flare-ups had more kidney disease, higher natriuretic peptide levels, and more previous episodes. The riskiest combination was prior episodes plus unstructured follow-up, nearly tripling the hazard of another event. The study makes a concrete case that how follow-up is organized after discharge is itself a treatment decision.
pmc-11728710:
Dongxu Wang and co-authors made a light-driven material that strips ammonia from dirty water under visible light. Ammonia from farms, factories, and fish ponds builds up in rivers and lakes and threatens water safety. Using light to clean it is cheap, reusable, and kind to the environment, so better materials for the job are in demand.

Their material joins two parts: a carbon-based sheet and a cobalt compound. The best mix, with ten percent of the second part, removed about ninety-five percent of the ammonia in eighty minutes of light. Much of the ammonia turned into harmless nitrogen gas. The study shows a simple route to a strong cleaning material and explains why the pairing works so well.
pmc-11728910:
Gary Klinefelter, Michael Diamond, and Stephen Krawetz report, in a 2025 study, that a sperm protein called SP22 may help predict whether a man can father a child. The protein, made from the Park7 gene, was first tied to rat sperm fertility more than twenty years ago.

Using a targeted antibody, the team compared sperm from donors who achieved a live birth with sperm from donors who did not achieve a pregnancy. Levels of the protein were clearly lower in the second group. Parts of the gene also differed between the groups. The authors present the protein as the first sperm marker of this kind shown to track human fertility.
pmc-11729810:
Cancer patients often lose muscle mass and strength, a wasting called sarcopenia that worsens every outcome. Juliana Aparecida Braga Cruz and co-authors review whether inflammation drives that loss. Chronic inflammation floods the body with signaling proteins that break muscle down. The review asks whether those pro-inflammatory mediators can identify sarcopenia in cancer patients. It also checks whether studies measure the wasting in line with established guidelines.

The authors examine ten selected papers covering more than a thousand patients. Imaging and functional tools both appear, with uneven consistency. Their synthesis weighs which cytokine signals track muscle loss most credibly. The stakes are practical: a blood marker that flags sarcopenia early could trigger nutrition and exercise support before the wasting deepens.
pmc-11732610:
Rajyalakshmi Gogineni and co-authors read the blood of lung cancer patients stage by stage, looking for markers that track how far the disease has run. Their 2024 cross-sectional study enrolls 160 patients, evenly spread across the four clinical stages, and measures hormones, inflammation signals, and blood fats with standard assays.

Three markers climbed steeply with stage: parathyroid hormone rose dramatically, while C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 roughly doubled from earliest to latest disease. Blood fats shifted too, with protective cholesterol falling and triglycerides rising. Functional status worsened in step and tracked body mass closely. The authors argue this panel could help gauge severity where imaging is scarce or ambiguous. A single snapshot cannot show whether markers predict decline, only that they accompany it. Still, cheap blood tests that shadow stage this closely earn a place in the conversation about monitoring.
pmc-11736410:
A growth switch found on many cancers also turns up in bladder lining cancer, where it may flag worse disease and guide targeted drugs. Andong Guo and co-authors study that switch in a 2024 paper, pairing it with the cancer's sugar use. Records and tissue tests covered a group of patients at one Chinese hospital over two years.

Most tumors carried the switch. Its presence tracked with later stage disease and with high levels of an enzyme that marks fast sugar burning. It did not track with blood measures of insulin strain or a sugar-fat index. The authors read the pattern as a link between the switch and the cancer's hungry metabolism. They urge deeper work on the biology and on care plans that hit both the switch and the sugar path.
pmc-11759110:
Tjaša Ivošević and co-authors hunt for predictors of dangerous blood pressure spikes during neck surgery, in a 2023 study. Neck operations bleed heavily, so pressure surges are especially unwelcome. Knowing who will spike lets anesthetists prepare. Records from one hospital offered a large test bed.

Eight hundred eighty adults who had neck surgery under general anesthesia were reviewed. Pressure spikes struck a small share of patients. The sickest patients and the hardest intubations showed the highest rates. Sex, age, illness burden, and anesthesia choices were all weighed. Induced low pressure was among the factors studied. The results rank which warnings deserve action before incision. Anesthesia teams gain a focused checklist for a bleeding-prone surgery.
pmc-11760410:
Prajakta Anadeo and co-authors charted this 2024 anatomy survey of toddlers' mouths. Dentists know far less about baby teeth's arches and the lips above them than about adult mouths. Over six months, the team examined 135 children aged three to six, sorting lip shapes into three families and dental arches into ovoid, square, and tapered forms.

One lip subtype, a subtype of the arched family, led at about forty-four percent of children. Ovoid arches dominated both jaws, at seventy-nine percent up top and fifty-seven below. No significant link appeared between a child's lip shape and arch form. Baseline numbers like these help pediatric dentists spot the unusual early, in a dentition stage research often skips.
pmc-11769910:
Halladay and co-authors run thousands of models on teen drinking and mood in a 2024 paper. Past studies clash on how teen alcohol use and emotional woes link. Each study picks unlike measures and controls, which may drive the clash.

The team ran near eight thousand model variants on a long study of Australian teens. In bare cross time models, drinking and woes near all came as a pair. But how woes were scored, plus which controls were picked, swayed the links a lot. Mood woes looked more apt to lead to later drinking than the reverse.
pmc-11770010:
Hao Qu and co-authors present a 2024 study on why lung cancer that has spread to the brain resists a key chemotherapy drug. The drug is a first-line choice for these patients, yet resistance, early or acquired, blunts it often. A surface protein called CD146 had been tied to drug resistance and tumor growth in other settings.

Working with a brain-seeking line of lung cancer cells, the team found a subpopulation that strongly resisted the drug and carried far more of the protein. Blocking the protein restored drug sensitivity in cells and in animals. The protein acted through a known inflammatory signaling pathway. The findings nominate the protein as a target to pair with chemotherapy for brain metastases.
pmc-11772410:
Shaurya Dhingra and six co-authors describe a patient whose cancer marker shot up for a benign reason, in this 2024 case report and literature review. The marker, CA 19-9, is used to track cancers of the pancreas and bile ducts. A sixty-five year old woman with past gallbladder cancer showed a new liver spot on a check scan, and her marker read nearly six thousand.

Doctors drained the spot and gave antibiotics, and the marker fell fast. The lesion was an abscess, a pocket of infection, not a returning cancer. The authors review eight similar published cases where liver abscesses drove the same marker high. Their message is caution: a scary marker value can come from infection, and treating it as proof of cancer could lead to grave mistakes.
pmc-11773410:
Elie Karam and co-authors measured the mental health of Lebanon after the shocks of twenty twenty: the Beirut port blast, a financial collapse, and the pandemic, all at once. Between July and September twenty twenty-two, they interviewed a nationally representative sample of one thousand Lebanese by phone.

The rates were stark: about forty-eight percent screened positive for probable depression, forty-five percent for anxiety, and forty-four percent for probable post-traumatic stress. Region, jobs, and marital status showed no significant links in the adjusted models. One factor cut across everything: a composite score of financial strain influenced all three disorders. The authors describe a nation in a severe mental health crisis and call for nuanced, targeted policy responses.
pmc-11782210:
Chongjun Wu and co-authors set out a gene-first route for spotting a red-cell disorder in children with unexplained anemia. Hereditary spherocytosis makes red cells round and fragile, but in Jiangxi clinics its early signs blur into other anemias. The team sequenced thirty children whose anemia defied routine diagnosis.

Sequencing solved four fifths of cases: nineteen children carried the spherocytosis genes, and five carried other inherited anemia genes. At first visit, the spherocytosis cases looked much like the rest, underlining why blood tests alone miss them. The authors propose sequencing once common culprits such as nutrient deficiency and thalassemia are excluded, while noting the pathway needs refinement on larger cohorts.
pmc-11786010:
Shahab Kavousinejad and four co-authors use machine learning to judge growth maturity from neck X-rays. Their twenty twenty-four article serves orthodontics, where timing growth treatment right is key to good results. Classic checks rely on hand-wrist films or a dentist's subjective read of the neck bones.

The team gathered nine hundred eighty side head films from a Tehran dental school. Eight landmarks on the third and fourth neck vertebrae fed ratios into a stacked model, with an error-reduction function to sharpen landmark choice. Data augmentation widened the training set. On a held-out test set, the model called the maturation stage with near-perfect accuracy. The authors offer it as a semi-automated aid for clinics.
pmc-11786210:
Alireza Maleki and five co-authors published a 2024 study of retinopathy of prematurity, an eye disease of early-born infants, in southeastern Iran. The team reviewed 920 preterm infants referred to their eye hospital over one year. About 20 percent developed the retinopathy, and about 3.6 percent of all infants needed treatment for it.

Later gestational age and higher birth weight protected against the disease. A history of blood transfusion or phototherapy raised the risk of developing it. Phototherapy, though, lowered the need for treatment among those who did develop it. The authors say the pattern can guide screening and care in their region. They frame the work as a regional baseline for a preventable cause of infant blindness.
pmc-11788310:
Douaa Mugahid and a team of co-authors offer a practical guide to sharing biology data fairly, in two thousand twenty-four. Modern tools can gather many kinds of measures from the same sample at once. Yet much of that data sits in closed stores, in forms that other scientists and machines cannot read.

The guide sets out how to manage and share such multi-part data so others can find and reuse it. It lines up with current funder rules in the United States and Europe. Good sharing, the authors argue, lengthens the life of data and speeds discovery. The need grows sharper as artificial intelligence tools enter life science work.
pmc-11788410:
Garduno and co-authors set lab colony rules for the Chilean degu in Alzheimer's research. Degus are social, day-active rodents that live five to eight years. They can develop age-linked brain changes like Alzheimer's disease. No standard colony methods existed across labs before. That gap hurts repeatability of degu studies.

The guide covers housing, handling, and group care by species traits. Ecology and life history shape each rule given. Steps for Apoe gene work are detailed as well. Behavior test methods for aging studies are laid out. The authors aim for healthy colonies and comparable results.
pmc-11794210:
Shengxin Wang and co-authors pooled brain scan studies of Tai Chi in a meta-analysis published in 2024. Tai Chi is a slow exercise known to help body and mind. The team asked how it changes brain activity compared with other exercise or therapy. They screened hundreds of papers and kept eighteen that met strict rules.

The kept studies held 677 people, with an average age in the mid-fifties. One brain area stood out: the superior frontal gyrus showed changed activity. That region supports planning and self-control. The pooled result gives a firmer base than any single small study. It also points to where future scans should look.
pmc-11795210:
Junbin Liao and co-authors link diet and disability in older adults in this 2024 study from Guangzhou, China. Disability in later life limits daily tasks and care planning, and food may play a part through inflammation. The team scored each person's diet with an index that rates how inflammation-friendly the eating pattern is, then compared scores with the level of disability.

The study covered two hundred sixty-two older adults with mild to severe disability in two districts. Not exercising, having stopped exercising, stroke, and dementia each tied to deeper disability. After accounting for other factors, people with the most inflammation-heavy diets faced notably higher odds of severe disability than those with the lowest scores. The authors suggest that diet quality deserves a place in care plans for older adults.
pmc-11798810:
Yin and co-authors test a simple blood ratio as a predictor of diabetes risk in a large US survey sample. The ratio joins uric acid to HDL, the so-called good cholesterol. Past work linked the ratio to diabetes, but proof in big, varied groups was thin. The team used health survey data from 30,813 people gathered from 2005 to 2018. They modeled the link between the ratio and diabetes while adjusting for other factors.

Selection methods flagged the strongest predictors to include. Curve tools checked whether the ratio's link to risk bends at some level. The authors judged the model by accuracy, calibration, and clinical value. A cheap ratio that works across groups could aid early screening.
pmc-11801310:
Anthony Onwuegbuzie revisits quantitizing in an article published in 2024, returning to a widely cited piece from two thousand nine. Quantitizing means turning words based data, such as interview text, into numbers. The method has spread less than expected, and the author argues it lacks a clear guide.

He offers a broad framework built around why, when, what, where, how, and who. Inside it, a model sorts the work into four types, covering description, inference, measurement, and exploration. The article argues the method can serve many research styles, while noting that views on knowledge and values shape how scholars use it.
pmc-11802810:
Yasir Khan and co-authors surveyed medical and veterinary workers in a study published in 2024, though listed under 2025. Their topic was leishmaniasis, a disease passed between animals and humans, and the One Health idea that links human and animal care. Over five thousand people took part.

Knowledge of the disease was high, with most naming its cause and its animal-to-human spread. Attitudes to One Health were also positive, and most knew its zoonotic nature. Just over half used sandfly control, most often bed nets. Younger people scored better than older ones, and vets and state hospital staff scored best. The authors call for more teaching and community control.
pmc-11810910:
Masaki Tomonaga asks whether chimpanzees, like people, see faces in random noise. This quirk is called face pareidolia. It can come from a fast, rough scan for face like shapes, or from an active hunt for faces. Chimps seem to use the rough scan, but the active hunt was unclear.

Chimps were trained to pick a pattern hiding a face or a letter from a set of three. In test rounds, no true target was present at all. The patterns they picked, when averaged, still held a faint face like structure. Chance picking would leave no such trace. Tomonaga reads this as a sign that chimps do hunt for faces on purpose, not just by reflex.
pmc-11812510:
Indubala Maurya, Ayush Lohiya, and Ashish Solanki make the case for trial sequential analysis as a quality check on meta-analysis, using their own journal's recent output as the test bed. Their 2024 commentary counts nineteen systematic reviews from one year of the Indian Journal of Anaesthesia. Twelve carried a meta-analysis, and five of those added the sequential check.

In two of the five, the check confirmed the pooled result and the needed sample size was already met, marking the answer firm. In three, the trials fell short of the needed size, so a headline-significant pool still cannot be called settled. The authors explain how the method watches evidence build in sequence and guards against the random errors that mislead pooled studies.
pmc-11835910:
Soheil Shapouri and Yasaman Rafiee tested in 2024 whether ecological threats explain why some cultures are more collectivist, putting group needs above the individual. Disease outbreaks and natural disasters have been proposed as drivers, since both demand cooperation. The team used old and new measures of germ stress and disasters across 188 countries.

After accounting for national wealth, neither disasters nor infectious disease predicted collectivism scores. The null result held across different threat measures. The authors argue that past positive findings likely came from small, unrepresentative culture samples. They urge data-driven exploration over theory-only picks in cross-cultural work, to avoid unreliable claims about universal patterns.
pmc-11865210:
Yang Zhao and co-authors study deaths in hospital after heart bypass surgery in patients with weak hearts, in work published in 2024. The patients all had an ejection fraction below forty percent, meaning the heart pumped poorly. Data came from 765 patients treated between 2019 and 2023 at two hospitals in China.

Thirty-eight patients died in hospital, and the team compared them with survivors to find risk factors. Short-term prognosis in this fragile group guides surgical decisions. Knowing which traits predict death helps teams counsel patients and focus intensive care where risk is highest.
pmc-11907710:
Kwetepe Gladys Mafolo, Lindiwe Cele, and Mmampedi Mathibe study HIV treatment results in a 2024 paper from South Africa. Keeping the virus level in blood very low is the key sign that treatment works. Global targets push for that result, yet many patients still fall short for varied reasons.

Files of 379 adults on first line treatment at clinics in the city of Ekurhuleni were reviewed. The team counted how many had a suppressed virus level and which traits went with success or failure. South Africa carries one of the heaviest HIV loads in the world, so local data on what blocks success can guide clinic support.
pmc-11928310:
Ashwin Karnan and Anjana Ledwani present a case of mercury vapor poisoning in a 2024 clinical image article. A thirty-year-old laboratory worker arrived with two weeks of cough, chest pain, and breathlessness after four months of routine work around mercury vapor, with no other illness to explain it.

Chest CT showed strikingly dense deposits scattered through both lungs and kidneys, and blood and urine mercury ran high. Treatment combined oxygen, steroids, a chelating drug, and fluids. He recovered enough for discharge but was warned that lung scarring may follow. The article reviews how mercury's form and dose shape its damage across brain, lung, and kidney.
pmc-11934910:
Fada Guan and ten co-authors tested in 2024 a faster way to check whether a radiation plan made for one treatment machine fits its twin. Cancer centers buy beam-matched machines so patients can switch mid-course when one breaks down. Standard checks are slow, so the team tried a three-dimensional gamma score, computed with an open software kit.

Plans for many disease sites were rebuilt for the second machine and compared dose by dose. The gamma score flagged real differences beyond the usual point checks. A passing score gives clinics confidence to move a patient without replanning from scratch.
pmc-12180910:
Nathaniel Merrill and co-authors ask what clean coastal water is worth to people who swim, boat, and fish in New England. Their study appeared in 2024. The team paired a survey of residents with a large data set on shore traits, water clarity, and germ counts in the water.

Using a travel cost model, the authors found that clarity and germ levels both change what a trip is worth. A one-meter gain in clarity added about 4.5 dollars per trip in their units. They then used test cases for Narragansett Bay and Cape Cod to show how better water could bring large gains, and they share lessons for future studies of this kind.
pmc-12400310:
Hu studies how one Chinese city can give old people better care. Hengyang faces fast aging, weak home care, and too few care staff. Town groups, aid groups, and trained staff now try to work as one team. Yet smart tools see low use, and skilled staff stay scarce.

Hu asks if a chain model plus online care can fix those gaps. In that model, town staff keep lists of care needs. Aid groups give day-to-day help, and trained staff draw up care plans. Hu drew on case work and talks with staff. The aim is to share funds and staff more fairly and raise care quality.
pmc-12453410:
Katarzyna Okurowska and co-authors compare eye infection models in a 2024 study. A germ that infects the cornea, often through contact lenses, is tested on donated corneas in the lab before drugs reach patients. Pig and sheep corneas stand in for human ones, but their thickness differs, and storage and culture conditions vary between labs.

Those gaps could distort how infection takes hold and how drugs appear to work. Human, pig, and sheep corneas were infected side by side under matched conditions. Colonization and tissue response were compared across the three species. The verdict tells labs how far animal stand ins can be trusted for drug screening.
pmc-12527410:
Blanca Carlos-Ortega and four co-authors set out the traits of the grave skin cancer melanoma in Mexican patients at a large state center. Their study, from two thousand twenty-four, reads a long span of past cases.

The cancer is the third most common skin kind in the land, and takes most skin-cancer deaths. A scope tool lifts early finds past the bare eye. The team read near two hundred proved cases from a long past span. They logged sex, age, skin tone kind, past facts, the wound's place, its scope marks, spread at find, and its tissue kind. Two depth scores were read as well. Their aim is a full face of the disease as it lands there.
pmc-12660310:
Runways on frozen ground face a thaw threat as the world warms. Xiaolan Liu and co-authors tested a vented road bed design to keep the cold in, in work from twenty twenty-five. Flat, wide runways soak up heat, which softens the frozen base. Their design runs pierced vents side by side under the surface.

A computer model was checked against past lab data on air speed, rock layers, and heat depth curves. With warming and earth heat both in play, the vented bed held ground below ten meters in a frozen state for thirty years. The chill effect fades with depth and over time, then levels off. The rock layer gained most from the vents. The team offers the design as a base for lasting polar builds.
pmc-12660810:
Mohsen Moslehi and co-authors develop an epoxy material that absorbs microwaves well. Their 2025 paper joins carbon nanotubes, tiny carbon tubes, with a nickel-zinc iron oxide coating. Absorbing materials cut interference between devices and improve safety in communication systems.

The team made the coating and confirmed it with X-ray and chemical tests. The coated tubes showed strong magnetism with almost no leftover magnetization, a trait suited to absorption. Images showed the crystals spread over the tube surfaces. The filler share ranged from very low to a third of the mix, letting the team tune performance. Such composites can shield electronics, radar systems, and wireless gear. The work adds a recipe to a field chasing thinner, lighter absorbers.
pmc-12661710:
Leila Hamze and co-authors test how well standard disinfectants kill a hardy hospital bacterium, and how its slime layer shields it. Their 2025 study deals with Acinetobacter baumannii, a germ that haunts intensive care units. Many strains resist last resort antibiotics, and they persist on surfaces by forming biofilms. The team gathered sixty four isolates from hospitals, sick animals, and food. Five common biocides were tested with standard methods.

Killing doses for free floating bacteria sat below the strengths sold in products. Adding a protein to mimic dirt raised the needed doses. Biofilm growth protected the bacteria much further. Isolates spanned many types, including members of global outbreak clones. Food isolates were drug sensitive while clinical ones were resistant. The authors tie survival on surfaces to biofilm, urging cleaning regimes that account for it.
pmc-12661810:
Jun Hu and Wei Xiao test a heart patch made from cleaned heart tissue as a home for growing heart muscle cells, in a 2025 study. Patches meant to repair the heart often trigger immune rejection and inflammation. Their patch is a hydrogel of decellularized heart matrix, the scaffold left after cells are stripped away, and they compared it with a hyaluronic acid gel and plain culture dishes.

Cells in the heart-matrix gel stayed most viable, nearly tripling relative to controls after five days. Two genes tied to calcium handling, central to heartbeat strength, also switched on at higher levels than in the other settings. The authors conclude the natural matrix gel helps heart cells grow.
pmc-12662210:
In a 2025 study, Recep A. Ozdemir and co-authors investigate brain signals in early Alzheimer's disease. Animal work shows overexcited neurons and broken networks, but proof in people was thin. The team probed the default mode network, a web of regions active at rest, using magnetic pulses paired with brain wave recording.

Plain resting brain waves showed general slowing and weaker synchrony, signs spread across the whole brain. The pulse method found something sharper: the back part of the network was locally overexcited, and its link to the front part was disrupted. Those measures predicted specific thinking problems and carried the effect of brain structure on cognition. The approach may one day mark early disease and drug effects.
pmc-12662810:
Jiuhong Li and co-authors build a light-scan system to find nerve tumour edges during surgery, in work from twenty twenty-five. Cutting neural tumours safely hinges on knowing exactly where tumour ends. Optical coherence scans give live, touch-free images of tissue depth. A swept-source system with a fast micro scanner is built for the task. Human tumour samples and animal tumours test the system.

Light fades more slowly through glioma tissue than through nearby tissue. Brightness and slope measures split tumour from normal tissue clearly. The system spots nerves and their sheaths buried under two tumour types. Those deep structures appear as bright tubes or crescents on screen. Accuracy scores for the human glioma split run high in testing. A handheld theatre tool for precise cuts is the end goal.
pmc-12663110:
James Njunge and co-authors follow children discharged from hospital in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia to see what slows their growth. Children in low-resource settings often gain weight poorly after an illness, for reasons that stay unclear. Their 2025 cohort study spans six countries and tracks weight gain over ninety days after discharge.

Blood markers at discharge tied inflammation to the growth system itself. Inflammation pressed on the growth hormone and IGF-1 axis and on bone metabolism more than on other pathways. Gut damage and growth mediators were measured alongside, to untangle the chain. The picture points to inflammation as a driver, not a bystander. Child health teams get a target for post-discharge care, beyond food alone.
pmc-12663210:
Radhakrishnan and colleagues build in twenty twenty-five a wound dressing from shell-derived gel loaded with green tea and catechu extracts, aimed at diabetic foot ulcers. These ulcers strike many diabetics and resist healing, with infection and drug resistance common. Freeze-drying made a sponge scaffold whose pores soak up fluid strongly, and tests confirmed the plant extracts sat inside with their chemistry intact.

The dressing killed a broad range of germs found in such wounds. In animal tests it was safe on tissue and closed wounds almost fully, far ahead of untreated controls. Microscopy showed more skin cells, collagen, surface regrowth, and blood vessels. The authors see clinical promise but call for long studies before human use.
pmc-12663310:
Anas Arafa and five co-authors solve a fractional wave equation, the Fornberg Whitham type, with a step by step method that stays partly in closed form. Fractional forms let the math hold a memory of past states. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

The method is built for two senses of the fractional step, one of Caputo type and one with a broader kernel. The authors prove that a solution exists and is the only one, and they check that their steps converge. At whole order, results match known exact solutions. The broader kernel form held memory effects more strongly and settled faster, they report.
pmc-12663410:
Villads Nielsen and Thomas Just Sørensen redraw a classic map of the energy levels of lanthanide ions in water. Chemists have read these f-block elements from Dieke diagrams since 1968, but the tools behind those charts were crude by modern standards. Their 2025 work measures all thirteen trivalent lanthanide ions afresh, using glow spectroscopy at very cold temperatures.

The cold, sharper spectra let the team fit energy levels directly and split apart forms that older room-temperature work had to lump into bands. Several levels printed in the classic tables turned out to be artifacts and are dropped. For each glowing ion they also describe the ground state pattern in full. The authors offer the new diagram as a benchmark for lanthanide chemistry, a reference the field has lacked for half a century.
pmc-12664210:
Yanling Wei, Hongqiu Pan, Fuhui Lu, Xiaowei Deng, and Jianming Wang use single-cell RNA sequencing to study immune cells in active tuberculosis. Their 2025 study drew blood from three patients with active disease and two healthy controls.

The team profiled peripheral blood mononuclear cells and mapped cell types, gene activity, and cell-to-cell signals. Patients had more myeloid cells and platelets and fewer natural killer cells than controls. CD8 effector T cells and other groups showed signs of poor function, and the contact networks between cells looked rewired. The work is exploratory, but it points to where immune control breaks down in active tuberculosis.
pmc-12666210:
Linge Jian and co-authors link a blood sugar control score to eye disease risk in a large cohort study from two thousand twenty-five. Lower scores mean the body resists insulin more. The cohort held over two hundred thousand adults in the United Kingdom with early stages of a heart, kidney, and body-chemistry syndrome.

Higher scores went with lower risk of two eye diseases in a straight-line way. Cataract risk formed a U shape, and one diabetes eye disease formed an L shape. Top versus bottom score groups split risk most for that diabetes eye disease. Links grew stronger at later syndrome stages.
pmc-12669910: Julian Brummer and co-authors boil current physical activity guidance down to a slogan and a picture. The slogan reads: Move, Mix It Up, Make It Fun. Each part carries one strand of the advice: get moving, vary the kind of activity, and keep it enjoyable. The team also designed an infographic that draws the three ideas for use in public campaigns, so the guidance can be grasped at a glance.
pmc-12682910:
Kamil Rapacz, Jaroslaw Szymanski, Armour Forse, and Tomasz Rogula published a 2025 comparison of robotic and standard keyhole gastric bypass in patients with very severe obesity. A body mass index of 60 or more makes weight-loss surgery riskier and technically harder. Robots give surgeons steadier, more precise movements, but their value at this size was unproven.

The study drew on a national database covering 233,828 bypass patients from 2020 to 2023. Patients at the highest weights had more complications and more emergency visits than lighter patients. Within the heaviest group, robotic and keyhole surgery had the same 30-day complication rate. Robotic operations took longer, but patients left hospital sooner. The authors call for careful multi-centre trials to settle which approach is best.
pmc-12684110:
Ezgi Ulas and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on what adding immunotherapy does to the lymph nodes that drain a lung tumor. Those nodes teach the immune system to attack the cancer, yet they sit near the tumor and often catch radiation. The team compared nodes from twenty-five patients who got chemo-radiation plus two immune drugs before surgery with nodes from twenty-five matched patients who got chemo-radiation alone. Nodes were sorted by the radiation dose they had absorbed.

The immunotherapy group's nodes showed strong type I immune responses and more killer and regulatory T cells, at every dose level. The effect ran strongest in the hardest-hit nodes. High-dose nodes also showed scarring and long inflammation signatures, which the drugs partly softened. The authors stress the surprise: heavy radiation did not blunt the nodes' immune work.
pmc-12686410:
Kun Lin and co-authors map the cells of joint lining tissue in hemophilic arthritis. The illness comes from repeat bleeding into joints in people with hemophilia. It wears the joint down, yet its cell profile was largely unknown. The team read single-cell gene activity in lining tissue taken during knee replacement surgery. They compared the map with maps from two other joint diseases.

The hemophilic map stood apart from both other diseases. Mast cells, rare in the others, were active here and may start leaks from vessels. Iron left by blood drove a cell death form called ferroptosis in vessel and support cells. One vessel cell type may steer support cells toward easing that death. The map names fresh targets for gene-based care.
pmc-12687510:
Rogate Phinias, Mikidadi Muhanga, and Joshua Malago studied health data quality in Tanzania in a 2025 paper. Good care depends on records that are accurate, complete, consistent, and on time, yet the workers who type in patient data can introduce errors. The team asked which traits of those workers predict better data.

They surveyed 336 data-entering health workers at eight regional referral hospitals between August and October 2024. Older workers produced more accurate, complete, and timely records. Sex and schooling also mattered, with education linked above all to accuracy and completeness. The authors suggest training and support should be shaped with these patterns in mind, since errors in patient data can put lives at risk.
pmc-12690410:
Rahul Kanade and co-authors read, in a 2025 study, ten years of mitral valve surgery at one center where the valve ring had grown hard with calcium. That build-up, MAC, twists the valve's shape and makes surgery a hard call. The team read 172 such patients, and scored the build-up in 67 of them with a 10-point scan scale. Main outcomes were death, return, new surgery, stroke, long vent need, kidney loss, and deep chest infection at 30 days. A match group had valve swaps with no build-up in the same span.

Death at 30 days ran near twice the match rate: 9.9 against 4.2 percent. Stroke and long vent need also ran high in the build-up group. The team splits the finds by valve disease type and by scan score to guide picks.
pmc-12691010:
Sita Liu and co-authors link a sleep posture to learning flexibility in young calves in this 2025 study. Sleep aids brain growth, but its tie to thinking in farm animals is little studied. A curled posture in calves signals a REM-like sleep state and can be scored from video without touching the animals.

Twenty two-month-old calves were filmed for 48 hours, then given learning tasks with color cues tied to sweet or sour fluids. Fifteen calves passed the first learning stage. That stage showed no link to sleep posture time. Calves with more daily posture time, though, needed fewer rounds to reverse the learned rule, which signals greater flexibility. The authors suggest posture checks as a welfare tool.
pmc-12691810:
Felix-Mircea Brehar and seven co-authors review how water channels in the brain may shape many brain diseases. Their review is from two thousand twenty-five. A channel called AQP4 sits mostly on the feet of star-shaped brain cells, right next to blood vessels. From there it helps move fluid, clear waste, and keep the vessel wall seal tight.

When these channels drift away from the vessel side, that order is lost. The review links this loss to swelling, inflammation, and early signs of brain decline.
