It also covers what holds the channels in place and what can knock them loose. These include vessel stress, injury, and low energy in cells. The authors see the pattern as one thread in a larger web.
pmc-12692110:
Maria Lidia Iancu and co-authors tune a chickpea-avocado puree by a grid of tests, in a study from 2025. A new food's feel in the mouth is half its fate, and guess-work tunes it slow. A factorial grid lets three knobs be turned at once and read as one math form.

The knobs were chickpea share, avocado share, and the sweet-to-sour scale. Nine brews from the grid were graded by tool feel, tongue feel, and sour. Each knob and each pair and the full trio swayed feel marks with clear weight; sour claims on one knob pair could not be held. Kind math proof blessed the form. The best brew of the nine stands as the first build.
pmc-12693210:
Stefano Kayali and co-authors study how lockdown life reshaped irritable bowel symptoms in a 2025 survey paper. Nearly three thousand Italians reported diet, sleep, stress, and gut symptoms before and during the 2020 lockdown. The forced cocoon changed routines in opposite directions at once.

Among patients, nearly half improved. Lower general stress, more fiber, and longer sleep each raised the odds of symptoms resolving, while anxiety pill use cut them. New cases sprang up in about five percent of healthy respondents, driven by inactivity, work stress, and anxiety medication. Less alcohol protected. The gut, the authors show, mirrors the whole lifestyle.
pmc-12694910:
Pengxu Wang and co-authors present a 2025 study of gene marks that may shape pancreatic cancer risk. Chemical marks on DNA can change gene work without changing the code. The team used a gene based method that mimics a trial to test if such marks in blood track with this cancer.

They scanned marks across the full mark set, then ran checks with changed rules and in fresh data sets to test the strength of each hit. Hundreds of marks passed the checks, and a large share held up in at least one repeat test. A final pooled test kept a core set, with four marks backed most strongly. One top mark sits in a gene known from past cancer work. The authors offer the marks as leads for study.
pmc-12695810:
Ying Zhang and co-authors survey college students in northwest China in a 2025 study on mpox. The illness has spread westward in China, and students form a high risk group. The team asked what students know about the disease, how they view it, and whether they would accept a vaccine.

A set survey went to nine schools over two weeks in October 2024. A total of 3,483 students took part. Gaps in knowledge and in vaccine willingness stood out across groups. The findings give health staff a base for targeted teaching and vaccine plans on campus, rather than one broad message for all students.
pmc-12698710:
Xiaoyan Wang and a team of co-authors knit a smart hydrogel patch that tracks heart and breath through marathon misery. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Sweat, heat, and motion wreck most wearable sensors long before the finish line.

The gel mixes a common polymer with plant nanofibers, laced with MXene sheets and borax. It stayed stable for thirty-five days in storage and stretched to eight times its length with keen sensitivity. The MXene also killed over ninety-nine percent of bacteria. In simulated marathon heat and humidity, the patch held steady for six hours. Heart rate and breathing read cleanly throughout. The authors target early warning of heart and lung trouble in endurance sport.
pmc-12699710:
Tao Lin and a large team of co-authors set out the protocol for a head-to-head pooling of two talk therapies for depression, in a 2025 paper. Cognitive behavioural therapy and interpersonal psychotherapy both lift depression, but how they compare on wider outcomes, over the long term, and for which patients is less clear. The planned review will gather the raw, person-level data behind past trials rather than just their printed summaries.

Searches across four databases will find trials that pitted the two therapies against each other in adults. Trial teams will be asked to share anonymized data. Joint models will then compare results at treatment end and beyond, and test which starter traits tilt the balance. The authors expect the work to guide matching patients to the therapy likeliest to help them.
pmc-12699910:
A colonoscopy that cannot finish means repeat procedures, delays, and extra cost. Carla Rognoni and co-authors price a new magnetic balloon add-on that helps complete hard colonoscopies in a 2025 budget study set in Italy.

The device assists the scope through difficult bends of the bowel. The analysis compares its pathway with standard care for cases that would otherwise be left incomplete. Per patient, the device path cost slightly less from both the hospital view and the national health system view. If use grew from two to ten percent of incomplete cases over five years, savings would mount. Early budget work of this kind helps hospitals judge whether a promising gadget pays for itself.
pmc-12700410:
Tianyu Li leads a team of eight authors in 2025 in designing a lighter network for image super-resolution, the task of rebuilding a sharp picture from a small one. Existing networks do this well but demand heavy computing and memory, which keeps them off phones and other edge devices.

Their network, R2GDN, reuses features across dense residual blocks and borrows a reparameterization layer based on the lean RepGhost design. Cheap operations squeeze extra features out of the ones already computed, and the training-time structure folds away for fast running. The result targets clear upscaling that modest hardware can actually run.
pmc-12701210:
Paris Liokatis and nine colleagues wrote a surgical study in twenty twenty-five on rebuilding the mandibular condyle, the knob at the jaw joint, after a break healed in the wrong place. Such bad unions can spoil a patient's bite and make chewing hard, and surgery to fix them was long seen as hard to predict. The study tested whether digital planning changes that.

Each patient got a plan made on a computer and implants made for them alone by CAD/CAM methods. The team then set the planned joint surface against the real one after surgery. The gap between plan and result averaged 2.27 millimeters by one measure. Most patients ended with good jaw movement, opening their mouths about thirty-seven millimeters on average, and no lasting loss of feeling was reported. Close agreement of this kind turns a once wayward fix into a precise one.
pmc-12702610:
Steven George and co-authors describe care patterns for new shoulder pain in the United States military health system, in work from 2025. Shoulder trouble is common and drives many visits, yet system-wide care patterns were unknown. The cohort held 456,241 people with a fresh episode of shoulder pain.

Care in the first three months was sorted by scan use, drug use, and hands-on care, and by seven diagnosis groups. Most people never got a scan. Pain drugs of one common class were the top drug choice, and therapy was the top hands-on care. For some groups, civilian clinics used more scans and steroid shots and less therapy than military clinics. The authors say most patterns matched across settings, with clear gaps in a few groups.
pmc-12703010:
Abu Bocus and co-authors report a case where bleeding into the lungs hid behind a familiar diagnosis. An elderly woman with lupus arrived breathless and anemic, with cloudy lungs on imaging. The first call was pneumonia, and antibiotics began. She did not improve, and every germ test came back negative, forcing a rethink.

Deeper immune testing found antibodies pointing to a different disease: microscopic polyangiitis, a vessel inflammation that can overlap with lupus. The lung problem was hemorrhage from inflamed vessels, not infection. The authors use the case to warn clinicians that lung bleeding in lupus patients is not always a lupus flare. When respiratory illness refuses to resolve, especially with autoimmune disease in the background, the diagnosis deserves a second, wider look.
pmc-12703410:
Carlos Blanco-Camarillo and Carlos Rosales review a puzzling subgroup of white blood cells called low-density neutrophils. Their 2025 paper gathers what is known about these cells in health and disease. Neutrophils were once seen as a uniform defense cell. These lighter cells break that view. They turn up among a blood layer where they do not normally belong, and their numbers surge in several diseases.

In lupus, the cells readily cast out web-like traps and release strong signals that drive swelling. In cancer, the same label covers cells that calm immune defense instead. That clash has sown confusion about what the cells truly are and do. The authors sort the disputes over how to spot and name them. They also weigh the cells as possible markers of disease and as targets for future care.
pmc-12704310:
Sebastian Bogner and three colleagues published a review and combined analysis in two thousand twenty-five on suicide risk in colorectal cancer. A cancer diagnosis is known to raise suicide risk, but past studies on this cancer type disagreed. The team gathered the world evidence to settle the picture.

They searched six databases for studies comparing patients with people free of cancer. Forty-four studies qualified, covering more than nine million patients. Most reported standardised death ratios, which the team pooled in a combined analysis. The review weighs how factors like disease stage may shape risk. It gives clinicians and planners a firmer base for spotting patients who may need mental health support.
pmc-12705210:
Shannon Charlebois, Ken Flegel, and Matthew B. Stanbrook wrote a 2025 editorial against Quebec's Bill 2, a health law on access to care. The province had pledged that each resident would have a family doctor. Close to two million people still lack one, even though Quebec has many doctors for its size.

Instead of hiring more staff, the law shifts blame to doctors, the editors argue. It orders them to take on more patients and work harder, with no new support or funds. The editors back Quebec doctors who oppose the law. They call on the province to rethink it with doctors, not against them.
pmc-12706010:
Chuan Liu and co-authors show in 2025 that a fractal surface helps kidney podocytes mature in the lab. Podocytes are highly branched cells in the kidney filter, and tissues in the body often form self similar fractal patterns that flat lab dishes do not copy. The team first showed fractal traits in the kidney filter and its podocytes.

They then made culture surfaces that copy patterns drawn from tissue images of that filter. Podocytes grown on the fractal surface showed higher levels of function markers and clearer cell polarity than cells on flat ground. Gene data pointed to more laying down and reshaping of the material around cells, plus signs of added stress. The authors suggest fractal plates could become a simple tool for more faithful cell culture.
pmc-12706910:
Joseph Kwon and co-authors present a 2025 study checking a widely used children's quality-of-life questionnaire in Australian children. The tool has twenty-three items across body, feelings, social life, and school, and children answer it themselves. Before scores can be trusted for policy or care, the tool's measurement quality must be proven in the local population.

The team drew a random sample of five hundred children aged eleven to twelve from a long-running national study. Using a strict measurement model from Rasch theory, they tested whether each item behaves as a proper ruler should. The work shows whether the child self-report version measures one clean trait in this group.
pmc-12707010:
Hiroshi Kobayashi and eleven colleagues weigh two prognostic signals in a rare soft tissue cancer, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. Doctors have few tools to judge who will fare badly after surgery for a contained tumor. Blood inflammation scores and the immune cells inside the tumor both looked promising.

The team reviewed 103 patients with tumors of the limbs or trunk. They computed several blood ratios and stained tumors for CD8 killer T cells. One score, the systemic inflammatory response index, leaned toward predicting worse survival and spread. High CD8 counts leaned toward less spread, though not firmly. Only tumor size over ten centimeters clearly predicted spread. The authors call for bigger studies.
pmc-12708710:
Dong-Hye Suh, Jae Eun Choi, Sang Jun Lee, and Hei Sung Kim evaluate a small-tip radiofrequency device for tightening upper eyelids in Asian patients who want to avoid surgery. Sagging eyelids mark aging and bother many people, yet scalpel procedures deter them. Gentle heat can contract skin and spur collagen, offering a needle-and-knife-free route.

Fourteen subjects received one session with a quarter-square-centimeter tip, over the upper lid and the outer eye corner, with numbing cream and a protective lens. Every subject improved on photographs and physician scoring. By two months, seventy-three percent of patients reported more than half improvement, and satisfaction kept rising. Safety held throughout. Small tips suit delicate eyelid skin.
pmc-12709010:
Ke-Jun Liu and co-authors compare lung cancer drugs against a resistant change using computer simulations in a 2025 paper. Insertions in exon 20 of the EGFR gene make tumors respond unevenly to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. The team used models of the receptor's structure to see why this is so.

They modeled the normal receptor and three representative insertion forms in molecular dynamics runs. They then examined how an older drug, osimertinib, and a newer one bind each form. Work at this fine scale can guide which patients should get which drug. It can also guide how better drugs for this change might be designed.
pmc-12709710:
Meghan Hill and six colleagues publish the design of a New Zealand trial testing whether a familiar abortion drug can help people with a previous caesarean start labor naturally. Spontaneous labor is safest after a uterine scar, because the standard induction drug raises rupture risk. Mifepristone blocks progesterone and may make the uterus responsive to its own signals.

Participants with one prior lower-segment caesarean are randomized to a single dose of mifepristone or placebo near term. The trial needs at least 168 participants to detect labor starting within forty-eight hours rising from ten to thirty percent. A positive result could change how post-caesarean births are managed.
pmc-12709810:
Shiqi Ren and co-authors review amino acid metabolism in 2025 as a target for cancer care. Tumors rewire how they use amino acids, the building blocks of protein, to fuel growth, survival, invasion, and escape from the immune system. These nutrients also shape how immune cells switch on.

The review maps how amino acids feed the cell's central energy cycle and its recycling system. It then surveys attack routes: blocking the enzymes that process amino acids, diet-based plans, and nano-sized delivery systems. The authors aim to ground future trials that starve tumors of what they crave.
pmc-12710510:
Xianqiu Chen and seven co-authors report two cases of a stubborn lung mold infection cured with a fat-wrapped form of an older antifungal drug. Their 2025 paper covers adults whose immune systems were normal, a group in which this mold, Aspergillus flavus, is seldom suspected. Both patients stayed ill through rounds of antibacterial drugs.

Gene-based tests and tissue checks pinned down the mold. Once the wrapped drug, liposomal amphotericin B, was added, symptoms eased and lung images cleared in both cases. The authors pair the cases with a review of past reports. They urge doctors to test for fungi early when lung infections resist standard drugs, and they voice more trust in this gentler form of the drug.
pmc-12710710:
Zixiao Zhu and a team of co-authors present a way to print soft robots with built in motion and sensing in a 2025 paper. Soft robots need motors and sensors spread through a stretchy body, but stiff electronics clash with soft materials. The team combine two printing methods to build robots and their electronics in one automated process.

Design tricks such as lattice structures, wavy wiring, and split circuit boards keep the electronics working under large bends. Their demo robots show several modes of motion, touch sensing in real time, wireless links, and self guided obstacle avoidance. The authors offer the approach as a path to self reliant soft robots.
pmc-12711910:
Yangwon Chae and co-authors test whether balls of fat derived stem cells inside printed scaffolds can regrow bone, in work from 2025. Bone heals well on its own, but large gaps with complex shapes need help. Printed scaffolds can be shaped to fit such gaps exactly.

Stem cells from fat can turn into bone forming cells. Single cells grown flat lose vigor over time, while cells grown as 3D balls survive better and form bone more strongly. The team placed those balls in a printed plastic and mineral scaffold. They tested the pairing in a rabbit arm bone defect model.
pmc-12713810:
Astrid Zamora and co-authors study how tea and other diet habits relate to sleep in midlife women in Mexico City. Their twenty twenty-four paper mixes deep interviews with survey math. Little was known about how women themselves link food and drink to rest.

Thirty working-class women from a long health cohort gave detailed accounts of sleep and diet. Field notes and transcripts were sorted by theme. Tea stood out as a habit women tied to sleep, for good or ill. Guided by that hint, the team tested tea against sleep length in the wider cohort. The paired design lets lived words shape the numbers that follow.
pmc-12714110:
Saran Lal Ajai Mokan Dasan and Ramesh reported a rare case in two thousand twenty-five where a liver abscess caused a block of blood flow out of the liver. The abscess came from amoebic infection, a common tropical problem, but the flow block, called Budd-Chiari syndrome, is seldom tied to it. Their patient was a man aged thirty-seven with poorly controlled type one diabetes.

He arrived with fever, belly pain, and swelling. Scans showed a left liver abscess plus clots in the liver vein and the great vein below it. Drainage, strong antimicrobials, and blood thinners led to recovery and reopened vessels. Early checks can prevent lasting liver harm.
pmc-12714410:
Xiu Feng and colleagues surveyed the genetics of snow trout relatives, a group of fishes found only in the upper Yellow River and nearby waters on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. These high-altitude fishes are sensitive to human pressure and climate change, yet their population health was unmeasured. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team sequenced two mitochondrial gene stretches in hundreds of fish from many sites. The sites cover a great lake, canyon and source stretches of the river, and two neighboring drainages.

Diversity ran highest in the lake and the main river stretches and lowest in one isolated drainage by one measure. Dam-affected populations with little restocking showed thinned diversity, while stocked ones matched undisturbed levels. All fish sorted into three deep lineages with distinct geographic homes. The authors offer the map as a base for conservation planning.
pmc-12714710:
Tirthankar Bandyopadhyay, Baidehi Basu, and Pabitra Parua study how a chemical tag on a DNA-packing protein times the end of gene reading. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five, using fission yeast as the model.

Gene reading runs through start, stretch, and stop phases, and the handoff to stopping was murky. The team tracked proteins along genes with a binding-and-reading method. A driver protein left the reading complex near the stop signal, while a partner that resets tags grew beyond it. The histone tag steered that swap: it drew the driver in during the stretch phase and let it go at the stop signal. Upsetting the tag flipped the pattern of the reset partner and of several reading marks. The work clarifies a switch that ends messages cleanly.
pmc-12715410:
Pranav Unnikrishnan and co-authors run a 13-generation evolution experiment in bulb mites to learn why a gene keeps two versions in the wild, in a 2025 study. The gene 6Pgdh comes in S and F forms: S males breed better and S takes over in lab jars, yet both persist in nature. Temperature and mating competition were suspected equalizers.

Populations evolved under two temperatures and two sex ratios. At the cooler temperature with stronger male competition, the F form gained ground, defying the usual S advantage. A head-to-head breeding test found no direct gap, hinting selection also acts through survival. The authors conclude that a three-way interplay of gene, climate, and social setting can hold both versions in play.
pmc-12715510:
Keneth Mugume and four co-authors survey herbal medicine use among adults with high blood pressure in Uganda in a 2025 paper. Herbal products are widely used for heart conditions, but they can cause harm or clash with prescribed drugs. The team studied patients at a referral hospital in the capital area to see how common such use is and in what forms.

Every patient in the sample had used herbal medicine for blood pressure at some point, and most had used it in the past year. Most took it as a liquid by mouth, often alongside prescribed drugs, and family was the top source of advice. Ease of access and a belief that the herbs are safe and free of side effects drove use.
pmc-12715710:
Xinpeng Wang and co-authors test a feed supplement for largemouth bass in 2025. Replacing fishmeal with soybean meal can inflame the gut and stunt growth in this fish. A paired amino acid supplement may ease that harm.

Three diets were fed to young fish for eight weeks in repeated tanks. Fish on the supplement grew faster and heavier than fish on plain soybean diet. Their blood held more of several key amino acids. Gut folds grew taller with more mucus cells, and cell damage seen on the plain diet was eased. Gut microbe diversity rose as well.
pmc-12715910:
Caley Mikesell and co-authors describe a pilot in 2025 of a tiered mental health model for children that is built to be trauma aware. Childhood hardship and trauma are common roots of mental health trouble. Their model sorts care into levels, so mild needs are met in primary care and deeper needs move up to specialists.

The team works at a large academic medical center, in its child clinics for both levels of care. They merged three record sets for the year from July 2023 to June 2024. Plain analyses of the merged data show who was served and how care flowed. The paper sets out the ideas behind the model, the local setting that shaped it, and what the pilot showed. A tiered model that screens for trauma could catch needs earlier in places families already visit.
pmc-12716510:
Anna Kalbarczyk leads a ten-author team studying women leaders' influence on health policy across sub-Saharan Africa, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Women form seventy percent of the region's health workforce but hold only thirty-eight percent of ministry leadership posts. Evidence about what women leaders actually change has been thin.

The mixed-methods study combined a multicountry online survey with in-depth interviews. Leaders of all genders answered the survey; a subset of women leaders sat for interviews. Fields covered reproductive, maternal, child and adolescent health, nutrition, and immunisation. The authors explore how women leaders are perceived to shape policy and gender equity. Their aim is evidence that can support widening women's path into health leadership.
pmc-12717310:
Zhenzhen Zhang and co-authors compare two ways of delivering a triple therapy for advanced bile duct cancer inside the liver, in this 2025 study. Sixty-seven patients with inoperable tumors got either liver-artery infusion chemotherapy or standard body-wide chemotherapy, each paired with the same targeted drug and immune drug. The infusion route bathes the liver in high drug levels while sparing the rest of the body.

Infusion patients responded far more often and shrank their tumors more. After statistical balancing of the groups, they also lived longer overall and stayed progression-free longer. Local and distant control both favored the infusion arm. Side effects stayed manageable, and immune side effects tracked with slower progression. The authors back the infusion route for this cancer when the team and tools allow.
pmc-12717810:
Bin-bin Zhao, Hui Wang, Nan Luo, and Zhuan-Zhuan Zhang interview parents of children with strabismus in a 2025 study. Crossed or wandering eyes affect family life well beyond vision. Twelve parents of children aged four to eleven took part in deep interviews in early 2025, framed by family systems theory, which treats the household as one interlocked unit. A seven-step method distilled the transcripts into themes.

Four themes emerged. Parents described raw emotional distress, from anxiety to guilt, and the family's adjustment strategies, like sharing labor. They also named a pile-up of challenges, including conflict between relatives, and the support they say they need. Services that treat only the child's eyes miss the household strain the interviews expose.
pmc-12718510:
Gang Chen and colleagues published a 2025 study hunting breast cancer prognosis markers in genetic data. Immune activity shapes how breast cancer progresses. The team combined several genetic databases. A method using inherited variants tested causal links. One gene, involved in cell shape, rose to the top.

Lab work checked the gene in patient tissue. Its levels related to immune cell infiltration. Cell experiments tested growth, sticking, and invasion. Changing the gene altered cancer cell behavior. Protein tests traced its working pathway. A validated marker could help predict outcomes. It might also suggest new treatment angles for aggressive cases.
pmc-12719310:
Ring-shaped RNA strands, closed into loops, are unusually tough for RNA, and cancer cells use them to dodge the immune system and resist drugs. Quan Dai, Xiaoli Yuan, Hang Dong, and Haiyi Xue review this double game in a 2025 paper. Some rings help tumors hide, while others wake the immune system up and make therapy work better.

On the dark side, rings shield a key brake protein on cancer cells, pass quieting signals to immune cells in tiny sacs, and starve killer cells of fuel. On the bright side, some rings trip alarm paths inside cells and push cancer cells toward a death the immune system can see. The review also weighs rings as blood markers and as drug targets, while listing the hard steps left before clinic use.
pmc-12719610:
Gong and co-authors study how the plant compound dauricine affects bladder cancer through the immune cells around the tumor. Macrophages of the M2 type help tumors grow and spread. Dauricine, from a Chinese herb, can slow several tumor types. Its effect on the tumor setting was unclear. Lab tests showed dauricine blocked M2 shifting in macrophages. It also pushed those cells toward an iron-driven form of cell death.

The effect ran through a protein called HCK and its downstream partner IDO1. Cancer cells under treatment also showed more ferritin breakdown. Together the changes slowed tumor progress in the models. The work names a pathway that future bladder cancer drugs might target.
pmc-12721110:
José Luis Andrade Valencia and co-authors report an emergency brain bypass after a planned aneurysm fix in a 2025 paper. A blocked basilar artery threatens the brainstem and needs fast flow return. Scope clot pulls are the norm, but some cases need open surgery.

A sixty nine year old man had an aneurysm clipped by plan. Eight hours later the basilar artery shut in the hyperacute phase. The team joined a scalp artery to a cerebellar artery as a bypass. Flow return halted stroke growth and woke the patient sharply. Set watch rules and ready microsurgery made the save possible.
pmc-12722210:
Dina Thole and co-authors build a light-driven material for clean hydrogen in a 2025 paper. Demand for green energy keeps growing, and hydrogen made from formic acid is one route. The team combined a copper-based porous crystal with carbon nanotubes to make a catalyst that works under light.

Tests of the blend's structure and heat behaviour confirmed the two parts had joined well. Under light, the material split formic acid and produced gas that was three-quarters hydrogen. After the reaction, the team also found it had captured carbon dioxide, and its light response could be reused. The authors present the blend as a promising, recyclable option for making hydrogen while trapping the main greenhouse gas, though the work stays at lab scale.
pmc-12722310:
Liang Ma and nine co-authors engineer flaws into a crystal to make sunlight clean polluted water faster. The crystal is a bismuth tungstate used as a photocatalyst, a material that uses light to drive chemical attack on pollutants. Their 2025 study places two kinds of missing-atom flaws in set regions: tungsten gaps at the edges and oxygen gaps at the center. That uneven layout bends the internal electric field, making it nearly three times stronger, and adds active sites at the surface.

The boosted material fully broke down stubborn agents used in salt-lake mineral processing, which resist normal cleanup. The team calls the paired flaws a defect dipole, since the two regions pull in opposite ways. They present region-wise flaw design as a new lever for catalyst builders.
pmc-12722510:
Cancer doctors face a flood of new evidence, and language models promise help keeping up. An eight-author team staged a blinded contest: five AI systems answered fifty clinical scenarios about multiple myeloma, a blood cancer, covering diagnosis, staging, and treatment. Three expert oncologists scored the answers for accuracy, relevance, completeness, invented facts, and readiness for clinical use.

A system built as an agentic workflow, coordinating several tools and steps, won clearly, reaching 82 percent accuracy. Raw chatbots scored far lower, and a retrieval-augmented system sat between. Invented facts were uncommon everywhere, at roughly 3 to 10 percent. Yet readiness for real clinical use was low for every system, topping out near 25 percent. The authors conclude the tools can support doctors but cannot yet be trusted unsupervised.
pmc-12722610:
Pancreatic cancer surgery too often leaves tumor at the cut edge, and Gianella Cornejo and thirteen co-authors added radiation twice to change that, in a 2025 study. Fifteen patients with resectable or borderline tumors received focused beam radiation before surgery, then an electron dose delivered inside the open abdomen during the operation itself.

Two-thirds had borderline tumors and most also received chemotherapy first. The strategy cleared the margins in 86.7 percent of patients, and two patients with BRCA2-mutated tumors had no cancer left at all in the removed tissue. Median survival reached 30 months, with 16 months before progression. The authors read the numbers as a case for double radiation in a disease where local recurrence usually writes the ending, and call for wider testing.
pmc-12723410:
Augusto Cesar Hunt-Serracin and five co-authors study how a germ that causes lung disease builds its wall. Their work from twenty twenty-five looks at two proteins, MurA and CwlM. MurA helps make the wall, and CwlM can turn it on.

The team used a computer model to find where the two proteins meet. That spot has charge and sits far from a known switch site. Tests with changed proteins showed the boost needs this spot. In live cells, though, the harm from change was mild. Other unknown parts may help MurA work.
pmc-12723910:
Adam Staadig and co-authors compare three gene typing assays on hard forensic samples, such as old bone and teeth from missing person cases, in a study from 2025. Such samples hold tiny amounts of worn DNA, a problem shared with ancient DNA work.

Two targeted assays pulled far more gene calls from the worn samples than whole genome sequencing did. Added tricks, such as deeper reads and filling gaps from patterns, can lift the whole genome route. The authors say ancient DNA methods earn a firm place in forensic labs when samples are badly worn.
pmc-12724010:
Lei and co-authors track plant strategy shifts as karst vegetation recovers. The CSR frame sorts plants by competition, stress tolerance, and disturbance use. Five recovery stages ran from herbs to tree forest. Each stage held five large plots with four subplots each. Leaf traits came from 2,503 plants of 160 woody species.

A strategic trade-off showed as succession advanced. Early stages leaned one way, and later stages leaned another. Diversity and leaf traits both tied to the shift. Random forest and redundancy tools mapped the links. The authors say strategy mix marks recovery stage in karst lands.
pmc-12728210:
Sharafeldin, Marzouk, and Abdelghany pulse water through a solar heater and count the gains in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Flat plate collectors are a workhorse of solar heat. Pulsing the flow, rather than running it steady, may stir heat transfer. The team built a full test rig outdoors. They measured pressure, flow, sunlight, and temperatures in and out.

They scored the setup three ways: energy quality, money, and emissions saved. Pulsing at the best setting pushed the top efficiency figure well above steady flow. Disorder measures fell too. The cost of the heat produced was worked out per unit. Such triple checks help buyers judge a tweak beyond raw heat. Solar engineers are the readers.
pmc-12729010:
Yan Chen and ten colleagues sorted septic shock patients into blood-flow subphenotypes and asked who benefits from fluids. Aggressive fluid resuscitation is standard, yet evidence on which circulation patterns gain most is thin. The twenty twenty-five retrospective study covered 691 patients monitored with PiCCO devices at a Chinese tertiary hospital. Latent profile modelling grouped patients using all measured hemodynamic parameters.

A four-profile model fit best. One group was hyperdynamic, with high cardiac output and low vascular resistance. Another carried the highest preload, and a third was hypodynamic with low output and high resistance. The team then tested how forty-eight-hour fluid balance related to intensive care death within each group. The approach aims to match fluid strategy to a patient's circulation pattern rather than treating all shock alike.
pmc-12729110:
Five authors, led by Luis Pablo Hervé-Claude, surveyed pig farmers in 2025 on five Caribbean islands about African swine fever, a deadly pig illness. The disease returned to the Americas in 2021 and rages in two nearby lands. Island farmers would be key to stopping its spread, yet little was known about their habits.

Most farms proved small and backyard run, with lively trade within each island and weak disease guards. Fewer than a third of farmers knew anything of the fever. The survey maps gaps in knowledge and daily practice. Health teams can use the results to target training and guards before the disease lands.
pmc-12729210:
Fatemeh Araste, Marzieh Akbarzadeh, and Maryam Sadat Nabavinia review bubble like carriers that ferry cancer drugs and can also aid diagnosis. Carriers promise targeted delivery, fewer side effects, and stabler drugs. Their 2025 review covers three families: lab made carriers such as liposomes, natural cell released vesicles, and hybrids that merge both.

Each family is weighed for strengths and pitfalls, including stability, hard manufacturing, and toxicity. Recent studies and case reports show how the carriers improve treatment results in practice. The authors stress that more work is needed to fix the weak points before clinics can use these carriers widely. They frame the field as promising but unfinished, with safety and scale up as the main hurdles.
pmc-12729310:
Elisabetta Tumminelli and co-authors present a 2025 study on using whole olive pruning waste, branches and leaves together, as a source of healthy compounds. Olive growing makes heaps of prunings, but most recovery efforts chase leaves only, and sorting leaves out is costly. The team asked whether the unsorted mix gives extracts as strong as leaf-only ones.

Using a designed set of thirteen extraction runs, they tuned solvent mix, heat, and time. Scaled-up extracts were then tested in chemical assays and on skin cells facing oxidative stress. The mixed-waste extracts matched leaf extracts in antioxidant strength. The authors present unsorted waste as a simpler, greener feedstock.
pmc-12729810:
Ten authors map the high blood pressure chain in a poor Accra zone in a 2025 home survey. The chain runs rate, know, treat, and hold, and gaps show where care leaks. A random 854 adults aged 25 and up in Ga Mashie gave pressure reads and life logs.

Near half held the ill, yet under half of those knew it, and just 16 percent held it in check. Weight gain and a kin past of sugar ill tied to high rates. Sugar ill and drink use tied to good hold in odd splits. Pre-stage rates ran near 28 percent more.
pmc-12731110:
Wang and three co-authors probe how speech and reading link in the brains of three-tongue speakers in this twenty twenty-five study. The group spoke Uyghur first, then Chinese, then English, a mix that pulls apart age of learning from daily use. That split lets the team test which force shapes each skill.

Inside, one hundred forty-four speakers named pictures in one tongue, then judged words in a second tongue. Words heard in speech sped word calls across tongues, which shows a shared word store. Speech pull was ruled by how early a tongue was learned, with the first tongue on top. Word uptake was ruled by how much a tongue is used, with the town-dominant tongue on top.
pmc-12731310:
Jinghui Zhang and seven colleagues run a randomized trial of ultrasound-guided lung treatment for early-born babies, in a twenty twenty-five study. Babies born before thirty-two weeks often lack lung surfactant, a soapy layer that keeps air sacs open. Standard guides dose it by symptoms and oxygen need. The team instead dosed by lung ultrasound scans and a scan score in eighty-nine infants.

The scan group needed breathing machines less often and for fewer days. They also used less surfactant, got the first dose sooner, and faced fewer X-ray exposures. The authors say scan guidance sharpens both diagnosis and dosing for this common newborn problem, sparing babies radiation and drug.
pmc-12731410:
Natassia Rodrigo and colleagues study how weight loss before pregnancy shapes the placenta in obese mice. Obesity in pregnancy can harm how the placenta handles food and signals for the growing young. Female mice fed a rich diet lost weight either by a switch to plain food or by a drug that curbs hunger. The team then read the chemistry and gene activity of the placenta late in pregnancy.

The rich diet lowered key building blocks for protein and raised signs of stress and inflammation. The plain-food switch eased both. The drug eased signs of metabolic stress but not inflammation. The paper weighs how each route to weight loss lands on the placenta.
pmc-12731510:
Glory Madu and co-authors test in this 2025 study whether a standard kids' motor test should weigh its twelve skills equally. The test scores running-style and ball skills for children; its totals assume each skill counts the same, though checks suggest otherwise. With eighty-two children in guided active play, the team derived data-driven weights and raced both scoring styles against fitness and activity measures.

The data-backed weights shifted which skills mattered, yet both styles explained play activity and fitness about equally well. High ball-skill scores still paired with more vigorous play under either scheme. The authors judge both scorings fit for school and clinic use, with weighted scores promising for targeted programs.
pmc-12731610:
Jannat Akram and co-authors review how pancreatic beta cells respond to low oxygen in a 2025 paper. Beta cells make insulin and need much oxygen to do so. Low oxygen can arise when blood supply is disrupted, when islets are isolated for transplant, or in diseases such as type 2 diabetes and sleep apnea.

The review explains how oxygen sensing factors shift the cells from efficient energy use to a simpler sugar burning mode. It also covers links with nutrient sensing, redox balance, and survival paths such as cell recycling. Candidate protectors range from gut hormones to oxygen carrying proteins. For transplantation, oxygen delivery tools, preconditioning, and encapsulation may ease injury and help grafts survive.
pmc-12731710:
Daeyoung Hong and co-authors published a study in 2025 on predicting stomach cancer risk from health records. Finding high-risk people early could prompt timely scope exams and referrals. The team reasoned that cancers of the gut and nearby organs share signals that can aid learning. They built a method that first learns from other such cancers, then adapts to stomach cancer.

The work used records from one hospital database, with five hundred and eight stomach cancer cases in the target group. The transfer method beat basic models on the main scores and held up best when labels were cut back. The authors note that all data came from one center, so checks at more sites are needed before real use.
pmc-12731810:
Researchers report a 2025 study on blood immune checks for people with multiple sclerosis who take anti-CD20 drugs. These drugs lower B cells and can raise infection risk. The team asked whether some immune measures can flag who will get infections or respond well.

The study followed 55 patients at one center who began one of two such drugs between 2017 and 2023. Blood tests tracked T, B, and NK cells plus antibody levels over 24 months. About 64 percent of patients had infections, most from COVID-19. Low IgG antibody levels stood out as the main risk factor for infection. Three patients also developed a lung condition the authors name in full.
pmc-12731910: Shuta Ohara and Kenichi Suda wrote this 2025 review on liquid biopsy, the testing of blood and other fluids for signs of cancer. The method has advanced quickly as a tool of precision oncology. Instead of cutting tissue, clinicians read molecular traces that tumors shed, catching changes in the cancer's makeup and burden over time with little burden on the patient. The review surveys where the approach now stands and the challenges still ahead before it can fully guide care.
pmc-12732010:
Sinthia Vidal-Canas and co-authors report an odd mind-first case of a fungal brain ill in a 2025 study. The fungus preys on people whose immune guard is worn down, and its classic marks are headache, fever, and a stiff neck. In long-suppressed patients it can strike the mind first, which slows the call.

Their patient was a 53-year-old man with joint disease on two immune-damping drugs. For a week he sank into low mood, lost joy, shunned company, and grew sharp with kin. The report shows how the team reached the true cause, and urges care with odd mind signs.
pmc-12732110:
Taein Lee and co-authors test a gene-silencing strategy against kidney cancer in mice in a 2025 study. The target is EphA2, a receptor that helps tumor cells behave badly. The team grew kidney tumor cells with the gene knocked down and implanted them under the kidney capsule of mice, the organ's true site.

Tumors with the gene silenced grew far less than controls, weighed much less at harvest, and showed more cell death. Two partner signals that drive malignant behavior, FAK and RhoA, also quieted. The authors read the pathway as a promising drug target for renal cell carcinoma and call for work toward treatments that block it.
pmc-12732610:
Elena Gabriele and six co-authors report a large real-world survey of a medical food product for metabolic syndrome, in a 2025 paper. The product, a gel that slows nutrient absorption, had shown promise for both full syndrome and early imbalances. Over three and a half years, an online platform collected reports from more than twenty-two hundred patients, plus physicians, pharmacists, and caregivers of children.

Nearly all patients said their condition improved. Most doctors and pharmacists rated the product good or excellent for effectiveness, and safety ratings were similarly high. It was used mostly alone or alongside diet and exercise. Quality of life also gained, patients reported. The authors call the survey evidence of real-world value, while its design, self-reported and uncontrolled, limits how firmly cause can be assigned to the product.
pmc-12733010:
Olukunmi Balogun and co-authors review trials of apps and connected devices for women's health in rich countries, in a 2025 paper. Digital tools are widely touted for health gains, yet proof for non-pregnant women was scattered. Six databases were searched through February 2023.

From more than 18,000 papers, six studies in seven reports qualified. Participants were women with excess weight, women past menopause, or breast cancer patients in early stages. Tools ranged from wearables to sensor-based trackers. Quality was graded with a standard bias tool, and results were woven together in words rather than pooled. The thin, varied yield shows enthusiasm for connected health running ahead of hard trial proof for this group.
pmc-12733310:
A fat-handling protein on mouth cancer cells may mark the tumors most likely to spread and return. Kotaro Sakurai and co-authors test that idea in this 2025 study of 55 patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma. They stained tumor samples for the protein CD36 and scored its level against stage, growth pattern, and outcome.

Higher CD36 went with later stage, more invasive growth, poorer cell maturity, and relapse. It stood as an independent risk factor for the cancer coming back. Gene data hint that CD36-rich tumors also switch on fat-burning and cell-migration programs. The authors propose CD36 as a warning marker for this cancer's aggression. It may one day guide how hard doctors treat and watch such patients.
pmc-12733810:
Qinjian Xu and co-authors present a 2025 study on left-right differences in the taekwondo back kick. The back kick scores often in matches, yet the two legs rarely work the same way. Knowing where the dominant and non-dominant legs diverge can sharpen training and cut injury risk.

Twelve elite athletes performed kicks with each leg in a lab. Motion capture, force plates, and muscle sensors recorded the movement in sync. During the lift phase, the non-dominant attacking leg produced more hip and knee power, while the dominant side bent the knee more. The support leg split its duties differently across sides as well. The kicking phase showed its own pattern of contrasts. Coaches get a joint-by-joint map of the asymmetry.
pmc-12734510:
Songyuan Yan and co-authors present a 2025 chip method that sorts plastic-making cyanobacteria from a rival strain. The target strain makes PHB, a bioplastic precursor, while its cousin does not. In mixed cultures, rivals can crowd out the maker strain. Keeping the maker pure matters for cheap production.

Their tool uses dielectrophoresis, where electric fields push cells by their makeup and shape. A cascade of electrodes enriches the target strain step by step. The two strains differ in form and in how they respond to the field. Repeated passes raise purity with each stage. Cleaner cultures could lower the cost of bioplastic from sunlight and air.
pmc-12735110:
Ligang Ni and seven co-authors scanned the genomes of a Chinese pig breed in a 2025 study. Fengjing pigs are prized for large litters, but their numbers have fallen, raising fears of inbreeding. The team looked at stretches of DNA where both copies are the same, a sign of shared ancestry, to measure that risk.

They re-read the full genomes of 105 pigs and found about twenty-three such stretches per animal. The overall inbreeding level came out near one tenth. Three genome regions carried these stretches in many animals, a mark of past selection. Those regions held sixty-four genes, including fourteen tied to traits farmers care about, like litter size and meat quality. On one chromosome, six known trait regions overlapped the pattern. The findings give breeders targets for keeping the breed productive without losing its diversity.
pmc-12735410:
Hongyan Cheng and co-authors published this study in 2025. It follows soil microbes across forty-five years of tree planting on once-open land. The focus is carbon use efficiency: how much carbon microbes keep for growth versus breathing out. That balance helps decide whether soil gains or loses carbon. The team paired a tracer method with gene surveys along the planting timeline.

Efficiency rose as the forest aged, and it rose alongside soil carbon stores. Gene patterns explain part of the shift. Microbes rich in resource-gathering genes used carbon more efficiently. Those rich in stress-tolerance genes used it less so. The authors read this as a strategy shift: as conditions ease, microbes spend less on defense and more on growth and yield. That shift may help planted forests lock carbon away.
pmc-12736010:
Ewa Skała and Agnieszka Kicel published this study in 2025. It grows shoots of maral root, a Siberian medicinal plant, in a temporary-immersion bioreactor and measures their output of caffeoylquinic acids, antioxidant compounds prized from the plant. Wild supply is limited, so bioreactor production matters.

Two dials were tested: growing time, three versus five weeks, and how often the shoots were dunked in nutrient fluid. Five weeks with ninety-minute dunk cycles gave the most biomass. Three-hour cycles gave the best compound yield per reactor, led by chlorogenic acid, the family's best-known member. The extract scavenged three kinds of damaging radicals in test-tube assays. The authors conclude the PlantForm bioreactor suits this species well, and that immersion rhythm is a real production variable, not a detail. Tuning it lets growers trade bulk against potency for the market they serve.
pmc-12736510:
Eun-Hye Kim and co-authors map the genes of a spreading weed in South Korea in 2025. Curly dock grows worldwide and now serves there as a food, a medicine, and a plant for restoring riverbanks, yet its gene background was little known. The team built nineteen new gene markers from its genome to read variation across groups.

They tested 120 plants from six riverbank groups and found 166 gene variants in total. The groups showed signs of inbreeding and only mild splits between them, though finer tests found six gene units. Partial blocks to gene flow seem to shape the pattern. The results can guide both control of the weed and its careful use.
pmc-12736610:
Nadin Habash, Ahmad Abu Alqumsan, and Tao Zhou published a survey in 2025 on real-time object detection from aerial platforms. Drones and other aircraft need light detectors that run on board with little compute, memory, and power. The survey focuses on methods built for that tight setting. It first reviews the main aerial datasets and their hard traits, such as tiny objects and complex backgrounds.

Recent work is grouped by theme: light backbones, fine feature handling, multi-scale fusion, and adapted transformer parts. The survey also covers hardware-aware tricks like quantization and pruning, plus automated design search for drone limits. Large pre-trained models and their compressed forms are reviewed for onboard use.
pmc-12737710:
Bovine leukemia virus infects cattle for life, usually silently, yet sometimes ends in lymphoma. Doucet and co-authors review why this retrovirus is so hard for the immune system to beat. The virus targets B cells and spreads two ways: by making new virus particles and by driving infected cells to copy themselves. Immunity curbs the first route but not the second, so infected clones slowly expand.

Viral factors such as the Tax protein, small viral RNAs, and changes in the host cell's own genome stack up over years. The result is a slow, multistep march toward cancer that the authors use to model viral persistence.
pmc-12738610:
Bingxin Zhong and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on tar-like pollutants in the mud of lagoons in Lingshui County, Hainan. The lagoons form the island's first marine special reserve, yet little was known about these pollutants there. The team sampled surface mud in spring and sorted out where the pollution comes from and how much risk it poses.

Levels ran from low to middling, with six-ring forms making up over half the total. Math models pointed to burning of fossil fuels and plant matter as the main sources. Risk scores came out low to moderate for lagoon life. The study gives local managers a baseline and a source map for keeping the reserve clean.
pmc-12738710:
Seyed Rahman Soleimani Nadaf and three co-authors design a lean blockchain system for patient records that can grow without slowing to a crawl, in a 2025 paper. Blockchains promise tamper-proof, shared health records, but classic designs buckle under hospital-scale volume and delay.

Their model, DHC, keeps each facility’s daily records in local dynamic blocks gathered into a local chain. Those chains periodically anchor into the wider network, while bulk data live off-chain under integrity checks. New data structures keep retrieval fast and storage light. The design targets the real constraints of clinics: privacy for patients, quick access in emergencies, and trust between institutions that do not fully trust each other.
pmc-12742110:
Bo Li and co-authors build a deep learning model to spot severe mitral stenosis on chest X-rays in this 2025 paper. A narrowed heart valve is hard to diagnose from an X-ray alone, yet X-rays are cheap and common everywhere. An automated reader could screen for the disease where specialists are scarce.

The team trained the model on 515 chest images, 285 from patients with the disease and 230 from healthy controls, split into training, tuning, and test sets. The model scored near-perfect discrimination on both held-out sets, with accuracy of 0.96 and 0.94. Heat maps showed it focused on regions matching known X-ray signs of the disease. The authors offer it as a screening aid.
pmc-12745510:
Benjamin Shwartzman, Noel Tomy, and Leonard Shvartzman report rebuilding a nose defect that spanned three facial zones after cancer surgery. Their 2025 case report follows a sixty-year-old woman with an invasive skin cancer of the left nostril wing. Seven staged scrapings cleared the tumor.

The hole left behind, about three and a half by two and a half centimeters, took the whole nostril wing, side wall, and inner cheek. Repair came in layers: a twin-stalked lining flap inside, a cartilage graft from the ear's bowl for support, and a forehead flap for cover. Staged touch-ups refined shape and airway. The authors draw lessons on planning by facial subunit for such layered repairs.
pmc-12746010:
Ahmed Abdirahman Ahmed, Gökçen Yıldız, and Adadi Parise test ways to dry mango into powder faster without losing its good traits. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Drying method shapes both the cost of the powder and how much of the fruit's value survives.

The team paired ultrasound pre-treatment with three drying routes: hot air, microwave, and a mix of both. Thirty minutes of ultrasound plus the mixed route cut drying time by eighty percent. Plain microwave drying kept the most health-linked compounds, while hot air alone gave the powder the best handling traits, like density and flow. Ultrasound also made the powder dissolve and swell better. The authors frame the choice as a trade-off by goal.
pmc-12747910:
Wang and co-authors review the case for finerenone, a newer hormone-blocking drug, in heart failure where the heart still pumps with preserved strength. This form of heart failure has tangled causes and few proven treatments. Overactive mineralocorticoid receptors help drive it, and blocking them is the strategy under review.

Finerenone is a non-steroidal blocker, more selective than older drugs such as spironolactone, with stronger anti-scarring and anti-inflammatory action in early studies. Kidney trials in diabetes first showed heart and kidney benefits, and the FINEARTS-HF trial extended the gains to this heart failure group. The review also weighs pairing finerenone with two other modern drug classes and surveys trials now under way. The authors call for a direct head-to-head trial against spironolactone with heart outcomes as the main measure.
pmc-12748610:
Moh Sofi'ul Anam and colleagues pool thirty-six trials on feeding microalgae to laying hens, in this meta-analysis from twenty twenty-five. Microalgae bring omega-3 fats, pigments, and antioxidants to the feed bag, but trial results have been patchy. The pooled verdict sorts the real effects from the noise.

The hens ate no more or less, yet laid more and heavier eggs, with stronger shells and better internal quality scores. Yolks turned deeper and redder in color. Their fat profile shifted the way nutritionists hope: more of the prized omega-3s, including EPA and DHA, and less omega-6, cutting the ratio between them. Blood cholesterol and liver enzymes fell, suggesting healthier livers. The authors conclude microalgae earn their place as a functional feed additive that upgrades both hen and egg.
pmc-12749210:
Feng Zhou and co-authors build a language model tool that finds viral traces in tumor gene data, in work from twenty twenty-five. Viruses may help start or drive some cancers, so finding them in tumor samples matters. Older tools align sequences, but fast viral change and gaps in viral genomes limit them.

The tool, called ViTrace, learns from DNA context, position links, and protein code data at once. It trained on just thirteen species yet recalled most strains from hundreds of unseen species in tests. Applied to single cell data from two throat area cancers, it showed virus patterns by tumor, cell, and patient. Some viruses found were not reported before. The frame could guide precise cancer care.
pmc-12749510:
Yan and co-authors use a mouse model in this 2025 study to learn how an eye disease called choroideremia harms sight. The disease runs in families and slowly takes vision. It stems from loss of a protein that helps move other proteins to the right place in eye cells, but the chain of damage was unclear.

The team bred mice that lack the protein in the eye and studied the light-sensing layer. That layer thinned early in life, and the links between its cells broke down. Light tests showed weak signals, and gene tests showed drops in key sight genes. The work also found immune cells switched on in the eye, which hints at a path for future treatment.
pmc-12749610:
Israel and Parnas build a fruit fly system to study how nerve circuits remodel as the animal grows in twenty twenty-five. One named neuron drives backward walking in adults. The team shows its circuit persists from larva to adult in conserved form. That span lets them watch remodeling live across life stages.

A gene control mechanism for outgrowth is described in the system. A causal link from remodeling to behavior is also shown. The circuit is small, well mapped, and tied straight to motor output. Driver lines give precise access to its cells. The authors offer it as a clean lab bench for circuit change.
pmc-12749810:
Eloisa Torchia and co-authors present a 2025 method for making cell culture gels with robots, aimed at drug testing. Cells grown on flat plastic or glass behave unlike cells in the body, which weakens drug forecasts. Richer models like organoids mimic the body better but do not scale to mass screening.

Their system, HYDRA, uses liquid-handling robots to lay thin, flat gel films inside standard test plates. The robot lays down a small volume and pulls it back at once, pinning the edge so no curved rim forms. Films from fish gelatin worked in standard 96- and 384-well plates with plate-wide quality checks. Drug dose tests on the films kept their sensitivity, and imaging stayed clear. The method bridges body-like conditions and factory-scale testing.
pmc-12750010:
Gabriela Colaneri and co-authors show how a cell-cycle protein, once switched on by a growth signal, helps melanoma resist chemotherapy, in a 2025 study. The protein, p21, is usually cast as a brake on cell division, yet in melanoma its abundance predicts poor outcomes. Tumors that spread carried more p21, including more of it parked in the cell's cytoplasm, than early tumors did.

Experiments and computer analysis traced the wiring: the growth enzyme AKT tags p21 with a phosphate, and the tagged protein moves and behaves differently. Cutting p21 levels made melanoma cells respond better to the drug dacarbazine. The axis from AKT to p21 thus explains part of this cancer's stubbornness and marks a drug target: block the tag, and standard chemotherapy may bite again.
pmc-12750310:
A rare and fast-growing nose tumor is reported by Xie and co-authors in a 2025 case study with a literature review. The tumor mixes several tissue types and is hard to name correctly. Gene tests in this patient found a missing gene segment and a changed partner gene, which may help explain how the tumor arose.

Surgery could not remove the whole tumor, so focused radiation with a rotating beam method was paired with chemotherapy. The tumor shrank to a full response and stayed gone for more than forty-seven months, with side effects the patient could bear. The authors suggest the gene marks may aid diagnosis and that this radiation method merits wider use.
pmc-12750610:
Luciana Sobral and a large team track tuberculosis spread to children and teenagers living with lung TB patients in Brazil. Their prospective cohort study was published in twenty twenty-five. Young contacts are prime targets for preventive treatment, if infection is caught.

Five hundred and sixty-two close contacts aged eighteen or under were followed for six months across several centers. Checks included exams, chest imaging, and a blood test for TB infection. A positive test at start or a switch to positive by month six counted as infection. About three in ten contacts were infected. Models then weighed which household and patient traits raised a child's risk.
pmc-12750710:
Shengyang Chen and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a coarse-to-fine classifier that predicts what microbial proteins do, with special care for rare functions. Knowing protein jobs drives probiotic discovery and biotechnology, but function labels form deep family trees and most branches are rare. Standard deep learning flattens that tree and fails on the long tail. The authors' network instead climbs the tree level by level, letting parent and child labels inform each other.

For one label system the cascade follows the official hierarchy directly. For the other, it builds a hierarchy from meaning-based clustering of the terms themselves, then attends across levels. Skewed training data is rebalanced on the fly, and rare labels get extra weight in the loss. Across all major categories the system beat both classic sequence matching and rival neural tools.
pmc-12750910: Jian-xian Zhang and three co-authors report a single case in 2025 of a rare hernia treated with keyhole surgery that uses a three dimensional view. The patient was a woman in her sixties with chest tightness and short breath for more than ten years, worse in the past year. Her repair combined a tension free mesh method with work to free stuck tissue inside the belly, and she recovered smoothly after the operation.
pmc-12751010:
Vikas Ashokrao Sadaphal, Hsin-Ru Wu, and Rai-Shung Liu report a gold-driven reaction in this twenty twenty-five chemistry paper. They joined two kinds of starting material: a chain with both a double and a triple bond, and a nitrone, a nitrogen-oxygen compound. Gold steered the joining.

The reaction adds carbon and nitrogen groups side by side along the chain, then cuts the double bond. Tracing the steps, the team found an early attack by a nitrogen partner, followed by a cascade with the nitrone before the cut. Such routes can build complex molecules for drug and material research in fewer steps.
pmc-12751410:
Yang Liao and co-authors set out a trial protocol testing calligraphy training for stroke recovery in a 2025 paper. Stroke often leaves lasting problems with thinking and arm movement. Standard rehabilitation helps but can be costly, hard to reach, and easy to drop. Calligraphy practice combines fine hand movement with attention and memory, which may aid both domains at once.

The trial will enroll ninety-three patients in early recovery at one Shanghai hospital. Patients are assigned by chance to calligraphy plus routine care, a reading control, or routine care alone, over four weeks. A light-based brain imaging method will track activity changes in the cortex. Thinking, arm function, grip, and daily living skills are also measured. The authors aim to reveal both whether the training works and how the brain changes with it.
pmc-12751510:
Tala Tamim El Jarkass and co-authors rapidly review how social conditions shape Long COVID outcomes, in a 2025 paper. Long COVID affects tens of millions of people, yet the role of income, schooling, work, and place is poorly mapped. The team searched three databases for observational studies with original data. Seventy-one studies qualified, and their quality was scored with a standard scale.

Female sex and older age tied consistently to higher risk and heavier symptoms. Black and Hispanic patients faced Long COVID more often than white patients. Lower schooling and money insecurity also tracked with greater burden. Frontline and essential workers carried extra risk. Place-based gaps appeared but shifted between rural and urban settings. The authors call for targeted public health action and a shared case definition.
pmc-12752110:
Jinlong Liu and six co-authors studied a card tool for teaching end-of-life care in a 2025 paper. Nursing students often learn hospice care from lectures, which can leave a gap between theory and the emotional side of practice. The tool, a set of Heart to Heart Cards, invites students to talk through feelings and choices in a guided way.

Seventeen students in a hospice course were interviewed in depth about using the cards. Their answers grouped into three themes. Students shared first impressions of the cards and ideas to improve them. They described deep learning that came from a themed session built around the cards. They also named the hard parts of carrying card-based practice from classroom drills into real wards. The authors conclude the cards help bridge theory and practice and build communication skill.
pmc-12752310:
Sakina Banoo, Aijaz Hassan Ganie, and Anzar Ahmad Khuroo report a 2025 study of plant knowledge in Drass valley, a cold high valley in Ladakh cut off for months each year. Local groups have built deep plant lore over many generations. The team spoke with sixty people from three ethnic groups in their own languages.

They recorded well over a hundred plant species in use. About a third served as medicine, most often leaves taken by mouth. The rest fed people or stock, gave fuel, or served in rites. Thirteen species had uses not known before in print. The authors urge lab checks on those plants and fair sharing of gains with local people.
pmc-12752510:
Deleting one injury switch makes healed muscle grow fat instead of fiber, Catriona Logan and co-authors show in a 2025 study. Two Wnt genes switch on after injury in lung and muscle, sitting head-to-head on one chromosome. Between them lies a shared enhancer that lights up after damage.

Mice missing that enhancer made less of both Wnt signals after injury. Their repaired muscles carried extra fat, a sign of poor regeneration. The enhancer needs known stress-response binding sites to fire. Tissue repair thus leans on a single shared switch, whose loss tilts healing toward fat.
pmc-12753410:
Jia-Yang Chen and three co-authors test polyethylene glycol, a common polymer, as a repair aid after spinal cord injury in mice, in a 2025 study. A cut cord triggers inflammation and oxidative stress that block recovery. The polymer is known to seal torn nerve membranes and limit scarring, making it a candidate fusogen that might reconnect fibers.

The team used a mouse model in which the cord is fully transected. Treatment effects were tracked alongside measures of inflammatory response and oxidative stress factors, to tie any functional gain to its mechanism. If a cheap, widely available polymer truly helps cords heal, it could move toward trials faster than a bespoke new drug.
pmc-12754010:
Samuel Chong and nine co-authors trace how COVID-19 moved up a tower block in a 2025 study. High-rise flats stack homes over shared shafts and drains, which may ferry a breath-borne virus floor to floor. In dense Singapore, where towers are the norm, screening data offered a rare clean read.

Blocks put through mass testing showed a clear pattern: flats in the same vertical stack as a known case faced far higher risk than others. A fluid flow model of one block then chased the path, testing how air and drain flows could carry the virus upward. The pair of reads guides tower safety plans.
pmc-12754510:
Lu and five co-authors review magnesium alloys as biodegradable materials for bone defects in a 2025 paper. Bone defects arise from tumors, injury, tissue death, and birth conditions. They cause much suffering and cost. Materials that break down as tissue regrows are strong candidates for repair.

Magnesium alloys offer adjustable breakdown rates, good fit with the body, useful strength, and support for bone growth. Polymers are also used, but metals fill a distinct role. Problems remain: magnesium can degrade too fast and may not drive bone growth strongly enough. The review covers uses and recent advances. It also maps strategies to improve performance for clinical bone repair.
pmc-12755110:
Bom Lee and co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, tiny drug ships built to calm the immune self in autoimmune disease. Such ills rise in count and spread in the world. Known drugs mute the whole immune set and bring harm, like more germs caught. Nano ships can take drugs to hot spots and lymph hubs, and shield them on the way. The path in counts too: vein, skin, muscle, or mouth each has its own gains. The review reads known care's flaws first.

It then walks the ship work by path in. Lab tests by vein, skin, muscle, and mouth beat plain care in force and dose saved. Calm of the immune self, not its full mute, is the aim.
pmc-12756110:
Felipe de Sousa and co-authors lay out in 2025 how to diagnose the most common heart disease of cats. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the heart wall thickens, sometimes silently, sometimes ending in heart failure. No single blood test proves it, so vets must combine several kinds of evidence.

The paper walks through that combination: history and hands-on exam first, then blood markers that support but cannot confirm the diagnosis. Heart tracings can hint at conduction trouble. Ultrasound of the heart remains the gold standard, confirming the thickening and guiding staging and treatment. The authors argue that an integrated workup prevents missed or wrong diagnoses and improves care for affected cats.
pmc-12756210:
Yanjun Fang and six co-authors trace how a model plant moves zinc from its roots to the rest of its body. Their 2025 study matters because zinc-poor soil leads to zinc-poor crops, and then to zinc-poor diets for people. The team studied a transporter protein, ZIP2, that carries zinc between sheath cells in the root.

They found that sensor and kinase proteins switch ZIP2 on by adding a phosphate mark at one key spot on the protein. Without that spot, the transporter stops working, as tests in yeast and in plants both showed. Plants given the switched forms of ZIP2 and a sibling transporter stood up better to low zinc. The switch network is a target for breeding crops that hold more zinc.
pmc-12756310:
Nabin Lamichhane and co-authors screen rice landraces for drought tolerance in Nepal in a 2025 study. Drought resilient varieties matter more as climate change brings more frequent droughts. Twelve landraces from three climate zones of far west Nepal faced control, intermittent drought, and complete drought treatments. Yield and several drought tolerance indices were measured for each variety.

All varieties lost yield under drought, but losses varied widely. Some landraces from each zone lost significantly more than average, while others held up better. Three varieties stood out with consistently higher tolerance index values. Grouping analyses revealed distinct response patterns, supporting use of many traits together. Readers see local landraces as a reservoir for breeding climate ready rice.
pmc-12756510:
One to three of every thousand newborns suffer oxygen shortage to the brain, and doctors lack fast markers of how bad the injury is. Runci Li and co-authors test a gentle idea in mice: rinse the eye and collect the tiny vesicles cells shed into the fluid. Pups that endured mild or severe oxygen shortage showed clear changes in those vesicles.

Counts rose, sizes shifted, and the protein cargo changed in ways that map onto pathways for immunity, energy, and brain signaling, with some changes unique to severe injury. Because eye fluid is easy to sample without needles, such vesicle signatures could one day flag at-risk newborns early.
pmc-12757110:
Sathyaseelan Arumugam and four co-authors review surgery choices for two uncommon colon cancer sites in a 2025 paper. Cancers of the transverse colon and the splenic bend are rarer than other colon cancers. Surgeons still debate how much bowel to remove and how widely to clear lymph nodes.

The review follows standard reporting rules across seven databases through mid-2024. Seven studies covering hundreds of cases compared limited segment removal with extended removal. Robotic, keyhole, and open techniques all appear in the limited approach group. Safety around surgery and long-term cancer outcomes were weighed side by side. The synthesis helps surgical teams judge whether smaller operations cost patients anything in cure odds.
pmc-12764110:
Ye Li and eight co-authors build computer models to flag a thyroid problem in sepsis patients in a 2025 study. In severe illness the thyroid often slows even though the gland itself is healthy, a state called non-thyroidal illness syndrome. Finding which sepsis patients face this state, and which may die, could guide care.

The team drew records from 963 patients and trained eight learning methods. One method best predicted who would develop the syndrome, while another best predicted death among those who had it. Low thyroid hormone levels marked higher risk, and factors such as breathing machines and organ failure marked death risk. The authors warn that one hospital's data limits the findings.
pmc-12764210:
Tiara Resmi, Oki Suwarsa, and Irna Sufiawati report a rare case of a blistering form of lupus that struck mainly inside the mouth, in this 2025 case report. The disease, bullous lupus, affects fewer than five in a hundred lupus patients, and mouth involvement is usually mild. Heavy mouth disease as the lead sign is very uncommon and hard to pin down.

Their patient was a twenty-nine-year-old woman with a week of severe mouth ulcers, fever, and painful swallowing. Tissue samples showed the split-under-the-surface pattern of the disease, letting the team diagnose it without an advanced test they lacked. Treatment mixed mouth care with steroid infusions and an immune-calming drug. All lesions healed fully within four weeks. The case shows careful clinic work can both name and tame this rare presentation.
pmc-12766810:
Marcelo Gobbo Jr and co-authors built a short quality-of-life scale for doctors in Brazil, in this 2025 study. A nationwide web survey drew 2,005 doctors from all regions. The new 13-item scale was checked in split samples with factor and item-response methods.

The scale split into three parts: life quality, support at work, and felt stress. Scores matched a known world quality-of-life scale well. Women reported more stress than men, and doctors working 60 or more hours a week reported more stress than those on shorter weeks. Well-being rose with income up to a point, then leveled off. The authors offer the index for tracking doctor welfare.
pmc-12767410:
Yaxin Weng and co-authors charted world research on jaw joint disorders in children and teens in 2025. Temporomandibular disorders affect the jaw joint and chewing muscles. The team traced papers from 2000 to 2024 in a major citation database, mapping authors, centers, lands, and hot topics.

Over 2,200 papers fit the field, and yearly output and citations rose steeply. One Danish author led on output, while a Swedish author led on citations. The United States led on volume and joint work, while many Asian lands cooperated less. Recent hot topics include diagnostic criteria, 3D cone scans, and jaw involvement in juvenile arthritis. Psychosocial factors also drew growing attention.
pmc-12768610:
Erica Suzumura and four co-authors test whether a middle ear implant offers good value for adults in Brazil with nerve based hearing loss. People who cannot use standard hearing aids for medical reasons have no publicly funded option in the country. The implant sits in the middle ear and boosts sound directly.

A lifetime model compared implant care with no treatment. The implant cost far more up front but added about one and a half years of life in full health. The cost per such year fell below Brazil's accepted limit, and repeat model runs mostly agreed. The authors say funding the implant would promote fair access to hearing care.
pmc-12768710:
Tais Galvao and Marcus Silva present this 2025 conference abstract on what a Brazilian health journal has published in health technology assessment. The journal, run by the health ministry, spreads proof for the national health system. The team gathered its abstracts from 2016 to 2024 and sorted the assessment-relevant ones by word patterns.

Of 674 abstracts, 409 counted as relevant. Clustering split them into six themes: risk factors, health services, infections and clinical services, death trends, causes of death, and one more group on birth defects. Health services formed the largest share, at about a third. The authors weigh the journal's spread against a standard assessment model to judge its service to policy.
pmc-12768810:
Annapoorna Prakash and co-authors wrote a 2025 study that tries to settle what counts as a digital health tool. Groups that judge new health tools need a shared set of words, but each country has used its own terms. The lack of a shared set of terms has slowed work on fair rules for judging these tools.

The team read past work and found 328 ways the term had been defined. Three parts came up again and again: what the tool is for, who uses it, and the tech behind it. The team also found nine ways that countries sort these tools into groups. A two-round survey of experts then backed the three parts and backed sorting tools by what they are for. The shared words should help groups in many countries judge tools in the same way.
pmc-12771710:
