Wekesa and co-authors field-test a new wall spray against malaria in Siaya County, Kenya, in a 2025 study. Spraying inner walls kills the mosquitoes that spread the disease. Old sprays lose force as the insects gain strength against them, so a spray with a fresh mode of attack was due.

Crews sprayed 25 homes with the new spray and 25 with a standard one, plus five with plain water. Month by month for six months, test insects were held against the walls. The new spray killed nearly all test insects through month six and beat the standard spray. Homes liked it, and no side effects were logged for it.
pmc-12771910:
Keyhole womb surgery needs gas pumped into the belly and the body tipped head down, both of which can raise pressure in the skull. Huiman Ji and co-authors test two sleep drugs for that risk in a 2025 trial. Sixty women were split by lot to get one drug or the other.

The team tracked skull pressure with sound scans of the sheath round the eye nerve. That sheath swelled in both groups once gas and tilt were in place. The size of the swell was much the same for the new drug and the old one at each check. Sick feelings and head pain after surgery were also logged. The new drug, the team finds, acts much like the old on skull pressure.
pmc-12772010:
Liying Wang and co-authors explore how women with ovarian cancer experience cancer-related thinking problems, in this 2025 study. Such impairment is among the most common and lasting symptoms these patients report. Thirty-one women at a Shanghai cancer center gave in-depth interviews about a year after diagnosis on average. The team coded the accounts using symptom management theory.

Four themes emerged. Women described subtle decline in memory and attention, though some barely noticed change. They blamed surgery anesthesia, chemotherapy, and tangled symptom clusters, while also withdrawing socially. Daily life disruption felt contained, but confidence in their own ability eroded. Coping meant cutting mental load, using compensating tricks, or passive acceptance. The authors call for culturally sensitive, patient-centered support for this symptom.
pmc-12772210:
Handuo Shi and co-authors model how a bacterial filament senses the shape of the cell surface it clings to in a 2025 paper. The filament, a relative of actin called MreB, guides wall building in rod-shaped bacteria and gathers where the surface curves in certain ways. Why it prefers those spots was not known.

Their model weighs the energy of twisting and bending a filament against the geometry of the surface beneath it. It predicts that a strongly twisted filament favors spots with lower values of two curvature measures. Simulations of the filament's stiffness gave length scales matching real cells. The preference held even without motion or rebuilding cycles. The findings suggest plain energy balance explains the pattern, and they offer design ideas for shape-sensing nano materials.
pmc-12774910:
Sledge and co-authors report a 2025 study of why a breast cancer drug stops working over time. The drug is trastuzumab deruxtecan, used for cancers with low or high levels of a growth protein. The team used gene and protein data from tumor samples to look for signs linked to drug failure.

Working with records from 2,799 patients, the team found that higher levels of the growth protein gene and lower levels of a pump gene were linked to longer survival on the drug. Changes in a few genes grew more common after treatment. The results point to ways doctors may spot failure early and plan next steps.
pmc-12775410:
Sudhakar and Muthucumaraswamy report a study from two thousand twenty-five on using machine learning to improve footwear production. Factories track defects, downtime, energy use, and output speed. The team asked whether tuning a prediction model could lift all of these at once on a real shop floor.

They refined a logistic regression model until its accuracy rose and it classified every defect-free output correctly. It beat rival methods such as support vector machines and naive Bayes on several scores. The gains in prediction led to real process gains: higher throughput, less equipment downtime, and lower energy use. The authors argue that tuned classifiers joined with live factory data can make shoe production both leaner and greener.
pmc-12775610:
Meera Dhodapkar and co-authors tell how nerve monitoring caught a hidden bleed during neck spine surgery. A 77-year-old man had a laminoplasty to free his squeezed spinal cord. Mid-operation, the monitoring traces shifted. The change pointed to injury below the worked levels. Their 2025 case report follows the rapid response. Emergency scans found a spontaneous blood pocket pressing on the cord.

The team rushed back in and cleared the pocket. The man was back to his pre-surgery nerve state within a day. Such bleeds are rare but can cripple if missed. The authors argue that live monitoring earns its keep by catching harm far from the cut. They call for more study of its reach in spine work.
pmc-12775710:
Yichen Sun leads a team of thirteen in a 2025 study that pits two immune drugs against each other before lung surgery. Both drugs free the immune system to attack cancer, and each pairs with chemo to shrink a lung tumor before the cut. Which one does better had not been faced off.

Records from two hospitals covered 366 patients from 2018 to 2024, some on each drug. Matching on patient traits leveled the field. The team then compared shrink rates, full tumor death in the cut tissue, and how the surgery went. Early answers guide a choice that clinics now make blind.
pmc-12780410:
Targeted lung cancer drugs work only when the tumor carries the right mutation, so doctors need to know how common those mutations are locally. Edgar Amorin Kajatt and eight co-authors measured EGFR mutations in Latin American patients in a 2025 study. All patients had non-small cell lung cancer removed by surgery at stages I to III.

The study enrolled 80 patients between March 2021 and October 2022. Two-thirds were women, and over half had never smoked. Most tumors were stage I, and all were adenocarcinoma, the subtype where these mutations cluster. Of those tested, 39.5 percent carried an EGFR mutation, a rate that shapes drug planning in the region. The team also charted mutation subtypes and treatment patterns. Their data fill a gap, since biomarker counts for Latin America have been scarce.
pmc-12783310:
Grahmm A Funk and co-authors compared two bone cements as local carriers for a cancer drug, in a study published in 2025. After a bone tumor is removed, cement fills the gap and steadies the bone. Loading that cement with the drug doxorubicin could attack leftover cancer cells right where they hide.

The standard cement weakened when the drug was mixed in, and drug released from it killed cancer cells less well in dishes. The likely cause is a clash between the drug and the cement's hardening chemistry. A newer cement based on different chemistry kept its strength with the drug aboard, and its released drug worked at full strength. The authors present the newer material as a strong candidate where bones must bear load and deliver treatment at once.
pmc-12784910:
August Cesarec and co-authors weigh the cost of colon cancer screening in Croatia in this 2025 study. Colon cancer is the most often diagnosed cancer in Croatia and the second by deaths. A national program started in 2007 invites people aged 50 to 74 for a stool blood test every two years.

The team built a model for 10,000 people aged 50, followed for five years. It compared no screening with the current stool test and with a newer stool test. Treating advanced cancer cost far more per patient than the average across all stages. Both screening options gave better health at lower cost than no screening. The newer test was preferred, with higher sensitivity and lower costs.
pmc-12785110:
Labeling cell types in single-cell data often means borrowing labels from a reference set, but batch differences between labs distort the patterns. Ming Zhang and co-authors present PLKD in this 2025 paper, a method that learns biological patterns instead of raw gene readings.

A large teacher model groups genes into sets that each stand for a biological function, then passes its knowledge to a small, fast student model. Working at the pattern level makes the labels steadier across batches, and the student stays robust to noise. Benchmarks show accurate annotation, and the design also handles data that mixes several measurement types.
pmc-12785310: Emilia Konował and Anna Modrzejewska-Sikorska introduce a special journal issue on metal nanoparticles, in a 2025 editorial. Nanotechnology builds and studies structures smaller than one hundred nanometers across, and metal particles at that scale gain unusual optical, chemical, and electrical traits. Those traits open uses from medicine to catalysis and sensing. The editors frame the issue as a bridge from basic studies to new applications, and the short introduction sets the scope rather than reporting new data.
pmc-12785510:
Ruizhe Xue and co-authors review how AI can untangle the health effects of non microbial food contaminants through gut microbes in a 2025 paper. Heavy metals, pesticide residues, antibiotics, plastics, and lasting organic pollutants all enter the body in daily food. Their effects are subtle, chronic, and increasingly tied to the gut community. The links among exposures, microbes, their products, and health outcomes are highly non linear.

The review first sums up how each contaminant class shifts gut microbes and, through them, gut barrier strength, immunity, metabolism, and disease risk. It then covers machine and deep learning and network methods that join exposure and multi omics data. Those tools hunt for microbe and metabolite signatures of single contaminants and guess at causal paths. Data messiness, small samples, and hard to read models are named as the key limits to beat.
pmc-12786010:
Bahar Yola and five co-authors build a sensor that sniffs a weed killer in drinking water, in a 2025 paper. The herbicide, glyphosate, is sprayed widely and tied to cancer risk over long exposure. Their sensor stacks three materials on a carbon tip, then stamps the surface with a plastic mold shaped by the target itself. When the target slips back into its mold, the current shifts and betrays it.

The stamped tip read the herbicide across a narrow low range with a very small detection floor. Spiked drinking water gave back nearly all the added dose. Rival chemicals barely moved the needle, and repeat runs held steady. The authors offer the stamped-sensor recipe as a cheap, sharp tool for water checks, in place of slow lab machines.
pmc-12786610:
Krzysztof Żerdziński and four co-authors survey systematic reviews of artificial intelligence in intensive care and grade how ready the field is for real use, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Critical care is time-pressed and data-rich, fertile ground for AI support, but weak validation makes it risky too.

Thirty-four reviews across five ICU domains fed the overview. Prediction and early warning tools dominated, mostly in adults and built on health records. Reports touted accuracy ranges, yet calibration and bedside usefulness were rarely addressed. Readiness signals clustered at low to middling levels, with no sign of routine regulated deployment. The authors call for outside validation, real-world impact trials, fuller reporting, and governance work.
pmc-12787210:
Michał Kawiak and co-authors test how hydrogen weakens rail steel welds in a 2025 study. Pearlite steel rails and their thermite welds can absorb hydrogen during welding and service. The gas makes steel crack sooner, a risk for long-lived track.

Welded samples absorbed a small amount of hydrogen during welding itself. When samples were loaded with more hydrogen, the desired fatigue crack formed in far fewer load cycles. Fracture toughness also fell, with hydrogenated samples breaking at lower stress intensity. Sample orientation barely mattered for plain rail steel. The work feeds plans to add crack-resistant inserts made by additive manufacturing at weak spots.
pmc-12787410: Khan and co-authors frame a review, published in 2025, on greener ways to feed crops and manage farmland. Feeding the world while soils thin and the climate shifts is a defining problem of the century. The review argues that how plants are nourished, and how their surroundings are managed, decides whether farming can last. It surveys approaches that keep yields up while cutting the damage that heavy chemical use causes.
pmc-12787610:
Traces of medicines are turning up in drinking water around the world, and the diabetes drug metformin is one of them. Abeer Aljadaani, Amr Yakout, and Hany Abdel-Aal build a sponge-like material to pull it out of water. Their material anchors copper and zinc oxide particles on treated graphene oxide sheets.

Several forces hold the drug on the surface at once: binding at the copper sites, stacking against the carbon sheets, and hydrogen bonds. Together they gave a high uptake, about 233 milligrams per gram, and the water cleared in only 25 minutes. After five rounds of cleaning and reuse, the material lost only about 4 percent of its power. It removed nearly all the drug from river, tap, and bottled water samples. The authors offer it as a strong option for treating drug-laced wastewater.
pmc-12788510:
Four authors, led by Mahesh Shenoy, wrote this 2025 study of gum health in patients who also live with other diseases. Periodontitis is an infection of the tissues that hold the teeth in place. Body-wide illness can harm those tissues, and gum disease can in turn affect the body.

The team used a retrospective design and read patient files from the past ten years. The patients had sought dental care at teaching hospitals in Riyadh City. Only patients with a medical condition, such as diabetes, heart disease, or a suppressed immune system, and with full gum records were included. The authors compared groups with a chi-square test. Overall, they found no clear difference between the groups, except when plaque was taken into account. The study maps how gum status looks in medically frail dental patients.
pmc-12788610:
Aiswarya Gopinath and co-authors test how root canal sealers hold after retreatment in a 2025 lab study. A tight seal keeps germs from creeping back, and its grip is gauged by how hard a plug pushes out of the canal.

Ninety premolars were filled, then retreated with one of two solvents, with or without sound wave stirring of the rinse. Slices from the root tip went under a testing press. The sealer gripped hardest after the gentler solvent paired with sound activation. The pairing shapes up as the better prep for refilling.
pmc-12790810:
Courage O Idahor and co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, radiofrequency ablation as a treatment for chronic pain. The method uses heat from radio waves, sent through a needle, to disrupt the nerve paths that carry pain. It serves pain from the spine, damaged nerves, and even cancer that resists other care. Many patients get too little relief from drugs, or suffer side effects they cannot bear.

The review traces the method from early brain surgery roots to its modern forms: standard, pulsed, cooled, and bipolar. It explains how lesions form, compares where each form fits, and weighs trial and guideline evidence. Newer tools such as live imaging, robotic help, and pairing with healing therapies are also covered. Safety risks and fair access close the authors' account.
pmc-12794410:
Caroline Osoro and Jenny Hill wrote this 2025 perspective on a sudden funding shock for malaria control in Africa. In 2025 the United States ended most of its global health programs, and several European donors cut aid too. African programs had few backup plans, even though the continent carries ninety-four percent of world malaria cases. Bed net drives, seasonal drug campaigns, and surveys all took hits.

The authors urge African leaders and regional bodies to take charge. Some governments already pledge more private-sector fundraising. A continental strategy pushes higher health budgets with clear accounting. Without fresh domestic money, the authors warn, hard-won gains against malaria could slip into resurgence. The piece is a call for self-reliant funding.
pmc-12795710:
Seven authors in the Philippines test a fast drug assay for rifampicin in a 2025 paper. Generic forms of the tuberculosis drug must prove they match the reference product, and that proof needs a quick, exact blood test. The team checked an ultra high performance liquid chromatography method against rules at home and abroad.

Plasma was cleaned by protein precipitation with methanol and ascorbic acid, then run through a compact column with ultraviolet detection. The three minute run used a shifting mix of water and acetonitrile at set temperatures. Checks covered selectivity, linearity, sensitivity, accuracy, precision, and carry over, and the results met the bioanalytical standards in the rules. The method now readies the lab for bioequivalence trials of generic rifampicin.
pmc-12796410:
Nadezhda Sutormina, Inna Kalabina, Victoria Efimova, and Elena Nikolaeva studied brain links in young children and how they tie to memory and screen use, in twenty twenty-five. They recorded brain waves from thirty-one children aged five to seven, just before and just after a short smartphone game. They then gauged how brain areas link up, using graph measures of how tight and how spread the web is.

The brief game did not shift the link patterns in any clear way. Children with stronger working memory showed a more locally grouped and less globally linked pattern in slow brain waves. In faster waves, the stronger group also showed more local grouping. The authors say these brain wave measures can mark real gaps in memory skill between young children, even if a short game leaves no trace.
pmc-12797810:
Dingding Wang and co-authors study muscle loss risk across a combined syndrome spectrum in a 2025 paper. Sarcopenia, the steady loss of muscle, drives disability and raises death risk. Heart, kidney, and metabolic problems each feed it, but their joint effect was unmapped.

The analysis uses a national United States survey of more than four thousand adults from 2011 to 2018. A new five-stage framework grades combined heart-kidney-metabolic burden. Muscle loss was judged by a standard national criteria set. Statistical models test how risk grows by stage and whether inactivity multiplies it. The multisystem view may help clinics spot high-risk patients earlier and target activity programs where they count most.
pmc-12800310:
Tianxiao Liu and co-authors test a sleep drug as a guard for the brain after stroke in a 2025 study of rats. A stroke cuts blood to the brain; when flow returns, swelling and cell death can worsen the harm. A cell alarm system called the inflammasome helps drive that second wave.

The drug, remimazolam, shrank dead brain area and eased movement faults in rats with blocked brain arteries. In dish-grown brain cells starved of oxygen, it kept more cells alive. A fiery form of cell death dropped in both setups. Gene and protein tests showed the drug turned down the alarm path, from its NF-kB switch to the inflammasome parts. The work hints at a new use for a known drug.
pmc-12801510:
Dawei Yang, Haifang Wang, Yuguo Zhang, and Bingzheng Yan test adding a blood-vessel blocker to artery-delivered chemotherapy for advanced liver cancer. When tumor invades the portal vein, options shrink fast. Chemoembolization starves the tumor through its artery; bevacizumab chokes the new vessels tumors grow to survive.

One hundred eighty patients were randomized evenly. After two years of follow-up, the added drug shrank tumors more and cut vessel growth signals deeper. Time without progression stretched from about six to ten and a half months. Median survival reached nineteen months against thirteen. Severe high blood pressure and low platelets rose in the drug group, the trade the authors weigh in its favor.
pmc-12802010:
Nongnuch Jindarattanaporn and co-authors study in 2025 how ultra processed food companies in Thailand shape health through business power. These firms have grown fast, hold weight in the economy, and build networks with political actors to press their interests. Their products are linked to obesity and other long term diseases, a rising public concern in Thailand.

The team reviewed public records for fifteen national and global firms over six years and interviewed dozens of field experts. National firms used all seven strategy types in their framework, from political and marketing moves to science shaping and reputation work. Global firms used all but the labor strategy. Theme based analysis ties those moves together as a playbook. The case gives health policy a concrete map of how food industry power works in one middle income country.
pmc-12802210:
Where a bowel cancer starts, left side or right, has long predicted survival once it spreads. Tsung-Chiao Tsai and co-authors ask whether that rule survives the cancer's rarest journey, to the brain, in a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis. They pooled studies of patients whose colorectal cancer had metastasized to the brain and who were tracked by primary tumor site.

Ten studies with 1,792 patients qualified. Left-sided colon cancer patients lived longer after brain spread than right-sided ones, with a hazard ratio of 0.71, and the studies agreed closely. Rectal cancers, by contrast, showed no significant survival difference from colon cancers in this setting. The authors conclude that sidedness keeps its meaning even in the brain, a refinement for counseling patients with this grim complication.
pmc-12804710:
Ling Huang and six co-authors compared two strengths of red light therapy in two thousand twenty-five for slowing short-sight in guinea pigs. Repeated low-level red light is used to curb myopia, but the safer lower dose must prove it works as well as the higher one. Forty-eight pigs were split into control, untreated myopia, and two light groups.

Both light strengths cut eye elongation and the myopic shift by a wide margin versus untreated animals. Both restored the thickness and blood flow of a key eye layer, kept the wall structure sound, and prevented cell death in the retina. No clear gap split the two doses, backing the lower dose as both safe and effective.
pmc-12804810:
Dongying Zhao and Maofa Jiang wrote a paper in twenty twenty-five on how steel plants can manage their energy loads with a fuzzy decision method. Making steel uses huge amounts of energy, so the choice among load plans shapes both cost and how green the plant is. The plans must be weighed on many points at once, and expert views are often vague.

The pair built a model on the Fermatean fuzzy FUCA method, which ranks options even when judgments are vague. They scored fifteen plans on gains and costs, with input from experts in the field. The model picked out the plans that work best and can be done, and dropped ones that cost too much or are hard to run. When they changed the weights, the rankings stayed much the same. Checks against like methods backed the model too.
pmc-12804910:
Mariana Nabais and six colleagues butcher turtles, raw and roasted, to read the habits of ancient hunters, in a 2025 experimental study. Turtles and tortoises were a known Stone Age food in the Mediterranean, and fire's role in processing them was unclear.

Roasting in the shell made the animals far easier and faster to take apart, whatever the butcher's experience. Raw carcasses collected more cut and percussion marks, while roasted shells showed heavy heat damage. Stone tool edges picked up wear much like tools used on other small game. Chemical tests could not reliably detect light heating. The authors read fire as labor-saving know-how, passed down and planned, in early human groups.
pmc-12805710:
Krishna Adeshara and co-authors test a blood marker for sorting risk in a hard-to-treat diabetes group, in this 2025 study. The marker is a soluble form of a receptor tied to inflammation and cell stress. Their patients had type 1 diabetes plus blood pressure that resisted treatment, a mix that sharply raises heart and kidney danger.

Over a median of twelve years, sixty-two of the resistant patients developed coronary artery disease. Higher marker levels tracked with greater risk of that outcome and of end-stage kidney failure. Much of the signal faded once kidney function was counted, though the trend remained. The authors suggest the marker, read alongside standard kidney tests, can flag the patients in most danger.
pmc-12807910:
Tobias Peters, Kai Biermeier, and Ingrid Scharlau test eye attention as a trust gauge in a paper whose head is dated 2025. Healthy distrust means using AI help yet staying alert for its errors. Past checks lean on stated trust and reliance, which may miss quiet doubt.

That cut, though, did not clearly help later calls on the labels. The authors weigh what gaze can and cannot prove about trust. The work adds a covert lens to a mostly self-report field.
pmc-12808210:
Zhang and co-authors redesign the blockchain for the internet of vehicles, where cars generate mountains of data but cannot store a full ledger each. Classic blockchains demand every full node keep everything, an impossible ask for vehicle hardware. Coded chains compress blocks, but fixed codes cope badly when cars join and leave. Their scheme uses rateless Raptor codes, which can spin out the redundancy the moment needs, and adjusts its settings on the fly, without re-encoding stored data.

A lightweight consensus method based on verifiable randomness keeps agreement cheap. The authors report storage savings near 98 percent, a vanishingly small chance of failed decoding, and a system holding up as the network churns. The work is a design with analysis rather than a road trial. For engineers building vehicle data networks, it offers a ledger whose storage cost bends with the fleet instead of breaking.
pmc-12808310:
Tiwen Lu and co-authors report a new way to make a 3D-printed alloy stay strong and stretchy at very low temperatures, in a 2025 paper. Tiny hard particles can strengthen metals, but laser printing leaves little control over how they form. The team starts with powder grains of a cobalt-chromium-nickel alloy coated with nanoparticles of titanium carbide.

During printing, the first laser pass melts the coating into the alloy. Later passes reheat the metal, and the particles form again in place, small and evenly spread. These particles block the slip that weakens metals, adding about 312 units of tensile strength while letting the metal keep stretching without cracking early. At near-liquid-helium cold, the printed alloy pairs high strength with high ductility, and the team says the trick should transfer to other printed alloys.
pmc-12808710:
Hudabia Murtaza and co-authors compute what happens when one site in a hydrogen-storing crystal is left empty. The material, a potassium-based double perovskite hydride, is a candidate for clean energy storage because it can hold hydrogen in solid form. Using first-principles calculations, the team compared the intact crystal with a version missing its aluminum site.

Both versions proved structurally and thermodynamically stable by their energy and tolerance checks. The vacancy made the crystal softer against strain, though it stayed brittle either way. Electronically the two differ sharply: the intact material is a wide-gap insulator, while the vacancy version behaves like a metal. Their light responses also split, with the intact crystal polarizing more at high energies. The study maps how a single defect class could tune hydrides for green energy uses.
pmc-12809610:
Liza Boyar leads a team of nine authors in 2025 in asking who uses meal kits. These are boxed ingredient services that promise a home-cooked dinner without the shopping. Data came from an international food policy survey run in five countries in 2022.

The team measured how many people had used a kit in the past week. They modeled what went with it: age, income, cooking skill, home cooking habits, and eating out. Healthy eating, weight change, and green efforts also entered. Population-level answers show whether kits serve the time-pressed, the keen cook, or the struggling one, evidence for both marketers and health planners.
pmc-12810310: A crystal structure note by Eric Hosten and Richard Betz, published in 2025, pins down the hydrogen atoms of a small chlorinated ring compound. The molecule is a protected form of a chlorine-bearing aldehyde. Its aliphatic ring sits in a chair shape. In the crystal, weak carbon-hydrogen to oxygen contacts pair the molecules into symmetric dimers. Such notes feed structure databases that chemists search when planning syntheses.
pmc-12811810:
Ali Alameri and seven co-authors review how facial trauma affects dental implant looks in a 2025 paper. Trauma often knocks out front teeth and tears nearby tissue. Implants in such spots must please the eye for years. Whether old trauma hurts soft tissue outcomes was unclear.

With grafting and careful placement, outcomes matched uninjured sites. Prompt placement with grafting held contours steady in trauma cases. Some series kept that stability past a decade. Small, mixed studies limit the certainty, they warn.
pmc-12812710:
Chao Han, Dahai Yu, Xueli Sun, and Ziyan Liang track in 2025 how mind and life quality change for young and mid life stroke patients through rehab training. First strokes in this age band can derail work and family life, so gains in mood matter as much as gains in movement. Their study followed just over two hundred patients in China.

The program mixed body therapy, task therapy, and counseling, five days a week for six to eight weeks. Standard scales scored life quality, mental state, and low mood before and after. Patients were split by whether each score began in the impaired range. Changes were then compared.
pmc-12812910:
Oksana Zayachkivska and three co-authors wrote a 2026 essay on obesity care and the balance between two kinds of body fat. White fat stores energy, while brown fat burns it to make heat. The essay argues that how these two fats trade places may shape how well a person holds up against weight gain and disease.

They point to a newer view that puts fat tissue at the center of how obesity is defined and found early. More than 75 medical groups back that view. The essay asks how strength and repair in the body, at the level of fat, could guide care that finds risk sooner and fits each patient better.
pmc-12815410:
Bedrana Muracevic-Begovic, Amra Mujkanovic-Dzino, and Jasmin Hodzic report a twin pregnancy case involving Down syndrome in one twin in a 2025 case report. When one twin carries a severe anomaly, ending that twin's life can protect the mother and the healthy twin. Law and access, though, vary sharply by country.

Since the procedure is not legal in Bosnia and Herzegovina, she was referred to a center in Serbia. After ethics approval, the affected twin was treated late in pregnancy, and delivery days later gave one healthy baby. Follow-up at one month was normal.
pmc-12815910:
Takashi Sasaki and co-authors identify a small protein that keeps fast muscles working, in a 2025 study. Muscle contraction runs on calcium: it floods the cell to trigger a pull, then a pump called SERCA1 clears it so the muscle can relax. A tiny peptide normally brakes that pump.

The new protein, named MCARE, sits in the cell membrane of fast-twitch muscle and blocks the brake. With the brake off, the pump clears calcium faster and relaxation speeds up. Mice lacking the protein developed wasting and weakness in fast muscles that looked like muscular dystrophy. The find names a fresh target for diseases where muscle relaxation and strength fail.
pmc-12816210:
Khuzin Dinislam and co-authors review, in a study published in 2025, a cell protein called SIRT1 as a key player in heart and vessel disease. Such disease is the leading cause of death worldwide, covering many heart and vessel disorders. SIRT1 is an enzyme that depends on a common fuel carrier, and it steers many basic cell tasks.

Through those tasks, it shapes vessel lining health, cell stress, swelling, aging, and the growth and failure of the heart muscle. The diseases it touches include heart failure, artery clogging, high blood pressure, and heart attack. The review gathers recent findings on what SIRT1 does in health and in disease. It also explores whether drugs aimed at SIRT1 and its sister proteins could treat these conditions. That makes it a map for drug hunters.
pmc-12816610:
Zhou and a large team build a battery free, wireless patch and implant that tracks body pressure signals in twenty twenty-five. Brain pressure and pulse matter for spotting disease early, but wired implants risk infection. Their sensor is a hair thin crystal film that sings at a set pitch. Body pressure bends the film and shifts the pitch, read from outside.

As a wearable, it followed pulse and breathing pauses. As an implant, it sensed brain pressure down to tiny levels across a wide range. Rat tests caught true pressure rises in a swollen brain model. Long implants stayed body friendly. The team sees broad use in pressure watch care.
pmc-12816710:
Rangaswamy Venkatesh and co-authors build and test a nickel Schiff base complex in a 2025 study. Such azomethine linked compounds draw note as drug leads. The team made the nickel complex and read it by light spectra and nuclear resonance, backed by density functional math.

The shape came out square planar, tied through nitrogen and oxygen. Charge flow between metal and ligand ran strong, with a tight energy gap that hints at high reactivity. Docking placed it snug in a target pocket, past a standard drug. Germ tests beat Escherichia coli and kin, with fair action on Staphylococcus aureus.
pmc-12817410:
Qiuyu Zhu and co-authors describe a rare pile-up of lung disasters in a COVID-19 patient who never went on a ventilator. The fifty-six-year-old man with COVID pneumonia developed air loose in the chest center, a collapsed lung, and air trapped under the skin, all at once. A large blood clot in the lung then landed on top of the damage.

Alongside standard COVID care, the team cut a small vent in the chest wall and hooked it to a vacuum dressing, a trick that draws trapped air out. His condition improved quickly once the vent was working. Blood thinners treated the clot, and he went home in stable shape. The case warns doctors to watch for these air leaks even without a breathing machine.
pmc-12817510:
Juan Izquierdo-Condoy and co-authors measure high-risk HPV infection in Ecuadorian women, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. HPV drives cervical cancer, and past Ecuador counts swung widely. Screening program data held over sixteen thousand valid tests from health centers across the land.

About eleven percent tested positive for the virus. Women in their thirties made up the largest share of positives. One pooled group of five types led the finds, at over forty percent of positives. About one in seven positive women carried several types at once. Rates sat below past national claims but above global norms.
pmc-12817810:
Muhammad Saifullah, Simin Sharafi, and Reza Ghanei Gheshlagh pool the evidence on self-medication in Pakistan. Their 2025 review and meta-analysis searched six databases for studies published since 2000, following standard review rules. Eligible studies all came from 2008 onward. The pooled estimate gives one national figure for how common the practice is, while the analysis hunts for why rates differ across regions and groups. The authors aim to give health planners a firm number and a map of where the habit runs strongest.
pmc-12819010:
Inês Carvalho and four co-authors report a case of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, a bile duct cancer arising in the liver, that spread to rare locations in a younger patient. The cancer is usually diagnosed in late middle age, often at an advanced stage, and is fast to spread. Their 2025 case is a 41-year-old woman with three days of double vision, blurred vision, and headache. Imaging showed metastases far beyond the usual pattern.

They also note a possible rise among younger patients, who may fare worse.
pmc-12819310:
Ozge Buyukahisha and co-authors report a skin condition triggered by an immune therapy drug, in a case report published in 2025. Their patient had early stage triple negative breast cancer. pmc-12819410:
Tim Wehnes and co-authors present a 2025 study of mouth bacteria, body age, and thinking in the oldest old. The group held 311 adults aged 85 and up, most of them Chinese, living in the community. Body age was read from DNA marks by four known aging clocks. Mouth bacteria were typed by gene reads, and mind and body function were scored by standard tests.

Mouth care may join the map of healthy late aging.
pmc-12819710:
Yuxuan Su, Fang Zhao, Shuang Liu, Zheqin Dong, and Dongxu Liu build a smart gel for chronic skin wounds in a paper whose text is dated 2025. Such wounds stall with lasting swelling, poor cell regrowth, and weak blood supply. Plain dressings only cover the wound and can tear new tissue when changed.

Their gel joins two networks and a dose of strontium ions. One network sets fast under light, the other adds antioxidant power from a dopamine based part. Lab tests track cell growth, cell movement, and vessel tube forming. Tests in animals, the authors report, show the gel aids skin regrowth by boosting vessels and steering immune cells toward healing.
pmc-12820110:
Tao Liu and co-authors design a metal alloy electrode that could let solid-state lithium batteries charge fast. Thick electrodes tend to crack as they swell, breaking the paths that ions and electrons travel. Their 2025 paper uses a three-metal alloy of indium, tin, and bismuth as the negative electrode.

As lithium enters, the alloy forms several phases in steps, which spreads stress and limits cracks. The paths for charge stay intact, and the changes reverse cleanly on discharge. The electrode stored about 724 milliamp-hours per gram and survived very high currents. A full cell kept 87.5 percent of its capacity after 1,300 cycles at fast charge. pmc-12820210:
Qiqi Lu, Zhongming Zhao, and co-authors build a score for how mixed the immune cells inside a tumor are, in a 2025 study. Tumors hold many kinds of immune cells in varied spots and states. How that mix links to growth and care was still hard to gauge with one number.

Their score counts the spread of cell types in each tumor. Low scores went with worse survival, more growth linked traits, and weaker response to immune care. The score beat older marks in tests, such as counts of tumor mutations. The team reads low mix as a sign of tumors in a late stage.
pmc-12820310:
Prince Paul and co-authors published a study in 2025 on concrete reinforced with waste natural fibers, such as jute, coir from coconut husks, and bamboo. They compiled 444 concrete mix designs from the literature, each described by seven input variables. Six machine learning algorithms were trained and tuned on the data. A gradient boosting model performed best, with the strongest fit and the lowest prediction error. pmc-12820510:
Soraia Pereira and co-authors set out, in a 2025 trial protocol, a program to make primary care nursing safer by improving the work environment itself. Happier, better-supported nurses keep patients safer and stay in their jobs longer, a chain shown by many past studies.

The program runs six training sessions of three hours each, aimed at empowering nurses in their daily practice. Before and after, nurses rate the safety climate and their work setting. The trial asks whether fixing the environment moves safety more than training skills alone.
pmc-12820610:

pmc-12821310:

pmc-12821710:
Chesmi Kumbalatara and co-authors survey vape and tobacco use in college students in this 2025 study. Vaping spread fast on campuses in the late twenty-tens, and its aerosols carry nicotine plus fine particles. The team asks what drives first use and steady use.

Tobacco was most often the first product tried, at a younger age than vaping. Tree and regression models name school year, income, job status, and first-use age as key predictors of steady vaping. The authors urge tailored campus programs.
pmc-12821810:

pmc-12822010:

Statistical models adjusted for age, parity, stage of pregnancy, education, and whether the pregnancy was planned. Correlations and regressions mapped the association. pmc-12822210:
Fanghua He and co-authors link kidney markers with syphilis activity and brain spread in a 2025 study. Three hundred ninety HIV negative patients with syphilis entered the analysis. Higher urea and creatinine tracked with stronger disease activity marks. Filtration estimates moved the other way. Top third kidney marker groups faced roughly double the odds of brain spread. pmc-12822310:

pmc-12824210:
Jiaqi Liu and co-authors design in 2025 a material that flashes fast and bright when hit by radiation, for use in detectors. One crystal gave a response under a nanosecond and a high light yield, beating leading commercial materials. Those traits allowed very precise timing in a scan for positrons and sharp X-ray images. Readers in materials science see a design rule that favors fast flashes over long lived trapped states.
pmc-12824310:
Mohammad Hossein Davoudi and Hossein Kamran Haghighi pull zinc out of toxic lead plant waste, in a study from 2025. The waste, from a smelter in Zanjan, Iran, holds much zinc plus lead, arsenic, and salts. Left as is, it threats soil and water; cleaned, it is a source of a prized metal.

Their route washes out salts, then leaches the zinc into acid. A solvent wash with an agent called D2EHPA then grabs the zinc in stages. The wash cut arsenic to a trace far too low to block the next step, while zinc rose to a rich level fit for plating out as pure metal. pmc-12824410:

The new approach maps each strained molecule onto a single defined reference while keeping its structure intact. The reference comes from models trained on flat ring compounds. Tests on carbon belts, spirals, bowls, tubes, and ball-shaped molecules showed the method to be accurate and broad. It needs only one main calculation per molecule, which speeds up design work.
pmc-12826810:
Marcel D'Eon bids farewell in 2025 after eleven years editing the Canadian Medical Education Journal, and uses his last editorial to tell its survival story. Under his watch the journal grew from two issues a year to six, a pace kept since 2020. Citations climbed past nine hundred a year, submissions past three hundred, and readership split evenly between Canada and the United States. Inside, he built section editor teams and partnerships with national medical bodies. Even the logo has a story, adapted from artwork submitted to the journal's images section. pmc-12827110:

The study checks that promise directly.
pmc-12827410:

pmc-12827510:

pmc-12829010:

Four feature selection methods narrowed the predictors, and eleven learning algorithms competed to classify risk. Performance was judged with accuracy curves, calibration, and decision analysis, and the best model became a web calculator. The authors propose it as a triage step before colposcopy in low-resource settings.
pmc-12829110:
Solveig Reeh and nine co-authors report, in 2025 work, a grave rare harm after a routine tooth pull in a cat. Vet tooth work is safe as a rule, yet harms, when they come, can be fierce, with eye wounds the known risk. This case ran far past the eye.

pmc-12830510:

After the trial, patients received a paper survey with their own report in the new designs. They rated how clear and useful each feature was and named their preferences. The team compared answers between the trial's two arms and across chart features. The findings point to designs that patients can read at a glance, a step toward reports that truly inform care talks.
pmc-12830610:
Masoumeh Safkhani and Mahmoud Ghorbani Fard propose two secure login protocols for the Internet of Drones, in a 2025 paper.
