The new protocols aim to patch those weak spots directly. They authenticate drones and control stations before data flows. Security goals span privacy, secrecy, and resistance to replay. Formal and informal analysis checks the designs. Drone network builders gain vetted blueprints for safe communication. The work fits a fast-growing layer of airspace infrastructure.
pmc-12830810:
Pouria Feizabadi and co-authors test whether a lab value from flu tests can warn of rising flu cases, in a 2025 study from Iran. The value, called a cycle threshold, reflects how much virus is in a sample. Lower values mean more virus. The team ask whether weekly averages of that value move before national case counts.

Data cover one year, from March 2023 to March 2024. Average threshold values ran about four weeks ahead of case counts, with a moderate link between the two. Models that used the lagged value predicted weekly incidence well. The authors suggest that tracking this lab value at national scale could give health officials up to four weeks of warning. That lead time could help them staff clinics, stock supplies, and time public messages before a surge peaks.
pmc-12830910:
Yue Fang and seven co-authors build a soft motion sensor in a 2025 paper. Wearable trackers feed health checks and virtual reality systems. Their sensor mimics the ion based sensing of human skin. Earlier versions were too faint and read bending in only one direction.

The new fiber sensor pairs a water rich gel with tuned ion effects. Two forces, dipole attraction and size blocking, widen the ion flow gap on bending. Sensitivity hit a record level for this sensor class. A square prism shape with paired electrodes reads bends in several directions. Math models of gel mechanics and ion drift backed the design. The team demoed it driving a digital twin in a virtual world.
pmc-12831310:
Daniel Molnar, Virginie Metoukam Bauquis, and Christine Clavien test a card game that gets people planning for future health crises, in a 2025 study. Advance care planning is often put off, and the game was built to open the conversation.

At a 90-minute public event, 124 attendees learned about advance directives and tried the game, which helps players name fears, hopes, and priorities. One hundred eighteen, average age 75, answered surveys before and after. Only 32 returned the final survey weeks later. The team tracked attitudes, felt readiness, and actions taken or planned. They also asked how players rated the game and whether they preferred the app or paper cards. Conversation tools, they suggest, can move planning from paper to practice.
pmc-12835010:
Nandimalla Vishnu and co-authors build a pH sensor from a conducting polymer in 2025. The polymer is usually made in acid or non-water settings, which limits green production. Their method forms it at neutral pH on a carbon-coated electrode instead.

Cycling the coated electrode in a neutral buffer built the active polymer film. Microscope and light checks confirmed the film's form and makeup. The sensor responded in a clean, near-ideal way to pH shifts and ignored common biochemicals. Under tuned settings, it read pH in several food samples, with a path to small online monitors.
pmc-12836810:
Benjamin Lieser, Georgy Belousov, and Johannes Soding present a 2025 paper on a faster tool for family tree studies of genes. Such studies model how letters in a gene swap over time. Richer models that let each column of an alignment have its own swap rates are too slow to fit. The heavy part is a math step that must run for each column.

Their tool, PhyloGrad, speeds that step up a great deal. It ran 30 to 100 times faster than a standard learning library in their tests. It also used far less memory. Even for a single shared model, it beat a leading tree tool by a wide margin. The tool is written in Rust with links for Python use.
pmc-12836910:
Wu Liu and six co-authors weighed in 2025 when heart surgery should happen for patients with infected heart valves. The infection destroys valve tissue and still kills many patients despite better care. Custom waits four to six weeks while drugs control the infection, but early surgery reports keep appearing with mixed results.

The team reviewed one hundred sixty-six surgical patients over six years. They split them by how soon after admission they went to surgery: within a week, in the second week, or in weeks three and four. Comparing survival and complications across the bands helps surgeons judge the trade between waiting and acting.
pmc-12837010:
Benjamin Kaß and co-authors price a six-week therapy that treats the bond between struggling parents and their babies, and ask whether the health system gets its money's worth. Parent-infant psychotherapy builds parental sensitivity, the soil of infant resilience. German insurers, though, pay for outcomes per euro.

Two randomized trials in the SKKIPPI project tested the short program against usual care: one with mothers facing postpartum mental disorders, one with infants showing regulation problems in the first three years. Costs and effects were tallied side by side. Early relationships compound for decades; showing they are also a bargain is how such programs move from pilot to standard coverage.
pmc-12837110:
Nathalie Ouare and co-authors published this malaria study in 2025 from Nanoro, Burkina Faso. Dams and irrigation fight hunger and thirst, but still water can breed the mosquitoes that carry malaria. The team ran monthly household surveys from March 2022 to February 2023 in five villages set three to forty kilometers from the Soum dam. Blood from 13,786 people was checked for the main malaria parasite.

Silent carriage, at 24.5 percent, beat frank illness, at 19.5 percent. The village by the dam ran highest, near forty-two percent, and the far village lowest. Teens carried the most infection in every village. Rain, oddly, tied to lower risk once other traits were weighed. The authors urge joint action across health, water, and farming to blunt the dam's malaria cost.
pmc-12837210:
Vivek Kaliraman and Joni Watson survey acute care nurses on patient handoffs at shift change in a 2025 study. Handoffs, where care facts pass from one nurse to the next, are a known safety risk when communication is uneven. National rules require a standard handoff process, yet proof on handoff quality between nurses was thin.

An online survey with twenty four questions ran in mid 2024 and drew more than a thousand replies. After screening, 688 direct care nurses in United States hospitals were kept for analysis. The survey covered missed facts, completeness, patient involvement, and problem shift changes. More than one in four nurses agreed with at least one concern.
pmc-12837410:
Philumena Bauer and co-authors review how hospitals and care groups steer their green and social duties with management controls. Health care emits a real share of world carbon output, and funds and rules squeeze groups from all sides. Leaders need tools that turn broad pledges into daily practice.

The review scans world studies on sustainability management controls in care settings. Green topics rule the field, far ahead of social and governance ones. Cultural and administrative controls get the most ink. Budget-style controls, planning, and reward links stay little studied. Studies also show a weak bridge between big strategy and ward-level work. The authors sketch a framework to help leaders wire pledges into budgets, targets, and staff routines, and they name the gaps scholars should fill next.
pmc-12837810:
Yan Liu and co-authors teach an AI to forecast which diabetes patients will answer eye treatment. Their 2025 study targets diabetic macular edema, a swelling of the retina that steals sight, and the injected drugs that block a growth factor to dry it out.

Their model reads two kinds of eye imaging together, four hundred two eyes in all, and learns with an attention method shaped to mimic clinical reasoning. It outlined disease markers with solid accuracy and predicted treatment response at an area under the curve of about eighty-four percent, beating rival methods. The design choices also make its reasoning easier to inspect. The authors offer it as a step toward precise, explainable treatment choices in eye clinics.
pmc-12838010:
Luyi Ying and co-authors published a 2025 case report of an eye infection blamed on human herpesvirus 7, a virus not known to affect the eye. The virus is a relative of the cold-sore virus family. It was known to target immune blood cells. No case in the cornea, the clear front of the eye, had been reported.

The patient was a thirty-two-year-old man who had received a corneal graft for a cone-shaped flaw. Twelve days later, a branching sore grew on the graft, the mark of the cold-sore virus family. Tear tests found the DNA of this virus, and none of its relatives. Drugs by mouth and drops cleared the surface in two weeks, as the viral markers fell. Pale bumps then appeared as he healed. At five weeks the virus was gone, and the eye stayed clear for eight months.
pmc-12838410:
Xiaoqin Yuan, Shanshan Zhang, and Yufeng Tang report a new gene variant in a Chinese family, in work from 2025. Hereditary spastic paraplegia covers many genetic diseases that stiffen and weaken the legs. Variants in one motor protein gene already link to several nerve diseases, but not yet to this family pattern.

Family members had full nerve exams, brain scans, and electrical studies of nerve and muscle. Whole exome sequencing found a rare missense change in that gene in the lead patient. Checks in parents and computer tools supported a likely harmful effect on the protein. Illness showed as dominant complex disease with strong spasticity and ataxia. The report widens the known range for this gene.
pmc-12838510:
Iriagbonse Osaigbovo and three co-authors explore research capacity among allied health professionals in Nigeria, in a 2025 qualitative study. Most prior work on this topic focuses on physicians, not on cadres such as pharmacists, laboratory scientists, radiographers and physiotherapists. Data come from six focus groups and four key informant interviews at the University of Benin Teaching Hospital.

Six themes emerged, from narrow early research exposure to weak funding, training gaps and ethics delays. Staff showed strong drive tied to career growth and patient care, but workload and time pressure held them back. Suggested fixes include protected time, small internal grants, mentorship and department research units. Multisite work is proposed next.
pmc-12841810:
Two seed bug species look so alike that a puzzling in-between form has stirred doubt about where one species ends and the other begins. Chenguang Zheng and co-authors settled the question in this 2025 study by combining body form, gene data, and habitat data. Several established species-splitting methods were applied to the same samples.

Most methods agreed on how to draw the boundary, clarifying what the in-between form really is. Without gene data, the form had defied sorting for years. Clear species limits matter beyond naming: these bugs feed on crops and trees, and control advice depends on knowing which species is present. The study shows how layering three kinds of evidence can end a long taxonomic dispute.
pmc-12843410:
Cristian-Sorin Hariga and co-authors review migraine care from a plastic surgeon's view in a paper from 2025. Migraine is a common, disabling nerve disorder with many causes. Drugs remain the base of care, yet some patients keep having attacks.

In select patients, squeezed nerves outside the skull feed the pain. The review covers how to map trigger sites and test them with nerve blocks or botulinum toxin. Surgery to free those nerves can then help stubborn cases. The authors argue for care that joins drugs with targeted surgery. They close with future paths for this combined approach. Patient selection is framed as the key to good results.
pmc-12844910:
Patricia Pérez-Pérez and a large team look for free-living amoebae in dry lands on a Spanish island. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. These tiny life forms live in soil and water all over the world. Some kinds can cause disease in people, so their spread near homes is a health concern.

They test soil and water samples from Fuerteventura with culture and gene tests. One genus ruled in soil, and one kind ruled in water. Gene tests were faster and cheaper, while culture proved the amoebae were alive and caught more kinds. Checks also found mixed germ loads in the water. The team urges care, since risky kinds live near people.
pmc-12846410:
Whitley and co-authors look past headline coverage rates to ask when Australian children actually get their measles shots. National figures are snapshots, so delays can hide between them. Using the national register, they track over 53,000 children in one New South Wales health district, born between 2015 and 2019, with an Aboriginal researcher co-leading the work.

Coverage passes the 95 percent target, and Aboriginal children beat the national rates. Most children are vaccinated on time, and late ones usually catch up within six months. Still, a few pockets of low coverage appear in smaller areas. The authors argue that timing data like this helps aim catch-up efforts where they matter.
pmc-12847910:
Matthaeus Schwarz-Schilling and co-authors make a bacterium's protein building machinery copy itself in a 2025 study. A synthetic cell that can renew itself needs its translation machinery, the system that reads genes and builds proteins, to be born inside a cell free setup.

First the team found, for each of the thirty proteins involved, how much was needed for that protein to build itself from its own gene. Making several at once stalled, since the parts spread too thin. Anchoring the genes densely on a surface fixed that: genes, machinery, messages, and fresh proteins stayed close together. Groups of proteins, up to all thirty, then regenerated themselves on the surface.
pmc-12848010:
Yan You and co-authors turn a polluting solvent into useful fuel with an electric catalyst in this 2025 study. Dichloromethane contaminates water and resists cleanup. Electrochemical stripping of its chlorine could make hydrocarbons instead of waste, but the halfway fragments are unstable.

Their catalyst pairs cobalt phthalocyanine with sulfur-doped graphene. Sulfur oxide groups grip the cobalt centers and donate electrons, lowering the energy barrier. That steadies the fragile fragments long enough to finish the conversion. The setup works at moderate voltages. Cleaner water plus a sellable product is the prize. The study details why the pairing performs so well.
pmc-12848310:
Akbar and co-authors design an electric vehicle motor that uses carbon nanotube and copper windings, in a 2025 engineering study. Induction motors are popular for electric cars because they are cheap, flexible to control, and handle heat well. The team built a 5 horsepower, three-phase motor design in simulation software and compared the new winding material with plain copper. The composite promises better conductivity, heat stability, and lower weight.

Finite element simulations reported efficiency, output power, torque, and magnetic flux in the air gap. The composite version beat the copper design on the electrical and mechanical measures checked. The authors conclude the material is a viable path to lighter, more efficient traction motors. The work is simulation-based, so bench tests would be the next step.
pmc-12849110:
Abi Crane, Juan Benito, Albert Chen, Daniel Ksepka, and Daniel Field use bird jaw bones to test fossil relationships. Their study from twenty twenty-five concerns the origin of crown birds. Fossils near that origin remain hard to place. Jaw bones hold useful clues, but their fused parts hid detail before.

High-resolution scans separated the jaw elements in young crown birds and fossils. The team then compared support for rival family trees. Evidence from Asteriornis favoured gamebird-like relatives over primitive bird groups. Other fossils showed striking jaw similarities with each other. Those shared traits raise fresh questions about their placement. The work shows lower jaws deserve more weight in bird evolution studies.
pmc-12849310:
Shigehiko Yumura and co-authors watch actomyosin flow in detached cells in a 2025 study of how cells crawl and divide. In stuck-down cells this backward flow is well known, but its drivers in free cells were unclear.

Using slime mold cells lifted off the surface, the team saw strong flows of actin and myosin at the same speed. Surface parts did not move, so the flow comes from the cell cortex, not the membrane. Blocking actin growth killed the flow, while blocking myosin barely slowed it. Flow speed and crawl speed moved in opposite ways, backing the clutch model. During division, flows toward the middle surged. Cell biologists get a clear driver story.
pmc-12852810:
Anxin Chen and co-authors built a machine learning tool to predict alopecia areata, the patchy hair-loss disease, from gene activity data, in a 2025 study. The disease recurs easily and is hard to catch early. The team pulled six public datasets, mapped the disease's biology, and used two feature-picking methods to shortlist genes.

Five datasets formed the training set and one the test set. Three genes emerged as the key features, tied to immune response, nerve inflammation, and stress pathways. Five learning algorithms were compared, and the gradient-boosted tree model won. An explanation method showed which features drove each prediction, and the team published the model as a free web tool.
pmc-12853910:
Fan He and colleagues profiled genes and proteins in myeloid cancers in 2025. Myeloid diseases overlap in their biology. Chronic forms can turn into acute leukemia. That turn brings poor prognosis quickly. Treatment options stay limited after transformation. Combined gene and protein data were analysed.

Shared features crossed disease boundaries clearly. A gene signature split prognosis groups. One growth pathway stood out strongly. That pathway looked druggable in models. A known inhibitor drug was tested. Animal models backed the inhibition effect. Risk sorting gains a new tool. Pathway therapy gains fresh rationale.
pmc-12856010:
Five authors, led by Faten Derouez, test in 2025 which social and climate forces drive desert spread in Saudi Arabia, using three decades of data. Land drying threatens farms and water across the kingdom. Past work lacked long, joined time series for the country, so the team built one from 1990 to 2023.

Their models weigh green energy use, growth, carbon output, heat shifts, and plant cover. Green energy trimmed desert spread by a small share, while plant cover gains cut it far more. Growth and carbon output made spread worse. The authors urge faster green energy growth and yearly replanting to square with national plans.
pmc-12859910:
During knee replacement surgery, giving just enough strong painkiller matters: too much slows recovery, too little leaves pain. Fengrong Liu and four co-authors ran a small randomized trial in 2025 testing a brain-and-body pain index that guides dosing of a fast painkiller. Eighty-four patients were split between guided dosing and the usual approach.

Guided patients used less of the drug, woke faster, and far fewer reported strong pain soon after surgery, about 17 percent versus 56 percent. Recovery scores, nausea, and hospital stay were similar. The authors present the index-guided approach as a safe way to trim opioid use.
pmc-12865010:
Bohong Cai and co-authors polled surgeons in 2025 on the skills and practice tools needed for a keyhole spine operation. The operation, PTED, slips a scope through the side to fix a slipped disc. A thirty-eight-item survey, drafted by experts, went to spine surgeons through chat groups and two large meetings. One hundred fifty-four replies came back from most of China's provinces.

Brain skills, knowing the steps and the anatomy, ranked as the most vital. Cadaver practice was the favored training, but young surgeons could rarely get it. High-grade physical models and virtual reality rigs were the top stand-ins. Booked practice time was short on average. The team urges wider access to the stand-ins for the next wave of surgeons.
pmc-12868710:
Ferns are ancient plants with few sequenced genomes, which hampers both evolutionary study and conservation. Zengqiang Xia and co-authors present in 2025 the genome of Brainea insignis, an endangered cycad fern and the only species in its genus. Assembled to chromosome level, the genome runs 8.62 billion bases. It is huge, the team finds, mainly because repeated sequences piled up recently. An ancient genome doubling, shared by its fern lineage, also plays a part.

Resequencing across the species' range revealed three lineages shaped by ice-age refuges and limited spread afterward. Shrinking populations show inbreeding and a growing load of harmful variants, with too little time to purge them. Genes tied to local climates suggest adaptation, and projected climate shifts put the southwestern Indochina populations at highest risk. The authors argue for conservation that keeps habitats connected and lets adaptive genes flow.
pmc-12875910:
Gabrielle Turcotte and co-authors wrote a study, dated 2025 in its text, on how horse competition organizers in Ontario handle biosecurity. Horses gather in large groups at events, where infections can spread fast. Organizers carry the duty of setting and enforcing the protective rules. The team interviewed ten organizers of English-style events, both sanctioned and not, about their experience.

Two themes emerged. First, biosecurity is a balancing act, weighed against cost, convenience, and the show's other demands. Second, the groups who share the duty, organizers, vets, riders, and governing bodies, often work at cross purposes. The authors note their sample may lean toward organizers already keen on the topic. Even so, they found broad willingness to cooperate on better practice. The study frames safer events as a shared project that needs every party's buy-in.
pmc-12876910:
Wenjun Shan and co-authors review mitochondrial cleanup as an anti aging target in a 2025 paper. Faulty mitochondria drive aging through reactive oxygen buildup, DNA mutations, and energy imbalance. Cells normally clear the damaged units by a selective autophagy route, through two known pathways, and that cleanup slows with age, letting damage pile up in a vicious cycle.

Raising cleanup with drugs or exercise can restore cell energy and slow aging signs, the review argues. Yet the tool cuts both ways, too much or faulty cleanup speeds disease instead. Future work must find the right dose per tissue and keep the balance dynamic, not fixed.
pmc-12882510:
Fatemeh Gabeleh, Mohammad Mahdavi, Mohammad Hadi Karbalaie Niya, and Mehrdad Ravanshad published this study in 2025. It tracks two common viruses in children who received heart transplants. Drugs that protect the new heart also weaken defenses, so dormant viruses can wake and cause harm.

The team followed twenty-eight children, testing blood at surgery and one and two months later, plus urine and donor heart tissue. Every child already carried antibodies to one virus, cytomegalovirus, and about two-thirds carried the other, Epstein-Barr virus. Active infection showed in roughly one in ten blood samples for the first virus. The second virus appeared in about a quarter of samples. Some donor hearts carried virus too. The authors urge long-term monitoring and preventive treatment for these children.
pmc-12886810:
Xin Jin and co-authors rework light-based sensors in a paper on surface-enhanced Raman scattering. Raman signals grow hugely near sharp metal shapes, but the field's shared view held that isolated lithographic structures could not reach single-molecule sensitivity without near-touching pairs that makers cannot yet make.

Using field modeling, the team improved isolated structures step by step. Changes brought a no-loss sticking layer, flatter faces, high-curve oval shapes, and tuned thin-film bases. Their best designs lifted the field boost from modest values to several hundred. These signal boosts approach what single-molecule spotting needs, with shapes simple enough to make at scale.
pmc-12890510:
Deepthi Ashok and co-authors traced heart rhythm damage after COVID in two thousand twenty-five. Arrhythmias rise during and long after infection. The mechanism inside the heart was unknown. Hamsters were infected and monitored by telemetry. Heart tracings and breathing were recorded for weeks. The heart's own wiring system was examined closely.

Slow rhythms and persistent conduction blocks appeared fast. Immune genes switched on inside the wiring tissue. Macrophages moved into that tissue as well. No viral protein was found in the heart itself. Damage thus comes from immune activation, not direct infection. Mitochondrial stress signals joined the picture. The model explains post-COVID rhythm complaints.
pmc-12895910:
David Wagaba and co-authors pool studies on brucellosis in people and livestock across Sub-Saharan Africa, in this 2025 paper. The neglected disease spreads from animals through milk, meat, and contact with birth materials. It burdens both health and farm incomes in the region.

The review searched six databases for studies from 2012 to 2024. Two hundred forty-two papers from twenty-five countries met the rules. Pooling their results gives a regional rate of past infection in humans and in farm animals. Such a map is a first step toward control plans that join human and animal health efforts.
pmc-12896010:
Gholampour and co-authors present a 2025 snapshot study of movement and eating in older women with high blood pressure in Iran. Activity and diet both steer blood pressure, so the team charted real habits. Three hundred thirty-four women at hospitals and health centers in Ardabil filled food and activity questionnaires. Body measures were taken on site.

Average age was near seventy, and most women were married. Six in ten reported high activity levels, a surprise for this age group. More activity tracked with lower systolic pressure. Daily intake averaged about two thousand calories. Body mass index emerged as one predictor of the top pressure number in their models.
pmc-12908310:
Masih Kameh Khosh and four co-authors describe a rare skin cancer that imitates breast cancer in this two thousand twenty-five case report. The tumor is a primary cutaneous apocrine carcinoma, a cancer of sweat gland type cells in the skin. It can look and stain under the microscope much like breast carcinoma. That likeness risks a wrong diagnosis and wrong treatment. Their patient was a sixty-year-old man who came to a breast clinic.

The team walks through the tests that separated skin origin from breast origin. Location, history, and marker patterns all played a part. The case warns doctors to keep this rare tumor in mind when a breast-like cancer appears in skin. Pathologists and breast specialists are the audience.
pmc-12909810:
Acute myeloid leukemia often returns after chemotherapy, and growing evidence ties this resistance to an unhealthy gut microbiome. The authors review how gut microbes may help leukemia cells survive treatment. Bacteria can alter drugs directly, tune the immune system, and release metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids and kynurenine, that favor cell survival and epigenetic change. Clinical studies link low microbial diversity, loss of Faecalibacterium, and overgrowth of Enterococcus with worse outcomes for patients.

Possible countermeasures include fecal transplants, probiotics, and diet changes, all of which show early promise. The authors stress that methods vary widely between studies, which makes results hard to compare. They call for standard study designs and for pinning down the exact microbe-metabolite paths that drive resistance. Such knowledge, they argue, should guide the next round of clinical trials.
pmc-12913710:
Amelia Anshar and co-authors test a tropical fish as an early-warning species for plastic pollution in two thousand twenty-five. Styrene, a plastic building block, now shows up in tropical fresh waters at levels nearing harm. The Celebes medaka, a small fish native to Southeast Asia, could serve as a local sentinel.

Adult fish swam in four styrene doses for ninety-six hours. Their livers were scored for cell damage: hollowed cells, dead patches, swelling cells crowding in, and congestion. Stress gene reads tracked detox, antioxidant, and inflammation markers. The paired tissue and gene data judge both the harm styrene does at low doses and the fish's worth as a monitor for the region's waters.
pmc-12916410:
Rosa Eckert and eleven co-authors published a stroke study in twenty twenty-six on the dangerous hours after heart surgery, when a clot can fly to the brain. At a large academic heart center, thirty-nine patients received mechanical clot removal for major artery strokes following cardiac procedures between twenty eighteen and twenty twenty-two. The team charted who they were and how they fared.

Strokes clustered after assist-device surgery most often, then bypass grafting and valve replacement. Half the cases were wake-up strokes, found on waking rather than witnessed. Successful reopening rates and neurological outcomes are reported against procedure type. The authors supply scarce real numbers for a complication every heart team fears and few centers see often.
pmc-12926110:
In this personal essay, animal physiologist Walter Gay Bottje looks back on a career shaped as much by chance as by planning. A snowstorm that shut down highways and rail lines led him to meet his wife. A high school swim coach steered him to a university whose strong biology program quietly prepared him for graduate work.

He recounts detours through ruminant nutrition and rumen microbiology before circling back to his true interest, physiology, and to heat stress work in broiler chickens. The essay's title names his research threads: blood flow, glutathione, oxidative stress, and mitochondria. Bottje offers the story as a reminder that luck, seized well, is part of a scientific life.
pmc-12926710:
Jia Liu and co-authors work on a delivery trick that could carry antibody drugs to the moist linings where many viruses attack. Published in 2025, their study targets a receptor that normally ferries one antibody type, IgA, across mucosal walls. The drug industry prefers the IgG type, which the receptor ignores, so IgG treatments miss the surfaces where infections like RSV begin.

The team studies single-domain antibodies that grip the receptor, aiming to hitch IgG cargo across the wall with them. Binding traits are tuned so the cargo loads, crosses, and lets go on the far side. The goal is richer IgG at the airway surface, where it can meet the virus first.
pmc-12937510:
Dongxue Chen and six co-authors show that a common enzyme deficiency leaves people open to hepatitis E, in this 2025 study. The missing enzyme, called G6PD, normally shields red cells from oxidative damage, and its absence affects about four hundred million people. Such patients catch viruses more easily, but the hepatitis E link was uncharted.

Infection rates ran far higher in patients with the deficiency, about twenty-four percent against under one percent in a comparison group. Infected deficient patients also showed more jaundice and more pneumonia. In lab cells with the enzyme knocked down, the virus entered more easily and stress rose, while a viral protein was shown to grip the enzyme directly. The authors conclude the deficiency both invites the virus in and deepens the liver injury it causes.
pmc-12955710:
Matthias Pfeifer and seven colleagues present a study published in 2025 on breeding apples that resist powdery mildew. The fungus is among the worst diseases of apple orchards, but a Siberian crabapple called Malus baccata 'Jackii' shrugs it off. Earlier work had located its resistance, named Plbj, on one chromosome arm; this team set out to map it precisely and build breeder-ready markers.

Crossing the resistant crabapple with a dessert variety, they scored offspring for disease over several seasons and built genetic maps from dense markers. The resistance locus landed on linkage group ten, narrowed to a stretch of about three point three million DNA letters containing candidate defense genes. New quick tests now let breeders select resistant seedlings directly, speeding resistant variety development.
pmc-12961410:
Mircea Andriescu and co-authors advance a child's own urethra to fix a birth defect of the penis in a 2025 study. In distal hypospadias the urinary opening sits short of the tip, and dozens of repairs compete, many rebuilding the tube with stitched tissue and its attendant complications. Mobilization takes the opposite bet: free the native urethra and slide it forward into place.

Seventy cases from one center, operated between 2022 and 2025, form the series. The dissection frees the urethra with its spongy surround in a pyramid pattern, drops the complex into a groove split between the erectile bodies, and advances it to the tip. Outcomes satisfied on function and appearance, with four boys developing a narrowed opening afterward. The authors argue that using the child's own tube, unstitch­ed, dodges the classic failure modes of reconstructed urethras.
pmc-12967010:
Aya Elsayed Abdelwahed and a large team of co-authors surveyed people across the Arab region about using AI chatbots for health help, in a 2025 study. Chatbots can coach patients and answer health questions at any hour, but careless use can also mislead. The team wanted to know who uses them, for what, and with what attitudes.

The web survey drew 12,886 valid replies from twenty-one Arab countries, mostly from young, city-dwelling, well-schooled respondents. About seven in ten knew of health chatbots, yet only about one in four had used one. Users turned to them chiefly for health coaching, self-medication, and self-diagnosis, and ChatGPT was the most common choice. Training in AI was the strongest sign of use. The authors say these patterns can guide safer roll-out of chatbots in health care.
pmc-12991710:
Taskin Khan and co-authors measure how snacks and drinks change mouth acidity in preschool children, in a 2025 study. Acid dips after eating wear on young teeth. Many parents and children do not know which foods drive the deepest dips. The team wanted both the size of the change and how long food lingered.

Over seven days, 150 children each received a different snack or drink. Saliva acidity was read with a digital meter at intervals up to thirty minutes. Every test food caused a clear drop right after eating. Most food cleared the mouth within the half hour. The results give dentists concrete numbers for guiding families on snack choices.
pmc-13037610:
Quan Nguyen, Phung Le, and Ngoan Le test fiber-rich tropical feeds for pigs in a lab digestion model. Their 2025 study runs eight local feedstuffs through a three-step simulation of stomach, small intestine, and hindgut. Banana stem, brewery waste, cassava parts, cabbage waste, sweet potato vines, taro, tofu waste, and a foliage plant take part.

Two feeds barely digest in the small intestine, but tofu waste makes it up in the hindgut with the highest acid output of the set. Its protein also digests well early, keeping hindgut ammonia modest. Test diets mostly trail the control on digestible protein, except the tofu diet. Banana stem and cassava leaf diets boost hindgut fermentation. The authors map which local scraps can realistically stretch pig diets.
pmc-13086410:
Kamal Kolluri and three co-authors wrote a 2026 case report on liver cancer that spread to the large bowel. A 70-year-old man had been treated for hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer, with several local therapies. Nearly six years after diagnosis, a blood marker began to rise again.

pmc-13122210:

pmc-13128610:
Jose Castro and co-authors tally the public cost of Hansen's disease in Brazil in a 2026 study. pmc-13130610:
Rafael Mariante and co-authors sum up a joint Brazilian and international meeting on toxoplasmosis, in a commentary published in 2026. pmc-13130710:
Joseph Cornelius and Fabio Rinaldi test whether fake clinical notes can train software that scrubs real ones, in a paper dated 2026. Flavio Chierichetti and co-authors study recommendation limits on content platforms in a 2026 paper. Platforms show users small sets of items picked from a huge catalog by learned models. The models aim to match each user's tastes as closely as possible.

pmc-13135910:

pmc-13136210:
Dominik Schröder and co-authors validate a German quality of life scale in heart patients in a 2026 paper. Adults born with heart defects live long lives needing care. The WHOQOL-BREF scale is wide used, but unchecked in this group.

pmc-13136510:

pmc-13138210:

pmc-13138710:

pmc-13144410:

pmc-13144810:

pmc-13145110:

pmc-13145810:

pmc-13146210:

pmc-13162210:
Publication bias, the tendency for positive studies to appear in print more often, can distort meta-analyses. The framework avoids continuity corrections and runs in standard software at low cost. Simulations checked how well it adjusts for bias against rival methods, and several real data sets show its range across odds ratios and proportions with rare outcomes. The authors offer it as a practical way to gauge how much selective publication might be bending a rare-event meta-analysis.
pmc-13163710:
Jia-Wei Liu and co-authors test gene sequencing for stubborn skin infections in a 2026 pilot study. The culprits are nontuberculous mycobacteria, slow germs whose skin disease looks vague under the microscope and grows poorly in culture. Twenty patients at a Beijing hospital, each confirmed infected, gave tissue for both culture and metagenomic sequencing.

Sequencing found the germ in nineteen of twenty patients; culture managed six. It also returned answers faster. Fish-bone injuries explained most cases of the leading species, which favors fingers and forearms. All biopsies showed the same granulomatous tissue pattern. One patient with an immune defect carried body-wide infection. Tailored antibiotics succeeded in seventeen patients, though seven suffered drug side effects. The authors urge pairing sequencing with clinical judgment for these infections.
pmc-13163810:
Yu-Hsun Chang, Kun-Chi Wu, and Dah-Ching Ding study, in twenty twenty-six, how two forms of a hormone receptor act in pre-cancer cells of the fallopian tube. Ovarian cancer is the most deadly cancer of the female reproductive tract. Its most common form is thought to start in these tube cells. The receptor responds to progesterone, a hormone. One form of it links to better outcomes, but its role in early cells was unclear.

The team raised each form in lab cells that lack two key guard genes. The first form slowed growth, drove cell death, and aged the cells. The second form sped growth. With hormone treatment, both forms halted the cell cycle and drove death.
pmc-13165110:
Adam Mańka, Krzysztof Aniołek, Andrzej Hełka, and Jan Rak published a study in 2026 on how heat from electric current ages the copper wires that feed trains. Contact wires carry huge currents to locomotives, and the current itself warms the wire. The team asked at what point that warming starts to change the metal for good.

They heated wire samples in the lab with currents of about fifteen hundred amps, reaching up to roughly two hundred eighty degrees. Between one hundred twenty and two hundred degrees the metal's mechanical traits barely moved. Above two hundred degrees, hardness and stiffness fell clearly. Long hot running, the authors warn, can soften wires, invite permanent bending, and raise both failure risk and upkeep costs for rail networks.
pmc-13172810:
Jiwon Hwang, Mi Yeon Lee, and Joong Kyong Ahn ask whether gaining muscle and gaining fat pull blood uric acid in opposite directions, in a 2026 study. High uric acid feeds gout and tracks with obesity, but muscle is the body's main store of the raw material that becomes uric acid. The team followed healthy Korean adults who had checkups between 2015 and 2017, tracking body makeup over two years.

The group held 39,505 adults, split among men and women before and after menopause. Body scans sorted each person by whether muscle, fat, and waist-to-hip ratio rose, fell, or stayed flat. Uric acid changed in step with those shifts, in a dose-like pattern. The title gives the headline: muscle and fat changes push the level in opposing ways. The results may refine how doctors read weight change in patients at gout risk.
pmc-13172910:
Leigha MacNeill and co-authors test a risk calculator for mental health in young children. Their 2026 study aims to make the tool fit for routine care. Data came from two groups. One held 2,763 children from the general public. The other held 323 children at higher risk. Risks and strengths were checked in the toddler and early preschool years.

Later preschool checks measured illness of the mind. A past model used basic facts, irritability, and bad childhood events. It held up in both groups, with the same score for accuracy. The team then tested if child and parenting strengths added value. That fits a strengths based view, they note. Next steps for use in clinics are also discussed.
pmc-13173010:
Nuran Golbasi and co-authors test sound wave imaging as a gentle way to judge nail disease. Their 2026 study uses quantitative ultrasound on finger and toe nails. Nail disease is hard to name because signs overlap. A biopsy is invasive. The team scanned patients with a fungal nail illness, with swelling based nail disease, and healthy controls.

In all, 26 patients and 152 nails were scanned. Raw sound data gave three measures of tissue form. Sick finger nails showed a clear drop in one measure, largest in fungal cases. Other measures rose in set patterns, one in fungal disease and one in a scarring nail illness. Toe nail results are also reported. The authors test whether the method is steady and fit for clinic use.
pmc-13173210:
Katia Noyes and eight co-authors study short skill badges for research staff in a 2026 abstract. Such badges, called micro-credentials, let learners gain skills at their own pace with no due dates. A Buffalo center for team science offers four of them, on teaching, sound trial practice, honest research, and science writing.

Each badge grows out of a yearly class chain of three to five long sessions. The study tracks when learners start and finish each badge next to the school term and other center events. The aim is to time badge offers so busy staff can truly use them.
pmc-13175010:
Uwe Kierdorf and Patrick Barrière report in 2026 only the second known case of a deer growing an antler from its cheek bone. A male rusa deer, about seven years old, was shot in New Caledonia carrying normal velvet antlers on top. Below his left eye, a second small antler, about five centimeters, sprouted from the cheek bone on its own stalk.

The little antler wore normal velvet and sat in a bony socket under ordinary scalp skin. During cleaning it detached, suggesting its base joined the skull by cartilage rather than bone. A bump above the right eye may have been a third growth, but the shot destroyed that region. The authors blame old injury to the bone skin. They suggest any skull membrane bone in deer can sprout an antler if provoked.
pmc-13176610:
Hurong Shen and ten co-authors review plant-derived vesicle-like particles for immune regulation and disease therapy, in a paper from 2026. These natural nano carriers, above all from herbal medicine, carry active ingredients across species lines. They circulate longer and penetrate tissue better than many small drugs, with low immune reaction.

The review maps disease-specific immune settings to guide therapy choice. It weighs how each particle type regulates varied immune cells to restore balance in inflammatory and immune diseases. Engineering tricks to sharpen targeting are also evaluated. One open risk is immune reaction to foreign plant proteins in humans.
pmc-13177810:
Orla McBride and co-authors test a way to recruit families into a new United Kingdom birth cohort. Their 2024 study aimed to link birth and maternity records across all four nations. That linked frame would let the team invite about two thousand families. An opt out approach was essential, since families would be contacted unless they declined.

Each nation needed its own path, due to distinct laws on second use of data. Long talks with data approval panels were required. Public dialogue was held with data holders, data users, and parents. People were keen on a new cohort, the team found. They broadly accepted use of records to build the frame. Most valued that it would include a wide mix of family life.
pmc-13178910:
Anindya Mukherjee and co-authors report real-world results for two breast cancer drugs, palbociclib and ribociclib, used in India. These drugs block cell-cycle enzymes called CDK4 and CDK6 and are given with hormone therapy to patients whose tumors feed on hormones but lack the HER2 marker. The team pulled hospital records for patients treated in first-line or later settings between 2021 and 2023.

For both drugs, patients who were more active, whose cancer was new rather than returned, who got hormone therapy first, and who had no earlier chemotherapy stayed free of disease growth longer. On combined analysis, fitness level, the line of hormone therapy, and prior chemotherapy each mattered on their own. The authors present the study as a picture of how these drugs perform outside trials in Indian practice.
pmc-13179210:
Yoichi Shimizu, Katsunori Tsuji, Akiko Hanai, and Mai Hosokawa review activity pacing for cancer fatigue, in a paper published in 2026. Pacing means balancing activity and rest across the day, rather than pushing through or stopping altogether. It is widely used alongside exercise advice, but its benefit for cancer-related fatigue was unproven.

Searching four databases, the team found ten studies that fit, seven of them randomized trials. Pooled results showed a small effect that could be chance overall, with wide variation between studies. One subgroup stood out: patients on chemotherapy, mostly with breast cancer, gained a moderate, clear benefit. The common techniques were goal setting, social support, and graded tasks that grow step by step. The authors say pacing deserves a place for patients in active treatment.
pmc-13179510:
Minu Shilpakar and co-authors catalog the larval flukes living inside freshwater snails in the southwestern Kathmandu Valley, where snail-borne parasites threaten people and livestock but local data are patchy. Over one monsoon season they collected nearly nineteen hundred snails from swamps, ditches, paddies, and canals, covering five species, and coaxed the parasite larvae out with light.

Four snail species carried infections, about three percent overall, with one species clean. Nine larval types were found, including some that can infect humans. Infection peaked in July and August and in grazing swamps, and bigger snails were infected more often. The authors recommend seasonal, habitat-focused surveillance and further work on the animals that complete the parasites' life cycles.
pmc-13179610:
Lukas Geis, Dennis Hecker, Martin Hoefer, Ulrich Meyer, and Marcel Schulz study how to pick the set of transcription factors with the greatest sway over a target gene set. Transcription factors are the switches of genes. Such choices matter when scientists perturb cells and want the strongest, clearest effect. In the network view, switches and genes form a two-sided graph of influences.

The authors frame the search as a probing problem. A researcher tests some switches, learns from the outcome, and chooses the next probes wisely. They compare adaptive strategies, which react to results, with fixed ones on simulated networks. Then they run the methods on real data for genes in T-cell immunity. The work links computer science with gene regulation planning.
pmc-13179710:
Writing in reply to a letter about their study of hypertensive urgency, Prado, Bea, and Martínez explain how treatment choices were made in their emergency department data. Care followed each doctor's judgment, weighing blood pressure level, symptoms, heart risk, and signs of organ damage, rather than a fixed protocol. They add a new comparison of treated and untreated patients.

The groups matched on age, sex, and symptoms, but untreated patients started with lower blood pressure, which suggests doctors treated by severity. Admission rates were alike. The authors agree that rest and repeat readings matter, and they note that follow-up outcome studies are under way.
pmc-13179910:
In cervical dystonia, the neck muscles contract on their own, and the cerebellum seems to lose its normal braking power over the motor cortex. Franca Peemöller and co-authors test whether gentle electric stimulation of the cerebellum can restore that brake in a 2026 trial. Fifteen patients with the isolated form of the condition took part.

Each patient received positive, negative, and sham stimulation in a blinded crossover design. Before and after each session, magnetic pulses probed three braking circuits in the sensorimotor network, and symptom severity was scored. At baseline the cerebellar brake was indeed missing while other brakes worked. The title gives the outcome plainly: the stimulation did not modulate the inhibitory circuits.
pmc-13180110:
Yan Zheng, Tingfen Han, Yanjun Wu, Tingting Wang, and Jinbo Wang mine twenty years of drug safety reports for medicines tied to a kidney syndrome, in a 2026 study. The syndrome damages the kidney's filters and leaks protein. Drug causes are a growing safety concern. The team used the United States adverse event database from 2004 to 2024. Four statistical methods hunted for drug-event signals. Onset timing was also analyzed.

Nearly four thousand cases were found. Fifty-four medicines showed strong positive signals. Cancer drugs made up the largest group. One weight-loss drug and one vessel drug ranked highest by one method. Anti-inflammatory drugs appeared as a notable group too. Cancer drugs acted fastest, at about four months on average. Inflammatory drugs took longest. The authors call this the first large-scale map of the problem. It gives prescribers a watch list for kidney monitoring.
pmc-13180310:
Daniel Schonberger and co-authors report a 2026 study of metabolism scaling in dragonflies and damselflies. Among warm blooded animals, metabolic rate scales with body size to the power of about three quarters, long read as a fixed law. Insects, though, are little studied on this point.

With family tree methods, the team traced the scaling slope across this old insect order. The slope came out near one, a straight isometry, not the classic fraction. Rates evolved in a gradual way with weak pull back and several shifts in peak values. Cell size and surface area did not explain the steep slope. The authors credit the high oxygen demand of flight and growth by cell count, not cell size.
pmc-13180410:
Ans Alamami and co-authors describe a heart and lung machine used as a bridge in a man with stubborn shock and severe acid buildup, in a 2026 case report. The patient, aged forty-seven, had diabetes and took a drug that can raise acid levels. Infection was also suspected.

Despite a breathing machine, strong germ drugs, and high dose pressor drugs, his heart failed and organs shut down. On the second day the team started the external circuit plus a blood cleaning machine. Blood flow steadied, acid cleared, and organ work improved. He left the hospital alive, though his heart stayed weak. The authors stress care in picking such high risk cases.
pmc-13180910:
Yue Sun and co-authors build a lab method to measure fertility drug potency in a 2026 paper. Menotropins, drawn from the urine of postmenopausal women, mix several hormones. Standards today rely on animal tests that vary widely and cannot weigh the strongest fractions well.

Their chromatography method measures the shared alpha subunit of three hormones plus one hormone's own content. A lab-made standard anchors the numbers. Purity comes from the share of the target peaks. Validation followed strict international guidelines. A reliable bench method could steady batch quality without animal testing. The work targets a long-standing gap in how this drug class is controlled.
pmc-13182110:
Emily MacLean and co-authors survey tuberculosis lab services in a 2026 regional report. Seven high burden countries of the Western Pacific faced review. Fast, exact diagnosis and strong lab networks make or break TB care, yet resources vary wildly across the region. In 2024 the World Health Organization's regional office ran the assessment the paper reports.

The survey mapped which tests each country offers and how lab services are organized. Gaps found this way can steer funding to the weakest links first. Regional comparison also lets countries borrow fixes from neighbors with like burdens. The report gives health ministries a shared starting picture for upgrading TB diagnosis.
pmc-13183610:
Cao and Wu describe nursing care for a transplant patient facing two lethal threats at once. Their patient, an 18-year-old woman, had severe aplastic anemia, where the marrow stops making blood cells, plus a stubborn fungal infection eating into her face. She received a salvage stem cell transplant from a donor.

A nurse-led team built care on four pillars: layered infection control, wound care pairing antifungal drugs with local dressings, early watch for complications, and staged mental support. The Omaha System framed each problem and response. The graft took hold, the infection was contained, the facial wound shrank, and a severe immune reaction was weathered. A year on, she was doing well.
pmc-13184010:
Hamad Algamaiah, writing alone, reviews a dental method that seals exposed dentin right after a tooth is prepared for a crown, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Sealing at once, rather than at the fitting visit, aims for stronger bonds and less pain after care. Algamaiah searched three databases for lab and clinical studies on the method and its variants.

The proof shows better bond strength and longer bond life than late sealing. Sealed teeth also let less fluid through and hurt less after care. Several glue styles and extra resin layers were weighed. Clinical studies report good comfort and lasting repairs. The author backs the method but notes study flaws and calls for longer trials.
pmc-13185910:
Öztürk and Bulut present a case report, published in 2026, on a rare cause of belly pain in a teenager. The condition is a twisting of the omentum, the fatty apron that hangs inside the abdomen. About 400 cases exist in the medical literature, and few are caught before surgery. Children account for only a small share. Its signs are vague and usually point doctors toward appendicitis instead. Their patient was a 15-year-old boy with five days of abdominal pain.

Tests suggested inflammation, but scans showed a normal appendix. A CT scan then revealed two telling signs: a twisted vessel stalk and a whirlpool pattern in the fat. With that lead, the team operated and confirmed the twist. The case shows how one good scan can spare a child the wrong operation. It also adds a rare pediatric case to the record.
pmc-13186210:
Raymond Tucker and co-authors build a short survey that tracks how suicidal desire rises and falls, in a 2026 study. Most surveys ask how strong the desire is, not how much it swings over a week. Swings may carry their own signal about risk and care needs, so the team set out to measure them.

They draft 17 items and test them in three groups of adults and students with recent suicidal thoughts. The survey settles into nine items in two parts: one for desire that shifts a lot, and one for desire that stays flat. Scores link in modest ways to mood swings and show little tie to how strong the desire is. In a third study, scores matched phone-based daily reports fairly well. The tool gives clinicians a quick way to ask about change, not just level.
pmc-13186510:
Julián Rondón-Carvajal and four co-authors report a rare case in which a returning chest tumor brought on a dangerous drop in blood sugar, in this 2026 case report. The tumor, a solitary fibrous tumor of the lining around the lung, can in a small share of cases trigger this effect, known as Doege-Potter syndrome. Reports of the syndrome at relapse are scarce.

The case is presented as the first of its kind in Colombia where the relapsed tumor stayed benign. The authors stress that a relapse must always be checked for a turn toward cancer, which happens in up to about twelve percent of cases. Tumor size, cell features under the microscope, and marker stains all feed that judgment. The report adds a data point for doctors facing the same odd pairing.
pmc-13187510:
Yoonyoung Jang and ten co-authors weigh fat rates in Koreans with HIV in a 2026 study. Weight gain is a rising care point as virus care lengthens lives. Whether such adults run fatter than the wider crowd, and how that gap moved over a decade, was not charted.

Health-check files held near 11,000 adults with the virus, set against near 77,000 from a land-wide poll, for 2009 to 2020. Weight bands were read year by year for both. The virus group's plump share sat past a quarter. Trend maps help aim weight care in virus clinics.
pmc-13187610:
Vandeputte and co-authors test whether two simple blood ratios forecast survival in bile duct cancer. Patients with unresectable disease now receive two chemotherapy drugs plus an immune therapy as standard first-line care, but markers of who will do poorly are scarce. Data from 509 patients at thirty-nine sites in eleven countries are gathered retrospectively.

Both ratios, neutrophils to eosinophils and neutrophils to lymphocytes, are measured before treatment. Patients with the second ratio above the median die sooner and progress sooner, with about double the hazard in adjusted models. The authors suggest these cheap, routine ratios could help stratify patients in trials and counsel them in clinic, pending confirmation.
pmc-13189010:
Sisse Rudkjøbing and co-authors describe how patients with gliomas, a type of brain tumor, use specialized palliative care in Denmark. These patients face fast-moving nerve and thinking symptoms, and timely referral to comfort-focused care matters. The study reviews records for patients treated at Odense University Hospital from 2016 to 2020, drawing on medical files and the national palliative care database.

Of 443 patients, 185 start specialized palliative care, generally seven months after diagnosis. Patients with the most severe grade of tumor receive it for a median of 2.5 months before death. Every such patient sees a palliative physician and a named contact nurse. About 63 percent also use at least one other professional, most often a physiotherapist. Younger patients use more of these services than older ones. The authors conclude referrals still come late in the disease course.
pmc-13189210:
Takeya Oda, Amirmahmoud Houshmand Chatroudi, and Yuko Yotsumoto asked what makes a flickering image feel like it lasts longer than it does, in a 2026 study. This flicker-induced time dilation is a sturdy illusion, but whether meaning in the image matters, beyond the flicker itself, was unknown. The team made flickers from faces and houses, plus scrambled versions with no meaning, at three speeds, and had people judge durations and rate how striking each stimulus felt.

Faster flicker reliably stretched felt duration. Meaning never did, at any speed, with or without brightness pulsing. Yet meaningful images did feel more striking, and strikingness rose with flicker speed too. The split shows that feeling an image is vivid is not what stretches time. The authors conclude the illusion is driven by low-level timing signals in early vision, not by higher-level processing of content.
pmc-13190210:
Jiangping Fu and four co-authors set out a trial of heritage sport for health change in young adults. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The Haian Flower Drums, a folk drum act with roots as a heritage art, is the sport in test. The plan rests on a theory that ties what students expect and value to what they do.

Hundreds of university students join a two-arm trial of over a year, with a three-year tail watch on one arm. The lead aim is to check a model that links class level, bodily skill, and a teach-practise-play path. Side reads map the mind traits that shift as habits change. Skill and mood facts are logged across set waves, with mixed models for the main read.
pmc-13190910:
Yuan Zhang and co-authors design a gel-like electrolyte for sodium metal batteries, in a 2026 study. Sodium batteries promise fast charging and high safety, but their quasi-solid electrolytes move sodium ions too slowly. Flow is sluggish both inside the material and at its faces. The team pairs two mediator salts that lock together in their effects.

One salt starts a controlled building of the gel network, while the other slows that growth to keep it even. The result conducts almost purely by sodium ions and resists puncture well. During use, each salt builds a helpful skin on one battery face. Those skins speed ion flow and limit wear. Cells gain fast charging with a long life in tests.
pmc-13192010:
Yulong Zhang and co-authors compare two antibody treatments for hard-to-treat kidney disease in this 2026 study. The disease, primary membranous nephropathy, scars the kidney's filters and often relapses. One group got obinutuzumab alone, a strong B-cell clearing drug. The other got rituximab plus tacrolimus. The team reviewed twenty-eight patients from one center over twenty-four months.

Standard kidney measures did not differ between the groups. Remission rates were alike, at about ninety percent in both. Immune remission, meaning the disease antibody cleared, ran higher with obinutuzumab alone. That gap reached statistical significance. The obinutuzumab group had also been ill far longer before treatment. The authors back B-cell clearing as the core strategy and call for longer studies of lasting benefit.
pmc-13192310:
Alistair Boxall and co-authors set out a plan for making pharmacy safe for the planet as well as for patients, in this 2026 paper. Drug ingredients heal people but leak into water and soil, where they harm wildlife and breed drug-resistant microbes. By the authors' measure, current practice already breaches the Earth system limit for such new chemical entities.

The team proposes a framework of four broad tests and twelve sub-tests covering a drug's whole life, from design to disposal. Judged against it, today's practices align only partly or poorly. Weak points include ignoring environmental effects at the design stage and thin data from poorer countries. The paper stresses the burden on Indigenous and marginalized communities whose lands and livelihoods suffer from contamination. A ten-point road map aims at a fair, sustainable system by 2050, with greener chemistry and upgraded waste treatment.
pmc-13194110:
Yuzhe Guo, Anna Cheng, and Yujuan Huang review pore-based gene reading for sick children in a 2026 paper. Germ hunts in child emergency care must be swift and true, since hours can cost lives. Stock tests are slow and blind to many germs at once.

Pore reading streams a germ's code in real time, reads long spans, and fits in a small box at the bedside. It can name whole germ crowds from thin samples. The review walks its base rules and fresh tweaks for hard child samples. Care-point gene hunts may soon be plain kit.
pmc-13194210:
Masaki Iino, writing alone in 2026, proposes a concept called Integrative Intelligence, a way of describing how people judge well when time, roles, and body signals must be held together at once. It is not a new ability or stage, Iino argues, but a mode already hidden in ordinary judgment that shows under the right conditions.

The study uses self-ethnography, the author studying his own experience, drawing on mountaineering logs, body data, dialogues with an AI, and later reflections. Four linked lenses are developed, including an inner conference of viewpoints and AI as a reflective surface. Three mountain cases show the same constraint pattern producing distinct modes of judgment, supporting the claim that the mode is context-sensitive.
pmc-13194510:
Sabine Kruijer and co-authors study pain care for residents with dementia in a 2026 paper. Brain changes blunt how residents voice pain, so pain shows in odd ways and is easily missed. Care homes in the Netherlands hold many such residents, yet full studies of pain practice there are scarce.

A national survey drew near four hundred staff, managers, and family caregivers, followed by twenty deep interviews. Questions covered how pain is spotted and which drug and non-drug steps follow. Answers were tallied and read for shared themes. The study maps daily practice so gaps between guidance and ward reality can be named and closed.
pmc-13194610:
Sihui Wen and ten co-authors trace a gene control chain behind age-related hearing loss in this two thousand twenty-six paper. This hearing loss is permanent and grows more common as populations age. Chemical marks on DNA-packaging proteins, called epigenetic changes, are emerging drivers. The team found a chain that links one such mark to a gene and then to small RNA regulators. That chain controls autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning process, in the ear's hair cells.

In aging models, the mark and the gene moved in opposite directions. Tuning the chain changed waste buildup and cell death in hair cells. A broad multi-omics scan mapped the wider effects. The work names a possible drug target for a condition with no cure.
pmc-13194710:
Tamara Büttner and co-authors published this study in 2026. It shows how low oxygen limits virus therapy inside tumors. Adenoviruses are being honed as cancer killers, but solid tumors are starved of oxygen inside. In flat cell cultures, low oxygen cut the virus's protein output in pancreatic cancer cells. The team then grew the cells as 3D balls, which form natural oxygen slopes like real tumors.

When virus was added as the balls formed, infection stayed trapped in the well-fed outer rim. When cells were infected first in normal air, the virus spread evenly through the ball. The pattern shows timing and oxygen together shape the attack. The authors urge that virus therapies be tested in such 3D, low-oxygen models. Flat dishes, they warn, flatter the virus.
pmc-13194910:
Bijaya Kumar Muni leads a 2026 signal processing paper on estimating the direction of arriving signals, a task used in radar, sonar, and wireless networks. The classic MUSIC algorithm locates signal sources precisely but falters in chaotic, noisy, or highly correlated conditions. The authors set out to harden it.

Their method adds a robust cost function, Tukey Biweight, which down-weights wild data points, and models chaotic signal behavior with a Chebyshev-based generator. Monte Carlo simulations, repeated random trials, compared four variants. The combined chaotic and robust version consistently gave the best accuracy and resolution, especially at low signal-to-noise ratios and high signal correlation. The authors propose it for practical wireless and radar systems.
pmc-13197110:
Hiwot Abebe Haileslassie and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study of a pulse food toolkit for preschool children. Pulses are dry beans, peas, and lentils. Early tastes shape later eating, so the toolkit aimed to make pulses familiar in childcare centers.

The program ran three months in two centers in Saskatoon, with fifty children and eight staff. It mixed weekly lessons, new recipes, a food guide for cooks, and parent newsletters. Children got slightly better at naming chickpeas, beans, and peas, though gains were not firm proof. Children still ate more of the usual dishes than the pulse dishes. Staff views and food content checks round out the pilot's lessons.
pmc-13197710:
Estela Emiliano and co-authors test what a rule change does to leukemia care in a 2026 Brazilian study. In 2022 the World Health Organization redrew the map of chronic myeloid leukemia, dropping the accelerated phase that once sat between chronic phase and blast crisis.

The team re-scored 139 newly diagnosed patients, all started on imatinib, under both the old and new rules. Eight patients once called accelerated phase became chronic phase under the new scheme. Survival came out much the same either way, while blast crisis patients still fared far worse. The study reassures clinics that dropping the middle stage does not hide risk or change who needs urgent care.
pmc-13198510:
Jefté Peper-Nascimento and colleagues studied stress and sepsis effects on rat brain growth factors in a 2026 paper. Sepsis is a life-threatening body-wide response to infection. Long mild stress can reshape brain chemistry, so the team asked whether the two combine to lower nerve support proteins.

Rats went through a sepsis procedure, then thirty days of mild stress drills. Blood and two brain areas were tested for five support proteins and two stress hormones. Stress raised both hormones, while sepsis alone did not. Stress lowered four support proteins in both brain areas, with or without sepsis. Sepsis alone also lowered several, with strength by protein and region. No combined boost appeared.
pmc-13198610:
Xinpeng Zuo and six co-authors study gene control in a single-celled organism in this two thousand twenty-six paper. The organism, Paramecium tetraurelia, carries two kinds of nuclei in one cell. Small germline nuclei pass genes to offspring, while one big somatic nucleus runs daily life. During sex, the germline nuclei divide by meiosis and the big nucleus breaks apart. The team focused on a family of transcription factors called TFDP.

They found sixteen members of the family, a striking expansion. Two of them play double roles in the process. They guide meiosis in the germline nuclei and also steer the fragmentation of the somatic one. The work shows how one cell juggles two nuclear fates. Cell biologists who study reproduction are the readers.
pmc-13199410:
Christina Sauter and colleagues studied hidden neck spread in nose and sinus cancers across centers in a 2026 review. These cancers are rare, and no standard rule guides neck surgery when scans look clear. Doctors must choose between preventive neck dissection, removing neck nodes, and watchful scanning.

The study pooled 438 patients treated from 2012 to 2022. Hidden spread appeared in eight percent of patients whose necks looked clear on scans. One fourth got preventive neck surgery. Squamous cell type was the sole early risk flag for hidden spread. Patients with hidden spread had far worse five-year disease-free survival. Given the low spread rate, the authors question routine preventive surgery and urge case-by-case calls.
pmc-13199710:
Shujuan Chen and Qing-Wei Chen wrote a 2026 letter on parent roles in autism therapy for children. A study in Jordan, by Al-Dwaikat and co-authors, was the first of its kind there. It found parents accepted applied behavior analysis well but knew little about it, and knowledge linked to greater involvement in therapy.

The letter praises the work but lists gaps to fix. A figure box names acceptance where it should name involvement. The Arabic versions of the two surveys lack full reports of their accuracy checks, and sharing them would aid repeat studies. The model could also rest on known behavior theories, which the writers suggest testing with the same data. They urge openness and firmer theory.
pmc-13199810:
Eline van de Kamp, Francine Schneider, Hein Daanen, and Maud Huynen compare how high-risk Dutch groups lived through a heatwave, in a 2026 survey study. Five hundred fourteen adults over fifty in Limburg answered right after a July 2023 heatwave, and risk groups were carved out by age, sex, health, income, and social contact. The team linked those traits to discomfort, protective habits, and how dangerous people judged the heat.

Poor health and low income, more than age alone, tracked with discomfort and strain. Lower-income respondents protected themselves more but with cheap measures, while the least healthy did not step up protection, perhaps for physical reasons. Risk piled up as disadvantages stacked.
pmc-13200610: Yefei Zhang and colleagues are authors of a 2013 article retracted by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, as recorded in a 2026 notice. The article claimed a small RNA molecule blocked cell death in vessel lining cells exposed to oxidized cholesterol. An inquiry found image editing and duplication shared with another paper submitted at the same time by a different group. The board lost trust in the findings and retracted the work. The authors were informed and gave no comment.
pmc-13200810:
Jarbas da Silva Ziani and co-authors studied why HIV treatment gets interrupted during hospital stays in a 2026 paper from Brazil. Steady antiretroviral therapy keeps the virus suppressed, and gaps can let it rebound. Hospital admission is a risky moment, when routines break and records scatter.

The team reviewed records of just over two hundred patients hospitalized at a mid-sized hospital in Rio Grande do Sul from 2022 to 2024. They tested which patient and care factors tracked with therapy interruption. Findings point to fixable causes, such as missing medication lists or slow restarts. Hospitals get evidence for checklists that keep HIV therapy running through an admission, protecting both the patient and long-term treatment options.
pmc-13201610:
Worries about fertility after cancer can weigh heavily on survivors, and a 2026 study headed by Shaimaa Mohamed Amin examines how a partner's support fits into that burden. The research article tests whether partner support carries part of the link between reproductive health concerns and psychological distress.

The cross-sectional study surveyed 202 married female cancer survivors, aged twenty to forty-nine, attending oncology departments at Tanta University Hospital in Egypt. Greater reproductive concerns came with greater distress, while stronger partner support came with less of both. Statistical mediation analysis supported a partial indirect effect through partner support, leading the authors to recommend couple-focused counselling in survivorship care.
pmc-13202010:
Removing excess fluid is delicate when septic shock has weakened the heart, and a 2026 study protocol by Jing-Chao Luo sets out to test a hormone treatment for that phase. The protocol describes a single-center trial of recombinant human brain natriuretic peptide in adults recovering from septic shock with cardiac dysfunction and volume overload.

Thirty patients will receive a bolus followed by an infusion lasting up to seventy-two hours, with monitoring already in place. The main measure is the within-patient change in a venous return pressure gradient shortly after treatment begins. Secondary measures cover heart function, tissue perfusion, and congestion, with blood pressure instability as the key safety endpoint.
pmc-13202210:
Ewnetu and co-authors survey hidden malaria infections in Ethiopia's highlands, where transmission was long thought minimal, in a 2026 study. They tested more than twelve hundred people without symptoms at eight sites between about 1,900 and 2,900 meters of altitude, using sensitive lab tests, and collected travel histories.

One parasite species faded with altitude, from sixty-seven percent infected at the lowest site to sixteen percent at the highest. The other ranged from ten to thirty-four percent with no altitude pattern. Recent travel explained few infections, suggesting the parasites now circulate locally. The authors argue sites up to 2,500 meters should be treated as endemic, with stronger control efforts.
pmc-13202410:
Melanie Ambler, Mukta Awasthi, Lynn Gerber, Bryant Lin, and Claire Wakefield pilot in a 2026 study a bedside music legacy program in palliative care. Patients near life's end, and their loved ones, often face pain, stress, and fear. Sharing life stories set to music may ease that strain and leave a keepsake.

The program ran at three California hospitals with live bedside recording sessions. A clinician musician improvised as patients told stories, then families got an edited recording. One hundred patients and loved ones were invited into the mixed methods pilot. Among 79 patients assessed, pain fell 1.58 points on a ten point scale after sessions. Stress also dropped sharply, and mood gains showed in the interview material.
pmc-13202510:
Samantha Murray and co-authors present a 2026 study of virtual reality therapy for people with mild intellectual disability and substance use problems. This group faces higher addiction risk and finds talk therapy hard, since it leans on abstract words and memory. Virtual reality offers safe, real-feeling scenes to practice skills in context.

Two small studies ran at a Dutch inpatient clinic, each with ten adults. The first mapped alcohol triggers through interviews: home routines, supermarkets, social pressure, and travel all ranked high. Patients wanted to use the scenes to spot triggers and practice refusal. The second study had nicotine users practice coping in craving scenes. The work feeds design of a full therapy program.
pmc-13202710:
Negative skin tests do not always rule out drug allergy, and a 2026 case report by Nur Betül Baştuğ İnan shows that gap for the antibiotic teicoplanin. The article presents a patient whose skin prick and intradermal tests for teicoplanin were negative, yet who reacted during a supervised drug challenge.

The 66-year-old woman had been referred with suspected drug allergy after treatment that included teicoplanin a week earlier. During provocation testing she developed an immediate skin reaction despite the reassuring earlier test results. The authors note that reports of IgE-mediated teicoplanin allergy are rising, and they argue this case tempers claims that skin testing reliably predicts such reactions.
pmc-13202810:
Phuong Thao Nguyen and Sahara review how single-cell methods expose the wiring faults behind congenital heart disease. The condition strikes about one percent of newborns. It remains the top birth-defect killer of infants. Gene causes alone have not explained it. Reading cells one by one shows which cells talk and which fall silent.

The authors reanalyze a dataset of 157,273 heart cell nuclei from children with five diagnoses. Each disease rewired cell chatter in its own way. Some overfired growth and metabolism signals. One major type showed broad signal shutdown and broken links. Endothelial and muscle cells sit at the network hubs. The maps point to fresh drug targets per subtype.
pmc-13204310:
Anna Makowska and Udo Kontny review natural killer cells as a cancer treatment platform in this 2026 paper. These immune cells kill without needing a prior lesson about their target, and they carry a gentler side-effect profile than engineered T cells. The review gives special weight to nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a virus-driven throat cancer.
