One kidney came from a cat with early chronic kidney disease, the other from a matched healthy cat. Such ultra-strong scans have barely been tried in cat medicine.

The sick kidney lost the clear border between its outer and inner zones on scans. Water-motion measures ran lower in its outer zone, matching heavier scarring seen under the microscope. Values in the deepest zone ran higher instead. The authors say these scan signs track tissue scarring well, a step toward gentler checks for kidney disease in cats.
pmc-13314110:
Akeem Moradehun Bamiro and co-authors run a 2026 pilot study on whether a routine blood ratio can predict survival in rats with chemically induced tongue cancer. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio forecasts outcomes in human cancers, but its value inside preclinical models was undefined. Female rats drank water laced with a carcinogen for twenty weeks, then had blood counts taken. Eighteen animals entered a 42-day survival watch. The team tested three inflammatory ratios for their power to separate survivors from non-survivors.

Only the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio worked. Its discrimination score reached 0.901 on the analysis curve, while the platelet and monocyte ratios performed poorly. Rats above a ratio of roughly 0.55 died at a starkly different rate, eight of nine against one of nine below the line. The authors suggest this cheap count could help researchers in resource-limited settings stratify animals and design larger confirmatory studies.
pmc-13314210:
Tri Widyawati and co-authors feed soybean and cabbage extracts to malnourished rats in a 2025 study. Protein-energy malnutrition still burdens many regions, and local crops might supply affordable recovery foods. Rats were starved of protein for two weeks, then dosed with the extracts alone or combined for four weeks.

All treated groups gained weight, most strongly at high combined doses, while blood measures stayed stable and iron rose. A gut transporter that absorbs protein pieces switched on more strongly, especially with the cabbage extract. That extract also carried more plant chemicals and stronger antioxidant punch. The authors see the pair as promising functional foods for recovery diets.
pmc-13315110:
Ming-Ray Liao and six co-authors test number sense in peafowl in a 2026 study. Many animals can tell larger groups from smaller ones. Peacocks grow trains with many eyespots, which females inspect. That display raises the question of whether the birds count well.

Captive peafowl faced a touchscreen with two squares of circles. Pecking the square with more circles earned a reward. Circle size, density, and total area were varied to fool shortcuts. The birds still tracked the number itself in most trials. Their accuracy followed the ratio between the two counts, as classic law predicts. Performance stayed above chance across the quantity changes. The authors say peafowl may use number in mate choice.
pmc-13315510:
Shao-Chun Li and co-authors train an explainable imaging model to spot bone marrow involvement in follicular lymphoma, in a 2026 paper. Knowing whether lymphoma has reached the marrow shapes treatment, but the proof usually needs a biopsy. Baseline PET/CT scans might carry the answer noninvasively.

The study gathered 187 newly diagnosed patients, ninety-three with proven marrow involvement. From their scans the team drew clinical details, standard imaging measures, radiomic textures, and deep learning features, within two region frameworks: pelvis alone, or spine plus pelvis. Screening funnels cut the feature flood, and six model designs competed. The best performer is judged on independent validation data. The comparison also shows how much the wider spine window adds.
pmc-13316210:
Alberto De Lorenzo and a very large team studied in 2026 how treatment choices for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy vary across Italian centers over time. The nerve disease is treatable and immune driven, yet real-world evidence on strategies and their change over the years was limited.

The multicentre study mixed prospective and retrospective observation to chart prescription patterns, check alignment with international guidelines, and find clinical, structural, and time factors tied to decisions and outcomes. Wide center-to-center variation in such a treatable disease flags room to standardize care and share best practice.
pmc-13316410:
A rare disease called pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 7 stunts brain growth and kills in early childhood. Lizette Zavala, Magdalena Sobien, and Cassandra Hayne studied the gene behind it in 2026, called TOE1, which makes an enzyme that trims small RNA molecules as they mature. Over a dozen gene changes in TOE1 have been linked to the disease, but how they harm the enzyme was unclear.

The team tested eleven disease-linked variants of the enzyme in the lab. Eight variants made the protein less stable under heat, and nearly all cut its trimming activity. One variant also changed how the enzyme groups together. The catalog of damaged variants may guide future treatment ideas and basic studies.
pmc-13316610:
Donnie Mategula heads a very large team behind a 2026 multi-country cohort study of diarrhoea outcomes in young children, centered on Shigella, a leading cause in poorer settings. The study asks what follows a clinic visit for Shigella diarrhoea: lingering illness, hospital care, or slowed growth.

Between June 2022 and August 2024, clinics in seven countries enrolled 8,756 children aged 6 to 35 months with fresh diarrhoea episodes. Stool testing by culture and gene methods sorted Shigella cases from children with no germ found. Follow-up visits at four weeks and three months track long diarrhoea, admissions, and height growth. The design gives health planners firm ground on the hidden costs of this infection.
pmc-13317410:
Monica Sciacco and a large team test a high-plex imaging tool on muscle samples in inflammatory muscle disease. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. These diseases are a mixed group of immune ills of muscle, each with its own marks. A biopsy is a key test, but old stain methods can show only a few markers at once, with low detail.

Their tool runs many rounds of stain and scan on one slice, to map many proteins in place. Signal stays strong and tissue shape holds through all rounds. Early maps show distinct patterns of immune cells, matrix change, and vessel change by disease kind. The pilot shows the route works for muscle.
pmc-13317510:
Nicolas Colmano and colleagues explain, in a 2026 study, how faults in the sodium-potassium pump's alpha1 subunit cause low magnesium with seizures that resist treatment. The pump sits in every cell membrane, and its many variants cause a family of diseases.

Every variant tied to the low-magnesium seizure picture carried a stray leak current, worked weakly, and reached the cell surface in smaller numbers. A frozen-structure image of one variant, W931R, suggests the leaks slip through the seam where protein meets membrane fat. The shared leak gives doctors a unifying mechanism and a target: plug the seam or boost surface delivery, and several pump diseases might ease at once.
pmc-13318210:
Megan Hare and Kathryn Humphreys track, in a 2026 study, how new mothers' and fathers' depressive symptoms feed each other across the first eighteen months after birth. Postpartum depression in fathers is understudied, and couples may pass low mood back and forth.

The study followed 119 couples with advanced panel modeling. Mothers' symptoms held steady across every check, while fathers' steadied only later. A relay emerged: mothers' one-month symptoms predicted fathers' at six months, which in turn predicted mothers' at twelve months. Mothers who recalled emotional or physical neglect in childhood entered pregnancy with heavier symptoms, and emotional neglect echoed again at one month. Screening, the authors argue, should treat the couple as one system.
pmc-13318610:
Lukas Retzer and Cornelia Niessen offer a 2026 qualitative interview study. They ask what workers expect from future workplace robots. The focus is social skills and independence. Twenty workers from hospitality, manufacturing, and care jobs were interviewed. The authors also built a taxonomy of robot social skills.

Workers could state clear preferences about future robot use. Basic social skills were widely wanted. Polite, readable behaviour could be built in broadly. Freedom to act alone needed careful tuning to task and setting. Too little social skill risks negative reactions. Too much independence carries the same risk. The authors turn these views into provisional design requirements. They aim them at developers of workplace robots.
pmc-13319110:
Xi Li leads a large team presenting, in 2026, an end-to-end AI system that reads surgical video and links movement patterns to patient outcomes. The system, called Frame-to-Outcome, turns dissection footage into gesture sequences. Testing used the nerve-sparing step of robot prostate surgery. Transformer models classified actions frame by frame.

The system detected short gestures of about two seconds reliably. Accuracy reached an AUC of 0.80 at frame level and 0.81 at video level in their tests. Features like gesture frequency, duration, and transitions predicted outcomes about as well as human labels. Effect directions matched across 25 shared features, with a strong correlation of 0.96 between the two. Longer tissue peeling and lower energy use tied to better erectile recovery. The authors see a base for data-driven surgical feedback.
pmc-13320110:
Juan Antonio Valera-Calero and colleagues set out, in 2026, to analyse where ChatGPT disagrees with human researchers when scoring trial quality in physiotherapy. The PEDro scale rates experimental studies on items such as randomisation, blinding and follow-up, and systematic reviews depend on those scores. Whether an artificial intelligence system can reproduce them reliably was unclear.

Rather than scoring trials fresh, the team used item-level scores already published inside systematic reviews, where dual independent appraisal and consensus had strengthened the reference standard. Eligible reviews came from indexed journals over a recent ten-year window. Blinded assessors prompted the model once per article with standard instructions and asked for brief justifications. A statistician blinded to score sources then compared item by item, so disagreement patterns could be traced to specific scale items.
pmc-13320410:
Fang-Chin Hsu and co-authors test mucus swabbed from the scope as a source for bowel growth checks in a 2026 pilot study. Bowel cancer ranks high in both new cases and deaths in the world, and early growths that may turn bad need sharp, low burden checks. Mucus that coats the bowel wall may trap loose DNA shed right at the growth site, richer than blood or stool.

A gene change tied to bowel growths was hunted in that mucus DNA in a first small group. The test caught cancer and advanced early growths with high catch rates at a low signal floor in the pilot counts, though false alarms rose as well. It beat a stool blood test and a blood marker on catch rate in this early contrast. Wider trials must set its true place.
pmc-13320510:
Rick R.A. Hendriks and colleagues adapt a climate and health survey for Dutch nurses in a 2026 study. Nurses link the public with health care and will face more heat, storm, and infection risks tied to a changing climate. No checked Dutch tool existed to gauge nurses' awareness, concern, drive, and habits on climate and health.

The team followed six stages, with forward and back translation, expert review, and field pre-testing, then checks of how well the survey held together. Nurses across the Netherlands were reached through the national nurses group and other networks from June 2025. A sound Dutch version gives leaders a baseline for training and for planning climate ready care.
pmc-13320710:
Carley Dearing and co-authors report a rat study, published in 2026, on brain circuits that guard blood sugar under stress. Long term stress raises the risk of diabetes, and a path from the front of the brain to the brainstem helps control stress hormones. The team blocked signals along that path in male and female rats, then put the animals through repeated varied stress.

After the circuit was blocked, unstressed females handled a glucose load poorly, with higher blood sugar and weaker insulin response. Stressed females also cleared glucose more slowly and showed higher stress hormone levels. The results suggest the circuit is needed for healthy glucose control, with effects that differ by sex and by stress history.
pmc-13320810:
Ting Li and colleagues present, in 2026, a case where a three-dimensional printed model guided hip surgery for a nine-year-old girl. Developmental dysplasia means the hip socket forms too shallow for the ball of the thigh bone, causing subluxation and early joint damage. Her case was complicated by a cystic lesion inside the socket bone.

The girl had an abnormal gait for a year, hip pain and a shorter left leg. Imaging showed a shallow socket, a partly deformed femoral head and a cyst roughly two centimetres across. Surgeons printed a life-size model of her pelvis and rehearsed a Pemberton osteotomy, a reshaping cut, on it before operating. The authors review why printed models can shorten operating time, improve visualisation and reduce radiation in such tailored paediatric surgery.
pmc-13321010:
Suhaib Muflih and colleagues review antibiotic use before caesarean birth across Jordan in a 2026 national records study. Antibiotics given before surgery help prevent wound infection, yet compliance data from lower income settings are scarce. Records covered 60,212 women who had caesarean births from 2015 to 2022 in 20 health ministry hospitals.

Only 19.4 percent received preventive antibiotics as guidelines advise, though the monthly rate crept up over time. Planned surgery and a longer wait after admission raised the chance of proper cover. Women who got proper cover had 41 percent lower odds of returning to hospital with a wound infection. The gap points to clear room for routine improvement.
pmc-13321810:
Jun-Jie Chen and co-authors report a light driven route to fluorinated ring systems for drug design in a 2026 chemistry study. Small bicyclic scaffolds can stand in for benzene rings in medicines, but fluorinated versions are hard to build by standard methods. The team used visible light and energy transfer catalysis to fold flat ring starting materials into three dimensional shapes.

The dearomative cycloaddition joins gem-difluoro alkenes carrying varied heteroaromatic rings into bicyclo[2.1.1]hexane products. Conditions were mild, yields were good, and shape selectivity was excellent across many ring types. Mechanism checks pointed to triplet diradical steps. The route opens fluorinated stand-ins that older carbene or cycloaddition methods reach poorly.
pmc-13322910:
Zihan Zhang and colleagues describe a vasculitis case that first looked like a middle ear problem, in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a 50-year-old woman, had severe secretory otitis media with hearing loss, facial nerve palsy, ear pain and high fever, and was treated for infection for a long period.

Testing later showed granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a rare disease where inflamed small vessels and granulomas harm the airways, kidneys and other tissue. No other typical signs were present at first, which explains the delay. The authors urge ear specialists to consider body-wide disease behind stubborn ear cases, since early treatment and team care can prevent lasting damage.
pmc-13323110:
Justin C Deme and co-authors picture the bacterial Tat transport core in action, in a 2026 structural study. The twin-arginine system moves folded proteins across membranes and matters for bacterial virulence and for plant photosynthesis.

Cryo-electron microscopy gave resting structures of TatBC complexes from Escherichia coli and two other bacteria, plus substrate-bound forms at early transport stages. Cargo proteins touch the core only through their N-terminal signal peptides, whose targeting parts contact TatC while TatB clamps the peptide body. Strongly tilted helices thin the membrane sharply at the site. With lab tests alongside, the authors propose a step-by-step model for how transport begins.
pmc-13323310:
Simone Sarti and co-authors review whole network analysis of health behaviour, in a 2026 systematic review covering smoking, alcohol use, physical activity and diet. Unlike personal network studies, this method maps every tie inside a defined group, showing how habits spread and settle.

Searching six databases under PRISMA guidance, they kept 27 empirical studies with full network data. Peer influence, similarity-based bonding, cohesion and central positions recurred as structural drivers across all four behaviours. Behaviour clusters and joint change in ties and habits stood out, and long-term actor-based models best separated choosing similar friends from copying them. The authors commend the method for designing group-level health interventions.
pmc-13323810:
Mohamed Wishahi and Mohamed Badawy write a 2026 letter to the editor on the 2025 European guidelines for urinary infections. They respond to a study by Yadav and others that built a prediction nomogram from patient factors beyond the urine sample itself.

The new European Association of Urology scheme sorts infections as localised or systemic by symptoms and signs, replacing the older split between uncomplicated and complicated infection. Care follows that clinical setup rather than culture results alone, with localised cases managed as outpatients. The writers stress that symptoms, examination, labs and imaging all feed diagnosis, and that antibiotic effects on gut and urinary microbes deserve weight in treatment choice.
pmc-13324310:
Hongyue Lin and Ying Huang identify the enzyme USP48 as a brake on colorectal cancer, in a 2026 study built around its partner protein SELENBP1. Both proteins track with better clinical outcomes in this common and deadly cancer, whose aggressive behaviour resists standard care.

Raising USP48 levels suppressed malignant behaviour in colorectal cancer cells in their experiments, covering growth and stem-like traits. The enzyme works by stabilising SELENBP1, removing the ubiquitin tags that would send it for disposal. That places USP48 on the opposite side from several related enzymes that drive this cancer. The authors propose USP48 as a marker of how malignant a tumour is and as a lead for new treatment design.
pmc-13324410:
Sergey A Belokobylskij, Deokseo Ku and Hye-Rin Lee describe six new parasitoid wasp species from the Korean Peninsula, in a 2026 taxonomic paper on the braconid genus Aleiodes. These rogadine wasps parasitise caterpillars and mummify their hosts, a striking life cycle within a huge and varied genus.

The six newcomers span three subgenera and are each named, described and illustrated in full, with the authors credited inside the species names. Material came from the Korean fauna, long less documented than tropical Asian and American faunas for this group. A key to the Palaearctic subgenera of Aleiodes rounds out the paper, giving identifiers a route into a genus holding over six hundred described species.
pmc-13324510:
Åsa Carlsund and colleagues explore how specialist nurses counsel patients at risk of type 2 diabetes in a 2026 interview study from Swedish primary care. Food advice sits at the heart of prevention, but little was known about how nurses tailor it.

Semi-structured interviews ran from August to November 2025, and content analysis yielded four themes with 12 subthemes. Nurses stressed empathy, person-centered talk, and small-step goals shaped by gender, culture, and daily life. Short visits, low drive, money limits, and cultural gaps still blocked good advice. The nurses asked for training in cultural competence, fresh tools, and stronger backing from their organizations. Better support could make prevention advice fit real lives.
pmc-13325910:
Juan Aguilar-Gonzalez and team systematically tested pyrocarbon implants in shoulder arthroplasty. Their 2026 review and meta-analysis searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane, Scopus, and Web of Science in April 2025, comparing chrome-cobalt, pyrocarbon, and ceramic options for humeral head replacement. Pyrocarbon use is growing, including interposition arthroplasty and hemiarthroplasty, yet whether results differ by material had stayed unclear.

The review assessed implant survival, functional scores including the Constant score and Subjective Shoulder Value, pain scores, revision rates defined as reoperation involving implant removal, replacement, or conversion, complications, and radiological change. Prior reports suggested strong short-to-mid-term results, such as 93% survival at two years in one study and single-digit complication and revision rates in another, but long-term data remain limited. The authors aim to give surgeons a fuller picture of cumulative revision and complication rates across implant types.
pmc-13326310:
Parisa Kohnepoushi and co-authors pool in a 2026 analysis how well machine learning flags suicide related outcomes. Clinicians need plain numbers on hits, misses, and false alarms before such tools can aid care. Single studies give scattered answers, so a pooled read helps.

Four data banks were searched for work from January 2010 to December 2024 with at least 100 people per study. Of 500 records screened, 22 studies met the rules for pooling. Blend models scored best on the standard curve scale, at 0.95 overall. Their pooled specificity hit 0.97, but sensitivity sat at just 0.50, a wide and weak band. Bias checks used a standard quality tool for test studies throughout.
pmc-13326810:
Clare L. Tolley and colleagues ask how best to warn vulnerable people about dirty air in a 2026 qualitative study. Those with prior illness, city poverty, or minority backgrounds carry the highest exposure risk.

Interviews and focus groups gathered 50 participants from varied at-risk groups in North East England. From their views the team built a theory-based communication framework. Messages must tailor risk facts to each group and pair them with doable protective steps. Trusted voices matter: health workers and community peers outrank distant agencies. Channels such as text messages and local networks widen reach. Behavior change trials are the next test.
pmc-13327610:
Phage therapy needs a fast test for whether a virus can infect a patient's bacteria. Xiao Han and co-authors built one on Raman light fingerprints of bacterial chemistry. Their test reads how infection reshapes the cell's molecules, without waiting for visible lysis. Four Raman markers merge into one infection index. The test told susceptible from resistant bacteria within about an hour. It matched plaque assays in twenty-four of twenty-five checks.

The index also ranks how strongly a phage attacks a shared host. Tracking it over dose and time finds the lowest dose that keeps infection self-spreading. That floor defines a sane starting dose for therapy. The platform turns a yes-no test into a dosing tool.
pmc-13328010:
Carla Estrada-Muñoz and co-authors validate the Internet Addiction Test for wildland firefighters in a 2026 study. Digital tools now saturate emergency work, blurring needed use and harmful overuse that can erode attention and sleep. They gave the test to 205 firefighters and checked its structure and reliability.

Two factors emerged, one for broad problematic engagement and one for loss of control, and the confirmatory model fit very well, with CFI and TLI both at 0.997 on their report. The two factors overlapped heavily, limiting how cleanly they separate, yet the scale held up as a screening tool. The authors advise pairing scores with device logs and fatigue measures before judging any firefighter's use.
pmc-13330110:
Xiaoling Lin and colleagues describe building a phone-based self-care tool for bipolar disorder in a 2026 study. Bipolar illness often returns despite drug care, so support between visits matters. The tool, Mood Calm, runs as a WeChat mini program with six modules, from symptom and drug tracking to crisis spotting and thinking training.

Design drew on cognitive behaviour theory, prior literature, and an expert panel, with wearable links planned for sleep and activity. A four-week early trial then ran with five patients in remission, testing core modules only. All five finished and praised ease of use in the report. System data hinted at weaker drug routine logging. A larger randomised trial is planned next.
pmc-13330310:
Soichiro Kano and co-authors report the case of a 19-year-old man whose heart stopped after drowning in a river. A friend pulled him out, called for help, and started chest compressions at once. By the time crews arrived, his heart had restarted, and he flew to hospital care.

His blood oxygen kept falling despite standard care. The team placed him early on a lung support machine that adds oxygen to blood outside the body. With that support plus full intensive care, he left the hospital with no brain harm. The authors suggest early use of the machine may help in like cases.
pmc-13330510:
Sandeep R. Reddy, Manjunatha Bangeppagari, and Prabhakar Kamarthy test potassium bromate harm in zebrafish in a 2026 study. The chemical is a food additive and pollutant known to damage genes and drive oxidation in mammals, but fish data were thin. Short tests ran for 96 hours and longer tests for 21 days.

The median lethal level at 96 hours came to 1052.6 mg per litre in the reported estimate. Short exposure slowed swimming and exploration and pushed fish toward the tank bottom. Longer exposure raised blood sugar and damaged liver tissue, with cell swelling, widened spaces, decay, and dead areas. Harm arose below lethal levels, giving baseline data for water risk work.
pmc-13330610:
Mohamed Omar Osman and colleagues pool evidence on dengue fever in Ethiopia in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Dengue reports have risen in parts of the country, yet national pooled figures were missing. Searches followed standard review rules, and the protocol was registered in advance. Thirteen studies met the entry rules.

Eight cross-sectional studies fed the prevalence pool, which came to 25 percent in the reported estimate. Rates looked higher before 2020 than after in subgroup checks. Risk links included not wearing long sleeves, not using nets, open water storage, and no recent insecticide spraying. Spread between studies was high for risk links. Targeted community teaching and mosquito control are urged.
pmc-13330810:
Khaleel Ahmed and colleagues report the crystal structure of a long-chain aromatic ester in a 2026 article. Such phenyl benzoate systems matter for liquid crystals and drug research, where rigid cores plus flexible chains govern packing and phase shifts. Fluorine atoms in the mix can tune polarity and stability.

The central ring tilts against its two neighbours, with the first tilt measured at 74.19 degrees in the reported structure and the second at 67.86 degrees in the same analysis. The fourteen-carbon chain stretches out straight. In the crystal, weak hydrogen bonds to oxygen and fluorine link molecules into endless chains along one axis. Two chain patterns repeat through the solid.
pmc-13330910:
Dustin C. Brown and colleagues synthesise and study paired ruthenium carbonyl complexes in a 2026 article. Such phosphine-supported pairs can catalyse small-molecule changes, from alkene shifts to hydrogenation. Fluorinated acetate bridges give the metal centres a fresh electronic setting that may tune that activity.

One trifluoroacetate-bridged compound was made by two routes and its structure was solved. Measured and computed traits are set beside three kin compounds that vary the bridge and phosphine parts. Past work links the twist angle between phosphines to alkene shift activity, though one study found no such link and pointed to electron donation instead. The new data add a fluorinated case to that debate.
pmc-13331710:
Georgios Mavrogenis and colleagues present a 2026 technique report on removing a stubborn recurrent growth from the duodenum of a 70-year-old woman. The 1.5 cm adenoma had regrown after several earlier removal attempts and sat in heavy scar tissue, which makes cutting in the thin duodenal wall risky.

Their combined method filled the bowel with salt water, used clip-and-band traction to hold the tissue taut, and applied a hook-and-drag cutting motion in the scarred areas. Working under general anesthesia with surgical backup, they removed the growth in one piece, closed the site with clips, and the patient recovered without problems. The authors suggest the mix of methods can make such fibrotic duodenal cases safer to treat.
pmc-13332010:
Dandan Li and colleagues synthesize 2026 evidence on sex differences in omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid levels. Sex hormones may shape how the body makes these fats, but it has stayed unclear how steady any male-female gaps are across blood and tissue pools. The team searched Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register through late February 2026 for cross-sectional reports giving both sexes' levels in healthy adults with mean age up to fifty. They pooled unadjusted male-female gaps with random-effects models.

Sixty-seven publications qualified, yielding 85 comparisons and 71 fatty acid markers across plasma, red cell, and adipose tissue pools. The review matters for nutrition research, since a marker read one way in men may not read the same way in women. Clearer sex-specific norms should sharpen risk estimates and keep diet studies from mixing unlike measures.
pmc-13332710:
Yu Kuei Lin and co-authors surveyed United States adults with type 1 diabetes in 2026 on how low blood sugar still affects daily life despite modern monitoring and pump technology. Nearly everyone using continuous glucose monitors or hybrid closed-loop pumps still feels the drag of hypoglycaemia.

The analysis covered 796 adults recruited through the T1D Exchange, 23 percent using monitors alone and 77 percent using closed-loop systems, who completed a 12-domain impact questionnaire. Overall, 96 percent reported at least one life domain harmed, and 31 percent reported harm in 10 or more domains, led by sleep, leisure, emotional well-being, spontaneity, and exercise. Closed-loop users surprisingly reported worse impacts than monitor-only users in leisure, fitness, spontaneity, sex life, and work. The authors urge routine clinical attention to low-sugar burden and more work on why technology alone does not lift it.
pmc-13333110:
Bader Jad Allah and colleagues report a 2026 case in which pulmonary embolism opened the door to a paradoxical thalamic stroke through a patent foramen ovale. Paradoxical clots through that heart opening are an uncommon but important cause of acute ischemic stroke, notably when lung clots are present. The patient was a 46-year-old man with bilateral grade C3-R pulmonary embolism who then developed focal nerve deficits, including word-finding difficulty.

CT lung scans confirmed the clot, and heart ultrasound with a bubble study found a patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunting. Contrast brain MRI then showed an acute left thalamic infarct consistent with paradoxical embolic stroke, after other causes were excluded. Blood-thinner and closure decisions were made through a mixed-field process with the patient. The case urges suspicion for paradoxical embolism when clot, heart opening, and new nerve symptoms coincide.
pmc-13333410:
Elena Uyy and a team profiled the blood of diabetic foot patients in a 2026 study, looking for a pattern of damage signals rather than stray markers. Diabetic foot syndrome mixes poor circulation, chronic inflammation, and wounds that will not heal, yet its molecular footprint was ill defined.

The team used high-resolution protein measurement on plasma from diabetic patients with and without the foot syndrome, including degrees of limb ischemia. They found a set of acute-phase and stress proteins shifted together. The set includes serum amyloid A1 and A2, amyloid P component, and S100A8. It also includes defensin alpha 1B, fibrinogen chains, a heat shock protein, thymosin beta 4, fibronectin, and tenascins. In diabetic mice with ischemic wounds, blocking the danger sensor TLR4 changed several of the proteins, lowering some amyloid-linked ones. The authors frame the signature as evidence that damage-associated signals drive inflammation in this complication.
pmc-13333510:
Guangbi Fu and colleagues report a counterintuitive link in a 2026 cross-sectional study: among type 2 diabetes patients, higher vitamin B12 levels went with more diabetic retinopathy, not less. B12 shortfalls are common in diabetes and earlier work tied deficiency to eye damage, so the direction of the finding cuts against habit.

The analysis reused data on 413 adults with type 2 diabetes seen in Guangdong between December 2017 and November 2018, with eye disease graded by ophthalmologists. After adjustment for confounders, each 100-unit rise in B12 carried 49 percent higher odds of retinopathy. Patients in the top third of B12 levels, at or above 398, showed higher odds than the bottom third, at an odds ratio of 11.83. Curve modelling confirmed a straight-line relationship, and no subgroup, by sex, age, or kidney function, changed the pattern. The authors stress a snapshot cannot prove B12 causes eye disease, only that the association runs the unexpected way.
pmc-13333710:
ShangJun Li, Avijit Deb Nath, and Md. Hadi Al-amin authored a 2026 computational study of how cooperation evolves in repeated games between self-interested agents. They focus on memory-two strategies, which respond to the last two rounds of play between both sides.

Their framework joins a Q-learning multi-agent engine with Moran, Wright-Fisher, and replicator selection rules, tested across eight simulation experiments. Under standard Prisoner's Dilemma payoffs, play settled at a high cooperation rate near 0.814 on average. Memory-two strategies made up 61.0 percent of the settled population and always took over when invading a fully defecting population. Cooperation survived moderate noise but collapsed past a clear threshold. The results map where long-memory reciprocity can hold in artificial and human systems.
pmc-13333810:
Jing Luo and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol testing Tiao Shen Li Yan acupuncture for swallowing problems after stroke. Acupuncture often improves swallowing in this group, yet nobody has mapped how it reorganizes brain networks.

The randomized, single-blind, sham-controlled trial will enroll 46 patients with post-stroke dysphagia, split evenly between real and sham acupuncture given 30 minutes a day, five days a week, for six weeks. Resting-state functional MRI and diffusion imaging will track connectivity changes, while swallowing assessments, a videofluoroscopy-based measure, cognition testing, and a quality-of-life questionnaire capture clinical change. Twenty healthy volunteers provide reference scans. As a protocol, the article reports the design and planned outcomes rather than results.
pmc-13334010:
Entidhar Jasim Khamees and colleagues made tiny selenium particles in two ways and tested them against germs and cancer cells. One batch came from a chemical process, the other from pulsed laser blasts in liquid. Both gave round, stable particles of like size, checked by microscope and light tests.

Both batches slowed four kinds of bacteria, with strength rising by dose and strain. Against colon cancer cells in dishes, both killed more cells as the dose rose. The laser-made batch reached the same kill at a lower dose. The authors present selenium particles as candidates for germ-fighting and cancer uses, pending much more testing.
pmc-13334410:
Manuel Jesús Enciso-Ripoll and co-authors mapped Spain's public dental workforce in a 2026 cross-sectional analysis. Spain has one of Europe's densest dentist supplies, yet public coverage is thin and uneven across regions.

Data came from transparency requests to all 17 autonomous communities plus Ceuta and Melilla, registration records, and health ministry sources. In 2024-2025 Spain counted 42,860 active dentists, about 84.68 per 100,000 people, but only 1,685 salaried public dentists, leaving an average load near 31,590 residents per public dentist. The public share ranged from 2.0 percent in Madrid to 7.6 percent in Castilla-La Mancha. Another 6,810 accredited private providers joined public programs in mixed-model regions. The numbers frame a planning problem about equity, not raw supply.
pmc-13334810:
Tanmoy Dutta and co-authors build a lab model of fatty liver disease in a 2026 paper. The disease, tied to body metabolism, affects about 32 percent of people worldwide. It ranges from simple fat buildup in the liver to swelling, scarring, and in the end liver failure or cancer. How simple fat turns into the worse forms is still poorly known.

Older lab models miss key traits of a real liver. Cell lines grown flat do not act like tissue, and stem-cell models need long checks. The team instead grew small balls of real human liver cells. They mixed the main liver cells with star-shaped support cells at the ratio found in the body. Fed a fat-rich mix, the balls took on traits of the disease.
pmc-13335010:
Aurélien Stab and six co-authors wrote a 2026 study that screens organophosphate chemicals for harm to hormones with computer models. They are used on farms and in home electronics. Their hormone effects were checked for just a few old types, so most of the family had not been looked at.

The team joined three tools in one pipeline: work on shape, structure-activity algorithms, and molecular docking. It was tuned to 97 percent sensitivity for estrogen receptor disruptors and checked against lab assays. Of 42 compounds and mixtures, 88 percent upset the estrogen or androgen receptor at sub-toxic levels. Aryl types hit hardest, often both at once. Docking showed them tucked in the pocket of the first receptor much like estradiol, but with weaker polar contacts. Their scores matched known reproductive toxicity. One rigid cluster stayed inactive.
pmc-13335210:
Huthaifa Atallah and co-authors weigh two bedside tests for people learning to walk on a prosthetic leg. Sixty-three adults in Jordan with one lower-limb amputation took both the Amputee Mobility Predictor, a scored task battery, and the Timed Up and Go, a stand-walk-turn drill against the clock. The team then checked how scores lined up with age, cause of amputation, and fall risk.

The two tests moved in near-lockstep in opposite directions, as better battery scores meant faster drill times. More than half the group screened as at risk of falls, and each extra point on the battery cut fall odds sharply. Age and the cause of amputation shaped results, while time since amputation did not. The authors back using both tests together in clinic.
pmc-13335710:
Youfeng Guo and co-authors find that a common pain drug can help or harm disc cells in the spine, based on dose. Their paper from 2026 deals with worn spinal discs, a main cause of low back pain. The drug, celecoxib, is wide used for that pain, but its direct effect on disc cells was not mapped.

At low doses the drug calmed swelling in disc cells and kept their scaffold sound in cell and rat tests. At high doses it set off a copper based cell death path through two proteins named in the study. That path built up copper, stressed the cell power plants, and broke the scaffold down. Blocking the path reversed the harm in rats.
pmc-13335810:
Shan-Shan Rao and co-authors identified a gut bacterial protein that protects bone in a 2026 study of the gut-skeleton axis. Signals from gut microbes reach distant organs, but the actual messenger molecules were unknown.

The protein, Amuc_1473, rides in vesicles shed by the commensal bacterium Akkermansia muciniphila. It directly encourages bone formation and restrains bone-eating cells by binding two regulators, NELF-E and RPL26, that govern transcription pausing and protein production. Levels of the protein fell in bone and blood across many bone-loss settings, from aging and estrogen loss to smoking, chronic stress, alcohol, and high-fat diet. Intermittent fasting restored the bacterium, the protein, and bone quality in these models, tying a popular diet pattern to a concrete microbial mechanism.
pmc-13336010:
Guangping Li and colleagues study 2026 ligand-defined surface science enabling instant and any-sequence DNA sticking on gold nano-bits . A clear mechanism view for DNA sticking on gold nano-bits remains unclear. The authors show that ligand-defined surface charge control, with weakly charged vitamin C ligands, greatly lowers the speed barrier for DNA sticking on gold nano-bits.

In near-neutral settings, this interface rapidly coats gold nano-bits with sulfur-tagged and non-sulfur-tagged short DNA strands by simple vortex mixing. This works even for DNA containing only a single end adenine. The vitamin C interface also overcomes the clash between butanol drying and non-sulfur-tagged DNA. It enables any-sequence round nucleic acid formation under drying settings across several nano-bit systems. Vitamin C reduces surface electric pushback while promoting H-bond-aided surface links.
pmc-13336110:
Chang Zhang and colleagues study 2026 HNRNPU K181 lactate tagging driving cervix cancer growth by raising PHGDH and rewiring serine use. Cervix cancer remains a major global health burden, yet gene workings driving its metabolic rewiring are not fully known. The authors find mixed nuclear protein U as a novel non-histone substrate of lysine lactate tagging that links lactate buildup to serine use and tumor growth.

They show that lactate tagging at lysine 181 steadies HNRNPU, enhances its binding to PHGDH mRNA, and maintains the exon 1 PHGDH transcript and mRNA hold. This keeps PHGDH levels and switches on the serine making pathway. This rewiring promotes redox balance, DNA-block making, and cervix cancer cell growth both in vitro and in vivo. In detail, they reveal a rival link between lactate tagging and NAA50 tagging at lysine 181. This establishes a dynamic after-making switch that fine-tunes HNRNPU function.
pmc-13336510:
Yixin Zhu and co-authors built a deep learning system that proposes new near-infrared fluorescent dyes in a 2026 study. Near-infrared imaging sees deep into tissue with little background glow, but finding good fluorophores by hand is slow, expensive labor.

Their system runs two modules: a predictive one, sharpened by transfer learning to cope with scarce data, estimates optical properties, while a generative module drafts candidates that chemists can actually synthesize. Three suggested molecules, NTDT-TPA, NPA-BTD, and DPP-TPA, were made and tested to validate the pipeline. NTDT-TPA was packed into nanoparticles and performed in cells and living animals as a fluorescence imaging agent. Knowledge transfer between tasks let the small dataset punch above its weight.
pmc-13336910:
Jiawen Chen leads a large 2026 team wrapping boron carriers in macrophage skin to treat glioblastoma. This brain tumor resists cures because the blood-brain barrier blocks drugs and the tumor stifles immunity. Boron neutron capture therapy kills tumor cells selectively, but standard boron agents reach the brain too weakly.

The membrane coat crosses the barrier, homes to tumors, and dodges immune clearance using the macrophage's own tricks. In mouse gliomas it delivered 53.15 µg per gram of boron-10 to tumors, a level 3.09-fold above uncoated particles in the study comparison. Neutron shots extended survival by 50 days and woke up immunity in the reported model. Adding anti-PD-1 therapy cleared tumors fully in half the mice.
pmc-13337110:
Xiangyu Xu and co-authors reveal how dividing cells share their endoplasmic reticulum fairly in a 2026 study. This membrane network, sheets near the nucleus and tubes at the edges, must split evenly between daughter cells. At division entry the pattern reverses: tubes gather around the centrosomes while sheets move outward.

A division kinase tags the tube-shaping protein RTN4, which then partners with Rab11 and rides dynein motors toward the centrosomes. That gathering tubes the nearby network and guarantees symmetric inheritance, which in turn helps other organelles split evenly and division proceed faithfully. Fair organelle sharing turns out to be actively engineered, not left to chance.
pmc-13337410:
Fatih Mehmet Uğurlu and colleagues survey earthquake trauma among athletes in Turkey in a 2026 study. The sample held 359 athletes living in 11 provinces hit by the Kahramanmaraş earthquakes of February 6, 2023, reached by snowball sampling. A standard scale measured post-earthquake trauma levels alongside personal details.

Average trauma scored 65.84 on the scale used, above the midpoint and classed as above-average by the authors. Women reported more symptoms than men. Athletes who lost relatives or lost a home also scored markedly higher than those who did not. The authors conclude that athletic life alone does not buffer disaster trauma, and that bereavement and housing loss deserve targeted mental health support after quakes.
pmc-13337510:
Marthe Sophie Kilian leads a 2026 team measuring late kidney damage after radiation that grazes the kidneys. Precise ablative radiotherapy for kidney tumors controls cancer well, but long-term renal safety data are thin. The retrospective cohort screened 731 trunk radiotherapy patients and kept 232 whose kidneys received meaningful incidental dose, tracking kidney function over time.

Worsening kidney disease appeared in 46.98% of patients during a median follow-up of 170 days in the cohort analysis. Higher mean and maximum kidney doses independently predicted decline, with a steady dose-response and risk cut-offs near 18.7 Gy and 19.0 Gy in the exploratory analysis. Female sex also raised risk. Severe toxicity stayed rare, supporting careful, kidney-sparing treatment planning.
pmc-13337710:
Jeong-Hoo Lee and colleagues test two yogurt-related bacteria as possible oral probiotics in a 2026 study. Streptococcus mutans and Streptococcus sobrinus help drive tooth decay by building plaque biofilms. Blocking settlement, rather than killing bacteria outright, is the strategy explored here.

Strains DM287 and DM294 of Streptococcus thermophilus came from yogurt and from the tongue coating of healthy adults. Both cut plaque mass by about three quarters in a wire model assay reported by the authors. They also lowered pathogen biofilm and reduced sticking under test conditions. Growth tests suggested the effect was not mainly from killing, supporting a gentler route to decay prevention.
pmc-13338210:
Razan A Alenezi, Abdulhameed Alsarraf, and Mahmoud K AL-Omiri studied how mouth diseases affect daily life for patients at an oral medicine clinic in Kuwait. Their study, published in 2026, compared people with diseases of the soft tissue inside the mouth against matched controls without such disease. Each person filled in a short survey on pain, discomfort, and limits in daily life.

The study covered 103 patients and 103 controls. Patients scored worse on mental discomfort and related measures than controls, and women reported worse scores than men. People with growths that could turn into cancer fared worst of all. The authors argue that care for these patients should include support for mental health, not only treatment of the mouth itself.
pmc-13338410:
Ahmed A. Alawi Al-Naghi and colleagues built a clear machine learning tool in 2026 to forecast the crush strength of coconut fibre concrete. Plant fibres boost bend and crack resistance, but coconut fibre makes tangled links that muddy strength forecasts. Six regression methods were tuned with particle swarm search on 586 test mixes.

Nested grouped cross checks guarded model choice, and a locked test set gave the last check. The best mix, extreme gradient boosting with particle swarm tuning, hit an R squared of 0.963 in cross checks. Sound strength forecasts help builders trust green coconut fibre concrete more in real designs.
pmc-13339010:
Yidian Wang and Piero Macchi simulate missing-link defects in a metal-organic framework in a 2026 study. Ultra-low dielectric materials are vital for smaller electronics, and the framework HKUST-1 is a candidate. Removing some links might lower its dielectric response further.

A polarizable force field was tuned against the clean material, then applied to flawed versions. Defects cut dielectric susceptibility by up to about 30 percent in the reported simulations, reaching a constant near 1.5 as modeled. Response fell in a straight line as defects rose, driven by lower polarizability. Even few defects sped dielectric relaxation, suggesting deliberate flaws as a design tool.
pmc-13339710:
Hongyun Ruan and colleagues weighed surgery routes in 2026 for thymoma removal at Beijing Chest Hospital from 2005 to 2024. Keyhole chest surgery is now common, yet its long term worth against open chest cuts stayed in doubt. In all, 317 patients were split by route: keyhole surgery for 178, side chest cut for 73, and breastbone cut for 66.

Weighting balanced baseline gaps, and op measures plus long term outcomes were weighed. Keyhole surgery may mean a faster return home, but only if tumour control and safety match open surgery. The head to head test helps chest surgeons pick routes that balance return home speed against cancer control.
pmc-13339910:
Mohamed R. Kady and Robert A. Britton resequence two probiotic bacterial genomes in a 2026 report. Public genomes for Limosilactobacillus reuteri conflicted with new reads of a sticking protein gene called cmbA. Hybrid long and short sequencing closed both genomes anew.

Two regions totaling 40 kbp, thought missing from the type strain, proved intact as reported. The cmbA gene is the longest in both genomes and holds a repeated stretch: 11 repeats in one strain and 8 in the other as counted. Gel and mass tests confirmed a matching 160 kDa protein band, fixing the reference record.
pmc-13340510:
Qun He and co-authors dope a cobalt catalyst with palladium to make ammonia from nitrate at factory scale currents. Their paper from 2026 tackles a weak point of the electric route: it fades at the high currents real plants need. Their rebuilt catalyst held over ninety eight percent ammonia yield share at a very high current density and ran steady past one hundred seventy hours.

Live spectra and sums point to a twin boost. The doping lowers the energy step that gates the rate. It also rebuilds the water layer at the surface, drawing in ions and lining water up to pass protons and steady the mid steps. The palladium role here differs from its role in copper systems, the authors note.
pmc-13340910:
Christopher G Rohner and Andrew Trom told of a rare neurosyphilis case in 2026 in a 42 year old man, as syphilis rises again across the United States. The patient went to the emergency room twice within 60 days with vague, on and off numbness and tingling in hands and feet, which he first brushed off. Signs grew to balance trouble, ear ringing, poor focus, low attention, odd behaviour, waxing confusion, and one hallucination.

The first emergency workup about three weeks earlier had a clear head CT, yet the shifting picture pointed to neurosyphilis. The case reminds doctors that syphilis can show up as shifting nerve and mind signs. Early suspicion and spinal fluid tests matter before lasting harm sets in.
pmc-13341210:
Kim and co-authors compare two spine fusion methods for worn lumbar joints. One method uses a scope with two cages through a side path. The other is the standard open fusion from the back. Records covered 115 patients treated from 2021 to 2024. All had one-level disease and failed 12 weeks of basic care.

The scope group held 58 patients and the open group 57. Scope cases lost less blood and took less time. Cage height and angle ran slightly higher with the scope. Pain eased faster after scope surgery in the first weeks. Scores at 6 and 12 months matched between the groups.
pmc-13341510:
Dementia reframed as a failure of the body's memory is proposed by Samuel Ruesga Mundo in a 2026 hypothesis paper. Decades of amyloid- and tau-centered work have produced few disease-changing therapies, and puzzles like pathology without symptoms motivate a broader frame.

His Hierarchical-Circular Model runs on the principle signal, plasticity, stable state, across five levels from genetic programming and epigenetic memory to allostatic load, a psycho-neuro-endocrine-immune network, and interoceptive brain integration. Disturbance at any level can ripple both ways and lock in harmful stable states that surface as dementia. The write-up draws on multisystem studies from 2010 to 2025.
pmc-13341710:
Saudi teen athletes live differently from their non-sporting peers, in a 2026 cross-sectional study by Fahad Bin Radhyan and colleagues. The Riyadh project surveyed 124 boys aged 16 to 17, 70 athletes and 54 non-athletes, with a validated 47-item Arab teen lifestyle questionnaire.

Athletes nearly all met activity guidelines, 98.6% of them versus 55.6% of the non-athlete group, and carried lower body mass index, 23.64 in athletes versus 29.69 in the comparison group, both in kg/m2. More athletes ate fruit on five or more days weekly, 54.3% of athletes versus 33.3% of the other boys. Oddly, athletes slept less, 9.06 hours a night versus 11.28 hours for the non-athletes, though both groups cleared 8 hours. Screen time did not differ, complicating any simple sport-is-healthier story.
pmc-13341810:
Aristotle's hunch that arm swing speeds runners gets biomechanical backing from Jiahua Li and colleagues in a 2026 study. One world-class sprinter performed laboratory arm-swing modification sessions on a pressure treadmill while motion capture and force data fed forward and inverse dynamics models.

With the modified swing, cadence and peak ground force fell, step length grew, and forward and vertical impulse integrals rose, while sideways impulse shrank. Center of mass movement stayed consistent, and energy estimates matched standard equations. A brief technique intervention thus measurably improved propulsion in the lab, suggesting coaches can train arm action as more than decoration.
pmc-13342110:
Cheng Luo and five co-authors achieve a long-sought trick in radical chemistry, in this 2026 paper. Kinetic resolution separates a mixed pair of mirror-image molecules by reacting one faster than the other, leaving enriched product. Radicals are so reactive that chemists thought resolution among them was out of reach.

Guided by a chiral acid catalyst under visible light, the team resolved Minisci reactions, where glycine-based partners add to ring-shaped nitrogen compounds. Yields and mirror purity were both high, for products and for recovered starting material. A second case coupled aldehydes with olefins to build molecules with both an axis of twist and a distant center of chirality. The authors call the work a conceptual breakthrough and hope it opens racemic feedstocks, the cheapest kind, to asymmetric radical chemistry.
pmc-13342510:
Dong Hoon Shin and co-authors build a similarity search chip in a 2026 paper. Hashing methods turn data into short codes so near matches can be found fast, but fixed cutoffs and wasteful analog coding have kept them off dedicated hardware.

Their design, named DASH, uses a grid of transistors paired with memory resistors that works in both analog and digital modes. In analog mode it projects data at random while maximizing code entropy and adjusting its own bias from the data. Digital mode then measures code distances cheaply. On synthetic three dimensional clusters the chip kept groups apart and raised code quality. On a large digit set it beat fixed hashing on recall and noise tolerance.
pmc-13342710:
Bhavana Kushwaha and Ruoning Wang comment in 2026 on work by You and colleagues about a mitochondrial protein called OPA1 in tumor dendritic cells. Their commentary centers on conventional type 1 dendritic cells, key immune cells that often lose strength inside solid tumors and fail to rally an attack.

You and colleagues found that falling OPA1 levels track with weaker mitochondria and fading cell function, acting through a signaling path involving NRF1. Giving mice dendritic cells with polarized, fitter mitochondria sparked strong immune responses against tumors. Kushwaha and Wang frame the result as metabolic immunotherapy: fixing immune cell energy systems might rescue treatments that most patients currently resist.
pmc-13343710:
Aashay Prasad Pande and five co-authors test whether MRI measures can predict graft size in ACL reconstruction, in a study published in 2026. Surgeons need grafts thick enough for a stable knee, and size is hard to know before harvest. Fifty-two patients were split evenly between hamstring tendon and peroneus longus tendon grafts, with tendon area measured on scans at set points.

Ankle-level area did the same job for the peroneus tendon, and the authors claim the first such cutoff for that tendon. Both thresholds sorted adequate grafts with high accuracy in this group.
pmc-13344210:
Christina M Ackerman-Banks and co-authors ask whether treating depression in pregnancy protects the heart after birth, in a 2026 claims study from Maine. Depression during pregnancy is known to raise new cardiovascular disease risk within two years of delivery, but whether care itself softens that risk was open.

Treated patients faced a 25 percent lower risk of new cardiovascular disease across the first 24 months after delivery. New chronic high blood pressure, though, showed no link to treatment. The authors urge deeper study of the pathways tying mood care to heart protection.
pmc-13346010:
Keith Nishihara, Nikitha Reddy, and Kevin S Tang review dangerous heart complications of chest-center masses in 2026. Lumps in the mediastinum sit against the heart, great veins, and windpipe. Pressure from them can trigger fluid crushing the heart, vena cava blockage, or blocked heart outflow. Yet no guideline covers these emergencies.

Searching PubMed work through late 2025, the authors outline how often such masses appear, what causes them, and how each life-threatening syndrome shows up and gets confirmed. Definitive care targets the mass itself once the patient is stabilized. A team approach spanning anesthesia, surgery, and critical care, they argue, should be standard for every such patient.
pmc-13346110:
Angie Zuleidi Mayorquin and co-authors chase the scent schedule of a twilight passionflower in 2026. Passiflora pohlii opens at dawn, smells strongly of citrus, and relies on crepuscular Ptiloglossa bees. The team located its scent glands, timed its emissions, and read its perfume chemistry across the morning.

Outer crown filaments house the osmophores, the scent-making tissue, and emissions peaked exactly at dawn before collapsing by 90 percent later in anthesis while flowers still looked fresh. Microscopy showed scent-cell organelles breaking down in step with the fade. Monoterpenes ruled the bouquet, led by geraniol and its kin, a package tuned tightly to one bee's size, senses, and flight hour.
pmc-13346610:
Fulong Ma and co-authors model the slow deformation of warm, ice-rich frozen sand in a 2026 study. Frozen ground under roads and pipelines creeps over time, and warm ice-rich soils flow most. Predicting that creep needs tests on realistic samples and a model that respects the soil's mix.

The team devised a way to prepare ice-rich specimens, then ran compression creep tests at two ice contents. Saturated and very icy sands crept quite differently. Their model blends soil skeleton, ice, and unfrozen water, with ice-cement bonds that break progressively. It matched the tests across ice contents and stress levels, a tool for cold-region engineering.
pmc-13348210:
Dargham Hammad and Fadyia Al-Ameedy study circular RNAs and cytokine levels in postmenopausal women with osteoarthritis. Their twenty twenty-six case-control study compares seventy-five patients with seventy-five healthy peers. Osteoarthritis wears joints down amid steady low-grade inflammation.

If their levels track the disease, they could serve as blood biomarkers. That would aid early finds in a group where joint pain is often waved off as age. The design also weighs how the RNAs may steer cytokine output.
pmc-13348410:
Harvey K. Kamboyi and a large team report genomes for anthrax bacteria from the 2023 Zambia outbreak, in an announcement from 2026. The outbreak ran May to November with 834 suspected human cases and four deaths, plus 390 livestock and 39 wildlife deaths in the official tallies. Strains came from three patients and one soil sample where a cow had died.

Cases spread across 44 districts in nine provinces, with a non-endemic southern district as the hot centre holding 35 percent of cases in the reported split. Public genomes from linked human and soil strains support tracing of spread paths and vaccine or test matching for a disease that returns yearly in western Zambia.
pmc-13348610:
Abubakari, Faisal, and Asuma model factors tied to infant death in Ghana's Northern Region. Infant mortality stays a major public health concern in Ghana, above all in the north. Survival analysis with Kaplan-Meier curves compared groups by traits such as child sex, maternal schooling, residence, marital status, and occupation. Most traits showed no statistically clear survival gap between groups. At least one factor did stand out, guiding where child health efforts may focus.
pmc-13348810:
Ruixue Tao and colleagues study the two resistance plasmids riding in one hospital Klebsiella, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The strain is an ST15 multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae from a clinical case. It carried plasmids named pKPA1-1 and pKPA1-2. Both could conjugate, copying themselves into new bacteria.

The two differed in character. The first moved freely, passing into both Klebsiella and Escherichia coli. The second moved only within Klebsiella, but stayed more stable once it arrived. Their drug resistance menus were near-identical. Oddly, gaining either plasmid made the bacterium less virulent, a fitness trade the authors note. The study matters because such plasmids are the courier network of hospital resistance. Knowing their range, stability, and cost helps predict where resistance travels next.
pmc-13349710:
Jin Yong Kim reviews a 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, in a review from 2026. Andes virus stands out among hantaviruses for repeated person-to-person spread and severe lung-heart illness in South America. So world and regional agency reports were gathered to trace how infection moved through a crowded, enclosed ship after departure from Ushuaia on April 1.

By May 27, a total of 13 people were infected, with 11 confirmed and 2 probable cases, and 3 had died in the reported tally. Gene reads differed by at most one change, pointing to onboard spread after few spillovers, while older age near 65 years, shared cabins, and close care contact fed transmission.
pmc-13350610:
Drugs that block PD-1 have cut deaths from advanced melanoma, yet only a share of patients gain from them. Yu Wang and co-authors set out in their 2026 paper to predict, before treatment, whose survival would be good or poor on PD-1 blockade alone. They built simple scoring charts, called nomograms, from gene mutation and copy number data in two patient cohorts.

Their top chart rests on five genes and split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups with clearly apart survival times. The same split meant nothing in two cohorts who never got the drug, which shows the chart forecasts drug benefit rather than general fate. The charts are free online, and the authors offer them as an aid for doctors choosing treatment for metastatic melanoma.
pmc-13350710:
Bryant Morocho and Steve Kwon compared prediction tools for gastrointestinal stromal tumours in a 2026 review. These tumours vary widely, with five-year survival reported between 59 and 81.3 percent and recurrence between 3.8 and 37.5 percent, so one prognosis never fits all.

Large pooled analyses show stomach tumours relapsing less than intestinal ones, and women faring somewhat better than men. The review organises rival nomograms so clinicians can see which inputs matter, which tool suits which question, and where the numbers remain shaky.
pmc-13351010:
Lara Delbene and co-authors weigh school plans that prep nurses for disaster work in a 2026 review of teach forms. Disasters grow more oft and more harsh, so care nets must stand ready to act with skill. Nurses man the front line and need firm drills to face grave events with skill and calm.

A fast proof sweep pools past work on such drills for nurses and their students in schools. Set search rules and a check flow pick the pool from world sources in a clear way. Teach forms that lift ready skill are the core of the sweep and its finds.
pmc-13351710:
Shasha Wang, Ye Qi, and Dan Yao compare picky eating levels in preschool children with autism in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Picky eating is common in autism, but how its degree affects diet and behaviour is unclear. The study enrolled 130 children aged 3 to 6 years who met DSM-5 criteria.

Height and weight were measured, diet variety and eating behaviour were scored with validated scales, and intake came from three 24-hour recalls. Growth did not differ clearly between low and high picky eating groups, and most children grew within the normal range. Diet variety, nutrient intake, and eating behaviour did differ, with the low picky eating group showing higher total diet variety.
pmc-13351910:
Heejoung Kim leads a 2026 prospective study using DNA from lung wash fluid to estimate tumour mutation burden in advanced lung cancer. Getting enough tumour tissue for gene tests is often hard. Patients with stage IV disease who received pembrolizumab at three Korean centres gave wash fluid and matched tumour tissue before treatment.

Mutation burden was measured by whole-exome sequencing of DNA from tiny vesicles in the wash fluid. Of 64 patients, 53 had usable fluid results and 46 had usable tissue results. DNA amount and read depth were similar between sources. The team compared the two measures and linked fluid burden to survival and response over median follow-up of 17.0 months.
pmc-13352610:
Qifei Zhu and co-authors built reference ranges in 2026 for blood tests in Chinese local donkeys. Vets read such tests against normal ranges, but no standard ranges built to international rules existed for these donkeys, which limits care and disease tracking.

Blood came from healthy donkeys on five farms with different conservation status and raising systems. More than 1,100 serum samples were tested for twenty measures covering protein, liver, energy, minerals, and kidney function. Blood cell counts came from more than 900 donkeys on one farm. Farm origin drove most of the variation in the chemistry measures, more than age or sex. The ranges are offered for clinical use.
pmc-13352810:
Lianci Peng and co-authors vet two bacteria from fermented vegetables as possible probiotics in a 2026 study. Lactic acid bacteria live in pickles, guts, and dairy, and many help health, but a strain must prove both useful and safe before use. The team sequenced the full genomes of the two isolates and ran lab tests on their behavior.

The genomes held gene clusters for making natural antibiotics and protective compounds, yet lacked the classic machinery of harmful bacteria. Both strains survived strong acid and bile, conditions that mimic the stomach and gut, and they made acid vigorously. Such traits suit bacteria meant to reach the intestine alive and crowd out germs. The careful genome check also sets a safety template for turning food microbes into health products.
pmc-13355710:
Antonio Vicidomini and co-authors tested a tolerance-promoting nanoparticle treatment in 2026 in young mice with a urea cycle disorder. pmc-13356410:
Jingyu Zhong and co-authors test how stable MRI texture measures are in a 2026 study. Such measures, called radiomic features, are used to turn scans into numbers for research and care. Deep learning tools now rebuild scans and outline organs, but their effect on those numbers was not fully known.

They extracted 107 features per region. Agreement scores across scans were low for both manual and automatic outlines. The findings warn that scan and outline choices can shift radiomic results, so studies must control them with care.
pmc-13356910:
Nikunj Barvadiya and co-authors review pancreatic pseudocysts in 2026, fluid-filled pockets that often form after pancreas injury or pancreatitis. Some pockets clear on their own, while others cause infection, bleeding, or blockage. Older rules urged surgery for any cyst lasting six weeks or growing past six centimeters.

Newer scans and studies have overturned that rule, showing size and age alone poorly predict outcome. The review lays out a stepwise plan: watchful waiting, tube drainage, endoscopic drainage, or surgery, chosen by symptoms, harm, duct shape, and timing rather than size alone. A team-based, patient-by-patient approach aims for the best outcome with the least needless intervention.
pmc-13358510:
Liming Chen and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on a plant-based drug for scarred lungs. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis slowly stiffens the lungs and has few good treatments. Rats given the tablets showed less lung scarring than untreated rats, alone or paired with a steroid drug. The team traced changes in lung tissue, blood signals, and a group of immune cells tied to inflammation. The results hint the drug works by calming a key scarring pathway, a lead for future care.
pmc-13358610:
Woo Hyeon Son and co-authors study exercise and metabolic syndrome in a 2026 paper from South Korea. They used national health screening data grouped by age, covering 2014 to 2023. Hard exercise tied to lower rates of high blood pressure and high blood sugar. A decision tree model then sorted the groups to flag who sits at high risk, a step toward health advice shaped for each age group.
pmc-13359710:
Estelle Manguin and co-authors study asthma treatment in horses in a 2026 paper. Horses with severe equine asthma are treated with airway-opening drugs, sometimes plus inhaled steroids. The team compared lung microbe samples from horses on airway drugs alone versus horses also given inhaled steroids. Bacterial load and some microbe groups shifted differently between the treatments even though breathing improved in both. Whether these microbe changes help or harm the lung remains open, a question for longer studies.
pmc-13359910:
Wei-Zhe Li and co-authors separate two puzzles of HIV persistence in a 2026 study. Even on early treatment, HIV hides in a reservoir of infected cells. A smaller reservoir tracked with natural killer cell function, part of the fast innate arm. Faster shrinkage instead tracked with restored HIV-specific T-cell responses, the adaptive arm. pmc-13360810:

pmc-13365210:

pmc-13365510:

pmc-13369110:
Charles Zhang and co-authors published a case series in 2026 on eye infection after an artificial cornea implant. The implant restores sight in badly scarred eyes, but infection inside the eye is a feared risk. The team gathered proven cases at one referral center.

pmc-13369810:
Daniel Grasso and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, how starved pancreatic cancer cells use tiny parcels to switch on a survival trick in their neighbors. pmc-13370010:

Iron and a kin metal peak at year one, dip, then rise a new, a wave short tests miss. One crop food good stays hid, bound by those metals. The char runs rich in lime and lifts soil base. Long watch shows char work is a wave, not a step.
pmc-13371210:

pmc-13371510:
Richard Muñoz, Danilo Oliveira, and Alejandro Arrieta validate, published in 2026, a Portuguese version of a hospital safety culture survey across a Brazilian hospital system. Every item loaded on the general factor. Communication about error, response to error, and staffing pace drove the general score most. The authors judge the tool valid and reliable for Brazilian hospitals, ready to guide improvement work.
pmc-13371610:
Sha Zhao and colleagues report early treprostinil use in a high-risk child with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension. Their 2026 case concerns a 14-year-old girl with congenital heart disease. pmc-13372410:
Dayong Yan and colleagues trace a signalling chain that drives mouth cancer spread and drug resistance in a 2026 study. pmc-13372810:

pmc-13374010:

pmc-13374310:

pmc-13374810:

pmc-13375410:

pmc-13375610:
José A García and co-authors tell of a moved bone graft in a sick girl in a 2026 case report. The girl, aged six in 2025, had spine TB in 2021. A cut took out a bad chest bone and a leg bone graft, about two cm long, filled the gap. Full germ drug care then cured the ill.
