pmc-13375810:
Chang-Hyun Kim and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, how place shapes the gut bacteria of a common mosquito in Illinois. Gut microbes affect the mosquito's nutrition, breeding, and immunity, yet city growth may shift them. The team sampled female mosquitoes from homes and woods in two towns and read their gut bacteria by gene sequencing.

Woodland mosquitoes held richer and more varied gut bacteria than those from homes. The woods near one town showed the richest mix of all. Both town and habitat type shaped the results, and they interacted as well. The authors urge care in reading the data, since stray contamination could not be fully ruled out.
pmc-13376210:
Xingjin Wang and co-authors compared, in a 2026 computer study, two neck fusion cages that fix with two screws or four. The surgery joins neck bones from the front after a worn disc is removed. Slim cages that sit flush are popular, but which screw count holds better was unclear.

The team built a 3D model of the neck from scan data and placed each cage at one disc level. Loads mimicked bending and twisting of the neck. The two-screw cage took more stress on its cage and plate but less on its screws. Stress on nearby bones looked much the same for both. After fusion, the two designs acted alike. The simpler two-screw cage may serve as well, though long-term clinic data is still needed.
pmc-13376410:
Ethan Belnap and co-authors screened, in a 2026 study, food pantry visitors in Chicago for cholesterol problems they did not know they had. Dyslipidemia drives heart disease yet hides quietly, and food-insecure people see doctors least. Screenings at West Chicago pantries between 2023 and 2025 gathered 389 participants with lipid panels and vital signs.

Nearly seven in ten met criteria for dyslipidemia at screening, most often the mixed pattern. Over 72 percent had never reported the condition, and two thirds of those unaware tested positive, making unreported disease alone 49 percent. Among people who did report it, 73 percent were uncontrolled. The pattern skewed toward high triglycerides and low protective cholesterol, a fingerprint, the authors say, of cheap high-carbohydrate diets.
pmc-13376510:
Gut germs in cattle oft host sleepy virus guests that can wake on cue, yet few such guests from rumen strains have been caught live. Seon Young Park and co-authors wake one in a 2026 study. The host strain came from cattle and sits in a group long tied to gut health and to some ills.

The waked guest kills kin strains and some milk germs as well. Its form is the long tail kind, with a short wait, a big burst, and good strength in sour, hot gut states. It also breaks biofilms well. Its code, near thirty eight thousand marks, holds fifty eight genes and tracks the sleepy guests guessed in kin strains. The read charts virus range in this host group.
pmc-13377410:
Yi Jin and a large team of co-authors present a 2026 study on mouth bacteria migrating to the gut in advanced liver cirrhosis. Cirrhosis scrambles the partnership between the body and its microbes. Pairing mouth and stool gene data with computer models of microbial metabolism, the team tracked how the two communities change as the disease worsens. Their functional profiling showed the mouth and gut microbiomes growing metabolically more alike.

Species that had apparently translocated from mouth to gut were predicted to produce extra ammonia and acetate. Community and host models suggested these shifts ripple into energy use and redox balance in the liver, brain, and muscle. The authors propose an acetate-ammonia axis linking microbial migration to the whole-body metabolic stress of cirrhosis. The work is modeling-based, offering a mechanism for later testing.
pmc-13377710:
Xiao-Jun Xiang and colleagues link blood sugar swings to death risk after coronary stenting in critically ill patients in a 2026 study. Glycaemic variability has been tied to poor outcomes in critical illness, yet its value after stent implantation was unclear. The team analysed 2,427 adults who had coronary stents and were admitted to coronary or cardiovascular intensive care, using MIMIC-IV data, with external validation in the eICU database.

Variability was defined as the coefficient of variation of blood glucose. Patients in the highest variability quarter faced markedly higher in-hospital death risk, hazard ratio near 2.58, and higher one-year death risk, near 1.77, against the lowest quarter. The study suggests that steady glucose control, not only average glucose, matters for survival after stenting.
pmc-13377810:
Tam Ngo Thi and others assess AI readiness among first-year pharmacy students in Vietnam in a 2026 mixed-methods study. The team surveyed 220 students on AI readiness across cognition, ability, vision, and ethics, plus perceptions and usage, with interviews in a purposive subsample. Regression models tested factors linked to engagement.

Overall readiness was moderate, with cognition and ability stronger than vision and ethics. AI use was common, mainly for academic tasks, with ChatGPT the most used tool. Positive views of AI in education predominated, alongside worries about academic integrity and over-reliance. Higher digital reading skill and urban residence tracked with greater readiness. Students called for structured, pharmacy-specific AI teaching that pairs practical skills with ethical guidance.
pmc-13379410:
Domingo reviews the evidence that pollution feeds Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 neurology synthesis. Alzheimer's is the world's commonest neurodegenerative disorder, and its burden is projected to more than double by 2050, passing 150 million people. Most cases arise late in life from genes interacting with changeable exposures. The review assembles findings from human cohorts, animal experiments, and cell systems across pollutant classes: airborne particles, heavy metals, pesticides, PFAS chemicals, and microplastics now found in human tissues.

The 2024 Lancet Commission on dementia listed 14 changeable risk factors, with air pollution explicitly among them, framing exposure control as prevention. Domingo highlights studies finding Alzheimer-type brain changes in children and young adults living amid heavy city pollution, suggesting damage begins decades before symptoms. Shared mechanisms run through inflammation, oxidative stress, and blood vessel injury. The review argues that cleaning air and water is a concrete lever against a disease doctors still cannot cure.
pmc-13380110:
Paik, Kalligeros, Zelber-Sagi, Paik, Alqahtani, and Younossi trace how national food systems feed into fatty liver disease worldwide. Their 2026 study covers MASLD, a metabolic liver condition, across 204 countries. The team asks whether the path from food environment to liver outcomes differs between poorer and richer nations.

Data from global burden, nutrition, and food statistics were ordered in time: food exposures first, metabolic risks later, disease and liver deaths last. Countries split by a development index. In lower-development settings, city growth raised ultra-processed food retail exposure, which tracked with more obesity. Calorie surplus in turn tracked with disease prevalence. Structural models separated direct from indirect paths.
pmc-13380710:
Alexandru Marian Bologa and a large team present a 2026 study of a very rare condition that gives the face a mask-like appearance. The condition is linked to small missing pieces of chromosome 8, yet some people with overlapping deletions do not show the mask-like face. That puzzle suggests a second mechanism is at work.

The team compared 30 previously reported people with deletions in that region, grouped by whether the face was affected, and added a new case from Romania. They examined how the genome folds in three dimensions. A recurring folding pattern brought a cluster of conserved control elements near a gene called GDF6 in affected people. That pattern is a candidate explanation for the distinctive face.
pmc-13380810:
Dana Klatt Shaw shows that hungry immune cells drive spinal cord repair in zebrafish, in a 2026 study. In mammals, sluggish debris clearance and chronic swelling stall recovery after spinal cord injury. The fish, by contrast, mount brief immune activation and clear debris fast, then regrow.

Gene readouts and cell removal proved the fish macrophages are highly cell-eating and required for regrowth. The gene tcim emerged as an immune-rich repair factor: deleting it weakened debris eating and repair and switched white blood cells toward a pro-swelling profile. Expressing tcim in mouse macrophages also boosted fat use and retraining of precursors into active eaters, marking eating capacity as a lever for repair.
pmc-13385810:
José Gerardo Silos García and co-authors forecast electricity demand for future super smart grids with an explainable neural network, in a 2026 paper. Planning such grids needs demand estimates that use social data as well as past consumption, since older methods lean too hard on one region's time series. Their model runs two networks in parallel over the two data streams and fuses them with an attention mechanism.

Tested on ninety-two Australian suburban zones, the method cut forecast error to under two percent, beating standard recurrent models when social metrics were included in training. Two explanation tools then reveal which inputs drove each forecast. The authors link better, fairer forecasts to pricing and supply choices that serve all zones.
pmc-13385910:
Xiaotao Yang, Lijun Liu, and Zebin Cao study how the edge of the western North American craton has changed over time. A craton is the old, stable core of a continent, and its edge shapes hills, volcanoes, and metal deposits. Past work focused on the Colorado Plateau and blamed water from a sinking slab. The team instead built a sharp three-dimensional map of wave speed below the whole margin.

The map shows the deep keel of the craton pulling back as depth grows, all along the margin. Two narrow weak zones run far into the craton, reaching the Black Hills. Their match with strong flow below suggests that flow can wear the craton away. Rock data point to slow thinning that moves volcanoes and lifts the land.
pmc-13388710:
Jiatong Ji's team built a single-nucleus atlas of human and mouse cortex after severe traumatic brain injury, tracing how each cell type responds across injury stages and swelling. The human data showed a polarised oligodendrocyte state, a myelin-backing cell type, that did not appear in injured mice.

That state carried higher ABCA1, a lipid-handling gene, plus adhesion genes, and tracked with worsening oedema, while lab tests tied it to lipid handling that kept myelin markers intact. Microglial signals through CALM2 and HMGB1 appeared to drive the program. The authors caution that mouse models may miss key human injury biology.
pmc-13390410:
Tianyu Qu and co-authors trace how a long non-coding RNA drives dangerous lung vessel disease under low oxygen. Their 2026 study focuses on pulmonary hypertension, where vessel walls thicken until the heart strains. The RNA, called Snhg18, rises sharply in the muscle cells of lung arteries when oxygen falls.

Blocking Snhg18 slowed cell growth in dishes and in a live animal model. The team found two switches behind its rise: extra gene copies and a transcription factor that binds its promoter. Snhg18 then partners with a reader protein to stabilize the message for a glycolysis enzyme. More of that enzyme means more sugar burning, which fuels the growth. The chain offers a fresh target for treatment.
pmc-13390610:
Navin Raj Ramamurthy and colleagues contrast, in 2026, two teenagers whose similar surface bleeding hid different platelet disorders. Bleeding from gums and skin usually points to faults in the first stage of clotting, while deep bleeding points to the second stage, but some diseases blur that split.

One patient, with repeated gum bleeding yet normal platelet counts and near-normal clotting tests, proved to have Glanzmann thrombasthenia, where platelets cannot clump properly. The second had type 2 von Willebrand disease, a fault in a key clotting helper protein. Haematology readers gain a paired lesson in separating look-alike bleeding disorders with targeted testing.
pmc-13390810:
Katrina Volgemute and a large team set norms, in 2026, for a short Latvian personality survey for use with athletes. Traits shape who takes up sport and how far they go. Yet many surveys used in sport lack sound tests in athlete groups or fair norms to judge scores by.

Two linked studies examined and refined the shortened inventory in 925 athletes aged fifteen to forty-five across 84 sports. The team checked how well the tool works and built norms fit for athletes. They also probed links between traits and the level each athlete had reached. Sport psychologists gain a tested tool with score bands from athletes themselves. Old norms came from the public at large and could misjudge rivals. The norms come from the group who will use them, which makes each score fair to read.
pmc-13391010:
Chieh-Ni Kuo's team reviews nuclear magnet echo marker work in child care, where high-detail mapping has tracked age-related energy-use-linked change and its ties to growth, food, and disease risk. Mass scans dominate marker work, yet NMR offers gentle, fast analysis of diverse body fluids with minimal prep.

Specific pulse patterns such as CPMG and NOESY, plus tools like NMRProcFlow and MetaboAnalyst, streamline signal analysis and reading. Clinically, NMR signatures have lit up early birth, growth, allergy, lipid disorders, infection, and brain conduct, including childhood allergic asthma, despite limits on low-level markers.
pmc-13392410:
Yoshimi Murakami and co-authors describe a toddler whose drooping right eyelid and limited eye movement turned out to be the first sign of an inherited brain vessel disorder. Genetic testing found a new variant in PDCD10, the gene tied to the most severe form of familial cerebral cavernous malformation. The report appeared in 2026.

Scans first showed many calcified spots in the brain, and magnetic resonance imaging then revealed multiple cavernous malformations. Follow-up imaging a year later showed fresh lesions, including one near the pons, plus bleeding beside the nerve that moves the eye. Because new lesions can appear quickly and bleeding risk stays high, the authors stress close monitoring over time.
pmc-13392910:
Khalid F Alhejaili and three colleagues report a 21-year-old woman who arrived coughing blood with severe breathing failure from bleeding across both lungs. A week earlier she had lost hearing in both ears without explanation. Scans showed widespread hazy shadowing in the lungs, and washed lung fluid confirmed alveolar bleeding, a dangerous emergency with several possible triggers.

Blood tests found the p-ANCA antibody pattern tied to small-vessel vasculitis. Rival markers came back negative, and kidney function stayed normal throughout. That pairing is unusual, since kidney damage usually travels with this disease. Strong steroid pulses calmed the illness fast enough for her to leave the ventilator within five days. The authors propose the hearing loss was an early vasculitis clue, and argue that unexplained hearing loss before lung bleeding deserves antibody testing.
pmc-13393710:
Getulio Pereira de Oliveira leads a twelve-author comparison of glioblastoma cells grown flat in dishes versus as three-dimensional balls. The team tracked how culture shape changes the vesicles cells shed and their resistance to the standard drug temozolomide. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive primary brain tumour, and shed vesicles are suspected couriers of resistance. Protein lists were built for cells and their vesicles under drug stress in both formats.

Spheroids secreted more, smaller vesicles and carried a stem-like, drug-resistant protein profile, while flat cultures reshaped their proteins more deeply, loading them with DNA repair and stress adaptation families. Several modifying enzymes dropped inside cells yet were kept in vesicles on purpose, a sign of active sorting. Vesicle cargo mirrored how each culture adapted and matched protein families tied to patient outcomes, which the authors propose as sorting markers and anti-resistance targets.
pmc-13393810:
Hyo Jung Lee and coauthors explore what a good death means to older Singaporeans in a 2026 study. As Singapore ages and grows more diverse, end-of-life planning must reflect culturally specific views, yet those views had been little documented.

The paper draws on older adults' perspectives on dying well and on care preferences, including willingness to discuss death and to plan ahead. Findings aim to inform advance care planning, family conversations, and policy on end-of-life decisions. Readers gain insight into how older Singaporeans weigh comfort, family, and control at life's end.
pmc-13396110:
Yue Li and colleagues gathered records from six medical centers in China on 60 people with myasthenia gravis treated with eculizumab, a drug that blocks part of the immune system. Their 2026 real-world study fills a gap, since most proof for the drug comes from tightly run trials.

Charts yielded daily-living scores, strength scores, and steroid doses at the start, at weeks one, four, and eight, and at final follow-up. By week eight, about 31 percent had reached minimal symptoms or better, rising to about 33 percent at last check. Daily-living scores fell, and the authors also report steroid use and side effects over the course.
pmc-13396810:
Ramona Haji-Seyed-Javadi and co-authors define a second job for HELZ, an enzyme that unwinds RNA-DNA knots called R-loops, in a 2026 study that complements parallel work on the same protein. Untangling these knots matters most where DNA breaks, since stranded RNA can block the repair crew.

The team found HELZ through a screen for genes whose loss makes cells hypersensitive to break-causing drugs. HELZ gathers at break sites and prefers hybrids with a loose single-stranded tail. By clearing R-loops, it helps recruit BRCA1, a lead repair protein, which allows the end trimming that homologous recombination repair needs. Without it, damage lingers and genome stability suffers.
pmc-13397010:
Jongbeom Kim and co-authors review add-ons that let cryogenic electron microscopes report chemistry, not just shape, in a 2026 article. Cryo-EM has revolutionized biology by picturing molecules near atom-level detail in their natural setting. Yet a density map alone says little about which elements sit where, or in what chemical state.

The review covers scanning modes and spectroscopies bolted onto the microscope. These include contrast schemes that weigh atoms, X-ray emission analysis, and energy-loss spectroscopy, which reads how electrons shed energy in the sample. Together they map elements and chemical states without labels, even in fragile frozen specimens, pointing structural biology toward samples whose story is partly chemical.
pmc-13397510:
Hayeem Rudy and co-authors measure how breast shape drifts after reduction surgery that keeps the lower tissue stalk, a change surgeons call bottoming out. Their 2026 study follows patients over six months with phone-based three-dimensional scans. Until now, no one had put numbers on how the upper and lower parts of the breast change over time.

Fifteen patients of one surgeon were scanned at one week, then at one, three and six months after surgery. By six months the lower part had grown about 7 percent in surface area while the upper part shrank by about 8 percent on average. The shift became clear between one and three months, and key distances on the chest lengthened by roughly a centimetre.
pmc-13397710:
Paula Fernanda Morais de Sousa and colleagues document the arrival of cat-spread sporotrichosis in Castanhal, a town in Pará state in Brazil's Eastern Amazon. Their 2026 report covers a fungal skin disease passed through scratches, bites or contact with soil and plants. Long neglected, the illness has lately broken out in several regions and proved hard to stamp out.

Of 23 animals suspected of carrying the fungus, 20 were confirmed by lab culture, all showing the expected sores and signs. Cases clustered in animals allowed outdoors and in areas near forest or newly settled land. The team urges fast diagnosis and control steps, since infected cats can pass the fungus to people.
pmc-13397810:
Al-Hassan Alkhafaji and colleagues screened cancer patients receiving chemotherapy in Yemen for thinking problems, distress, and quality of life. Their 2026 study took place at the National Oncology Center in Sana'a during June and July 2025, where cancer care data and resources are scarce. Chemotherapy can affect memory, mood, and daily function, yet little was known about how often these effects appear in Yemeni patients.

Among 167 adults, most with advanced cancer, only 6 percent showed normal cognition on screening, while 94 percent screened positive for impairment, mainly in language and visual-spatial skills. About one in five showed borderline or abnormal anxiety or depression, and quality-of-life scores ran below average. Older age, male sex, and smoking tracked with lower cognition, while more education tracked with higher scores. The paper calls for routine screening and support in Yemeni oncology care.
pmc-13399310:
Ana Homšek Ilić and co-authors asked which mathematical model best predicts infliximab drug levels in patients with inflammatory bowel disease, in a 2026 pharmacology study. Infliximab dosing is increasingly guided by measured blood levels. Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease also differ in where and how deeply they inflame the gut, so one model may mislead in the other.

Working retrospectively at a university hospital in Belgrade, the team tested twenty published models across five datasets. These covered all patients together and four subgroups, including acute severe ulcerative colitis and fistulizing Crohn's disease. No single model met every accuracy criterion. Before any individual data were fed in, the Matsuoka model performed best overall, while the Xu model suited Crohn's patients. Once patient measurements were included, the Ternant 2008 model led overall. The authors argue for choosing the model to fit each patient's disease type and severity.
pmc-13399410:
Jonathan W Leigh and colleagues describe the design of Text4HF in a 2026 protocol paper, a pilot trial of tailored text messages meant to improve self-care in people living with heart failure. Daily self-care strongly shapes whether these patients stay out of hospital, yet many struggle with it. Texting was chosen because it is simple and familiar, especially for older adults who may not manage apps well.

The single-site trial plans to randomize 30 community-dwelling adults aged 50 or older with stage C heart failure and weak self-care scores. Half get twelve weeks of tailored messages plus usual care, and half get usual care alone. Recruitment began in September 2024, and 26 participants with a mean age of 60 had enrolled when the protocol was written. Completion is expected in June 2026.
pmc-13399810:
Hélder Pereira and Takuji Yokoe describe harvesting graft cartilage from a small accessory bone at the back of the ankle to repair cartilage damage on the talus, in a 2026 technical note. The os trigonum, an extra bone present in roughly a fifth of people, and the neighboring posterolateral talar process carry viable cartilage that can serve as an alternative donor. Removing them also treats posterior ankle impingement.

The best candidates have both a talar lesion and a symptomatic os trigonum, though even a silent one can be harvested with the patient's consent. Because the donor site sits outside the load-bearing joint, taking it carries minimal risk of the donor-site soreness that plagues grafts taken from the knee. The harvested cartilage is minced and implanted into the prepared talar defect in the same operation. The authors argue the approach is a valid option worth considering.
pmc-13400010:
Harrison Volaski and colleagues examined whether patients who use cannabis around the time of ankle fracture surgery end up needing more opioids afterward, in a 2026 retrospective study. The team identified adults who had open reduction and internal fixation of traumatic ankle fractures between 2016 and 2022 under five surgeons at one academic institution. They then telephoned them between December 2023 and May 2024 to ask, with consent, about perioperative cannabis use in any form.

The headline result is a negative one: self-reported cannabis use was not an independent predictor of complications after surgery or of how long patients kept using opioids after their ankle surgery. The authors are open about the measurement limits. Cannabis exposure was recalled retrospectively by phone, sometimes years after surgery, and the interview never asked about frequency, dose, formulation, or route. Within those limits, the study adds a reassuring data point for surgeons counseling ankle fracture patients.
pmc-13400310:
Christopher J Williamson and Andrew J Tedstone model, in 2026, algal blooms across the whole Greenland Ice Sheet over two decades. Dark algae grow on melting ice, support other microbes and darken the surface. Darker ice absorbs more sun and melts faster, raising sea level.

Their computer runs covered the years 2000 to 2022 and tested how key settings changed the results. Conditions fit for algal growth appeared around all ice sheet edges every year. Total bloom area rose by a small trend across the period, tied to how much bare ice each melt season exposed. Northern sectors stood out as places where large blooms may grow yet remain little sampled.
pmc-13400510:
Paula Cristina de Magalhães, Andrei Giacchetto Felice and Siomar de Castro Soares analyze, in 2026, the full gene sets of Rickettsia bacteria. These germs live inside host cells and spread by ticks and other arthropods. They cause diseases such as spotted fever and typhus. Because they are hard to grow in labs, computer analysis carries much of the research load.

The team compared 165 genomes from 31 species drawn from a public database. The genus as a whole has an open pangenome, meaning new genes keep appearing as genomes are added. Core genes handled vital tasks, while rare genes often tied to mobility and gene swapping. Some species stayed highly conserved, while others showed extensive reshuffling of their DNA.
pmc-13400610:
Simon W Samouel and colleagues make, in 2026, cobalt oxide nanoparticles using aloe vera leaf extract, comparing three green production routes. The tiny particles can act as catalysts that release hydrogen, a clean fuel, from chemical stores. Plant-based synthesis avoids harsh chemicals, but the method chosen can change particle shape and power.

Hydrothermal, microwave and precipitation routes all yielded pure crystals, confirmed by X-ray and surface analysis, with flower-like or capsule shapes depending on method. All versions catalyzed both hydrogen release from sodium borohydride and the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide. The hydrothermal batch gave the fastest hydrogen rate in one reaction, while the precipitation batch excelled in the other with a lower energy barrier.
pmc-13400910:
Jiaojiao Hong and colleagues pool, in 2026, studies on whether losing the BAP1 protein predicts survival in malignant pleural mesothelioma, an aggressive cancer of the lung lining. BAP1 is an enzyme that regulates chromatin and cell death, and its loss is common in this cancer. Individual studies disagreed on what it means for patients.

Fourteen studies covering 1,835 patients met the criteria. Across both simple and adjusted analyses, tumors with BAP1 loss or mutation consistently fared better, with death risk roughly halved in unadjusted pooling. Time without progression also improved. The counterintuitive result, losing a protective gene yet living longer, may reflect distinct tumor biology, and the authors present it as a useful prognostic marker.
pmc-13401210:
Ali Akbar Heydari, Sepideh Elyasi, and Farshad Abedi describe a 2026 case of pan-drug resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae. The bacterium resisted every antibiotic on the local testing panel, and the team treated it with two oral drugs. Their patient was a 45-year-old man with bone infection at several sites and a wound that kept draining pus.

Broad antibiotics, repeated surgical cleaning, and two amputations had failed to clear the infection. A colistin and meropenem combination was stopped after it injured his kidneys. The team then gave oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily with rifampin 600 mg once daily as salvage therapy. The discharge dried up quickly and inflammation markers fell sharply. The authors suggest the pairing as a low-cost option when standard drugs cannot be had or cannot be tolerated.
pmc-13401610:
Yuting Qin and colleagues developed a 2026 oral nanovaccine made from dietary fibre that aims to teach lasting tolerance in allergic rhinitis rather than merely ease symptoms. Antihistamines and nasal steroids relieve the condition, which affects over 400 million people, but they do not cure it.

Their platform uses dextran fibre as both allergen carrier and food for gut bacteria. As intestinal microbes ferment it, short-chain fatty acids are released steadily alongside the allergen. Those acids, acting through the FFAR2 receptor, expand regulatory B and T cells, which then travel from gut to nasal lining. In mouse models the vaccine slowed disease progression, improved airway function, and cut allergen-specific IgE levels. The authors frame the gut-to-nose route as a path to durable protection against allergic airway disease.
pmc-13401710:
Ibrahim Antoun and co-authors wrote a 2026 review asking whether artificial intelligence can speed up care for acute type A aortic dissection. It is a tear in the inner wall of the body's main artery, where every delay raises the death toll. The review's title borrows the emergency mantra that time is aorta.

The authors searched medical databases and society sources through June 2026 for work on AI in diagnosis, imaging, triage, transfer, and surgical activation for this emergency. Delays creep in at recognition, imaging interpretation, interhospital transfer, and operating room activation. AI tools are proposed at each step, reading scans, flagging findings, and tightening team communication. The review weighs peer-reviewed studies, earlier reviews, and guidelines to judge whether the technology genuinely shortens the road to surgery or merely promises to.
pmc-13401810:
Chuchu Zhao and co-authors describe a 2026 case of granulomatous mastitis, a chronic inflammatory breast condition that mimicked infection for months. Their patient was a 24-year-old woman with right breast pain and a growing mass that lasted four months.

She was treated first as a breast abscess, through several antibiotic courses and surgical drainage. Steroid shots into the lesion brought no improvement, while new areas were hit too. A scan suggested an inflammatory lesion, tests stayed negative, and a core biopsy finally showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation, proving granulomatous mastitis. As things worsened despite all that, methotrexate, a drug that damps the immune system, was started, and at about seven weeks she felt broadly better. The authors stress early biopsy when a seeming abscess will not behave like one, and the hard call of when to switch from antibiotics to immune treatment.
pmc-13402010:
Ayodeji S Erubu and co-authors audited whether patients starting mental health medicines at a hospital in South-West Nigeria got the basic checks guidelines call for. Records covered first-contact patients seen from January 2024 through December 2025, judged against NICE and Royal College of Psychiatrists standards. Of 345 patients reviewed, 262 received at least one psychotropic medicine and entered the audit.

Simple bedside checks did well, with weight, vital signs, and movement screening recorded for every patient. Blood and heart tests lagged badly: kidney tests reached only about a quarter of patients, heart tracings about one in nine, and no one had prolactin checked. Inpatients scored far higher than outpatients. The authors call for local protocols, better access to tests, and repeat audits to close the gap.
pmc-13402310:
Konstantinos Kapelios and colleagues present bMINTY, a local web app that keeps the results of high-throughput sequencing studies tidy, searchable, and reusable. Gene studies produce huge result sets, and key facts often scatter across papers, supplements, and repositories, which blocks reuse. Most labs reuse ready gene expression tables rather than rerunning raw data, yet no single portable tool tied those tables to their study details.

bMINTY stores details for studies, assays, and result files, including workflow versions, genome annotation versions, and single-cell identities for cell-level work. Query results export as RO-Crate packages, machine-readable bundles that can ride along as publication supplements next to public analysis code. Kapelios and the team built the tool around FAIR goals: findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable data. The pitch is less new science than better housekeeping for science already done.
pmc-13402610:
Haoyin Zhong and co-authors give chemists a way to time the single steps of the oxygen evolution reaction, the slow half of water splitting that bottlenecks many energy devices. Catalyst design has leaned on bulk traits matched to overall activity, leaving the speed of each elementary step hidden. Their open-circuit voltage-pulse method pauses electron flow to the circuit while hydroxide keeps feeding electrons, isolating the step that forms the OOH intermediate.

Paired with a pulse method timing the OH deprotonation step, the framework shows dopants split the work: iron speeds OOH formation, while manganese speeds deprotonation instead. A nickel iron manganese catalyst built on that split improved both steps at once and performed better overall. The authors offer the step-timing approach as a practical ruler for finding strong electrocatalysts faster and with less guesswork.
pmc-13402810:
Luca Salvi and team asked how cells spot and quiet a brand-new jumping gene they have never met. Their 2026 work puts foreign DNA into fission yeast, Schizosaccharomyces pombe, to watch first-contact defense. Quieting of known jumping genes is well mapped, but spotting of novel invaders had stayed a puzzle.

The new element, called tj1, was hit by RNA interference and heterochromatin quieting, with success hinging on copy number and insertion site. RNA, not DNA, was sensed, and spotting tracked with antisense RNA levels from upstream transcripts. Even non-jumping genes could spark quieting. The authors propose that breaks in normal transcription patterns, rather than a set jumping-gene signal, alert host defenses. The model reframes genome defense in yeast.
pmc-13403010:
Tamas Toth and co-authors report a 600 gram girl born at about 25 weeks whose gut disease tore a hole in her stomach at 24 days old. Neonatal gastric perforation is a rare surgical emergency of premature, extremely low birth weight infants, with high mortality. She had developed necrotizing enterocolitis in her third week, then worsened with a swollen belly and free air inside.

Emergency surgery found a single hole in the back wall of the stomach ringed by dead tissue, exactly where the feeding tube tip sat. Surgeons trimmed the dead edge minimally and closed the hole in two layers. She survived a long intensive care course scarred by repeated sepsis, liver bile stasis, chronic lung disease, and a later adhesive blockage needing a second operation. The authors argue the necrotic margins favor ischemic injury from severe gut disease over tube trauma.
pmc-13404010:
Satoshi Yoneda and co-authors described in 2026 how a focused burn treatment stopped bleeding from neck-of-womb growths in three pregnant women. Such growths in pregnancy raise the risk of late miscarriage and early birth. All three cases looked like pregnancy-type growths on exam and ultrasound.

Doctors seared only the growth surface to stop the bleeding, alongside oral gut-support therapy. Bleeding stopped at once in all three women. The growths then shrank step by step until none could be seen. Each woman went on to deliver at full term. The gentle option deserves wider study, the team says.
pmc-13404310:
Agata J Barszcz and colleagues mapped the molecular network of RBMXL3, a primate-specific RNA-binding protein found mainly in the male gonad. Their 2026 study uses the human seminoma cell line TCam-2, used as a germline model. RBMXL3 function had been little known despite links to sperm formation, cancer, and a newborn breathing disorder. RNA metabolism in sperm development depends on such regulators.

Transcriptome and RNA-binding data showed RBMXL3 drives gene expression changes and alternative splicing, binding a wide range of RNA transcripts. Protein interaction data placed it in RNA metabolism networks, and a retrotransposition assay showed it suppresses LINE-1 jumping gene activity. The paper nominates RBMXL3 as a candidate regulator of human spermatogenesis, while in vivo fertility relevance still needs testing.
pmc-13405610:
Steffany Martins Moreira and colleagues study first foods beyond milk for babies in the western Brazilian Amazon, in a 2026 analysis. Data come from the MINA-Brazil birth cohort in Cruzeiro do Sul, Acre, with 774 children seen at one year and 854 at two years. Diet was captured by a day-long recall at each visit.

Quality indicators follow World Health Organization advice: food variety, meat or egg eating, ultra-processed food and days with no fruit or vegetables. Meat or egg eating reached 79 percent at age one and 89.9 percent at age two in the reported figures. Ultra-processed food was also common, a mixed picture. Social and health factors are modelled in layers from distant to close causes.
pmc-13406310:
Amina McDiarmid argues in a 2026 essay that Alzheimer's drug discovery must look beyond antibody treatments. Approved anti-amyloid immunotherapies clear brain plaques, yet how much real thinking and daily function they save stays disputed. Three named drugs anchor the discussion: aducanumab, lecanemab and donanemab.

Treatment slows decline by roughly twenty to thirty percent in some patient groups, the essay notes, but absolute gains remain modest. Benefit concentrates in early disease with low tau burden. Swelling and bleeding in the brain occur often enough to matter for safety and cost. McDiarmid warns that statistically clear trial results may not translate into meaningful real-world benefit.
pmc-13406810:
Mihaela Zaharie led a 2026 study of preterm babies who developed bloodstream infections caused by Gram-negative bacteria in a specialist newborn unit. The team looked back at cases from 2022 and 2023, covering both infections appearing soon after birth and those starting later.

Later-starting infections were more common, and Klebsiella pneumoniae was the organism found most often. Resistant bacteria were linked to about half the cases, and roughly one baby in four died in hospital. Among survivors checked at 18 to 24 months, about 38 percent showed developmental problems, mostly in language and thinking skills. Being born earlier stood out as the clearest predictor of both death and later impairment, pointing to early treatment and planned follow-up.
pmc-13407810:
Yuan-yuan Zhang and team mapped two decades of research on return of liver cancer after heat ablation. Their 2026 bibliometric work searches Web of Science from 2005 to 2025 for studies of hepatocellular carcinoma return after radiofrequency or microwave ablation, a major driver of long-term survival. The global map and shifting themes had not been charted in full.

Of 3,673 records, 969 met criteria, with yearly output growing fast and China supplying nearly half, forming a leading cluster with Japan and South Korea. Four theme pillars stood out: outlook and joined care, ablation versus resection, technique and safety, and precise image-guided therapy. Recent bursts highlight microwave ablation and head-to-head tests with liver resection. The work gives researchers and funders a map of where ablation-return science is heading.
pmc-13408110:
Morena Pappalardo and team weighed community pharmacists in early skin cancer spotting in Barcelona province. Their 2026 real-world work enrolls 184 pharmacists from 104 pharmacies, plus primary care doctors and skin specialists, to test a screening route. Spotting at-risk people is key for skin cancer screening, yet pharmacist roles alongside doctors and specialists had not been weighed in Spain.

Pharmacists recruited 340 volunteers, gave a risk survey, and checked upper limbs for pigmented spots over 2 millimeters. Among those checked by primary care, 74 were sent to skin specialists, where 15 malignant lesions were confirmed: one melanoma, one squamous cell carcinoma, plus 13 basal cell carcinomas. The work backs pharmacists as a front-line triage layer for skin cancer, while referral and follow-up routes need standard rules.
pmc-13408610:
D Meera Fathima and colleagues used a doll placement test to assess dental anxiety in young children with and without verbal communication challenges. Their 2026 study compares 82 children aged 3 to 7, half with normal verbal skills and half with limited verbal skills, in a miniature dental setup. Children who struggle to speak often feel greater dental fear, yet standard anxiety scales rely on words.

In the limited-verbal group, 82.9 percent chose a doll position signaling a need for parental presence, a significant difference. In the normal-verbal group, 82.9 percent showed clearly positive behavior in the dental chair. Anxiety measured by doll placement correlated with observed behavior in the operatory. The paper supports doll placement as a nonverbal anxiety signal to guide reassurance and parental presence for children with communication challenges.
pmc-13408710:
Steffen Herff and colleagues listen in 2026 to the forearm muscles of twenty-two drummers to learn what years of practice do to the electrical chatter of individual motor units. Surface sensors recorded two wrist muscles while drummers of widely varying experience played a steady one-handed pattern at five speeds. The team extracted the shape of each muscle spike and modelled how it changed with lifetime practice hours.

Experienced players kept steadier timing and struck more evenly between hands, as expected. Their muscle spikes also fired more often, lasted less time, and carried fewer peaks, a signature the authors read as more efficient muscle use rather than simply stronger contraction. The pattern depended on which muscle, which arm, and how fast the tempo ran. The results offer rare physiological evidence that long training refines the motor units themselves.
pmc-13410410:
Hafiza Aasia Malik and colleagues review in 2026 how bacterial membranes are being reshaped into cancer vaccine platforms. A bacterium's outer skin naturally alarms the immune system, which makes it a strong carrier. Engineers can also fix tumor markers onto that skin so the body learns both targets at once.

Forms covered include tiny shed vesicles, emptied bacterial shells, membrane pieces, and blends fused with tumor membranes. Tests in mice with melanoma, lung, breast, and brain tumors showed hotter immune attack inside tumors and help alongside other therapies. New tools, from gene editing to computer-guided antigen choice, speed design. Safety fixes such as softening toxic lipid parts remain central before human use.
pmc-13410610:
Zhouyang Gao and co-workers study in 2026 why some laying hens eat more than their body and eggs seem to need. The gap between actual feed use and expected use, called residual feed intake, reflects inborn metabolic differences. Breeding for a low gap could cut feed costs, yet late laying life was little studied.

Hens matched for weight and egg count were split into low-gap and high-gap groups. Low-gap hens used protein and dry matter better and showed stronger antioxidant defenses. Their gut walls also looked steadier, with firmer seal proteins and calmer immune signals. Chemical profiling of blood and droppings pointed to amino acid, fat, and energy pathways as the main ground of difference.
pmc-13410710:
Nicky Ahadi, Jeeyeon Kim, Daniel Whibley, and Maxwell Barnish weigh in 2026 the evidence that music-based therapy aids recovery in multiple sclerosis. Music methods range from walking to a beat to imagining movement while listening. Small studies have hinted at gains, yet the overall picture was scattered.

Six databases were searched, and 23 studies with 955 participants met the rules for inclusion. Motor function was the outcome checked most often, then quality of life. Beat-cued walking and music-guided movement imagery showed the most steady gains, covering speed, distance, stride, and symmetry of gait. Results for other outcomes stayed murky. Differences in methods and small samples cap how firm any claim can be.
pmc-13410810:
Jiazheng Lin and co-workers build in 2026 a personal genome for a liver cancer patient and use it to hunt tumor changes that standard references miss. Universal reference genomes hide patient-specific variation in repetitive or complex DNA stretches. Their approach assembled both copies of the patient's genome almost completely.

Long-read and chromosome-contact sequencing built paired assemblies from tumor and healthy tissue of the same person. Using the healthy assembly as the reference sharpened read alignment and cut ambiguous matches. Extra small and structural changes surfaced, including some in the hard-to-read centromere regions. Gene activity read by parental copy flagged candidate drivers, and lab tests backed two regulatory suspects for follow-up.
pmc-13412010:
Michael P Dorsch and colleagues report the ManageHF randomized trial in 2026, testing phone-app prompts that coach heart failure patients at home. About 900,000 older Americans are hospitalized for heart failure each year, and missed symptoms or salty diets often send patients back. The app sent just-in-time messages on spotting worsening symptoms and cutting dietary sodium, arranged in a two-by-two design with an active control group.

Recruitment faltered during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the trial stopped early with 62 patients enrolled and 43 finishing twelve weeks. Participants averaged 55 years of age, and most had a weakened heart pump. Too few patients finished for firm conclusions, so the authors stress better recruitment plans for future app trials.
pmc-13412310:
Teresa A Milner and five co-authors trace a brain pathway that may explain blood pressure rises after menopause, in this 2026 mouse study. Menopausal hypertension is common and harmful, and overactive sympathetic nerves seem involved. The hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, a control hub for those nerves, is their focus.

Ovarian failure was induced chemically to mimic post-menopause. In those mice, two weeks of angiotensin infusion raised pressure alongside stronger AMPA GluA1 currents, but not NMDA currents, in the nucleus. That boost ran through an estrogen receptor called GPER1 tied to a scaffolding protein, AKAP150. Male mice reached the same pressure rise yet by a classical kinase route. Estrogen receptor beta drugs changed nothing in the post-menopause animals.
pmc-13412410:
Lai, Liu, Lei, and Chen test, in 2026, whether adding the targeted drug lenvatinib to the dual immunotherapy nivolumab plus ipilimumab fixes that regimen's weak early tumor control in unresectable liver cancer. That flaw cost lives in the first year of the pivotal trial. Their retrospective Taipei series covered 104 patients, 82 on the doublet alone and 22 on the triple combination, with weighting methods to balance the groups.

The triple therapy controlled disease far more often, an 81.8 percent disease control rate against 39.0 percent for the doublet in the analyzed cohort, while responses lasted a similar 21.4 versus 21.8 months once achieved. Median progression-free survival stretched from 3.2 months to 10.2 months with lenvatinib added, and the adjusted hazard ratio of 0.44 confirmed the benefit, though overall survival did not significantly improve. High blood pressure, proteinuria, and mouth sores came more often with the triple regimen, while liver function scores stayed stable.
pmc-13412510:
Cem Terece, Simge Tezel Yozgat, and Volkan Karataşlı compare two stitch materials for cervical cerclage in a 2026 pilot study. Cerclage, a stitch that holds a weak cervix closed during pregnancy, is usually placed with braided polyester, and makers' versions differ in construction. Records covered 22 women who had McDonald cerclage at one centre during 2024 and 2025, split evenly between Mersilene and Uniester sutures.

Delivery timing, maternal complications, and newborn outcomes showed no significant differences between the material groups. Median delivery arrived near 35 weeks in both arms of the study. Operating time ran about three minutes shorter with Uniester, a gap short of statistical significance. Carrying twins emerged as the only independent predictor of early birth in their models.
pmc-13413910:
Bo Zhang, Ronggang Wang, and Feng Wang review in 2026 the state of forward osmosis, a way to clean water by pulling it through a film with a strong draw fluid. No pump pressure is used, so the method saves power and fouls less than reverse osmosis. Drawbacks stay real, though. Flow runs lower, few films are sold, and the draw fluid costs money and power to refresh. Their survey covers film types, draw fluid groups, fouling kinds, and live uses.

Applications span sea water desalting, power from mixed waters, and waste water reuse. Fouling comes in mineral, organic, lump, and germ forms, but lands more gently than in pumped systems. The authors see the field move toward pulling value from water, such as lithium from hot spring brine.
pmc-13415610:
Bruna Paviani and co-authors profile the chemistry of grape pomace, the skins and seeds left after winemaking, from four California varieties in 2026. White wine pomaces from Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc held more leftover sugar and wider sugar chain diversity than red pomaces from Pinot Noir and Merlot. Advanced mass spectrometry identified thirty-nine oligosaccharides, built mainly from six carbon and five carbon sugars.

Two flavanol compounds, catechin and its mirror form epicatechin, made up to half of measured phenolics in Chardonnay pomace and about 45 percent in Pinot Noir. Glucose and fructose dominated the sugar building blocks. The molecular map supports turning this winery residue into valuable ingredients.
pmc-13416110:
Rui Yin and colleagues built an interpretable fault-diagnosis system in 2026 for chemical plants, where black-box models often stall because operators cannot see why they flag a fault. Their Takagi-Sugeno-Kang fuzzy system groups sensor data into information granules that describe data patterns, then pairs those groups with nonlinear rules for each fault type.

Gradient-based tuning sharpened the system, and tests on the Tennessee Eastman process data confirmed it could diagnose faults while staying readable. Plant engineers gain a diagnostic aid they can inspect and trust, rather than a verdict they must take on faith.
pmc-13416810:
Ri-Xin Jiang and co-authors revise the ground beetle genus Broscosoma in China, in a 2026 taxonomic paper. The genus holds 62 known species across western Europe and east Asia, with China especially rich at 45 recorded forms. Their work describes seven species that are new to science, each from a different part of the country.

New species come from Guangdong, Sichuan, Guizhou, Zhejiang, Fujian, Hubei with Chongqing, and Chongqing alone. Drawings show body form and key traits for each one. A full checklist and a distribution map for species outside two major upland regions are included. The authors expect more diversity to emerge from wider work in south China.
pmc-13417710: A 2026 correction notice fixes significance marks in a figure of a study on transdiagnostic cognitive behavioural therapy and long term quality of life across anxiety and depression. The notice is a correction only, stating that one arrow value in the psychological quality of life model wrongly carried significance stars, while another value was missing stars it should have shown. A corrected figure replaces the original, and no results or conclusions are changed.
pmc-13418610:
Devkota and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a toddler whose Wilms tumor, the most common kidney cancer of childhood, first showed up as a blocked bowel. The boy was two and a half years old, with a week of belly pain, swelling, and vomiting. Scans showed a large tumor on the right kidney pressing where the small bowel begins.

Surgeons operated, removing the right kidney and adding a bypass from the stomach to the small bowel. Lab study confirmed stage III disease with favorable cell features. The child healed well and went on to drug treatment and radiation. Most Wilms tumors appear as a painless belly lump, so a blocked bowel as the first sign is rare. Doctors should keep this tumor in mind when a young child has an unexplained bowel block.
pmc-13419310:
Kevin McCarroll and colleagues report a 2026 case where undiagnosed overactive parathyroid glands caused both hip fractures without any fall. An 82-year-old woman arrived unable to bear weight after two months of left hip pain, and imaging showed a displaced left hip fracture plus a healing right hip fracture.

Blood tests showed high calcium and parathyroid hormone with low vitamin D, bone density scores were severely low, and no tumor or adenoma was found, so she received bone-strengthening drugs without surgery. The case reminds doctors to check parathyroid function when older adults break hips without trauma.
pmc-13419410:
Pamela S. Lee and colleagues gather infection prevention experts to test popular myths that keep single-use plastics flowing through hospitals. United States hospitals produce millions of tons of waste each year, much of it plastic from infection control work. Habits held for safety can drive heavy plastic use even when proof behind them is thin.

Eight experts from fields spanning infectious disease, prevention, quality, and sustainability built the list of myths together. A wider survey then asked infection specialists how they judged the same common practices. Each myth was weighed against current published evidence. Naming myths plainly gives hospitals cover to drop wasteful routines that add cost and emissions without making patients safer.
pmc-13420310:
Żurowska and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare eye case in a 76-year-old man treated for sleep apnoea with a CPAP machine. CPAP means a mask that blows air steadily to keep airways open at night. He came to an eye cancer clinic with suspected tumour, plus floaters, flashes, and tunnel-like vision in his left eye. Scans instead showed a large choroidal detachment, meaning fluid had lifted the eye's middle layer.

Eye pressure rose and sight worsened over the first weeks despite steroid and pupil-dilating drops. Doctors added pressure-lowering drops, and over sixteen weeks the detachment slowly settled. No tumour was found at any point. They advise eye teams to consider breathing therapy history when a detachment has no clear cause. The case also shows that careful watching and drops can succeed without surgery.
pmc-13420710:
Beyza Tağraf and colleagues run a randomized trial pairing a plant-rich ketogenic diet with intermittent fasting in early-to-mid Alzheimer's disease. Eating patterns that shift the brain toward ketone fuel may steady failing energy use in this disease. Cognition and brain structure were measured at the start and again at six months.

By a reliable-change yardstick, 93 percent of the diet group held stable, and 7 percent improved. Among controls, 70 percent held stable, and just over 3 percent improved in the same analysis. Group change scores differed firmly in statistical terms. Response tracked each person's metabolic type and brain integrity at entry. The authors present diet-plus-fasting as a candidate support, not a cure, and call for wider trials.
pmc-13421210:
Agostino Chiaravalloti and colleagues mapped blood tau markers against brain sugar metabolism in 2026 among 100 cognitively impaired patients. PET scans show where the brain burns less glucose in Alzheimer disease, and blood phosphorylated tau tests promise a simpler window, yet their voxel-by-voxel correspondence was uncharted.

Plasma p-tau181 and its ratio to amyloid tracked lower glucose use mainly in temporal brain regions, with the ratio measure most consistent, including in the 58 patients with spinal-fluid-confirmed Alzheimer disease. Clinicians gain a blood marker that mirrors the brain's metabolic map in the regions Alzheimer disease hits first.
pmc-13421310:
Abhinav Ayyadevara and ten colleagues write to the editor in 2026 about a drug target in Ph-like B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. This high-risk subtype relapses often. Three-year survival sits near 65 percent. They focus on BRG1, a motor protein of the SWI/SNF chromatin complex that early B cells need.

In solid tumours, losing a related gene makes cancers depend on BRG1's partner protein, yet blood cancers show the reverse pattern: they depend on BRG1 itself. The team's experiments found this leukaemia subtype selectively sensitive to BRG1 blockade. They present that sensitivity as a therapeutic vulnerability worth exploiting, since options after relapse remain poor.
pmc-13421610:
Angeliki Margoni, Kostas A Papavassiliou and Athanasios G Papavassiliou argue, in a 2026 paper, that care for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease should watch for kidney cancer as well as kidney failure. The disease affects roughly one person in a thousand. It is the leading inherited cause of end-stage kidney failure. Observational data also link it to about double the usual risk of renal cell carcinoma.

The authors caution that the risk estimate rests on mixed datasets, and that intensive scanning of cystic kidneys may simply find more cancers. They sketch the biological steps that could carry a cystic kidney toward cancer and propose risk modelling with a multistep, precision surveillance programme. Their aim is proportionate vigilance rather than alarm.
pmc-13422010:
Anders Thorsted and co-authors model how depemokimab, an ultra-long-acting antibody drug, moves through the body and lowers blood eosinophils in asthma and chronic sinus disease with nasal polyps. The drug targets interleukin-5 and is designed for twice-yearly dosing. Their 2026 analysis pools data from three early-phase and four phase III trials.

The pharmacokinetic analysis included 961 participants and the combined analysis 1,324 participants. The model predicted a half-life of 47 days with negligible build-up between doses. A single 100 milligram dose cut blood eosinophil counts to under a quarter of baseline, and levels stayed suppressed across the 26-week dosing interval, with a small rise at the end. No patient factors required dose adjustment. The authors conclude the modelling supports twice-yearly 100 milligram dosing.
pmc-13422810:
Megumi Hazumi leads a thirteen-author team following a Japanese community cohort for nineteen years, in a 2026 study, to test whether an irregular daily rhythm predicts earlier death. Social rhythm — the regularity of sleep, meals and activity — had been suspected of mattering, yet long-term evidence on specific causes of death was scarce.

Nearly one hundred thousand adults aged forty-five to seventy-four rated their rhythm at entry. Those calling it irregular died at consistently higher rates at every checkpoint, with a nineteen-year risk about a tenth higher in relative terms. Death by illness and accidental death both rose; suicide risk was elevated only at some horizons. National death records supplied the outcomes. The authors argue rhythm regularity belongs in preventive health thinking.
pmc-13423310:
Yacoby-Halevi and colleagues mined the United States FDA adverse event database from 2010 to 2024. They checked the safety of ticagrelor in adults aged 75 and older. Ticagrelor is a potent blood-thinning drug used after heart attacks. Its reported side effects were compared against clopidogrel, an older alternative. The comparison ran separately in younger and older patients.

The analysis covered 6,476 ticagrelor-related reports. Of those, 1,681, or 26 percent, involved older adults taking the drug. In that older group, ticagrelor showed no excess reporting of breathlessness, brain bleeding, complete heart block, or gout. That held against younger users. Acute kidney injury was the sole event reported more often in older adults. Its reporting odds ratio was 2.3, against 0.6 in younger patients. Gastrointestinal bleeding and several other bleeding events were reported less often in both age groups.
pmc-13423810:
Zeyuan Sun and a team of co-authors linked newborn brain scans to toddler development after very preterm birth in a 2026 paper. Babies born very early face high risk of developmental delay, but early signs of which child will struggle are scarce. The team studied MRI scans of 352 such infants taken near their due dates.

Outcomes were checked at eighteen to twenty-four months with a standard developmental scale. Toddlers with motor delays had smaller volume in the left rear cerebellum back at term age, even when other domains were accounted for. No clear volume differences appeared for thinking or language delays. The authors single out the cerebellum as an early marker for motor risk.
pmc-13424110:
Zhouen Peng and six colleagues test whether the support plate inside a basketball shoe, carbon fibre, nylon, or none, changes leg loading and muscle work during game movements. Twenty recreational male college players performed jumps, 45-degree cuts, and lateral shuffles in one standard shoe fitted three ways, while force plates and muscle sensors recorded the action.

Across tasks, outside forces and joint moments at the toe, ankle, and knee stayed broadly similar whatever the plate. Muscle activity differed only in narrow spots, most clearly in the thigh muscles during cutting, and joint co-contraction ratios held steady. The authors conclude plate material tunes feel and support without materially raising external loads, a useful boundary for shoe designers.
pmc-13424210:
Noora Said and three co-authors revisit, with post-pandemic calm, what is actually known about COVID-19 and diabetes. Early in the pandemic, diabetes stood out as a top predictor of severe illness and death. Later reports of diabetes appearing after infection raised a new possibility. Influence might run in both directions.

Their review weighs proposed mechanisms, from viral effects in the pancreas to changes in insulin-sensitive tissues. It also audits the big pooled analyses on new type 1 and type 2 diabetes after infection. Strengths and weaknesses of the underlying studies get explicit treatment. The authors separate findings that survived scrutiny from those born of the rush, giving clinicians a steadier map of the two-way link.
pmc-13424310:
Yeseul Kim leads a nineteen-author effort to find diagnoses for children with developmental delay or intellectual disability whose standard exome sequencing came back empty. Two newer technologies were applied to 87 such children: optical genome mapping, which photographs whole chromosomes for large rearrangements, and complete long-read sequencing, which reads long DNA stretches directly.

Six children gained a pathogenic or likely pathogenic answer, four large structural changes and two single-letter changes. The mapping method added diagnoses in 4.71% of cases and the long reads in 6.98%, each catching changes the other missed. Disputed cases were checked with further sequencing, and one deep intron variant was proven harmful in a lab assay. The authors propose a stepwise diagnostic route.
pmc-13424810:
Kurniawan and colleagues present a 2026 case of a baby girl with suspected Cornelia de Lange syndrome. The condition shapes growth, the face, and the limbs before birth. A twenty-eight-year-old mother was referred during pregnancy because her baby measured small. Ultrasound showed shortened forearm bones in both arms, slow growth, and excess fluid around the baby.

An elective caesarean at thirty-seven weeks delivered a girl weighing 1,446 grams. She showed the syndrome's facial signs, including thick eyebrows, a short nose with a sunken bridge, and a long, smooth groove above the lip, alongside the arm malformations. The authors review how such limb findings on prenatal ultrasound can point to the syndrome early. They stress that its severity varies widely, so prognosis depends on which organs and symptoms a given child has.
pmc-13424910:
Kawata and colleagues examined in 2026 whether a blood protein called transthyretin, measured before surgery, predicts recurrence after curative removal of stage I to III colorectal cancer. Transthyretin reflects both nutrition and inflammation and falls quickly when health declines. The team studied 536 patients treated at one hospital from 2014 to 2024, using sex-specific cutoff values for low levels.

Patients with low transthyretin had clearly worse recurrence-free survival than those with high levels. Low levels more than doubled the risk of recurrence after other factors were counted. The signal was not equal across ages, though. It was strongest in younger patients and faded steadily in older ones, and levels ran lower in women and dropped with age. The authors say the test helps most when read with the patient's age and sex in mind.
pmc-13426110:
Sofia Casado-Hoces, Delia Gonzalez-Tejedor, and Rebeca Martin-Velasco review the skin signs of diabetes in a 2026 paper. High blood sugar harms skin cells directly, and skin changes show in over thirty percent of patients at diagnosis and in nearly all over the illness. Some marks flag poor sugar control in known patients; others can be the first sign of the disease.

The review sorts lesions by cause: insulin resistance marks, infections, the disease's own damage, long term complications, and reactions to drugs or devices such as pumps and glucose sensors. Knowing the map, the authors argue, sharpens daily care and speeds treatment.
pmc-13426210:
Dianzhi Feng and colleagues evaluated planting performance of sandy soil solidified with biopolymer and plant fiber in a 2026 environmental study. Yellow River silt mixed with 1.5 percent xanthan gum and 0.6 percent jute fiber formed the growing medium, tested at three compaction levels with oat as the indicator plant. High biopolymer content can hinder growth, so the team proposed a layered structure of residual soil, solidified soil, a seed layer, and raw soil cover.

That structure produced germination above 85 percent, with moderate compaction growing best, soil temperature between 23 and 28 degrees, and moisture holding between 10 and 20 percent across depths. The design counters surface hardening while improving water and heat movement.
pmc-13426410:
Galí and colleagues showed in 2026 that winter convection in the Labrador and Irminger Seas injects fresh surface carbon deep into the ocean, a route missing from most carbon budgets. How much carbon the deep ocean receives matters for climate accounting. Drifting robot profilers in those seas caught repeated green pigment signals a kilometer down during strong mixing winters from 2014 to 2017, evidence that surface plankton were being carried down whole.

The deep particles looked like fresh plankton material, distinct from the usual sinking crumbs. Models tied the deep supply to how much water convection stirred. In strong years, mixing delivered roughly a third to nearly half of the combined carbon supply to the deep layer, rivaling sinking itself.
pmc-13427110:
Junge and co-authors describe the first nickel complexes holding tin and lead analogues of alkynes. Alkynes are the carbon triple-bond units found all through catalysis. Their heavy versions are extremely rare for the heavier elements of group 14. Direct mixing of the tin or lead dimers with a nickel starting material failed. So the team found another route.

Instead, they generated the heavy dimers inside nickel's coordination sphere. They used a reductive group elimination, with hydrogen release from tin hydride precursors bound to the metal. Structural measurements combined with computations showed the products are best described as sigma-complexes. In those, the metal binds the single bond between the two heavy atoms side-on. The authors call this a new bonding mode in organometallic chemistry. It expands how chemists can think about activating heavy-element bonds at transition metal centers for future catalysis.
pmc-13427810:
Jinbo Luo and co-authors search, in a 2026 study, for body-clock genes that matter in fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. Daily rhythm genes help run the liver, and their disruption may feed fat buildup and inflammation. The team combined two public datasets of liver samples with a list of 248 rhythm-related genes. Statistical filtering and network analysis narrowed the field to genes that shifted together with disease.

Machine learning settled on three key genes, named SOCS2, FBXO27, and HMMR. A scoring chart built from them separated patients from controls in both datasets. Immune cell checks tied two of the genes to mast cell activity, a clue about inflammation in the liver. Drug prediction pointed to compounds that might act on these genes. The work stays computational, yet it hands wet-lab teams a short, testable list.
pmc-13427910:
Jan Sönke Englbrecht and colleagues examine how a new German rule changed brain-death testing for potential organ donors on heart-lung support. Under the update, doctors skilled with ECMO must attend breath testing, and blood-flow methods no longer count as backup tests on venoarterial ECMO.

At University Hospital Münster, every potential donor on that support from 2021 to 2024 was compared before and after the rule. Eight people were found, brain death was set in seven, and four donations went ahead, equal to 15 percent of all donors in the period. Transplant teams get a plain account of what the stricter rule costs in practice.
pmc-13428210:
Mehran Mottahedi and co-authors report, in a 2026 case, emergency heart surgery during pregnancy in a teenager with Marfan syndrome. Marfan weakens the aorta, and pregnancy adds strain that can tear or balloon it. Their patient was 19, pregnant for the first time, and 15 weeks along when palpitations led to scans. Imaging showed a giant bulge of the aortic root and upper aorta, a leaking valve, and a weakened heart pump.

After counseling on risks to mother and baby, the team replaced the root and valve in a Bentall operation without ending the pregnancy. Heavy bleeding forced a delayed closing of the chest, plus transfusion support. Scans afterward showed the new valve working and the baby still alive. She went home on day 11, a rare outcome the authors credit to close teamwork.
pmc-13428310:
Lívia Maria Martins Aragão and co-authors pool, in a 2026 review, trials of light therapy for a chronic mouth condition called oral lichen planus. The disease causes sore, sometimes ulcered patches inside the mouth and has no cure. Standard steroid treatment helps but brings side effects with long use. Photobiomodulation uses low-level light to calm tissue without drugs. The team searched seven databases through March 2025 and kept 15 clinical trials.

Combined results showed light therapy eased pain slightly more than standard drug care. Disease severity and anxiety scores did not differ clearly between approaches. Light therapy did bring higher rates of complete healing of the mouth lining and fewer returns of lesions in the erosive form. No side effects were reported for the light treatment. Stronger trials are still wanted before firm guidance follows.
pmc-13428610:
Abdullah Aman, Ahmed Raza, and Shahzadi Gulfishan write to the editor about how sports heart screening in children should be judged. A recent study screened young athletes with ECG and ultrasound at a referral center and found cardiac issues in 9.3% of them. The letter praises the topic and then questions the design. A single hospital-based sample of referred children can inflate rates against the general athletic population.

No control group of screened children with normal findings was included for contrast. Screening yields swing with who is screened and where, the writers note. They urge broader risk detection goals past sudden death alone.
pmc-13428710:
Jessica L. Fernandes and co-authors explore, in a 2026 study, how anxiety disorders pair with body chemistry during the pandemic years. More than 300 million people live with an anxiety disorder, and oxidative stress may play a part. Oxidative stress means harm from reactive molecules outruns the body's defenses. The team compared 116 adults with an anxiety diagnosis against 234 adults without one, recruited in Brazil between September 2020 and July 2021.

Standard scales scored anxiety, low mood, stress, daily rhythms, thinking, and day-to-day function. The anxiety group fared worse on all of them, with more stress and more broken daily rhythms. Blood tests showed lower total antioxidant capacity in the anxiety group at first pass. Once the team corrected for the many tests run, that blood gap no longer held up. The authors keep oxidation as a thread worth more study, while the mood and rhythm findings stand on firmer ground.
pmc-13429110:
Qiu, Wu, and Liu reviewed in 2026 urinary tract infections among hospital patients with gynaecological cancers at a hospital in Meizhou, China. Such infections can halt cancer treatment, stretch stays, and raise costs. The team pulled records for 659 patients treated in 2024, covering tumor type, treatment, and infection details, and screened the data for risk factors with layered statistics.

Qiu found cervical cancer was the largest group, followed by womb lining and ovarian cancers. Just over half the patients had a ureter stent placed, and nearly three in ten kept a urine catheter for a week or more. The infection rate was about six in a hundred patients. Three factors raised risk on their own: a catheter kept a week or longer, which roughly quadrupled the odds, obesity, and having fewer than two deliveries. The authors use the findings to target prevention at catheter care and high-risk patients.
pmc-13429810:
McClure and five co-authors study how an injected antibiotic reaches the tear film of dogs in this two thousand twenty-six paper. The drug, cefovecin, is given under the skin and lasts for weeks, so the team asked whether enough of it seeps into tears to fight eye infections.

Six beagles received one injection after mild conjunctivitis was induced, and tear samples were collected for two weeks. Inflamed eyes held far more drug than calm ones, and levels stayed detectable the whole period. Tears beat the amounts needed to stop streptococcus bacteria throughout, helped against staphylococcus for a few days, but never reached levels for pseudomonas. The findings guide vets treating bacterial eye ulcers in dogs.
pmc-13430710:
Yang Yang and colleagues search chrysanthemum genomes for drought tolerance, a trait that limits one of the world's most popular cut flowers as climates dry. The genetic basis and causal genes for withstanding water shortage were largely unknown.

Two hundred cut-flower lines, typed at 330,710 high-quality DNA markers, were analysed with a multi-locus genome-wide method. Single-environment work found 43 stable marker-trait links, while multi-environment work added 18 stable links and 115 interactions. Eleven nearby genes matched known drought regulators in other plants, including WRKY57, MYB121, and GH3.6, giving breeders named targets.
pmc-13430810:
Weicong Fan and Xinlei Ma study how an enzyme, NAT10, drives aggression in bowel cancer by tagging a message RNA. NAT10 adds an acetyl mark called ac4C to RNA, a change seen across tumours, and the team asks how it steers bowel cancer growth.

High NAT10 in bowel cancer was first spotted in a public gene data set, then ac4C levels were checked by dot blot and NAT10 levels by a gene test. Cell growth, spread, invasion, and movement were measured, and the link between NAT10 and SERPINA1 was checked by binding tests and a reporter assay. The work traces a chemical tag from enzyme to target to tumour behaviour.
pmc-13431010:
Mukoma and colleagues reported in 2026 on the views of biokineticists, specialists in exercise therapy, about early detection of long-term diseases in rural South Africa. Diseases such as diabetes and heart disease hit rural areas hard because care is far away and diagnosis comes late. The team interviewed ten registered biokineticists, chosen on purpose, about screening, referrals, teamwork, and barriers in the health system.
