pmc-13535210:
Elyssa Grogan and co-authors argue that two new federal quality measures for hospital boarding work at cross purposes in this 2026 paper. Boarding, holding admitted patients in the emergency department for want of a bed, endangers patients, above all older ones. Medicare's agency has answered with two measures born in different programs.

One measure asks hospitals to attest they have protocols to cut boarding for older patients. The other will make hospitals report the share of boarded patients overall. Because the pair grew up apart, their definitions drift, inviting uneven counting and gaming. The authors urge the agency to align the two, and to split the reporting measure by age so it reinforces the older-adult focus. Older patients, they note, are the group boarding harms most, and the measures should say so consistently.
pmc-13535410:
Toni Choueiri and nine co-authors lay out a phase 3 trial for kidney cancer that returns after immune care, in a 2026 conference abstract. A post-surgery immune drug is now standard for high-risk patients, yet some still relapse. No drug has been tested head-on for that moment. The trial pits a pair of drugs against the current go-to single drug in patients whose cancer came back during or after that early immune care.

One arm joins an oxygen-sensor blocker with a broad kinase blocker. The other arm uses the standard kinase blocker alone. The study is open-label and runs at many centers, with entry open to adults with the clear-cell form of the disease. The pair's promise rests on strong phase 2 hints in related settings. Results will set the care rule for a growing patient group.
pmc-13537510:
Bethany Boyd and a large team describe a movement disorder in Dachshund dogs in a 2026 study of sixty-two cases from 2017 to 2025. The disorder brings sudden episodes of stiff, twisted movement, and it had not been described in this breed before. The team gathered records from many clinics and added a survey of owners.

Most dogs first showed signs at about three years old. Episodes often moved from limb to limb and could bring tremors, drooling, vomiting, or lip smacking. All cases fit one known type of the disorder. A gluten-free diet was the most common response, and about half of the dogs with follow-up had fewer or milder episodes.
pmc-13538410:
Estelle Barbier and co-authors hunt for drug targets in compulsive alcohol use in a 2026 rat study. Only some drinkers slide into addiction, drinking on despite punishment. Earlier work from the team tied that slide, in male rats, to a set of neurons in the central amygdala, a brain hub for threat and reward.

The team read gene activity in single nuclei from that hub. Changes clustered in a few neuron types, including the key set. Network analysis flagged a growth factor receptor, FGFR1, as a druggable driver of the altered pattern. Silencing that receptor in the key neurons cut punishment-resistant drinking. A drug that blocks the receptor, given body-wide, did the same. The receptor now stands as a candidate target.
pmc-13538510:
Marios Impraimakis, Daniel Vazquez, and Feiyu Zhou add a trust layer to fast object detection in a 2026 study. Detectors label objects quickly yet hide whether each confidence score deserves trust in blurry or blocked scenes. A curve-based network modeled trust from seven shape and meaning features tied to each detection, keeping every feature influence visible. A vision-language model also captioned scenes without disturbing the trust layer.

Tests on a large public photo set and campus images showed the layer correctly flagging low-trust calls under blur, blocking, or weak texture. Smooth feature maps revealed exactly when confidence stood on solid ground and when it wobbled. The authors offer the system as a transparent perception piece for self-driving and mixed-media tools that must justify acceptance or review.
pmc-13538710:
Sunyong Park, Kwang Cheol Oh, and DaeHyun Kim compare heating fuels for Korean greenhouses across climates in a 2026 cost assessment. Diesel, raw biomass, and two grades of heat-treated biomass were weighed for seven horticultural regions and three crops with distinct warmth needs. Fuel use and yearly cost were modeled with price sensitivity, equal efficiency, transport distance, and break-even checks.

Heating demand ran lowest in the warmest region and highest in the coldest for every crop, rising from strawberry to tomato to pepper. The most heavily treated biomass needed least fuel and cost least across all crops and regions under baseline terms. Its edge survived equal efficiency and transport tests, yet price mapping showed rivals winning in many price corners. The authors frame results as screening guidance, not farm bill forecasts.
pmc-13539210:
Nine researchers build a precision dosing model for a transplant drug in a paper from 2026. Tacrolimus prevents liver rejection but has a narrow safe range. A gene called CYP3A5 varies in both donor and recipient and changes how fast the drug clears. The team analyzed more than one hundred patients with thousands of drug level readings. They compared model structures and searched for factors that shift clearance.

A standard two-compartment model fit well without exotic kinetics. Combined donor and recipient gene types cut clearance in steps. An antifungal drug lowered clearance by a third, while a steroid raised it slightly. Simulations produced tailored dose ranges for each setting. The authors offer an algorithm for model-guided dosing.
pmc-13539710:
Daniel W Nebert, Zijuan Liu, and Vasilis Vasiliou argue in a 2026 invited review that self-copying lipid droplets preceded genomes at life's origin. Evidence hints the last universal ancestor already carried a sizable genome surprisingly soon after Earth formed, during an era of molten surfaces and heavy bombardment. The puzzle is how fragile molecules survived such violence long enough to evolve.

Under a lipid-first view, tiny fat droplets that copy themselves could have crowded deep sea vents and turbulent surface waters within Earth's first few hundred million years. Acting as protective capsules, they would shelter early nucleic acids and proteins while evolution proceeded inside. The authors frame today's human genome as the culmination of over four billion years of that process, driven by shifting pressures to eat, escape, and breed.
pmc-13539810:
Tom Osborn and ten co-authors present a 2026 study validating a ten-question survey on harmful childhood experiences for young people in Kenya. Such experiences are tied to later mental illness, yet most measurement work comes from wealthier countries.

Data came from 2,842 students aged 11 to 25 at 42 secondary schools across four Kenyan counties. Statistical checks supported a two-part structure for the questionnaire, and higher scores tracked with more depression, more anxiety, and more bullying. The link with bullying ran stronger among boys. The authors call for care that recognises past trauma, plus more study of what protects young people against these effects.
pmc-13539910:
Cheng and colleagues pilot a combined look at kidneys, toxins, and thinking in chronic kidney disease. Their 2026 study enrols twelve outpatients with stage three to five disease and early cognitive decline, none on dialysis. The team measured two uremic toxins that build up as kidneys fail, indoxyl sulfate and p-cresyl sulfate, alongside computerised cognitive tests and brain MRI scans.

Both toxin levels rose as kidney filtration fell, though with only twelve patients those correlations were not statistically firm. One clear signal appeared: better filtration tracked with stronger strategy use on a spatial working memory task, a correlation of about 0.70 that did reach significance. No clear link emerged between thinking scores and the severity of artery narrowing in the brain scans. The authors present the work as a pilot, mapping which measures deserve a properly powered follow-up study.
pmc-13540110:
Jameson Mori and co-authors test whether a deer disease stays detectable as tissue rots in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Chronic wasting disease is a prion disease of deer and kin, tracked through lymph node tests. Samples from the field often arrive in poor shape, and one standard test needs intact tissue structure.

The team stored known positive lymph nodes from wild white-tailed deer at two temperatures for up to twelve months. The other standard test, ELISA, needs no intact structure, only mashed tissue. It still found the prions in every node after a full year of decay at both temperatures, though rates within groups varied over time. The authors say the test can support disease tracking even with badly degraded samples.
pmc-13540510:
Rujuan Dai and four colleagues examine, in a 2026 mouse study, an unusual class of T cells that pile up in lupus yet stay poorly understood. These double negative T cells carry neither of the two usual surface markers, CD4 or CD8.

Deleting a gene called Egr2 in the lymphocytes of lupus-prone mice sharply shrank the main double negative population. The deletion also changed which inflammatory signals the cells produced and normalised several surface markers toward healthy levels. Single-cell sequencing showed distinct cell clusters shifting with the deletion. Production of these cells fell both in the thymus and from mature cells in culture, placing EGR2 at two stages of their making.
pmc-13540810:
Yixuan Ma and five colleagues review, in a 2026 single-centre study, short-term results of blinatumomab for high-risk B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in China. The drug links T cells to leukaemia cells bearing CD19, and trial success needed real-world confirmation in this harder-to-treat group.

Twenty-nine patients received cycles lasting one to four weeks. After a single cycle, measurable residual disease had vanished in about eighty-three percent of patients. Every patient with the Ph-like subtype cleared disease, while results weakened sharply for two genetic patterns: a T315I change in the BCR::ABL1 fusion and an E2A::PBX1 rearrangement. Serious blood toxicity touched nearly half the cohort.
pmc-13540910:
Majd Abdullah Kalloumeh and five colleagues review, in a 2026 systematic review, how orthodontists keep upper front teeth from tipping too far while pulling them backward into space left by extracted premolars. Protruding upper incisors are a frequent problem, and trials disagreed on the best mechanics.

Twenty randomised trials with 568 patients aged twelve to thirty-five were pooled. Every technique tipped the incisor crowns backward significantly, with loop-based mechanics tipping slightly more than sliding mechanics, a gap too small to matter clinically. Pulling all front teeth at once versus in two steps showed no clear difference. Evidence on vertical movement was patchy and weak, the authors report.
pmc-13541610:
Feride Neva Yüngül and Seda Keskin used machine learning to hunt gas-sorting membranes that beat the usual limits. Published in 2026, the study paired tiny-scale mock-ups with learning models to forecast gas flow through 104,196 mixed-matrix membranes. Plastic-only membranes must trade flow for choosiness, and testing every metal-organic frame mix by mock-up costs too much.

Mock-ups supplied gas uptake and spread data for 3,982 made frameworks and 4,701 dreamed-up ones. Three learning models then forecast flow for four gases and were checked against both mock-ups and lab measures. Many mixes beat the old upper bounds with very high carbon dioxide flow, and framework shape and chemistry steered results most. Readers get a fast route to top films for natural gas cleaning, flue gas work, and hydrogen capture.
pmc-13542010:
Qiyuan Chen, Jiali Yang, and their co-authors review how tiny antenna like structures on cancer cells may help tumors spread. Their 2026 review concerns primary cilia, small signaling compartments on the cell surface whose presence changes with cell state. Spreading cancer cells must change identity, survive after tearing free from their base, and keep the ability to seed new tumors.

Evidence from breast models links some identity shifting states to more cilia and to signals that support stem like traits and treatment resistance. Ciliary signals also cross pathways for adhesion and survival after detachment. The authors caution that these networks are not specific to cilia, and direct proof that cilia cause survival after detachment is still thin. The review maps a possible unifying thread in metastasis.
pmc-13542110:
Kaitlin Merkowsky and colleagues expose mice in a 2026 study. The mice were female. Exposures were glyphosate weedkiller, bacterial lipopolysaccharide, or both. The goal was to test lung inflammation from farm air. Women in agriculture breathe dust and pesticides daily. Most inhalation research has used male animals.

Twenty mice got nose-delivered treatments for five days. The combined exposure gave the worst picture. Airways grew tighter, and inflammatory signals rose. More cells flooded the air spaces. Airway lining damage showed on special X-ray images. Those images came from a synchrotron facility. Glyphosate alone did far less harm. The authors suggest adaptation may begin within five days.
pmc-13542210:
Nan Li and colleagues tied age-related Y chromosome loss to death risk after major heart attacks. Published in 2026, the study tracked 928 men treated with urgent artery-opening procedures for ST-elevation heart attacks. Y loss in blood cells, common with aging, was already linked to heart disease, but its role right after such attacks was murky.

Over a median near-four-year follow-up, 93 men died. Men with Y loss in at least 18 percent of blood cells faced roughly double to two-and-a-half times the death risk at one, two, and three years versus men below that line. Age and other factors were allowed for. The link held for men without a prior attack but not for those with one. The authors present high Y loss as a new risk-sorting marker after such attacks.
pmc-13543010:
Kaijia Zhao and a large team of co-authors study how other ills and poor nutrition, alone and joined, shape outlook for cancer patients. Both are common as people age and chronic disease spreads. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Data came from a large multi center cohort of near thirteen thousand cancer patients in China. Other ill burden was scored by a known index, and poor nutrition by a global rule set. Most patients had poor nutrition, and most had a high other ill burden. The two linked firmly only in the earliest cancer stage. The authors then weigh how each, and both together, track survival, short term death, long stays, and costs.
pmc-13543610:
Aby Charles and colleagues published a 2026 education study using a simulated trauma ultrasound module to teach abdominal anatomy to first-year medical students. The module rehearsed the EFAST scan, the emergency ultrasound survey used after road accidents, under an emergency physician's supervision. Two cohorts, of ninety-one and ninety-seven students, took knowledge tests before and after on ultrasound use, clinical reasoning, and anatomy, and joined focus groups about the experience.

Scores rose by about thirty-one percent overall, with the largest gains in ultrasound and clinical-scenario questions and a smaller, real gain in anatomy. One cohort improved by over forty percent and the other by over twenty-one percent. Students welcomed the hands-on format and reported clear educational value. Learning anatomy through a simulated emergency, the authors argue, ties structure to purpose from the very first year of training.
pmc-13543910:
Richard Dzeha and Owusu Amponsah published a 2026 retrospective analysis of measles cases and vaccine coverage in one district of Ghana, covering 2019 to 2024. Measles can be prevented by vaccination, yet it still flares where coverage dips. The team set out to chart the disease run and the two-dose vaccine schedule.

They worked from district surveillance and immunization records, six years of them. Over one hundred sixty suspected cases were logged, and about a sixth were confirmed by laboratory test. Two in three suspected cases were in children under five. Suspected counts peaked in the middle of the run; confirmed counts peaked a year later. The first vaccine dose reached its target in only one year of six. The second dose fell short in four of six years. Dropout from the first to the second dose ran above one in ten in four years, then eased.
pmc-13544710:
Kuperstein and co-authors look for hidden heart damage in patients with blunt traumatic brain injury. A blow to the brain can stun the heart, but echo measures can miss it: most such patients keep a normal ejection fraction. The team reviewed 105 adults scanned within two days of admission at one trauma center, excluding those with heart disease. They focused on fractional shortening, a measure of how much the heart's main chamber narrows.

Twenty-three patients had low fractional shortening, and in most of them the ejection fraction still looked preserved. That low-shortening group stayed longer in intensive care, died more often in hospital, and needed skull surgery more often. Bleeding under the brain's surface layer was their most common scan finding. The authors propose the simpler measure as a warning flag the standard one misses. The study is retrospective and single-center, so the flag needs prospective testing.
pmc-13545010:
Rachel Maina and ten co-authors present a 2026 study testing whether a broad cognitive test battery works for older adults in Kenya. Dementia screening tools built abroad often fit local language and culture poorly. The team adapted a battery spanning memory, attention, fluency, and visual skills, on paper and tablet.

The tests were translated into Swahili, checked by back translation, and tuned with community input. They then went to 148 adults aged 45 to 79 who showed no cognitive impairment. Completion ran high and users judged the tests relevant and welcome. Participants asked for simpler wording, short breaks, and free choice of language. The paper maps the battery's internal structure.
pmc-13545110:
Daniel Rodrigo Serbena and co-authors pooled fifty-three studies on AI for neuroblastoma, a childhood nerve cancer, in a 2026 review. The team searched five databases and sorted models into plain machine learning and hybrid nomograms that marry statistics with clinical facts. The questions were diagnosis, risk grouping, outlook, and gene traits.

Machine learning edged radiologists on telling this cancer from look-alikes, though not by a clear margin. Hybrid nomograms grouped risk well, and AI nomograms and gene signatures beat classic outlook markers on paper. Predicting chemo response stayed below clinical usefulness everywhere. Only a third of models reported calibration, and a quarter had any outside check. The authors call the field promising but premature, and urge prospective trials in children before bedside use.
pmc-13545610:
Duo Sun and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how a nuclear medicine scan of the lymph system performs in kaposiform hemangioendothelioma, a rare vascular tumor seen mostly in infants and young children. The scan, lymphoscintigraphy, traces lymph flow and can reveal blockage and swelling. Records covered 25 patients, nearly all with a tumor on a limb.

Abnormal scans appeared in 22 of the 24 limb cases, and every abnormal case showed lymph stasis inside the tumor, with swelling only on the tumor side. Flow looked restricted in about two thirds of abnormal cases. Among six patients scanned again later, five showed no real improvement in drainage. The authors see the scan as useful for diagnosis and for following lasting swelling.
pmc-13546010:
Dolores Lopez Bernal, Gines Gea Martinez, and Jose Javier Garcia-Medina run a 2026 pilot study of ozonated oil drops around cataract surgery. Each of 33 patients had one eye on the oil drops and the other eye on standard care, across 60 eyes in all. Drops ran from three days before surgery to three weeks after.

No infections arose in either group, and most eye surface scores matched at three weeks and three months. Fewer oil-eye patients felt a gritty eye at three weeks, though the gap was not firm in test terms. All patients found the drops easy to bear, so larger trials are warranted.
pmc-13546210:
Donnenfeld and co-authors report real-world results for two enhanced single-focus lenses implanted at cataract surgery in the United States. The lenses stretch the range of sharp focus a little beyond a standard implant, aiming at useful mid-range sight. Six surgeons contributed cases: 141 eyes from 84 patients, split between the plain lens and its astigmatism-correcting twin.

At the last check, sharp corrected distance vision was reached by about ninety-seven and ninety-five percent of the two groups. Uncorrected mid-range vision at the set level reached about seventy-seven and ninety-three percent, and every patient reached it with both eyes together. No serious side effects appeared in the records, and the surgeons rated their experience well. The authors call the results a good real-world showing.
pmc-13546710:
Maksuda Aktar and co-authors fed a Bangladeshi crossbred duck, the BAU Black and White, four different protein levels in 2026 to find the ration that grows the best birds. Starting with 264 day-old ducklings, the groups received feed containing protein from about 16.5 percent up to 21 percent. Weight, feed use, blood measures, carcass traits, and meat quality were recorded through ten weeks of age.

The middle-high ration, near 19.5 percent protein, gave the heaviest birds, the fastest daily gain, and the most efficient feed conversion, along with the best carcass and breast meat weights. Meat differed mainly in water loss and color, and blood counts were mostly unchanged. The authors recommend that protein level for raising this duck.
pmc-13546810:
Jinglei Tan and Caiqiang Chen test a stem cell secretion gel to speed burn wound healing in rats. The gel comes from bone marrow stem cells pretreated with berberine, a natural plant compound with antibacterial, anti inflammatory, and vessel growth traits. Conditioned medium carries the healing signals without transplanting live cells.

Burned rats receive placebo gel, standard stem cell medium gel, berberine pretreated medium gel, or a standard silver cream. The pretreated gel closes wounds fastest, with better skin regrowth, more ordered collagen, and higher capillary density at day 21. Wound tissue shows raised collagen levels and activation of a known growth signaling pathway. The results support pretreated cell medium as a burn therapy candidate.
pmc-13547210:
Movahed, Toosi, and Nael teach feature selection to adapt while a model learns. Their 2026 paper tackles multi-label learning in high-dimensional data. Items often carry several labels at once here. Redundant and noisy features drag accuracy down badly. Standard selection methods pick features once and freeze them.

Their framework, called PG-GFE, treats selection as a staged decision process. A mixed graph links features, labels, and data instances together. A graph neural network scores each feature's reliability live. Uncertainty estimates feed those scores throughout training. An evolutionary step then removes weak features in stages. Eight benchmark datasets tested the approach thoroughly. Two standard classifiers, MLkNN and BR, ran the comparisons. Hamming loss and ranking loss both fell noticeably. Average precision and F1 scores rose at the same time. Statistical tests confirmed the gains were robust. Very large datasets strain memory, the authors concede.
pmc-13547410:
Natela M. Shanidze and co-authors linked lifetime noise exposure to hearing test results in 2026 using a structured interview that tallies work, leisure, and firearm noise across a whole life. Fifty-four adults aged 23 to 82 gave their noise histories, self-rated their hearing, and completed tone and speech tests. Statistical models separated the effect of accumulated noise from the effect of age itself.

Age raised hearing thresholds at every frequency, as expected. Heavier lifetime noise independently worsened low-frequency hearing in both ears together, specific tones in each ear, and speech reception in the worse ear. The authors present the interview as a practical clinical tool and read the results as evidence that lifetime noise speeds age-related hearing decline.
pmc-13547810:
Koen Rummens and Sofie Beier test what helps readers spot tricky relationships in bar charts in a 2026 study. Earlier work found that placing the two bars of a misleading comparison side by side makes the trick far easier to catch. Color highlighting might rescue the harder interleaved layout, the team reasoned.

The adjacency advantage replicated cleanly in the first experiment. In the second, the key bars were painted red, either statically or fading in from gray. Neither cue improved detection over plain gray bars. Layout, not color, governs what chart readers see, a caution for designers who lean on highlighting.
pmc-13548110:
Szymon Stupnicki and co-authors review a hidden cause of shoulder pain in a 2026 paper. The state, subcoracoid impingement, arises when two shoulder bones squeeze the tendon that runs between them. It is often missed or read as another shoulder fault.

Pain flares when the arm lifts, crosses in, and turns down, which shrinks the gap the tendon needs. That gap is the key measure for diagnosis. Sports with overhead loads, like freestyle swimming and throwing, raise the risk. Scans and scopes help confirm the squeeze. The review gathers current knowledge so clinicians spot the state sooner and treat it with more care.
pmc-13548210:
Gamage, Hettiarachchi, Amarasekara, Jayawardena, and Wasalathanthri gather the views of care staff on weight support for young adults with obesity in Sri Lanka, in a study from twenty twenty-six. What care staff in cities think about such care was a gap in the evidence. Eight staff from the fields of diet, activity, behavior, and medicine are asked for their views. The talks go on till no new themes come up.

Blocks include gaps in staff knowledge, staff attitudes, and scarce resources. Client drive, sticking with care, and cultural myths also hold care back. Plans stress early spotting, with sound paths to send clients on to the right help. Care fit to each person, broad in scope, with steady follow-up, is urged. A supportive social setting rounds out the advice.
pmc-13548610:
Mateusz Jundzill and co-authors grade genome note tools across thousands of species in a 2026 study. Annotation turns raw microbe genome reads into gene maps, but head to head proof for tool picks was thin. The team ran four open tools, Prokka, Bakta, EggNOG-mapper, and PGAP, over a huge genome haul.

More than 156,000 genomes went through the bench, from clean lab strains to broken and mixed assemblies. Bakta led on top grade bacterial genomes. PGAP won on archaeal genomes and rough assemblies, and gave the widest term cover. EggNOG-mapper packed more terms per trait. The guide ties tool choice to genome grade and origin.
pmc-13548710:
Mei Feng and colleagues identify a mouth bacterium living inside cervical tumors as an active driver of the cancer's aggression, in a 2026 integrative study. Fusobacterium nucleatum is known for promoting gut cancers, but its role in the cervix was unexplored. Combining computing analysis with gene sequencing of patient tissue, the team located the bacterium inside tumor cells, confirming its presence with imaging and electron microscopy.

Tumors rich in the bacterium belonged to patients with worse survival. In culture, the bacterium invaded cervical cancer cells, spurred their growth and spread, blocked their death, and sped tumor growth in mice. It worked by raising a protein called HMGB1 and switching on an inflammatory relay that released two signaling molecules. The authors cast the bacterium as a prognostic marker and a possible treatment target in cervical cancer.
pmc-13548810:
Lu Xing and Xueqi Wu reviewed smart computer tools in child nutrition in a 2026 mini review. These tools now help judge diets, forecast poor nutrition, aid clinic choices, suggest meals, coach by chat, and watch food settings. All of these uses land in one place: what a child eats each day.

The review sorts the tools into two roles. In one role, the tool turns health, diet, and setting data into scores and forecasts. In the other, it takes part in food choice itself, shaping taste, talk, and family habits. The authors weigh both gains and risks for kids. Their map helps health teams use such tools with care.
pmc-13549010:
Daniel Meleschko and colleagues forge a double bond between cobalt and antimony, one of the heaviest stable elements, in a 2026 chemistry paper. Multiple bonds joining transition metals to heavy group fifteen elements are notoriously hard to isolate, unlike their lighter nitrogen and phosphorus cousins. The team started from a molecule with an antimony and antimony double bond and used carbene reagents to split it into single antimony-bearing units.

Passing one unit to a cobalt center produced a terminal cobalt stibinidene with an exceptionally short bond. Several independent measures, from bond order calculations to orbital analysis, agreed the link is a genuine covalent double bond, the first of its kind. The compound reacted with an alkyne and with an azide to form small rings, echoing lighter-element behavior. The authors offer the cleavage route as a general recipe for heavy multiple bonds.
pmc-13549610:
Siyu Yang and four co-authors report three cases where a heart-lung machine supported patients whose airways were blocked by cancer. Their article came out in 2026. The machine, called VV-ECMO, takes over gas exchange from the lungs and can keep a patient alive during risky airway procedures.

All three patients had breathing failure because tumors narrowed or blocked the main airway, and normal intubation could not keep oxygen up. The team ran the machine without heparin, a blood thinner, to lower bleeding risk. Doctors then cleared tumor tissue or placed airway stents through a scope. Oxygen improved at once in all three cases. The authors stress careful patient selection and teamwork across specialties.
pmc-13549710:
Sarah Clarke and co-authors study fear of recurrence in survivors of a torn heart artery in this 2026 paper. The condition, SCAD, causes heart attacks by splitting an artery wall. Recovery carries a heavy mental load, survivors report. Fear that it will happen again, or worsen, is common. Uncertainty about the condition may color how that fear lands. The team tested whether uncertainty changes the fear's link to mental health.

Anxiety, depression, and heart-related distress were the outcomes. If uncertainty amplifies fear's harm, easing uncertainty becomes a treatment target. Clear information and follow-up plans are cheap tools for that. The study draws on survivor survey data. It argues mental care belongs in cardiac follow-up for this group. SCAD mostly strikes younger women, a group cardiac rehab often underserves.
pmc-13549810:
Koji Masuda, Harumi Gomi, and co-authors run a drug staff led teach push to curb a broad germ drug in Japan, in work from 2026. Germ drug wise use needs habit change, not facts lone, in ward staff. A work set teach plan built on habit science was the tool tried here.

All full time docs take a clip and test once pre launch. Each use of the drug then needs a writ cause at the desk. Use days drop by more than a fifth past the push in checks. Like drops hold in same season match spans as well. Desk prompts may steer drug habits with light cost.
pmc-13550110:
Arzu Dinç Yavaş and Sümeyye Akçay compare three low doses of injected ozone gas for knee osteoarthritis in forty-five patients treated weekly for three weeks. Ozone therapy is used for joint pain, but the best concentration is unsettled. Groups received the lowest, middle, or highest of three low doses.

Pain and function scores improved significantly in every group by week four, with no significant differences between doses on the main scales. The lowest-dose group did gain more walking distance than the highest-dose group, an exploratory finding the authors treat cautiously. No adverse events appeared. Given the retrospective design, they call for larger prospective trials before dose recommendations harden.
pmc-13550510:
Einstein Francisco Camargos, Raphael Lopes Olegário, and Otávio Toledo Nóbrega write to a journal questioning a new brain scan index, in a 2026 letter. The index claims to measure the glymphatic system, the brain's waste-clearing flow, from diffusion scans.

Brain waste clearance is real and important, but measuring it without invasive tools is unsolved. The new index refines an older one using genetic programming, a search method that evolves formulas. The letter grants the work is elegant and timely. Its worry is construct validity: whether the number truly tracks the plumbing it names. History warns that scan measures can drift from the biology beneath them. The authors urge validation against firmer standards before clinical use.
pmc-13550610:
Sara Milijanovic, leading nine colleagues, published a 2026 comparison of extracts from Gentiana dinarica, an endangered Balkan plant, grown wild and in laboratory culture. Chemical makeup can shift with growing conditions, so the team tested extracts from leaves and roots of both sources. They measured antioxidant, antibacterial, tumor-cell, and immune effects.

Cultured shoots carried more of two compound families and killed bacteria and tumor cells differently from wild leaves, while also flipping an immune response from calming to stimulating in spleen cells. Cultured roots lacked compounds found in wild roots yet scavenged free radicals most strongly. Effects could rise, fall, or vanish by source, so the authors urge detailed checks before cultured plants substitute for wild ones.
pmc-13550710:
Ronan Gleeson and co-authors use spectroscopy and microkinetic modeling to find the active-site distribution in a palladium single-atom catalyst. Their paper deals with metal-doped carbon materials, whose making creates varied local settings.

It is palladium on nitrogen-doped graphene, tested for the oxygen reduction reaction. Core-level data from past papers were joined with density functional calculations and kinetic modeling to screen possible site structures. A heat-and-energy analysis and X-ray absorption data ruled out edge and porous sites, for poor match with lab data. The basal site mix that is left explains the ensemble effect on activity.
pmc-13551410:
Mathias Krogh Pedersen, leading nine colleagues, published a 2026 study checking whether two preservative allergens still appear in Danish cosmetics ten years after European regulation. Methylchloroisothiazolinone and methylisothiazolinone, known as MCI and MI, prevent spoilage in water-based products but cause contact allergy. Using a Danish product database, the team found 257 products listing them, then chemically analyzed thirty shampoos and liquid soaps.

Most identified products were shampoos and conditioners. Two of twenty-five labeled products exceeded the 15 parts per million limit for rinse-off goods, and four missed the required ratio between the two preservatives. Since allergy remains common despite rare use, the authors suggest the legal limit may still be too high to protect users.
pmc-13551510:
Rong Guo, Boyang Ni, and Megan L. Fritz published a 2026 genome-wide study of smell genes in the moth Chloridea virescens, part of the Heliothinae group. Two gene families, odorant receptors and odorant-binding proteins, let insects detect scents for feeding and mating. The team catalogued both families across the moth genome and compared them with relatives.

They found 81 receptor genes and 49 binding protein genes, the latter sorted into three types by a structural pattern. The receptor favors one partner protein inside the cell, a detail the structures now explain.

In tumors, CD97 helps some cancers keep stem-like traits, spread, and survive stress, though its role shifts with tumor type. Drug ideas include antibody-drug conjugates, which showed early promise in dishes, and engineered immune cells that slowed two cancers in animals. A catch is that healthy immune and other cells also carry CD97, so harm to normal tissue is a real risk. The review weighs that balance and lists early ideas, from RNA treatments to structure-guided drugs.
pmc-13565110:
Palak Mehta, Erik Moore, Alekha Dash, and Surabhi Shukla review fat bubble carriers for getting drugs into the eye, in a paper from 2026. Eye disease blinds or impairs about two billion people worldwide. Yet less than five percent of a standard eye drop dose reaches its target, because tears, the cornea, and inner barriers wash or block most of it.

The carriers, called liposomes, are tiny spheres of fat that can hold a drug and shield it. Changing their surface can help them cross the cornea and linger in the eye. The review sorts those surface tricks and weighs their gains and limits. It also covers the eye's barriers in brief, so readers can see why each trick is needed. The goal is eye care that works at lower doses.
pmc-13565310:
Costanza Franchini and six co-authors track anxiety and depression in students after brief counseling, in a paper dated 2026. University students are prone to both conditions, yet proof for short psychodynamic counseling is thin. Their program ran just four weekly sessions, with one follow-up meeting three months later.

The study followed 108 students, most in their early twenties, and measured symptoms at four points: first visit, treatment start, treatment end, and three months on. Standard Beck scales tracked both depression and anxiety. Symptoms held steady during the wait before treatment, setting a baseline for judging change. The design tests whether gains arrive during the brief course and whether they last. The title's hint is that change takes time.
pmc-13565510:
Xiao Zhang and co-authors feed goji berry sugar chains to cats and watch their chemistry shift in a 2026 study. The polysaccharide from goji is famed for antioxidant and gut effects, but feline data were missing. Twenty four adult cats ate plain food or food spiked with three dose levels for eight weeks.

Weight, appetite, blood counts, and standard chemistry stayed unmoved, a clean safety sign. Deeper scans told another story: blood metabolites shifted along fat and amino acid pathways, and gut microbe diversity and membership changed measurably. Several bacterial groups tracked with the altered metabolites. The authors conclude the supplement remodels metabolism and gut ecology in cats without visible harm.
pmc-13565710:
Nan Ji, Yong Liu, and Ying Wang study how feelings shape medical choices, in a 2026 paper. Patients decide about care based on more than facts; trust in the doctor, a sense of being understood, and mood all play a part. The team surveyed six hundred adult patients at a traditional Chinese medicine hospital in Wuxi.

Patients answered thirty questions covering good and bad feelings, trust, empathy, involvement in choices, and how decisions turned out. Good feelings, trust, and empathy each went with stronger involvement, while bad feelings went with weaker involvement. Involvement in turn helped explain how those factors linked to decision outcomes. The authors note the study captures links at one moment in one hospital, so wider and longer studies are needed before firm claims can be made.
pmc-13565910:
Mirza Muhammad Hadeed Khawar and co-authors check whether a diabetes drug class links to safer heart surgery, in a 2026 study. The drugs, SGLT2 inhibitors, help the heart and kidneys in people with diabetes and heart failure. Whether taking them before major heart procedures helps or hurts was unclear. The team mined a large United States health record network for answers.

They found more than 150,000 patients who had major cardiac procedures. Patients who had used the drugs in the prior year were matched with like non-users, forming over seven thousand pairs. The drug group had lower death rates in the first 30 days after surgery. They also saw fewer cases of acute kidney injury. The authors stress that records can only hint at cause, and they call for proper randomized trials of the drugs around surgery.
pmc-13566410:
Cristina Marrocchio, Michele Ligorio, and Nicola Sverzellati review, in a 2026 article, precision imaging for interstitial lung diseases, a family of more than two hundred disorders that scar lung tissue. Standard high-resolution scans and breathing tests can miss mild change and depend heavily on patient effort. The authors survey computer-measured scan features and AI tools instead.

Newer programs now beat older ones at diagnosis, measuring disease extent, and predicting outlook, with better agreement between readers. Routine clinical use still lags behind the published results. Radiologists get a balanced view of tools that could standardize lung assessment once proof and workflow hurdles are cleared.
pmc-13566610:
Edilma Sanabria and co-authors study drug movement in water mixes in a 2026 chemistry paper. Two front line tuberculosis drugs were dissolved with a ring shaped synthetic molecule that can host other molecules. How the three move together in water shapes how a drug carrier of this kind might behave.

Flow spread tests at room temperature measured how each part drifts alone and how it drags the others. The cross terms came out clearly nonzero, a sign of real coupling between the drugs and the ring host. Magnetic resonance readings backed the picture. Such transport data help judge whether the host could carry both drugs at once.
pmc-13566910:
Jiming Li and three co-authors tuned in 2026 how much zirconium a common aluminum alloy should carry. Tiny zirconium-rich grains pin the metal's crystal boundaries, keeping grains small and defects few. The team cast the alloy at several zirconium levels and compared structure and rust resistance.

A mid dose, six hundredths of a percent, gave the finest grains and the strongest defense, beating both a higher and a lower dose. Its surface film stayed dense and blocked chloride attack. Too little zirconium under-refines the metal; too much clumps the grains. The result guides alloy recipes for foil and sheet.
pmc-13567310:
Shinichi Nakagawa and Akira Yamamoto present a 2026 study on how a persona prompt skews AI estimates of food nutrition. Vision-language models judge nutrients from meal photos, and portion size is their biggest error source. The team tested six models from three vendors on Japanese cafeteria dishes and American meal photos. Each model judged photos with no persona, with a Japanese-dietitian persona, or with an American-dietitian persona.

The Japanese-dietitian prompt lowered energy estimates in every model and both data sets. It left the balance of nutrients roughly intact. The American persona shifted estimates only slightly and inconsistently. A direct order to assume smaller portions behaved differently and less steadily. The persona's effect cut error on the small-portion Japanese set but was neutral on the larger-portion American one. The authors warn the trick needs testing on each target domain before use.
pmc-13567810:
Mohamed Ahmed El Maghawry and co-authors review seven years of therapeutic plasma exchange at a large Egyptian hospital. The treatment filters and replaces a patient's plasma, and it serves diseases across many organ systems. Real-world data from lower-income countries are scarce. They studied two hundred twenty-one patients treated between 2016 and 2022, grouping them by kidney, nerve, blood, and metabolic conditions.

The commonest reasons were a nerve disease, a blood clotting disorder, and a muscle weakness crisis. About seventy-eight percent of patients responded, and about fifteen percent died. Nerve cases responded well, while kidney cases had the lowest response and highest deaths. Side effects hit about a third of patients but stayed mild or moderate. Needing a ventilator, weak kidneys, and low blood counts each predicted death. The results match the treatment's standing as a first-line option for its top-rated uses.
pmc-13569610:
A single snapshot of brain wiring can miss how networks shift moment to moment in early psychosis. Romain Aubonnet, Mahmoud Hassan, Paolo Gargiulo, Stefano Seri, and Giorgio Di Lorenzo track those shifts in a 2026 study. Brain waves from 78 patients and 60 healthy peers were sorted into five network states.

Static reads showed weaker alpha links in patients overall. The dynamic view found one state whose path length varied less in patients. That hints at stiffer switching in a key resting network. Drug status split the state patterns further. State measures tied to social scores and thought disorder, unlike static ones.
pmc-13569910:
Seven surgeons in France describe a hybrid graft technique for revision knee ligament surgery in a 2026 paper. Fascia lata grafts are proven for rebuilding the anterior cruciate ligament, but graft thinness or a second tendon harvest can limit them. Their method wraps a narrow fascia strip around a synthetic ligament.

The composite reaches eight millimeters, pairing living tissue with a six millimeter synthetic core for strength. A thinner harvest lets the donor site close more easily. The combined operation also adds a lateral stabilizing step outside the joint. The authors present the technique as a simple, repeatable option for revision cases where a patient's own tissue is in short supply.
pmc-13570010:
Noemie Gross, Anna Molto, and Renaud Felten review spondyloarthritis in the span near birth. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. This joint ill oft hits women of child age, yet facts on birth odds, course, and post-birth flare stay split. The team searched a large base with no date cap for English and French work.

Of more than three hundred finds, near half fit. Some women show low egg store and long wait to conceive, in part from pain drugs. Course in birth is most oft firm for one form and mixed for the spine form. Birth fates are most oft sound, with small lifts in early birth risk. Post-birth flares are common.
pmc-13570410:
Paula Duarte D'Ambrosio and seven co-authors report a robotic surgery case for a tumor that came back, in a case report from 2026. A forty-one-year-old woman had a thymoma, a tumor near the heart, return in the lining of her chest three years after her first surgery.

Surgeons used a robot to remove the chest lining and the tumor spots. They then bathed the chest cavity in heated chemotherapy drugs. The patient went home after seven days with no major problems. Two years later she was still free of disease. The authors say this combined, low-impact approach may suit carefully chosen patients, though larger studies are needed.
pmc-13570610:
Cybele Lara Abad and Raymund Razonable review whether a transplant drug raises viral infection risks in this 2026 paper. Belatacept helps prevent kidney rejection, but its long-term safety record is incomplete. The team pooled sixty-four studies on three threats: two viruses and a virus-linked lymph disorder.

In randomized trials, infection risks on the drug matched those on the standard drug class. One exception appeared after year two: a stronger dose doubled one virus's infection rate. In real-world studies, two viruses showed roughly double the risk on belatacept. Reports of the lymph disorder did not rise clearly in trials. The authors caution that the real-world studies carry limits. They advise vigilance for viral infections in long-term users.
pmc-13571310:
Siddiqui and co-authors measure how much health care people in England with a rare vessel inflammation disease use, and what it costs. Real world cost data for the disease, called EGPA, were scarce. Their 2026 study follows 486 patients from diagnosis and matches them against general and severe asthma comparison groups in linked primary and hospital records.

Use of every care type ran higher for EGPA patients, above all in the first year. Yearly costs averaged near fourteen thousand pounds, about eight times the general group and four times the asthma group, with hospital stays the biggest driver. Patients with a worse severity score used more care, and those relapsing or stable cost more than those in remission. The authors frame the disease as a heavy burden on services.
pmc-13571410:
Anna Jones and co-authors report real-world results for a targeted ovarian cancer drug in a 2026 study. Mirvetuximab soravtansine is an antibody-drug conjugate that homes to folate receptor alpha, found on most ovarian cancers, and delivers its payload there. Trials showed good results under strict entry rules. This review covered sixty-six patients treated for recurrent disease at one university cancer center and its partner hospital between late 2022 and spring 2025.

Survival with and without progression was charted, and side effects catalogued from the records. Adjusted models hunted for traits tied to longer survival. Real-world cohorts include the frailer patients trials skip, so these numbers tell oncologists what to expect in the clinic.
pmc-13571610:
Tamer Othman and Ibrahim Aldoss present a 2026 literature review of immune therapies for adult B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Returned or resistant disease once left adults with poor odds, and transplant in a second remission was the only path to cure. Three immune treatments changed that picture in the last decade.

The review sums the key trials of blinatumomab, inotuzumab ozogamicin, and CAR T-cell therapy, weighing benefit and side effects for each. All three improved outcomes in returned disease while cutting reliance on harsh chemotherapy, and all are moving into first-line care. The authors add their own guidance on fitting the drugs into practice.
pmc-13571710:
Almeida Souto and co-authors tracked a 2026 cohort of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension patients diagnosed before and after a pulmonary embolism response team was set up. This form of high lung pressure can often be cured, yet diagnosis often drags for years after the first clot. The single centre study took place in a general hospital in Argentina.

Among twenty-nine patients, those diagnosed after the team launched reached diagnosis far sooner after their pulmonary embolism. Median time fell from 256 weeks to forty-three weeks, a sharp drop Almeida Souto reports. The later group also trended toward lower risk levels at diagnosis, though that gap was not significant. The authors credit team follow-up after embolism for catching the condition beyond specialist centres.
pmc-13572010:
Wilfred Aniagyei and co-authors probe why type 1 diabetes in Ghana so often breaks the textbook pattern. Many African patients keep producing some insulin, a retained C-peptide level that hints at a different disease path, yet the T-cell side of these forms was unexplored. Their 2026 paper focuses on CD25, the receptor part that lets T cells hear interleukin-2, and on its gene, IL2RA.

Patients were grouped by low, mid, and high C-peptide and compared with healthy controls, in body and after lab stimulation. Diabetes groups showed more CD25 on both major T-cell kinds, tracking age, C-peptide, and blood sugar control. The gene itself varied little and did not explain the receptor levels. A distinctive double-marked T-cell population expanded in the mid and high groups, and in the low group once ages were matched. The authors chart immune variety behind the clinical variety.
pmc-13572210:
Haruna Iriyama and thirteen colleagues published a case report in two thousand twenty-six on treating two diseases at once. A forty-two-year-old woman had triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive type. She was also taking an immune-suppressing antibody for multiple sclerosis, which raised doubts about adding a second immune drug.

After consulting a nerve specialist, the team gave standard chemotherapy plus the immune drug pembrolizumab before surgery. Scans then showed a complete response. Surgery removed part of the breast, and lab checks confirmed no cancer remained. Her multiple sclerosis has not flared so far. The authors present the case as evidence the combination can be given safely in such patients.
pmc-13572310:
Joshua Reitz and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, whether diabetes and weight-loss drugs that mimic the gut hormone GLP-1, including newer dual-action versions, could also treat alcohol use disorder. Heavy drinking and metabolic dysfunction overlap heavily and together drive liver disease, making a shared treatment attractive.

The drugs are already approved for diabetes and obesity and are under study for fatty liver disease. Evidence so far suggests they may cut alcohol intake while steadying metabolism, with the dual approach possibly filling a gap for people carrying both problems. The authors map ongoing trials and open questions, framing addiction care around metabolic circuits rather than willpower alone.
pmc-13572410:
Dongyang Yang and co-authors realize a long hunted state of matter: a Mott insulator at the Dirac point of a graphene like band. Published in 2026, the study twists two layers of molybdenum selenide into a honeycomb moiré pattern. The twist slows the band's fermions nearly a hundredfold, letting repulsion between charges dominate where in true graphene speed wins.

Light based sensing, pairing two exciton techniques, detects a charge gap at the Dirac point lasting up to 110 kelvin. Further correlated states appear at full and fractional fillings, one with weak magnetism. The platform keeps a clean symmetry that theorists prize. The authors offer it as a sandbox for quantum many body physics in twisted materials.
pmc-13572510:
Minjae Cho and Chuangchuang Sun present a 2026 method that helps robot learning agents pick up new tasks fast. Agents that learn by trial and error often forget old skills when a new task clashes with them. The method stacks three levels: one reads the task, one finds broad moves that fit many tasks, and one picks fine actions.

The broad moves, called macro-actions, are found on their own and stripped of task-specific detail, so they can be reused across jobs. They point the fine policy toward goal states and ease the load on each level. Each level trains on its own tailored scheme, which keeps the stack stable. On the MetaWorld test suite, the method learned with fewer trials and won more often than past leaders. Code is posted online for others to check.
pmc-13572610:
Claudia Peters and five co-authors surveyed health and social care staff in two thousand twenty-six about work and mental health after the COVID-19 pandemic. Five hundred seventy-six staff took part in two thousand twenty-three. Most were women, with an average age of forty-nine, and more than half were front-line health workers such as nurses and doctors.

Health workers rated their ability to work lower than other staff. They reported more strain, time pressure, and clash between work and private life, and more thoughts of leaving. About one in five of all staff had moderate to severe mental distress. The authors urge strong steps to guard staff mental health.
pmc-13572710:
Meili Li and Shuai Xu study why giving rural schools AI tools does not by itself make students feel more able to learn. Their 2026 paper covers six rural lower-secondary schools in China. It blends survey data from 486 students and 24 teachers with 32 interviews of students, teachers, parents, and school leaders, giving the interviews the lead role.

The authors frame the story with two theories: one about the resources families and schools hold, and one about what people can actually do with them. How often students used AI, and how much teachers guided that use, varied with family resources and home internet. Teacher guidance, planned study use of AI, and confidence in judging AI output tied most strongly to feeling capable. The interviews showed a routine that worked: try, get feedback, hear an explanation, revise. Access alone, the authors argue, converts to learning only through such teaching.
pmc-13572810:
Aoife Warren and colleagues link childhood trauma, brain links, and working memory, in work published in 2026. Schizophrenia involves altered frontoparietal connectivity that supports higher thought and memory. Childhood trauma also links with altered connectivity and weaker cognition in patients and healthy people alike.

Brain scans during a memory task came from patients and a larger control group. Higher physical neglect scores predicted poorer working memory across all participants. One prefrontal link pattern predicted better memory scores in the data. Patients showed wide connectivity gaps versus controls, but trauma level alone showed no such gaps. Connectivity did not carry the trauma to memory effect, though diagnosis shaped both links.
pmc-13573310:
Anna Macova and co-authors mapped the family tree of gut parasites that infect shrews in Europe and Asia, in work published in 2026. Shrews are protected and play a large role in nature, yet their parasites are poorly known. Stool samples came from almost two hundred shrews of four groups.

Parasites were found in about a quarter of samples, usually at low levels. Gene reads sorted them into four clusters. Three clusters stuck to one host group, while one was shared across three groups. Some worm like patterns in shape did not match the gene tree. The authors conclude that jumps between hosts happen more often in these parasites than was once thought.
pmc-13573710:
Fayha Salah Ahmed, Mohammad Imteyaz Ahmad, Mohamedi Begum, Deepa Rao, and Sheifa Joan wrote a study in 2026 on LDL cholesterol and machine learning. LDL is the bad form that guides heart risk care. The old Friedewald equation can miss the true mark, most of all when triglycerides run high. The team used more than 96,000 lipid profiles from Dubai Health to test new ways to get the mark.

Five learning models took in just three inputs: total cholesterol, HDL, and triglycerides. In the normal range for triglycerides, the models matched direct lab tests more closely than three standard equations. Past that range, all ways lost ground, the models and the old math alike. The team had no external validation of the work. So they frame the models as aids to the old math, not as swaps for it. That weak spot is the next task.
pmc-13574210:
Kohei Kamikawa and five co-authors reported in 2026 a case of severe anorexia in a teenage girl with Turner syndrome. Turner syndrome brings short stature and late puberty, which can weigh heavily on a teenager's body image. The link between the syndrome and anorexia was unclear.

The girl, followed since early childhood, grew distressed by her differences from peers and by body changes when hormone therapy began. A classmate's remark about her neck set off strict food restriction, and she lost much weight in six months. The case urges clinics to watch eating closely in this group.
pmc-13574310:
Stefanie Ewald and co-authors pilot a digital parenting program, Daily Growth, that sends help at the moment parents need it. Parenting programs can cut child mental health problems, but few parents join or stick with them. This program sends short videos matched to a recent hard moment at home.

Australian parents of toddlers were randomized to the program or to a parenting website for two weeks, with brief surveys twice a day. Most parents finished the follow-up survey and kept up with the daily check-ins. Despite technical glitches, most said they would recommend the program, use its skills, and found it easy to use. The authors judge the prototype feasible and ready for a larger trial.
pmc-13574410:
Jie Yuan and co-authors report long term care of a rare bleed from swollen veins near a stoma. Their case report from 2026 deals with high pressure in the liver veins, which can open odd vein paths. No standard plan exists for such bleeds, so each case is a hard call.

The patient had blood in the urine from veins around a bladder made from gut tissue. A tube through the liver was used to block the veins in April 2018, and the bleeding stopped at once. It came back at sixteen and twenty months as the veins reopened under lasting pressure. A second block in February 2022 stopped it again, with no new bleed for close to four years.
pmc-13575010:
Deepthi Jayan and three co-authors test solar cells built for space in a 2026 study. The cells pair silicon with a layered material called MXene. Radiation in orbit chews up normal silicon cells fast, so a tougher design could extend satellite life.

Under proton and electron blasts, the paired cells kept over eighty-four percent of their starting power. Plain silicon cells kept only fifty-five percent under the same dose. Imaging and probe tools showed the MXene layer shielding the joint from damage. A digital twin model, trained on the decay data, forecast cell performance with high accuracy for mission planning.
pmc-13575210:
Avinash Singh and Mohammad Soyeb Alam model ground sinking above an underground copper mine in India in a 2026 study. Mining out ore can let the surface sag, harming buildings, land, and safety. The mine uses blast-hole stoping, a method that removes ore in large blocks.

Their three-dimensional computer model built in faults, rock joints, and the planned mining sequence. It simulated the untouched state, current workings, and forecasts five and ten years ahead. Rock properties were tuned by matching the model back against observed behaviour, which sharpened the predictions. Output maps show strain and movement in all directions for each phase. The authors present the approach as a practical route to site-specific subsidence forecasts for working mines.
pmc-13575310:
Jing Zhou and ten co-authors published a plant pathology study in twenty twenty-six on how the late blight pathogen rewires potato defenses from inside the nucleus. A Phytophthora effector protein was already known to target the potato transcription factor StKNOX3. The new work shows what that factor normally partners with.

StKNOX3 binds two enzymes that tag histone proteins, stabilizing them in the nucleus, and the trio together helps the pathogen infect. The effector strengthens the trio's assembly, raising the histone tag and switching defense genes off. Genome-wide binding and expression maps showed the factor repressing genes for cell walls, hormones, and stress responses. The study exposes an epigenetic lever the pathogen pulls to disarm its host.
pmc-13575510:
Jun He and co-authors link a brain vessel variant to stroke severity in a 2026 study. Some people are born with a fetal-type rear brain artery, a variant in how blood reaches the back of the brain. The team asked if that variant tracks with worse strokes in that region.

Records covered 161 patients at two hospitals with fresh strokes in the rear brain. Scans sorted them by whether the variant was present. Severity was scored on a standard stroke scale at admission. The variant group showed higher rates of mid-to-severe stroke. Blood sugar and uric acid also differed by severity. After full adjustment, the variant stayed tied to worse strokes, with odds about five times higher.
pmc-13575610:
Penghua Zhang and Yang Gu test whether pairing two scans improves breast cancer diagnosis, in a 2026 study. One scan uses ultrasound with stiffness measures, which flag hard tissue. The other is magnetic resonance imaging, which shows blood flow and structure. The team compared each alone and both together in sixty patients with cancer and forty with harmless lumps.

Judged against tissue results, the combined reading caught the most cancers and was also best at clearing harmless cases. Stiffness scores and related ratios ran higher in cancerous tissue, and the MRI signs of dense vessels and fast enhancement did too. The authors conclude that the two scans correct each other's misses, and that pairing them gives a sharper, more trustworthy diagnosis.
pmc-13575910:
Weerapong Lilitwat and Prakreeti Bhandari lay out a precision playbook for a runaway immune storm in sick children, in a 2026 review. Old checklists name the disease but cannot say which gear drives it in one child. Their frame matches trigger and body pattern to pathway marks and drugs.

One signal mark backs a drug that blocks interferon gamma. Another pair backs a dampener used in macrophage storms. Wider signaling calls for a kinase blocker in stubborn cases, and a sixth interleukin drug fits a sibling storm from cell therapy. The authors stress these marks guide, not govern. Antibiotics, organ support, and early transplant planning run beside every targeted move, with a hard reassessment inside three days.
pmc-13576210:
Lorena Maestre and colleagues assembled an antibody panel that identifies blood-cell types across many animal species, a long-standing gap in veterinary medicine. Their 2026 study tested 69 antibodies on lymph node, spleen, and bursa tissue from 13 domestic and 28 exotic or wild species, plus human lymph node.

Sixteen antibodies survived the screen, covering T cells, B cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells through markers including CD3, CD4, CD8, CD20, and CD163. The panel enables precise detection of the main haematopoietic populations in diverse species. The authors present it as a versatile tool for veterinary diagnosis and research, and a step toward diagnostic accuracy in animals matching human standards.
pmc-13576310:
Linlin Wang leads a 2026 study building a prediction score for a common snag in heart stent work: loss of blood flow in a side branch after the main vessel is stented. Forked artery narrowings are frequent and tricky to treat. Records covered 830 patients treated at one Chinese hospital between 2022 and 2023.

Four factors made the final score: age, plaque position on the same side as the branch, flow grade before stenting, and a heart stress blood marker. The chart-style model scored 0.651 on the accuracy curve, easing to 0.641 after internal correction, a modest level of discrimination. Calibration checks showed predictions matched observed rates well. The authors offer the score for sorting risk before the procedure and choosing a strategy, while noting its limits.
pmc-13577110:
Se Kye Kim and co-authors present a 2025 journal article comparing the genomes of a reference Escherichia coli strain and its plasmid-cured offspring. The parent strain, ATCC 43894, is a standard for studying enterohemorrhagic disease, and the offspring lost its large virulence plasmid. Researchers had assumed the pair share one genetic background apart from that plasmid.

Whole genome reads showed the expected plasmid difference, plus surprises. The parent carried extra mutations, including a 2.5-thousand-letter deletion that removed two acid resistance genes and a third gene. The authors warn that the cured strain is not a clean match, which matters for past and future experiments.
pmc-13577210:
Shen and co-authors tested in 2026 whether low blood counts or low blood protein flag the risk of mental side effects from a TB drug in a shortened oral regimen. Drug-resistant tuberculosis now gets nine-month all-oral plans, and one common drug, cycloserine, can cause nerve and psychiatric harm. Who is at risk was poorly defined.

The cohort in Kazakhstan followed three standard regimens that shared a core of three drugs, with one adding cycloserine. Events of special interest were nerve damage, seizures, and psychosis. Logistic models tested whether anemia or low albumin at the start predicted those events. The byline is a large team, framed here by its lead author. Readers get a cheap, baseline screen that clinics can run before choosing a regimen.
pmc-13577510:
Mengyao Li, Yongchun Guo, and Su Wang study walls printed from titanium alloy with a mixed laser and arc heat source, in a paper from 2026. The method lays molten wire layer by layer to build metal parts. Settings like laser power shape the wall's grain and strength. The team varied the settings and then pulled, struck, and probed the printed walls.

More laser power widened each layer and shrank its height. At a middle power, strength ran near even in both test directions. That balance matters for parts loaded from many sides. The top of each wall proved harder than its middle. Break stretch also stayed close across directions at the sweet setting. The authors give builders a tested base for printing flight-grade titanium parts.
pmc-13578110:
Marta Skowron Volponi and co-authors test whether a moth that looks like a hornet also copies the hornet's scent. The hornet clearwing moth resembles the European hornet in shape and sound, which may keep predators away. The team asks whether the match extends to the waxy chemicals, called cuticular hydrocarbons, that coat both insects. These chemicals often serve as recognition cues between insects.

Comparing the chemical profiles, the authors find no sign of copying. The moth carries about six times less of the coating than the hornet, and it lacks alkenes entirely, a class of these compounds that predators use to spot prey. Related moth families show very different profiles as well. The authors suggest the moth's thin, simple coating may instead make it harder to detect at all. They note that trials with real predators are still needed to test that idea.
pmc-13578610:
Alexander Hiden and co-authors look back in 2026 at habits tied to large weight loss in adults with severe obesity in a structured program. Lasting loss needs a steady cut in energy intake plus more activity.

Records were checked at the start and at six and twelve months for adults who began with a very high body mass index. The team sorted patients by how much they lost and compared the habits each group reported. Those who lost at least fifteen percent of their weight more often reported eating less, cutting fat and sugar, and staying active. They also reported using more of the known winning strategies in total.
pmc-13578710:
Miao Xie and colleagues present a two unit tracked machine that bolts mine tunnel roofs in tight spaces, in a 2026 study. The hard part is keeping the front and rear units moving as one. A physics model of track and ground contact feeds a motion simulator, run under matched, squeezed, and pulling modes. A full size prototype matched the simulator within a few percent on average. The authors offer the design as a safer path for the bulk of tunnels that big rigs cannot enter.
pmc-13578910:
Farzad Hekmatifar and co-authors adapt a stroke mind test into Persian in 2026 and check how well it works. The study held 136 stroke patients and 60 matched healthy adults. Scores tracked a standard mind test with a strong link. Stroke and healthy groups split by a wide gap, as a sound test should. pmc-13579110:
Timoth Mkilima sketches a testable design for light-programmed microbial power systems, in a 2026 review. Microbial electrochemical cells let germs trade electrons with electrodes while they eat waste or fix carbon dioxide. Their output sags for known reasons: uneven biofilms, transport gradients, electrode drift, and community change. The proposed design wraps the cell in clear reactors, electrodes that light can address, shaped light delivery, and dense sensing.

They then form a tight seal on a sac and open it into a whole-sac recording mode. The protocol points readers to the pair's earlier work for full detail on use.
pmc-13579610: Jacq, Picherit, and Bas reported in twenty twenty-six how a printed jaw model helped a girl aged nine and her folks grasp her jaw cyst care. She has a rare inborn ill that oft brings such cysts, and two large ones showed on scans. Talk and scan pics left the folks unsure, with a tongue gap in the way. A life-size print with cysts in color made the plan plain at last. The folks then gave clear consent and kept the checks.
pmc-13579810:
Hatice Çalişkan Burgucu and co-authors study two proteins in adrenal tumors in a 2026 paper. The tumors make excess cortisol and cause Cushing syndrome. The team checked tissue levels of apelin and of a growth factor tied to blood vessel growth, then compared tumor tissue with normal adrenal cortex from controls.

The study covered 11 patients with the tumors and 15 controls, using stained tissue sections scored for both strength and share of positive cells. Apelin staining strength was clearly higher in tumor tissue, though the share of positive cells and combined scores did not differ. The strength measure alone separated the groups fairly well. pmc-13580110:
Marleen van Greevenbroek and Leendert Trouw review how chemically altered proteins can switch on the complement system, part of the immune system's first response, in a 2026 article. pmc-13580310:
Danielle Naegeli and co-authors present a 2026 study of how culture shapes the silent gestures people invent to say who did what to whom. Two groups played a gesture game in pairs, passing their signs down a chain: Dutch players and Balinese players. Balinese chains mostly kept one type and shunned that abstract space move. The authors tie the split to the earth-fixed frame, not to a stage of growth. pmc-13581010:
Qian Wu and five co-authors review how artificial intelligence has been used for a lung condition called PRISm, in a 2026 paper. AI tools have spread into lung diagnosis and prognosis, yet work on this condition is still new. The team searched six major medical databases for matching studies.

Nine appeared in the last two years, and results showed strong performance. The review maps a young field and points to where better studies are needed.
pmc-13581410:
Juan Chen, Hui-Hong Wang, En-Wei Tian, and Nian-He Xia name a new plant species in 2026, found in Guangxi in China. Gene trees place it near one kin from seed genes and near the other from leaf genes, with weak backing. Its few wild stands face a fall in grown plants, so the team rates it as at risk. The work helps shops check that raw herbs are what labels claim.
pmc-13581610:
Computers usually fight errors with constant, costly vigilance. Tristan Sterin and co-authors build one that relaxes into correctness instead. Their scaffolded DNA computer lets molecules settle toward the lowest-energy state, and the right answer is that state. They ran ten programs on it, including multiplication by three, division by two, and addition of twenty-five-bit numbers. The largest run handled a hundred bits of computation.

pmc-13581810:
Xiaochen Xiang and co-authors wrote a trial report from 2026 on a talk-based program to cut risky sex among men who have sex with men. Such acts raise the risk of HIV and other infections. The program rests on a form of talk therapy that links thoughts to acts. It was given over the internet and aimed at the patterns that drive high-risk acts.

Before the program, close to half of the men took high risks even though they knew the dangers well. After the program, the treated group had less unprotected sex than the comparison group. The team also saw shifts in gut germs that may track the change in acts, but they stress that this part is early and needs more work.
pmc-13581910:
David Vaz, Sarah Ibrahim, and Aleksandra Pikula scan medical schools in Canada in a 2026 study for lessons on healthy living as medicine. Such lessons teach how food, movement, sleep, and ties with others can prevent long-term disease. No one had mapped how much of this the schools now teach.
