Food, mental well-being, and activity came up most, while sleep and social ties lagged. The map gives schools a base from which to grow this teaching.
pmc-13582110:
Vivekanand Vimal and co-authors show that balancing in two directions at once is far harder than the sum of its parts. Their 2026 study seats participants in a motion simulator rigged to topple like an inverted pendulum, joystick in hand, and asks them to stay upright. Tilting about two axes hurt performance super-additively, beyond what either axis alone predicts.

Vision softened the deficit only slightly, and the two-axis penalty beat even a no-gravity-cue version of the task. Two days of practice, though, brought performance nearly to the one-axis level. The finding bears on flight mishaps and on falls: our balance system does not scale gracefully from one plane of tilt to two.
pmc-13582310:
Nermeen H Lashine and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on losartan, a blood pressure drug, against chemical brain injury in rats. Carbon tetrachloride, an industrial solvent, reaches the brain and drives oxidative stress and a cell death program called necroptosis. Twenty-four rats split into control, poisoned, drug, and nanoparticle drug groups.

The solvent raised damage markers and lowered antioxidant defenses, and it switched on the necroptosis gene chain. Brain tissue showed lost Purkinje cells and thinned layers. Both drug forms eased the chemical, gene, and tissue changes. The nanoparticle version was included to test whether packaging sharpens the protection.
pmc-13582410:
Kunxiang Wang and five co-authors published a case report in twenty twenty-six on a kidney tumor in an adult that turned out to be a childhood cancer. Wilms tumor is the commonest malignant kidney tumor in children but is exceptionally rare in adults. Bigger tumors and later diagnosis give adults worse odds, and no adult-specific treatment standard exists.

The patient's kidney mass was presumed to be clear-cell carcinoma, and the kidney was removed. Pathology instead showed nephroblastoma. Treatment then followed a children's oncology regimen with combined modalities. One year after finishing, the patient felt well and scans showed no leftover or returning disease. The case argues adult kidney masses deserve a wider differential.
pmc-13582710:
Shah and colleagues published a 2026 study on flipped classrooms in medical microbiology teaching. In flipped classes, students study material first and use class time to apply it. The team split exam questions by thinking depth using Bloom's levels. They compared 204 flipped-class students with 200 taught by plain lectures.

Both groups scored alike on basic recall questions in the exams. Flipped students scored clearly higher on application and problem-solving questions. That pattern suggests class time built deeper learning, not more facts. Most students, 88 percent, rated the flipped approach positively overall. The authors tie gains to prework covering basics before class time. Prework used videos and readings prepared by the course directors themselves. The course covered microbiology for second-year medical students specifically.
pmc-13583410:
Jake Cravino and co-authors get to the root of a lab trick that seems to break the rules in a 2026 paper. The trick splits the flow at the mouth of a column used to sort drugs, and it has been said to cut pressure, sharpen peaks, and boost the read.

The team gauged pressure, ran flow mocks, and built small stand-in models of the mouth. Most of the cut in pressure came from past the column, not in it. The split mouth broke the usual funnel of out-flow and skimmed the flow that hugs the wall. In a model of a worn column that skim cut the spread of peaks and raised their height by near a fifth. The boost in the read held when flow was held out of the count. The gains are real but mixed in cause.
pmc-13583510:
Gianvincenzo Zuccotti and co-authors lay out a pilot plan in a 2026 paper to catch child maltreatment earlier. Spotting, recording, and reporting suspect cases should be routine across hospitals and clinics, yet uneven training and patchy records let cases slip.

Their Sentinel project pairs a digital registry, built on a standard research data tool, with structured training for children's doctors and other health staff. The pilot runs for twenty-four months in one hospital-and-community network in Italy. Staff skills and case handling are measured before and after. The team wants to learn whether the system is usable, workable, and strong enough to spread, before any larger rollout is planned.
pmc-13583610:
The gland where immune cells mature may help drive ALS, not just suffer from it. Julia Pereira Lemos and co-authors studied that gland, the thymus, in ALS-model mice in a 2026 paper. Regulatory T cells, which calm immune attack and protect neurons, are raised there. The team tracked gland structure and T cell growth across disease stages.

Late in the disease, the gland had shrunk and held fewer young and regulatory cells. The regulatory cells that remained suppressed poorly in lab tests. The gland's teaching cells also thinned, and young protectors sat in the wrong zones. Death of those cells ran high. The authors cast the thymus as a maintainer of the disease.
pmc-13583710:
Seven researchers in France measure the environmental cost of urine testing in a 2026 paper. Urinalysis is the most common infection workup, and labs have merged onto automated lines without knowing the footprint. A life cycle assessment compared manual, semi automated, and fully automated workflows for one standard test battery.

Carbon cost per test ran 1.9, 2.6, and 1.1 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent across the three workflows. Antibiotic susceptibility testing drove most emissions in every arm. The fully automated line scored lowest on twelve of eighteen impact measures and on human health harm. Scaled to fifty thousand tests a year, rankings shifted on some measures but not on the health endpoint.
pmc-13583810:
A large team reviews heart surgery results for children in Pakistan in a 2026 paper. The cases came through a state funded program in Punjab that pays for care for heart defects present at birth. The team used the program registry for cases from the start of 2024 to mid 2025.

More than five thousand patients had close to six thousand procedures, split between open surgery and tube based work. Most patients were children, with a median age of six years. Death rates climbed steeply as procedures grew more complex, from near one percent to near thirty. Wealth measures and other traits were also weighed for their links to death and hospital stay.
pmc-13584210:
Hansel Canagarajah and co-authors survey in 2026 how UK rheumatology professionals view and use artificial intelligence in their work. About forty percent used AI daily or weekly in clinic or research. Looking up medical facts with chatbots was the top clinical use. Eighty-six percent expected AI to reshape practice within five years. Administrative tasks and imaging of muscles and joints were seen as the biggest impact areas.
pmc-13584610:
Zukang Miao leads a team of nine authors from 2026 in a study of the fillers used after dead bone is cleaned out of a hip joint. The bone loss is called osteonecrosis of the femoral head. The team looked at how well patients did in care and what X-ray scans showed. By ranking the whole field at once, the work can name a top choice for care. pmc-13585410:
Kefan Cui, Renjie Zhu, and Jingmeng Li chart, in 2026 work, how lung cancer learns to beat a key targeted drug. The drug is the standard for patients whose tumours carry a set gene change, but the cancer finds ways around it in time. Gene tests after that point found a spread of escape routes. A fresh change in the target gene led, with side paths through other growth genes next. In about a fourth, more than one route ran at once. Some tumours changed type outright, and those patients fared worst. Lab cell tests backed one side path's role. pmc-13585810:
Ahmed Abd Rab El Rasool and co-authors ask whether a common ADHD drug is truly safe for the heart. Their 2026 study uses forty children with a new diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Forty healthy children matched by age and sex served as controls. pmc-13586110:
Lian Wu and colleagues find a gene that sets how widely rice leaves lean out from the stem. Leaf angle shapes how light falls through a rice canopy and thus how much grain a dense field can yield. pmc-13586410:

pmc-13586510:

pmc-13586710:

pmc-13586910:

pmc-13587310:

pmc-13587610:

pmc-13587810:

pmc-13587910:

pmc-13588110:

pmc-13588310:

pmc-13588510:

pmc-13588910:

pmc-13589610:

pmc-13589710:

pmc-13590210:

pmc-13590710:
Abdalrhman Alanizi and co-authors present a case report from 2026 about a teen girl with obesity who got acute biliary pancreatitis after her dose of a weight loss drug was raised. pmc-13591010:
Bibek Devkota, Marcus Wilson, and Babita Bhattarai report a sudden blood pressure crash after a routine reversal drug, in a 2026 case report. pmc-13591110:

pmc-13591210:

pmc-13593310:

The team used survey data from 2011 and 2015 in China. All men were aged 45 or more at the start. They weighed uric acid at the start against new prostate growth years later. Math models took age and health traits into account. They also checked if the link bends at high levels or shifts by group.
pmc-13594010:

pmc-13594510:

Tests on nine hundred thirteen compounds beat classic machine learning and single-view models. Adding true 3D shape gave a steady gain over flat maps alone. The joined view shows how much geometry adds when data are scarce.
pmc-13609610:
Qing Wang leads an eight-author team simulating the electric arc inside a magnesium smelting furnace. Electrofusion furnaces melt magnesite with a direct-current arc between a top electrode and the furnace bottom, and short arcs behave differently from the long arcs most models describe. The team built a two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic model coupling electromagnetic, heat, and flow fields, validated against classic free-arc experiments.

The simulated arc squeezes into a tight column with its hottest, fastest region near the center. Because the short arc reaches the anode before its jet can spread, momentum lands concentrated on the pool surface, producing sharp pressure peaks. Raising current heated the arc, sped the jet, and strengthened pressure and shear on the pool. Lengthening the arc did the opposite, and arc length mattered more than current overall. The authors offer the results as guidance for furnace operation and energy use in magnesium production.
pmc-13610310:
Xiaoping Wu and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on grading rice seed strength with a special camera. Seed strength, called vigor, tells how well a seed will sprout and grow. The camera reads light past the red end of the spectrum, which can show the seed's state without harming it. The snag is that each rice type reflects light in its own way, so a model trained on one type often fails on the next.

The team built a method that trains on one main type and then adapts to new types with few samples. They used nine hundred seeds from three types in all. Their method sorted seeds of the new types far more truly than a direct transfer of the old model. It also stayed steady when the main-type share changed. The team sees it as a tool for seed checks that do no harm.
pmc-13610810:
Bianca Simionescu and co-authors review plant-based diets in teenagers, weighing heart and metabolic gains against growth risks. Teen years fix eating habits while the body still needs much fuel for growth, bone building, and brain development. Plant diets are rising fast among the young.

The review stresses that plant-based is not one exposure. Diets built on whole grains, beans, and nuts track with better blood pressure, sugar, and fats. Diets built on refined grains and sweet processed items track with the opposite. Gaps in key vitamins and minerals recur in the proof. Added nutrients in fortified foods can close many gaps. The authors urge quality checks over labels. A well-built plant diet can serve teens; a sloppy one can harm.
pmc-13610910:
İbrahim Gecili and ten co-authors test two plant compounds in rats in a 2026 study of Alzheimer-like harm. A drug injected into the brain can mimic the sporadic form of the disease, raising a brain signal chemical and harming memory. The team asked whether early dosing with the two acids could blunt that harm.

Sixty-four female rats were split into eight groups, with doses given by mouth for twenty-one days. Treated rats did better on maze and memory tests than untreated ones. Brain tissue showed less cell damage and lower levels of the harmful signals. Higher doses helped more, and one acid at its top dose looked strongest.
pmc-13611110:
Zhao and six co-authors presented an optical encoding scheme in twenty twenty-six for wide-field infrared cameras that stack several views onto one detector. Folding views together saves hardware, but a small target in the merged image no longer shows which view it came from.

The scheme tags each view twice: once by the shape of its blur spot, and once by a light pattern called polarization. The team tested the idea in a detailed computer simulation with realistic noise and light loss. In twenty-five thousand locked trials, the combined code named the right view about ninety-six percent of the time. Shape alone and polarization alone each scored far lower. The authors note the results come from simulation only. Bench tests with real infrared parts must come before the method can be trusted in the field.
pmc-13611210:
Yuhong Li and ten co-authors test how tiny plastic bits affect the gut of young horseshoe crabs, a marine species already under strain. They kept fifth- and sixth-stage young crabs in water with polystyrene particles at levels like those found in the sea, for one week and for three weeks. The team then checked the gut for trapped plastic, stress markers, immune activity, and the mix of gut microbes.

Exposure threw the crabs' gut chemistry off balance and shifted their gut microbes in harmful ways. Helpful bacteria fell while groups linked to disease rose. The younger crabs were hit harder than the older ones, and longer exposure made the effects worse. The authors warn that plastic waste in coastal waters may harm young sea life at a stage when it is least able to cope.
pmc-13611310:
Duohu Gong and co-authors model how fault gases spread inside sealed high-voltage switchgear so sensors can be placed well. When insulation fails, the filling gas breaks down into marker gases that drift through the chamber. Old checks are offline and slow. The team built a simulation joining heat, flow, and gas spread, then checked it against a real test chamber.

Fault position shaped how fast each sensor smelled the gas. Four marker gases drifted in distinct ways. One spot, labeled M4, scored best for a single sensor. The work gives utilities a base for live fault watch.
pmc-13611610:
Billy Camacho and co-authors test a chitosan gel that soaks up heavy metals from water, in a 2026 study. Chitosan is a natural polymer drawn from shell material. The gel was challenged with mercury, nickel, and copper ions, alone and in pairs. Experiments ran at three temperatures and a fixed acidity.

Lab spectra confirmed the gel's makeup and showed metals bound inside it. In paired tests, the metals fought over binding sites, so each was taken up less than alone. Mercury was captured most strongly overall. Computer modeling at the molecular level, using density functional theory, explained the pull of each metal. Heat raised uptake for all three. Water treatment designers get a cheap, well-mapped option.
pmc-13611910:
Katarina Lund and co-authors track what happens when hepatitis B patients stop their daily antiviral pills, in a 2026 study. Long term pill therapy rarely clears a key surface marker of the virus. Stopping can wake the immune system and clear it, but it can also spark a flare. The team followed patients who had taken the pills for at least three years.

Of 25 who stopped, five cleared or nearly cleared the marker and seven reached calm immune control. Six had severe flares and had to restart, and one needed a liver transplant. A related viral marker at the stop date flagged the flare group. The authors urge close, fast blood checks after any stop.
pmc-13612010:
Chiara Bozzola and co-authors test digital training for hearing horse heart sounds in a 2026 study. Listening to the heart is a core skill for vets, but students get few chances to hear the full range of abnormal sounds. The team asked whether adding recorded heart sounds to written study would sharpen students' skill more than text alone.

Forty-one students at two Italian universities were split into two groups for four weeks of self-study; thirty finished the final test. Both groups improved, but the group with recordings gained more on the task of telling one abnormal sound from another. Total scores did not differ by a clear margin. The authors say recordings look like a useful add-on to written study for this skill.
pmc-13612210:
Shuo Zhang leads an eight-author team pinning down a helper protein behind aphid insecticide resistance. The spirea aphid, Aphis spiraecola, damages orchards worldwide and has grown resistant to both neonicotinoid and pyrethroid sprays. Detox enzymes called P450s do the chemical work, but need electrons from one partner protein, NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase. The team cloned the aphid's version of that gene and measured where and when it switches on, across strains.

The gene ran highest in wingless adults, especially in blood and gut tissue, and both insecticides provoked it, raising expression about fivefold. Silencing it cut P450 activity by roughly 17 to 18 percent in resistant strains. Sensitivity snapped back accordingly: the lethal dose fell 57.6 percent for imidacloprid and 49.8 percent for lambda-cyhalothrin. The authors also produced the protein in vitro to confirm activity. This single reductase underwrites resistance to two insecticide families at once, making it an attractive target.
pmc-13612510:
Aldana Cepeda Dean, Natalia Rego, and Luisa Berná argue that bioinformatics is not the meritocracy it imagines itself to be in this 2026 opinion article. The field works with data and code, which feels neutral. Yet women's careers in it leak away at every stage, and their work is cited less and credited less, a pattern named the Matilda effect.

The authors trace the gaps through hiring, recognition, and the slow attrition of the pipeline. They add a newer twist: the field's own tools can bake the bias in, since datasets and algorithms learn from a skewed record. Fixing individuals will not fix this, they argue. Only sustained action by institutions and the community, on credit, hiring, and tool design, can close gaps that effort alone has not.
pmc-13612710:
Sang Hee Kim and colleagues present a 2026 South Korean study comparing nerve-related side effects of two groups of cancer immunotherapy drugs in people with lung cancer. One group blocks a protein called PD-1, and the other blocks its partner, PD-L1. Such side effects are uncommon, yet they can be serious, so knowing whether one drug group carries more risk helps doctors choose and monitor treatment.

Using nationwide health data and a design that mimics a clinical trial, the team matched 931 patients in each group. Nerve problems in the limbs were more common with PD-L1 drugs overall, at 19.2 percent against 14.1 percent. Timing differed too: early problems within 30 days were more common with PD-1 drugs, while the pattern shifted after three months.
pmc-13613010:
Aishwarya Bhowmik and four co-authors examine what chronic methamphetamine does to brain mitochondria in a 2026 paper. The drug kills dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra, the region lost in Parkinson's disease, through oxidative stress driven by one enzyme. Whether the neurons' power plants pile up or break down during chronic exposure was unclear.

Male mice received the drug or saline daily for twenty-eight days. Two proteins that run mitochondrial recycling fell in the target region, hinting the cleanup system was impaired. Sure enough, mitochondrial density inside dopamine neurons rose, and the rise depended on the same enzyme tied to the damage. Breathing tests on the tissue then checked whether the extra mitochondria actually worked. The emerging picture is a traffic jam: damaged power plants accumulate because disposal falters, stressing the very neurons the drug destroys. The study links a street drug's toxicity to a Parkinson's-like cellular failure.
pmc-13613410:
Reinaldo Giudici wrote a 2026 study of a trap in measuring reaction rates in loop reactors. In such rigs the reaction runs in a tube while samples are drawn from a stirred tank. If the whole rig is treated as a plain batch tank, the rate values that come out are false.

Giudici works through the math for set reaction orders and gives plain formulas that link the false values to the true ones. At low pass conversion the order stays right but the rate reads low. At high conversion the false form collapses to first order, ruled by the tank.
pmc-13613510:
Dolores-San Juan and co-authors feed in a 2026 rat study high-fat diets to juveniles and adults and find the young brain's alarm center suffers more. The amygdala, still maturing in adolescence, helps run stress and appetite. Four weeks of fatty food made both age groups overeat modestly.

In juveniles, stress hormone signals in the amygdala fell while inflammation markers rose in blood and brain, immune cells there stirred, and dopamine handling shifted. Adults showed glial shape changes without that full inflammatory profile. Both ages behaved alike in the end, but the young brain paid a deeper molecular price.
pmc-13614310:
Lenin Kumar Verdhi and Nicolai Cramer report a cobalt-catalysed reaction that joins carbon and nitrogen onto allene molecules. The reaction keeps tight control over the product's handedness, a long-standing challenge in this corner of chemistry. Starting from a mixed, racemic set of allenyl esters, their chiral cobalt catalyst picks out one form and builds valuable chiral products called enamido esters. Yields reached 88 percent, with near-perfect handedness ratios above 99 to 1.

The reaction works by kinetic resolution, meaning the catalyst reacts faster with one mirror form and leaves the other behind in enriched purity. Tuning pushed that sorting power to a factor of 138. As a showpiece, the team resolved a natural compound that acts as the male bean weevil's pheromone, a scent chemical of farm interest. Chemists gain a selective route to building blocks that are hard to make cleanly by older means.
pmc-13614810:
Alok Kumar Sahoo and colleagues report a 2026 study of anxiety in Indian parents whose children were having planned surgery at a large hospital. Parental worry before a child's operation is common, yet it is rarely treated as part of care, even though it can affect how the whole episode goes. The study followed 216 parents and scored their anxiety at admission, just before surgery, and at discharge using two standard scales.

Clear anxiety before surgery showed in 56 percent of parents, and mothers scored higher than fathers, at 67.3 percent against 56.9 percent on one measure. Schooling, income, past surgery in the family, and the type of operation all played a part. Naming the parents at highest risk gives hospitals a way to offer calm, clear information where it is needed most.
pmc-13615710:
Büşra Tetik Dinçer and co-authors study blood tests in a rare bone illness of childhood. Their twenty twenty-six paper deals with chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis, where bone swells without germs. Blood markers of swelling can be mild, mid-level, or very high in these children.

The team reviewed cases at one center and split them by marker level at diagnosis. Very high levels can point to look-alike diseases, not this illness. They compared scans, signs, and treatments across the two groups. The work helps doctors judge when high markers should cast doubt on the diagnosis and prompt more checks.
pmc-13616510:
Richard Milani and Carl Lavie write a sharp editorial on a care gap that brackets each heart attack. Drugs that cut bad cholesterol are cheap, safe, and proved, yet most patients reach their attack with that risk long in view and long untreated. The piece, from 2026, reads a study of just under two thousand attack cases at Yale from 2018 to 2022.

Under half the patients were on any such drug when the attack hit. Nine in ten held bad cholesterol past the low goal, and just one in twenty left on paired drugs. No mark gains ground across the five years. The pair call the stall a fail on both sides of the event. Their fix starts with treat-first habits long pre-attack.
pmc-13616610:
Anthony L. Carbone and colleagues present a case report of a 19-year-old man in high-intensity Air Force special warfare training. His vague back, thigh, and foot pain hid an extreme spread of bone stress injuries. Such overuse injuries are common in athletes and trainees, yet they usually strike one or two bones with pain matching the damage. Scans showed grade 3 and 4a stress injuries, near the top of the severity scale, across numerous bones in both legs.

The mismatch drives the report: widespread, severe bone injury with oddly mild, diffuse symptoms. The authors also weigh whether low physical activity during his teenage years left his bones under-built for the sudden training load. Trainers and military doctors are urged to image early when a trainee's pain is vague but stubborn, since stress injury can be silently extensive.
pmc-13616710:
Jiaxin Bai and co-authors build a flu vaccine from a less-used viral surface protein, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. That protein changes less across strains than the usual target, which makes it a hopeful base for a broad vaccine. Proteins for three season strains were made in insect cells.

A nano-scale fat adjuvant boosted the vaccine in mouse tests. Antibody and T cell responses rose, and more immune cells made key signals. The three-part vaccine guarded mice against several flu strains, among them a bird flu strain. The team backs the multi-part design as a path toward a universal flu shot.
pmc-13616810:
Arielle Langer comments on long-term outcomes after blood clots in the veins linked to estrogen, and on the treatment fork they create. The fork is simple: stop blood thinners after a set time, or continue them for life. A large registry study in younger patients without cancer found low recurrence for this group once off treatment.

Langer notes that bleeding on thinners, driven largely by uterine bleeding, ran far higher than recurrence off them for these women. She questions whether estrogen must stop the moment a clot is found, since staying on it during treatment does not seem to raise recurrence. The value of inherited clotting tests for this decision also comes under scrutiny. The piece weighs clot risk against bleeding harm.
pmc-13617210:
Liya Hou and four colleagues survey animal models of aortic valve disease, a growing cause of death for which no drug treatment yet works in the clinic. The disease, covering valve calcification, narrowing, and malformation, makes up more than sixty percent of all valve heart disease. Because its mechanisms remain poorly understood, researchers rely on animal models to test ideas before human trials.

The review walks through the major model types, explaining how each is created, what valve damage it produces, and where it fits best in research. Every model is weighed for strengths and weaknesses, since none copies human disease perfectly. Tables and comparisons aim to help basic and preclinical researchers pick the right model for a given question. The authors hope better model choices will speed the search for drug targets.
pmc-13617610:
Ellen Oudkerk-Sodia and eight colleagues introduce nanolipogels, hybrid lipid and polymer nanoparticles designed to deliver messenger RNA into cells more cheaply and gently than current carriers. Existing carriers can need costly multi-step synthesis, vary between batches, or provoke immune reactions. The particles start from a synthetic phospholipid made in a single enzyme-catalyzed step, then polymerize in water in one pot.

Two partner chemicals give either a permanently charged or an acidity-responsive shell for loading the negatively charged RNA. The finished particles measure under two hundred nanometers, capture more than three quarters of their RNA cargo, and release it steadily over seven days in cell-like conditions. In human and mouse cell tests they kept cells alive as well as optimized liposome controls and far better than a common commercial reagent. One version produced about eleven times more reporter protein than the commercial reagent.
pmc-13618910:
Michelle Heck and five colleagues test whether human sign-trackers, people whose eyes lock onto reward-predicting cues rather than the reward's location, also show stronger bias toward alcohol. Animal work links sign-tracking to addiction vulnerability, and this Pavlovian framework is being translated to human eye-movement tasks. One hundred fifty-nine volunteers completed the cue task, an alcohol attention test, and questionnaires on drinking and personality.

Sign-trackers showed a tendency toward greater alcohol bias than intermediate responders, though not compared with goal-trackers. No differences in alcohol consumption appeared across the behavioral profiles, failing to replicate earlier reports. The authors blame a weak setup: fictitious token rewards and a passive task likely muted the effects. They call the support for the theory preliminary and small. They urge better paradigms with more engaging stimuli and real rewards before the framework's boundary conditions can be judged.
pmc-13619010:
Longfang Chen and co-authors published a 2026 study of a rare gene variant that fires up a cell-death pathway and drives a Still-like inflammatory illness in one family line. Still disease is a whole-body inflammatory illness of the immune system, with no clear root. Family clusters of it had not been reported. This family broke that pattern: three people in three generations bore the illness.

Gene sequencing of the family found one variant, in RIPK3, a gene that runs a bursting form of cell death called necroptosis. Laboratory tests showed the variant is a gain of function: the gene product works too hard and clumps, firing the death pathway. Blood readings from one patient showed two inflammatory pathways lit high and two inflammatory markers raised. A drug blocking it damped the inflammation. The team presents the case as an inherited form of the illness.
pmc-13619210:
Yan Wang and co-authors link childhood loneliness to later heart and vessel disease in Chinese women with low education, in a 2026 study. Data came from a national ageing survey that followed more than four thousand women aged forty-five and older from 2011 to 2020. Loneliness in childhood was recalled at the start.

About five percent reported frequent childhood loneliness with no close friend. Over nine years, about half developed high blood pressure, a third heart disease, and a tenth had a stroke. Lonely children faced notably higher hazards of high blood pressure and heart disease as adults, after wide adjustment. The stroke link was elevated but not firm. The authors stress early social life as part of lifelong heart health.
pmc-13619310:
Roman Krawetz and co-authors checked blood and joint fluid in 2026 for signs of immune attack on joint tissue. In joint diseases, the immune system can make antibodies against its own matrix proteins, the stuff that pads and links joints. The team focused on two such proteins and the antibodies aimed at them. Samples came from healthy people and from patients with three forms of joint disease.

Levels of the two proteins and their antibodies differed by disease and by sample type. One protein ran low in the blood of patients with one disease and high in another. Antibodies to both proteins were raised in most disease groups. In one disease, protein and antibody levels in joint fluid rose together, hinting at a local immune drive.
pmc-13619410:
Jue Wang and co-authors report, in a 2026 case paper, a fast full response in a hard form of rectal cancer. The man, 61, had stage IIIB disease of a kind that most times shrugs off immune drugs: stable satellites and sound repair genes. Care mixed a dual immune drug, which hits PD-1 and CTLA-4 at once, with the XELOX drug pair and rays at 45 gray in 25 hits. Check paths were touch exams, scans, scope views, and tissue bits. Scans at week 12 first showed a full clear. Scope and tissue proof at week 20 backed the call.

No grave immune ill came. At the last check, in March 2026, no return had shown. The team casts the mix as a path to spare the organ.
pmc-13619810:
Five authors led by Rommel Gutierrez read how students roam online course halls while keeping their raw trails at home. Course platforms log each click, yet pooled logs put student life on show. Their frame trains the model in split form across sites, then asks a glass-box lens why it calls a trail roam-rich. Near thirty thousand student-course units were rebuilt from near eleven million clicks.

A clear rule-built roam score serves as the check mark for the build. Top sort scores thus read as a cap on rule catch, not as sight of new truth. With the rule parts cut out, scores stayed high in a lean run. Split-form training kept pace with pooled training in the tests.
pmc-13619910:
Xiaoyi Wang and co-authors study in 2026 self-stigma among adolescents in conflict with the law, and how beliefs about meritocracy shape it. If society is seen as rewarding merit, young offenders may blame themselves doubly, as both offenders and failures. Two studies test that idea with survey and experimental designs.

In the survey of 322 adolescents, stronger meritocracy beliefs predicted higher self-stigma. A path through group self-esteem and social disconnection appeared. In the experiment with 254 participants, only social disconnection carried the effect. The authors suggest boosting social connection as a near-term buffer against self-stigma.
pmc-13620210:
Julieta Benítez-Malvido and seven colleagues studied how gut worms affect male and female spur-thighed tortoises differently across southern Spain. The team sampled tortoises in five land types, from Mediterranean shrubland to farm fields and pine plantations, and measured body traits, growth, and the roundworm communities living in each animal's hindgut.

Worm burden and spread looked similar in both sexes, yet the costs split sharply. Heavier infestation tracked with smaller size and slower growth only in males, while females kept growing steadily. Females also carried more diverse and evenly spread worm communities, arranged in networks that suggest easier transmission among them. Infestation fell in both sexes where unproductive land made up more of the landscape. The authors argue tortoise conservation should plan for the sexes separately, since females seem harder for worms to drag down.
pmc-13623010:
Tadahiko Ohtsuru leads a study comparing one injection against three injections of a freeze-dried platelet concentrate for knee osteoarthritis, the wear-and-tear joint disease that limits walking in older adults. The concentrate, made from the patient's own blood platelets, aims to ease pain without surgery. Earlier work tested single shots only, so the benefit of repeat dosing was unknown.

Patients chose their schedule with their doctors: 1,054 took one injection and 317 took three. Both groups reported pain and function on a standard knee survey over twelve months. The three-injection group edged ahead in the first month, and the edge lasted longer for early-stage disease but not for advanced disease. After adjusting for patient differences, the repeat group more often met the bar for a real clinical response at one year. Side effects per injection were similar, which the authors read as acceptable safety.
pmc-13623110:
Lele Chang and co-authors test a drug pairing for recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer that carries a PIK3CA mutation, a common gene change. The pairing combines immune checkpoint inhibitors, which release the immune system to attack tumours, with tyrosine kinase inhibitors, which block growth signals. No standard approach targets this mutation group.

Data came from two prospective trials plus hospital records, covering fifty-five patients. Twenty-seven received the pairing and twenty-eight received doctor-chosen conventional treatment. Tumours shrank in most patients on the pairing, more often than on conventional care, and the time before cancer grew again more than doubled. Survival leaned the same way without reaching statistical ground. Side effects such as high blood pressure, rash, and thyroid problems were more common with the pairing but were managed, with no treatment-related deaths. The authors call the results a strong case for larger trials.
pmc-13623410:
Julian Schoch and three co-authors argue that dry soil sets a hard limit on how trees recover water at night, in a 2026 paper. Trees balance carbon gain against water loss through leaf pores. Most models stress daytime flows and skip night recovery. The team extends one such model to add storage that buffers day gaps and refills at night, then tests it on field data from a downy oak.

As soil dried, night refill slowed. Below a soil water threshold, refill could not finish before dawn. Leaf pore closing began near that same threshold. The authors say water use is capped not just by day demand but by the length of the night.
pmc-13623710:
Zhenghan Luo and co-authors build a field test for the two deadliest bird flu subtypes. Their 2026 paper pairs fast gene copying with a CRISPR reader to spot H5 and H7 viruses. Both subtypes kill at high rates and threaten public health. The kit needs little gear and runs two reactions per sample.

Adding the CRISPR step sharpened detection a hundred to a thousand times over copying alone. It reached just a few copies per microliter for H7. The test fired only on the target viruses, ignoring look-alike lung pathogens. Primer pairs were tuned for each subtype. The authors pitch the assay as a screening tool for clinics and farms far from big labs.
pmc-13623810:
Samir J Sheth and colleagues published a 2026 follow-up survey of long-term results after a sixty-day nerve stimulation treatment for chronic low back pain. Thin wires placed through the skin deliver stimulation to nerves in the lower back for two months, then come out. Earlier studies hinted the relief could outlast the treatment, and this survey tests that idea in everyday practice.

The survey reached 602 patients who had responded to the treatment, at times ranging from six months to over five years later. Four in five had needed no follow-up procedure such as nerve burning, a permanent implant, or surgery. Among those who avoided further procedures, most reported pain relief or clear gains in quality of life, movement, mood, or sleep. People hoping to dodge surgery or a permanent implant succeeded. The authors present the short treatment as a possible long-lasting, low-risk option.
pmc-13623910:
Fan Zhu and three colleagues published a cohort study in two thousand twenty-six on uric acid swings in kidney disease. Average uric acid is a known risk marker, but how much it bounces between visits may signal instability. Its link to near-term death in chronic kidney disease was unclear.

Over ten thousand five hundred adults with at least three uric acid readings were followed. Higher swing levels tracked with clearly higher short-term mortality, even after full adjustment. No such link appeared for kidney events or heart events. Most deaths came within ninety days, and the signal vanished beyond that window. A large intensive care database reproduced the short-term pattern. The authors read variability as a warning sign of fragile health.
pmc-13624110:
Jin Huang and co-authors test caffeinated chewing gum during repeated sprints in thin air, in this 2026 Europe PMC study. Ten team-sport athletes chewed gum with caffeine or a placebo on separate days, then ran a two-half intermittent sprint test simulating altitude. Each half packed twenty short all-out sprints with brief recoveries.

Total work rose with caffeine in both halves, and peak and mean power were higher. Brain blood measures also rose in both halves; muscle oxygen measures improved in the first half. The gum delivered caffeine fast and sustained performance in low oxygen, a setting where endurance usually suffers.
pmc-13624310:
Jiaxin Li leads a study of how colorectal tumours recruit neutrophils and turn their web-like DNA traps into a spreading weapon. The white cells cast these traps, called NETs, to catch microbes, yet inside tumours the same webs help cancer cells spread. The team focused on a tumour protein, MIIP, known to restrain cancer growth.

In patient tissue, tumours low in MIIP carried neutrophil loads and traps, and patients showed more distant spread and fared worse. In dish experiments, fluid from low-MIIP cancer cells drew neutrophils and triggered trap release, and the traps made the cancer cells more mobile. Tracing the wiring, MIIP binds a signalling protein and damps a pathway that produces a neutrophil-summoning chemical. In a mouse model of liver spread, a trap-dissolving enzyme slowed metastasis, and restoring MIIP strengthened that effect. The authors propose the traps as a treatment target.
pmc-13624410:
Chronic low back pain from worn spinal discs limits daily life, and one posture-based method, known as GDS, is usually taught in person. Haroon Mansha, Saleh Shah, Muhammad Naveed Babur, and Muhammad Junaid Ijaz deliver it through a smartphone app in a small 2026 pilot study. Fifteen patients used the app for six weeks, following video guidance and daily reminders, with pain and quality-of-life surveys taken before and after.

Every quality-of-life domain improved significantly, the disability score shifted by about 40 percent, and four in five patients kept up at least five sessions a week. The authors call the early results promising but say larger studies must pin down the program's settings before wider use.
pmc-13625210:
Lucas Berger Munaro, Daniel J Tolhurst, and Jessica E Rutkoski show how a profit-based scorecard can steer wheat breeding in Illinois. Breeders often pick lines by yield alone, yet farmers earn from test weight and maturity too. The team priced each trait from the region's cropping system and grain price rules. They then fed a genomic model data on 2,995 wheat lines, five traits, and twelve test settings from 2022 to 2024.

The combined multi-trait model explained most inherited variation and predicted breeding values with high accuracy. Picking by the profit index returned about 120 dollars per hectare, beating both a single-trait model and yield-only picking, which returned under 100 dollars. Trait links also shifted with setting, a warning that one fixed recipe fits poorly.
pmc-13626210:
Walt Adamson and co-authors present a 2026 study of what sets the level of a protein in blood that is tied to kidney disease risk. Variants of this protein's gene are major risk factors for chronic kidney disease in people with recent African ancestry. Yet how gene type and nearby control variants shape the protein's blood level was not well defined.

The team measured the protein in over forty thousand UK Biobank members. Levels varied in a dose-like way with known gene variants, one of which had the largest effect. Even after gene type was counted, levels stayed higher in Black participants. The study maps coding, modifier, and regulatory effects on the protein.
pmc-13626510:
Kapil Singhal and co-authors survey sleep among India's anaesthesiologists, where broken nights are part of the job. Irregular shifts, on-call duty, and high stress eat into rest, and poor sleep dulls the judgment patients depend on. Of 728 doctors answering the online survey, more than sixty percent slept under seven hours, and over half scored in the poor range on a sleep quality index.

Several factors independently predicted bad sleep: being female, taking more than three night or on-call duties a month, a sedentary lifestyle, high stress at home, and an existing sleep disorder. Respondents blamed irregular hours and work-life imbalance, and asked for systematic fixes rather than personal tips. The authors argue the findings are a patient-safety issue, not only a wellness one. They recommend structured rosters and attention to lifestyle and stress as the first steps toward a rested workforce.
pmc-13626910:
Haifu Zhang, Shuojun Li, Yonghang Feng, and Biyun Xie weigh intensive insulin therapy for fat-driven pancreatitis in a review from 2026. Very high blood triglycerides can inflame the pancreas badly. Standard tools pooled the results. Registered in advance, the review followed a set plan. The pooled verdict can settle ward arguments about drip intensity. Emergency care for a rising condition needs that clarity.
pmc-13627110:

pmc-13627810:

pmc-13628210:

pmc-13628610:
Qinghao Ge and co-authors build a pocket test kit that sniffs out mercury in seafood and water by color change, in a 2026 paper. Mercury rides the food chain into fish and shellfish and harms nerves and kidneys. Lab grade detection is slow and bench bound.

pmc-13628910:

pmc-13629010:
Zeliha Yılmaz and co-authors study health anxiety in mothers of young children in hospital, in a 2026 paper. The worry pattern, called cyberchondria, grows when mothers search symptoms online under stress and doubt. The team asked how tiredness and felt support from nurses link to its five sides.

The authors urge clear, planned talks between nurses and parents.
pmc-13629410:

pmc-13629510:
Morgan Walker and Chris Baugh walk through a case of hemolytic anemia in an emergency department, where the urgent work up led to a hidden cause. This anemia, from red cell breakdown inside or outside vessels, is rare but can kill. The report came out in twenty twenty-six.

A man in his sixties came in with two weeks of breathlessness on effort and fatigue, with steady vital signs. Lab work showed low hemoglobin and red cell share, plus marks of cell breakdown. pmc-13629810:
Kah Shuen Thong and ten colleagues audited the use of antibacterial drugs among COVID-19 patients in northern Malaysia. The audit covered ten government hospitals. Their study sampled 476 patients from over nineteen thousand hospital stays. The span ran from February 2020 to December 2021.

Drug use rose and fell with surges in admissions. Severe disease drove the ordering. So did conditions like diabetes and chronic lung or kidney disease. pmc-13630510:
Jinjin Wang and co-authors test blood sugar markers as signs of early blood vessel aging in this 2026 study. pmc-13630710:
Hernia repair with mesh is common, and where the mesh sits may shape later surgery in the belly. Elisa Pelfini and co-authors lay out the ORION study plan in 2026. The study will follow patients across European centers who need new keyhole belly surgery after an earlier mesh repair. One group had a hernia return, and the other needs surgery for other reasons. Data will be gathered over one year from March 2026. The hernia group gets extra checks at thirty and ninety days. Results should show how the first mesh choice affects the second operation.
pmc-13630810:
Rex Fernando and two colleagues present a protocol that lets a network of computers reach agreement. It works even when up to a third of the members are malicious. That is a standard, well-studied hardness base for post-quantum cryptography. It still needs a public key setup and a shared reference string. Its route runs through a generic use of batched argument systems. The authors frame the result as scalable agreement on conservative foundations.
pmc-13631310:
Ricardo Gutiérrez and colleagues traced a decade of drug-proof gene spread in Costa Rica. Genome analysis showed both plasmid and chromosome homes, with a world-shared plasmid backbone splitting into multi-drug-proof giant plasmids. Gutiérrez and colleagues urge steady genomic watch.
pmc-13631810: Giacomo Marzi, Marco Balzano, and Davide Marchiori reply in 2026 to a comment on their free tool for a rater-agreement score. The comment flagged a flaw in one part of the tool's ratio-scale maths, while other scale types stand untouched. A fixed build is now out in open stores, data sets whose least value is one were never hit, and the tool stays free with a public log of fixes.
pmc-13632510:
Emily Gracey, Sylvie Kandel, and Jed Lampe build a lab model for newborn drug safety in a 2026 paper. Testing drugs in newborns is ethically hard, and no good human cell model existed for how a newborn liver handles drugs. Babies in intensive care often get many drugs off-label, raising the risk of harm. The team grew liver-like cells from adult stem cells that keep a fetal enzyme active.

The cells showed a mix of fetal markers and newborn drug-handling genes, distinct from mature liver cells. They processed a key hormone and a common sedative in the same pattern as newborn liver cells. The model also responded to drug interaction tests, offering a platform for this fragile group.
pmc-13632610:
Mette Østergaard Thunbo and co-authors study bladder infection treatment in pregnancies after gastric bypass in a 2026 Danish cohort study. Bypass surgery reshapes the gut and may blunt absorption of oral antibiotics, risking failed cures.

Bypass patients claimed cystitis antibiotics far more often, about a quarter versus about an eighth of pregnancies. Among treated women, bypass history tied to notably higher odds of repeat prescriptions within two weeks and of hospital-recorded bladder infection. Severe complications stayed rare in both groups. The authors read the pattern as weaker drug effect or a harder course, and advise closer monitoring for these mothers.
pmc-13632810:
Anja I. Frei and seven colleagues published this 2026 study of aggression and violence against intensive care nurses in Basel. pmc-13633110:

pmc-13633510:

pmc-13634210:

pmc-13634710:

pmc-13637610:

pmc-13642110:

pmc-13643810:

pmc-13645610:

pmc-13645810:

pmc-13646110:

pmc-13646210:

pmc-13647310:

pmc-13648310:

pmc-13649410:

pmc-13649510:

pmc-13650010:

pmc-13650710:

pmc-13650810:

pmc-13651610:

pmc-13651910:

pmc-13652510:

pmc-13653010:

pmc-13654110:

pmc-13655410:

pmc-13657210:

pmc-13658710:
Yiming Zhong and co-authors review the cell's protein cleanup system and hearing loss in a 2026 paper. The cleanup system tags worn proteins and breaks them down in a shredder unit. pmc-13659210:

pmc-13661810:

pmc-13662510:

pmc-13662610:
Zaheer A Rana and co-authors study how nerve signals set muscle speed in a 2026 paper. Muscles come in fast and slow types, and nerve firing patterns help pick which type a fiber acts like. Fast fibers respond to short, rapid bursts of signal, while slow fibers respond to long, slow ones. Less was known about which gene switches turn on the fast program.

The team gave muscles fast and slow signal patterns and tracked gene changes. One switch, called Ets2, rose fast only under the rapid pattern and moved into cell nuclei. Blocking that switch cut fast gene activity in fast muscles. The work names Ets2 as a key driver of the fast muscle program.
pmc-13663910:
Theodoros Xanthos reviews how telling a patient a diagnosis shapes what happens next, in this 2026 paper. A correct diagnosis does not guarantee the patient grasps it or gets the right follow-up care. Xanthos sorts the evidence on labels, explanations of test results, the nocebo effect, and what happens when a diagnosis is later revised.

Experiments show that wording alone can shift how severe an illness feels and what treatment people say they want, though often in made-up settings. Warnings about side effects can themselves breed symptoms, a mechanism the review is careful not to pin on any one patient. Follow-up studies expose a plainer failure: correct or revised findings often never reach the care that follows. Xanthos urges judging communication by understanding and completed care, not symptom relief alone.
pmc-13664610:
Claire Lloyd-Davies and Abdul Kasem review in 2026 the joint use of two tracing tools for breast cancer that cannot be felt by touch. Finding the tumor and its first draining lymph node has grown less invasive with new tools. One tool is a radar reflector placed in the tumor before drug therapy starts. The other is a magnetic tracer, given before surgery, that marks the sentinel node.

The team looked back at patients treated at a London hospital from late 2022 to mid 2026. All had breast conserving surgery with sentinel node biopsy using both tools. The record shows how the pair performed together in real practice. A reliable pair lets surgeons plan calmer surgery dates, since neither tool needs same day injections.
pmc-13665010:
Ana María Correa-Basurto and co-authors review a ring based chemical family as a source of new type two diabetes drugs, in a paper from 2026. Diabetes joins high blood sugar with insulin resistance and slow harm to vessels large and small.

Lab compounds from this family hit many diabetes targets, from sugar cutting enzymes to hormone and fat sensors. Small swaps on the ring, such as added halogens or fused partner rings, swung strength and selectivity a great deal. Some matched or beat standard drugs in lab tests. No member has yet proven itself in patients, the authors stress.
pmc-13666010:
Vaughn and colleagues introduce in 2026 a fast method for mapping electrical synapses in living brain tissue. Electrical coupling is widespread, but mapping it normally needs slow multi-electrode recordings. Their technique pairs light stimulation of engineered neurons with a spike-timing computation that scores coupling strength. They call it opto-delta-L.

In the thalamus, coupled networks reached across a hundred micrometers and mixed neuron subtypes freely. Each hub cell coupled to a few neighbors. In cortex, somatostatin neurons were coupled most strongly. The authors say the method can speed study of how electrical synapses shape circuits, behavior, and thought.
pmc-13667410:
Shin-Rou Yin and co-authors build artificial borders inside a crystal film in this 2026 study. The material can hold electric charge in a set direction, a trait used in memory devices. In real samples, borders between crystal grains affect how the charge flips, but those borders are hard to study one by one.

The team lifted thin films and joined them at set angles, making borders they could control. The border area needed a stronger push to flip and leaked more current than the grain area. Leakage rose sharply as the join angle grew. Tests also showed the border acts as a high-flow path, with a very low energy bar for charge flow.
pmc-13669210:
Kiseleva and co-authors study how water droplets jump off textured surfaces as they condense, in this 2026 paper. On water-repelling surfaces, merging droplets can leap away on their own, clearing the surface fast. That helps anti-fogging, water harvesting, and heat transfer.

The team varied the spacing of tiny cone arrays while keeping cone shape the same. They found a spacing threshold that separates jumping from non-jumping behavior. Tight arrays let very small droplets depart cleanly, while wider spacing left droplets partly stuck and slowed removal. Microscope evidence tied the difference to how fully each droplet rests on the texture. The results give designers a clear rule for building better condensing surfaces.
pmc-13670410:
Schmeising-Barnes, Lidington, Moschopoulou, Trivedi, and Waller interview people with chronic heartburn about a swallowable sponge test. The test could screen for food pipe cancer without a camera scope. It samples cells that flag a precancerous change called Barrett's. Forty British adults on regular reflux medicine talked through their views. All sat in the age bands a screening program would target.

Most liked the quick, simple, low-invasion test, yet not all felt able or willing to take it. Three themes ran through the talks. People described how they share reflux care with clinicians. They showed a dislike of uncertainty that the test could both feed and calm. Their views of who counts as a worthy candidate also varied. The 2026 authors urge planners to design around those concerns.
pmc-13674310:
Predicting complex traits like disease from limited data is the problem behind a 2026 methods paper by Baining Shen and co-authors. Their tool, called mBoost, checks whether the features fed into a model are good ones and whether the chosen model itself is a poor fit. The work targets disease prediction, where costly data collection keeps sample sizes small.

Using tests on simulated data and real examples, the team shows mBoost picking the right size for a neural network in a drug study and spotting weak models in gut microbiome cohorts. It also gives a confidence measure for a model's results and a way to judge whether a trained model can be trusted on new data. For researchers stuck switching models in hope of better results, that kind of check can save time and point to a model worth keeping.
pmc-13675110:
Mingyou Yu and co-authors report a 2026 rat study on stem cells from human umbilical cords as a treatment for brain bleeding in newborns. Bleeding inside the brain's fluid spaces can badly injure preterm infants. The team tested whether these cells protect the young brain and spur repair.

Preterm rats were split into healthy, injured, and treated groups. The cells were placed into the brain's fluid spaces after the bleed was induced. The researchers tracked weight, behavior, tissue state, cell death, and signal proteins tied to growth. One growth pathway named in the title links the cells to nerve regrowth. Early animal results like these form the base for any later move toward care for infants.
pmc-13675610:
Anna Novoseltseva and co-authors report a 2026 study on how the wait between death and tissue fixing harms myelin, the fatty wrap on nerve fibers. In human brain studies that wait varies and can fake or hide disease signs. The team held brains from five aged rhesus monkeys in the cold and imaged them at death, one day, and three days, using two light-based methods that read fiber order.

Longer waits brought steady decay: order signals fell in both white and gray matter, scatter rose, and defects per area climbed, seen as swellings, bubbles, and breaks. The authors say the changes are easy to measure with light tools, so brain banks should log and standardize the wait.
pmc-13675810:
Nan Chen and Liang'an Huo model how illness news and illness itself spread together in a 2027 paper. People move between places, hear word both online and in person, and carry both news and germs as they go.

Their model stacks three layers: online news, offline news, and the epidemic, all tied by travel. Math yields the tipping point where an outbreak takes off, and test runs check the math. Travel speeds news spread, the runs show. Both news channels hold the illness back, lifting the tipping point and shrinking outbreaks. Denser, faster news flow helps more.
pmc-13676110:
Manaf Aljishi and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a new use for the drug finerenone in a rare genetic kidney disease. The disease scars the kidney's filters and often ignores standard immune-calming drugs. It stems from a fault in making coenzyme Q, a cell energy helper.

The patient was a 35-year-old woman with lasting protein in her urine after pregnancy and a strong family history of early kidney failure. Gene tests found the faulty gene, and standard drugs plus a supplement had failed or were not tolerated. After finerenone began in May 2024, her urine protein measure improved greatly. A single case cannot prove a treatment, but it flags an option for a disease with few choices left.
pmc-13676210:
Abdulla Albastaki and Judith Smith review if soil germ maps can place crime soil in court, in work from 2026. Soil is a top trace in outdoor violent crime. New gene scans plus smart sorts claim they can split soils that old tests cannot tell apart.

High scores in past work come from small closed test sets, not true source proof. Key germs may also shift in store or transit, which clouds court use. The pair sets a least data list for court files. Germ maps should back old soil tests for now, not swap them out.
pmc-13676410:
Dominik Hoch and co-authors turn a wood-derived building block into strong adhesives with a masked-ring trick. The block, guaiacol, is a core unit of lignin, the polymer that stiffens wood. Softwood lignin could feed a vast stream of it. Their 2026 work wakes the block with an oxidant, phenyliodine diacetate, which forms a masked ortho-quinone in minutes at room temperature.

Three woken blocks join into one starter unit, and sulfur-rich partners link them into a glue network. Lap-shear tests on the new adhesives reached up to 16.9 megapascals, a professional-grade mark. The trick also works straight on raw technical lignin. Those brews glued aluminum at 9.1 megapascals. The team pitches the masked ring as a green bridge from wood waste to high-performance materials.
pmc-13678110:
A one-stop desk that handles all outpatient errands in one place may lift how patients rate a hospital. Gong Xue and co-authors surveyed that idea at a large hospital in a 2026 study. Over one thousand outpatients or family members from fifteen departments answered in spring 2025. The survey covered booking, talks with doctors, and overall satisfaction. Two scores summed up ease of the one-stop service and quality of communication.

Overall satisfaction ran high, near nine in ten patients. Both ease and communication tracked strongly with the total score. In layered tests, each one predicted satisfaction on its own. The authors say smooth errands and clear talk are twin levers for better visits. The study is one hospital's snapshot, offered as a base for wider checks.
pmc-13679810:
Meron Biza and co-authors report a rare case of a chest infection that sprang from a severe swelling of the gullet, with no injury or surgery behind it. Their 2026 case report describes a 75-year-old woman with diabetes who had just had bad pneumonia. She came in with chest pain that stung when she breathed, plus short breath.

A scan ruled out a lung clot but showed a thickened gullet wall, streaks in the fat around it, and fluid near the lung. The picture fit the rare gullet illness and a spread to the space between the lungs. Since she was stable, the team held off on a scope that might tear a weak spot. Fourteen days of strong vein-fed drugs cleared both her signs and her scans.
pmc-13680310:
Ingmar Brilmayer, Philip Georgis, and Petra Schumacher wire pairs of talkers for gaze and brain waves at once in a 2026 study. In talk, a listener must pick which thing a word points to, fast. Labs can now track eyes and brain signals together, live, as two people chat.

In a simplified director game, one partner told the other to move objects while both wore the gear. Brain ripples tied to words and to glances were pulled apart from the talk's overlap. A target with a hidden rival drew a stronger late brain wave, a sign of harder work. Looks led the brain's answer, the records show.
pmc-13680610:
Viacheslav Korolev leads a team of twelve in a 2026 physics study on light bursts from solids under strong laser fields. When a fierce laser drives a semiconductor, it can emit high-order harmonics, a route to compact fast light sources. A quick fading of the driven state caps how bright and clean that light can be.

The team measured how the yield shifts with laser color in thin and bulk crystals, then ran deep calculations of how electrons scatter off lattice vibrations. Only when the math used scatter rates that vary across the crystal's momentum map did the yield match. Carriers race into zones where scattering is fierce.
pmc-13682410:
Yolanda Lau and co-authors study how often people with multiple sclerosis in England develop diabetes, and what that pairing does to their outcomes, in a cohort study from 2026. The data came from linked primary care, hospital, and death records. Each person with the nerve disease was matched with up to ten people without it.

Over an average of fifteen years of follow-up, diabetes arose more often in the sclerosis group. Once diabetes appeared, hospital visits rose sharply and stays grew much longer, a median of twelve days against two. Death risk also climbed by a strong margin. Similar patterns held in the comparison group. The authors argue that preventing diabetes matters greatly in this population.
pmc-13682610:
Christenson and co-authors fed extra methionine to pregnant beef cattle in late gestation in a 2026 study. Methionine is an amino acid that may support growth and later calf performance. Two three-year studies covered artificially bred heifers and naturally bred cows on winter range.

Heifers given grain supplements, with or without the amino acid, ended heavier and gained more than hay-only heifers. Unsupplemented cows on range had lower body condition and weight than all supplemented groups, and lower pregnancy rates. Calf outcomes and carcass traits barely differed across groups. Protein supplements mattered, the authors conclude, but the extra methionine itself gave no clear gain for mothers or calves.
pmc-13682810:
Liqin Cao and co-authors review how new drugs and cell therapies feed into transplant for stubborn leukemia in a 2026 paper. Relapsed acute myeloid leukemia carries a grim outlook. A donor stem cell transplant is the only cure for most. Getting patients to transplant in remission is the battle.

Fresh mutation checks at relapse pick the targets. FLT3 blockers bridge patients to transplant and guard them after. IDH inhibitors serve their mutation carriers. The BCL2 blocker venetoclax anchors salvage regimens. Cellular immunotherapy joins the toolkit as well. The review sequences these weapons around the transplant, aiming to turn a disastrous prognosis into a curable one.
pmc-13682910:
Seungwoo Cha and co-authors used brain imaging to predict how well a stroke patient's arm will work, in a 2026 study. Early prediction helps therapists plan personal rehabilitation. The team studied two hundred and forty-two patients with a fresh stroke from a blocked brain artery, all of whom had brain scans and arm function tests. Software measured the damaged area and its overlap with movement paths automatically.

Adding the imaging measures clearly improved prediction of arm scores, and damage to the motor tract stood out as the key factor. A grouping analysis then found three kinds of patients: younger people with mild problems, older people with many other illnesses, and people with severe deficits and large strokes. Outcomes differed sharply across the groups. The authors say the profiles can guide personal care plans.
pmc-13683910:
Samantha Biglieri and co-authors review the evidence in a 2025 paper on communities that work well for people with dementia. Such communities aim to include and support residents with dementia and their care partners, rather than push them to the margins. The team gathered past reviews across many fields to see what builds and sustains these places.

Working across groups and fields stood out as vital, as did raising awareness and cutting stigma. Rules and planning guides play a key role, and street and building design can ease daily navigation. Social and community supports foster connection and wellbeing. One gap stood out: few reviews probed the policy and political conditions such communities need. The authors call that the next frontier.
pmc-13685610:
Younis and co-authors test whether the actin shell of white blood cells is needed for them to stick to vessel walls. Sticking is the first key step when these cells leave the blood to fight inflammation. Prior work in cystic fibrosis cells hinted the shell helps integrins cluster.

The team used a drug that blocks actin growth in human and mouse monocytes. The drug cut shell formation after chemokine signals, yet left total actin levels in place. Early results split two jobs: the shell seems needed for integrin clustering, not for switching integrins on. That split may explain sticking defects in some diseases.
pmc-13688910:
Nine authors sequence bacteria from a recycled water plant in this 2026 study. Reusing treated wastewater matters more as the climate shifts, but counting Escherichia coli, the standard safety check, says nothing about which strains survive treatment or what risks they carry.

The team sequenced 180 isolates taken along the plant, from inflow to final outflow. They found eighty-eight strain types across eight family groups, with more variety entering than leaving. The survivors' virulence and drug resistance gene profiles looked much like those upstream, even though total counts fell by over ninety percent. Matches with animal, bird, and human strains hinted at many sources feeding the plant.
pmc-13689010:
Francesca Cristetti and co-authors track the microbes at work in wine made from Nebbiolo grapes grown in several vineyards, in work published in 2026. The fungi and bacteria on grapes at harvest help drive the ferment and shape the wine. They also carry marks of the place the grapes grew. Whether those marks last once a commercial starter yeast is added was not clear.

The team charted fungi and bacteria through the ferments and paired those charts with measures of the wine's chemistry and aroma. The mix of microbes shifted over time in clear patterns of succession, and marks tied to region held up from start to finish. The wines' chemical and aroma profiles differed in step with the microbes. The findings show that a sense of place stays readable in the wine even when a starter is used.
pmc-13689210:
Harrison and a team including Pandher hunt Ontario soils for bacteria that feed common bean plants in twenty twenty-six. Beans partner with root bacteria that pull nitrogen from the air, but the pairing often underperforms. The team trapped over two hundred strains from farm soils using four bean types. Full genomes sorted the catch into eleven species, two of them new.

Soil source shaped which species turned up far more than bean type did. One new species fixed nitrogen best on average in greenhouse tests. Strong strains appeared across several species, though. The genome library now stands ready for picking starter strains tuned to Ontario fields, the authors say.
pmc-1852410:
Gupta, Stamatoyannopoulos, Bailey, and co-authors explain Tomtom, a method for comparing DNA motifs. Motifs are short patterns in DNA that proteins recognise when switching genes on or off. New patterns are found often, but judging whether one matches a known pattern needs sound statistics.

Tomtom measures how similar two motifs are and tests whether that likeness could arise by chance. Users can search a database of known motifs with a newly found one as the query. Reliable matching helps researchers name the proteins likely to bind a site and plan follow-up tests.
pmc-2707010:
Liberati, Altman, Tetzlaff, and co-authors explain the PRISMA Statement for reporting systematic reviews. Systematic reviews and pooled analyses judge whether health care treatments work. Readers can only trust such reviews if the methods are reported fully and clearly.

This long companion paper explains each item of the updated PRISMA guidance and gives examples. It shows authors what to report about searching, selecting, and combining studies. Journals worldwide adopted PRISMA, so the explanation shaped how evidence summaries in medicine are written and checked to this day.  Checklists in the paper show authors exactly which details reviewers will seek.
pmc-2816710:
Larsen, Vogensen, van den Berg, and co-authors compare gut microbes in adults with type 2 diabetes and adults without it. Recent evidence had suggested a link between metabolic disease and the bacterial populations living in the gut. Whether diabetic gut communities truly differ was still an open question.

The team assessed the make-up of intestinal microbes in both groups as controls against each other. Finding real differences would support the idea that gut bacteria play a role in diabetes, not merely reflect diet or drugs. The study helped launch wide interest in microbe-based diabetes care.
pmc-2946910:
Huynh-Thu, Irrthum, Wehenkel, and co-authors test tree-based methods for inferring gene regulatory networks from expression data. Rebuilding the wiring diagram of which genes control which others is a pressing open problem in systems biology. Gene expression measurements from microarrays offer clues, but the network itself stays hidden.

The authors assess their approach within a community benchmarking effort for reverse engineering networks. Tree-based methods treat each gene's activity as something to predict from other genes. Knowing which methods recover real networks best guides the search for drug targets and disease mechanisms.
pmc-3965110:
Finn, Bateman, Clements, and their co-authors described Pfam in 2014, a database of protein families. A protein family is a set of proteins that share a common part and often a common job. Pfam is served from sites in the United Kingdom and the United States and is used worldwide.

Release twenty-seven held close to fifteen thousand entries, each checked by hand by an expert. Users can search a new protein sequence and learn which known families it belongs to. That match gives a strong first clue to what the protein does, which guides lab work on genes, disease, and drug targets.
pmc-4402510:
Ritchie, Phipson, Wu, and their co-authors described limma for RNA sequencing in 2015. Limma is an R and Bioconductor package that gives an integrated way to analyze gene expression data. It handles complex study designs and borrows information across genes to cope with small sample sizes.

The paper shows how limma's methods, first built for microarrays, were extended to RNA-seq counts. Borrowing strength across genes steadies results when only a few samples exist. That is the common case in costly patient studies. Limma became a core tool for finding genes that differ between healthy and diseased tissue or before and after treatment.
pmc-4614810:
Eren, Esen, Quince, and their team presented Anvi'o in 2015, a platform for omics data. High-throughput sequencing and related technologies were transforming studies of natural microbial communities. Full study of microbial lifestyles needs ways to organize and view genetic information interactively.

Anvi'o lets users explore genomes and metagenomes together with their own added data layers. Researchers can inspect, compare, and share analyses through a visual interface. That interactivity helps teams form and test ideas while looking at the data, not after. The platform supports work on how microbes live, interact, and drive processes in oceans, soils, and hosts.
pmc-5715110:
Peter Bankhead and colleagues introduced QuPath, open source software for digital pathology, in 2017. Pathologists now scan whole slides into large digital images, but viewing and measuring them by hand is slow. A free, flexible tool was missing for research use.

QuPath lets users view whole slides, mark regions, and train the software to find tumor areas. It can measure large numbers of cells in a batch and export the results for statistics. Because the code is open, labs can adapt it and share methods. The tool helped make digital slide analysis routine in cancer research.
pmc-6004510:
Godfred Boateng, Torsten Neilands, Edward Frongillo, and colleagues wrote best practices for building survey scales in 2018. Health and social research depends on scales that measure attitudes, symptoms, and behaviors. Building a sound scale takes many steps that are easy to do badly.

The primer walks through item writing, expert review, pilot testing, and checks for structure and reliability. It explains common traps, such as too few items or samples that are too narrow. Each stage has clear advice a small team can follow. New researchers can use it to produce measures that others can trust and reuse.
pmc-7618010:
George Seed and a large team study acquired resistance to PARP inhibitors in advanced prostate cancer, in work from 2024. These drugs work against tumors with defects in homologous recombination repair, but resistance emerges. Samples came from patients in the TOPARP-B trial with metastatic castration-resistant disease, tracked to the end of treatment.

Reversion mutations that restore BRCA2 or PALB2 appeared in most such tumors by treatment end. Many reversions bore marks of a specific repair route involving POLQ. Their count and timing linked to survival outcomes. For tumors with full BRCA2 deletion, rare cells without the deletion were selected instead. The data point to restored repair as the core need in resistance.
pmc-7619410:
Britain has some of the world's highest rates of drinking during pregnancy, so the long-term effects on children matter. Parsonage and four co-authors use a large British birth cohort to ask whether alcohol exposure before birth shapes risky behavior at sixteen. They study 6,752 teenagers and compare no exposure with infrequent, frequent, and binge-level exposure, tracking seven risk behaviors.

Teenagers with infrequent or frequent exposure were more likely to drink hazardously at sixteen, with the strongest link for frequent exposure. Those exposed to binge drinking were more likely to have underage sex and scored higher on total risk behavior. The authors back the official guidance that avoiding alcohol in pregnancy is safest. They call for more research on how exposure before birth echoes into the next generation's choices.
pmc-8012210:
Jeffrey Granja and co-authors introduced ArchR in 2021, a software package for studying how accessible the DNA is inside single cells. Methods that profile chromatin accessibility one cell at a time can map the regulatory landscape of a tissue in fine detail. The data grew faster than the tools, leaving researchers with huge datasets and slow ways to read them.

ArchR was built to handle that scale, pulling biological meaning out of accessibility data quickly and in an integrated workflow. The authors describe how the package aligns cells, finds marker regions, and links them to genes. For labs working with single-cell regulatory data, it turned an unwieldy analysis into a manageable routine.
podcast-joerogan-ZkJjqGLoK10:
Director Neill Blomkamp talks about eternal recurrence in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Blomkamp, who made District 9, is known for gritty science fiction with real-world teeth. Here the subject is an old idea: that time loops, and all things return exactly as they were.

He and Rogan test the notion against his films, his life, and the strange pull of patterns that repeat. Rogan asks whether living as if life recurs would change how a person acts. The segment is the filmmaker's most philosophical hour on the show, a break from craft talk into the deep structure of time itself.
podmore-newer-spiritualism-1910:
Frank Podmore took his keen tools to fresh marvels in The Newer Spiritualism, his book of 1910.
