New stars of the dark room then drew crowds with forms that took shape and things that moved at no touch. Podmore sat, watched, and checked each claim as he had for years. His finds are grave for the faith's fans.

Trick ropes, hid hands, and stage craft fill his case. He grants the odd scrap, yet finds the new wave weak. The book is the best bust of its age. It ends his long watch with a sigh.
pound-provenca-1910:
Provença, published in Boston in 1910, is Pound's early collection of translations and originals drawn from the troubadours of medieval Provence. Before Pound was a modernist leader, he was a scholar of these twelfth-century love poets, and this book shows why.

He renders Arnaut Daniel, Bertran de Born, and others into English verse that strains to keep their music and difficulty. Original poems in the same manner stand beside the translations. Pound believed modern poetry had to pass through this medieval discipline. The book is the record of that apprenticeship, and of a young poet finding his masters.
price-cost-indexes-from-1875-to-1989-est:
Michael S. Hart, the founder of Project Gutenberg, wrote this essay on price and cost indexes running from 1875 toward 2010. First published as a column called the Rate of Change of the Rate of Change in the Electronic Journal of Virtual Culture and expanded for release in November 1993. His opening paradox sets the argument: computers look like an incredible bargain. They are twice the bargain they seem, because the dollars themselves keep shrinking.

Hart works the arithmetic of his own drives, where each year's gear is cheaper and faster than the last. His tables of indexes turn anecdote into series, an early attempt to measure deflation in information goods. The essay is also a Gutenberg manifesto in disguise: if computing power halves in price while doubling in worth, free digital libraries become inevitable.
prize-money-sailor-s-knots-part-10:
W. W. Jacobs placed a comic tale from his Sailors' Knots of 1909 in the tap-room of the Cauliflower inn at Claybury, where an old man holds court by the fire. Snow lies on the fields, horses steam outside, and talk turns to how Claybury men amuse themselves.

The old man rails against Bob Pretty, whom he calls the biggest rascal and poacher in the village, and hints at a story about a prize hamper. Jacobs builds the tale from pub talk, sly tricks, and village rivalry. Readers get his well-known blend of dry humour and seaside character.
promptuarium-alchemiae-das-ist-vornehmer: A German title page, worn and hard to read in the scan, announces a storehouse of writings on the stone of the wise. The book gathers choice pieces by learned philosophers, with skilled alchemist hand-work and tested ways of making medicines. Its sources come from animals, plants, minerals, and metals, offered as needful to alchemists and doctors alike. The page carries a grant of privilege and names its publisher, the front door of an old German work on hidden arts.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
Charivaria fronts Punch for March 10, 1920, in volume 158, gathering short comic notes on Ireland, Poland, boxing, and dentistry. The London weekly kept its peacetime readers supplied with a joke for nearly every headline.

London is said to hold one hundred thousand more people than New York, though they are only just living. A warning that the Home Rule Bill would cause friction in Ireland is met with sorrow at the very thought. Poland's finance minister asks for a loan of three thousand million francs, Dempsey faces a draft-dodging charge, and gold in the mouth is declared out of date.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: A publisher's header alone introduces the tenth volume of The Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte in the pages shown. Title, author, and language are its whole news: the work is Constant's, and the text is English. No preface explains this part, no contents page maps it, and no opening line of narrative is printed. What Constant recounts in volume ten, and at what point of Napoleon's life it begins, are facts that these opening pages do not supply.
ricardo-high-price-bullion-1810:
David Ricardo made his name with The High Price of Bullion, a pamphlet of 1810. Britain's Bank Restriction had freed the Bank of England from paying gold for notes. Bullion prices rose, and Ricardo blamed paper money issued in excess. His tract applies the quantity theory of money to the case.

Too many notes, he argues, cheapen each one against gold and goods. The cure was a return to cash payments under strict rule. The pamphlet's clarity won him a hearing among statesmen and thinkers. It set the terms of the great bullion debate. Economists still cite it as a model pamphlet. Ricardo the theorist enters history here.
rilke-malte-laurids-brigge-1910:
Die Aufzeichnungen des Malte Laurids Brigge, Rilke's only novel, appeared in German in 1910. The text here is the German original; the first English translation came in 1930 and is not in the public domain. Malte, a young Danish nobleman without money, lives in a cheap Paris room and writes what he sees.

Fear walks with him through hospitals, crowds, and streets full of the poor. Memories of his childhood home in Denmark break into the Paris notes without warning. Rilke breaks the tale into fragments, more diary than plot. The book became the first great German novel of modern city consciousness. Its dread and pity still feel new.
robinson-town-down-the-river-1910:
Edwin Arlington Robinson published The Town Down the River in 1910, returning to the Tilbury Town portraits that had made his reputation. By then Robinson had won powerful admirers, including President Theodore Roosevelt, who found him a government job. This volume is the essential middle collection of his career.

New townsfolk join the gallery: failures, dreamers, and quiet sufferers rendered in exact, ironic verse. Robinson also includes poems on larger themes, among them a notable piece on the painter George Crabbe. His sympathy never turns soft, and his endings often twist the knife gently. Readers who want Robinson beyond the famous anthology pieces should start with this book and its haunted New England streets.
rolland-jean-christophe-cannan-vol1-1910:
Romain Rolland began his long novel Jean-Christophe in 1904, telling the life of a German composer. Gilbert Cannan translated the work into English, and volume one appeared in 1910. It holds the first four books: Dawn, Morning, Youth, and Revolt.

Young Jean-Christophe Krafft grows up in a small town on the Rhine, poor and gifted. Music becomes his refuge from a drunken father and a narrow world. He fights the stale taste of his elders and starts to find his own voice. Rolland wrote the cycle as a hymn to art, freedom, and the kinship of peoples. The full work later helped earn him the Nobel Prize in literature.
russell-philosophical-essays-1910:
Philosophical Essays, published in 1910, collects Russell's early papers from the decade when analytic philosophy was being invented. The subjects are truth, knowledge, and ethics, treated with the new logical tools he was forging with Whitehead.

The volume includes his essay on the elements of ethics and his engagements with pragmatism, whose theory of truth he resisted. Russell's prose here is already the famous instrument: lucid, cool, and quietly devastating. These papers bridge his Leibniz book and the Principia then in press. For readers of Russell, this is the workshop where the mature voice was made.
russell-principia-mathematica-vol-1-1910:
Principia Mathematica, published in three volumes between 1910 and 1913, was Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell's attempt to derive all of mathematics from logic. This first volume lays the foundations: propositional logic, classes, and relations.

Working in a dense forest of symbols, the authors build number and proof from a handful of primitive ideas. One famous proof, that one plus one equals two, arrives hundreds of pages in, with a note that the proposition is occasionally useful. The labor took a decade and changed both fields. Logicism, the program it founded, shaped a century of thought.
sbe-50-index-1910:
M. Winternitz made the General Index that ends the Sacred Books of the East. Book Fifty came out in 1910 and caps the whole vast set. The set ran to fifty books of texts from the faiths of Asia. Muller, its first head, had died ten years past.

The index lists names and themes from all the books in one A to Z run. A reader can trace a god, a rite, or a rule through the whole set at once. Short heads tell which faith and which book each text sits in. The book is the key that makes the great set of use.
scheible-das-kloster-vol10:
Band ten of Das Kloster, cells thirty-seven through forty, appeared in 1848 from Johann Scheible's Stuttgart house. Ten bands of complete reprints had made Scheible the keeper of Germany's folk print past. His rule never changed: print the whole text, however odd, however feared.

So the grimoires come entire, Faust books and Höllenzwänge among them, with nothing struck out. Folk charms hold their place beside works of high ritual, and chapbooks fill the gaps between. For the student of German magic, such fullness is the point. A cut text hides what its makers believed; Scheible's pages hide nothing, and band ten keeps that faith.
seligman-melanesians-of-british-new-guin:
Charles Gabriel Seligman led the Cambridge expedition's work in The Melanesians of British New Guinea, published in 1910. The volume reports on the Papuan coast: sorcery, secret societies, and mortuary ritual among the peoples studied. A chapter by F. R. Barton adds his own years of local knowledge to the team's findings.

Seligman's party worked village by village, recording custom before deep change reached the coast. Masks, feasts of merit, and the handling of the dead pass in careful detail. The book stands as a standard early ethnography of Papua, exact and humane in equal measure.
shahnama-warner-vol-5-1910:
Volume 5 of the Warner brothers' Shahnama of Firdausi appeared in 1910, midway through their nine-volume English version. Firdausi spent decades on the Book of Kings, Persia's national epic. The Warners matched his patience with a translation project that ran from 1905 into the 1920s.

Kings rise and fall in this volume as the epic moves from legend toward firmer history. Battles, embassies, and family feuds fill the verse, along with wise counsel from viziers and elders. The translators added notes to guide readers through names and customs. The middle volume holds the epic's long arc together, linking the heroes of myth to the shahs of record.
shaker-testimony-christs-second-appearin:
The Shakers set out their whole faith in the Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing, first printed in 1808 and reissued in 1810. The United Society of Believers speaks here as one voice. Mother Ann Lee, their foundress, is presented as the vessel of Christ's second appearing, the hinge of their system.

Celibacy, shared goods, and confession of sin flow from that claim, and the book argues each from scripture. It is systematic, dense, and meant to answer critics who saw only dancing and strangeness. As the charter theology of American Shakerism, it remains the movement's fullest statement of itself.
spr-proceedings-vol23-1909-1910:
Volume twenty three binds parts fifty eight and fifty nine, for 1909 and 1910. The Society for Psychical Research carries its record into the years before the Great War. Thought transference trials appear with new statistical checks. The census tradition still governs how spontaneous cases are gathered.

Trance sittings with Piper and her successors in the files fill long sections. Investigators try proxy sitters and other guards against hidden knowledge. Apparition reports continue, each tied to named witnesses. Volume twenty three sustains the primary archive of the evidential debate. Its tone is sober where its subject is strange. That contrast defines the whole Proceedings run.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5010:
George Washington gives eight yearly addresses, from January 8, 1790, to December 7, 1796, parted by three stars. The first opens with glad thanks for the bright state of public affairs. North Carolina has lately joined the Constitution, the country's credit and good name rise, and concord, peace, and plenty bless the land, all happy signs for the nation's future.

Washington tells Congress that the work of the last session pleased their voters as well as the newness and weight of the task let them hope. More will be asked in this grave session, and cool, firm wisdom must do it. Among the objects before them, he singles out the common defense as fit for special care. To be ready for war, he holds, is one of the surest ways to keep peace, and a free folk should be both armed and trained.
striking-hard-deep-waters-part-10:
Striking Hard belongs to Deep Waters, a set of comic tales by W. W. Jacobs about sailors and waterside folk. Mr. Porter comes home and tells his wife, busy at her ironing, that the men have struck at last, after standing more than flesh and blood could bear.

Mrs. Porter is not impressed. She recalls the last strike, when everything they had saved for a rainy day went bit by bit, and asks what they will live on now. Her husband trusts the committee and its speakers; she suggests he practice singing in the street. Jacobs draws the humor from the gap between dockyard pride and kitchen sense.
suso-eternal-wisdom-1910:
A Little Book of Eternal Wisdom, by Blessed Henry Suso, was printed at London by Burns, Oates and Washbourne, publishers to the Holy See, with the church's approvals dated 14 April 1910. Walter Hilton's Parable of the Pilgrim is added at the back.

A foreword opens with the names Jesus and Mary, models of true manhood and true womanhood in the writer's mind. Suso, a fourteenth-century German Dominican mystic, cast the book as a dialogue between Eternal Wisdom and the servant who longs to follow Christ. Its short chapters teach suffering, detachment, and love of God in plain, tender speech, and it stayed a favorite of Catholic devotion for centuries.
suso-life-by-himself-1910:
The Life of Blessed Henry Suso by Himself was translated from the original German. Thomas Francis Knox, a priest of the Oratory, made the version. Burns, Lambert, and Oates printed it at London in 1865. Suso, a German Dominican of the fourteenth century, wrote the life as the record of his own road to holiness.

Knox's preface tells how Suso was born at Ueberlingen, near Constance. He was of noble stock on both sides. He took his mother's maiden name out of devotion to her holiness. He set his father's surname aside. His baptismal name was Henry; the preface adds that God later changed it to Amandus, or Beloved, a secret found among his papers after death. The life mixes outward events with visions and hard penances.
the-alchemy-of-happiness-by-al-ghazzali-: Al Ghazzali wrote The Alchemy of Happiness, here rendered from the Hindustani by Claud Field for the Wisdom of the East set, shaped by L. Cranmer-Byng and S. A. Kapadia and printed in London by John Murray in 1910. A motto from Abu'l Feda heads the title page: knowledge of a part is better than ignorance of the whole.
the-alchemy-of-thought-1910: L. P. Jacks, dean of Manchester College, Oxford, and editor of The Hibbert Journal, wrote The Alchemy of Thought, printed in London by Williams and Norgate of Henrietta Street in 1910. The front pages carry long praise for his Mad Shepherds and other human studies from The Times, Country Life, the Westminster Gazette, and The Daily News.
the-book-of-the-thousand-nights-and-a-ni: The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 9, is set down here under Richard F. Burton's name. Only the Project Gutenberg head pages are shown, with no page of the tales. They give the title, Burton's name, a release date of September 2002, and an edition note. They also say the file was scanned by J. C. Byers and proofread by Doris Ringbloom. The head pages warn readers that rights law shifts from land to land and urge them to check the law at home first.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-10:
Volume 10 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XIII inside the governor's house. The Vekeel treats the house as his own. All he finds there stirs his greed and his interest alike. His first aim is a document that might back his moves against Orion, and the seizure of Orion's estates, in the eyes of the rulers at Medina.

The more gold the Vekeel can soon send the new sovereign, the surer his favor. He goes room to room with a child's greed, testing pillows, smelling scents, and peering into scrolls he can't read. In the dead woman's trunks he finds costly jewels and gold coins. He sticks her finest diamond ring on his own gem-covered finger. His interpreter, who reads Greek, must render each document found, and at the last a basket of discarded tablets by the writing-table catches his eye.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-10:
Part X of The Caxtons turns on the mystery of Francis Vivian, as Pisistratus tells it. The narrator is the family's son, writing his own life as he goes. His scholar father and a shrewd uncle weigh the clues with him.

The uncle's guess about the parentage of Francis Vivian strikes the narrator as a true discovery. On that view, the willful boy made a bold love match no father would approve. Thwarted and stung, he threw himself on the world. The narrator likes this account because it clears Vivian of mean or criminal acts, leaving him rash and at fault, but not base.
the-complete-works-of-brann-the-iconocla: William Cowper Brann's Iconoclast writings reach volume 10 in this Gutenberg text of June 1996, etext 568. A header defect is worth noting: its inner line still calls the book volume 1. The header also says the full set runs to twelve volumes. Beyond that header nothing is present, so Brann's essays in this volume cannot be described.
the-complete-works-of-james-whitcomb-ril: Volume 10 of the complete works of James Whitcomb Riley was issued as a Project Gutenberg text in October 1996, etext number 692, as the second item in that series. Only the Gutenberg header is present here, with its standard notes on copyright, donations, and advance release dates.The book itself never opens here.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book X of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume X of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. The strength that a momentary effort gave Rousseau to quit the Hermitage left him the moment he was out of it.

Scarcely settled in his new habitation, he suffered often from retentions, joined by a new complaint, a rupture he had long felt without knowing what it was. The physician Thieiry, his old friend, came to see him and made him acquainted with his situation. The sight of all the apparatus of the infirmities of years taught him a hard lesson: when the body is no longer young, the heart cannot be young with impunity. The fine season did not restore him, and he passed the whole year 1758 in that state.
the-daisy-chain-or-aspirations-pg3610:
Charlotte Yonge's preface to The Daisy Chain, or Aspirations, dated February 22, 1856, calls the book an overgrown work of a mixed class. It is neither a tale for the young nor a novel for their elders. Begun as talk-like sketches, it outgrew both its first plan and the periodical where it started.

Yonge asks readers to take it as a family chronicle, a home record of the May family across the years when character is chiefly formed. It traces the effect of the aspirations every young nature holds. Its moral, she says, is that the young should ask whether their upward strivings truly point upward and rest on lowliness. Chapter I then opens with fifteen-year-old Ethel May, thin and trembling with pent-up eagerness, begging Miss Winter for an afternoon's long walk and bridling at the rebuke for her haste.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-h:
The last part of Hell in Dante's Vision, cantos thirty-two through thirty-four, comes in the Rev. H. F. Cary's verse. Dante wishes for rough, harsh rhymes fit for the pit where all rocks lean, and calls on the muses who helped Amphion wall Thebes. Below the giants' feet, a voice warns him not to tread on the heads of the wretched souls.

Traitors lie locked in ice, some gnawing each other in endless hate. At the center sits the great fallen angel, fixed in the frozen deep. The poets climb past him and turn toward the stars.
the-emperor-volume-10:
Volume ten of Georg Ebers's The Emperor opens at part two, chapter eighteen, with farewell and baptism. Selene and Helios have been baptized, and two days later Dame Hannah sails from Mareotis harbour with her adopted children and Mary, bound for a new home at Besa in Upper Egypt. A presbyter and a deacon escort the Nile boat.

One girl holds back a beat at the thought of Antinous, whom she may never see again, then says a firm yes. Clara Bell closes Ebers's tale in a key of faith, loss, and a river road south.
the-forerunner-volume-1-1909-1910: Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here, before the book itself begins. It names The Forerunner, Volume 1 (1909-1910), by Charlotte Perkins Gilman. The volume stands fifth in a series of her works. No title page shows up in these pages. No contents list or page of the magazine can be read either. So nothing about the essays, tales, or poems inside can be told from these opening pages alone.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It for March 10, 1898 is number 10 of volume 2, and number 70 of the whole run. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a publisher's notice. A year's subscription costs $1.50, and six months seventy-five cents. Foreign subscriptions cost two dollars and a quarter. It is published every Thursday from 3 and 5 West 18th Street, New York. Payment may be made by registered letter, check, or postal-order.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
John Ormsby translated this stretch of Cervantes' Don Quixote, Volume 1, Part 10. Chapter twenty-eight treats the strange and delightful adventure that befell the curate and the barber in the same Sierra. The chapter opens with praise for the times when Don Quixote was sent into the world.

Happy and fortunate, the narrator calls those times, since the daring knight's resolve brought him forth. The curate and barber, who have tracked the runaway into the mountains, now meet their own adventure there. Cervantes widens the Sierra Morena strand here, shifting focus from the knight to the friends who seek to bring him home.
the-journal-of-abnormal-psychology-volum: Volume 10 of The Journal of Abnormal Psychology keeps only its old etext header here. None of the journal's articles appear. The header gives the file as etext 1226. Release came in March 1998. Charles Keller scanned the volume. OmniPage Professional software did the reading. Beyond the title and volume number, nothing can be read. No contents, contributors, or arguments survive in the wrapper. The record holds the scanner's label, not the periodical. Early digitization sometimes kept the label and lost the text.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-10:
The return of the Kingmaker gives Book Ten, the portion in this record of Edward Bulwer Lytton novel, its title. Sibyll and her father have found a home at a farm looking over a field once strewn with war dead. Flocks now graze where soldiers fell.

Sibyll sets aside her embroidery and watches a winding lane from an upper room furnished with music, manuscripts, and bright cushions. Her face lights at a sight outside, and she rushes down past her father. Peace in the household stays fragile while Warwick return reshapes the kingdom beyond the farm gate.
the-laws-of-candy-beaumont-fletcher-s-wo: Beaumont and Fletcher wrote their tragi-comedy for the stage, and this record holds the third part of a ten part works edition edited by A. R. Walker. Only the cast list and the start of act one are present here, naming General Cassilanes, his son Antinous, Prince Philander of Cyprus, and the imperious Princess Erota. The scene is Candy, and principal actor names from an early company also appear. The dialogue itself does not appear in this record.
the-little-dream-an-allegory-in-six-scen: John Galsworthy's The Little Dream, an allegory in six scenes, appears here with only its title page and list of characters, so the dialogue itself does not appear. The title page calls it No. 1 of Galsworthy's second series of plays, while a companion record calls the same play No. 2. The characters are Seelchen, a mountain girl, Lamond, a climber, and Felsman. Figures in the dream include three mountains, the Great Horn, Cow Horn, and Wine Horn, and flowers such as the Edelweiss, Alpenrose, and Gentian.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Volume 10 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction opens with its number for Saturday, July 7, 1827, priced at twopence. The lead article presents an engraving of His Majesty's pony phaeton. George IV, the article explains, seldom lets a fine day pass at his Windsor cottage without driving the Long Walk and Virginia Water in the little carriage. Windsor Park, fourteen miles in circumference, supplies the setting.

The article walks readers through the park's geography: the Little Park, Queen Elizabeth's Walk, the Queen's Lodge, and gardens enlarged under the late king. After describing the engraving, it promises anecdotes of the king's life and prints an original letter of the former Prince of Wales. The letter was written to Alexander Davison on the death of Lord Nelson. Readers of 1827 got a loyal magazine that treated the king's carriage drive as national news.

The Mirror's No. 338, dated Saturday, November 1, 1828, prints a correspondent's letter about Nelson's monument at Liverpool. The writer thanks the editor for the town hall engraving in No. 270 and now supplies a view of the monument in the Liverpool Exchange Buildings. Richard Westmacott executed the bronze group, completed in October 1823. The subscription raised about 9,000 pounds, and the bronze weighs upwards of twenty-two tons.

Four captive figures sit at the marble pedestal's base for Nelson's victories. Bronze bas-reliefs between them show his great naval actions. Lions' heads and laurel festoons enrich the pedestal, and brass letters carry the Trafalgar signal: England expects every man to do his duty. The main group joins Nelson with Victory and Death, his country mourning and his navy eager to avenge him. Readers get civic sculpture decoded emblem by emblem.

The Mirror's No. 375, dated Saturday, June 13, 1829, completes the Regent's Park architectural series with Cumberland Terrace. The editors call it the most magnificent terrace in the circuit. It stands above the road behind a carriage sweep and handsome balustrades, with a garden promenade below for residents. Nash, its architect, was so lavish of ornament that the whole range resembles a triumphal temple.

Centre and wings join by two handsome arches of four Doric columns each. Allegorical figures of the Seasons, the Quarters of the Globe, and the Arts and Sciences line the balustrade, twenty-seven figures in the whole range. A central colonnade of twelve columns carries an entablature under a pediment crowned by Painting and companions. Readers close the park series at its most theatrical address, stucco pretending to be a temple of empire.

Lydford Bridge in Devon is pictured in No. 574 of The Mirror, dated November 3, 1832. Lydford, a poor decayed village of rude cottages seven miles north of Tavistock, was once a place of real importance. In Domesday Book it was rated alongside London itself, and its castle keep served as court and prison for offenders against the Stannary Laws, the rules governing tin mining.

The bridge itself is one rough arch across a narrow rocky chasm near Dartmoor. The chasm drops nearly eighty feet from road level, with the small River Lyd rattling through its tight channel below. The writers compare it with the Devil's Bridge in Wales. Passing over shows little, they warn; the scene must be viewed from the crags.
the-occult-sciences-sketches-of-traditio: The opening pages present here are not the work itself. They are badly garbled publisher's advertisements for the Cabinet Edition of the Encyclopaedia Metropolitana. The adverts list volumes on political economy, the history of the Jews, Greek literature, and moral philosophy, with prices in shillings. Much of the type cannot be read with confidence. No title page, author, or passage on the occult sciences can be read in what is present. The book's own contents therefore cannot fairly be described.
the-parisians-volume-10:
Book X of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens with a letter to Graham Vane. M. Renard writes after months of silence, and his letter is translated for the reader. He reports at last a piece of information that may lead to a greater discovery. After their fruitless search in Vienna, both men had concluded that Madame Marigny and Madame Duval had exchanged names.

Renard reasons that the handsome monsieur who visited the false Duval knew of the exchange. If his name and whereabouts can be found, he likely knows what became of the missing lady. Renard kept his plan quiet to avoid disappointing an honorable client. The search turns back to Vienna and to the mysterious lover.
the-point-of-view-pg5310:
Elinor Glyn's The Point of View, issued in the Author's Press Series of her works, shares its title exactly with Henry James's book of letters in the sibling record. The two works have nothing else in common. Glyn's is a novel, and Chapter I is set in Rome at the end of May. The Grand Hotel restaurant is filling up late, and the season's entertainments are lessening.

Stella Rawson enters with her uncle and aunt, Canon and Mrs. Ebley. The party takes a secluded corner. They look and feel out of place among the gay company, but the Grand Hotel's drains were beyond question. The Canon judged typhoid fever a worse risk than worldly company. The women wear subdued black fastened to the throat. For Stella, twenty-one and fresh from an English cathedral close of gossip and tea-parties, a first fashionable restaurant feels almost deliciously wrong.
the-wandering-jew-volume-10:
Volume ten of Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew contains book ten, its chapters moving through confessions, rivals, two carriages, anonymous letters, a golden city, and a test. Chapter thirty-three, Confessions, stays close to Adrienne de Cardoville during a painful scene just described.

Adrienne has grown pale and thin with sorrow, her full cheeks hollowed and a faint azure line circling her large black eyes. She has thrown aside her bonnet to tend Mother Bunch more easily, rubbing the poor sempstress's thin ivory hands. Mother Bunch had fainted from emotion and weakness rather than suffocation, and the freshness of the air plus Adrienne's smelling salts revive her. Sue dwells on beauty worn down by suffering and service.
the-white-cat-captains-all-book-10:
W. W. Jacobs tells The White Cat, from his Captains All collection, in the tap-room of the Cauliflower inn. Rain falls outside while a traveller strokes a cat by the fire and an ancient on the settle talks. The inn's cat is a good mouser, the old man says, but Claybury once had a cat you could not buy for a hundred golden sovereigns.

That white cat had one yellow eye and one blue, and belonged to old Clark, who called it his blue-eyed darling and made a sinful fuss over it. Young Joe Clark hated the animal, yet stood in his uncle's will for five cottages and land worth forty pounds a year. Joe therefore fed it cream and tit-bits, hiding his feelings, and was promised the cat with the property.
the-world-s-best-orations-vol-1-of-10: Volume one of The World's Best Orations is shown here through its advisory council list alone. Council members include Sir Charles Wentworth Dilke of London. Professors from the University of Pennsylvania, Columbia, and Johns Hopkins appear. William Draper Lewis and Richard Gottheil are among them. Sheldon Jackson of the Bureau of Education also serves. The orations themselves do not appear in the pages included here.
tob-0010:
A second book of Enoch survives not in Ethiopia but among medieval Slavic Christians, who copied it in their own tongue. Called 2 Enoch, or the Slavonic Enoch, it tells how the patriarch rose through layer after layer of heaven. It stands apart from the better-known Ethiopian book of the same hero.

Enoch meets angels, sees the stores of snow and dew, and learns the calendar by which the cosmos runs. Visions of judgment close the ascent. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The Slavonic survival itself is the marvel: a lost Jewish apocalypse kept alive by Slavic monks.
tob-0039-d10:
Another installment of the Doctors' Trial record, Roll 11 continues the microfilm transcript of the Nuremberg proceedings of 1946 to 1947. The case against the Nazi doctors turned on experiments done on prisoners who could not refuse. The tribunal sat under American authority in occupied Germany.

On this roll, more of the evidence unfolds in session order: the experiments described, the defendants' roles examined, the verdicts still ahead. Reading transcript is slow work, but it shows how proof was laid before judges in real time. The full filmed record, of which this roll is part, remains a primary source for the trial and for the ethics rules it forced into being.
tob-0110:
Nicholas Barnaud gathered the Book of Lambspring, a set of fifteen emblems with verses, in the late sixteenth century. A dragon, a sphinx, and a two-bodied hermaphrodite appear among its figures. Each picture poses a riddle about the alchemical work, and the verses deepen rather than solve it.

Poetry and image work as one, in the manner of the great emblem books. Lambspring became a jewel of that genre, reprinted in the famous collections of alchemical art. This entry draws on a verified pre-1930 edition. Readers who enjoy puzzles in picture form will find few finer examples from the period.
tob-10110:
Ali ibn Usman al-Hujviri wrote the Kashf al-Mahjub in the eleventh century, in Persian, and Reynold A. Nicholson translated it into English. Its subtitle in translation, The Unveiling of the Veiled, names its aim. One of the oldest surviving manuals of Sufism, it explains Islam's mystical path for the general reader.

Hujviri sets out Sufi doctrines and practices, defines technical terms, and recounts lives of early saints and teachers. He also weighs rival claims and corrects abuses he saw among pretenders. Nicholson's version made the manual a cornerstone of Western Sufi studies, and it remains a clear early map of Sufi teaching.
tob-10810:
Maurice Maeterlinck brought the fourteenth-century Flemish mystic Ruysbroeck to French readers in Ruysbroeck and the Mystics, introducing translated selections with his own reflections. Maeterlinck, himself a poet of quiet and silence, called Ruysbroeck's writings the most lovely mystic prose he knew. Where scholars analyze, the Belgian poet marvels.

Selections from Ruysbroeck carry the substance: contemplation, the inner life, and union with God described in rich imagery. Maeterlinck's framing essays connect the medieval prior to modern seekers after stillness. Readers who met Ruysbroeck through Underhill's analysis or Scully's biography will find here a fellow artist's appreciation, valuable for tone as much as information.
tob-12910:
Rabindranath Tagore's Gitanjali, or Song Offerings, presents English prose-poems adapted from his Bengali originals. The collection won Tagore the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first awarded to an Asian writer. Its poems are love songs to God, simple and luminous on the surface, drawn from devotional traditions of Bengal.

A singer offers his life, his work, and his emptiness to a divine presence who is king, friend, and beloved by turns. Western readers met modern India's spiritual voice in these pages and responded with enormous enthusiasm. A century later the fervor has cooled into respect, and the best poems still shine quietly.
tob-4110:
Mencius, called the Second Sage of Confucianism, receives a full volume in Legge's Chinese Classics. Legge prints the Chinese text, his English version, long notes, and a life of the thinker. Mencius taught in the fourth century BC, when China was split among warring states.

He insists that human nature is good, as water by nature flows down. Rulers who feed and teach their people earn the right to rule; tyrants may justly be cast off, a bold claim he makes to kings' faces. His talks with rulers are sharp, warm, and funny by turns. Verified from the 1919 edition, Legge's Mencius remains standard.
tob-4210:
Kashmir Shaivism's central verses, the Spanda Karikas, survive here in their Sanskrit text. Spanda means the divine pulse or throb of creative energy said to vibrate in all things. The short verses ascribe the world's play to that single trembling of consciousness.

Commentators in Kashmir built a whole philosophy on these lines, reading them as a map of how the absolute becomes the many and returns. The entry carries the verified Sanskrit alone, without translation, so readers will want a rendering alongside. Even so, the bare text matters: Sanskritists and students of Shaivism can work from the source words themselves.
uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-volume-:
Volume ten of Uarda opens at chapter forty-two, on the plain of Pelusium at night. Thousands of tents shine white as snow hillocks under bright stars and calm moonlight. The camp has feasted: three great flower-garlanded vats of wine, drawn by thirty oxen, rolled through the tent streets all evening.

Behind the Regent Ani's magnificent pavilion stands a screened tent where old Hekt, the witch, lies hidden. Only Katuti and Ani's closest servants know who she is. She breathes with difficulty from a failing heart, a sick hawk crouched on her lap. While the banquet proceeds in the great pavilion, the hidden witch fades in the dark, and the romance nears its close.
un-ga-res-410:
War had wrecked Korea by the fall of 1950, and Resolution 410, adopted on 1 December 1950, builds a UN plan to feed and rebuild it. The Assembly recalls its October vote on Korea's freedom. A report from the Economic and Social Council lay before it. North Korea's attack, and the war waged against the UN force sent to restore peace, had left vast ruin the Korean people could not fix alone.

The people of Korea stand in dire need, the text holds: of relief goods, of stock, and of help to rebuild their trade and farms. A UN programme of relief and rebuilding for Korea is called a must. It would serve both lasting peace in the land and the base of wealth a free, united Korea needs.
un-ga-res-a-69-10: Joint work with a bloc of former Soviet states fills Resolution A/69/10, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Commonwealth of Independent States had held observer status at the Assembly since 1994. The text welcomes the bloc's work toward aims that match the pledges of the UN Charter. It also recalls a point the Security Council has stressed: strong links between the UN and regional groups serve peace.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 10, adopted on 9 February 1946 at the twenty-seventh plenary meeting, is one brief procedural sentence. The Assembly asked the Secretary-General to send the provisional rules of procedure of the Trusteeship Council, drawn from the Preparatory Commission's report, to that Council as soon as it was set up.

General Assembly Resolution 410 (V), adopted at the fifth session in 1950, created the United Nations Korean Reconstruction Agency for the relief and rebuilding of Korea. The Assembly noted the vast ruin left by the fighting. It held that a United Nations programme was needful both for lasting peace and for the groundwork of a united, free Korea.

The agency, known as UNKRA, was placed under an Agent General answerable to the Assembly. He worked beside the unification commission. Its policy put food, clothing, and shelter first. Then came farm output and the repair of transport and power. Aid was shared fairly across the whole population, with no political strings attached.

Resolution 69/10 of the General Assembly, from its sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns cooperation between the United Nations and the Commonwealth of Independent States. The Commonwealth has held observer status since 1994. The Assembly notes the Commonwealth's regional work in trade, health, environment, crime, and drug control. It asks the Secretary-General to consult regularly with its leadership. He is to report to the seventy-first session. It invites United Nations agencies and financial institutions to deepen their cooperation with it.
un-sc-res-10: Security Council Resolution 10 was adopted on November 4, 1946, in the council's first year, when its members were still learning how the new body would work. The record in this catalog names no subject, and the resolution's topic should be taken from the official text rather than guessed at. It stands as one of the early formal decisions of the council, preserved in the UN's official record. It dates from the season when the wartime alliance was being recast as a peacetime system for settling disputes.
un-sc-res-110: The United Nations Charter faced its ten-year review moment in 1955. Article 109 allowed a general conference to revise the Charter. The General Assembly had decided such a conference should meet at a fitting time. On 16 December 1955 the Security Council stated its agreement with that decision. The whole resolution is that single act of concurrence. In the end, no review conference was ever held.
un-sc-res-1310:
Israel had pulled its forces out of southern Lebanon weeks earlier. On 27 July 2000 the Security Council extended UNIFIL, its Lebanon force, for six months. The new term ran until 31 January 2001. The Secretary-General had confirmed that Israel had cleared the withdrawal line. Lebanon now planned to send more of its own troops south.

The Council backed the force deploying across its whole area. It restated Lebanon's sovereignty and independence. It condemned every act of violence, above all attacks on the force itself. It also pressed armed groups in the south to stop fighting. The aim was a calm border while Lebanon rebuilt its authority there.
un-sc-res-1410:
Independence for East Timor brought a successor mission from the Security Council on 17 May 2002. The people of East Timor had chosen a constituent assembly in August 2001 and a president in April 2002 by peaceful vote. The transitional administration, UNTAET, had led the territory to the point of statehood. The Secretary-General warned that the new institutions were still fragile.

The Council created the United Nations Mission of Support in East Timor, UNMISET, from 20 May 2002 for an initial twelve months. Its mandate covered help with administration, law enforcement, and security while Timorese bodies took over. Under Chapter VII, the mission could take the actions needed to do its work. Over two years it would hand all operational duties to the East Timorese authorities as milestones were met. The drawdown was reviewed against real progress, not a fixed date.
un-sc-res-1510:
Afghanistan's security force outgrew Kabul in the autumn of 2003. On 13 October 2003 the Security Council let ISAF expand across the country. Until then the force had guarded the capital and its surroundings. Now it could support Afghan authorities in other areas, as resources allowed. The aim was to let the United Nations and aid groups work safely nationwide. Afghans themselves held the chief duty for security, the text notes.

The Council also extended ISAF's mandate for twelve months. Member states in the force could take all needed measures. The force had to keep working closely with Afghan leaders. It also had to coordinate with the United States-led coalition. The expansion marked a turning point in the war.
un-sc-res-1610:
UNAMSIL received its final extension on 30 June 2005. The Secretary-General's report of 26 April set out the drawdown schedule he advised. A strong United Nations presence was still needed after the peacekeepers left. The Council praised the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's work and thanked the Special Court. Sierra Leone's forces would take full charge of security when the mission closed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended UNAMSIL's mandate for a final six months, to 31 December 2005. The Secretary-General had to finish planning for a follow-on United Nations office to start in January 2006. UNAMSIL and the country team were encouraged to work as one in the mission's last phase. Sierra Leone's army and police had to be ready to guard the country alone. The Council underlined the need to keep the Special Court's premises secure. The government was urged to keep building its forces with outside help.
un-sc-res-1710:
UNMEE was extended for four months as the border deadlock deepened on 29 September 2006. The Secretary-General's report of 19 September lay before the Council. Both parties had accepted the Boundary Commission's rulings as final and binding, yet marking the line had not begun. The mission was praised for doing its duties in hard conditions.

The Council extended UNMEE's mandate for four months. It restated its demands from resolution 1640 (2005): Eritrea had to lift its limits on the mission, and Ethiopia had to accept the border ruling without delay. Both parties had to give UNMEE full access, help, and protection. The Council voiced regret at the lack of progress on demarcation. It called on both sides to cooperate with the Commission and start the work of marking the border. If it found no real movement, the Council meant to review the mission's future at the mandate's end.
un-sc-res-1810:
The 1540 Committee gained three more years on 25 April 2008. Resolution 1540 (2004) had ordered every state to bar non-state actors from weapons of mass destruction. Resolution 1673 (2006) had kept the committee working. The spread of nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons was restated as a threat to international peace. Peaceful uses of the same science had to stay open, the Council stressed.

The Council restated every decision and duty in resolution 1540. States that had not yet filed a first report were called again to do so without delay. States that had reported were urged to add fresh detail whenever asked. Voluntary summary action plans were encouraged. States needing help were told to send their requests to the committee. The Council extended the 1540 Committee's mandate for three years, to 25 April 2011. A full report on states' compliance was due.
un-sc-res-1910: Kept under number 1910, a Security Council resolution is preserved in official-record form through a Wikisource transcription. The document is built to outlast its meeting: governments not in the room must still be able to read exactly what was required of them. That durability is on display here, in a complete text kept word for word.
un-sc-res-2010:
Somalia reached the Council's table and drew Resolution 2010, adopted on 30 September 2011. Famine gripped the country that summer. Al-Shabaab had pulled out of most of Mogadishu, yet attacks went on. The African Union force, called AMISOM, still stood below its authorized strength of 12,000 troops.

The Council keeps AMISOM deployed until 31 October 2012. The African Union must raise the force to its full 12,000 level fast. United Nations logistical support runs for the same period. Somali leaders must follow the new road map of tasks, or future support is at risk. A guard unit will shield the growing number of officials working in Mogadishu.
un-sc-res-210: The United Nations Security Council issued Resolution 210 as one of its formal decisions, and the catalog carries it under the year 1965. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them.
un-sc-res-310: Number 310 marks this Security Council text in the official record, catalogued here at 1972. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-410: Year 1977 in the catalog holds Resolution 410, a formal Security Council decision of the United Nations. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Spain under General Franco troubled the young United Nations in 1946. Many members saw his regime as a leftover of Europe's fascist era. The Council had kept Spain's situation on its active list. Resolution 10, adopted unanimously at the Council's 79th meeting, changed the handling of that question.

The members took Spain off the Council's list of seized matters. All records and papers on the case went to the General Assembly. The Secretary-General had to notify the Assembly of the transfer. The question of Franco's Spain thus moved arenas. It became an Assembly debate, where pressure on the regime continued through resolutions on membership and diplomacy.

Should the UN Charter itself be rewritten? Ten years after its birth, that debate came due. The Charter said a review meeting must be held if both big UN bodies agreed. On 21 November 1955 the General Assembly voted for such a meeting, at a fit time. Resolution 110 gave the Council's answer on 16 December 1955.

Nine members backed the Assembly's choice. The Soviet Union voted no. France held back. The Council thus agreed that a review meeting should take place one day. In the end, no such meeting was ever held. The Charter stayed as written in 1945, barring small tweaks. This text preserves the one formal step ever taken toward a full review.

Israel's pull-out from south Lebanon reshaped this force renewal of 2000. On 27 July, the Council adopted Resolution 1310 without dissent. Six weeks before, the Secretary-General had confirmed the pull-out. It met the terms of Resolution 425 from 1978. Lebanon asked the force to stay while Beirut sent its own troops south.

The text backs the plan for UNIFIL to spread through its whole zone. Lebanon will add troops and police in the south at the same time. The mandate then runs six months, to 31 January 2001. Strong backing for Lebanon's land, freedom, and self-rule is restated. The force stayed an interim one, the text stresses, even after twenty-two years.

Resolution 1410, adopted unanimously on 17 May 2002, designs the UN mission that would stand beside a newborn Timor-Leste. East Timorese voters had chosen a constituent assembly in August 2001 and a president in April 2002, completing the road to independence set for 20 May. The Council praised their courage and vision, and the UN administration that had run the territory since 1999.

In place of that administration it established a successor support mission, UNMISET, for an initial twelve months from independence day. The new mission's job was narrower: help fragile young institutions with administration, policing, and defense capacity while Timorese officials took command. The resolution frames independence not as an ending but as a handover.

Kabul alone had UN-backed guards after the Taliban fell. The force called ISAF watched the capital and its edge. By 2003, Afghan leaders wanted that shield spread wider. Their foreign minister wrote to ask for help on 10 October. NATO, which ran the force, wrote too. Resolution 1510 passed with no dissent on 13 October 2003.

The Council let ISAF work past Kabul, as means allowed. Its task was to keep the peace so aid and rebuilding could go on. The force's mandate grew by twelve months. States in ISAF could use all steps needed to do the job. Reports were due each three months. The move marked the first big growth of the Afghan mission.

Resolution 1610, adopted on 30 June 2005, sets the endgame for the UN mission in Sierra Leone. Security was steadily improving, and the Secretary-General's April report laid out a drawdown schedule for UNAMSIL, with a strong UN presence to remain after the troops left. The Council praised the truth and reconciliation commission's work and urged the government to spread its report widely.

UNAMSIL's mandate was extended for a final six months, to the end of 2005, so the withdrawal could be completed in order. The Special Court trying Sierra Leone's war criminals was called essential work, and all states were urged to make sure its indictees actually appeared before it. Peace in Sierra Leone, the text insists, also depended on calm next door in Liberia.

The border dispute between Ethiopia and Eritrea drives Resolution 1710, adopted on 29 September 2006. The UN Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, watched the Temporary Security Zone between them. A boundary commission had ruled on the border under the Algiers Agreements, but marking the line on the ground had stalled, and Eritrea was limiting the mission's movement.

The Council extends UNMEE for four months, until 31 January 2007. It demands that Eritrea lift all limits on the mission at once and that Ethiopia accept the boundary ruling fully and let marking begin. It warns that if no progress is shown by the deadline, it may reshape or change the mission, and it plans a review before 30 November 2006.

Keeping weapons of mass destruction away from armed groups is the aim of Resolution 1810, adopted on 25 April 2008. It builds on Resolution 1540 from 2004, which ordered every state to block non-state actors from getting nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons. A committee, the 1540 Committee, tracked how states were doing, but many had not yet filed their first reports.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council repeats that all states must fully carry out Resolution 1540. It extends the 1540 Committee, with expert help, for three years until 25 April 2011. States that have not reported must do so without delay. The committee is told to match offers of help with states that need it, run outreach events, and deliver a full review of progress by set dates.

Somalia had a weak interim government and an ongoing armed conflict when the Council adopted Resolution 1910 on 28 January 2010. The resolution concerns AMISOM, the African Union Mission in Somalia. Its soldiers, mainly from Uganda and Burundi, were protecting the interim authorities in the capital, Mogadishu.

The Council allowed African Union member states to keep AMISOM in Somalia until 31 January 2011. It asked the Union to build the force up toward its planned strength of eight thousand troops. United Nations logistical support for the mission would continue. Donor countries were urged to pay for the force. The text also pushed for more training of Somali police and security forces, and it set reports to the Council every four months.

AMISOM is extended and pressed to reach full strength in Resolution 2010, adopted on 30 September 2011. Mogadishu's security had improved, the Kampala Accord of June 2011 had deferred Somali elections to August 2012, and a September roadmap set the transitional institutions twelve months of tasks. Drought and famine were at their worst.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes African Union member states to maintain AMISOM until 31 October 2012. It urges the AU to raise it to its mandated 12,000 uniformed personnel. The Secretary-General must keep providing the UN logistical support package for up to 12,000 troops. The package includes a guard force for UN and international staff in Mogadishu and counter-IED and ordnance disposal work. Future Council support for the transitional institutions is made contingent on completing the roadmap's tasks, and the Council signals it will review AMISOM's troop levels once the mission reaches 12,000.

India and Pakistan were at war over Kashmir in September 1965, and the fighting was spreading. A cease-fire call two days earlier, in Resolution 209, had not stopped it. The Council adopted Resolution 210 unanimously on 6 September 1965. It said the wider fighting made the crisis far more serious.

The Council called on both sides to stop all hostilities at once, across the whole area of conflict. Every soldier was to pull back to the positions held before 5 August 1965. The Secretary-General was told to push hard to make the cease-fire take effect. He also had to strengthen the United Nations observer group in the area and keep the Council informed without delay.

African contract workers in Namibia went on strike in early 1972, and South Africa answered with harsh repression. South Africa was still occupying Namibia, although the United Nations had ended its mandate years before. Leaders of African states and of the United Nations Council for Namibia addressed the Council. Resolution 310 was adopted on 4 February 1972.

The Council strongly condemned South Africa's refusal to obey the United Nations decisions on Namibia. It restated that the occupation was illegal and harmful to the Namibian people. The repression of the workers was condemned as well. South Africa was told to end it and to scrap any labor system that clashed with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It also had to pull its police, military forces, and civilian staff out of Namibia at once. Further steps would follow if it refused.

Cyprus in 1977 was calm in part, but its peacekeeping force still could not move freely in the north of the island. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 7 June, called the force essential. It helped maintain quiet and made the continued search for a settlement easier. Talks between the two communities offered the best hope. Resolution 410 was adopted on 15 June 1977.

The Council extended the force's stationing to 15 December 1977. It repeated its call for urgent progress on a settlement. That call rested on the General Assembly's plan for Cyprus and on Resolution 367. Both sides were urged to show restraint. The Secretary-General was to continue his mission of good offices between the communities. He had to report on this resolution by 30 November 1977.

Latvia followed its Baltic neighbor through the same door in 1991. On 12 September, the Council adopted Resolution 710 without a vote. The same meeting handled Estonia's bid. The Republic of Latvia had declared its freedom restored in August. The Soviet Union was falling apart around it. Most Western states had never called the 1940 seizure lawful.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Latvia. Admission followed days later, with Estonia and Lithuania as well. Latvia framed its return as a state restored, not a state born. That claim rested on the view that its 1918 republic had never died in law.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
The fourth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/4210, covers the force in 1958 and 1959. UNEF was still a young experiment, holding the line between Egypt and Israel after the Suez Crisis. Its camps and patrol routes were now set, and its routines were taking shape.

The report describes the force's strength, its observation work, and talks with both parties. It also takes up the thorny question of who should pay. The document belongs to the years when peacekeeping was being invented in practice, one report at a time.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s15-10: Section 15.10 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sits in the part on services to federal agencies by the Federal Register. It covers information on drafting and publication. The Director of the Federal Register may prepare information and instructions, and pass them to agencies. The aim is good compliance with the Federal Register laws and rule-making laws named in the text. The Director may also run programs of technical instruction.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s18-10:
Section 18.10 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers illustrations, tabular material, and forms in documents for the Federal Register. It sits in Part 18 of Title 1, on the drafting of documents, in the electronic Code as of October 2026. The issuing body is the Administrative Committee of the Federal Register.

Where a form or illustration must be published, a clear and readable original, or a clear and fully readable copy of about eight and a half by eleven inches, must be included. It goes in the original document and in each certified copy. A second clause deals with tabular material. A document that includes such material may be assigned to the deferred publication schedule, under the section the text cites.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s21-10: Section 21.10 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations, in the part on preparing documents for the Code, states the basic building block of the Code. The normal divisions of a part are sections. Sections are the basic units of the Code. When a section needs room inside it, it may be split into paragraphs. Paragraphs may in turn be split further, using the lettering scheme set out in the next section of the same part. The rule keeps the shape of federal rules the same across agencies.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s304-10:
Section 304.10 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets a rule for keeping records tied to information requests. It sits in Part 304, on disclosure of records or information, for the Administrative Conference of the United States. The agency must keep all letters about requests it gets under that part. It must also keep copies of all records it was asked for.

Such material is kept until its disposal is allowed by Title 44 or by the national archives records schedule named in the text. No record may be thrown out while it is the subject of a live request, appeal, or court case under the freedom of information law. If an outside body holds records for the agency, the agency must say so in its guide and tell how to ask for them.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s426-210:
Section 426.210 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets fees for records requests. It belongs to the Freedom of Information Act rules of the National Commission on Military, National, and Public Service. The Commission charges the requester for handling a request, under the section and the budget office's guidelines.

The Act sets three requester classes: commercial users, schools and news media, and all others. Fees differ by class, and a requester may seek a fee waiver. No fee is charged when the cost of handling the request falls below twenty-five dollars. The Commission usually collects all fees before sending copies. Payment is by check or money order made out to the Treasury of the United States, or by another method the Commission names.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s457-110:
Section 457.110 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations requires self evaluation under handicap bias rules for one commission. The body is the National Capital Planning Commission. The rule sits in its part on enforcing bans on such bias in its own programs. The hosted text is current in twenty twenty six.

By a date in August nineteen eighty seven, the agency had to evaluate its current policies and practices, the rule states. It had to weigh their effects where they did not, or might not, meet the part's requirements. Changes were then to be made to the extent set in the rule. A dated self audit is the engine that drives later compliance.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s5-10: Section 5.10 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations is headed Forms of publication and sits in Part 5 of Title 1, on general rules for the Federal Register. The issuing body is the Administrative Committee of the Federal Register, and the text comes from the electronic Code as of October 2026. The evidence shown for this entry is brief. The part given states how the Federal Register is published. It is published in paper and online, at the govinfo website, under section 4101 of Title 44.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s500-110:
Section 500.110 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations requires a self-review by the National Commission for Employment Policy. It sits in the part on fair treatment regardless of handicap in that agency's programs. By 24 August 1987, the agency had to weigh its current policies and ways of working, and their effects, where they might fall short of the part. Where change was needed, the agency had to make it.

Interested persons had to be given a chance to take part. That includes handicapped persons and groups speaking for them, by spoken or written comments. For three years after the review, the agency must keep on file, open to the public, a note of the areas weighed and problems found, and of any changes made.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s601-10: Section 601.10 of Title 1 of the federal rules sets traits of a light review class. The class is for acts of the National Capital Planning Commission. Acts in the class have no big effect on the human setting. Four traits mark the acts that fit the class in the rule. They have small or no effect on the setting. They bring no real change to the state of things. Their joint effects stay small as a whole. They match acts weighed in past studies.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s602-10:
Section 602.10 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers secret and controlled records in the Freedom of Information Act rules of the National Capital Planning Commission. Where a request seeks a record classified by another agency, or fit for such treatment, the Commission hands the task of answering to that agency. The same referral applies where the classifying agency should weigh the record, or has the chief interest in it.

Records marked as Controlled Unclassified Information by another agency are also referred to that agency. But the choice to release or withhold such material rests on the Act's own exemptions. It does not rest on the controlled marking itself.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s603-10:
Section 603.10 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets the conditions for disclosing a person's record. The agency is the National Capital Planning Commission. The default rule is strict. No record in a system of records may be disclosed, by any means, to any person or agency.

The bar lifts if prior written consent is obtained from the individual the record concerns. A list of exceptions then follows. Disclosure to Commission employees for use in their duties is allowed. Disclosure required by the Freedom of Information Act is allowed. Disclosures for a routine use described in a system notice are allowed. Transfers to the Bureau of the Census for statistical purposes are allowed, in a form that bars identification of individuals. Transfers for statistical or research use carry the same safeguard. The hosted text is from the electronic Code as of late October 2026.
uslaw-usc-t1-s110:
Section 110 of Title 1 of the United States Code is a saving clause for the Revised Statutes. It sits in Chapter 2, on acts and resolutions and the forms of their making. The rule deals with laws that set a time bar on a case or a suit. Such laws are in the Revised Statutes and are hit by the repeal in that work. The clause says that the repeal is not to touch them.

Suits and cases, in the courts of law or on a charge of crime, are thus kept safe. They cover acts done before the repeal was made. They may be started and run in the same span of time as if the repeal had not been made. The rule thus guards old rights of suit from the sweep of a new book of laws.
uslaw-usc-t1-s210: Section 210 of Title 1 sits in Chapter 3, which covers the Code of Laws and its supplements. The Superintendent of Documents distributes copies of the District of Columbia code and the supplements provided for by section 202 and section 203. Distribution follows the same manner used for bound volumes of the Statutes at Large. A closing proviso adds that slip or pamphlet copies need not be printed or distributed.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1110:
Section 1110 of Title 2 of the United States Code is the appropriations section for one chapter of Title 2. That chapter covers the John C. Stennis Center for Public Service Training and Development. The center trains people for public service careers.

The whole section is a single line of law. It appropriates a fixed sum to the fund named in the chapter. The sum is 7,500,000 dollars, given to carry out the chapter's purposes. No yearly renewal is written into the text. The line stands as a one-time endowment by statute for a training center named for a senator.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1410: Section 1410 of Title 2 of the United States Code bars court review of most acts under the Congressional Accountability chapter. Save as plainly allowed by three named sections of the title, no court may review compliance or noncompliance with the chapter. The bar also covers any act taken under the chapter. It sits in the part on office and court dispute steps for that chapter. The hosted text is the full section, stated in one sentence.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1610:
Section 1610 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers estimates based on the tax reporting system. It sits in Chapter 26 of that title, on the disclosure of lobbying activities. Part (a) deals with bodies covered by section 6033(b) of Title 26. A person, other than a lobbying firm, that must report lobbying outlay under that tax section may act in a set way.

Such a person may make a good faith estimate, by class of dollar value, of the sums at stake. The estimate is for the right quarter of the year. It serves to meet the terms of sections 1603(a)(3) and 1604(b)(4) of Title 2. The section adds terms for all other ends as well. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1910:
Section 1910 of Title 2 of the United States Code requires the United States Capitol Police to report its spending to Congress twice a year. It sits in the chapter on the Capitol Police, in the part covering organization and administration.

Within sixty days after each six-month period ends, the Chief of the Capitol Police must send Congress a detailed report. The report must list what the force spent on its operations, item by item. It names every person or firm paid and the amount. It also describes the services rendered and their dates. A further statement covers all sums appropriated to, received, or spent by the force, plus any unspent balances. Each report is printed as a House document.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2010:
Section 2010 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers assignment of rooms in the House Office Building. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the rules for care of the Capitol complex, in the House subchapter. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. Office space in Congress is scarce and prized.

Assignment and reassignment of rooms and other space in that building are subject to House control, the text states. That control may be exercised by rule, resolution, order, or otherwise. A saving clause adds that nothing in the linked sections limits that control. The House thus keeps final say over its own office map.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4110:
Section 4110 of Title 2 of the United States Code provides for monuments to deceased Senators and House Members buried in the Congressional Cemetery. It sits in Chapter 41 of Title 2, on congressional officers and administration. The version here is current through Public Law 119-134.

Whenever a deceased Senator or Member of the House is in fact buried in the Congressional Cemetery, a duty arises. The Sergeant at Arms of the Senate, for a Senator, or of the House, for a Member, must have a monument raised. The monument is to be of granite, with fitting inscriptions. Its cost is a charge on the contingent funds of the Senate or of the House, whichever the deceased belonged to, and is paid out of those funds.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5310:
Section 5310 of Title 2 keeps members' pay certificates moving while Congress is away. The Clerk of the House is authorized and directed to sign them during a set recess window. The window runs from the recess after the first session until the first day of the second session.

The certificates are for the monthly compensation of Members and Delegates in Congress. They must be in the form in use on August 15, 1876, by the text's own reference. A certificate signed by the Clerk under this section has the like force and effect as the certificate of the Speaker. The section sits in Chapter 53 of Title 2, on Members of the House. It falls in the subchapter on member pay. The hosted Code text is published by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel, current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5510:
Section 5510 of Title 2 of the United States Code lets the House call in outside help after a computer security attack. If the Speaker, with the agreement of the Minority Leader, finds that an attack has happened and that handling it goes beyond the House's own means, a set power opens. Despite any other law, rule, or order, the Speaker may ask the head of any executive or military department, or free-standing body, for help.

The head asked must start giving fit help within twenty-four hours of the request. Help includes, where needed, bringing the House's information systems back to a working state. That state must let the law-making process go on and let Members, officers, and staff work.
uslaw-usc-t2-s610:
Section 610 of Title 2 of the United States Code, in the chapter on the Congressional Budget Office, lets that office help pay off staff student loans. The Director may set up a program, from 12 November 2001, to recruit or retain qualified staff. Under it, the Office may agree to repay, by direct payments for the employee, all or part of a student loan the employee took out earlier.

The Director may apply, by regulation, such parts of the general personnel statute as are needed to run the program. The regulations must cap payments at 6,000 dollars for any employee in any calendar year, and 40,000 dollars in total for any one employee. The Office may not reimburse loan payments an employee made before an agreement was signed.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6510:
Section 6510 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with pays for goods from the Senate fund. It sits in Chapter 65, on Senate officers, in a general part of the chapter. The pays in view are for goods and stores, with fuel in the list. Those goods must have been bought on or past 8 July 1935. The buys must have been made through the Administrator of General Services. The pays are to be made by a cheque, on a bill that has been passed.

The bill must be passed by the Committee on Rules and Administration of the Senate. The rule is thus a short one on the form of pay for a set of buys. The fund in view is the contingent fund of the Senate, the pool for the daily costs of the Senate.
wattles-science-being-well-1910:
Wattles turned his Certain Way toward the body in The Science of Being Well, the 1910 companion to his prosperity book. Health, he argues, follows the same law as wealth: think health, act as the well act, and trust the life principle within. Worry and gloomy images count as real dangers here.

Eating, bathing, breathing, and sleep all get chapters shaped by his mental-science rules. The tone stays practical, closer to a handbook than a sermon. Together with its sister volume, the book shows New Thought at its most confident, promising readers command over fortune and flesh alike.
wattles-science-getting-rich-1910:
Wallace D. Wattles promised a method, not a mystery, in The Science of Getting Rich, printed in 1910. His New Thought classic teaches thinking in the Certain Way. Hold the picture of what you want, act with faith, and give every person more than you take. Gratitude keeps the channel open, in his scheme.

The short book speaks to clerks and strivers who felt the age's wealth passing them by. Its plain chapters made it the most cited prosperity text of the whole movement in time. A century of success literature drinks from Wattles and his Certain Way, often without knowing his name at all.
what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-10:
Book ten of Lord Lytton's What Will He Do With It? opens with Jasper Losely on the move. We last left him resting at a small town near Fawley. In the morning he walks on to the old manor house. At the gate he sees a hired carriage drive past, and Lady Montfort looks out in tears.

Losely knows her face at once, though she does not see him. He asks what her sad visit could mean for his old fraud. At the gate latch he halts again, unsure how to gain entry to Darrell. His own name would bar the door. Lytton sets a villain's bold plan against a house full of grief.
wisdom-of-the-east-the-alchemy-of-happin: The scan pages here show the title pages, partly garbled, of The Alchemy of Happiness by Al Ghazzali, with the text itself not present. Claud Field translated the work from the Hindustani. It belongs to the Wisdom of the East series, edited by L. Cranmer-Byng and S. A. Kapadia. John Murray printed it in London. A line from Abu'l Feda heads the title: knowledge of a part beats ignorance of the whole. Library stamps from the Archaeological Survey of India mark the copy.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol10:
Volume X of the Journal of Discourses rounds the first ten of the set, printed at Liverpool in 1863. Stenographic reports carry the voices of Brigham Young, his counsellors, the Twelve Apostles, and other speakers of the day. A full decade of Utah preaching now stood in print, sermon upon sermon, for readers everywhere.

The talks range across belief and behavior, from God's nature to the care of orchards, homes, and families. That breadth is the record's charm and its use: a whole society thinks aloud in these pages. Volume X closes the set's first stretch, with sixteen volumes of the same record still to come.
